general.Choice A: Two policies can create similar price and quantity effects but differ in who receives the transfer
general.Choice B: Two policies with matching price and quantity effects must give their revenue or rents to the same recipients.
general.Choice C: Two policies with matching import quantities must raise equal government revenue, even when quota licenses are given away.
general.Choice D: Two policies can raise the same domestic price, but only the quota distorts domestic production and consumption.
general.Correct Answer: A — Two policies can create similar price and quantity effects but differ in who receives the transfer
general.Feedback: An equivalent tariff and binding quota can produce similar prices and quantities, yet tariff revenue goes to government while quota rents go to the holders of import rights unless those rights are auctioned. Both can distort production and consumption. Policy design must therefore track who receives revenue or rents as well as efficiency effects.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: An import quota is:
general.Choice A: A legal limit on the quantity of a good that may be imported
general.Choice B: A tax collected on every domestic sale
general.Choice C: A subsidy for foreign producers
general.Choice D: A minimum price set below the world price
general.Correct Answer: A — A legal limit on the quantity of a good that may be imported
general.Feedback: A quota directly limits import quantity.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: A binding import quota normally causes the domestic price to:
general.Choice A: Fall below the world price
general.Choice B: Rise above the world price
general.Choice C: Remain permanently at the world price
general.Choice D: Equal zero
general.Correct Answer: B — Rise above the world price
general.Feedback: Restricted imports create scarcity in the domestic market.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: Quota rents are:
general.Choice A: The government’s tariff revenue in every quota system
general.Choice B: The entire loss of consumer surplus
general.Choice C: The price gap created by the quota multiplied by the permitted import quantity
general.Choice D: Domestic producers’ total revenue
general.Correct Answer: C — The price gap created by the quota multiplied by the permitted import quantity
general.Feedback: Quota rents accrue to whoever holds the valuable import rights.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: When does the government receive quota rents?
general.Choice A: Whenever any quota is binding
general.Choice B: Only when imports fall to zero
general.Choice C: Whenever foreign exporters own the licenses
general.Choice D: When it auctions the import licenses and keeps the proceeds
general.Correct Answer: D — When it auctions the import licenses and keeps the proceeds
general.Feedback: Rent distribution depends on who owns or sells the import rights.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: At an importing country's request, a foreign government caps shipments and gives its exporters the rights free. Which restriction is this?
general.Choice A: A voluntary export restraint (VER)
general.Choice B: An import tariff collected by the importing treasury
general.Choice C: An import-license auction held by the importing treasury
general.Choice D: A subsidy paid on domestic production
general.Correct Answer: A — A voluntary export restraint (VER)
general.Feedback: A VER limits exports from the supplying country. With free rights assigned to foreign exporters, those exporters can capture the scarcity rents.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: In the displayed trade graph, what domestic price results under the import quota?
general.Feedback: The graph marks the domestic price under the quota at $6.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: What world price is shown in the displayed trade graph?
general.Feedback: The green world-price line is drawn at $3.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: A binding import quota directly limits:
general.Choice A: Domestic supply at every price
general.Choice B: The quantity that may be imported
general.Choice C: The world price in every country
general.Choice D: Domestic demand at every price
general.Correct Answer: B — The quantity that may be imported
general.Feedback: A quota is a quantitative restriction on imports.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: When a binding quota raises the domestic price above the world price, domestic producers generally:
general.Choice A: Gain producer surplus
general.Choice B: Lose producer surplus
general.Choice C: Receive no price effect
general.Choice D: Become foreign producers
general.Correct Answer: A — Gain producer surplus
general.Feedback: The higher domestic price benefits domestic sellers.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: Quota rent is the value created by:
general.Choice A: The gap between domestic demand and domestic supply at autarky only
general.Choice B: Total consumer surplus before trade
general.Choice C: Government tax revenue collected on all domestic production
general.Choice D: The gap between the domestic price and world price on the units allowed to be imported
general.Correct Answer: D — The gap between the domestic price and world price on the units allowed to be imported
general.Feedback: Import licenses can carry value because permitted imports can be bought at the world price and sold at the higher domestic price.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: Refer to the quota graph. How many units are imported under the quota?
general.Choice A: 20 units
general.Choice B: 10 units
general.Choice C: 30 units
general.Choice D: 40 units
general.Correct Answer: A — 20 units
general.Feedback: The horizontal distance between Qs=20 and Qd=40 is 20.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: Refer to the quota-rent graph. What is the value of rectangle R?
general.Feedback: The domestic-world price gap is $10 across 20 imported units.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: If domestic license holders receive the quota rents in the displayed trade graph, total quota rents equal:
general.Choice A: $50 thousand
general.Choice B: $225 thousand
general.Choice C: $150 thousand
general.Choice D: $300 thousand
general.Correct Answer: C — $150 thousand
general.Feedback: The $3 price wedge times 50 thousand imports produces $150 thousand in quota rents.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: A quota permits 30 imports and creates an $8 domestic-world price gap. What is the total quota rent?
general.Feedback: Quota rent is $8 × 30 = $240.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: Under a voluntary export restraint, foreign firms receive free rights to supply 45 units. Buyers pay $27 while the unchanged world price is $23. Who receives the $180 scarcity rent?
general.Choice A: The importing government as tariff revenue
general.Choice B: Domestic producers in addition to their producer surplus
general.Choice C: Domestic consumers as a price rebate
general.Choice D: The foreign firms holding the export rights
general.Correct Answer: D — The foreign firms holding the export rights
general.Feedback: The price wedge is $4 and 45 units cross the border: $180. The foreign holders of the free rights receive the rents; the importing treasury collects no tariff.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: A tariff and a quota initially reduce imports to the same amount. Demand then rises. Which policy automatically permits more imports?
general.Choice A: The tariff, because the import quantity can adjust at the tariff-inclusive price
general.Choice B: The quota, because its quantity cap rises automatically
general.Choice C: Neither, because demand cannot shift under trade
general.Choice D: Both always preserve the same price and imports
general.Correct Answer: A — The tariff, because the import quantity can adjust at the tariff-inclusive price
general.Feedback: A fixed quota holds imports constant; a tariff allows quantity to adjust.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: At the quota-induced domestic price of $6 in the displayed trade graph, domestic producers supply:
general.Choice A: 75 thousand
general.Choice B: 175 thousand
general.Choice C: 150 thousand
general.Choice D: 200 thousand
general.Correct Answer: C — 150 thousand
general.Feedback: The $6 line intersects supply at Q = 150 thousand.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: At the quota-induced domestic price of $6 in the displayed trade graph, domestic consumers demand:
general.Choice A: 150 thousand
general.Choice B: 175 thousand
general.Choice C: 275 thousand
general.Choice D: 200 thousand
general.Correct Answer: D — 200 thousand
general.Feedback: The $6 line intersects demand at Q = 200 thousand.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: What import quantity is permitted by the quota shown in the displayed trade graph?
general.Choice A: 50 thousand
general.Choice B: 75 thousand
general.Choice C: 125 thousand
general.Choice D: 200 thousand
general.Correct Answer: A — 50 thousand
general.Feedback: At $6, imports equal Qd − Qs = 200 − 150 = 50 thousand.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: What is the per-unit quota rent implied by the displayed trade graph?
general.Choice A: $1 per unit
general.Choice B: $3 per unit
general.Choice C: $6 per unit
general.Choice D: $9 per unit
general.Correct Answer: B — $3 per unit
general.Feedback: The domestic price is $6 while the world price is $3, creating a $3 price wedge per imported unit.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: A quota allows 30 imported units. The domestic price is $18 and the world price is $14. What is total quota rent?

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: A tariff and quota produce the same domestic price and import quantity. What determines whether their national welfare effects are identical?
general.Choice A: Whether producers earn any surplus
general.Choice B: Who receives the quota rents
general.Choice C: Whether domestic consumers exist
general.Choice D: Whether the world price is positive
general.Correct Answer: B — Who receives the quota rents
general.Feedback: A tariff creates government revenue; a quota can create equivalent rents that may go to domestic or foreign license holders.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: A binding quota is tightened. In the standard import model, which combination is most likely?
general.Choice A: Domestic price rises and imports fall
general.Choice B: Domestic price falls and imports rise
general.Choice C: Domestic price and imports both remain fixed
general.Choice D: Domestic price falls and exports rise
general.Correct Answer: A — Domestic price rises and imports fall
general.Feedback: A tighter quantity limit restricts import supply further and pushes the domestic price upward.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: A binding quota permits 24 imports and creates a $7 price gap. Calculate total quota rent.
general.Feedback: Quota rent is $7×24=$168.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: An import quota is administered by first-come, first-served licenses. What additional concern arises?
general.Choice A: The quota cannot bind
general.Choice B: License allocation may reward speed or connections rather than lowest distribution cost
general.Choice C: Consumers receive all rents automatically
general.Choice D: Domestic price must equal zero
general.Correct Answer: B — License allocation may reward speed or connections rather than lowest distribution cost
general.Feedback: Administrative allocation can create inefficiency and rent-seeking.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: Assuming quota rents remain domestic, what total deadweight loss is shown by the displayed trade graph?
general.Choice A: $112.5 thousand
general.Choice B: $150 thousand
general.Choice C: $225 thousand
general.Choice D: $450 thousand
general.Correct Answer: C — $225 thousand
general.Feedback: The two $112.5-thousand distortion triangles sum to $225 thousand.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: The domestic government auctions all import licenses competitively with no administrative costs. What is the value of rectangle R in the quota graph, and how does it enter domestic welfare?
general.Choice A: R is $100 of government revenue, a domestic transfer rather than deadweight loss.
general.Choice B: R is $200 of deadweight loss because domestic firms pay it to the government.
general.Choice C: R is $200 of government revenue, a domestic transfer rather than deadweight loss.
general.Choice D: R is $100 of deadweight loss because domestic firms pay it to the government.
general.Correct Answer: C — R is $200 of government revenue, a domestic transfer rather than deadweight loss.
general.Feedback: Rectangle R has height $40 - $30 = $10 and width 40 - 20 = 20 imported units, so its value is $200. A competitive domestic government auction collects this rent as government revenue. The payment transfers income within the country; it is not destroyed surplus or deadweight loss.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: Compare the free-trade import gap with the quota import gap. By how much do imports fall?
general.Choice A: 50 thousand
general.Choice B: 125 thousand
general.Choice C: 200 thousand
general.Choice D: 150 thousand
general.Correct Answer: D — 150 thousand
general.Feedback: Imports fall from 275 − 75 = 200 thousand to 50 thousand, a decline of 150 thousand.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: The quota raises domestic production from 75 thousand to 150 thousand. What is the production-side deadweight loss in the displayed trade graph?
general.Choice A: $112.5 thousand
general.Choice B: $75 thousand
general.Choice C: $150 thousand.
general.Choice D: $225 thousand
general.Correct Answer: A — $112.5 thousand
general.Feedback: The production triangle is 1/2 × $3 × 75 thousand = $112.5 thousand.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: Use the quota graph to calculate the consumption-side deadweight loss.
general.Choice A: $50 thousand
general.Choice B: $112.5 thousand
general.Choice C: $150 thousand.
general.Choice D: $225 thousand
general.Correct Answer: B — $112.5 thousand
general.Feedback: The consumption triangle is 1/2 × $3 × 75 thousand = $112.5 thousand.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: A tariff and a voluntary export restraint each allow 45 imports at a domestic price of $27; the world price stays $23. Foreign firms get the VER rights free. How much higher is importing-country surplus under the tariff, holding quantities and other costs equal?
general.Choice A: $0, because identical prices imply identical national welfare
general.Choice B: $1,215, because all spending on imports is government revenue
general.Choice C: $180, because the tariff removes both distortion losses
general.Choice D: $180, because the price-wedge receipts stay in the importing country
general.Correct Answer: D — $180, because the price-wedge receipts stay in the importing country
general.Feedback: Both restrictions have the same production and consumption distortions. The difference is $4 × 45 = $180: tariff receipts stay domestic while the specified VER rents go abroad.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: A quota is set at the current free-trade import quantity and is fully binding only if import demand later rises. Compared with a fixed tariff, what feature makes the quota potentially more restrictive after a demand increase?
general.Choice A: The tariff fixes import quantity while the quota fixes price
general.Choice B: A quota cannot affect price after it is set
general.Choice C: The quota fixes import quantity while the domestic price can rise further
general.Choice D: The quota automatically lowers the world price to zero
general.Correct Answer: C — The quota fixes import quantity while the domestic price can rise further
general.Feedback: A quantitative ceiling does not expand automatically when import demand rises, so the domestic price can adjust upward.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: A small importer has Qd = 100 - P and Qs = P - 20. Pw is $30. A $10 tariff and a quota initially allow 40 imports. Demand then becomes Qd = 120 - P. With all else unchanged, which comparison is correct?
general.Choice A: Tariff: price $50 and 40 imports; quota: price $40 and 60 imports
general.Choice B: Tariff: price $40 and 60 imports; quota: price $50 and 40 imports
general.Choice C: Both keep price $40 and imports 40
general.Choice D: Both raise price to $50 because a demand increase must raise the world price
general.Correct Answer: B — Tariff: price $40 and 60 imports; quota: price $50 and 40 imports
general.Feedback: The tariff keeps domestic price at 30 + 10 = 40, where imports are 80 - 20 = 60. Under the cap, 120 - P - (P - 20) = 40 implies P = 50.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: A quota allows 36 imports at $29 while Pw remains $24. Consumers lose $310 and domestic producers gain $94. Foreign exporters receive the rights free. Relative to free trade, what are the national loss and the global distortion loss, ignoring other effects?
general.Choice A: $36 national loss; $216 distortion loss
general.Choice B: $180 for both because the rents are the only loss
general.Choice C: $216 national loss; $36 distortion loss
general.Choice D: $310 for both because every dollar lost by consumers disappears
general.Correct Answer: C — $216 national loss; $36 distortion loss
general.Feedback: Rents are (29 - 24) × 36 = 180. Domestic surplus falls 310 - 94 = 216. Of this, 180 is transferred abroad; the remaining 36 is destroyed surplus.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: Two quota systems have the same price and import quantity. Rents total $240. System A auctions rights competitively and spends $20 of real resources administering them; system B gives rights free to domestic importers at no resource cost. Ignoring other effects, which comparison is correct?
general.Choice A: A raises national surplus by $240 because auction receipts are new gains
general.Choice B: B loses $240 nationally because private domestic rents leave the country
general.Choice C: Both have identical national surplus because administrative costs are transfers
general.Choice D: A raises $240 for government, but national surplus is $20 lower than under B
general.Correct Answer: D — A raises $240 for government, but national surplus is $20 lower than under B
general.Feedback: Both keep the $240 rent inside the country; auctioning changes its recipient. The stated real administrative cost makes A $20 worse nationally than B.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: At Pw = $18, Qd = 54 and Qs = 20. A quota is set at 34 imports, with no initial price premium. Demand then increases by 10 at every price. If Qd falls by 2 and Qs rises by 3 for each $1 price increase, what does the unchanged quota do?
general.Choice A: Price remains $18 and imports rise to 44 because the quota was initially harmless
general.Choice B: Price rises to $23 because only the demand response matters
general.Choice C: Price rises to $20; the initially zero-rent cap now creates $68 in rents
general.Choice D: $34 of rents appears because rent always equals the quota quantity
general.Correct Answer: C — Price rises to $20; the initially zero-rent cap now creates $68 in rents
general.Feedback: At the old price the new import gap is 44, ten above the cap. Each $1 rise closes the gap by 5, so price rises $2. Rents are $2 × 34 = $68.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: Using the world-price and quota-price outcomes, calculate the consumer-surplus loss caused by the quota.
general.Choice A: $337.5 thousand
general.Choice B: $562.5 thousand
general.Choice C: $1,400 thousand
general.Choice D: $712.5 thousand
general.Correct Answer: D — $712.5 thousand
general.Feedback: Consumer surplus falls by 1,512.5 − 800 = 712.5 thousand dollars.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: With Qd = 110 - P, Qs = P - 10 and Pw = $30, a quota is auctioned to allow 40 imports. A $10 tariff is proposed instead. Demand then rises by 20 at every price. With competitive licensing and no administration costs, which post-shift outcome is correct?
general.Choice A: Quota: price $50 and receipts $800; tariff: price $40 and receipts $600
general.Choice B: Both: price $40 and receipts $400
general.Choice C: Quota: price $40 and receipts $600; tariff: price $50 and receipts $800
general.Choice D: Both: price $50 and receipts $800
general.Correct Answer: A — Quota: price $50 and receipts $800; tariff: price $40 and receipts $600
general.Feedback: After the shift, Qd = 130 - P. A 40-unit cap requires 140 - 2P = 40, so P = 50 and auction rents are 20 × 40 = 800. The tariff keeps P = 40, allows 60 imports and raises 600.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: An importing market has Qd = 96 - P, Qs = P - 16 and Pw = $28. A voluntary export restraint gives foreign firms free rights to ship 32 units. Compared with free trade, what are the importing-country welfare loss and the part transferred abroad?
general.Choice A: $144 lost nationally, with no foreign transfer
general.Choice B: $528 lost nationally, including $384 in foreign rents
general.Choice C: $384 lost nationally, all of it destroyed surplus
general.Choice D: $912 lost nationally, including a second deduction for the same rents
general.Correct Answer: B — $528 lost nationally, including $384 in foreign rents
general.Feedback: The cap implies P = (96 + 16 - 32)/2 = 40, a $12 wedge. Rents are 12 × 32 = 384. Straight curves each change quantity by 12, creating total distortion of 144. National loss is 384 + 144 = 528.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: An importer initially has Qd = 92 - P, Qs = P - 12 and Pw = $26. A $10 tariff and a 32-unit quota initially match. Demand then falls by 28 at every price. Which outcome follows?
general.Choice A: Both keep price $36 because initially equivalent restrictions remain equivalent
general.Choice B: The quota keeps imports at 32 even when buyers want only 24 at the world price
general.Choice C: The quota becomes nonrestrictive at $26 with 24 imports; the tariff still raises price to $36 with 4 imports
general.Choice D: The tariff becomes nonrestrictive while the quota raises price above $36
general.Correct Answer: C — The quota becomes nonrestrictive at $26 with 24 imports; the tariff still raises price to $36 with 4 imports
general.Feedback: New demand is 64 - P. At Pw = 26 the desired import gap is 38 - 14 = 24, below the cap. Under the tariff P = 36 and imports are 28 - 24 = 4. A cap is a maximum, not a required shipment.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: Compared with free trade, how does the quota in the graph change consumer surplus, producer surplus, quota rents, and total welfare? Assume domestic license holders receive the quota rents.
general.Choice A: Consumers lose $712.5k; producers gain $337.5k; quota rents are $150k; net welfare falls $225k
general.Choice B: Consumers lose $825k; producers gain $337.5k; quota rents are $150k; net welfare falls $337.5k
general.Choice C: Consumers lose $712.5k; producers gain $337.5k; quota rents are $225k; net welfare falls $150k
general.Choice D: Consumers lose $712.5k; producers gain $225k; quota rents are $150k; net welfare falls $337.5k
general.Correct Answer: A — Consumers lose $712.5k; producers gain $337.5k; quota rents are $150k; net welfare falls $225k
general.Feedback: The quota raises price from $3 to $6. Quantities are in thousands: consumption falls from 275 to 200, while domestic production rises from 75 to 150. Consumer surplus falls by $3 x (275 + 200) / 2 = $712.5k; producer surplus rises by $3 x (75 + 150) / 2 = $337.5k. Imports under the quota are 200 - 150 = 50 thousand, so rents are $3 x 50 = $150k. Domestic license holders receive those rents, making the net welfare change -$712.5k + $337.5k + $150k = -$225k, the sum of the two $112.5k distortion triangles.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: Using the phone-case quota graph, replace free domestic import licenses with a voluntary export restraint that gives foreign firms the same rights free. Prices and quantities remain unchanged, with no additional costs. Relative to free trade, what is the domestic welfare loss, and how much of it is transferred abroad?
general.Choice A: $300 thousand loss, including $150 thousand transferred abroad
general.Choice B: $375 thousand loss, including $150 thousand transferred abroad
general.Choice C: $375 thousand loss, including $225 thousand transferred abroad
general.Choice D: $450 thousand loss, including $225 thousand transferred abroad
general.Correct Answer: B — $375 thousand loss, including $150 thousand transferred abroad
general.Feedback: The price gap is $6-$3=$3 and quota imports are 200-150=50 thousand, so foreign firms receive $150 thousand. Production and consumption each change by 75 thousand, giving total deadweight loss of 0.5*$3*(75+75)=$225 thousand. Domestic loss is $225 thousand plus $150 thousand, or $375 thousand.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: The phone-case quota graph shows free trade and a quota with domestic rights holders. If the import cap is raised from the displayed amount to 100 thousand, with both linear demand and supply curves and the world price unchanged, which result follows?
general.Choice A: Domestic price $6; rents $300 thousand; distortion loss $225 thousand
general.Choice B: Domestic price $4; rents $100 thousand; distortion loss $25 thousand
general.Choice C: Domestic price $5; rents $200 thousand; distortion loss $100 thousand
general.Choice D: Domestic price $5; rents $100 thousand; distortion loss $200 thousand
general.Correct Answer: C — Domestic price $5; rents $200 thousand; distortion loss $100 thousand
general.Feedback: The curves imply Qd = 350 - 25P and Qs = 25P. A gap of 100 requires 350 - 50P = 100, so P = 5. The wedge is 2 and rents 200 thousand. Production rises 50 and consumption falls 50 relative to Pw = 3, giving DWL 100 thousand.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: Refer to the graph. Which quantity combination is correct under the import quota?
general.Choice A: Qs = 75 thousand; Qd = 275 thousand; imports = 200 thousand
general.Choice B: Qs = 200 thousand; Qd = 150 thousand; exports = 50 thousand
general.Choice C: Qs = Qd = 175 thousand; imports = 0
general.Choice D: Qs = 150 thousand; Qd = 200 thousand; imports = 50 thousand
general.Correct Answer: D — Qs = 150 thousand; Qd = 200 thousand; imports = 50 thousand
general.Feedback: At the quota-induced price of $6, domestic supply is 150 thousand and demand is 200 thousand, leaving 50 thousand imports.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: A binding quota permits 20 imports and raises domestic price $10 above world price. One-quarter of the licenses are given to foreign exporters; the rest go to domestic residents. Production and consumption distortions total $100, and no resources are spent obtaining licenses. What is the domestic welfare loss?
general.Choice A: $300: $100 of distortions plus every $200 of quota rents, regardless of ownership.
general.Choice B: $100: rent ownership never affects domestic welfare because all rents are transfers worldwide.
general.Choice C: $250: $100 of distortions plus $150 of rents retained by domestic residents.
general.Choice D: $150: $100 of distortions plus $50 of rents going abroad; $150 of rents stay domestic.
general.Correct Answer: D — $150: $100 of distortions plus $50 of rents going abroad; $150 of rents stay domestic.
general.Feedback: Total rent is 20×10=200. Foreign recipients receive 0.25×200=50, while domestic recipients retain 150. For domestic welfare, add exported rents to the 100 resource distortion loss: 150.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: Two binding quota systems create the same $200 of rents and $100 of production/consumption distortions. A costless government auction captures all rents. Free domestic licenses instead induce $30 of real lobbying expenses. Which comparison is correct?
general.Choice A: Auction loss is $100 and free-license loss $130; the ownership transfer is not a resource loss, but lobbying dissipates resources.
general.Choice B: Auction loss is $300 and free-license loss $130; government revenue must be added to deadweight loss.
general.Choice C: Auction loss is $100 and free-license loss -$70; private rents are an extra national gain over the auction.
general.Choice D: Both losses are $100; lobbying uses money and therefore cannot consume real resources.
general.Correct Answer: A — Auction loss is $100 and free-license loss $130; the ownership transfer is not a resource loss, but lobbying dissipates resources.
general.Feedback: Auction receipts and domestic private rents are domestic transfers. With identical market distortions, only the $30 real lobbying difference changes national loss: 100 versus 130.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: A quota generates $200 of rents that currently go to foreign exporters, plus $100 of domestic production/consumption distortions. A reform auctions all rights domestically without changing price or imports, but uses $60 of real administrative resources. What is the change in domestic welfare?
general.Choice A: A $300 gain: recover foreign rents and eliminate both distortion triangles even though price and imports are unchanged.
general.Choice B: A $140 gain: recover $200 in foreign-held rents, then subtract $60 of administration; the $100 distortion remains.
general.Choice C: A $60 loss: rent ownership cannot affect domestic welfare, so only administration changes.
general.Choice D: A $240 loss: auction payments and administration must both be subtracted from consumers’ unchanged position.
general.Correct Answer: B — A $140 gain: recover $200 in foreign-held rents, then subtract $60 of administration; the $100 distortion remains.
general.Feedback: The market distortion is unchanged. National loss falls from 100+200=300 to 100+60=160, an improvement of 140. Capturing previously foreign rents changes domestic income even though the physical allocation stays fixed.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: A small country has Qs=P-20, initial Qd=80-P and world price $30. A $10 tariff initially produces the same imports as a quota of 20. Demand then becomes Qd=100-P. Which comparison follows?
general.Choice A: With the tariff, P=$50 and imports=20; with the quota, P=$40 and imports=40.
general.Choice B: Both policies keep P=$40 and imports=20 because they were initially equivalent.
general.Choice C: With the tariff, P=$40 and imports=40; with the quota, P=$50 and imports=20.
general.Choice D: Both policies raise P=$50 and imports=40 because demand increases equally under each.
general.Correct Answer: C — With the tariff, P=$40 and imports=40; with the quota, P=$50 and imports=20.
general.Feedback: The nonprohibitive tariff keeps P=30+10=40; new imports are (100-40)-(40-20)=40. The quota fixes Qd-Qs=20: 100-P-(P-20)=20, giving P=50. Initial equivalence does not imply equal responses to shocks.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: A small country has Qd=100-P, Qs=P-20 and a binding quota of 20 imports. World price falls from $30 to $20 while domestic schedules and the quota are unchanged. What happens to domestic price and quota rents?
general.Choice A: Domestic price falls from $50 to $40; rents stay $400 because a quota fixes the price wedge.
general.Choice B: Domestic price stays $50; rents fall from $400 to $200 because import cost is lower.
general.Choice C: Domestic price falls to $20; unlimited foreign supply removes the binding quota automatically.
general.Choice D: Domestic price stays $50; total rents rise from $400 to $600 because the import-right price gap widens.
general.Correct Answer: D — Domestic price stays $50; total rents rise from $400 to $600 because the import-right price gap widens.
general.Feedback: The quota-clearing equation 100-P-(P-20)=20 gives P=50 at either world price. Rents rise from (50-30)×20=400 to (50-20)×20=600. The quantity cap, not a fixed wedge, is held constant.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: Demand rises in a small importing country. Under a nonprohibitive fixed tariff, unlimited foreign supply holds domestic price at world price plus tariff. Under a binding quota, the maximum imports cannot rise. Which adjustment difference is most accurate?
general.Choice A: Tariff imports absorb the extra demand at the unchanged price; quota price rises, inducing more domestic output and restraining consumption.
general.Choice B: Tariff price must rise because imports are fixed; quota imports absorb the change because its price wedge is fixed.
general.Choice C: Both domestic prices must rise equally; greater demand determines price independently of the trade-policy instrument.
general.Choice D: Quota price rises only if domestic supply is vertical; otherwise domestic firms can absorb any demand increase at the same price.
general.Correct Answer: A — Tariff imports absorb the extra demand at the unchanged price; quota price rises, inducing more domestic output and restraining consumption.
general.Feedback: At a fixed tariff-inclusive world price, imports can expand. A binding quota prevents that import response, so price adjusts until more domestic supply and less quantity demanded close the gap. Upward-sloping domestic supply does not keep price fixed.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.5 — Analyze quotas, quota rents, and tariff-versus-quota differences.
general.Question: In the quota-rent graph, import licenses are initially given free to foreign firms. The domestic government instead sells all licenses at a costless competitive auction, with the quota and prices unchanged. What domestic welfare gain follows, and how much deadweight loss remains relative to free trade?
general.Choice A: Gain of $100; remaining deadweight loss $100
general.Choice B: Gain of $200; remaining deadweight loss $200
general.Choice C: Gain of $400; remaining deadweight loss $200
general.Choice D: Gain of $200; remaining deadweight loss $100
general.Correct Answer: D — Gain of $200; remaining deadweight loss $100
general.Feedback: Rectangle R has height $40-$30=$10 and width 40-20=20 imports, so the auction brings $200 home instead of transferring it abroad. Each distortion triangle is half of $10 times 10 units, or $50. Their $100 total remains because prices and quantities are unchanged.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: Why does possible compensation not prove losers are compensated?
general.Choice A: Compensation occurs automatically through the world price
general.Choice B: Losers have no measurable loss
general.Choice C: Total surplus cannot fund transfers
general.Choice D: A transfer requires an actual policy or agreement
general.Correct Answer: D — A transfer requires an actual policy or agreement
general.Feedback: Feasibility and implementation are different.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: What is missing from the claim “protection saves jobs”?
general.Choice A: Effects on consumers, downstream industries, exports, and alternative uses of resources
general.Choice B: The protected industry’s name
general.Choice C: The number of foreign countries only
general.Choice D: A promise that prices never change
general.Correct Answer: A — Effects on consumers, downstream industries, exports, and alternative uses of resources
general.Feedback: A complete analysis includes opportunity costs and spillovers.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: What is the proper response to a national-security claim?
general.Choice A: Accept every claim automatically
general.Choice B: Evaluate the specific risk, policy cost, and narrower alternatives
general.Choice C: Reject every claim automatically
general.Choice D: Count only tariff revenue
general.Correct Answer: B — Evaluate the specific risk, policy cost, and narrower alternatives
general.Feedback: Security arguments require evidence and proportionality.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: What efficiency question should be separated from the equity question in trade?
general.Choice A: Whether total surplus rises versus how gains and losses are distributed
general.Choice B: Whether imports equal exports versus whether prices exist
general.Choice C: Whether firms earn revenue versus whether consumers buy
general.Choice D: Whether quotas are legal versus whether supply slopes upward
general.Correct Answer: A — Whether total surplus rises versus how gains and losses are distributed
general.Feedback: Efficiency asks whether trade raises total surplus. Equity asks how the resulting gains and losses are distributed across people, firms, industries, or regions.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: Why might adjustment assistance be discussed even when trade raises total surplus?
general.Choice A: Trade eliminates all consumer gains
general.Choice B: Some workers and communities can bear concentrated transition costs
general.Choice C: Efficiency requires equal outcomes
general.Choice D: Imports always reduce total employment
general.Correct Answer: B — Some workers and communities can bear concentrated transition costs
general.Feedback: Trade can raise total surplus while imposing concentrated transition costs on particular workers and communities. Adjustment assistance addresses those distributional costs without denying the aggregate gains.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: How does evaluating protection connect positive and normative economics?
general.Choice A: Positive economics decides which distribution is fair
general.Choice B: Normative economics calculates tariff revenue mechanically
general.Choice C: The two approaches are identical in trade policy
general.Choice D: Positive analysis estimates costs and benefits; normative judgment weighs goals and distribution
general.Correct Answer: D — Positive analysis estimates costs and benefits; normative judgment weighs goals and distribution
general.Feedback: Trade-policy evaluation separates what a policy does from judgments about whether its goals justify those effects.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: Why is “a tariff protects jobs” incomplete economic analysis?
general.Choice A: The statement is sufficient because preserving employment in the protected sector captures the main national welfare effect
general.Choice B: It ignores higher consumer costs, resource shifts, and jobs affected in other industries
general.Choice C: Employment effects can be evaluated from the protected industry because tariff costs are unlikely to spill into other sectors
general.Choice D: The key missing issue is the effect on foreign workers; domestic consumer and input costs are secondary to that effect
general.Correct Answer: B — It ignores higher consumer costs, resource shifts, and jobs affected in other industries
general.Feedback: A complete analysis traces costs and effects beyond the protected industry.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: Which is the strongest way to evaluate a national-security argument for protection?
general.Choice A: Assume every industry is essential
general.Choice B: Reject the argument because trade is always harmless
general.Choice C: Compare the security benefit with the policy cost and less costly alternatives
general.Choice D: Count only the protected firms’ profits
general.Correct Answer: C — Compare the security benefit with the policy cost and less costly alternatives
general.Feedback: Security can be legitimate, but the claim still requires evidence and comparison.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: New domestic pump makers request temporary protection while they learn to match established foreign firms' costs. Which argument are they using?
general.Choice A: National-security argument
general.Choice B: Jobs argument based only on existing employment
general.Choice C: Retaliation against a partner's trade barrier
general.Choice D: Infant-industry argument
general.Correct Answer: D — Infant-industry argument
general.Feedback: The infant-industry argument claims temporary learning can make a new industry competitive. The label alone does not establish that future benefits exceed current costs.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: Why can retaliation make a tariff more costly?
general.Choice A: Trading partners may restrict the country’s exports, harming additional producers and workers
general.Choice B: Trading partners may tax imports from the country, but the proceeds go into the original country’s treasury.
general.Choice C: Trading partners may tax imports from the country, making its goods cheaper for foreign customers to buy.
general.Choice D: Trading partners may restrict imports from the country, increasing sales opportunities for the country’s exporters.
general.Correct Answer: A — Trading partners may restrict the country’s exports, harming additional producers and workers
general.Feedback: Retaliation can restrict sales of the country’s exports in foreign markets. Export producers and their workers can therefore lose business in addition to the costs created by the original tariff.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: Which statement separates efficiency from equity in trade analysis?
general.Choice A: An efficient outcome must divide gains equally
general.Choice B: Trade can raise total surplus while distributing gains and losses unevenly
general.Choice C: Equity is measured only by import quantity
general.Choice D: If consumers gain, fairness is settled
general.Correct Answer: B — Trade can raise total surplus while distributing gains and losses unevenly
general.Feedback: Efficiency concerns total surplus; equity concerns distribution.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: A national-security concern applies to one narrowly defined input. Which policy is most economically targeted?
general.Choice A: A focused resilience policy for that input rather than broad protection across unrelated goods
general.Choice B: A tariff on every imported good
general.Choice C: A permanent quota on all consumer goods
general.Choice D: No comparison of alternatives
general.Correct Answer: A — A focused resilience policy for that input rather than broad protection across unrelated goods
general.Feedback: Targeting reduces collateral costs while addressing the stated risk.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: Which evidence would most directly support an infant-industry argument?
general.Choice A: A promise that protection will never end
general.Choice B: Current producer profits alone
general.Choice C: A credible path showing temporary learning lowers future costs enough to exceed protection costs
general.Choice D: A claim that consumers do not respond to prices
general.Correct Answer: C — A credible path showing temporary learning lowers future costs enough to exceed protection costs
general.Feedback: The argument requires a temporary, evidence-based learning mechanism and net benefits.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: Workers in an import-competing industry lose jobs while consumers gain from lower prices. Which conclusion is strongest?
general.Choice A: Trade has no gains because some workers lose
general.Choice B: Every consumer gain should be ignored
general.Choice C: Efficiency proves no assistance can be justified
general.Choice D: Trade creates aggregate gains but may justify debate over adjustment assistance
general.Correct Answer: D — Trade creates aggregate gains but may justify debate over adjustment assistance
general.Feedback: Aggregate gains and adjustment costs can coexist.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: A domestic industry argues for protection because foreign competition will reduce its employment. What is the main economic weakness in stopping the analysis there?
general.Choice A: Tariffs never affect prices
general.Choice B: It ignores consumer costs and jobs/resources created elsewhere
general.Choice C: Employment can never fall in an import-competing industry
general.Choice D: Foreign competition always raises domestic producer surplus
general.Correct Answer: B — It ignores consumer costs and jobs/resources created elsewhere
general.Feedback: A complete welfare analysis includes costs to consumers, resource reallocation, and economy-wide effects.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: A new domestic battery industry asks for five years of protection while firms learn a production process. Which finding would give the request the strongest economic case?
general.Choice A: Documented learning-by-doing is expected to lower future costs enough to offset the temporary protection cost
general.Choice B: The firms would earn higher profits whenever imports are restricted
general.Choice C: Consumers prefer the domestic brand even at a higher price
general.Choice D: The industry wants protection with no expiration date
general.Correct Answer: A — Documented learning-by-doing is expected to lower future costs enough to offset the temporary protection cost
general.Feedback: A defensible infant-industry case requires a credible temporary learning benefit large enough to justify the cost of protection.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: A national-security case for protecting a product is strongest when:
general.Choice A: Domestic producers simply want higher profits
general.Choice B: Imports come from any foreign country regardless of risk
general.Choice C: The protected industry has falling employment
general.Choice D: The product is genuinely critical and dependence creates a specific strategic vulnerability
general.Correct Answer: D — The product is genuinely critical and dependence creates a specific strategic vulnerability
general.Feedback: National-security arguments need a concrete strategic externality or vulnerability, not a generic dislike of imports.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: Which statement correctly treats potential compensation from trade?
general.Choice A: Losers are automatically compensated through prices
general.Choice B: Aggregate gains may make compensation feasible, but actual policy is required for losers to receive it
general.Choice C: Potential compensation proves no one loses
general.Choice D: Compensation is impossible whenever trade raises total surplus
general.Correct Answer: B — Aggregate gains may make compensation feasible, but actual policy is required for losers to receive it
general.Feedback: A Kaldor-Hicks gain does not itself transfer resources.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: Which statement about a trade deficit is economically valid?
general.Choice A: It does not by itself measure whether individual trades create gains from exchange
general.Choice B: It proves imports have zero consumer value
general.Choice C: It proves every domestic industry is shrinking
general.Choice D: It equals tariff deadweight loss
general.Correct Answer: A — It does not by itself measure whether individual trades create gains from exchange
general.Feedback: The trade balance is not the surplus test for a particular market.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: A quota-holder spends resources lobbying to obtain import rights. How does rent seeking affect welfare?
general.Choice A: It turns all rents into consumer surplus
general.Choice B: It can dissipate some quota rents and create additional social cost
general.Choice C: It removes the domestic price increase
general.Choice D: It guarantees efficient license allocation
general.Correct Answer: B — It can dissipate some quota rents and create additional social cost
general.Feedback: Resources spent capturing rents can add to the policy cost.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: Which comparison best tests whether protection is the least-cost response to worker displacement?
general.Choice A: Compare it with wage insurance, retraining, mobility aid, and targeted income support
general.Choice B: Compare only protected-firm profits
general.Choice C: Compare only import quantity before and after
general.Choice D: Assume no alternative policies exist
general.Correct Answer: A — Compare it with wage insurance, retraining, mobility aid, and targeted income support
general.Feedback: Adjustment goals can be pursued through policies with different efficiency costs.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: A proposed tariff would save 2,000 jobs in one industry but raise costs for downstream firms and millions of consumers. What is the best economic evaluation?
general.Choice A: Compare protected wages with tariff revenue, treating higher input prices as transfers that cannot affect downstream output.
general.Choice B: Compare protected jobs with downstream jobs, treating consumer purchasing-power losses as irrelevant when employment rises.
general.Choice C: Compare protected-job benefits with consumer, downstream, retaliation and efficiency costs before judging the policy.
general.Choice D: Compare imports before and after the tariff, treating fewer imports as the net national benefit of protection.
general.Correct Answer: C — Compare protected-job benefits with consumer, downstream, retaliation and efficiency costs before judging the policy.
general.Feedback: Saved jobs are one effect. Consumer costs, input-using industries, retaliation and resource distortions can offset benefits; import reductions or selected employment counts do not measure net welfare.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: An industry requests “temporary” protection but has received it for 25 years and has no measurable productivity improvement. What does this evidence do to the infant-industry argument?
general.Choice A: It proves consumers receive the tariff revenue
general.Choice B: It weakens it because the promised temporary learning benefit has not materialized
general.Choice C: It strengthens it because longer protection proves the industry is important
general.Choice D: It is irrelevant because infant-industry protection should be permanent
general.Correct Answer: B — It weakens it because the promised temporary learning benefit has not materialized
general.Feedback: Persistent protection without learning or an exit condition undermines the standard infant-industry rationale.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: A country imposes a tariff to reduce dependence on a strategic input, but domestic production cannot expand and allied suppliers are available. Which conclusion is strongest?
general.Choice A: If domestic output cannot expand, the tariff may do little to make supply more reliable; compare buying from several allied suppliers with the tariff’s added costs.
general.Choice B: Higher producer prices establish greater resilience immediately, even if domestic capacity cannot expand.
general.Choice C: Lower import dependence is sufficient for resilience, regardless of whether the remaining supply comes from one supplier.
general.Choice D: Allied suppliers remove every security risk, making evaluation of diversification costs and reliability unnecessary.
general.Correct Answer: A — If domestic output cannot expand, the tariff may do little to make supply more reliable; compare buying from several allied suppliers with the tariff’s added costs.
general.Feedback: The tariff cannot quickly create the missing domestic capacity. Buying from several reliable allied suppliers may address the specific risk at lower cost, but its reliability and costs still require comparison.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: A tariff raises domestic producer surplus by $60 million, government revenue by $20 million, and lowers consumer surplus by $105 million. Ignoring other effects, what is the strongest conclusion?
general.Choice A: National surplus rises by $185 million because all three figures should be added
general.Choice B: National surplus rises by $25 million because producer gains exceed revenue
general.Choice C: The tariff is efficient because government receives revenue
general.Choice D: National surplus falls by $25 million even though protected producers gain
general.Correct Answer: D — National surplus falls by $25 million even though protected producers gain
general.Feedback: The net change is +60 +20 -105 = -25 million; distributional gains do not erase the aggregate loss.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: A protection proposal benefits a small organized industry by $50 per person while costing a very large number of consumers $2 each. Why can the policy still attract strong political support?
general.Choice A: Small individual consumer losses establish a smaller total cost, so support reflects a necessarily positive net benefit.
general.Choice B: A large consumer population creates stronger per-person lobbying incentives even when each person loses only a little.
general.Choice C: A larger individual stake gives beneficiaries stronger organizing incentives even when small dispersed losses sum to more.
general.Choice D: Organized support reveals higher aggregate willingness to pay, so the policy’s national efficiency follows from its passage.
general.Correct Answer: C — A larger individual stake gives beneficiaries stronger organizing incentives even when small dispersed losses sum to more.
general.Feedback: Concentrated stakes can make organizing worthwhile for beneficiaries while small individual losses discourage consumers from organizing. Political support does not establish aggregate net benefits.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: Import access raises consumer surplus by $640 and reduces producer surplus by $390. A proposal uses a $390 lump-sum transfer to restore producers and consumes $35 in real adjustment resources. Which result separates efficiency from distribution?
general.Choice A: $250 remains because transfers and real adjustment costs are both ignored
general.Choice B: $605 remains because the producer transfer creates additional national surplus
general.Choice C: $215 of net gain remains, and compensation occurs only because the proposal provides it
general.Choice D: $175 is lost because both producer losses and compensation must be subtracted
general.Correct Answer: C — $215 of net gain remains, and compensation occurs only because the proposal provides it
general.Feedback: The trade gain is 640 - 390 = 250. The transfer reallocates that surplus; the real resource cost reduces it to 215. Potential compensation is distinct from this stipulated actual compensation.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: A politician says, “Imports destroy domestic production, so imports destroy value.” What is the best response?
general.Choice A: Imports can lower domestic production, and that loss of domestic output by itself establishes that national welfare falls
general.Choice B: Domestic production creates value for the country, whereas imported consumption contributes little to domestic consumer surplus
general.Choice C: Imports create net value when the imported quantity is smaller than the domestic production displaced by trade
general.Choice D: Imports replace domestic units whose marginal cost exceeds the world price while expanding consumption valued above that price
general.Correct Answer: D — Imports replace domestic units whose marginal cost exceeds the world price while expanding consumption valued above that price
general.Feedback: The welfare gain comes from lower-cost sourcing and additional mutually beneficial consumption.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: A politician says, “Exports make the country poorer because goods leave.” What is the best response?
general.Choice A: Exports move units to buyers willing to pay the higher world price, raising producer and total surplus despite domestic consumer losses
general.Choice B: Exports raise the domestic price, so producer gains are offset dollar-for-dollar by losses to domestic consumers
general.Choice C: Exports shift goods abroad without changing domestic willingness to pay or opportunity cost, leaving welfare unchanged
general.Choice D: Because residents consume fewer units after trade, the country's welfare falls despite the higher world price
general.Correct Answer: A — Exports move units to buyers willing to pay the higher world price, raising producer and total surplus despite domestic consumer losses
general.Feedback: Export welfare analysis compares valuations and costs, not just physical flows.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: A protected pump industry reports falling average costs. The same decline occurred in unprotected firms using a newly available machine. What additional evidence is needed to show that protection encouraged learning and that the resulting benefits justified its costs?
general.Choice A: Evidence that protected firms still employ workers, regardless of the source of cost reductions
general.Choice B: Evidence that protection generated additional learning whose future benefits exceed its costs
general.Choice C: Evidence that import prices exceed zero, proving domestic learning is valuable
general.Choice D: Evidence that production increased, proving the tariff caused every cost reduction
general.Correct Answer: B — Evidence that protection generated additional learning whose future benefits exceed its costs
general.Feedback: A common technology improvement weakens the claim that protection caused the learning. The case needs an additional benefit attributable to the policy and comparison with its costs.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: A tariff preserves 2,000 jobs in one sector but raises input costs in downstream firms. What analysis is still required?
general.Choice A: The protected-sector employment effect should be compared with consumer costs, while downstream employment can be treated as secondary
general.Choice B: Tariff revenue and protected-sector payroll provide enough information to determine whether the policy raises national welfare
general.Choice C: Net employment, consumer costs, fiscal effects, retaliation, and alternative adjustment policies
general.Choice D: The job count settles the welfare question once the preserved positions are valued at their current wage payments
general.Correct Answer: C — Net employment, consumer costs, fiscal effects, retaliation, and alternative adjustment policies
general.Feedback: Concentrated benefits do not erase dispersed costs.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: Why can a bilateral tariff reduce the protected country’s exports?
general.Choice A: Foreign retaliation reduces imports into the protected country while higher input prices raise its exporters’ productivity.
general.Choice B: The tariff directly taxes domestic export sales while retaliation lowers the world price of every protected input.
general.Choice C: Reduced imports mechanically require equal export losses in each industry while input costs remain unchanged.
general.Choice D: Foreign retaliation can reduce market access while tariffed inputs raise domestic exporters’ costs.
general.Correct Answer: D — Foreign retaliation can reduce market access while tariffed inputs raise domestic exporters’ costs.
general.Feedback: Exports can fall through retaliatory barriers abroad and higher costs of imported inputs at home. Neither an industry-by-industry identity nor direct taxation of exports is required.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: A tariff is removed gradually rather than immediately. Which tradeoff is most relevant?
general.Choice A: A slower phaseout accelerates consumer gains but concentrates all employment adjustment into the first year.
general.Choice B: A slower phaseout preserves tariff revenue without delaying efficiency gains because the announced endpoint is unchanged.
general.Choice C: A slower phaseout can ease short-run adjustment but prolong higher prices and distortions relative to immediate removal.
general.Choice D: A slower phaseout removes distributional losses by spreading them across years, leaving only consumer gains to compare.
general.Correct Answer: C — A slower phaseout can ease short-run adjustment but prolong higher prices and distortions relative to immediate removal.
general.Feedback: Timing affects adjustment capacity as well as how long tariffs distort prices and quantities. Gradual removal can soften disruption while delaying gains; it does not erase distributional losses.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: A quota causes a $520 consumer loss, a $170 domestic producer gain and $280 of rents. Domestic firms hold the rights and spend $60 of real resources competing for them. A competitive auction would yield the same rents and use $15 of real resources. How much would switching to the auction improve national welfare?
general.Choice A: $280; all auction proceeds are newly created surplus
general.Choice B: $325; add auction proceeds to the resource saving
general.Choice C: $60; auctions have no resource cost regardless of the stated data
general.Choice D: $45; it saves resources while changing who receives an existing transfer
general.Correct Answer: D — $45; it saves resources while changing who receives an existing transfer
general.Feedback: Distortion before rent-seeking is 520 - 170 - 280 = 70. The present system loses 70 + 60 = 130; the auction loses 70 + 15 = 85. National welfare improves by 45, not by the rent amount.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: Officials propose a tariff on emergency valves because a foreign supply outage could halt hospitals. Domestic firms cannot expand within five years; audited reserves and two independent allied suppliers could cover an outage sooner at lower resource cost. Which assessment is best?
general.Choice A: The security label alone establishes that any tariff improves resilience
general.Choice B: The security concern can be real, but the evidence favors reserves and diversified supply over this tariff
general.Choice C: The tariff must solve the outage risk because it raises domestic producer surplus
general.Choice D: All resilience spending is wasteful because the small-country trade model has gains from trade
general.Correct Answer: B — The security concern can be real, but the evidence favors reserves and diversified supply over this tariff
general.Feedback: Evaluate whether the instrument actually reduces the stated risk and whether another instrument does so at lower cost. A legitimate objective does not make an ineffective tariff the preferred response.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: A new sensor industry predicts learning gains worth $18 million in present value. Protection would cost $24 million in present-value consumer surplus, transfer $9 million to domestic producers and yield $5 million of tariff revenue. Suppose learning is additional and there are no other effects. Which evaluation is correct?
general.Choice A: The modeled net loss is $6 million because all consumer loss is destroyed
general.Choice B: The modeled net gain is $32 million because producer gains and revenue are additional to learning
general.Choice C: The modeled net gain is $8 million, but the case depends on the learning forecast being credible
general.Choice D: The policy is proven desirable regardless of whether learning occurs
general.Correct Answer: C — The modeled net gain is $8 million, but the case depends on the learning forecast being credible
general.Feedback: Static national loss is 24 - 9 - 5 = 10 million. Additional learning of 18 gives a modeled gain of 8. If the learning is not caused by protection or does not materialize, the conclusion can reverse.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: A tariff preserves 240 jobs in an input industry but eliminates 160 downstream jobs. Retaliation would eliminate another 120 export jobs if it occurs; its probability is one-half. What follows from these employment estimates alone?
general.Choice A: Expected employment rises by 80, so the tariff necessarily raises welfare
general.Choice B: Expected employment falls by 40 because retaliation is certain
general.Choice C: Expected employment rises by 240 because losses outside the protected industry are irrelevant
general.Choice D: Expected employment rises by 20, but this alone does not establish a national welfare gain
general.Correct Answer: D — Expected employment rises by 20, but this alone does not establish a national welfare gain
general.Feedback: Expected job change is 240 - 160 - 0.5 × 120 = 20. Employment counts alone do not measure consumer surplus, resource costs or other welfare effects.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: A minister defends a tariff by citing $12 million of domestic producer gains. It also raises $8 million in revenue and costs consumers $17 million. Retaliation causes a separate $7 million net loss to domestic exporters. Ignoring other effects, which conclusion follows?
general.Choice A: National surplus falls $4 million; the protected industry does not capture the whole policy effect
general.Choice B: National surplus rises $3 million because retaliation affects only foreigners
general.Choice C: National surplus rises $12 million because the protected producers are the relevant group
general.Choice D: National surplus falls $24 million because producer gains and revenue cannot offset consumer losses
general.Correct Answer: A — National surplus falls $4 million; the protected industry does not capture the whole policy effect
general.Feedback: Include all the stated domestic effects once: 12 + 8 - 17 - 7 = -4 million. Retaliation transmits costs beyond the original protected industry; producer gains alone do not establish a national gain.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: Opening trade gives consumers $720 and costs producers $420. A plan transfers $420 from consumers to producers but uses $75 of real resources delivering assistance. Compared with autarky, which statement is correct?
general.Choice A: Consumers retain $300 because assistance resources are just transfers
general.Choice B: Producers can be restored and consumers retain $225; compensation and efficiency must both be evaluated
general.Choice C: National surplus rises $720 because producer compensation cancels the original loss without cost
general.Choice D: National surplus falls $195 because compensation must be subtracted twice
general.Correct Answer: B — Producers can be restored and consumers retain $225; compensation and efficiency must both be evaluated
general.Feedback: The initial national gain is 720 - 420 = 300. The transfer restores producers but changes no total; resource use reduces the gain to 225. The result presumes the assistance is actually delivered.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: Trade raises total surplus but lowers income in one region. This illustrates:
general.Choice A: Trade has no efficiency gain
general.Choice B: Equity is identical to total surplus
general.Choice C: Efficiency and equity can point to different concerns
general.Choice D: Imports must be banned
general.Correct Answer: C — Efficiency and equity can point to different concerns
general.Feedback: Trade can increase total surplus while imposing concentrated losses on particular regions or groups, so efficiency and equity are separate questions.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: Potential compensation means:
general.Choice A: Losers are automatically paid
general.Choice B: No one loses
general.Choice C: The government must impose a quota
general.Choice D: Winners gain enough in aggregate that compensation could be possible
general.Correct Answer: D — Winners gain enough in aggregate that compensation could be possible
general.Feedback: If total surplus rises, the winners gain enough in aggregate that compensation could be possible, but compensation occurs only if an actual transfer or policy is implemented.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: Protection would preserve 2,000 jobs for a year at a real efficiency cost of $60 million to consumers and firms that use the protected product, with no other benefits in this exercise. A targeted transition program costs $20 million and enables 1,500 workers to obtain equally valued jobs that year. How do the two policies compare in cost per worker helped and number of workers helped?
general.Choice A: Protection costs $13,333 per preserved job; transition costs $30,000 per worker and leaves no employment gap.
general.Choice B: Protection is necessarily best because it preserves all 2,000 jobs; consumer and downstream costs are irrelevant to an employment goal.
general.Choice C: Protection costs $30,000 per preserved job; transition costs about $13,333 per reemployed worker but leaves 500 more workers needing help.
general.Choice D: Transition is necessarily best because its total cost is lower; differences in the number of workers helped need not be reported.
general.Correct Answer: C — Protection costs $30,000 per preserved job; transition costs about $13,333 per reemployed worker but leaves 500 more workers needing help.
general.Feedback: Protection costs 60000000/2000=30000 per job-year, versus 20000000/1500≈13333. The targeted program costs less per worker but reaches fewer. Advice should state both the efficiency comparison and the remaining distributional need.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: A strategic input faces an outage risk. A broad tariff costs $40 million in expected efficiency losses and would reduce expected outage losses by $15 million. A reserve program costs $12 million and would reduce those losses by $25 million. Both estimates already include operating costs. Which evaluation is best on the stated evidence?
general.Choice A: The tariff nets $55 million while reserves net $37 million; security benefits should be added to policy costs.
general.Choice B: The reserve program nets $25 million while the tariff nets $15 million; resource costs are irrelevant once security is the objective.
general.Choice C: The tariff is preferable whenever it reduces imports, even if the reserve program has larger net security benefits.
general.Choice D: The reserve program nets $13 million while the tariff nets -$25 million; a real security concern does not establish that broad protection is the best instrument.
general.Correct Answer: D — The reserve program nets $13 million while the tariff nets -$25 million; a real security concern does not establish that broad protection is the best instrument.
general.Feedback: Net expected benefits are 25-12=13 million for reserves and 15-40=-25 million for the tariff. The national-security goal is evaluated by the policy’s actual risk reduction and resource cost, not the protection label.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
general.Question: Temporary protection was justified by a forecast that three years of learning would cut unit resource cost from $12 to $8, below a $9 world price. After five years, audited cost remains $12. Firms request renewal based only on past subsidies and current jobs. Which evidence would most strengthen a renewed learning case?
general.Choice A: A credible, independently testable mechanism and timetable for additional learning gains exceeding the new consumer and resource costs.
general.Choice B: The total subsidy already spent, because recovering sunk public expenditure establishes future learning benefits.
general.Choice C: The number of years protection has lasted, because longer duration demonstrates that costs are approaching the target.
general.Choice D: Current protected employment alone, because retaining jobs proves unit productivity has improved despite the audited cost.
general.Correct Answer: A — A credible, independently testable mechanism and timetable for additional learning gains exceeding the new consumer and resource costs.
general.Feedback: The promised cost reduction has not occurred, weakening the original rationale. Renewal requires prospective, credible learning evidence and a comparison with additional costs. Sunk subsidies, duration and employment do not establish future productivity gains.

general.Learning Objective: ITP.6 — Evaluate trade-policy arguments using efficiency, distribution, and evidence.
