general.Question: A proposed tariff is estimated to create $40 million of domestic producer gains, $25 million of revenue and $80 million of consumer losses. Retaliation would additionally reduce domestic exporters’ net surplus by $20 million. These export losses are additional to the gains and losses already listed. What is the overall effect on national welfare?
general.Choice A: Net gain is $5 million; retaliation can be ignored because export firms are outside the protected industry.
general.Choice B: Net loss is $35 million; retaliation adds a separate export-market loss to the initial $15 million tariff loss.
general.Choice C: Net loss is $60 million; government revenue is an extra resource loss rather than a domestic transfer.
general.Choice D: Net loss is $15 million; every export loss is automatically included in consumer losses from the original tariff.
general.Correct Answer: B — Net loss is $35 million; retaliation adds a separate export-market loss to the initial $15 million tariff loss.
general.Feedback: The initial national change is 40+25-80=-15 million. Adding the explicitly separate export loss gives -35 million. Revenue is a domestic transfer, while retaliation can impose additional losses in other markets.

general.Question: A decision should continue when:
general.Choice A: Marginal benefit is at least marginal cost
general.Choice B: Total cost is zero
general.Choice C: Average cost is falling
general.Choice D: Demand is perfectly elastic
general.Correct Answer: A — Marginal benefit is at least marginal cost
general.Feedback: Marginal reasoning compares the next benefit with the next cost.

general.Common Misconception: Using totals or averages instead of the next order’s values.
general.Question: A delivery service considers accepting one more order. The order adds $28 in revenue and $19 in delivery cost. What should it do?
general.Choice A: Accept because the added benefit exceeds the added cost
general.Choice B: Reject because any additional cost makes the order harmful
general.Choice C: Accept only if total daily revenue exceeds total daily cost
general.Choice D: Reject unless average delivery cost falls after the order
general.Correct Answer: A — Accept because the added benefit exceeds the added cost
general.Feedback: The additional order adds $9 in net benefit.

general.Common Misconception: Missing the one-more-unit focus of marginal analysis.
general.Question: A student asks whether one more study hour is worthwhile by comparing its expected grade improvement with the fatigue it creates. What reasoning is being used?
general.Choice A: Marginal reasoning about one additional hour
general.Choice B: Average reasoning about all study hours combined
general.Choice C: Sunk-cost reasoning about time already spent
general.Choice D: Total-benefit reasoning without considering added cost
general.Correct Answer: A — Marginal reasoning about one additional hour
general.Feedback: The question compares the benefit and cost created by one additional hour.

general.Question: If the marginal benefit of an action is $30 and the marginal cost is $20, what should a rational person do?
general.Choice A: Take the action
general.Choice B: Avoid the action
general.Choice C: Ignore the marginal benefit
general.Choice D: Choose only by total cost
general.Correct Answer: A — Take the action
general.Feedback: Because marginal benefit is greater than marginal cost, the action is worth taking.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring the displaced alternative or adding costs and benefits.
general.Question: A cyber-security team can run one more audit. It costs 90 staff-hours and is expected to prevent 120 hours of incident response, but the audit also displaces training worth 20 hours. What is the net marginal effect?
general.Choice A: A gain of 10 staff-hours
general.Choice B: A gain of 30 staff-hours
general.Choice C: A loss of 70 staff-hours
general.Choice D: A gain of 210 staff-hours
general.Correct Answer: A — A gain of 10 staff-hours
general.Feedback: Net marginal effect is 120 minus 90 direct hours minus 20 displaced training hours.

general.Question: A business owner already spent $2,000 on a project. Finishing the project costs another $500 and will bring in $800. What should matter for the decision?
general.Choice A: The extra $500 cost and extra $800 benefit
general.Choice B: The full $2,500 spent across the whole project
general.Choice C: Only the sunk $2,000
general.Choice D: Only whether the project feels successful
general.Correct Answer: A — The extra $500 cost and extra $800 benefit
general.Feedback: The decision should compare the additional cost of finishing with the additional benefit.

general.Question: A firm already spent $5,000 designing a product. It can spend $1,200 more to launch it and earn $1,700 in revenue. What should it do if it is using marginal reasoning?
general.Choice A: Launch, because the marginal benefit exceeds the marginal cost by $500
general.Choice B: Do not launch, because total spending is $6,200
general.Choice C: Do not launch, because the $5,000 sunk cost is too large
general.Choice D: Launch only if total revenue exceeds all past costs
general.Correct Answer: A — Launch, because the marginal benefit exceeds the marginal cost by $500
general.Feedback: The $5,000 is sunk. The launch decision compares the extra $1,200 cost with the extra $1,700 revenue.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring probability or including sunk research spending.
general.Question: A vaccine trial can enroll one more site. The site has a 60% chance of producing evidence worth $50,000 and costs $24,000 to operate. Ignoring other effects, what does expected marginal analysis recommend?
general.Choice A: Enroll because expected marginal benefit is $30,000, above cost
general.Choice B: Reject because the full $50,000 benefit is uncertain
general.Choice C: Enroll only if earlier research spending is recovered
general.Choice D: Reject because the $24,000 cost raises total trial spending
general.Correct Answer: A — Enroll because expected marginal benefit is $30,000, above cost
general.Feedback: Expected added benefit is 0.60 × $50,000 = $30,000, which exceeds $24,000.

general.Common Misconception: Using total, average, or sunk values instead of next-hour changes.
general.Question: A bookstore considers staying open one more hour. The hour adds $240 in sales margin and $170 in staffing and utility cost. Which comparison matters?
general.Choice A: The $240 added benefit versus the $170 added cost
general.Choice B: Total yearly sales versus total yearly operating and staffing cost
general.Choice C: Average hourly sales versus the original opening expense
general.Choice D: Past rent payments versus today’s entire revenue
general.Correct Answer: A — The $240 added benefit versus the $170 added cost
general.Feedback: Marginal analysis isolates what changes during the additional hour.

general.Question: A business can earn $900 from one more project, but completing it costs $650. What should it do?
general.Choice A: Complete it because marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost
general.Choice B: Reject the project because any cost is bad
general.Choice C: Ignore the extra revenue
general.Choice D: Complete the project only if GDP rises
general.Correct Answer: A — Complete it because marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost
general.Feedback: The marginal benefit is greater than the marginal cost, so the project adds net benefit.

general.Common Misconception: Reversing the MB-MC rule or using averages and totals.
general.Question: A nurse can make one more follow-up call. The expected patient benefit is 12 points and the fatigue cost is 8 points. What should the nurse do?
general.Choice A: Make the call because its marginal benefit exceeds its marginal cost
general.Choice B: Skip the call because fatigue creates any positive cost
general.Choice C: Make the call only if average benefit per call rises
general.Choice D: Skip the call unless total benefit exceeds all past costs
general.Correct Answer: A — Make the call because its marginal benefit exceeds its marginal cost
general.Feedback: The next call adds 4 points of net benefit.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring a cost component or adding benefit and cost.
general.Question: A grocer can stock one more crate. Expected sales margin is $45, spoilage risk costs $12, and shelf labor costs $18. What should the grocer do?
general.Choice A: Stock it because the $45 benefit exceeds the $30 added cost
general.Choice B: Reject it because spoilage risk makes total benefit uncertain
general.Choice C: Stock it only if the store’s average profit increases
general.Choice D: Reject it because adding the crate increases total store costs.
general.Correct Answer: A — Stock it because the $45 benefit exceeds the $30 added cost
general.Feedback: Marginal cost is $30, leaving $15 in net marginal benefit.

general.Question: A vendor already spent 100 tokens setting up a stall. Staying open one more hour costs 12 tokens and brings in 20 tokens. What should matter now?
general.Choice A: The extra 12-token cost and extra 20-token benefit
general.Choice B: The full 112 tokens spent
general.Choice C: Only the original 100-token setup cost
general.Choice D: Only whether the stall looks impressive
general.Correct Answer: A — The extra 12-token cost and extra 20-token benefit
general.Feedback: The setup cost is sunk. The current decision compares the extra cost and extra benefit of staying open.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring avoided costs or relying on total and average values.
general.Question: A warehouse has packed 900 orders; that work is irreversible. The last 100 avoid $2,100 of penalties if completed tonight. Overtime costs $1,600 and displaces training worth $700. An outside packer can finish them for $1,900 without using warehouse staff. Which decision maximizes incremental value?
general.Choice A: Use the outside packer: its $200 gain exceeds overtime’s $200 loss and leaving the orders unfinished.
general.Choice B: Use overtime: its $500 gain exceeds the outside packer’s $200 gain because training is not a cash payment.
general.Choice C: Leave them unfinished: both methods cost more than zero, and previous packing costs must be recovered first.
general.Choice D: Use overtime: the 900 completed orders make finishing the final 100 worthwhile regardless of displaced training.
general.Correct Answer: A — Use the outside packer: its $200 gain exceeds overtime’s $200 loss and leaving the orders unfinished.
general.Feedback: Relative to leaving the orders unfinished, overtime yields 2100-1600-700=-200; outsourcing yields 2100-1900=200. The prior 900 orders are sunk. The relevant choice compares complete incremental costs across feasible methods.

general.Common Misconception: Letting sunk investment override a negative next increment.
general.Question: A software firm has spent $2 million irreversibly. Updating costs $90,000 and adds $70,000 in revenue. Canceling avoids the update but triggers a $35,000 support-termination payment. Selling the unfinished code yields $15,000 and requires $10,000 of handover work, with no termination payment. Which option is best from today?
general.Choice A: Sell: its $5,000 net receipt exceeds updating’s $20,000 loss and cancellation’s $35,000 loss.
general.Choice B: Update: its $70,000 revenue exceeds the sale receipt, so the remaining $90,000 cost should be ignored.
general.Choice C: Cancel: avoiding the $90,000 update cost is sufficient even though selling has a positive net receipt.
general.Choice D: Update: the $2 million already spent makes the smallest additional cash outlay the relevant criterion.
general.Correct Answer: A — Sell: its $5,000 net receipt exceeds updating’s $20,000 loss and cancellation’s $35,000 loss.
general.Feedback: Future net values are 70-90=-20 thousand for updating, -35 thousand for canceling and 15-10=5 thousand for selling. The historical $2 million is common to every alternative and cannot justify continuation.

general.Common Misconception: Stopping early or continuing after MB falls below MC.
general.Question: A transit line can add up to three buses in order. Their direct marginal benefits are $140k, $105k and $78k; each costs $100k. Adding any buses requires $30k of dispatch setup. Only a three-bus plan also enables transfers worth $60k. Which plan has the highest net benefit?
general.Choice A: Three buses: net benefit is $53k, exceeding $15k for two and $10k for one.
general.Choice B: Two buses: stop before the third because its direct $78k benefit is below its $100k cost.
general.Choice C: One bus: its $40k direct surplus exceeds the second bus’s $5k direct surplus.
general.Choice D: No buses: dispatch setup makes every positive-size plan have negative net benefit.
general.Correct Answer: A — Three buses: net benefit is $53k, exceeding $15k for two and $10k for one.
general.Feedback: One bus nets 140-100-30=10. Two net 140+105-200-30=15. Three net 140+105+78+60-300-30=53. The third enables a complementary benefit, so its relevant incremental benefit is 78+60.

general.Common Misconception: Confusing marginal, total, and average values.
general.Question: Marginal benefit is:
general.Choice A: The added benefit from one more unit.
general.Choice B: A past benefit that cannot change.
general.Choice C: Average benefit per unit.
general.Choice D: Total benefit from all units.
general.Correct Answer: A — The added benefit from one more unit.
general.Feedback: Marginal benefit measures the change from one additional unit.

general.Common Misconception: Calling future or avoidable costs sunk.
general.Question: A cost is sunk when it:
general.Choice A: Will occur only if one more unit is chosen.
general.Choice B: Has already occurred and cannot be recovered.
general.Choice C: Changes with the current decision.
general.Choice D: Equals the next-best alternative.
general.Correct Answer: B — Has already occurred and cannot be recovered.
general.Feedback: Sunk costs are past and unrecoverable.

general.Common Misconception: Using totals, averages, or sunk costs.
general.Question: The marginal rule says to continue while:
general.Choice A: Marginal benefit is at least as large as marginal cost.
general.Choice B: Average cost is falling
general.Choice C: Total benefit is positive
general.Choice D: Past spending is large.
general.Correct Answer: A — Marginal benefit is at least as large as marginal cost.
general.Feedback: The next unit should be chosen when its added benefit covers its added cost.

general.Common Misconception: Reporting total or average benefit instead of the change.
general.Question: Total benefit is 50 and average benefit is 10. One more unit raises total benefit to 57. What is marginal benefit?
general.Feedback: Marginal benefit is 57 minus 50.

general.Common Misconception: Reversing the marginal rule or adding MB and MC.
general.Question: Marginal cost is $12 and marginal benefit is $17. What should happen?
general.Choice A: Take the next unit because benefit exceeds cost
general.Choice B: Stop because the unit has a positive cost
general.Choice C: Add $12 and $17 before deciding
general.Choice D: Use average cost instead of marginal cost
general.Correct Answer: A — Take the next unit because benefit exceeds cost
general.Feedback: Compare MB with MC; the next unit adds $5 in net benefit.

general.Common Misconception: Treating an average per unit as the next unit’s change.
general.Question: Which value is average rather than marginal?
general.Choice A: Total cost divided by all units produced
general.Choice B: The change in cost from one more unit
general.Choice C: The benefit added by the next unit
general.Choice D: A future cost avoided by stopping now
general.Correct Answer: A — Total cost divided by all units produced
general.Feedback: Average divides a total across units; marginal measures a change.

general.Common Misconception: Calling a recoverable or avoidable cost sunk.
general.Question: A $100 fee is refundable if a project stops today. Is it sunk for today’s decision?
general.Choice A: No, because stopping can still recover it
general.Choice B: Yes, because it was paid in the past
general.Choice C: Yes, because every prior payment is sunk
general.Choice D: No, because future costs can never matter
general.Correct Answer: A — No, because stopping can still recover it
general.Feedback: A cost is sunk only if the current choice cannot recover or avoid it.

general.Common Misconception: Adding benefit and cost or reporting gross revenue.
general.Question: One more sale brings $30 in revenue and requires $22 in added cost. What is net marginal benefit?
general.Feedback: Net marginal benefit equals $30 minus $22.

general.Common Misconception: Failing to connect scarce-resource tradeoffs to the next increment.
general.Question: Scarcity limits a community’s emergency crews. How does marginal analysis help decide whether to assign one more crew-hour to inspections?
general.Choice A: Compare the added inspection benefit with the best use of that crew-hour forgone
general.Choice B: Add the value of every program the community cannot fund
general.Choice C: Use total inspection benefit without considering the next hour’s cost
general.Choice D: Treat all prior emergency spending as the next hour’s marginal cost
general.Correct Answer: A — Compare the added inspection benefit with the best use of that crew-hour forgone
general.Feedback: Scarcity makes the crew-hour costly; marginal analysis tests whether its added inspection benefit covers that cost.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring the best alternative use of the next increment.
general.Question: A worker could earn $25 during one more study hour. How does opportunity cost enter the marginal study decision?
general.Choice A: The forgone $25 is part of the marginal cost of that hour
general.Choice B: The $25 is a sunk cost because work has not occurred
general.Choice C: All lifetime wages become the marginal cost of studying
general.Choice D: Opportunity cost matters only for the first study hour
general.Correct Answer: A — The forgone $25 is part of the marginal cost of that hour
general.Feedback: The next hour’s opportunity cost belongs in its marginal cost.

general.Common Misconception: Using totals or fixed costs instead of incremental profit.
general.Question: A firm expands output while the revenue from one more unit exceeds the cost of that unit. How does this connect marginal analysis to profit maximization?
general.Choice A: Each positive marginal contribution raises profit until the next unit turns negative
general.Choice B: Profit is maximized whenever total revenue is positive
general.Choice C: Fixed cost determines whether every additional unit is produced
general.Choice D: Average revenue must exceed total cost for the next unit
general.Correct Answer: A — Each positive marginal contribution raises profit until the next unit turns negative
general.Feedback: Profit rises while marginal revenue covers marginal cost.

general.Common Misconception: Leaving external incremental harm out of social decisions.
general.Question: A factory’s next unit creates pollution damage not paid by the factory. How does that affect marginal analysis?
general.Choice A: The external damage belongs in social marginal cost
general.Choice B: The damage is sunk because outsiders bear it
general.Choice C: Only private production cost can be marginal
general.Choice D: External damage matters only after all output is produced
general.Correct Answer: A — The external damage belongs in social marginal cost
general.Feedback: Social marginal analysis counts costs imposed on others.

general.Common Misconception: Replacing the next increment with totals or averages.
general.Question: A public program considers one additional service. How does marginal analysis implement cost-benefit reasoning?
general.Choice A: Compare the added social benefit with the added social cost
general.Choice B: Compare lifetime total program spending with the current year’s available budget
general.Choice C: Add average benefit and average cost together
general.Choice D: Continue whenever any participant receives a benefit
general.Correct Answer: A — Compare the added social benefit with the added social cost
general.Feedback: Cost-benefit analysis at the margin asks whether the next increment creates net social benefit.

general.Common Misconception: Failing to transfer marginal comparison to an individual purchase.
general.Question: A consumer buys another unit while its added satisfaction exceeds the price and other next-unit costs. What connection is being made?
general.Choice A: Consumer choice can use the same MB-versus-MC rule
general.Choice B: Consumer choice depends only on total satisfaction accumulated from every prior purchase
general.Choice C: The price becomes sunk before the purchase decision
general.Choice D: Average satisfaction determines every additional purchase
general.Correct Answer: A — Consumer choice can use the same MB-versus-MC rule
general.Feedback: The consumer continues while the next unit’s marginal benefit covers its marginal cost.

general.Common Misconception: Rejecting any costly unit or using averages and sunk costs.
general.Question: A food truck can serve one more customer for $11 in added revenue and $8 in added food and labor cost. Which choice follows the marginal rule?
general.Choice A: Serve the customer because marginal benefit covers marginal cost
general.Choice B: Stop because the customer creates a positive cost
general.Choice C: Serve only if average revenue for the day rises
general.Choice D: Stop unless earlier setup expenses have been recovered
general.Correct Answer: A — Serve the customer because marginal benefit covers marginal cost
general.Feedback: The next customer adds $3 in net benefit, so service should continue.

general.Common Misconception: Letting an unrecoverable past cost control a current choice.
general.Question: A student has already paid a nonrefundable fee for a course. When deciding whether to continue, the fee should be treated as:
general.Choice A: The opportunity cost of attending the next class meeting
general.Choice B: A benefit of continuing because the fee has already been paid
general.Choice C: A sunk cost that does not change the current marginal decision.
general.Choice D: A reason to continue so the payment is not wasted.
general.Correct Answer: C — A sunk cost that does not change the current marginal decision.
general.Feedback: Only future benefits and future costs should guide the current decision.

general.Common Misconception: Reporting the new total or an average instead of the change.
general.Question: A clinic adds one appointment and total patient benefit rises from 40 to 47 points. What is the marginal benefit of that appointment?
general.Choice A: 7 benefit points
general.Choice B: 47 total benefit points
general.Choice C: 40 prior benefit points
general.Choice D: 43.5 average benefit points
general.Correct Answer: A — 7 benefit points
general.Feedback: Marginal benefit is the change in total benefit: 47 minus 40.

general.Common Misconception: Comparing the next-hour benefit with total or past costs.
general.Question: A café should remain open for one extra hour if the extra revenue from that hour:
general.Choice A: Exceeds average revenue for the day.
general.Choice B: Covers yesterday’s losses.
general.Choice C: Exceeds total daily cost.
general.Choice D: Exceeds the extra operating cost for that hour.
general.Correct Answer: D — Exceeds the extra operating cost for that hour.
general.Feedback: The extra hour should be judged by its additional revenue and additional cost.

general.Common Misconception: Rejecting a positive-net increment or using averages and sunk effort.
general.Question: A student considers studying one more hour. Expected exam benefit is 6 points and fatigue cost is 4 points. What should the student do?
general.Choice A: Study because the added benefit exceeds the added cost
general.Choice B: Stop because any fatigue makes studying harmful
general.Choice C: Study only if average grades rise
general.Choice D: Stop unless prior study time is recovered
general.Correct Answer: A — Study because the added benefit exceeds the added cost
general.Feedback: The extra hour adds 2 points of net benefit.

general.Common Misconception: Adding benefit and cost or reporting only one side.
general.Question: A restaurant can serve one more table for $70 in added revenue and $52 in added cost. Which amount is net marginal benefit?
general.Feedback: Net marginal benefit is $70 minus $52.

general.Common Misconception: Assigning a fixed past payment to the next-hour decision.
general.Question: A store has already paid monthly rent. When deciding whether to stay open one more hour, how should that rent be treated?
general.Choice A: As a sunk cost that does not change with the hour
general.Choice B: As the marginal cost of every extra hour
general.Choice C: As the marginal benefit of added sales
general.Choice D: As an avoidable cost only if sales are low
general.Correct Answer: A — As a sunk cost that does not change with the hour
general.Feedback: Only costs that change with the additional hour are marginal.

general.Common Misconception: Substituting total, average, or historical values for the next increment.
general.Question: A clinic can treat one more patient. Which question is marginal?
general.Choice A: What added benefit and added cost will this patient create?
general.Choice B: What have all patients cost since the clinic opened?
general.Choice C: What is average benefit across all patients?
general.Choice D: How large was the clinic’s original construction budget?
general.Correct Answer: A — What added benefit and added cost will this patient create?
general.Feedback: Marginal analysis asks what changes because of one additional patient.

general.Common Misconception: Escalating commitment based on past effort.
general.Question: A software team has spent six months on a feature. Completing it requires 200 more hours and is expected to save users 140 hours. The strongest decision is:
general.Choice A: Stop unless there are additional future benefits not yet counted.
general.Choice B: Continue because six months have already been invested.
general.Choice C: Ignore the remaining 200 hours because the project is nearly done.
general.Choice D: Continue because users receive some benefit.
general.Correct Answer: A — Stop unless there are additional future benefits not yet counted.
general.Feedback: Past effort is sunk; the remaining cost exceeds the identified future benefit.

general.Common Misconception: Using total or average values instead of the next unit.
general.Question: The marginal benefit of the fourth unit is $18 and its marginal cost is $14. The fourth unit should be:
general.Choice A: Produced or consumed because marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost.
general.Choice B: Rejected because any positive marginal cost makes the unit undesirable
general.Choice C: Accepted only if no sunk costs were incurred earlier
general.Choice D: Rejected unless average benefit also rises.
general.Correct Answer: A — Produced or consumed because marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost.
general.Feedback: The fourth unit adds $4 in net benefit.

general.Common Misconception: Including sunk development spending in the marginal comparison.
general.Question: A firm has already spent $50,000 developing a product. Finishing it will cost another $12,000 and is expected to generate $18,000. The firm should:
general.Choice A: Cancel because total spending would reach $62,000
general.Choice B: Finish so the original $50,000 is not wasted
general.Choice C: Finish the product because the future benefit exceeds the future cost.
general.Choice D: Ignore the $18,000 expected revenue because it is uncertain.
general.Correct Answer: C — Finish the product because the future benefit exceeds the future cost.
general.Feedback: The $50,000 is unrecoverable; the relevant comparison is $18,000 versus $12,000.

general.Common Misconception: Using totals or fixed costs rather than incremental values.
general.Question: A museum stays open an extra hour. The added admissions revenue is $900 and added staffing and utility cost is $1,100. Marginal analysis says:
general.Choice A: Stay open because total daily revenue is high
general.Choice B: Stay open to recover fixed building costs
general.Choice C: Close at the normal time because marginal cost exceeds marginal benefit.
general.Choice D: Close only if average cost rises.
general.Correct Answer: C — Close at the normal time because marginal cost exceeds marginal benefit.
general.Feedback: The extra hour reduces net benefit by $200.

general.Common Misconception: Using average or total cost instead of the added cost.
general.Question: A factory’s average cost is $14, while producing unit 101 raises total cost from $1,400 to $1,418. Which cost is relevant to the unit-101 decision?
general.Choice A: The $18 marginal cost of unit 101
general.Choice B: The $14 average cost of existing output
general.Choice C: The $1,418 total cost after production
general.Choice D: The $1,400 cost already incurred
general.Correct Answer: A — The $18 marginal cost of unit 101
general.Feedback: Unit 101 changes total cost by $18; that increment is its marginal cost.

general.Common Misconception: Adding benefit and cost or reporting only one side.
general.Question: A student studies an additional hour. The expected grade benefit is valued at 9 points and fatigue cost at 6 points. The net marginal benefit is:
general.Choice A: 3 points.
general.Choice B: 15 points.
general.Choice C: 6 points.
general.Choice D: 9 points.
general.Correct Answer: A — 3 points.
general.Feedback: Net marginal benefit equals 9 minus 6.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring the displaced incremental alternative.
general.Question: A platform can add one feature now for $80,000. It yields $95,000 in direct benefit but delays a security upgrade worth $25,000. What is the feature’s net marginal effect?
general.Feedback: $95,000 minus $80,000 direct cost minus $25,000 opportunity cost equals -$10,000.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring congestion cost or adding benefit and costs.
general.Question: Adding one more flight would bring in $80,000 in revenue, incur $54,000 in operating costs, and impose $18,000 in expected delay costs on other flights. What is its net marginal benefit?

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring forgone training or adding values.
general.Question: A police department considers one more patrol. Crime reduction is valued at $120,000, added payroll is $75,000, and the officers would forgo training worth $38,000. What is net marginal benefit?

general.Common Misconception: Comparing totals or adding the two marginal changes.
general.Question: Total benefit rises from $140 to $158 when a fifth unit is added, while total cost rises from $92 to $107. What is the fifth unit’s net marginal benefit?
general.Feedback: MB is $18 and MC is $15, so net marginal benefit is $3.

general.Common Misconception: Using average cost instead of the next box’s cost.
general.Question: A warehouse’s average handling cost is $9 per box. Handling the next box costs $13 and brings in $15 after other variable costs have been deducted, but before deducting this handling cost. What should it do?
general.Choice A: Handle it because $15 exceeds the $13 marginal cost
general.Choice B: Reject it because marginal cost exceeds average cost
general.Choice C: Handle it only if average cost falls below $9
general.Choice D: Reject it because total handling cost rises
general.Correct Answer: A — Handle it because $15 exceeds the $13 marginal cost
general.Feedback: The box adds $2 in profit even though its marginal cost exceeds average cost.

general.Common Misconception: Stopping early or continuing after MB falls below MC.
general.Question: A firm can run up to four ads. Their marginal benefits are $90, $70, $45, and $20; each ad costs $50. How many ads should run?
general.Choice A: Two ads
general.Choice B: One ad
general.Choice C: Three ads
general.Choice D: Four ads
general.Correct Answer: A — Two ads
general.Feedback: Only the first two ads have marginal benefit at least $50.

general.Common Misconception: Including sunk design cost or ignoring the cancellation alternative.
general.Question: A project has an unrecoverable $8,000 design cost. Finishing costs $3,000 and yields $4,200; cancellation costs $400. Which comparison is relevant?
general.Choice A: Finish for a $1,200 future gain versus paying $400 to cancel
general.Choice B: Compare the full $11,000 spending with $4,200 revenue
general.Choice C: Finish only to recover the $8,000 design cost
general.Choice D: Cancel because any remaining cost is harmful
general.Correct Answer: A — Finish for a $1,200 future gain versus paying $400 to cancel
general.Feedback: The future choices are a $1,200 net gain from finishing or a $400 cancellation cost.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring avoided cost as benefit or using totals and averages.
general.Question: A sixth quality inspection lowers expected defect losses by $260 and costs $210 in labor. What is the correct next-step decision?
general.Choice A: Perform it because avoided loss is a marginal benefit above cost
general.Choice B: Skip it because inspection creates a positive labor cost
general.Choice C: Perform it only if total defect losses become zero
general.Choice D: Skip it unless average inspection cost falls
general.Correct Answer: A — Perform it because avoided loss is a marginal benefit above cost
general.Feedback: The inspection creates $50 in net marginal benefit.

general.Common Misconception: Omitting a cost component or reporting gross output.
general.Question: One more worker adds $620 in output but requires $480 in wages and $90 in added equipment use. What is the worker’s net marginal contribution?
general.Feedback: $620 minus $480 minus $90 equals $50.

general.Common Misconception: Installing every beneficial unit without comparing the final unit’s marginal cost.
general.Question: A factory’s next three pollution-control units have marginal benefits of $90, $70, and $45 and marginal costs of $40, $65, and $60. How many units should be installed?
general.Choice A: One unit.
general.Choice B: Three units.
general.Choice C: Zero units.
general.Choice D: Two units.
general.Correct Answer: D — Two units.
general.Feedback: The first two units have MB at least as large as MC; the third does not.

general.Common Misconception: Continuing after marginal cost exceeds marginal benefit.
general.Question: A firm can produce units with marginal benefits of $20, $16, $12, and $8 and marginal costs of $6, $10, $13, and $15. How many units maximize net benefit?
general.Choice A: Two units.
general.Choice B: Four units.
general.Choice C: One unit.
general.Choice D: Three units.
general.Correct Answer: A — Two units.
general.Feedback: The first two units add net benefit; the third and fourth would reduce it.

general.Common Misconception: Using sunk design cost to justify a negative future decision.
general.Question: A city has spent $4 million on a stadium design. Construction will cost another $30 million and generate benefits valued at $24 million. What should marginal analysis recommend?
general.Choice A: Build because total benefits are positive.
general.Choice B: Do not build because the future cost exceeds the future benefit.
general.Choice C: Ignore construction cost because design work is complete.
general.Choice D: Build because abandoning the design wastes $4 million.
general.Correct Answer: B — Do not build because the future cost exceeds the future benefit.
general.Feedback: The $4 million is sunk; the relevant comparison is $24 million in benefits versus $30 million in future cost.

general.Common Misconception: Using total benefit without checking each additional hour.
general.Question: A clinic can extend hours. The first extra hour has MB $5,000 and MC $2,000; the second has MB $3,000 and MC $2,500; the third has MB $1,500 and MC $2,200. The optimal extension is:
general.Choice A: Zero hours.
general.Choice B: Three hours.
general.Choice C: One hour.
general.Choice D: Two hours.
general.Correct Answer: D — Two hours.
general.Feedback: Extend through the second hour and stop before the third, where MC exceeds MB.

general.Common Misconception: Using average profitability to justify a negative marginal transaction.
general.Question: A company’s average profit per customer is positive, but the next customer is expected to cost $140 to serve and generate $110 in revenue. The company should:
general.Choice A: Accept the customer to spread fixed costs over more customers
general.Choice B: Accept because average profit is positive
general.Choice C: Accept because total revenue will increase.
general.Choice D: Reject the next customer because marginal cost exceeds marginal benefit.
general.Correct Answer: D — Reject the next customer because marginal cost exceeds marginal benefit.
general.Feedback: The next customer lowers profit by $30.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring a relevant marginal cost borne by others.
general.Question: A farmer has already applied fertilizer. One additional unit raises crop value by $45 and costs $38, but also causes $10 in expected runoff damage. Including the external cost, the farmer should:
general.Choice A: Ignore runoff because it is not paid directly by the farmer.
general.Choice B: Apply because total crop value is positive.
general.Choice C: Apply because private marginal cost is only $38.
general.Choice D: Not apply the additional unit because marginal social cost is $48.
general.Correct Answer: D — Not apply the additional unit because marginal social cost is $48.
general.Feedback: The added social cost is $38 plus $10, which exceeds the $45 marginal benefit.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring expected downstream marginal cost.
general.Question: A hospital considers one more diagnostic test. Expected patient benefit is $420, direct test cost is $250, and expected false-positive follow-up cost is $190. Taking all the listed benefits and costs into account, should the hospital add the test?
general.Choice A: Ignore false-positive costs because they occur later.
general.Choice B: Do not add the test because total marginal cost is $440.
general.Choice C: Add because the direct cost is below the benefit.
general.Choice D: Add because some patients benefit.
general.Correct Answer: B — Do not add the test because total marginal cost is $440.
general.Feedback: Relevant marginal cost includes direct and expected follow-up costs.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring opportunity cost or adding benefit and costs.
general.Question: An airline can sell one more seat for $240. Added catering and handling cost $35, and carrying the passenger means giving up $170 in net earnings from cargo. What is net marginal benefit?
general.Feedback: The added passenger brings $240 in revenue, costs $35 to serve, and replaces cargo that would have earned $170 net. The net marginal benefit is $240 - $35 - $170 = $35.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring an external marginal cost.
general.Question: A city considers a third congestion-reduction measure. Driver time savings are $1.4 million, implementation costs $900,000, and added neighborhood noise costs $600,000. What should it do?
general.Choice A: Reject because marginal social cost is $1.5 million
general.Choice B: Adopt because private implementation cost is below benefit
general.Choice C: Adopt because total time savings remain positive
general.Choice D: Reject only if average program cost rises
general.Correct Answer: A — Reject because marginal social cost is $1.5 million
general.Feedback: Implementation plus noise costs exceed the next measure’s benefit.

general.Common Misconception: Using positive total or average profit instead of the next unit.
general.Question: Total revenue at 200 units is $18,000 and at 201 units is $18,075. Total cost rises from $14,400 to $14,482. Should unit 201 be produced?
general.Choice A: No, because marginal revenue $75 is below marginal cost $82
general.Choice B: Yes, because total revenue remains above total cost
general.Choice C: Yes, because average profit is positive
general.Choice D: No, because total cost rises when the unit is produced
general.Correct Answer: A — No, because marginal revenue $75 is below marginal cost $82
general.Feedback: Unit 201 reduces profit by $7.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring the next-best alternative use of staff time.
general.Question: A hospital can add a night shift. Expected benefit is $31,000; added payroll is $22,000; and using the nurses displaces training worth $11,000. Which decision is best?
general.Choice A: Do not add it because relevant marginal cost is $33,000
general.Choice B: Add it because payroll alone is below benefit
general.Choice C: Add it because total hospital benefit is large
general.Choice D: Do not add it because any displaced activity is sunk
general.Correct Answer: A — Do not add it because relevant marginal cost is $33,000
general.Feedback: Payroll plus forgone training exceeds the shift’s expected benefit.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring probability or including sunk grant spending.
general.Question: A research grant has spent $2 million. Another experiment costs $180,000 and has a 40% chance of producing evidence worth $600,000. Ignoring other outcomes, should it run?
general.Choice A: Run because expected marginal benefit is $240,000
general.Choice B: Stop because the $600,000 benefit is uncertain
general.Choice C: Run only to justify the $2 million already spent
general.Choice D: Stop because total spending would rise
general.Correct Answer: A — Run because expected marginal benefit is $240,000
general.Feedback: Expected added benefit exceeds the $180,000 experiment cost.

general.Common Misconception: Crossing a negative increment to reach a smaller later positive one.
general.Question: A retailer’s first three added inventory batches have net marginal benefits of $6,000, $2,000, and -$1,500. A fourth would have +$500 only if the third is purchased. How many additional batches should the retailer buy?
general.Choice A: Buy two batches
general.Choice B: Buy four batches
general.Choice C: Buy three batches
general.Choice D: Buy one batch
general.Correct Answer: A — Buy two batches
general.Feedback: Buying batches three and four together would reduce net benefit by $1,000.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring a relevant external or opportunity cost.
general.Question: A pollution rule’s next reduction step yields $4.8 million in health benefits, costs firms $3.6 million, and reduces recreational value by $1.5 million. Based on social marginal analysis, should the additional reduction be required?
general.Choice A: Do not require it because social marginal cost is $5.1 million
general.Choice B: Require it because compliance cost alone is below benefit
general.Choice C: Require it because total prior health benefits are large
general.Choice D: Do not require it because all environmental policy is costly
general.Correct Answer: A — Do not require it because social marginal cost is $5.1 million
general.Feedback: The next step’s combined social costs exceed its benefit.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring a nonbudget marginal cost.
general.Question: A utility considers one more conservation rebate. Expected energy savings are $130, rebate administration costs $90, and customer hassle is valued at $45. What is the social decision?
general.Choice A: Do not offer it because marginal social cost is $135
general.Choice B: Offer it because administrative cost is below savings
general.Choice C: Offer it because total energy savings remain positive
general.Choice D: Do not offer it because rebates are transfers
general.Correct Answer: A — Do not offer it because marginal social cost is $135
general.Feedback: The next rebate’s social cost exceeds its benefit by $5.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring the alternative assignment of the next team.
general.Question: An emergency agency can pre-position one more team. Expected response benefit is $500,000, deployment costs $320,000, and the team’s best alternative assignment is worth $210,000. What should it do?
general.Choice A: Do not deploy because relevant marginal cost is $530,000
general.Choice B: Deploy because direct cost is below expected benefit
general.Choice C: Deploy because emergency benefits are not monetary
general.Choice D: Do not deploy because prior readiness spending is sunk
general.Correct Answer: A — Do not deploy because relevant marginal cost is $530,000
general.Feedback: Direct plus opportunity cost exceeds expected response benefit.

general.Common Misconception: Using only private marginal cost.
general.Question: A farm’s next fertilizer application raises crop value by $1,100, costs $760, and increases expected water cleanup by $390. Which statement is correct?
general.Choice A: Do not apply because marginal social cost exceeds benefit by $50
general.Choice B: Apply because private marginal profit is $340
general.Choice C: Apply because total crop revenue is positive
general.Choice D: Do not apply because fertilizer cost is sunk
general.Correct Answer: A — Do not apply because marginal social cost exceeds benefit by $50
general.Feedback: Combined marginal cost is $1,150, above the $1,100 benefit.

general.Common Misconception: Treating unpaid resources as zero marginal cost.
general.Question: A nonprofit is considering one more meal-delivery route. The route would generate $900 in attributable donations, cost $620 for food and fuel, and use volunteer time that would otherwise provide tutoring worth $310. Should the nonprofit add the route?
general.Choice A: Do not add it because relevant marginal cost is $930
general.Choice B: Add it because direct cost is below donations
general.Choice C: Add it because volunteer time is unpaid
general.Choice D: Do not add it because total program costs are high
general.Correct Answer: A — Do not add it because relevant marginal cost is $930
general.Feedback: Direct plus forgone volunteer value exceeds added donations.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring the next-best use of salaried labor.
general.Question: A data center’s next cooling upgrade saves $140,000 in expected outages, costs $100,000, and uses technicians who could complete security work worth $50,000. What should it do?
general.Choice A: Do not upgrade because relevant marginal cost is $150,000
general.Choice B: Upgrade because outage savings exceed direct cost
general.Choice C: Upgrade because technicians are already salaried
general.Choice D: Do not upgrade because total cooling spending is high
general.Correct Answer: A — Do not upgrade because relevant marginal cost is $150,000
general.Feedback: Direct and opportunity costs exceed the expected outage savings.

general.Common Misconception: Skipping a required increment or using gross and average values.
general.Question: A school intervention’s next class has gross benefit 44 points, delivery cost 30, and teacher fatigue cost 9. A later class would yield gross benefit 50 but requires this class first. What should the school do now?
general.Choice A: Deliver the next class because its net marginal benefit is 5
general.Choice B: Skip to the later class because its gross benefit is higher
general.Choice C: Stop because combined cost is positive
general.Choice D: Deliver only if average class benefit rises
general.Correct Answer: A — Deliver the next class because its net marginal benefit is 5
general.Feedback: The current required class has positive net marginal benefit.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring the relevant alternatives after a sunk cost.
general.Question: A project already cost $8 million. Finishing costs $5 million. Expected future benefits are $4 million, but cancellation requires a $0.5 million cleanup cost. What is the best choice?
general.Choice A: Cancel, because cancellation costs $0.5 million while finishing has a $1 million negative future net benefit.
general.Choice B: Finish because future benefits exceed the $0.5 million cleanup cost
general.Choice C: Cancel because total project cost exceeds total benefit
general.Choice D: Finish so the $8 million already spent is not wasted.
general.Correct Answer: A — Cancel, because cancellation costs $0.5 million while finishing has a $1 million negative future net benefit.
general.Feedback: Compare future choices: finish yields -$1 million; cancel costs $0.5 million.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring opportunity cost, counting sunk expense, or comparing total rather than incremental profit.
general.Question: A training firm must decide whether to accept one additional client. A nonrefundable $4,000 license fee is already paid, and existing contracts will earn $50,000 profit either way. The new client will pay $18,000 with probability 0.75 and $10,000 otherwise. Service costs $11,000, support costs $2,000, and using the specialists forgoes another job's $4,000 net profit. All figures concern the firm; there are no other effects. Which marginal decision maximizes expected profit?
general.Choice A: Reject: relevant expected marginal profit is -$1,000.
general.Choice B: Accept: relevant expected marginal profit is +$3,000.
general.Choice C: Reject: relevant expected marginal profit is -$5,000.
general.Choice D: Accept: relevant expected marginal profit is +$49,000.
general.Correct Answer: A — Reject: relevant expected marginal profit is -$1,000.
general.Feedback: Expected marginal revenue is 0.75 × $18,000 + 0.25 × $10,000 = $16,000. Relevant marginal cost is $11,000 + $2,000 + $4,000 = $17,000, so accepting lowers expected profit by $1,000. The paid license fee is sunk and the $50,000 from existing contracts is unchanged. Omitting the forgone job, adding the sunk fee, or including existing profit gives the distractor results.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring probability or external marginal cost.
general.Question: A flood barrier segment has a 30% chance of preventing $10 million in damage, costs $2.4 million, and creates $900,000 in expected habitat loss. What does social marginal analysis recommend?
general.Choice A: Do not build because expected benefit is $3 million and social cost is $3.3 million
general.Choice B: Build because expected damage avoided exceeds construction cost
general.Choice C: Build because the possible gross benefit is $10 million
general.Choice D: Do not build because uncertain benefits should count as zero
general.Correct Answer: A — Do not build because expected benefit is $3 million and social cost is $3.3 million
general.Feedback: Expected benefit is below construction plus habitat cost.

general.Common Misconception: Stopping at the first negative increment without evaluating feasible complementary later steps.
general.Question: A project's next three stages have benefits of 14, 8 and 19 points and costs of 9, 12 and 10 points. Stages must occur in order. A manager would stop after stage one because stage two loses points. What is the best decision?
general.Choice A: Complete all three; their total net benefit is 10 points
general.Choice B: Stop after one; any negative increment rules out later stages
general.Choice C: Complete only stage three; it has the largest net benefit
general.Choice D: Complete two; positive total benefits justify the second stage
general.Correct Answer: A — Complete all three; their total net benefit is 10 points
general.Feedback: Feasible cumulative net benefits are 0, 5, 1 and 10. Stages two and three together add 5 points. The last stage cannot be taken alone.

general.Common Misconception: Comparing gross future revenue without considering the alternative and remaining cost.
general.Question: A firm spent $12 million on a prototype. Completing it costs $7 million. Selling the finished product yields $6 million, while selling the unfinished prototype now yields $1.5 million. How much better is the best current choice than completing it?
general.Choice A: $4.5 million better by completing
general.Choice B: $10.5 million better by selling now
general.Choice C: $2.5 million better by selling now
general.Choice D: $1 million better by selling now
general.Correct Answer: C — $2.5 million better by selling now
general.Feedback: Completion yields $6m - $7m = -$1m from now; selling now yields $1.5m. Selling is better by $2.5m. The $12m already spent is common and sunk.

general.Common Misconception: Using total profit or average cost rather than the marginal comparison.
general.Question: A producer earns a positive total profit. The next indivisible batch adds $320 in revenue and $350 in cost, but is required for a second batch adding $410 in revenue and $340 in cost. Which choice maximizes additional profit?
general.Choice A: Produce both batches for a $40 gain
general.Choice B: Produce neither because the first batch loses $30
general.Choice C: Produce the second batch alone for a $70 gain
general.Choice D: Produce the first alone to spread fixed cost
general.Correct Answer: A — Produce both batches for a $40 gain
general.Feedback: The feasible additions yield $0, -$30 and +$40. Although the first batch loses money, the required pair gains $40. The second batch is not independently feasible.

general.Common Misconception: Letting sunk spending or an irrelevant total comparison drive the decision.
general.Question: A policy has already spent $2 billion. Continuing for one year costs $600 million and produces expected benefits of $520 million; ending it costs $30 million in transition expenses. Should the policy continue for another year or end now?
general.Choice A: End the policy: ending costs $30 million, while continuing would cost $80 million more than it provides in benefits.
general.Choice B: End because total cost since the program began exceeds total benefit
general.Choice C: Continue so the $2 billion already spent is not wasted
general.Choice D: Continue because the $520 million in benefits exceeds the $30 million transition cost.
general.Correct Answer: A — End the policy: ending costs $30 million, while continuing would cost $80 million more than it provides in benefits.
general.Feedback: The decision should compare future alternatives: continue loses $80 million; ending costs $30 million.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring the best alternative use of the next slot.
general.Question: A hospital evaluates all benefits and costs using the same points scale. One treatment provides 88 benefit points and has a 42-point supply cost. The staff could instead remain available for emergencies, an alternative valued at 35 points. A different treatment method reduces the supply cost by 8 points but also reduces the benefit by 12 points. Which treatment method provides the greater net benefit compared with keeping the staff available for emergencies?
general.Choice A: The original treatment, with an 11-point net gain
general.Choice B: The cheaper method, with a 15-point net gain
general.Choice C: Neither, because readiness must be added to benefit
general.Choice D: Both versions give the same gain because both save supplies
general.Correct Answer: A — The original treatment, with an 11-point net gain
general.Feedback: Original net gain is 88 - 42 - 35 = 11. The cheaper method gives 76 - 34 - 35 = 7. Both beat the alternative, but cost saving alone does not make the revised method better.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring probability or displaced maintenance.
general.Question: A software team’s next round of development work has a 50% chance of creating $180,000 in value and costs $70,000. It also delays maintenance worth $25,000. What should it do?
general.Choice A: Do not run it because expected benefit $90,000 is below relevant cost $95,000
general.Choice B: Run it because possible benefit is $180,000
general.Choice C: Run it because development cost alone is below expected benefit
general.Choice D: Do not run it because uncertainty makes expected benefit zero
general.Correct Answer: A — Do not run it because expected benefit $90,000 is below relevant cost $95,000
general.Feedback: Expected benefit is $90,000; direct plus opportunity cost is $95,000.

general.Common Misconception: Continuing after MC exceeds MB or stopping too soon.
general.Question: The next two maintenance zones add benefits of 18 and 13 points and operating costs of 10 and 11 points. Opening either requires a one-time setup cost of 9 points. Zones must be opened in order. Which option has the greatest net benefit?
general.Choice A: Open both zones, gaining 1 point
general.Choice B: Open neither, because the first zone alone loses 1 point
general.Choice C: Open only the first, gaining 8 points
general.Choice D: Open both, gaining 10 points
general.Correct Answer: A — Open both zones, gaining 1 point
general.Feedback: Including setup once, one zone gives 18 - 10 - 9 = -1; both give 31 - 21 - 9 = 1. The second zone covers the remaining setup loss and adds a net gain.

general.Common Misconception: Using favorable totals instead of unfavorable margins.
general.Question: Total benefit at five inspection stations is $900,000 and total cost is $610,000. At six they are $970,000 and $688,000. Station six also displaces a separate activity worth $9,000. How much added benefit would make station six break even?
general.Feedback: Station six adds $70,000 in benefit and $78,000 in direct cost plus $9,000 forgone value. It is short by $17,000; the positive total surplus does not settle the incremental choice.

general.Common Misconception: Stopping at the first negative increment without evaluating feasible complementary later steps.
general.Question: Sequential grants have expected net benefits of $2.0m, $0.7m, -$0.4m and $0.6m. Each later grant requires all earlier grants. How many maximize total expected net benefit?
general.Choice A: Four grants, yielding $2.9m
general.Choice B: Two grants, yielding $2.7m
general.Choice C: Three grants, yielding $2.3m
general.Choice D: One grant, yielding $2.0m
general.Correct Answer: A — Four grants, yielding $2.9m
general.Feedback: Feasible totals for zero through four grants are 0, 2.0, 2.7, 2.3 and 2.9 million. Grants three and four jointly add $0.2m, so stopping at the first negative increment misses the best feasible package.

general.Common Misconception: Using an average benchmark instead of MB versus MC.
general.Question: A program's average benefit is 16 points per participant. The next participant adds 9 benefit points and 7 cost points; accommodating that participant also lowers benefits to existing participants by 3 points. What is the correct marginal decision?
general.Choice A: Reject; the overall incremental net benefit is -1 point
general.Choice B: Accept; 9 exceeds the direct cost of 7
general.Choice C: Reject solely because 9 is below the average of 16
general.Choice D: Accept; a positive average establishes a positive marginal gain
general.Correct Answer: A — Reject; the overall incremental net benefit is -1 point
general.Feedback: Count the 3-point loss to existing participants as an added consequence: 9 - 7 - 3 = -1. The existing average is not the relevant comparison.

general.Common Misconception: Allocating fixed or total cost to the next-unit rule.
general.Question: A plant's prepaid lease is unchanged. An extra order earns $760 and needs $490 in materials and $140 in overtime. It also occupies capacity that could earn $160 net on another order. What minimum price increase makes accepting it break even?
general.Feedback: Relevant cost is $490 + $140 + $160 = $790, against $760 in revenue. Another $30 reaches break-even; the unchanged lease does not enter.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring probability or including sunk campaign spending.
general.Question: A campaign has already spent $400,000. A final placement costs $60,000 and yields additional revenue of $100,000 if it succeeds, otherwise zero. With no other effects, which success probability makes the placement break even?
general.Choice D: A probability above 100% because past spending must be recovered
general.Feedback: Set expected incremental revenue equal to avoidable cost: p times $100,000 = $60,000, so p = 0.60. Past campaign expenditure is sunk.

general.Common Misconception: Comparing totals or reporting one marginal change.
general.Question: At 12 trips a route has total benefits of 840 points and costs of 610. At 13 trips these become 892 and 655. At 14 they become 930 and 699. With no later trips available, which expansion from 12 is best?
general.Choice A: Add one trip; the two increments net +7 and -6 points
general.Choice B: Add two trips because total benefit still exceeds total cost
general.Choice C: Add neither because both trips raise total cost
general.Choice D: Add two trips because 14 trips has the highest total benefit
general.Correct Answer: A — Add one trip; the two increments net +7 and -6 points
general.Feedback: Trip 13 adds 52 - 45 = 7 points. Trip 14 adds 38 - 44 = -6. Relative to 12 trips, the feasible gains are 0, 7 and 1; add only trip 13.

general.Common Misconception: Comparing gross future costs or sunk totals instead of future alternatives.
general.Question: A university pilot has spent $6 million. Extending it costs $900,000 and yields $1.1 million in expected benefit, while ending now requires $250,000 in transition cost. What is best?
general.Choice A: Extend because its future net gain exceeds the cost of ending
general.Choice B: End because total spending is already too high
general.Choice C: Extend only to avoid wasting the $6 million
general.Choice D: End because transition cost is less than extension cost
general.Correct Answer: A — Extend because its future net gain exceeds the cost of ending
general.Feedback: Extending gains $200,000, while ending loses $250,000.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring changing external costs or continuing one unit too far.
general.Question: A city adds park lighting in blocks. Marginal benefits are 100, 82, 61, and 40; private costs are 55 each, but marginal light-pollution costs are 10, 18, 25, and 32. How many blocks should be lit?
general.Choice A: Two blocks
general.Choice B: One block
general.Choice C: Three blocks
general.Choice D: Four blocks
general.Correct Answer: A — Two blocks
general.Feedback: Social MC is 65, 73, 80, and 87; only the first two pass.

general.Common Misconception: Using gross possible savings or ignoring probability.
general.Question: An inspection costs $70,000 and prevents $500,000 in repairs if it finds a defect in time, otherwise saving nothing. It displaces work worth $20,000. What detection probability makes the inspection break even?
general.Feedback: Expected benefit is p times $500,000. Direct plus opportunity cost is $90,000, so break-even requires p = 90,000 / 500,000 = 18%.

general.Common Misconception: Rejecting a unit whenever it has any cost.
general.Question: The next unit has marginal benefit $24 and marginal cost $19. What should happen?
general.Choice A: Continue only because past costs are sunk.
general.Choice B: Stop because cost is positive.
general.Choice C: Stop unless average benefit rises.
general.Choice D: Produce or consume the next unit.
general.Correct Answer: D — Produce or consume the next unit.
general.Feedback: The next unit adds $5 in net benefit.

general.Common Misconception: Using a blanket rule without checking whether the cost is truly sunk.
general.Question: A fee has already been paid, but its refund terms have not yet been checked. When should it affect the current decision?
general.Choice A: Only if some part of it can still be recovered or avoided.
general.Choice B: Only when total benefits are positive.
general.Choice C: Always, because past spending must be recovered.
general.Choice D: Never, even if a refund remains available.
general.Correct Answer: A — Only if some part of it can still be recovered or avoided.
general.Feedback: Check whether the current choice changes how much of the fee can be recovered. A refund available under one choice but not another is relevant; a payment that cannot be recovered or changed is sunk. Having paid the fee does not by itself establish that it is irrelevant, and a desire to recover past spending is not a marginal benefit.

general.Common Misconception: Comparing totals or averages instead of their changes.
general.Question: A school considers one more tutoring session. Total benefit would rise from 72 to 80 points and total cost from 48 to 54 points. Which values should be compared?
general.Choice A: Marginal benefit 8 and marginal cost 6
general.Choice B: Total benefit 80 and total cost 54
general.Choice C: Average benefit 76 and average cost 51
general.Choice D: Prior benefit 72 and prior cost 48
general.Correct Answer: A — Marginal benefit 8 and marginal cost 6
general.Feedback: The additional session adds 8 benefit points and 6 cost points.

general.Common Misconception: Using positive average profit instead of the next order’s margin.
general.Question: A firm’s average profit is positive. The next order adds $180 in revenue and $205 in avoidable cost. What should it do?
general.Choice A: Reject the order because its marginal contribution is negative
general.Choice B: Accept because average profit across all prior orders remains positive
general.Choice C: Accept because total revenue will rise
general.Choice D: Reject only if fixed cost also rises
general.Correct Answer: A — Reject the order because its marginal contribution is negative
general.Feedback: The order reduces profit by $25.

general.Common Misconception: Using totals or treating any added cost as disqualifying.
general.Question: Total benefit rises from 300 to 336 with one more unit; total cost rises from 210 to 242. What should happen?
general.Choice A: Add the unit because MB 36 exceeds MC 32
general.Choice B: Stop because total cost rises by 32
general.Choice C: Add only if average benefit increases
general.Choice D: Stop because total cost remains positive
general.Correct Answer: A — Add the unit because MB 36 exceeds MC 32
general.Feedback: The next unit adds 4 in net benefit.

general.Common Misconception: Continuing after marginal cost first exceeds marginal benefit.
general.Question: MB values for units 1 through 4 are 30, 22, 14, and 8; MC values are 10, 16, 15, and 12. Which production plan is optimal?
general.Choice A: Produce only unit 1
general.Choice B: Produce all four units
general.Choice C: Produce the first three units
general.Choice D: Produce the first two units
general.Correct Answer: D — Produce the first two units
general.Feedback: Units 1 and 2 add net benefit; unit 3 would reduce it.

general.Common Misconception: Escalating commitment based on sunk cost.
general.Question: A project has spent $5 million irreversibly. Finishing now costs $3 million and produces $2 million in future benefits. Abandoning it costs $1.5 million in required restoration, with no future benefits. Delaying changes neither future cost nor benefit. Which choice minimizes the remaining loss?
general.Choice A: Abandon: $2 million of benefits is below $3 million of cost, regardless of the restoration alternative.
general.Choice B: Finish: the $5 million already spent must be counted as an additional benefit from completion.
general.Choice C: Finish: the $1 million future loss is smaller than the $1.5 million abandonment loss.
general.Choice D: Delay: postponement removes the restoration cost even though the stated future alternatives are unchanged.
general.Correct Answer: C — Finish: the $1 million future loss is smaller than the $1.5 million abandonment loss.
general.Feedback: Finishing nets 2-3=-1 million. Abandoning nets -1.5 million. Finishing is preferable by 0.5 million, despite its negative standalone future net value, because the feasible alternative is worse. Sunk spending is irrelevant.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring a displaced private profit opportunity or counting an unavoidable sunk fee.
general.Question: A firm can accept a rush order for $30,000 or decline it. Internal production requires $16,000 in materials and labor plus $2,000 in extra maintenance, and displaces a job with $9,000 net profit. Outsourcing costs $24,000 plus $1,000 for inspection and leaves that other job intact. A $6,000 design fee is already paid and nonrefundable under every choice. Both production methods are feasible and give the same revenue. Which plan maximizes incremental private profit?
general.Choice A: Produce internally; incremental profit is $12,000.
general.Choice B: Outsource production; incremental profit is $5,000.
general.Choice C: Reject the order; the best production option loses $1,000.
general.Choice D: Produce internally; incremental profit is $3,000.
general.Correct Answer: B — Outsource production; incremental profit is $5,000.
general.Feedback: Internal production adds $30,000 - $16,000 - $2,000 - $9,000 = $3,000 after accounting for the displaced job. Outsourcing adds $30,000 - $24,000 - $1,000 = $5,000 and preserves that job, so outsourcing is best. The $6,000 design fee is sunk and does not enter either comparison.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring the displaced project or including sunk spending.
general.Question: A project has $10 million in sunk spending. Completion costs $3 million, yields $3.4 million, and displaces another project worth $0.6 million. What is the decision?
general.Choice A: Do not complete because relevant marginal cost is $3.6 million
general.Choice B: Complete because future revenue exceeds direct cost
general.Choice C: Complete to recover the $10 million
general.Choice D: Do not complete because total project cost is high
general.Correct Answer: A — Do not complete because relevant marginal cost is $3.6 million
general.Feedback: Direct plus opportunity cost exceeds future benefit.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring an external marginal cost.
general.Question: One more factory inspection avoids expected losses of $95,000, costs $62,000, and creates $38,000 in delay costs for customers. What is the social choice?
general.Choice A: Skip it because marginal social cost is $100,000
general.Choice B: Perform it because direct cost is below avoided loss
general.Choice C: Perform it because total quality benefit is positive
general.Choice D: Skip it because all delay costs are sunk
general.Correct Answer: A — Skip it because marginal social cost is $100,000
general.Feedback: The inspection’s combined added cost exceeds avoided loss.

general.Common Misconception: Continuing after MC exceeds MB or stopping early.
general.Question: A city can buy sensors sequentially. Direct MBs are 90, 72, 50 and 31; MCs are 40, 60, 55 and 48. A linked alert system worth 25 becomes feasible only with at least three sensors and costs no more. Which number maximizes total net benefit?
general.Choice A: Three: totals are 50, 62, 82 and 65 for one through four sensors.
general.Choice B: Two: the third direct MB is below MC, so any linked benefit must be excluded.
general.Choice C: Four: four sensors have the largest total direct benefit regardless of incremental cost.
general.Choice D: One: its individual net benefit is largest, so later positive gains should be ignored.
general.Correct Answer: A — Three: totals are 50, 62, 82 and 65 for one through four sensors.
general.Feedback: Cumulative direct net gains are 50, 62, 57 and 40. Add 25 for plans with at least three sensors: 82 and 65. Three is optimal because the third unlocks an additional benefit while the fourth does not.

general.Common Misconception: Comparing gross future costs or sunk totals instead of net alternatives.
general.Question: A project has spent $5 million irreversibly. Finishing costs $900,000 and yields $1 million. Canceling costs $180,000. Selling the project as-is brings $350,000 but requires $120,000 of transfer work and avoids cancellation fees. Which choice is best?
general.Choice A: Sell: its $230,000 future net value exceeds finishing’s $100,000 and canceling’s -$180,000.
general.Choice B: Finish: the $1 million receipt is the largest, and the sunk investment should be recovered before considering a sale.
general.Choice C: Cancel: its $180,000 outlay is below finishing cost, so the sale receipt should not affect the comparison.
general.Choice D: Finish: the relevant sale alternative is $350,000 minus the entire $5 million already spent.
general.Correct Answer: A — Sell: its $230,000 future net value exceeds finishing’s $100,000 and canceling’s -$180,000.
general.Feedback: Compare future net values: 1,000,000-900,000=100,000; -180,000; 350,000-120,000=230,000. Selling wins. The historical $5 million is unchanged by the decision.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring the forgone use of the next resource increment.
general.Question: A hospital can add a mobile unit with expected benefits of $700,000 and direct costs of $520,000. Its team would abandon prevention work worth $210,000. Hiring temporary prevention staff costs $140,000 and preserves all that work; no other constraints change. Which plan maximizes incremental benefit?
general.Choice A: Add the unit and hire temporary staff: net gain is $40,000, versus a $30,000 loss if prevention is displaced.
general.Choice B: Do not add the unit: the $210,000 prevention value must be lost under every plan.
general.Choice C: Add the unit without replacement: its $180,000 cash surplus establishes the largest social gain.
general.Choice D: Add the unit and hire staff: net gain is $250,000 because preserved prevention is an extra benefit above the baseline.
general.Correct Answer: A — Add the unit and hire temporary staff: net gain is $40,000, versus a $30,000 loss if prevention is displaced.
general.Feedback: Without replacement the incremental gain is 700-520-210=-30 thousand. With replacement it is 700-520-140=40 thousand; the preserved prevention service is already in the baseline, not an extra 210 gain.

general.Common Misconception: Omitting a cost component or reporting gross output.
general.Question: A manufacturer can hire a worker for one job that adds $1,400 in output. Wages are $980 and equipment costs $260 but can be resold for $100 after the job. The worker’s workstation could instead be rented out for $190 during the job. Which net contribution is relevant?
general.Choice A: $70: subtract wages, net equipment cost and forgone workstation rent.
general.Choice B: $260: subtract wages and net equipment cost but ignore the owned workstation.
general.Choice C: $160: subtract wages and the full equipment purchase but ignore resale and rent.
general.Choice D: -$30: subtract wages, the full equipment purchase and rent, ignoring resale.
general.Correct Answer: A — $70: subtract wages, net equipment cost and forgone workstation rent.
general.Feedback: Net equipment use costs 260-100=160. Relevant contribution is 1400-980-160-190=70. Ownership does not remove forgone rental income, and recoverable resale value reduces the equipment cost.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring external marginal cost.
general.Question: A cleanup method yields $500 in health benefits, costs the operator $370 and damages habitat by $150. A gentler method gives the same health benefit, costs $430 and causes $20 of habitat damage. Which method is socially preferable, and what would an operator ignoring habitat costs choose?
general.Choice A: Society prefers the gentler method ($50 net); the operator prefers the original ($130 private net versus $70).
general.Choice B: Society prefers the original ($130 net); the operator prefers the gentler method because its habitat damage is lower.
general.Choice C: Both prefer the original because its cash cost is lower and habitat losses are transfers between users.
general.Choice D: Both reject cleanup because the original method’s $520 social cost proves every available method has negative net benefit.
general.Correct Answer: A — Society prefers the gentler method ($50 net); the operator prefers the original ($130 private net versus $70).
general.Feedback: Original social net benefit is 500-370-150=-20; gentler net benefit is 500-430-20=50. Ignoring habitat, private nets are 130 and 70, so private and social rankings differ.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring probability or sunk testing expenditure.
general.Question: A preventable failure has a 25% probability and would cost $800,000. Prevention costs $170,000 and eliminates the loss. A perfect test costs $20,000 and permits prevention only when failure would otherwise occur. For a risk-neutral decision maker, which strategy has the lowest expected cost?
general.Choice A: Test then prevent if needed: $62,500, versus $170,000 for unconditional prevention and $200,000 for no action.
general.Choice B: Prevent unconditionally: $170,000, versus $220,000 for testing because testing cannot change the failure probability.
general.Choice C: Take no action: $0, because a 25% possible loss is not a current cash outlay.
general.Choice D: Test then prevent if needed: $190,000, because prevention must be paid even after a negative test.
general.Correct Answer: A — Test then prevent if needed: $62,500, versus $170,000 for unconditional prevention and $200,000 for no action.
general.Feedback: No action costs 0.25×800000=200000 in expectation. Unconditional prevention costs 170000. Testing allows conditional prevention, costing 20000+0.25×170000=62500. Information has value because it changes action in the no-failure state.

general.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
general.Question: Refer to the graph. Compare two adjustment paths from D to B: demand changes first in one path; supply changes first in the other. Which claim about the intermediate quantity and final equilibrium is correct?
general.Choice A: Demand first takes quantity to A; supply first takes it to C; both paths end at B.
general.Choice B: Demand first takes quantity to C; supply first takes it to A; both paths end at B.
general.Choice C: Demand first takes quantity to C; supply first takes it to A; the paths end at different equilibria.
general.Choice D: Either first shift keeps quantity at D; only the second shift moves quantity to B.
general.Correct Answer: B — Demand first takes quantity to C; supply first takes it to A; both paths end at B.
general.Feedback: With S0 fixed, D0 to D1 moves the market from D to C. With D0 fixed, S0 to S1 moves it from D to A. The final D1/S1 intersection is B regardless of order; the intermediate quantities differ.

general.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
general.Question: Refer to the graph. The taco market begins at point D. Tacos are a normal good. Consumer income rises while the cost of an important production input increases. Which labeled point is the new equilibrium after both changes?
general.Choice A: B — the intersection of D1 and S1
general.Choice B: C — the intersection of D1 and S0
general.Choice C: A — the intersection of D0 and S1
general.Choice D: D — the intersection of D0 and S0
general.Correct Answer: A — B — the intersection of D1 and S1
general.Feedback: Because tacos are a normal good, higher consumer income shifts demand from D0 to D1. The higher input cost shifts supply from S0 to S1. The new D1-S1 equilibrium is point B.

general.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
general.Question: An analyst attributes the move from B back to A to cheaper streaming substitutes and lower theater operating costs. Which evaluation correctly connects these events to the changes shown in the movie-ticket graph?
