general.Common Misconception: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
general.Question: A restaurant-demand model assumes nearby competitors stay open, but two close. What should happen to the forecast?
general.Choice A: Reconsider it because a held-constant condition changed
general.Choice B: Keep it because assumptions do not affect forecasts
general.Choice C: Reject all demand models as permanently useless
general.Choice D: Treat competitor closures as a moral judgment
general.Correct Answer: A — Reconsider it because a held-constant condition changed
general.Feedback: Competitor closures violate the forecast’s fixed-competition assumption and may shift demand toward the restaurant.

general.Common Misconception: Choosing by complexity or preference instead of purpose.
general.Question: One model explains short-run layoffs; another explains long-run hiring. How should a firm choose?
general.Choice A: Always select the model with more variables and equations
general.Choice B: Average both answers without checking assumptions
general.Choice C: Use whichever model supports its preferred plan
general.Choice D: Match the model to the time horizon and question
general.Correct Answer: D — Match the model to the time horizon and question
general.Feedback: The firm should match model horizon to its decision: the layoff model for short-run adjustment and the hiring model for long-run planning.

general.Common Misconception: Transferring a result without checking context or omitted factors.
general.Question: A model predicts well in rural areas but not dense cities. What is the first question to ask?
general.Choice A: Would adding any variable guarantee success
general.Choice B: Are city outcomes outside economic analysis
general.Choice C: Do its assumptions fit both settings equally well
general.Choice D: Must every rural observation be discarded
general.Correct Answer: C — Do its assumptions fit both settings equally well
general.Feedback: The first review is whether density changes a key mechanism or assumption that held in rural markets.

general.Common Misconception: Treating shared historical fit as proof of one mechanism.
general.Question: Two models fit past data, but only one predicts behavior after a new fee. What evidence best separates them?
general.Choice A: The recommendation preferred by the policymaker
general.Choice B: Evidence from the new fee setting where predictions differ
general.Choice C: More past outcomes both models already reproduce
general.Choice D: The relative length of the two model descriptions
general.Correct Answer: B — Evidence from the new fee setting where predictions differ
general.Feedback: The new fee creates an out-of-sample case where the models disagree, so observed post-fee behavior can distinguish them.

general.Common Misconception: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
general.Question: A policy conclusion disappears when one plausible assumption changes. What is the strongest evaluation?
general.Choice A: The conclusion is sensitive and should be qualified
general.Choice B: The original conclusion remains fully robust
general.Choice C: The alternate assumption should be hidden from users
general.Choice D: The model is useless for every other question
general.Correct Answer: A — The conclusion is sensitive and should be qualified
general.Feedback: A conclusion that disappears under one plausible assumption is fragile and should be reported with that sensitivity clearly stated.

general.Common Misconception: Assuming additional detail automatically improves a model.
general.Question: A larger model fits old data better but predicts new data worse. What does this show?
general.Choice A: Historical fit proves the larger model is superior
general.Choice B: Prediction quality depends only on equation length
general.Choice C: The smaller model must omit every relevant mechanism
general.Choice D: Added complexity can overfit rather than improve transfer
general.Correct Answer: D — Added complexity can overfit rather than improve transfer
general.Feedback: Better historical fit paired with worse new-data prediction is evidence of overfitting rather than a general gain from complexity.

general.Common Misconception: Transferring a result without checking context or omitted factors.
general.Question: A labor model predicts a payroll subsidy lowers hiring costs and expands employment at flexible wages. In a new region, bargaining agreements guarantee workers the entire subsidy as higher wages while firms’ net hiring costs stay unchanged. Which transfer of the model is defensible?
general.Choice A: Keep the original employment forecast; a subsidy of the same statutory size must have the same effect under any bargaining rule.
general.Choice B: Reject the original model in its own region; failure to transfer proves flexible wages never mattered for employment.
general.Choice C: Rework the wage-setting mechanism; the unchanged net hiring cost removes the model’s stated employment-expansion channel.
general.Choice D: Predict an equal employment contraction; workers receiving the subsidy necessarily shifts firms’ labor demand left by the same amount.
general.Correct Answer: C — Rework the wage-setting mechanism; the unchanged net hiring cost removes the model’s stated employment-expansion channel.
general.Feedback: The original mechanism depends on a reduction in firms’ net labor cost. If wage bargaining absorbs the subsidy completely, that channel is absent. The model may still describe its original institutions, but needs revision for the new setting.

general.Common Misconception: Treating shared historical fit as proof of one mechanism.
general.Question: Two models fit past recessions equally well. One says reduced credit supply cuts investment; the other says weak expected sales reduce both borrowing and investment. A new policy randomly expands credit access for some otherwise comparable firms. Which observation best distinguishes the proposed mechanisms?
general.Choice A: Borrowing and investment remain correlated in the historical sample after adding more recession years.
general.Choice B: Investment rises among newly credit-eligible firms relative to controls without a prior relative improvement in expected sales.
general.Choice C: Both models continue to predict the same national investment total during the experiment.
general.Choice D: Firms with the strongest expected sales borrow most before the randomized eligibility change.
general.Correct Answer: B — Investment rises among newly credit-eligible firms relative to controls without a prior relative improvement in expected sales.
general.Feedback: Randomized credit access creates variation separate from firms’ preexisting sales outlook. A relative investment response supports the credit-supply channel; historical co-movement alone is compatible with both mechanisms.

general.Common Misconception: Assuming additional detail automatically improves a model.
general.Question: A simple model forecasts regional employment with a 5% error on data that were not used to build it. It recommends policy A across a plausible range of numerical assumptions. A more complex model reduces that error to 4.8%, but small, plausible changes in its assumptions reverse whether it recommends A or B. The policy would be costly and difficult to reverse. What should policymakers do before choosing a policy?
general.Choice A: Report the modest prediction gain and unstable ranking, test the assumptions that change the recommendation, and assess whether the policy choice is reliable enough for this decision.
general.Choice B: Choose the complex model because any lower forecast error establishes a more reliable policy ranking.
general.Choice C: Choose A solely because the simple model is stable, treating stability as proof that its mechanism and recommendation are correct.
general.Choice D: Average the two point recommendations without examining the assumptions, because averaging eliminates uncertainty about how the models represent the economy.
general.Correct Answer: A — Report the modest prediction gain and unstable ranking, test the assumptions that change the recommendation, and assess whether the policy choice is reliable enough for this decision.
general.Feedback: Forecast accuracy and the reliability of a policy recommendation are different concerns. A small improvement in forecast accuracy may not justify a costly, hard-to-reverse decision when reasonable changes in assumptions reverse the recommendation. Policymakers should test those assumptions and explain the uncertainty.

general.Common Misconception: Treating a conditional assumption as a universal fact.
general.Question: What role does an assumption play in a model?
general.Choice A: It replaces the evidence used to test predictions
general.Choice B: It makes the model a policy recommendation
general.Choice C: It states a condition used to focus the analysis
general.Choice D: It guarantees that every result is factually certain
general.Correct Answer: C — It states a condition used to focus the analysis
general.Feedback: An assumption states a condition held fixed or treated as given so the model can trace a particular relationship.

general.Common Misconception: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
general.Question: Must a model be rejected because it simplifies reality?
general.Choice A: No; but only when the model includes a graph
general.Choice B: No; judge whether the simplification fits its purpose
general.Choice C: Yes; useful models reproduce every real-world detail
general.Choice D: Yes; evidence cannot support a simplified explanation
general.Correct Answer: B — No; judge whether the simplification fits its purpose
general.Feedback: Simplification is a design feature; rejection is warranted only when omitted details undermine the model’s purpose or performance.

general.Common Misconception: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
general.Question: A demand model predicts fewer purchases after a price increase. How should this positive prediction be evaluated?
general.Choice A: Compare the conditional prediction with observed evidence
general.Choice B: Treat the prediction as a statement of what ought to happen
general.Choice C: Accept the mechanism because the prediction sounds plausible
general.Choice D: Reject all models whenever one observation differs
general.Correct Answer: A — Compare the conditional prediction with observed evidence
general.Feedback: The demand model makes a testable positive prediction, but its conclusion should be limited to settings where its assumptions describe the relevant buying decision.

general.Common Misconception: Treating a focused representation as a literal copy of reality.
general.Question: A manager uses a two-factor model of sales rather than listing every detail of the store. Why?
general.Choice A: To prove omitted details never affect sales
general.Choice B: To avoid comparing predictions with evidence
general.Choice C: To focus on relationships relevant to the decision
general.Choice D: To guarantee that every forecast is exact
general.Correct Answer: C — To focus on relationships relevant to the decision
general.Feedback: The manager simplifies to two influential sales drivers so the model remains usable for the decision it is meant to inform.

general.Common Misconception: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
general.Question: An economist studies how price affects purchases while holding income constant. Why hold income constant?
general.Choice A: To turn a positive claim into a value judgment
general.Choice B: To isolate the price-purchase relationship
general.Choice C: To claim household income never changes
general.Choice D: To eliminate uncertainty from all forecasts
general.Correct Answer: B — To isolate the price-purchase relationship
general.Feedback: Holding income constant isolates the effect of price instead of mixing a price response with an income-driven demand shift.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring the role of an assumption when applying a model.
general.Question: A model predicts that a tax reduces quantity traded, assuming no evasion. Actual evasion is widespread. What should an analyst conclude?
general.Choice A: The model is useless for every purpose.
general.Choice B: The prediction may need revision because a key behavioral assumption fails.
general.Choice C: Evasion has no effect on incentives.
general.Choice D: The original prediction becomes a normative statement.
general.Correct Answer: B — The prediction may need revision because a key behavioral assumption fails.
general.Feedback: Model conclusions depend on whether important assumptions are reasonable in the setting.

general.Common Misconception: Treating model complexity as the sole quality criterion.
general.Question: Two models answer different questions about the same market. How should an economist choose between them?
general.Choice A: Always choose the more complicated model.
general.Choice B: Use whichever gives the preferred answer.
general.Choice C: Use the model whose mechanisms and assumptions fit the question.
general.Choice D: Assume one model must be universally correct.
general.Correct Answer: C — Use the model whose mechanisms and assumptions fit the question.
general.Feedback: Model choice depends on purpose, relevant mechanisms, and evidence.

general.Common Misconception: Applying a model without checking context.
general.Question: A simple model omits a factor that is small in one setting but large in another. What follows?
general.Choice A: Any omission makes the model worthless.
general.Choice B: The factor must be irrelevant everywhere.
general.Choice C: The model becomes a definition rather than an explanation.
general.Choice D: The model may work in the first setting and fail in the second.
general.Correct Answer: D — The model may work in the first setting and fail in the second.
general.Feedback: The importance of an omitted factor depends on the situation.

general.Common Misconception: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
general.Question: A model uses an unrealistic assumption but predicts well in a narrow setting. What is the strongest evaluation?
general.Choice A: Judge whether the abstraction serves that narrow purpose
general.Choice B: Reject the model because every assumption must be literal
general.Choice C: Accept the model for all settings without further checks
general.Choice D: Treat predictive fit as proof of the assumed mechanism
general.Correct Answer: A — Judge whether the abstraction serves that narrow purpose
general.Feedback: A simplifying assumption need not be literally realistic if the model predicts well for the narrow question and setting in which it is used.

general.Common Misconception: Assuming past empirical relationships are invariant.
general.Question: A model fits historical data but fails after institutions change. Which limitation is most relevant?
general.Choice A: Relationships estimated under old rules may not remain stable.
general.Choice B: Historical data can never be useful.
general.Choice C: Institutions are outside economics.
general.Choice D: Model assumptions matter only for graphs.
general.Correct Answer: A — Relationships estimated under old rules may not remain stable.
general.Feedback: Institutional change can alter incentives and the parameters of a model.

general.Common Misconception: Hiding dependence on uncertain assumptions.
general.Question: A service model favors shorter forms when training is unchanged, but favors the current forms when a plausible training delay is included. What should the analyst report?
general.Choice A: A definite preference for shorter forms because simplification is the model's purpose
general.Choice B: The ranking depends on the training assumption and needs evidence about that condition
general.Choice C: Only the original ranking because the delay is not certain
general.Choice D: An average recommendation without identifying why the ranking changed
general.Correct Answer: B — The ranking depends on the training assumption and needs evidence about that condition
general.Feedback: A plausible change in training conditions reverses the result. Report that sensitivity and seek evidence about the condition instead of presenting either conditional ranking as guaranteed.

general.Common Misconception: Assuming complexity automatically improves a model.
general.Question: A highly detailed model predicts poorly because many parameters are estimated imprecisely. What does this illustrate?
general.Choice A: Simple models always predict perfectly.
general.Choice B: Parameters have no role in models.
general.Choice C: More complexity can add noise and does not guarantee better prediction.
general.Choice D: Prediction quality depends only on graphics.
general.Correct Answer: C — More complexity can add noise and does not guarantee better prediction.
general.Feedback: Extra detail can create estimation problems and overfitting.

general.Common Misconception: Choosing models by fit alone when mechanisms differ.
general.Question: Two queue models fit an office before appointments are introduced. One assumes arrivals cluster; the other assumes service is slow. Appointments spread arrivals without changing service time. Which result best distinguishes them?
general.Choice A: A large wait reduction favors the arrival-clustering explanation
general.Choice B: Unchanged service time proves both explanations equally well
general.Choice C: The prior fit establishes that slow service caused the queues
general.Choice D: Any remaining wait refutes the arrival-clustering explanation
general.Correct Answer: A — A large wait reduction favors the arrival-clustering explanation
general.Feedback: Appointments change arrival clustering while service time stays fixed. A large reduction therefore supports clustering as a mechanism, although other sources of waiting may remain.

general.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
general.Question: Between equilibrium A and equilibrium B, which curve shifts, and what quantity change reflects movement along the other curve?
general.Choice A: Demand shifts right; quantity supplied increases by 100 thousand along S0.
general.Choice B: Supply shifts right; quantity demanded increases by 50 thousand along D0.
general.Choice C: Supply shifts right; quantity demanded increases by 100 thousand along D0.
general.Choice D: Demand shifts right; quantity supplied increases by 50 thousand along S0.
general.Correct Answer: D — Demand shifts right; quantity supplied increases by 50 thousand along S0.
general.Feedback: Demand shifts right from D0 to D1 while S0 stays fixed. Equilibrium moves from A at 200 thousand tickets to B at 250 thousand, so quantity supplied rises by 50 thousand along S0. A higher quantity supplied does not mean supply itself shifted.

general.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
general.Question: Use the graph. Which explanation of the move from A to B is supported by comparing what sellers offer at the price marked at A?
general.Choice A: Supply decreases: at that same price, sellers offer 100 thousand fewer tickets on S1 than on S0.
general.Choice B: Supply decreases: at that same price, sellers offer 50 thousand fewer tickets on S1 than on S0.
general.Choice C: Only quantity supplied decreases: a lower ticket price moves sellers along S0 by 100 thousand tickets.
general.Choice D: Only quantity supplied decreases: a lower ticket price moves sellers along S0 by 50 thousand tickets.
general.Correct Answer: A — Supply decreases: at that same price, sellers offer 100 thousand fewer tickets on S1 than on S0.
general.Feedback: At A’s $10 price, S0 offers 200 thousand tickets and S1 offers 100 thousand. Offering 100 thousand fewer tickets at the same price is a decrease in supply. A movement along S0 would instead be a change in quantity supplied caused by a price change. In the graph, the A-to-B price actually rises.

general.Question: If choosing one option means giving up the next-best alternative, the value given up is:
general.Choice A: Opportunity cost
general.Choice B: A sunk cost
general.Choice C: A price ceiling
general.Choice D: Consumer surplus
general.Correct Answer: A — Opportunity cost
general.Feedback: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative forgone.

general.Common Misconception: Using total forgone options or explicit price only.
general.Question: Opportunity cost is the value of:
general.Choice A: Every rejected alternative added together.
general.Choice B: The next-best alternative given up.
general.Choice C: A past cost that cannot be recovered.
general.Choice D: Only the money price of the choice.
general.Correct Answer: B — The next-best alternative given up.
general.Feedback: Opportunity cost is the value of the single next-best forgone alternative.

general.Common Misconception: Equating zero price with zero opportunity cost.
general.Question: A free event can have an opportunity cost because:
general.Choice A: Only paid activities have opportunity costs
general.Choice B: Attending uses time that could have been used elsewhere.
general.Choice C: Past spending determines the opportunity cost of attending
general.Choice D: Because the event is free, attending uses no scarce resources.
general.Correct Answer: B — Attending uses time that could have been used elsewhere.
general.Feedback: Time and other resources have alternative uses even when admission is free.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring forgone rental income.
general.Question: An owner uses a building that could rent for $2,000 per month. The implicit cost is:
general.Choice A: The original purchase price each month.
general.Choice B: All possible rents added together.
general.Choice C: $2,000 per month.
general.Choice D: $0 because the owner owns it.
general.Correct Answer: C — $2,000 per month.
general.Feedback: The best forgone rental income is an implicit opportunity cost.

general.Common Misconception: Adding all rejected alternatives or selecting the least valuable.
general.Question: A person rejects options valued at $30, $20, and $5. If another activity is chosen, which rejected value determines its opportunity cost?
general.Choice A: $30, the highest-valued rejected option
general.Choice B: $55, the sum of all rejected options
general.Choice C: $5, the least-valued rejected option
general.Choice D: $20, the middle rejected option
general.Correct Answer: A — $30, the highest-valued rejected option
general.Feedback: Opportunity cost uses one alternative: the highest-valued option forgone.

general.Common Misconception: Assuming opportunity cost must be monetary.
general.Question: Why can spending an hour in a free park have an opportunity cost?
general.Choice A: The hour could have been used for another valued activity
general.Choice B: Parks always collect a hidden entrance payment
general.Choice C: Only travel spending can create opportunity cost
general.Choice D: Free time has no alternative uses
general.Correct Answer: A — The hour could have been used for another valued activity
general.Feedback: Time is scarce and can have a valuable next-best use even when no money changes hands.

general.Common Misconception: Treating an unrecoverable past payment as a current opportunity cost.
general.Question: A nonrefundable ticket was bought last month. When deciding whether to attend tonight, what should be treated as sunk?
general.Choice A: The amount already paid for the ticket
general.Choice B: The best activity available tonight
general.Choice C: Income that could be earned during the event
general.Choice D: A resale price still available tonight
general.Correct Answer: A — The amount already paid for the ticket
general.Feedback: A sunk payment cannot be changed; current alternatives and recoverable values remain relevant.

general.Common Misconception: Assuming owned resources have no opportunity cost.
general.Question: An owner uses a room that could be rented to someone else. Why is the room not costless?
general.Choice A: Using it gives up possible rental income
general.Choice B: Ownership requires paying its purchase price again
general.Choice C: Every imaginable room use must be added together
general.Choice D: Only borrowed rooms can have opportunity costs
general.Correct Answer: A — Using it gives up possible rental income
general.Feedback: The best forgone use of an owned resource is an implicit cost.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring duration or assuming unpaid time has no opportunity cost.
general.Question: A worker takes two unpaid hours off instead of working for $18 per hour. What wage value is forgone?
general.Feedback: Two forgone work hours at $18 each equal $36.

general.Common Misconception: Seeing scarcity and opportunity cost as unrelated definitions.
general.Question: Scarcity means a community cannot fund every valued program. If the community funds a clinic, what determines the clinic’s opportunity cost?
general.Choice A: Funding the clinic requires giving up the best alternative program
general.Choice B: Scarcity makes the clinic’s historical spending a sunk cost
general.Choice C: Opportunity cost disappears once officials approve a budget
general.Choice D: Every unfunded program must be added together as the cost
general.Correct Answer: A — Funding the clinic requires giving up the best alternative program
general.Feedback: Scarcity forces a choice; the best forgone use created by that choice is its opportunity cost.

general.Common Misconception: Failing to connect a production tradeoff with opportunity cost.
general.Question: Moving along a production possibilities frontier from more food toward more machinery requires giving up food. What does the food forgone measure?
general.Choice A: The opportunity cost of the additional machinery
general.Choice B: The sunk cost of previously produced food
general.Choice C: The money price of machinery in the product market
general.Choice D: The total value of all unattainable production points
general.Correct Answer: A — The opportunity cost of the additional machinery
general.Feedback: The output surrendered when production shifts measures the opportunity cost along a PPF.

general.Common Misconception: Assigning comparative advantage to absolute output or higher opportunity cost.
general.Question: Two producers can make the same goods, but one gives up fewer shirts for each bicycle. How does opportunity cost identify comparative advantage?
general.Choice A: The producer giving up fewer shirts has comparative advantage in bicycles
general.Choice B: The producer making more total goods in both industries must have comparative advantage
general.Choice C: The producer with the higher bicycle opportunity cost should specialize
general.Choice D: Comparative advantage depends only on money prices of the goods
general.Correct Answer: A — The producer giving up fewer shirts has comparative advantage in bicycles
general.Feedback: Comparative advantage belongs to the producer with the lower opportunity cost.

general.Common Misconception: Using sunk or total values instead of additional benefit and cost.
general.Question: A firm considers producing one additional unit. How does opportunity cost enter a marginal decision?
general.Choice A: The forgone value of resources used for that unit is compared with its added benefit
general.Choice B: Every past expense and every earlier unit’s benefit are added to the next unit’s marginal cost
general.Choice C: The total benefit of all earlier units determines the next unit’s cost
general.Choice D: Opportunity cost matters only before the first unit is produced
general.Correct Answer: A — The forgone value of resources used for that unit is compared with its added benefit
general.Feedback: Marginal analysis compares added benefit with the opportunity cost of the next unit.

general.Common Misconception: Treating owner-supplied inputs as free when moving from accounting to economic profit.
general.Question: An entrepreneur uses a personally owned building and unpaid owner labor. How do these opportunity costs connect to economic profit?
general.Choice A: Forgone rent and salary are implicit costs subtracted from accounting profit
general.Choice B: Owned inputs disappear from both accounting and economic analysis
general.Choice C: Historical purchase prices plus every owner cash withdrawal are charged again each period
general.Choice D: Economic profit subtracts every rejected business idea
general.Correct Answer: A — Forgone rent and salary are implicit costs subtracted from accounting profit
general.Feedback: Implicit opportunity costs explain why economic profit can be below accounting profit.

general.Common Misconception: Failing to interpret forgone output as the cost of additional production.
general.Question: A workshop gives up progressively more chairs for each additional table. What connection does this create between opportunity cost and the production tradeoff?
general.Choice A: The opportunity cost of later tables rises as more chairs are forgone
general.Choice B: Opportunity cost stays equal to the money price of a table in every production decision
general.Choice C: Past chair production becomes a sunk cost of every table
general.Choice D: The tradeoff disappears because both goods use the same workshop
general.Correct Answer: A — The opportunity cost of later tables rises as more chairs are forgone
general.Feedback: The amount of one good forgone measures the opportunity cost of producing more of the other.

general.Common Misconception: Treating an owned resource as costless or adding both options.
general.Question: A library can use its only meeting room for a job workshop or a tax-help clinic this evening. It chooses the workshop. What is the opportunity cost?
general.Choice A: The value of the tax-help clinic that cannot be held
general.Choice B: The original cost of constructing and maintaining the meeting room over time
general.Choice C: The value of both events added together
general.Choice D: Zero because the library already owns the room
general.Correct Answer: A — The value of the tax-help clinic that cannot be held
general.Feedback: The clinic is the next-best use forgone when the room hosts the workshop.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring a nonmonetary forgone alternative.
general.Question: A student spends two hours volunteering instead of preparing for tomorrow’s exam. Which item belongs in the opportunity cost of volunteering?
general.Choice A: The value of the study time the student gives up
general.Choice B: Only the bus fare paid to reach the volunteer site
general.Choice C: Every activity the student could have imagined doing
general.Choice D: The volunteer work itself because it was the chosen activity
general.Correct Answer: A — The value of the study time the student gives up
general.Feedback: The next-best use of the student’s time can be an opportunity cost without a money price.

general.Common Misconception: Looking only for an explicit money payment.
general.Question: A student can spend Saturday working for $80 or attending a free concert. If the student attends the concert, the opportunity cost is:
general.Choice A: The $80 in forgone earnings.
general.Choice B: The concert ticket price of $0.
general.Choice C: Only the cost of transportation.
general.Choice D: Every activity the student could imagine doing.
general.Correct Answer: A — The $80 in forgone earnings.
general.Feedback: The next-best alternative is working, so the forgone $80 is the opportunity cost.

general.Common Misconception: Treating owned resources as costless.
general.Question: A city uses an empty lot for a playground instead of a community garden. The opportunity cost of the playground is:
general.Choice A: The original purchase price of the lot.
general.Choice B: The value of the community garden that is not built.
general.Choice C: Zero because the city already owns the land.
general.Choice D: The total value of every possible project.
general.Correct Answer: B — The value of the community garden that is not built.
general.Feedback: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best use of the lot.

general.Common Misconception: Equating a zero price with zero opportunity cost.
general.Question: A parent attends a free evening class and gives up two hours of family time. Why can the class still have an opportunity cost?
general.Choice A: The family time is a valued alternative use of those hours
general.Choice B: Free classes always charge an unannounced cash fee
general.Choice C: Only the building’s operating expense counts as a cost
general.Choice D: A zero tuition price eliminates every competing use of the parent’s time
general.Correct Answer: A — The family time is a valued alternative use of those hours
general.Feedback: Time has valued alternative uses even when an activity charges no fee.

general.Common Misconception: Adding all rejected options or selecting the least-valued one.
general.Question: A resident can spend Saturday repairing a porch, helping at a food pantry, or hiking. Helping at the pantry is chosen, and porch repair was valued most among the rejected options. What is the relevant forgone alternative?
general.Choice A: Repairing the porch
general.Choice B: Hiking only
general.Choice C: Both rejected activities added together
general.Choice D: The food-pantry shift that was chosen
general.Correct Answer: A — Repairing the porch
general.Feedback: Opportunity cost uses the single highest-valued rejected alternative.

general.Common Misconception: Using the chosen activity instead of the forgone alternative.
general.Question: A nurse can use a lunch break to take a walk or finish a required report. She finishes the report. What is the opportunity cost?
general.Choice A: The value of the walk she gives up
general.Choice B: The value of the completed report
general.Choice C: The value of both lunch-break activities added together
general.Choice D: Zero because the break is unpaid
general.Correct Answer: A — The value of the walk she gives up
general.Feedback: The walk is the alternative surrendered when the report is chosen.

general.Common Misconception: Confusing the selected benefit with the best option forgone.
general.Question: A family spends its last $50 of entertainment money on a museum visit instead of the next-best choice, a movie night. What is the opportunity cost?
general.Choice A: The value the family placed on movie night
general.Choice B: The value of the museum visit itself
general.Choice C: Every activity available in the city
general.Choice D: Only the family’s earlier spending on unrelated entertainment choices
general.Correct Answer: A — The value the family placed on movie night
general.Feedback: Movie night is the next-best alternative given up.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring the alternative output of an already-employed worker.
general.Question: A bakery assigns its only decorator to a wedding cake, so a birthday-cake order cannot be completed. Which item is forgone?
general.Choice A: The value of the birthday-cake order
general.Choice B: The decorator’s entire annual salary plus all bakery overhead
general.Choice C: Both cake orders added together
general.Choice D: Nothing because the decorator remains employed
general.Correct Answer: A — The value of the birthday-cake order
general.Feedback: The birthday-cake order is the best displaced use of the decorator’s time.

general.Common Misconception: Treating a donated or owned resource as costless.
general.Question: A nonprofit uses a donated room for tutoring instead of leasing it to a neighborhood group. Which item can be an opportunity cost?
general.Choice A: The rental value the nonprofit gives up
general.Choice B: The donor’s original cost of the room
general.Choice C: Zero because the room was donated
general.Choice D: Every possible future use combined
general.Correct Answer: A — The rental value the nonprofit gives up
general.Feedback: Forgone rental value is an implicit opportunity cost of using the room.

general.Question: A student can earn $120 working Saturday or attend a free exam review session. If attending the session raises her expected exam score enough to be worth $180 to her, what is the net benefit of attending the review?
general.Feedback: The opportunity cost is the $120 in forgone wages. Net benefit is $180 - $120 = $60.

general.Common Misconception: Counting only explicit money costs.
general.Question: A laboratory assistant works an extra Saturday shift and gives up a study group that would improve preparation for a licensing exam. Which interpretation is best?
general.Choice A: The value of improved exam preparation is part of the shift’s opportunity cost
general.Choice B: The earned wage offsets the study group’s benefit in the opportunity-cost calculation
general.Choice C: Transportation and other out-of-pocket expenses make up the shift’s opportunity cost
general.Choice D: The opportunity cost combines the values of several unchosen Saturday activities
general.Correct Answer: A — The value of improved exam preparation is part of the shift’s opportunity cost
general.Feedback: A valuable nonmonetary alternative can be the next-best option forgone.

general.Question: A worker can produce 10 reports or 5 presentations in a day. What is the opportunity cost of one presentation?
general.Choice A: 2 reports
general.Choice B: 5 reports
general.Choice C: 10 reports
general.Choice D: 50 reports
general.Correct Answer: A — 2 reports
general.Feedback: Giving up 10 reports to gain 5 presentations means each presentation costs 2 reports.

general.Common Misconception: Summing all rejected alternatives or using the chosen benefit.
general.Question: A consultant can accept Project A for a net benefit of $18,000, Project B for $15,000, or Project C for $9,000. If Project A is chosen, its opportunity cost is:
general.Feedback: Project B is the highest-valued forgone alternative.

general.Common Misconception: Failing to update opportunity cost when the next-best alternative changes.
general.Question: A worker’s hourly wage rises from $20 to $32. Holding preferences constant, how does this change the opportunity cost of taking an unpaid hour off?
general.Choice A: Stays at zero because no payment is made.
general.Choice B: Equals the combined value of every alternative activity.
general.Choice C: Rises by $12 because the forgone hourly wage is higher.
general.Choice D: Falls because leisure is now more valuable.
general.Correct Answer: C — Rises by $12 because the forgone hourly wage is higher.
general.Feedback: The forgone wage from an hour of work is now larger.

general.Common Misconception: Equating acquisition price with current opportunity cost.
general.Question: A nonprofit receives a donated building and chooses to use it as offices rather than lease it for $90,000 annually. Which statement is correct?
general.Choice A: The opportunity cost is the donor’s original purchase price
general.Choice B: The opportunity cost is zero because the building was donated
general.Choice C: The donation has no purchase price, but office use carries a $90,000 annual opportunity cost.
general.Choice D: The opportunity cost is the sum of the values of all possible future uses.
general.Correct Answer: C — The donation has no purchase price, but office use carries a $90,000 annual opportunity cost.
general.Feedback: Current opportunity cost is based on the best forgone use, here the lease income.

general.Common Misconception: Adding all forgone alternatives.
general.Question: A worker can take a one-day class, work an overtime shift earning $180, or attend a recreational event valued at $120. If the worker takes the class, the opportunity cost is:
general.Choice A: $300, the sum of both rejected alternatives.
general.Choice B: $180, the value of the next-best alternative.
general.Choice C: $120, because recreation is not work.
general.Choice D: Zero if the class has no tuition.
general.Correct Answer: B — $180, the value of the next-best alternative.
general.Feedback: The overtime shift is the most valuable forgone option, so it determines opportunity cost.

general.Common Misconception: Counting only tuition or only forgone earnings.
general.Question: A student pays $12,000 in tuition and gives up $24,000 in earnings to attend school for a year. The opportunity cost is at least:
general.Feedback: The full opportunity cost includes explicit tuition and forgone earnings.

general.Common Misconception: Using the difference rather than the value of the next-best alternative.
general.Question: A farmer can plant wheat worth $42,000 or soybeans worth $50,000 on the same field. If wheat is planted, the opportunity cost is:
general.Choice A: $42,000, the value of the wheat that is chosen
general.Choice B: $92,000, the combined value of wheat and soybeans
general.Choice C: $8,000, the difference between the two crop values.
general.Choice D: $50,000 in forgone soybean output.
general.Correct Answer: D — $50,000 in forgone soybean output.
general.Feedback: The next-best alternative is the soybean crop worth $50,000.

general.Common Misconception: Treating owned resources as free.
general.Question: A firm uses a warehouse it owns for storage instead of renting it out for $30,000 per year. The storage decision has an implicit cost of:
general.Choice A: The building’s recorded depreciation expense.
general.Choice B: $0 because ownership avoids a rental payment.
general.Choice C: The difference between neighborhood property values.
general.Choice D: $30,000 per year.
general.Correct Answer: D — $30,000 per year.
general.Feedback: Forgone rental income is an implicit opportunity cost.

general.Common Misconception: Assuming a mandated or strategic choice has no opportunity cost.
general.Question: Military engineers can repair a base runway, restore a civilian bridge worth $18 million, or reinforce a dam worth $23 million. The runway is selected for strategic reasons. Which economic statement follows?
general.Choice A: Its opportunity cost is the $23 million dam reinforcement
general.Choice B: Its opportunity cost is every civilian project added together
general.Choice C: Strategic importance eliminates opportunity cost
general.Choice D: Its opportunity cost is the lower-valued bridge project
general.Correct Answer: A — Its opportunity cost is the $23 million dam reinforcement
general.Feedback: Even a required choice forgoes the highest-valued feasible alternative use.

general.Common Misconception: Assuming identical time requirements imply identical opportunity costs.
general.Question: A free municipal charging station requires a two-hour wait. One driver could earn $35 per hour during that time; another values the same two hours at $20 total. Which statement is best?
general.Choice A: The first driver faces the larger time opportunity cost
general.Choice B: Both drivers face zero cost because charging is free
general.Choice C: Both drivers face the same cost because the wait is identical
general.Choice D: The second driver faces the larger cost because leisure is nonmonetary
general.Correct Answer: A — The first driver faces the larger time opportunity cost
general.Feedback: Opportunity cost depends on the value of each person’s best alternative use of time.

general.Common Misconception: Adding rejected options or selecting the chosen or least-valued alternative.
general.Question: A photographer can accept a portrait job worth $500, an event job worth $650, or spend the day editing a personal project valued at $420. If the portrait job is chosen, what is its opportunity cost?
general.Choice A: $650 from the event job
general.Choice B: $1,070 from both rejected options
general.Choice C: $500 from the chosen portrait job
general.Choice D: $420 from the least valuable alternative
general.Correct Answer: A — $650 from the event job
general.Feedback: The $650 event job is the highest-valued option forgone.

general.Common Misconception: Omitting either forgone earnings or an explicit cost.
general.Question: A free certification exam takes five hours. A worker would otherwise earn $25 per hour and also pays $15 for transit. Ignoring other effects, what is the opportunity cost?
general.Choice A: $140 from forgone wages plus transit
general.Choice B: $125 from forgone wages only
general.Choice C: $15 because only cash payments count
general.Choice D: $110 after subtracting transit from wages
general.Correct Answer: A — $140 from forgone wages plus transit
general.Feedback: Five hours of wages equal $125; adding $15 transit gives $140.

general.Common Misconception: Using the value difference or treating owned equipment as free.
general.Question: A printer owned by a design firm can produce client brochures worth $9,000 or internal marketing materials worth $6,500. If it produces internal materials, what is the opportunity cost?
general.Choice A: $9,000 in forgone client work
general.Choice B: $2,500 as the difference in values
general.Choice C: $6,500 from the chosen materials
general.Choice D: Zero because the firm owns the printer
general.Correct Answer: A — $9,000 in forgone client work
general.Feedback: The best forgone use of the printer is the $9,000 client work.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring duration or assuming zero price means zero cost.
general.Question: A student spends three hours at a free festival instead of tutoring for $22 per hour. Ignoring other costs, what is the opportunity cost?
general.Choice A: $66 in forgone tutoring wages
general.Choice B: $22 because only one hourly wage counts
general.Choice C: $0 because festival admission is free
general.Choice D: $88 from adding the chosen event’s value
general.Correct Answer: A — $66 in forgone tutoring wages
general.Feedback: Three forgone tutoring hours at $22 each equal $66.

general.Common Misconception: Substituting a sunk payment for the best current alternative.
general.Question: A club paid a nonrefundable $2,000 deposit for a banquet. Today it can hold the banquet or use the date for a fundraiser expected to net $3,500. Which amount is the opportunity cost of holding the banquet now?
general.Choice A: $3,500 from the forgone fundraiser
general.Choice B: $2,000 from the nonrefundable deposit
general.Choice C: $5,500 from adding both amounts
general.Choice D: $1,500 from subtracting the deposit
general.Correct Answer: A — $3,500 from the forgone fundraiser
general.Feedback: The deposit cannot be changed; the fundraiser is the current alternative forgone.

general.Common Misconception: Failing to update the next-best alternative.
general.Question: A mechanic plans to repair personal equipment, giving up a customer job worth $300. Before work begins, a $450 emergency job becomes available. If the personal repair remains the choice, what is its opportunity cost?
general.Choice A: $450 because the best available alternative changed
general.Choice B: $300 because the original plan fixes the cost
general.Choice C: $750 because both customer jobs are forgone
general.Choice D: $150 because only the increase matters
general.Correct Answer: A — $450 because the best available alternative changed
general.Feedback: The new $450 job replaces the $300 job as the best option forgone.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring opportunity costs of owner-supplied assets and labor.
general.Question: A software founder uses a personally owned server for a new service. The server could instead be leased for $18,000, and the founder could earn $70,000 at another firm. Which costs are missing from a cash-expense-only analysis?
general.Choice A: Forgone lease income and forgone salary
general.Choice B: Only the server’s historical purchase price
general.Choice C: Every possible technology investment added together
general.Choice D: No costs because neither resource requires a new payment
general.Correct Answer: A — Forgone lease income and forgone salary
general.Feedback: Owned capital and owner labor have valuable alternative uses that are implicit costs.

general.Common Misconception: Freezing opportunity cost when the best available alternative changes.
general.Question: A researcher initially gives up consulting worth $900 to spend a weekend on a paper. A new consulting request worth $1,400 then becomes available before the weekend begins. If the paper remains the choice, how does its opportunity cost change?
general.Choice A: It rises from $900 to $1,400 because the next-best alternative changed
general.Choice B: It remains $900 because only the original alternatives matter
general.Choice C: It becomes $2,300 because both consulting offers must be added
general.Choice D: It falls to zero because research produces future benefits
general.Correct Answer: A — It rises from $900 to $1,400 because the next-best alternative changed
general.Feedback: Opportunity cost is forward-looking and updates when the next-best feasible alternative changes.

general.Common Misconception: Treating a sunk design expense as the current opportunity cost.
general.Question: A theater has already spent $40,000 designing a production. It can use the booked dates to stage that production, spending $25,000 more for an expected $20,000 return, or use the same dates for a concert expected to net $12,000. If it stages the production, what is the opportunity cost of using those dates, measured by the best forgone use of the dates?
general.Choice A: $12,000 from the forgone concert
general.Choice B: $40,000 already spent on design
general.Choice C: $52,000 from adding design and concert values
general.Choice D: $5,000 because the remaining production return is below its added cost
general.Correct Answer: A — $12,000 from the forgone concert
general.Feedback: Using the dates for the production forgoes the concert's $12,000 net value. The $40,000 design expense is sunk. The production's future spending and return matter for deciding whether to stage it, but they are not the value of the alternative use of the dates.

general.Common Misconception: Using the purchase budget or adding rejected uses.
general.Question: A government owns a vacant parcel valued on its books at $20 million and uses it for a courthouse. The land could instead be sold for $14 million or used for housing valued at $18 million. The opportunity cost is:
general.Choice A: $32 million.
general.Choice B: $20 million.
general.Choice C: $14 million.
general.Choice D: $18 million.
general.Correct Answer: D — $18 million.
general.Feedback: The housing project is the most valuable forgone use.

general.Common Misconception: Adding alternatives or using the lower cash-based option.
general.Question: A retailer uses an owned parcel for parking. The parcel could be leased for $70,000 or used for pickup lockers expected to net $85,000. Parking produces a benefit valued at $90,000. What is the opportunity cost of parking?
general.Choice A: $85,000 from the locker project
general.Choice B: $155,000 from both rejected uses
general.Choice C: $5,000 as parking’s net advantage
general.Choice D: $70,000 because leasing is a cash transaction
general.Correct Answer: A — $85,000 from the locker project
general.Feedback: The locker project is the most valuable feasible use forgone.

general.Common Misconception: Omitting explicit costs or failing to credit a benefit received.
general.Question: A one-year program charges $18,000 tuition and $2,000 for required supplies. A student gives up a $44,000 job but gains employer-independent health coverage valued at $4,000 while enrolled. Ignoring future benefits, what is the net opportunity cost?
general.Choice A: $60,000 after crediting the gained coverage
general.Choice B: $64,000 from tuition, supplies, and wages
general.Choice C: $44,000 because only forgone earnings count
general.Choice D: $20,000 because only explicit payments count
general.Correct Answer: A — $60,000 after crediting the gained coverage
general.Feedback: Costs total $64,000; subtracting the $4,000 gained benefit leaves $60,000.

general.Common Misconception: Adding rejected projects or using chosen value or value difference.
general.Question: A government funds a coastal barrier valued at $30 million. The same engineers could instead complete a water system valued at $34 million or road repairs valued at $21 million. Which statement is correct?
general.Choice A: The barrier’s opportunity cost is the $34 million water system
general.Choice B: $55 million is the cost because both alternatives are rejected
general.Choice C: $4 million is the cost because it is the value difference
general.Choice D: $30 million is the cost because it is the chosen project’s value
general.Correct Answer: A — The barrier’s opportunity cost is the $34 million water system
general.Feedback: The water system is the highest-valued alternative use of the engineers.

general.Common Misconception: Using historical purchase price or the value difference as opportunity cost.
general.Question: A factory bought a machine for $500,000 five years ago. It can now use one shift for parts worth $28,000 or rent the shift to another firm for $31,000. What is the current opportunity cost of producing parts?
general.Choice A: $31,000 in forgone rental income
general.Choice B: $500,000 from the historical purchase
general.Choice C: $3,000 as the difference between uses
general.Choice D: $28,000 because that is the chosen output
general.Correct Answer: A — $31,000 in forgone rental income
general.Feedback: The purchase price is sunk; current opportunity cost is the best alternative return.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring repeated time or the explicit project fee.
general.Question: A researcher devotes ten hours per week for six weeks to an unpaid project instead of consulting at $75 per hour. She also pays a one-time $120 data fee. Ignoring benefits, what is the total opportunity cost?
general.Choice A: $4,620 from forgone consulting plus the fee
general.Choice B: $4,500 from forgone consulting only
general.Choice C: $870 from one week of time plus the fee
general.Choice D: $120 because the project pays no wage
general.Correct Answer: A — $4,620 from forgone consulting plus the fee
general.Feedback: Sixty consulting hours cost $4,500; adding the $120 fee gives $4,620.

general.Common Misconception: Including an alternative that does not compete for the constrained resource.
general.Question: A nonprofit has 400 skilled volunteer-hours. A tax clinic would use all hours and create value estimated at $30,000. The best alternative is a housing clinic worth $34,000; a food program worth $20,000 uses different volunteers. What is the tax clinic’s opportunity cost?
general.Choice A: $34,000 from the housing clinic
general.Choice B: $54,000 from both other programs
general.Choice C: $4,000 as the difference in clinic values
general.Choice D: $30,000 from the tax clinic itself
general.Correct Answer: A — $34,000 from the housing clinic
general.Feedback: Only feasible competing uses of the same volunteer-hours matter; housing is the best one.

general.Common Misconception: Comparing with the wrong land use or adding alternative returns.
general.Question: A farmer plants berries on land that could yield corn worth $48,000 or solar-lease income of $55,000. Berries are expected to net $62,000 after new expenses. Compared with the next-best use of the land, what is the net benefit of planting berries?
general.Feedback: The solar lease is the $55,000 opportunity cost; $62,000 minus $55,000 equals $7,000.

general.Common Misconception: Using a prepaid sunk fee or the difference rather than the forgone project.
general.Question: A cloud platform uses reserved computing capacity for fraud detection worth $1.8 million. The capacity could instead support search improvements worth $2.1 million or recommendation improvements worth $1.9 million. Reservation fees were prepaid and nonrefundable. What is the current opportunity cost?
general.Choice A: $2.1 million from search improvements
general.Choice B: The nonrefundable reservation fee
general.Choice C: $4.0 million from both rejected systems
general.Choice D: $0.3 million as the difference from search
general.Correct Answer: A — $2.1 million from search improvements
general.Feedback: The prepaid fee is sunk; search is the highest-valued alternative use of capacity.

general.Common Misconception: Using an irreversible past expenditure instead of the best current alternative.
general.Question: A museum has already paid a nonrefundable $30,000 deposit for an exhibit. It can proceed for another $12,000 and earn $9,000, or use the gallery for a lecture series worth $7,000. Which item is the opportunity cost of proceeding?
general.Choice A: The $7,000 lecture series forgone
general.Choice B: The $30,000 nonrefundable deposit
general.Choice C: The $42,000 total of past and future spending
general.Choice D: Zero because the deposit cannot be recovered
general.Correct Answer: A — The $7,000 lecture series forgone
general.Feedback: The deposit is sunk; the lecture series is the best forgone current use.

general.Common Misconception: Confusing the chosen project, the least-valued option, or the sum of alternatives with opportunity cost.
general.Question: A county can assign an emergency team to wildfire prevention valued at $1.4 million, flood preparation valued at $1.1 million, or routine inspections valued at $0.8 million. Political rules require the flood project. What is its opportunity cost?
general.Choice A: $1.4 million in forgone wildfire prevention
general.Choice B: $2.2 million from both rejected programs
general.Choice C: $1.1 million because that is the chosen project’s value
general.Choice D: $0.8 million because routine inspections cost the least
general.Correct Answer: A — $1.4 million in forgone wildfire prevention
general.Feedback: The wildfire program is the most valuable feasible alternative forgone.

general.Common Misconception: Comparing gross returns without subtracting conversion cost and the next-best alternative.
general.Question: A firm owns a machine that can produce Product X, earning $75,000 in revenue after variable costs, or Product Y, earning $92,000 after variable costs. Converting it to Product Z would earn $100,000 after variable costs but requires an additional $15,000 conversion cost. If the firm chooses Z, what is its net benefit compared with the next-best alternative?
general.Feedback: Z nets $85,000, which is $7,000 below the $92,000 next-best use.

general.Common Misconception: Allowing sunk construction to replace forward-looking incremental costs and alternatives.
general.Question: A port authority has already installed specialized foundations for a terminal. It can complete the terminal for $40 million and obtain benefits of $55 million, or redirect crews to storm protection worth $22 million. Which comparison is relevant now?
general.Choice A: Terminal net benefit of $15 million versus $22 million forgone storm protection
general.Choice B: All foundation spending plus $40 million versus terminal benefits
general.Choice C: Terminal benefits of $55 million versus foundation spending alone
general.Choice D: Only the irreversible foundations because they created the current choice
general.Correct Answer: A — Terminal net benefit of $15 million versus $22 million forgone storm protection
general.Feedback: Past foundations are sunk; completing nets $15 million and forgoes storm protection worth $22 million.

general.Common Misconception: Treating posted price as total economic cost.
general.Question: A popular clinic charges no appointment fee, but patients must wait four hours. A nearby clinic charges $80 with almost no wait. Which claim correctly compares the options?
general.Choice A: The free clinic can have a higher full cost for a patient whose time is especially valuable
general.Choice B: The free clinic must have zero opportunity cost because its posted price is zero
general.Choice C: The paid clinic always has the higher full cost regardless of time values
general.Choice D: Waiting time is a sunk cost and cannot affect a current clinic choice
general.Correct Answer: A — The free clinic can have a higher full cost for a patient whose time is especially valuable
general.Feedback: The opportunity cost of waiting time can outweigh the difference in money price.

general.Common Misconception: Omitting forgone earnings or nonmoney value.
general.Question: A fellowship costs $9,000 in new fees. The student could instead take a job paying $32,000 with $4,000 in work-only expenses, or an assistantship netting $24,000. A $2,000 nonrefundable deposit is already paid under either choice. What current full cost must the fellowship's benefits exceed?
general.Feedback: The best alternative nets $32,000 - $4,000 = $28,000. Add $9,000 in avoidable fellowship fees: $37,000. The deposit is sunk; do not add the rejected assistantship.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring the development cost or comparing with the wrong alternative.
general.Question: A firm can use a patent internally for expected profit of $3.2 million, license it for $3.8 million, or sell it for $3.5 million. Internal use requires an additional $0.4 million development cost. Relative to the next-best alternative, internal use has a net advantage of:
general.Choice A: $3.4 million.
general.Choice B: -$1.0 million.
general.Choice C: -$0.2 million.
general.Choice D: $0.6 million.
general.Correct Answer: B — -$1.0 million.
general.Feedback: Internal use nets $2.8 million; licensing at $3.8 million is the next-best alternative.

general.Common Misconception: Using the difference or summing all forgone alternatives.
general.Question: A field team has six weeks. One rejected survey uses all six weeks and is worth 90 points. Two compatible surveys each use three weeks and are worth 52 and 46 points. If the team selects a different six-week project, what value is forgone?
general.Choice A: 52 points
general.Choice B: 98 points
general.Choice C: 90 points
general.Choice D: 188 points
general.Correct Answer: B — 98 points
general.Feedback: The feasible pair yields 52 + 46 = 98 points, exceeding the single survey's 90. Compare feasible plans; do not sum mutually exclusive plans.

general.Common Misconception: Adding rejected alternatives or netting chosen benefits against opportunity cost.
general.Question: A student keeps a research placement. A rejected job offers $29,000 but requires $5,000 in extra travel. Another rejected placement pays $20,000 and supplies training valued at $6,000. All other costs and benefits are equal. Which alternative sets the opportunity cost?
general.Choice A: The other placement, worth $26,000 net
general.Choice B: The job, worth its $29,000 salary
general.Choice C: Both alternatives together, worth $50,000 net
general.Choice D: The job, worth $24,000 net
general.Correct Answer: A — The other placement, worth $26,000 net
general.Feedback: The job nets $24,000; the other placement totals $26,000. The best feasible rejected option sets the cost, including noncash training value.

general.Common Misconception: Letting sunk design work displace the best current alternative.
general.Question: A firm has prepaid a nonrefundable software license. It can use it for an internal project, sell the transferable access for $18,000, or use it for a client job earning $25,000 with $9,000 in new expenses. What is the opportunity cost of internal use?
general.Choice A: $18,000 from resale
general.Choice B: $25,000 from the client's gross payment
general.Choice C: $16,000 from the client's net payment
general.Choice D: Zero because the license fee is sunk
general.Correct Answer: A — $18,000 from resale
general.Feedback: The original payment is sunk, but resale is feasible. Resale yields $18,000, more than the client job's $16,000 net, so $18,000 is forgone.

general.Common Misconception: Assuming opportunity cost must be money or only a value difference.
general.Question: A volunteer can cover one six-hour shift valued at 15 service points or two compatible three-hour shifts valued at 9 points each. A new placement uses all six hours and requires travel time valued at 2 points, with no other costs. What benefit would make it strictly preferable?
general.Choice A: More than 20 points
general.Choice B: More than 17 points
general.Choice C: More than 18 points, ignoring travel
general.Choice D: More than 35 points
general.Correct Answer: A — More than 20 points
general.Feedback: The best alternative is the pair, worth 18 points. The new placement must also cover 2 points of added travel cost, so strict preference requires benefit above 20.

general.Common Misconception: Adding mutually exclusive alternatives or using the difference in values.
general.Question: A council selects project A. Rejected B is worth 80 points and uses the full budget; C and D are worth 47 and 40 points and fit the budget together, but require the same exclusive specialist slot. What is A's opportunity cost?
general.Choice A: 80 points
general.Choice B: 87 points
general.Choice C: 167 points
general.Choice D: 47 points
general.Correct Answer: A — 80 points
general.Feedback: C and D cannot be combined because of the specialist constraint. Among feasible alternatives, B's 80 points is highest; budget feasibility alone is insufficient.

general.Common Misconception: Adding alternatives or privileging a cash return over a higher noncash value.
general.Question: An owned studio could be leased for $44,000 with $8,000 in landlord expenses, or used for workshops earning $53,000 with $19,000 in new expenses. A chosen community project also needs $7,000 in supplies. What is its full current economic cost?
general.Feedback: Leasing nets $36,000 and workshops net $34,000. Add the community project's $7,000 avoidable supplies to the best forgone use: $43,000.

general.Common Misconception: Adding alternative uses or reporting the value difference.
general.Question: A resource stays assigned to project A. Alternative B would yield 76 points before a required setup cost of x; C yields 61 points net. For what values of x would C have a higher net value than B and therefore determine A’s opportunity cost?
general.Choice A: x greater than 15 points
general.Choice B: x greater than 61 points
general.Choice C: x less than 15 points
general.Choice D: x greater than 76 points
general.Correct Answer: A — x greater than 15 points
general.Feedback: Compare B's 76 - x with C's 61. They tie at x = 15; above 15, C is the strictly better forgone use.

general.Common Misconception: Using selected value, summed alternatives, or the difference.
general.Question: A firm assigns its specialist to defect prevention. The best rejected production project nets $96,000; an energy project nets $82,000. A new tool raises the energy project's net value by $20,000 and leaves other options unchanged. What happens to defect prevention's opportunity cost?
general.Choice A: It rises by $6,000 to $102,000
general.Choice B: It rises by $20,000 to $116,000
general.Choice C: It remains $96,000 because the chosen project is unchanged
general.Choice D: It becomes $178,000 by adding the original alternatives
general.Correct Answer: A — It rises by $6,000 to $102,000
general.Feedback: The best alternative changes from production at $96,000 to energy at $102,000. Opportunity cost rises by $6,000, not the tool's full $20,000 gain.

general.Common Misconception: Omitting explicit cost or adding multiple rejected events.
general.Question: An arena uses a Saturday date for a youth championship valued at $160,000. A concert would net $210,000 and a convention would net $185,000. The championship also requires $15,000 in security spending. What is its full opportunity cost?
general.Choice A: $225,000 from the concert plus security
general.Choice B: $210,000 from the concert alone
general.Choice C: $410,000 from both rejected events plus security
general.Choice D: $65,000 from the value difference plus security
general.Correct Answer: A — $225,000 from the concert plus security
general.Feedback: The best forgone event is $210,000; adding $15,000 security gives $225,000.

general.Common Misconception: Reversing or ignoring the output tradeoff ratio.
general.Question: A machine can make 90 filters or 60 pumps per shift at a constant tradeoff. A new contract takes half a shift for pumps and requires calibration that uses another one-sixth of a shift without output. How many filters does accepting the contract forgo?
general.Choice A: 60 filters
general.Choice B: 45 filters
general.Choice C: 30 filters
general.Choice D: 15 filters
general.Correct Answer: A — 60 filters
general.Feedback: The contract uses two-thirds of a shift: one-half production plus one-sixth calibration. At 90 filters per shift, the forgone output is 60 filters.

general.Common Misconception: Using the controller quantity directly or reversing the ratio.
general.Question: A shift can produce 150 sensors or 100 controllers at a constant tradeoff. A rush order for 40 controllers also prevents a separate setup-free run worth 12 sensors. How many sensors must the order's benefit exceed to justify accepting it?
general.Choice A: 72 sensors
general.Choice B: 60 sensors
general.Choice C: 52 sensors
general.Choice D: 112 sensors
general.Correct Answer: A — 72 sensors
general.Feedback: Forty controllers use 40% of the shift and forgo 60 sensors. Add the separate 12-sensor opportunity: total forgone output is 72 sensors.

general.Common Misconception: Treating a no-longer-feasible alternative as the current opportunity cost.
general.Question: A researcher keeps a public-interest project. Its best rejected contract netted $41,000. That contract is canceled; a replacement pays $38,000 but requires $9,000 in new expenses, while teaching nets $31,000. How does the opportunity cost change?
general.Choice A: It falls by $10,000
general.Choice B: It falls by $3,000
general.Choice C: It falls by $12,000
general.Choice D: It rises to $60,000
general.Correct Answer: A — It falls by $10,000
general.Feedback: After cancellation, teaching at $31,000 beats the replacement's $29,000 net. The cost falls from $41,000 to $31,000, a $10,000 decrease.

general.Common Misconception: Selecting the highest-valued infeasible bundle or using gross rather than net alternative value.
general.Question: A lab chooses Compound A, which uses its entire allocation of 12 scientist-months and 5 sequencer slots. Instead, Platform B would use all 12 months and 5 slots for $11 million net value. Three smaller projects each need 6 scientist-months: C uses 3 slots and yields $8 million before $2 million in new costs; D uses 2 slots and yields $7 million before $2 million in new costs; E uses 3 slots and yields $10 million before $2 million in new costs. Projects are indivisible, compatible if both resource limits are met, and their net values add. What is the opportunity cost of assigning the resources to Compound A?
general.Choice A: $13 million: the net value of projects D and E.
general.Choice B: $14 million: the net value of projects C and E.
general.Choice C: $11 million: the net value of the full Platform B.
general.Choice D: $17 million: the gross value of projects D and E.
general.Correct Answer: A — $13 million: the net value of projects D and E.
general.Feedback: Net values are C = $6m, D = $5m and E = $8m. D plus E uses 12 scientist-months and 5 slots and yields $13m. C plus E would yield $14m but needs 6 slots, so it is infeasible. C plus D and Platform B each yield $11m. The best feasible alternative forgone is therefore D plus E, worth $13m net.

general.Common Misconception: Confusing a consequence of the chosen timing with the alternative forgone.
general.Question: A transportation agency can use its team to start a bus redesign now or use that same team for a safety audit this year and start the redesign next year. The audit has $6 million in benefits, while the one-year delay would add $2 million to redesign costs. These are the only differences between the plans. If the agency starts the redesign now, what is the value of the forgone audit benefits alone, before accounting for the delay-related cost difference?
general.Choice A: $6 million in forgone safety-audit benefits.
general.Choice B: $2 million in avoided redesign-delay costs.
general.Choice C: $4 million after netting out delay costs.
general.Choice D: $8 million after adding the delay costs.
general.Correct Answer: A — $6 million in forgone safety-audit benefits.
general.Feedback: The question asks specifically for the audit benefits forgone, which are $6m. The $2m delay cost is a separate consequence avoided by starting now. If comparing the two complete plans instead, doing the audit first would provide $6m in benefits less $2m in added redesign costs, a $4m net advantage.

general.Common Misconception: Using the first unit’s cost or cumulative cost for the next unit.
general.Question: A workshop's first table forgoes 3 chairs and its second forgoes 5 more. A buyer offers 4 chairs for each table. Producing both tables just breaks even in chairs, yet producing only the first is better. Why?
general.Choice A: The second table loses one chair at the margin, offsetting the first table's gain
general.Choice B: The second table's opportunity cost equals the average cost of four chairs
general.Choice C: Breaking even on the pair proves both tables individually add net benefit
general.Choice D: The first table's forgone chairs become a reason to accept the second
general.Correct Answer: A — The second table loses one chair at the margin, offsetting the first table's gain
general.Feedback: The first table gains 4 - 3 = 1 chair; the second gains 4 - 5 = -1. The average hides the unfavorable incremental tradeoff.

general.Common Misconception: Comparing gross rather than net alternatives or summing rejected options.
general.Question: A studio chooses an educational stream. A sports broadcast would earn $94,000 before a $21,000 rights fee; a concert nets $77,000. A discount reduces the rights fee by $6,000. What happens to the educational stream's opportunity cost?
general.Choice A: It rises from $77,000 to $79,000
general.Choice B: It rises from $73,000 to $79,000
general.Choice C: It stays $77,000 because the concert is unchanged
general.Choice D: It rises by $6,000 to $83,000
general.Correct Answer: A — It rises from $77,000 to $79,000
general.Feedback: Initially the concert beats sports' $73,000 net. After the discount, sports nets $79,000 and becomes the best alternative. The opportunity cost rises by $2,000.

general.Common Misconception: Using the chosen activity or treating assigned staff as costless.
general.Question: A recreation center assigns its only instructor to swimming lessons instead of the next-best option, a safety workshop. What is the opportunity cost?
general.Choice A: The value of the safety workshop that is not offered
general.Choice B: The instructor’s wage plus every rejected program
general.Choice C: Zero because the instructor is already employed
general.Choice D: The value of the swimming lessons that were chosen
general.Correct Answer: A — The value of the safety workshop that is not offered
general.Feedback: The safety workshop is the next-best use of the instructor’s time.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring the displaced output of an already-paid worker.
general.Question: A café manager moves one employee from taking orders to preparing deliveries. The next-best use of that employee was serving counter customers. What is forgone?
general.Choice A: The value of the counter service the employee would have provided
general.Choice B: Every task performed anywhere in the café that day
general.Choice C: Only the employee’s past training expense
general.Choice D: Nothing because the employee remains on the payroll
general.Correct Answer: A — The value of the counter service the employee would have provided
general.Feedback: An employee’s time has an opportunity cost equal to its best forgone use.

general.Common Misconception: Assuming no new cash payment means no opportunity cost.
general.Question: A student uses a prepaid transit pass to travel to a debate tournament instead of visiting a grandparent. Which item can be part of the tournament’s opportunity cost?
general.Choice A: The value of the forgone family visit
general.Choice B: Only an additional transit fare paid today
general.Choice C: The original price of the transit pass in every case
general.Choice D: Zero because the pass makes the trip free at the margin
general.Correct Answer: A — The value of the forgone family visit
general.Feedback: The valued family visit is a forgone alternative even without a new fare.

general.Question: An instructor gives three choices: work for $80, study for a test worth $60, or attend a free concert. If the student chooses the concert, what is the opportunity cost?
general.Choice D: $0 because the concert is free
general.Feedback: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative, not every alternative added together. The next best option is the $80 shift.

general.Common Misconception: Assuming only money payments create opportunity cost.
general.Question: A student spends a free afternoon practicing piano instead of the next-best option, visiting a friend. What is the opportunity cost?
general.Choice A: The value of the friend visit that is forgone
general.Choice B: Zero because neither activity requires payment
general.Choice C: The value of both activities added together
general.Choice D: The value of piano practice because it was chosen
general.Correct Answer: A — The value of the friend visit that is forgone
general.Feedback: The valued friend visit is the next-best use of the afternoon forgone.

general.Common Misconception: Adding every rejected option or selecting the lower-valued one.
general.Question: A musician spends an evening rehearsing and gives up both a paid performance worth $220 and family time valued at $160. Which alternative determines the opportunity cost?
general.Choice A: The $220 performance because it is the more valuable forgone option
general.Choice B: The $160 family time because nonmonetary options always rank first
general.Choice C: Both alternatives added together for a total of $380
general.Choice D: Zero because rehearsal may improve future performance
general.Correct Answer: A — The $220 performance because it is the more valuable forgone option
general.Feedback: Only the highest-valued forgone alternative determines opportunity cost.

general.Common Misconception: Treating owned resources as costless.
general.Question: A firm uses owned office space that could rent for $24,000. What implicit cost belongs in the decision?
general.Choice A: The average rent of all comparable office spaces.
general.Choice B: $24,000 in forgone rent.
general.Choice C: $0 because the space is owned.
general.Choice D: The building’s original purchase price.
general.Correct Answer: B — $24,000 in forgone rent.
general.Feedback: Forgone rent is the opportunity cost of using the space.

general.Common Misconception: Counting only explicit or implicit cost.
general.Question: Tuition is $10,000 and forgone earnings are $30,000. The minimum opportunity cost of attending school is:
general.Feedback: Both tuition and forgone earnings are part of the full cost.

general.Common Misconception: Adding uses, privileging cash rent, or treating ownership as costless.
