general.Question: A business uses its owned van for deliveries instead of renting it out for $900 or using it for service calls worth $1,100. What is the delivery decision’s opportunity cost?
general.Choice A: $1,100 from the service calls
general.Choice B: $2,000 from both rejected uses
general.Choice C: $900 because rental income is explicit cash
general.Choice D: $0 because the business owns the van
general.Correct Answer: A — $1,100 from the service calls
general.Feedback: Service calls are the highest-valued alternative use of the van.

general.Common Misconception: Omitting either forgone wages or an explicit cost.
general.Question: A worker attends a free six-hour workshop instead of a shift paying $24 per hour and pays $12 for parking. Ignoring benefits, what is the opportunity cost?
general.Choice A: $156 from forgone wages plus parking
general.Choice B: $144 from forgone wages only
general.Choice C: $12 because the workshop is free
general.Choice D: $132 after subtracting parking
general.Correct Answer: A — $156 from forgone wages plus parking
general.Feedback: Six hours at $24 equals $144; adding $12 parking gives $156.

general.Common Misconception: Ignoring joint resource constraints or choosing only the largest single alternative.
general.Question: A city assigns its only crew and an $8 million project budget to a rail extension that uses all 12 available crew-weeks. Alternative projects are indivisible and can be sequenced; their resource use and net benefits add. Water repairs need 12 weeks and $8 million, with $24 million net benefit. Drainage needs 5 weeks and $3 million, with $14 million net benefit. Bridge work needs 7 weeks and $5 million, with $15 million net benefit. A hospital upgrade needs 6 weeks and $5 million, with $20 million net benefit. All net benefits already deduct project spending. What is the best feasible alternative forgone by selecting rail?
general.Choice A: Drainage plus the hospital upgrade, worth $34 million net.
general.Choice B: Bridge work plus the hospital upgrade, worth $35 million net.
general.Choice C: Drainage plus bridge work, worth $29 million net.
general.Choice D: The water-repair project alone, worth $24 million net.
general.Correct Answer: A — Drainage plus the hospital upgrade, worth $34 million net.
general.Feedback: Drainage plus the hospital upgrade fits: 11 crew-weeks and $8m, yielding $34m net. Bridge work plus the hospital upgrade would yield $35m but needs 13 weeks and $10m, exceeding both limits. Drainage plus bridge work fits but yields $29m; water repairs yield $24m. The rail choice forgoes the best feasible bundle, worth $34m; do not deduct project spending again.

general.Common Misconception: Adding alternatives or using the chosen project’s value.
general.Question: An owned parcel can support a clinic worth $12 million, housing worth $15 million, or parking worth $5 million. Choosing the clinic has an opportunity cost of:
general.Choice A: $12 million.
general.Choice B: $3 million.
general.Choice C: $20 million.
general.Choice D: $15 million.
general.Correct Answer: D — $15 million.
general.Feedback: Housing is the highest-valued forgone use.

general.Common Misconception: Treating sunk design spending as the current alternative forgone.
general.Question: A university has already spent $4 million designing a laboratory. It can finish the lab or assign the same construction team to a residence project valued at $11 million. What is the current opportunity cost of finishing the lab?
general.Choice A: $11 million in forgone residence value
general.Choice B: $4 million already spent on design
general.Choice C: $15 million from adding both amounts
general.Choice D: Zero because laboratory design is complete
general.Correct Answer: A — $11 million in forgone residence value
general.Feedback: The design expense is sunk; the residence project is the current best alternative use of the team.

general.Common Misconception: Counting only the workshop fee or only the forgone earnings.
general.Question: A consultant can attend a workshop or take one of two mutually exclusive Saturday jobs: one pays $480 with $40 travel cost; the other pays $430 remotely. Workshop admission costs $120, including a $50 nonrefundable deposit already paid, and attendance requires $20 travel. From now, what is attendance’s relevant economic cost?
general.Choice A: $580: the full $120 workshop fee, $20 travel and $440 net job earnings.
general.Choice B: $960: $90 of attendance spending plus both jobs’ combined $870 net earnings.
general.Choice C: $90: only attendance requires a new payment, so foregone work is not a current cost.
general.Choice D: $530: $90 of avoidable workshop/travel spending plus the best forgone job’s $440 net earnings.
general.Correct Answer: D — $530: $90 of avoidable workshop/travel spending plus the best forgone job’s $440 net earnings.
general.Feedback: The remaining fee is 120-50=70; add 20 travel. The best alternative nets max(480-40,430)=440. Relevant cost is 90+440=530. The nonrefundable deposit is sunk and mutually exclusive jobs are not added.

general.Common Misconception: Using the first unit’s cost or cumulative cost for the next unit.
general.Question: A factory reallocates a shift from valves to pumps. The first 30 pumps displace 40 valves; the next 30 displace 60 more. It needs 45 pumps. A supplier offers those 45 pumps in exchange for 65 valves. Assume constant tradeoffs within each stated block. Which source uses fewer valve-equivalent resources?
general.Choice A: Make them internally: apply the first-block ratio to all 45 pumps, for a cost of 60 valves.
general.Choice B: Make them internally: one pump displaces one valve, for a cost of 45 valves.
general.Choice C: Use the supplier: internal production sacrifices 70 valves, compared with 65 through exchange.
general.Choice D: Use the supplier: producing any of the second block requires giving up all 100 valves.
general.Correct Answer: C — Use the supplier: internal production sacrifices 70 valves, compared with 65 through exchange.
general.Feedback: The first 30 pumps cost 40 valves. The next 15 cost 15×(60/30)=30 valves, totaling 70. The supplier costs 65, saving 5. Rising opportunity cost requires using the appropriate segment rather than one overall ratio.

general.Common Misconception: Using personal value or the original ticket price instead of forgone resale value.
general.Question: A student owns a concert ticket bought for $90. Selling it now would yield $140 less a $10 selling fee. Attending requires $20 parking and rules out a $100 evening job; she can both sell the ticket and work if she skips. What is the relevant economic cost of attending?
general.Choice A: $160: the $140 posted resale price and parking, excluding the compatible work alternative.
general.Choice B: $210: the original $90 purchase, $100 forgone earnings and parking.
general.Choice C: $150: the better of resale or work, plus parking, treating those alternatives as mutually exclusive.
general.Choice D: $250: $130 net resale value, $100 forgone earnings and $20 parking.
general.Correct Answer: D — $250: $130 net resale value, $100 forgone earnings and $20 parking.
general.Feedback: If she skips, selling and working are compatible and yield 140-10+100=230. Attendance also costs 20 parking, for a relevant total of 250. The original purchase price is sunk; net resale value remains a current opportunity cost.

general.Common Misconception: Selecting the highest-valued infeasible bundle or using gross rather than net alternative value.
general.Question: A foundation has $10 million and one evaluation team. Health uses the full budget and team and yields benefits valued at $14 million. Education yields $13 million using both resources. Two small programs together yield $16 million within the budget, but need two teams. Hiring a second team costs $3 million beyond the available budget. With no borrowing, what is the best feasible alternative forgone if health is chosen?
general.Choice A: Education at $13 million; the $16 million package is infeasible under the joint budget and staffing limits.
general.Choice B: The two-program package at $16 million; a larger benefit makes its extra staffing feasible.
general.Choice C: Education plus the small programs at $29 million; all rejected benefits belong in opportunity cost.
general.Choice D: $1 million; opportunity cost is health’s gain relative to education rather than the alternative itself.
general.Correct Answer: A — Education at $13 million; the $16 million package is infeasible under the joint budget and staffing limits.
general.Feedback: Opportunity cost is the value of the best feasible forgone alternative. Education fits both constraints; the two-program package would require unaffordable staffing. The difference in benefits is not the opportunity cost.

general.Common Misconception: Choosing a capacity-infeasible bundle or failing to compare feasible net-return bundles.
general.Question: A studio selects a film that uses both of its release slots and all 8 available editor-weeks. Its alternatives are indivisible. A documentary uses 1 slot and 3 editor-weeks for $6 million net return. A series uses 1 slot and 5 editor-weeks for $9 million net return. A concert uses 1 slot and 4 editor-weeks, earning $12 million before $2 million of new costs. A festival package uses both slots and 8 editor-weeks for $14 million net return. Projects can be combined when both capacity limits are met, and net returns add. What is the best feasible alternative forgone by selecting the film?
general.Choice A: The documentary and concert, with $16 million net return.
general.Choice B: The series and concert, with $19 million net return.
general.Choice C: The documentary and series, with $15 million net return.
general.Choice D: The festival package alone, with $14 million net return.
general.Correct Answer: A — The documentary and concert, with $16 million net return.
general.Feedback: The concert nets $10m. Combining it with the documentary yields $16m and uses 2 slots and 7 editor-weeks. The series plus concert would yield $19m but requires 9 editor-weeks, so it is infeasible. The documentary plus series yields $15m, and the festival package yields $14m. The best feasible use forgone is the $16m documentary-concert bundle.

general.Common Misconception: Assuming a mandate eliminates opportunity cost or adding rejected projects.
general.Question: A city has one engineering team for this year. A stadium roof must eventually be repaired, but an approved one-year deferral is feasible at an expected cost of $4 million. Deferring would allow a flood barrier worth $26 million or a transit repair worth $19 million; the same team cannot do both. If the city repairs the roof now, what current alternative value is forgone?
general.Choice A: $22 million: the flood-barrier benefit net of the feasible deferral cost.
general.Choice B: $26 million: the flood-barrier benefit with the cost of making that alternative feasible ignored.
general.Choice C: $41 million: both public-project benefits minus the deferral cost.
general.Choice D: Zero: an eventual roof requirement removes every feasible current alternative.
general.Correct Answer: A — $22 million: the flood-barrier benefit net of the feasible deferral cost.
general.Feedback: The best current deferral plan yields 26-4=22 million; transit would yield 19-4=15. The future repair obligation does not erase a feasible timing alternative, but its associated cost must be included.

general.Common Misconception: Reversing the output ratio or using the required pump count directly.
general.Question: A machine can make 420 filters or 280 pumps per day at a constant tradeoff. A contract needs 70 pumps; each forgone filter has net value $8. Buying all pumps externally costs $700 plus $80 delivery and leaves the machine free for filters. Which fulfillment method has the lower relevant cost?
general.Choice A: Buy externally: $780 is below the $840 value of the 105 filters forgone by making pumps.
general.Choice B: Make internally: 70 filters are forgone, costing $560 compared with $780 externally.
general.Choice C: Make internally: owned machine time has zero current cost, so only the external bill is relevant.
general.Choice D: Buy externally: 210 filters are forgone internally, making its relevant cost $1,680.
general.Correct Answer: A — Buy externally: $780 is below the $840 value of the 105 filters forgone by making pumps.
general.Feedback: Each pump sacrifices 420/280=1.5 filters; 70 pumps cost 105 filters worth 840. External fulfillment costs 700+80=780 and saves 60 in resource value. Machine ownership does not remove its alternative use.

general.Common Misconception: Failing to update opportunity cost when a better feasible alternative appears.
general.Question: Maintenance uses a weekend that could otherwise produce a certain $40,000 net value. Before the decision, an urgent order becomes available: a 50% chance of $80,000 net value and a 50% chance of zero; it cannot be combined with the regular order. A guarantee costing $6,000 would make the urgent order’s $80,000 certain. For a risk-neutral manager, what is the opportunity cost of maintenance?
general.Choice A: $74,000: the guaranteed urgent order is the best feasible alternative after its guarantee cost.
general.Choice B: $120,000: add the regular order and the urgent order’s expected value plus its guaranteed gain.
general.Choice C: $40,000: the original plan fixes opportunity cost even after a better alternative becomes feasible.
general.Choice D: $80,000: use the guaranteed receipt while ignoring the resources needed to obtain the guarantee.
general.Correct Answer: A — $74,000: the guaranteed urgent order is the best feasible alternative after its guarantee cost.
general.Feedback: The regular and unguaranteed urgent orders each have expected net value 40,000. The guaranteed order nets 80,000-6,000=74,000 and is feasible before maintenance is chosen. Mutually exclusive alternatives are compared, not added.

general.Question: The economist's role in policy analysis is primarily to:
general.Choice A: Clarify likely tradeoffs and consequences
general.Choice B: Choose everyone's values
general.Choice C: Guarantee a policy works
general.Choice D: Eliminate scarcity
general.Correct Answer: A — Clarify likely tradeoffs and consequences
general.Feedback: Economics can analyze consequences and tradeoffs, while value judgments remain separate choices.

general.Common Misconception: Giving economists authority to choose society’s values.
general.Question: An economist estimates a policy’s effects, then recommends adoption. What two roles appear?
general.Choice A: Scientist for the estimate and adviser for the recommendation
general.Choice B: Adviser for both because policy is mentioned
general.Choice C: Scientist for both because evidence is used
general.Choice D: Legislator for the estimate and judge for the advice
general.Correct Answer: A — Scientist for the estimate and adviser for the recommendation
general.Feedback: Economists can estimate consequences; recommendations also require value judgments.

general.Question: A policy tradeoff occurs when:
general.Choice A: Improving one goal makes another goal harder to achieve
general.Choice B: A policy has no consequences
general.Choice C: Supply equals demand
general.Choice D: A tax is legally paid by sellers
general.Correct Answer: A — Improving one goal makes another goal harder to achieve
general.Feedback: Policies often require balancing competing goals rather than delivering only benefits.

general.Question: A positive statement is best described as:
general.Choice A: A testable claim about how the world is
general.Choice B: A claim about how the world should be
general.Choice C: A statement that is always good
general.Choice D: A policy recommendation
general.Correct Answer: A — A testable claim about how the world is
general.Feedback: Positive statements describe or predict how the world is.

general.Question: A statement using 'should' is usually:
general.Choice A: Positive
general.Choice B: Normative
general.Choice C: A demand shifter
general.Choice D: A supply schedule
general.Correct Answer: B — Normative
general.Feedback: Normative statements make value judgments about what should happen.

general.Common Misconception: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
general.Question: A price-support study predicts more output, then recommends the policy as fair. How should these two claims be evaluated?
general.Choice A: Test the output prediction separately from the fairness judgment
general.Choice B: Ignore the prediction once advice appears
general.Choice C: Treat both parts as positive because evidence exists
general.Choice D: Treat both parts as normative because policy is involved
general.Correct Answer: A — Test the output prediction separately from the fairness judgment
general.Feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

general.Question: An analyst writes: "A congestion charge will reduce downtown car trips by 10%. That reduction is worth the added financial burden on commuters." How are the two claims classified?
general.Choice A: First normative; second positive.
general.Choice B: Both positive.
general.Choice C: First positive; second normative.
general.Choice D: Both normative.
general.Correct Answer: C — First positive; second normative.
general.Feedback: The 10% traffic prediction can be tested against evidence, whether or not it proves true. Saying the reduction is worth the burden ranks competing outcomes; that judgment needs a value premise that traffic data alone cannot establish.

general.Common Misconception: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
general.Question: A transit study predicts that a lower fare will increase ridership. Why is this positive?
general.Choice A: Evidence could test the predicted change
general.Choice B: The prediction must be socially desirable
general.Choice C: The result is guaranteed to be true
general.Choice D: Transit policy contains no value judgment
general.Correct Answer: A — Evidence could test the predicted change
general.Feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

general.Common Misconception: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
general.Question: A council member says parks should receive more funding because access is fair. Why is this normative?
general.Choice A: It includes a government budget
general.Choice B: It ranks outcomes using a value judgment
general.Choice C: It predicts a measurable funding change
general.Choice D: It must be supported by all voters
general.Correct Answer: B — It ranks outcomes using a value judgment
general.Feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

general.Question: Which statement is positive?
general.Choice A: The city should make rent cheaper.
general.Choice B: Rent control is unfair.
general.Choice C: A binding rent ceiling reduces apartment supply
general.Choice D: The best policy is always lower rent.
general.Correct Answer: C — A binding rent ceiling reduces apartment supply
general.Feedback: This is positive because it makes a testable claim about what the policy will do.

general.Question: An economist says, 'The city should accept some efficiency loss to make housing more affordable.' What makes this normative?
general.Choice A: It can be tested with rental data alone
general.Choice B: It uses a value judgment about what policy should do
general.Choice C: It describes only current prices
general.Choice D: It states the law of demand
general.Correct Answer: B — It uses a value judgment about what policy should do
general.Feedback: The statement recommends what policy should do, so it is normative.

general.Question: Which statement is positive rather than normative?
general.Choice A: A binding rent ceiling reduces the quantity of rental housing supplied
general.Choice B: The city should cap rents to protect tenants
general.Choice C: Housing is too important to leave to markets
general.Choice D: Fair rents matter more than landlord profits
general.Correct Answer: A — A binding rent ceiling reduces the quantity of rental housing supplied
general.Feedback: The claim that a binding rent ceiling reduces the quantity of rental housing supplied is a testable prediction. The other claims prescribe what the city should do or express judgments about fairness and priorities.

general.Question: An economist says, 'A higher minimum wage will reduce employment among low-skill workers.' What kind of statement is this?
general.Choice A: Positive
general.Choice B: Normative
general.Choice C: A price floor
general.Choice D: A circular-flow claim
general.Correct Answer: A — Positive
general.Feedback: This is positive because it makes a testable claim about cause and effect.

general.Common Misconception: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
general.Question: A commissioner says the city ought to favor safer streets even if travel takes longer. What makes this normative?
general.Choice A: The ability to measure travel time
general.Choice B: The ranking of safety against travel time
general.Choice C: The prediction that streets can change
general.Choice D: The reference to a city decision
general.Correct Answer: B — The ranking of safety against travel time
general.Feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

general.Question: An economist says, 'A rent ceiling below equilibrium will reduce housing quality over time.' Another says, 'The city should accept that cost to help low-income renters.' Which pairing is correct?
general.Choice A: First is positive; second is normative
general.Choice B: First is normative; second is positive
general.Choice C: Both are positive
general.Choice D: Both are normative
general.Correct Answer: A — First is positive; second is normative
general.Feedback: The first is testable. The second recommends what policy should do, so it is normative.

general.Question: A report predicts that extending library hours will increase weekly visits. Another recommends the extension because access is worth the staffing cost. Which assessment is correct?
general.Choice A: The visit prediction is testable; the recommendation adds a value judgment
general.Choice B: Both claims are normative because a public agency is involved
general.Choice C: The recommendation is positive because staffing costs can be measured
general.Choice D: The visit prediction is normative until the extension occurs
general.Correct Answer: A — The visit prediction is testable; the recommendation adds a value judgment
general.Feedback: Evidence can test the predicted visit change. Calling improved access worth its cost also ranks outcomes; future predictions can be positive before observation.

general.Question: An evaluator says, "Option A saves more staff time, so it is the best policy." Which reply separates the testable component from the hidden value premise?
general.Choice A: Measure the time savings, then ask why that objective should outrank other consequences
general.Choice B: Treat the entire sentence as positive because staff time is measurable
general.Choice C: Treat the time-saving estimate as normative because it supports a recommendation
general.Choice D: Conclude more accurate timing data will uniquely determine the preferred policy
general.Correct Answer: A — Measure the time savings, then ask why that objective should outrank other consequences
general.Feedback: Time savings can be tested. Moving from that estimate to "best" requires a criterion for weighing time against other outcomes.

general.Question: A board ranks plans only by the number of people served and selects A. New evidence shows B serves more people but offers less privacy. Which conclusion distinguishes logic from values?
general.Choice A: Choosing A would necessarily show the new service count is false
general.Choice B: Its stated rule now favors B; preferring A would require changing or qualifying that rule
general.Choice C: The privacy difference makes the service-count evidence normative
general.Choice D: More people served proves B is morally superior under every criterion
general.Correct Answer: B — Its stated rule now favors B; preferring A would require changing or qualifying that rule
general.Feedback: A fixed criterion has implications that evidence can change. Preferring privacy can justify a different criterion, but does not refute the service-count evidence.

general.Question: A forecast says a digitization plan will reduce waiting. A recommendation says it should be adopted only if access for people without internet is protected. Waiting falls but offline access worsens. Which inference is sound?
general.Choice A: Observed waiting reductions prove the plan satisfies the value criterion
general.Choice B: The forecast becomes normative because implementation affected access
general.Choice C: The forecast is supported, while the recommendation's stated condition is unmet
general.Choice D: The failed access condition refutes the waiting-time forecast
general.Correct Answer: C — The forecast is supported, while the recommendation's stated condition is unmet
general.Feedback: The observed waiting result bears on the positive claim. Protecting offline access is a separate condition in the recommendation; success on one outcome does not satisfy it.

general.Question: A report states that volunteers prefer evening shifts and therefore evening-only service is fair. A representative survey confirms the preference. What remains unresolved?
general.Choice A: Whether a confirmed preference statement can count as positive
general.Choice B: Whether using a survey converts the fairness conclusion into a measured fact
general.Choice C: Whether the fairness judgment proves daytime users have no unmet needs
general.Choice D: Whether fairness should be judged by volunteer preferences rather than users' access
general.Correct Answer: D — Whether fairness should be judged by volunteer preferences rather than users' access
general.Feedback: A preference claim is empirically testable. The move from measured volunteer preferences to fairness requires a value premise about whose interests count.

general.Question: A rule gives priority to people facing the greatest hardship. New data show that a different group meets that description. What change is consistent with keeping the same normative principle?
general.Choice A: Change the priority group because the evidence changed who satisfies the criterion
general.Choice B: Keep the old group because normative principles cannot use evidence
general.Choice C: Declare hardship measurement normative solely because it informs policy
general.Choice D: Treat the data as proof that greatest-hardship priority is the only fair principle
general.Correct Answer: A — Change the priority group because the evidence changed who satisfies the criterion
general.Feedback: A stable value criterion can lead to a different recommendation when facts change. Evidence identifies its beneficiaries without uniquely establishing the criterion itself.

general.Question: A researcher predicts that simplifying an application raises completion when eligibility is unchanged. A trial simplifies the form and broadens eligibility; completion rises. Which statement is justified?
general.Choice A: Only recommendations can be evaluated when two policies change together
general.Choice B: The prediction is positive, but the joint change does not isolate the form's effect
general.Choice C: The rise proves the form alone caused every added completion
general.Choice D: The extra eligibility change makes the original claim normative
general.Correct Answer: B — The prediction is positive, but the joint change does not isolate the form's effect
general.Feedback: The conditional causal prediction is testable. Because eligibility changed too, the observation does not by itself identify the effect of form simplification.

general.Question: What is a positive statement?
general.Choice A: A testable claim about how the world is
general.Choice B: A claim about how the world should be
general.Choice C: A statement that is always morally good
general.Choice D: A policy recommendation
general.Correct Answer: A — A testable claim about how the world is
general.Feedback: A positive statement describes or predicts how the world is.

general.Question: An instructor presents this claim: 'A price ceiling below equilibrium creates a shortage.' What kind of statement is this?
general.Choice A: Normative
general.Choice B: Positive
general.Choice C: A value judgment
general.Choice D: A policy recommendation
general.Correct Answer: B — Positive
general.Feedback: This is positive because it is a testable cause-and-effect claim.

general.Question: An instructor gives two claims. Claim 1: 'Rent control reduces housing supply.' Claim 2: 'The city should use rent control anyway.' Which pairing is correct?
general.Choice A: Claim 1 is normative; Claim 2 is positive
general.Choice B: Both claims are positive
general.Choice C: Claim 1 is positive; Claim 2 is normative
general.Choice D: Both claims are normative
general.Correct Answer: C — Claim 1 is positive; Claim 2 is normative
general.Feedback: The first claim is testable. The second claim recommends what should happen, so it is normative.

general.Question: An adviser predicts a wage rule raises employed teenagers’ annual income by $8 million but reduces teenage employment by 3%. She recommends it because the income gain is worth the employment loss. A pilot instead finds a 1% job loss. Which conclusion separates evidence from values?
general.Choice A: The pilot makes the original employment prediction normative because a positive statement cannot be contradicted by data.
general.Choice B: The pilot challenges the size of the positive employment prediction; it does not by itself establish the adviser’s tradeoff criterion.
general.Choice C: The smaller loss proves the recommendation objectively correct, regardless of how the affected teenagers value work and income.
general.Choice D: The recommendation makes both numerical predictions normative, so neither can be evaluated using pilot evidence.
general.Correct Answer: B — The pilot challenges the size of the positive employment prediction; it does not by itself establish the adviser’s tradeoff criterion.
general.Feedback: Predictions about income and employment are testable positive claims even when inaccurate. Calling one outcome worth another introduces a value judgment. New evidence informs the tradeoff but cannot supply the normative weighting by itself.

general.Common Misconception: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
general.Question: A report states: (1) a tax reduces cigarette purchases; (2) the tax burden falls heavily on low-income smokers; (3) therefore the tax is unjust. Which classification is correct?
general.Choice A: All three are positive, because technical wording removes every value judgment
general.Choice B: Only statement 1 is positive
general.Choice C: Statements 1 and 2 are positive; statement 3 is normative
general.Choice D: Statements 2 and 3 are normative
general.Correct Answer: C — Statements 1 and 2 are positive; statement 3 is normative
general.Feedback: The first two claims can be tested empirically. The conclusion that the policy is unjust is normative.

general.Common Misconception: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
general.Question: Does positive mean good or favorable?
general.Choice A: Yes; positive means the outcome is desirable
general.Choice B: Yes; positive claims support the policy being discussed
general.Choice C: No; it means testable in principle
general.Choice D: Yes; positive claims are facts that must be true.
general.Correct Answer: C — No; it means testable in principle
general.Feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

general.Common Misconception: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
general.Question: Does false automatically mean normative?
general.Choice A: Yes; normative claims are the claims that turn out to be false
general.Choice B: Yes; positive claims must be factually correct
general.Choice C: Yes; a claim becomes normative once evidence rejects it.
general.Choice D: No; a false claim can still be testable
general.Correct Answer: D — No; a false claim can still be testable
general.Feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

general.Common Misconception: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
general.Question: Is every policy statement normative?
general.Choice A: No; policy predictions can be positive
general.Choice B: Yes; any statement about government policy is normative
general.Choice C: Yes; policy effects cannot be tested with evidence
general.Choice D: Yes; mentioning a recommendation makes every related claim normative.
general.Correct Answer: A — No; policy predictions can be positive
general.Feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

general.Common Misconception: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
general.Question: Does technical tone guarantee a positive claim?
general.Choice A: Yes; technical language makes a statement factual
general.Choice B: No; technical wording can conceal a value judgment
general.Choice C: Yes; numerical language removes value judgments
general.Choice D: Yes; professional wording means the claim can be tested.
general.Correct Answer: B — No; technical wording can conceal a value judgment
general.Feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

general.Common Misconception: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
general.Question: An economist predicts job losses and recommends against a rule. What additional judgment turns the prediction into policy advice?
general.Choice A: The existence of a measurable employment effect
general.Choice B: The fact that the rule is a government policy
general.Choice C: The recommendation adds a value judgment about the predicted cost
general.Choice D: The use of an economic forecast.
general.Correct Answer: C — The recommendation adds a value judgment about the predicted cost
general.Feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

general.Common Misconception: Assuming objective wording alone makes a claim positive.
general.Question: A model predicts a tax effect under stated assumptions. Why is it positive?
general.Choice A: Because the prediction supports the tax
general.Choice B: Because the model is written in technical language
general.Choice C: Because the prediction must be true if the assumptions are stated.
general.Choice D: Evidence could test the conditional prediction
general.Correct Answer: D — Evidence could test the conditional prediction
general.Feedback: Identify what observation could support or contradict the testable component.

general.Common Misconception: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
general.Question: A library reports that Sunday hours increased visits. What makes this positive?
general.Choice A: The increase in visits is a desirable outcome
general.Choice B: Library officials support Sunday hours
general.Choice C: The report is written confidently, so the claim must be true.
general.Choice D: Visit records could test the claimed increase
general.Correct Answer: D — Visit records could test the claimed increase
general.Feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

general.Common Misconception: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
general.Question: “The library should stay open Sundays because access matters.” Why is this normative?
general.Choice A: It recommends a choice using a value judgment
general.Choice B: Sunday visits can be counted
general.Choice C: The statement concerns a public institution
general.Choice D: Evidence could show whether Sunday hours increase attendance.
general.Correct Answer: A — It recommends a choice using a value judgment
general.Feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

general.Common Misconception: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
general.Question: A forecast that later proves false can still be positive when:
general.Choice A: The forecast was made by an expert
general.Choice B: Evidence could in principle have tested it
general.Choice C: The forecast described an outcome people wanted
general.Choice D: The forecast was stated with certainty.
general.Correct Answer: B — Evidence could in principle have tested it
general.Feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

general.Common Misconception: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
general.Question: Which claim is normative in a school debate?
general.Choice A: Average class size fell by two students last year
general.Choice B: Smaller classes increased per-student spending
general.Choice C: The district ought to favor smaller classes despite higher costs
general.Choice D: Enrollment is projected to rise next year.
general.Correct Answer: C — The district ought to favor smaller classes despite higher costs
general.Feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

general.Common Misconception: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
general.Question: Which claim is positive in a transit debate?
general.Choice A: The city should make transit more affordable
general.Choice B: Lower fares are fairer to low-income riders
general.Choice C: Expanding transit access is more important than balancing the transit budget.
general.Choice D: A lower fare increased weekday ridership
general.Correct Answer: D — A lower fare increased weekday ridership
general.Feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

general.Common Misconception: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
general.Question: A report says a fee reduced waste and therefore is fair. What is normative?
general.Choice A: The claim that the fee reduced waste
general.Choice B: The measured amount of waste reduction
general.Choice C: The judgment that the fee is fair
general.Choice D: The fact that a fee was imposed.
general.Correct Answer: C — The judgment that the fee is fair
general.Feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

general.Common Misconception: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
general.Question: A weakly supported prediction later fails. What classification remains possible?
general.Choice A: Normative, because the prediction turned out to be false
general.Choice B: Normative, because the evidence supporting it was weak
general.Choice C: Neither positive nor normative until the prediction is confirmed.
general.Choice D: Positive, because testability does not require truth
general.Correct Answer: D — Positive, because testability does not require truth
general.Feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

general.Common Misconception: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
general.Question: “Costs rose 8%, so the city should respond.” What is present?
general.Choice A: A positive measurement plus a normative recommendation
general.Choice B: A purely positive statement because it includes a measured percentage
general.Choice C: A purely normative statement because it recommends action
general.Choice D: Two positive claims because both parts refer to economic conditions.
general.Correct Answer: A — A positive measurement plus a normative recommendation
general.Feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

general.Common Misconception: Assuming objective wording alone makes a claim positive.
general.Question: A program “works,” but no outcome is named. What is missing?
general.Choice A: A statement that the program is desirable
general.Choice B: A measurable claim that evidence could contradict
general.Choice C: A recommendation about whether the program should continue
general.Choice D: A larger sample of people who support the program.
general.Correct Answer: B — A measurable claim that evidence could contradict
general.Feedback: Identify what observation could support or contradict the testable component.

general.Common Misconception: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
general.Question: “Equal access matters more than maximum output.” What is this?
general.Choice A: A positive claim because access and output can both be measured
general.Choice B: A positive claim because it compares two economic outcomes
general.Choice C: A normative ranking of competing values
general.Choice D: Neither positive nor normative because no policy is named.
general.Correct Answer: C — A normative ranking of competing values
general.Feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

general.Common Misconception: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
general.Question: A tax study uses the word efficient for a measurable revenue criterion. Is it necessarily normative?
general.Choice A: Yes; the word efficient always expresses a value judgment
general.Choice B: Yes; any claim about taxes is normative
general.Choice C: Yes; a policy criterion cannot be evaluated with evidence.
general.Choice D: No; the stated criterion can be tested with evidence
general.Correct Answer: D — No; the stated criterion can be tested with evidence
general.Feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

general.Common Misconception: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
general.Question: A subsidy is predicted to raise enrollment and is therefore recommended. Which split is correct?
general.Choice A: Both parts are positive because enrollment can be measured
general.Choice B: Both parts are normative because a subsidy is a policy
general.Choice C: The forecast is positive; the recommendation is normative
general.Choice D: The forecast is normative; the recommendation is positive.
general.Correct Answer: C — The forecast is positive; the recommendation is normative
general.Feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

general.Common Misconception: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
general.Question: “The policy benefits most residents, so it is just.” Where is the normative step?
general.Choice A: The claim that most residents benefit
general.Choice B: The number of residents affected by the policy
general.Choice C: The measured size of the benefits.
general.Choice D: Calling the distribution just
general.Correct Answer: D — Calling the distribution just
general.Feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

general.Common Misconception: Assuming objective wording alone makes a claim positive.
general.Question: What could test the claim that a road fee reduces congestion?
general.Choice A: Traffic counts around comparable fee changes
general.Choice B: A survey asking whether drivers think the fee is fair
general.Choice C: A city council vote on the fee
general.Choice D: A statement from officials that the fee will work.
general.Correct Answer: A — Traffic counts around comparable fee changes
general.Feedback: Identify what observation could support or contradict the testable component.

general.Common Misconception: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
general.Question: When can “the project has positive net benefits” be positive?
general.Choice A: Always, because net benefits are measured in dollars
general.Choice B: When inputs and the net-benefit rule are empirically checkable
general.Choice C: Never, because the word benefits is inherently normative
general.Choice D: Only when everyone agrees the project is desirable.
general.Correct Answer: B — When inputs and the net-benefit rule are empirically checkable
general.Feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

general.Common Misconception: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
general.Question: “The only acceptable policy is universal access.” Why is this normative?
general.Choice A: Universal access can be measured
general.Choice B: The statement refers to a policy outcome
general.Choice C: It embeds a value standard despite objective wording
general.Choice D: The sentence does not include a numerical prediction.
general.Correct Answer: C — It embeds a value standard despite objective wording
general.Feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

general.Common Misconception: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
general.Question: A rule lowers costs but is called morally wrong. What can evidence settle?
general.Choice A: Both the cost effect and whether the rule is morally wrong
general.Choice B: Only whether the rule is morally wrong
general.Choice C: Neither claim, because the rule is a policy.
general.Choice D: The cost effect, but not the moral conclusion by itself
general.Correct Answer: D — The cost effect, but not the moral conclusion by itself
general.Feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

general.Common Misconception: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
general.Question: A report defines success only as maximum total surplus. What choice is normative?
general.Choice A: Calculating total surplus from observed prices and quantities
general.Choice B: Selecting total surplus as the sole ranking criterion
general.Choice C: Measuring how total surplus changes after the policy
general.Choice D: Estimating the policy’s effect on output.
general.Correct Answer: B — Selecting total surplus as the sole ranking criterion
general.Feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

general.Common Misconception: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
general.Question: Two analysts agree that an archive plan preserves more records but delays public access. One recommends it; the other rejects it. What additional finding would show a factual disagreement as well as a value disagreement?
general.Choice A: They agree on the delay but differ on whether it is acceptable
general.Choice B: They use the same probabilities but prefer different distributions of access
general.Choice C: They assign different probabilities to permanent record loss under the alternative
general.Choice D: They give different ethical priority to immediate public access
general.Correct Answer: C — They assign different probabilities to permanent record loss under the alternative
general.Feedback: Probabilities of record loss are empirical assessments. The other differences concern how agreed consequences should be valued.

general.Common Misconception: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
general.Question: A report finds that a shuttle saves travelers time but increases neighborhood noise. It recommends adoption using travelers' gains alone. Which critique is precise?
general.Choice A: Time savings become normative when expressed in money
general.Choice B: Adding more precise effect estimates removes the need to decide whose welfare counts
general.Choice C: The effects are testable; excluding neighbors from the recommendation embeds a value choice
general.Choice D: Noise estimates are normative because neighbors dislike the outcome
general.Correct Answer: C — The effects are testable; excluding neighbors from the recommendation embeds a value choice
general.Feedback: Time and noise effects can be measured. Counting only travelers when recommending a policy assigns standing to one group and excludes another, which is a value choice.

general.Common Misconception: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
general.Question: Two forecasts disagree about whether a new scheduling rule will shorten next year's queues. Both specify measurable waiting times and comparable staffing. What would change their status as positive claims?
general.Choice A: The forecast with the larger benefit is positive; the other is normative
general.Choice B: Both become normative until next year's data exist
general.Choice C: Agreement by the forecasters is required before evidence can test them
general.Choice D: Neither disagreement nor the future date changes their testable status
general.Correct Answer: D — Neither disagreement nor the future date changes their testable status
general.Feedback: Positive status depends on empirical testability, not agreement, truth, desirability or whether the outcome has occurred. Later evidence can support one forecast over the other.

general.Common Misconception: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
general.Question: An analyst rejects a delivery plan because predicted delays exceed her stated acceptable limit. Better evidence places delays below that limit, but she still rejects it on privacy grounds. Which interpretation fits?
general.Choice A: The factual case changed, and the rejection now requires an additional value criterion
general.Choice B: The original delay forecast was normative because it supported rejection
general.Choice C: The unchanged decision proves the new delay estimate is irrelevant to the original argument
general.Choice D: Privacy concerns establish that the revised forecast is false
general.Correct Answer: A — The factual case changed, and the rejection now requires an additional value criterion
general.Feedback: The delay objection no longer follows from the updated evidence and original threshold. A privacy objection can support rejection, but it is a separate normative premise.

general.Common Misconception: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
general.Question: A planner defines "optimal" as maximizing visits, then claims the chosen schedule is objectively best. Another schedule serves fewer visitors but reaches people with greater need. Which statement is most defensible?
general.Choice A: A numerical criterion cannot contain a value judgment
general.Choice B: Visit maximization identifies an optimum under one criterion, not a uniquely justified social ranking
general.Choice C: Calling a result optimal makes its criterion empirically true
general.Choice D: The need difference disproves the measured visit counts
general.Correct Answer: B — Visit maximization identifies an optimum under one criterion, not a uniquely justified social ranking
general.Feedback: Optimization can be objective conditional on a criterion. Choosing visits rather than need as the social objective remains a normative judgment.

general.Common Misconception: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
general.Question: “A bus lane reduced travel time.” What kind of claim is this?
general.Choice A: Positive and empirically testable
general.Choice B: Normative because reduced travel time is desirable
general.Choice C: Normative because the statement concerns transportation policy
general.Choice D: Neither, because one observed result cannot be tested.
general.Correct Answer: A — Positive and empirically testable
general.Feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

general.Common Misconception: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
general.Question: “The city ought to accept higher costs for cleaner air.” What kind?
general.Choice A: Positive because costs and air quality can be measured
general.Choice B: Normative because it ranks a tradeoff
general.Choice C: Positive because the statement describes a policy tradeoff
general.Choice D: Neither, because the statement contains no numerical estimate.
general.Correct Answer: B — Normative because it ranks a tradeoff
general.Feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

general.Common Misconception: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
general.Question: When does a false forecast remain positive?
general.Choice A: Only when the forecast describes a desirable outcome
general.Choice B: Only when an expert made the forecast
general.Choice C: When evidence could have tested the forecast
general.Choice D: Never; a false claim cannot be positive.
general.Correct Answer: C — When evidence could have tested the forecast
general.Feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

general.Common Misconception: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
general.Question: A report predicts gains and calls them worth unequal losses. What is normative?
general.Choice A: The judgment that gains justify the losses
general.Choice B: The prediction that the policy creates gains
general.Choice C: The estimated size of the gains
general.Choice D: The measured distribution of gains and losses.
general.Correct Answer: A — The judgment that gains justify the losses
general.Feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

general.Common Misconception: Assuming objective wording alone makes a claim positive.
general.Question: What best tests “a fee reduces congestion”?
general.Choice A: A survey asking whether residents support the fee
general.Choice B: Traffic counts before and after comparable changes
general.Choice C: A council vote to adopt the fee
general.Choice D: A statement from officials that congestion will fall.
general.Correct Answer: B — Traffic counts before and after comparable changes
general.Feedback: Identify what observation could support or contradict the testable component.

general.Common Misconception: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
general.Question: Why is “Policy A is responsible” not automatically positive?
general.Choice A: The statement mentions a policy
general.Choice B: The word responsible refers to a measurable outcome
general.Choice C: Responsible may hide an unstated value standard
general.Choice D: Any sentence about policy performance is positive.
general.Correct Answer: C — Responsible may hide an unstated value standard
general.Feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

general.Common Misconception: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
general.Question: School plan A is predicted to raise scores by 6 points and reduce free time by 4 hours weekly. Plan B raises scores by 4 points and reduces free time by 1 hour. A board declares A preferable because each extra score point is worth at least 2 hours of free time. Which statement correctly distinguishes the predictions from the board’s value judgment?
general.Choice A: The outcome predictions are normative; the board’s numerical weighting is positive, and A’s extra 2 points cost 3 hours.
general.Choice B: All claims are positive because they contain numbers; A dominates B on both scores and free time.
general.Choice C: The weighting is normative, so the score and time predictions cannot be tested against observed outcomes.
general.Choice D: The outcome predictions are positive; the board’s weighting is normative, and A’s extra 2 points cost 3 hours relative to B.
general.Correct Answer: D — The outcome predictions are positive; the board’s weighting is normative, and A’s extra 2 points cost 3 hours relative to B.
general.Feedback: Comparative predictions imply A adds 2 score points while costing 3 more hours, or 1.5 hours per extra point. Whether that is worthwhile depends on the board’s stated value criterion, not merely on the accuracy of the predictions.

general.Question: On a PPF, opportunity cost is measured by:
general.Choice A: What must be given up to gain more of the other good
general.Choice B: The money price of the good only
general.Choice C: The legal maximum price
general.Choice D: The tax paid by buyers
general.Correct Answer: A — What must be given up to gain more of the other good
general.Feedback: Opportunity cost on a PPF is what must be given up to get more of another good.

general.Common Misconception: Confusing movement toward the frontier with a shift of productive capacity.
general.Question: An economy moves from inside its PPF to the frontier without new resources. What changed?
general.Choice A: Productive capacity necessarily expanded
general.Choice B: Unused resources were employed more efficiently
general.Choice C: The frontier shifted outward
general.Choice D: Opportunity cost disappeared
general.Correct Answer: B — Unused resources were employed more efficiently
general.Feedback: Moving from inside the PPF to its frontier uses idle or misallocated resources more fully; productive capacity and the frontier remain unchanged.

general.Question: A bowed-out PPF shows that as more Good X is produced:
general.Choice A: The opportunity cost of Good X rises
general.Choice B: The opportunity cost of Good X falls to zero
general.Choice C: The economy escapes scarcity
general.Choice D: The PPF becomes a price floor
general.Correct Answer: A — The opportunity cost of Good X rises
general.Feedback: A bowed-out PPF shows increasing opportunity cost as resources are shifted toward one good.

general.Question: Why does opportunity cost usually rise along a bowed-out PPF?
general.Choice A: Resources are perfectly identical in every use
general.Choice B: Resources are not equally well suited to producing both goods
general.Choice C: Scarcity disappears at high output levels
general.Choice D: Prices are fixed by government
general.Correct Answer: B — Resources are not equally well suited to producing both goods
general.Feedback: Opportunity cost rises because resources are specialized and become less well suited as they are shifted into the other good.

general.Question: An economy is producing inside its PPF. What is the best interpretation?
general.Choice A: The point is unattainable
general.Choice B: The point is efficient
general.Choice C: The point is attainable but inefficient
general.Choice D: The point eliminates scarcity
general.Correct Answer: C — The point is attainable but inefficient
general.Feedback: A point inside the PPF can be produced, but resources are not being used efficiently.

general.Question: A workshop makes chairs and desks. Better scheduling lets previously idle machines produce more of both until no further increase in either is possible without reducing the other. Labor, machines and technology are unchanged. How does this appear on its PPF?
general.Choice A: An outward shift of the frontier.
general.Choice B: A move from one frontier point to another.
general.Choice C: A move beyond the unchanged frontier.
general.Choice D: A move from inside to the unchanged frontier.
general.Correct Answer: D — A move from inside to the unchanged frontier.
general.Feedback: Idle machines initially put production inside the PPF. Using existing capacity fully moves production to the frontier. The unchanged resources and technology mean capacity has not expanded, so the frontier does not shift.

general.Question: An economy gains more capital and better technology. What happens to its PPF?
general.Choice A: It shifts outward
general.Choice B: It shifts inward
general.Choice C: It becomes a demand curve
general.Choice D: It creates a binding price floor
general.Correct Answer: A — It shifts outward
general.Feedback: More resources or better technology increase productive capacity, shifting the PPF outward.

general.Question: A natural disaster destroys factories and equipment. What happens to the PPF?
general.Choice A: It shifts outward
general.Choice B: It shifts inward
general.Choice C: The economy moves to a different point on the same PPF.
general.Choice D: Opportunity cost disappears
general.Correct Answer: B — It shifts inward
general.Feedback: A loss of productive resources reduces what the economy can produce, shifting the PPF inward.

general.Question: Moving along a PPF gives up 18 units of Good Y to gain 6 units of Good X. What is the opportunity cost per unit of Good X?
general.Choice A: 6 units of Good Y
general.Choice B: 18 units of Good Y
general.Choice C: 3 units of Good Y
general.Choice D: 108 units of Good Y
general.Correct Answer: C — 3 units of Good Y
general.Feedback: Opportunity cost per Good X is what is given up divided by what is gained: 18 / 6 = 3.

general.Question: A PPF move gains 5 units of Good X but gives up 20 units of Good Y. What is the opportunity cost per additional Good X?
general.Choice A: 5 units of Good Y
general.Choice B: 20 units of Good Y
general.Choice C: 0.25 units of Good Y
general.Choice D: 4 units of Good Y
general.Correct Answer: D — 4 units of Good Y
general.Feedback: The economy gives up 20 units of Good Y to gain 5 units of Good X, so 20 / 5 = 4.

general.Question: A production possibilities frontier shows:
general.Choice A: The exact market price of each good
general.Choice B: Government’s preferred production mix
general.Choice C: The economy’s current unemployment rate
general.Choice D: Currently feasible combinations of two goods
general.Correct Answer: D — Currently feasible combinations of two goods
general.Feedback: A PPF shows possible production combinations with current resources and technology.

general.Question: A point inside the PPF usually means:
general.Choice A: Resources are not being used efficiently
general.Choice B: The point is unattainable
general.Choice C: The economy has no tradeoffs
general.Choice D: The economy is beyond its resources
general.Correct Answer: A — Resources are not being used efficiently
general.Feedback: A point inside the PPF is attainable but inefficient.

general.Question: A point outside the PPF is:
general.Choice A: Efficient but always chosen
general.Choice B: Unattainable with current resources and technology
general.Choice C: A price floor
general.Choice D: A market surplus
general.Correct Answer: B — Unattainable with current resources and technology
general.Feedback: A point outside the PPF cannot be reached with current resources and technology.

general.Question: Moving along a PPF usually means:
general.Choice A: Producing more of every good without cost
general.Choice B: Creating a tax wedge
general.Choice C: Producing more of one good and less of another
general.Choice D: Changing only the price level
general.Correct Answer: C — Producing more of one good and less of another
general.Feedback: Moving along the PPF shows a tradeoff between two goods.

general.Question: An outward shift of the PPF usually represents:
general.Choice A: A shortage
general.Choice B: A binding price ceiling
general.Choice C: A decrease in demand
general.Choice D: Economic growth
general.Correct Answer: D — Economic growth
general.Feedback: An outward shift means the economy can produce more than before.

general.Question: If moving from point A to point B on a PPF gives up 6 units of corn to gain 3 units of wheat, the opportunity cost per wheat is:
general.Choice A: 2 units of corn
general.Choice B: 3 units of corn
general.Choice C: 6 units of corn
general.Choice D: 18 units of corn
general.Correct Answer: A — 2 units of corn
general.Feedback: Opportunity cost per wheat is corn given up divided by wheat gained: 6 / 3 = 2.

general.Question: A PPF is bowed outward. Moving from low production of Good X to high production of Good X requires giving up larger and larger amounts of Good Y. What principle does this show?
general.Choice A: Increasing opportunity cost
general.Choice B: Constant opportunity cost
general.Choice C: A binding price floor
general.Choice D: A tax wedge
general.Correct Answer: A — Increasing opportunity cost
general.Feedback: A bowed-out PPF shows increasing opportunity cost as resources are shifted toward one good.

general.Question: A student says, 'This point is inside the PPF, so it is impossible.' What is the correction?
general.Choice A: Inside the PPF is unattainable
general.Choice B: Inside the PPF is efficient
general.Choice C: Inside the PPF means economic growth
general.Choice D: Inside the PPF is attainable but inefficient
general.Correct Answer: D — Inside the PPF is attainable but inefficient
general.Feedback: A point inside the PPF can be produced, but it wastes or underuses resources.

general.Question: A student says, 'This point is outside the PPF, so it is efficient.' What is the correction?
general.Choice A: Outside the PPF is unattainable with current resources and technology
general.Choice B: Outside the PPF is inefficient but possible
general.Choice C: Outside the PPF means unemployment and underused resources.
general.Choice D: Outside the PPF means a binding ceiling
general.Correct Answer: A — Outside the PPF is unattainable with current resources and technology
general.Feedback: Outside the PPF means the economy cannot reach that point with current resources and technology.

general.Question: With a constant production tradeoff, a country can produce either 80 units of food or 40 units of machinery. What is the opportunity cost of one unit of machinery?
general.Choice A: 0.5 unit of machinery per unit of food
general.Choice B: 2 units of food per unit of machinery
general.Choice C: 2 units of machinery per unit of food
general.Choice D: 80 units of food per unit of machinery
general.Correct Answer: B — 2 units of food per unit of machinery
general.Feedback: Divide the 80 units of food forgone by the 40 units of machinery gained: 80 / 40 = 2 units of food per unit of machinery. The inverse ratio, 0.5 unit of machinery per unit of food, answers the opposite question; 80 is the total endpoint sacrifice, not the cost per machinery unit.

general.Question: A storm destroys factories and equipment. What happens to the economy's PPF?
general.Choice A: It shifts outward
general.Choice B: The economy moves along the same PPF only
general.Choice C: It shifts inward
general.Choice D: The PPF becomes a demand curve
general.Correct Answer: C — It shifts inward
general.Feedback: A loss of productive resources reduces what the economy can produce, shifting the PPF inward.

general.Question: Worker training improves human capital and shifts the PPF outward for both goods. Which economic relationship does this illustrate?
general.Choice A: A price ceiling creates a shortage
general.Choice B: Human capital raises productive capacity
general.Choice C: A tax wedge reduces market size
general.Choice D: A positive statement becomes normative
general.Correct Answer: B — Human capital raises productive capacity
general.Feedback: Better worker training improves human capital and can shift the PPF outward.

general.Question: A student says, “A point outside the PPF is inefficient because the economy is not producing there.” What is wrong with that statement?
general.Choice A: A point outside the PPF is always efficient
general.Choice B: A point outside the PPF shows idle resources
general.Choice C: It is unattainable with current resources, not merely inefficient.
general.Choice D: A point outside the PPF means opportunity cost is zero
general.Correct Answer: C — It is unattainable with current resources, not merely inefficient.
general.Feedback: Inside the PPF is inefficient. Outside the PPF is unattainable with current resources and technology.

general.Question: An economist uses a PPF to show how producing more military goods requires producing fewer consumer goods. What is the model showing?
general.Choice A: Tradeoffs and opportunity cost
general.Choice B: Tax incidence
general.Choice C: A binding price ceiling
general.Choice D: A market surplus
general.Correct Answer: A — Tradeoffs and opportunity cost
general.Feedback: The PPF shows tradeoffs because producing more of one good requires giving up some of another.

general.Question: An economy moves from a point inside its PPF to a point on the PPF. What happened?
general.Choice A: It reached an unattainable point
general.Choice B: It used idle resources more efficiently
general.Choice C: It created a tax wedge
general.Choice D: It shifted demand left
general.Correct Answer: B — It used idle resources more efficiently
general.Feedback: Moving from inside the PPF to the frontier means resources are being used more efficiently.

general.Question: An economy gets better technology for producing both goods. What happens to its PPF?
general.Choice A: It shifts inward
general.Choice B: It becomes a price ceiling
general.Choice C: It shifts outward
general.Choice D: It creates a shortage
general.Correct Answer: C — It shifts outward
general.Feedback: Better technology increases productive capacity, shifting the PPF outward.

general.Question: A point is outside the PPF today but becomes attainable after an increase in capital and technology. What changed?
general.Choice A: The market price was fixed
general.Choice B: Demand decreased
general.Choice C: The economy moved inside the PPF
general.Choice D: The economy's productive capacity increased
general.Correct Answer: D — The economy's productive capacity increased
general.Feedback: More capital and better technology increase what the economy can produce.

general.Question: Which list contains all and only the efficient production points labeled in the PPF graph?
general.Choice A: A, B, C, D, E
general.Choice B: A, B, C, D, F
general.Choice C: A, B, C, E, G
general.Choice D: A, B, D, E, F
general.Correct Answer: A — A, B, C, D, E
general.Feedback: A, B, C, D, and E lie on the production possibilities frontier. F lies inside it and is inefficient; G lies outside it and is currently unattainable.

general.Question: Refer to the PPF graph. Which point is attainable but inefficient?
general.Choice A: G
general.Choice B: F
general.Choice C: C
general.Choice D: E
general.Correct Answer: B — F
general.Feedback: Point F is inside the PPF, so it is attainable but inefficient.

general.Question: Refer to the PPF graph. Which point is currently unattainable?
general.Choice A: F
general.Choice B: A
general.Choice C: G
general.Choice D: D
general.Correct Answer: C — G
general.Feedback: Point G is outside the PPF, so it is unattainable with current resources and technology.

general.Question: Refer to the PPF graph. Moving from B to C increases production of Good X by how many units?
general.Feedback: Point B has 8 units of Good X and point C has 15, so Good X increases by 7 units.

general.Question: Refer to the PPF graph. Moving from B to C requires giving up how many units of Good Y?
general.Feedback: Good Y falls from 45 at B to 35 at C, so the economy gives up 10 units of Good Y.

general.Question: Refer to the PPF graph. What is the opportunity cost of moving from C to D?
general.Choice A: 6 units of Good X
general.Choice B: 15 units of Good Y
general.Choice C: 20 units of Good Y
general.Choice D: 21 units of Good X
general.Correct Answer: B — 15 units of Good Y
general.Feedback: Moving from C to D raises Good X from 15 to 21, but Good Y falls from 35 to 20. The opportunity cost is 15 units of Good Y.

general.Question: Refer to the PPF graph. What is the opportunity cost per additional unit of Good X when moving from C to D?
general.Choice A: 6 units of Good Y
general.Choice B: 15 units of Good Y
general.Choice C: 2.5 units of Good Y
general.Choice D: 0.4 units of Good Y
general.Correct Answer: C — 2.5 units of Good Y
general.Feedback: Moving from C to D gains 6 units of Good X and gives up 15 units of Good Y, so 15 / 6 = 2.5 units of Good Y per Good X.

general.Question: Use the graph. Compare the opportunity cost of Good X over A to B and D to E. Which numerical evidence and conclusion fit the PPF?
general.Choice A: The costs are 0.5 and 4 Y per X; opportunity cost rises as more X is produced.
general.Choice B: The costs are 0.625 and 5 Y per X; opportunity cost stays constant as more X is produced.
general.Choice C: The costs are 0.5 and 4 Y per X; opportunity cost stays constant as more X is produced.
general.Choice D: The costs are 0.625 and 5 Y per X; opportunity cost rises as more X is produced.
general.Correct Answer: D — The costs are 0.625 and 5 Y per X; opportunity cost rises as more X is produced.
general.Feedback: A to B gives up 5 Y for 8 X, so the cost is 0.625 Y per X. D to E gives up 20 Y for 4 X, so the cost is 5 Y per X. This larger sacrifice per additional X shows increasing opportunity cost along the bowed frontier.

general.Question: Refer to the PPF graph. If the economy moves from F to C, what has happened?
general.Choice A: The economy has moved from inefficient production to efficient production
general.Choice B: The economy has moved from unattainable production to attainable production
general.Choice C: The economy has reduced both goods
general.Choice D: The economy has moved outside the PPF
general.Correct Answer: A — The economy has moved from inefficient production to efficient production
general.Feedback: Point F is inside the PPF and point C is on the PPF, so the economy moved from inefficient to efficient production.

general.Question: A country invests more in capital goods today, sacrificing consumer goods. In a PPF framework, what is the likely long-run implication?
general.Choice A: More future growth because capital accumulation can expand productive capacity
general.Choice B: No future effect because PPF choices never matter
general.Choice C: Immediate elimination of scarcity because future productive capacity will be larger.
general.Choice D: A binding price floor in the capital market
general.Correct Answer: A — More future growth because capital accumulation can expand productive capacity
general.Feedback: Choosing more capital goods today can increase future productive capacity and shift the PPF outward later.

general.Question: An economy moves from inside its PPF to a point on the PPF and then later shifts the PPF outward. What sequence is correct?
general.Choice A: First scarcity disappears, then opportunity cost disappears
general.Choice B: First efficiency improves, then productive capacity grows
general.Choice C: First demand shifts, then price controls bind
general.Choice D: First the economy becomes unattainable, then efficient
general.Correct Answer: B — First efficiency improves, then productive capacity grows
general.Feedback: Moving from inside to the frontier is improved efficiency. Shifting the frontier outward is growth.

general.Question: A new technology improves only production of medical devices, not food. Which PPF interpretation is best?
general.Choice A: The entire frontier must shift inward
general.Choice B: The economy moves inside the PPF
general.Choice C: The frontier rotates outward on the medical-device axis
general.Choice D: The law of demand no longer applies
general.Correct Answer: C — The frontier rotates outward on the medical-device axis
general.Feedback: Technology that improves only one good expands capacity for that good, rotating the PPF outward along that axis.

general.Question: A PPF table shows that moving from Bundle B to Bundle C increases wheat from 40 to 55 but reduces corn from 90 to 60. What is the opportunity cost per additional unit of wheat?
general.Choice A: 15 units of corn
general.Choice B: 30 units of corn
general.Choice C: 2 units of corn
general.Choice D: 0.5 units of corn
general.Correct Answer: C — 2 units of corn
general.Feedback: Wheat rises by 15 and corn falls by 30. Opportunity cost per wheat is 30 / 15 = 2 corn.

general.Question: An economy is producing inside its PPF because some labor and capital are idle. Which change moves it toward the frontier without shifting the frontier?
general.Choice A: Discovering a new technology
general.Choice B: Putting unemployed resources back to work
general.Choice C: Increasing the capital stock
general.Choice D: Expanding the labor force permanently
general.Correct Answer: B — Putting unemployed resources back to work
general.Feedback: Using idle resources moves the economy toward the existing PPF. New technology or more resources shift the PPF outward.

general.Question: A new technology improves only the production of Good X, not Good Y. What happens to the PPF?
general.Choice A: It shifts inward equally for both goods
general.Choice B: It creates a shortage of Good Y
general.Choice C: It becomes a price ceiling
general.Choice D: It rotates outward on the Good X axis
general.Correct Answer: D — It rotates outward on the Good X axis
general.Feedback: Technology that helps only one good expands production possibilities for that good, rotating the PPF outward on that axis.

general.Question: Refer to the PPF graph. What is the opportunity cost per additional unit of Good X when production moves from A to B?
general.Choice A: 1.6 units of Good Y
general.Choice B: 5 units of Good Y
general.Choice C: 8 units of Good Y
general.Choice D: 0.625 units of Good Y
general.Correct Answer: D — 0.625 units of Good Y
general.Feedback: Moving from A to B gains 8 units of Good X and gives up 5 units of Good Y, so opportunity cost per Good X is 5 / 8 = 0.625.

general.Question: Refer to the PPF graph. What is the opportunity cost per additional unit of Good X when production moves from B to C?
general.Choice A: About 1.43 units of Good Y
general.Choice B: 0.7 units of Good Y
general.Choice C: 7 units of Good Y
general.Choice D: 10 units of Good Y
general.Correct Answer: A — About 1.43 units of Good Y
general.Feedback: Moving from B to C gains 7 units of Good X and gives up 10 units of Good Y, so 10 / 7 is about 1.43.

general.Question: Refer to the PPF graph. What is the opportunity cost per additional unit of Good X when production moves from D to E?
general.Choice A: 4 units of Good Y
general.Choice B: 5 units of Good Y
general.Choice C: 0.2 units of Good Y
general.Choice D: 20 units of Good Y
general.Correct Answer: B — 5 units of Good Y
general.Feedback: Moving from D to E gains 4 units of Good X and gives up 20 units of Good Y, so 20 / 4 = 5.

general.Question: Refer to the PPF graph. Which move has the highest opportunity cost per additional unit of Good X?
general.Choice A: A to B
general.Choice B: D to E
general.Choice C: B to C
general.Choice D: C to D
general.Correct Answer: B — D to E
general.Feedback: The move from D to E gives up 20 units of Good Y to gain only 4 units of Good X, the highest cost per unit among the listed moves.

general.Question: Refer to the PPF graph. Compare the opportunity cost per additional unit of Good X from A to B with the cost from D to E. Which calculation and conclusion are supported?
general.Choice A: A to B costs 0.625 Y per X, while D to E costs 5 Y per X; opportunity cost rises
general.Choice B: A to B costs 5 Y per X, while D to E costs 0.625 Y per X; opportunity cost falls
general.Choice C: Both moves cost 1 Y per X; opportunity cost remains constant
general.Choice D: A to B costs 8 Y per X, while D to E costs 4 Y per X; opportunity cost falls
general.Correct Answer: A — A to B costs 0.625 Y per X, while D to E costs 5 Y per X; opportunity cost rises
general.Feedback: The graph shows A to B gives up 5 Y for 8 X, or 0.625 Y per X. D to E gives up 20 Y for 4 X, or 5 Y per X, demonstrating increasing opportunity cost.
