micro.Choice D: CS and PS must be equal
micro.Correct Answer: C — Buyer value must be at least seller cost
micro.Feedback: An exchange creates positive gains only when the buyer’s value is at least as large as the seller’s cost.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: Buyer value is $17 and seller cost is $22. Efficient action?
micro.Choice A: Exchange at any price
micro.Choice B: Exchange only at $39
micro.Choice C: Produce two units
micro.Choice D: No exchange
micro.Correct Answer: D — No exchange
micro.Feedback: Because the buyer values the unit at $17 while the seller’s cost is $22, the exchange would destroy $5 of total surplus and should not occur.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: A learner keeps producing after the next seller’s cost exceeds the next buyer’s value. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
micro.Choice A: Keep producing because more output always raises surplus
micro.Choice B: Ignore seller cost when buyers still want the good
micro.Choice C: Produce until consumer surplus becomes zero
micro.Choice D: Stop before units whose marginal cost exceeds marginal willingness to pay
micro.Correct Answer: D — Stop before units whose marginal cost exceeds marginal willingness to pay
micro.Feedback: Units with cost above value reduce total surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: A learner allocates scarce units to the lowest-value buyers because they “need a bargain.” What does efficiency require?
micro.Choice A: Allocate units to the highest-cost sellers
micro.Choice B: Efficiency requires equal surplus for every buyer
micro.Choice C: Allocate units to the highest willingness-to-pay buyers, holding other assumptions fixed
micro.Choice D: Allocate units randomly regardless of value
micro.Correct Answer: C — Allocate units to the highest willingness-to-pay buyers, holding other assumptions fixed
micro.Feedback: The standard surplus criterion maximizes gains by placing goods with the highest-value users.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: A learner assigns production to the highest-cost sellers because they need the highest price. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
micro.Choice A: Efficiency requires identical costs across firms
micro.Choice B: Use lower-cost sellers first
micro.Choice C: Use higher-cost sellers first
micro.Choice D: Seller cost does not affect total surplus
micro.Correct Answer: B — Use lower-cost sellers first
micro.Feedback: Producing with lower opportunity-cost sellers preserves more surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: A learner calls the buyer with the highest willingness to pay the marginal buyer. What is the correction?
micro.Choice A: The marginal buyer is the last buyer just willing to purchase at the market price
micro.Choice B: The marginal buyer is always the richest buyer
micro.Choice C: The marginal buyer is the first buyer in the market
micro.Choice D: The marginal buyer is a seller at the equilibrium quantity
micro.Correct Answer: A — The marginal buyer is the last buyer just willing to purchase at the market price
micro.Feedback: Marginal refers to the edge of participation, not the maximum willingness to pay.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: A learner says an outcome is efficient whenever consumer surplus is maximized. What is missing?
micro.Choice A: Efficiency ignores sellers entirely
micro.Choice B: Consumer surplus and total surplus are identical
micro.Choice C: Efficiency means price must be zero
micro.Choice D: Efficiency uses total surplus, including producer surplus
micro.Correct Answer: D — Efficiency uses total surplus, including producer surplus
micro.Feedback: Market efficiency is judged by combined buyer and seller gains.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: A learner says the efficient quantity is where price is lowest. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
micro.Choice A: Efficiency depends only on fixed cost
micro.Choice B: The efficient quantity is always zero under scarcity
micro.Choice C: The efficient quantity is where marginal buyer value and marginal seller cost cross
micro.Choice D: The lowest price always maximizes total surplus
micro.Correct Answer: C — The efficient quantity is where marginal buyer value and marginal seller cost cross
micro.Feedback: Efficiency compares marginal willingness to pay with marginal willingness to accept.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: Why does equilibrium quantity matter for surplus?
micro.Choice A: It guarantees equal incomes
micro.Choice B: It maximizes price
micro.Choice C: The final included unit has value equal to cost
micro.Choice D: It eliminates scarcity
micro.Correct Answer: C — The final included unit has value equal to cost
micro.Feedback: At the efficient competitive quantity, the marginal buyer’s willingness to pay equals the marginal seller’s cost; additional units would not create positive gains.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: The first three units have marginal benefits $20, $15 and $9, and marginal costs $6, $10 and $12. With no other effects, how many units maximize total surplus?
micro.Feedback: The first two units create positive gains (14 and 5); the third destroys 3. Stop after two.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: How does efficient allocation connect to opportunity cost?
micro.Choice A: Use resources where buyer value exceeds the opportunity cost by the greatest amount
micro.Choice B: Ignore opportunity cost once a market price exists
micro.Choice C: Give production to the highest-cost supplier
micro.Choice D: Allocate goods to minimize consumer surplus
micro.Correct Answer: A — Use resources where buyer value exceeds the opportunity cost by the greatest amount
micro.Feedback: Surplus measures the value created above the opportunity cost of resources used.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: Why do the marginal buyer and seller help identify equilibrium efficiency?
micro.Choice A: They determine the money supply
micro.Choice B: They set every firm’s fixed cost
micro.Choice C: They identify the highest consumer income
micro.Choice D: They mark the edge where willingness to pay and willingness to accept determine whether one more trade adds gains
micro.Correct Answer: D — They mark the edge where willingness to pay and willingness to accept determine whether one more trade adds gains
micro.Feedback: The last feasible trade reveals the marginal gain from extending quantity.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: A price control changes the quantity traded away from the competitive quantity. What efficiency question should surplus analysis ask?
micro.Choice A: Did every buyer pay the same tax?
micro.Choice B: Did nominal GDP change?
micro.Choice C: Are mutually beneficial trades lost or inefficient trades created?
micro.Choice D: Did the legal price change labels on the graph?
micro.Correct Answer: C — Are mutually beneficial trades lost or inefficient trades created?
micro.Feedback: Efficiency focuses on how the policy changes the set of value-creating trades.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: At Q=4, marginal benefit is $18 and marginal cost is $12; at Q=5 they are both $15; at Q=6 they are $12 and $18. With smooth declining MB and rising MC, where is the efficient output?
micro.Correct Answer: B — Q=5
micro.Feedback: At Q=5 the marginal value equals marginal cost. Below it an expansion adds gains; above it extra units cost more than they are worth.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: At the market price, the marginal buyer is the buyer who:
micro.Choice A: Has the highest willingness to pay
micro.Choice B: Receives the largest consumer surplus
micro.Choice C: Would buy every unit
micro.Choice D: Is just willing to purchase the last unit traded
micro.Correct Answer: D — Is just willing to purchase the last unit traded
micro.Feedback: The marginal buyer is at the trading cutoff.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: At the market price, the marginal seller is the seller who:
micro.Choice A: Is just willing to provide the last unit traded
micro.Choice B: Has the lowest cost
micro.Choice C: Receives the largest producer surplus
micro.Choice D: Would supply every unit
micro.Correct Answer: A — Is just willing to provide the last unit traded
micro.Feedback: The marginal seller is at the trading cutoff.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: A voluntary exchange creates gains when:
micro.Choice A: Seller cost exceeds buyer value
micro.Choice B: The buyer’s willingness to pay is at least the seller’s willingness to accept
micro.Choice C: Price exceeds both value and cost
micro.Choice D: Buyer and seller surplus are equal
micro.Correct Answer: B — The buyer’s willingness to pay is at least the seller’s willingness to accept
micro.Feedback: Value must cover cost.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: In the standard competitive model, the efficient quantity is reached where:
micro.Choice A: Every buyer receives zero surplus
micro.Choice B: Every seller receives equal surplus
micro.Choice C: Marginal willingness to pay equals marginal willingness to accept
micro.Choice D: The price is judged fair
micro.Correct Answer: C — Marginal willingness to pay equals marginal willingness to accept
micro.Feedback: Efficiency stops where marginal value equals marginal cost.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: When two identical units are available, which buyer allocation maximizes measured surplus?
micro.Choice A: Give them to the two buyers with the lowest willingness to pay
micro.Choice B: Give them to the two buyers with the highest willingness to pay
micro.Choice C: Assign them randomly regardless of value
micro.Choice D: Give both to the marginal seller
micro.Correct Answer: B — Give them to the two buyers with the highest willingness to pay
micro.Feedback: Higher buyer values create greater total surplus when costs are unchanged.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: In an efficient allocation, a unit should be produced when:
micro.Choice A: The market price is below zero
micro.Choice B: Consumer and producer surplus must be equal
micro.Choice C: The buyer’s willingness to pay is at least the seller’s willingness to accept
micro.Choice D: The seller’s willingness to accept exceeds every buyer’s willingness to pay
micro.Correct Answer: C — The buyer’s willingness to pay is at least the seller’s willingness to accept
micro.Feedback: Production creates a nonnegative gain when value to the buyer covers the seller’s opportunity cost.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: Efficiency requires goods to go to buyers who:
micro.Choice A: Always pay the highest possible price
micro.Choice B: Value them most highly as measured by willingness to pay
micro.Choice C: Have the lowest willingness to pay
micro.Choice D: Arrive first regardless of value
micro.Correct Answer: B — Value them most highly as measured by willingness to pay
micro.Feedback: Allocating units to higher-value buyers maximizes measured gains from consumption.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: Efficiency requires production by sellers who:
micro.Choice A: Can supply at the lowest opportunity cost
micro.Choice B: Have the highest willingness to accept
micro.Choice C: Charge the highest price
micro.Choice D: Receive the largest fixed subsidy
micro.Correct Answer: A — Can supply at the lowest opportunity cost
micro.Feedback: Using lower-cost sellers preserves more surplus from each unit produced.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: Once the next seller’s willingness to accept exceeds the next buyer’s willingness to pay, producing one more unit would:
micro.Choice A: Increase total surplus
micro.Choice B: Leave total surplus unchanged by definition
micro.Choice C: Create consumer surplus with no cost
micro.Choice D: Reduce total surplus
micro.Correct Answer: D — Reduce total surplus
micro.Feedback: The next unit costs more to produce than the buyer values it, so it destroys surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: The efficient quantity is the quantity that:
micro.Choice A: Maximizes consumer surplus only
micro.Choice B: Guarantees equal incomes
micro.Choice C: Maximizes total surplus
micro.Choice D: Maximizes producer surplus only
micro.Correct Answer: C — Maximizes total surplus
micro.Feedback: Efficiency in this model is defined by maximizing the combined gains from exchange.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: If the next unit has willingness to pay of $26 and willingness to accept of $20, producing that unit would:
micro.Choice A: Have no effect on total surplus
micro.Choice B: Add $6 to total surplus
micro.Choice C: Reduce total surplus by $6
micro.Choice D: Transfer $46 from buyer to seller
micro.Correct Answer: B — Add $6 to total surplus
micro.Feedback: The gain from the unit is $26 - $20 = $6.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: Marginal willingness to pay is $18 and marginal cost is $12. Which adjustment raises surplus?
micro.Choice A: Decrease output
micro.Choice B: Keep output fixed because price is absent
micro.Choice C: Increase output; the next unit adds $6
micro.Choice D: Raise price without changing output
micro.Correct Answer: C — Increase output; the next unit adds $6
micro.Feedback: MB exceeds MC by $6.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: Marginal willingness to pay is $14 and marginal cost is $21. Which adjustment raises surplus?
micro.Choice A: Increase output
micro.Choice B: Keep output fixed because both are positive
micro.Choice C: Lower price without changing output
micro.Choice D: Decrease output; the last unit destroys $7
micro.Correct Answer: D — Decrease output; the last unit destroys $7
micro.Feedback: MC exceeds MB by $7.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: Allocation A gives two units to buyers valuing them at $40 and $32; B gives them to buyers valuing them at $35 and $28. Costs are equal. Which is better?
micro.Choice A: Allocation A by $9
micro.Choice B: Allocation B by $9
micro.Choice C: Allocation A by $5
micro.Choice D: They are equal
micro.Correct Answer: A — Allocation A by $9
micro.Feedback: A has $72 value versus $63.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: Plan A uses sellers with costs $9 and $15; Plan B uses costs $12 and $19. Buyers are unchanged. Which is better?
micro.Choice A: Plan B by $7
micro.Choice B: Plan A by $7
micro.Choice C: Plan A by $3
micro.Choice D: They are equal
micro.Correct Answer: B — Plan A by $7
micro.Feedback: A costs $24 versus $31.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: A buyer values a unit at $31 and a seller can provide it at a cost of $18. What total gain from exchange is available?
micro.Choice A: The buyer must receive all $13
micro.Choice B: The seller must receive all $13
micro.Choice C: The market price must equal $13
micro.Choice D: The trade can create $13 in total gains
micro.Correct Answer: D — The trade can create $13 in total gains
micro.Feedback: Buyer value minus seller cost gives the total gain from the exchange: $31 − $18 = $13.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. A student argues that the allocation at E is efficient only if buyers and sellers receive equal surplus. Which quantity and explanation correctly evaluate this claim under the standard competitive assumptions?
micro.Choice A: 6 units: marginal willingness to pay equals marginal cost; equal surplus shares are not required.
micro.Choice B: 8 units: equality of buyer and seller surplus is the condition required for efficiency.
micro.Choice C: 6 units: equality of buyer and seller surplus is the condition required for efficiency.
micro.Choice D: 8 units: marginal willingness to pay equals marginal cost; equal surplus shares are not required.
micro.Correct Answer: D — 8 units: marginal willingness to pay equals marginal cost; equal surplus shares are not required.
micro.Feedback: Demand and supply intersect at E, with quantity 8 and marginal value and cost both $10. This equality identifies the efficient quantity. Efficiency concerns total gains from trade, not an equal division of those gains.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. A student argues that the allocation at E is efficient only if buyers and sellers receive equal surplus. Which quantity and explanation correctly evaluate this claim under the standard competitive assumptions?
micro.Choice A: 6 units: marginal willingness to pay equals marginal cost; equal surplus shares are not required.
micro.Choice B: 8 units: total surplus is maximized only because the buyer’s payment equals the seller’s receipt.
micro.Choice C: 8 units: the market price is itself the total social gain from those trades.
micro.Choice D: 8 units: marginal willingness to pay equals marginal cost; equal surplus shares are not required.
micro.Correct Answer: D — 8 units: marginal willingness to pay equals marginal cost; equal surplus shares are not required.
micro.Feedback: At E, quantity is 8 and marginal value equals marginal cost at $14. That marginal equality identifies efficiency under the stated assumptions. Equal transfer payments or equal surplus shares do not establish efficiency.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. A student argues that the allocation at E is efficient only if buyers and sellers receive equal surplus. Which quantity and explanation correctly evaluate this claim under the standard competitive assumptions?
micro.Choice A: 4 units: marginal willingness to pay equals marginal cost; equal surplus shares are not required.
micro.Choice B: 5 units: equality of buyer and seller surplus is the condition required for efficiency.
micro.Choice C: 4 units: equality of buyer and seller surplus is the condition required for efficiency.
micro.Choice D: 5 units: marginal willingness to pay equals marginal cost; equal surplus shares are not required.
micro.Correct Answer: D — 5 units: marginal willingness to pay equals marginal cost; equal surplus shares are not required.
micro.Feedback: Demand and supply intersect at E, with quantity 5 and marginal value and cost both $14. This equality identifies the efficient quantity. Efficiency concerns total gains from trade, not an equal division of those gains.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: There are four tablets and buyers value one unit each at [40, 34, 27, 19, 12]. Which allocation maximizes buyer-side surplus for any common price low enough to sell all available units?
micro.Choice A: Allocate the units to the 4 lowest-value buyers
micro.Choice B: Allocate the units randomly to avoid unequal outcomes
micro.Choice C: Allocate the units to buyers with values [40, 34, 27, 19]
micro.Choice D: Allocate to buyers whose values are closest to the average
micro.Correct Answer: C — Allocate the units to buyers with values [40, 34, 27, 19]
micro.Feedback: For a fixed number of units and common price, allocating to the highest-value buyers maximizes total willingness to pay and consumer surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: When allocating four tablets, a buyer who values one unit at $19 receives the last unit. A buyer who did not receive a unit and values it at $12 replaces that buyer. What happens to total surplus if production cost is unchanged?
micro.Choice A: Total surplus rises by $7
micro.Choice B: Total surplus is unchanged because the price is unchanged
micro.Choice C: Producer surplus falls by $19
micro.Choice D: Total surplus falls by $7
micro.Correct Answer: D — Total surplus falls by $7
micro.Feedback: Replacing a higher-value recipient with a lower-value recipient reduces total willingness to pay by the difference, while production cost is unchanged.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: Four buyers value permits at $28, $22, $16, and $10. At a price of $16, who is marginal?
micro.Choice A: The buyer with willingness to pay of $16
micro.Choice B: The $28 buyer
micro.Choice C: The $10 buyer
micro.Choice D: All four buyers

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: Four sellers have costs of $5, $9, $13, and $18. At a price of $13, who is marginal?
micro.Choice A: The $5 seller
micro.Choice B: The seller with a cost of $13
micro.Choice C: The $18 seller
micro.Choice D: All sellers below $18
micro.Correct Answer: B — The seller with a cost of $13

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: A buyer values a service at $40 and seller cost is $24. What gain is available?
micro.Feedback: Buyer value minus seller cost is $16.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: A buyer values a service at $18 and seller cost is $23. Which conclusion follows?
micro.Choice A: The exchange creates $5
micro.Choice B: The exchange creates $41
micro.Choice C: Any price from $18 to $23 is efficient
micro.Choice D: The exchange should not occur because it would reduce total surplus by $5
micro.Correct Answer: D — The exchange should not occur because it would reduce total surplus by $5
micro.Feedback: Cost exceeds value by $5.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: Why is output below the efficient quantity inefficient?
micro.Choice A: Every seller has negative surplus

micro.Choice C: Some units valued above cost are not traded
micro.Choice D: Consumer and producer surplus must be equal

micro.Choice C: Producer surplus must be zero
micro.Choice D: Some units cost more than buyers value them

micro.Choice A: Require a fourth unit without any value/cost evidence because more trades always raise total surplus.

micro.Choice C: Allow only the first two units: it removes a third-unit loss of $4 while retaining positive gains of $20 and $6.
micro.Choice D: Keep all three because payments from buyers necessarily cover social opportunity costs.
micro.Correct Answer: C — Allow only the first two units: it removes a third-unit loss of $4 while retaining positive gains of $20 and $6.
micro.Feedback: The three marginal gains are $20, $6 and −$4. Efficiency retains positive-gain trades and rejects the negative one rather than maximizing quantity alone.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: Four trades have marginal gains $18, $9, $2 and −$4. Policy A allows the efficient trades; Policy B requires all four. Both transfer $10 from sellers to buyers and use $3 of administration. Which net-surplus comparison follows?
micro.Choice A: A yields $36 and B $32; include the transfer as an extra social benefit.
micro.Choice B: A yields $26 and B $22; the common transfer cancels and the forced fourth trade accounts for the $4 difference.
micro.Choice C: Both yield $26 because administration and distribution are identical.
micro.Choice D: A yields $16 and B $12; subtract the transfer as a resource cost.
micro.Correct Answer: B — A yields $26 and B $22; the common transfer cancels and the forced fourth trade accounts for the $4 difference.
micro.Feedback: The efficient first three gains sum to $29. A uses $3, leaving $26. B also includes the −$4 trade, leaving $22 after administration.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.3 — Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
micro.Question: A policy keeps the goods and buyer allocation unchanged, saves $12 in production resources, but requires $5 of new search effort. It also transfers $20 from buyers to sellers. What is the total-surplus change?
micro.Choice A: A $27 increase: add the transfer to the net resource saving.
micro.Choice B: A $13 decrease: subtract the transfer from the net resource saving.
micro.Choice C: A $12 increase: search effort has no resource value.
micro.Choice D: A $7 increase: count the $12 saving and $5 search cost, while the $20 transfer cancels.
micro.Correct Answer: D — A $7 increase: count the $12 saving and $5 search cost, while the $20 transfer cancels.
micro.Feedback: The unchanged allocation preserves gross buyer value. Net resource use falls $12−$5=$7. The $20 payment affects the split of gains rather than their total.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: A price change moves $12 from consumers to producers with quantity fixed. What occurred?
micro.Choice A: A $24 deadweight loss
micro.Choice B: A $12 total-surplus gain
micro.Choice C: A transfer, not a $12 deadweight loss
micro.Choice D: Elimination of producer surplus
micro.Correct Answer: C — A transfer, not a $12 deadweight loss
micro.Feedback: With quantity unchanged, the $12 shift from consumers to producers is a transfer of surplus rather than a $12 deadweight loss.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: A learner treats consumer surplus and producer surplus as competing measures and keeps only the larger one. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
micro.Choice A: Only consumer surplus counts toward efficiency
micro.Choice B: Total surplus adds both buyer and seller surplus
micro.Choice C: Total surplus always equals the larger side
micro.Choice D: Producer surplus replaces consumer surplus at equilibrium
micro.Correct Answer: B — Total surplus adds both buyer and seller surplus
micro.Feedback: The efficiency measure combines gains on both sides of the market.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: A learner says any voluntary trade creates gains even when seller cost exceeds buyer value. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
micro.Choice A: A trade creates positive total gains only when buyer value is at least seller cost
micro.Choice B: Voluntary exchange always creates positive measured surplus regardless of values
micro.Choice C: Seller cost is irrelevant to gains from trade
micro.Choice D: Buyer value matters only after the trade occurs
micro.Correct Answer: A — A trade creates positive total gains only when buyer value is at least seller cost
micro.Feedback: The buyer-seller value gap determines whether the exchange adds surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: Demand rises, raising price and quantity. What should surplus analysis examine?
micro.Choice A: Only the price rise
micro.Choice B: Only firm revenue
micro.Choice C: Whether scarcity disappears
micro.Choice D: How new buyer value and expanded exchanges change CS, PS, and total surplus
micro.Correct Answer: D — How new buyer value and expanded exchanges change CS, PS, and total surplus
micro.Feedback: A demand increase changes buyer willingness to pay, equilibrium price, and quantity, so surplus analysis should track the resulting changes in consumer, producer, and total surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: Supply falls, raising price and lowering quantity. What should surplus analysis examine?
micro.Choice A: Higher marginal costs, redistributed surplus, and lost gains
micro.Choice B: Only ownership
micro.Choice C: Only buyer count
micro.Choice D: Whether demand becomes vertical
micro.Correct Answer: A — Higher marginal costs, redistributed surplus, and lost gains
micro.Feedback: A decrease in supply reflects higher marginal costs, raises price, reduces quantity, redistributes surplus, and can eliminate mutually beneficial trades.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: A price change along unchanged demand and supply curves should be analyzed first by asking:
micro.Choice A: Whether every buyer pays a different price
micro.Choice B: How consumer surplus, producer surplus, and quantity traded change
micro.Choice C: Whether the graph axes should be reversed
micro.Choice D: Whether total surplus equals total revenue
micro.Correct Answer: B — How consumer surplus, producer surplus, and quantity traded change
micro.Feedback: A price change should be evaluated by tracking consumer surplus, producer surplus, and quantity traded so transfers can be separated from changes in total surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: Why can flatter demand change the size of a consumer-surplus response?
micro.Choice A: Consumer surplus disappears
micro.Choice B: Supply becomes fixed
micro.Choice C: Quantity responds more, affecting continuing and entering or exiting buyers
micro.Choice D: Price stops mattering
micro.Correct Answer: C — Quantity responds more, affecting continuing and entering or exiting buyers
micro.Feedback: With flatter demand, quantity demanded responds more to a price change, so the number of continuing and entering or exiting buyers changes more and affects the size of the consumer-surplus change.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: Why can steeper supply change the size of a producer-surplus response?
micro.Choice A: Producer surplus equals revenue
micro.Choice B: Demand disappears
micro.Choice C: All sellers have equal cost
micro.Choice D: Quantity responds less, changing seller participation and area
micro.Correct Answer: D — Quantity responds less, changing seller participation and area
micro.Feedback: With steeper supply, quantity supplied responds less to a price change, changing seller participation and the size of the producer-surplus response.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: A market graph shows consumer surplus of $45 and producer surplus of $35. There are no external effects. What is total surplus?
micro.Feedback: Add the two gains: 45+35=$80. Revenue is not an additional surplus component.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: How does opportunity cost enter gains-from-exchange analysis?
micro.Choice A: Only buyer income determines whether trade creates gains
micro.Choice B: Gains exist whenever price is positive
micro.Choice C: Seller willingness to accept reflects the value of resources given up
micro.Choice D: Opportunity cost is excluded from producer decisions
micro.Correct Answer: C — Seller willingness to accept reflects the value of resources given up
micro.Feedback: Exchange gains compare buyer value with seller opportunity cost.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: A policy reduces buyer surplus from $50 to $38 and raises seller surplus from $30 to $42, with no other effects. What happens to total surplus?
micro.Choice A: It falls by $12.
micro.Choice B: It stays at $80.
micro.Choice C: It rises by $12.
micro.Choice D: It falls by $24.
micro.Correct Answer: B — It stays at $80.
micro.Feedback: The $12 reduction for buyers exactly matches the $12 gain for sellers; 38+42=50+30=80.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: Why does comparative advantage ultimately matter for gains from exchange?
micro.Choice A: Specialization can create additional mutually beneficial trades and larger total gains
micro.Choice B: Comparative advantage guarantees equal surplus for everyone
micro.Choice C: It eliminates opportunity cost
micro.Choice D: It makes all world prices identical
micro.Correct Answer: A — Specialization can create additional mutually beneficial trades and larger total gains
micro.Feedback: Comparative advantage expands the potential gains available from exchange.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: Total surplus measures the combined gains received by:
micro.Choice A: Sellers only
micro.Choice B: Government only
micro.Choice C: Buyers and sellers
micro.Choice D: Buyers only
micro.Correct Answer: C — Buyers and sellers
micro.Feedback: Total surplus is the sum of consumer and producer surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: A market creates $40 of gains for buyers and $35 of gains for sellers. Which welfare measure combines both sets of gains?
micro.Choice A: Total revenue
micro.Choice B: Total surplus
micro.Choice C: Consumer surplus
micro.Choice D: Producer surplus
micro.Correct Answer: B — Total surplus
micro.Feedback: Total surplus combines the gains received by buyers and sellers.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: A trade creates $12 of consumer surplus and $9 of producer surplus. The gain from that trade is:
micro.Feedback: The total gain from exchange is the sum of the buyer’s and seller’s surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: A voluntary trade is mutually beneficial when:
micro.Choice A: The seller’s willingness to accept exceeds the buyer’s willingness to pay
micro.Choice B: The market price is zero
micro.Choice C: Consumer surplus must equal producer surplus
micro.Choice D: The buyer’s willingness to pay is at least as high as the seller’s willingness to accept
micro.Correct Answer: D — The buyer’s willingness to pay is at least as high as the seller’s willingness to accept
micro.Feedback: A trade can create gains when the buyer values the unit at least as much as the seller’s opportunity cost.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: If a transaction creates no consumer surplus but $6 of producer surplus, total surplus from that transaction is:
micro.Choice B: Cannot be positive unless both sides receive surplus
micro.Feedback: Total surplus adds the gains of both sides; one side may receive all of the measured surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: Which statement about total surplus is correct?
micro.Choice A: It ignores all gains from voluntary exchange
micro.Choice B: It can rise even if one side receives a smaller share of the gains
micro.Choice C: It rises only when consumer and producer surplus rise by identical amounts
micro.Choice D: It is the same thing as total revenue
micro.Correct Answer: B — It can rise even if one side receives a smaller share of the gains
micro.Feedback: Efficiency concerns the size of total gains, not whether those gains are split evenly.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: If a mutually beneficial trade is prevented, the unrealized gain is best described as:
micro.Choice A: Lost total surplus
micro.Choice B: A transfer from buyer to seller
micro.Choice C: Higher total revenue
micro.Choice D: Producer surplus that still exists
micro.Correct Answer: A — Lost total surplus
micro.Feedback: Preventing a beneficial trade destroys the buyer-seller gain that would otherwise be created.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: Consumer surplus falls by $8 while producer surplus rises by $8 and no trades are lost. Total surplus:
micro.Choice A: Falls by $16
micro.Choice B: Rises by $16
micro.Choice C: Must become zero
micro.Choice D: Does not change
micro.Correct Answer: D — Does not change
micro.Feedback: An equal transfer between buyers and sellers changes distribution but not the combined surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: After the price of event admissions falls to $15, one additional buyer with willingness to pay $25 enters and one additional seller with cost $10 can supply the unit. What is the gain from this additional trade?
micro.Feedback: The gain from an additional trade is the buyer’s willingness to pay minus the seller’s cost, not either side’s individual surplus alone.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: After the price of equipment rentals falls to $12, one additional buyer with willingness to pay $20 enters and one additional seller with cost $8 can supply the unit. What is the gain from this additional trade?
micro.Feedback: The gain from an additional trade is the buyer’s willingness to pay minus the seller’s cost, not either side’s individual surplus alone.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: After the price of market boxes falls to $17, one additional buyer with willingness to pay $32 enters and one additional seller with cost $10 can supply the unit. What is the gain from this additional trade?
micro.Feedback: The gain from an additional trade is the buyer’s willingness to pay minus the seller’s cost, not either side’s individual surplus alone.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: After the price of clinic slots falls to $28, one additional buyer with willingness to pay $34 enters and one additional seller with cost $25 can supply the unit. What is the gain from this additional trade?
micro.Feedback: The gain from an additional trade is the buyer’s willingness to pay minus the seller’s cost, not either side’s individual surplus alone.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: If price rises while the same units continue to trade, what usually happens?
micro.Choice A: Some consumer surplus is transferred to producers
micro.Choice B: Total surplus must rise
micro.Choice C: Producer surplus falls
micro.Choice D: All consumer surplus becomes deadweight loss
micro.Correct Answer: A — Some consumer surplus is transferred to producers
micro.Feedback: With unchanged trades, price redistributes surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: If price falls while the same units continue to trade, what usually happens?
micro.Choice A: Total surplus must fall
micro.Choice B: Some producer surplus is transferred to consumers
micro.Choice C: Consumer surplus falls
micro.Choice D: All producer surplus becomes deadweight loss
micro.Correct Answer: B — Some producer surplus is transferred to consumers
micro.Feedback: With unchanged trades, price redistributes surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: Consumer surplus rises from $80 to $95 while producer surplus falls from $60 to $40. Total surplus:
micro.Choice A: Rises by $15
micro.Choice B: Falls by $20
micro.Choice C: Is unchanged
micro.Choice D: Falls by $5
micro.Correct Answer: D — Falls by $5
micro.Feedback: Total changes from $140 to $135.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: A market change raises consumer surplus by $18 and lowers producer surplus by $10. What happens to total surplus?
micro.Choice A: It is unchanged
micro.Choice B: It rises by $28
micro.Choice C: It rises by $8
micro.Choice D: It falls by $28
micro.Correct Answer: C — It rises by $8
micro.Feedback: The net change in total surplus is +$18 - $10 = +$8.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: A buyer values a unit at $70, a seller’s willingness to accept is $52, and they trade at $60. What is total surplus from the trade?
micro.Feedback: Consumer surplus is $10 and producer surplus is $8; their sum equals the $18 gain from exchange.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: Two possible trades have WTP/WTA pairs of $50/$32 and $40/$38. If both trades occur, what is total gain from exchange?
micro.Feedback: The gains are $18 and $2, totaling $20.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: A rule transfers $15 of surplus from consumers to producers but also prevents trades worth $6 in total gains. What is the net change in total surplus?
micro.Choice A: An increase of $9
micro.Choice B: An increase of $15
micro.Choice C: No change because transfers never matter
micro.Choice D: A decrease of $6
micro.Correct Answer: D — A decrease of $6
micro.Feedback: The $15 transfer changes distribution only; the prevented trades destroy $6 of total surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: A buyer values a good at $50 and the seller's cost is $20. At a market price of $23, which statement is correct?
micro.Choice A: Total surplus $30; buyer receives $3; seller receives $27.
micro.Choice B: Total surplus $50; buyer receives $27; seller receives $23.
micro.Choice C: Total surplus $23; buyer receives $27; seller receives $-4.
micro.Choice D: Total surplus $30; buyer receives $27; seller receives $3.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Total surplus $30; buyer receives $27; seller receives $3.
micro.Feedback: Total surplus is $50−$20=$30. The buyer receives $50−$23=$27, and the seller receives $23−$20=$3; the two shares add to $30.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Output is limited to 6 units. What is true about units 7 and 8?
micro.Choice A: Their cost exceeds value, so omitting them raises surplus
micro.Choice B: Their marginal value exceeds marginal cost, so omitting them loses $4 of total surplus
micro.Choice C: They transfer $4 from producers to consumers
micro.Choice D: No loss can be measured
micro.Correct Answer: B — Their marginal value exceeds marginal cost, so omitting them loses $4 of total surplus
micro.Feedback: Between Q=6 and Q=8, demand lies above supply; the missing triangle is $4.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Output is pushed to 10 units. What is true about units 9 and 10?
micro.Choice A: Their value exceeds cost, so they add $4
micro.Choice B: They transfer $4 from consumers to producers
micro.Choice C: Their marginal cost exceeds value, so producing them destroys $4 of total surplus
micro.Choice D: More output is always efficient
micro.Correct Answer: C — Their marginal cost exceeds value, so producing them destroys $4 of total surplus
micro.Feedback: Between Q=8 and Q=10, supply lies above demand; the excess-cost triangle is $4.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: A price change raises producer surplus by $30 and lowers consumer surplus by $30, with no quantity change. Total surplus:
micro.Choice A: Rises by $30
micro.Choice B: Falls by $30
micro.Choice C: Falls by $60
micro.Choice D: Is unchanged
micro.Correct Answer: D — Is unchanged
micro.Feedback: The equal gain and loss are a transfer.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: A restriction raises producer surplus by $24 and lowers consumer surplus by $39. The change in total surplus is:
micro.Choice A: A decrease of $15
micro.Choice B: An increase of $24
micro.Choice C: A decrease of $39
micro.Choice D: No change
micro.Correct Answer: A — A decrease of $15
micro.Feedback: Add +$24 and -$39.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: A price rise causes one low-value buyer to leave and one high-cost seller to enter. Why can total surplus change?
micro.Choice A: Any price rise raises total surplus
micro.Choice B: Surplus stops existing
micro.Choice C: The set of exchanges changes, so the effect is not only a transfer
micro.Choice D: The outcome becomes equitable
micro.Correct Answer: C — The set of exchanges changes, so the effect is not only a transfer
micro.Feedback: Participation changes can create or destroy gains.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Demand shifts from D1 to D2. Which statement is correct?
micro.Choice A: Producer surplus falls to zero
micro.Choice B: Total surplus stays $64
micro.Choice C: Quantity remains 8
micro.Choice D: Consumer surplus, producer surplus, and total surplus all rise; total surplus becomes $100
micro.Correct Answer: D — Consumer surplus, producer surplus, and total surplus all rise; total surplus becomes $100
micro.Feedback: The new equilibrium has two $50 surplus triangles.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Supply shifts from S1 to S2. Which statement is correct?
micro.Choice A: Consumer surplus, producer surplus, and total surplus all fall; total surplus becomes $36
micro.Choice B: Consumer surplus rises because price rises
micro.Choice C: Producer surplus rises because price rises
micro.Choice D: Total surplus stays $64
micro.Correct Answer: A — Consumer surplus, producer surplus, and total surplus all fall; total surplus becomes $36
micro.Feedback: Higher marginal cost reduces quantity and both surplus areas.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: A buyer values a good at $35 and the seller's cost is $11. If the market price rises from $20 to $26, what changes?
micro.Choice A: Consumer surplus falls $6, producer surplus rises $6, and total surplus stays $24
micro.Choice B: Consumer and total surplus both fall $6
micro.Choice C: Producer and total surplus both rise $6
micro.Choice D: Both sides gain $6
micro.Correct Answer: A — Consumer surplus falls $6, producer surplus rises $6, and total surplus stays $24
micro.Feedback: Price redistributes the fixed value-cost gain.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: Before a restriction, consumer surplus is $45 and producer surplus is $35. The restriction prevents exchanges with combined gains of $12 and has no other effects. What is total surplus afterward?
micro.Feedback: Initial total surplus is $45 + $35 = $80. The prevented beneficial exchanges remove $12, leaving $68. The question specifies that the reported CS and PS precede the restriction.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. How much total surplus is lost by producing from Q = 8 through Q = 10?
micro.Feedback: The inefficient triangular region has base 2 and height 4, so the lost total surplus is $4.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: The price of event admissions falls from $24 to $15, and exactly 40 units continue to trade between the same buyers and sellers. Holding quantity and participants fixed, what happens to surplus?
micro.Choice A: Consumer surplus rises by $360, producer surplus falls by $360, and total surplus is unchanged
micro.Choice B: Consumer surplus rises by $360 and total surplus rises by $360
micro.Choice C: Producer surplus falls by $360 and total surplus falls by $360
micro.Choice D: Both consumer and producer surplus rise by $360
micro.Correct Answer: A — Consumer surplus rises by $360, producer surplus falls by $360, and total surplus is unchanged
micro.Feedback: With the same trades still occurring, the price change transfers surplus dollar for dollar from sellers to buyers; it does not change total surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: A classmate says the lower price for event admissions must increase total surplus because buyers pay less. Which correction is strongest?
micro.Choice A: A lower price always lowers total surplus because sellers receive less
micro.Choice B: Total surplus depends only on the posted price, not the traded quantity
micro.Choice C: A lower price redistributes surplus; total surplus rises only if additional beneficial trades occur
micro.Choice D: Consumer surplus and total surplus are the same measure
micro.Correct Answer: C — A lower price redistributes surplus; total surplus rises only if additional beneficial trades occur
micro.Feedback: Price changes and quantity changes must be separated. A pure transfer changes distribution, while new beneficial trades change total surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: The price of equipment rentals falls from $18 to $12, and exactly 30 units continue to trade between the same buyers and sellers. Holding quantity and participants fixed, what happens to surplus?
micro.Choice A: Consumer surplus rises by $180 and total surplus rises by $180
micro.Choice B: Producer surplus falls by $180 and total surplus falls by $180
micro.Choice C: Both consumer and producer surplus rise by $180
micro.Choice D: Consumer surplus rises by $180, producer surplus falls by $180, and total surplus is unchanged
micro.Correct Answer: D — Consumer surplus rises by $180, producer surplus falls by $180, and total surplus is unchanged
micro.Feedback: With the same trades still occurring, the price change transfers surplus dollar for dollar from sellers to buyers; it does not change total surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: The price of market boxes falls from $22 to $17, and exactly 50 units continue to trade between the same buyers and sellers. Holding quantity and participants fixed, what happens to surplus?
micro.Choice A: Consumer surplus rises by $250 and total surplus rises by $250
micro.Choice B: Producer surplus falls by $250 and total surplus falls by $250
micro.Choice C: Consumer surplus rises by $250, producer surplus falls by $250, and total surplus is unchanged
micro.Choice D: Both consumer and producer surplus rise by $250
micro.Correct Answer: C — Consumer surplus rises by $250, producer surplus falls by $250, and total surplus is unchanged
micro.Feedback: With the same trades still occurring, the price change transfers surplus dollar for dollar from sellers to buyers; it does not change total surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: The price of clinic slots falls from $35 to $28, and exactly 20 units continue to trade between the same buyers and sellers. Holding quantity and participants fixed, what happens to surplus?
micro.Choice A: Consumer surplus rises by $140 and total surplus rises by $140
micro.Choice B: Consumer surplus rises by $140, producer surplus falls by $140, and total surplus is unchanged
micro.Choice C: Producer surplus falls by $140 and total surplus falls by $140
micro.Choice D: Both consumer and producer surplus rise by $140
micro.Correct Answer: B — Consumer surplus rises by $140, producer surplus falls by $140, and total surplus is unchanged
micro.Feedback: With the same trades still occurring, the price change transfers surplus dollar for dollar from sellers to buyers; it does not change total surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: A price rises by $5. Ten existing buyers continue, and two buyers leave. Why can the consumer-surplus loss exceed $50?
micro.Choice A: Continuing buyers lose $50, and departing buyers lose their former surplus too
micro.Choice B: Multiply $5 by every potential buyer
micro.Choice C: Producer surplus is subtracted twice
micro.Choice D: Total surplus always falls by $5
micro.Correct Answer: A — Continuing buyers lose $50, and departing buyers lose their former surplus too
micro.Feedback: The loss includes the rectangle on continuing units plus lost surplus of exiting buyers.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: A price falls by $4. Eight sellers continue, and two high-cost sellers exit. Why can the producer-surplus loss exceed $32?
micro.Choice A: Multiply $4 by all firms
micro.Choice B: Continuing sellers lose $32, and exiting sellers lose their former surplus too
micro.Choice C: Consumer surplus is counted as a seller loss
micro.Choice D: Total surplus always falls by $4
micro.Correct Answer: B — Continuing sellers lose $32, and exiting sellers lose their former surplus too
micro.Feedback: The loss includes continuing and exiting sellers.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Repealing the restriction at the marked quantity left of E restores E and transfers $9 from producers to consumers on continuing trades. Assuming efficient allocation and no other effects, which total-surplus change and explanation are correct?
micro.Choice A: Total surplus rises $8; the $9 transfer changes its distribution.
micro.Choice B: Total surplus rises $4; the $9 transfer changes its distribution.
micro.Choice C: Total surplus rises $4; the $9 transfer is an additional resource gain.
micro.Choice D: Total surplus rises $8; the $9 transfer is an additional resource gain.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Total surplus rises $4; the $9 transfer changes its distribution.
micro.Feedback: The omitted triangle has width 8−6 = 2 and height 12−8 = $4, so restoring trade creates $4. The $9 transfer increases CS and decreases PS equally, leaving their sum unchanged apart from the recovered trades.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: The price of equipment rentals falls by $6 on 30 continuing rentals, transferring $180 to renters. Two additional rentals create gains of $9 and $4. What is the total-surplus change?
micro.Choice A: Total surplus rises by $193
micro.Choice B: Total surplus rises by $13
micro.Choice C: Total surplus rises by $180
micro.Choice D: Total surplus falls by $167
micro.Correct Answer: B — Total surplus rises by $13
micro.Feedback: The $180 is a transfer on continuing rentals. Only the $9 and $4 gains from new rentals raise total surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: The price of market boxes falls, but quantity and the identities of buyers and sellers do not change. Which evidence would be needed to claim an efficiency gain?
micro.Choice A: Evidence that additional value-above-cost trades now occur
micro.Choice B: Evidence that buyers pay less
micro.Choice C: Evidence that sellers receive less
micro.Choice D: Evidence that consumer surplus rises
micro.Correct Answer: A — Evidence that additional value-above-cost trades now occur
micro.Feedback: A price transfer alone does not raise total surplus. New beneficial trades would.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: The price of clinic slots falls by $7 on 20 continuing appointments. One new appointment has buyer value $42 and provider cost $31. What happens to total surplus?
micro.Choice A: It rises by $151
micro.Choice B: It rises by $140
micro.Choice C: It falls by $129
micro.Choice D: It rises by $11
micro.Correct Answer: D — It rises by $11
micro.Feedback: The $140 on continuing appointments is transferred surplus. The new appointment adds $42 − $31 = $11.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Starting at the marked quantity through A and B, what change in total surplus would expanding output to E cause, and why?
micro.Choice A: A $8 gain: it adds trades whose value exceeds their resource cost.
micro.Choice B: A $4 gain: it adds trades whose value exceeds their resource cost.
micro.Choice C: A $4 gain: the change transfers that amount from sellers to buyers.
micro.Choice D: An $8 gain: the change transfers that amount from sellers to buyers.
micro.Correct Answer: B — A $4 gain: it adds trades whose value exceeds their resource cost.
micro.Feedback: The restricted quantity is 6 and E is at 8. At Q = 6, value is $12 and cost $8. The surplus gain is 0.5 × 2 × 4 = $4. A transfer by itself does not change total surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Starting at the marked quantity through A and B, what change in total surplus would reducing output to E cause, and why?
micro.Choice A: A $8 gain: it avoids producing units whose cost exceeds their value.
micro.Choice B: A $4 gain: the change transfers that amount from sellers to buyers.
micro.Choice C: A $4 gain: it avoids producing units whose cost exceeds their value.
micro.Choice D: An $8 gain: the change transfers that amount from sellers to buyers.
micro.Correct Answer: C — A $4 gain: it avoids producing units whose cost exceeds their value.
micro.Feedback: The restricted quantity is 10 and E is at 8. At Q = 10, cost is $12 and value $8. The surplus gain is 0.5 × 2 × 4 = $4. A transfer by itself does not change total surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. As price moves from P1 to P2, a report counts only the gain on units already traded. Which full consumer-surplus change and explanation correct the omission?
micro.Choice A: An increase of $32, including $28 on original units and $4 on additional units.
micro.Choice B: An increase of $40; it consists entirely of the gain on original units.
micro.Choice C: An increase of $32; it consists entirely of the gain on original units.
micro.Choice D: An increase of $40, including $32 on original units and $8 on additional units.
micro.Correct Answer: D — An increase of $40, including $32 on original units and $8 on additional units.
micro.Feedback: Demand intercept $20; (Q, P) changes from (8, 12) to (12, 8). Consumer surplus rises from $32 to $72, an increase of $40. The price change on existing units contributes $32; the additional-unit triangle contributes $8.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. As price moves from P1 to P2, a report counts only the gain on units already traded. Which full producer-surplus change and explanation correct the omission?
micro.Choice A: An increase of $32, including $24 on original units and $8 on additional units.
micro.Choice B: An increase of $24, including $20 on original units and $4 on additional units.
micro.Choice C: An increase of $32; it consists entirely of the gain on original units.
micro.Choice D: An increase of $24; it consists entirely of the gain on original units.
micro.Correct Answer: A — An increase of $32, including $24 on original units and $8 on additional units.
micro.Feedback: Supply intercept $2; (Q, P) changes from (6, 8) to (10, 12). Producer surplus rises from $18 to $50, an increase of $32. The price change on existing units contributes $24; the additional-unit triangle contributes $8.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. By how much does consumer surplus rise when price falls from P1 to P2?
micro.Feedback: Consumer surplus rises from $32 to $72.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. By how much does producer surplus rise when price rises from P1 to P2?
micro.Feedback: Producer surplus rises from $18 to $50.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: A price change transfers $20 from buyers to sellers with no quantity change. Total surplus:
micro.Choice A: Does not change
micro.Choice B: Rises $20
micro.Choice C: Falls $20
micro.Choice D: Falls $40
micro.Correct Answer: A — Does not change
micro.Feedback: With quantity unchanged, the $20 shift from buyers to sellers is only a transfer of surplus. Total surplus does not change.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: Consumer surplus rises $18 and producer surplus falls $27. Total surplus:
micro.Choice A: Rises $18
micro.Choice B: Falls $9
micro.Choice C: Falls $27
micro.Choice D: Is unchanged
micro.Correct Answer: B — Falls $9
micro.Feedback: The net change in total surplus is $18 - $27 = -$9, so total surplus falls by $9.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Output is 6 rather than 8. Total-surplus loss is:
micro.Feedback: Stopping at Q = 6 leaves $4 of mutually beneficial gains unrealized relative to the efficient quantity Q = 8.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. At the overproduction outcome, how much total surplus is lost relative to the efficient quantity?
micro.Feedback: Producing beyond the efficient quantity creates $4 of deadweight loss because marginal cost exceeds marginal willingness to pay on the extra units.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. After demand shifts from D1 to D2, total surplus is:
micro.Feedback: After demand shifts to D2, the consumer- and producer-surplus regions sum to $100 of total surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. After supply shifts from S1 to S2, total surplus is:
micro.Feedback: After supply shifts to S2, the higher marginal costs reduce the efficient quantity and leave $36 of total surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: A buyer values a unit at $52 and seller cost is $18. Price falls from $45 to $25 with the same buyer and seller. A second proposed cut to $15 would leave the seller unwilling to produce and there is no subsidy. Which comparison is right?
micro.Choice A: Both cuts only redistribute surplus because price can never affect whether a trade occurs.
micro.Choice B: The first cut redistributes a $34 gain; the second prevents the trade and loses that $34 gain.
micro.Choice C: The first cut creates $20 of new total surplus; the second creates another $10 even without production.
micro.Choice D: The first cut loses $20 of total surplus; the second restores it by lowering consumer spending.
micro.Correct Answer: B — The first cut redistributes a $34 gain; the second prevents the trade and loses that $34 gain.
micro.Feedback: At $25 the seller still covers the $18 cost, so total gains remain $34. At $15 production is not privately viable without other support; if the trade disappears, its positive gain is lost.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.4 — Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
micro.Question: A trade creates $24 of total gains. A price rule shifts $7 from seller to buyer without changing the trade, while enforcing the rule consumes $5 of real resources. Which result separates distribution from the resource effect?
micro.Choice A: The $7 changes the split, while net total surplus falls from $24 to $19 because of enforcement.
micro.Choice B: Net total surplus rises to $26 because the $7 transfer is a benefit and enforcement costs $5.
micro.Choice C: Net total surplus falls to $12 because both the transfer and enforcement are social losses.
micro.Choice D: Net total surplus stays $24 because both enforcement and the payment rule are transfers.
micro.Correct Answer: A — The $7 changes the split, while net total surplus falls from $24 to $19 because of enforcement.
micro.Feedback: The buyer’s $7 gain is the seller’s $7 loss, canceling in the total. Enforcement uses $5 of resources, leaving $19.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: A student says efficiency requires equal gains. Which statement corrects this mistake?
micro.Choice A: Efficiency maximizes total surplus; equal division is equity
micro.Choice B: Efficiency requires zero PS
micro.Choice C: Equity means largest quantity
micro.Choice D: Efficiency and equity are identical
micro.Correct Answer: A — Efficiency maximizes total surplus; equal division is equity
micro.Feedback: Efficiency concerns maximizing total surplus. Whether the gains are divided equally is an equity question.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: A market maximizes total surplus but distributes gains unevenly. Accurate statement?
micro.Choice A: It cannot be efficient
micro.Choice B: It can be efficient while raising equity concerns
micro.Choice C: It has zero total surplus
micro.Choice D: WTP equals need
micro.Correct Answer: B — It can be efficient while raising equity concerns
micro.Feedback: An allocation can maximize total surplus and still distribute those gains unevenly, so efficiency does not settle equity.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: A learner says the market outcome with the highest consumer-plus-producer surplus must also be the fairest. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
micro.Choice A: Highest total surplus guarantees equal distribution
micro.Choice B: Fairness is measured only by producer surplus
micro.Choice C: Equity is identical to willingness to pay
micro.Choice D: Efficiency and equity are separate criteria
micro.Correct Answer: D — Efficiency and equity are separate criteria
micro.Feedback: Total surplus measures efficiency, while fairness requires additional value judgments.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: Why should willingness to pay not be a complete measure of need?
micro.Choice A: WTP is always zero
micro.Choice B: Budget constraints can limit the dollar amount expressed
micro.Choice C: Demand has no preference information
micro.Choice D: Only sellers face constraints
micro.Correct Answer: B — Budget constraints can limit the dollar amount expressed
micro.Feedback: Willingness to pay can be constrained by income and purchasing power, so it is not a complete measure of need or fairness.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: Why can producer surplus differ from profit?
micro.Choice A: Profit excludes fixed costs
micro.Choice B: Producer surplus excludes revenue
micro.Choice C: Consumer surplus determines fixed cost
micro.Choice D: Producer surplus may cover variable costs but not fixed costs
micro.Correct Answer: D — Producer surplus may cover variable costs but not fixed costs
micro.Feedback: Producer surplus is revenue above variable opportunity cost, but profit must also account for fixed costs, so the two measures can differ.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: How does surplus analysis connect to normative economics?
micro.Choice A: Any efficient market is normatively fair
micro.Choice B: Equity is determined mechanically by the equilibrium price
micro.Choice C: Efficiency can be measured with surplus, but equity judgments require values about distribution
micro.Choice D: Normative economics eliminates the need to measure efficiency
micro.Correct Answer: C — Efficiency can be measured with surplus, but equity judgments require values about distribution
micro.Feedback: The efficiency result is positive analysis; deciding whether the distribution is fair adds a normative criterion.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: Why might an externality require extending ordinary consumer-plus-producer surplus analysis?
micro.Choice A: Externalities matter only for income distribution
micro.Choice B: Third-party costs or benefits are not fully captured by private surplus
micro.Choice C: Externalities automatically raise consumer surplus
micro.Choice D: Producer surplus already includes every social cost
micro.Correct Answer: B — Third-party costs or benefits are not fully captured by private surplus
micro.Feedback: Social surplus must include effects on people outside the transaction.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: Which statement correctly distinguishes efficiency from equity?
micro.Choice A: Both require equal surplus
micro.Choice B: Efficiency concerns only price
micro.Choice C: Equity always maximizes total surplus
micro.Choice D: Efficiency concerns total surplus; equity concerns distribution
micro.Correct Answer: D — Efficiency concerns total surplus; equity concerns distribution
micro.Feedback: Efficiency and equity answer different questions.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: A market can maximize total surplus and still be criticized because:
micro.Choice A: The gains may be distributed very unevenly
micro.Choice B: Every efficient market has zero consumer surplus
micro.Choice C: Efficiency requires identical incomes
micro.Choice D: Producer surplus must exceed consumer surplus
micro.Correct Answer: A — The gains may be distributed very unevenly
micro.Feedback: Efficiency does not settle fairness.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: Which statement is an efficiency claim?
micro.Choice A: Every buyer should receive the same quantity
micro.Choice B: Low-income buyers deserve priority
micro.Choice C: Gains should be split equally
micro.Choice D: Reassigning production to lower-cost sellers raises total surplus
micro.Correct Answer: D — Reassigning production to lower-cost sellers raises total surplus
micro.Feedback: Lower cost is an efficiency argument.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: Which statement is an equity claim?
micro.Choice A: A larger share of gains should go to lower-income households
micro.Choice B: Highest-value buyers should receive units
micro.Choice C: Lowest-cost sellers should produce
micro.Choice D: Exchange continues while value exceeds cost
micro.Correct Answer: A — A larger share of gains should go to lower-income households
micro.Feedback: Distribution across income groups is equity.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: A market outcome can maximize total surplus but still raise concerns about:
micro.Choice A: Whether buyers have preferences
micro.Choice B: Equity or distribution
micro.Choice C: Whether any exchange occurred
micro.Choice D: Whether prices exist
micro.Correct Answer: B — Equity or distribution
micro.Feedback: Efficiency and equity are different criteria; maximizing total gains does not determine how those gains are shared.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: Why can willingness to pay understate the importance of a good to a low-income consumer?
micro.Choice A: Ability to pay can constrain the amount the consumer can bid
micro.Choice B: Willingness to pay never reflects preferences
micro.Choice C: Low-income consumers always have zero consumer surplus
micro.Choice D: Market prices automatically correct income differences
micro.Correct Answer: A — Ability to pay can constrain the amount the consumer can bid
micro.Feedback: Observed willingness to pay reflects both preferences and purchasing power.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: Surplus analysis by itself does not determine whether an outcome is:
micro.Choice A: Efficient in the total-surplus sense
micro.Choice B: Based on voluntary exchange
micro.Choice C: Associated with gains from trade
micro.Choice D: Fair
micro.Correct Answer: D — Fair
micro.Feedback: Total surplus is an efficiency measure, not a complete theory of fairness.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: A policy transfers $100 of surplus from producers to consumers while all the same units continue to trade. What can surplus analysis establish?
micro.Choice A: Distribution changes; total surplus increases by $100
micro.Choice B: Distribution changes; total surplus decreases by $100
micro.Choice C: Distribution changes; total surplus is unchanged by the transfer
micro.Choice D: Distribution is unchanged; both sides gain $100 in surplus
micro.Correct Answer: C — Distribution changes; total surplus is unchanged by the transfer
micro.Feedback: A pure transfer changes who receives surplus, not its total.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: Why can producer surplus differ from accounting profit even when both are measured in dollars?
micro.Choice A: Profit ignores revenue
micro.Choice B: Producer surplus subtracts all fixed costs twice
micro.Choice C: Consumer surplus determines accounting profit
micro.Choice D: Producer surplus can include amounts used to cover fixed costs
micro.Correct Answer: D — Producer surplus can include amounts used to cover fixed costs
micro.Feedback: Producer surplus is revenue above variable or marginal cost; accounting profit also subtracts fixed cost.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: Which statement correctly links the demand curve, supply curve, and total surplus?
micro.Choice A: Demand represents consumer surplus directly and supply represents producer surplus directly
