micro.Choice B: Demand represents marginal willingness to pay, supply represents marginal cost, and total surplus sums value minus cost over traded units
micro.Choice C: Price alone determines total surplus regardless of quantity
micro.Choice D: Efficiency requires the two surplus regions to be equal
micro.Correct Answer: B — Demand represents marginal willingness to pay, supply represents marginal cost, and total surplus sums value minus cost over traded units
micro.Feedback: Demand represents marginal willingness to pay and supply represents marginal cost. Total surplus sums the value-minus-cost gains created by the units that trade.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: Why can willingness to pay be an incomplete measure of social importance?
micro.Choice A: It can reflect ability to pay as well as value
micro.Choice B: It is identical for every buyer
micro.Choice C: It measures seller cost
micro.Choice D: It cannot be expressed in money
micro.Correct Answer: A — It can reflect ability to pay as well as value
micro.Feedback: Income can constrain dollar willingness to pay.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: Why is producer surplus not always accounting profit?
micro.Choice A: Revenue is excluded from producer surplus
micro.Choice B: Fixed costs may reduce profit even when producer surplus is positive
micro.Choice C: Producer surplus counts buyer value
micro.Choice D: Profit ignores costs
micro.Correct Answer: B — Fixed costs may reduce profit even when producer surplus is positive
micro.Feedback: Profit also subtracts fixed costs.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: Two policies generate the same total surplus, but one gives nearly all gains to high-income buyers while the other spreads gains broadly. Surplus analysis alone can conclude that:
micro.Choice A: The second policy is necessarily more efficient because gains are spread broadly
micro.Choice B: Neither policy can be compared in any way
micro.Choice C: They are equally efficient by total surplus, but it cannot settle the equity comparison
micro.Choice D: The first policy is necessarily better because buyers have more income
micro.Correct Answer: C — They are equally efficient by total surplus, but it cannot settle the equity comparison
micro.Feedback: Equal total surplus means equal measured efficiency, while distribution requires an additional normative criterion.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: Suppose a market creates pollution costs not borne by buyers or sellers. Why can ordinary consumer-plus-producer surplus overstate social surplus?
micro.Choice A: It automatically subtracts taxes from surplus
micro.Choice B: It omits part of the external cost
micro.Choice C: It counts willingness to pay twice
micro.Choice D: It treats every seller as identical
micro.Correct Answer: B — It omits part of the external cost
micro.Feedback: Private surplus measures can miss costs imposed on third parties.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: A rich buyer outbids a poor buyer for a scarce medicine even though the poor buyer’s health benefit would be larger. What limitation does this illustrate?
micro.Choice A: Willingness to pay depends partly on ability to pay
micro.Choice B: Total surplus can never be calculated
micro.Choice C: Producer surplus is always negative in health markets
micro.Choice D: Efficiency and scarcity are unrelated
micro.Correct Answer: A — Willingness to pay depends partly on ability to pay
micro.Feedback: Dollar willingness to pay is constrained by income and may not measure all dimensions of social value.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: An economist reports that Policy A yields $500 of total surplus and Policy B yields $470. What can be concluded without additional value judgments?
micro.Choice A: Policy A is necessarily fairer
micro.Choice B: Policy B must have more consumer surplus
micro.Choice C: Policy A must make every person better off
micro.Choice D: Policy A has higher measured efficiency under the surplus criterion
micro.Correct Answer: D — Policy A has higher measured efficiency under the surplus criterion
micro.Feedback: The total-surplus comparison speaks to measured efficiency, not fairness or individual gains.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: Which claim is strongest about an efficient market outcome?
micro.Choice A: It guarantees equal surplus
micro.Choice B: It maximizes measured total surplus under the assumptions but need not be the fairest distribution
micro.Choice C: It proves willingness to pay measures need perfectly
micro.Choice D: It eliminates every market failure
micro.Correct Answer: B — It maximizes measured total surplus under the assumptions but need not be the fairest distribution
micro.Feedback: Efficiency is conditional and distribution-neutral.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: A low-income buyer can pay $12 for a vital item while a wealthy buyer will pay $40 for convenience. What limitation appears?
micro.Choice A: Consumer surplus cannot use dollars
micro.Choice B: Producer surplus is always negative
micro.Choice C: Willingness to pay can reflect ability to pay, not only need
micro.Choice D: Demand measures seller cost
micro.Correct Answer: C — Willingness to pay can reflect ability to pay, not only need
micro.Feedback: Income can constrain measured willingness to pay.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: A scarce good is allocated to the buyers with the highest willingness to pay. Which limitation of surplus analysis should be kept in mind?
micro.Choice A: Surplus analysis cannot compare alternative allocations.
micro.Choice B: Market prices eliminate all distributional concerns.
micro.Choice C: Willingness to pay measures need independently of income.
micro.Choice D: Willingness to pay can reflect ability to pay as well as preferences, so measured efficiency does not by itself settle fairness.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Willingness to pay can reflect ability to pay as well as preferences, so measured efficiency does not by itself settle fairness.
micro.Feedback: Willingness to pay is measured in dollars and can be constrained by purchasing power. A surplus-maximizing allocation can therefore be efficient without resolving questions of need or fairness.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: Market A has consumer surplus of $80 and producer surplus of $70, but production creates $40 of external damage. Market B has consumer surplus of $75 and producer surplus of $65 with no external damage. Which statement is strongest?
micro.Choice A: B is necessarily unfair because producer surplus is lower
micro.Choice B: External damage should be ignored because it is outside buyer and seller surplus
micro.Choice C: Private surplus favors A, but including the stated external damage gives B higher social surplus
micro.Choice D: A is necessarily socially efficient because its private surplus is larger
micro.Correct Answer: C — Private surplus favors A, but including the stated external damage gives B higher social surplus
micro.Feedback: A has $150 private surplus but $110 after the external cost; B has $140 and no stated external cost.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: Two allocations produce the same total surplus. Allocation X gives almost all gains to one household; Allocation Y distributes gains across many households. Which conclusion is economically defensible from surplus data alone?
micro.Choice A: The allocations cannot have equal total surplus if distributions differ
micro.Choice B: They are tied on measured efficiency, while choosing between distributions requires an equity judgment
micro.Choice C: X is more efficient because concentrated gains are larger per person
micro.Choice D: Y is more efficient because more people receive gains
micro.Correct Answer: B — They are tied on measured efficiency, while choosing between distributions requires an equity judgment
micro.Feedback: Total surplus measures the size of the pie; distribution of the pie is a separate criterion.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: Why is “a higher price always benefits society” wrong?
micro.Choice A: A higher price can redistribute surplus and alter quantity; total surplus is what matters
micro.Choice B: Higher prices always reduce producer surplus
micro.Choice C: Higher prices erase willingness to pay
micro.Choice D: Society benefits only when consumer surplus is zero
micro.Correct Answer: A — A higher price can redistribute surplus and alter quantity; total surplus is what matters
micro.Feedback: Price alone does not determine efficiency.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: Why is “a lower price always benefits society” wrong?
micro.Choice A: Lower prices always raise cost
micro.Choice B: Consumers may gain while producers lose, and quantity effects can change total gains
micro.Choice C: Lower prices erase demand
micro.Choice D: Society benefits only when producer surplus is zero
micro.Correct Answer: B — Consumers may gain while producers lose, and quantity effects can change total gains
micro.Feedback: Count both sides and quantity effects.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: A seller has marginal cost $12 per unit and a $1,000 fixed license fee. Why can producer surplus be positive while profit is negative?
micro.Choice A: Producer surplus may cover variable costs but not the fixed fee
micro.Choice B: Producer surplus subtracts the fee twice
micro.Choice C: Profit ignores fixed costs
micro.Choice D: Marginal cost includes all fixed costs
micro.Correct Answer: A — Producer surplus may cover variable costs but not the fixed fee
micro.Feedback: Fixed cost can exceed producer surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: A scarce good goes to the highest bidders. What concern can remain despite maximum measured surplus?
micro.Choice A: The allocation cannot be efficient
micro.Choice B: Producer surplus must be negative
micro.Choice C: Low-income buyers may have high need but limited dollar willingness to pay
micro.Choice D: Price cannot be observed
micro.Correct Answer: C — Low-income buyers may have high need but limited dollar willingness to pay
micro.Feedback: Measured willingness to pay does not fully resolve need or fairness.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: A market allocation maximizes total surplus, but most surplus goes to a small group. Which conclusion follows?
micro.Choice A: The allocation can be efficient without being equitable
micro.Choice B: The allocation cannot be efficient unless surplus is equal
micro.Choice C: Efficiency proves the distribution is morally best
micro.Choice D: Total surplus must be zero
micro.Correct Answer: A — The allocation can be efficient without being equitable
micro.Feedback: Efficiency concerns the size of the combined gains; equity concerns their distribution.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: Two buyers have the same need, but one has greater ability to pay and therefore higher measured willingness to pay. What limitation does this reveal?
micro.Choice A: Willingness to pay is always an objective measure of need
micro.Choice B: Willingness to pay can reflect purchasing power as well as preference
micro.Choice C: Consumer surplus cannot be calculated in dollars
micro.Choice D: Producer surplus must therefore be negative
micro.Correct Answer: B — Willingness to pay can reflect purchasing power as well as preference
micro.Feedback: Dollar willingness to pay need not rank need independently of income.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: Why is maximizing total surplus not a complete social objective by itself?
micro.Choice A: It cannot compare buyer values with seller costs
micro.Choice B: It requires consumer and producer surplus to be equal
micro.Choice C: It always recommends zero production
micro.Choice D: It does not specify how gains are distributed or weigh other values
micro.Correct Answer: D — It does not specify how gains are distributed or weigh other values
micro.Feedback: Total surplus is an efficiency measure, not a full ethical framework.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: A market reaches the quantity where marginal willingness to pay equals marginal cost. Which claim goes too far?
micro.Choice A: The outcome is therefore fair to every participant
micro.Choice B: No additional unit has positive net gain
micro.Choice C: Reducing output would miss beneficial trades
micro.Choice D: Increasing output would add units whose cost exceeds value
micro.Correct Answer: A — The outcome is therefore fair to every participant
micro.Feedback: The marginal condition supports efficiency, not universal fairness.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: A buyer values a unit at $50 but cannot afford the market price. What does standard surplus analysis record?
micro.Choice A: The buyer automatically receives $50 of consumer surplus
micro.Choice B: The buyer’s measured willingness to pay must represent both willingness and ability to pay
micro.Choice C: The market price becomes zero
micro.Choice D: The seller must treat need as payment
micro.Correct Answer: B — The buyer’s measured willingness to pay must represent both willingness and ability to pay
micro.Feedback: Measured willingness to pay is constrained by ability and willingness to pay.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: Two allocations create the same total surplus but distribute it differently. What does efficiency analysis alone say?
micro.Choice A: The more equal allocation is automatically less efficient
micro.Choice B: The producer-favored allocation is automatically efficient
micro.Choice C: It cannot choose between them without an additional distributional criterion
micro.Choice D: Both allocations must have identical prices
micro.Correct Answer: C — It cannot choose between them without an additional distributional criterion
micro.Feedback: Equal total surplus means efficiency alone does not resolve the distributional choice.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. A proposal would redistribute surplus solely because the current buyer and seller shares differ. Which calculation and efficiency judgment evaluate that justification?
micro.Choice A: CS = $48 and PS = $24; unequal shares alone do not establish inefficiency.
micro.Choice B: CS = $64 and PS = $32; unequal shares alone establish inefficiency.
micro.Choice C: CS = $48 and PS = $24; unequal shares alone establish inefficiency.
micro.Choice D: CS = $64 and PS = $32; unequal shares alone do not establish inefficiency.
micro.Correct Answer: D — CS = $64 and PS = $32; unequal shares alone do not establish inefficiency.
micro.Feedback: E gives Q = 8 and P = $14. CS = 0.5 × 8 × 16 = $64; PS = 0.5 × 8 × 8 = $32. Marginal value equals marginal cost at E, so unequal shares do not establish an efficiency problem. Redistribution may reflect an equity objective.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. A student uses the surplus shares at E to argue that every efficient market must divide its gains equally. Which reading and judgment are correct?
micro.Choice A: CS and PS are each $25; their equality here does not establish a general efficiency requirement.
micro.Choice B: CS and PS are each $20; their equality here does not establish a general efficiency requirement.
micro.Choice C: CS and PS are each $25; their equality here establishes a general efficiency requirement.
micro.Choice D: CS and PS are each $20; their equality here establishes a general efficiency requirement.
micro.Correct Answer: A — CS and PS are each $25; their equality here does not establish a general efficiency requirement.
micro.Feedback: At E, Q = 5 and P = $14, with demand and supply intercepts $24 and $4. Each area is 0.5 × 5 × 10 = $25. Efficiency depends on marginal value equaling marginal cost, not equal surplus shares.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: Allocation A creates $500 of total surplus split $450 to buyers and $50 to sellers. Allocation B creates $480 split evenly. Which conclusion can efficiency analysis support by itself?
micro.Choice A: Allocation B is more efficient because it is equal
micro.Choice B: Allocation A is more efficient, but efficiency alone cannot settle whether its distribution is preferable
micro.Choice C: Allocation A is both more efficient and necessarily fairer
micro.Choice D: The allocations are equally efficient because both sides gain
micro.Correct Answer: B — Allocation A is more efficient, but efficiency alone cannot settle whether its distribution is preferable
micro.Feedback: Efficiency ranks the totals, while distribution requires a separate equity judgment.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: Two patients value the only available treatment at $100 and $70. Production cost is $20, but the $70 patient has greater measured medical need and less income. Policy A sells to the highest bidder; Policy B assigns it to the higher-need patient at the same production cost. Which comparison separates measured surplus from equity?
micro.Choice A: A creates $100 and B $70 because production cost is a transfer; the higher need cannot enter any policy judgment.
micro.Choice B: Both create $80 because medical need and willingness to pay must give the same ranking.
micro.Choice C: A creates $80 of willingness-to-pay surplus and B $50; favoring B can reflect an equity judgment rather than a claim that B maximizes this dollar measure.
micro.Choice D: B creates more measured willingness-to-pay surplus because greater need necessarily implies higher dollar willingness to pay.
micro.Correct Answer: C — A creates $80 of willingness-to-pay surplus and B $50; favoring B can reflect an equity judgment rather than a claim that B maximizes this dollar measure.
micro.Feedback: Subtract the common $20 resource cost from each willingness to pay: $80 versus $50. Income can affect willingness to pay, so a different equity criterion may support the lower-dollar-surplus allocation.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: An efficient trade creates $40 of total surplus, split $2 to the buyer and $38 to the seller. A proposed transfer gives $15 from seller to buyer without changing production or use, but implementing it consumes $3 of real resources. Which assessment is correct?
micro.Choice A: The split becomes $17/$23 and total surplus rises to $55 because the buyer receives more.
micro.Choice B: The transfer itself destroys $15 of surplus, so net total surplus is $22.
micro.Choice C: Total surplus remains $40 after administration because every policy payment is a transfer.
micro.Choice D: Before administration the split becomes $17/$23 with the same $40 total; after the $3 resource cost, net total surplus is $37, so distribution improves by a chosen equity criterion at a measured efficiency cost.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Before administration the split becomes $17/$23 with the same $40 total; after the $3 resource cost, net total surplus is $37, so distribution improves by a chosen equity criterion at a measured efficiency cost.
micro.Feedback: The $15 payment redistributes the existing $40. The $3 administrative resource use reduces net total surplus to $37. Whether the distributional change is worth that cost requires an equity judgment.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: A rule reallocates $200 of existing surplus from one group to another without changing any trade. A revision would also restore one excluded trade with buyer value $50 and seller cost $32 but require $6 of real resources. What incremental effect comes from the revision beyond the original redistribution?
micro.Choice A: It adds $12 of total surplus: $50−$32−$6; the $200 transfer is not counted again.
micro.Choice B: It adds $212 of total surplus because both the transfer and restored trade create new resources.
micro.Choice C: It reduces surplus by $188 because the transfer is a loss that offsets the new trade.
micro.Choice D: It adds $18 because the $6 real implementation cost does not affect surplus.
micro.Correct Answer: A — It adds $12 of total surplus: $50−$32−$6; the $200 transfer is not counted again.
micro.Feedback: The original transfer leaves total surplus unchanged. The extra trade creates $18 of gains and uses $6 of implementation resources, adding $12 beyond that redistribution.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: A price change reduces consumer surplus by $160 and raises producer surplus by $160, with quantity and participants unchanged. A related restriction then prevents a trade worth $25 to its buyer and costing $18 to supply. A student reports a $160 social loss. Which correction is complete?
micro.Choice A: The total social loss is $167 because both the transfer and foregone trade reduce total surplus.
micro.Choice B: The total social loss is $25 because the excluded seller’s cost is irrelevant.
micro.Choice C: There is no social loss because the initial consumer and producer changes offset every later effect.
micro.Choice D: The price change is a transfer; the excluded trade creates a separate $7 social loss.
micro.Correct Answer: D — The price change is a transfer; the excluded trade creates a separate $7 social loss.
micro.Feedback: The −$160 and +$160 cancel. Preventing a trade with value $25 and cost $18 sacrifices $7 of gains, a distinct quantity effect.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: Efficiency and equity differ because:
micro.Choice A: Both require equal surplus
micro.Choice B: Efficiency concerns only price
micro.Choice C: Efficiency concerns total gains; equity concerns distribution
micro.Choice D: Equity concerns only quantity
micro.Correct Answer: C — Efficiency concerns total gains; equity concerns distribution
micro.Feedback: They answer different questions.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: Why is producer surplus not automatically profit?
micro.Choice A: Fixed costs may still need to be subtracted
micro.Choice B: Producer surplus excludes revenue
micro.Choice C: Profit ignores costs
micro.Choice D: Consumer surplus determines profit
micro.Correct Answer: A — Fixed costs may still need to be subtracted
micro.Feedback: Producer surplus does not subtract fixed costs, while economic profit does. Fixed costs can therefore make profit smaller than producer surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: Why can willingness to pay be an imperfect guide to fairness?
micro.Choice A: It is identical across buyers
micro.Choice B: It can depend on ability to pay
micro.Choice C: It measures production cost
micro.Choice D: It cannot be observed
micro.Correct Answer: B — It can depend on ability to pay
micro.Feedback: Willingness to pay can reflect ability to pay as well as preferences, so a surplus-maximizing allocation does not by itself resolve questions of fairness.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: A competitive market allocates goods to the highest willingness to pay, but some users impose uncompensated disposal harm and low-income households receive few goods. Which assessment separates efficiency assumptions from equity?
micro.Choice A: Competition rules out unpriced harm, while unequal access alone proves that all trades reduce total surplus.
micro.Choice B: Correcting harm necessarily gives every household an equal share, so no separate equity judgment remains.
micro.Choice C: The highest willingness-to-pay rule establishes social efficiency regardless of external harm and income differences.
micro.Choice D: Unpriced harm can invalidate the private surplus benchmark; unequal access raises a distinct equity question even after that harm is corrected.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Unpriced harm can invalidate the private surplus benchmark; unequal access raises a distinct equity question even after that harm is corrected.
micro.Feedback: Private willingness to pay and cost omit the external harm. Internalizing that cost targets efficiency, while deciding whether the resulting distribution is fair is a separate judgment.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.5 — Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
micro.Question: Two policies preserve the same trades and total production cost. Policy A leaves $90 of surplus with sellers and $10 with buyers. Policy B leaves $60 with sellers and $40 with buyers. Which conclusion follows from surplus accounting alone?
micro.Choice A: B yields more total surplus because buyers receive a larger share.
micro.Choice B: A yields more total surplus because sellers receive a larger share.
micro.Choice C: Both yield $100 of total surplus; choosing between distributions requires an equity criterion beyond the sum.
micro.Choice D: Neither can be efficient because the two groups do not receive equal shares.
micro.Correct Answer: C — Both yield $100 of total surplus; choosing between distributions requires an equity criterion beyond the sum.
micro.Feedback: The totals are 90+10=100 and 60+40=100. With production and allocation fixed, the difference is distribution rather than measured total efficiency.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A policy transfers $20 to consumers and prevents $6 of gains. Total-surplus loss?
micro.Feedback: The $20 transfer changes who receives surplus, while the $6 of prevented gains is the actual loss in total surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A learner counts a $20 transfer from consumers to producers as a $20 deadweight loss. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
micro.Choice A: A transfer changes who receives surplus; deadweight loss requires gains that disappear
micro.Choice B: Every transfer is a deadweight loss
micro.Choice C: Producer gains are excluded from total surplus
micro.Choice D: Consumer losses never affect welfare
micro.Correct Answer: A — A transfer changes who receives surplus; deadweight loss requires gains that disappear
micro.Feedback: Efficiency loss comes from destroyed gains, not from a dollar merely moving between groups.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A tax creates a wedge between the buyer price and seller receipt. What surplus question comes first?
micro.Choice A: How the wedge changes consumer surplus, producer surplus, revenue, and completed trades
micro.Choice B: Whether all buyers have identical income
micro.Choice C: Whether fixed cost equals market price
micro.Choice D: Whether the demand curve becomes vertical
micro.Correct Answer: A — How the wedge changes consumer surplus, producer surplus, revenue, and completed trades
micro.Feedback: The first task is to account for the two effective prices, tax revenue, and any lost trades.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A tax reduces consumer surplus by $50 and producer surplus by $30, while government collects $60. With no other effects, what is the deadweight loss?
micro.Feedback: Total surplus changes by −50−30+60=−20. Government revenue is included as a transfer, not counted again as a loss.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: Before a tax total surplus is $120. Afterward CS is $45, PS $35, and revenue $28. Loss?
micro.Feedback: Post-tax total surplus is $45 + $35 + $28 = $108. Compared with the original $120, total surplus falls by $12.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A tax reduces quantity traded from 10 units to 8. Which measure captures the resulting loss of gains from trade?
micro.Choice A: The form of the tax law
micro.Choice B: The relationship between the tax rate and tax revenue
micro.Choice C: The best overall tax policy for the country
micro.Choice D: The reduction in total surplus when quantity falls from 10 to 8
micro.Correct Answer: D — The reduction in total surplus when quantity falls from 10 to 8
micro.Feedback: The surplus question is how much total surplus disappears when the tax reduces quantity from 10 units to 8.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A binding price ceiling helps some buyers and hurts sellers. What else must a surplus analysis examine?
micro.Choice A: Whether fewer beneficial trades occur
micro.Choice B: Whether consumer and producer surplus become equal
micro.Choice C: Whether every buyer gains
micro.Choice D: Whether the legal price equals total surplus
micro.Correct Answer: A — Whether fewer beneficial trades occur
micro.Feedback: Distributional gains and losses are incomplete without checking quantity and unrealized gains from exchange.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: Why can a floor raise seller surplus yet reduce total surplus?
micro.Choice A: Higher prices destroy all PS
micro.Choice B: It can prevent value-above-cost exchanges for units no longer sold
micro.Choice C: CS is not in total surplus
micro.Choice D: Quantity becomes infinite
micro.Correct Answer: B — It can prevent value-above-cost exchanges for units no longer sold
micro.Feedback: A price floor can raise producer surplus for some sellers while preventing trades for which buyer value exceeds seller cost, reducing total surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A ceiling transfers $16 from sellers to buyers and prevents trades worth $5 in combined surplus. Enforcement uses $2 of real resources. What is the total-surplus change?
micro.Feedback: The transfer cancels across buyers and sellers. Lost gains and real enforcement costs reduce total surplus by 5+2=$7.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: When evaluating how a price control affects total surplus, which change should an economist examine?
micro.Choice A: How every method of rationing works
micro.Choice B: The city’s long-run construction plans
micro.Choice C: The best way to enforce the control
micro.Choice D: Whether the control changes the number of mutually beneficial exchanges
micro.Correct Answer: D — Whether the control changes the number of mutually beneficial exchanges
micro.Feedback: Surplus analysis asks whether the price control changes the number of mutually beneficial exchanges and therefore changes total surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: If a policy merely transfers $10 of surplus from buyers to sellers and no trades change, total surplus:
micro.Choice A: Must equal zero
micro.Choice B: Is unchanged
micro.Choice C: Falls by $10
micro.Choice D: Rises by $10
micro.Correct Answer: B — Is unchanged
micro.Feedback: A pure transfer changes who receives surplus, not the combined amount.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: If a policy prevents mutually beneficial trades, total surplus generally:
micro.Choice A: Falls
micro.Choice B: Rises
micro.Choice C: Is guaranteed to stay constant
micro.Choice D: Becomes equal to government revenue
micro.Correct Answer: A — Falls
micro.Feedback: Prevented beneficial exchanges eliminate gains that would otherwise exist.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: When market price rises and the same units continue to trade, consumer surplus generally:
micro.Choice A: Rises
micro.Choice B: Must stay constant
micro.Choice C: Becomes producer surplus one-for-one in every case
micro.Choice D: Falls
micro.Correct Answer: D — Falls
micro.Feedback: Buyers pay more for the same units, reducing their value-minus-price gains.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: When market price rises and the same units continue to trade, producer surplus generally:
micro.Choice A: Must stay constant
micro.Choice B: Becomes consumer surplus
micro.Choice C: Rises
micro.Choice D: Falls
micro.Correct Answer: C — Rises
micro.Feedback: Sellers receive a higher price relative to their willingness to accept.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A policy causes some trades with positive gains to disappear. The value of those lost gains is:
micro.Choice A: Guaranteed government revenue
micro.Choice B: A loss in total surplus
micro.Choice C: A pure transfer between buyers and sellers
micro.Choice D: Additional consumer surplus
micro.Correct Answer: B — A loss in total surplus
micro.Feedback: Lost mutually beneficial trades reduce the combined gains available in the market.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: Consumer surplus falls $60, producer surplus rises $44, and revenue rises $10. Total surplus:
micro.Choice A: Falls by $16
micro.Choice B: Rises by $54
micro.Choice C: Falls by $6
micro.Choice D: Falls by $26
micro.Correct Answer: C — Falls by $6
micro.Feedback: Include government revenue once: −$60 + $44 + $10 = −$6. The $10 received by government is a transfer of surplus, not another loss. Total surplus falls by $6.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: Consumer surplus rises $35, producer surplus falls $50, and administration uses $4 of resources. Total surplus:
micro.Choice A: Falls by $15
micro.Choice B: Rises by $31
micro.Choice C: Falls by $54
micro.Choice D: Falls by $19
micro.Correct Answer: D — Falls by $19
micro.Feedback: The consumer and producer changes sum to $35 − $50 = −$15. Administration consumes another $4 of real resources, so the total change is −$19. A resource cost reduces surplus; it is not just a payment transferred to another participant.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A tax leaves $40 consumer surplus, $30 producer surplus, and $20 revenue. Without it, total surplus is $100. Deadweight loss is:
micro.Feedback: Post-tax total is $90.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: Why is the entire producer loss from a price ceiling not necessarily deadweight loss?
micro.Choice A: Producer losses never matter
micro.Choice B: All consumer gains are deadweight loss
micro.Choice C: Deadweight loss equals price
micro.Choice D: Part may be transferred to buyers; only net destroyed gains are deadweight loss
micro.Correct Answer: D — Part may be transferred to buyers; only net destroyed gains are deadweight loss
micro.Feedback: Separate transfers from destroyed gains.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: Consumer surplus falls by $70 and producer surplus falls by $50 after a tax, while tax revenue equals $100. What is the reduction in total surplus?
micro.Feedback: The $120 decline in private surplus includes $100 transferred as revenue, leaving a $20 reduction in total surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A $3 per-unit tax lowers private surplus by $45 and creates $36 in tax revenue. What happened to total surplus?
micro.Choice A: It fell by $45
micro.Choice B: It fell by $9
micro.Choice C: It rose by $36
micro.Choice D: It was unchanged
micro.Correct Answer: B — It fell by $9
micro.Feedback: The $45 private-surplus reduction includes a $36 transfer to tax revenue, leaving a $9 reduction in total surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A $4 per-unit tax creates a wedge between the buyer price and seller receipt. Which values are used to compute consumer and producer surplus?
micro.Choice A: Consumer surplus uses the buyer price; producer surplus uses the seller receipt
micro.Choice B: Both use the tax revenue
micro.Choice C: Both use the midpoint of the two prices
micro.Choice D: Consumer surplus uses seller receipt and producer surplus uses buyer price
micro.Correct Answer: A — Consumer surplus uses the buyer price; producer surplus uses the seller receipt
micro.Feedback: The two sides face different effective prices after the wedge.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A per-unit tax causes two previously beneficial trades not to occur. What part of the total-surplus change is not merely a transfer?
micro.Choice A: All tax revenue
micro.Choice B: The gains from those two trades that disappear
micro.Choice C: The entire reduction in consumer surplus
micro.Choice D: The entire reduction in producer surplus
micro.Correct Answer: B — The gains from those two trades that disappear
micro.Feedback: Tax revenue is transferred surplus; gains from trades that no longer occur are lost total surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: Why can a tax reduce total surplus even when the government keeps every dollar collected?
micro.Choice A: The wedge can prevent trades whose buyer value exceeded seller cost
micro.Choice B: Government revenue is excluded from every welfare calculation
micro.Choice C: The tax makes willingness to pay equal zero
micro.Choice D: The tax forces every seller to leave
micro.Correct Answer: A — The wedge can prevent trades whose buyer value exceeded seller cost
micro.Feedback: The efficiency loss comes from beneficial trades that no longer occur, not from revenue merely changing hands.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A binding price ceiling lowers the legal price, and the same quantity continues to reach the same buyers from the same sellers. What is the immediate surplus effect?
micro.Choice A: Consumer surplus and total surplus both rise by the same amount
micro.Choice B: Surplus transfers from producers to consumers while total surplus is unchanged
micro.Choice C: Producer surplus and total surplus both fall by the same amount
micro.Choice D: Both sides gain surplus
micro.Correct Answer: B — Surplus transfers from producers to consumers while total surplus is unchanged
micro.Feedback: With quantity and participants fixed, the lower price is a transfer.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A binding price floor raises the price and leaves quantity traded unchanged. What follows?
micro.Choice A: Total surplus rises because the price is higher
micro.Choice B: Total surplus falls by the entire consumer loss
micro.Choice C: Producer surplus and consumer surplus both rise
micro.Choice D: Some surplus transfers from consumers to producers, but total surplus is unchanged
micro.Correct Answer: D — Some surplus transfers from consumers to producers, but total surplus is unchanged
micro.Feedback: A price change alone redistributes surplus when the same trades occur.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A supply decrease reduces the efficient quantity. Why?
micro.Choice A: Higher marginal cost leaves fewer units with value above cost
micro.Choice B: Higher marginal cost lowers every buyer’s willingness to pay
micro.Choice C: Higher marginal cost makes every remaining trade create a loss
micro.Choice D: Higher marginal cost raises marginal benefit by the same amount
micro.Correct Answer: A — Higher marginal cost leaves fewer units with value above cost
micro.Feedback: When marginal cost rises, the positive-gain range of output shrinks.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A policy transfers $22 of surplus from consumers to producers and, separately, prevents trades worth $9 in total gains. Compared with the original market, total surplus changes by:
micro.Feedback: The $22 transfer changes distribution only; the separately lost trades reduce total surplus by $9.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A price change transfers $30 from consumers to producers and also reduces mutually beneficial trades by $12. What is the efficiency effect?
micro.Choice A: Total surplus rises by $18
micro.Choice B: Total surplus falls by $42
micro.Choice C: Total surplus is unchanged
micro.Choice D: Total surplus falls by $12
micro.Correct Answer: D — Total surplus falls by $12
micro.Feedback: The $30 is a transfer; only the $12 of lost gains reduces total surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A rule lowers consumer surplus by $25 and raises producer surplus by $19. If there are no other gains or losses, what happened to total surplus?
micro.Choice A: It rose by $6
micro.Choice B: It was unchanged
micro.Choice C: It fell by $6
micro.Choice D: It rose by $44
micro.Correct Answer: C — It fell by $6
micro.Feedback: Add the changes: -$25 + $19 = -$6.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A ceiling increases surplus for continuing buyers by $25, but buyers who lose access forfeit $5 of prior surplus. Producer surplus falls by $40. There are no search costs or other effects. What happens to total surplus?
micro.Choice A: It falls by $15
micro.Choice B: It rises by $20
micro.Choice C: It falls by $20
micro.Choice D: It falls by $70
micro.Correct Answer: C — It falls by $20
micro.Feedback: Count all consumers: their net change is +$25 − $5 = +$20. Adding the $40 producer loss gives a $20 total-surplus loss. Counting only successful buyers understates the loss.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A price ceiling transfers $18 from producers to consumers and prevents $7 of gains. Total surplus:
micro.Choice A: Rises by $18
micro.Choice B: Falls by $7
micro.Choice C: Falls by $25
micro.Choice D: Is unchanged
micro.Correct Answer: B — Falls by $7
micro.Feedback: The transfer cancels; the lost gains remain.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A tax sends $40 to government revenue and eliminates $9 of gains. Ignoring administration, total surplus:
micro.Choice A: Falls by $49
micro.Choice B: Rises by $40
micro.Choice C: Falls by $9
micro.Choice D: Is unchanged
micro.Correct Answer: C — Falls by $9
micro.Feedback: Revenue is a transfer; eliminated gains are a loss.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A tax reduces consumer surplus by $80 and producer surplus by $50 while raising $110 in revenue. Which accounting is correct?
micro.Choice A: It reduces total surplus by $130
micro.Choice B: It increases total surplus by $110
micro.Choice C: It only transfers surplus and causes no loss
micro.Choice D: The tax transfers $110 and reduces total surplus by $20
micro.Correct Answer: D — The tax transfers $110 and reduces total surplus by $20
micro.Feedback: The $130 private-surplus reduction includes $110 transferred as revenue and $20 that disappears.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A binding price floor causes unsold output. Why is unsold production not automatically producer surplus?
micro.Choice A: Producer surplus requires a price received for a unit that is actually sold
micro.Choice B: Producer surplus equals the posted price on every produced unit
micro.Choice C: Unsold units create consumer surplus
micro.Choice D: The supply curve is irrelevant once a floor exists
micro.Correct Answer: A — Producer surplus requires a price received for a unit that is actually sold
micro.Feedback: No sale means no revenue from that unit; a posted price does not create surplus by itself.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A market starts with CS of $180 and PS of $120. Tax A leaves CS of $110 and PS of $70 and raises $96. Tax B leaves CS of $100 and PS of $65 and raises $112. With no externalities or administrative costs, which tax preserves more total surplus?
micro.Choice A: Tax A by $15, because its private surplus is higher
micro.Choice B: Tax B by $16, equal to its extra revenue
micro.Choice C: Tax B by $1, even though private surplus is lower
micro.Choice D: They tie, because tax revenue is only a transfer
micro.Correct Answer: C — Tax B by $1, even though private surplus is lower
micro.Feedback: Include revenue once: A yields $110 + $70 + $96 = $276; B yields $100 + $65 + $112 = $277. Against the $300 baseline, the losses are $24 and $23. Lower private surplus alone does not rank efficiency.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A binding price ceiling reduces the quantity traded. Which missing transactions reduce total surplus?
micro.Choice A: Only transactions with buyer value below seller cost
micro.Choice B: All transactions completed below the ceiling
micro.Choice C: Transactions where buyer willingness to pay exceeded seller cost
micro.Choice D: Only transactions involving the marginal seller
micro.Correct Answer: C — Transactions where buyer willingness to pay exceeded seller cost
micro.Feedback: Lost beneficial trades are the source of reduced total surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A linear market has demand P = 28 − Q and supply P = 4 + Q. Demand then becomes P = 32 − Q. With supply unchanged, which statement correctly compares the two equilibria?
micro.Choice A: Price rises by $2, so CS falls by $24 and TS stays unchanged
micro.Choice B: Price rises by $2, while CS rises by $26 and TS rises by $52
micro.Choice C: Price rises by $4, while CS rises by $26 and TS rises by $26
micro.Choice D: Price rises by $2, while CS rises by $2 and TS rises by $4
micro.Correct Answer: B — Price rises by $2, while CS rises by $26 and TS rises by $52
micro.Feedback: Initially Q = 12 and P = $16, giving CS = PS = $72. After the demand change, Q = 14 and P = $18, giving CS = PS = $98. CS rises by $26 and TS by $52. Higher willingness to pay changes the surplus comparison even though the price rises.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: Demand is P = 27 − Q. Supply changes from P = 3 + Q to P = 7 + Q because production costs rise. Which comparison correctly separates producer surplus from price changes?
micro.Choice A: Price rises by $2, so PS rises by $20 and TS is unchanged
micro.Choice B: Price rises by $4, while PS falls by $22 and TS falls by $22
micro.Choice C: Price rises by $2, but PS falls by $22 and TS falls by $44
micro.Choice D: Price rises by $2, so PS rises by $24 and TS rises by $48
micro.Correct Answer: C — Price rises by $2, but PS falls by $22 and TS falls by $44
micro.Feedback: The original equilibrium is Q = 12, P = $15, with CS = PS = $72. After the cost increase, Q = 10 and P = $17, with CS = PS = $50. Thus PS falls $22 and TS falls $44. The higher selling price does not offset higher costs and fewer trades.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: Demand rises from P = 24 − Q to P = 28 − Q while supply remains P = 4 + Q. At the new efficient equilibrium, total surplus is $44 higher. How is this increase explained?
micro.Choice A: $44 from additional trades and nothing from the original units
micro.Choice B: $20 transferred from sellers and $24 from additional trades
micro.Choice C: $40 of additional spending and $4 of tax revenue
micro.Choice D: $40 of higher value on the original ten units and $4 from additional trades
micro.Correct Answer: D — $40 of higher value on the original ten units and $4 from additional trades
micro.Feedback: The original efficient quantity is 10 and the new quantity is 12. Willingness to pay rises $4 on each of the original ten units, adding $40. The two new units add a triangle of 0.5 × 2 × $4 = $4. A demand increase can raise gains on existing units as well as create new beneficial trades.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A rule changes the market price but not the set of completed trades. Which test prevents confusing redistribution with an efficiency change?
micro.Choice A: Check whether consumers paid a lower price
micro.Choice B: Check whether any units with positive value-minus-cost gains were added or lost
micro.Choice C: Check whether producers received a higher price
micro.Choice D: Check whether consumer and producer surplus are equal
micro.Correct Answer: B — Check whether any units with positive value-minus-cost gains were added or lost
micro.Feedback: Efficiency changes when the set of beneficial trades changes; price alone can merely redistribute surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A tax reduces consumer surplus by $140 and producer surplus by $90, generating $190 of revenue. Proposal A returns all revenue as lump-sum transfers with no administrative cost. Proposal B returns it but uses $15 of real resources. Which comparison is correct?
micro.Choice A: The original tax loses $40 of total surplus; A leaves that loss unchanged and B increases it to $55.
micro.Choice B: The original tax loses $230; either rebate restores all lost surplus because revenue is a social benefit twice.
micro.Choice C: The original tax loses $40; A eliminates the loss by redistributing revenue and B leaves only $15 of loss.
micro.Choice D: The original tax gains $190; B adds another $15 of surplus because administration is spending.
micro.Correct Answer: A — The original tax loses $40 of total surplus; A leaves that loss unchanged and B increases it to $55.
micro.Feedback: Initial total-surplus change is −140−90+190=−$40. Rebating a transfer does not recreate the lost trades. Real administrative costs add $15 to the loss.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A ceiling transfers $75 from continuing sellers to buyers but prevents trades worth $30 of gains. A proposed rationing lottery additionally sends one unit to a buyer valuing it at $18 instead of an otherwise served buyer valuing it at $28, with production unchanged. What is the combined total-surplus effect?
micro.Choice A: A $115 loss: add the $75 transfer, $30 prevented gains and $10 misallocation.
micro.Choice B: A $40 loss: $30 from prevented trades plus $10 from misallocation; the $75 transfer is not an additional social loss.
micro.Choice C: A $35 gain: the $75 transfer offsets $40 of real losses.
micro.Choice D: A $30 loss: any reassignment at unchanged quantity leaves total surplus unchanged.
micro.Correct Answer: B — A $40 loss: $30 from prevented trades plus $10 from misallocation; the $75 transfer is not an additional social loss.
micro.Feedback: Prevented trades lose $30. The reassigned unit loses $28−$18=$10 of use value with the same cost. The $75 changes distribution, so total lost surplus is $40.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A price floor transfers $60 from buyers to sellers and induces excess production with resource cost $25 above buyer value. A reform removes the excess production but preserves the $60 distributional transfer through a lump-sum payment costing $8 to administer. Compared with the floor, what changes?
micro.Choice A: Total surplus rises $77 because preserving the transfer adds a new $60 social benefit.
micro.Choice B: Total surplus falls $8 because reducing excess output cannot recover resource costs.
micro.Choice C: Total surplus rises $17; the same intended transfer remains, but eliminating $25 of waste uses $8 in administration.
micro.Choice D: Total surplus rises $25 because administrative resources are only a transfer.
micro.Correct Answer: C — Total surplus rises $17; the same intended transfer remains, but eliminating $25 of waste uses $8 in administration.
micro.Feedback: Relative to the floor, recover $25 of wasted resources and subtract $8 of administration, for +$17. Keeping the transfer does not add or subtract another $60 of total surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A tax collects $10 on each of 12 units after reducing trade from 15 units. The three lost trades would have generated gains of $8, $5, and $2. Which statement is correct?
micro.Choice A: Tax revenue is $150 and total surplus is $120 lower
micro.Choice B: Tax revenue is $120 and total surplus is unchanged
micro.Choice C: Tax revenue is $15 and total surplus is $120 lower
micro.Choice D: Tax revenue is $120 and total surplus is $15 lower because of the lost trades
micro.Correct Answer: D — Tax revenue is $120 and total surplus is $15 lower because of the lost trades
micro.Feedback: Revenue equals $10 times 12. Lost total surplus is the sum of gains on the three trades: $15.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A ceiling lowers the price by $6 on 20 units that still trade and eliminates two trades with gains of $9 and $4. What is the best accounting?
micro.Choice A: It transfers $120 on continuing trades and reduces total surplus by $13
micro.Choice B: It raises total surplus by $107
micro.Choice C: It reduces total surplus by $133
micro.Choice D: It transfers $13 and reduces total surplus by $120
micro.Correct Answer: A — It transfers $120 on continuing trades and reduces total surplus by $13
micro.Feedback: The price change transfers $6 × 20 = $120. The two lost trades reduce total surplus by $13.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: Consumer surplus falls $48, producer surplus rises $31, and revenue is $12. Total surplus:
micro.Choice A: Falls $5
micro.Choice B: Falls $17
micro.Choice C: Rises $43
micro.Choice D: Falls $29
micro.Correct Answer: A — Falls $5
micro.Feedback: The net change is -$48 + $31 + $12 = -$5, so total surplus falls by $5.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A price ceiling raises consumer surplus by a net $22 before search costs, reduces producer surplus by $34, and creates $3 of real search costs not included in either surplus figure. What is the change in total surplus?
micro.Choice A: Falls $12
micro.Choice B: Falls $15
micro.Choice C: Rises $19
micro.Choice D: Falls $37
micro.Correct Answer: B — Falls $15
micro.Feedback: Add the net consumer-surplus change to the producer-surplus change and subtract the separately stated real search cost: $22−$34−$3=−$15. A transfer component alone would not measure the full consumer-surplus change.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A policy lowers producer surplus by $80, raises consumer surplus by $45 and generates $25 of government revenue. It uses no additional administrative resources. What is the social loss, and why is it not $80?
micro.Choice A: $80; producer-surplus losses are always identical to social losses.
micro.Choice B: $150; add every group’s change without signs.
micro.Choice C: $10; $70 of the producer loss appears as gains to consumers and government.
micro.Choice D: $0; any government revenue exactly offsets all private losses.
micro.Correct Answer: C — $10; $70 of the producer loss appears as gains to consumers and government.
micro.Feedback: Total-surplus change is −$80+$45+$25=−$10. Transfers to other groups explain why the loss to one group is not the total social loss.

micro.Learning Objective: CPS.6 — Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.
micro.Question: A policy raises consumer surplus by $90 and reduces producer surplus by $65, but requires a $40 government payment. With no other resource effects, which conclusion correctly counts taxpayers?
micro.Choice A: Net total surplus rises $25: ignore the government payment when adding private surplus.
micro.Choice B: Net total surplus rises $90 because the consumer gain alone measures the benefit.
micro.Choice C: Net total surplus falls $105 because consumer gains cannot count toward welfare.
micro.Choice D: Net total surplus falls $15: $90−$65−$40.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Net total surplus falls $15: $90−$65−$40.
micro.Feedback: Consumers, producers and government must be included consistently. The government payment is a cost to taxpayers: 90−65−40=−15. The net loss remains after internal transfers cancel.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.1 — Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.
micro.Question: A business owner says, “My time is free because I do not pay myself.” What correction is needed?
micro.Choice A: Owner time is a fixed cost of zero
micro.Choice B: Only taxes count as costs
micro.Choice C: The owner’s forgone alternative earnings are an implicit cost
micro.Choice D: The statement is correct
micro.Correct Answer: C — The owner’s forgone alternative earnings are an implicit cost
micro.Feedback: Owner-supplied resources still have opportunity costs.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.1 — Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.
micro.Question: Which cost belongs in economic cost but not recorded accounting cost?
micro.Choice A: Employee wages
micro.Choice B: Electricity payment
micro.Choice C: Purchased materials
micro.Choice D: Forgone rent on an owner-occupied building
micro.Correct Answer: D — Forgone rent on an owner-occupied building
micro.Feedback: Forgone rent is an implicit opportunity cost.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.1 — Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.
micro.Question: Accounting profit is $60,000 and implicit costs are $45,000. What is economic profit?
micro.Feedback: Economic profit subtracts implicit cost from accounting profit.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.1 — Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.
micro.Question: A firm earns zero economic profit. What has it covered?
micro.Choice A: Explicit costs only
micro.Choice B: Explicit and implicit costs, including normal profit
micro.Choice C: No owner compensation
micro.Choice D: Variable costs but not fixed costs
micro.Correct Answer: B — Explicit and implicit costs, including normal profit
micro.Feedback: Zero economic profit means all opportunity costs are covered.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.1 — Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.
micro.Question: A learner says, “If the owner did not write a check, the resource has no cost.” Which statement corrects this claim?
micro.Choice A: Only variable resources have economic costs
micro.Choice B: Every implicit cost must appear on an invoice
micro.Choice C: Opportunity cost matters only for consumers
micro.Choice D: Owner-supplied resources can have implicit opportunity costs even without a cash payment
micro.Correct Answer: D — Owner-supplied resources can have implicit opportunity costs even without a cash payment
micro.Feedback: Economic cost includes the value of the next-best use of owner-supplied resources.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.1 — Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.
micro.Question: A learner subtracts the owner’s forgone salary when calculating accounting profit. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
micro.Choice A: The forgone salary should be added to revenue
micro.Choice B: Accounting profit ignores explicit costs
micro.Choice C: Accounting profit subtracts explicit costs; the forgone salary is implicit
micro.Choice D: Accounting profit subtracts all opportunity costs
micro.Correct Answer: C — Accounting profit subtracts explicit costs; the forgone salary is implicit
micro.Feedback: Implicit costs matter for economic profit, not the accounting-profit calculation.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.1 — Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.
micro.Question: A learner says economic profit equals accounting profit plus implicit costs. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
micro.Choice A: Economic profit and accounting profit are always equal
micro.Choice B: Economic profit equals accounting profit minus implicit costs
micro.Choice C: Economic profit equals accounting profit plus explicit costs
micro.Choice D: Economic profit ignores owner opportunity costs
micro.Correct Answer: B — Economic profit equals accounting profit minus implicit costs
micro.Feedback: Implicit costs reduce economic profit relative to accounting profit.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.1 — Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.
micro.Question: A learner calls zero economic profit a “loss.” Which statement corrects this claim?
micro.Choice A: Zero economic profit means all explicit and implicit costs, including normal profit, are covered
micro.Choice B: Zero economic profit means revenue is zero
micro.Choice C: Zero economic profit means explicit costs exceed revenue
micro.Choice D: Zero economic profit excludes owner compensation
micro.Correct Answer: A — Zero economic profit means all explicit and implicit costs, including normal profit, are covered
micro.Feedback: Normal profit is included in economic cost, so zero economic profit can be a sustainable outcome.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.1 — Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.
micro.Question: A learner finds accounting profit of $50,000 and implicit cost of $70,000, then reports economic profit of $20,000. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
micro.Choice A: $20,000 is correct because profit cannot be negative
micro.Choice B: Economic profit is $120,000
micro.Choice C: Implicit cost should be ignored
micro.Choice D: Economic profit is −$20,000
micro.Correct Answer: D — Economic profit is −$20,000
micro.Feedback: Economic profit equals $50,000 − $70,000 = −$20,000.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.1 — Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.
micro.Question: A proprietor uses a personally owned storefront. How does opportunity cost enter production cost?
micro.Choice A: The building has no cost
micro.Choice B: Only depreciation counts
micro.Choice C: Forgone market rent is an implicit cost
micro.Choice D: Forgone rent is revenue
micro.Correct Answer: C — Forgone market rent is an implicit cost
micro.Feedback: Owner-supplied property has an opportunity cost.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.1 — Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.
micro.Question: An entrepreneur leaves a $70,000 job to run a firm. In economic-cost analysis, the $70,000 is:
micro.Choice A: An explicit wage payment
micro.Choice B: A sunk cost
micro.Choice C: Producer surplus
micro.Choice D: An implicit cost
micro.Correct Answer: D — An implicit cost
micro.Feedback: The forgone salary is the next-best alternative.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.1 — Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.
micro.Question: A firm has $90,000 revenue, $60,000 explicit costs and $20,000 forgone owner income. What is economic profit?
micro.Feedback: Economic profit subtracts explicit and implicit costs: 90,000−60,000−20,000=$10,000.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.1 — Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.
micro.Question: An owner earns $25,000 accounting profit and forgoes $25,000 in its best alternative use of time and capital. What does economic profit equal?
micro.Choice A: $25,000: forgone returns are ignored.
micro.Choice B: $0: the owner’s opportunity cost is covered.
micro.Choice C: −$25,000: the accounting return does not count.
micro.Choice D: $50,000: add the two returns.
micro.Correct Answer: B — $0: the owner’s opportunity cost is covered.
micro.Feedback: Economic profit is accounting profit minus implicit opportunity cost: 25,000−25,000=0.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.1 — Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.
micro.Question: Producer surplus differs from accounting profit partly because:
micro.Choice A: Producer surplus subtracts consumer surplus
micro.Choice B: Accounting profit excludes revenue
micro.Choice C: They are always identical
micro.Choice D: Producer surplus is tied to variable or marginal costs, while accounting profit also subtracts fixed costs
micro.Correct Answer: D — Producer surplus is tied to variable or marginal costs, while accounting profit also subtracts fixed costs
micro.Feedback: The measures use different cost concepts.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.1 — Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.
micro.Question: An owner uses a building that could instead earn $12,000 in annual rent. No rent check is paid by the owner’s business. What annual cost should economic analysis include?
micro.Choice A: $0 because no payment occurs
micro.Choice B: $12,000 explicit wage cost
micro.Choice C: $12,000 implicit opportunity cost
micro.Choice D: $24,000 because both uses count at once
micro.Correct Answer: C — $12,000 implicit opportunity cost
micro.Feedback: Using the building sacrifices the $12,000 rental alternative even without a cash payment.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.1 — Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.
micro.Question: Accounting profit is $42,000 and the owner forgoes a $35,000 outside salary, with no other implicit costs. What is economic profit?
micro.Feedback: Subtract the forgone owner return: 42,000−35,000=$7,000.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.1 — Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.
micro.Question: Why is normal profit connected to the idea of opportunity cost?
micro.Choice A: It is identical to producer surplus
micro.Choice B: It compensates entrepreneurial resources for what they could earn in their next-best use
micro.Choice C: It is a tax on accounting profit
micro.Choice D: It measures consumer willingness to pay
micro.Correct Answer: B — It compensates entrepreneurial resources for what they could earn in their next-best use
micro.Feedback: Normal profit is the implicit opportunity cost required to keep entrepreneurial resources in the firm.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.1 — Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.
micro.Question: How does marginal decision-making differ from comparing total economic profit?
micro.Choice A: Marginal analysis focuses on changes from one more action, while economic profit compares total revenue with all opportunity costs
micro.Choice B: Marginal analysis compares total revenue with total explicit costs, while economic profit isolates the value of the next unit
micro.Choice C: Economic profit evaluates the next incremental action, while marginal analysis measures the return on the entire project
micro.Choice D: Both methods compare total revenue and total cost, but marginal analysis reports the result per unit of output
micro.Correct Answer: A — Marginal analysis focuses on changes from one more action, while economic profit compares total revenue with all opportunity costs
micro.Feedback: The two tools answer different questions: one about incremental choices and one about overall return after opportunity costs.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.1 — Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.
micro.Question: Which item is an explicit cost?
micro.Choice A: A payment to a materials supplier
micro.Choice B: The owner’s forgone salary
micro.Choice C: Forgone interest on owner savings
micro.Choice D: Unpaid owner management time
micro.Correct Answer: A — A payment to a materials supplier
micro.Feedback: Explicit costs are direct monetary payments.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.1 — Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.
micro.Question: Which item is an implicit cost?
micro.Choice A: A wage paid to an employee
micro.Choice B: The salary an owner gives up elsewhere
micro.Choice C: A utility bill
micro.Choice D: A lease payment
micro.Correct Answer: B — The salary an owner gives up elsewhere
micro.Feedback: Implicit costs are forgone alternatives of owner-supplied resources.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.1 — Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.
micro.Question: Accounting profit equals:
micro.Choice A: Revenue minus explicit and implicit costs
micro.Choice B: Explicit costs minus revenue
micro.Choice C: Revenue minus explicit costs
micro.Choice D: Revenue divided by output
micro.Correct Answer: C — Revenue minus explicit costs
micro.Feedback: Accounting profit subtracts explicit costs.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.1 — Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.
micro.Question: Economic profit equals:
micro.Choice A: Revenue minus explicit costs only
micro.Choice B: Accounting profit plus implicit costs
micro.Choice C: Revenue minus fixed cost only
micro.Choice D: Revenue minus explicit and implicit costs
micro.Correct Answer: D — Revenue minus explicit and implicit costs
micro.Feedback: Economic profit subtracts all opportunity costs.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.1 — Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.
micro.Question: Zero economic profit means:
micro.Choice A: All explicit and implicit costs are covered
micro.Choice B: Revenue is zero
micro.Choice C: Accounting profit is zero
micro.Choice D: The owner receives no compensation
micro.Correct Answer: A — All explicit and implicit costs are covered
micro.Feedback: Zero economic profit includes normal profit.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.1 — Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.
micro.Question: An owner uses a building she could rent to another business for $2,000 per month. In economic-cost analysis, the forgone rent is:
micro.Choice A: An implicit cost
micro.Choice B: An explicit cost
micro.Choice C: Accounting revenue
micro.Choice D: A sunk cost
micro.Correct Answer: A — An implicit cost
micro.Feedback: Using an owner-supplied resource sacrifices its next-best return, so the forgone rent is an implicit cost.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.1 — Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.
micro.Question: Which cost is explicit for a small restaurant?
micro.Choice A: The owner’s forgone salary at another job
micro.Choice B: The interest the owner could have earned on invested savings
micro.Choice C: The rent the owner could earn from an owned building
micro.Choice D: The monthly payment to its food supplier
micro.Correct Answer: D — The monthly payment to its food supplier
micro.Feedback: An explicit cost is a direct monetary payment made by the firm.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.1 — Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.
micro.Question: Economic cost includes:
micro.Choice A: Only payments that vary with output
micro.Choice B: Only costs paid in cash this month
micro.Choice C: Both explicit payments and implicit opportunity costs
micro.Choice D: Only costs recorded by an accountant
micro.Correct Answer: C — Both explicit payments and implicit opportunity costs
micro.Feedback: Economic cost counts both recorded payments and the value of forgone alternatives.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.1 — Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.
micro.Question: A firm has $150,000 in revenue and $110,000 in explicit costs. Its accounting profit is:
micro.Feedback: Accounting profit equals revenue minus explicit costs.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.1 — Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.
micro.Question: Economic profit is calculated as:
micro.Choice A: Revenue minus explicit and implicit costs
micro.Choice B: Revenue minus explicit costs only
micro.Choice C: Accounting profit plus implicit costs
micro.Choice D: Revenue minus fixed cost only
micro.Correct Answer: A — Revenue minus explicit and implicit costs
micro.Feedback: Economic profit subtracts all opportunity costs, including implicit costs.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.1 — Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.
micro.Question: Normal profit is best understood as:
micro.Choice A: A guaranteed positive economic profit
micro.Choice B: Revenue remaining after variable cost only
micro.Choice C: A payment excluded from economic cost
micro.Choice D: The return needed to keep owner-supplied resources in their current use
micro.Correct Answer: D — The return needed to keep owner-supplied resources in their current use
micro.Feedback: Normal profit is part of implicit cost and represents the opportunity cost of entrepreneurial resources.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.1 — Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.
micro.Question: If accounting profit is $60,000 and implicit costs are $25,000, economic profit is:
micro.Feedback: Economic profit equals accounting profit minus implicit costs.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.1 — Distinguish explicit cost, implicit cost, accounting profit, economic profit, and normal profit.
micro.Question: A firm earning zero economic profit is:
micro.Choice A: Producing with zero revenue
micro.Choice B: Covering both explicit and implicit opportunity costs
micro.Choice C: Failing to cover explicit costs
micro.Choice D: Necessarily earning zero accounting profit
micro.Correct Answer: B — Covering both explicit and implicit opportunity costs
