micro.Feedback: The level of MC relative to ATC, not merely MC’s direction, controls ATC.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.4 — Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.
micro.Question: A firm’s MC equals AVC at Q=40 and equals ATC at Q=55. Which conclusion is correct?
micro.Choice A: Both averages are minimized at 40
micro.Choice B: Minimum AVC occurs at 40 and minimum ATC at 55
micro.Choice C: Both averages are minimized at 55
micro.Choice D: AFC is minimized at 55
micro.Correct Answer: B — Minimum AVC occurs at 40 and minimum ATC at 55
micro.Feedback: Each average is minimized where MC crosses it.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.4 — Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.
micro.Question: Northstar Bakery output schedule through worker 2 is 0:0, 1:8, 2:20. Worker 2 has MP 12. Compared with AP after worker 1, what happens to AP when worker 2 is added?
micro.Choice A: AP rises to 10 units per worker
micro.Choice B: AP falls to 12 units per worker
micro.Choice C: AP rises to 20 units per worker
micro.Choice D: AP is unchanged at 8 units per worker
micro.Correct Answer: A — AP rises to 10 units per worker
micro.Feedback: Compare the new worker’s MP with the prior AP, then compute the new AP.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.4 — Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.
micro.Question: Harbor Roasters output schedule through worker 4 is 0:0, 1:10, 2:23, 3:36, 4:47. Worker 4 has MP 11. Compared with AP after worker 3, what happens to AP when worker 4 is added?
micro.Choice A: AP falls to 11 units per worker
micro.Choice B: AP rises to 47 units per worker
micro.Choice C: AP falls to 11.75 units per worker
micro.Choice D: AP is unchanged at 12 units per worker
micro.Correct Answer: C — AP falls to 11.75 units per worker
micro.Feedback: Compare the new worker’s MP with the prior AP, then compute the new AP.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.4 — Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.
micro.Question: Blue Peak Printing output schedule through worker 6 is 0:0, 1:7, 2:18, 3:31, 4:43, 5:53, 6:61. Worker 6 has MP 8. Compared with AP after worker 5, what happens to AP when worker 6 is added?
micro.Choice A: AP falls to 10.17 units per worker
micro.Choice B: AP falls to 8 units per worker
micro.Choice C: AP rises to 61 units per worker
micro.Choice D: AP is unchanged at 10.6 units per worker
micro.Correct Answer: A — AP falls to 10.17 units per worker
micro.Feedback: Compare the new worker’s MP with the prior AP, then compute the new AP.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.4 — Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.
micro.Question: Juniper Foods output schedule through worker 2 is 0:0, 1:8, 2:19. Worker 2 has MP 11. Compared with AP after worker 1, what happens to AP when worker 2 is added?
micro.Choice A: AP falls to 11 units per worker
micro.Choice B: AP rises to 19 units per worker
micro.Choice C: AP rises to 9.5 units per worker
micro.Choice D: AP is unchanged at 8 units per worker
micro.Correct Answer: C — AP rises to 9.5 units per worker
micro.Feedback: Compare the new worker’s MP with the prior AP, then compute the new AP.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.4 — Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.
micro.Question: Maple Street Media output schedule through worker 4 is 0:0, 1:6, 2:15, 3:26, 4:37. Worker 4 has MP 11. Compared with AP after worker 3, what happens to AP when worker 4 is added?
micro.Choice A: AP rises to 9.25 units per worker
micro.Choice B: AP falls to 11 units per worker
micro.Choice C: AP rises to 37 units per worker
micro.Choice D: AP is unchanged at 8.67 units per worker
micro.Correct Answer: A — AP rises to 9.25 units per worker
micro.Feedback: Compare the new worker’s MP with the prior AP, then compute the new AP.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.4 — Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.
micro.Question: Lakeside Ceramics output schedule through worker 6 is 0:0, 1:9, 2:22, 3:36, 4:48, 5:58, 6:66. Worker 6 has MP 8. Compared with AP after worker 5, what happens to AP when worker 6 is added?
micro.Choice A: AP falls to 8 units per worker
micro.Choice B: AP rises to 66 units per worker
micro.Choice C: AP falls to 11 units per worker
micro.Choice D: AP is unchanged at 11.6 units per worker
micro.Correct Answer: C — AP falls to 11 units per worker
micro.Feedback: Compare the new worker’s MP with the prior AP, then compute the new AP.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.4 — Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.
micro.Question: Refer to the MP–AP graph. Between which two worker counts does MP cross AP, and why does the crossing locate the average-product maximum?
micro.Choice A: Between five and six; marginal output switches from pulling the average up to pulling it down.
micro.Choice B: Between four and five; marginal output switches from pulling the average up to pulling it down.
micro.Choice C: Between four and five; equality of marginal and average output makes total output zero.
micro.Choice D: Between five and six; equality of marginal and average output makes total output zero.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Between four and five; marginal output switches from pulling the average up to pulling it down.
micro.Feedback: MP is above AP at four workers and below AP at five, placing the plotted crossing between them. A marginal value above an average raises it; a marginal value below lowers it. Equality does not imply zero TP.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.4 — Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Which statement correctly combines its reading at Q = 25 with the marginal-average cost rule?
micro.Choice A: MC is about $17; the next units cost less than either average and lower both AVC and ATC.
micro.Choice B: MC is about $15; the next units cost less than either average and lower both AVC and ATC.
micro.Choice C: MC is about $17; the next units cost more than either average and raise both AVC and ATC.
micro.Choice D: MC is about $15; the next units cost more than either average and raise both AVC and ATC.
micro.Correct Answer: A — MC is about $17; the next units cost less than either average and lower both AVC and ATC.
micro.Feedback: Q = 25: MC ≈ 17 below AVC ≈ 21 and ATC ≈ 30. Both avc and atc fall. A marginal cost below an average lowers it; a marginal cost above an average raises it.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.4 — Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Which statement correctly combines its reading at Q = 35 with the marginal-average cost rule?
micro.Choice A: MC is about $19; the next units cost more than AVC but less than ATC, raising AVC and lowering ATC.
micro.Choice B: MC is about $21; the next units cost more than AVC but less than ATC, raising AVC and lowering ATC.
micro.Choice C: MC is about $21; AVC falls while ATC rises.
micro.Choice D: MC is about $19; AVC falls while ATC rises.
micro.Correct Answer: B — MC is about $21; the next units cost more than AVC but less than ATC, raising AVC and lowering ATC.
micro.Feedback: Q = 35: AVC ≈ 18, MC ≈ 21, ATC ≈ 23. Avc rises while atc falls. A marginal cost below an average lowers it; a marginal cost above an average raises it.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.4 — Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Which statement correctly combines its reading at Q = 50 with the marginal-average cost rule?
micro.Choice A: MC is about $40; the next units cost more than either average and raise both AVC and ATC.
micro.Choice B: MC is about $46; both AVC and ATC fall.
micro.Choice C: MC is about $46; the next units cost more than either average and raise both AVC and ATC.
micro.Choice D: MC is about $40; both AVC and ATC fall.
micro.Correct Answer: C — MC is about $46; the next units cost more than either average and raise both AVC and ATC.
micro.Feedback: Q = 50: MC ≈ 46 above both averages. Both avc and atc rise. A marginal cost below an average lowers it; a marginal cost above an average raises it.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.4 — Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Which statement correctly combines its reading at Q = 40 with the marginal-average cost rule?
micro.Choice A: MC is about $30; ATC falls because MC remains below it.
micro.Choice B: MC is about $34; ATC rises merely because MC is rising.
micro.Choice C: MC is about $30; ATC rises merely because MC is rising.
micro.Choice D: MC is about $34; ATC falls because MC remains below it.
micro.Correct Answer: D — MC is about $34; ATC falls because MC remains below it.
micro.Feedback: Q = 40: MC ≈ 34 below ATC ≈ 38. Atc falls because mc remains below it. A marginal cost below an average lowers it; a marginal cost above an average raises it.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.4 — Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.
micro.Question: Refer to the TP graph. The firm hires an eighth worker at a positive wage. Which output change and production implication follow?
micro.Choice A: Output falls from 62 to 60; this hire cannot be a way to produce additional output.
micro.Choice B: Output falls from 64 to 62; this hire cannot be a way to produce additional output.
micro.Choice C: Output falls from 62 to 60; the positive wage ensures that this hire increases output.
micro.Choice D: Output falls from 64 to 62; the positive wage ensures that this hire increases output.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Output falls from 62 to 60; this hire cannot be a way to produce additional output.
micro.Feedback: TP falls from 62 at seven workers to 60 at eight, so the eighth worker has MP = −2. Paying more for labor on this segment lowers rather than expands production.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.4 — Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. At Q = 40, which ordering holds, and what does it imply about a small increase in output?
micro.Choice A: MC < AVC < AC; the next units cost less than either average, lowering both AVC and AC.
micro.Choice B: AVC < MC < AC; the next units cost more than AVC but less than AC, lowering AVC and raising AC.
micro.Choice C: MC < AVC < AC; the next units cost less than either average, raising both AVC and AC.
micro.Choice D: AVC < MC < AC; the next units cost more than AVC but less than AC, raising AVC and lowering AC.
micro.Correct Answer: D — AVC < MC < AC; the next units cost more than AVC but less than AC, raising AVC and lowering AC.
micro.Feedback: At Q = 40, MC lies above AVC but below AC. A marginal cost above an average pulls that average up; a marginal cost below an average pulls it down. Thus AVC rises and AC falls.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.4 — Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.
micro.Question: If MP exceeds AP, AP:
micro.Choice A: Falls
micro.Choice B: Rises
micro.Choice C: Is at its minimum
micro.Choice D: Becomes zero
micro.Correct Answer: B — Rises
micro.Feedback: A marginal above the average raises it.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.4 — Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.
micro.Question: If MP equals AP, AP is:
micro.Choice A: Necessarily zero
micro.Choice B: At a local minimum
micro.Choice C: At a local maximum in the standard product-curve relationship
micro.Choice D: Equal to total product
micro.Correct Answer: C — At a local maximum in the standard product-curve relationship
micro.Feedback: MP crosses AP at maximum AP.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.4 — Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.
micro.Question: MC is below AVC. AVC:
micro.Choice A: Falls
micro.Choice B: Rises
micro.Choice C: Is at its maximum
micro.Choice D: Equals AFC
micro.Correct Answer: A — Falls
micro.Feedback: A below-average marginal lowers the average.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.4 — Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.
micro.Question: MC equals AVC. AVC is:
micro.Choice A: At its maximum
micro.Choice B: At its minimum
micro.Choice C: Zero
micro.Choice D: Equal to ATC
micro.Correct Answer: B — At its minimum
micro.Feedback: MC crosses AVC at minimum AVC.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.4 — Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.
micro.Question: MC is rising but below ATC. ATC:
micro.Choice A: Must rise
micro.Choice B: Must be constant
micro.Choice C: Still falls
micro.Choice D: Equals MC
micro.Correct Answer: C — Still falls
micro.Feedback: Even though MC is rising, it remains below ATC, so the marginal cost still pulls average total cost downward.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.4 — Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.
micro.Question: Why does AFC fall continuously?
micro.Choice A: TFC falls with output
micro.Choice B: MC falls forever
micro.Choice C: AVC becomes zero
micro.Choice D: A fixed total is spread over more units
micro.Correct Answer: D — A fixed total is spread over more units
micro.Feedback: The numerator is fixed while Q rises.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.4 — Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.
micro.Question: At a fixed wage, MP falls. MC:
micro.Choice A: Falls
micro.Choice B: Is unchanged
micro.Choice C: Rises
micro.Choice D: Becomes TFC
micro.Correct Answer: C — Rises
micro.Feedback: MC and MP move inversely.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.4 — Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.
micro.Question: Use the graph to complete the cost identity TC = TVC + ____. Which amount and explanation fit the missing term?
micro.Choice A: $120 of total fixed cost; TC equals TVC plus this constant amount.
micro.Choice B: $240 of marginal cost; TC equals TVC plus the cost of the next unit.
micro.Choice C: $120 of marginal cost; TC equals TVC plus the cost of the next unit.
micro.Choice D: $240 of total fixed cost; TC equals TVC plus this constant amount.
micro.Correct Answer: D — $240 of total fixed cost; TC equals TVC plus this constant amount.
micro.Feedback: The horizontal fixed-cost line is at $240. TC starts at $240 while TVC starts at zero. Their difference is $240 at every output because TC = TVC+TFC. This is a total, not a marginal or per-unit cost.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.4 — Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.
micro.Question: Refer to the average-cost graph. Approximately how large is the ATC–AVC gap at Q = 20, and why is the gap smaller at Q = 70?
micro.Choice A: About $12 per unit; the same fixed cost is spread over more units.
micro.Choice B: About $6 per unit; the same fixed cost is spread over more units.
micro.Choice C: About $12 per unit; total fixed cost falls as output rises.
micro.Choice D: About $6 per unit; total fixed cost falls as output rises.
micro.Correct Answer: A — About $12 per unit; the same fixed cost is spread over more units.
micro.Feedback: At Q = 20 the gap and the AFC curve are about $12; by Q = 70 they are about $3.4. The gap is AFC = TFC/Q. With TFC = $240 unchanged, a larger denominator reduces fixed cost per unit.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.4 — Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Where does MC cross ATC, and what do the marginal-average relationships imply at the crossing?
micro.Choice A: At roughly Q = 30; the next units switch from lowering to raising the relevant average because MC crosses it from below.
micro.Choice B: At roughly Q = 39; the next units switch from lowering to raising the relevant average because MC crosses it from below.
micro.Choice C: At roughly Q = 39; the next units switch from raising to lowering the relevant average because MC crosses it from below.
micro.Choice D: At roughly Q = 30; the next units switch from raising to lowering the relevant average because MC crosses it from below.
micro.Correct Answer: B — At roughly Q = 39; the next units switch from lowering to raising the relevant average because MC crosses it from below.
micro.Feedback: MC crosses ATC at roughly Q = 39. Before each crossing MC is below that average and pulls it down; after the crossing MC is above it and pulls it up. Thus the crossing identifies a minimum, not a maximum.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.4 — Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. At Q = 120, which cost identity is demonstrated by Points A, B, and C?
micro.Choice A: A = B − C
micro.Choice B: A = B + C
micro.Choice C: B = A + C
micro.Choice D: C = A + B
micro.Correct Answer: B — A = B + C
micro.Feedback: $1,200=$800+$400, illustrating TC=TVC+TFC.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.4 — Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.
micro.Question: Why can a higher fixed cost leave MC unchanged?
micro.Choice A: MC excludes all cost
micro.Choice B: Fixed cost is revenue
micro.Choice C: MC measures the change in TC, and fixed cost does not change with output
micro.Choice D: Output is long run
micro.Correct Answer: C — MC measures the change in TC, and fixed cost does not change with output
micro.Feedback: A constant addition to TC cancels in ΔTC.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.4 — Explain relationships among production measures and short-run cost curves.
micro.Question: A plant’s output schedule shows falling MP. At constant wages, which cost pattern follows?
micro.Choice A: Falling MC
micro.Choice B: Constant MC
micro.Choice C: Falling TFC
micro.Choice D: Rising MC
micro.Correct Answer: D — Rising MC
micro.Feedback: Less output per worker raises cost per extra unit.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A fixed license fee rises. Which curves shift?
micro.Choice A: AVC and MC only
micro.Choice B: All curves
micro.Choice C: AFC and ATC only
micro.Choice D: MC only
micro.Correct Answer: C — AFC and ATC only
micro.Feedback: A pure fixed-cost change leaves variable and marginal cost unchanged.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: The wage rises. Which curves shift upward?
micro.Choice A: AFC only
micro.Choice B: TFC and AFC only
micro.Choice C: LRATC only by definition
micro.Choice D: AVC, ATC, and MC
micro.Correct Answer: D — AVC, ATC, and MC
micro.Feedback: The wage is a variable-input price.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A learner says a higher fixed insurance premium shifts AVC and MC upward. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
micro.Choice A: All short-run curves shift by the same amount
micro.Choice B: A fixed-cost increase lowers ATC
micro.Choice C: A pure fixed-cost increase shifts AFC and ATC, not AVC or MC
micro.Choice D: A fixed-cost increase shifts only MC
micro.Correct Answer: C — A pure fixed-cost increase shifts AFC and ATC, not AVC or MC
micro.Feedback: Fixed cost does not change the variable cost of current output or the incremental cost of another unit.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A learner says, “Fixed cost and sunk cost mean the same thing.” Which statement corrects this claim?
micro.Choice A: A fixed cost can be avoidable in a future decision; a sunk cost is unrecoverable
micro.Choice B: Every sunk cost varies with output
micro.Choice C: Every fixed cost has already been paid forever
micro.Choice D: Sunk costs are always implicit
micro.Correct Answer: A — A fixed cost can be avoidable in a future decision; a sunk cost is unrecoverable
micro.Feedback: Fixed describes how cost behaves with current output; sunk describes whether it can be recovered.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A learner includes a nonrefundable past payment when comparing two current options that both leave the payment unchanged. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
micro.Choice A: Double the payment to reflect risk
micro.Choice B: Treat it as marginal cost
micro.Choice C: Convert it into future revenue
micro.Choice D: Ignore the payment because it is sunk and identical across the options
micro.Correct Answer: D — Ignore the payment because it is sunk and identical across the options
micro.Feedback: Only costs and benefits that differ across current alternatives should affect the choice.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A learner calls a cancelable future lease payment sunk because the lease is a fixed cost. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
micro.Choice A: Only variable costs can be avoided
micro.Choice B: A lease payment is always implicit
micro.Choice C: The future payment is avoidable if canceling the lease eliminates it
micro.Choice D: All fixed costs are sunk
micro.Correct Answer: C — The future payment is avoidable if canceling the lease eliminates it
micro.Feedback: A cost can be fixed with respect to output yet avoidable with respect to a future decision.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A productivity improvement raises output per worker. With wages unchanged, what happens to labor cost per unit?
micro.Choice A: It rises
micro.Choice B: It becomes fixed
micro.Choice C: It falls
micro.Choice D: It equals revenue
micro.Correct Answer: C — It falls
micro.Feedback: More output from the same wage lowers unit cost.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A factory produces the same output with fewer labor hours. Which cost most directly falls?
micro.Choice A: Sunk cost
micro.Choice B: Past fixed cost
micro.Choice C: Forgone owner salary
micro.Choice D: Variable cost
micro.Correct Answer: D — Variable cost
micro.Feedback: Labor-hours savings lower current variable cost.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: Cost curves can be reused across market structures because:
micro.Choice A: Every firm faces the same price
micro.Choice B: All firms earn zero profit
micro.Choice C: Market structure determines fixed cost
micro.Choice D: Production technology and input costs determine cost independently of the firm’s demand conditions
micro.Correct Answer: D — Production technology and input costs determine cost independently of the firm’s demand conditions
micro.Feedback: Revenue conditions differ, but cost construction follows production and input prices.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A higher wage paid for labor directly raises:
micro.Choice A: Variable and marginal production costs
micro.Choice B: Only implicit cost
micro.Choice C: Only TFC
micro.Choice D: Consumer surplus
micro.Correct Answer: A — Variable and marginal production costs
micro.Feedback: Labor is the variable input in the standard short-run model.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: If the rental price of an adjustable machine service rises, what happens to cost?
micro.Choice A: All sunk costs fall
micro.Choice B: The cost of outputs using that service rises
micro.Choice C: Marginal product automatically doubles
micro.Choice D: Economic cost excludes it
micro.Correct Answer: B — The cost of outputs using that service rises
micro.Feedback: An input-price increase raises production cost.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A monopoly and a competitive firm may use the same cost schedule. Which conditions differ when they determine revenue and choose output?
micro.Choice A: Their revenue and demand conditions, not the cost identities
micro.Choice B: TC=TFC+TVC only for competition
micro.Choice C: Monopoly has no marginal cost
micro.Choice D: Competition has no fixed cost
micro.Correct Answer: A — Their revenue and demand conditions, not the cost identities
micro.Feedback: The same cost relationships apply to both firms, but the demand and marginal revenue they face differ.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: How does the sunk-cost rule connect to marginal analysis?
micro.Choice A: Both rules say fixed costs are always irrelevant
micro.Choice B: Both focus the current choice on additional costs and benefits that change across alternatives
micro.Choice C: Marginal analysis requires adding all past costs
micro.Choice D: Sunk cost is another term for marginal cost
micro.Correct Answer: B — Both focus the current choice on additional costs and benefits that change across alternatives
micro.Feedback: Past unrecoverable costs do not change the marginal consequences of the current decision.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: How can a cost be fixed with respect to current output but still relevant to a future decision?
micro.Choice A: It may be avoidable if choosing a different plan eliminates the future payment
micro.Choice B: Every fixed cost is permanently sunk
micro.Choice C: Fixed costs always change one-for-one with output
micro.Choice D: Future fixed costs are excluded from economic cost
micro.Correct Answer: A — It may be avoidable if choosing a different plan eliminates the future payment
micro.Feedback: Cost behavior with output and recoverability across decisions are different classifications.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: Why is “recovering what we already spent” a poor reason by itself to continue a project?
micro.Choice A: Continuing can convert past spending into a relevant marginal benefit if enough future revenue is earned
micro.Choice B: Past spending should be added to expected future benefits because the project needs to recover its historical cost
micro.Choice C: A project should continue when accounting profit remains positive, even if future incremental costs exceed benefits
micro.Choice D: Past unrecoverable spending is unchanged by the current choice, so the decision should compare future incremental benefits and costs
micro.Correct Answer: D — Past unrecoverable spending is unchanged by the current choice, so the decision should compare future incremental benefits and costs
micro.Feedback: The relevant comparison is forward-looking, not an attempt to reverse an unrecoverable past payment.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A fixed-cost increase raises:
micro.Choice A: AVC and MC
micro.Choice B: MC only
micro.Choice C: AVC only
micro.Choice D: AFC and ATC
micro.Correct Answer: D — AFC and ATC
micro.Feedback: Fixed cost affects AFC and ATC.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A higher wage raises:
micro.Choice A: TVC, AVC, ATC, and MC
micro.Choice B: TFC and AFC only
micro.Choice C: AFC only
micro.Choice D: No cost curves
micro.Correct Answer: A — TVC, AVC, ATC, and MC
micro.Feedback: A wage is a variable-input price.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A sunk cost:
micro.Choice A: Changes with output
micro.Choice B: Can be avoided immediately
micro.Choice C: Cannot be recovered
micro.Choice D: Exists only in the long run
micro.Correct Answer: C — Cannot be recovered
micro.Feedback: Sunk costs are unrecoverable.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A sunk cost is a cost that:
micro.Choice A: Exists only when economic profit is negative
micro.Choice B: Has already been incurred and cannot be recovered
micro.Choice C: Always varies with current output
micro.Choice D: Can always be avoided by shutting down today
micro.Correct Answer: B — Has already been incurred and cannot be recovered
micro.Feedback: A sunk cost is unrecoverable and should not be changed by the current decision.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: An avoidable cost is a cost that:
micro.Choice A: Can be eliminated by choosing a particular alternative
micro.Choice B: Has already been paid and cannot be recovered
micro.Choice C: Must be fixed in every time period
micro.Choice D: Is excluded from economic cost
micro.Correct Answer: A — Can be eliminated by choosing a particular alternative
micro.Feedback: Avoidable costs differ across the alternatives being considered.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A nonrefundable $2,000 design fee was paid last month. For today’s continue-or-cancel decision, the fee is:
micro.Choice A: Avoidable
micro.Choice B: Marginal revenue
micro.Choice C: An implicit future cost
micro.Choice D: Sunk
micro.Correct Answer: D — Sunk
micro.Feedback: The payment cannot be recovered regardless of the current choice.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A monthly service contract can be canceled before next month with no penalty. Next month’s payment is:
micro.Choice A: An implicit cost only
micro.Choice B: A past fixed cost
micro.Choice C: Avoidable
micro.Choice D: Sunk
micro.Correct Answer: C — Avoidable
micro.Feedback: A future cost that disappears under one option is relevant to the decision.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A specialized mold has no resale value after purchase. For a current output decision, its purchase price is:
micro.Choice A: Variable cost
micro.Choice B: Sunk and irrelevant to marginal cost
micro.Choice C: Marginal revenue
micro.Choice D: Avoidable fixed cost
micro.Correct Answer: B — Sunk and irrelevant to marginal cost
micro.Feedback: The unrecoverable payment does not change with current output.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A fixed-cost increase shifts ATC upward more at low output than at high output. Why?
micro.Choice A: The additional payment raises marginal cost as output rises
micro.Choice B: The additional fixed payment is spread over more units
micro.Choice C: The additional payment reduces variable cost as output rises
micro.Choice D: The additional payment becomes a variable cost at high output
micro.Correct Answer: B — The additional fixed payment is spread over more units
micro.Feedback: The vertical ATC shift is ΔTFC/Q.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A constant per-unit input-cost increase creates approximately parallel shifts in AVC and MC. Why?
micro.Choice A: The fixed payment is spread across increasing output
micro.Choice B: Higher productivity offsets part of each unit’s extra cost
micro.Choice C: The same added cost applies to each additional unit
micro.Choice D: Average fixed cost rises by the same amount as MC
micro.Correct Answer: C — The same added cost applies to each additional unit
micro.Feedback: A per-unit variable charge adds to average variable and marginal cost.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: Use the graph. Refer to the shift from MC1 to MC2. At Q = 20, approximately how does marginal cost change, and what productivity inference follows if the wage is fixed and labor is the variable input?
micro.Choice A: From $18 to $8; marginal product rises.
micro.Choice B: From $14 to $4; marginal product falls.
micro.Choice C: From $18 to $8; marginal product falls.
micro.Choice D: From $14 to $4; marginal product rises.
micro.Correct Answer: D — From $14 to $4; marginal product rises.
micro.Feedback: At Q = 20, MC1 is about $14 and MC2 about $4. With a fixed wage and labor as the variable input, MC = w/MP. Lower marginal cost therefore corresponds to higher marginal product, not a reduction in fixed cost.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: An annual business-license fee doubles. At a fixed positive Q, what changes?
micro.Choice A: AFC and ATC rise; AVC and MC are unchanged
micro.Choice B: AVC and MC rise; AFC and ATC are unchanged
micro.Choice C: All four per-unit cost measures rise by the same amount
micro.Choice D: TFC rises; TC and all per-unit cost measures are unchanged
micro.Correct Answer: A — AFC and ATC rise; AVC and MC are unchanged
micro.Feedback: A fixed fee changes total and average fixed cost.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A $3 per-unit packaging charge is introduced. What changes?
micro.Choice A: TFC rises $3Q; AFC and ATC rise $3
micro.Choice B: TVC rises $3Q; AVC, ATC, and MC rise $3
micro.Choice C: TVC rises $3; AVC and MC rise $3Q
micro.Choice D: TC rises $3Q; ATC rises $3 but MC is unchanged
micro.Correct Answer: B — TVC rises $3Q; AVC, ATC, and MC rise $3
micro.Feedback: A constant per-unit charge is variable and marginal.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A machine purchase already made has no resale value. A new output plan is considered. How should the purchase price enter the plan?
micro.Choice A: Add it to MC for every unit
micro.Choice B: Treat it as a wage
micro.Choice C: Exclude it from marginal comparison because it is sunk
micro.Choice D: Subtract it from revenue twice
micro.Correct Answer: C — Exclude it from marginal comparison because it is sunk
micro.Feedback: Unrecoverable past cost does not vary with the current plan.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A $50,000 market study cannot be resold or refunded. The firm is choosing among future plants. The study cost is:
micro.Choice A: Sunk for the plant choice
micro.Choice B: A variable cost of each unit
micro.Choice C: A marginal benefit
micro.Choice D: Avoidable after the choice
micro.Correct Answer: A — Sunk for the plant choice
micro.Feedback: The past unrecoverable payment is common to all future options.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A fixed-cost increase leaves AVC unchanged because:
micro.Choice A: Fixed cost is not part of TVC
micro.Choice B: AVC equals MC
micro.Choice C: Wages fell
micro.Choice D: Output is long run
micro.Correct Answer: A — Fixed cost is not part of TVC
micro.Feedback: A pure fixed-cost change does not affect AVC.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A higher wage shifts MC upward because:
micro.Choice A: AFC rises
micro.Choice B: Added output now requires more variable spending
micro.Choice C: Plant size changes
micro.Choice D: Accounting profit rises
micro.Correct Answer: B — Added output now requires more variable spending
micro.Feedback: The wage is a variable-input cost.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: Higher productivity lowers costs because:
micro.Choice A: Fixed cost becomes sunk
micro.Choice B: Profit is included in cost
micro.Choice C: More output comes from the same inputs
micro.Choice D: Demand shifts
micro.Correct Answer: C — More output comes from the same inputs
micro.Feedback: Productivity lowers cost per unit.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A theater paid $5,000 for an advertising campaign that cannot be refunded. It is deciding whether to hold an event tomorrow. How should the $5,000 enter the decision?
micro.Choice A: It should determine the ticket price
micro.Choice B: It should be ignored because it is sunk
micro.Choice C: It should be charged again to tomorrow’s event
micro.Choice D: It should be treated as marginal cost of each ticket
micro.Correct Answer: B — It should be ignored because it is sunk
micro.Feedback: The advertising payment is unrecoverable and identical under either current choice.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A firm can cancel a future equipment rental and save $3,000 if it stops a project. The $3,000 is:
micro.Choice A: An avoidable cost relevant to the stop-or-continue choice
micro.Choice B: A sunk cost because equipment is fixed
micro.Choice C: An implicit cost with no monetary payment
micro.Choice D: Irrelevant because it is a fixed monthly amount
micro.Correct Answer: A — An avoidable cost relevant to the stop-or-continue choice
micro.Feedback: Future fixed commitments can be avoidable if the decision eliminates them.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A company spent $40,000 developing software that now has no resale value. A new update would cost $8,000 and generate an expected $11,000 benefit. Ignoring other effects, what should the firm do?
micro.Choice A: Reject the update because total spending would become $48,000
micro.Choice B: Reject the update because sunk costs must be recovered first
micro.Choice C: Buy the update only if the original $40,000 is refunded
micro.Choice D: Buy the update because the $40,000 is sunk and the incremental benefit exceeds the incremental cost
micro.Correct Answer: D — Buy the update because the $40,000 is sunk and the incremental benefit exceeds the incremental cost
micro.Feedback: The current decision compares the $11,000 additional benefit with the $8,000 additional cost.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A store’s current lease payment is nonrefundable, but the lease ends this month. The owner is deciding whether to renew for another year. Which cost is relevant?
micro.Choice A: Both payments are sunk
micro.Choice B: Neither payment because rent is fixed
micro.Choice C: The future renewal payment
micro.Choice D: The current nonrefundable payment
micro.Correct Answer: C — The future renewal payment
micro.Feedback: The current payment is sunk; the future renewal is avoidable and differs across options.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A firm owns a specialized machine with no resale value. Its original purchase price is irrelevant to whether to use it for a new order because the purchase price is:
micro.Choice A: Marginal revenue
micro.Choice B: Sunk
micro.Choice C: Variable
micro.Choice D: Avoidable
micro.Correct Answer: B — Sunk
micro.Feedback: An unrecoverable past expenditure does not change across the current alternatives.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A firm receives a property-tax increase that does not depend on output. Which immediate short-run curve change is correct?
micro.Choice A: AVC and MC shift upward together
micro.Choice B: Only MC shifts upward
micro.Choice C: All curves shift downward
micro.Choice D: ATC shifts upward while AVC is unchanged
micro.Correct Answer: D — ATC shifts upward while AVC is unchanged
micro.Feedback: A property tax is fixed with respect to output.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: The wage paid to every production worker rises. Which curve combination shifts upward?
micro.Choice A: AVC, ATC, and MC
micro.Choice B: AFC and ATC only
micro.Choice C: AFC and MC only
micro.Choice D: TFC and AFC only
micro.Correct Answer: A — AVC, ATC, and MC
micro.Feedback: The wage changes variable and marginal costs.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A process improvement raises output from every labor level. With input prices unchanged, the most defensible cost prediction is:
micro.Choice A: AFC rises and MC is unchanged
micro.Choice B: MC and ATC shift downward over the affected output range
micro.Choice C: TFC becomes zero
micro.Choice D: All costs rise because output rises
micro.Correct Answer: B — MC and ATC shift downward over the affected output range
micro.Feedback: More output from the same inputs reduces marginal and average cost.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A machine lease can be canceled next month without penalty, but the current month’s payment is already made. For a decision next month, the lease is:
micro.Choice A: A sunk cost forever
micro.Choice B: A variable cost per unit
micro.Choice C: A fixed but avoidable cost
micro.Choice D: An implicit cost
micro.Correct Answer: C — A fixed but avoidable cost
micro.Feedback: Future fixed commitments can be avoidable even when current payments are sunk.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: Which change can lower MC without changing TFC?
micro.Choice A: A higher building lease
micro.Choice B: A higher marginal product of labor
micro.Choice C: A larger sunk advertising payment
micro.Choice D: A higher annual license fee
micro.Correct Answer: B — A higher marginal product of labor
micro.Feedback: Higher MP means fewer variable-input dollars per extra unit.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: Harbor Roasters TFC rises by $120 while Q=47 and variable spending are unchanged. How do average costs and marginal cost change? Round per-unit changes to cents.
micro.Choice A: AFC and ATC rise $2.55; AVC and MC are unchanged
micro.Choice B: AVC and MC rise $2.55; AFC is unchanged
micro.Choice C: AFC rises $120; ATC and MC rise $2.55
micro.Choice D: ATC and MC rise $120; AFC and AVC are unchanged
micro.Correct Answer: A — AFC and ATC rise $2.55; AVC and MC are unchanged
micro.Feedback: The fixed-cost increase adds $120/47 = $2.55 to AFC and ATC. AVC and MC are unchanged because the payment does not vary with output.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: Riverbend Textiles TFC rises by $120 while Q=80 and variable spending are unchanged. How do average costs and marginal cost change? Round per-unit changes to cents.
micro.Choice A: AVC and MC rise $1.50; AFC is unchanged
micro.Choice B: AFC rises $120; ATC and MC rise $1.50
micro.Choice C: ATC and MC rise $120; AFC and AVC are unchanged
micro.Choice D: AFC and ATC rise $1.50; AVC and MC are unchanged
micro.Correct Answer: D — AFC and ATC rise $1.50; AVC and MC are unchanged
micro.Feedback: The fixed-cost increase adds $120/80 = $1.50 to AFC and ATC. AVC and MC are unchanged because the payment does not vary with output.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: Maple Street Media TFC rises by $120 while Q=37 and variable spending are unchanged. How do average costs and marginal cost change? Round per-unit changes to cents.
micro.Choice A: AVC and MC rise $3.24; AFC is unchanged
micro.Choice B: AFC rises $120; ATC and MC rise $3.24
micro.Choice C: AFC and ATC rise $3.24; AVC and MC are unchanged
micro.Choice D: ATC and MC rise $120; AFC and AVC are unchanged
micro.Correct Answer: C — AFC and ATC rise $3.24; AVC and MC are unchanged
micro.Feedback: The fixed-cost increase adds $120/37 = $3.24 to AFC and ATC. AVC and MC are unchanged because the payment does not vary with output.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: Prairie Solar TFC rises by $120 while Q=94 and variable spending are unchanged. How do average costs and marginal cost change? Round per-unit changes to cents.
micro.Choice A: AVC and MC rise $1.28; AFC is unchanged
micro.Choice B: AFC and ATC rise $1.28; AVC and MC are unchanged
micro.Choice C: AFC rises $120; ATC and MC rise $1.28
micro.Choice D: ATC and MC rise $120; AFC and AVC are unchanged
micro.Correct Answer: B — AFC and ATC rise $1.28; AVC and MC are unchanged
micro.Feedback: The fixed-cost increase adds $120/94 = $1.28 to AFC and ATC. AVC and MC are unchanged because the payment does not vary with output.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: Harbor Roasters TFC rises by $120 while Q=56 and variable spending are unchanged. How do average costs and marginal cost change? Round per-unit changes to cents.
micro.Choice A: AFC and ATC rise $2.14; AVC and MC are unchanged
micro.Choice B: AVC and MC rise $2.14; AFC is unchanged
micro.Choice C: AFC rises $120; ATC and MC rise $2.14
micro.Choice D: ATC and MC rise $120; AFC and AVC are unchanged
micro.Correct Answer: A — AFC and ATC rise $2.14; AVC and MC are unchanged
micro.Feedback: The fixed-cost increase adds $120/56 = $2.14 to AFC and ATC. AVC and MC are unchanged because the payment does not vary with output.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: Riverbend Textiles TFC rises by $120 while Q=85 and variable spending are unchanged. How do average costs and marginal cost change? Round per-unit changes to cents.
micro.Choice A: AVC and MC rise $1.41; AFC is unchanged
micro.Choice B: AFC rises $120; ATC and MC rise $1.41
micro.Choice C: ATC and MC rise $120; AFC and AVC are unchanged
micro.Choice D: AFC and ATC rise $1.41; AVC and MC are unchanged
micro.Correct Answer: D — AFC and ATC rise $1.41; AVC and MC are unchanged
micro.Feedback: The fixed-cost increase adds $120/85 = $1.41 to AFC and ATC. AVC and MC are unchanged because the payment does not vary with output.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A firm has already paid a nonrefundable $6,000 permit fee. Completing a project requires $14,000 more and will generate $17,000 in additional revenue. What is the correct decision logic?
micro.Choice A: Complete the project because the relevant incremental gain is $3,000
micro.Choice B: Cancel because total cost is $20,000
micro.Choice C: Cancel because the permit fee must be recovered
micro.Choice D: Complete only if revenue exceeds $23,000
micro.Correct Answer: A — Complete the project because the relevant incremental gain is $3,000
micro.Feedback: The sunk permit is irrelevant; compare $17,000 additional revenue with $14,000 avoidable completion cost.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A plant pays $10,000 per month on a contract. If it closes now, $7,000 can be canceled but $3,000 must still be paid. For the close-or-operate choice, how much of the monthly contract is avoidable?
micro.Feedback: Only the portion that disappears when the plant closes is avoidable.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A publisher spent $25,000 editing a book. It can print the book for an additional $12,000 and expects $15,000 in additional sales. Which statement is correct?
micro.Choice A: The editing cost should be allocated to each future copy before deciding
micro.Choice B: The firm must recover all $25,000 before printing
micro.Choice C: Printing adds $3,000 to profit relative to not printing, because the editing cost is sunk
micro.Choice D: Printing loses $22,000 because total cost is $37,000
micro.Correct Answer: C — Printing adds $3,000 to profit relative to not printing, because the editing cost is sunk
micro.Feedback: The current decision compares the $15,000 incremental revenue with the $12,000 avoidable printing cost.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A fixed annual license can be surrendered halfway through the year for a $4,000 refund. For a midyear shutdown decision, which amount is relevant?
micro.Choice A: Only variable labor cost can be relevant
micro.Choice B: $4,000 because shutting down recovers it
micro.Choice C: $0 because every fixed cost is sunk
micro.Choice D: The full original license price regardless of refund
micro.Correct Answer: B — $4,000 because shutting down recovers it
micro.Feedback: The recoverable amount differs across choices and is therefore avoidable rather than sunk.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: TFC rises by $1,000. At Q=100, which statement is correct?
micro.Choice A: All four per-unit curves rise by $10
micro.Choice B: Only MC rises by $10
micro.Choice C: AFC and ATC each rise by $10; AVC and MC do not change
micro.Choice D: AVC rises but ATC does not
micro.Correct Answer: C — AFC and ATC each rise by $10; AVC and MC do not change
micro.Feedback: The fixed-cost increase per unit is $1,000/100.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A per-unit royalty of $4 is added to production. Which immediate effect is correct?
micro.Choice A: AFC and ATC rise by $4
micro.Choice B: Only TFC rises
micro.Choice C: MC falls by $4
micro.Choice D: AVC, ATC, and MC rise by $4 at every positive output
micro.Correct Answer: D — AVC, ATC, and MC rise by $4 at every positive output
micro.Feedback: A constant per-unit cost adds $4 to variable and marginal cost.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A firm’s fixed insurance premium is refundable if the plant closes. Which description is best?
micro.Choice A: Fixed in the current production range but not sunk
micro.Choice B: Variable and sunk
micro.Choice C: Implicit and marginal
micro.Choice D: Always avoidable at every moment
micro.Correct Answer: A — Fixed in the current production range but not sunk
micro.Feedback: Fixed and sunk are different classifications.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A new scheduling system reduces idle time without changing wages or plant rent. Which curves should fall?
micro.Choice A: AFC only
micro.Choice B: TFC and AFC only
micro.Choice C: AVC, ATC, and MC; AFC is unchanged
micro.Choice D: All costs including TFC
micro.Correct Answer: C — AVC, ATC, and MC; AFC is unchanged
micro.Feedback: Higher labor productivity reduces variable and marginal cost.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A company installs automation that raises fixed cost but lowers variable cost. Which result is necessarily true?
micro.Choice A: AFC rises at each positive output
micro.Choice B: MC rises at each output
micro.Choice C: ATC rises at every output
micro.Choice D: AVC is unchanged
micro.Correct Answer: A — AFC rises at each positive output
micro.Feedback: The fixed-cost component per unit rises; the net ATC effect depends on both changes.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A lease payment is fixed for the year. Why can it still matter for a long-run plant decision?
micro.Choice A: All fixed costs are always marginal
micro.Choice B: The firm may avoid renewing it when all inputs become adjustable
micro.Choice C: Sunk costs become variable automatically
micro.Choice D: The short run lasts exactly one year
micro.Correct Answer: B — The firm may avoid renewing it when all inputs become adjustable
micro.Feedback: A current fixed commitment may become avoidable over a longer horizon.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A firm’s wage doubles while MP also doubles at every labor level. What happens to labor-based MC?
micro.Choice A: It doubles
micro.Choice B: It is cut in half
micro.Choice C: It remains unchanged
micro.Choice D: It becomes fixed cost
micro.Correct Answer: C — It remains unchanged
micro.Feedback: MC=wage/MP; proportional changes cancel.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A firm compares two technologies. Technology A has higher fixed cost and lower MC. Which statement is defensible without revenue information?
micro.Choice A: A has lower ATC at low output but higher ATC at high output; lower MC matters most when few units are produced.
micro.Choice B: A has lower ATC at every output; the lower MC offsets the fixed-cost difference by the same amount at every scale.
micro.Choice C: A has higher ATC at every output; the higher fixed cost increases the cost of each additional unit.
micro.Choice D: A may have lower ATC at high output but higher ATC at low output; the fixed-cost burden is spread as production expands.
micro.Correct Answer: D — A may have lower ATC at high output but higher ATC at low output; the fixed-cost burden is spread as production expands.
micro.Feedback: The fixed-versus-variable tradeoff depends on output.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: The wage rises 20%, but MP rises 20% after training. What happens to labor-based MC?
micro.Choice A: It rises 20%
micro.Choice B: It falls 20%
micro.Choice C: It remains unchanged
micro.Choice D: It becomes fixed
micro.Correct Answer: C — It remains unchanged
micro.Feedback: The wage-to-MP ratio is unchanged.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: The wage rises 25% while MP falls 20%. Which statement is strongest?
micro.Choice A: MC falls
micro.Choice B: MC is unchanged
micro.Choice C: Only AFC changes
micro.Choice D: MC rises by more than 25%
micro.Correct Answer: D — MC rises by more than 25%
micro.Feedback: A higher numerator and lower denominator both raise wage/MP.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: Automation raises TFC $20,000 and lowers AVC $4. At Q=2,000, what happens to ATC?
micro.Choice A: ATC rises $6 per unit
micro.Choice B: ATC falls $4
micro.Choice C: ATC rises $10
micro.Choice D: ATC is unchanged
micro.Correct Answer: A — ATC rises $6 per unit
micro.Feedback: AFC rises $10 while AVC falls $4, for a net $6 increase.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: Automation raises TFC by $20,000 and lowers AVC by $4. At Q=10,000, what happens to ATC?
micro.Choice A: ATC rises $6
micro.Choice B: ATC falls $2 per unit
micro.Choice C: ATC rises $2
micro.Choice D: ATC is unchanged
micro.Correct Answer: B — ATC falls $2 per unit
micro.Feedback: AFC rises $2 while AVC falls $4.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A packaging plant must pay its current $24,000 lease whether it operates or closes. Next year it can renew at $24,000 or lease a larger plant for $42,000. At the planned output of 9,000 units, variable cost would be $8 per unit in the old plant or $5 in the larger plant. Which decision correctly treats the time horizon?
micro.Choice A: The current lease is avoidable; next year the old plant costs $18,000 less in total
micro.Choice B: The current lease is sunk, so exclude both possible lease payments next year
micro.Choice C: The larger plant is cheaper at every output because its variable cost is lower
micro.Choice D: The current lease is unavoidable; next year the larger plant costs $9,000 less in total
micro.Correct Answer: D — The current lease is unavoidable; next year the larger plant costs $9,000 less in total
micro.Feedback: The current commitment does not disappear with shutdown. Next year total cost is $24,000 + $8 × 9,000 = $96,000 in the old plant and $42,000 + $5 × 9,000 = $87,000 in the larger one. Future capacity costs are avoidable choices. The larger plant saves $9,000 at this output, not at every output.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Using Q = 400 as the baseline, suppose fixed cost doubles while the variable-cost schedule is unchanged. What would AC be at Q = 400?
micro.Feedback: Baseline AFC is $8. Doubling fixed cost doubles AFC to $16, while AVC stays $12; AC becomes $28.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. At Q = 120, suppose variable input costs raise TVC by 25% while TFC is unchanged. What new pair of totals follows?
micro.Choice B: TVC=$800 and TC=$1,400
micro.Feedback: TVC rises from $800 to $1,000; adding unchanged TFC=$400 gives TC=$1,400.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. At Q = 120, suppose TFC rises from $400 to $600 while the variable-cost curve is unchanged. Approximately what would ATC become?
micro.Choice A: $11.67 per unit
micro.Choice B: $8.33 per unit
micro.Choice C: $10.00 per unit
micro.Choice D: $13.33 per unit
micro.Correct Answer: A — $11.67 per unit

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: At Northstar Bakery, 3 workers each earn $120 per production period, and total fixed cost is $240 per period. The last worker raises output from 20 to 34 units; labor is the only variable input. A recurring fixed fee adds $240 per period and pay rises $15 per worker. Output, employment and productivity remain unchanged. Which new cost values are correct? Round final results to cents.
micro.Feedback: The new fixed cost is $480 and the wage bill is 3×$135=$405. Divide each by 34 for AFC and AVC; ATC uses their unrounded sum. The last worker adds 14 units, so MC=$135/14=$9.64.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: At Ironwood Furniture, 4 workers each earn $135 per production period, and total fixed cost is $300 per period. The last worker raises output from 29 to 41 units; labor is the only variable input. A recurring fixed fee adds $240 per period and pay rises $15 per worker. Output, employment and productivity remain unchanged. Which new cost values are correct? Round final results to cents.
micro.Feedback: The new fixed cost is $540 and the wage bill is 4×$150=$600. Divide each by 41 for AFC and AVC; ATC uses their unrounded sum. The last worker adds 12 units, so MC=$150/12=$12.50.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: At Harbor Roasters, 5 workers each earn $105 per production period, and total fixed cost is $180 per period. The last worker raises output from 47 to 56 units; labor is the only variable input. A recurring fixed fee adds $240 per period and pay rises $15 per worker. Output, employment and productivity remain unchanged. Which new cost values are correct? Round final results to cents.
micro.Feedback: The new fixed cost is $420 and the wage bill is 5×$120=$600. Divide each by 56 for AFC and AVC; ATC uses their unrounded sum. The last worker adds 9 units, so MC=$120/9=$13.33.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.

micro.Question: At Summit Glassworks, 6 workers each earn $160 per production period, and total fixed cost is $480 per period. micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: At Maple Street Media, 3 workers each earn $100 per production period, and total fixed cost is $195 per period. Output, employment and productivity remain unchanged. Which new cost values are correct? Round final results to cents.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: At Granite Toolworks, 4 workers each earn $145 per production period, and total fixed cost is $390 per period. Output, employment and productivity remain unchanged. Which new cost values are correct? Round final results to cents.
micro.Feedback: The new fixed cost is $630 and the wage bill is 4×$160=$640. Divide each by 52 for AFC and AVC; ATC uses their unrounded sum. The last worker adds 13 units, so MC=$160/13=$12.31.

micro.Question: At Lakeside Ceramics, 5 workers each earn $115 per production period, and total fixed cost is $225 per period. Output, employment and productivity remain unchanged. Which new cost values are correct? Round final results to cents.

micro.Question: At Prairie Solar, 6 workers each earn $155 per production period, and total fixed cost is $450 per period. The last worker raises output from 74 to 85 units; labor is the only variable input. A recurring fixed fee adds $240 per period and pay rises $15 per worker. Output, employment and productivity remain unchanged. Which new cost values are correct? Round final results to cents.
micro.Feedback: The new fixed cost is $690 and the wage bill is 6×$170=$1020. Divide each by 85 for AFC and AVC; ATC uses their unrounded sum. The last worker adds 11 units, so MC=$170/11=$15.45.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A fixed tax rises. Which curves move?
micro.Choice A: AFC and ATC
micro.Choice B: AVC and MC
micro.Choice C: MC only
micro.Choice D: AVC only
micro.Correct Answer: A — AFC and ATC
micro.Feedback: Fixed cost does not enter AVC or MC.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A per-unit materials price rises. Which curves move?
micro.Choice A: AFC only
micro.Choice B: AVC, ATC, and MC
micro.Choice C: TFC only
micro.Choice D: AFC and MC only
micro.Correct Answer: B — AVC, ATC, and MC
micro.Feedback: Per-unit materials are variable and marginal costs.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A $900 annual fee is already paid and cannot be refunded. For today’s output decision it is:
micro.Choice A: A variable cost
micro.Choice B: Marginal cost
micro.Choice C: A sunk cost
micro.Choice D: Avoidable revenue
micro.Correct Answer: C — A sunk cost
micro.Feedback: The payment is unrecoverable.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A monthly lease can be canceled next month. For next month’s plant decision it is:
micro.Choice A: Sunk forever
micro.Choice B: A per-unit variable cost
micro.Choice C: An implicit cost only
micro.Choice D: Avoidable even if fixed with respect to output
micro.Correct Answer: D — Avoidable even if fixed with respect to output
micro.Feedback: Fixed does not automatically mean sunk.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A wage rises while plant rent stays fixed. Which measures rise?
micro.Choice A: TVC, AVC, ATC, and MC
micro.Choice B: TFC and AFC only
micro.Choice C: AFC only
micro.Choice D: No cost measures
micro.Correct Answer: A — TVC, AVC, ATC, and MC
micro.Feedback: The wage is a variable-input price.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A property tax rises while output is unchanged. Which measures rise?
micro.Choice A: TVC, AVC, and MC
micro.Choice B: TFC, AFC, TC, and ATC
micro.Choice C: MC only
micro.Choice D: AP and MP
micro.Correct Answer: B — TFC, AFC, TC, and ATC
micro.Feedback: A fixed-cost increase affects total and average fixed components.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: Technology raises MP with wages unchanged. Which relationship is expected?
micro.Choice A: MC rises
micro.Choice B: TFC falls necessarily
micro.Choice C: MC falls
micro.Choice D: AFC rises
micro.Correct Answer: C — MC falls
micro.Feedback: Higher MP lowers variable input cost per extra unit.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.5 — Analyze how fixed costs, input prices, and productivity changes affect cost curves.
micro.Question: A firm automates production, raising TFC but lowering AVC. Which conclusion is certain?
micro.Choice A: ATC falls at every output
micro.Choice B: AFC rises at each positive output
micro.Choice C: MC rises at every output
micro.Choice D: TFC becomes sunk by definition
micro.Correct Answer: B — AFC rises at each positive output
micro.Feedback: Only the fixed-cost component’s direction is certain.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Diminishing MP and diseconomies of scale differ because:
micro.Choice A: The first is short run with fixed inputs; the second is long run with all inputs variable
micro.Choice B: They are identical
micro.Choice C: The first concerns demand
micro.Choice D: The second requires negative output
micro.Correct Answer: A — The first is short run with fixed inputs; the second is long run with all inputs variable
micro.Feedback: The concepts apply to different horizons and input changes.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: MES is best defined as:
micro.Choice A: The largest feasible output
micro.Choice B: The smallest output attaining minimum LRATC
micro.Choice C: The point where MP becomes negative
micro.Choice D: The lowest total cost
micro.Correct Answer: B — The smallest output attaining minimum LRATC
micro.Feedback: MES is the first output on the minimum-LRATC range.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: A learner treats LRAC as the ATC curve of one fixed plant. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
micro.Choice A: LRAC is total variable cost per unit only
micro.Choice B: LRAC reflects the lowest attainable ATC across alternative plant sizes
micro.Choice C: LRAC is the same as AFC
micro.Choice D: LRAC fixes every input forever
micro.Correct Answer: B — LRAC reflects the lowest attainable ATC across alternative plant sizes
micro.Feedback: The long run permits plant adjustment, so LRAC summarizes least-cost choices across plants.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: A learner says economies of scale mean total cost must fall as output rises. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
micro.Choice A: Economies of scale mean average cost falls; total cost can still rise
micro.Choice B: Economies mean output falls
micro.Choice C: Economies mean fixed cost becomes zero
micro.Choice D: Economies require marginal product to be negative
micro.Correct Answer: A — Economies of scale mean average cost falls; total cost can still rise
micro.Feedback: The concept concerns cost per unit, not necessarily the level of total cost.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: A learner says diseconomies of scale begin when marginal product first falls in the short run. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
micro.Choice A: Diseconomies and diminishing marginal product are the same event
micro.Choice B: Diseconomies require one input to remain fixed
micro.Choice C: Diseconomies mean LRAC is falling
micro.Choice D: Diseconomies concern long-run expansion of all inputs and rising LRAC
micro.Correct Answer: D — Diseconomies concern long-run expansion of all inputs and rising LRAC
micro.Feedback: The two concepts refer to different horizons and different input adjustments.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: A learner reads a downward-sloping LRAC segment as diseconomies of scale. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
micro.Choice A: LRAC slope says nothing about scale
micro.Choice B: A downward-sloping LRAC segment requires negative output
micro.Choice C: A downward-sloping LRAC segment represents economies of scale
micro.Choice D: A downward-sloping LRAC segment represents constant returns
micro.Correct Answer: C — A downward-sloping LRAC segment represents economies of scale
micro.Feedback: Falling long-run average cost as output expands is economies of scale.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: A learner says rising LRAC means output itself must be falling. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
micro.Choice A: Rising LRAC means total cost is falling
micro.Choice B: LRAC can rise while output expands; the issue is rising cost per unit at larger scale
micro.Choice C: Rising LRAC requires zero output
micro.Choice D: Output and LRAC always move in opposite directions
micro.Correct Answer: B — LRAC can rise while output expands; the issue is rising cost per unit at larger scale
micro.Feedback: Diseconomies describe a higher average cost at greater output, not a fall in output.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: A learner chooses the largest output on a flat minimum-LRAC segment as MES. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
micro.Choice A: MES is always the largest efficient output
micro.Choice B: MES is where LRAC first begins to fall
micro.Choice C: MES is where total cost is smallest
micro.Choice D: MES is the smallest output that attains the minimum LRAC
micro.Correct Answer: D — MES is the smallest output that attains the minimum LRAC
micro.Feedback: The definition focuses on the minimum scale required to achieve the lowest long-run unit cost.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: A learner says a flat LRAC means output is not changing. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
micro.Choice A: Flat LRAC means economies of scale
micro.Choice B: Flat LRAC means fixed cost is constant in the short run
micro.Choice C: Output can rise while LRAC stays constant; that range reflects constant returns to scale
micro.Choice D: Flat LRAC means output must be zero
micro.Correct Answer: C — Output can rise while LRAC stays constant; that range reflects constant returns to scale
micro.Feedback: Constant returns refers to proportional changes in all inputs and output, leaving long-run cost per unit unchanged.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: How can better organization create economies of scale?
micro.Choice A: Specialization and coordination may lower LRATC over an output range
micro.Choice B: It guarantees negative MP
micro.Choice C: It raises every input price
micro.Choice D: It eliminates opportunity cost
micro.Correct Answer: A — Specialization and coordination may lower LRATC over an output range
micro.Feedback: Scale can permit productive specialization.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: How does specialization connect to economies of scale?
micro.Choice A: A larger scale can support specialized workers or capital that lowers cost per unit
micro.Choice B: Specialization always creates diminishing marginal product
micro.Choice C: Specialization raises fixed cost per unit forever
micro.Choice D: Specialization eliminates opportunity cost
micro.Correct Answer: A — A larger scale can support specialized workers or capital that lowers cost per unit
micro.Feedback: Scale can make specialized tasks and equipment economical, lowering LRAC over a range.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: How do coordination problems connect organizational size to diseconomies of scale?
micro.Choice A: Coordination problems reduce all input prices
micro.Choice B: They guarantee constant returns to scale
micro.Choice C: They turn fixed cost into sunk cost
micro.Choice D: Communication and management complexity can raise cost per unit as the organization grows
micro.Correct Answer: D — Communication and management complexity can raise cost per unit as the organization grows
micro.Feedback: Very large scale can create managerial inefficiencies that push LRAC upward.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: How does the short-run/long-run distinction connect SRATC curves to LRAC?
micro.Choice A: SRATC includes implicit cost but LRAC does not
micro.Choice B: The curves differ only because of revenue
micro.Choice C: Each SRATC holds a plant size fixed, while LRAC allows the firm to choose the least-cost plant for each output
micro.Choice D: LRAC fixes plant size while SRATC changes every input
micro.Correct Answer: C — Each SRATC holds a plant size fixed, while LRAC allows the firm to choose the least-cost plant for each output
micro.Feedback: Long-run flexibility over plant size is what lets LRAC trace the least-cost envelope.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: How is economies of scale different from spreading a fixed short-run cost over more units?
micro.Choice A: Falling AFC is a long-run scale effect only
micro.Choice B: Economies of scale is a long-run change in cost per unit when all inputs can vary; falling AFC is a short-run arithmetic effect
micro.Choice C: They are identical concepts
micro.Choice D: Economies of scale requires one input to remain fixed
micro.Correct Answer: B — Economies of scale is a long-run change in cost per unit when all inputs can vary; falling AFC is a short-run arithmetic effect
micro.Feedback: Both can lower average cost, but they arise from different mechanisms and horizons.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: How can productivity improvements affect long-run average cost?
micro.Choice A: If the same inputs can produce more output, attainable cost per unit can fall
micro.Choice B: Higher productivity necessarily raises LRAC
micro.Choice C: Productivity affects revenue but never cost
micro.Choice D: Productivity makes all costs sunk
micro.Correct Answer: A — If the same inputs can produce more output, attainable cost per unit can fall
micro.Feedback: More output from a given bundle of resources can lower the cost required per unit.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: How does MES build on the idea of economies of scale?
micro.Choice A: MES is the largest feasible plant regardless of cost
micro.Choice B: MES marks the smallest output at which the firm has exhausted the available LRAC reductions
micro.Choice C: MES is where diseconomies first begin at zero output
micro.Choice D: MES measures short-run AFC
micro.Correct Answer: B — MES marks the smallest output at which the firm has exhausted the available LRAC reductions
micro.Feedback: Before MES, additional scale can still lower long-run average cost; at MES the minimum has been reached.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: How does constant returns to scale differ from short-run diminishing marginal product?
micro.Choice A: Constant returns is a long-run proportional change in all inputs; diminishing marginal product varies one input with others fixed
micro.Choice B: They are identical concepts
micro.Choice C: Constant returns requires a fixed plant
micro.Choice D: Diminishing marginal product requires all inputs to change proportionally
micro.Correct Answer: A — Constant returns is a long-run proportional change in all inputs; diminishing marginal product varies one input with others fixed
micro.Feedback: The concepts apply to different production experiments and time horizons.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
