micro.Question: Why can MES matter when comparing efficient firm scale with the size of a market?
micro.Choice A: It determines consumer demand directly
micro.Choice B: It fixes the market price by law
micro.Choice C: It measures accounting profit rather than cost
micro.Choice D: It indicates the minimum output needed to achieve the lowest available long-run unit cost
micro.Correct Answer: D — It indicates the minimum output needed to achieve the lowest available long-run unit cost
micro.Feedback: MES summarizes how much output a firm must reach before it captures all available scale economies.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Economies of scale mean LRATC:
micro.Choice A: Rises
micro.Choice B: Is always constant
micro.Choice C: Equals MC
micro.Choice D: Falls as output expands
micro.Correct Answer: D — Falls as output expands
micro.Feedback: Scale economies lower LRATC.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Diseconomies of scale mean LRATC:
micro.Choice A: Rises as output expands
micro.Choice B: Falls
micro.Choice C: Is constant
micro.Choice D: Equals zero
micro.Correct Answer: A — Rises as output expands
micro.Feedback: Scale diseconomies raise LRATC.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Minimum efficient scale is:
micro.Choice A: The largest possible output
micro.Choice B: The smallest output at minimum LRATC
micro.Choice C: The first positive MP
micro.Choice D: The output with lowest TFC
micro.Correct Answer: B — The smallest output at minimum LRATC
micro.Feedback: MES is the first minimum-LRATC output.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. At what output does LRAC reach its minimum?
micro.Choice A: 30 units
micro.Choice B: 90 units
micro.Choice C: 60 units
micro.Choice D: 120 units
micro.Correct Answer: C — 60 units
micro.Feedback: The LRAC curve bottoms out at Q=60.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: A firm can build one of several plants. Why is LRATC sometimes called an envelope?
micro.Choice A: It averages every plant curve
micro.Choice B: It is always tangent at every point to every plant
micro.Choice C: It excludes capital costs
micro.Choice D: It traces the least-cost portions available across plant choices
micro.Correct Answer: D — It traces the least-cost portions available across plant choices
micro.Feedback: The long-run curve summarizes the best plant choice at each output.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Long-run average cost shows the lowest attainable average cost when:
micro.Choice A: Output must remain constant
micro.Choice B: Only labor can change
micro.Choice C: All inputs can be varied
micro.Choice D: At least one input is fixed
micro.Correct Answer: C — All inputs can be varied
micro.Feedback: The long run allows the firm to choose among plant sizes and adjust all inputs.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: LRAC falls from $28 per unit to $21 per unit as a firm expands its long-run output. This pattern indicates:
micro.Choice A: Diminishing marginal product from a fixed plant
micro.Choice B: Economies of scale
micro.Choice C: Diseconomies of scale
micro.Choice D: Constant returns to scale
micro.Correct Answer: B — Economies of scale
micro.Feedback: Falling long-run average cost as scale expands indicates economies of scale.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: A very large firm becomes harder to coordinate, and its long-run cost per unit rises as it expands further. This is:
micro.Choice A: Diseconomies of scale
micro.Choice B: Economies of scale
micro.Choice C: Constant returns to scale
micro.Choice D: A fall in total product caused by one fixed input
micro.Correct Answer: A — Diseconomies of scale
micro.Feedback: Rising unit cost at greater scale is diseconomies of scale; coordination problems are a common source.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: The LRAC curve is often described as an envelope because it:
micro.Choice A: Adds all short-run fixed costs together
micro.Choice B: Shows the highest ATC at every output
micro.Choice C: Is identical to one short-run ATC curve
micro.Choice D: Traces the lowest attainable ATC across available plant sizes
micro.Correct Answer: D — Traces the lowest attainable ATC across available plant sizes
micro.Feedback: In the long run, the firm can choose the least-cost plant for each output level.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Which is a common source of economies of scale?
micro.Choice A: Management becoming harder to coordinate
micro.Choice B: A fall in marginal product caused by one fixed input
micro.Choice C: Greater specialization as the firm expands
micro.Choice D: A fixed input becoming more crowded
micro.Correct Answer: C — Greater specialization as the firm expands
micro.Feedback: Larger scale can support specialization of labor and capital that lowers average cost.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Which is a common source of diseconomies of scale?
micro.Choice A: Bulk purchasing discounts
micro.Choice B: Coordination and communication problems in a very large organization
micro.Choice C: Spreading fixed cost over more units only
micro.Choice D: Workers specializing in narrower tasks
micro.Correct Answer: B — Coordination and communication problems in a very large organization
micro.Feedback: Large scale can raise organizational and coordination costs per unit.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Why can a firm choose a different plant size in long-run cost analysis?
micro.Choice A: All inputs are variable in the long run
micro.Choice B: Plant size is always variable in the short run
micro.Choice C: Fixed cost is zero at every output
micro.Choice D: Marginal cost determines plant size automatically
micro.Correct Answer: A — All inputs are variable in the long run
micro.Feedback: The long run is defined by enough time to adjust all inputs, including plant capacity.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Minimum efficient scale is the:
micro.Choice A: Largest output the firm can physically produce
micro.Choice B: Output where total cost is lowest
micro.Choice C: First output where marginal product is positive
micro.Choice D: Smallest output at which minimum LRAC is attained
micro.Correct Answer: D — Smallest output at which minimum LRAC is attained
micro.Feedback: MES marks the first output level that reaches the minimum long-run average cost.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: A flat LRAC over a range of output is associated with:
micro.Choice A: Diseconomies of scale throughout the range
micro.Choice B: Diminishing marginal product only
micro.Choice C: Constant returns to scale
micro.Choice D: Economies of scale throughout the range
micro.Correct Answer: C — Constant returns to scale
micro.Feedback: A flat long-run average cost means proportional expansion does not change cost per unit.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: If LRAC first reaches its minimum at 5,000 units and remains flat until 8,000, MES is:
micro.Choice A: 13,000 units
micro.Choice B: 5,000 units
micro.Choice C: 8,000 units
micro.Choice D: 6,500 units
micro.Correct Answer: B — 5,000 units
micro.Feedback: MES is the smallest output that attains the minimum LRAC.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: With constant returns to scale, doubling all inputs tends to:
micro.Choice A: Double output
micro.Choice B: More than double output
micro.Choice C: Increase output by less than double
micro.Choice D: Force output to remain unchanged
micro.Correct Answer: A — Double output
micro.Feedback: Constant returns means output changes in the same proportion as all inputs.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: A large firm’s coordination burden raises LRATC. This is:
micro.Choice A: Diseconomies of scale, not diminishing marginal product
micro.Choice B: Diminishing marginal product only
micro.Choice C: A fixed-cost shift
micro.Choice D: A sunk-cost effect
micro.Correct Answer: A — Diseconomies of scale, not diminishing marginal product
micro.Feedback: The problem arises while all inputs and scale can change.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: A factory’s LRATC reaches $18 at 40,000 units and stays at $18 through 70,000 units. MES is:
micro.Choice A: 70,000 units
micro.Choice B: 40,000 units
micro.Choice C: 55,000 units
micro.Choice D: The output with minimum MC
micro.Correct Answer: B — 40,000 units
micro.Feedback: MES is the smallest output attaining minimum LRATC.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Refer to the LRATC graph. Between which outputs is average cost constant, and how should the regions on either side be interpreted?
micro.Choice A: About 30 to 60; economies of scale precede this interval and diseconomies follow it.
micro.Choice B: About 45 to 80; economies of scale precede this interval and diseconomies follow it.
micro.Choice C: About 45 to 80; diseconomies of scale precede this interval and economies follow it.
micro.Choice D: About 30 to 60; diseconomies of scale precede this interval and economies follow it.
micro.Correct Answer: B — About 45 to 80; economies of scale precede this interval and diseconomies follow it.
micro.Feedback: LRATC falls until about Q = 45, is flat through Q = 80, then rises. Falling, constant and rising long-run average cost represent economies, constant returns and diseconomies of scale, respectively.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Refer to the LRATC graph. What output is marked, and what does it represent for the firm’s scale?
micro.Choice A: 80 units; minimum efficient scale.
micro.Choice B: 60 units; the largest output the firm is technologically able to produce.
micro.Choice C: 60 units; minimum efficient scale.
micro.Choice D: 80 units; the largest output the firm is technologically able to produce.
micro.Correct Answer: C — 60 units; minimum efficient scale.
micro.Feedback: The marker is at Q = 60, the lowest point of LRATC. Minimum efficient scale is the smallest output attaining minimum long-run average cost; it is not a technological capacity ceiling.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Refer to the plant-cost graph. At Q = 75, which available plant has the lowest average cost, and how should a firm able to choose its plant use that comparison?
micro.Choice A: Plant 2; choose the lowest available plant cost at the required output.
micro.Choice B: Plant 3; average all three plant costs to find the cost of the best plant.
micro.Choice C: Plant 2; average all three plant costs to find the cost of the best plant.
micro.Choice D: Plant 3; choose the lowest available plant cost at the required output.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Plant 3; choose the lowest available plant cost at the required output.
micro.Feedback: At Q = 75, SRATC3 lies below SRATC2 and SRATC1. The least-cost plant choice uses the minimum available cost at that output, not the mean of plant costs.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Better software reduces coordination errors as scale expands. Which long-run effect is plausible?
micro.Choice A: The diseconomies-of-scale region begins at a higher output
micro.Choice B: Diminishing MP begins sooner by definition
micro.Choice C: TFC becomes zero
micro.Choice D: MES must become the largest output
micro.Correct Answer: A — The diseconomies-of-scale region begins at a higher output
micro.Feedback: Improved coordination can delay rising LRATC.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: A key input price falls for every plant size. Which long-run effect is most defensible?
micro.Choice A: Only AFC shifts
micro.Choice B: LRATC shifts downward
micro.Choice C: LRATC becomes vertical
micro.Choice D: Diseconomies disappear by definition
micro.Correct Answer: B — LRATC shifts downward
micro.Feedback: Lower input prices reduce the least attainable cost across scales.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Assume input prices are unchanged. All inputs rise 25% and output rises 40%. Which classification fits?
micro.Choice A: Constant returns
micro.Choice B: Diseconomies
micro.Choice C: Economies of scale
micro.Choice D: Diminishing MP only
micro.Correct Answer: C — Economies of scale
micro.Feedback: With unchanged input prices, total input cost rises in proportion to inputs while output rises by a larger percentage, so long-run average cost falls—consistent with economies of scale.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: All inputs rise 50% and output rises 50%. Which classification fits?
micro.Choice A: Economies
micro.Choice B: Diseconomies
micro.Choice C: Negative MP
micro.Choice D: Constant returns to scale
micro.Correct Answer: D — Constant returns to scale
micro.Feedback: Output and input changes are proportional.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Assume input prices are unchanged. All inputs double and output rises 70%. Which classification fits?
micro.Choice A: Diseconomies of scale
micro.Choice B: Economies
micro.Choice C: Constant returns
micro.Choice D: Increasing MP
micro.Correct Answer: A — Diseconomies of scale
micro.Feedback: With unchanged input prices, total input cost rises in proportion to inputs while output rises by a smaller percentage, so long-run average cost rises—consistent with diseconomies of scale.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: LRATC falls from $30 at 10,000 units to $24 at 20,000 units. The firm is in:
micro.Choice A: A diseconomies range
micro.Choice B: An economies-of-scale range
micro.Choice C: A constant-returns range
micro.Choice D: A diminishing-MP proof
micro.Correct Answer: B — An economies-of-scale range
micro.Feedback: Falling LRATC identifies economies.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: LRATC reaches its minimum of $18 at 40,000 units and remains at that minimum through 70,000 units. Which statement is correct?
micro.Choice A: MES is 70,000; the plateau exhibits constant returns
micro.Choice B: MES is 40,000; the plateau exhibits increasing returns
micro.Choice C: MES is 40,000; the plateau exhibits constant returns
micro.Choice D: MES is 70,000; the plateau exhibits decreasing returns
micro.Correct Answer: C — MES is 40,000; the plateau exhibits constant returns
micro.Feedback: The first minimum is MES; flat LRATC is constant returns.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: LRATC rises after 90,000 units because management layers slow decisions. This is:
micro.Choice A: Diminishing MP from fixed capital
micro.Choice B: A fixed-cost shift only
micro.Choice C: An implicit cost omission
micro.Choice D: A coordination-based diseconomy of scale
micro.Correct Answer: D — A coordination-based diseconomy of scale
micro.Feedback: All inputs and organizational scale are changing.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: A large plant spreads a specialized laboratory over more units. This can create:
micro.Choice A: Economies of scale
micro.Choice B: Negative MP
micro.Choice C: A higher AFC at every output
micro.Choice D: A sunk-cost fallacy
micro.Correct Answer: A — Economies of scale
micro.Feedback: Indivisible specialized resources can lower unit cost at scale.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: A firm can choose plants with ATC $26, $22, and $25 at a target output. LRATC there is:
micro.Feedback: Choose the lowest attainable ATC.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: A small plant is cheapest at low Q and a large plant at high Q. What does this show?
micro.Choice A: The large plant always has lower fixed cost
micro.Choice B: The small plant has no variable cost
micro.Choice C: Optimal plant size depends on intended output
micro.Choice D: LRATC averages plant costs
micro.Correct Answer: C — Optimal plant size depends on intended output
micro.Feedback: Long-run choice matches capacity to output.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: A firm’s minimum LRATC is achieved from 30,000 to 55,000 units. Which output is MES?
micro.Choice D: The output with minimum TFC
micro.Feedback: MES is the smallest output at minimum LRATC.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: A firm triples all inputs and output also triples. If input prices are unchanged, LRATC:
micro.Choice A: Remains unchanged
micro.Choice B: Falls by two-thirds
micro.Choice C: Triples
micro.Choice D: Becomes zero
micro.Correct Answer: A — Remains unchanged
micro.Feedback: Cost and output rise proportionally.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: The downward LRATC region represents:
micro.Choice A: Diminishing MP
micro.Choice B: A fixed-cost increase
micro.Choice C: Negative MP
micro.Choice D: Economies of scale
micro.Correct Answer: D — Economies of scale
micro.Feedback: Falling LRATC is economies of scale.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Approximately what LRAC does the graph show at Q=30?
micro.Choice A: About $12
micro.Choice B: About $28
micro.Choice C: About $44
micro.Choice D: About $20
micro.Correct Answer: D — About $20
micro.Feedback: At Q=30, the curve is near the $20 gridline.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. What LRAC is shown at Q = 90?
micro.Choice A: About $20
micro.Choice B: About $8
micro.Choice C: About $12
micro.Choice D: About $36
micro.Correct Answer: A — About $20
micro.Feedback: At Q=90, the curve is again near $20.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Assume input prices are unchanged. A distribution network uses 40% more labor, buildings, and equipment but can handle 60% more shipments. This pattern is consistent with:
micro.Choice A: Diseconomies of scale
micro.Choice B: Constant returns to scale
micro.Choice C: A fixed short-run production function
micro.Choice D: Economies of scale
micro.Correct Answer: D — Economies of scale
micro.Feedback: With unchanged input prices, total input cost rises in proportion to inputs while output rises by a larger percentage, so long-run average cost falls—consistent with economies of scale.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Assume input prices are unchanged. A company expands every input by 25%, but output increases by only 10%. Which scale result does this suggest?
micro.Choice A: Constant returns to scale
micro.Choice B: A reduction in total cost
micro.Choice C: Diseconomies of scale
micro.Choice D: Economies of scale
micro.Correct Answer: C — Diseconomies of scale
micro.Feedback: With unchanged input prices, total input cost rises in proportion to inputs while output rises by a smaller percentage, so long-run average cost rises—consistent with diseconomies of scale.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Plant A has ATC $18 at 500 units and Plant B has ATC $15 at 500 units. If both plants are feasible in the long run, LRAC at 500 units cannot exceed:
micro.Feedback: The firm can choose the lower-cost plant, so the long-run attainable average cost is at most $15.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: LRAC falls from $24 to $18 as output rises from 2,000 to 4,000 units. The firm is operating in a range of:
micro.Choice A: Economies of scale
micro.Choice B: Diseconomies of scale
micro.Choice C: Constant returns to scale
micro.Choice D: Negative marginal product
micro.Correct Answer: A — Economies of scale
micro.Feedback: Average cost is falling as the scale of production expands.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: LRAC rises from $14 to $17 as output rises from 8,000 to 10,000 units. The firm is experiencing:
micro.Choice A: Economies of scale
micro.Choice B: Constant returns to scale
micro.Choice C: Falling total cost
micro.Choice D: Diseconomies of scale
micro.Correct Answer: D — Diseconomies of scale
micro.Feedback: Rising long-run average cost with greater scale indicates diseconomies of scale.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Which statement best distinguishes LRAC from a single SRATC curve?
micro.Choice A: LRAC is total cost rather than average cost
micro.Choice B: SRATC always lies below LRAC
micro.Choice C: LRAC reflects the least-cost plant choice at each output; a SRATC holds plant size fixed
micro.Choice D: LRAC holds all inputs fixed while SRATC varies all inputs
micro.Correct Answer: C — LRAC reflects the least-cost plant choice at each output; a SRATC holds plant size fixed
micro.Feedback: Long-run cost allows plant adjustment; a particular short-run curve corresponds to a given plant.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: A larger factory permits dedicated machinery and specialized teams that reduce unit cost. This is an example of:
micro.Choice A: A sunk-cost effect
micro.Choice B: Economies of scale
micro.Choice C: Diseconomies of scale
micro.Choice D: Diminishing marginal product from a fixed plant
micro.Correct Answer: B — Economies of scale
micro.Feedback: Specialization and indivisible technologies can lower LRAC as scale expands.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: LRAC is $18 at 2,000 units, $14 at 3,000, $12 at 4,000, $12 at 5,000, and $13 at 6,000. MES is:
micro.Choice A: 5,000 units
micro.Choice B: 6,000 units
micro.Choice C: 3,000 units
micro.Choice D: 4,000 units
micro.Correct Answer: D — 4,000 units
micro.Feedback: The minimum LRAC is $12, first reached at 4,000 units.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: A firm increases all inputs by 25% and output also rises by 25%. This is consistent with:
micro.Choice A: Diseconomies of scale
micro.Choice B: Diminishing marginal product caused by fixed capital
micro.Choice C: Constant returns to scale
micro.Choice D: Economies of scale
micro.Correct Answer: C — Constant returns to scale
micro.Feedback: Output changes in the same proportion as all inputs.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: A firm’s LRAC reaches a flat minimum from 10,000 to 14,000 units. Which output is the minimum efficient scale?
micro.Feedback: MES is the first output on the minimum-cost range.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: LRAC is $16 at both 20,000 and 30,000 units, and the curve is flat between them. Over that range the firm experiences:
micro.Choice A: Constant returns to scale
micro.Choice B: Economies of scale
micro.Choice C: Diseconomies of scale
micro.Choice D: Negative returns to labor
micro.Correct Answer: A — Constant returns to scale
micro.Feedback: An unchanged long-run cost per unit over a range is consistent with constant returns to scale.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Why is the largest output on a flat minimum-LRAC segment not the MES?
micro.Choice A: MES is always the midpoint of the flat segment
micro.Choice B: MES is the output with highest total cost
micro.Choice C: MES requires LRAC to begin rising
micro.Choice D: MES is defined as the smallest output that attains minimum LRAC
micro.Correct Answer: D — MES is defined as the smallest output that attains minimum LRAC
micro.Feedback: Larger outputs may also be efficient, but MES identifies the minimum scale needed to achieve the lowest unit cost.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. A firm currently produces 30 units at an LRAC of about $20. Which move most directly approaches minimum efficient scale?
micro.Choice A: Expand toward 60 units
micro.Choice B: Contract toward zero output
micro.Choice C: Expand toward 120 units
micro.Choice D: Remain at 30 because LRAC is already minimized
micro.Correct Answer: A — Expand toward 60 units
micro.Feedback: The minimum occurs at Q=60, so moving from 30 toward 60 approaches MES.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Where LRATC is flat over an output interval, the firm experiences:
micro.Choice A: Diminishing marginal product
micro.Choice B: Constant returns to scale
micro.Choice C: Rising AFC
micro.Choice D: Negative marginal product
micro.Correct Answer: B — Constant returns to scale
micro.Feedback: A flat LRATC indicates unchanged cost per unit as all inputs and output expand proportionally.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: The first output at which the flat minimum begins is:
micro.Choice A: The largest feasible scale
micro.Choice B: Maximum efficient scale
micro.Choice C: Minimum efficient scale
micro.Choice D: The first positive marginal product
micro.Correct Answer: C — Minimum efficient scale
micro.Feedback: MES is the smallest output attaining minimum LRATC.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: The LRATC envelope represents:
micro.Choice A: The average of all SRATC curves
micro.Choice B: The highest fixed cost at each output
micro.Choice C: A firm’s demand curve
micro.Choice D: The lowest attainable ATC among available plant sizes at each output
micro.Correct Answer: D — The lowest attainable ATC among available plant sizes at each output
micro.Feedback: In the long run the firm can choose the least-cost plant for each output.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Assume input prices are unchanged. A firm doubles every input and output rises by only 70%. This is evidence of:
micro.Choice A: Diminishing marginal product
micro.Choice B: Economies of scale
micro.Choice C: Constant returns to scale
micro.Choice D: Diseconomies of scale
micro.Correct Answer: D — Diseconomies of scale
micro.Feedback: With unchanged input prices, total input cost rises in proportion to inputs while output rises by a smaller percentage, so long-run average cost rises—consistent with diseconomies of scale.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Assume input prices are unchanged. A firm doubles every input and output more than doubles. LRATC should generally:
micro.Choice A: Fall
micro.Choice B: Rise
micro.Choice C: Remain fixed by definition
micro.Choice D: Equal marginal product
micro.Correct Answer: A — Fall
micro.Feedback: With unchanged input prices, output rises more than proportionally to total input cost, so long-run average cost falls.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. If output expands from about 30 toward 60 units, what happens to LRAC?
micro.Choice A: LRAC rises, indicating diseconomies of scale
micro.Choice B: LRAC falls, indicating economies of scale
micro.Choice C: LRAC stays constant
micro.Choice D: LRAC falls, indicating diseconomies of scale
micro.Correct Answer: B — LRAC falls, indicating economies of scale
micro.Feedback: The left side of the U-shaped LRAC slopes downward toward its minimum.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Refer to the LRAC graph. If the firm expands all adjustable inputs to raise output from about 60 toward 90 units, what happens to LRAC?
micro.Choice A: LRAC falls, indicating economies of scale
micro.Choice B: LRAC stays at the minimum of about $12
micro.Choice C: LRAC rises, indicating diseconomies of scale
micro.Choice D: LRAC rises, indicating economies of scale
micro.Correct Answer: C — LRAC rises, indicating diseconomies of scale
micro.Feedback: To the right of the minimum, LRAC rises as scale expands.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: At Q = 1,000 the lowest ATC among three plants is $22; at Q = 2,000 it is $17; at Q = 3,000 it is $19. Which sequence best describes LRAC over these outputs?
micro.Choice A: It falls and then rises
micro.Choice B: It rises and then falls
micro.Choice C: It is constant
micro.Choice D: It must equal the ATC of the smallest plant
micro.Correct Answer: A — It falls and then rises
micro.Feedback: LRAC takes the lowest attainable ATC at each output, producing $22, $17, then $19.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: A firm increases every input by 50%, while output rises by 80%. Holding input prices constant, what should happen to average cost?
micro.Choice A: Average cost should rise
micro.Choice B: Average cost must remain unchanged
micro.Choice C: Average cost becomes fixed cost only
micro.Choice D: Average cost should fall
micro.Correct Answer: D — Average cost should fall
micro.Feedback: Output rises more than proportionally to total input use, spreading cost over a larger proportional output increase.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: A manager blames rising LRAC at very large scale on “diminishing marginal product of labor.” What is the best correction?
micro.Choice A: Diseconomies require total product to fall
micro.Choice B: Diminishing marginal product and diseconomies are identical definitions
micro.Choice C: Diseconomies of scale are a long-run phenomenon involving changes in all inputs, not crowding one variable input against fixed inputs
micro.Choice D: The explanation is correct because the long run always has fixed capital
micro.Correct Answer: C — Diseconomies of scale are a long-run phenomenon involving changes in all inputs, not crowding one variable input against fixed inputs
micro.Feedback: Diminishing marginal product is a short-run concept; diseconomies concern scale when all inputs can vary.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: LRAC values are $22 at Q=1, $18 at Q=2, $15 at Q=3, $15 at Q=4, and $17 at Q=5. If quantities are thousands of units, which statement is correct?
micro.Choice A: MES is 5 thousand units because LRAC rises there
micro.Choice B: MES is 2 thousand units because LRAC is already falling
micro.Choice C: MES is 3 thousand units and constant returns hold from 3 to 4 thousand
micro.Choice D: MES is 4 thousand units because it is the largest minimum-cost output
micro.Correct Answer: C — MES is 3 thousand units and constant returns hold from 3 to 4 thousand
micro.Feedback: The minimum $15 first appears at 3 and remains unchanged through 4.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: A firm triples every input and output also triples. If input prices are unchanged, what happens to LRAC?
micro.Choice A: It must rise
micro.Choice B: It remains unchanged
micro.Choice C: It falls to one-third
micro.Choice D: It triples
micro.Correct Answer: B — It remains unchanged
micro.Feedback: Proportional output and input expansion implies constant returns to scale and unchanged long-run unit cost.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: A firm can produce 6,000 units at LRAC $20, 8,000 at $16, 10,000 at $16, and 12,000 at $18. What is the strongest conclusion?
micro.Choice A: MES is 8,000 units; 8,000–10,000 is a minimum-cost range
micro.Choice B: MES is 10,000 units because output is larger
micro.Choice C: MES is 12,000 units because LRAC turns upward there
micro.Choice D: There is no MES because two outputs share the minimum
micro.Correct Answer: A — MES is 8,000 units; 8,000–10,000 is a minimum-cost range
micro.Feedback: MES is the smallest output attaining the minimum $16 LRAC.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Assume input prices are unchanged. A firm expands all inputs 50% and output expands 50%. Which long-run result follows?
micro.Choice A: Diminishing MP and rising LRATC
micro.Choice B: Economies of scale and falling LRATC
micro.Choice C: Negative MP
micro.Choice D: Constant returns to scale and unchanged LRATC
micro.Correct Answer: D — Constant returns to scale and unchanged LRATC
micro.Feedback: With unchanged input prices, proportional increases in all inputs and output leave long-run average cost unchanged, consistent with constant returns to scale.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Two plant sizes have ATC of $22 and $19 at Q=30,000. What does LRATC equal at that quantity if both are feasible?
micro.Feedback: LRATC selects the lowest attainable short-run ATC.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Which observation alone does not prove economies of scale?
micro.Choice A: Total cost rises as output rises
micro.Choice B: LRATC falls as output rises
micro.Choice C: Output more than doubles when all inputs double
micro.Choice D: Average cost falls after plant expansion
micro.Correct Answer: A — Total cost rises as output rises
micro.Feedback: Total cost normally rises with output even under economies of scale.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: The graph gives roughly the same LRAC at Q=30 and Q=90. Which statement distinguishes those two positions?
micro.Choice A: Expanding from either output lowers LRAC at the same rate
micro.Choice B: Expanding from either output raises LRAC at the same rate
micro.Choice C: LRAC stays flat throughout the interval from Q=30 to Q=90
micro.Choice D: Expanding from Q=30 lowers LRAC, while expanding from Q=90 raises LRAC
micro.Correct Answer: D — Expanding from Q=30 lowers LRAC, while expanding from Q=90 raises LRAC
micro.Feedback: Q=30 lies on the economies-of-scale side; Q=90 lies on the diseconomies side.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: A bottler can renew a compact plant with annual cost TC = 18000 + 9Q or lease an automated plant with TC = 42000 + 5Q. Both can supply either forecast: 4,000 or 8,000 units. Which long-run plan minimizes cost across those forecasts?
micro.Choice A: Use the automated plant at both forecasts because its variable cost is lower
micro.Choice B: Use the compact plant at both forecasts because its fixed cost is lower
micro.Choice C: Use the compact plant at 8,000 and the automated plant at 4,000; the switch occurs at 6,000 units
micro.Choice D: Use the compact plant at 4,000 and the automated plant at 8,000; the switch occurs at 6,000 units
micro.Correct Answer: D — Use the compact plant at 4,000 and the automated plant at 8,000; the switch occurs at 6,000 units
micro.Feedback: Set the two total costs equal: $24,000 = $4Q, so the crossover is 6,000. At 4,000 units costs are $54,000 versus $62,000; at 8,000 they are $90,000 versus $82,000. Long-run planning selects the lower attainable cost at each output; this comparison does not infer diminishing marginal returns.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Output doubles while long-run total cost rises only 70%. What happens to LRATC?
micro.Choice A: It rises 30%
micro.Choice B: It is unchanged
micro.Choice C: It doubles
micro.Choice D: It falls 15%
micro.Correct Answer: D — It falls 15%
micro.Feedback: New LRATC is 1.7/2=0.85 of the original.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Output doubles while long-run total cost rises 140%. What happens to LRATC?
micro.Choice A: It rises 20%
micro.Choice B: It falls 30%
micro.Choice C: It is unchanged
micro.Choice D: It rises 140%
micro.Correct Answer: A — It rises 20%
micro.Feedback: New LRATC is 2.4/2=1.2 of the original.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Diminishing MP is observed when labor rises with capital fixed. Can this alone establish diseconomies of scale?
micro.Choice A: Yes, always
micro.Choice B: Yes, if MP is positive
micro.Choice C: No, because scale analysis varies all inputs
micro.Choice D: No, because costs never depend on product
micro.Correct Answer: C — No, because scale analysis varies all inputs
micro.Feedback: Short-run and long-run input experiments differ.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: A firm doubles labor and capital; output triples. If input prices are unchanged, what happens to LRATC?
micro.Choice A: It doubles
micro.Choice B: It rises by 50%
micro.Choice C: It is unchanged
micro.Choice D: It falls by one-third
micro.Correct Answer: D — It falls by one-third
micro.Feedback: Cost doubles while output triples, so average cost becomes two-thirds of the original.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Assume input prices are unchanged. A factory expands every input 100%, but coordination problems limit output growth to 50%. Which combined statement is correct?
micro.Choice A: Diminishing MP and falling LRATC
micro.Choice B: Diseconomies of scale and rising LRATC
micro.Choice C: Constant returns and fixed LRATC
micro.Choice D: Economies and falling LRATC
micro.Correct Answer: B — Diseconomies of scale and rising LRATC
micro.Feedback: With unchanged input prices, input cost doubles while output rises only 50%, so long-run average cost rises; the firm experiences diseconomies of scale.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Two firms have similar LRAC: one operates near Q = 30 and the other near Q = 90. If each increases output slightly, what happens to LRAC?
micro.Choice A: Both firms’ LRAC falls as output expands slightly
micro.Choice B: The first firm’s LRAC falls; the second firm’s LRAC rises
micro.Choice C: Both firms’ LRAC rises as output expands slightly
micro.Choice D: The first firm’s LRAC rises while the second firm’s LRAC falls
micro.Correct Answer: B — The first firm’s LRAC falls; the second firm’s LRAC rises
micro.Feedback: The firms are on opposite sides of the LRAC minimum at Q=60.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: All inputs and total cost double while output rises from 1,000 to 2,400 units. LRAC begins at $30. New LRAC?
micro.Feedback: Cost becomes $60,000 and output 2,400.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Long-run TC is $480,000 at 12,000 units and $675,000 at 15,000 units. Which has lower LRAC, and by how much?
micro.Choice A: 15,000 units, by $5 per unit
micro.Choice B: 12,000 units, by $5 per unit
micro.Choice C: 12,000 units, by $15 per unit
micro.Choice D: Equal LRAC
micro.Correct Answer: B — 12,000 units, by $5 per unit
micro.Feedback: LRAC is $40 versus $45.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Assume input prices are unchanged. All inputs double and output more than doubles. The firm experiences:
micro.Choice A: Diminishing marginal product
micro.Choice B: Diseconomies of scale
micro.Choice C: Negative marginal product
micro.Choice D: Economies of scale
micro.Correct Answer: D — Economies of scale
micro.Feedback: With unchanged input prices, total input cost rises in proportion to inputs while output rises by a larger percentage, so long-run average cost falls—consistent with economies of scale.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Assume input prices are unchanged. All inputs and output double. The firm experiences:
micro.Choice A: Constant returns to scale
micro.Choice B: Economies of scale
micro.Choice C: Diseconomies of scale
micro.Choice D: Diminishing marginal product
micro.Correct Answer: A — Constant returns to scale
micro.Feedback: With unchanged input prices, proportional increases in all inputs and output leave long-run average cost unchanged, consistent with constant returns to scale.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Assume input prices are unchanged. All inputs double and output rises 60%. The firm experiences:
micro.Choice A: Economies of scale
micro.Choice B: Diseconomies of scale
micro.Choice C: Constant returns to scale
micro.Choice D: Increasing MP
micro.Correct Answer: B — Diseconomies of scale
micro.Feedback: With unchanged input prices, total input cost rises in proportion to inputs while output rises by a smaller percentage, so long-run average cost rises—consistent with diseconomies of scale.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: LRATC first reaches its minimum at 25,000 units and remains flat through 40,000. MES is:
micro.Choice A: 40,000 units
micro.Choice B: 32,500 units
micro.Choice C: 25,000 units
micro.Choice D: The largest possible output
micro.Correct Answer: C — 25,000 units
micro.Feedback: MES is the first minimum-cost output.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: At a given output, three plants have ATC of $28, $24, and $31. LRATC is:
micro.Feedback: Choose the least-cost feasible plant.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Which long-run force can create diseconomies of scale?
micro.Choice A: Coordination and communication problems
micro.Choice B: Spreading fixed cost only
micro.Choice C: Early specialization only
micro.Choice D: A decline in TFC
micro.Correct Answer: A — Coordination and communication problems
micro.Feedback: Organizational complexity can raise LRATC.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Which long-run force can create economies of scale?
micro.Choice A: Negative MP by definition
micro.Choice B: Specialization and use of indivisible equipment
micro.Choice C: Higher coordination burden
micro.Choice D: A rise in every input price
micro.Correct Answer: B — Specialization and use of indivisible equipment
micro.Feedback: Scale can spread specialized resources and indivisible inputs.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: The LRATC envelope is below available SRATC curves because:
micro.Choice A: It excludes variable cost
micro.Choice B: It averages only fixed cost
micro.Choice C: The firm selects the least-cost plant at each output
micro.Choice D: Every plant is efficient at every output
micro.Correct Answer: C — The firm selects the least-cost plant at each output
micro.Feedback: Long-run flexibility permits plant choice.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Refer to the LRATC graph. What output is marked, and what does it represent for the firm’s scale?
micro.Choice A: 80 units; minimum efficient scale.
micro.Choice B: 60 units; the largest output the firm is technologically able to produce.
micro.Choice C: 80 units; the largest output the firm is technologically able to produce.
micro.Choice D: 60 units; minimum efficient scale.
micro.Correct Answer: D — 60 units; minimum efficient scale.
micro.Feedback: The marker is at Q = 60, the lowest point of LRATC. Minimum efficient scale is the smallest output attaining minimum long-run average cost; it is not a technological capacity ceiling.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. What output represents minimum efficient scale?
micro.Choice A: 30 units
micro.Choice B: 90 units
micro.Choice C: 60 units
micro.Choice D: 120 units
micro.Correct Answer: C — 60 units
micro.Feedback: MES is the smallest output attaining minimum LRAC; here that point is Q=60.

micro.Learning Objective: COP.6 — Evaluate long-run average cost, economies of scale, diseconomies of scale, and minimum efficient scale.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Which claim is NOT supported by the LRAC curve?
micro.Choice A: LRAC falls as output approaches 60 from the left side
micro.Choice B: LRAC rises as output moves above 60 on the right side
micro.Choice C: The minimum LRAC occurs at approximately Q=60
micro.Choice D: There is a broad flat interval of constant returns to scale
micro.Correct Answer: D — There is a broad flat interval of constant returns to scale
micro.Feedback: The graph has a single rounded minimum rather than a visibly flat minimum-cost interval.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: Which event shifts demand?
micro.Choice A: Consumer income changes
micro.Choice B: The good's own price changes
micro.Choice C: Quantity supplied changes
micro.Choice D: There is movement along the demand curve.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Consumer income changes
micro.Feedback: Income is a demand shifter. The good's own price causes movement along demand.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: If consumer income rises and tablets are a normal good, what happens?
micro.Choice A: Demand for tablets increases
micro.Choice B: Quantity demanded falls
micro.Choice C: Supply of tablets increases
micro.Choice D: Demand for tablets decreases
micro.Correct Answer: A — Demand for tablets increases
micro.Feedback: For a normal good, higher income increases demand.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: When only the price of a good changes, what happens on the demand curve?
micro.Choice A: There is movement along the demand curve
micro.Choice B: The demand curve shifts right
micro.Choice C: The demand curve shifts left
micro.Choice D: Supply shifts right
micro.Correct Answer: A — There is movement along the demand curve
micro.Feedback: A good's own price changes quantity demanded, not demand.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: The price of coffee falls. What is the most precise result?
micro.Choice A: Quantity demanded of coffee increases
micro.Choice B: Demand for coffee increases
micro.Choice C: Supply of coffee decreases
micro.Choice D: Demand for coffee decreases
micro.Correct Answer: A — Quantity demanded of coffee increases
micro.Feedback: Because coffee's own price changed, buyers move along the demand curve.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: Consumers expect the price of laptops to rise next month, so they buy more laptops today. What happens today?
micro.Choice A: Current demand increases
micro.Choice B: Current quantity demanded falls
micro.Choice C: Supply decreases
micro.Choice D: Demand stays fixed because only current price matters
micro.Correct Answer: A — Current demand increases
micro.Feedback: Expectations about future prices can shift current demand.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: A recession lowers consumer income. If restaurant meals are a normal good, what happens to demand for restaurant meals?
micro.Choice A: Demand decreases
micro.Choice B: Demand increases
micro.Choice C: Quantity demanded increases because price changed
micro.Choice D: Supply increases
micro.Correct Answer: A — Demand decreases
micro.Feedback: For a normal good, lower income decreases demand.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: The price of streaming subscriptions rises, and fewer subscriptions are purchased. What is the most precise explanation?
micro.Choice A: Quantity demanded decreased because the good's own price changed
micro.Choice B: Demand decreased because the curve shifted left
micro.Choice C: Supply increased because sellers charged more
micro.Choice D: Demand increased because price rose
micro.Correct Answer: A — Quantity demanded decreased because the good's own price changed
micro.Feedback: The good's own price changed, so this is a movement along demand and a change in quantity demanded.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: Bus fares fall, while a campus adds students who use the bus. Considering each change separately, how does it affect demand for bus rides?
micro.Choice A: Lower fares shift demand right; more students move buyers along demand.
micro.Choice B: Lower fares move buyers along demand; more students shift demand left.
micro.Choice C: Both changes move buyers along the same demand curve.
micro.Choice D: Lower fares move buyers along demand; more students shift demand right.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Lower fares move buyers along demand; more students shift demand right.
micro.Feedback: The fare is the ride's own price, so its fall increases quantity demanded along a curve. More potential riders are a non-price determinant: at each fare, the campus buys more rides, shifting demand right.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: The price of peanut butter rises. If jelly is a complement, what happens to demand for jelly?
micro.Choice A: Demand for jelly decreases
micro.Choice B: Demand for jelly increases
micro.Choice C: Supply of jelly decreases
micro.Choice D: Quantity supplied of jelly increases
micro.Correct Answer: A — Demand for jelly decreases
micro.Feedback: Complements are used together. If peanut butter becomes more expensive, demand for jelly falls.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: The price of bus rides rises. If subway rides are substitutes, what happens to demand for subway rides?
micro.Choice A: Demand for subway rides increases
micro.Choice B: Demand for subway rides decreases
micro.Choice C: Supply of subway rides increases
micro.Choice D: Quantity demanded of bus rides increases
micro.Correct Answer: A — Demand for subway rides increases
micro.Feedback: When the price of a substitute rises, demand for the other good increases.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: The law of demand says that, other things equal:
micro.Choice A: As price falls, quantity demanded rises
micro.Choice B: As price falls, demand always shifts left
micro.Choice C: As price rises, supply shifts left
micro.Choice D: As price rises, quantity demanded rises
micro.Correct Answer: A — As price falls, quantity demanded rises
micro.Feedback: The law of demand says price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: When the price of a good falls, what happens to quantity demanded?
micro.Choice A: Quantity demanded increases
micro.Choice B: Demand decreases
micro.Choice C: Supply increases
micro.Choice D: The demand curve shifts left
micro.Correct Answer: A — Quantity demanded increases
micro.Feedback: A change in the good's own price causes movement along the demand curve.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: A change in which factor would shift the demand curve?
micro.Choice A: Consumer income
micro.Choice B: The good's own price
micro.Choice C: Movement along the curve
micro.Choice D: Quantity supplied
micro.Correct Answer: A — Consumer income
micro.Feedback: Income is a demand shifter. The good's own price changes quantity demanded.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: If income rises and tablets are a normal good, what happens to demand for tablets?
micro.Choice A: Demand increases
micro.Choice B: Demand decreases
micro.Choice C: Quantity demanded decreases because price changed
micro.Choice D: Supply decreases
micro.Correct Answer: A — Demand increases
micro.Feedback: For a normal good, higher income increases demand.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: Two goods are substitutes when:
micro.Choice A: One good can be used in place of the other
micro.Choice B: The goods are typically consumed together
micro.Choice C: The goods use the same raw material in production
micro.Choice D: A price change for one good leaves demand for the other unrelated
micro.Correct Answer: A — One good can be used in place of the other
micro.Feedback: Substitutes are goods that can replace one another.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: Two goods are complements when:
micro.Choice A: They are commonly used together
micro.Choice B: One good can be used in place of the other
micro.Choice C: The goods are produced using the same inputs
micro.Choice D: A price change for one good leaves demand for the other unchanged.
micro.Correct Answer: A — They are commonly used together
micro.Feedback: Complements are goods used together.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: If the price of a substitute for iPhones falls, what happens to demand for iPhones?
micro.Choice A: Demand for iPhones decreases
micro.Choice B: Demand for iPhones increases
micro.Choice C: Supply of iPhones increases
micro.Choice D: Quantity demanded of iPhones increases because iPhone price fell
micro.Correct Answer: A — Demand for iPhones decreases
micro.Feedback: If a substitute gets cheaper, buyers shift away from the original good.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: If the price of printer ink rises, what likely happens to demand for printers?
micro.Choice A: Demand for printers decreases
micro.Choice B: Demand for printers increases
micro.Choice C: Supply of printers increases
micro.Choice D: Quantity supplied of printers increases
micro.Correct Answer: A — Demand for printers decreases
micro.Feedback: Printers and ink are complements, so higher ink prices reduce demand for printers.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
micro.Question: On the displayed gourmet-donut demand curve, what price and quantity are shown at point A?
micro.Choice A: $10 and 100 thousand donuts
micro.Choice B: $5 and 225 thousand donuts
micro.Choice C: $10 and 225 thousand donuts
micro.Choice D: $14 and 100 thousand donuts
micro.Correct Answer: A — $10 and 100 thousand donuts
micro.Feedback: At point A, the demand curve pairs a price of $10 with a quantity demanded of 100 thousand donuts.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
micro.Question: In the displayed coffee market, the move from D0 to D1 represents:
micro.Choice A: A decrease in demand
micro.Choice B: An increase in quantity demanded caused only by a lower price
micro.Choice C: An increase in demand
micro.Choice D: A decrease in supply
micro.Correct Answer: C — An increase in demand
micro.Feedback: D1 lies to the right of D0, showing that consumers demand more coffee at each common price.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
micro.Question: How should the change in the tea demand curve from D0 to D1 be classified?
micro.Choice A: A decrease in demand
micro.Choice B: An increase in demand
micro.Choice C: A decrease in quantity demanded caused only by a higher price
micro.Choice D: An increase in supply
micro.Correct Answer: A — A decrease in demand
micro.Feedback: D1 lies to the left of D0, showing that consumers demand less tea at each common price.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: The price of headphones falls from $80 to $60, and consumers buy more headphones. What is the most precise statement?
micro.Choice A: Quantity demanded increases
micro.Choice B: Demand increases
micro.Choice C: Supply increases
micro.Choice D: Demand shifts right
micro.Correct Answer: A — Quantity demanded increases
micro.Feedback: A change in the good's own price causes movement along demand, so quantity demanded changes.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: A consumer's income rises, and meal delivery is a normal good. At every price, consumers now want more meal delivery. What happened?
micro.Choice A: Demand increased
micro.Choice B: Quantity demanded increased because price fell
micro.Choice C: Supply increased
micro.Choice D: Demand decreased
micro.Correct Answer: A — Demand increased
micro.Feedback: Income is a demand shifter. For a normal good, higher income increases demand.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: Compare two changes: first, D1/S1 to D2/S1; second, D1/S1 to D1/S2. Which statement correctly classifies both changes and gives their ending equilibria?
micro.Choice A: First, demand increases and ends at (P3, Q2); second, quantity demanded increases along D1 and ends at (P1, Q2).
micro.Choice B: First, demand increases and ends at (P3, Q3); second, quantity demanded increases along D1 and ends at (P1, Q3).
micro.Choice C: First, quantity demanded changes along an unchanged demand curve and ends at (P3, Q2); second, demand shifts and ends at (P1, Q2).
micro.Choice D: First, quantity demanded changes along an unchanged demand curve and ends at (P3, Q3); second, demand shifts and ends at (P1, Q3).
micro.Correct Answer: A — First, demand increases and ends at (P3, Q2); second, quantity demanded increases along D1 and ends at (P1, Q2).
micro.Feedback: D1/S1 to D2/S1 switches demand curves, so demand increases; the ending intersection is (P3,Q2). D1/S1 to D1/S2 stays on D1: price falls and quantity demanded increases along that curve, ending at (P1,Q2). A change in quantity demanded along a curve differs from a change in demand itself.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: The price of tablets falls, and consumers buy more tablets. No non-price determinant changed. What happened?
micro.Choice A: Quantity demanded increased along the existing demand curve.
micro.Choice B: Demand increased and the curve shifted right
micro.Choice C: Supply increased and the curve shifted right
micro.Choice D: Demand decreased because price fell
micro.Correct Answer: A — Quantity demanded increased along the existing demand curve.
micro.Feedback: A change in the good's own price causes movement along demand, not a demand shift.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: A student says, 'Demand increased because the price rose.' What is the correct response?
micro.Choice A: A demand increase can raise price; a price rise alone moves along demand.
micro.Choice B: That is correct because demand always means the current price
micro.Choice C: That describes a supply increase
micro.Choice D: That proves the good is inferior
micro.Correct Answer: A — A demand increase can raise price; a price rise alone moves along demand.
micro.Feedback: A price rise can be caused by a demand increase, but the price rise itself does not shift demand.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: A market survey shows that at every possible price consumers now plan to buy more electric bikes than before. Which event cannot explain the change?
micro.Choice A: A subsidy to buyers
micro.Choice B: A rise in gasoline prices
micro.Choice C: A fall in the price of electric bikes itself
micro.Choice D: Stronger preferences for low-emission travel
micro.Correct Answer: C — A fall in the price of electric bikes itself
micro.Feedback: A change in the good’s own price causes movement along demand, not a shift of the entire demand curve.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: The price of streaming subscriptions rises, and consumers buy fewer subscriptions. What happened?
micro.Choice A: Quantity demanded decreased
micro.Choice B: Demand decreased
micro.Choice C: Supply increased
micro.Choice D: Demand shifted right
micro.Correct Answer: A — Quantity demanded decreased
micro.Feedback: A change in the good's own price changes quantity demanded, not demand.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: Consumers expect laptop prices to rise next month, so more laptops are purchased today. What happens to current demand for laptops?
micro.Choice A: Demand increases
micro.Choice B: Quantity demanded decreases
micro.Choice C: Supply decreases
micro.Choice D: Demand stays fixed because only current price matters
micro.Correct Answer: A — Demand increases
micro.Feedback: Expectations about higher future prices can increase demand today.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: A popular celebrity endorsement makes more buyers want a product at every price. What happens?
micro.Choice A: Demand shifts right
micro.Choice B: Quantity demanded falls
micro.Choice C: Supply shifts left
micro.Choice D: The product's own price changed
micro.Correct Answer: A — Demand shifts right
micro.Feedback: A change in tastes shifts demand; more buyers wanting the product shifts demand right.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: The price of tablets rises. What happens in the market for tablet cases, a complement?
micro.Choice A: Demand for tablet cases decreases
micro.Choice B: Demand for tablet cases increases
micro.Choice C: Supply of tablet cases increases
micro.Choice D: Quantity supplied of tablets decreases
micro.Correct Answer: A — Demand for tablet cases decreases
micro.Feedback: If tablets become more expensive, fewer tablets are bought, reducing demand for tablet cases.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: The price of tea rises. If coffee is a substitute for tea, what happens to demand for coffee?
micro.Choice A: Demand for coffee increases
micro.Choice B: Demand for coffee decreases
micro.Choice C: Quantity demanded of coffee decreases because coffee price changed
micro.Choice D: Supply of coffee decreases
micro.Correct Answer: A — Demand for coffee increases
micro.Feedback: When a substitute becomes more expensive, demand for the other good rises.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: The market initially clears at D1/S2. Consumer income rises for this normal good, while supply conditions remain unchanged. Which explanation and equilibrium movement fit the graph?
micro.Choice A: Demand shifts right; equilibrium moves from (P1, Q2) to (P2, Q3).
micro.Choice B: Demand shifts right; equilibrium moves from (P2, Q1) to (P3, Q2).
micro.Choice C: Demand shifts left; equilibrium moves from (P1, Q2) to (P2, Q3).
micro.Choice D: Demand shifts left; equilibrium moves from (P2, Q1) to (P3, Q2).
micro.Correct Answer: A — Demand shifts right; equilibrium moves from (P1, Q2) to (P2, Q3).
micro.Feedback: Higher income increases demand for a normal good. With supply fixed at S2, demand shifts right from D1 to D2, moving equilibrium from (P1,Q2) to (P2,Q3). This is a demand shift, not a supply change.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Common Misconception: Calling an across-the-board schedule change a movement along demand.
micro.Question: A survey shows buyers want more electric scooters at every listed price than they did last month. Which statement is most precise?
micro.Choice A: Quantity demanded increased because the scooter price fell.
micro.Choice B: Demand increased, so the entire demand schedule shifted right.
micro.Choice C: Demand increased only at the market price.
micro.Choice D: The law of demand stopped applying to electric scooters.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Demand increased, so the entire demand schedule shifted right.
micro.Feedback: Wanting more at every price is a rightward shift of demand, not a change in quantity demanded caused by the good’s own price.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
micro.Question: What economic change does the move from A to B in the donuts graph represent?
micro.Choice A: Price falls $5; quantity demanded increases by 100 thousand along the existing curve.
micro.Choice B: Price falls $5; quantity demanded increases by 125 thousand along the existing curve.
micro.Choice C: Price falls $5; demand increases by 125 thousand because the curve shifts right.
micro.Choice D: Price falls $5; demand increases by 100 thousand because the curve shifts right.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Price falls $5; quantity demanded increases by 125 thousand along the existing curve.
micro.Feedback: A is at $10 and 100 thousand donuts; B is at $5 and 225 thousand. Price falls $5 and quantity demanded rises 125 thousand. Because A and B lie on the same demand curve, this is a movement along demand rather than an increase in demand.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
micro.Question: Moving from point A to point B on the displayed demand curve changes quantity demanded by:
micro.Choice A: A decrease of 125 thousand donuts
micro.Choice B: An increase of 5 thousand donuts
micro.Choice C: An increase of 125 thousand donuts
micro.Choice D: An increase of 225 thousand donuts
micro.Correct Answer: C — An increase of 125 thousand donuts
micro.Feedback: Quantity demanded rises from 100 thousand at A to 225 thousand at B, an increase of 125 thousand.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
micro.Question: At a price of $10 on the displayed coffee graph, how does quantity demanded change when demand shifts from D0 to D1?
micro.Choice A: It decreases from 125 thousand to 50 thousand
micro.Choice B: It increases from 100 thousand to 175 thousand
micro.Choice C: It stays at 125 thousand
micro.Choice D: It increases from 50 thousand to 125 thousand
micro.Correct Answer: D — It increases from 50 thousand to 125 thousand
micro.Feedback: At $10, D0 shows 50 thousand units and D1 shows 125 thousand, so quantity demanded at that price rises by 75 thousand.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
micro.Question: Coffee is a normal good. At a price of $10, compare D0 and D1. Which income change and quantity change are consistent with the graph?
micro.Choice A: Income rises; quantity demanded rises by 75 thousand
micro.Choice B: Income rises; quantity demanded rises by 100 thousand
micro.Choice C: Income falls; quantity demanded falls by 75 thousand
micro.Choice D: Income falls; quantity demanded falls by 100 thousand
micro.Correct Answer: A — Income rises; quantity demanded rises by 75 thousand
micro.Feedback: At $10, D0 shows 50 thousand units and D1 shows 125 thousand. The 75-thousand increase at the same price is consistent with higher income for a normal good.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. At a price of $4, how does quantity demanded change as demand shifts from D0 to D1?
micro.Choice A: It increases from 100 thousand to 200 thousand
micro.Choice B: It decreases from 200 thousand to 100 thousand
micro.Choice C: It decreases from 300 thousand to 200 thousand
micro.Choice D: It stays at 100 thousand
micro.Correct Answer: B — It decreases from 200 thousand to 100 thousand
micro.Feedback: At $4, D0 shows 200 thousand units while D1 shows 100 thousand, a decrease of 100 thousand at the same price.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
micro.Question: Tea is a normal good. At a price of $4, compare D0 and D1. Which income change and quantity change are consistent with the graph?
micro.Choice A: Income falls; quantity demanded falls by 75 thousand
micro.Choice B: Income rises; quantity demanded rises by 100 thousand
micro.Choice C: Income falls; quantity demanded falls by 100 thousand
micro.Choice D: Income rises; quantity demanded rises by 75 thousand
micro.Correct Answer: C — Income falls; quantity demanded falls by 100 thousand
micro.Feedback: At $4, quantity demanded is 200 thousand on D0 and 100 thousand on D1. This 100-thousand decrease at the same price is consistent with lower income for a normal good.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: A product gets cheaper because supply increases. Students say demand increased because quantity sold rose. What is the error?
micro.Choice A: They confused an increase in quantity demanded with an increase in demand
micro.Choice B: They correctly identified a demand shift
micro.Choice C: They confused a price floor with a price ceiling
micro.Choice D: They ignored that supply can never change price
micro.Correct Answer: A — They confused an increase in quantity demanded with an increase in demand
micro.Feedback: If price falls because supply increases, buyers move along the demand curve. Quantity demanded rises, but demand itself does not shift.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: A product becomes cheaper and sales rise. A follow-up survey finds that buyers now want more at EVERY unchanged price after a favorable health report. A student attributes all extra purchases to movement along the old demand curve. Which correction uses the survey evidence?
micro.Choice A: Demand is unchanged; every increase in sales is a movement along demand.
micro.Choice B: Demand shifts left; lower prices mean buyers want less at each fixed price.
micro.Choice C: Supply must shift left; buyer surveys establish producers’ costs.
micro.Choice D: Demand shifts right; the price change alone cannot explain greater planned purchases at a fixed price.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Demand shifts right; the price change alone cannot explain greater planned purchases at a fixed price.
micro.Feedback: Unlike a supply-driven price fall alone, the survey reports greater demand at fixed prices after new health information. That identifies a demand shift, although the survey alone does not determine the separate supply change or how much of observed sales growth each cause explains.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: The price of peanut butter rises. If jelly is a complement, what happens in the jelly market?
micro.Choice A: Demand for jelly decreases
micro.Choice B: Demand for jelly increases
micro.Choice C: Supply of jelly decreases
micro.Choice D: Quantity demanded of jelly increases
micro.Correct Answer: A — Demand for jelly decreases
micro.Feedback: Peanut butter and jelly are complements. If peanut butter gets more expensive, demand for jelly falls.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: The price of bus rides rises. If subway rides are substitutes, what happens in the subway market?
micro.Choice A: Demand for subway rides increases
micro.Choice B: Demand for subway rides decreases
micro.Choice C: Supply of subway rides decreases
micro.Choice D: Quantity supplied of bus rides increases
micro.Correct Answer: A — Demand for subway rides increases
micro.Feedback: When the price of a substitute rises, demand for the other good increases.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: Consumers expect the price of coffee to fall next month. What happens to current demand for coffee, other things equal?
micro.Choice A: Current demand decreases
micro.Choice B: Current demand increases
micro.Choice C: Current quantity supplied increases
micro.Choice D: Supply shifts left
micro.Correct Answer: A — Current demand decreases
micro.Feedback: If buyers expect a lower future price, they delay purchases, reducing current demand.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: The market initially clears at D1/S1. A substitute becomes more expensive, while supply conditions remain unchanged. Which explanation and equilibrium movement fit the graph?
micro.Choice A: Demand shifts right; equilibrium moves from (P2, Q1) to (P3, Q2).
micro.Choice B: Demand shifts right; equilibrium moves from (P1, Q2) to (P2, Q3).
micro.Choice C: Demand shifts left; equilibrium moves from (P2, Q1) to (P3, Q2).
micro.Choice D: Demand shifts left; equilibrium moves from (P1, Q2) to (P2, Q3).
micro.Correct Answer: A — Demand shifts right; equilibrium moves from (P2, Q1) to (P3, Q2).
micro.Feedback: A higher substitute price increases demand for this good, shifting demand right from D1 to D2. With supply fixed at S1, the graph moves from (P2,Q1) to (P3,Q2). Both equilibrium price and quantity rise.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: The market initially clears at D2/S2. A close substitute becomes cheaper, while supply conditions remain unchanged. Which explanation and equilibrium movement fit the graph?
micro.Choice A: Demand shifts left; equilibrium moves from (P2, Q3) to (P1, Q2).
micro.Choice B: Demand shifts left; equilibrium moves from (P3, Q2) to (P2, Q1).
micro.Choice C: Demand shifts right; equilibrium moves from (P2, Q3) to (P1, Q2).
micro.Choice D: Demand shifts right; equilibrium moves from (P3, Q2) to (P2, Q1).
micro.Correct Answer: A — Demand shifts left; equilibrium moves from (P2, Q3) to (P1, Q2).
micro.Feedback: A cheaper substitute reduces demand for this good, shifting demand left from D2 to D1. On unchanged S2, equilibrium moves from (P2,Q3) to (P1,Q2). Both equilibrium price and quantity fall.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Question: The price of a substitute for coffee rises. What happens in the coffee market, holding other factors constant?
micro.Choice A: Demand for coffee increases, raising equilibrium price and quantity
micro.Choice B: Quantity demanded of coffee decreases along the same curve
micro.Choice C: Supply of coffee increases because coffee is now profitable
