micro.Choice D: As zero scarcity
micro.Correct Answer: A — As lower short-run demand elasticity
micro.Feedback: Inertia reduces the measured short-run quantity response.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: Economists use elasticity to measure:
micro.Choice A: How strongly one variable responds to a change in another
micro.Choice B: Only whether a variable rises or falls
micro.Choice C: The dollar value of every market transaction
micro.Choice D: The slope of any line without regard to units
micro.Correct Answer: A — How strongly one variable responds to a change in another
micro.Feedback: Elasticity is a responsiveness measure: percentage response divided by percentage change in a driver.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: Why is an elasticity coefficient usually unit-free?
micro.Choice A: It always uses dollars
micro.Choice B: It compares percentage changes
micro.Choice C: It divides quantity by price levels
micro.Choice D: It converts all values to index numbers
micro.Correct Answer: B — It compares percentage changes
micro.Feedback: Because both numerator and denominator are percentage changes, measurement units cancel.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: A price elasticity of demand equal to 1.8 is classified as:
micro.Choice A: Inelastic
micro.Choice B: Unit elastic
micro.Choice C: Elastic
micro.Choice D: Perfectly inelastic
micro.Correct Answer: C — Elastic
micro.Feedback: A demand elasticity greater than one means quantity responds proportionally more than price.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: A price elasticity of demand equal to 0.45 is classified as:
micro.Choice A: Elastic
micro.Choice B: Unit elastic
micro.Choice C: Perfectly elastic
micro.Choice D: Inelastic
micro.Correct Answer: D — Inelastic
micro.Feedback: A coefficient between zero and one is inelastic.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: A price elasticity of demand equal to 1 is:
micro.Choice A: Unit elastic
micro.Choice B: Perfectly elastic
micro.Choice C: Perfectly inelastic
micro.Choice D: Necessarily negative income elasticity
micro.Correct Answer: A — Unit elastic
micro.Feedback: Unit elasticity means equal proportional changes in price and quantity demanded.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: A vertical demand curve represents demand that is:
micro.Choice A: Perfectly elastic
micro.Choice B: Perfectly inelastic
micro.Choice C: Unit elastic everywhere
micro.Choice D: Elastic only at high prices
micro.Correct Answer: B — Perfectly inelastic
micro.Feedback: Quantity does not respond to price on a vertical demand curve, so elasticity is zero.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: A horizontal demand curve represents demand that is:
micro.Choice A: Perfectly inelastic
micro.Choice B: Unit elastic everywhere
micro.Choice C: Perfectly elastic
micro.Choice D: Inelastic because slope is zero
micro.Correct Answer: C — Perfectly elastic
micro.Feedback: A tiny price increase eliminates quantity demanded along a perfectly elastic demand curve.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: Demand is generally more elastic when consumers have:
micro.Choice A: Fewer alternatives
micro.Choice B: Less time to adjust
micro.Choice C: A smaller share of income at stake
micro.Choice D: Many close substitutes
micro.Correct Answer: D — Many close substitutes
micro.Feedback: Close substitutes make it easier to switch away when price rises.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: Compared with luxuries, necessities generally have demand that is:
micro.Choice A: Less elastic
micro.Choice B: More elastic
micro.Choice C: Perfectly elastic
micro.Choice D: Always unit elastic
micro.Correct Answer: A — Less elastic
micro.Feedback: Consumers have less ability to reduce purchases of necessities after a price increase.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: Compared with a broadly defined market, a narrowly defined market usually has:
micro.Choice A: Less elastic demand
micro.Choice B: More elastic demand
micro.Choice C: The same elasticity by definition
micro.Choice D: Perfectly inelastic demand
micro.Correct Answer: B — More elastic demand
micro.Feedback: Narrow markets have more close substitutes, which raises demand elasticity.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: Demand tends to be more elastic for a good that takes up:
micro.Choice A: A tiny share of the buyer’s budget
micro.Choice B: No time to compare alternatives
micro.Choice C: A large share of the buyer’s budget
micro.Choice D: A fixed legal quantity
micro.Correct Answer: C — A large share of the buyer’s budget
micro.Feedback: Large budget shares give buyers a stronger reason to adjust.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: Over a longer time horizon, demand for gasoline is likely to become:
micro.Choice A: Less elastic
micro.Choice B: Perfectly inelastic
micro.Choice C: Unrelated to available alternatives
micro.Choice D: More elastic
micro.Correct Answer: D — More elastic
micro.Feedback: Over time, drivers can change vehicles, locations, and travel habits.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: Which feature most directly makes demand for one brand of bottled water elastic?
micro.Choice A: Many nearly identical brands
micro.Choice B: Water is necessary for life
micro.Choice C: The product is sold in liters
micro.Choice D: The market price is positive
micro.Correct Answer: A — Many nearly identical brands
micro.Feedback: Brand-level demand is elastic because buyers can switch among close substitutes.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: Which purchase is most likely to have inelastic demand in the short run?
micro.Choice A: A vacation package
micro.Choice B: A required medication with few substitutes
micro.Choice C: A premium restaurant meal
micro.Choice D: One brand of breakfast cereal
micro.Correct Answer: B — A required medication with few substitutes
micro.Feedback: Necessity, limited substitutes, and short adjustment time all reduce elasticity.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: Which demand curve is steeper in the graph, and why is that visual slope different from price elasticity of demand?
micro.Choice A: D1 is steeper; slope uses the axis units, whereas elasticity compares percentage changes.
micro.Choice B: D2 is steeper; its numerical slope is also its price elasticity at every point.
micro.Choice C: D1 is steeper; changing dollars to cents leaves the numerical slope unchanged.
micro.Choice D: D2 is steeper; slope uses the axis units, whereas elasticity compares percentage changes.
micro.Correct Answer: D — D2 is steeper; slope uses the axis units, whereas elasticity compares percentage changes.
micro.Feedback: D2 is the steeper curve. A slope depends on the units on the axes. Elasticity uses percentage changes, so it is not the numerical slope and requires no unit-specific scale.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: Refer to the linear demand curve. Identify the price at C and classify demand as you move from C through B to A.
micro.Choice A: $12; demand changes from elastic to unit elastic to inelastic.
micro.Choice B: $10; demand changes from elastic to unit elastic to inelastic.
micro.Choice C: $12; demand changes from inelastic to unit elastic to elastic.
micro.Choice D: $10; demand changes from inelastic to unit elastic to elastic.
micro.Correct Answer: A — $12; demand changes from elastic to unit elastic to inelastic.
micro.Feedback: C is at a price of $12 on the upper half of demand. Demand is elastic there, unit elastic at the midpoint B, and inelastic at A on the lower half. Constant slope does not mean constant percentage responsiveness.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: A horizontal demand curve is the graphical form of:
micro.Choice A: Perfectly inelastic demand
micro.Choice B: Unit-elastic demand
micro.Choice C: Perfectly elastic demand
micro.Choice D: A supply curve
micro.Correct Answer: C — Perfectly elastic demand
micro.Feedback: A horizontal demand curve is the limiting case of perfectly elastic demand.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: What elasticity case is represented by the vertical demand curve?
micro.Choice A: Perfectly elastic demand
micro.Choice B: Unit-elastic demand
micro.Choice C: A perfectly elastic supply curve
micro.Choice D: Perfectly inelastic demand
micro.Correct Answer: D — Perfectly inelastic demand
micro.Feedback: A vertical demand curve means quantity demanded does not change when price changes.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: A linear demand curve intersects the price axis at $100 and the quantity axis at 1,000 units. Near the price intercept, which combination of elasticity and marginal revenue is expected?
micro.Choice A: Inelastic demand and negative marginal revenue
micro.Choice B: Unit-elastic demand and zero price
micro.Choice C: Elastic demand and positive marginal revenue
micro.Choice D: Perfectly inelastic demand and maximum quantity
micro.Correct Answer: C — Elastic demand and positive marginal revenue
micro.Feedback: Upper portions of a linear demand curve are elastic, where marginal revenue is positive.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: A linear demand curve intersects the axes. At a point near the quantity intercept, which combination is expected?
micro.Choice A: Elastic demand and positive marginal revenue
micro.Choice B: Unit-elastic demand and maximum price
micro.Choice C: Perfectly elastic demand and zero quantity
micro.Choice D: Inelastic demand and negative marginal revenue
micro.Correct Answer: D — Inelastic demand and negative marginal revenue
micro.Feedback: Lower portions are inelastic and adding sales reduces total revenue.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: A university raises parking prices and observes little first-semester change, but large declines after students revise housing and transit choices. This illustrates:
micro.Choice A: Demand becoming more elastic over time
micro.Choice B: Supply becoming perfectly inelastic
micro.Choice C: Income elasticity turning negative
micro.Choice D: A movement from elastic to inelastic demand
micro.Correct Answer: A — Demand becoming more elastic over time
micro.Feedback: The adjustment menu expands over time.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: A national market for all beverages is compared with demand for one flavor of one soda brand. Which statement is strongest?
micro.Choice A: The national beverage market is more elastic because it contains more products
micro.Choice B: The brand-flavor demand is more elastic because the market is defined narrowly
micro.Choice C: Both have identical elasticity because they use the same currency
micro.Choice D: The brand flavor is less elastic because it has fewer buyers
micro.Correct Answer: B — The brand-flavor demand is more elastic because the market is defined narrowly
micro.Feedback: Narrow definitions expose many close alternatives.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: A platform adds many alternative sellers, reducing buyers’ switching costs. What happens to seller-level demand?
micro.Choice A: It becomes more elastic
micro.Choice B: It becomes more inelastic
micro.Choice C: It becomes perfectly inelastic
micro.Choice D: It changes only income elasticity
micro.Correct Answer: A — It becomes more elastic
micro.Feedback: Lower switching costs and more alternatives raise responsiveness to seller price.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: A loyalty program causes customers to forfeit points if they switch sellers. What is the likely short-run effect on demand elasticity?
micro.Choice A: It raises supply elasticity
micro.Choice B: It makes income elasticity negative
micro.Choice C: It lowers demand elasticity by raising switching costs
micro.Choice D: It creates perfect competition
micro.Correct Answer: C — It lowers demand elasticity by raising switching costs
micro.Feedback: Switching penalties reduce immediate substitution.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: A commuter has few alternatives this week but can relocate or change vehicles over several years. Demand for gasoline is likely to be:
micro.Choice A: More elastic in the short run than in the long run
micro.Choice B: Equally elastic in both periods by definition
micro.Choice C: More elastic in the long run than in the short run
micro.Choice D: Perfectly elastic in both periods
micro.Correct Answer: C — More elastic in the long run than in the short run
micro.Feedback: Longer adjustment periods create more substitution possibilities.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: Demand for “food” is less elastic than demand for “restaurant lunches” mainly because:
micro.Choice A: Restaurant lunches are always necessities
micro.Choice B: Food has a steeper curve in every graph
micro.Choice C: Broad markets always have lower prices
micro.Choice D: Food is a broader market with fewer substitutes outside the category
micro.Correct Answer: D — Food is a broader market with fewer substitutes outside the category
micro.Feedback: Narrower definitions expose more alternatives within the broader category.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Starting at C, which initial price and sequence of elasticity classifications describe movement down the demand curve through B to A?
micro.Choice A: $10; demand changes from elastic to unit elastic to inelastic.
micro.Choice B: $12; demand changes from elastic to unit elastic to inelastic.
micro.Choice C: $12; demand changes from inelastic to unit elastic to elastic.
micro.Choice D: $10; demand changes from inelastic to unit elastic to elastic.
micro.Correct Answer: B — $12; demand changes from elastic to unit elastic to inelastic.
micro.Feedback: C is at a price of $12 on the upper half of demand. Demand is elastic there, unit elastic at the midpoint B, and inelastic at A on the lower half. Constant slope does not mean constant percentage responsiveness.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: At the midpoint of a linear demand curve, demand is typically:
micro.Choice A: Perfectly elastic
micro.Choice B: Perfectly inelastic
micro.Choice C: Unit elastic
micro.Choice D: Income inelastic
micro.Correct Answer: C — Unit elastic
micro.Feedback: For a linear demand curve, the midpoint separates elastic and inelastic regions.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: Refer to the demand curve. Which change in quantity per $1 price decrease and interpretation of elasticity are correct?
micro.Choice A: 5 units; the constant unit response does not imply constant percentage responsiveness.
micro.Choice B: 7.5 units; the constant unit response does not imply constant percentage responsiveness.
micro.Choice C: 7.5 units; the constant unit response implies constant percentage responsiveness.
micro.Choice D: 5 units; the constant unit response implies constant percentage responsiveness.
micro.Correct Answer: B — 7.5 units; the constant unit response does not imply constant percentage responsiveness.
micro.Feedback: The line connects P = 16, Q = 0 to P = 0, Q = 120, giving 120/16 = 7.5 additional units per $1 decrease. Elasticity also uses P/Q, which varies along the line. Constant slope is not constant elasticity.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: The upper and lower portions of the plotted demand curve have the same slope. Which point elasticities at C and A, and explanation, reconcile that slope with different percentage responses?
micro.Choice A: 2 at C and 1/2 at A; the price-to-quantity ratio changes even though slope is constant.
micro.Choice B: 3 at C and 1/3 at A; a constant slope means equal percentage responsiveness at both points.
micro.Choice C: 2 at C and 1/2 at A; a constant slope means equal percentage responsiveness at both points.
micro.Choice D: 3 at C and 1/3 at A; the price-to-quantity ratio changes even though slope is constant.
micro.Correct Answer: D — 3 at C and 1/3 at A; the price-to-quantity ratio changes even though slope is constant.
micro.Feedback: The intercepts are P = 16 and Q = 120, so |d Q/d P| = 7.5. At C, P = 12 and Q = 30 give 7.5 × 12/30 = 3; at A, P = 4 and Q = 90 give 7.5 × 4/90 = 1/3. Elasticity falls through one at B because percentage bases change, not because the straight line changes slope.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: A product has many substitutes, but buyers have signed one-year contracts. Which statement is most defensible?
micro.Choice A: Demand must be perfectly elastic immediately
micro.Choice B: Short-run demand can be inelastic; renewal demand more elastic
micro.Choice C: Contracts make long-run demand less elastic
micro.Choice D: Substitutes matter only for supply elasticity
micro.Correct Answer: B — Short-run demand can be inelastic; renewal demand more elastic
micro.Feedback: Contractual switching costs suppress short-run response but not necessarily later response.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: Refer to the linear demand graph. Which point elasticities at C and A illustrate the role of the price-to-quantity ratio in elasticity?
micro.Choice A: 2 at C and 1/2 at A; the price-to-quantity ratio changes even though slope is constant.
micro.Choice B: 3 at C and 1/3 at A; the price-to-quantity ratio changes even though slope is constant.
micro.Choice C: 3 at C and 1/3 at A; a constant slope means equal percentage responsiveness at both points.
micro.Choice D: 2 at C and 1/2 at A; a constant slope means equal percentage responsiveness at both points.
micro.Correct Answer: B — 3 at C and 1/3 at A; the price-to-quantity ratio changes even though slope is constant.
micro.Feedback: The intercepts are P = 16 and Q = 120, so |d Q/d P| = 7.5. At C, P = 12 and Q = 30 give 7.5 × 12/30 = 3; at A, P = 4 and Q = 90 give 7.5 × 4/90 = 1/3. Elasticity falls through one at B because percentage bases change, not because the straight line changes slope.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: A pharmaceutical patent expires and many close substitutes enter. Holding other determinants constant, what happens to the original brand’s demand elasticity and pricing power?
micro.Choice A: Demand becomes less elastic and markup rises
micro.Choice B: Demand becomes perfectly inelastic because medicine is necessary
micro.Choice C: Demand becomes more elastic and sustainable markup falls
micro.Choice D: Elasticity is unchanged because only price affects demand
micro.Correct Answer: C — Demand becomes more elastic and sustainable markup falls
micro.Feedback: Entry creates switching options, increasing responsiveness and limiting markup.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: A government taxes a product with inelastic demand partly to raise revenue. Which additional fact most threatens the stability of that revenue over time?
micro.Choice A: The product currently takes a small budget share
micro.Choice B: Supply is upward sloping
micro.Choice C: Close substitutes are developing rapidly
micro.Choice D: The statute requires sellers to remit the tax
micro.Correct Answer: C — Close substitutes are developing rapidly
micro.Feedback: New substitutes can make long-run demand substantially more elastic.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: A city evaluates a fuel tax using a one-month elasticity estimate. Why might this underestimate the tax’s eventual effect on fuel consumption?
micro.Choice A: Short-run demand always has more substitutes
micro.Choice B: Long-run elasticity must equal zero
micro.Choice C: Tax incidence eliminates time-horizon effects
micro.Choice D: Long-run demand allows vehicle, residence, and commuting adjustments
micro.Correct Answer: D — Long-run demand allows vehicle, residence, and commuting adjustments
micro.Feedback: Long-run behavioral and capital adjustments usually increase demand elasticity.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: A firm’s demand curve becomes flatter after a rival enters, but the axes are rescaled at the same time. What is required before concluding that demand became more elastic?
micro.Choice A: Only a visual comparison of slopes
micro.Choice B: Proof that the rival charges a lower nominal price
micro.Choice C: A unit-free elasticity calculation at comparable price-quantity points
micro.Choice D: A calculation of income elasticity
micro.Correct Answer: C — A unit-free elasticity calculation at comparable price-quantity points
micro.Feedback: Graph scaling can change apparent slope, so percentage responsiveness must be compared.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: Two products have identical slopes on graphs measured in different quantity units. Which conclusion is valid?
micro.Choice A: They have identical elasticity everywhere
micro.Choice B: The product with larger units is more elastic
micro.Choice C: Both must be unit elastic
micro.Choice D: No elasticity ranking follows without price and quantity information
micro.Correct Answer: D — No elasticity ranking follows without price and quantity information
micro.Feedback: Slope depends on units; elasticity also uses the point’s P/Q ratio.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: A demand estimate is elastic at the current price but the firm plans a large price cut. Why is using one constant coefficient risky?
micro.Choice A: Elasticity may change along the demand curve and outside the estimated range
micro.Choice B: Elasticity always becomes infinite after a price cut
micro.Choice C: Percentage changes cannot be calculated for price cuts
micro.Choice D: Only supply elasticity changes with price
micro.Correct Answer: A — Elasticity may change along the demand curve and outside the estimated range
micro.Feedback: A local or arc estimate may not extrapolate to a large move.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: A regression estimates how many units quantity demanded changes when price rises by one dollar. Why must this estimate be converted before it can be reported as a price elasticity?
micro.Choice A: Every regression coefficient is already unit-free
micro.Choice B: Convert it using the current price and quantity scale
micro.Choice C: Elasticity ignores the price coefficient
micro.Choice D: Only cross-price coefficients require conversion
micro.Correct Answer: B — Convert it using the current price and quantity scale
micro.Feedback: The estimate measures a change in units per dollar. Elasticity compares percentage changes, so the conversion also requires the current price and quantity.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: The graph shows otherwise comparable products D1 and D2 over the marked price decrease. Which revenue changes and explanation using substitute availability are consistent with midpoint elasticity?
micro.Choice A: D1: $400→$520; D2: $300→$280. More close substitutes is a plausible explanation for D1’s greater responsiveness.
micro.Choice B: D1: $450→$570; D2: $350→$330. More close substitutes is a plausible explanation for D1’s greater responsiveness.
micro.Choice C: D1: $450→$570; D2: $350→$330. More close substitutes is a plausible explanation for D2’s lower responsiveness.
micro.Choice D: D1: $400→$520; D2: $300→$280. More close substitutes is a plausible explanation for D2’s lower responsiveness.
micro.Correct Answer: B — D1: $450→$570; D2: $350→$330. More close substitutes is a plausible explanation for D1’s greater responsiveness.
micro.Feedback: On D1, revenue goes from 10 × 45 = $450 to 6 × 95 = $570, and midpoint elasticity is 1.43. On D2 it goes from 10 × 35 = $350 to 6 × 55 = $330, with elasticity 0.89. More close substitutes can explain greater responsiveness on D1, although the graph alone cannot establish the cause.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: A student says elasticity is just the direction of a change. What correction is needed?
micro.Choice A: Elasticity measures the size of a percentage response relative to a percentage change
micro.Choice B: Elasticity records only whether demand slopes down
micro.Choice C: Elasticity is the market price divided by income
micro.Choice D: Elasticity is another name for total revenue
micro.Correct Answer: A — Elasticity measures the size of a percentage response relative to a percentage change
micro.Feedback: Elasticity adds magnitude to direction by comparing percentage changes.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: Which coefficient represents the strongest demand response to price?
micro.Feedback: The larger absolute coefficient indicates greater responsiveness.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: Which change most likely makes brand-level demand more elastic?
micro.Choice A: Consumers become locked into annual contracts
micro.Choice B: The purchase becomes more necessary
micro.Choice C: Buyers have less time to adjust
micro.Choice D: Several close competing brands enter
micro.Correct Answer: D — Several close competing brands enter
micro.Feedback: More close substitutes increase switching.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: Which product characteristic most likely reduces demand elasticity?
micro.Choice A: The item is a necessity with few substitutes
micro.Choice B: The item is a luxury with many substitutes
micro.Choice C: The market is narrowly defined
micro.Choice D: The purchase takes a large budget share
micro.Correct Answer: A — The item is a necessity with few substitutes
micro.Feedback: Necessity and few substitutes limit response.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: Why is demand for one brand of salt more elastic than demand for salt as a category?
micro.Choice A: Salt is measured in pounds
micro.Choice B: The brand has many close substitutes within the category
micro.Choice C: Category demand has a flatter slope in every graph
micro.Choice D: Brand demand ignores consumer preferences
micro.Correct Answer: B — The brand has many close substitutes within the category
micro.Feedback: Narrower markets have more alternatives.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: A vertical demand curve has elasticity:
micro.Choice A: One
micro.Choice B: Infinity
micro.Choice C: Zero
micro.Choice D: A value that rises with price
micro.Correct Answer: C — Zero
micro.Feedback: Quantity is fixed as price changes.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: A horizontal demand curve has elasticity:
micro.Choice A: Zero
micro.Choice B: One
micro.Choice C: Negative one
micro.Choice D: Effectively infinite
micro.Correct Answer: D — Effectively infinite
micro.Feedback: An arbitrarily small price increase causes demand to vanish.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: Which displayed demand curve has zero price elasticity?
micro.Choice A: D2
micro.Choice B: D1
micro.Choice C: Both D1 and D2
micro.Choice D: Neither D1 nor D2
micro.Correct Answer: A — D2
micro.Feedback: D2 is vertical, so quantity does not respond to price and elasticity is zero.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: A product is a necessity but one brand has many rivals. Which elasticity comparison is correct?
micro.Choice A: Both must be inelastic
micro.Choice B: Brand demand can be elastic while category demand remains inelastic
micro.Choice C: Category demand must be more elastic
micro.Choice D: Necessity eliminates market-definition effects
micro.Correct Answer: B — Brand demand can be elastic while category demand remains inelastic
micro.Feedback: The relevant substitute set differs by market definition.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: A regression slope is −200 units per dollar. Why is this not enough to classify elasticity?
micro.Choice A: Negative slopes are always elastic
micro.Choice B: All slopes below −1 are elastic
micro.Choice C: Elasticity also requires the current price and quantity scale
micro.Choice D: Elasticity uses only units per dollar
micro.Correct Answer: C — Elasticity also requires the current price and quantity scale
micro.Feedback: Point elasticity scales the slope by P/Q.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: A price-comparison service makes close substitutes easier to find. Before its launch a 5% price increase reduced sales by 2%; afterwards the same increase reduces sales by 8%, over equal adjustment periods. Which interpretation and revenue prediction fit the evidence?
micro.Choice A: Absolute demand elasticity falls from 2.5 to 0.625; a small price increase now tends to raise revenue.
micro.Choice B: Demand becomes more elastic solely because the firm moves upward along an unchanged demand curve; comparison information plays no role.
micro.Choice C: Absolute demand elasticity rises from 0.4 to 1.6; a small price increase now tends to reduce revenue because buyers can switch more easily.
micro.Choice D: Demand remains inelastic because both tests use the same price increase; quantity responses cannot change the classification.
micro.Correct Answer: C — Absolute demand elasticity rises from 0.4 to 1.6; a small price increase now tends to reduce revenue because buyers can switch more easily.
micro.Feedback: The response ratios are 2/5=0.4 and 8/5=1.6. Easier comparison improves substitution options. Above unit elasticity, the percentage quantity loss outweighs a small price increase.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: A seller forecasts that a 5% price rise will raise revenue using today’s demand elasticity of 0.4. A close substitute launches before the planned price rise. Which revision and test would make the forecast more defensible?
micro.Choice A: Reestimate demand after entry; if elasticity rises above one, the predicted revenue effect can reverse.
micro.Choice B: Keep 0.4 because elasticity is a permanent property of the product; test only whether accounting costs changed.
micro.Choice C: Raise the revenue forecast automatically because a new substitute always increases demand for this seller’s product.
micro.Choice D: Use supply elasticity in place of demand elasticity because another producer has entered.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Reestimate demand after entry; if elasticity rises above one, the predicted revenue effect can reverse.
micro.Feedback: The new substitute changes buyers’ alternatives. The revenue prediction depends on responsiveness at the time of the price change, so an estimate above one can overturn the old inelastic-demand forecast.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: A supply increase occurs in a market with highly elastic demand. Compared with inelastic demand, what happens?
micro.Choice A: Quantity rises less and price falls more
micro.Choice B: Price and quantity do not change
micro.Choice C: Total revenue must always rise
micro.Choice D: Quantity rises more and price falls less
micro.Correct Answer: D — Quantity rises more and price falls less
micro.Feedback: Elastic buyers absorb added supply with a larger quantity response and smaller price decline.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: Two customer groups buy the same product at the same price. A 4% price increase reduces Group A’s purchases by 2% and Group B’s by 8%. Both groups have the same adjustment period. B spends a larger income share on the product and has more substitutes. Which conclusion is justified?
micro.Choice A: A is less responsive than B, consistent with the stated budget-share and substitution differences; equal prices do not imply equal elasticities.
micro.Choice B: A is more responsive than B because a smaller quantity response gives the larger elasticity.
micro.Choice C: Both have the same elasticity because price and adjustment period are the same; the responses measure supply instead.
micro.Choice D: The comparison proves that time horizon explains the difference, despite the identical adjustment periods.
micro.Correct Answer: A — A is less responsive than B, consistent with the stated budget-share and substitution differences; equal prices do not imply equal elasticities.
micro.Feedback: The absolute elasticities are 0.5 and 2. Greater budget exposure and more substitutes are plausible reasons for B’s stronger response; the equal time horizon rules out that particular explanation.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: A product is a necessity but has many close generic substitutes. Which determinant should dominate brand-level demand?
micro.Choice A: Brand demand can be elastic even if category demand is inelastic, because consumers can switch brands without giving up the necessity.
micro.Choice B: Brand demand should be less elastic than category demand, because a brand includes fewer possible purchases than the category.
micro.Choice C: Brand and category demand should have equal elasticity, because both purchases satisfy the same basic need.
micro.Choice D: Brand demand can be elastic only if the entire category is a luxury, because generic substitutes cannot change necessity status.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Brand demand can be elastic even if category demand is inelastic, because consumers can switch brands without giving up the necessity.
micro.Feedback: Elasticity depends on the defined choice set.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: A product has no close substitutes today but represents a large budget share. What is the best conclusion?
micro.Choice A: Few substitutes establish inelastic demand; budget share changes spending levels but cannot affect responsiveness.
micro.Choice B: Few substitutes restrain responsiveness while a large budget share encourages adjustment; estimate their combined effect in this market.
micro.Choice C: The large budget share establishes elastic demand; the absence of substitutes changes price but cannot affect responsiveness.
micro.Choice D: The two determinants imply unit elasticity; their opposing directions necessarily cancel quantitatively.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Few substitutes restrain responsiveness while a large budget share encourages adjustment; estimate their combined effect in this market.
micro.Feedback: Elasticity determinants are tendencies, not mechanical rules.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.1 — Foundations and determinants of elasticity
micro.Question: A climate policy raises energy prices, encourages substitution, induces innovation, and changes household location over a decade. What does this imply about short-run versus long-run demand elasticity?
micro.Choice A: Long-run elasticity should be smaller because consumers exhaust their easiest adjustments during the first month
micro.Choice B: Over a decade, innovation and relocation give households more ways to respond, so demand may be more elastic than a first-month estimate suggests
micro.Choice C: The policy changes supply responsiveness but leaves household demand responsiveness essentially unchanged over time
micro.Choice D: The first-month estimate remains the best long-run measure because later innovation and relocation are separate effects
micro.Correct Answer: B — Over a decade, innovation and relocation give households more ways to respond, so demand may be more elastic than a first-month estimate suggests
micro.Feedback: Technology, capital, and location adjustments expand long-run response.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: A learner calculates different elasticity values for A-to-B and B-to-A. Which statement best corrects the error?
micro.Choice A: Use midpoint averages in both percentage-change denominators
micro.Choice B: Use the first point in both directions
micro.Choice C: Average the two elasticity answers after rounding
micro.Choice D: Use only the larger endpoint
micro.Correct Answer: A — Use midpoint averages in both percentage-change denominators
micro.Feedback: The midpoint method is symmetric.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: A learner divides percentage price change by percentage quantity change for demand. Which statement best corrects the error?
micro.Choice A: The ratio is price change divided by income change
micro.Choice B: Divide percentage quantity change by percentage price change
micro.Choice C: Either ratio is acceptable
micro.Choice D: Use total revenue divided by price
micro.Correct Answer: B — Divide percentage quantity change by percentage price change
micro.Feedback: Quantity response belongs in the numerator.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: A learner reports demand elasticity as negative and classifies the good as inferior. Which statement best corrects the error?
micro.Choice A: Negative price elasticity proves inferiority
micro.Choice B: Change the sign to identify complements
micro.Choice C: Use absolute price elasticity; income elasticity identifies inferiority
micro.Choice D: Price elasticity must be zero
micro.Correct Answer: C — Use absolute price elasticity; income elasticity identifies inferiority
micro.Feedback: The demand-law sign is conventionally ignored for magnitude classification.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: Consumer surplus changes after a price increase. Which elasticity fact predicts whether quantity contracts a little or a lot?
micro.Choice A: Price elasticity of supply only
micro.Choice B: Price elasticity of demand
micro.Choice C: Income elasticity of supply
micro.Choice D: The GDP deflator
micro.Correct Answer: B — Price elasticity of demand
micro.Feedback: Demand elasticity governs the quantity response that shapes surplus loss.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: A budget line rotates after a price change. Which elasticity summarizes the resulting proportional quantity response for one good?
micro.Choice A: Price elasticity of supply
micro.Choice B: Cross-price elasticity of firms
micro.Choice C: Price elasticity of demand
micro.Choice D: Tax elasticity
micro.Correct Answer: C — Price elasticity of demand
micro.Feedback: Consumer choice generates the demand response summarized by elasticity.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: A price change creates both substitution and income effects. Which measure summarizes their combined percentage quantity response?
micro.Choice A: Price elasticity of demand
micro.Choice B: Price elasticity of supply
micro.Choice C: Tax incidence
micro.Choice D: Producer surplus
micro.Correct Answer: A — Price elasticity of demand
micro.Feedback: Observed demand elasticity reflects the total quantity response.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: The midpoint method calculates percentage changes using:
micro.Choice A: Only the starting value
micro.Choice B: The average of the starting and ending values
micro.Choice C: Only the ending value
micro.Choice D: The larger value in both denominators
micro.Correct Answer: B — The average of the starting and ending values
micro.Feedback: Using averages makes the elasticity estimate symmetric for increases and decreases.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: At point B on the displayed linear demand curve, what price and quantity are shown?
micro.Choice A: $8 and 60 units
micro.Choice B: $12 and 30 units
micro.Choice C: $4 and 90 units
micro.Choice D: $8 and 90 units
micro.Correct Answer: A — $8 and 60 units
micro.Feedback: Point B is marked at P = $8 and Q = 60.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: Which labeled point is the midpoint of the displayed linear demand curve?
micro.Choice A: Point A
micro.Choice B: Point B
micro.Choice C: Point C
micro.Choice D: None of the labeled points
micro.Correct Answer: B — Point B
micro.Feedback: The line runs from P = $16, Q = 0 to P = $0, Q = 120, so its midpoint is P = $8, Q = 60 at B.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: Which labeled point lies in the inelastic portion of the displayed linear demand curve?
micro.Choice A: Point B
micro.Choice B: Point C
micro.Choice C: Point A
micro.Choice D: All three points are equally elastic
micro.Correct Answer: C — Point A
micro.Feedback: Below the midpoint of a linear demand curve, quantity is relatively large and price relatively small, so demand is inelastic; A is in that region.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: At a price of $10 in the displayed graph, which curve shows the larger quantity demanded?
micro.Choice A: D2, at 45 units
micro.Choice B: D1, at 35 units
micro.Choice C: D1, at 45 units
micro.Choice D: D2, at 55 units
micro.Correct Answer: C — D1, at 45 units
micro.Feedback: At P = $10, point B on D1 is Q = 45 while point D on D2 is Q = 35.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: When price is $6, which demand curve shows the larger quantity demanded?
micro.Choice A: D2, at 95 units
micro.Choice B: D1, at 55 units
micro.Choice C: D2, at 45 units
micro.Choice D: D1, at 95 units
micro.Correct Answer: D — D1, at 95 units
micro.Feedback: At P = $6, D1 is at point A with Q = 95, while D2 is at point C with Q = 55.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: The price elasticity coefficient of a perfectly inelastic demand curve is:
micro.Choice C: Infinity
micro.Feedback: With zero percentage change in quantity despite a price change, the elasticity coefficient is zero.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: A point elasticity is measured on a differentiable demand curve. Which expression combines slope with the current point?
micro.Choice A: The absolute value of (dP/dQ) × (P+Q)
micro.Choice B: Q divided by P only
micro.Choice C: The absolute value of (dQ/dP) × (P/Q)
micro.Choice D: The slope squared
micro.Correct Answer: C — The absolute value of (dQ/dP) × (P/Q)
micro.Feedback: Point elasticity scales the derivative by the current price-to-quantity ratio.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: A market researcher observes annual software licenses: price moves from $80 to $92, while quantity demanded moves from 5000 to 4100. Use the midpoint method to estimate elasticity and select the coefficient.
micro.Feedback: The midpoint estimate is about 1.42; this places the observation in the elastic range.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: A market researcher observes stadium club seats: price moves from $300 to $345, while quantity demanded moves from 900 to 720. Use the midpoint method to estimate elasticity and select the coefficient.
micro.Feedback: The midpoint estimate is about 1.59; this places the observation in the elastic range.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: A market researcher observes specialty insulin pumps: price moves from $5000 to $5400, while quantity demanded moves from 1200 to 1140. Use the midpoint method to estimate elasticity and select the coefficient.
micro.Feedback: The midpoint estimate is about 0.67; this places the observation in the inelastic range.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: A market researcher observes organic grocery boxes: price moves from $45 to $51, while quantity demanded moves from 1600 to 1360. Use the midpoint method to estimate elasticity and select the coefficient.
micro.Feedback: The midpoint estimate is about 1.3; this places the observation in the elastic range.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: A market researcher observes private tutoring hours: price moves from $60 to $72, while quantity demanded moves from 1000 to 760. Use the midpoint method to estimate elasticity and select the coefficient.
micro.Feedback: The midpoint estimate is about 1.5; this places the observation in the elastic range.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: A market researcher observes winter heating fuel: price moves from $3.2 to $3.8, while quantity demanded moves from 8000 to 7400. Use the midpoint method to estimate elasticity and select the coefficient.
micro.Feedback: The midpoint estimate is about 0.45; this places the observation in the inelastic range.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: A market researcher observes luxury handbags: price moves from $900 to $810, while quantity demanded moves from 450 to 585. Use the midpoint method to estimate elasticity and select the coefficient.
micro.Feedback: The midpoint estimate is about 2.48; this places the observation in the elastic range.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: A market researcher observes online news subscriptions: price moves from $12 to $15, while quantity demanded moves from 10000 to 7600. Use the midpoint method to estimate elasticity and select the coefficient.
micro.Feedback: The midpoint estimate is about 1.23; this places the observation in the elastic range.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: A market researcher observes commercial drone rentals: price moves from $200 to $230, while quantity demanded moves from 700 to 560. Use the midpoint method to estimate elasticity and select the coefficient.
micro.Feedback: The midpoint estimate is about 1.59; this places the observation in the elastic range.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: For perfectly elastic demand at a market price of $5, what is the idealized result if one seller tries to charge more than $5?
micro.Choice A: Quantity demanded remains fixed at 50
micro.Choice B: Quantity demanded rises without limit
micro.Choice C: Quantity demanded falls to zero
micro.Choice D: Demand becomes perfectly inelastic
micro.Correct Answer: C — Quantity demanded falls to zero
micro.Feedback: With perfectly elastic demand, buyers will not accept a price above the market price represented by the horizontal curve.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: A firm estimates demand elasticity at 2.5. Holding other factors constant, a 4 percent price cut is predicted to change quantity demanded by approximately:
micro.Choice A: A 1.6 percent increase
micro.Choice B: A 6.5 percent decrease
micro.Choice C: A 10 percent increase
micro.Choice D: A 10 percent decrease
micro.Correct Answer: C — A 10 percent increase
micro.Feedback: Quantity response is elasticity times the price change magnitude: 2.5 × 4% = 10%.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: A firm estimates demand elasticity at 0.3. A 10 percent price increase is predicted to reduce quantity demanded by approximately:
micro.Choice A: 30 percent
micro.Choice B: 13 percent
micro.Choice C: 0.3 percent
micro.Choice D: 3 percent
micro.Correct Answer: D — 3 percent
micro.Feedback: The predicted quantity response is 0.3 × 10% = 3%.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: For demand Q = 100 − 2P, what is elasticity at P = 20, where Q = 60?
micro.Choice A: About 1.50
micro.Choice B: About 2.00
micro.Choice C: About 40.00
micro.Choice D: About 0.67
micro.Correct Answer: D — About 0.67

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: For demand Q = 100 − 2P, what is elasticity at P = 40, where Q = 20?
micro.Feedback: 2 × 40/20 = 4, so demand is elastic near the price intercept.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: How do the absolute elasticity magnitudes of D1 and D2 compare?
micro.Choice A: Both equal one
micro.Choice B: D1 equals zero while D2 approaches infinity
micro.Choice C: Both equal zero
micro.Choice D: D1 approaches infinity while D2 equals zero
micro.Correct Answer: D — D1 approaches infinity while D2 equals zero
micro.Feedback: Perfectly elastic demand is the infinite-elasticity limiting case; perfectly inelastic demand has elasticity zero.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: A streaming service raises price by 5 percent and subscriptions fall by 12 percent. Demand is:
micro.Choice A: Elastic
micro.Choice B: Inelastic
micro.Choice C: Unit elastic
micro.Choice D: Perfectly inelastic
micro.Correct Answer: A — Elastic
micro.Feedback: Quantity changes proportionally more than price, so elasticity exceeds one.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: A clinic raises a required treatment price by 8 percent and visits fall by 2 percent. Demand is:
micro.Choice A: Elastic
micro.Choice B: Inelastic
micro.Choice C: Unit elastic
micro.Choice D: Perfectly elastic
micro.Correct Answer: B — Inelastic
micro.Feedback: Quantity changes proportionally less than price.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: A seller operating where demand is elastic lowers price. Which result is most likely?
micro.Choice A: Quantity rises by a larger percentage than price falls
micro.Choice B: Quantity rises by a smaller percentage than price falls
micro.Choice C: Quantity does not change
micro.Choice D: Total revenue must fall
micro.Correct Answer: A — Quantity rises by a larger percentage than price falls
micro.Feedback: Elastic demand means a proportionally larger quantity response.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: Why is the midpoint method preferred when comparing two price-quantity observations?
micro.Choice A: It always produces an elasticity of one
micro.Choice B: It removes the need for percentage changes
micro.Choice C: It gives one symmetric estimate in either direction
micro.Choice D: It uses only the lower price and quantity
micro.Correct Answer: C — It gives one symmetric estimate in either direction
micro.Feedback: Average denominators eliminate direction-dependent base values.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: A price increase reduces quantity demanded, so the raw price elasticity of demand is negative. Economists usually report:
micro.Choice A: Its square
micro.Choice B: Only the negative sign
micro.Choice C: Zero whenever price and quantity move oppositely
micro.Choice D: Its absolute value
micro.Correct Answer: D — Its absolute value
micro.Feedback: Demand elasticity is usually stated as a positive magnitude for classification.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: On D1, compare the labeled quantities at the two marked prices. What is the change in quantity demanded?
micro.Choice A: 50 units
micro.Choice B: 20 units
micro.Choice C: 40 units
micro.Choice D: 60 units
micro.Correct Answer: A — 50 units
micro.Feedback: The change is 95 − 45 = 50 units.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. How much does quantity demanded change between the two marked points on D2?
micro.Choice A: 50 units

micro.Choice C: Demand becomes vertical after large changes

micro.Correct Answer: A — Elasticity can vary along the curve and outside the estimated range
micro.Feedback: Local estimates may not extrapolate to large changes.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: Demand is perfectly inelastic: quantity demanded remains at the same positive amount when market price increases. A student correctly computes zero midpoint demand elasticity, then concludes that total revenue is unchanged. Which diagnosis is correct?
micro.Choice A: Zero quantity change gives zero elasticity, but the higher-price point has higher revenue because the same positive quantity sells at a higher price.
micro.Choice B: Zero elasticity also means zero price change, so equal revenue follows.
micro.Choice C: Zero elasticity means quantity rises enough to offset the price rise, so equal revenue follows.
micro.Choice D: A vertical demand curve has infinite elasticity, so the midpoint calculation must be reversed.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Zero quantity change gives zero elasticity, but the higher-price point has higher revenue because the same positive quantity sells at a higher price.
micro.Feedback: Quantity is unchanged while price increases, so the midpoint quantity-change numerator and demand elasticity are zero. Revenue is P×Q: with a positive fixed Q, the higher price produces higher revenue.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: A seller sees no quantity response after a tiny price test. Why is concluding perfectly inelastic demand premature?
micro.Choice A: The zero response estimates elasticity precisely at zero; repeat the same tiny test only to check the seller’s revenue arithmetic.
micro.Choice B: The test may hide a response because of noise, contracts or its size; vary the test and allow adjustment before treating demand as perfectly inelastic.
micro.Choice C: The test establishes elastic demand because buyers delayed purchases; a larger increase must therefore raise revenue.
micro.Choice D: The test establishes unit elasticity because quantity was stable; the next test should hold total revenue constant.
micro.Correct Answer: B — The test may hide a response because of noise, contracts or its size; vary the test and allow adjustment before treating demand as perfectly inelastic.
micro.Feedback: Observed response may be imprecise or constrained over the test window.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: An elasticity estimate is based on a period when income and competitor prices also changed. Why might the estimate fail to isolate the effect of price on quantity demanded?
micro.Choice A: The midpoint formula requires quantity to remain unchanged
micro.Choice B: A time series cannot contain movements along a demand curve
micro.Choice C: Income and competitor prices may also explain the quantity change
micro.Choice D: Changing income establishes that demand is perfectly elastic
micro.Correct Answer: C — Income and competitor prices may also explain the quantity change
micro.Feedback: Income and competitor prices can shift demand, so the observed quantity change cannot necessarily be attributed to the product’s own price alone.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: A firm’s price and quantity move in the same direction after a demand shift. Why can the observed ratio not be treated as price elasticity of demand?
micro.Choice A: The observations prove a positive own-price demand elasticity
micro.Choice B: The observations establish that the product is an inferior good
micro.Choice C: The observations are invalid unless supply is perfectly inelastic
micro.Choice D: The observations reflect a demand shift, not a fixed demand curve
micro.Correct Answer: D — The observations reflect a demand shift, not a fixed demand curve
micro.Feedback: Elasticity of demand requires isolating a price change along a given demand relationship.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: A supply shift causes price and quantity to move in opposite directions. Under what condition can the resulting arc approximate demand elasticity?
micro.Choice A: Demand stays unchanged, and a separate change in supply causes the price change
micro.Choice B: Demand also shifts at the same time
micro.Choice C: The legal tax payer is known
micro.Choice D: Income elasticity equals one
micro.Correct Answer: A — Demand stays unchanged, and a separate change in supply causes the price change
micro.Feedback: If demand stays unchanged, a price change caused by an independent change in supply traces a movement along the demand curve.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: A firm estimates the price elasticity of demand at 1.05, with a wide confidence interval spanning values below and above one. What is the prudent pricing conclusion?
micro.Choice A: The price increase should lower revenue because the point estimate exceeds one; the interval affects the size but cannot affect the sign.
micro.Choice B: The price increase should raise revenue because the interval includes inelastic values; the point estimate affects the size but cannot affect the sign.
micro.Choice C: Revenue should be unchanged because the interval includes one; averaging elastic and inelastic estimates guarantees unit elasticity.
micro.Choice D: The revenue effect of a small price change is uncertain because plausible elasticity values fall on both sides of one; use cautious testing.
micro.Correct Answer: D — The revenue effect of a small price change is uncertain because plausible elasticity values fall on both sides of one; use cautious testing.
micro.Feedback: Sampling uncertainty around one makes the revenue prediction ambiguous.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: Two reports describe the same demand estimate as −2.3 and 2.3. A manager says they predict opposite sales responses to a 2% price increase. Which diagnosis is appropriate if the second report uses the absolute-value convention?
micro.Choice A: Both imply an approximate 4.6% sales decline; the second reports magnitude rather than an upward-sloping demand response.
micro.Choice B: One predicts a 4.6% decline and the other a 4.6% rise because absolute values reverse economic behavior.
micro.Choice C: Both predict a 2.3% sales decline because elasticity should not be multiplied by the price change.
micro.Choice D: Neither permits a revenue prediction because opposite printed signs prove the data disagree.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Both imply an approximate 4.6% sales decline; the second reports magnitude rather than an upward-sloping demand response.
micro.Feedback: The signed estimate gives −2.3×2%=−4.6%. Reporting |Ed|=2.3 retains that downward-demand interpretation; it changes notation, not the estimated behavior.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: Using the midpoint method, calculate the price elasticity of demand for digital music downloads when price rises from $1.00 to $1.20 and quantity demanded falls from 50,000 to 39,000.
micro.Feedback: Midpoint elasticity is approximately 1.36.

micro.Question: Calculate midpoint price elasticity of demand for monthly parking permits when price changes from $75 to $85 and quantity demanded changes from 1200 to 1030.
micro.Feedback: Midpoint elasticity is approximately 1.22.

micro.Question: Using the midpoint method, calculate the price elasticity of demand for prepared-meal subscriptions when price rises from $40 to $46 and quantity demanded falls from 2,200 to 1,800.
micro.Feedback: Midpoint elasticity is approximately 1.43.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: Calculate midpoint price elasticity of demand for regional airline tickets when price changes from $220 to $250 and quantity demanded changes from 900 to 720.
micro.Feedback: Midpoint elasticity is approximately 1.74.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: Calculate midpoint price elasticity of demand for language-learning apps when price changes from $10 to $8 and quantity demanded changes from 5000 to 6500.
micro.Feedback: Midpoint elasticity is approximately 1.17.
