micro.Question: Calculate midpoint price elasticity of demand for home-cleaning visits when price changes from $100 to $115 and quantity demanded changes from 700 to 570.
micro.Feedback: Midpoint elasticity is approximately 1.47.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: Calculate midpoint price elasticity of demand for ski-lift tickets when price changes from $80 to $72 and quantity demanded changes from 1500 to 1800.
micro.Feedback: Midpoint elasticity is approximately 1.73.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: Calculate midpoint price elasticity of demand for online game passes when price changes from $25 to $30 and quantity demanded changes from 4000 to 3150.
micro.Feedback: Midpoint elasticity is approximately 1.31.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: Calculate midpoint price elasticity of demand for coworking day passes when price changes from $30 to $36 and quantity demanded changes from 1800 to 1380.
micro.Feedback: Midpoint elasticity is approximately 1.45.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.2 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
micro.Question: Calculate midpoint price elasticity of demand for specialty running shoes when price changes from $140 to $126 and quantity demanded changes from 800 to 1000.
micro.Feedback: Midpoint elasticity is approximately 2.11.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A learner says a price increase always raises revenue. Which statement best corrects the error?
micro.Choice A: Revenue always falls after a price increase
micro.Choice B: Revenue is unrelated to elasticity
micro.Choice C: Revenue rises only when supply is elastic
micro.Choice D: Revenue rises only when demand is inelastic over the relevant range
micro.Correct Answer: D — Revenue rises only when demand is inelastic over the relevant range
micro.Feedback: The quantity response determines whether the price gain dominates.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A learner says unit elasticity means total revenue is zero. Which statement best corrects the error?
micro.Choice A: Unit elasticity leaves total revenue approximately unchanged
micro.Choice B: Unit elasticity means quantity is zero
micro.Choice C: Unit elasticity means price is zero
micro.Choice D: Unit elasticity means marginal cost is zero
micro.Correct Answer: A — Unit elasticity leaves total revenue approximately unchanged
micro.Feedback: Unit elasticity marks the revenue maximum, not zero revenue.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A learner says marginal revenue is positive on inelastic demand. Which statement best corrects the error?
micro.Choice A: Marginal revenue is always positive
micro.Choice B: Marginal revenue is negative in the inelastic range
micro.Choice C: Marginal revenue equals price everywhere
micro.Choice D: Marginal revenue depends only on supply
micro.Correct Answer: B — Marginal revenue is negative in the inelastic range
micro.Feedback: Expanding sales in the inelastic region reduces total revenue.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A learner calculates total revenue by adding price and quantity. Which statement best corrects the error?
micro.Choice A: Divide price by quantity
micro.Choice B: Add consumer and producer surplus
micro.Choice C: Multiply price by quantity sold
micro.Choice D: Subtract quantity from price
micro.Correct Answer: C — Multiply price by quantity sold
micro.Feedback: Total revenue is P × Q.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A learner says a price cut always lowers total revenue because each unit sells for less. What is missing?
micro.Choice A: A price cut always makes demand inelastic
micro.Choice B: Quantity may rise enough to increase revenue when demand is elastic
micro.Choice C: Quantity demanded never changes with price
micro.Choice D: Revenue depends only on fixed cost
micro.Correct Answer: B — Quantity may rise enough to increase revenue when demand is elastic
micro.Feedback: The total-revenue test compares the price change with the percentage quantity response.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A learner says marginal revenue must be positive everywhere on a downward-sloping demand curve. Which statement best corrects the error?
micro.Choice A: Marginal revenue becomes zero near unit elasticity and negative on the inelastic portion
micro.Choice B: Marginal revenue is always equal to price
micro.Choice C: Marginal revenue is negative only when demand is perfectly elastic
micro.Choice D: Elasticity has no relationship to marginal revenue
micro.Correct Answer: A — Marginal revenue becomes zero near unit elasticity and negative on the inelastic portion
micro.Feedback: For a standard downward-sloping demand curve, MR is positive on the elastic portion, zero near unit elasticity, and negative on the inelastic portion.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A demand point has price $12 and quantity 50. What is total revenue at that point?
micro.Feedback: Multiply price by units sold: $12×50=$600.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A firm cuts price and total revenue rises. What does this imply about demand over that price range?
micro.Choice A: Quantity demanded must have fallen
micro.Choice B: Price and quantity effects always cancel
micro.Choice C: Customers were responsive enough for the quantity gain to dominate
micro.Choice D: Demand was perfectly inelastic
micro.Correct Answer: C — Customers were responsive enough for the quantity gain to dominate
micro.Feedback: The total-revenue test translates elasticity into a practical pricing signal.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: Why is unit elasticity a useful benchmark for revenue management on a linear demand curve?
micro.Choice A: It makes demand perfectly horizontal
micro.Choice B: It is near the point where total revenue is maximized
micro.Choice C: It guarantees profit is maximized regardless of cost
micro.Choice D: It makes marginal cost zero
micro.Correct Answer: B — It is near the point where total revenue is maximized
micro.Feedback: At unit elasticity the price and quantity percentage effects offset, marking the revenue peak on a standard linear demand curve.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A seller is on a smooth downward-sloping demand segment with |Ed|=2. Is selling a little more output associated with positive or negative marginal revenue?
micro.Choice A: Positive: the quantity gain outweighs the price reduction’s effect on revenue.
micro.Choice B: Negative: every price reduction lowers total revenue.
micro.Choice C: Zero: every point on demand maximizes revenue.
micro.Choice D: Negative: elastic demand means quantity barely responds.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Positive: the quantity gain outweighs the price reduction’s effect on revenue.
micro.Feedback: On an elastic segment, a small price reduction raises total revenue, so the extra output has positive MR.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A tax raises the price buyers pay. Why can demand elasticity matter for the seller’s revenue response?
micro.Choice A: It fixes the statutory tax rate
micro.Choice B: It determines the seller’s fixed cost
micro.Choice C: It guarantees producer surplus rises
micro.Choice D: It determines how strongly quantity demanded falls as the buyer price rises
micro.Correct Answer: D — It determines how strongly quantity demanded falls as the buyer price rises
micro.Feedback: Revenue consequences depend on the quantity response to the effective price change.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A seller receives $18 per unit and sells 400 units after a change. What is its total revenue?
micro.Feedback: Total revenue is 18×400=$7,200, regardless of costs.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: Total revenue equals:
micro.Choice A: Price divided by quantity sold
micro.Choice B: Quantity sold minus price
micro.Choice C: Price multiplied by quantity sold
micro.Choice D: Elasticity multiplied by price
micro.Correct Answer: C — Price multiplied by quantity sold
micro.Feedback: Total revenue is P × Q.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: When demand is elastic, a price increase usually causes total revenue to:
micro.Choice A: Rise
micro.Choice B: Remain unchanged
micro.Choice C: Become zero
micro.Choice D: Fall
micro.Correct Answer: D — Fall
micro.Feedback: With elastic demand, the percentage drop in quantity is larger than the percentage price increase.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: When demand is inelastic, a price increase usually causes total revenue to:
micro.Choice A: Rise
micro.Choice B: Fall
micro.Choice C: Remain unchanged
micro.Choice D: Equal marginal revenue
micro.Correct Answer: A — Rise
micro.Feedback: With inelastic demand, quantity falls proportionally less than price rises.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: When demand is unit elastic, a price change leaves total revenue:
micro.Choice A: Always higher
micro.Choice B: Approximately unchanged
micro.Choice C: Always lower
micro.Choice D: Equal to zero
micro.Correct Answer: B — Approximately unchanged
micro.Feedback: Equal proportional price and quantity changes offset in total revenue.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A seller cuts price and total revenue rises. Over that price range, demand is most likely:
micro.Choice A: Inelastic
micro.Choice B: Perfectly inelastic
micro.Choice C: Unrelated to price
micro.Choice D: Elastic
micro.Correct Answer: D — Elastic
micro.Feedback: When demand is elastic, the percentage quantity increase outweighs the percentage price decrease, raising total revenue.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A seller cuts price and total revenue falls. Over that price range, demand is most likely:
micro.Choice A: Perfectly elastic
micro.Choice B: Necessarily unit elastic
micro.Choice C: Inelastic
micro.Choice D: Elastic
micro.Correct Answer: C — Inelastic
micro.Feedback: With inelastic demand, quantity rises proportionally less than price falls, so total revenue declines.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: If a price change leaves total revenue approximately unchanged, demand over that range is closest to:
micro.Choice A: Income elastic
micro.Choice B: Unit elastic
micro.Choice C: Perfectly inelastic
micro.Choice D: Perfectly elastic
micro.Correct Answer: B — Unit elastic
micro.Feedback: At unit elasticity, the percentage price and quantity effects approximately offset.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A firm sells 200 units at $15 each. Which expression gives total revenue?
micro.Feedback: Total revenue equals price multiplied by quantity sold.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: On a linear demand curve, total revenue is typically highest near the point where demand is:
micro.Choice A: Perfectly inelastic
micro.Choice B: Most inelastic possible
micro.Choice C: Defined only by income elasticity
micro.Choice D: Unit elastic
micro.Correct Answer: D — Unit elastic
micro.Feedback: For a standard linear demand curve, total revenue reaches its maximum around unit elasticity.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A price increase raises total revenue. Which demand condition is consistent with that result?
micro.Choice A: Demand must be perfectly elastic
micro.Choice B: Demand must have positive income elasticity
micro.Choice C: Demand is inelastic over the relevant range
micro.Choice D: Demand is elastic over the relevant range
micro.Correct Answer: C — Demand is inelastic over the relevant range
micro.Feedback: With inelastic demand, the price effect dominates the smaller quantity decline.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: At the exact unit-elastic point on a smooth demand curve, approximately what effect does a very small price change have on total revenue?
micro.Choice A: A guaranteed large increase
micro.Choice B: Approximately no effect
micro.Choice C: A guaranteed large decrease
micro.Choice D: It makes total revenue equal total cost
micro.Correct Answer: B — Approximately no effect
micro.Feedback: At unit elasticity, opposing price and quantity percentage changes offset.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: Why does maximum total revenue not necessarily identify the profit-maximizing output?
micro.Choice A: Revenue and profit are always identical
micro.Choice B: Elasticity cannot be used by firms
micro.Choice C: Profit also depends on production costs and marginal cost
micro.Choice D: The revenue maximum occurs only under perfect competition
micro.Correct Answer: C — Profit also depends on production costs and marginal cost
micro.Feedback: Profit maximization compares marginal revenue with marginal cost.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A theater cuts ticket price and total revenue rises. This reveals that demand over that range is:
micro.Choice A: Inelastic
micro.Choice B: Perfectly inelastic
micro.Choice C: Elastic
micro.Choice D: Necessarily unit elastic
micro.Correct Answer: C — Elastic
micro.Feedback: A price cut raises revenue only when quantity responds more than proportionally.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A toll road raises its fee and total revenue also rises. Demand over that range is most likely:
micro.Choice A: Elastic
micro.Choice B: Perfectly elastic
micro.Choice C: Negative income elastic
micro.Choice D: Inelastic
micro.Correct Answer: D — Inelastic
micro.Feedback: Revenue moving with price indicates inelastic demand.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A firm raises price while operating on the elastic portion of its demand curve. Total revenue will:
micro.Choice A: Increase
micro.Choice B: Stay constant
micro.Choice C: Equal total cost
micro.Choice D: Decrease
micro.Correct Answer: D — Decrease
micro.Feedback: The percentage quantity loss exceeds the percentage price gain.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: Why might a seller avoid operating on the inelastic portion of a demand curve when marginal cost is positive?
micro.Choice A: Raising price would increase revenue and reduce quantity-related cost
micro.Choice B: Cutting price would increase both revenue and profit automatically
micro.Choice C: Marginal revenue is positive there
micro.Choice D: Demand becomes perfectly elastic there
micro.Correct Answer: A — Raising price would increase revenue and reduce quantity-related cost
micro.Feedback: On the inelastic region, a price increase raises revenue while fewer units are produced.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: Marginal revenue is positive when demand is:
micro.Choice A: Inelastic
micro.Choice B: Elastic
micro.Choice C: Perfectly inelastic
micro.Choice D: At the quantity intercept
micro.Correct Answer: B — Elastic
micro.Feedback: Selling another unit raises total revenue on the elastic portion.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: Marginal revenue equals zero where demand is:
micro.Choice A: Perfectly elastic
micro.Choice B: Perfectly inelastic
micro.Choice C: Unit elastic
micro.Choice D: Income elastic
micro.Correct Answer: C — Unit elastic
micro.Feedback: Total revenue is maximized and locally unchanged at unit elasticity.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A drought reduces farm output, causing price to rise sharply while farmers’ total revenue rises. This pattern is consistent with:
micro.Choice A: Inelastic demand for the crop
micro.Choice B: Elastic demand for the crop
micro.Choice C: Perfectly elastic crop supply
micro.Choice D: Unit income elasticity
micro.Correct Answer: A — Inelastic demand for the crop
micro.Feedback: A supply reduction raises price; with inelastic demand, the price effect dominates the quantity loss.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. What is total revenue at point C?
micro.Feedback: At C, P = $12 and Q = 30, so total revenue is $12 × 30 = $360.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. What is total revenue at point B?
micro.Feedback: At B, P = $8 and Q = 60, so total revenue is $480.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Compare points C and B and calculate total revenue at each. What does the change imply about demand over that interval?
micro.Choice A: Demand is inelastic
micro.Choice B: Demand is elastic
micro.Choice C: Demand is perfectly inelastic
micro.Choice D: Demand is unit elastic throughout the interval
micro.Correct Answer: B — Demand is elastic
micro.Feedback: When a price cut raises total revenue, demand is elastic over the interval.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Use the price, quantity, and total-revenue change from C to B. Which elasticity conclusion follows?
micro.Choice A: Demand is inelastic over C–B
micro.Choice B: Demand is perfectly inelastic over C–B
micro.Choice C: Demand is elastic over C–B
micro.Choice D: Demand must have elasticity of zero
micro.Correct Answer: C — Demand is elastic over C–B
micro.Feedback: A price decrease that raises total revenue signals elastic demand.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Moving from B to A, use the change in total revenue to classify demand over that segment.
micro.Choice A: Demand is elastic over B–A
micro.Choice B: Demand is perfectly elastic over B–A
micro.Choice C: Demand has constant unit elasticity over B–A
micro.Choice D: Demand is inelastic over B–A
micro.Correct Answer: D — Demand is inelastic over B–A
micro.Feedback: A price decrease that lowers total revenue signals inelastic demand.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Which total revenue at B and interpretation of a small movement in either direction along demand are correct?
micro.Choice A: $480; revenue is maximized there because demand is unit elastic.
micro.Choice B: $360; revenue is maximized there because demand is unit elastic.
micro.Choice C: $480; revenue is maximized there because demand is perfectly inelastic.
micro.Choice D: $360; revenue is maximized there because demand is perfectly inelastic.
micro.Correct Answer: A — $480; revenue is maximized there because demand is unit elastic.
micro.Feedback: B has P = 8 and Q = 60, so revenue is $480. It is the midpoint of the linear demand curve, with unit elasticity. Revenue decreases for a small movement to either side, though its first-order change is zero at the maximum.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: Calculate total revenue at the two labeled points on D1. What does the change confirm about elasticity?
micro.Choice A: D1 is inelastic over B–A
micro.Choice B: D1 is perfectly inelastic over B–A
micro.Choice C: D1 is elastic over B–A
micro.Choice D: D1 has zero elasticity over B–A
micro.Correct Answer: C — D1 is elastic over B–A
micro.Feedback: A price cut that increases total revenue indicates elastic demand.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: Apply the total-revenue test to the two marked points on D2. How should this interval be classified?
micro.Choice A: D2 is elastic over D–C
micro.Choice B: D2 is perfectly elastic over D–C
micro.Choice C: D2 is unit elastic over D–C
micro.Choice D: D2 is inelastic over D–C
micro.Correct Answer: D — D2 is inelastic over D–C
micro.Feedback: A price cut that reduces total revenue indicates inelastic demand.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A seller cuts price by 8 percent and quantity demanded rises by 5 percent. Which conclusion is correct?
micro.Choice A: Demand is inelastic and total revenue falls
micro.Choice B: Demand is elastic and total revenue rises
micro.Choice C: Demand is unit elastic and total revenue is unchanged
micro.Choice D: Demand is perfectly inelastic and quantity cannot change
micro.Correct Answer: A — Demand is inelastic and total revenue falls
micro.Feedback: Elasticity is about 0.625. With inelastic demand, a price cut reduces total revenue.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A seller raises price by 6 percent and quantity demanded falls by 15 percent. Which conclusion is correct?
micro.Choice A: Demand is inelastic and total revenue rises
micro.Choice B: Demand is elastic and total revenue falls
micro.Choice C: Demand is unit elastic and total revenue is unchanged
micro.Choice D: Demand is income elastic
micro.Correct Answer: B — Demand is elastic and total revenue falls
micro.Feedback: Elasticity is 2.5, so the proportionally larger quantity loss reduces revenue.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A garden workshop compares admission prices. Holding demand conditions fixed, price changes from $40 to $48 and quantity demanded from 150 to 135. Using midpoint elasticity in absolute value, which calculation and revenue decision are supported for these two prices?
micro.Choice A: About 0.58, elastic; $40 raises revenue by $480.
micro.Choice B: About 0.58, inelastic; $48 raises revenue by $480.
micro.Choice C: About 1.73, elastic; $40 raises revenue by $480.
micro.Choice D: About 0.58, inelastic; $40 raises revenue by $480.
micro.Correct Answer: B — About 0.58, inelastic; $48 raises revenue by $480.
micro.Feedback: Midpoint elasticity is |(135 - 150) / ((135 + 150) / 2)| divided by |(48 - 40) / ((48 + 40) / 2)|, about 0.58. Revenue is $6,000 at $40 and $6,480 at $48. Compare these feasible prices; the interval does not establish a global optimum.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A digital lesson service compares subscription prices. Holding demand conditions fixed, price changes from $9 to $12 and quantity demanded from 900 to 600. Using midpoint elasticity in absolute value, which calculation and revenue decision are supported for these two prices?
micro.Choice A: About 1.40, elastic; $9 earns $900 more than $12.
micro.Choice B: About 1.40, elastic; $12 earns $900 more than $9.
micro.Choice C: About 0.71, inelastic; $12 earns $900 more than $9.
micro.Choice D: About 1.40, unit elastic; the prices earn equal revenue.
micro.Correct Answer: A — About 1.40, elastic; $9 earns $900 more than $12.
micro.Feedback: Midpoint elasticity is |(600 - 900) / ((600 + 900) / 2)| divided by |(12 - 9) / ((12 + 9) / 2)|, about 1.4. Revenue is $8,100 at $9 and $7,200 at $12. Compare these feasible prices; the interval does not establish a global optimum.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A repair service can charge $50 for 120 jobs or $45 for 140 jobs, with enough capacity for either. Holding other demand factors fixed, use midpoint elasticity to choose the higher-revenue price.
micro.Choice A: About 1.46, elastic; choose $50 because elastic demand favors a higher price.
micro.Choice B: About 0.68, inelastic; choose $50 because revenue is $6,300 rather than $6,000.
micro.Choice C: About 1.00, unit elastic; choose either because the revenues are equal.
micro.Choice D: About 1.46, elastic; choose $45 because revenue is $6,300 rather than $6,000.
micro.Correct Answer: D — About 1.46, elastic; choose $45 because revenue is $6,300 rather than $6,000.
micro.Feedback: The midpoint changes are 20/130 for quantity and 5/47.5 for price, giving about 1.46. Revenue is 45 × 140 = $6,300 versus 50 × 120 = $6,000. The price cut raises revenue over this interval.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A monopolist currently operates where demand elasticity is 0.7 and marginal cost is positive. Which adjustment is most likely to increase profit?
micro.Choice A: Raise price and reduce output
micro.Choice B: Lower price and expand output
micro.Choice C: Hold output because marginal revenue is positive
micro.Choice D: Move farther into the inelastic region
micro.Correct Answer: A — Raise price and reduce output
micro.Feedback: In the inelastic region, marginal revenue is negative; raising price increases revenue and reduces cost.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A tour operator can serve all customers at either quoted price: $24 attracts 250 buyers and $20 attracts 320. Other demand conditions are fixed. Which midpoint estimate and revenue advice follow?
micro.Choice A: About 1.35, elastic; use $20, which raises revenue by $400.
micro.Choice B: About 1.35, elastic; use $24, which raises revenue by $400.
micro.Choice C: About 0.74, inelastic; use $24, which raises revenue by $400.
micro.Choice D: About 1.00, unit elastic; the two prices earn the same revenue.
micro.Correct Answer: A — About 1.35, elastic; use $20, which raises revenue by $400.
micro.Feedback: Midpoint elasticity is (70/285)/(4/22) ≈ 1.35. The lower price earns 20 × 320 = $6,400 instead of 24 × 250 = $6,000. The larger proportional quantity response offsets the price cut.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A firm sells 2,000 units at $15. After raising price to $17, it sells 1,700 units. Which statement is correct?
micro.Choice A: Total revenue rises, indicating inelastic demand
micro.Choice B: Total revenue falls from $30,000 to $28,900, indicating elastic demand over the range
micro.Choice C: Revenue is unchanged, indicating unit elasticity
micro.Choice D: The change reveals income elasticity
micro.Correct Answer: B — Total revenue falls from $30,000 to $28,900, indicating elastic demand over the range
micro.Feedback: Revenue falls when price rises, so quantity responded strongly enough to indicate elastic demand.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: Moving down a linear demand curve past the midpoint, what happens to elasticity, marginal revenue, and total revenue?
micro.Choice A: Elasticity falls below one, marginal revenue becomes negative, and total revenue declines as quantity expands
micro.Choice B: Elasticity rises above one, marginal revenue stays positive, and revenue rises
micro.Choice C: Elasticity remains one and marginal revenue remains zero
micro.Choice D: Demand becomes perfectly elastic and revenue becomes infinite
micro.Correct Answer: A — Elasticity falls below one, marginal revenue becomes negative, and total revenue declines as quantity expands
micro.Feedback: Below the midpoint, demand is inelastic and additional sales reduce total revenue.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A farm product has inelastic demand. A bumper crop shifts supply right. What likely happens to farmers’ total revenue?
micro.Choice A: It rises because output always raises revenue
micro.Choice B: It is unchanged because supply shifted
micro.Choice C: It falls because the price decline dominates the quantity increase
micro.Choice D: It becomes equal to consumer surplus
micro.Correct Answer: C — It falls because the price decline dominates the quantity increase
micro.Feedback: With inelastic demand, lower price reduces revenue even as quantity rises.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A farm product has elastic demand. A weather shock shifts supply left. What likely happens to farmers’ total revenue?
micro.Choice A: It rises because price rises
micro.Choice B: It is unchanged because demand did not shift
micro.Choice C: It equals tax revenue
micro.Choice D: It falls because the quantity loss dominates the price increase
micro.Correct Answer: D — It falls because the quantity loss dominates the price increase
micro.Feedback: With elastic demand, the percentage quantity reduction exceeds the price increase.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: Why must the absolute demand elasticity exceed one for a standard positive-markup monopolist with positive marginal cost?
micro.Choice A: Because demand would be upward sloping
micro.Choice B: Because total revenue would be zero
micro.Choice C: Because supply would become perfectly elastic
micro.Choice D: Otherwise marginal revenue would be nonpositive at the chosen output
micro.Correct Answer: D — Otherwise marginal revenue would be nonpositive at the chosen output
micro.Feedback: Profit maximization with positive marginal cost requires positive marginal revenue, which occurs on the elastic region.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. A seller at A can choose the posted price at A, B, or C and can serve all buyers. It wants higher revenue while retaining at least 50 unit sales. Which price is best, and what explains the result?
micro.Choice A: The price at C; its highest posted price also gives the highest revenue and meets the minimum.
micro.Choice B: The price at A; its largest quantity necessarily gives the highest revenue.
micro.Choice C: The price at B; revenue rises by 120 while sales remain above the minimum.
micro.Choice D: The price at B; revenue stays unchanged but sales rise above their level at A.
micro.Correct Answer: C — The price at B; revenue rises by 120 while sales remain above the minimum.
micro.Feedback: A earns 4 × 90 = 360, B earns 8 × 60 = 480, and C earns 12 × 30 = 360. B raises revenue by 120 and sells 60 units. C also fails the 50-unit minimum. The A-to-B interval is inelastic, so the price increase raises revenue.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A seller initially charges the price at C. Capacity is 70 units, and sales equal the smaller of demand and capacity. Using the graph, which alternative price earns more revenue, and why does the capacity constraint matter?
micro.Choice A: B earns $400 versus $210 at A; using all quantity demanded at A would overstate actual sales.
micro.Choice B: B earns $480 versus $280 at A; demand elasticity guarantees all units demanded can be sold despite capacity.
micro.Choice C: B earns $400 versus $210 at A; demand elasticity guarantees all units demanded can be sold despite capacity.
micro.Choice D: B earns $480 versus $280 at A; using all quantity demanded at A would overstate actual sales.
micro.Correct Answer: D — B earns $480 versus $280 at A; using all quantity demanded at A would overstate actual sales.
micro.Feedback: B has P = 8, Qd = 60: sales are 60 and revenue $480. A has P = 4, Qd = 90: only 70 can be sold, earning $280. Capacity leaves B unconstrained but limits A. Demand elasticity describes desired purchases, not a seller’s capacity.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A seller raises price and total revenue falls. What does the total-revenue test imply?
micro.Choice A: Demand is elastic
micro.Choice B: Demand is inelastic
micro.Choice C: Demand is perfectly inelastic
micro.Choice D: Supply is elastic
micro.Correct Answer: A — Demand is elastic
micro.Feedback: Revenue moving opposite price indicates elastic demand.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A seller raises price and total revenue rises. What does the total-revenue test imply?
micro.Choice A: Demand is elastic
micro.Choice B: Demand is inelastic
micro.Choice C: Demand is unit elastic
micro.Choice D: Income elasticity is positive
micro.Correct Answer: B — Demand is inelastic
micro.Feedback: Revenue moving with price indicates inelastic demand.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: Which statement about unit-elastic demand is correct?
micro.Choice A: Quantity does not respond to price
micro.Choice B: A price increase always raises revenue
micro.Choice C: The percentage changes offset, leaving total revenue about unchanged
micro.Choice D: Demand is horizontal
micro.Correct Answer: C — The percentage changes offset, leaving total revenue about unchanged
micro.Feedback: Unit elasticity leaves revenue approximately unchanged for small changes.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A price cut raises quantity 18 percent while price falls 9 percent. What happens to total revenue?
micro.Choice A: It rises because demand is elastic
micro.Choice B: It falls because demand is inelastic
micro.Choice C: It remains unchanged because both variables changed
micro.Choice D: It cannot be determined without income
micro.Correct Answer: A — It rises because demand is elastic
micro.Feedback: Elasticity is 2, so quantity rises proportionally more than price falls.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A price increase of 12 percent reduces quantity by 3 percent. Which conclusion follows?
micro.Choice A: Demand is elastic, so total revenue falls
micro.Choice B: Demand is inelastic, so total revenue likely rises
micro.Choice C: Demand is unit elastic
micro.Choice D: Demand is perfectly elastic
micro.Correct Answer: B — Demand is inelastic, so total revenue likely rises
micro.Feedback: Elasticity is 0.25; the price effect dominates revenue.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: At the midpoint of a linear demand curve, which pair is correct?
micro.Choice A: Perfect inelasticity and zero revenue
micro.Choice B: Elastic demand and negative marginal revenue
micro.Choice C: Unit elasticity and maximum total revenue
micro.Choice D: Inelastic demand and positive marginal revenue
micro.Correct Answer: C — Unit elasticity and maximum total revenue
micro.Feedback: The midpoint of a linear demand curve is unit elastic and revenue-maximizing.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A firm operates on the inelastic portion of demand with positive marginal cost. Why is that inconsistent with profit maximization?
micro.Choice A: A price cut would necessarily raise profit
micro.Choice B: Marginal revenue is positive there
micro.Choice C: Demand must be horizontal
micro.Choice D: A price increase would raise revenue while reducing output cost
micro.Correct Answer: D — A price increase would raise revenue while reducing output cost
micro.Feedback: Inelastic demand implies negative marginal revenue.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. As price falls from C through B to A, which total-revenue sequence and economic explanation are correct?
micro.Choice A: $300, $400, $300; price cuts raise revenue above the midpoint and lower it below the midpoint.
micro.Choice B: $360, $480, $360; price cuts raise revenue above the midpoint and lower it below the midpoint.
micro.Choice C: $360, $480, $360; price cuts raise revenue when demand is inelastic and lower it when elastic.
micro.Choice D: $300, $400, $300; price cuts raise revenue when demand is inelastic and lower it when elastic.
micro.Correct Answer: B — $360, $480, $360; price cuts raise revenue above the midpoint and lower it below the midpoint.
micro.Feedback: C = (30, 12), B = (60, 8) and A = (90, 4), giving revenues 360,480,360. Above the midpoint demand is elastic, so quantity gains outweigh price cuts. Below it demand is inelastic, so the price loss dominates.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A farm quota reduces quantity 5% and raises price 8%, with no other change. A student says fewer sales must lower revenue. Which correction is right using the exact stated percentage changes?
micro.Choice A: Revenue falls 5% because the price increase does not affect revenue per sale.
micro.Choice B: Revenue rises exactly 13% because the magnitudes of both percentage changes should be added.
micro.Choice C: Revenue stays unchanged because all quota policies imply unit elasticity.
micro.Choice D: Revenue rises about 2.6% because 1.08×0.95=1.026; quantity falls proportionately less than price rises.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Revenue rises about 2.6% because 1.08×0.95=1.026; quantity falls proportionately less than price rises.
micro.Feedback: Revenue is price times quantity. The new revenue factor is 1.08×0.95=1.026, so revenue rises 2.6%; a lower quantity alone does not determine revenue.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A seller faces downward-sloping demand with absolute elasticity 0.8 at its current output. An analyst proposes a small output expansion to raise total revenue. Which response follows from elasticity, without needing a cost model?
micro.Choice A: Reject the revenue claim: the current range is inelastic, so marginal revenue is negative and a small output reduction raises revenue.
micro.Choice B: Accept the claim: any positive price makes marginal revenue positive regardless of elasticity.
micro.Choice C: Reject the claim because marginal revenue is zero whenever elasticity is below one.
micro.Choice D: Accept the claim because inelastic demand means quantity changes proportionately more than price.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Reject the revenue claim: the current range is inelastic, so marginal revenue is negative and a small output reduction raises revenue.
micro.Feedback: In the inelastic range, expanding sales requires a proportionately large price reduction, reducing revenue. Thus MR is negative; the conclusion is about revenue rather than a complete profit choice.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A 10 percent price increase lowers quantity 20 percent. Cost per unit is unchanged. Which revenue-profit statement is best supported?
micro.Choice A: Both revenue and profit must rise
micro.Choice B: Profit must fall by exactly 10 percent
micro.Choice C: Revenue is unchanged
micro.Choice D: Revenue falls, but profit direction still requires cost information
micro.Correct Answer: D — Revenue falls, but profit direction still requires cost information
micro.Feedback: Elasticity determines revenue direction, but profit also depends on costs.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A seller wants to maximize revenue with one uniform price. What information about elasticity is needed beyond knowing its value at the current price?
micro.Choice A: Only whether the product is normal
micro.Choice B: Only supply elasticity
micro.Choice C: Elasticity at the current point and along the curve
micro.Choice D: The statutory tax rate
micro.Correct Answer: C — Elasticity at the current point and along the curve
micro.Feedback: Revenue is maximized where elasticity reaches one, requiring location-specific information.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: A crop quota reduces sales from 1,000 to 900 units and raises price from $10 to $12. Farmers’ variable production cost falls by $300, while administering the quota uses $1,200 of their resources. Which comparison avoids confusing revenue with profit?
micro.Choice A: Revenue rises by $800 and profit must rise by $800 because the demand response is inelastic.
micro.Choice B: Revenue rises by $800, but net producer profit falls by $100 after cost savings and administration.
micro.Choice C: Revenue falls by $1,000 and profit falls by $1,900 because fewer units are sold.
micro.Choice D: Revenue rises by $1,200 and profit rises by $300 because the calculation uses the old quantity at the new price.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Revenue rises by $800, but net producer profit falls by $100 after cost savings and administration.
micro.Feedback: Revenue changes from $10,000 to $10,800. Profit changes by +800+300−1,200=−$100. Inelastic response can raise revenue without making an administratively costly policy profitable.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: For museum tickets, price and quantity move from $12 and 1000 units to $10 and 1280 units. Which total-revenue calculation is correct?
micro.Choice A: Total revenue changes from $15,360 to $10,000
micro.Choice B: Total revenue changes from $12,000 to $12,800
micro.Choice C: Total revenue remains $12,000
micro.Choice D: Total revenue changes from $12,800 to $12,000
micro.Correct Answer: B — Total revenue changes from $12,000 to $12,800
micro.Feedback: Compute P × Q at each point: $12,000 initially and $12,800 afterward.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: For streaming plans, price and quantity move from $15 and 4000 units to $18 and 3500 units. Which total-revenue calculation is correct?
micro.Choice A: Total revenue changes from $52,500 to $72,000
micro.Choice B: Total revenue remains $60,000
micro.Choice C: Total revenue changes from $60,000 to $63,000
micro.Choice D: Total revenue changes from $63,000 to $60,000
micro.Correct Answer: C — Total revenue changes from $60,000 to $63,000
micro.Feedback: Compute P × Q at each point: $60,000 initially and $63,000 afterward.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: For parking fees, price and quantity move from $8 and 2000 units to $10 and 1800 units. Which total-revenue calculation is correct?
micro.Choice A: Total revenue changes from $14,400 to $20,000
micro.Choice B: Total revenue remains $16,000
micro.Choice C: Total revenue changes from $18,000 to $16,000
micro.Choice D: Total revenue changes from $16,000 to $18,000
micro.Correct Answer: D — Total revenue changes from $16,000 to $18,000
micro.Feedback: Compute P × Q at each point: $16,000 initially and $18,000 afterward.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: For event passes, price and quantity move from $50 and 600 units to $45 and 720 units. Which total-revenue calculation is correct?
micro.Choice A: Total revenue changes from $30,000 to $32,400
micro.Choice B: Total revenue changes from $36,000 to $27,000
micro.Choice C: Total revenue remains $30,000
micro.Choice D: Total revenue changes from $32,400 to $30,000
micro.Correct Answer: A — Total revenue changes from $30,000 to $32,400
micro.Feedback: Compute P × Q at each point: $30,000 initially and $32,400 afterward.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.3 — Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
micro.Question: For software licenses, price and quantity move from $100 and 900 units to $110 and 790 units. Which total-revenue calculation is correct?
micro.Choice A: Total revenue changes from $79,000 to $99,000
micro.Choice B: Total revenue changes from $90,000 to $86,900
micro.Choice C: Total revenue remains $90,000
micro.Choice D: Total revenue changes from $86,900 to $90,000
micro.Correct Answer: B — Total revenue changes from $90,000 to $86,900
micro.Feedback: Compute P × Q at each point: $90,000 initially and $86,900 afterward.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: A learner calculates supply elasticity with consumer income in the denominator. Which statement best corrects the error?
micro.Choice A: Supply elasticity uses income change
micro.Choice B: Supply elasticity uses a rival’s price
micro.Choice C: Price elasticity of supply uses the good’s own price change
micro.Choice D: Supply elasticity equals quantity supplied
micro.Correct Answer: C — Price elasticity of supply uses the good’s own price change
micro.Feedback: Supply elasticity connects output response to output price.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: A learner says short-run supply is always more elastic. Which statement best corrects the error?
micro.Choice A: Short-run supply is always perfectly elastic
micro.Choice B: Time affects demand only
micro.Choice C: Supply elasticity falls whenever firms enter
micro.Choice D: Longer time usually gives producers more capacity and input adjustments
micro.Correct Answer: D — Longer time usually gives producers more capacity and input adjustments
micro.Feedback: Adjustment options expand over time.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: After calculating a 12% increase in quantity supplied from an 8% price increase, a student reports PES = 0.67. Which step is wrong?
micro.Choice A: The ratio was inverted; PES = 12%/8% = 1.5
micro.Choice B: The supply response should be given a negative sign
micro.Choice C: The percentage changes should be added to get 20
micro.Choice D: The calculation should use the original price level instead
micro.Correct Answer: A — The ratio was inverted; PES = 12%/8% = 1.5
micro.Feedback: Price elasticity of supply divides the percentage change in quantity supplied by the percentage change in price, so 12%/8% = 1.5.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: A learner says unused production capacity makes supply less elastic. What is the correction?
micro.Choice A: Unused capacity fixes quantity supplied at one level
micro.Choice B: Unused capacity affects demand elasticity but not supply
micro.Choice C: Unused capacity guarantees perfectly elastic supply
micro.Choice D: Unused capacity usually makes it easier to expand output, increasing supply elasticity
micro.Correct Answer: D — Unused capacity usually makes it easier to expand output, increasing supply elasticity
micro.Feedback: Spare capacity lets firms respond to higher prices without first building entirely new capacity.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: A learner says input mobility has no effect on supply elasticity. Which statement corrects this mistake?
micro.Choice A: Only demand-side substitutes affect elasticity
micro.Choice B: Input mobility changes the sign of supply elasticity
micro.Choice C: Inputs that can be reallocated easily generally make supply more elastic
micro.Choice D: Input mobility makes supply perfectly inelastic
micro.Correct Answer: C — Inputs that can be reallocated easily generally make supply more elastic
micro.Feedback: Flexible inputs let producers change output more readily when price changes.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: A learner gets PES = 0.4 and calls supply elastic. What should be corrected?
micro.Choice A: The sign alone determines elastic versus inelastic
micro.Choice B: A coefficient below one is inelastic over the measured range
micro.Choice C: Any positive coefficient is elastic
micro.Choice D: A coefficient below one is perfectly elastic
micro.Correct Answer: B — A coefficient below one is inelastic over the measured range
micro.Feedback: For PES, magnitude below one means quantity supplied responds proportionally less than price.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: A binding rent ceiling creates a shortage. Which elasticity determines how strongly quantity supplied shrinks over time?
micro.Choice A: Income elasticity of demand
micro.Choice B: Price elasticity of supply
micro.Choice C: Cross-price elasticity only
micro.Choice D: Elasticity of money supply
micro.Correct Answer: B — Price elasticity of supply
micro.Feedback: Long-run housing supply elasticity drives the supply response.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: A minimum price raises quantity supplied. Which elasticity predicts the surplus expansion from the supply side?
micro.Choice A: Price elasticity of demand only
micro.Choice B: Income elasticity
micro.Choice C: Price elasticity of supply
micro.Choice D: Cross-price elasticity
micro.Correct Answer: C — Price elasticity of supply
micro.Feedback: Supply elasticity predicts output expansion.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: A commodity price rises 10% and quantity supplied rises 15%. What does this imply about the responsiveness of producers?
micro.Choice A: Producers show an elastic supply response
micro.Choice B: Producers show an inelastic supply response
micro.Choice C: Quantity supplied did not respond
micro.Choice D: The result measures demand, not supply
micro.Correct Answer: A — Producers show an elastic supply response
micro.Feedback: A 15% quantity response to a 10% price change gives PES above one.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: Why does a longer time horizon often connect supply elasticity to investment decisions?
micro.Choice A: Longer horizons make all prices fixed
micro.Choice B: Firms lose the ability to change inputs over time
micro.Choice C: Supply becomes unrelated to marginal cost
micro.Choice D: Firms have more time to add capacity and reorganize production
micro.Correct Answer: D — Firms have more time to add capacity and reorganize production
micro.Feedback: Investment and capacity adjustment make long-run supply more responsive.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: How does inventory management connect to supply elasticity?
micro.Choice A: Inventory affects only consumer demand
micro.Choice B: Stored goods make supply vertical by definition
micro.Choice C: Stored inventory can be released when price rises, increasing quantity responsiveness
micro.Choice D: Inventory prevents firms from reacting to price
micro.Correct Answer: C — Stored inventory can be released when price rises, increasing quantity responsiveness
micro.Feedback: Storage creates another margin through which sellers can respond to price changes.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: A market has highly mobile labor and equipment. What does that suggest about the supply response to a price increase?
micro.Choice A: The price increase cannot affect production
micro.Choice B: Output can adjust more strongly because inputs can move toward the market
micro.Choice C: Output must remain fixed because mobile inputs leave the market
micro.Choice D: Demand becomes more elastic while supply is unchanged
micro.Correct Answer: B — Output can adjust more strongly because inputs can move toward the market
micro.Feedback: Input mobility links production flexibility to greater supply elasticity.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: Price elasticity of supply measures how quantity supplied responds to a change in:
micro.Choice A: Consumer income
micro.Choice B: The price of a complement in consumption
micro.Choice C: The good’s price
micro.Choice D: Buyer preferences
micro.Correct Answer: C — The good’s price
micro.Feedback: Price elasticity of supply compares the percentage change in quantity supplied with the percentage change in the good’s price.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: Why is supply generally more elastic over a longer time horizon?
micro.Choice A: Less time to adjust production
micro.Choice B: No unused capacity
micro.Choice C: Inputs fixed by law
micro.Choice D: More time to adjust production
micro.Correct Answer: D — More time to adjust production
micro.Feedback: A longer time horizon gives producers more time to expand capacity, change inputs, and otherwise adjust production.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: A firm with substantial unused capacity is likely to have short-run supply that is:
micro.Choice A: More elastic supply
micro.Choice B: Less elastic supply
micro.Choice C: Perfectly inelastic supply
micro.Choice D: No possible quantity change
micro.Correct Answer: A — More elastic supply
micro.Feedback: Unused capacity makes output easier to expand.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: Which product is likely to have more elastic short-run supply?
micro.Choice A: Seats at tonight’s sold-out concert
micro.Choice B: A storable manufactured good
micro.Choice C: Fresh fish already caught today
micro.Choice D: Land in a fixed downtown block
micro.Correct Answer: B — A storable manufactured good
micro.Feedback: Storage and adjustable production make supply more responsive.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: At a price of $8, what quantity is supplied on the short-run supply curve?
micro.Choice A: 60 units
micro.Choice B: 100 units
micro.Choice C: 70 units
micro.Choice D: 40 units
micro.Correct Answer: C — 70 units
micro.Feedback: Point A on the short-run supply curve is Q = 70 at P = $8.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Starting from P = $4 and Q = 60, which supply curve shows the larger increase in quantity supplied when price rises to $8?
micro.Choice A: Short-run supply
micro.Choice B: Both show the same response
micro.Choice C: Neither curve responds
micro.Choice D: Long-run supply
micro.Correct Answer: D — Long-run supply
micro.Feedback: Long-run supply reaches Q = 100, compared with Q = 70 in the short run.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: A bakery owns an unused oven and can add a second production shift quickly. Other things equal, its short-run supply is likely to be:
micro.Choice A: More elastic because output can expand without major new investment
micro.Choice B: More inelastic because unused capacity prevents adjustment
micro.Choice C: Perfectly inelastic because the bakery has fixed equipment
micro.Choice D: Unit elastic because capacity and price are unrelated
micro.Correct Answer: A — More elastic because output can expand without major new investment
micro.Feedback: Unused capacity makes it easier to raise output when price rises.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: Which situation generally makes supply more price elastic?
micro.Choice A: Production requires a fixed harvest already in the ground
micro.Choice B: All firms are operating at absolute capacity
micro.Choice C: The good must be supplied at one fixed quantity
micro.Choice D: Inputs can be moved easily into the industry
micro.Correct Answer: D — Inputs can be moved easily into the industry
micro.Feedback: Mobile inputs let producers expand or contract output more readily.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: A fresh strawberry farmer has only today to respond to a sudden price increase. Compared with supply over several growing seasons, today’s supply is usually:
micro.Choice A: Perfectly elastic
micro.Choice B: Exactly unit elastic
micro.Choice C: Less elastic
micro.Choice D: More elastic
micro.Correct Answer: C — Less elastic
micro.Feedback: The very short run gives the farmer little time to change acreage, plants, or harvest capacity.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: A seller can store a product cheaply and release inventory when price rises. Cheap storage generally makes supply:
micro.Choice A: Unrelated to price
micro.Choice B: More elastic
micro.Choice C: Less elastic
micro.Choice D: Perfectly inelastic
micro.Correct Answer: B — More elastic
micro.Feedback: Inventory can be shifted toward periods with higher prices, increasing quantity responsiveness.

micro.Question: Use the graph. Refer to the common starting point and the higher marked price on the two supply curves. Which short-run and long-run quantity increases, and elasticity interpretation, are supported?

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: The price of beachfront rentals rises from $250 to $300. In the short run, quantity supplied rises from 1,200 to 1,260. Which midpoint elasticity and interpretation are correct?

micro.Correct Answer: C — About 0.27; inelastic supply, so producers respond proportionally less than price

micro.Feedback: The midpoint coefficient is about 1.43; the magnitude determines the classification.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: Over one week, the price of a crate of fresh strawberries rises from $30 to $36, while quantity supplied rises from 5,000 to 5,450 crates. Which midpoint elasticity and interpretation are correct?
micro.Choice A: About 0.47; inelastic supply, so producers respond proportionally less than price

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: A planning model assumes a 9 percent output-price increase with supply elasticity 1.5. Which forecast is most consistent with the elasticity estimate?

micro.Choice C: Quantity supplied falls about 13.5 percent
micro.Choice D: Quantity supplied rises exactly 1.5 percent

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply

micro.Question: For supply Q = −20 + 4P, what is point elasticity at P = 10, where Q = 20?

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: A supply curve passes through the origin and is linear. What is point elasticity along the positive portion?

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: A farmer cannot change this season’s planted acreage after a price increase. Short-run supply is likely:
micro.Choice A: Relatively elastic
micro.Choice B: Perfectly elastic
micro.Choice C: Unrelated to production constraints
micro.Choice D: Relatively inelastic
micro.Correct Answer: D — Relatively inelastic
micro.Feedback: Fixed acreage and biological lags limit immediate output response.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: Housing supply is typically more elastic in a growing suburb than in a fully built downtown because the suburb has:
micro.Choice A: More available land and expansion capacity
micro.Choice B: More inelastic demand
micro.Choice C: A necessarily higher price level
micro.Choice D: No construction time
micro.Correct Answer: A — More available land and expansion capacity
micro.Feedback: Available land and development capacity make quantity more responsive.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: Supply of seats for tonight’s concert is:
micro.Choice A: Highly elastic
micro.Choice B: Nearly perfectly inelastic
micro.Choice C: Unit elastic by definition
micro.Choice D: Perfectly elastic after the show starts
micro.Correct Answer: B — Nearly perfectly inelastic
micro.Feedback: The number of seats cannot expand for that event.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. When price rises from $4 to $8, how much does quantity supplied rise in the short run?
micro.Choice A: 10 units
micro.Choice B: 40 units
micro.Choice C: 30 units
micro.Choice D: 70 units
micro.Correct Answer: A — 10 units
micro.Feedback: Short-run quantity rises from 60 to 70, a 10-unit increase.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: Use the graph. Refer to the common starting point and the higher marked price on the two supply curves. Which short-run and long-run quantity increases, and elasticity interpretation, are supported?
micro.Choice A: 20 and 60 units; the larger long-run response reflects more time to adjust inputs and capacity.
micro.Choice B: 10 and 40 units; the larger long-run response reflects more time to adjust inputs and capacity.
micro.Choice C: 10 and 40 units; the larger long-run increase proves every input can adjust fully in the short run.
micro.Choice D: 10 and 100 units; compare the short-run change with the long-run final level to measure responsiveness.
micro.Correct Answer: B — 10 and 40 units; the larger long-run response reflects more time to adjust inputs and capacity.
micro.Feedback: Both curves start at Q = 60, P = 4. At P = 8, short-run A has Q = 70 and long-run B has Q = 100. The increases are 10 and 40. With the same starting point and price change, more adjustment time yields the larger quantity response and greater supply elasticity.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: Firm A can add workers and rent extra machines within a month. Firm B needs two years to build a new plant. For the same one-month price increase, whose supply should be more elastic?
micro.Choice A: Firm A’s, because it can adjust capacity sooner
micro.Choice B: Firm B’s, because long construction times create flexibility
micro.Choice C: Both equally, because price changes determine elasticity by themselves
micro.Choice D: Neither, because supply elasticity applies only to agriculture
micro.Correct Answer: A — Firm A’s, because it can adjust capacity sooner
micro.Feedback: Faster capacity adjustment makes quantity supplied more responsive in the relevant time period.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: A concert venue has 20,000 fixed seats for tonight but can schedule additional shows next month. Supply of seats is likely to be:
micro.Choice A: More elastic tonight than next month
micro.Choice B: Equally elastic in both periods
micro.Choice C: Perfectly elastic tonight and perfectly inelastic next month
micro.Choice D: More inelastic tonight than next month
micro.Correct Answer: D — More inelastic tonight than next month
micro.Feedback: Tonight’s capacity is fixed, while a longer horizon permits additional performances.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: Two firms face the same price increase. One has idle machinery; the other is already using every machine around the clock. Which response is most likely?
micro.Choice A: Both must have the same percentage increase in output
micro.Choice B: Neither can change output because price does not affect supply
micro.Choice C: The firm with idle machinery has the larger percentage increase in output
micro.Choice D: The capacity-constrained firm has the larger percentage increase in output
micro.Correct Answer: C — The firm with idle machinery has the larger percentage increase in output
micro.Feedback: Unused capacity makes output easier to expand, increasing supply elasticity.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: Suppose lumber producers can quickly redirect logs among several mills, while a specialized chemical plant requires dedicated equipment. Other things equal, supply should be:
micro.Choice A: Perfectly inelastic in both industries in every time period
micro.Choice B: More elastic for lumber because inputs are easier to reallocate
micro.Choice C: More elastic for the chemical because specialized equipment raises flexibility
micro.Choice D: Equally elastic because both industries sell physical goods
micro.Correct Answer: B — More elastic for lumber because inputs are easier to reallocate
micro.Feedback: Ease of reallocating inputs is a major determinant of supply responsiveness.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: A 10% increase in price causes quantity supplied to rise by only 3%. What does that imply about supply?
micro.Choice A: Supply is inelastic over the measured range
micro.Choice B: Supply is elastic over the measured range
micro.Choice C: Supply is unit elastic over the measured range
micro.Choice D: Supply is perfectly elastic over the measured range
micro.Correct Answer: A — Supply is inelastic over the measured range
micro.Feedback: A percentage quantity response smaller than the percentage price change gives PES below one.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Calculate the midpoint price elasticity of supply for the larger long-run quantity response shown.
micro.Feedback: The midpoint quantity change is 40/80 = 50% and the price change is 4/6 ≈ 66.7%, giving PES ≈ 0.75.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: Using the midpoint method, the price of artisan bread loaves changes from $4 to $5 and quantity supplied changes from 900 to 1080. What is price elasticity of supply?
micro.Feedback: The midpoint calculation gives a supply elasticity of about 0.82, classified as inelastic.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: Using the midpoint method, the price of rental bicycles changes from $12 to $15 and quantity supplied changes from 300 to 390. What is price elasticity of supply?
micro.Feedback: The midpoint calculation gives a supply elasticity of about 1.17, classified as elastic.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: Using the midpoint method, the price of greenhouse tomatoes changes from $3 to $4 and quantity supplied changes from 1000 to 1180. What is price elasticity of supply?
micro.Feedback: The midpoint calculation gives a supply elasticity of about 0.58, classified as inelastic.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: Using the midpoint method, the price of cloud-server capacity rises from $40 to $50 per unit, and quantity supplied rises from 500 to 700 units. What is the price elasticity of supply?
micro.Feedback: The midpoint calculation gives a supply elasticity of about 1.5, classified as elastic.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: Using the midpoint method, the price of hotel rooms rises from $150 to $180, and short-run quantity supplied rises from 800 to 840 rooms. What is the price elasticity of supply?
micro.Feedback: The midpoint calculation gives a supply elasticity of about 0.27, classified as inelastic.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Using the common starting point and point A on the short-run supply curve, calculate the midpoint price elasticity of supply.
micro.Feedback: The midpoint quantity change is 10/65 ≈ 15.4% and the price change is 4/6 ≈ 66.7%, giving PES ≈ 0.23.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: A linear supply curve intersects the quantity axis at a positive quantity. Along its positive-price region, supply elasticity tends to be:
micro.Choice A: Less than one
micro.Choice B: Greater than one
micro.Choice C: Exactly one at every point
micro.Choice D: Negative
micro.Correct Answer: A — Less than one
micro.Feedback: With Q = a + bP and a > 0, bP/Q < 1.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: A linear supply curve has a negative quantity intercept and crosses the price axis above zero. Along its positive-quantity region, supply elasticity tends to be:
micro.Choice A: Less than one
micro.Choice B: Greater than one
micro.Choice C: Exactly zero
micro.Choice D: Negative because the intercept is negative
micro.Correct Answer: B — Greater than one
micro.Feedback: With Q = −a + bP, bP/Q exceeds one where Q is positive.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: An agricultural innovation makes crop supply more elastic. After a demand increase, compared with the old supply curve, equilibrium will show:
micro.Choice A: A smaller quantity increase and a larger price increase
micro.Choice B: No quantity change
micro.Choice C: A larger quantity increase and a smaller price increase
micro.Choice D: An equal price and quantity change by definition
micro.Correct Answer: C — A larger quantity increase and a smaller price increase
micro.Feedback: More elastic supply absorbs demand shifts through quantity rather than price.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: At a price of $80, 200 equipment-rental days are supplied. At $100, supply is 220 days this month and 280 after firms expand their fleets. Use midpoint elasticity. Which conclusion fits a buyer seeking 250 rental days at $100?
micro.Choice A: Supply is about 1.50 this month and 0.43 after expansion; only current capacity meets the requirement.
micro.Choice B: Supply is about 0.43 this month and 1.50 after expansion; only the expanded fleet meets the requirement.
micro.Choice C: Supply is about 0.43 in both periods because the price change is the same.
micro.Choice D: Supply is about 1.50 in both periods because any quantity increase is elastic.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Supply is about 0.43 this month and 1.50 after expansion; only the expanded fleet meets the requirement.
micro.Feedback: The common midpoint price change is 20/90. Quantity changes are 20/210 this month and 80/240 after expansion. PES is about 0.43 and 1.50. At $100, 220 is below the required 250, while 280 exceeds it.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. A buyer needs 90 units when price has risen from the common starting point to $8. Using midpoint supply elasticities, which comparison and procurement conclusion are supported?
micro.Choice A: Short run about 0.75, long run 0.23; 90 units can be supplied only in the short run.
micro.Choice B: Short run about 0.23, long run 0.75; 90 units can be supplied only after the longer adjustment.
micro.Choice C: Short run about 0.23, long run 0.75; neither horizon can supply 90 units at $8.
micro.Choice D: Short run about 0.23, long run 1.33; longer-run supply is elastic because it is flatter.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Short run about 0.23, long run 0.75; 90 units can be supplied only after the longer adjustment.
micro.Feedback: Starting quantity is 60 at $4. At $8, short-run quantity is 70 and long-run quantity is 100. Midpoint PES is (10/65)/(4/6) ≈ 0.23 and (40/80)/(4/6) = 0.75. Both are inelastic over this interval, but only the long run reaches the 90-unit requirement.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: Which situation most likely has highly inelastic short-run supply?

micro.Choice C: A storable manufactured input
micro.Choice D: Tickets for a stadium event already underway

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: Supply becomes more elastic over time mainly because producers can:

micro.Choice B: Make demand shift automatically
micro.Choice C: Eliminate scarcity
micro.Choice D: Set any price without losing buyers
micro.Correct Answer: A — Change capacity, enter, exit, and substitute inputs
micro.Feedback: Longer horizons expand production adjustments.
