micro.Question: Use the graph. Refer to the common starting point and the higher marked price on the two supply curves. Which short-run and long-run quantity increases, and elasticity interpretation, are supported?
micro.Choice A: 10 and 40 units; the larger long-run response reflects more time to adjust inputs and capacity.
micro.Choice B: 20 and 60 units; the larger long-run response reflects more time to adjust inputs and capacity.
micro.Choice C: 10 and 40 units; the larger long-run response implies less percentage responsiveness over time.
micro.Choice D: 20 and 60 units; the larger long-run response implies less percentage responsiveness over time.
micro.Correct Answer: A — 10 and 40 units; the larger long-run response reflects more time to adjust inputs and capacity.
micro.Feedback: Both curves start at Q = 60, P = 4. At P = 8, short-run A has Q = 70 and long-run B has Q = 100. The increases are 10 and 40. With the same starting point and price change, more adjustment time yields the larger quantity response and greater supply elasticity.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: Supply is Q=20+2P. At P=$20, a planner uses the slope 2 as elasticity and forecasts a 20% quantity rise after a small 10% price increase. Which correction is correct?
micro.Choice A: Elasticity is 2 because slope and elasticity are equal for any straight line; the 20% forecast is correct.
micro.Choice B: Elasticity is 60/20=3; the quantity response is approximately 30%.
micro.Choice C: Elasticity is 2×20/60≈0.67; the approximate quantity response is 6.7%, not 20%.
micro.Choice D: Elasticity is 0.67, so quantity falls 6.7% when price rises.
micro.Correct Answer: C — Elasticity is 2×20/60≈0.67; the approximate quantity response is 6.7%, not 20%.
micro.Feedback: At P=20, Q=60. Elasticity multiplies slope by P/Q: 2×20/60=2/3. The forecast quantity response is (2/3)×10%≈6.7%.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: Using the midpoint formula and the displayed short-run and long-run endpoints, which approximate pair correctly compares supply elasticity?
micro.Choice A: Short run 0.75; long run 0.23
micro.Choice B: Short run 1.00; long run 1.00
micro.Choice C: Short run 3.25; long run 0.75
micro.Choice D: Short run 0.23; long run 0.75
micro.Correct Answer: D — Short run 0.23; long run 0.75
micro.Feedback: The short-run response is about 0.23 and the long-run response about 0.75, so long-run supply is more elastic.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: A product has very elastic demand and very inelastic supply. A demand increase occurs. Which short-run outcome is most likely?
micro.Choice A: A small price rise and large quantity rise, given elastic demand
micro.Choice B: A large price fall and small quantity rise, given inelastic supply
micro.Choice C: A large price rise and small quantity rise, given inelastic supply
micro.Choice D: An unchanged price and quantity, given opposing elasticities
micro.Correct Answer: C — A large price rise and small quantity rise, given inelastic supply
micro.Feedback: For a demand shift, supply elasticity governs how much output can expand; inelastic supply yields a large price response.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: A demand shift causes price and quantity supplied to move in the same direction. Under what condition can the resulting arc approximate supply elasticity?
micro.Choice A: Supply shifts at the same time as demand
micro.Choice B: Supply stays unchanged, and a separate change in demand causes the price change
micro.Choice C: Demand is perfectly inelastic over the price range considered
micro.Choice D: The product is a normal good for its buyers
micro.Correct Answer: B — Supply stays unchanged, and a separate change in demand causes the price change
micro.Feedback: If supply stays unchanged, a price change caused by an independent change in demand traces a movement along the supply curve.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: A national housing-supply estimate is 1.2 over ten years. City A has little buildable land and a one-year planning horizon; City B has available land and a ten-year horizon. Which use of the estimate is defensible?
micro.Choice A: Apply 1.2 to both cities because a national elasticity incorporates each local constraint equally.
micro.Choice B: Apply a larger elasticity to A because scarce land makes each price increase more valuable to owners.
micro.Choice C: Treat it as a starting point, not a common local forecast; A likely faces tighter short-run constraints, while B has more adjustment possibilities.
micro.Choice D: Apply zero elasticity to B because a longer horizon fixes the housing stock more tightly.
micro.Correct Answer: C — Treat it as a starting point, not a common local forecast; A likely faces tighter short-run constraints, while B has more adjustment possibilities.
micro.Feedback: Supply responsiveness depends on available resources and adjustment time. A national long-horizon estimate cannot identify either city’s elasticity without local evidence, particularly A’s constrained short-run response.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: A producer’s price rises 8%. Its short-run supply elasticity is 0.25 and its long-run elasticity is 1.5, each applicable near the initial price. Which forecast and explanation fit, with other determinants held constant?
micro.Choice A: Quantity supplied rises 12% in the short run and 2% in the long run because time reduces adjustment options.
micro.Choice B: Quantity supplied rises 8% in both periods because elasticity measures the direction but not the size of the response.
micro.Choice C: Quantity supplied falls 2% then 12% because the higher output price raises the firm’s input costs by definition.
micro.Choice D: Quantity supplied rises about 2% in the short run and 12% in the long run as capacity and inputs can adjust.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Quantity supplied rises about 2% in the short run and 12% in the long run as capacity and inputs can adjust.
micro.Feedback: Supply response is elasticity times the price change: 0.25×8%=2% and 1.5×8%=12%. Longer adjustment time can allow greater output response.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply

micro.Question: Calculate midpoint price elasticity of supply for electricity from peaker plants: price changes from $70 to $84, and quantity supplied changes from 1000 to 1320.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: Calculate midpoint price elasticity of supply for downtown parking spaces this hour: price changes from $10 to $14, and quantity supplied changes from 800 to 816.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.4 — Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
micro.Question: Using the midpoint method, calculate the price elasticity of supply for custom furniture pieces when price rises from $900 to $990 and quantity supplied rises from 100 to 116.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A learner drops the negative sign from income elasticity. Which statement best corrects the error?
micro.Choice A: Keep the sign because negative income elasticity identifies an inferior good
micro.Choice B: Always use absolute value for every elasticity
micro.Choice C: A negative sign indicates substitutes
micro.Choice D: The sign affects only supply elasticity
micro.Correct Answer: A — Keep the sign because negative income elasticity identifies an inferior good
micro.Feedback: Income-elasticity sign carries classification information.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A learner says cross-price elasticity below one means goods are unrelated. Which statement best corrects the error?
micro.Choice A: One is the required cutoff for related goods
micro.Choice B: The sign identifies substitutes or complements; magnitude indicates strength
micro.Choice C: Only values above one are substitutes
micro.Choice D: Negative values are calculation errors
micro.Correct Answer: B — The sign identifies substitutes or complements; magnitude indicates strength
micro.Feedback: Cross-price classification is based on sign, not a one-unit cutoff.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A learner sees income elasticity of -0.5 and labels the good a necessity. Which statement best corrects the error?
micro.Choice A: The negative sign identifies an inferior good for the measured consumers
micro.Choice B: Any coefficient below one identifies a normal necessity
micro.Choice C: Negative income elasticity means the goods are complements
micro.Choice D: The coefficient measures price responsiveness, not income responsiveness
micro.Correct Answer: A — The negative sign identifies an inferior good for the measured consumers
micro.Feedback: Negative income elasticity means demand falls when income rises.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: Income rises 10% and quantity demanded rises 5%. A learner reports income elasticity of 2. What went wrong?
micro.Choice A: The sign should be negative because income rose
micro.Choice B: The correct value is 15 because percentages are added
micro.Choice C: Income elasticity cannot be calculated from percentage changes
micro.Choice D: The ratio was reversed; the elasticity is 0.5
micro.Correct Answer: D — The ratio was reversed; the elasticity is 0.5
micro.Feedback: Income elasticity is %ΔQd divided by %Δincome, so 5%/10% = 0.5.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A learner sees cross-price elasticity of +0.9 and says the goods are complements. Which statement best corrects the error?
micro.Choice A: A positive coefficient indicates complements
micro.Choice B: The sign identifies normal versus inferior goods
micro.Choice C: Cross-price elasticity cannot classify related goods
micro.Choice D: A positive coefficient indicates substitutes
micro.Correct Answer: D — A positive coefficient indicates substitutes
micro.Feedback: Demand for one good moves with the other good’s price when the goods are substitutes.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: The price of good Y rises 8% and demand for good X rises 4%. A learner reports cross-price elasticity of 2. Which statement best corrects the error?
micro.Choice A: The ratio is 12 because the percentages are added
micro.Choice B: Cross-price elasticity uses X’s own price change
micro.Choice C: The ratio is 4%/8% = 0.5
micro.Choice D: The ratio must be negative because price rose
micro.Correct Answer: C — The ratio is 4%/8% = 0.5
micro.Feedback: Cross-price elasticity divides the percentage change in demand for X by the percentage change in the price of Y.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A grocery chain expects household incomes to rise. Which use of income elasticity is most direct?
micro.Choice A: Calculate the money multiplier
micro.Choice B: Find the slope of the supply curve
micro.Choice C: Forecast which product categories may gain or lose demand
micro.Choice D: Determine the legal incidence of a sales tax
micro.Correct Answer: C — Forecast which product categories may gain or lose demand
micro.Feedback: Income elasticity helps firms anticipate demand shifts as consumer income changes.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A category has income elasticity 1.4. How does that connect to business forecasting during an expansion?
micro.Choice A: The category must be a complement to every other good
micro.Choice B: Demand may grow more than proportionally with income
micro.Choice C: Demand must fall as income rises
micro.Choice D: Quantity supplied must fall by 1.4%
micro.Correct Answer: B — Demand may grow more than proportionally with income
micro.Feedback: An elasticity above one indicates a strong positive demand response to income growth.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: Why can income elasticity help explain changes in the mix of goods consumers buy as an economy grows?
micro.Choice A: Normal, luxury, and inferior goods respond differently to rising income
micro.Choice B: All goods have identical income responses
micro.Choice C: Income elasticity measures only producer costs
micro.Choice D: It fixes consumer preferences at one bundle
micro.Correct Answer: A — Normal, luxury, and inferior goods respond differently to rising income
micro.Feedback: Different income responses shift the composition of demand as purchasing power changes.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A coffee shop tracks the price of a nearby competitor’s drinks. Why is cross-price elasticity useful?
micro.Choice A: It determines the legal tax rate
micro.Choice B: It indicates how the competitor’s price may shift demand for the shop’s drinks
micro.Choice C: It measures the shop’s fixed cost
micro.Choice D: It identifies the money supply
micro.Correct Answer: B — It indicates how the competitor’s price may shift demand for the shop’s drinks
micro.Feedback: Cross-price elasticity connects substitute pricing to demand shifts.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A console maker lowers console prices. Why might a game publisher care about cross-price elasticity?
micro.Choice A: Negative cross-price elasticity would imply game demand rises as console price falls
micro.Choice B: Positive income elasticity guarantees game demand falls
micro.Choice C: Supply elasticity determines whether consoles and games are complements
micro.Choice D: Cross-price elasticity is unrelated to complementary products
micro.Correct Answer: A — Negative cross-price elasticity would imply game demand rises as console price falls
micro.Feedback: Complementary goods connect through opposite movements between one price and the other good’s demand.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: Two brands have cross-price elasticity near +2. What strategic connection does that suggest?
micro.Choice A: They are strong complements
micro.Choice B: They are unrelated goods
micro.Choice C: They must have identical marginal costs
micro.Choice D: Their demand is strongly linked as substitutes
micro.Correct Answer: D — Their demand is strongly linked as substitutes
micro.Feedback: A large positive cross-price coefficient signals a strong substitution relationship.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A positive income elasticity usually identifies a:
micro.Choice A: Inferior good
micro.Choice B: Complement
micro.Choice C: Normal good
micro.Choice D: Perfectly inelastic good
micro.Correct Answer: C — Normal good
micro.Feedback: Demand for a normal good rises as income rises.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A negative income elasticity usually identifies an:
micro.Choice A: Normal good
micro.Choice B: Substitute good
micro.Choice C: Unit-elastic good
micro.Choice D: Inferior good
micro.Correct Answer: D — Inferior good
micro.Feedback: Demand for an inferior good falls as income rises.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A positive cross-price elasticity indicates that two goods are:
micro.Choice A: Substitutes
micro.Choice B: Complements
micro.Choice C: Both inferior
micro.Choice D: Both perfectly inelastic
micro.Correct Answer: A — Substitutes
micro.Feedback: When the price of one rises, demand for its substitute rises.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A negative cross-price elasticity indicates that two goods are:
micro.Choice A: Substitutes
micro.Choice B: Complements
micro.Choice C: Both normal
micro.Choice D: Both elastic
micro.Correct Answer: B — Complements
micro.Feedback: When the price of one rises, demand for its complement falls.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: Household income rises and demand for bus rides falls. This pattern is most consistent with bus rides being:
micro.Choice A: A normal good with positive income elasticity
micro.Choice B: A luxury with income elasticity above one
micro.Choice C: A substitute good identified by cross-price elasticity
micro.Choice D: An inferior good for these consumers
micro.Correct Answer: D — An inferior good for these consumers
micro.Feedback: Demand moving opposite income implies negative income elasticity and an inferior good.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: Demand for restaurant meals rises when consumer income rises. The income elasticity of demand is therefore most likely:
micro.Choice A: Exactly zero by definition
micro.Choice B: A measure of supply responsiveness
micro.Choice C: Positive
micro.Choice D: Negative
micro.Correct Answer: C — Positive
micro.Feedback: Normal goods have positive income elasticity because demand moves with income.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: If demand for a good changes very little when income changes, its income elasticity is likely to be:
micro.Choice A: The same as its price elasticity
micro.Choice B: Close to zero
micro.Choice C: Necessarily greater than one
micro.Choice D: Necessarily negative
micro.Correct Answer: B — Close to zero
micro.Feedback: A small percentage demand response relative to income means an income elasticity near zero.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: The price of butter rises and demand for margarine rises. Butter and margarine are most likely:
micro.Choice A: Unrelated because cross-price effects cannot shift demand
micro.Choice B: Substitutes
micro.Choice C: Complements
micro.Choice D: Inferior goods
micro.Correct Answer: B — Substitutes
micro.Feedback: Demand for one good moving in the same direction as the other good’s price implies positive cross-price elasticity.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: The price of game consoles falls and demand for compatible games rises. Consoles and games are most likely:
micro.Choice A: Complements
micro.Choice B: Substitutes
micro.Choice C: Both inferior goods
micro.Choice D: Goods with zero cross-price elasticity
micro.Correct Answer: A — Complements
micro.Feedback: Demand for games moves opposite the console price, indicating negative cross-price elasticity.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: If a change in the price of one good has almost no effect on demand for another, their cross-price elasticity is probably:
micro.Choice A: Strongly positive
micro.Choice B: Strongly negative
micro.Choice C: Always equal to one
micro.Choice D: Near zero
micro.Correct Answer: D — Near zero
micro.Feedback: Little demand response to the other good’s price implies little economic relationship between the goods.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: Income changes by 5 percent and demand for premium gym memberships changes by 8 percent. What is income elasticity of demand?
micro.Feedback: Income elasticity equals 8% ÷ 5% = 1.6.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: Income changes by 6 percent and demand for instant noodles changes by -3 percent. What is income elasticity of demand?
micro.Feedback: Income elasticity equals -3% ÷ 6% = -0.5.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: Income changes by 10 percent and demand for public transit rides changes by -4 percent. What is income elasticity of demand?
micro.Feedback: Income elasticity equals -4% ÷ 10% = -0.4.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: Income changes by 4 percent and demand for fine dining meals changes by 7 percent. What is income elasticity of demand?
micro.Feedback: Income elasticity equals 7% ÷ 4% = 1.75.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: Income changes by 8 percent and demand for basic groceries changes by 3 percent. What is income elasticity of demand?
micro.Feedback: Income elasticity equals 3% ÷ 8% = 0.38.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: The price of coffee rises by 10 percent, and quantity demanded for tea rises by 6 percent. What is the cross-price elasticity of demand between coffee and tea?
micro.Feedback: Cross-price elasticity equals 6% ÷ 10% = 0.6.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: The price of printer ink rises by 8 percent, and quantity demanded for printers falls by 12 percent. What is the cross-price elasticity of demand between printer ink and printers?
micro.Feedback: Cross-price elasticity equals -12% ÷ 8% = -1.5.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: The price of gasoline rises by 20 percent, and quantity demanded for bus rides rises by 5 percent. What is the cross-price elasticity of demand between gasoline and bus rides?
micro.Feedback: Cross-price elasticity equals 5% ÷ 20% = 0.25.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: The price of hot-dog buns falls by 10 percent, and quantity demanded for hot dogs rises by 7 percent. What is the cross-price elasticity of demand between hot-dog buns and hot dogs?
micro.Feedback: Cross-price elasticity equals 7% ÷ -10% = -0.7.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: The price of a national-brand product falls by 5 percent, and quantity demanded for the store-brand alternative falls by 8 percent. What is the cross-price elasticity of demand between the two products?
micro.Feedback: Cross-price elasticity equals -8% ÷ -5% = 1.6.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A retailer observes positive cross-price elasticity between its store brand and a national brand. The national brand cuts price. What should the retailer expect for store-brand demand?
micro.Choice A: A decrease
micro.Choice B: An increase
micro.Choice C: No change because the goods are substitutes
micro.Choice D: A shift in store-brand supply
micro.Correct Answer: A — A decrease
micro.Feedback: For substitutes, a fall in one price reduces demand for the other.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A restaurant observes negative cross-price elasticity between entrées and desserts. It sharply raises entrée prices. What is the predicted effect on dessert demand?
micro.Choice A: Dessert demand rises
micro.Choice B: Dessert demand falls
micro.Choice C: Dessert demand is unchanged because desserts have their own price
micro.Choice D: Dessert supply shifts right
micro.Correct Answer: B — Dessert demand falls
micro.Feedback: Complements are consumed together, so fewer entrées reduce dessert demand.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A firm forecasts income growth of 4 percent and estimates income elasticity for its product at 1.5. Holding other factors constant, demand is predicted to:
micro.Choice A: Increase about 2.7 percent
micro.Choice B: Decrease about 6 percent
micro.Choice C: Increase about 6 percent
micro.Choice D: Increase exactly 1.5 percent
micro.Correct Answer: C — Increase about 6 percent
micro.Feedback: Multiply the income change by the elasticity: 4% × 1.5 = 6%.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: During a recession, income falls 3 percent. A product has income elasticity −0.8. Demand is predicted to:
micro.Choice A: Decrease about 2.4 percent
micro.Choice B: Increase about 0.27 percent
micro.Choice C: Remain unchanged because the coefficient is below one
micro.Choice D: Increase about 2.4 percent
micro.Correct Answer: D — Increase about 2.4 percent
micro.Feedback: A negative coefficient times negative income growth produces a positive demand change.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: The price of Product Y rises 10 percent. Cross-price elasticity of demand for Product X is −0.5. Demand for X is predicted to:
micro.Choice A: Fall about 5 percent
micro.Choice B: Rise about 5 percent
micro.Choice C: Fall about 20 percent
micro.Choice D: Remain unchanged because the value is negative
micro.Correct Answer: A — Fall about 5 percent
micro.Feedback: A negative coefficient indicates complements: 10% × −0.5 = −5%.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: The price of Product Y falls 8 percent. Cross-price elasticity of demand for Product X is 1.25. Demand for X is predicted to:
micro.Choice A: Rise about 10 percent
micro.Choice B: Fall about 10 percent
micro.Choice C: Fall about 6.4 percent
micro.Choice D: Remain unchanged because both are substitutes
micro.Correct Answer: B — Fall about 10 percent
micro.Feedback: For substitutes, a price decline in Y lowers demand for X: 1.25 × −8% = −10%.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A positive income elasticity of 2.2 for international vacations means that a recession is likely to cause demand to:
micro.Choice A: Rise because vacations are inferior
micro.Choice B: Fall more than proportionally to income
micro.Choice C: Remain unchanged because the coefficient is positive
micro.Choice D: Fall less than proportionally to income
micro.Correct Answer: B — Fall more than proportionally to income
micro.Feedback: A positive coefficient above one identifies an income-elastic normal good.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A cross-price elasticity between ride-share trips and subway rides is 0.2. Which inference is best supported?
micro.Choice A: They are strong complements
micro.Choice B: They are unrelated because 0.2 is below one
micro.Choice C: They are weak substitutes in the observed range
micro.Choice D: Both are inferior goods
micro.Correct Answer: C — They are weak substitutes in the observed range
micro.Feedback: The positive sign indicates substitutes; the small magnitude indicates a weak relationship.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A cross-price elasticity between game consoles and compatible games is −1.4. Which inference is best supported?
micro.Choice A: They are substitutes because the magnitude exceeds one
micro.Choice B: The console is an inferior good
micro.Choice C: Demand for games is perfectly inelastic
micro.Choice D: They are relatively strong complements
micro.Correct Answer: D — They are relatively strong complements
micro.Feedback: The negative sign indicates complements, and the magnitude suggests a strong link.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: Household income changes by 5 percent and demand for discount groceries changes by -2 percent. Which estimate and classification are correct?
micro.Choice A: Income elasticity is -2.5; the product is classified from the reciprocal
micro.Choice B: Income elasticity is 0.4; the sign has no economic meaning
micro.Choice C: Income elasticity is -0.4; the product is an inferior good
micro.Choice D: The product cannot be classified because price is not provided
micro.Correct Answer: C — Income elasticity is -0.4; the product is an inferior good
micro.Feedback: Divide the demand percentage change by the income percentage change: -0.4. The sign and magnitude identify an inferior good.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: Household income changes by 6 percent and demand for private college housing changes by 5 percent. Which estimate and classification are correct?
micro.Choice A: Income elasticity is 1.2; the product is classified from the reciprocal
micro.Choice B: Income elasticity is 0.83; the sign has no economic meaning
micro.Choice C: The product cannot be classified because price is not provided
micro.Choice D: Income elasticity is 0.83; the product is an income-inelastic normal good
micro.Correct Answer: D — Income elasticity is 0.83; the product is an income-inelastic normal good
micro.Feedback: Divide the demand percentage change by the income percentage change: 0.83. The sign and magnitude identify an income-inelastic normal good.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: Household income changes by 8 percent and demand for used clothing changes by -4 percent. Which estimate and classification are correct?
micro.Choice A: Income elasticity is -0.5; the product is an inferior good
micro.Choice B: Income elasticity is -2; the product is classified from the reciprocal
micro.Choice C: Income elasticity is 0.5; the sign has no economic meaning
micro.Choice D: The product cannot be classified because price is not provided
micro.Correct Answer: A — Income elasticity is -0.5; the product is an inferior good
micro.Feedback: Divide the demand percentage change by the income percentage change: -0.5. The sign and magnitude identify an inferior good.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: Household income changes by 3 percent and demand for premium home renovations changes by 7.5 percent. Which estimate and classification are correct?
micro.Choice A: Income elasticity is 0.4; the product is classified from the reciprocal
micro.Choice B: Income elasticity is 2.5; the product is an income-elastic normal good
micro.Choice C: Income elasticity is 2.5; the sign has no economic meaning
micro.Choice D: The product cannot be classified because price is not provided
micro.Correct Answer: B — Income elasticity is 2.5; the product is an income-elastic normal good
micro.Feedback: Divide the demand percentage change by the income percentage change: 2.5. The sign and magnitude identify an income-elastic normal good.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: The price of tablet cases changes by 15 percent, and demand for tablets changes by -18 percent. Which cross-price result is correct?
micro.Choice A: Cross-price elasticity is -1.2; the goods are complements
micro.Choice B: Cross-price elasticity is -0.83; the reciprocal defines the relationship
micro.Choice C: Cross-price elasticity is 1.2; the goods are substitutes regardless of sign
micro.Choice D: The goods are unrelated because neither quantity supplied nor income is given
micro.Correct Answer: A — Cross-price elasticity is -1.2; the goods are complements
micro.Feedback: The coefficient is -18% ÷ 15% = -1.2. Its sign identifies complements.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: The price of coffee creamer changes by 20 percent, and demand for coffee changes by -7 percent. Which cross-price result is correct?
micro.Choice A: Cross-price elasticity is -2.86; the reciprocal defines the relationship
micro.Choice B: Cross-price elasticity is 0.35; the goods are substitutes regardless of sign
micro.Choice C: Cross-price elasticity is -0.35; the goods are complements
micro.Choice D: The goods are unrelated because neither quantity supplied nor income is given
micro.Correct Answer: C — Cross-price elasticity is -0.35; the goods are complements
micro.Feedback: The coefficient is -7% ÷ 20% = -0.35. Its sign identifies complements.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A planning model assumes a 7 percent income increase with income elasticity 1.3. Which forecast is most consistent with the elasticity estimate?
micro.Choice A: Demand rises about 5.4 percent
micro.Choice B: Demand rises about 9.1 percent
micro.Choice C: Demand falls about 9.1 percent
micro.Choice D: Demand rises exactly 1.3 percent
micro.Correct Answer: B — Demand rises about 9.1 percent
micro.Feedback: Multiply 7% by 1.3.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A planning model assumes a 12 percent increase in a substitute’s price with cross-price elasticity 0.75. Which forecast is most consistent with the elasticity estimate?
micro.Choice A: Demand falls about 9 percent
micro.Choice B: Demand rises about 16 percent
micro.Choice C: Demand rises about 9 percent
micro.Choice D: Demand is unchanged because 0.75 is below one
micro.Correct Answer: C — Demand rises about 9 percent
micro.Feedback: Positive cross elasticity means demand moves with the substitute price: 12% × 0.75 = 9%.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A planning model assumes a 10 percent increase in a complement’s price with cross-price elasticity −0.6. Which forecast is most consistent with the elasticity estimate?
micro.Choice A: Demand rises about 6 percent
micro.Choice B: Demand falls about 16.7 percent
micro.Choice C: Demand is unchanged because the coefficient is negative
micro.Choice D: Demand falls about 6 percent
micro.Correct Answer: D — Demand falls about 6 percent

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A coffee shortage raises coffee prices, and demand for tea rises sharply. What does this indicate about the relationship between coffee and tea and the sign of their cross-price elasticity?
micro.Choice A: Coffee and tea are complements
micro.Choice B: Tea is an inferior good
micro.Choice C: Coffee supply must be perfectly elastic
micro.Choice D: Tea substitutes for coffee, so cross-price elasticity is positive
micro.Correct Answer: D — Tea substitutes for coffee, so cross-price elasticity is positive
micro.Feedback: Switching to tea reveals substitution and a positive cross-price relationship.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: The price of smartphones falls, and demand for mobile data plans rises. Which coefficient captures this relationship?
micro.Choice A: A negative cross-price elasticity between phones and data plans
micro.Choice B: A positive income elasticity for phones
micro.Choice C: Price elasticity of phone supply
micro.Choice D: A positive cross-price elasticity because both demands rose
micro.Correct Answer: A — A negative cross-price elasticity between phones and data plans
micro.Feedback: A lower phone price raises data-plan demand, so the percentage changes have opposite signs.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: An inferior good has income elasticity −0.2. How should the magnitude be interpreted?
micro.Choice A: The good is a strong luxury because the magnitude is below one
micro.Choice B: Demand responds weakly to income changes, but in the opposite direction
micro.Choice C: Demand is perfectly income inelastic
micro.Choice D: The good must be a complement
micro.Correct Answer: B — Demand responds weakly to income changes, but in the opposite direction
micro.Feedback: The negative sign indicates inferior; the small magnitude indicates weak responsiveness.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A normal good has income elasticity 0.9. A boom raises income. What is most likely?
micro.Choice A: Demand falls because the coefficient is below one
micro.Choice B: Demand rises more than proportionally
micro.Choice C: Demand rises, but less than proportionally
micro.Choice D: Demand is unaffected
micro.Correct Answer: C — Demand rises, but less than proportionally
micro.Feedback: Positive but below one means an income-inelastic normal good.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A firm estimates a cross-price elasticity of nearly zero between two products. What is the best supported conclusion?
micro.Choice A: They are definitively unrelated in every market and period
micro.Choice B: They are complements because zero is not positive
micro.Choice C: They are both necessities
micro.Choice D: Their demands show little observed relationship in the sampled range
micro.Correct Answer: D — Their demands show little observed relationship in the sampled range
micro.Feedback: Near zero indicates weak measured interaction, not an eternal structural claim.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A researcher reports income elasticity of −2.3. Should the sign be discarded as with price elasticity of demand?
micro.Choice A: Yes; the magnitude alone identifies a luxury good
micro.Choice B: No; the negative sign identifies an inferior good
micro.Choice C: No; the negative sign identifies complementary goods
micro.Choice D: Yes; income elasticities are reported as absolute values
micro.Correct Answer: B — No; the negative sign identifies an inferior good
micro.Feedback: Income and cross-price signs carry classification information.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: An income elasticity of 1.6 suggests the good is:
micro.Choice A: An inferior good
micro.Choice B: A complement
micro.Choice C: A normal good whose demand is income elastic
micro.Choice D: A normal good whose demand is income inelastic
micro.Correct Answer: C — A normal good whose demand is income elastic
micro.Feedback: Positive income elasticity above one is often associated with a luxury-type normal good.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: An income elasticity of 0.4 suggests the good is:
micro.Choice A: An inferior good
micro.Choice B: A substitute
micro.Choice C: A normal good whose demand falls as income rises
micro.Choice D: A normal good whose demand rises less than proportionally with income
micro.Correct Answer: D — A normal good whose demand rises less than proportionally with income
micro.Feedback: The positive sign indicates normal; magnitude below one indicates income inelasticity.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A cross-price elasticity of 0.8 between tea and coffee implies they are:
micro.Choice A: Substitutes
micro.Choice B: Complements
micro.Choice C: Both inferior
micro.Choice D: Unrelated because the value is below one
micro.Correct Answer: A — Substitutes
micro.Feedback: A positive cross-price coefficient indicates substitutes; magnitude measures strength.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A cross-price elasticity of −0.6 between printers and ink cartridges implies they are:
micro.Choice A: Substitutes
micro.Choice B: Complements
micro.Choice C: Both normal goods
micro.Choice D: Perfectly inelastic
micro.Correct Answer: B — Complements
micro.Feedback: A negative cross-price coefficient means demand moves opposite the other good’s price.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A good has income elasticity of 0.35. Which description fits best?
micro.Choice A: A normal necessity whose demand rises less than proportionally with income
micro.Choice B: An inferior good whose demand falls as income rises
micro.Choice C: A luxury whose demand rises more than proportionally with income
micro.Choice D: A substitute whose demand responds to another good’s price
micro.Correct Answer: A — A normal necessity whose demand rises less than proportionally with income
micro.Feedback: Positive income elasticity below one is commonly associated with necessities.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: Income rises 8% and quantity demanded for a service rises 12%. Based on these changes, the service is best classified as:
micro.Choice A: An inferior good
micro.Choice B: A normal necessity with elasticity below one
micro.Choice C: A complement identified by cross-price elasticity
micro.Choice D: A normal luxury
micro.Correct Answer: D — A normal luxury
micro.Feedback: Demand rises more than proportionally with income, so income elasticity exceeds one.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A retailer estimates income elasticity for its store brand at -0.6. During a strong income expansion, the retailer should expect demand for the store brand to:
micro.Choice A: Remain fixed because elasticity is negative
micro.Choice B: Move only if the store changes its own price
micro.Choice C: Fall, other things equal
micro.Choice D: Rise more than income
micro.Correct Answer: C — Fall, other things equal
micro.Feedback: Negative income elasticity indicates an inferior good, so higher income reduces demand.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: Cross-price elasticity between streaming service A and streaming service B is +1.3. What is the best interpretation?
micro.Choice A: They are unrelated because only the sign of price elasticity matters
micro.Choice B: They are inferior goods because the coefficient is positive
micro.Choice C: They are substitutes and demand for one is fairly responsive to the other’s price
micro.Choice D: They are complements because the coefficient is greater than one
micro.Correct Answer: C — They are substitutes and demand for one is fairly responsive to the other’s price
micro.Feedback: A positive cross-price elasticity signals substitutes; the magnitude indicates a meaningful response.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: Cross-price elasticity between printers and ink cartridges is -0.7. If printer prices rise, demand for ink cartridges should generally:
micro.Choice A: Become perfectly elastic
micro.Choice B: Fall
micro.Choice C: Rise
micro.Choice D: Stay unchanged by definition
micro.Correct Answer: B — Fall
micro.Feedback: A negative cross-price elasticity indicates complements, so higher printer prices reduce demand for ink.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: The price of tea rises 5% and demand for coffee rises 2%. Which conclusion is best?
micro.Choice A: Coffee and tea are substitutes with a positive cross-price elasticity
micro.Choice B: Coffee and tea are complements with a negative cross-price elasticity
micro.Choice C: Coffee is inferior because its demand increased
micro.Choice D: Tea supply is elastic because coffee demand changed
micro.Correct Answer: A — Coffee and tea are substitutes with a positive cross-price elasticity
micro.Feedback: The demand response is in the same direction as the other good’s price change, so cross-price elasticity is positive.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: Holding prices fixed, a 4% income increase raises demand for Product A by 6% and lowers demand for Product B by 2%. If income next falls 2%, use the same local elasticities to forecast the two demands approximately.
micro.Choice A: A rises 3% and B falls 1%; A is normal and B is inferior.
micro.Choice B: A falls 3% and B rises 1%; A is normal and B is inferior.
micro.Choice C: A falls 3% and B falls 1%; discard both income-elasticity signs.
micro.Choice D: A falls 1.33% and B rises 4%; use income change divided by demand change.
micro.Correct Answer: B — A falls 3% and B rises 1%; A is normal and B is inferior.
micro.Feedback: Income elasticities are 6/4 = 1.5 for A and -2/4 = -0.5 for B. Multiplying each signed coefficient by -2% gives -3% and +1%. The signs must be retained for income elasticity.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: Holding other factors fixed, an 8% increase in camera prices reduces demand for a compatible lens by 6%. A supplier next forecasts a 4% camera-price decrease. Which cross-price estimate and approximate lens-demand forecast are consistent?
micro.Choice A: +0.75; lenses and cameras are substitutes, and lens demand falls about 3%.
micro.Choice B: -0.75; lenses and cameras are complements, and lens demand falls about 3%.
micro.Choice C: -0.75; lenses and cameras are complements, and lens demand rises about 3%.
micro.Choice D: -1.33; lenses and cameras are complements, and lens demand rises about 5.33%.
micro.Correct Answer: C — -0.75; lenses and cameras are complements, and lens demand rises about 3%.
micro.Feedback: Cross-price elasticity is -6/8 = -0.75. The negative sign indicates complements. Applying the same local estimate to a -4% camera-price change gives (-0.75)(-4%) = +3% lens demand.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A controlled price test finds that an 8% increase in Service Y’s price raises demand for Service X by 10%. If Y next cuts price 4%, which estimate, relationship, and approximate forecast follow?
micro.Choice A: -1.25, complements; demand for X rises about 5%.
micro.Choice B: +1.25, substitutes; demand for X rises about 5%.
micro.Choice C: +0.80, substitutes; demand for X falls about 3.2%.
micro.Choice D: +1.25, substitutes; demand for X falls about 5%.
micro.Correct Answer: D — +1.25, substitutes; demand for X falls about 5%.
micro.Feedback: Cross-price elasticity is 10/8 = +1.25. Its positive sign indicates substitutes. Applying that signed estimate to -4% gives a -5% change in X demand, with other factors fixed.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: Two rival brands have cross-price elasticity +0.8 for A’s demand with respect to B’s price. Brand A expects B to cut price 5%, while income and A’s own price remain fixed. A proposes stocking 4% more units because the coefficient is positive. Evaluate the plan.
micro.Choice A: The sign identifies substitutes and predicts a 4% demand increase, so the stock increase matches the forecast.
micro.Choice B: The sign identifies substitutes, but the forecast is a 4% demand decrease, so the proposed stock increase reverses the response.
micro.Choice C: The sign identifies complements and predicts a 4% demand decrease, so the stock increase reverses the response.
micro.Choice D: The sign identifies substitutes but predicts a 6.25% demand decrease, so division gives the correct forecast.
micro.Correct Answer: B — The sign identifies substitutes, but the forecast is a 4% demand decrease, so the proposed stock increase reverses the response.
micro.Feedback: A positive cross-price coefficient means X demand moves in the same direction as the other product’s price. Here 0.8 × (-5%) = -4%. A cheaper substitute reduces demand for A; positive elasticity does not mean demand always increases.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A positive income elasticity identifies:
micro.Choice A: An inferior good
micro.Choice B: A normal good
micro.Choice C: Complements
micro.Choice D: Perfectly inelastic demand
micro.Correct Answer: B — A normal good
micro.Feedback: Demand for a normal good moves with income.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A negative income elasticity identifies:
micro.Choice A: A normal good
micro.Choice B: Substitutes
micro.Choice C: An inferior good
micro.Choice D: Elastic supply
micro.Correct Answer: C — An inferior good
micro.Feedback: Demand for an inferior good moves opposite income.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A positive cross-price elasticity identifies:
micro.Choice A: Complements
micro.Choice B: Inferior goods
micro.Choice C: Perfectly elastic goods
micro.Choice D: Substitutes
micro.Correct Answer: D — Substitutes
micro.Feedback: Demand for one rises with the other’s price when goods substitute.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A negative cross-price elasticity identifies:
micro.Choice A: Complements
micro.Choice B: Substitutes
micro.Choice C: Normal goods
micro.Choice D: Unrelated goods by definition
micro.Correct Answer: A — Complements
micro.Feedback: Demand for one falls when the other’s price rises.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A 5 percent income increase raises demand 7.5 percent. What is income elasticity?

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: The price of tea rises 10 percent and demand for coffee rises 6 percent. What is cross-price elasticity?
micro.Feedback: 6 ÷ 10 = 0.6, indicating substitutes.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: The price of printers rises 8 percent and demand for ink falls 12 percent. What is cross-price elasticity?
micro.Feedback: −12 ÷ 8 = −1.5, indicating complements.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A rival’s 10% price cut reduces a firm’s sales by 15%, with its own price held fixed. Using the resulting cross-price elasticity, what would a small 4% rival price increase predict, and what relationship is indicated?
micro.Choice A: About a 6% sales increase; the goods are substitutes because the cross-price elasticity is +1.5.
micro.Choice B: About a 6% sales decline; the goods are complements because the original sales change was negative.
micro.Choice C: About a 1.5% sales increase; elasticity is already a percentage forecast.
micro.Choice D: About a 2.7% sales increase; use the reciprocal of the observed response ratio.
micro.Correct Answer: A — About a 6% sales increase; the goods are substitutes because the cross-price elasticity is +1.5.
micro.Feedback: The ratio is (−15%)/(−10%)=+1.5. A 4% rival-price rise predicts 1.5×4%=6% more sales, consistent with substitution.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: Income falls 4% and product demand rises 6%, with prices and other determinants unchanged. If the estimated income elasticity applies to a subsequent small 2% income increase, what is the forecast and classification?
micro.Choice A: Demand rises about 3%; discard the negative sign when using income elasticity.
micro.Choice B: Demand falls about 3%; the good is inferior over the observed range.
micro.Choice C: Demand falls about 1.5%; the elasticity coefficient itself is the forecast percentage.
micro.Choice D: Demand rises about 8%; add the observed quantity change to the new income change.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Demand falls about 3%; the good is inferior over the observed range.
micro.Feedback: Income elasticity is 6/(−4)=−1.5. Multiplying by the new +2% income change gives −3%. Its negative sign identifies an inferior good over this range.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A rival cuts its price 10%. Your product’s cross-price elasticity with that rival is +1.5, while your own-price elasticity is −0.5. Holding your price and other determinants fixed, which forecast and interpretation fit?
micro.Choice A: Your sales rise about 15%; positive cross-price elasticity means the goods are complements.
micro.Choice B: Your sales fall about 15%; the positive cross-price elasticity indicates substitutes.
micro.Choice C: Your sales rise about 5%; use own-price elasticity with the rival’s price cut.
micro.Choice D: Your sales fall about 0.15%; multiply by the elasticity as though it were already a percentage.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Your sales fall about 15%; the positive cross-price elasticity indicates substitutes.
micro.Feedback: Use the cross-price coefficient for a rival’s price: 1.5×(−10%)=−15%. The positive relationship between rival price and own sales is the substitute pattern.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: Income is forecast to rise 5%. Transit demand has income elasticity −0.6; leisure-rail demand has income elasticity +1.4. Prices and other determinants are fixed. Which forecast separates the sign from responsiveness?
micro.Choice A: Transit demand rises about 3%, while leisure-rail demand rises about 7%; discard the minus sign before forecasting.
micro.Choice B: Transit demand falls about 0.6%, while leisure-rail demand rises about 1.4%; coefficients are percentage changes themselves.
micro.Choice C: Transit demand falls about 3%, while leisure-rail demand rises about 7%; the estimates classify transit as inferior over this range.
micro.Choice D: Both demands rise 5% because the income shock is common to the two markets.
micro.Correct Answer: C — Transit demand falls about 3%, while leisure-rail demand rises about 7%; the estimates classify transit as inferior over this range.
micro.Feedback: Multiply each coefficient by the 5% income rise: −0.6×5%=−3% and 1.4×5%=7%. For income elasticity, the sign identifies the direction and must be retained.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.5 — Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
micro.Question: A product has cross-price elasticity −0.9 with a companion service. The service price falls 10%. An analyst discards the minus sign and forecasts a 9% product-sales decline. Which correction is right?
micro.Choice A: Discard the sign: product sales fall about 9%, consistent with the purchases being substitutes.
micro.Choice B: Keep the sign: product sales fall about 0.9%, because the coefficient already contains the 10% price change.
micro.Choice C: Keep the sign: product sales rise about 9%, consistent with the two purchases being complements.
micro.Choice D: Discard both signs: product sales are unchanged because cross-price elasticity cannot predict quantity.
micro.Correct Answer: C — Keep the sign: product sales rise about 9%, consistent with the two purchases being complements.
micro.Feedback: For cross-price elasticity the sign distinguishes complements from substitutes. (−0.9)×(−10%)=+9%, so a cheaper complement raises demand for the product.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: A learner says the side that sends the tax payment to the government bears the entire tax burden. Which statement best corrects the error?
micro.Choice A: Sellers always bear excise taxes
micro.Choice B: Buyers always bear sales taxes
micro.Choice C: Relative elasticity determines incidence, not remittance
micro.Choice D: The burden is always equal
micro.Correct Answer: C — Relative elasticity determines incidence, not remittance
micro.Feedback: Market price adjustments distribute the burden.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: A learner says inelastic markets have no tax burden because quantity changes little. Which statement best corrects the error?
micro.Choice A: No quantity change means no one pays
micro.Choice B: Inelasticity eliminates price changes
micro.Choice C: Only elastic markets generate revenue
micro.Choice D: Small deadweight loss can coexist with substantial tax burden
micro.Correct Answer: D — Small deadweight loss can coexist with substantial tax burden
micro.Feedback: Burden and efficiency loss are different outcomes.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: A learner predicts profit direction from the total-revenue test alone. Which statement best corrects the error?
micro.Choice A: Revenue and profit are identical
micro.Choice B: Revenue direction is known; profit still requires costs
micro.Choice C: Profit depends only on elasticity
micro.Choice D: Costs affect demand rather than profit
micro.Correct Answer: B — Revenue direction is known; profit still requires costs
micro.Feedback: Elasticity informs revenue; cost completes profit analysis.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: A learner says a price-based policy will reduce quantity by the same percentage in every market. Which statement best corrects the error?
micro.Choice A: Elasticity affects revenue but not policy responses
micro.Choice B: Quantity response depends on the relevant elasticity
micro.Choice C: Every market has unit-elastic demand
micro.Choice D: Only supply shifts can change quantity
micro.Correct Answer: B — Quantity response depends on the relevant elasticity
micro.Feedback: More elastic buyers or sellers respond more strongly to price incentives.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: A learner says labor demand elasticity is unrelated to substitution possibilities. Which statement corrects this mistake?
micro.Choice A: More available substitutes for a type of labor generally make labor demand more elastic
micro.Choice B: Substitutes make labor demand perfectly inelastic
micro.Choice C: Factor demand elasticity depends only on worker preferences
micro.Choice D: Substitution changes labor supply but never labor demand
micro.Correct Answer: A — More available substitutes for a type of labor generally make labor demand more elastic
micro.Feedback: Employers can respond more strongly to wage changes when alternative inputs are available.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: A learner says supply elasticity does not matter when the price received for an export rises. Which statement best corrects the error?
micro.Choice A: Export prices affect demand only
micro.Choice B: Supply elasticity matters only in closed markets
micro.Choice C: More elastic supply means output cannot change
micro.Choice D: More elastic supply allows a larger output response to the higher price
micro.Correct Answer: D — More elastic supply allows a larger output response to the higher price
micro.Feedback: Trade price changes generate larger production responses when supply is more elastic.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: Demand elasticity has magnitude 0.3 and supply elasticity is 1.2 in a competitive market. Which side bears more of a small per-unit tax?
micro.Choice A: Sellers, because supply is more elastic.
micro.Choice B: Both equally, because the tax is per unit.
micro.Choice C: Buyers, because demand is less elastic.
micro.Choice D: The side legally sending the payment, regardless of elasticity.
micro.Correct Answer: C — Buyers, because demand is less elastic.
micro.Feedback: Buyers adjust quantity less readily than sellers; the less elastic side bears more of the tax.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: Two competitive markets receive the same $4 per-unit tax and have linear curves with no other distortions. Quantity falls by 10 units in A and 30 in B. Which has the greater deadweight loss?
micro.Choice A: A: $40 versus B: $120
micro.Choice B: Both: $4
micro.Choice C: B: $120 versus A: $40
micro.Choice D: B: $60 versus A: $20
micro.Correct Answer: D — B: $60 versus A: $20
micro.Feedback: DWL is half the tax wedge times lost quantity: A=0.5×4×10=$20 and B=0.5×4×30=$60.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: A monopolist faces less elastic demand. Which market-structure result is most consistent with that condition?
micro.Choice A: The firm can sustain a larger markup
micro.Choice B: The market becomes perfectly competitive
micro.Choice C: Marginal cost becomes zero
micro.Choice D: Consumer surplus must rise
micro.Correct Answer: A — The firm can sustain a larger markup
micro.Feedback: Market power is stronger when buyers have fewer substitutes.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: A tariff raises the domestic price of an import. Which elasticity predicts the size of the import decline?
micro.Choice A: Income elasticity of domestic supply
micro.Choice B: Price elasticity of money demand
micro.Choice C: Elasticity of import demand
micro.Choice D: Labor-supply elasticity only
micro.Correct Answer: C — Elasticity of import demand
micro.Feedback: Import-demand responsiveness drives the quantity effect.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: Labor-demand elasticity is −0.8. With other conditions fixed, use the small-change approximation to predict employment after a 5% wage increase.
micro.Choice A: Employment rises about 4%.
micro.Choice B: Employment falls about 6.25%.
micro.Choice C: Employment rises about 5%.
micro.Choice D: Employment falls about 4%.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Employment falls about 4%.
micro.Feedback: Percentage employment change is −0.8×5%=−4%; labor is the input demanded.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: A factory’s output imposes an unpriced $3 external cost per unit. A corrective tax raises its relevant per-unit cost, and output demand is price-responsive. Which outcome is consistent with the purpose of the tax?
micro.Choice A: Output falls as the firm faces more of the social cost of production.
micro.Choice B: Output rises because an external cost is an extra benefit.
micro.Choice C: The tax is justified only if output cannot change.
micro.Choice D: The external cost disappears solely because tax revenue is collected.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Output falls as the firm faces more of the social cost of production.
micro.Feedback: The unpriced harm motivates correction; incorporating that cost can reduce output and associated harm. Revenue collection itself is not removal of the physical externality.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: Strategic rivals in an oligopoly may match a price cut. Why does this complicate a firm’s elasticity estimate?
micro.Choice A: Elasticity applies only to monopoly
micro.Choice B: Rival reactions and substitution jointly shape the response
micro.Choice C: Rival reactions make demand vertical
micro.Choice D: Price changes no longer affect quantity
micro.Correct Answer: B — Rival reactions and substitution jointly shape the response
micro.Feedback: Strategic response changes the residual demand facing the firm.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: A firm’s marginal cost rises. Which elasticity helps predict how much the firm can pass through in price?
micro.Choice A: Income elasticity alone
micro.Choice B: Elasticity of demand facing the firm
micro.Choice C: Supply elasticity of consumers
micro.Choice D: GDP elasticity
micro.Correct Answer: B — Elasticity of demand facing the firm
micro.Feedback: Less elastic customer demand supports greater pass-through.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: A public good is financed through taxation. Which elasticities help determine how strongly the tax distorts the market being taxed?
micro.Choice A: The public good’s nonrivalry alone
micro.Choice B: Income elasticity of government
micro.Choice C: Demand and supply elasticities in the tax base
micro.Choice D: Cross-price elasticity of money
micro.Correct Answer: C — Demand and supply elasticities in the tax base
micro.Feedback: Tax-base responsiveness determines the lost transactions.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: Comparative advantage predicts gains from specialization. Which elasticity determines how strongly trade quantities react to changes in relative prices?
micro.Choice A: Income elasticity only
micro.Choice B: Trade-related demand and supply elasticities
micro.Choice C: Perfectly inelastic domestic demand by assumption
micro.Choice D: No elasticity is relevant to trade volumes
micro.Correct Answer: B — Trade-related demand and supply elasticities
micro.Feedback: Comparative advantage explains gains; elasticity shapes the size of quantity adjustments.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: A per-unit tax is generally borne more heavily by the side of the market that is:
micro.Choice A: More elastic
micro.Choice B: Legally required to mail the payment
micro.Choice C: Less elastic
micro.Choice D: Represented by the flatter curve in every case
micro.Correct Answer: C — Less elastic
micro.Feedback: The less elastic side has fewer ways to avoid the taxed transaction.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: If demand is much less elastic than supply, buyers usually bear:
micro.Choice A: None of the tax burden
micro.Choice B: Exactly half of every tax by rule
micro.Choice C: More of a per-unit tax burden
micro.Choice D: Less of a per-unit tax burden
micro.Correct Answer: C — More of a per-unit tax burden
micro.Feedback: The less elastic side of the market changes quantity less and bears more of the tax burden.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: If supply is much less elastic than demand, sellers usually bear:
micro.Choice A: Only the administrative cost of the tax
micro.Choice B: More of a per-unit tax burden
micro.Choice C: Less of a per-unit tax burden
micro.Choice D: None of the tax burden
micro.Correct Answer: B — More of a per-unit tax burden
micro.Feedback: The less elastic side has fewer alternatives and bears more of the tax burden.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: A business facing highly elastic demand should be especially cautious about:
micro.Choice A: Raising price
micro.Choice B: Expanding output
micro.Choice C: Tracking competitors
micro.Choice D: Estimating variable cost
micro.Correct Answer: A — Raising price
micro.Feedback: With elastic demand, a price increase can cause a proportionally larger loss of quantity demanded.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: A business facing very inelastic demand can raise price with a relatively small percentage decline in:
micro.Choice A: Fixed cost
micro.Choice B: Supply elasticity
micro.Choice C: Producer technology
micro.Choice D: Quantity demanded
micro.Correct Answer: D — Quantity demanded
micro.Feedback: Inelastic demand means quantity demanded responds proportionally less than price.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: Other things equal, a tax reduces the quantity traded by more when demand and supply are:
micro.Choice A: Perfectly vertical
micro.Choice B: Unrelated to price
micro.Choice C: More elastic
micro.Choice D: More inelastic
micro.Correct Answer: C — More elastic
micro.Feedback: More responsive buyers and sellers reduce traded quantity more when a tax wedge is introduced.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: A policy that raises price will reduce consumption most strongly when demand is:
micro.Choice A: Independent of price
micro.Choice B: More elastic
micro.Choice C: More inelastic
micro.Choice D: Perfectly inelastic
micro.Correct Answer: B — More elastic
micro.Feedback: Elastic demand produces a larger percentage quantity response to a given percentage price change.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: An export industry can expand output more after a world-price increase when its supply is:
micro.Choice A: More elastic
micro.Choice B: More inelastic
micro.Choice C: Perfectly inelastic
micro.Choice D: Measured only by income elasticity
micro.Correct Answer: A — More elastic
micro.Feedback: More elastic supply allows producers to respond more strongly to the higher price.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: If employers can easily substitute machines for a type of labor when wages rise, demand for that labor is likely to be:
micro.Choice A: More inelastic
micro.Choice B: Perfectly inelastic
micro.Choice C: Unrelated to substitution possibilities
micro.Choice D: More elastic
micro.Correct Answer: D — More elastic
micro.Feedback: Availability of substitutes makes factor demand more responsive to its price.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: A city wants a fee to sharply reduce use of a service. The fee is more likely to change behavior when demand for the service is:
micro.Choice A: Perfectly inelastic
micro.Choice B: Vertical at every price
micro.Choice C: Elastic
micro.Choice D: Inelastic
micro.Correct Answer: C — Elastic
micro.Feedback: Elastic demand means usage responds strongly to a price-like charge.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: A tax is imposed in a market with perfectly inelastic demand and upward-sloping supply. Who bears the economic burden?
micro.Choice A: Sellers bear the entire tax
micro.Choice B: The burden is necessarily split equally
micro.Choice C: Buyers bear the entire tax
micro.Choice D: The government bears the tax
micro.Correct Answer: C — Buyers bear the entire tax
micro.Feedback: Buyers cannot change quantity, so the consumer price rises by the full tax.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: A tax is imposed in a market with perfectly inelastic supply and downward-sloping demand. Who bears the economic burden?
micro.Choice A: Buyers bear the entire tax
micro.Choice B: The burden is necessarily split equally
micro.Choice C: No one bears the tax because quantity is fixed
micro.Choice D: Sellers bear the entire tax
micro.Correct Answer: D — Sellers bear the entire tax
micro.Feedback: Suppliers cannot withdraw quantity, so the net price they receive falls by the full tax.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: A planning model assumes a 20 percent wage increase with labor-demand elasticity 0.8. Which forecast is most consistent with the elasticity estimate?
micro.Choice A: Employment rises about 16 percent
micro.Choice B: Employment falls about 16 percent
micro.Choice C: Employment falls about 25 percent
micro.Choice D: Employment is unchanged because labor is a factor market
micro.Correct Answer: B — Employment falls about 16 percent
micro.Feedback: The demand response is 0.8 × 20% = 16% in the opposite direction.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: A labor tax is imposed where workers’ labor supply is much less elastic than firms’ labor demand. Who bears most of the burden?
micro.Choice A: Firms through higher labor cost only
micro.Choice B: The government
micro.Choice C: Whichever party receives the tax form
micro.Choice D: Workers through lower after-tax compensation
micro.Correct Answer: D — Workers through lower after-tax compensation
micro.Feedback: The less elastic side—workers in this case—has fewer avoidance options.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: A subsidy is offered to buyers in a market with perfectly inelastic supply. Who captures the subsidy?
micro.Choice A: Sellers through a higher market price
micro.Choice B: Buyers through a permanently lower net price
micro.Choice C: The benefit splits equally
micro.Choice D: No one because quantity cannot rise
micro.Correct Answer: A — Sellers through a higher market price
micro.Feedback: With fixed supply, competition among buyers bids the subsidy into seller receipts.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: A minimum wage has a larger employment effect in one industry than another. Which explanation is most directly elasticity-based?
micro.Choice A: Workers are legally required to pay the wage
micro.Choice B: Labor demand is more elastic in the industry with the larger employment response
micro.Choice C: The industry has higher nominal revenue
micro.Choice D: Labor supply slopes upward in both industries
micro.Correct Answer: B — Labor demand is more elastic in the industry with the larger employment response
micro.Feedback: More elastic labor demand produces a larger quantity-of-labor response to wage changes.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: Why is labor demand often more elastic when machinery can easily substitute for labor?
micro.Choice A: Machinery makes labor supply more elastic
micro.Choice B: Wages become a smaller unit of measurement
micro.Choice C: Firms can change input mix more strongly after a wage increase
micro.Choice D: The output demand curve becomes vertical
micro.Correct Answer: C — Firms can change input mix more strongly after a wage increase
micro.Feedback: Input substitutability raises the responsiveness of labor demanded.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: A country’s export demand is highly elastic. Its currency appreciates, raising foreign-currency export prices. What is the likely quantity effect?
micro.Choice A: A relatively large decline in exports
micro.Choice B: A small decline because export demand is elastic
micro.Choice C: No change because exchange rates affect only supply
micro.Choice D: An increase in exports
micro.Correct Answer: A — A relatively large decline in exports
micro.Feedback: Elastic foreign demand responds strongly to the higher effective price.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: Import supply to a small country is nearly perfectly elastic at the world price. A tariff is introduced. Which side is likely to bear most of the tariff?
micro.Choice A: Foreign suppliers
micro.Choice B: Domestic import buyers
micro.Choice C: The burden must be equal
micro.Choice D: Domestic exporters
micro.Correct Answer: B — Domestic import buyers
micro.Feedback: The highly elastic foreign supply side can redirect goods, leaving domestic buyers with the price increase.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: A tariff reduces imports much more than forecast. Which prior assumption was probably too low?
micro.Choice A: The income elasticity of domestic supply
micro.Choice B: The slope of the world price line in dollars
micro.Choice C: The price elasticity of import demand
micro.Choice D: The statutory tariff rate
micro.Correct Answer: C — The price elasticity of import demand
micro.Feedback: A larger-than-expected quantity response indicates more elastic import demand.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: A policy analyst uses demand elasticity to predict a quota’s price effect. What additional elasticity is essential?
micro.Choice A: Income elasticity only
micro.Choice B: Cross-price elasticity only
micro.Choice C: No other elasticity is relevant
micro.Choice D: Supply elasticity
micro.Correct Answer: D — Supply elasticity
micro.Feedback: The equilibrium price response depends on responsiveness on both sides.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: A binding production quota reduces market quantity. In which demand case is the price increase likely largest?
micro.Choice A: More inelastic demand
micro.Choice B: More elastic demand
micro.Choice C: Perfectly elastic demand
micro.Choice D: Demand with many substitutes
micro.Correct Answer: A — More inelastic demand
micro.Feedback: When buyers reduce quantity little, price must rise more to clear the restricted supply.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: Demand is very inelastic and supply is relatively elastic. Which side of the market will bear most of a new excise tax?
micro.Choice A: Sellers
micro.Choice B: The government
micro.Choice C: Buyers
micro.Choice D: Whichever side writes the check
micro.Correct Answer: C — Buyers
micro.Feedback: Buyers have fewer ways to avoid the taxed market.

micro.Learning Objective: ELAS.6 — Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions
micro.Question: Demand is relatively elastic and supply is very inelastic. Which side of the market will bear most of a new tax?
micro.Choice A: Buyers
