micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: A student sees producer losses from imports and concludes total surplus must fall. What corrects the error?
micro.Choice A: Producer losses are not real
micro.Choice B: Imports never lower producer surplus
micro.Choice C: Consumer gains can exceed producer losses
micro.Choice D: Government revenue always offsets the loss
micro.Correct Answer: C — Consumer gains can exceed producer losses
micro.Feedback: Net welfare depends on both sides of the market.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: Why do consumers gain when a lower world price opens an import market?
micro.Choice A: They pay more and purchase less
micro.Choice B: Domestic supply shifts right automatically
micro.Choice C: Tariff revenue rises
micro.Choice D: They pay less and purchase more
micro.Correct Answer: D — They pay less and purchase more
micro.Feedback: Both the price and quantity effects raise consumer surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: A student says exports benefit everyone because producers gain. What is the correction?
micro.Choice A: Domestic consumers may lose from the higher price
micro.Choice B: Producers never gain from exports
micro.Choice C: The domestic price falls
micro.Choice D: Exports eliminate domestic consumption
micro.Correct Answer: A — Domestic consumers may lose from the higher price
micro.Feedback: Export gains are unevenly distributed.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: Why can total surplus rise even when domestic consumers lose from exports?
micro.Choice A: Consumer losses are ignored
micro.Choice B: Producer gains can exceed consumer losses
micro.Choice C: Foreign surplus is counted as domestic government revenue
micro.Choice D: Domestic demand becomes vertical
micro.Correct Answer: B — Producer gains can exceed consumer losses
micro.Feedback: The net change is what matters for total surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: A student says “gains from trade” means every person gains. What does the term actually mean?
micro.Choice A: Every wage rises
micro.Choice B: Every producer expands
micro.Choice C: Total surplus rises
micro.Choice D: Imports and exports are equal
micro.Correct Answer: C — Total surplus rises
micro.Feedback: Aggregate gains do not imply universal gains.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: A learner says free trade cannot create net gains if one domestic group loses. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
micro.Choice A: Distributional losses are never counted
micro.Choice B: Net gains can be positive when winners gain more than losers lose
micro.Choice C: Any losing group makes total surplus negative
micro.Choice D: Trade gains require every person to gain
micro.Correct Answer: B — Net gains can be positive when winners gain more than losers lose
micro.Feedback: Aggregate gains and distribution are separate: a market can have positive net gains and identifiable losers.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: How does consumer surplus connect to an import market?
micro.Choice A: It becomes tariff revenue
micro.Choice B: It equals domestic production
micro.Choice C: A lower world price expands the area below demand and above price
micro.Choice D: It disappears whenever imports occur
micro.Correct Answer: C — A lower world price expands the area below demand and above price
micro.Feedback: In an importing market, the lower world price increases consumer surplus by lowering the price buyers pay and increasing the quantity they purchase.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: How does producer surplus connect to an import market?
micro.Choice A: It always becomes zero
micro.Choice B: It equals imports
micro.Choice C: It becomes consumer expenditure
micro.Choice D: A lower domestic price shrinks the area above supply and below price
micro.Correct Answer: D — A lower domestic price shrinks the area above supply and below price
micro.Feedback: In an importing market, the lower world price reduces producer surplus because domestic sellers receive a lower price and sell a smaller quantity.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: How does total surplus identify gains from trade?
micro.Choice A: Compare consumer plus producer surplus before and after trade
micro.Choice B: Compare imports with exports only
micro.Choice C: Count producer revenue only
micro.Choice D: Count the physical number of goods leaving
micro.Correct Answer: A — Compare consumer plus producer surplus before and after trade
micro.Feedback: Gains from trade equal the increase in total domestic surplus, found by comparing consumer plus producer surplus before and after trade.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: Why can trade raise total surplus while hurting one group?
micro.Choice A: Group losses are not counted
micro.Choice B: A larger gain to one side can exceed the other side’s loss
micro.Choice C: Prices do not affect surplus
micro.Choice D: Total surplus measures equality
micro.Correct Answer: B — A larger gain to one side can exceed the other side’s loss
micro.Feedback: Trade can raise total surplus when the gains to the winning side exceed the losses borne by the losing side.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: How can demand elasticity affect consumer losses from an export-driven price increase?
micro.Choice A: Elasticity fixes the world price
micro.Choice B: Elasticity determines license ownership
micro.Choice C: More responsive quantity demanded changes the lost-consumption area and surplus reduction
micro.Choice D: Elasticity makes consumer surplus constant
micro.Correct Answer: C — More responsive quantity demanded changes the lost-consumption area and surplus reduction
micro.Feedback: When demand is more elastic, domestic quantity demanded responds more to an export-driven price increase, changing the size of the consumer-surplus loss.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: How does the surplus framework connect free-trade winners and losers to the efficiency conclusion?
micro.Choice A: Add consumer and producer surplus changes to determine the net gain
micro.Choice B: Count only the group that gains
micro.Choice C: Ignore producer surplus in importing markets
micro.Choice D: Treat every redistribution as deadweight loss
micro.Correct Answer: A — Add consumer and producer surplus changes to determine the net gain
micro.Feedback: The surplus framework converts distributional changes into a net total-surplus comparison.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: Opening an importing market to a lower world price normally causes domestic consumer surplus to:
micro.Choice A: Decrease
micro.Choice B: Increase
micro.Choice C: Remain unchanged
micro.Choice D: Become equal to producer surplus
micro.Correct Answer: B — Increase
micro.Feedback: Consumers pay less and purchase more.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: Opening an importing market to a lower world price normally causes domestic producer surplus to:
micro.Choice A: Increase
micro.Choice B: Remain unchanged
micro.Choice C: Decrease
micro.Choice D: Become tariff revenue
micro.Correct Answer: C — Decrease
micro.Feedback: Domestic producers receive a lower price and sell less.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: Opening an exporting market to a higher world price normally causes domestic consumer surplus to:
micro.Choice A: Increase
micro.Choice B: Remain unchanged
micro.Choice C: Become quota rent
micro.Choice D: Decrease
micro.Correct Answer: D — Decrease
micro.Feedback: Domestic consumers pay the higher world price and buy less.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: Opening an exporting market to a higher world price normally causes domestic producer surplus to:
micro.Choice A: Increase
micro.Choice B: Decrease
micro.Choice C: Remain unchanged
micro.Choice D: Become government revenue
micro.Correct Answer: A — Increase
micro.Feedback: Domestic producers receive a higher price and sell more.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: What does “gains from trade” mean in the standard surplus model?
micro.Choice A: Every domestic consumer and producer gains
micro.Choice B: Total surplus is higher with trade than without trade
micro.Choice C: Imports become larger than domestic production
micro.Choice D: The government receives tariff revenue
micro.Correct Answer: B — Total surplus is higher with trade than without trade
micro.Feedback: Gains from trade are measured by the increase in total surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: Which statement is correct when total surplus rises after trade opens?
micro.Choice A: Every domestic person must be better off
micro.Choice B: Domestic producers must always gain
micro.Choice C: Some domestic groups may still lose even though the aggregate gain is positive
micro.Choice D: Domestic consumers must always lose
micro.Correct Answer: C — Some domestic groups may still lose even though the aggregate gain is positive
micro.Feedback: Aggregate gains do not imply universal gains.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: When an importing country opens to a lower world price, domestic buyers generally:
micro.Choice A: Lose because imports reduce choice
micro.Choice B: Are unaffected because only producers trade
micro.Choice C: Pay the old domestic price by definition
micro.Choice D: Gain because they pay a lower price
micro.Correct Answer: D — Gain because they pay a lower price
micro.Feedback: The lower domestic price raises consumer surplus for buyers.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: When an importing country opens to trade at a lower price, domestic producers generally:
micro.Choice A: Are unaffected by the lower domestic price
micro.Choice B: Receive tariff revenue automatically
micro.Choice C: Lose some producer surplus
micro.Choice D: Gain producer surplus because imports raise price
micro.Correct Answer: C — Lose some producer surplus
micro.Feedback: Domestic sellers receive a lower price and sell less, reducing producer surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: When an exporting country opens to a higher world price, domestic producers generally:
micro.Choice A: Pay the world price to consumers
micro.Choice B: Gain producer surplus
micro.Choice C: Lose producer surplus
micro.Choice D: Are unaffected because exports go abroad
micro.Correct Answer: B — Gain producer surplus
micro.Feedback: The higher domestic price and larger domestic production raise producer surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: The standard small-country model predicts that opening to free trade:
micro.Choice A: Raises total surplus even though some domestic groups can lose
micro.Choice B: Makes every domestic person better off
micro.Choice C: Always lowers consumer surplus
micro.Choice D: Always lowers producer surplus
micro.Correct Answer: A — Raises total surplus even though some domestic groups can lose
micro.Feedback: Trade creates net gains while redistributing surplus between buyers and sellers.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: An importing country opens to trade. Consumer surplus rises by $900 and producer surplus falls by $500. What is the gain from trade?
micro.Feedback: The net increase in total surplus is $900 minus $500 = $400.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: An exporting country opens to trade. Producer surplus rises by $760 and consumer surplus falls by $460. What happens to total surplus?
micro.Choice A: It falls by $300
micro.Choice B: It rises by $1,220
micro.Choice C: It does not change
micro.Choice D: It rises by $300
micro.Correct Answer: D — It rises by $300
micro.Feedback: The producer gain exceeds the consumer loss by $300.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: After an importing market opens, domestic consumers gain $90 of surplus while domestic producers lose $55. Which statement describes the national welfare effect in the standard model?
micro.Choice A: Total surplus falls by $145 because one group loses
micro.Choice B: Total surplus is unchanged because gains and losses offset by definition
micro.Choice C: Producer surplus rises by $35 because imports expand
micro.Choice D: Total surplus rises by $35 even though producers lose
micro.Correct Answer: D — Total surplus rises by $35 even though producers lose
micro.Feedback: The consumer gain exceeds the producer loss by $35, so national total surplus rises while distribution shifts toward consumers.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: Opening an export market gives domestic producers $70 more surplus but costs domestic consumers $46 of surplus. What is the best summary?
micro.Choice A: There is no national gain because both groups must benefit
micro.Choice B: Consumers gain $24 because the world price is higher
micro.Choice C: The country has a $24 net gain while consumers lose
micro.Choice D: The country has a $116 net loss because consumers lose
micro.Correct Answer: C — The country has a $24 net gain while consumers lose
micro.Feedback: Producer gains exceed consumer losses by $24, illustrating how trade can raise total surplus without making every group better off.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: Why can free trade raise total surplus even when domestic producers in an importing industry lose?
micro.Choice A: Consumer surplus is always larger than producer surplus
micro.Choice B: Consumer gains can exceed producer losses
micro.Choice C: Producer losses are not counted in welfare analysis
micro.Choice D: Imports automatically create government revenue
micro.Correct Answer: B — Consumer gains can exceed producer losses
micro.Feedback: The efficiency result is based on the net change in combined surplus, not on every group winning.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: Why can free trade raise total surplus even when domestic consumers in an exporting industry lose?
micro.Choice A: Producer gains can exceed consumer losses
micro.Choice B: Consumer losses are ignored when goods are exported
micro.Choice C: Exports eliminate scarcity
micro.Choice D: The domestic price must fall under exports
micro.Correct Answer: A — Producer gains can exceed consumer losses
micro.Feedback: Higher export prices redistribute surplus toward producers while creating a positive net gain in the standard model.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: After trade opens, one group gains $120 and another loses $85. Which statement is best?
micro.Choice A: There is a $205 net gain because gains and losses are both positive numbers
micro.Choice B: There is no net gain because someone loses
micro.Choice C: The losing group’s loss should not be counted
micro.Choice D: There is a $35 net gain, but the distributional conflict is real
micro.Correct Answer: D — There is a $35 net gain, but the distributional conflict is real
micro.Feedback: Net welfare is the gain minus the loss, while distribution identifies who bears the loss.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: A policy analyst says “trade is beneficial, so nobody can be harmed by opening the market.” What is wrong with the statement?
micro.Choice A: Only exporters can gain from trade
micro.Choice B: Consumer and producer surplus never change with trade
micro.Choice C: Net gains do not imply every group gains

micro.Feedback: Producer surplus falls from $450 to $32, a loss of $418.

micro.Choice B: A loss of $800
micro.Choice C: A loss of $400
micro.Choice D: No change
micro.Correct Answer: C — A loss of $400

micro.Question: In Bellora's export market, no-trade consumer surplus is $578 and open-trade consumer surplus is $162. Calculate the consumer-surplus change.

micro.Choice B: A loss of $256
micro.Choice C: No change
micro.Choice D: A loss of $416
micro.Correct Answer: D — A loss of $416

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: In Caspia's export market, no-trade consumer surplus is $450 and open-trade consumer surplus is $72. Calculate the consumer-surplus change.
micro.Choice A: A loss of $378
micro.Choice B: A gain of $378

micro.Question: In Arden's export market, no-trade producer surplus is $450 and open-trade producer surplus is $1250. Calculate the producer-surplus change.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: In Caspia's export market, no-trade producer surplus is $450 and open-trade producer surplus is $1152. Calculate the producer-surplus change.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: Bellora's total surplus is $1156 without trade and $1480 with imports. Calculate gains from trade.

micro.Question: Caspia's total surplus is $900 without trade and $1384 with imports. Calculate gains from trade.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: Which group normally gains from a lower import price?
micro.Choice A: Domestic import-competing producers
micro.Choice B: Only the government
micro.Choice C: Domestic consumers
micro.Choice D: No domestic group
micro.Correct Answer: C — Domestic consumers
micro.Feedback: A lower import price benefits domestic consumers because they pay less and purchase more, increasing consumer surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: Which group normally gains from a higher export price?
micro.Choice A: Domestic consumers
micro.Choice B: Only the government
micro.Choice C: No domestic group
micro.Choice D: Domestic producers
micro.Correct Answer: D — Domestic producers
micro.Feedback: A higher export price benefits domestic producers because they receive a higher price and expand production, increasing producer surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: Gains from trade refer to:
micro.Choice A: An increase in total surplus
micro.Choice B: A gain for every person
micro.Choice C: A rise in tariff revenue
micro.Choice D: A fall in all domestic production
micro.Correct Answer: A — An increase in total surplus
micro.Feedback: Gains from trade are measured by the increase in total surplus after trade opens.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: Which statement is true?
micro.Choice A: Trade raises total surplus only if everyone gains
micro.Choice B: Trade can create winners and losers while raising total surplus
micro.Choice C: Imports always lower total surplus
micro.Choice D: Exports always lower total surplus
micro.Correct Answer: B — Trade can create winners and losers while raising total surplus
micro.Feedback: Trade can raise total surplus even though it creates domestic winners and losers.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: Consumer surplus rises by $780 and producer surplus falls by $460. Total surplus changes by:
micro.Feedback: Total surplus rises by $780 − $460 = $320.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: Producer surplus rises by $900 and consumer surplus falls by $540. Total surplus changes by:
micro.Feedback: Total surplus rises by $900 − $540 = $360.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: At Pw=$30 in the import graph, consumer surplus equals:
micro.Feedback: At Pw = $30, consumer surplus is the triangle below demand and above price: ½ × 50 × 50 = $1,250.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: At Pw=$30 in the import graph, producer surplus equals:
micro.Feedback: At Pw = $30, producer surplus is the triangle above supply and below price: ½ × 10 × 10 = $50.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: At Pw=$70 in the export graph, consumer surplus equals:
micro.Feedback: At Pw = $70, consumer surplus is the triangle below demand and above price: ½ × 10 × 10 = $50.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: At Pw=$70 in the export graph, producer surplus equals:
micro.Feedback: At Pw = $70, producer surplus is the triangle above supply and below price: ½ × 50 × 50 = $1,250.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: No-trade total surplus is $900 and open-trade total surplus is $1,300. Gains from trade are:
micro.Feedback: Gains from trade equal the increase in total surplus: $1,300 − $900 = $400.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: Which is a transfer rather than a net loss?
micro.Choice A: A mutually beneficial trade prevented by policy
micro.Choice B: High-cost production replacing imports
micro.Choice C: Consumption valued above world cost that no longer occurs
micro.Choice D: A shift of surplus from consumers to producers
micro.Correct Answer: D — A shift of surplus from consumers to producers
micro.Feedback: A shift of surplus from consumers to producers is a transfer between domestic groups. Prevented mutually beneficial trades and inefficient production are net social losses.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: Why do import gains exceed producer losses in the standard model?
micro.Choice A: Lower-cost sourcing and added consumption create extra surplus
micro.Choice B: Producer losses are excluded
micro.Choice C: Imports raise domestic price
micro.Choice D: Domestic production expands
micro.Correct Answer: A — Lower-cost sourcing and added consumption create extra surplus
micro.Feedback: With imports, lower-cost foreign supply replaces some higher-cost domestic production and the lower price creates additional consumption gains. Together those gains exceed the producer-surplus loss.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: Why do export gains exceed consumer losses in the standard model?
micro.Choice A: Consumer losses are excluded
micro.Choice B: Higher-value foreign sales and added production create extra surplus
micro.Choice C: Exports lower domestic price
micro.Choice D: Domestic production contracts
micro.Correct Answer: B — Higher-value foreign sales and added production create extra surplus
micro.Feedback: With exports, additional domestic production is sold where the world price exceeds marginal cost, and those production gains exceed the consumer-surplus loss from the higher domestic price.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: In an import market, domestic price falls from $50 to $30. Which group loses?
micro.Choice A: Domestic producers
micro.Choice B: Domestic consumers
micro.Choice C: Foreign consumers only
micro.Choice D: The government automatically
micro.Correct Answer: A — Domestic producers
micro.Feedback: A lower import price reduces the price domestic producers receive and the quantity they sell, so domestic producers lose surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: In an export market, domestic price rises from $50 to $70. Which group loses?
micro.Choice A: Domestic producers
micro.Choice B: Domestic consumers
micro.Choice C: Foreign producers only
micro.Choice D: The government automatically
micro.Correct Answer: B — Domestic consumers
micro.Feedback: A higher export price raises the price domestic consumers pay and reduces the quantity they buy, so domestic consumers lose surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: Which measure is needed for national gains from trade?
micro.Choice A: Change in import quantity alone
micro.Choice B: Change in producer revenue alone
micro.Choice C: Change in total domestic consumer plus producer surplus
micro.Choice D: Change in the physical trade balance alone
micro.Correct Answer: C — Change in total domestic consumer plus producer surplus
micro.Feedback: National gains from trade are measured by the change in total domestic surplus: consumer surplus plus producer surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.3 — Calculate and interpret consumer, producer, and total-surplus changes from trade.
micro.Question: Why is every-person-gains not required for aggregate gains?
micro.Choice A: Individual losses are ignored
micro.Choice B: Prices do not matter
micro.Choice C: Only firms count
micro.Choice D: Total surplus sums gains and losses across groups
micro.Correct Answer: D — Total surplus sums gains and losses across groups
micro.Feedback: Aggregate gains require total gains to exceed total losses; they do not require every person or group to gain.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: A small importing country faces a world price of $20 per unit and imposes a $4 per-unit tariff. The country cannot affect the world price, and imports continue after the tariff. What domestic price results?
micro.Choice A: $24 per unit
micro.Choice B: $16 per unit
micro.Choice C: $20 per unit
micro.Choice D: $4 per unit
micro.Correct Answer: A — $24 per unit
micro.Feedback: With imports continuing, domestic price equals world price plus the per-unit tariff: $20 + $4 = $24. The tariff adds to the domestic price; it is not subtracted from the world price.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: A tariff raises domestic production and lowers domestic consumption. What happens to imports?
micro.Choice A: They rise
micro.Choice B: They fall
micro.Choice C: They are unchanged
micro.Choice D: They equal domestic production
micro.Correct Answer: B — They fall
micro.Feedback: The gap between demand and supply shrinks.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: A student labels tariff revenue as deadweight loss. What is wrong?
micro.Choice A: Revenue belongs to consumers
micro.Choice B: Deadweight loss equals producer gain
micro.Choice C: Revenue is a transfer; deadweight loss is lost surplus
micro.Choice D: Tariffs never collect revenue
micro.Correct Answer: C — Revenue is a transfer; deadweight loss is lost surplus
micro.Feedback: Separate transfers from net losses.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: Which two effects create tariff deadweight loss?
micro.Choice A: Producer surplus and tariff revenue
micro.Choice B: Imports and exports
micro.Choice C: Consumer surplus and quota rent
micro.Choice D: Production distortion and consumption distortion
micro.Correct Answer: D — Production distortion and consumption distortion
micro.Feedback: The tariff causes too much high-cost domestic production and too little consumption.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: A learner calculates tariff revenue using all domestic consumption rather than imported units. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
micro.Choice A: Multiply the tariff by domestic production plus imports
micro.Choice B: Use the world price times all consumption
micro.Choice C: Tariff revenue equals consumer surplus lost
micro.Choice D: Multiply the tariff per unit by the quantity imported
micro.Correct Answer: D — Multiply the tariff per unit by the quantity imported
micro.Feedback: The tariff is collected on imported units, not on every unit consumed.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: A learner says all consumer surplus lost under a tariff is deadweight loss. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
micro.Choice A: Producer gains are not part of total surplus
micro.Choice B: Government revenue is always deadweight loss
micro.Choice C: Some loss is transferred to producers and government; only the unrecovered portion is deadweight loss
micro.Choice D: All consumer loss disappears from national welfare
micro.Correct Answer: C — Some loss is transferred to producers and government; only the unrecovered portion is deadweight loss
micro.Feedback: Tariff welfare analysis separates transfers from production and consumption distortions.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: What surplus concept separates tariff revenue from deadweight loss?
micro.Choice A: All consumer losses are deadweight loss
micro.Choice B: All producer gains are deadweight loss
micro.Choice C: Transfers change recipients; deadweight loss removes mutually beneficial trades
micro.Choice D: Revenue is never part of welfare
micro.Correct Answer: C — Transfers change recipients; deadweight loss removes mutually beneficial trades
micro.Feedback: Tariff revenue is a transfer to the government, while deadweight loss represents gains from trade that disappear because the tariff distorts production and consumption.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: How can supply elasticity affect domestic production response to a tariff?
micro.Choice A: Elasticity eliminates tariff revenue
micro.Choice B: Elasticity fixes import quantity under every policy
micro.Choice C: Elasticity makes marginal cost irrelevant
micro.Choice D: More responsive supply creates a larger production increase and distortion
micro.Correct Answer: D — More responsive supply creates a larger production increase and distortion
micro.Feedback: When domestic supply is more responsive to price, the tariff-induced price increase produces a larger increase in domestic output and therefore a larger production distortion, other things equal.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: How is a tariff connected to a tax wedge?
micro.Choice A: It creates a gap between the domestic buyer price and the world resource price
micro.Choice B: It creates a gap between domestic quantity supplied and domestic quantity demanded, measured as tax per unit.
micro.Choice C: It creates a gap between the government’s total tariff receipts and the per-unit price paid for imports.
micro.Choice D: It creates a gap between the lower domestic buyer price and the unchanged world price after the tariff.
micro.Correct Answer: A — It creates a gap between the domestic buyer price and the world resource price
micro.Feedback: In the small-country importing model, a tariff raises the domestic price above the world price while imports continue. That price difference is the per-unit tax wedge. The import quantity and total tariff revenue are different measures, and the tariff does not lower the domestic buyer price.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: How is tariff deadweight loss connected to lost gains from exchange?
micro.Choice A: It equals tariff revenue
micro.Choice B: The tariff prevents beneficial imports and induces higher-cost production
micro.Choice C: It equals all consumer expenditure
micro.Choice D: It is a payment to foreign firms
micro.Correct Answer: B — The tariff prevents beneficial imports and induces higher-cost production
micro.Feedback: The tariff prevents some imports whose value to domestic buyers exceeds their world resource cost and also induces higher-cost domestic production. Those foregone gains create deadweight loss.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: How does a tariff connect to the tax-wedge idea from domestic markets?
micro.Choice A: It guarantees the legal and economic burden are identical
micro.Choice B: It creates a wedge between the world price and the domestic buyer/seller price
micro.Choice C: It eliminates the role of price
micro.Choice D: It shifts world demand only
micro.Correct Answer: B — It creates a wedge between the world price and the domestic buyer/seller price
micro.Feedback: A tariff acts like a tax on imports and raises the domestic price above the world price in the small-country model.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: How does tariff deadweight loss connect to surplus analysis?
micro.Choice A: It is the total surplus destroyed by production and consumption distortions
micro.Choice B: It is the full transfer from consumers to producers
micro.Choice C: It equals tariff revenue
micro.Choice D: It is producer surplus after the tariff
micro.Correct Answer: A — It is the total surplus destroyed by production and consumption distortions
micro.Feedback: The surplus framework identifies the trades and resource uses that no longer maximize gains.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: A tariff is:
micro.Choice A: A legal maximum on exports
micro.Choice B: A payment to domestic consumers
micro.Choice C: A tax on all domestic production
micro.Choice D: A tax on imported goods
micro.Correct Answer: D — A tax on imported goods
micro.Feedback: A tariff taxes imported units.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: In the basic small-country import model, a tariff normally causes the domestic price to:
micro.Choice A: Rise above the world price
micro.Choice B: Fall below the world price
micro.Choice C: Remain at the world price
micro.Choice D: Become equal to the no-trade quantity
micro.Correct Answer: A — Rise above the world price
micro.Feedback: The tariff creates a wedge between the world price and domestic price.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: A tariff that raises the domestic price generally causes imports to:
micro.Choice A: Increase
micro.Choice B: Decrease
micro.Choice C: Remain unchanged
micro.Choice D: Equal domestic quantity demanded
micro.Correct Answer: B — Decrease
micro.Feedback: Domestic production rises and domestic consumption falls, shrinking imports.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: Tariff revenue equals:
micro.Choice A: Domestic price multiplied by domestic production
micro.Choice B: Consumer surplus minus producer surplus
micro.Choice C: Tariff per imported unit multiplied by the number of imported units
micro.Choice D: The two tariff deadweight-loss triangles
micro.Correct Answer: C — Tariff per imported unit multiplied by the number of imported units
micro.Feedback: Government revenue is the tariff rate times post-tariff imports.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: Why is tariff revenue not deadweight loss?
micro.Choice A: Tariff revenue is retained by domestic firms, so it remains part of producer surplus rather than a social loss
micro.Choice B: Deadweight loss is the portion of consumer surplus transferred to producers and the government after the tariff
micro.Choice C: Tariff revenue offsets the production distortion, leaving the consumption distortion as the remaining deadweight loss
micro.Choice D: Revenue is a transfer to the government, while deadweight loss is surplus that disappears
micro.Correct Answer: D — Revenue is a transfer to the government, while deadweight loss is surplus that disappears
micro.Feedback: A transfer changes who receives surplus; deadweight loss is a net loss.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: In the displayed trade graph, what domestic price results from the $4 world price plus the tariff?
micro.Feedback: The graph marks the tariff-inclusive domestic price at $6.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: What is the per-unit tariff shown in the displayed trade graph?
micro.Feedback: The domestic price rises from the $4 world price to $6, so the tariff is $2 per unit.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: In a small importing country, a tariff usually causes domestic production of the protected good to:
micro.Choice A: Decrease
micro.Choice B: Remain fixed by definition
micro.Choice C: Fall to zero
micro.Choice D: Increase
micro.Correct Answer: D — Increase
micro.Feedback: The tariff raises the domestic price, encouraging domestic producers to supply more.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: In a small importing country, a tariff usually causes domestic consumption of the protected good to:
micro.Choice A: Remain fixed by definition
micro.Choice B: Become equal to exports
micro.Choice C: Decrease
micro.Choice D: Increase
micro.Correct Answer: C — Decrease
micro.Feedback: The higher domestic price reduces quantity demanded.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: Government tariff revenue is generated by:
micro.Choice A: The tariff multiplied by domestic consumption whether imported or not
micro.Choice B: The tariff per imported unit multiplied by the quantity imported
micro.Choice C: The world price multiplied by domestic production
micro.Choice D: Consumer surplus multiplied by producer surplus
micro.Correct Answer: B — The tariff per imported unit multiplied by the quantity imported
micro.Feedback: Tariff revenue equals the tax rate per imported unit times the number of units still imported.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: Refer to the tariff graph. What are post-tariff imports?
micro.Choice A: 10 units
micro.Choice B: 30 units
micro.Choice C: 40 units
micro.Choice D: 20 units
micro.Correct Answer: D — 20 units
micro.Feedback: At Pt=$40, Qd=40 and Qs=20, so imports are 20.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: A $6 tariff applies to 40 imported units. How much tariff revenue is collected?
micro.Feedback: Tariff revenue is $6 × 40 = $240.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: After a tariff, domestic production rises from 25 to 35 units while domestic consumption falls from 70 to 60 units. What happens to imports?
micro.Choice A: They rise from 45 to 95 units
micro.Choice B: They fall from 45 to 25 units
micro.Choice C: They fall from 70 to 60 units
micro.Choice D: They stay at 45 units
micro.Correct Answer: B — They fall from 45 to 25 units
micro.Feedback: Imports change from 70−25=45 to 60−35=25.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: A trade policy creates $300 of producer gains, $180 of government revenue, and $620 of consumer losses. What is the net welfare effect?
micro.Choice A: A $140 gain
micro.Choice B: A $140 loss
micro.Choice C: A $500 gain
micro.Choice D: No net change
micro.Correct Answer: B — A $140 loss

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: At the tariff-inclusive price of $6 in the displayed trade graph, domestic production is:
micro.Choice A: 50 thousand
micro.Choice B: 150 thousand
micro.Choice C: 100 thousand
micro.Choice D: 200 thousand
micro.Correct Answer: C — 100 thousand
micro.Feedback: The $6 line intersects domestic supply at Q = 100 thousand.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. At the tariff-inclusive price shown, what is domestic quantity demanded?
micro.Choice A: 100 thousand
micro.Choice B: 150 thousand
micro.Choice C: 250 thousand
micro.Choice D: 200 thousand
micro.Correct Answer: D — 200 thousand
micro.Feedback: The $6 line intersects demand at Q = 200 thousand.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: After the tariff in the displayed trade graph, imports equal:
micro.Choice A: 100 thousand
micro.Choice B: 50 thousand
micro.Choice C: 150 thousand
micro.Choice D: 200 thousand
micro.Correct Answer: A — 100 thousand
micro.Feedback: At $6, Qd = 200 thousand and Qs = 100 thousand, so imports are 100 thousand.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: Compared with free trade at Pw = $4, the tariff in the displayed trade graph reduces imports by:
micro.Choice A: 50 thousand
micro.Choice B: 100 thousand
micro.Choice C: 150 thousand
micro.Choice D: 200 thousand
micro.Correct Answer: B — 100 thousand
micro.Feedback: Free-trade imports are 250 − 50 = 200 thousand; after the tariff they are 100 thousand.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: A tariff raises the domestic price from $20 to $24. Domestic production rises while domestic consumption falls. What happens to imports?
micro.Choice A: They fall
micro.Choice B: They rise
micro.Choice C: They must stay unchanged
micro.Choice D: They become exports automatically
micro.Correct Answer: A — They fall
micro.Feedback: Imports equal domestic consumption minus domestic production; both changes shrink that gap.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: A $3 tariff is collected on 40 imported units. How much tariff revenue does the government receive?
micro.Feedback: Revenue is $3 × 40 = $120.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: Why does a small-country tariff reduce total surplus even though it creates government revenue?
micro.Choice A: Producer surplus always falls under a tariff
micro.Choice B: The world price rises by the full tariff
micro.Choice C: Some lost consumer surplus becomes deadweight loss rather than a transfer
micro.Choice D: Government revenue is never part of national surplus
micro.Correct Answer: C — Some lost consumer surplus becomes deadweight loss rather than a transfer
micro.Feedback: Part of the consumer loss is transferred to producers and government; the production and consumption distortions are net losses.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: Arden imposes an $8 tariff and imports 24 units after the tariff. Calculate tariff revenue.
micro.Feedback: Revenue is $8×24=$192.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: Bellora imposes a $10 tariff and imports 16 units after the tariff. Calculate tariff revenue.
micro.Feedback: Revenue is $10×16=$160.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: In Arden, an $8 tariff raises domestic production from 10 to 18. Calculate the production-side deadweight loss.
micro.Feedback: The triangle is ½×$8×8=$32.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: In Bellora, a $10 tariff raises domestic production from 16 to 26. Calculate the production-side deadweight loss.
micro.Feedback: The triangle is ½×$10×10=$50.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: An $8 tariff reduces domestic consumption from 50 to 42. Calculate the consumption-side deadweight loss.
micro.Feedback: The triangle is ½×$8×8=$32.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: A tariff creates a $45 production-side deadweight loss and a $55 consumption-side deadweight loss. Calculate total tariff deadweight loss.
micro.Feedback: Total tariff deadweight loss is the sum of the two distortion losses: $45+$55=$100.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: A tariff shifts $400 from consumers to domestic producers and $250 to government, while destroying $120 of surplus. What is the consumer loss?
micro.Feedback: Consumer loss equals producer gain + revenue + deadweight loss: 400+250+120=770.

micro.Learning Objective: ITP.4 — Analyze tariff effects on price, quantities, revenue, and total surplus.
micro.Question: Why is the tariff production-side deadweight loss a social loss?
micro.Choice A: Domestic firms receive revenue
micro.Choice B: Consumers buy imported goods
micro.Choice C: The government collects tariff revenue
micro.Choice D: Higher-cost domestic units replace lower-cost imported units
micro.Correct Answer: D — Higher-cost domestic units replace lower-cost imported units
micro.Feedback: The resource cost rises for units shifted to less efficient domestic production.
