micro.Question: A campaign has already spent $400,000. A final placement costs $60,000 and yields additional revenue of $100,000 if it succeeds, otherwise zero. With no other effects, which success probability makes the placement break even?
micro.Choice D: A probability above 100% because past spending must be recovered
micro.Feedback: Set expected incremental revenue equal to avoidable cost: p times $100,000 = $60,000, so p = 0.60. Past campaign expenditure is sunk.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.3
micro.Common Misconception: Comparing totals or reporting one marginal change.
micro.Question: At 12 trips a route has total benefits of 840 points and costs of 610. At 13 trips these become 892 and 655. At 14 they become 930 and 699. With no later trips available, which expansion from 12 is best?
micro.Choice A: Add one trip; the two increments net +7 and -6 points
micro.Choice B: Add two trips because total benefit still exceeds total cost
micro.Choice C: Add neither because both trips raise total cost
micro.Choice D: Add two trips because 14 trips has the highest total benefit
micro.Correct Answer: A — Add one trip; the two increments net +7 and -6 points
micro.Feedback: Trip 13 adds 52 - 45 = 7 points. Trip 14 adds 38 - 44 = -6. Relative to 12 trips, the feasible gains are 0, 7 and 1; add only trip 13.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.3
micro.Common Misconception: Comparing gross future costs or sunk totals instead of future alternatives.
micro.Question: A university pilot has spent $6 million. Extending it costs $900,000 and yields $1.1 million in expected benefit, while ending now requires $250,000 in transition cost. What is best?
micro.Choice A: Extend because its future net gain exceeds the cost of ending
micro.Choice B: End because total spending is already too high
micro.Choice C: Extend only to avoid wasting the $6 million
micro.Choice D: End because transition cost is less than extension cost
micro.Correct Answer: A — Extend because its future net gain exceeds the cost of ending
micro.Feedback: Extending gains $200,000, while ending loses $250,000.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.3
micro.Common Misconception: Ignoring changing external costs or continuing one unit too far.
micro.Question: A city adds park lighting in blocks. Marginal benefits are 100, 82, 61, and 40; private costs are 55 each, but marginal light-pollution costs are 10, 18, 25, and 32. How many blocks should be lit?
micro.Choice A: Two blocks
micro.Choice B: One block
micro.Choice C: Three blocks
micro.Choice D: Four blocks
micro.Correct Answer: A — Two blocks
micro.Feedback: Social MC is 65, 73, 80, and 87; only the first two pass.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.3
micro.Common Misconception: Using gross possible savings or ignoring probability.
micro.Question: An inspection costs $70,000 and prevents $500,000 in repairs if it finds a defect in time, otherwise saving nothing. It displaces work worth $20,000. What detection probability makes the inspection break even?
micro.Feedback: Expected benefit is p times $500,000. Direct plus opportunity cost is $90,000, so break-even requires p = 90,000 / 500,000 = 18%.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.3
micro.Common Misconception: Rejecting a unit whenever it has any cost.
micro.Question: The next unit has marginal benefit $24 and marginal cost $19. What should happen?
micro.Choice A: Continue only because past costs are sunk.
micro.Choice B: Stop because cost is positive.
micro.Choice C: Stop unless average benefit rises.
micro.Choice D: Produce or consume the next unit.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Produce or consume the next unit.
micro.Feedback: The next unit adds $5 in net benefit.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.3
micro.Common Misconception: Using a blanket rule without checking whether the cost is truly sunk.
micro.Question: A fee has already been paid, but its refund terms have not yet been checked. When should it affect the current decision?
micro.Choice A: Only if some part of it can still be recovered or avoided.
micro.Choice B: Only when total benefits are positive.
micro.Choice C: Always, because past spending must be recovered.
micro.Choice D: Never, even if a refund remains available.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Only if some part of it can still be recovered or avoided.
micro.Feedback: Check whether the current choice changes how much of the fee can be recovered. A refund available under one choice but not another is relevant; a payment that cannot be recovered or changed is sunk. Having paid the fee does not by itself establish that it is irrelevant, and a desire to recover past spending is not a marginal benefit.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.3
micro.Common Misconception: Comparing totals or averages instead of their changes.
micro.Question: A school considers one more tutoring session. Total benefit would rise from 72 to 80 points and total cost from 48 to 54 points. Which values should be compared?
micro.Choice A: Marginal benefit 8 and marginal cost 6
micro.Choice B: Total benefit 80 and total cost 54
micro.Choice C: Average benefit 76 and average cost 51
micro.Choice D: Prior benefit 72 and prior cost 48
micro.Correct Answer: A — Marginal benefit 8 and marginal cost 6
micro.Feedback: The additional session adds 8 benefit points and 6 cost points.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.3
micro.Common Misconception: Using positive average profit instead of the next order’s margin.
micro.Question: A firm’s average profit is positive. The next order adds $180 in revenue and $205 in avoidable cost. What should it do?
micro.Choice A: Reject the order because its marginal contribution is negative
micro.Choice B: Accept because average profit across all prior orders remains positive
micro.Choice C: Accept because total revenue will rise
micro.Choice D: Reject only if fixed cost also rises
micro.Correct Answer: A — Reject the order because its marginal contribution is negative
micro.Feedback: The order reduces profit by $25.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.3
micro.Common Misconception: Using totals or treating any added cost as disqualifying.
micro.Question: Total benefit rises from 300 to 336 with one more unit; total cost rises from 210 to 242. What should happen?
micro.Choice A: Add the unit because MB 36 exceeds MC 32
micro.Choice B: Stop because total cost rises by 32
micro.Choice C: Add only if average benefit increases
micro.Choice D: Stop because total cost remains positive
micro.Correct Answer: A — Add the unit because MB 36 exceeds MC 32
micro.Feedback: The next unit adds 4 in net benefit.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.3
micro.Common Misconception: Continuing after marginal cost first exceeds marginal benefit.
micro.Question: MB values for units 1 through 4 are 30, 22, 14, and 8; MC values are 10, 16, 15, and 12. Which production plan is optimal?
micro.Choice A: Produce only unit 1
micro.Choice B: Produce all four units
micro.Choice C: Produce the first three units
micro.Choice D: Produce the first two units
micro.Correct Answer: D — Produce the first two units
micro.Feedback: Units 1 and 2 add net benefit; unit 3 would reduce it.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.3
micro.Common Misconception: Escalating commitment based on sunk cost.
micro.Question: A project has spent $5 million irreversibly. Finishing now costs $3 million and produces $2 million in future benefits. Abandoning it costs $1.5 million in required restoration, with no future benefits. Delaying changes neither future cost nor benefit. Which choice minimizes the remaining loss?
micro.Choice A: Abandon: $2 million of benefits is below $3 million of cost, regardless of the restoration alternative.
micro.Choice B: Finish: the $5 million already spent must be counted as an additional benefit from completion.
micro.Choice C: Finish: the $1 million future loss is smaller than the $1.5 million abandonment loss.
micro.Choice D: Delay: postponement removes the restoration cost even though the stated future alternatives are unchanged.
micro.Correct Answer: C — Finish: the $1 million future loss is smaller than the $1.5 million abandonment loss.
micro.Feedback: Finishing nets 2-3=-1 million. Abandoning nets -1.5 million. Finishing is preferable by 0.5 million, despite its negative standalone future net value, because the feasible alternative is worse. Sunk spending is irrelevant.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.3
micro.Common Misconception: Ignoring a displaced private profit opportunity or counting an unavoidable sunk fee.
micro.Question: A firm can accept a rush order for $30,000 or decline it. Internal production requires $16,000 in materials and labor plus $2,000 in extra maintenance, and displaces a job with $9,000 net profit. Outsourcing costs $24,000 plus $1,000 for inspection and leaves that other job intact. A $6,000 design fee is already paid and nonrefundable under every choice. Both production methods are feasible and give the same revenue. Which plan maximizes incremental private profit?
micro.Choice A: Produce internally; incremental profit is $12,000.
micro.Choice B: Outsource production; incremental profit is $5,000.
micro.Choice C: Reject the order; the best production option loses $1,000.
micro.Choice D: Produce internally; incremental profit is $3,000.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Outsource production; incremental profit is $5,000.
micro.Feedback: Internal production adds $30,000 - $16,000 - $2,000 - $9,000 = $3,000 after accounting for the displaced job. Outsourcing adds $30,000 - $24,000 - $1,000 = $5,000 and preserves that job, so outsourcing is best. The $6,000 design fee is sunk and does not enter either comparison.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.3
micro.Common Misconception: Ignoring the displaced project or including sunk spending.
micro.Question: A project has $10 million in sunk spending. Completion costs $3 million, yields $3.4 million, and displaces another project worth $0.6 million. What is the decision?
micro.Choice A: Do not complete because relevant marginal cost is $3.6 million
micro.Choice B: Complete because future revenue exceeds direct cost
micro.Choice C: Complete to recover the $10 million
micro.Choice D: Do not complete because total project cost is high
micro.Correct Answer: A — Do not complete because relevant marginal cost is $3.6 million
micro.Feedback: Direct plus opportunity cost exceeds future benefit.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.3
micro.Common Misconception: Ignoring an external marginal cost.
micro.Question: One more factory inspection avoids expected losses of $95,000, costs $62,000, and creates $38,000 in delay costs for customers. What is the social choice?
micro.Choice A: Skip it because marginal social cost is $100,000
micro.Choice B: Perform it because direct cost is below avoided loss
micro.Choice C: Perform it because total quality benefit is positive
micro.Choice D: Skip it because all delay costs are sunk
micro.Correct Answer: A — Skip it because marginal social cost is $100,000
micro.Feedback: The inspection’s combined added cost exceeds avoided loss.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.3
micro.Common Misconception: Continuing after MC exceeds MB or stopping early.
micro.Question: A city can buy sensors sequentially. Direct MBs are 90, 72, 50 and 31; MCs are 40, 60, 55 and 48. A linked alert system worth 25 becomes feasible only with at least three sensors and costs no more. Which number maximizes total net benefit?
micro.Choice A: Three: totals are 50, 62, 82 and 65 for one through four sensors.
micro.Choice B: Two: the third direct MB is below MC, so any linked benefit must be excluded.
micro.Choice C: Four: four sensors have the largest total direct benefit regardless of incremental cost.
micro.Choice D: One: its individual net benefit is largest, so later positive gains should be ignored.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Three: totals are 50, 62, 82 and 65 for one through four sensors.
micro.Feedback: Cumulative direct net gains are 50, 62, 57 and 40. Add 25 for plans with at least three sensors: 82 and 65. Three is optimal because the third unlocks an additional benefit while the fourth does not.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.3
micro.Common Misconception: Comparing gross future costs or sunk totals instead of net alternatives.
micro.Question: A project has spent $5 million irreversibly. Finishing costs $900,000 and yields $1 million. Canceling costs $180,000. Selling the project as-is brings $350,000 but requires $120,000 of transfer work and avoids cancellation fees. Which choice is best?
micro.Choice A: Sell: its $230,000 future net value exceeds finishing’s $100,000 and canceling’s -$180,000.
micro.Choice B: Finish: the $1 million receipt is the largest, and the sunk investment should be recovered before considering a sale.
micro.Choice C: Cancel: its $180,000 outlay is below finishing cost, so the sale receipt should not affect the comparison.
micro.Choice D: Finish: the relevant sale alternative is $350,000 minus the entire $5 million already spent.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Sell: its $230,000 future net value exceeds finishing’s $100,000 and canceling’s -$180,000.
micro.Feedback: Compare future net values: 1,000,000-900,000=100,000; -180,000; 350,000-120,000=230,000. Selling wins. The historical $5 million is unchanged by the decision.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.3
micro.Common Misconception: Ignoring the forgone use of the next resource increment.
micro.Question: A hospital can add a mobile unit with expected benefits of $700,000 and direct costs of $520,000. Its team would abandon prevention work worth $210,000. Hiring temporary prevention staff costs $140,000 and preserves all that work; no other constraints change. Which plan maximizes incremental benefit?
micro.Choice A: Add the unit and hire temporary staff: net gain is $40,000, versus a $30,000 loss if prevention is displaced.
micro.Choice B: Do not add the unit: the $210,000 prevention value must be lost under every plan.
micro.Choice C: Add the unit without replacement: its $180,000 cash surplus establishes the largest social gain.
micro.Choice D: Add the unit and hire staff: net gain is $250,000 because preserved prevention is an extra benefit above the baseline.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Add the unit and hire temporary staff: net gain is $40,000, versus a $30,000 loss if prevention is displaced.
micro.Feedback: Without replacement the incremental gain is 700-520-210=-30 thousand. With replacement it is 700-520-140=40 thousand; the preserved prevention service is already in the baseline, not an extra 210 gain.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.3
micro.Common Misconception: Omitting a cost component or reporting gross output.
micro.Question: A manufacturer can hire a worker for one job that adds $1,400 in output. Wages are $980 and equipment costs $260 but can be resold for $100 after the job. The worker’s workstation could instead be rented out for $190 during the job. Which net contribution is relevant?
micro.Choice A: $70: subtract wages, net equipment cost and forgone workstation rent.
micro.Choice B: $260: subtract wages and net equipment cost but ignore the owned workstation.
micro.Choice C: $160: subtract wages and the full equipment purchase but ignore resale and rent.
micro.Choice D: -$30: subtract wages, the full equipment purchase and rent, ignoring resale.
micro.Correct Answer: A — $70: subtract wages, net equipment cost and forgone workstation rent.
micro.Feedback: Net equipment use costs 260-100=160. Relevant contribution is 1400-980-160-190=70. Ownership does not remove forgone rental income, and recoverable resale value reduces the equipment cost.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.3
micro.Common Misconception: Ignoring external marginal cost.
micro.Question: A cleanup method yields $500 in health benefits, costs the operator $370 and damages habitat by $150. A gentler method gives the same health benefit, costs $430 and causes $20 of habitat damage. Which method is socially preferable, and what would an operator ignoring habitat costs choose?
micro.Choice A: Society prefers the gentler method ($50 net); the operator prefers the original ($130 private net versus $70).
micro.Choice B: Society prefers the original ($130 net); the operator prefers the gentler method because its habitat damage is lower.
micro.Choice C: Both prefer the original because its cash cost is lower and habitat losses are transfers between users.
micro.Choice D: Both reject cleanup because the original method’s $520 social cost proves every available method has negative net benefit.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Society prefers the gentler method ($50 net); the operator prefers the original ($130 private net versus $70).
micro.Feedback: Original social net benefit is 500-370-150=-20; gentler net benefit is 500-430-20=50. Ignoring habitat, private nets are 130 and 70, so private and social rankings differ.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.3
micro.Common Misconception: Ignoring probability or sunk testing expenditure.
micro.Question: A preventable failure has a 25% probability and would cost $800,000. Prevention costs $170,000 and eliminates the loss. A perfect test costs $20,000 and permits prevention only when failure would otherwise occur. For a risk-neutral decision maker, which strategy has the lowest expected cost?
micro.Choice A: Test then prevent if needed: $62,500, versus $170,000 for unconditional prevention and $200,000 for no action.
micro.Choice B: Prevent unconditionally: $170,000, versus $220,000 for testing because testing cannot change the failure probability.
micro.Choice C: Take no action: $0, because a 25% possible loss is not a current cash outlay.
micro.Choice D: Test then prevent if needed: $190,000, because prevention must be paid even after a negative test.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Test then prevent if needed: $62,500, versus $170,000 for unconditional prevention and $200,000 for no action.
micro.Feedback: No action costs 0.25×800000=200000 in expectation. Unconditional prevention costs 170000. Testing allows conditional prevention, costing 20000+0.25×170000=62500. Information has value because it changes action in the no-failure state.

micro.Topic: Marginal Product And Value Of Marginal Product
micro.Learning Objective: FM.3 — Calculate Value of Marginal Product
micro.Common Misconception: Forgets that VMP equals output price times marginal product under the competitive-output-market assumption.
micro.Question: A bakery worker adds 7 loaves per hour, and each sells for $6. What is the worker's VMP?
micro.Choice A: $42 per hour
micro.Choice B: $7 per hour
micro.Choice C: $6 per hour
micro.Choice D: $13 per hour
micro.Correct Answer: A — $42 per hour
micro.Feedback: VMP equals output price times MPL: $6 × 7 = $42 per hour. MPL is physical output; VMP expresses that contribution in dollars.

micro.Topic: Marginal Product And Value Of Marginal Product
micro.Learning Objective: FM.3 — Calculate Value of Marginal Product
micro.Common Misconception: Forgets that VMP equals output price times marginal product under the competitive-output-market assumption.
micro.Question: The marginal product of a worker at a greenhouse is 10 plant flats. With an output price of $4, calculate the value of marginal product.
micro.Choice A: $40 per hour
micro.Choice B: $10 per hour
micro.Choice C: $4 per hour
micro.Choice D: $14 per hour
micro.Correct Answer: A — $40 per hour
micro.Feedback: VMP equals output price times MPL: $4 × 10 = $40 per hour. MPL is physical output; VMP expresses that contribution in dollars.

micro.Question: The marginal product of a worker at a landscaping firm is 3 yards. With an output price of $20, calculate the value of marginal product.
micro.Choice A: $3 per hour
micro.Choice B: $20 per hour
micro.Choice C: $60 per hour
micro.Choice D: $23 per hour
micro.Correct Answer: C — $60 per hour
micro.Feedback: VMP equals output price times MPL: $20 × 3 = $60 per hour. MPL is physical output; VMP expresses that contribution in dollars.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.7 — Marginal Rate of Substitution
micro.Question: Refer to the graph above. If the consumer's MRS were greater than 2 at a nearby affordable point, what adjustment would raise utility?
micro.Choice A: Choose more X and less Y
micro.Choice B: Choose less X and more Y
micro.Choice C: Keep the bundle because every boundary point is optimal
micro.Choice D: Buy an unaffordable amount of both goods
micro.Correct Answer: A — Choose more X and less Y
micro.Feedback: Valuing X more highly than its market tradeoff makes moving toward X beneficial until the tradeoffs match.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.7 — Marginal Rate of Substitution
micro.Question: MUx is 12 and MUy is 6. What does MRSx,y measure?
micro.Choice A: The consumer's marginal willingness to give up Y for X, equal to 12/6
micro.Choice B: The market price ratio regardless of preferences
micro.Choice C: Total utility 18
micro.Choice D: Income divided by 12
micro.Correct Answer: A — The consumer's marginal willingness to give up Y for X, equal to 12/6
micro.Feedback: For differentiable utility, MRSx,y = MUx/MUy and describes the slope magnitude of the indifference curve.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.7 — Marginal Rate of Substitution

micro.Learning Objective: CC.7 — Marginal Rate of Substitution
micro.Question: At the interior tangency in the graph, what is the consumer’s marginal willingness to give up Y for one more X, and which condition explains it?
micro.Choice A: Two units of Y; MRS equals the price ratio.
micro.Choice B: One unit of Y; total utility equals income.
micro.Choice C: One unit of Y; MRS equals the price ratio.
micro.Choice D: Two units of Y; total utility equals income.
micro.Correct Answer: C — One unit of Y; MRS equals the price ratio.
micro.Feedback: The budget has intercepts 20 and 20, so its slope has magnitude one. At C the indifference curve is tangent to it: the consumer’s MRS equals Px/Py = 1. This equality concerns marginal tradeoffs, not utility measured in dollars.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.10 — Marginal Utility per Dollar
micro.Question: MUx/Px is 9.0 and MUy/Py is 5.2. How should spending adjust?
micro.Choice A: Shift spending toward X and away from Y
micro.Choice B: Shift spending toward Y
micro.Choice C: Equalize marginal utilities without regard to price
micro.Choice D: Maximize spending rather than utility
micro.Correct Answer: A — Shift spending toward X and away from Y
micro.Feedback: A dollar should be moved toward the good with the higher marginal utility per dollar until the ratios are equal or a corner intervenes.

micro.Question: At the smooth interior optimum shown, the price of X falls while income and Y’s price stay fixed. What is the old price ratio Px/Py, and what adjustment is initially supported at the old bundle, assuming diminishing marginal utility and an interior new optimum?
micro.Choice A: One; MUx/Px rises relative to MUy/Py, favoring more spending on X subject to the new budget.
micro.Choice B: Two; MUx/Px rises relative to MUy/Py, favoring more spending on X subject to the new budget.
micro.Choice C: Two; MUx/Px falls relative to MUy/Py, favoring less spending on X subject to the new budget.
micro.Choice D: One; MUx/Px falls relative to MUy/Py, favoring less spending on X subject to the new budget.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Two; MUx/Px rises relative to MUy/Py, favoring more spending on X subject to the new budget.
micro.Feedback: The budget intercepts are 20 for X and 40 for Y, so Px/Py = 40/20 = 2. At the old tangency MUx/Px = MUy/Py. Lower Px raises MUx/Px at the unchanged bundle. Reallocation toward X helps restore equality, while the final bundle must satisfy the new budget.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.6
micro.Question: A market failure occurs when:
micro.Choice A: Market outcomes do not efficiently allocate resources
micro.Choice B: Every buyer and seller agrees on price
micro.Choice C: Demand slopes downward
micro.Choice D: A firm earns profit
micro.Correct Answer: A — Market outcomes do not efficiently allocate resources
micro.Feedback: Market failure describes cases where decentralized market outcomes are inefficient.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.6
micro.Question: Pollution from a factory that harms nearby residents is an example of:
micro.Choice A: A price floor
micro.Choice B: A negative externality
micro.Choice C: A perfectly efficient market
micro.Choice D: A positive externality.
micro.Correct Answer: B — A negative externality
micro.Feedback: Pollution affects bystanders, so it is a negative externality.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.6
micro.Question: A public good is usually:
micro.Choice A: Always sold by one monopoly firm
micro.Choice B: A legal maximum price
micro.Choice C: Hard to exclude people from and shared by many users
micro.Choice D: A substitute for every other good
micro.Correct Answer: C — Hard to exclude people from and shared by many users
micro.Feedback: Public goods are generally nonexcludable and nonrival.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.6
micro.Question: A seller with substantial influence over the market price has:
micro.Choice A: A price ceiling
micro.Choice B: A PPF
micro.Choice C: A circular flow
micro.Choice D: Market power
micro.Correct Answer: D — Market power
micro.Feedback: Market power exists when a buyer or seller can influence price.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.6
micro.Question: Which situation is most likely a market failure?
micro.Choice A: A factory pollutes a river used by nearby households
micro.Choice B: A buyer voluntarily purchases coffee
micro.Choice C: A seller lowers price during a sale
micro.Choice D: A student chooses to study
micro.Correct Answer: A — A factory pollutes a river used by nearby households
micro.Feedback: Pollution that harms third parties is a market failure because the full cost is not reflected in the market.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.6
micro.Common Misconception: Calling an effect on a buyer or seller a third-party spillover.
micro.Question: A delivery truck creates noise for residents who are not customers. Why is this an externality?
micro.Choice A: The cost falls on third parties outside the delivery exchange
micro.Choice B: The firm pays for fuel and driver time
micro.Choice C: Customers receive packages they ordered
micro.Choice D: The service operates in a city market
micro.Correct Answer: A — The cost falls on third parties outside the delivery exchange
micro.Feedback: An externality affects people outside the transaction.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.6
micro.Question: A market has one dominant seller that can influence price. Why might the market outcome be inefficient?
micro.Choice A: Scarcity disappears when one seller dominates
micro.Choice B: Market power can distort price and quantity
micro.Choice C: Opportunity cost no longer applies
micro.Choice D: The dominant seller must produce the efficient quantity.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Market power can distort price and quantity
micro.Feedback: Market power can allow a seller to influence price and reduce market efficiency.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.6
micro.Question: A market is efficient before a pollution externality is considered. Once pollution costs to bystanders are included, the market produces too much. What changed?
micro.Choice A: Private costs differed from social costs
micro.Choice B: Demand became perfectly inelastic
micro.Choice C: The PPF shifted outward
micro.Choice D: A price floor became nonbinding
micro.Correct Answer: A — Private costs differed from social costs
micro.Feedback: A negative externality means the market ignores some social costs, so private production can exceed the efficient level.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.6
micro.Question: A government responds to pollution with a tax. Which chain best explains the logic?
micro.Choice A: External cost → market underproduction → price ceiling raises quantity
micro.Choice B: External cost → market overproduction → corrective tax raises private cost → quantity falls
micro.Choice C: Scarcity disappears → supply increases → tax revenue falls to zero
micro.Choice D: Tax burden depends only on who writes the check
micro.Correct Answer: B — External cost → market overproduction → corrective tax raises private cost → quantity falls
micro.Feedback: A corrective tax makes private decision makers face more of the social cost, reducing overproduction.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.6
micro.Question: What is market failure?
micro.Choice A: Any situation where prices change, even though both sides hold the same relevant information
micro.Choice B: Any voluntary trade between buyers and sellers
micro.Choice C: A situation where the market fails to allocate resources efficiently
micro.Choice D: A point on the PPF
micro.Correct Answer: C — A situation where the market fails to allocate resources efficiently
micro.Feedback: Market failure occurs when the market does not allocate resources efficiently.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.6
micro.Question: A factory pollutes a river used by nearby residents. What kind of market failure is this?
micro.Choice A: A negative externality
micro.Choice B: A public good
micro.Choice C: A price floor
micro.Choice D: A positive externality.
micro.Correct Answer: A — A negative externality
micro.Feedback: Pollution harms bystanders who are not part of the transaction, so it is a negative externality.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.6
micro.Question: An instructor asks: which case is not automatically a market failure?
micro.Choice A: A factory pollutes a river, because inequality alone proves allocative inefficiency
micro.Choice B: A buyer voluntarily pays a high price for coffee
micro.Choice C: A seller has market power
micro.Choice D: A public good is underprovided
micro.Correct Answer: B — A buyer voluntarily pays a high price for coffee
micro.Feedback: A high voluntary price is not automatically a market failure. Externalities, public goods, and market power are stronger market-failure cases.

micro.Common Misconception: Calling every disliked, unequal, or expensive outcome a market failure.
micro.Question: Is every undesirable outcome a market failure?
micro.Choice A: The outcome is disliked but no incentive wedge is identified
micro.Choice B: Inequality alone proves productive inefficiency
micro.Choice C: No; a specific efficiency mechanism must be identified
micro.Choice D: A high price by itself establishes market failure
micro.Correct Answer: C — No; a specific efficiency mechanism must be identified
micro.Feedback: Market failure requires a specific reason private incentives diverge from efficient social outcomes.

micro.Common Misconception: Calling every disliked, unequal, or expensive outcome a market failure.
micro.Question: Does inequality alone define market failure?
micro.Choice A: The outcome is disliked but no incentive wedge is identified
micro.Choice B: Inequality alone proves productive inefficiency
micro.Choice C: A high price by itself establishes market failure
micro.Choice D: No; distribution and efficiency are distinct questions
micro.Correct Answer: D — No; distribution and efficiency are distinct questions
micro.Feedback: Market failure requires a specific reason private incentives diverge from efficient social outcomes.

micro.Common Misconception: Calling an effect on a buyer or seller a third-party spillover.
micro.Question: What makes an effect an externality?
micro.Choice A: It spills onto a third party outside the transaction
micro.Choice B: The outcome is a public good by definition
micro.Choice C: A large firm merely changes its own cost
micro.Choice D: The effect falls only on the buyer and seller
micro.Correct Answer: A — It spills onto a third party outside the transaction
micro.Feedback: An externality affects people outside the transaction.

micro.Common Misconception: Confusing market power with an externality or merely a large firm.
micro.Question: How does market power differ from an externality?
micro.Choice A: Market power requires a third-party spillover outside the transaction
micro.Choice B: It influences market terms rather than imposing a third-party spillover
micro.Choice C: Market power makes the good nonrival and nonexcludable
micro.Choice D: Market power occurs only when income is distributed unequally.
micro.Correct Answer: B — It influences market terms rather than imposing a third-party spillover
micro.Feedback: Market power can restrict mutually beneficial trades by influencing price or quantity.

micro.Common Misconception: Treating identified failure as proof that any intervention is superior.
micro.Question: Does finding market failure prove any intervention is better?
micro.Choice A: Any intervention is automatically costless
micro.Choice B: Identifying failure proves one remedy is optimal
micro.Choice C: No; feasible remedies also have costs and limits
micro.Choice D: Administrative incentives and information do not matter
micro.Correct Answer: C — No; feasible remedies also have costs and limits
micro.Feedback: Compare feasible responses, administrative costs, information limits, and unintended effects.

micro.Common Misconception: Calling an effect on a buyer or seller a third-party spillover.
micro.Question: Pollution changes a firm’s private marginal choice. What connection matters?
micro.Choice A: The effect falls only on the buyer and seller
micro.Choice B: Marginal analysis can compare private and social cost
micro.Choice C: The outcome is a public good by definition
micro.Choice D: A large firm merely changes its own cost
micro.Correct Answer: B — Marginal analysis can compare private and social cost
micro.Feedback: Marginal analysis compares the private marginal incentives facing the firm with the social marginal cost that includes the pollution spillover.

micro.Common Misconception: Confusing public goods with common resources or government-provided goods.
micro.Question: A public-good rule changes incentives to contribute. What connection matters?
micro.Choice A: It is nonrival but easy to exclude
micro.Choice B: It is rival with fully enforceable private access
micro.Choice C: Free-riding incentives can reduce voluntary provision
micro.Choice D: It is a private good supplied by government
micro.Correct Answer: C — Free-riding incentives can reduce voluntary provision
micro.Feedback: Because nonpayers can still benefit from a public good, contribution rules affect free-riding incentives and therefore voluntary provision.

micro.Common Misconception: Treating identified failure as proof that any intervention is superior.
micro.Question: A policy addresses hidden quality but is costly to administer. What should advisers do?
micro.Choice A: Administrative incentives and information do not matter
micro.Choice B: Any intervention is automatically costless
micro.Choice C: Identifying failure proves one remedy is optimal
micro.Choice D: Compare information gains with implementation tradeoffs
micro.Correct Answer: D — Compare information gains with implementation tradeoffs
micro.Feedback: Compare feasible responses, administrative costs, information limits, and unintended effects.

micro.Common Misconception: Calling an effect on a buyer or seller a third-party spillover.
micro.Question: A neighbor bears smoke from a restaurant exhaust fan. What feature identifies an externality?
micro.Choice A: The outcome is a public good by definition
micro.Choice B: A third party bears a cost outside the transaction
micro.Choice C: A large firm merely changes its own cost
micro.Choice D: The effect falls only on the buyer and seller
micro.Correct Answer: B — A third party bears a cost outside the transaction
micro.Feedback: An externality affects people outside the transaction.

micro.Common Misconception: Confusing public goods with common resources or government-provided goods.
micro.Question: A storm-warning signal can serve another listener without reducing its value and nonpayers are hard to exclude. What is it?
micro.Choice A: It is rival with fully enforceable private access
micro.Choice B: It is a private good supplied by government
micro.Choice C: A public good
micro.Choice D: It is nonrival but easy to exclude
micro.Correct Answer: C — A public good
micro.Feedback: Public goods are nonrival and nonexcludable; common resources are rival and hard to exclude.

micro.Common Misconception: Confusing market power with an externality or merely a large firm.
micro.Question: A seller can profitably influence price by restricting output. What concern appears?
micro.Choice A: A negative externality imposed on third parties
micro.Choice B: A public-good free-rider problem
micro.Choice C: A common-resource overuse problem.
micro.Choice D: Market power
micro.Correct Answer: D — Market power
micro.Feedback: Market power can restrict mutually beneficial trades by influencing price or quantity.

micro.Common Misconception: Calling any uncertainty asymmetric information.
micro.Question: A hospital knows treatment quality better than patients. What broad failure may arise?
micro.Choice A: Both sides possess the same relevant information
micro.Choice B: Relevant information is asymmetric across the transaction
micro.Choice C: The problem is only that future outcomes are uncertain
micro.Choice D: A spillover harms an unrelated third party
micro.Correct Answer: B — Relevant information is asymmetric across the transaction
micro.Feedback: Asymmetric information means one side holds relevant information the other lacks.

micro.Common Misconception: Confusing public goods with common resources or government-provided goods.
micro.Question: A navigation app is nonrival after creation but can exclude unpaid users. What is the best conclusion?
micro.Choice A: It is rival with fully enforceable private access
micro.Choice B: It is a private good supplied by government
micro.Choice C: It is nonrival but easy to exclude
micro.Choice D: It is not a pure public good because exclusion is feasible
micro.Correct Answer: D — It is not a pure public good because exclusion is feasible
micro.Feedback: The app is nonrival but excludable, so it is not a pure public good; it is closer to a club good.

micro.Common Misconception: Confusing public goods with common resources or government-provided goods.
micro.Question: An open-access aquifer is depleted. What private-social divergence occurs?
micro.Choice A: It is nonrival but easy to exclude
micro.Choice B: It is rival with fully enforceable private access
micro.Choice C: Each user ignores depletion costs shared by others
micro.Choice D: It is a private good supplied by government
micro.Correct Answer: C — Each user ignores depletion costs shared by others
micro.Feedback: Each user receives the private benefit of pumping water but bears only part of the depletion cost imposed on other users, creating an incentive to overuse the aquifer.

micro.Common Misconception: Calling any uncertainty asymmetric information.
micro.Question: A used-device seller knows battery quality that buyers cannot see. What can follow?
micro.Choice A: A spillover harms an unrelated third party
micro.Choice B: Both sides possess the same relevant information
micro.Choice C: The problem is only that future outcomes are uncertain
micro.Choice D: Hidden quality can drive better devices from the market
micro.Correct Answer: D — Hidden quality can drive better devices from the market
micro.Feedback: Asymmetric information means one side holds relevant information the other lacks.

micro.Common Misconception: Calling an effect on a buyer or seller a third-party spillover.
micro.Question: Why may a busy road be overused when access is free?
micro.Choice A: Drivers share congestion costs imposed on one another
micro.Choice B: The effect falls only on the buyer and seller
micro.Choice C: The outcome is a public good by definition
micro.Choice D: A large firm merely changes its own cost
micro.Correct Answer: A — Drivers share congestion costs imposed on one another
micro.Feedback: When each driver considers the private benefit of the trip but not the congestion delay imposed on other drivers, road use can exceed the socially efficient level.

micro.Common Misconception: Confusing public goods with common resources or government-provided goods.
micro.Question: Why may a privately funded flood barrier receive too little support?
micro.Choice A: It is nonrival but easy to exclude
micro.Choice B: People can benefit without paying
micro.Choice C: It is rival with fully enforceable private access
micro.Choice D: It is a private good supplied by government
micro.Correct Answer: B — People can benefit without paying
micro.Feedback: Because households can receive protection without contributing, each has an incentive to free ride, weakening private funding and causing underprovision.

micro.Common Misconception: Calling any uncertainty asymmetric information.
micro.Question: Why can hidden borrower risk reduce lending to reliable applicants?
micro.Choice A: A spillover harms an unrelated third party
micro.Choice B: Both sides possess the same relevant information
micro.Choice C: Lenders lack information borrowers possess
micro.Choice D: The problem is only that future outcomes are uncertain
micro.Correct Answer: C — Lenders lack information borrowers possess
micro.Feedback: Asymmetric information means one side holds relevant information the other lacks.

micro.Common Misconception: Confusing market power with an externality or merely a large firm.
micro.Question: A dominant platform blocks entry and reduces trades. What is the core concern?
micro.Choice A: Blocking entry makes the platform nonexcludable
micro.Choice B: Reducing trades creates a public-good free-rider problem
micro.Choice C: The platform’s size by itself proves a negative externality.
micro.Choice D: Market power can keep quantity below the efficient level
micro.Correct Answer: D — Market power can keep quantity below the efficient level
micro.Feedback: Market power can restrict mutually beneficial trades by influencing price or quantity.

micro.Common Misconception: Calling every disliked, unequal, or expensive outcome a market failure.
micro.Question: A product is expensive because its inputs are scarce. Is that alone market failure?
micro.Choice A: No; high cost alone does not identify an efficiency wedge
micro.Choice B: The outcome is disliked but no incentive wedge is identified
micro.Choice C: Inequality alone proves productive inefficiency
micro.Choice D: A high price by itself establishes market failure
micro.Correct Answer: A — No; high cost alone does not identify an efficiency wedge
micro.Feedback: Market failure requires a specific reason private incentives diverge from efficient social outcomes.

micro.Common Misconception: Calling every disliked, unequal, or expensive outcome a market failure.
micro.Question: A city dislikes unequal restaurant access. What must be shown for textbook market failure?
micro.Choice A: Inequality alone proves productive inefficiency
micro.Choice B: A mechanism causing private incentives to diverge from social efficiency
micro.Choice C: A high price by itself establishes market failure
micro.Choice D: The outcome is disliked but no incentive wedge is identified
micro.Correct Answer: B — A mechanism causing private incentives to diverge from social efficiency
micro.Feedback: Market failure requires a specific reason private incentives diverge from efficient social outcomes.

micro.Common Misconception: Confusing public goods with common resources or government-provided goods.
micro.Question: A lake is rival in use but access is difficult to restrict. Which problem fits?
micro.Choice A: It is rival with fully enforceable private access
micro.Choice B: It is a private good supplied by government
micro.Choice C: A common-resource overuse problem
micro.Choice D: It is nonrival but easy to exclude
micro.Correct Answer: C — A common-resource overuse problem
micro.Feedback: Public goods are nonrival and nonexcludable; common resources are rival and hard to exclude.

micro.Common Misconception: Calling any uncertainty asymmetric information.
micro.Question: An insurer cannot observe customers’ risk types before pricing. What issue fits?
micro.Choice A: Both sides possess the same relevant information
micro.Choice B: The problem is only that future outcomes are uncertain
micro.Choice C: A spillover harms an unrelated third party
micro.Choice D: Asymmetric information may distort participation
micro.Correct Answer: D — Asymmetric information may distort participation
micro.Feedback: Asymmetric information means one side holds relevant information the other lacks.

micro.Common Misconception: Treating identified failure as proof that any intervention is superior.
micro.Question: A fishery uses quotas, but regulators cannot observe illegal catch. What complicates the remedy?
micro.Choice A: Enforcement and information constraints affect performance
micro.Choice B: Any intervention is automatically costless
micro.Choice C: Identifying failure proves one remedy is optimal
micro.Choice D: Administrative incentives and information do not matter
micro.Correct Answer: A — Enforcement and information constraints affect performance
micro.Feedback: Compare feasible responses, administrative costs, information limits, and unintended effects.

micro.Common Misconception: Calling every disliked, unequal, or expensive outcome a market failure.
micro.Question: A poor neighborhood lacks groceries because operating costs are high. Why is failure not automatic?
micro.Choice A: Undesirability alone does not prove an efficiency wedge
micro.Choice B: The outcome is disliked but no incentive wedge is identified
micro.Choice C: Inequality alone proves productive inefficiency
micro.Choice D: A high price by itself establishes market failure
micro.Correct Answer: A — Undesirability alone does not prove an efficiency wedge
micro.Feedback: Market failure requires a specific reason private incentives diverge from efficient social outcomes.

micro.Common Misconception: Treating identified failure as proof that any intervention is superior.
micro.Question: A subsidy addresses a spillover but attracts costly gaming. What follows?
micro.Choice A: Any intervention that targets a spillover is automatically costless.
micro.Choice B: Identifying failure proves one remedy is optimal
micro.Choice C: Correcting one failure can create implementation costs and distortions
micro.Choice D: Administrative incentives and information do not matter
micro.Correct Answer: C — Correcting one failure can create implementation costs and distortions
micro.Feedback: Compare feasible responses, administrative costs, information limits, and unintended effects.

micro.Common Misconception: Calling every disliked, unequal, or expensive outcome a market failure.
micro.Question: A monopoly also pollutes. Why separate the mechanisms?
micro.Choice A: Inequality alone proves productive inefficiency
micro.Choice B: A high price by itself establishes market failure
micro.Choice C: The outcome is disliked but no incentive wedge is identified
micro.Choice D: Output restriction and third-party harm imply different wedges
micro.Correct Answer: D — Output restriction and third-party harm imply different wedges
micro.Feedback: Market failure requires a specific reason private incentives diverge from efficient social outcomes.

micro.Common Misconception: Calling an effect on a buyer or seller a third-party spillover.
micro.Question: A festival can run late, end early, or run late with sound insulation. Relative to ending early, running late adds $1,000 of gains to attendees and organizers and $1,400 of resident harm. Insulation costs $600 and reduces that harm to $200. Ignore bargaining costs. Which arrangement maximizes net gains, and what remains to be negotiated?
micro.Choice A: End early; all late operation has negative social value even with insulation.
micro.Choice B: Run late without insulation; the $1,000 private gain establishes efficiency.
micro.Choice C: Run late with insulation; divide its $200 net gain through compensation.
micro.Choice D: Run late with insulation; resident compensation itself adds another $200 of social benefit.
micro.Correct Answer: C — Run late with insulation; divide its $200 net gain through compensation.
micro.Feedback: Late without insulation yields 1000 - 1400 = -$400. Late with insulation yields 1000 - 600 - 200 = $200 relative to ending early. Compensation can distribute gains but is not an additional resource benefit.

micro.Common Misconception: Confusing market power with an externality or merely a large firm.
micro.Question: An exclusive right lets an innovator charge above marginal cost. Removing it would expand current access but could reduce future investment in similar products. Which evidence is needed before claiming removal raises welfare?
micro.Choice A: Only the current markup, because all markups equal net profit and total social loss.
micro.Choice B: Only the innovator’s revenue, because consumer gains are transfers that cannot affect welfare.
micro.Choice C: Only the number of new buyers, because future incentives are unrelated to exclusive rights.
micro.Choice D: Gains from additional current trades and the size of any resulting loss of valuable future innovation.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Gains from additional current trades and the size of any resulting loss of valuable future innovation.
micro.Feedback: Market power can exclude mutually beneficial current purchases, while expected returns can affect investment. A welfare comparison needs both margins and cannot be settled by the markup or seller revenue alone. This asks about incentives, not a legal test.

micro.Common Misconception: Calling an effect on a buyer or seller a third-party spillover.
micro.Question: A health agency observes that a vaccine subsidy increases vaccinations but an unrelated change also reduces exposure to infection. Which additional evidence is needed to judge whether the subsidy improves efficiency?
micro.Choice A: Only the subsidy budget, because larger transfers imply larger social gains.
micro.Choice B: The marginal spillover benefit at the new quantity, the real cost of extra doses, and policy implementation costs.
micro.Choice C: Only the number of new doses, because each added dose must be efficient.
micro.Choice D: Only recipients’ private willingness to pay, because the outside benefit is already in every purchase.
micro.Correct Answer: B — The marginal spillover benefit at the new quantity, the real cost of extra doses, and policy implementation costs.
micro.Feedback: A quantity increase is consistent with correcting underconsumption but does not prove optimal scale. Changed exposure can alter marginal external benefits. Evaluate incremental social benefits and real resource/implementation costs; the payment budget alone is not welfare.

micro.Common Misconception: Calling every disliked, unequal, or expensive outcome a market failure.
micro.Question: A crop price rises after a drought reduces harvests. A separate processing plant also discharges unpriced waste into a river. Which diagnosis and targeted response distinguish scarcity from market failure?
micro.Choice A: The crop price can signal genuine scarcity; a policy aimed at the waste should target its external cost rather than treating the high price alone as proof of failure.
micro.Choice B: Both are market failures solely because prices and waste increased, so a price ceiling necessarily corrects both.
micro.Choice C: Neither can be market failure because any outcome with a market price is efficient.
micro.Choice D: The drought is asymmetric information and the waste is merely a transfer between buyers and sellers.
micro.Correct Answer: A — The crop price can signal genuine scarcity; a policy aimed at the waste should target its external cost rather than treating the high price alone as proof of failure.
micro.Feedback: A supply loss can raise a competitive price without creating a distortion. Unpriced harm omits social cost from the private decision and calls for a response to that specific wedge.

micro.Common Misconception: Calling any uncertainty asymmetric information.
micro.Question: Buyers cannot observe product risk before purchase. Mandatory disclosure accurately reports it, but only in a format most buyers cannot interpret. A simplified tested label helps buyers compare risks at lower reading cost. Which comparison is defensible?
micro.Choice A: Accurate disclosure necessarily eliminates the problem regardless of comprehension, so testing the label adds no information.
micro.Choice B: Both address an information problem, but the tested label can improve usable information more effectively; accuracy alone does not establish that the first format changes decisions.
micro.Choice C: The unreadable format solves an externality while the label creates monopoly power.
micro.Choice D: Neither addresses market failure because information costs cannot affect mutually beneficial trades.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Both address an information problem, but the tested label can improve usable information more effectively; accuracy alone does not establish that the first format changes decisions.
micro.Feedback: The original problem is an information gap about risk. Disclosure must be usable to affect choices; evidence about comprehension and behavior distinguishes formal disclosure from an effective remedy.

micro.Common Misconception: Treating identified failure as proof that any intervention is superior.
micro.Question: A corrective policy would prevent $120 of external harm while using $35 of compliance resources and $100 of administrative resources. A simpler policy prevents $80 of harm and uses $20 in total resources. Which recommendation follows from these estimates alone?
micro.Choice A: The full policy is preferable because it prevents more harm, regardless of implementation cost.
micro.Choice B: Both policies are equally desirable because each reduces a market failure.
micro.Choice C: The full policy has net benefit −$15 and the simpler policy +$60; the simpler remedy is preferable to both the full policy and doing nothing.
micro.Choice D: Doing nothing is preferable because any administrative cost makes intervention inefficient.
micro.Correct Answer: C — The full policy has net benefit −$15 and the simpler policy +$60; the simpler remedy is preferable to both the full policy and doing nothing.
micro.Feedback: Net benefits are 120−35−100=−15 and 80−20=60. The scale of the original failure does not make every proposed correction worthwhile.

micro.Common Misconception: Calling every disliked, unequal, or expensive outcome a market failure.
micro.Question: A platform has market power and users create privacy spillovers. What is the best diagnosis?
micro.Choice A: Separate the output distortion from third-party privacy costs
micro.Choice B: A high price by itself establishes market failure
micro.Choice C: The outcome is disliked but no incentive wedge is identified
micro.Choice D: Inequality alone proves productive inefficiency
micro.Correct Answer: A — Separate the output distortion from third-party privacy costs
micro.Feedback: Market failure requires a specific reason private incentives diverge from efficient social outcomes.

micro.Common Misconception: Confusing public goods with common resources or government-provided goods.
micro.Question: A nonrival, nonexcludable water-quality alert system would generate $12,000 in total benefits and cost $8,000 to operate. Individual fee collection would cost $5,000; a binding cooperative funding agreement would cost $1,000. Both could fund the same service. Which evaluation is correct if there are no other effects?
micro.Choice A: Individual collection creates $4,000 of net gains because collection uses no resources.
micro.Choice B: The cooperative creates $3,000 of net gains; individual collection costs exceed the $4,000 operating surplus.
micro.Choice C: Both methods create $12,000 of net gains because users benefit whether or not they pay.
micro.Choice D: Neither can work because a private agreement cannot finance a nonexcludable service.
micro.Correct Answer: B — The cooperative creates $3,000 of net gains; individual collection costs exceed the $4,000 operating surplus.
micro.Feedback: Before funding costs the gain is 12,000 - 8,000 = $4,000. Net gains are -$1,000 with individual collection and $3,000 with the agreement. Nonexcludability complicates funding but does not rule out every institution.

micro.Common Misconception: Treating identified failure as proof that any intervention is superior.
micro.Question: A disclosure rule is forecast to prevent $90 of harm at $20 resource cost. A pilot finds that confusion causes $35 of additional harm and that only $50 of the original harm is actually prevented. A simpler label prevents $40 at $10 cost with no added confusion. Which comparison uses the observed performance?
micro.Choice A: The original rule has +$70 net benefit because forecasts should replace contradictory pilot evidence.
micro.Choice B: The original rule has +$30 net benefit because confusion is only a transfer, making it equivalent to the simpler label.
micro.Choice C: The original rule has net benefit −$5, while the simpler label has +$30; revise the policy despite its initially plausible mechanism.
micro.Choice D: Neither can be compared because any information rule guarantees an efficient outcome.
micro.Correct Answer: C — The original rule has net benefit −$5, while the simpler label has +$30; revise the policy despite its initially plausible mechanism.
micro.Feedback: Use the pilot’s actual effects: 50−35−20=−5. The alternative yields 40−10=30. The intended mechanism is relevant, but implementation evidence determines the net result.

micro.Common Misconception: Treating identified failure as proof that any intervention is superior.
micro.Question: A fishery’s paper quota is strict, but hidden catches make actual harvest high. A feasible alternative combines verified landing reports with transferable catch rights. What evidence would establish that this alternative improves net social benefit?
micro.Choice A: The new quota is numerically smaller, regardless of hidden catches or enforcement costs.
micro.Choice B: Quota holders receive valuable rights, so their transfer income equals the total welfare gain.
micro.Choice C: Trading occurs frequently, so actual harvest must equal the legally allowed total.
micro.Choice D: Reduced depletion losses exceed added monitoring and adjustment costs, while transfers permit lower-cost compliance.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Reduced depletion losses exceed added monitoring and adjustment costs, while transfers permit lower-cost compliance.
micro.Feedback: Evaluate actual behavior, not just the announced cap. Verification can reduce hidden harvest; transfers can lower compliance costs. Net improvement requires avoided resource losses to exceed real implementation and adjustment costs.

micro.Common Misconception: Calling every disliked, unequal, or expensive outcome a market failure.
micro.Question: A market maximizes measured total surplus but distributes it unequally; no externality, information gap, market power or public-good problem is identified. Policy A transfers $30 between participants without resource cost or changed behavior. Policy B makes the same transfer but destroys $8 of gains through changed allocation. Which assessment is correct?
micro.Choice A: Inequality motivates a separate equity judgment; A preserves measured surplus while B trades $8 of it for the same intended redistribution.
micro.Choice B: Both policies correct a demonstrated efficiency failure because any unequal outcome is inefficient.
micro.Choice C: B must be more efficient because changing allocation proves it addresses a market failure.
micro.Choice D: A raises total surplus by $30 while B raises it by $22 because transfers are new resources.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Inequality motivates a separate equity judgment; A preserves measured surplus while B trades $8 of it for the same intended redistribution.
micro.Feedback: An unequal split does not by itself demonstrate a missing efficiency condition. The costless transfer changes distribution; B additionally sacrifices $8 of gains. Whether that tradeoff is acceptable requires an equity judgment.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.6
micro.Common Misconception: Calling every market effect an externality.
micro.Question: An externality is:
micro.Choice A: A cost or benefit affecting a third party outside the transaction.
micro.Choice B: Any change in the market price.
micro.Choice C: A government expenditure.
micro.Choice D: A cost paid fully by the buyer.
micro.Correct Answer: A — A cost or benefit affecting a third party outside the transaction.
micro.Feedback: Externalities spill over to people not directly involved in the exchange.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.6
micro.Common Misconception: Using the provider rather than the good’s characteristics.
micro.Question: A public good is defined by:
micro.Choice A: Government ownership alone.
micro.Choice B: Nonrival consumption and difficulty excluding nonpayers.
micro.Choice C: A high market price.
micro.Choice D: Private benefits only.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Nonrival consumption and difficulty excluding nonpayers.
micro.Feedback: Public-good status depends on rivalry and excludability.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.6
micro.Common Misconception: Failing to transfer shared-resource incentives to everyday settings.
micro.Question: A shared office kitchen is repeatedly left dirty because each worker expects others to clean it. This resembles:
micro.Choice A: A common-resource or collective-action problem.
micro.Choice B: A perfectly enforced private property right.
micro.Choice C: A positive price signal.
micro.Choice D: A competitive firm’s shutdown decision.
micro.Correct Answer: A — A common-resource or collective-action problem.
micro.Feedback: Shared access and dispersed responsibility can encourage overuse or under-maintenance.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.6
micro.Common Misconception: Misclassifying an external cost.
micro.Question: A factory’s pollution harms nearby residents without compensating them. This is:
micro.Choice A: A public good.
micro.Choice B: A positive consumption externality.
micro.Choice C: A negative production externality.
micro.Choice D: A competitive price signal with no omitted cost.
micro.Correct Answer: C — A negative production externality.
micro.Feedback: The factory imposes a cost on third parties outside the transaction.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.6
micro.Common Misconception: Confusing government provision with the economic definition of a public good.
micro.Question: Which feature makes national defense a public good?
micro.Choice A: It is sold by one private firm.
micro.Choice B: Its marginal cost is always zero.
micro.Choice C: Consumers can be excluded easily.
micro.Choice D: It is broadly nonrival and difficult to exclude nonpayers.
micro.Correct Answer: D — It is broadly nonrival and difficult to exclude nonpayers.
micro.Feedback: Public goods are characterized by nonrivalry and nonexcludability.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.6
micro.Common Misconception: Treating a corrective tax as unrelated to marginal incentives.
micro.Question: At the next unit of a competitive product, a buyer values it at $18, the producer uses $14 of resources, and pollution harms neighbors by $6. Which outcome does a $6 per-unit tax encourage?
micro.Choice A: Forgo the unit: private gains are $4 but net social benefit is -$2.
micro.Choice B: Produce the unit: the $4 private gain measures its full social benefit.
micro.Choice C: Produce the unit: $6 of tax revenue makes its net social benefit $4.
micro.Choice D: Forgo the unit: every taxed unit has zero social benefit.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Forgo the unit: private gains are $4 but net social benefit is -$2.
micro.Feedback: The trade has a private gain of 18 - 14 = $4, but net social benefit is 18 - 14 - 6 = -$2. A $6 tax makes the relevant private cost $20, above willingness to pay. Revenue is a transfer, not an extra resource benefit.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.6
micro.Common Misconception: Confusing common resources with public goods.
micro.Question: Why can a common resource be overused?
micro.Choice A: It is nonrival and nonexcludable.
micro.Choice B: Users receive the private benefit while sharing depletion costs with others.
micro.Choice C: Its price is always above marginal cost.
micro.Choice D: No one can access it.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Users receive the private benefit while sharing depletion costs with others.
micro.Feedback: Common resources are rival but difficult to exclude, creating overuse incentives.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.6
micro.Common Misconception: Treating market power as only a distributional issue.
micro.Question: A dominant seller withholds an additional unit that a buyer values at $25 even though producing it uses $18 of resources. There are no externalities. Which mechanism explains the lost efficiency?
micro.Choice A: The withheld trade creates a $7 external pollution cost paid by a third party.
micro.Choice B: The seller’s lost sales revenue equals the social gain, regardless of production cost.
micro.Choice C: Restricting output can preserve the seller’s price while forgoing a trade with $7 of social gains.
micro.Choice D: Any price above resource cost proves that expanding output would reduce total surplus.
micro.Correct Answer: C — Restricting output can preserve the seller’s price while forgoing a trade with $7 of social gains.
micro.Feedback: The omitted unit has willingness to pay above marginal resource cost by 25 - 18 = $7. Market power can make restricting output privately attractive even though the unit would add social surplus. No third-party spillover is required.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.6
micro.Common Misconception: Ignoring information differences between parties.
micro.Question: A seller knows a used car’s quality, but buyers cannot distinguish good cars from bad ones. What problem can result?
micro.Choice A: A public-good free-rider problem.
micro.Choice B: A positive production externality.
micro.Choice C: A binding price floor by definition.
micro.Choice D: Adverse selection from asymmetric information.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Adverse selection from asymmetric information.
micro.Feedback: Hidden quality can drive high-quality goods from the market.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.6
micro.Common Misconception: Failing to distinguish private and social benefits.
micro.Question: Vaccination creates an external benefit, but a fixed number of appointments is already fully used. A subsidy is introduced without expanding capacity or changing how appointments are allocated. Which assessment best separates the externality diagnosis from this policy’s current effect?
micro.Choice A: Private demand rises, but vaccinations cannot rise yet; additional spillover benefits require more capacity or a better allocation.
micro.Choice B: The subsidy necessarily raises vaccinations to the efficient quantity despite the fixed appointment limit.
micro.Choice C: Fixed capacity means the external benefit disappears and the original externality diagnosis is false.
micro.Choice D: Subsidy spending itself equals new transmission benefits even when the vaccinated group is unchanged.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Private demand rises, but vaccinations cannot rise yet; additional spillover benefits require more capacity or a better allocation.
micro.Feedback: The external benefit can justify stronger private incentives, but supply is constrained here. With both quantity and recipients fixed, subsidizing existing appointments changes payments rather than the transmission benefit. Capacity and allocation matter for the feasible remedy.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.6
micro.Common Misconception: Choosing a policy that strengthens overuse incentives.
micro.Question: A fishery is open to many boats, and each boat ignores how its catch reduces future stocks for others. Which policy logic fits?
micro.Choice A: Subsidize every additional catch.
micro.Choice B: Limit or price access so users face more of the depletion cost.
micro.Choice C: Remove all information about stocks.
micro.Choice D: Set a price ceiling on fish without limiting harvest.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Limit or price access so users face more of the depletion cost.
micro.Feedback: Access rules, quotas, or charges can internalize the shared depletion cost.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.6
micro.Common Misconception: Ignoring the pricing and cost-recovery tradeoff.
micro.Question: A broadband network has high fixed cost and low marginal cost. Marginal-cost pricing would expand valuable access but leave a financing deficit. Average-cost pricing can cover costs but excludes some users whose value exceeds marginal cost. Public support has a real collection cost. What information is needed to choose between the two rules?
micro.Choice A: Only whether marginal-cost pricing creates an accounting loss, because loss proves social inefficiency.
micro.Choice B: Only whether average-cost pricing breaks even, because break-even proves maximum social surplus.
micro.Choice C: The extra access benefits net of resource cost, compared with the real cost of financing the deficit.
micro.Choice D: Only the subsidy payment, because every transferred dollar is a destroyed social resource.
micro.Correct Answer: C — The extra access benefits net of resource cost, compared with the real cost of financing the deficit.
micro.Feedback: The financing problem and the access distortion are distinct. Compare additional gains from valuable access with financing’s real costs under feasible support arrangements. Accounting losses and transfer amounts do not alone rank the rules.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.6
micro.Common Misconception: Misidentifying the source of market failure.
micro.Question: Which case is a negative externality?
micro.Choice A: Noise from a venue reducing nearby residents’ well-being.
micro.Choice B: A buyer paying the posted price.
micro.Choice C: A student receiving private tutoring that affects only the student and tutor.
micro.Choice D: A firm lowering its own cost.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Noise from a venue reducing nearby residents’ well-being.
micro.Feedback: Noise that reduces nearby residents’ well-being imposes a cost on third parties outside the transaction, so it is a negative externality.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.6
micro.Common Misconception: Misidentifying the source of market failure.
micro.Question: Why might a public good be underprovided privately?
micro.Choice A: Use by one person prevents all others from using it.
micro.Choice B: People can benefit without paying, weakening voluntary funding.
micro.Choice C: Exclusion is effortless.
micro.Choice D: Every consumer reveals exact willingness to pay.
micro.Correct Answer: B — People can benefit without paying, weakening voluntary funding.
micro.Feedback: When nonpayers can benefit from the good, individuals have an incentive to free ride, so voluntary private funding can be below the efficient level.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.6
micro.Common Misconception: Misidentifying the source of market failure.
micro.Question: What is the standard efficiency concern with market power?
micro.Choice A: Every firm earns zero accounting profit.
micro.Choice B: All prices fall below marginal cost.
micro.Choice C: Output may be restricted below the level where buyer value exceeds production cost.
micro.Choice D: Products become nonrival when one firm sets the market price.
micro.Correct Answer: C — Output may be restricted below the level where buyer value exceeds production cost.
micro.Feedback: Market power can restrict output below the efficient quantity, leaving mutually beneficial trades unrealized and creating deadweight loss.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.4
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Compare two adjustment paths from D to B: demand changes first in one path; supply changes first in the other. Which claim about the intermediate quantity and final equilibrium is correct?
micro.Choice A: Demand first takes quantity to A; supply first takes it to C; both paths end at B.
micro.Choice B: Demand first takes quantity to C; supply first takes it to A; both paths end at B.
micro.Choice C: Demand first takes quantity to C; supply first takes it to A; the paths end at different equilibria.
micro.Choice D: Either first shift keeps quantity at D; only the second shift moves quantity to B.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Demand first takes quantity to C; supply first takes it to A; both paths end at B.
micro.Feedback: With S0 fixed, D0 to D1 moves the market from D to C. With D0 fixed, S0 to S1 moves it from D to A. The final D1/S1 intersection is B regardless of order; the intermediate quantities differ.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.4
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. The taco market begins at point D. Tacos are a normal good. Consumer income rises while the cost of an important production input increases. Which labeled point is the new equilibrium after both changes?
micro.Choice A: B — the intersection of D1 and S1
micro.Choice B: C — the intersection of D1 and S0
micro.Choice C: A — the intersection of D0 and S1
micro.Choice D: D — the intersection of D0 and S0
micro.Correct Answer: A — B — the intersection of D1 and S1
micro.Feedback: Because tacos are a normal good, higher consumer income shifts demand from D0 to D1. The higher input cost shifts supply from S0 to S1. The new D1-S1 equilibrium is point B.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.4
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
micro.Question: An analyst attributes the move from B back to A to cheaper streaming substitutes and lower theater operating costs. Which evaluation correctly connects these events to the changes shown in the movie-ticket graph?
micro.Choice A: Consistent: demand falls and supply rises; price falls $2 while quantity remains 200 thousand.
micro.Choice B: Consistent: demand and supply both fall; price falls $4 while quantity remains 200 thousand.
micro.Choice C: Consistent: demand falls and supply rises; price falls $4 while quantity remains 200 thousand.
micro.Choice D: Consistent: demand and supply both fall; price falls $2 while quantity remains 200 thousand.
micro.Correct Answer: C — Consistent: demand falls and supply rises; price falls $4 while quantity remains 200 thousand.
micro.Feedback: Cheaper streaming substitutes reduce demand for theater tickets, while lower operating costs increase supply. B is at $14 and 200 thousand tickets; A is at $10 and 200 thousand. Both shifts lower price, producing the $4 fall. Their opposite effects on quantity offset in this graph.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.6
micro.Question: In a market system, prices help allocate resources by:
micro.Choice A: Eliminating all tradeoffs
micro.Choice B: Coordinating buyers' and sellers' decisions
micro.Choice C: Fixing output at one level
micro.Choice D: Replacing incentives
micro.Correct Answer: B — Coordinating buyers' and sellers' decisions
micro.Feedback: Prices convey information and coordinate decentralized decisions about production and consumption.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.6
micro.Common Misconception: Calling every disliked, unequal, or expensive outcome a market failure.
micro.Question: A voluntary coffee purchase makes both participants better off. Does this show market failure?
micro.Choice A: No; gains for both parties do not establish market failure
micro.Choice B: Yes; buyers and sellers always have unequal power
micro.Choice C: Yes; every price excludes some consumers
micro.Choice D: No; market failure requires government ownership
micro.Correct Answer: A — No; gains for both parties do not establish market failure
micro.Feedback: Market failure requires a specific reason private incentives diverge from efficient social outcomes.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.6
micro.Question: Prices guide the use of resources without a central planner directing each decision. What is this describing?
micro.Choice A: A price ceiling
micro.Choice B: A GDP deflator
micro.Choice C: A discouraged worker
micro.Choice D: Market allocation
micro.Correct Answer: D — Market allocation
micro.Feedback: In market allocation, households and firms use prices and voluntary exchange to guide resource use.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.9 — Median Voter Theorem
micro.Question: Consider a case in which policy is multidimensional and voters' preferences are not single-peaked. Can median-voter convergence be assumed?
micro.Choice A: No; the theorem's key assumptions may fail
micro.Choice B: Yes, it holds under every preference domain
micro.Choice C: Yes, because mean and median are identical
micro.Choice D: No, because majority voting is impossible
micro.Correct Answer: A — No; the theorem's key assumptions may fail
micro.Feedback: The result depends on a one-dimensional policy space, single-peaked preferences, majority rule, and strategic conditions.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.9 — Median Voter Theorem
micro.Question: Evidence indicates that policy is multidimensional and voters' preferences are not single-peaked. Can median-voter convergence be assumed?
micro.Choice A: No; the theorem's key assumptions may fail
micro.Choice B: Yes, it holds under every preference domain
micro.Choice C: Yes, because mean and median are identical
micro.Choice D: No, because majority voting is impossible
micro.Correct Answer: A — No; the theorem's key assumptions may fail
micro.Feedback: The result depends on a one-dimensional policy space, single-peaked preferences, majority rule, and strategic conditions.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.9 — Median Voter Theorem
micro.Question: Consider a case in which two office-seeking candidates care only about winning and voters choose the closer one on a single policy dimension. What tendency follows?
micro.Choice A: Both move toward opposite extremes
micro.Choice B: Policy location becomes irrelevant
micro.Choice C: The candidate at the mean always loses
micro.Choice D: Both candidates have an incentive to move toward the median voter
micro.Correct Answer: D — Both candidates have an incentive to move toward the median voter
micro.Feedback: Moving toward the median can capture pivotal voters without losing those on the candidate's outer side.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.9 — Median Voter Theorem
micro.Question: A classroom example assumes that voters have single-peaked preferences over one tax-rate line and choose by majority rule. Which position is pivotal?
micro.Choice A: The mean income regardless of voting
micro.Choice B: The most extreme voter's ideal point
micro.Choice C: The median voter's ideal point
micro.Choice D: A randomly chosen policy
micro.Correct Answer: C — The median voter's ideal point
micro.Feedback: On a one-dimensional line with single-peaked preferences, the median ideal point defeats alternatives in pairwise votes.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.9 — Median Voter Theorem
micro.Question: Evidence indicates that two office-seeking candidates care only about winning and voters choose the closer one on a single policy dimension. What tendency follows?
micro.Choice A: Both move toward opposite extremes
micro.Choice B: Policy location becomes irrelevant
micro.Choice C: The candidate at the mean always loses
micro.Choice D: Both candidates have an incentive to move toward the median voter
micro.Correct Answer: D — Both candidates have an incentive to move toward the median voter
micro.Feedback: Moving toward the median can capture pivotal voters without losing those on the candidate's outer side.
