micro.Learning Objective: IBP.9 — Median Voter Theorem
micro.Question: Suppose that voters have single-peaked preferences over one tax-rate line and choose by majority rule. Which position is pivotal?
micro.Choice A: The mean income regardless of voting
micro.Choice B: The most extreme voter's ideal point
micro.Choice C: The median voter's ideal point
micro.Choice D: A randomly chosen policy
micro.Correct Answer: C — The median voter's ideal point
micro.Feedback: On a one-dimensional line with single-peaked preferences, the median ideal point defeats alternatives in pairwise votes.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.9 — Median Voter Theorem
micro.Question: In this setting, the decisive voter lies at the 50th percentile of ordered ideal points. Why is this voter called median?
micro.Choice A: The voter has average income
micro.Choice B: Half the ideal points lie on each side
micro.Choice C: The voter is indifferent among all policies
micro.Choice D: The voter dictates outcomes without elections
micro.Correct Answer: B — Half the ideal points lie on each side
micro.Feedback: Median refers to position in the ordered distribution of ideal points, not necessarily average demographics or income.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.9 — Median Voter Theorem
micro.Question: Five voters have single-peaked preferences over one spending level, with ideal points 1, 3, 4, 8 and 10. Which level is the median ideal point and defeats any alternative in pairwise majority voting under these assumptions?
micro.Feedback: The ordered middle ideal point is 4, not the mean 5.2. Single-peakedness makes the median proposal a majority winner.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.9 — Median Voter Theorem
micro.Question: A classroom example assumes that two office-seeking candidates care only about winning and voters choose the closer one on a single policy dimension. What tendency follows?
micro.Choice A: Both move toward opposite extremes
micro.Choice B: Policy location becomes irrelevant
micro.Choice C: The candidate at the mean always loses
micro.Choice D: Both candidates have an incentive to move toward the median voter
micro.Correct Answer: D — Both candidates have an incentive to move toward the median voter
micro.Feedback: Moving toward the median can capture pivotal voters without losing those on the candidate's outer side.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.9 — Median Voter Theorem
micro.Question: Suppose that the decisive voter lies at the 50th percentile of ordered ideal points. Why is this voter called median?
micro.Choice A: The voter has average income
micro.Choice B: Half the ideal points lie on each side
micro.Choice C: The voter is indifferent among all policies
micro.Choice D: The voter dictates outcomes without elections
micro.Correct Answer: B — Half the ideal points lie on each side
micro.Feedback: Median refers to position in the ordered distribution of ideal points, not necessarily average demographics or income.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.9 — Median Voter Theorem
micro.Question: A policy analyst notes that the decisive voter lies at the 50th percentile of ordered ideal points. Why is this voter called median?
micro.Choice A: The voter has average income
micro.Choice B: Half the ideal points lie on each side
micro.Choice C: The voter is indifferent among all policies
micro.Choice D: The voter dictates outcomes without elections
micro.Correct Answer: B — Half the ideal points lie on each side
micro.Feedback: Median refers to position in the ordered distribution of ideal points, not necessarily average demographics or income.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.9 — Median Voter Theorem
micro.Question: An economist observes that two office-seeking candidates care only about winning and voters choose the closer one on a single policy dimension. What tendency follows?
micro.Choice A: Both move toward opposite extremes
micro.Choice B: Policy location becomes irrelevant
micro.Choice C: The candidate at the mean always loses
micro.Choice D: Both candidates have an incentive to move toward the median voter
micro.Correct Answer: D — Both candidates have an incentive to move toward the median voter
micro.Feedback: Moving toward the median can capture pivotal voters without losing those on the candidate's outer side.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.9 — Median Voter Theorem
micro.Question: A median-voter prediction was derived for single-peaked preferences on one policy dimension. The election then adds a second independent policy dimension. What conclusion is warranted?
micro.Choice A: The arithmetic median on the first dimension must still win every multidimensional comparison.
micro.Choice B: Adding a dimension guarantees unanimous agreement.
micro.Choice C: The original theorem’s assumptions no longer suffice to guarantee a median policy winner.
micro.Choice D: All individual preferences must become cyclic.
micro.Correct Answer: C — The original theorem’s assumptions no longer suffice to guarantee a median policy winner.
micro.Feedback: The one-dimensional ordering supports the median-voter result. Moving to multiple dimensions removes that guarantee without proving that a cycle must occur.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.9 — Median Voter Theorem
micro.Question: In this setting, policy is multidimensional and voters' preferences are not single-peaked. Can median-voter convergence be assumed?
micro.Choice A: No; the theorem's key assumptions may fail
micro.Choice B: Yes, it holds under every preference domain
micro.Choice C: Yes, because mean and median are identical
micro.Choice D: No, because majority voting is impossible
micro.Correct Answer: A — No; the theorem's key assumptions may fail
micro.Feedback: The result depends on a one-dimensional policy space, single-peaked preferences, majority rule, and strategic conditions.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.3
micro.Question: Which question is macroeconomic?
micro.Choice A: How many workers should one coffee shop hire?
micro.Choice B: How should one consumer spend a gift card?
micro.Choice C: How fast is the nation's GDP growing?
micro.Choice D: How should one firm price one sandwich?
micro.Correct Answer: C — How fast is the nation's GDP growing?
micro.Feedback: GDP growth is an economy-wide issue, so it is macroeconomic.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.3
micro.Question: Which pairing correctly distinguishes macroeconomics from microeconomics?
micro.Choice A: GDP growth is micro; one firm's hiring decision is macro
micro.Choice B: Both are always micro
micro.Choice C: Both are always normative
micro.Choice D: GDP growth is macro; one firm's hiring decision is micro
micro.Correct Answer: D — GDP growth is macro; one firm's hiring decision is micro
micro.Feedback: GDP growth concerns the whole economy, while one firm's hiring decision is about an individual firm.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.2
micro.Question: A binding minimum wage raises pay for workers who keep jobs but reduces hiring for low-skill labor. What is the strongest policy interpretation?
micro.Choice A: The policy eliminates scarcity in labor markets
micro.Choice B: The policy guarantees higher employment and higher wages for all workers
micro.Choice C: The policy only changes CPI and has no employment effects
micro.Choice D: The policy creates a tradeoff between higher wages for some and job loss for others
micro.Correct Answer: D — The policy creates a tradeoff between higher wages for some and job loss for others
micro.Feedback: A binding wage floor can help workers who remain employed while making it harder for others to find jobs.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.2
micro.Question: At a $12 equilibrium wage, firms hire 1,000 workers and 1,000 workers want jobs. A $16 minimum wage leads firms to demand 850 workers while 1,250 workers want jobs. Prices then rise 20%. Which interpretation is strongest?
micro.Choice A: The nominal wage floor creates a 250-worker shortage, and inflation raises the real wage further
micro.Choice B: The nominal wage floor creates a 400-worker surplus, but the real value of the $16 wage is partly eroded by inflation
micro.Choice C: The nominal wage floor creates no unemployment because 1,250 workers want jobs
micro.Choice D: The nominal wage floor creates a 150-worker surplus because employment falls from 1,000 to 850
micro.Correct Answer: B — The nominal wage floor creates a 400-worker surplus, but the real value of the $16 wage is partly eroded by inflation
micro.Feedback: The labor surplus is 1,250 - 850 = 400 workers. Inflation also reduces the purchasing power of the higher nominal wage.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.2
micro.Question: A binding minimum wage raises labor costs in restaurants. Restaurants hire fewer low-skill workers and raise menu prices. Which chain best synthesizes the effect?
micro.Choice A: Price ceiling in labor market → labor shortage → lower production costs → lower CPI
micro.Choice B: Tax wedge in output market → more labor demanded → lower unemployment
micro.Choice C: Price floor in labor market → lower labor demanded → higher production costs → higher output prices
micro.Choice D: Substitution bias → higher labor productivity → no job loss
micro.Correct Answer: C — Price floor in labor market → lower labor demanded → higher production costs → higher output prices
micro.Feedback: A binding wage floor can reduce labor demanded and raise firms' costs, which can push output prices upward.

micro.Question: Why can a minimum wage help some workers while hurting others?
micro.Choice A: All workers are guaranteed jobs at the higher wage
micro.Choice B: Workers who keep jobs earn more, but some workers may be priced out of employment
micro.Choice C: Firms hire more workers because labor is now more expensive
micro.Choice D: The CPI stops measuring prices
micro.Correct Answer: B — Workers who keep jobs earn more, but some workers may be priced out of employment
micro.Feedback: A higher minimum wage can raise earnings for workers who remain employed, but reduce hiring for others.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.1
micro.Question: A price-ceiling model predicts a shortage. In practice, the city also sees black markets, quality cuts, and favoritism. What does that comparison reveal about economic models?
micro.Choice A: The model captures the core shortage logic, while real-world institutions shape how the shortage appears
micro.Choice B: The model is useless because it did not list every consequence
micro.Choice C: The model proves black markets cannot happen because the legal price is fixed.
micro.Choice D: The model becomes normative once real examples are added
micro.Correct Answer: A — The model captures the core shortage logic, while real-world institutions shape how the shortage appears
micro.Feedback: A simple model explains the core mechanism. Real-world details determine the specific form the shortage takes.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.1
micro.Question: A model uses a simplified diagram of households, firms, markets, and money flows. Why do economists use models like this?
micro.Choice A: To include every detail of the real economy
micro.Choice B: To eliminate scarcity
micro.Choice C: To simplify reality and focus on key relationships
micro.Choice D: To avoid making assumptions
micro.Correct Answer: C — To simplify reality and focus on key relationships
micro.Feedback: Models simplify reality so economists can focus on the most important relationships.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: A market has many small sellers and easy entry, but every seller offers exactly the same product. What key condition for monopolistic competition is missing?
micro.Choice A: A large number of sellers
micro.Choice B: Freedom of entry and exit
micro.Choice C: Independent ownership
micro.Choice D: Product differentiation
micro.Correct Answer: D — Product differentiation
micro.Feedback: Many sellers and easy entry are not enough. Monopolistic competition also requires differentiated products.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: A restaurant has many nearby rivals, but customers value its menu and atmosphere enough that a small price increase does not drive everyone away. What best explains this result?
micro.Choice A: Product differentiation gives the restaurant limited price-setting power
micro.Choice B: Free entry makes the restaurant a pure price taker
micro.Choice C: Many sellers make the restaurant demand curve perfectly elastic
micro.Choice D: The restaurant controls the entire market supply
micro.Correct Answer: A — Product differentiation gives the restaurant limited price-setting power
micro.Feedback: Differentiation makes the firm’s product an imperfect substitute, so its individual demand curve slopes downward.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: Several new coffee shops open offering very similar drinks and service. Holding other factors constant, what is most likely to happen to the demand facing one existing shop?
micro.Choice A: It becomes less elastic because the market has more sellers
micro.Choice B: It becomes vertical because each shop is now smaller
micro.Choice C: It becomes perfectly inelastic because products remain differentiated
micro.Choice D: It becomes more elastic because customers have more close substitutes
micro.Correct Answer: D — It becomes more elastic because customers have more close substitutes
micro.Feedback: More close substitutes make customers more responsive to one firm’s price.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: A city has dozens of independently owned fitness studios. Each offers a somewhat different mix of classes, and new studios can enter without major legal barriers. Which model is the best starting point?
micro.Choice A: Monopoly
micro.Choice B: Oligopoly
micro.Choice C: Monopolistic competition
micro.Choice D: Perfect competition
micro.Correct Answer: C — Monopolistic competition
micro.Feedback: Many sellers, differentiated products, and relatively easy entry are the defining combination.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: A dental practice competes mainly through evening hours, online scheduling, and unusually fast appointments. Which source of differentiation is most important?
micro.Choice A: Identical-product pricing
micro.Choice B: Service differentiation
micro.Choice C: Resource ownership
micro.Choice D: Patent protection
micro.Correct Answer: B — Service differentiation
micro.Feedback: The practice is differentiating the service experience rather than relying on a legal barrier or identical product.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: Firm A sells a differentiated snack with many close substitutes. Firm B holds an exclusive patent on a drug with no close substitute. Which comparison is most plausible?
micro.Choice A: Firm A faces more elastic demand than Firm B
micro.Choice B: Firm A faces less elastic demand than Firm B
micro.Choice C: Both firms face perfectly elastic demand
micro.Choice D: Both firms must face the same elasticity because each has a downward-sloping demand curve
micro.Correct Answer: A — Firm A faces more elastic demand than Firm B
micro.Feedback: Close substitutes make buyers more responsive to Firm A’s price, while the patent shields Firm B from close substitution.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: A boutique raises its price by 4 percent and loses 7 percent of its customers, but many buyers remain because they prefer its style. What does this pattern most strongly indicate?
micro.Choice A: The firm is a price taker with perfectly elastic demand
micro.Choice B: The firm has monopoly power protected by an entry barrier
micro.Choice C: The market must contain only a few strategically interdependent firms
micro.Choice D: The firm has limited market power, not complete control of demand
micro.Correct Answer: D — The firm has limited market power, not complete control of demand
micro.Feedback: Differentiation can give a firm some control over price while close substitutes still constrain it.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: A market has many sellers and easy entry. Each seller faces a downward-sloping demand curve for its own product. Which additional fact is most consistent with monopolistic competition?
micro.Choice A: A single legal franchise blocks all new rivals
micro.Choice B: A few firms closely track each rival’s strategic moves
micro.Choice C: Products are differentiated but remain close substitutes
micro.Choice D: Products are identical and firms accept one market price
micro.Correct Answer: C — Products are differentiated but remain close substitutes
micro.Feedback: Differentiation explains why an individual firm faces downward-sloping demand despite many sellers and easy entry.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: Food-delivery technology makes customers almost indifferent to which neighborhood a restaurant occupies. Other features are unchanged. What happens to location as a source of differentiation?
micro.Choice A: It turns the market into a natural monopoly
micro.Choice B: It becomes weaker because distance matters less to customers
micro.Choice C: It becomes stronger because delivery creates a new legal barrier
micro.Choice D: It guarantees each restaurant a perfectly inelastic demand curve
micro.Correct Answer: B — It becomes weaker because distance matters less to customers
micro.Feedback: When location matters less to buyers, location creates less product differentiation and less insulation from rivals.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: Suppose all meaningful brand, location, service, and quality differences among many sellers disappear while entry remains easy. Which competitive model does the market move toward?
micro.Choice A: Perfect competition
micro.Choice B: Monopoly
micro.Choice C: Natural monopoly
micro.Choice D: Oligopoly
micro.Correct Answer: A — Perfect competition
micro.Feedback: With many sellers, easy entry, and effectively identical products, the key remaining conditions resemble perfect competition.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.2 — Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.
micro.Question: A monopolistically competitive firm chooses its MR=MC output. At that output, price is below ATC but above AVC. What should the firm do in the short run?
micro.Choice A: Raise output until price equals ATC
micro.Choice B: Exit the industry immediately because price is below ATC
micro.Choice C: Continue producing and accept an economic loss
micro.Choice D: Shut down because any loss requires shutdown
micro.Correct Answer: C — Continue producing and accept an economic loss
micro.Feedback: If price covers AVC, producing helps pay some fixed cost even though the firm earns an economic loss.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.2 — Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.
micro.Question: A firm has MR=40−2Q and constant MC=12. At what output do these curves meet?
micro.Feedback: 40−2Q=12 gives 2Q=28 and Q=14.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.2 — Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.
micro.Question: At its best positive output a firm receives P=$20 and has AVC=$16, ATC=$23. Fixed costs are unavoidable now. What should it do this period?
micro.Choice A: Operate despite an economic loss.
micro.Choice B: Shut down because P is below ATC.
micro.Choice C: Operate because it earns positive economic profit.
micro.Choice D: Shut down because P exceeds AVC.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Operate despite an economic loss.
micro.Feedback: Each unit contributes $4 toward unavoidable fixed cost, so operation is better than shutdown despite the $3 per-unit total-cost loss.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.2 — Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.
micro.Question: A differentiated firm chooses 50 units with P=$18 and ATC=$20. What is economic profit?

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.5 — Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.
micro.Question: A fixed advertising bill increases but demand does not change. Why does the MR=MC output stay the same?
micro.Choice A: Advertising expenses never affect profit
micro.Choice B: The fixed cost does not directly shift MR or MC
micro.Choice C: The fixed cost lowers price by the same amount
micro.Choice D: The fixed cost raises MC at every unit
micro.Correct Answer: B — The fixed cost does not directly shift MR or MC
micro.Feedback: A pure fixed-cost change lowers profit but does not alter the marginal decision when demand is unchanged.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.5 — Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.
micro.Question: An ad tells buyers the product price and where to buy it. Why is this informational rather than persuasive?
micro.Choice A: It supplies facts that reduce search costs
micro.Choice B: It guarantees buyers will prefer the brand
micro.Choice C: It changes the product’s physical quality
micro.Choice D: It prevents consumers from switching brands
micro.Correct Answer: A — It supplies facts that reduce search costs
micro.Feedback: Informational advertising communicates useful facts instead of mainly trying to reshape preferences.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.5 — Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.
micro.Question: After a successful campaign, buyers purchase more at every possible price. Is this a movement along the firm’s demand curve?
micro.Choice A: Yes, because quantity demanded increased
micro.Choice B: Yes, because advertising changes the posted price
micro.Choice C: No, it is a leftward shift of supply
micro.Choice D: No, it is a rightward shift of demand
micro.Correct Answer: D — No, it is a rightward shift of demand
micro.Feedback: More demanded at every price is a demand shift. A movement along demand requires a change in the firm’s own price.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.5 — Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.
micro.Question: After a branding campaign, the magnitude of price elasticity falls from 2 to 0.5. Using the small-change approximation, what quantity response follows a 4% price increase after the campaign?
micro.Choice A: An 8% decrease
micro.Choice B: A 2% increase
micro.Choice C: A 2% decrease
micro.Choice D: A 0.5% decrease
micro.Correct Answer: C — A 2% decrease
micro.Feedback: The postcampaign response is −0.5×4%=−2%.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.5 — Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.
micro.Question: Cost analysis helps separate two advertising cases. Which selling expense acts most like variable cost?
micro.Choice A: A fixed monthly billboard lease
micro.Choice B: A fee charged on each unit sold
micro.Choice C: A flat annual sponsorship payment
micro.Choice D: A one-time logo redesign
micro.Correct Answer: B — A fee charged on each unit sold
micro.Feedback: A per-unit fee varies with output and therefore enters variable and marginal cost.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.5 — Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.
micro.Question: A new product feature earns short-run profit, but rivals can copy it and enter freely. What response would tend to erode the innovator’s profit?
micro.Choice A: Rivals introduce close alternatives that draw away some of its demand.
micro.Choice B: Rivals’ entry guarantees the innovator a permanent monopoly.
micro.Choice C: Imitation raises every buyer’s reservation value for the original by definition.
micro.Choice D: Entry eliminates the innovator’s fixed costs.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Rivals introduce close alternatives that draw away some of its demand.
micro.Feedback: Imitation and entry expand the alternatives available to buyers, weakening the original firm’s demand advantage.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.5 — Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.
micro.Question: An advertisement lists a store’s prices, hours, and warranty terms. What type of advertising is this primarily?
micro.Choice A: Predatory pricing
micro.Choice B: Price discrimination
micro.Choice C: Informational advertising
micro.Choice D: Persuasive advertising
micro.Correct Answer: C — Informational advertising
micro.Feedback: The message mainly reduces consumers’ information costs by providing facts.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.5 — Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.
micro.Question: A perfume ad links the brand with status and excitement but provides almost no factual product information. What type of advertising is this primarily?
micro.Choice A: Perfectly competitive promotion
micro.Choice B: Persuasive advertising
micro.Choice C: Informational advertising
micro.Choice D: Marginal-cost pricing
micro.Correct Answer: B — Persuasive advertising
micro.Feedback: The ad is trying to shape preferences and brand perception rather than mainly transmit facts.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.5 — Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.
micro.Question: A café upgrades ingredients and service rather than cutting price. Which strategy is it using?
micro.Choice A: Nonprice competition through quality
micro.Choice B: A price ceiling
micro.Choice C: Perfect price discrimination
micro.Choice D: Market exit
micro.Correct Answer: A — Nonprice competition through quality
micro.Feedback: Monopolistically competitive firms often compete through quality and service as well as price.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.5 — Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.
micro.Question: A shoe company introduces custom colors and faster delivery while leaving its posted price unchanged. This is an example of:
micro.Choice A: Collusive pricing
micro.Choice B: A shutdown decision
micro.Choice C: Perfect competition
micro.Choice D: Nonprice competition
micro.Correct Answer: D — Nonprice competition
micro.Feedback: The firm is competing through product features and service rather than changing price.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.5 — Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.
micro.Question: A firm buys a one-time advertising campaign that does not change demand. If the expense is fixed, which cost curve does it directly raise?
micro.Choice A: Average variable cost
micro.Choice B: Marginal revenue
micro.Choice C: Average total cost
micro.Choice D: Marginal cost
micro.Correct Answer: C — Average total cost
micro.Feedback: A fixed selling cost raises fixed and average total cost but does not directly raise MC or AVC.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.5 — Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.
micro.Question: A platform charges a promotional fee on every unit a seller sells. The fee acts most like an increase in:
micro.Choice A: Market demand
micro.Choice B: Variable cost
micro.Choice C: Fixed cost
micro.Choice D: Consumer income
micro.Correct Answer: B — Variable cost
micro.Feedback: A per-unit selling expense rises with output, so it behaves like a variable cost.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.5 — Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.
micro.Question: A successful brand campaign causes more buyers to want the firm’s product at every price. What happens to the firm’s demand curve?
micro.Choice A: It shifts to the right
micro.Choice B: There is a movement down the same demand curve
micro.Choice C: It becomes the market supply curve
micro.Choice D: It shifts left because advertising raises cost
micro.Correct Answer: A — It shifts to the right
micro.Feedback: A change in buyers’ willingness to purchase at each price is a demand shift, not a movement along demand.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.5 — Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.
micro.Question: A loyalty campaign makes customers less willing to switch to rival brands after a price increase. The firm’s demand has become:
micro.Choice A: More elastic
micro.Choice B: Perfectly elastic
micro.Choice C: Perfectly inelastic in every case
micro.Choice D: Less elastic
micro.Correct Answer: D — Less elastic
micro.Feedback: Greater brand loyalty reduces responsiveness to the firm’s price, making demand less elastic.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.5 — Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.
micro.Question: A firm develops a distinctive new feature that rivals have not yet copied. What is the most immediate competitive effect?
micro.Choice A: Perfectly elastic firm demand
micro.Choice B: Automatic long-run zero profit immediately
micro.Choice C: Temporary product differentiation
micro.Choice D: Guaranteed permanent monopoly
micro.Correct Answer: C — Temporary product differentiation
micro.Feedback: A distinctive feature can temporarily strengthen differentiation until rivals respond or imitate it.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.5 — Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.
micro.Question: A firm spends $20,000 on a fixed ad campaign. Demand shifts right, but MC is unchanged. Which statement is correct?
micro.Choice A: Profit must rise because demand shifted right
micro.Choice B: The profit-maximizing output may rise because MR changed, while the fixed ad cost also lowers profit
micro.Choice C: Output must stay unchanged because every advertising expense is fixed
micro.Choice D: MC shifts upward by exactly $20,000 at every output
micro.Correct Answer: B — The profit-maximizing output may rise because MR changed, while the fixed ad cost also lowers profit
micro.Feedback: The demand shift can change MR and output even though the fixed selling cost itself does not shift MC.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.5 — Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.
micro.Question: A comparison website makes it easier for buyers to compare nearly identical local services. What effect is most likely on each firm’s demand?
micro.Choice A: Demand becomes more elastic
micro.Choice B: Demand becomes less elastic
micro.Choice C: Demand becomes vertical
micro.Choice D: Demand becomes perfectly inelastic
micro.Correct Answer: A — Demand becomes more elastic
micro.Feedback: Better comparison makes substitution easier, increasing buyers’ responsiveness to one firm’s price.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.5 — Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.
micro.Question: A firm pays a $3 promotional fee for every unit sold, and demand is unchanged. What is the most direct short-run effect?
micro.Choice A: Only fixed cost rises, so output cannot change
micro.Choice B: Demand shifts right by $3 at every quantity
micro.Choice C: ATC falls because advertising spreads fixed cost
micro.Choice D: MC rises, so the MR=MC output tends to fall
micro.Correct Answer: D — MC rises, so the MR=MC output tends to fall
micro.Feedback: A per-unit selling cost raises marginal cost and tends to reduce the profit-maximizing output when demand is unchanged.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.5 — Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.
micro.Question: A restaurant improves food quality. Customers are willing to pay more, but marginal production cost also rises. What determines the new profit-maximizing output?
micro.Choice A: The cost increase alone
micro.Choice B: The old output because quality is nonprice competition
micro.Choice C: The new MR and MC curves together
micro.Choice D: The demand shift alone
micro.Correct Answer: C — The new MR and MC curves together
micro.Feedback: Quality improvement can affect both willingness to pay and cost, so the new optimum still requires comparing MR and MC.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.5 — Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.
micro.Question: A branding campaign leaves the number of buyers unchanged but makes them less price sensitive. What becomes more plausible, other things equal?
micro.Choice A: A lower willingness to pay at every quantity
micro.Choice B: A larger profit-maximizing markup
micro.Choice C: A perfectly competitive price
micro.Choice D: A horizontal firm demand curve
micro.Correct Answer: B — A larger profit-maximizing markup
micro.Feedback: Less elastic demand can support greater price-cost markup for a firm with market power.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.5 — Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.
micro.Question: Consumers cannot directly observe product durability before purchase. Why might heavy advertising sometimes be interpreted as a quality signal?
micro.Choice A: A high-quality seller may expect repeat business that helps justify the advertising expense
micro.Choice B: Advertising legally guarantees the product will be high quality
micro.Choice C: Only low-quality sellers are allowed to advertise heavily
micro.Choice D: Advertising eliminates all uncertainty before purchase
micro.Correct Answer: A — A high-quality seller may expect repeat business that helps justify the advertising expense
micro.Feedback: In signaling models, willingness to incur a visible selling cost can sometimes convey information when higher quality supports repeat sales.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.5 — Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.
micro.Question: Two campaigns cost the same fixed amount. Campaign A shifts demand right but leaves elasticity unchanged. Campaign B leaves demand quantity unchanged but makes demand less elastic. Why can the profit effects differ?
micro.Choice A: Fixed advertising cost always changes MC by the same amount
micro.Choice B: Only Campaign A can affect marginal revenue
micro.Choice C: Only Campaign B can affect the price the firm charges
micro.Choice D: The campaigns alter the firm’s revenue conditions in different ways even though both add the same fixed cost
micro.Correct Answer: D — The campaigns alter the firm’s revenue conditions in different ways even though both add the same fixed cost
micro.Feedback: A demand shift and an elasticity change can alter MR and optimal price/output differently, while the fixed cost enters profit separately.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.5 — Analyze advertising, branding, quality, and other forms of nonprice competition.
micro.Question: A firm can spend on product quality that shifts demand right but also raises MC. Which conclusion is economically sound before seeing the magnitudes?
micro.Choice A: Profit must fall because marginal cost increases
micro.Choice B: Optimal output cannot change because price was not directly altered
micro.Choice C: Profit may rise or fall because both revenue and marginal cost conditions change
micro.Choice D: Profit must rise because buyers value the improvement
micro.Correct Answer: C — Profit may rise or fall because both revenue and marginal cost conditions change
micro.Feedback: The net effect depends on how much the improvement changes willingness to pay relative to the increase in marginal cost.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.6 — Evaluate product variety, efficiency, welfare tradeoffs, and real-world market classifications.
micro.Question: A monopolistically competitive firm earns zero economic profit in long-run equilibrium. Does that prove the outcome is fully efficient?
micro.Choice A: Yes. Entry forces price to equal MC and minimum ATC
micro.Choice B: No. Zero economic profit means the firm should shut down
micro.Choice C: No. Price can still exceed MC and output can remain below the minimum-ATC quantity
micro.Choice D: Yes. Zero economic profit guarantees both allocative and productive efficiency
micro.Correct Answer: C — No. Price can still exceed MC and output can remain below the minimum-ATC quantity
micro.Feedback: Zero economic profit is an entry condition, not proof of allocative or productive efficiency.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.6 — Evaluate product variety, efficiency, welfare tradeoffs, and real-world market classifications.
micro.Question: Why can consumers value monopolistic competition even though firms may not produce at minimum ATC?
micro.Choice A: It guarantees the lowest possible price for every product
micro.Choice B: It eliminates all selling costs
micro.Choice C: It makes every firm a price taker
micro.Choice D: It offers product variety that can match different preferences
micro.Correct Answer: D — It offers product variety that can match different preferences
micro.Feedback: Differentiation can create consumer value through variety even when the standard model shows some productive inefficiency.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.6 — Evaluate product variety, efficiency, welfare tradeoffs, and real-world market classifications.
micro.Question: In the standard long-run model, which condition signals allocative inefficiency for a monopolistically competitive firm?
micro.Choice A: Marginal revenue equals marginal cost
micro.Choice B: Economic profit equals zero
micro.Choice C: Price exceeds marginal cost
micro.Choice D: Price equals average total cost
micro.Correct Answer: C — Price exceeds marginal cost
micro.Feedback: Allocative efficiency requires P=MC. A positive markup means some mutually beneficial trades may not occur.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.6 — Evaluate product variety, efficiency, welfare tradeoffs, and real-world market classifications.
micro.Question: A market has only three differentiated firms, and each changes strategy when a rival cuts price. Why may monopolistic competition be a poor model?
micro.Choice A: Price changes are impossible under monopolistic competition
micro.Choice B: Strategic interdependence points toward oligopoly
micro.Choice C: Differentiated products require perfect competition
micro.Choice D: Few firms automatically create a natural monopoly
micro.Correct Answer: B — Strategic interdependence points toward oligopoly
micro.Feedback: The monopolistic-competition model assumes many firms whose individual strategic reactions are usually not central.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.6 — Evaluate product variety, efficiency, welfare tradeoffs, and real-world market classifications.
micro.Question: Why is a larger number of brands not automatically socially better?
micro.Choice A: Additional variety can create benefits but also use resources and duplicate fixed costs
micro.Choice B: Every new brand necessarily lowers marginal cost
micro.Choice C: More brands guarantee P=MC for all firms
micro.Choice D: Product variety eliminates excess capacity
micro.Correct Answer: A — Additional variety can create benefits but also use resources and duplicate fixed costs
micro.Feedback: The welfare question compares the value of added variety with the resources used to create and sustain it.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.6 — Evaluate product variety, efficiency, welfare tradeoffs, and real-world market classifications.
micro.Question: A policy causes several niche brands to exit. Average production cost falls, but consumers lose valued variety. What is the correct welfare conclusion?
micro.Choice A: Welfare must rise because average cost fell
micro.Choice B: Welfare must fall because the number of brands fell
micro.Choice C: The change is irrelevant because firms earn zero economic profit
micro.Choice D: The net effect is ambiguous without comparing cost savings with lost variety benefits
micro.Correct Answer: D — The net effect is ambiguous without comparing cost savings with lost variety benefits
micro.Feedback: Efficiency analysis must weigh resource savings against the consumer value of differentiation and variety.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.6 — Evaluate product variety, efficiency, welfare tradeoffs, and real-world market classifications.
micro.Question: A textbook labels a market monopolistically competitive because it has many differentiated sellers. In one rural town, however, only two sellers actually serve customers. What is the best caution?
micro.Choice A: Two local sellers guarantee a natural monopoly
micro.Choice B: Differentiation becomes irrelevant whenever geography matters
micro.Choice C: The local market may display strategic interdependence that the broad model misses
micro.Choice D: The market must still be perfectly competitive locally
micro.Correct Answer: C — The local market may display strategic interdependence that the broad model misses
micro.Feedback: Market boundaries matter. A broad national description can hide a much more concentrated local competitive environment.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.6 — Evaluate product variety, efficiency, welfare tradeoffs, and real-world market classifications.
micro.Question: A long-run monopolistically competitive firm earns zero economic profit but charges P>$MC$. What does this show?
micro.Choice A: The firm is producing at minimum ATC
micro.Choice B: Zero economic profit does not imply allocative efficiency
micro.Choice C: The firm must be earning an accounting loss
micro.Choice D: Entry has failed to eliminate all market power
micro.Correct Answer: B — Zero economic profit does not imply allocative efficiency
micro.Feedback: Entry can eliminate economic profit while differentiation leaves a markup and P above MC.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.6 — Evaluate product variety, efficiency, welfare tradeoffs, and real-world market classifications.
micro.Question: Two markets have the same total production cost. Market A offers one standardized product; Market B offers several differentiated versions that consumers value. What can be said?
micro.Choice A: Market B may generate greater consumer benefit because variety itself can have value
micro.Choice B: Market A must be more allocatively efficient because it has fewer products
micro.Choice C: Market B must have higher deadweight loss because it has more brands
micro.Choice D: Both markets provide identical welfare because production cost is the same
micro.Correct Answer: A — Market B may generate greater consumer benefit because variety itself can have value
micro.Feedback: Equal production cost does not imply equal consumer benefit when differentiated varieties match heterogeneous preferences.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.6 — Evaluate product variety, efficiency, welfare tradeoffs, and real-world market classifications.
micro.Question: Suppose a regulator could force every differentiated firm to price at marginal cost, but doing so would reduce firms’ ability to cover fixed product-development costs and some varieties would disappear. What is the best conclusion?
micro.Choice A: Marginal-cost pricing must raise welfare because P=MC is always sufficient
micro.Choice B: Variety loss is irrelevant because all firms initially earned zero economic profit
micro.Choice C: The policy must lower welfare because regulation can never improve allocation
micro.Choice D: The welfare effect depends on the gain from lower markups relative to the loss of valued variety
micro.Correct Answer: D — The welfare effect depends on the gain from lower markups relative to the loss of valued variety
micro.Feedback: The standard markup is inefficient, but differentiated products may create variety benefits and require fixed costs. Both sides matter.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: A market has many sellers but all products are identical. Why is that not enough for monopolistic competition?
micro.Choice A: Many sellers automatically imply monopolistic competition
micro.Choice B: Entry must be prohibited
micro.Choice C: Product differentiation is also required
micro.Choice D: Demand must be perfectly inelastic
micro.Correct Answer: C — Product differentiation is also required
micro.Feedback: The model requires both many firms and differentiated varieties.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: Why is a differentiated firm’s demand downward sloping?
micro.Choice A: Some customers prefer its variety, but they can switch when price rises
micro.Choice B: The firm is a price taker
micro.Choice C: The product has no close substitutes, so buyers cannot switch when the firm raises its price
micro.Choice D: Marginal cost creates demand
micro.Correct Answer: A — Some customers prefer its variety, but they can switch when price rises
micro.Feedback: Differentiation gives limited market power.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: Many cafés sell differentiated drinks and new cafés can enter without major barriers. Which shared feature with perfect competition allows profit to attract new producers?
micro.Choice A: Identical products
micro.Choice B: Horizontal demand for each café
micro.Choice C: Relatively easy entry
micro.Choice D: Price equal to marginal cost by definition
micro.Correct Answer: C — Relatively easy entry
micro.Feedback: Entry can occur in both models even though café products are differentiated.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: A town has one water supplier with no close substitute and many restaurants offering differentiated meals. For which seller is switching to a close rival’s product generally easier?
micro.Choice A: A restaurant
micro.Choice B: The water supplier
micro.Choice C: Both have no substitutes
micro.Choice D: Neither, because differentiation prevents substitution
micro.Correct Answer: A — A restaurant
micro.Feedback: Restaurant alternatives are close substitutes despite differentiation; the water supplier is specified to lack a close substitute.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: Before close substitutes enter, a 5% price increase reduces a firm’s quantity by 2%. After entry, the same price increase reduces quantity by 8%. What happens to demand elasticity magnitude?
micro.Choice A: It falls from 1.6 to 0.4.
micro.Choice B: It stays at 5.
micro.Choice C: It rises from 0.4 to 1.6.
micro.Choice D: It rises from 2.5 to 4.
micro.Correct Answer: C — It rises from 0.4 to 1.6.
micro.Feedback: Use |%ΔQ/%ΔP|: 2/5=0.4 and 8/5=1.6. More substitutes are consistent with greater responsiveness.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: A brand changes perceived value without changing physical quality. Which concept is central?
micro.Choice A: Marginal product
micro.Choice B: Preference and perceived differentiation
micro.Choice C: Natural monopoly
micro.Choice D: Comparative advantage
micro.Correct Answer: B — Preference and perceived differentiation
micro.Feedback: Consumer perceptions can shape demand for a variety.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: Which combination best describes monopolistic competition?
micro.Choice A: Many firms, differentiated products, and relatively easy entry and exit
micro.Choice B: One seller, no close substitutes, and barriers that prevent every rival from entering
micro.Choice C: Many firms selling an identical product
micro.Choice D: A few strategically interdependent firms
micro.Correct Answer: A — Many firms, differentiated products, and relatively easy entry and exit
micro.Feedback: The model combines many firms and entry with differentiated products.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: What gives a monopolistically competitive firm limited market power?
micro.Choice A: It controls every key input
micro.Choice B: Its product is differentiated from close substitutes
micro.Choice C: Government fixes its price
micro.Choice D: A government franchise that prevents all potential competitors from entering the market
micro.Correct Answer: B — Its product is differentiated from close substitutes
micro.Feedback: Differentiation makes the firm’s own demand slope downward.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: A neighborhood café competes through atmosphere, menu, and location. Which feature is being illustrated?
micro.Choice A: Perfectly elastic demand
micro.Choice B: A legal monopoly
micro.Choice C: Product differentiation
micro.Choice D: Strategic collusion
micro.Correct Answer: C — Product differentiation
micro.Feedback: Atmosphere, menu, and location can distinguish one seller from close substitutes.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: Which example is physical product differentiation?
micro.Choice A: A salon opens closer to commuters
micro.Choice B: A hotel trains staff to provide faster service
micro.Choice C: A retailer creates a memorable logo
micro.Choice D: A shoe brand uses a more durable sole
micro.Correct Answer: D — A shoe brand uses a more durable sole
micro.Feedback: The durable sole changes a physical characteristic of the product.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: Which example is location differentiation?
micro.Choice A: Two similar pharmacies serve different neighborhoods
micro.Choice B: One pharmacy uses stronger packaging
micro.Choice C: One pharmacy offers a longer warranty
micro.Choice D: One pharmacy uses a nationally advertised brand and standardized package design
micro.Correct Answer: A — Two similar pharmacies serve different neighborhoods
micro.Feedback: Convenient location can differentiate otherwise similar sellers.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: Which example is service differentiation?
micro.Choice A: A shop changes its wall color
micro.Choice B: A repair shop guarantees same-day updates
micro.Choice C: A repair shop owns a patented machine that lowers the cost of each service call
micro.Choice D: A shop sells an identical commodity
micro.Correct Answer: B — A repair shop guarantees same-day updates
micro.Feedback: The guarantee changes the service experience.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: What does branding differentiation primarily create?
micro.Choice A: A perfectly horizontal demand curve
micro.Choice B: A legal prohibition on all entry
micro.Choice C: A perceived identity that may make buyers view close substitutes differently
micro.Choice D: A legal franchise that prevents rival brands from entering the relevant market
micro.Correct Answer: C — A perceived identity that may make buyers view close substitutes differently
micro.Feedback: Branding can shape perceived differences and loyalty.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: Products in monopolistic competition are best described as:
micro.Choice A: Perfect complements
micro.Choice B: Identical commodities
micro.Choice C: Products that buyers regard as identical commodities from interchangeable sellers
micro.Choice D: Close but imperfect substitutes
micro.Correct Answer: D — Close but imperfect substitutes
micro.Feedback: Consumers can switch, but they may not view every variety as identical.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: Why does an individual firm face downward-sloping demand?
micro.Choice A: Some buyers prefer its particular variety
micro.Choice B: The firm takes price as given
micro.Choice C: Every buyer views all rival products as identical and refuses to switch among sellers
micro.Choice D: The government assigns each customer
micro.Correct Answer: A — Some buyers prefer its particular variety
micro.Feedback: Differentiation allows price to affect quantity demanded for the firm’s variety.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: A firm’s close substitutes become more numerous. Its demand will generally become:
micro.Choice A: Perfectly inelastic
micro.Choice B: Vertical
micro.Choice C: Less responsive to price
micro.Choice D: More elastic
micro.Correct Answer: D — More elastic
micro.Feedback: More alternatives make switching easier.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: A clothing store raises price and loses some, but not all, customers to nearby brands. What does this imply?
micro.Choice A: It faces perfectly inelastic demand
micro.Choice B: It is a price-taking commodity seller facing a horizontal demand curve at the market price
micro.Choice C: It has no substitutes
micro.Choice D: Its firm demand is downward sloping and relatively elastic
micro.Correct Answer: D — Its firm demand is downward sloping and relatively elastic
micro.Feedback: Differentiation gives market power, while close substitutes keep demand responsive.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: Amber Café sells a differentiated product among many close substitutes. Which market feature explains its downward-sloping firm demand?
micro.Choice A: The firm takes price as given
micro.Choice B: Entry is legally prohibited
micro.Choice C: Some customers prefer its variety, but can switch to rivals
micro.Choice D: The product is identical to every rival’s
micro.Correct Answer: C — Some customers prefer its variety, but can switch to rivals
micro.Feedback: Differentiation creates limited market power.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: Birch Salon sells a differentiated product among many close substitutes. Which market feature explains its downward-sloping firm demand?
micro.Choice A: The firm takes price as given
micro.Choice B: Some customers prefer its variety, but can switch to rivals
micro.Choice C: Entry is legally prohibited
micro.Choice D: The product is identical to every rival’s
micro.Correct Answer: B — Some customers prefer its variety, but can switch to rivals
micro.Feedback: Differentiation creates limited market power.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: Cedar Fitness sells a differentiated product among many close substitutes. Which market feature explains its downward-sloping firm demand?
micro.Choice A: Some customers prefer its variety, but can switch to rivals
micro.Choice B: The firm takes price as given
micro.Choice C: Entry is legally prohibited
micro.Choice D: The product is identical to every rival’s
micro.Correct Answer: A — Some customers prefer its variety, but can switch to rivals
micro.Feedback: Differentiation creates limited market power.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: Drift Apparel sells a differentiated product among many close substitutes. Which market feature explains its downward-sloping firm demand?
micro.Choice A: The firm takes price as given
micro.Choice B: Entry is legally prohibited
micro.Choice C: The product is identical to every rival’s
micro.Choice D: Some customers prefer its variety, but can switch to rivals
micro.Correct Answer: D — Some customers prefer its variety, but can switch to rivals
micro.Feedback: Differentiation creates limited market power.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: Elm Bistro sells a differentiated product among many close substitutes. Which market feature explains its downward-sloping firm demand?
micro.Choice A: The firm takes price as given
micro.Choice B: Entry is legally prohibited
micro.Choice C: Some customers prefer its variety, but can switch to rivals
micro.Choice D: The product is identical to every rival’s
micro.Correct Answer: C — Some customers prefer its variety, but can switch to rivals
micro.Feedback: Differentiation creates limited market power.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.1 — Explain the characteristics of monopolistic competition and the sources of product differentiation.
micro.Question: Fjord Studio sells a differentiated product among many close substitutes. Which market feature explains its downward-sloping firm demand?
micro.Choice A: The firm takes price as given
micro.Choice B: Some customers prefer its variety, but can switch to rivals
micro.Choice C: Entry is legally prohibited
micro.Choice D: The product is identical to every rival’s
micro.Correct Answer: B — Some customers prefer its variety, but can switch to rivals
micro.Feedback: Differentiation creates limited market power.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.2 — Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.
micro.Question: For a downward-sloping firm demand curve, why is MR below price?
micro.Choice A: ATC is U-shaped
micro.Choice B: Selling more requires a lower price, creating a price effect
micro.Choice C: Entry raises fixed cost and therefore pushes marginal revenue below the firm’s demand curve
micro.Choice D: Products are identical
micro.Correct Answer: B — Selling more requires a lower price, creating a price effect
micro.Feedback: Added revenue is reduced by the lower price on units sold.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.2 — Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.
micro.Question: What is the correct sequence for short-run firm choice?
micro.Choice A: Choose P where demand equals MC, then read Q from MR
micro.Choice B: Choose minimum ATC, then set P=MC
micro.Choice C: Choose Q where MR=MC, then read P from demand
micro.Choice D: Choose the highest price on demand
micro.Correct Answer: C — Choose Q where MR=MC, then read P from demand
micro.Feedback: Quantity comes from the marginal rule; demand supplies price.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.2 — Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.
micro.Question: A table has no exact MR=MC equality. Which output should be selected?
micro.Choice A: No output can be chosen
micro.Choice B: The first unit whose MC exceeds price
micro.Choice C: The minimum-ATC output
micro.Choice D: The last unit whose MR is at least MC
micro.Correct Answer: D — The last unit whose MR is at least MC
micro.Feedback: The discrete marginal rule compares the added revenue and cost of each unit.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.2 — Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.
micro.Question: A firm has P>MC but P<ATC. Which statement is correct?
micro.Choice A: It has a markup but an economic loss
micro.Choice B: It earns economic profit because P>MC
micro.Choice C: It must have zero profit
micro.Choice D: It is allocatively efficient
micro.Correct Answer: A — It has a markup but an economic loss
micro.Feedback: Profit depends on P versus ATC, not P versus MC.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.2 — Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.
micro.Question: A firm has P<ATC but P>AVC. What should it do in the short run?
micro.Choice A: Shut down because P<ATC
micro.Choice B: Produce at MR=MC and minimize its loss
micro.Choice C: Exit immediately because any economic loss requires the firm to leave the market
micro.Choice D: Produce at minimum ATC
micro.Correct Answer: B — Produce at MR=MC and minimize its loss
micro.Feedback: Covering AVC allows production to contribute toward fixed cost.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.2 — Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.
micro.Question: A differentiated firm’s MR is $16 and MC is $12 for the next unit. Should it add that unit, holding other decisions fixed?
micro.Choice A: No; it subtracts $4 from profit.
micro.Choice B: Only if ATC is zero.
micro.Choice C: Yes; it adds $4 to profit.
micro.Choice D: Only if the demand curve is horizontal.
micro.Correct Answer: C — Yes; it adds $4 to profit.
micro.Feedback: The extra revenue exceeds the extra cost by $4.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.2 — Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.
micro.Question: At its best positive output a differentiated firm has P=$9, AVC=$11 and ATC=$15. Fixed cost is unavoidable this period. Should it produce now?
micro.Choice A: Yes; any revenue is better than shutdown.
micro.Choice B: Yes; price need only cover AFC.
micro.Choice C: No; producing always requires positive economic profit.
micro.Choice D: No; shutting down avoids a variable-cost loss.
micro.Correct Answer: D — No; shutting down avoids a variable-cost loss.
micro.Feedback: Revenue does not cover variable cost at the best positive output. Shutdown loses fixed cost only.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.2 — Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.
micro.Question: A differentiated firm’s MR and MC cross at Q=10. Demand shows P=$24 there, while MR=$16. What price corresponds to the profit-maximizing output?
micro.Feedback: MR=MC selects Q=10; demand, not MR, gives its selling price of $24.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.2 — Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.
micro.Question: For a monopolistically competitive firm, average revenue equals:
micro.Choice A: Marginal cost
micro.Choice B: Price
micro.Choice C: Average total cost
micro.Choice D: Economic profit
micro.Correct Answer: B — Price
micro.Feedback: Average revenue is total revenue divided by quantity, which equals price.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.2 — Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.
micro.Question: Why is marginal revenue below price for the firm?
micro.Choice A: Marginal cost is rising
micro.Choice B: Average total cost falls as fixed cost is spread across a larger number of units
micro.Choice C: Selling another unit generally requires a lower price on units sold
micro.Choice D: Entry is legally blocked
micro.Correct Answer: C — Selling another unit generally requires a lower price on units sold
micro.Feedback: The price effect makes added revenue smaller than the new unit’s price.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.2 — Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.
micro.Question: What output rule does a monopolistically competitive firm use in the short run?
micro.Choice A: Produce where marginal revenue equals marginal cost on rising MC
micro.Choice B: Produce where demand intersects average total cost at the lowest attainable unit cost
micro.Choice C: Produce at minimum average fixed cost
micro.Choice D: Produce where price is highest
micro.Correct Answer: A — Produce where marginal revenue equals marginal cost on rising MC
micro.Feedback: The firm applies the same marginal rule as other profit-maximizing firms.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.2 — Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.
micro.Question: After choosing output where MR equals MC, where does the firm find its price?
micro.Choice A: On the marginal-revenue curve at the quantity where marginal revenue equals marginal cost
micro.Choice B: On its demand curve at that output
micro.Choice C: At minimum AVC
micro.Choice D: On the market supply curve
micro.Correct Answer: B — On its demand curve at that output
micro.Feedback: Demand gives the price buyers will pay for the chosen quantity.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.2 — Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.
micro.Question: A firm earns positive economic profit when, at its chosen output:
micro.Choice A: Price exceeds marginal revenue
micro.Choice B: Marginal cost exceeds price
micro.Choice C: Price exceeds average total cost
micro.Choice D: Average variable cost exceeds price
micro.Correct Answer: C — Price exceeds average total cost
micro.Feedback: Profit per unit is price minus ATC.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.2 — Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.
micro.Question: A firm incurs an economic loss when, at its chosen output:
micro.Choice A: Marginal revenue lies below demand even though price still covers average total cost
micro.Choice B: Price is above marginal cost
micro.Choice C: Demand slopes downward
micro.Choice D: Price is below average total cost
micro.Correct Answer: D — Price is below average total cost
micro.Feedback: A price below ATC means revenue does not cover total economic cost.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.2 — Determine short-run output, price, profit, loss, and shutdown outcomes using marginal analysis.
micro.Question: In the short run, a loss-making firm should continue producing when:

micro.Choice B: Price falls below minimum average variable cost but remains above average total cost

micro.Choice D: Fixed cost is positive

micro.Feedback: Production can cover variable cost and part of fixed cost.

micro.Question: Compare the long-run outcome in the graph with an earlier profitable position. Which current price and change in incumbent demand describe the effect of entry?
micro.Choice A: $23; entry shifted incumbent demand inward until price equaled ATC at the MR = MC output.
micro.Choice B: $27; entry eliminated profit by making each firm choose minimum ATC regardless of demand and MR.
micro.Choice C: $23; entry eliminated profit by making each firm choose minimum ATC regardless of demand and MR.
micro.Choice D: $27; entry shifted incumbent demand inward until price equaled ATC at the MR = MC output.
micro.Correct Answer: D — $27; entry shifted incumbent demand inward until price equaled ATC at the MR = MC output.
micro.Feedback: The plotted profit-maximizing quantity is 36, where demand is tangent to ATC at $27. Entry reduces incumbent demand until economic profit is zero. The firm still chooses output using MR = MC, and the tangency lies below the minimum-ATC output.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.3 — Analyze how entry and exit change an existing firm’s demand and economic profit.
micro.Question: Use the graph. Suppose demand shifts outward from the plotted position while costs remain unchanged. Which original price and likely short-run-to-long-run adjustment are correct?
micro.Choice A: $60; the firm can earn economic profit before entry reduces incumbent demand.
micro.Choice B: $70; the firm can earn economic profit before entry reduces incumbent demand.
micro.Choice C: $70; an outward demand shift must leave economic profit zero immediately, so it cannot encourage entry.
micro.Choice D: $60; an outward demand shift must leave economic profit zero immediately, so it cannot encourage entry.
micro.Correct Answer: B — $70; the firm can earn economic profit before entry reduces incumbent demand.
micro.Feedback: The starting tangency is P = ATC = 70 at Q1 = 20. A higher demand curve can support price above cost and positive short-run profit. Entry then offers substitutes and reduces incumbent demand; it need not eliminate profit immediately.

micro.Learning Objective: MCMP.3 — Analyze how entry and exit change an existing firm’s demand and economic profit.
micro.Question: Use the graph. Suppose the plotted outcome follows an earlier period of short-run profit and entry. Which current price and description of the adjustment are correct?
micro.Choice A: $76; entry shifted incumbent demand inward until price equaled ATC at the MR = MC output.
micro.Choice B: $72; entry shifted incumbent demand inward until price equaled ATC at the MR = MC output.
micro.Choice C: $76; entry eliminates the price–MC markup whenever it eliminates economic profit.
micro.Choice D: $76; entry shifts each incumbent’s marginal cost down until its existing demand curve becomes tangent to ATC.
micro.Correct Answer: A — $76; entry shifted incumbent demand inward until price equaled ATC at the MR = MC output.
micro.Feedback: At Q = 24, P = ATC = $76 while MC = $49.60. Entry reduces incumbent demand until profit is zero, but markup and output below minimum ATC remain. Entry need not shift the firm’s cost curves.

micro.Question: Summit Coffee has demand P=118−2.2Q and MC=18+0.32Q. A new rival enters and lowers the demand intercept by $12. Demand slope and the entire cost function stay unchanged. Compared with the original profit-maximizing outcome, how do price and maximum economic profit change?
micro.Choice A: Price rises and profit falls: the lower quantity must raise the price along the original demand curve.
micro.Choice B: Price is unchanged and profit falls: unchanged MC fixes price at its original level.
micro.Choice C: Price falls and profit is unchanged: output adjustment fully offsets the demand reduction.
micro.Choice D: Both fall: weaker demand lowers the chosen price and the maximum profit obtainable from the unchanged cost curve.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Both fall: weaker demand lowers the chosen price and the maximum profit obtainable from the unchanged cost curve.
micro.Feedback: The lower demand intercept reduces MR and the optimal output. With the stated linear demand and upward-sloping MC, price also falls. Revenue is lower at every positive output while costs are unchanged, so reoptimizing does not preserve the original maximum profit.

micro.Choice B: Price rises and profit falls: the lower quantity must raise the price along the original demand curve.
micro.Choice C: Price is unchanged and profit falls: unchanged MC fixes price at its original level.
micro.Choice D: Price falls and profit is unchanged: output adjustment fully offsets the demand reduction.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Both fall: weaker demand lowers the chosen price and the maximum profit obtainable from the unchanged cost curve.
micro.Feedback: The lower demand intercept reduces MR and the optimal output. With the stated linear demand and upward-sloping MC, price also falls. Revenue is lower at every positive output while costs are unchanged, so reoptimizing does not preserve the original maximum profit.

micro.Choice A: Demand is tangent to ATC and economic profit is zero

micro.Choice D: MR is tangent to demand

micro.Choice D: The firm earns $12 of economic profit per unit
