micro.Feedback: Cost sharing leaves the insured with some financial consequence from loss, improving incentives at the margin.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.3 — Moral Hazard
micro.Common Misconception: Confuses hidden actions with hidden characteristics
micro.Question: A policy analyst notes that a deductible makes the customer pay the first part of a covered loss. Why can it reduce moral hazard?
micro.Choice A: It restores some marginal cost of risky behavior to the customer
micro.Choice B: It reveals every customer's innate risk type
micro.Choice C: It guarantees no accident occurs
micro.Choice D: It converts insurance into a public good
micro.Correct Answer: A — It restores some marginal cost of risky behavior to the customer
micro.Feedback: Cost sharing leaves the insured with some financial consequence from loss, improving incentives at the margin.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.3 — Moral Hazard
micro.Common Misconception: Confuses hidden actions with hidden characteristics
micro.Question: Suppose that insured drivers become less careful after receiving broad coverage. What problem is illustrated?
micro.Choice A: Adverse selection
micro.Choice B: The median voter result
micro.Choice C: Moral hazard
micro.Choice D: Loss aversion
micro.Correct Answer: C — Moral hazard
micro.Feedback: Coverage changes incentives for an action that is difficult for the insurer to observe after contracting.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.3 — Moral Hazard
micro.Common Misconception: Confuses hidden actions with hidden characteristics
micro.Question: An economist observes that a bank expects a guaranteed bailout and therefore chooses a riskier portfolio. What causes the distortion?
micro.Choice A: The bank's hidden type before borrowing
micro.Choice B: Perfect screening
micro.Choice C: A lower opportunity cost of voting
micro.Choice D: Protection shifts part of the downside to others
micro.Correct Answer: D — Protection shifts part of the downside to others
micro.Feedback: When decision makers do not bear the full marginal loss, post-protection risk taking can rise.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.3 — Moral Hazard
micro.Common Misconception: Confuses observation with enforceable incentives
micro.Question: In this setting, behavior is perfectly monitored and a contract can condition payment on every action. What happens to hidden-action moral hazard?
micro.Choice A: It becomes adverse selection automatically
micro.Choice B: It can be greatly reduced through enforceable incentives
micro.Choice C: It must increase
micro.Choice D: It makes insurance unnecessary in every case
micro.Correct Answer: B — It can be greatly reduced through enforceable incentives
micro.Feedback: Observable, contractible action allows terms to reward care or penalize risk, though monitoring itself may be costly.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.3 — Moral Hazard
micro.Common Misconception: Confuses hidden actions with hidden characteristics
micro.Question: A policy analyst notes that insured drivers become less careful after receiving broad coverage. What problem is illustrated?
micro.Choice A: Adverse selection
micro.Choice B: The median voter result
micro.Choice C: Moral hazard
micro.Choice D: Loss aversion
micro.Correct Answer: C — Moral hazard
micro.Feedback: Coverage changes incentives for an action that is difficult for the insurer to observe after contracting.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.3 — Moral Hazard
micro.Common Misconception: Confuses hidden actions with hidden characteristics
micro.Question: An economist observes that insured drivers become less careful after receiving broad coverage. What problem is illustrated?
micro.Choice A: Adverse selection
micro.Choice B: The median voter result
micro.Choice C: Moral hazard
micro.Choice D: Loss aversion
micro.Correct Answer: C — Moral hazard
micro.Feedback: Coverage changes incentives for an action that is difficult for the insurer to observe after contracting.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.3 — Moral Hazard
micro.Common Misconception: Confuses hidden actions with hidden characteristics
micro.Question: Two banks hold identical assets initially. Only one receives a credible promise that taxpayers will absorb large future losses. With other incentives fixed, which response is consistent with moral hazard?
micro.Choice A: The protected bank selects less risk because it bears all taxpayers’ losses.
micro.Choice B: Both banks must select identical risk because their initial assets match.
micro.Choice C: The unprotected bank becomes insured merely because another bank is protected.
micro.Choice D: The protected bank selects more risk because it bears less downside.
micro.Correct Answer: D — The protected bank selects more risk because it bears less downside.
micro.Feedback: The guarantee changes the protected bank’s marginal exposure to losses even though initial assets are equal.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.3 — Moral Hazard
micro.Common Misconception: Confuses hidden actions with hidden characteristics
micro.Question: An insurer reimburses all losses. It then adds a deductible that makes the insured bear part of each loss, holding information and all other terms fixed. Which incentive changes most directly?
micro.Choice A: The insured bears a smaller loss and therefore has less reason for care.
micro.Choice B: The insured has a stronger financial reason to prevent a loss.
micro.Choice C: The insurer learns every hidden characteristic before contracting.
micro.Choice D: The deductible guarantees no accident can occur.
micro.Correct Answer: B — The insured has a stronger financial reason to prevent a loss.
micro.Feedback: A deductible leaves some loss with the insured and can strengthen care incentives, without guaranteeing perfect care or revealing all types.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.3 — Moral Hazard
micro.Common Misconception: Confuses hidden actions with hidden characteristics
micro.Question: A classroom example assumes that insured drivers become less careful after receiving broad coverage. What problem is illustrated?
micro.Choice A: Adverse selection
micro.Choice B: The median voter result
micro.Choice C: Moral hazard
micro.Choice D: Loss aversion
micro.Correct Answer: C — Moral hazard
micro.Feedback: Coverage changes incentives for an action that is difficult for the insurer to observe after contracting.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.3 — Moral Hazard
micro.Common Misconception: Confuses hidden actions with hidden characteristics
micro.Question: An insured driver maintains exactly the same level of care before and after coverage. An accident then occurs. Does that accident alone establish moral hazard?
micro.Choice A: Yes; every insured loss proves reduced care.
micro.Choice B: Yes; the insurer’s payment establishes hidden precontract risk.
micro.Choice C: No; moral hazard is impossible in insurance.
micro.Choice D: No; the accident alone does not demonstrate a coverage-induced change in behavior.
micro.Correct Answer: D — No; the accident alone does not demonstrate a coverage-induced change in behavior.
micro.Feedback: A bad outcome can occur without a change in incentives or behavior. The stated unchanged care does not demonstrate moral hazard.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.3 — Moral Hazard
micro.Question: Monitoring costs $8 per policy and is expected to reduce real accident losses by $5, with no other benefits or costs. Is monitoring justified by net resource savings in this example?
micro.Choice A: Yes; every reduction in moral hazard exceeds its cost.
micro.Choice B: No; it costs $3 more than the expected loss reduction.
micro.Choice C: Yes; the net saving is $13.
micro.Choice D: No; the reduction in losses is a transfer rather than a resource benefit.
micro.Correct Answer: B — No; it costs $3 more than the expected loss reduction.
micro.Feedback: The resource gain is $5 and the cost is $8, giving net savings of −$3.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.3 — Moral Hazard
micro.Common Misconception: Confuses hidden actions with hidden characteristics
micro.Question: Consider a case in which insured drivers become less careful after receiving broad coverage. What problem is illustrated?
micro.Choice A: Adverse selection
micro.Choice B: The median voter result
micro.Choice C: Moral hazard
micro.Choice D: Loss aversion
micro.Correct Answer: C — Moral hazard
micro.Feedback: Coverage changes incentives for an action that is difficult for the insurer to observe after contracting.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.3 — Moral Hazard
micro.Common Misconception: Confuses hidden actions with hidden characteristics
micro.Question: In this setting, a bank expects a guaranteed bailout and therefore chooses a riskier portfolio. What causes the distortion?
micro.Choice A: The bank's hidden type before borrowing
micro.Choice B: Perfect screening
micro.Choice C: A lower opportunity cost of voting
micro.Choice D: Protection shifts part of the downside to others
micro.Correct Answer: D — Protection shifts part of the downside to others
micro.Feedback: When decision makers do not bear the full marginal loss, post-protection risk taking can rise.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.3 — Moral Hazard
micro.Common Misconception: Confuses hidden actions with hidden characteristics
micro.Question: Evidence indicates that insured drivers become less careful after receiving broad coverage. What problem is illustrated?
micro.Choice A: Adverse selection
micro.Choice B: The median voter result
micro.Choice C: Moral hazard
micro.Choice D: Loss aversion
micro.Correct Answer: C — Moral hazard
micro.Feedback: Coverage changes incentives for an action that is difficult for the insurer to observe after contracting.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.3 — Moral Hazard
micro.Common Misconception: Confuses hidden actions with hidden characteristics
micro.Question: If an insurer can observe every safety action and enforce contract terms that reward or penalize those actions, what happens to hidden-action moral hazard?
micro.Choice A: It can be greatly reduced through enforceable incentives
micro.Choice B: It automatically becomes adverse selection
micro.Choice C: It must increase
micro.Choice D: It makes every insurance contract unnecessary
micro.Correct Answer: A — It can be greatly reduced through enforceable incentives
micro.Feedback: When enforceable contract terms reward or penalize observed safety actions, they can reduce the hidden-action problem.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.3 — Moral Hazard
micro.Common Misconception: Confuses hidden actions with hidden characteristics
micro.Question: Why can a deductible reduce moral hazard?
micro.Choice A: It reveals every customer's risk type
micro.Choice B: The insured person bears part of the marginal cost of a loss
micro.Choice C: It guarantees that no accident occurs
micro.Choice D: It makes coverage a public good
micro.Correct Answer: B — The insured person bears part of the marginal cost of a loss
micro.Feedback: Cost sharing preserves some incentive to take care after coverage begins.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.3 — Moral Hazard
micro.Common Misconception: Confuses hidden actions with hidden characteristics
micro.Question: A bank expects rescue only if its losses become very large. Managers respond by choosing a riskier portfolio after financing is obtained. What makes this a moral-hazard mechanism?
micro.Choice A: The rescue reveals the bank’s hidden precontract type with certainty.
micro.Choice B: The risk increase is a fixed characteristic that cannot respond to incentives.
micro.Choice C: Rescue expectations raise the bank’s share of every possible loss.
micro.Choice D: The rescue expectation reduces the downside the bank bears and changes its later risk-taking.
micro.Correct Answer: D — The rescue expectation reduces the downside the bank bears and changes its later risk-taking.
micro.Feedback: Sharing or shifting losses can weaken incentives to avoid them; the stated change is in behavior after financing.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.3 — Moral Hazard
micro.Common Misconception: Confuses observation with enforceable incentives
micro.Question: An insurer can perfectly verify how carefully a driver behaves but cannot make enforceable contract terms or penalties depend on that behavior. Does observing the driver’s behavior alone remove the incentive to take less care?
micro.Choice A: Yes; seeing an action automatically changes the driver’s payoff.
micro.Choice B: Yes; observation refunds every premium.
micro.Choice C: No; the remaining issue must be hidden precontract type only.
micro.Choice D: No; observing an action does not ensure that contract terms can reward or penalize it, so incentives may remain unchanged.
micro.Correct Answer: D — No; observing an action does not ensure that contract terms can reward or penalize it, so incentives may remain unchanged.
micro.Feedback: Observation and enforceability are separate. Verified actions need enforceable consequences to change the described incentive.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.3 — Moral Hazard
micro.Common Misconception: Confuses observation with enforceable incentives
micro.Question: An insurer can cheaply monitor care and enforce a premium discount for verified care, but cannot observe a customer’s inherited risk before contracting. Which problem can the policy directly reduce, and which may remain?
micro.Choice A: It can reduce adverse selection; moral hazard must remain even with enforceable care incentives.
micro.Choice B: It can reduce hidden-action moral hazard; hidden-type adverse selection may remain.
micro.Choice C: It eliminates both problems because monitoring later care reveals inherited risk perfectly.
micro.Choice D: It eliminates neither problem because premiums cannot change behavior.
micro.Correct Answer: B — It can reduce hidden-action moral hazard; hidden-type adverse selection may remain.
micro.Feedback: A discount conditional on care changes the reward for a post-contract action. It does not, under the stated information limit, reveal the customer’s original risk type.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.3 — Moral Hazard
micro.Common Misconception: Confuses observation with enforceable incentives
micro.Question: A company can eliminate employees’ hidden shirking through monitoring. Monitoring would recover $18,000 of output but use $25,000 of real resources annually. A cheaper incentive contract recovers $12,000 at a $4,000 resource cost. Which comparison is correct?
micro.Choice A: Perfect monitoring gains $18,000 net and is preferable because its resource cost is irrelevant to incentives.
micro.Choice B: Perfect monitoring loses $7,000 net, while the incentive contract gains $8,000; eliminating all hidden action is not necessarily efficient.
micro.Choice C: The incentive contract loses $8,000 net because any remaining shirking makes a policy inefficient.
micro.Choice D: Both policies have the same net benefit because both address moral hazard.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Perfect monitoring loses $7,000 net, while the incentive contract gains $8,000; eliminating all hidden action is not necessarily efficient.
micro.Feedback: Net benefits are 18,000−25,000=−7,000 and 12,000−4,000=8,000. Better observability is useful only when its gains justify its resource cost.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.2
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
micro.Question: Between equilibrium A and equilibrium B, which curve shifts, and what quantity change reflects movement along the other curve?
micro.Choice A: Demand shifts right; quantity supplied increases by 100 thousand along S0.
micro.Choice B: Supply shifts right; quantity demanded increases by 50 thousand along D0.
micro.Choice C: Supply shifts right; quantity demanded increases by 100 thousand along D0.
micro.Choice D: Demand shifts right; quantity supplied increases by 50 thousand along S0.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Demand shifts right; quantity supplied increases by 50 thousand along S0.
micro.Feedback: Demand shifts right from D0 to D1 while S0 stays fixed. Equilibrium moves from A at 200 thousand tickets to B at 250 thousand, so quantity supplied rises by 50 thousand along S0. A higher quantity supplied does not mean supply itself shifted.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
micro.Question: Use the graph. Which explanation of the move from A to B is supported by comparing what sellers offer at the price marked at A?
micro.Choice A: Supply decreases: at that same price, sellers offer 100 thousand fewer tickets on S1 than on S0.
micro.Choice B: Supply decreases: at that same price, sellers offer 50 thousand fewer tickets on S1 than on S0.
micro.Choice C: Only quantity supplied decreases: a lower ticket price moves sellers along S0 by 100 thousand tickets.
micro.Choice D: Only quantity supplied decreases: a lower ticket price moves sellers along S0 by 50 thousand tickets.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Supply decreases: at that same price, sellers offer 100 thousand fewer tickets on S1 than on S0.
micro.Feedback: At A’s $10 price, S0 offers 200 thousand tickets and S1 offers 100 thousand. Offering 100 thousand fewer tickets at the same price is a decrease in supply. A movement along S0 would instead be a change in quantity supplied caused by a price change. In the graph, the A-to-B price actually rises.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: A market has three firms that closely track one another’s pricing. What feature matters most?
micro.Choice A: The number three by itself
micro.Choice B: Perfectly elastic firm demand
micro.Choice C: Strategic interdependence
micro.Choice D: Zero fixed cost
micro.Correct Answer: C — Strategic interdependence
micro.Feedback: Rival response is central.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Why can an industry with six firms still be oligopolistic?
micro.Choice A: Any market with more than two firms is competitive
micro.Choice B: Six firms means monopolistic competition automatically
micro.Choice C: Only product identity matters
micro.Choice D: A few firms may dominate sales and react strategically
micro.Correct Answer: D — A few firms may dominate sales and react strategically
micro.Feedback: Firm count alone is insufficient.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Which measure squares market shares?
micro.Choice A: HHI
micro.Choice B: Four-firm concentration ratio
micro.Choice C: Average market share
micro.Choice D: Total revenue
micro.Correct Answer: A — HHI
micro.Feedback: HHI sums squared percentage market shares, so larger firms receive more weight. The four-firm ratio instead adds the four largest shares without squaring.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: What does a four-firm concentration ratio do?
micro.Choice A: Squares all shares
micro.Choice B: Adds the four largest market shares
micro.Choice C: Measures marginal cost
micro.Choice D: Identifies collusion directly
micro.Correct Answer: B — Adds the four largest market shares
micro.Feedback: The ratio is a sum, not a proof of conduct.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: A student says a four-firm concentration ratio squares each firm’s market share. What is the correction?
micro.Choice A: The four-firm ratio averages all firms’ squared shares
micro.Choice B: The four-firm ratio simply adds the shares of the four largest firms
micro.Choice C: The four-firm ratio multiplies the market shares of the four largest firms and then converts the product to a percentage
micro.Choice D: The four-firm ratio subtracts fringe shares from 100
micro.Correct Answer: B — The four-firm ratio simply adds the shares of the four largest firms
micro.Feedback: Squaring shares is part of HHI, not the four-firm concentration ratio.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: A student describes oligopoly as “a market where each firm can safely ignore rivals.” What is the key error?
micro.Choice A: Oligopoly decisions are strategically interdependent because major rivals can respond
micro.Choice B: Oligopoly always has exactly two firms, so any market with three or more important firms belongs to another structure
micro.Choice C: Oligopoly requires identical products
micro.Choice D: Oligopoly firms are all price takers
micro.Correct Answer: A — Oligopoly decisions are strategically interdependent because major rivals can respond
micro.Feedback: The defining strategic feature is that a few important firms must account for likely rival reactions.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: An airline’s fare cut is profitable if its rival keeps fares fixed but unprofitable if the rival matches it. What must the airline consider when deciding?
micro.Choice A: Only the airline’s fixed cost
micro.Choice B: Only whether the firms sell identical products
micro.Choice C: The rival’s likely response
micro.Choice D: The fare cut’s effect assuming the rival cannot react
micro.Correct Answer: C — The rival’s likely response
micro.Feedback: The payoff depends on the other firm’s action, which is the strategic interdependence central to oligopoly.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Which behavior belongs to oligopoly rather than the basic monopolistic-competition model?
micro.Choice A: Choosing an action after anticipating a specific rival’s response
micro.Choice B: Product differentiation
micro.Choice C: Short-run economic profit
micro.Choice D: Entry after profit
micro.Correct Answer: A — Choosing an action after anticipating a specific rival’s response
micro.Feedback: The basic monopolistic-competition model abstracts from strategic interdependence.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Compared with perfect competition, oligopolistic firms are more likely to:
micro.Choice A: Take price as given
micro.Choice B: Recognize that their own actions affect rivals and market outcomes
micro.Choice C: Face horizontal demand individually
micro.Choice D: Have free entry eliminate market power
micro.Correct Answer: B — Recognize that their own actions affect rivals and market outcomes
micro.Feedback: Oligopolists possess market power and strategic influence.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: How do network effects affect oligopoly?
micro.Choice A: They guarantee perfect competition
micro.Choice B: They eliminate switching costs
micro.Choice C: They can strengthen incumbent advantages and concentration
micro.Choice D: They make HHI irrelevant
micro.Correct Answer: C — They can strengthen incumbent advantages and concentration
micro.Feedback: Network effects can reinforce entry barriers.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: A market has four dominant firms. Which feature would most strongly distinguish oligopoly from monopoly or perfect competition?
micro.Choice A: Assume four dominant firms automatically mean monopolistic competition because any market with multiple sellers and differentiated products fits that model
micro.Choice B: Classify the market only by whether products are identical
micro.Choice C: Treat every concentrated market as a legal monopoly
micro.Choice D: Focus on few-firm strategic interdependence rather than requiring one firm or many tiny price takers
micro.Correct Answer: D — Focus on few-firm strategic interdependence rather than requiring one firm or many tiny price takers
micro.Feedback: Oligopoly sits between monopoly and atomistic competition because a few large firms interact strategically.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: A market has three firms with percentage shares 50, 30 and 20. What is the HHI?

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Which characteristic most clearly distinguishes oligopoly from monopolistic competition?
micro.Choice A: Firms must account for likely rival responses
micro.Choice B: Products are always identical
micro.Choice C: Firms can enter and exit the market freely.
micro.Choice D: Each firm is a price taker
micro.Correct Answer: A — Firms must account for likely rival responses
micro.Feedback: Strategic interdependence is the defining behavioral feature of oligopoly.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: A duopoly is:
micro.Choice A: A monopoly with two products
micro.Choice B: An oligopoly with two firms
micro.Choice C: A market with two buyers
micro.Choice D: A perfectly competitive market
micro.Correct Answer: B — An oligopoly with two firms
micro.Feedback: Duopoly is the two-firm special case of oligopoly.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Products in an oligopoly may be:
micro.Choice A: Only standardized
micro.Choice B: Only differentiated products.
micro.Choice C: Standardized or differentiated
micro.Choice D: Always public goods
micro.Correct Answer: C — Standardized or differentiated
micro.Feedback: Oligopoly describes market structure, not a single product type.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Why do barriers to entry matter in oligopoly?
micro.Choice A: They make incumbent firms price takers.
micro.Choice B: They eliminate strategic behavior
micro.Choice C: They guarantee identical costs
micro.Choice D: They help a few incumbent firms retain large market shares
micro.Correct Answer: D — They help a few incumbent firms retain large market shares
micro.Feedback: Entry barriers help sustain concentration.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: A four-firm concentration ratio is calculated by:
micro.Choice A: Adding the market shares of the four largest firms
micro.Choice B: Squaring every firm’s market share
micro.Choice C: Averaging the four smallest firms
micro.Choice D: The sum of squared shares for every firm and competitive fringe participant
micro.Correct Answer: A — Adding the market shares of the four largest firms
micro.Feedback: A concentration ratio sums selected leading shares.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: The HHI is calculated by:
micro.Choice A: Adding the four largest shares only
micro.Choice B: Summing squared market shares
micro.Choice C: Dividing market demand by firm count
micro.Choice D: Squaring the concentration ratio
micro.Correct Answer: B — Summing squared market shares
micro.Feedback: HHI weights larger firms more heavily through squaring.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Why does market definition matter when measuring concentration?
micro.Choice A: It fixes the number of firms that must be included at four.
micro.Choice B: It determines the legal price ceiling
micro.Choice C: Changing product or geographic boundaries changes which firms and sales are included
micro.Choice D: It makes strategic behavior disappear
micro.Correct Answer: C — Changing product or geographic boundaries changes which firms and sales are included
micro.Feedback: Concentration depends on the boundaries of the relevant market.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Why does an oligopoly firm pay unusually close attention to a rival’s likely response before changing price?
micro.Choice A: Because a few large rivals can materially change the payoff from the firm’s decision
micro.Choice B: Because oligopoly firms are required to match every rival price change in order to remain in the market
micro.Choice C: Because oligopoly firms sell only identical products
micro.Choice D: Because market demand is perfectly elastic for each firm
micro.Correct Answer: A — Because a few large rivals can materially change the payoff from the firm’s decision
micro.Feedback: With only a few important firms, one firm’s action can provoke responses that change its own payoff.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Which condition most helps a few established firms remain dominant in an oligopoly?
micro.Choice A: Perfectly free entry by many small firms
micro.Choice B: A requirement that every product be identical
micro.Choice C: A horizontal demand curve for each individual firm
micro.Choice D: Significant barriers that make entry difficult
micro.Correct Answer: D — Significant barriers that make entry difficult
micro.Feedback: Entry barriers help preserve a market in which a small number of firms account for much of total sales.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: A four-firm concentration ratio of 82% means that:
micro.Choice A: The HHI must equal 8200
micro.Choice B: Eighty-two firms control the market
micro.Choice C: The four largest firms together account for 82% of market sales
micro.Choice D: Each of the four largest firms individually controls 82% of total market sales
micro.Correct Answer: C — The four largest firms together account for 82% of market sales
micro.Feedback: A concentration ratio adds the market shares of the specified number of largest firms.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: The firms’ market shares are 36%, 25%, 17%, 12%, 10%. What is the HHI?
micro.Feedback: HHI squares and sums all percentage shares: 36² + 25² + 17² + 12² + 10² = 2454. Adding unsquared shares would not measure HHI.

micro.Question: The firms’ market shares are 42%, 22%, 16%, 11%, 9%. What is the four-firm concentration ratio?
micro.Feedback: Rank the shares and add the four largest: 42 + 22 + 16 + 11 = 91%. The fifth firm is excluded; shares are not squared.

micro.Feedback: HHI squares and sums all percentage shares: 41² + 22² + 16² + 11² + 10² = 2642. Adding unsquared shares would not measure HHI.

micro.Feedback: Rank the shares and add the four largest: 29 + 27 + 18 + 15 = 89%. The fifth firm is excluded; shares are not squared.

micro.Feedback: HHI squares and sums all percentage shares: 34² + 25² + 17² + 12² + 12² = 2358. Adding unsquared shares would not measure HHI.

micro.Feedback: Rank the shares and add the four largest: 40 + 22 + 16 + 11 = 89%. The fifth firm is excluded; shares are not squared.

micro.Feedback: HHI squares and sums all percentage shares: 28² + 27² + 18² + 15² + 12² = 2206. Adding unsquared shares would not measure HHI.

micro.Question: The firms’ market shares are 33%, 25%, 17%, 12%, 13%. What is the four-firm concentration ratio?
micro.Feedback: Rank the shares and add the four largest: 33 + 25 + 17 + 13 = 88%. The fifth firm is excluded; shares are not squared.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: The firms’ market shares are 39%, 22%, 16%, 11%, 12%. What is the HHI?
micro.Feedback: HHI squares and sums all percentage shares: 39² + 22² + 16² + 11² + 12² = 2526. Adding unsquared shares would not measure HHI.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: The firms’ market shares are 27%, 27%, 18%, 15%, 13%. What is the four-firm concentration ratio?
micro.Feedback: Rank the shares and add the four largest: 27 + 27 + 18 + 15 = 87%. The fifth firm is excluded; shares are not squared.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Four firms have market shares of 35%, 25%, 20%, and 10%, with the remaining firms holding 10%. What is the four-firm concentration ratio?
micro.Feedback: Add the shares of the four largest firms.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: A market has shares of 50%, 25%, 15%, and 10%. Which measure gives especially heavy weight to the 50% firm?
micro.Choice A: Four-firm concentration ratio
micro.Choice B: Average market share
micro.Choice C: Total revenue
micro.Choice D: HHI
micro.Correct Answer: D — HHI
micro.Feedback: Squaring shares makes a very large firm count disproportionately.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: A merger combines firms with 20% and 15% market shares. By how much does the HHI rise if all other shares stay unchanged?
micro.Choice A: 600 points
micro.Choice B: 35 points
micro.Choice C: 225 points
micro.Choice D: 1,225 points
micro.Correct Answer: A — 600 points
micro.Feedback: The change is 2ab = 2(20)(15) = 600.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: A national market appears unconcentrated, but each rural town has only two local suppliers. What is the main lesson?
micro.Choice A: HHI is always invalid
micro.Choice B: Geographic market definition can conceal local concentration
micro.Choice C: National concentration always measures local competition accurately.
micro.Choice D: Imports must equal zero
micro.Correct Answer: B — Geographic market definition can conceal local concentration
micro.Feedback: The relevant geographic market can be narrower than the national market.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: A firm observes that its rival will respond aggressively to any price cut. This expectation most directly illustrates:
micro.Choice A: A dominant strategy that is best regardless of the rival’s action.
micro.Choice B: Free entry
micro.Choice C: Strategic interdependence
micro.Choice D: Accounting profit
micro.Correct Answer: C — Strategic interdependence
micro.Feedback: The firm’s best action depends on the expected response.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: A market has six firms, but two control 78% of sales and rivals closely watch one another. Which structure is most plausible?
micro.Choice A: Perfect competition
micro.Choice B: Pure monopoly
micro.Choice C: Oligopoly
micro.Choice D: A nonmarket allocation
micro.Correct Answer: C — Oligopoly
micro.Feedback: Dominant shares and strategic interdependence point to oligopoly.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: A grocery chain has only 8% of national grocery sales but 55% of sales in one isolated county. What does this example show about concentration measures?
micro.Choice A: They measure profit rather than market share
micro.Choice B: They depend on how the relevant market is defined
micro.Choice C: They are valid only for national markets
micro.Choice D: They ignore geographic differences and therefore always produce the same concentration result nationwide
micro.Correct Answer: B — They depend on how the relevant market is defined
micro.Feedback: The same firm can appear small or dominant depending on the economically relevant geographic and product market.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Two markets each have a four-firm concentration ratio of 80%. In Market A the four firms have nearly equal shares; in Market B one firm is much larger than the other three. Which statement is most accurate?
micro.Choice A: Market B can have a higher HHI because HHI gives more weight to large shares
micro.Choice B: Both markets must have the same HHI because an equal CR4 guarantees identical concentration among the leading firms
micro.Choice C: Market A must have the higher HHI because equal shares are squared
micro.Choice D: HHI cannot distinguish markets with the same CR4
micro.Correct Answer: A — Market B can have a higher HHI because HHI gives more weight to large shares
micro.Feedback: Squaring market shares makes HHI more sensitive to a very large firm even when CR4 is unchanged.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Three national wireless carriers dominate a market. Before one carrier cuts price, its managers estimate how the other two are likely to respond. Which feature of oligopoly is being illustrated?
micro.Choice A: Perfect information with no rivalry
micro.Choice B: Automatic collusion
micro.Choice C: Zero barriers to entry
micro.Choice D: Strategic interdependence
micro.Correct Answer: D — Strategic interdependence
micro.Feedback: The payoff from one firm’s choice depends partly on how a small number of major rivals react.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: An industry’s HHI rises after two sizable firms merge. What can the HHI increase tell an analyst directly?
micro.Choice A: The merger is automatically unlawful
micro.Choice B: The merged firm must now be a monopolist because any increase in HHI implies complete control of the market
micro.Choice C: Market concentration increased under the chosen market definition
micro.Choice D: Consumer welfare necessarily fell
micro.Correct Answer: C — Market concentration increased under the chosen market definition
micro.Feedback: HHI measures concentration; welfare and policy conclusions require additional evidence about competition and efficiencies.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Refer to the market-share chart. What is the four-firm concentration ratio?
micro.Feedback: Sum the four largest market shares.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Refer to the market-share chart. What is the four-firm concentration ratio?
micro.Feedback: Sum the four largest market shares.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Refer to market-share chart 3. Other combines smaller firms, each with a share below firm D. What is the four-firm concentration ratio?
micro.Feedback: The four largest individual firms are A, B, C and D under the stated fringe assumption. Add their shares; do not count an aggregate of smaller firms as one large firm. Here CR4 = 28 + 22 + 18 + 14 = 82%.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Refer to market-share chart 4. Other combines smaller firms, each with a share below firm D. What is the four-firm concentration ratio?
micro.Feedback: The four largest individual firms are A, B, C and D under the stated fringe assumption. Add their shares; do not count an aggregate of smaller firms as one large firm. Here CR4 = 50 + 20 + 12 + 8 = 90%.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Refer to the market-share chart for market 5. For this calculation, assume the bar labeled Other represents one additional firm, not several small firms. What is the HHI?
micro.Feedback: With Other specified as one firm, HHI = 26² + 24² + 20² + 15² + 15² = 2,102. Square individual firm shares, not an unspecified fringe total. If Other contained several firms, their separate shares would be needed for an exact HHI.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Refer to the market-share chart for market 6. For this calculation, assume the bar labeled Other represents one additional firm, not several small firms. What is the HHI?
micro.Feedback: With Other specified as one firm, HHI = 38² + 32² + 12² + 9² + 9² = 2,774. Square individual firm shares, not an unspecified fringe total. If Other contained several firms, their separate shares would be needed for an exact HHI.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Refer to the market-share chart for market 7. For this calculation, assume the bar labeled Other represents one additional firm, not several small firms. What is the HHI?
micro.Feedback: With Other specified as one firm, HHI = 31² + 29² + 17² + 13² + 10² = 2,360. Square individual firm shares, not an unspecified fringe total. If Other contained several firms, their separate shares would be needed for an exact HHI.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Refer to the market-share chart for market 8. For this calculation, assume the bar labeled Other represents one additional firm, not several small firms. What is the HHI?
micro.Feedback: With Other specified as one firm, HHI = 45² + 18² + 14² + 12² + 11² = 2,810. Square individual firm shares, not an unspecified fringe total. If Other contained several firms, their separate shares would be needed for an exact HHI.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Market shares are 46%, 22%, 14%, 10% and 8%. The two smallest firms merge, with no other share changes. Which calculation and interpretation is correct?
micro.Choice A: CR4 stays 92% and HHI rises to 3120 because combining two small firms cannot change the top four.
micro.Choice B: CR4 rises to 100% and HHI stays 2960 because the combined market share is unchanged.
micro.Choice C: CR4 rises by 18 percentage points and HHI rises by 18 because the merging shares should be added to both indexes.
micro.Choice D: CR4 rises from 92% to 100% and HHI rises from 2960 to 3120; the measures describe concentration, not a complete prediction of conduct.
micro.Correct Answer: D — CR4 rises from 92% to 100% and HHI rises from 2960 to 3120; the measures describe concentration, not a complete prediction of conduct.
micro.Feedback: After merger the four shares are 46,22,18,14, so CR4=100%. The HHI increment is 2×10×8=160, making 3120. Conduct also depends on entry, substitution and behavior.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Market shares are 33%, 29%, 17%, 12% and 9%. Compare merger A (33% with 9%) with merger B (17% with 12%), holding other shares fixed. Which comparison is correct?
micro.Choice A: Both give CR4=100%, but A raises HHI by 594 and B by 408; equal CR4 does not imply the same HHI change.
micro.Choice B: Both give CR4=100% and the same HHI increase because each merger removes one firm.
micro.Choice C: A raises HHI less than B because one of its partners is the smallest firm.
micro.Choice D: CR4 stays 91% under both mergers because the original four largest shares are unchanged.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Both give CR4=100%, but A raises HHI by 594 and B by 408; equal CR4 does not imply the same HHI change.
micro.Feedback: Each leaves four firms, so CR4 becomes 100%. HHI increments are 2×33×9=594 and 2×17×12=408. The product of the merging shares matters, not merely the smaller partner’s rank.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Market shares are 40%, 26%, 15%, 11% and 8%. The 40% firm is split into two independent competitors, each with 20%, and all other shares stay fixed. Which comparison with the original concentration measures is correct?
micro.Choice A: CR4 remains 92% and HHI remains 2686 because the two new firms have the same combined share.
micro.Choice B: CR4 falls from 92% to 81%, and HHI falls from 2686 to 1886; the new shares must be reranked.
micro.Choice C: CR4 falls to 72% and HHI falls by only 20 because one new share should be omitted.
micro.Choice D: CR4 rises to 100% and HHI rises to 3486 because there are more competitors.
micro.Correct Answer: B — CR4 falls from 92% to 81%, and HHI falls from 2686 to 1886; the new shares must be reranked.
micro.Feedback: The new top four shares are 26,20,20,15, totaling 81. Replace 40² by 20²+20², reducing HHI by 800 to 1886. Independence, not merely a new label, is required for this calculation.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Market shares are 28%, 25%, 20%, 17% and 10%. Five percentage points move from the largest firm to the smallest, with all other shares fixed. Which updated concentration measures follow?
micro.Choice A: CR4=90% and HHI=2198 because the total share remains 100%.
micro.Choice B: CR4=95% and HHI=2328 because a growing small firm raises concentration.
micro.Choice C: CR4=85% and HHI=2068; rerank the new shares 25,23,20,17,15.
micro.Choice D: CR4=85% and HHI=2193 because HHI falls by exactly five points.
micro.Correct Answer: C — CR4=85% and HHI=2068; rerank the new shares 25,23,20,17,15.
micro.Feedback: After the transfer shares are 23,25,20,17,15. The top four sum to 85. Squared shares sum to 529+625+400+289+225=2068.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Market shares are 52%, 18%, 12%, 10% and 8%. The 18% and 12% firms propose merging. A report says the resulting HHI alone proves a precise price increase. Which response combines the calculation with its limitation?
micro.Choice A: HHI rises from 3336 to 3366, and the 30-point change is exactly the percentage price increase.
micro.Choice B: HHI stays 3336 because the merged firm’s combined share is unchanged, so no price effect is possible.
micro.Choice C: HHI rises to 3768, which by itself proves prices rise exactly 432%.
micro.Choice D: HHI rises from 3336 to 3768, but the price effect still requires evidence about substitution, entry, conduct and efficiencies.
micro.Correct Answer: D — HHI rises from 3336 to 3768, but the price effect still requires evidence about substitution, entry, conduct and efficiencies.
micro.Feedback: The increment is 2×18×12=432, yielding 3768. HHI measures the distribution of market shares; it is not a formula converting concentration changes directly into price changes.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Calculate the four-firm concentration ratio for shares [36, 24, 18, 12, 10].
micro.Feedback: Add the four largest shares.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Calculate the four-firm concentration ratio for shares [31, 23, 19, 15, 12].
micro.Feedback: Add the four largest shares.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Calculate the four-firm concentration ratio for shares [44, 21, 14, 11, 10].
micro.Feedback: Add the four largest shares.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Calculate the four-firm concentration ratio for shares [29, 25, 20, 16, 10].
micro.Feedback: Add the four largest shares.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Calculate the HHI for market C1 with percentage shares [40, 25, 15, 10, 10].
micro.Feedback: Square each percentage share and sum the squares.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Calculate the HHI for market C2 with percentage shares [32, 28, 18, 12, 10].
micro.Feedback: Square each percentage share and sum the squares.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Calculate the HHI for market C3 with percentage shares [50, 20, 12, 10, 8].
micro.Feedback: Square each percentage share and sum the squares.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Calculate the HHI for market C4 with percentage shares [27, 24, 21, 16, 12].
micro.Feedback: Square each percentage share and sum the squares.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Calculate the HHI for market C5 with percentage shares [35, 30, 15, 10, 10].
micro.Feedback: Square each percentage share and sum the squares.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Which feature makes oligopoly strategy different from ordinary independent firm choice?
micro.Choice A: Products must be identical
micro.Choice B: Entry must be impossible
micro.Choice C: Each firm anticipates rival responses
micro.Choice D: Every firm takes price as given
micro.Correct Answer: C — Each firm anticipates rival responses
micro.Feedback: Strategic interdependence is central.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: What does the HHI do that a four-firm ratio does not?
micro.Choice A: It ignores all small firms
micro.Choice B: It proves collusion
micro.Choice C: It uses revenue instead of shares
micro.Choice D: It squares shares and therefore weights large firms more heavily
micro.Correct Answer: D — It squares shares and therefore weights large firms more heavily
micro.Feedback: HHI incorporates the full share distribution and squares shares.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.1 — Explain oligopoly, strategic interdependence, entry barriers, and market concentration.
micro.Question: Why can the same industry have different concentration measures under different definitions?
micro.Choice A: The included products, locations, and firms change
micro.Choice B: Costs become fixed
micro.Choice C: Payoffs reverse order
micro.Choice D: Marginal revenue changes slope automatically
micro.Correct Answer: A — The included products, locations, and firms change
micro.Feedback: Market boundaries determine the denominator and participants.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.2 — Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.
micro.Question: In payoff order (Row, Column), whose payoff is second?
micro.Choice A: The row player’s
micro.Choice B: The government’s
micro.Choice C: The column player’s
micro.Choice D: The combined payoff
micro.Correct Answer: C — The column player’s
micro.Feedback: Payoff order must be read consistently.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.2 — Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.
micro.Question: Why must payoff order be stated?
micro.Choice A: It changes market shares
micro.Choice B: It changes the number of strategies
micro.Choice C: It guarantees equilibrium
micro.Choice D: Reversing the order changes each firm’s incentives
micro.Correct Answer: D — Reversing the order changes each firm’s incentives
micro.Feedback: Each number belongs to a different player.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.2 — Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.
micro.Question: What is a best response?
micro.Choice A: The highest-payoff action given the rival’s action
micro.Choice B: The joint-payoff maximum
micro.Choice C: The action with the highest single payoff anywhere
micro.Choice D: Any announced strategy
micro.Correct Answer: A — The highest-payoff action given the rival’s action
micro.Feedback: Best responses are conditional.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.2 — Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.
micro.Question: What makes a strategy dominant?
micro.Choice A: It maximizes joint payoff once
micro.Choice B: It beats the player’s alternative under every rival action
micro.Choice C: It gives equal payoffs
micro.Choice D: It is selected first
micro.Correct Answer: B — It beats the player’s alternative under every rival action
micro.Feedback: Dominance requires comparison across rival actions.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.2 — Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.
micro.Question: What defines Nash equilibrium?
micro.Choice A: Maximum combined payoff
micro.Choice B: Equal payoffs
micro.Choice C: Mutual best responses
micro.Choice D: A written agreement
micro.Correct Answer: C — Mutual best responses
micro.Feedback: Nash is stability against unilateral deviation.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.2 — Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.
micro.Question: Can a Nash equilibrium be jointly inferior?
micro.Choice A: No, Nash always maximizes total payoff
micro.Choice B: Only if firms are price takers
micro.Choice C: Only if HHI is zero
micro.Choice D: Yes, individual incentives can lead to a lower combined payoff
micro.Correct Answer: D — Yes, individual incentives can lead to a lower combined payoff
micro.Feedback: Equilibrium and efficiency are distinct.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.2 — Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.
micro.Question: A payoff cell at row A and column Y is (7,3), with the row player listed first. What does it report?
micro.Choice A: Row chooses Y and earns 3; column chooses A and earns 7.
micro.Choice B: Both players earn the joint payoff 10.
micro.Choice C: Row chooses A and earns 7; column chooses Y and earns 3.
micro.Choice D: Row earns 3 and column earns 7.
micro.Correct Answer: C — Row chooses A and earns 7; column chooses Y and earns 3.
micro.Feedback: The row/column positions identify actions, and the stated payoff order assigns 7 to the row player and 3 to the column player.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.2 — Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.
micro.Question: A student keeps searching for one action that is always best, but the player’s preferred action changes with the rival’s move. What concept should the student use?
micro.Choice A: A guaranteed dominant strategy
micro.Choice B: Conditional best responses
micro.Choice C: Market concentration
micro.Choice D: Joint-profit maximization only
micro.Correct Answer: B — Conditional best responses
micro.Feedback: Best responses can vary with the rival’s action even when no dominant strategy exists.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.2 — Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.
micro.Question: A row player’s payoffs are: A against X=6, A against Y=4; B against X=3, B against Y=5. Does it have a strictly dominant action?
micro.Choice A: No; A is better against X but B is better against Y.
micro.Choice B: Yes; A because its highest payoff is 6.
micro.Choice C: Yes; B because it earns 5 against Y.
micro.Choice D: Yes; both A and B are strictly dominant.
micro.Correct Answer: A — No; A is better against X but B is better against Y.
micro.Feedback: Compare within each rival action: 6>3 favors A against X, but 5>4 favors B against Y. No one action wins both comparisons.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.2 — Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.
micro.Question: Payoffs (row, column) are A/X=(4,3), A/Y=(1,1), B/X=(2,0), B/Y=(3,2). Which outcomes are pure-strategy Nash equilibria?
micro.Choice A: A/Y and B/X
micro.Choice B: A/X only
micro.Choice C: B/Y only
micro.Choice D: A/X and B/Y
micro.Correct Answer: D — A/X and B/Y
micro.Feedback: Against X, row prefers A (4>2); against Y, row prefers B (3>1). Against A, column prefers X (3>1); against B, column prefers Y (2>0). The mutual best responses are A/X and B/Y.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.2 — Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.
micro.Question: A student found the cell with the largest combined payoff and calls it the Nash equilibrium. What must still be checked?
micro.Choice A: Whether the firms have equal market shares
micro.Choice B: Whether the cell lies on the main diagonal
micro.Choice C: Whether each player would choose to stay there given the other player’s action
micro.Choice D: Whether the two payoffs are both positive and add to more than the payoffs in every neighboring cell
micro.Correct Answer: C — Whether each player would choose to stay there given the other player’s action
micro.Feedback: Joint-payoff maximization and Nash stability are separate questions.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.2 — Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.
micro.Question: How does a noncooperative game differ from an assumed cartel solution?
micro.Choice A: The government chooses each firm’s strategy
micro.Choice B: Each firm follows its own incentives rather than committing to maximize joint profit
micro.Choice C: The firms necessarily choose identical actions because noncooperative behavior rules out different strategies
micro.Choice D: The firms ignore rivals completely
micro.Correct Answer: B — Each firm follows its own incentives rather than committing to maximize joint profit
micro.Feedback: Noncooperative analysis asks what individually rational strategies imply without assuming binding joint-profit coordination.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.2 — Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.
micro.Question: In game theory, a strategy is:
micro.Choice A: The payoff received by every player
micro.Choice B: The payoff a player receives after all firms choose.
micro.Choice C: The market concentration ratio
micro.Choice D: A possible action or plan available to a player
micro.Correct Answer: D — A possible action or plan available to a player
micro.Feedback: Strategies are the choices available to players.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.2 — Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.
micro.Question: In a payoff pair written (8, 5), the first number usually belongs to:
micro.Choice A: The row player
micro.Choice B: The column player
micro.Choice C: Both players combined
micro.Choice D: The government
micro.Correct Answer: A — The row player
micro.Feedback: The standard stated order is row player first, column player second.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.2 — Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.
micro.Question: A best response is:
micro.Choice A: The strategy that maximizes the firms’ combined payoff.
micro.Choice B: The strategy producing the highest payoff given the rival’s action
micro.Choice C: Any strategy chosen first
micro.Choice D: The strategy with the lowest fixed cost
micro.Correct Answer: B — The strategy producing the highest payoff given the rival’s action
micro.Feedback: A best response is conditional on what the other player does.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.2 — Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.
micro.Question: A dominant strategy is one that:
micro.Choice A: The action associated with the highest payoff in one isolated cell only
micro.Choice B: Always gives both firms equal payoffs
micro.Choice C: Produces a higher payoff than the player’s alternatives for every rival action
micro.Choice D: Requires a written agreement
micro.Correct Answer: C — Produces a higher payoff than the player’s alternatives for every rival action
micro.Feedback: Dominance is a comparison across every possible rival action.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.2 — Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.
micro.Question: A Nash equilibrium occurs when:
micro.Choice A: The firms maximize joint profit
micro.Choice B: Both players receive equal payoffs
micro.Choice C: The cell with the largest total payoff even though one player would deviate alone
micro.Choice D: Each player is choosing a best response to the other
micro.Correct Answer: D — Each player is choosing a best response to the other
micro.Feedback: No player can improve by changing alone.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.2 — Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.
micro.Question: Why can a Nash equilibrium be inefficient?
micro.Choice A: Mutual best responses need not maximize joint payoff
micro.Choice B: Equilibrium requires zero profit
micro.Choice C: The government sets every payoff
micro.Choice D: The cell with the largest total payoff even though one player would deviate alone
micro.Correct Answer: A — Mutual best responses need not maximize joint payoff
micro.Feedback: Individual incentives can lead to a jointly inferior outcome.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.2 — Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.
micro.Question: In a two-firm game, what does a payoff represent?
micro.Choice A: The slope of the industry demand curve
micro.Choice B: The outcome value a player receives from a particular combination of strategies
micro.Choice C: The maximum number of firms that regulators permit to enter the market under the industry’s legal rules
micro.Choice D: The market concentration ratio
micro.Correct Answer: B — The outcome value a player receives from a particular combination of strategies
micro.Feedback: A payoff records how well a player does under a particular combination of actions.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.2 — Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.
micro.Question: A payoff cell is written (14, 9), with Row’s payoff listed first. What is Column’s payoff?
micro.Feedback: With payoff order (Row, Column), the second number belongs to Column.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.2 — Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibria.
micro.Question: A best response is the action that:
micro.Choice A: Maximizes the two firms’ combined payoff regardless of incentives
micro.Choice B: Is chosen by every rival in the market
micro.Choice C: Always remains best no matter what the rival does
micro.Choice D: Gives a player the highest payoff given the rival’s chosen action

micro.Choice A: A/Y and B/X are equilibria; A/Y has joint profit 23 versus 21 at B/X, but the larger total does not eliminate B/X as an equilibrium.
micro.Choice B: A/X alone is an equilibrium; its joint profit 23 versus 21 at B/Y makes B/Y fail the Nash condition even without a profitable unilateral deviation.
micro.Choice C: A/Y alone is an equilibrium; its joint profit 23 versus 21 at B/X makes B/X fail the Nash condition even without a profitable unilateral deviation.
micro.Choice D: A/X and B/Y are equilibria; A/X has joint profit 23 versus 21 at B/Y, but the larger total does not eliminate B/Y as an equilibrium.
micro.Correct Answer: D — A/X and B/Y are equilibria; A/X has joint profit 23 versus 21 at B/Y, but the larger total does not eliminate B/Y as an equilibrium.
micro.Feedback: At A/X, neither Row (14 versus 1) nor Column (9 versus 2) wants to deviate. At B/Y, neither Row (8 versus 2) nor Column (13 versus 1) wants to deviate. The totals are 23 and 21. Nash equilibrium concerns unilateral incentives, not whether another cell has a larger sum.

micro.Question: Use the displayed payoff matrix as the baseline. An enforceable agreement deducts 3 from the row firm’s payoff whenever it chooses B and 3 from the column firm’s payoff whenever it chooses Y, in every cell. Which comparison with the original game is correct?
micro.Choice A: The unique Nash outcome remains (B,Y) because an output-independent agreement cannot change any payoff.
micro.Choice B: Both (A,X) and (B,Y) are Nash outcomes after the deductions because the penalty leaves best responses unchanged.
micro.Choice C: The unique Nash outcome changes from (B,Y) to (A,X); (A,X) also remains the joint-payoff maximum.
micro.Choice D: The unique Nash outcome becomes (A,Y), because only the row firm changes its response.
micro.Correct Answer: C — The unique Nash outcome changes from (B,Y) to (A,X); (A,X) also remains the joint-payoff maximum.
micro.Feedback: Originally each firm prefers its noncooperative action. After deductions, row payoffs are A/X=10, A/Y=6, B/X=9, B/Y=5, so A is best against either column. Column payoffs analogously make X best against either row. Thus (A,X) is the unique equilibrium and gives the highest combined payoff, 20.

micro.Question: Starting from the displayed matrix, a program adds 6 to each firm’s payoff only at A/X. All other payoffs stay fixed. Which pure equilibria and joint-payoff conclusion follow?

micro.Choice B: A/X and B/Y are both equilibria; A/X has the highest joint payoff, 36.
micro.Choice C: Only A/X is an equilibrium; its highest joint payoff of 32 automatically eliminates the unchanged B/Y equilibrium.
micro.Choice D: Only A/X is an equilibrium; its highest joint payoff of 36 automatically eliminates the unchanged B/Y equilibrium.

micro.Question: Refer to the payoff matrix. An analyst says that the joint-profit maximum must differ from every Nash equilibrium. Which assessment of this particular game is correct? Payoffs are ordered (Row, Column).
micro.Choice A: B/Y is the only pure equilibrium; A/X maximizes joint profit at 18, so the analyst’s claim holds
micro.Choice B: A/X is the only pure equilibrium because its joint profit of 18 exceeds 14 at B/Y
micro.Choice C: A/X and B/Y are both pure equilibria; A/X also maximizes joint profit at 18, so the analyst’s claim fails
micro.Choice D: Neither diagonal cell is an equilibrium because a joint-profit maximum cannot be individually stable
micro.Correct Answer: C — A/X and B/Y are both pure equilibria; A/X also maximizes joint profit at 18, so the analyst’s claim fails
micro.Feedback: Row prefers A against X and B against Y; Column prefers X against A and Y against B. Both A/X and B/Y are mutual best responses. Firm profits alone do not determine social welfare.

micro.Choice D: Cooperation requires the firms to have identical costs

micro.Feedback: A prisoner’s dilemma exists precisely because individual incentives can undermine a jointly better outcome.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.3 — Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.
micro.Question: A student calls any concentrated industry a cartel. What is the correction?
micro.Choice A: A cartel requires coordination among firms to restrict competition; concentration alone does not establish that
micro.Choice B: A cartel is simply any market with fewer than ten firms
micro.Choice C: A cartel exists whenever HHI is high
micro.Choice D: A cartel means one firm owns the entire market
micro.Correct Answer: A — A cartel requires coordination among firms to restrict competition; concentration alone does not establish that
micro.Feedback: Market structure and collusive conduct are different concepts; a concentrated market need not be a cartel.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.3 — Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.
micro.Question: Two firms form an effective cartel. Industry MR equals industry MC at a combined output of 40 units. If they divide output equally, how much does each produce?
micro.Choice A: 40 units
micro.Choice B: 80 units
micro.Choice C: 20 units
micro.Choice D: 10 units
micro.Correct Answer: C — 20 units
micro.Feedback: The cartel chooses joint monopoly output first, then divides 40 equally: 20 each.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.3 — Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.
micro.Question: A cartel faces industry MR=60−2Q and constant industry MC=20. What joint output maximizes profit?
micro.Feedback: Set industry MR=MC: 60−2Q=20, giving Q=20.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.3 — Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.
micro.Question: What prevents an oligopoly from automatically behaving like one monopolist?
micro.Choice A: Downward-sloping demand
micro.Choice B: Member incentives and rival strategic responses
micro.Choice C: Fixed cost
micro.Choice D: Consumer surplus
micro.Correct Answer: B — Member incentives and rival strategic responses
micro.Feedback: Independent firms may not sustain the joint outcome.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.3 — Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.
micro.Question: Why might a lower-cost cartel member receive more output?
micro.Choice A: It has the highest fixed cost
micro.Choice B: It faces the least elastic demand
micro.Choice C: It is always the largest firm
micro.Choice D: Allocating production toward lower MC reduces joint cost
micro.Correct Answer: D — Allocating production toward lower MC reduces joint cost
micro.Feedback: Joint cost minimization matters for cartel allocation.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.3 — Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.
micro.Question: Why might a cartel be harder to sustain when close substitutes exist outside it?
micro.Choice A: HHI must rise
micro.Choice B: Member MC becomes zero
micro.Choice C: Consumers can switch away from the cartel after price increases
micro.Choice D: Punishment becomes costless
micro.Correct Answer: C — Consumers can switch away from the cartel after price increases
micro.Feedback: Outside substitutes constrain cartel pricing.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.3 — Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.
micro.Question: Which basic incentive concept explains cartel cheating?
micro.Choice A: Scarcity disappears
micro.Choice B: A member compares its private marginal gain with expected punishment
micro.Choice C: All firms maximize social surplus
micro.Choice D: Fixed cost becomes variable
micro.Correct Answer: B — A member compares its private marginal gain with expected punishment
micro.Feedback: Private incentives can undermine collective agreements.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.3 — Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.
micro.Question: How can foreign suppliers weaken a domestic cartel?
micro.Choice A: Tariffs always lower cartel price
micro.Choice B: Imports provide alternative sources and can expand outside supply
micro.Choice C: World price eliminates strategic behavior
micro.Choice D: Foreign firms cannot enter
micro.Correct Answer: B — Imports provide alternative sources and can expand outside supply
micro.Feedback: Outside supply can destabilize domestic coordination.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.3 — Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.
micro.Question: A prisoner’s dilemma describes a situation in which:
micro.Choice A: Cooperation is always stable
micro.Choice B: Individually attractive choices can make all players worse off
micro.Choice C: There is only one player
micro.Choice D: The jointly best outcome is always a Nash equilibrium.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Individually attractive choices can make all players worse off
micro.Feedback: The conflict is between individual and collective incentives.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.3 — Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.
micro.Question: Collusion occurs when firms:
micro.Choice A: Independently choose the same price after a common cost shock.
micro.Choice B: Take price as given
micro.Choice C: Coordinate rather than compete independently
micro.Choice D: Sell only differentiated products
micro.Correct Answer: C — Coordinate rather than compete independently
micro.Feedback: Collusion involves coordinated conduct.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.3 — Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.
micro.Question: A cartel is:
micro.Choice A: A group of firms that happen to charge similar prices without coordinating.
micro.Choice B: A single price-taking firm
micro.Choice C: A market with free entry
micro.Choice D: A group of firms coordinating output or price
micro.Correct Answer: D — A group of firms coordinating output or price
micro.Feedback: A cartel attempts to act collectively like a monopoly.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.3 — Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.
micro.Question: A profit-maximizing cartel chooses total output where:
micro.Choice A: Industry marginal revenue equals industry marginal cost
micro.Choice B: Price equals average total cost
micro.Choice C: Market price equals industry marginal cost.
micro.Choice D: Each member’s price equals zero
micro.Correct Answer: A — Industry marginal revenue equals industry marginal cost
micro.Feedback: The cartel uses the monopoly marginal rule for joint output.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.3 — Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.
micro.Question: Why does a cartel member often want to cheat?
micro.Choice A: Cheating always raises joint profit
micro.Choice B: Selling extra output at the cartel price can raise its own profit
micro.Choice C: Cheating guarantees that other members keep cooperating forever.
micro.Choice D: Entry is impossible
micro.Correct Answer: B — Selling extra output at the cartel price can raise its own profit
micro.Feedback: Private incentives can conflict with the cartel’s collective restriction.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.3 — Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.
micro.Question: Which factor makes cartel cheating harder?
micro.Choice A: More secret discounts
micro.Choice B: More substitute products
micro.Choice C: Reliable monitoring of member prices and output
micro.Choice D: A shorter expected relationship among cartel members.
micro.Correct Answer: C — Reliable monitoring of member prices and output
micro.Feedback: Monitoring increases the chance that cheating is detected.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.3 — Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.
micro.Question: A cartel that successfully coordinates output tries to behave most like:
micro.Choice A: A single profit-maximizing monopolist for the industry
micro.Choice B: A group of independent price-taking firms
micro.Choice C: A perfectly contestable market with free entry
micro.Choice D: A regulator that sets the market price equal to marginal cost and assigns output to each participating firm
micro.Correct Answer: A — A single profit-maximizing monopolist for the industry
micro.Feedback: A successful cartel restricts joint output and chooses the industry outcome that maximizes combined profit.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.3 — Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.
micro.Question: Why can a cartel agreement be unstable even when all members gain from the agreement?
micro.Choice A: Every member must legally charge a different price
micro.Choice B: Cartels require marginal cost to equal zero
micro.Choice C: Joint profit is always lower under collusion than under competition because restricting output reduces total sales
micro.Choice D: An individual member may gain by secretly expanding sales while others keep output restricted
micro.Correct Answer: D — An individual member may gain by secretly expanding sales while others keep output restricted
micro.Feedback: The group can prefer restriction while each member has a private incentive to capture extra sales.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.3 — Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.
micro.Question: What does monitoring do for a cartel?
micro.Choice A: It makes each firm a price taker
micro.Choice B: It eliminates the need to restrict output
micro.Choice C: It helps members detect whether other members are cheating on the agreement
micro.Choice D: It guarantees that barriers to entry disappear once all cartel members can observe one another’s sales
micro.Correct Answer: C — It helps members detect whether other members are cheating on the agreement
micro.Feedback: Monitoring makes hidden deviations easier to discover and therefore easier to punish.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.3 — Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.
micro.Question: In a one-shot prisoner’s-dilemma-style pricing game, why might both firms cut price even though both would prefer that neither cut?
micro.Choice A: Both firms face perfectly inelastic demand
micro.Choice B: Each firm has an individual incentive to cut given the rival’s possible action
micro.Choice C: The firms are maximizing total industry profit because the individually attractive price cut also maximizes their joint payoff
micro.Choice D: Price cuts are legally required
micro.Correct Answer: B — Each firm has an individual incentive to cut given the rival’s possible action
micro.Feedback: Individual incentives can push both firms toward a lower-payoff noncooperative outcome.

micro.Question: Two airlines choose whether to cut fares. Each earns more from cutting when the rival holds fares, but both earn less when both cut. This structure is closest to:
micro.Choice A: Perfect coordination with no conflict
micro.Choice B: A price-taking market
micro.Choice C: A prisoner’s dilemma

micro.Correct Answer: C — A prisoner’s dilemma
micro.Feedback: Each airline has an individual incentive that can trigger a jointly harmful price war.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.3 — Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.
micro.Question: Two firms agree to restrict output, but one secretly offers rebates. The rebate is best described as:
