micro.Choice B: Price leadership.

micro.Choice D: Cheating on the collusive arrangement
micro.Correct Answer: D — Cheating on the collusive arrangement
micro.Feedback: Secret discounts undermine the coordinated price.

micro.Question: Why might a lower-cost cartel member receive a larger production quota?

micro.Choice B: It faces horizontal demand
micro.Choice C: It can produce part of joint output at lower cost

micro.Feedback: Efficient allocation places more output with lower-cost producers.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.3 — Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.
micro.Question: A cartel has already chosen its joint-profit-maximizing total output. Why might it assign more production to a member with lower marginal cost?
micro.Choice A: Shifting output toward the lower-cost producer can reduce the cartel’s total production cost
micro.Choice B: Equal quotas always maximize joint profit
micro.Choice C: Higher-cost firms must produce more to preserve competition
micro.Choice D: Output allocation cannot affect cartel profit once total output is fixed, even when members have different marginal costs
micro.Correct Answer: A — Shifting output toward the lower-cost producer can reduce the cartel’s total production cost
micro.Feedback: For a fixed cartel total, allocating more production to lower-marginal-cost members can raise combined profit.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.3 — Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.
micro.Question: Three firms agree to keep prices high. One firm quietly gives large rebates while publicly posting the agreed price. Economically, the rebates are best interpreted as:
micro.Choice A: Proof that the cartel has eliminated all competition because no member can gain market share without openly cutting the posted price
micro.Choice B: A required form of price leadership
micro.Choice C: A concentration measure
micro.Choice D: Cheating that captures extra sales while rivals maintain the collusive price
micro.Correct Answer: D — Cheating that captures extra sales while rivals maintain the collusive price
micro.Feedback: Secret rebates undermine the agreement by letting one member expand sales at the others’ expense.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.3 — Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.
micro.Question: Which market condition makes a cartel harder to sustain?
micro.Choice A: A small number of firms with similar objectives
micro.Choice B: A credible punishment system that quickly detects and penalizes members who secretly exceed their agreed output
micro.Choice C: Many opportunities for members to make secret sales that rivals cannot observe
micro.Choice D: Frequent transparent reporting of member sales
micro.Correct Answer: C — Many opportunities for members to make secret sales that rivals cannot observe
micro.Feedback: When cheating is hard to observe, deviations are easier and enforcement becomes weaker.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.3 — Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.
micro.Question: A cartel restricts total output below the competitive level. What is the intended effect on the market price?
micro.Choice A: Create a perfectly elastic industry demand curve so the cartel can sell any quantity at the higher price
micro.Choice B: Raise price by moving up the market demand curve
micro.Choice C: Force price down to marginal cost
micro.Choice D: Make price independent of demand
micro.Correct Answer: B — Raise price by moving up the market demand curve
micro.Feedback: Restricting industry output raises the price buyers are willing to pay along downward-sloping market demand.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.3 — Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.
micro.Question: Suppose cartel members can observe one another’s sales almost immediately. Why can this improve cartel stability?
micro.Choice A: It makes cheating easier to detect and respond to
micro.Choice B: It removes each member’s incentive to earn profit
micro.Choice C: It guarantees the cartel price equals marginal cost
micro.Choice D: It causes market concentration to fall
micro.Correct Answer: A — It makes cheating easier to detect and respond to
micro.Feedback: Fast observability reduces the chance that a member can profit from hidden deviations for long.

micro.Question: A cartel’s members all prefer the collusive outcome to the competitive outcome, yet the agreement repeatedly breaks down. Which explanation is most consistent with oligopoly incentives?
micro.Choice A: The cartel outcome cannot produce positive profit
micro.Choice B: Members have no information about market demand
micro.Choice C: A jointly preferred outcome is automatically a Nash equilibrium
micro.Choice D: Each firm can gain privately from expanding output if it expects rivals to keep restricting theirs

micro.Question: An effective cartel raises price from $30 to $42 and reduces quantity sold. Which statement best separates redistribution from efficiency loss?

micro.Choice C: Some consumer surplus becomes producer gain, while trades no longer made create deadweight loss
micro.Choice D: Every dollar of lost consumer surplus is deadweight loss
micro.Correct Answer: C — Some consumer surplus becomes producer gain, while trades no longer made create deadweight loss
micro.Feedback: A higher price transfers some surplus, but the output restriction also destroys gains from mutually beneficial trades.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.3 — Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.
micro.Question: Use the graph’s plotted demand and constant MC. Two identical cartel members split the joint-profit-maximizing output equally. One secretly adds one unit while the other holds its quota. Which profit comparison and incentive assessment are correct?
micro.Choice A: The deviator gains $14 while joint profit falls $2; the deviation is privately attractive despite harming the cartel.
micro.Choice B: The deviator gains $18 while joint profit falls $2; lower joint profit by itself removes the unilateral incentive.
micro.Choice C: The deviator gains $18 while joint profit falls $2; the deviation is privately attractive despite harming the cartel.
micro.Choice D: The deviator gains $14 while joint profit falls $2; lower joint profit by itself removes the unilateral incentive.
micro.Correct Answer: C — The deviator gains $18 while joint profit falls $2; the deviation is privately attractive despite harming the cartel.
micro.Feedback: Demand is P = 100−2 Q and MC = $20. MR = MC gives Q = 20, P = 60 and each member profit (60−20) × 10 = $400. Deviation gives Q = 21, P = 58 and deviator profit (58−20) × 11 = $418. Joint profit falls from $800 to $798. Individual incentives differ from the joint objective.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.3 — Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.
micro.Question: A cartel member could earn an extra $12 million this year by secretly expanding output. If detected, it loses future profit with a present value of $30 million; detection probability is 60%. If undetected, future profit is unchanged. Under risk neutrality, which comparison determines whether to deviate?
micro.Choice A: The expected punishment is $18 million; comply because it exceeds the current gain.
micro.Choice B: The expected punishment is $30 million; comply because the full punishment is certain.
micro.Choice C: The expected punishment is $18 million; deviate because a current gain outweighs a larger discounted expected loss.
micro.Choice D: The expected punishment is $12 million; compare it with the $12 million gain using the probability of escaping detection.
micro.Correct Answer: A — The expected punishment is $18 million; comply because it exceeds the current gain.
micro.Feedback: The future loss is already a present value. Multiply it by detection probability: 0.6×$30 million=$18 million. Net expected gain from deviation is $-6 million, so compliance is preferred under the stated assumptions.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.3 — Analyze prisoner’s-dilemma incentives, collusion, cartel behavior, and cheating.
micro.Question: Use the graph. The cartel faces the plotted demand and constant MC. Demand price falls $2.50 for each extra unit of total output. Two members split cartel output equally; one adds two units while the other holds its quota. Which incentive and deterrence threshold follow?
micro.Choice A: The deviator gains $35 and joint profit falls $10; an expected present-value punishment greater than $35 deters it.
micro.Choice B: The deviator gains $45 and joint profit falls $10; an expected present-value punishment greater than $45 deters it.
micro.Choice C: The deviator gains $45 and joint profit falls $10; a punishment just above the $10 joint loss is sufficient.
micro.Choice D: The deviator gains $35 and joint profit falls $10; a punishment just above the $10 joint loss is sufficient.
micro.Correct Answer: B — The deviator gains $45 and joint profit falls $10; an expected present-value punishment greater than $45 deters it.
micro.Feedback: The intercept is 140 and MC 30, so joint MR = 140−5 Q gives Q = 22, P 85. Each earns (85−30) × 11 = 605. Deviation gives total Q = 24, P 80 and deviator output 13, profit 650, a gain 45. Joint profit falls 1210→1200. Deterrence compares the deviator’s own gain with its expected discounted penalty.

micro.Choice B: The expected punishment is $10 million; comply because any possible punishment outweighs the gain.
micro.Choice C: The expected punishment is $30 million; compare it with the $18 million gain using the probability of escaping detection.
micro.Choice D: The expected punishment is $10 million; deviate because the current gain exceeds it.
micro.Correct Answer: D — The expected punishment is $10 million; deviate because the current gain exceeds it.
micro.Feedback: The future loss is already a present value. Multiply it by detection probability: 0.25×$40 million=$10 million. Net expected gain from deviation is $8 million, so deviation pays under the stated assumptions.

micro.Correct Answer: A — When future losses are large enough and punishment is credible

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.4 — Evaluate repeated interaction, punishment, credibility, tacit coordination, and price wars.
micro.Question: What makes a threat credible?

micro.Choice B: The threatening firm would rationally carry it out later
micro.Choice C: It was made publicly
micro.Choice D: It creates a high HHI
micro.Correct Answer: B — The threatening firm would rationally carry it out later
micro.Feedback: Credibility is tested at the future decision point.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.4 — Evaluate repeated interaction, punishment, credibility, tacit coordination, and price wars.
micro.Question: Does parallel pricing prove collusion?
micro.Choice A: Yes, identical prices are conclusive
micro.Choice B: No, collusion is impossible
micro.Choice C: No, firms may respond independently to common conditions
micro.Choice D: Yes, if products differ
micro.Correct Answer: C — No, firms may respond independently to common conditions
micro.Feedback: Parallel conduct needs context and evidence.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.4 — Evaluate repeated interaction, punishment, credibility, tacit coordination, and price wars.
micro.Question: What is price leadership?
micro.Choice A: The leader owns every rival
micro.Choice B: A binding government price
micro.Choice C: A dominant strategy in every game
micro.Choice D: Rivals follow a leading firm’s announced price without legal control
micro.Correct Answer: D — Rivals follow a leading firm’s announced price without legal control
micro.Feedback: Leadership can create a focal price.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.4 — Evaluate repeated interaction, punishment, credibility, tacit coordination, and price wars.
micro.Question: A student says tacit coordination and explicit collusion are identical. What is the key distinction?
micro.Choice A: Explicit collusion means firms ignore rivals
micro.Choice B: Only tacit coordination can affect price
micro.Choice C: Tacit coordination can emerge without an explicit agreement among firms
micro.Choice D: Tacit coordination always requires a written contract
micro.Correct Answer: C — Tacit coordination can emerge without an explicit agreement among firms
micro.Feedback: Tacit coordination refers to aligned behavior without the explicit agreement that defines collusion.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.4 — Evaluate repeated interaction, punishment, credibility, tacit coordination, and price wars.
micro.Question: A student understands a one-shot prisoner’s dilemma. What new consideration enters when the firms expect to interact again?
micro.Choice A: Market concentration falls with each round
micro.Choice B: Today’s action can change future responses and future payoffs
micro.Choice C: The payoff matrix no longer matters at all
micro.Choice D: Every cooperative promise becomes binding
micro.Correct Answer: B — Today’s action can change future responses and future payoffs
micro.Feedback: Repeated interaction links current choices to future rewards or punishments, which can alter incentives.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.4 — Evaluate repeated interaction, punishment, credibility, tacit coordination, and price wars.
micro.Question: Repeated interaction may support cooperation because:
micro.Choice A: Future punishment guarantees cooperation regardless of observability or credibility
micro.Choice B: It makes all threats credible
micro.Choice C: It removes entry barriers
micro.Choice D: Current cheating can trigger costly future punishment
micro.Correct Answer: D — Current cheating can trigger costly future punishment
micro.Feedback: Future consequences can change current incentives.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.4 — Evaluate repeated interaction, punishment, credibility, tacit coordination, and price wars.
micro.Question: A threat is credible when:

micro.Choice C: It would hurt only the rival
micro.Choice D: The announced response is credible because it sounds severe and harms the entrant
micro.Correct Answer: A — Carrying it out remains in the threatening firm’s interest later
micro.Feedback: Credibility requires sequential rationality.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.4 — Evaluate repeated interaction, punishment, credibility, tacit coordination, and price wars.

micro.Choice B: Reduce margins for several rival firms
micro.Choice C: Eliminate strategic interdependence
micro.Choice D: Create a monopoly immediately
micro.Correct Answer: B — Reduce margins for several rival firms
micro.Feedback: Aggressive price cutting can damage all firms’ profits.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.4 — Evaluate repeated interaction, punishment, credibility, tacit coordination, and price wars.
micro.Question: Tacit coordination differs from explicit collusion because tacit coordination:

micro.Choice B: Occurs only when every firm charges exactly the same price.

micro.Choice D: Requires identical products
micro.Correct Answer: C — Can occur without an explicit agreement
micro.Feedback: Tacit coordination can arise through expectations and repeated conduct.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.4 — Evaluate repeated interaction, punishment, credibility, tacit coordination, and price wars.

micro.Feedback: Following can occur without formal control.

micro.Correct Answer: D — A firm that cheats today may lose future cooperative gains
micro.Feedback: When future interaction matters, the short-run gain from cheating can be weighed against future losses after retaliation.

micro.Feedback: A short horizon weakens the future cost of cheating.

micro.Correct Answer: B — Price leadership
micro.Feedback: A leader’s announced price can become a focal point.

micro.Choice C: The market cannot be oligopolistic because prices moved together

micro.Feedback: Similar prices can arise from common incentives or observation of rivals; parallel behavior by itself is not proof of an agreement.

micro.Feedback: Following a recognized price leader can coordinate market behavior, but observation alone does not prove an explicit agreement.

micro.Feedback: Compute both present values and subtract.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.4 — Evaluate repeated interaction, punishment, credibility, tacit coordination, and price wars.
micro.Question: In a present-value calculation, future payoffs are weighted by multiplying by the same factor for each period ahead. Holding all current payoffs fixed, this factor rises from 0.40 to 0.85. What changes most directly?
micro.Choice A: HHI automatically rises
micro.Choice B: The one-shot Nash equilibrium disappears by definition
micro.Choice C: Current marginal cost falls
micro.Choice D: Future punishment becomes more important relative to a one-time cheating gain
micro.Correct Answer: D — Future punishment becomes more important relative to a one-time cheating gain
micro.Feedback: A higher factor gives future consequences more weight relative to current payoffs in the present-value calculation.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.4 — Evaluate repeated interaction, punishment, credibility, tacit coordination, and price wars.
micro.Question: Why does an indefinite horizon support cooperation better than a known final round?
micro.Choice A: Demand becomes horizontal
micro.Choice B: MC equals price
micro.Choice C: Market shares become equal
micro.Choice D: Future punishment retains value
micro.Correct Answer: D — Future punishment retains value
micro.Feedback: A longer expected relationship increases future stakes.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.4 — Evaluate repeated interaction, punishment, credibility, tacit coordination, and price wars.
micro.Question: What makes a punishment threat credible?
micro.Choice A: Punishment is optimal after cheating occurs
micro.Choice B: Punishment was announced
micro.Choice C: Punishment hurts the cheater
micro.Choice D: The cartel has four members
micro.Correct Answer: A — Punishment is optimal after cheating occurs
micro.Feedback: The punisher must rationally carry it out.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.4 — Evaluate repeated interaction, punishment, credibility, tacit coordination, and price wars.
micro.Question: Why can price wars persist after a mistake?
micro.Choice A: Firms become price takers
micro.Choice B: Each response can trigger another retaliation
micro.Choice C: HHI automatically falls to zero
micro.Choice D: Demand becomes perfectly inelastic
micro.Correct Answer: B — Each response can trigger another retaliation
micro.Feedback: Retaliation can create a destructive feedback loop.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.4 — Evaluate repeated interaction, punishment, credibility, tacit coordination, and price wars.
micro.Question: What distinguishes tacit coordination from explicit collusion?
micro.Choice A: Tacit coordination has no strategic behavior
micro.Choice B: Explicit collusion is always legal
micro.Choice C: Tacit coordination lacks an explicit agreement
micro.Choice D: Tacit coordination requires identical prices
micro.Correct Answer: C — Tacit coordination lacks an explicit agreement
micro.Feedback: Tacit coordination arises without an explicit pact.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.4 — Evaluate repeated interaction, punishment, credibility, tacit coordination, and price wars.
micro.Question: Why is parallel pricing ambiguous evidence?
micro.Choice A: Collusion never affects price
micro.Choice B: Prices cannot move together
micro.Choice C: HHI measures costs exactly
micro.Choice D: Common demand or cost shocks can produce similar independent responses
micro.Correct Answer: D — Common demand or cost shocks can produce similar independent responses
micro.Feedback: Parallel conduct can have competitive explanations.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.4 — Evaluate repeated interaction, punishment, credibility, tacit coordination, and price wars.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.5 — Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.
micro.Question: Does low pricing prove predation?
micro.Choice A: No, it may reflect low cost or vigorous competition
micro.Choice B: Yes, every price cut is exclusionary
micro.Choice C: No, low prices never affect entry
micro.Choice D: Yes, if HHI is high
micro.Correct Answer: A — No, it may reflect low cost or vigorous competition
micro.Feedback: Intent and recoupment cannot be inferred from low price alone.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.5 — Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.
micro.Question: Why can advertising matter in both structures?
micro.Choice A: It makes every firm a price taker
micro.Choice B: It removes entry barriers
micro.Choice C: It guarantees collusion
micro.Choice D: It can differentiate products and alter substitution
micro.Correct Answer: D — It can differentiate products and alter substitution
micro.Feedback: Advertising can shape demand in both markets.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.5 — Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.
micro.Question: How can excess capacity serve as a commitment?
micro.Choice A: Installed capacity can make a large post-entry output response more credible
micro.Choice B: It removes sunk cost
micro.Choice C: It guarantees a price ceiling
micro.Choice D: It eliminates marginal cost
micro.Correct Answer: A — Installed capacity can make a large post-entry output response more credible
micro.Feedback: A sunk capacity choice can alter later incentives.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.5 — Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.
micro.Question: Why does product differentiation sometimes soften price competition?
micro.Choice A: It makes marginal cost vertical
micro.Choice B: More loyal buyers make firm demand less elastic
micro.Choice C: It removes strategic interdependence
micro.Choice D: It forces price equal MC
micro.Correct Answer: B — More loyal buyers make firm demand less elastic
micro.Feedback: Lower elasticity reduces customer switching.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.5 — Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.
micro.Question: A student knows that talk alone may not deter entry. What can make an incumbent’s announced response more believable?
micro.Choice A: A costly action taken in advance that changes the incumbent’s future incentives
micro.Choice B: A vague promise that entry will be punished somehow
micro.Choice C: A larger concentration ratio by itself
micro.Choice D: A public statement with no change in capacity or costs
micro.Correct Answer: A — A costly action taken in advance that changes the incumbent’s future incentives
micro.Feedback: A commitment can make future behavior credible by changing what the incumbent will find profitable after entry.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.5 — Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.
micro.Question: A student has learned that oligopoly firms react strategically to price changes. What is the next step when firms compete through quality or advertising instead?
micro.Choice A: Ignore rivals because only prices create interdependence
micro.Choice B: Apply the same strategic logic to nonprice actions because rivals may respond there too
micro.Choice C: Assume nonprice choices have no effect on demand
micro.Choice D: Treat advertising as proof of collusion
micro.Correct Answer: B — Apply the same strategic logic to nonprice actions because rivals may respond there too
micro.Feedback: Strategic interdependence applies to quality, advertising, service, and other competitive dimensions as well as price.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.5 — Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.
micro.Question: Nonprice competition includes competition through:
micro.Choice A: Quality, service, design, or advertising
micro.Choice B: Coordinating output quotas with rival firms.
micro.Choice C: Only lower posted prices
micro.Choice D: Only government licenses
micro.Correct Answer: A — Quality, service, design, or advertising
micro.Feedback: Oligopolists often compete on several dimensions.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.5 — Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.
micro.Question: Limit pricing refers to:
micro.Choice A: Setting the monopoly price after entry occurs.
micro.Choice B: Keeping price low partly to discourage entry
micro.Choice C: A legal maximum price
micro.Choice D: Matching every rival’s advertising
micro.Correct Answer: B — Keeping price low partly to discourage entry
micro.Feedback: The incumbent may sacrifice current profit to affect entry.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.5 — Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.
micro.Question: What does the kinked-demand model primarily attempt to explain?
micro.Choice A: How firms determine the original market price.
micro.Choice B: Why every oligopoly colludes
micro.Choice C: Price rigidity around an existing price
micro.Choice D: Why demand becomes vertical
micro.Correct Answer: C — Price rigidity around an existing price
micro.Feedback: The model explains rigidity, not the initial price.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.5 — Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.
micro.Question: What makes a strategic threat credible?
micro.Choice A: The threat was announced publicly
micro.Choice B: The threat would be costly to both firms
micro.Choice C: Carrying it out would be in the threatening firm’s interest if the situation actually occurred
micro.Choice D: The threat sounds severe to the rival
micro.Correct Answer: C — Carrying it out would be in the threatening firm’s interest if the situation actually occurred
micro.Feedback: Credibility depends on whether the threatened response would actually be rational when the time comes to act.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.5 — Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.
micro.Question: An incumbent builds capacity that would be useful even if entry occurs. Why can this deter entry?
micro.Choice A: It eliminates every fixed cost
micro.Choice B: It turns the market into perfect competition
micro.Choice C: It guarantees a legal monopoly
micro.Choice D: The capacity can make an aggressive post-entry response credible
micro.Correct Answer: D — The capacity can make an aggressive post-entry response credible
micro.Feedback: A sunk commitment can alter the incumbent’s later incentives.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.5 — Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.
micro.Question: An incumbent threatens to cut price below variable cost after entry, but doing so would be very costly and temporary. The threat is likely:
micro.Choice A: Not credible
micro.Choice B: A dominant strategy
micro.Choice C: A concentration ratio
micro.Choice D: Automatically profitable
micro.Correct Answer: A — Not credible
micro.Feedback: The incumbent may not rationally carry out the threat later.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.5 — Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.
micro.Question: A firm maintains a lower price today to reduce expected entrant profit. What is the strategic cost?
micro.Choice A: It raises current monopoly profit automatically
micro.Choice B: It sacrifices some current profit
micro.Choice C: It eliminates marginal cost
micro.Choice D: It guarantees no future rivalry
micro.Correct Answer: B — It sacrifices some current profit
micro.Feedback: Limit pricing trades current profit for possible entry deterrence.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.5 — Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.
micro.Question: In the kinked-demand model, rivals are assumed to match:
micro.Choice A: Price increases but never cuts
micro.Choice B: Every advertising campaign
micro.Choice C: Price cuts more readily than price increases
micro.Choice D: All capacity expansions
micro.Correct Answer: C — Price cuts more readily than price increases
micro.Feedback: This asymmetry creates the kink.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.5 — Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.
micro.Question: If MC changes within the discontinuity in the kinked-demand MR curve, the model predicts:
micro.Choice A: Price must fall to zero
micro.Choice B: The demand kink disappears
micro.Choice C: The market becomes competitive
micro.Choice D: Price and output may remain unchanged
micro.Correct Answer: D — Price and output may remain unchanged
micro.Feedback: The same output can remain optimal while MC crosses the MR gap.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.5 — Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.
micro.Question: A firm increases product quality rather than cutting price. This is:
micro.Choice A: Nonprice competition
micro.Choice B: Tacit collusion automatically
micro.Choice C: A concentration-ratio calculation
micro.Choice D: A shutdown decision
micro.Correct Answer: A — Nonprice competition
micro.Feedback: Oligopolists can compete on quality and other dimensions.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.5 — Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.
micro.Question: Heavy advertising builds brand loyalty and reduces switching. What strategic effect is most plausible?
micro.Choice A: Every firm becomes a price taker
micro.Choice B: Price competition may soften because firm demand becomes less elastic
micro.Choice C: Entry barriers disappear
micro.Choice D: Marginal revenue equals price
micro.Correct Answer: B — Price competition may soften because firm demand becomes less elastic
micro.Feedback: Loyalty can reduce substitution among brands.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.5 — Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.
micro.Question: In the airlines market, an incumbent announces a severe post-entry price cut. Internal documents show the cut would reduce the incumbent’s own post-entry payoff below accommodation. What is the best interpretation?
micro.Choice A: The threat is credible because it hurts the entrant
micro.Choice B: The threat is not credible
micro.Choice C: The announcement creates a dominant strategy for the entrant
micro.Choice D: The market is perfectly competitive
micro.Correct Answer: B — The threat is not credible
micro.Feedback: A threat is noncredible when carrying it out is not optimal after entry.

micro.Question: In the kinked-demand model, a modest marginal-cost change occurs entirely within the discontinuity in marginal revenue. What does the model predict?

micro.Correct Answer: A — The profit-maximizing price can remain unchanged
micro.Feedback: The MR discontinuity is used to explain why a range of marginal-cost changes may leave the chosen price unchanged.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.5 — Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.
micro.Question: Rivals match fare cuts but not fare increases in the kinked-demand market shown. Constant MC rises from $48 to $54, with demand and fixed cost unchanged. Which fare, quantity and profit assessment follow?
micro.Choice A: Fare $72 and quantity 20 remain unchanged; profit falls $120 because MC stays within the MR gap.
micro.Choice B: Fare $72 and quantity 30 remain unchanged; profit is unchanged because price rigidity prevents costs from affecting profit.
micro.Choice C: Fare $72 and quantity 20 remain unchanged; profit is unchanged because price rigidity prevents costs from affecting profit.
micro.Choice D: Fare $72 and quantity 30 remain unchanged; profit falls $180 because MC stays within the MR gap.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Fare $72 and quantity 30 remain unchanged; profit falls $180 because MC stays within the MR gap.
micro.Feedback: The kink is at Q 30, P 72 and the MR gap 36–60. Both cost levels lie inside it, so output and price stay fixed. Costs rise 6 × 30 = $180, reducing economic profit by that amount.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.5 — Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.
micro.Question: Using the kinked demand and MR shown, compare raising constant MC to $45 with raising it to $55. Hold demand fixed. Which results and explanation are correct?
micro.Choice A: At $45: Q = 20, P = $60; at $55: Q = 15, P = $62.50. The first cost lies within the MR gap, while the second lies above it.
micro.Choice B: At $45: Q = 30, P = $60; at $55: Q = 25, P = $62.50. The first cost lies within the MR gap, while the second lies above it.
micro.Choice C: At $45: Q = 20, P = $60; at $55: Q = 15, P = $62.50. Any cost change inside the MR gap must change the profit-maximizing quantity.
micro.Choice D: At $45: Q = 30, P = $60; at $55: Q = 25, P = $62.50. Any cost change inside the MR gap must change the profit-maximizing quantity.
micro.Correct Answer: A — At $45: Q = 20, P = $60; at $55: Q = 15, P = $62.50. The first cost lies within the MR gap, while the second lies above it.
micro.Feedback: The kink is (20, 60) with MR dropping 50→30. MC 45 lies in the gap and keeps the kink optimal. The upper MR branch is 70−Q; MC 55 gives Q = 15 and P = 70−0.5 × 15 = 62.50. Rigidity applies within the gap, not to every cost change.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.5 — Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.
micro.Question: The firm starts at the kink shown. An input improvement lowers constant MC from $48 to $42, while a recurring license fee adds $300 to fixed cost. Demand is unchanged and the firm stays active. Which evaluation is correct?
micro.Choice A: Price and quantity stay at $72 and 20; the $120 variable-cost saving is smaller than the fee, reducing profit $180.
micro.Choice B: Price and quantity stay at $72 and 30; the $180 variable-cost saving is smaller than the fee, reducing profit $120.
micro.Choice C: Price and quantity stay at $72 and 30; the $300 fixed fee must enter MC and outweigh the $180 saving in the output rule.
micro.Choice D: Price and quantity stay at $72 and 20; the $300 fixed fee must enter MC and outweigh the $120 saving in the output rule.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Price and quantity stay at $72 and 30; the $180 variable-cost saving is smaller than the fee, reducing profit $120.
micro.Feedback: The kink is Q 30, P 72 with MR gap 36–60. MC 42 remains in the gap. Variable-cost savings are (48−42) × 30 = $180, less than the 300 fee, so profit falls 120. The fixed fee affects profit, not the marginal output decision.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.5 — Analyze entry deterrence, nonprice competition, price leadership, and supplemental oligopoly models.
micro.Question: Refer to the game tree. The incumbent threatens to fight if the entrant enters. What path does backward induction predict, and is the threat to fight credible?

micro.Correct Answer: A — Enter, then Accommodate; the threat to fight is not credible
micro.Feedback: Backward induction determines the actual response and whether the threat is credible.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: Does a higher post-merger HHI settle the welfare question?
micro.Choice A: Yes, concentration is the only issue
micro.Choice B: No, market power, entry, and efficiencies still require analysis
micro.Choice C: No, HHI has no value
micro.Choice D: Yes, every merger harms consumers
micro.Correct Answer: B — No, market power, entry, and efficiencies still require analysis
micro.Feedback: Concentration is one part of merger analysis.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: A student says “high concentration proves firms are colluding.” What is the correction?
micro.Choice A: Collusion is impossible in concentrated markets
micro.Choice B: Concentration measures directly record secret agreements
micro.Choice C: High concentration can make strategic interaction important, but it does not by itself prove an agreement or harmful conduct
micro.Choice D: High concentration means every firm charges marginal cost
micro.Correct Answer: C — High concentration can make strategic interaction important, but it does not by itself prove an agreement or harmful conduct
micro.Feedback: Structure can affect incentives, but conduct and welfare conclusions require additional evidence.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: A student treats every dollar of consumer-surplus loss from a cartel as deadweight loss. What should the student separate?
micro.Choice A: Accounting profit from total revenue
micro.Choice B: Surplus transferred to producers from surplus destroyed by trades that no longer occur
micro.Choice C: Price changes from quantity changes
micro.Choice D: HHI from the concentration ratio
micro.Correct Answer: B — Surplus transferred to producers from surplus destroyed by trades that no longer occur
micro.Feedback: A cartel can redistribute surplus and destroy surplus; only the destroyed gains from trade are deadweight loss.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: A student says a higher post-merger HHI proves the merger harms consumers. What is the better statement?
micro.Choice A: HHI measures concentration; consumer effects also depend on competition, entry, cost savings, and resulting price reductions
micro.Choice B: HHI directly measures the change in consumer surplus
micro.Choice C: Any HHI increase means the merged firm becomes a monopolist
micro.Choice D: HHI is unrelated to merger analysis
micro.Correct Answer: A — HHI measures concentration; consumer effects also depend on competition, entry, cost savings, and resulting price reductions
micro.Feedback: Concentration is an input to analysis, not a complete welfare conclusion.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: A student argues that high research spending proves a concentrated market is socially optimal. What is missing?
micro.Choice A: Research spending always lowers HHI
micro.Choice B: Innovation matters only in perfect competition
micro.Choice C: High research spending eliminates market power
micro.Choice D: Innovation benefits must be weighed against possible higher prices, weaker rivalry, and other welfare effects
micro.Correct Answer: D — Innovation benefits must be weighed against possible higher prices, weaker rivalry, and other welfare effects
micro.Feedback: Innovation can be beneficial without settling the overall welfare comparison.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: A student sees several firms charge the same price and immediately labels the behavior collusion. What is the key correction?
micro.Choice A: Price equality proves the firms have equal market shares
micro.Choice B: Collusion can occur only when prices differ
micro.Choice C: Similar prices can arise independently from common costs or market conditions, so evidence of coordination is still needed
micro.Choice D: Identical prices are impossible without a cartel
micro.Correct Answer: C — Similar prices can arise independently from common costs or market conditions, so evidence of coordination is still needed
micro.Feedback: Parallel conduct is not automatically evidence of an agreement because firms can respond similarly to the same public conditions.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: How does cartel price compare with the competitive benchmark?
micro.Choice A: It is always lower
micro.Choice B: It equals marginal cost
micro.Choice C: It is unrelated to output
micro.Choice D: It is typically higher because joint output is restricted
micro.Correct Answer: D — It is typically higher because joint output is restricted
micro.Feedback: Coordination can reproduce monopoly-like outcomes.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: Industry demand is P=50−Q and marginal cost is $10. What output gives the competitive efficiency benchmark for evaluating a cartel?
micro.Feedback: The benchmark sets marginal value equal to MC: 50−Q=10, so Q=40.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: A cartel omits two units whose buyer values are $25 and $20 and whose marginal costs are $10 and $12. What surplus is lost from omitting them?
micro.Feedback: The forgone gains are (25−10)+(20−12)=15+8=$23.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: On 10 units still traded, a cartel raises price by $3 per unit without changing costs. Ignoring any separately lost trades, what transfer occurs?
micro.Choice A: $30 from buyers to sellers
micro.Choice B: $30 from sellers to buyers
micro.Choice C: $3 from buyers to government
micro.Choice D: $30 of deadweight loss on these units
micro.Correct Answer: A — $30 from buyers to sellers
micro.Feedback: Buyers pay $3×10=$30 more and sellers receive the same amount; this is a transfer on the retained trades.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: Why does antitrust examine concentration?
micro.Choice A: Concentration proves guilt
micro.Choice B: HHI measures product quality
micro.Choice C: Firm size never matters
micro.Choice D: A concentrated structure may make coordination or unilateral market power easier
micro.Correct Answer: D — A concentrated structure may make coordination or unilateral market power easier
micro.Feedback: Structure can affect competitive risk.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: Why are merger efficiencies relevant?
micro.Choice A: Lower costs can offset some harm if savings are real and passed through
micro.Choice B: Efficiencies make concentration irrelevant
micro.Choice C: Every merger lowers price
micro.Choice D: Cost savings prove no market power
micro.Correct Answer: A — Lower costs can offset some harm if savings are real and passed through
micro.Feedback: Policy weighs market-power risk against verifiable benefits.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: Compared with competition, an effective cartel typically produces:
micro.Choice A: More output at a lower price
micro.Choice B: The same output at minimum ATC
micro.Choice C: Zero producer surplus
micro.Choice D: Less output at a higher price
micro.Correct Answer: D — Less output at a higher price
micro.Feedback: A successful cartel mimics monopoly restriction.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: Why is high concentration not enough by itself to prove harmful conduct?
micro.Choice A: Entry conditions, efficiencies, imports, and actual behavior also matter
micro.Choice B: A high HHI guarantees high economic profit.
micro.Choice C: HHI measures only product quality
micro.Choice D: Every concentrated market is regulated
micro.Correct Answer: A — Entry conditions, efficiencies, imports, and actual behavior also matter
micro.Feedback: Concentration is evidence, not a complete conclusion.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: Which statement best captures oligopoly outcomes?
micro.Choice A: They always reproduce the monopoly outcome.
micro.Choice B: They can range from intense rivalry to substantial coordination
micro.Choice C: They always equal perfect competition
micro.Choice D: They are determined only by firm count
micro.Correct Answer: B — They can range from intense rivalry to substantial coordination
micro.Feedback: Rules, payoffs, timing, and repetition shape outcomes.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: Compared with a competitive outcome, an effective cartel usually chooses:
micro.Choice A: Lower output and a higher price
micro.Choice B: Higher output and a lower price
micro.Choice C: The same output with zero profit
micro.Choice D: Price equal to minimum average total cost
micro.Correct Answer: A — Lower output and a higher price
micro.Feedback: A cartel acts like a joint monopolist, restricting output to raise price and combined profit.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: Why is a high HHI not enough by itself to prove consumers are being harmed?
micro.Choice A: HHI directly measures consumer surplus
micro.Choice B: A high HHI guarantees prices equal marginal cost
micro.Choice C: HHI is unrelated to market shares
micro.Choice D: Concentration measures structure, while welfare also depends on conduct, entry conditions, efficiencies, and rivalry
micro.Correct Answer: D — Concentration measures structure, while welfare also depends on conduct, entry conditions, efficiencies, and rivalry
micro.Feedback: Concentration is evidence about market structure, not a complete welfare verdict.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: If two firms merge and all other market shares remain unchanged, what happens to market concentration?
micro.Choice A: It cannot change unless market demand shifts
micro.Choice B: It becomes zero if the merged firm cuts price
micro.Choice C: It generally increases because two separate shares become one larger share
micro.Choice D: It must fall because there is one fewer firm
micro.Correct Answer: C — It generally increases because two separate shares become one larger share
micro.Feedback: Combining shares raises concentration measures such as HHI, all else equal.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: A concentrated industry charges high markups but also spends heavily on research. What is the soundest conclusion?
micro.Choice A: Concentration always increases total surplus
micro.Choice B: There may be a tradeoff between market-power costs and innovation benefits that requires evidence
micro.Choice C: High research spending proves the market is efficient
micro.Choice D: High markups prove innovation has no value
micro.Correct Answer: B — There may be a tradeoff between market-power costs and innovation benefits that requires evidence
micro.Feedback: Oligopoly welfare can involve competing effects rather than a one-variable verdict.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: What is the basic economic concern behind antitrust scrutiny of collusion?
micro.Choice A: Coordinated restriction of competition can raise price and reduce output below competitive levels
micro.Choice B: Collusion makes every firm a price taker
micro.Choice C: Collusion necessarily creates free entry
micro.Choice D: Collusion guarantees maximum consumer surplus
micro.Correct Answer: A — Coordinated restriction of competition can raise price and reduce output below competitive levels
micro.Feedback: The core welfare concern is reduced rivalry that raises prices, restricts output, and can create deadweight loss.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: Why should an economist be cautious about predicting one outcome for every oligopoly market?
micro.Choice A: Every oligopoly has the same payoff matrix
micro.Choice B: Oligopoly theory assumes firms never respond to rivals
micro.Choice C: Market concentration fully determines every price
micro.Choice D: Different numbers of firms, products, information, costs, and strategic settings can produce different behavior
micro.Correct Answer: D — Different numbers of firms, products, information, costs, and strategic settings can produce different behavior
micro.Feedback: Oligopoly is a strategic family of models, not a guarantee that every few-firm market behaves identically.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: Which statement best summarizes why oligopoly welfare analysis can be complicated?

micro.Choice C: Few firms may create market power, but rivalry, innovation, efficiencies, and entry conditions also matter
micro.Choice D: Any market with four firms is automatically inefficient
micro.Correct Answer: C — Few firms may create market power, but rivalry, innovation, efficiencies, and entry conditions also matter
micro.Feedback: A sound evaluation combines structure, strategic conduct, efficiency claims, and market responses.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: An effective cartel raises price and reduces output. Which part of lost consumer surplus is not transferred to producers?

micro.Choice B: Cartel profit
micro.Choice C: Fixed cost
micro.Choice D: Accounting revenue
micro.Correct Answer: A — Deadweight loss
micro.Feedback: Lost mutually beneficial trades create DWL.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: A merger raises HHI but also creates verified large cost savings. What is the sound conclusion?
micro.Choice A: The merger must be approved
micro.Choice B: Both increased market power and efficiencies must be evaluated
micro.Choice C: The merger must be blocked
micro.Choice D: HHI becomes irrelevant
micro.Correct Answer: B — Both increased market power and efficiencies must be evaluated
micro.Feedback: Concentration and efficiency evidence both matter.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: A merger lowers marginal cost, but the merged firm keeps price high because rivalry weakens. What does this show?
micro.Choice A: Every efficiency improves consumer surplus
micro.Choice B: Lower cost removes market power
micro.Choice C: Cost savings need not be passed fully to consumers
micro.Choice D: Merger concentration cannot matter
micro.Correct Answer: C — Cost savings need not be passed fully to consumers
micro.Feedback: Pass-through depends on competitive pressure.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: Why can foreign competition affect a domestic concentration assessment?
micro.Choice A: Imports are excluded from every market definition
micro.Choice B: Foreign firms never affect price
micro.Choice C: HHI measures only domestic costs
micro.Choice D: Imports may provide substitutes that constrain domestic firms
micro.Correct Answer: D — Imports may provide substitutes that constrain domestic firms
micro.Feedback: Relevant competitors may include foreign suppliers.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: Why can game theory yield different predictions across oligopoly markets?
micro.Choice A: Game theory assumes identical markets
micro.Choice B: Every oligopoly has one dominant strategy
micro.Choice C: Firm costs never matter
micro.Choice D: Payoffs, information, timing, and repetition differ
micro.Correct Answer: D — Payoffs, information, timing, and repetition differ
micro.Feedback: Strategic settings differ across industries.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: Two firms with market shares of 18% and 12% merge. Holding all other shares fixed, why does HHI rise?
micro.Choice A: The merger automatically removes all smaller rivals
micro.Choice B: The squared share of the combined 30% firm exceeds the sum of the two firms’ separate squared shares
micro.Choice C: HHI counts the merged firm twice
micro.Choice D: Every merger doubles total market sales
micro.Correct Answer: B — The squared share of the combined 30% firm exceeds the sum of the two firms’ separate squared shares
micro.Feedback: Because shares are squared, combining two positive shares increases HHI by the cross term 2ab.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: A proposed merger would eliminate the closest competitor but also reduce marginal cost substantially. What is the best economic approach?
micro.Choice A: Compare reduced competition with verified cost savings and how much they lower customer prices
micro.Choice B: Approve the merger automatically because costs fall
micro.Choice C: Block the merger automatically because concentration rises
micro.Choice D: Ignore cost effects because only the number of firms matters
micro.Correct Answer: A — Compare reduced competition with verified cost savings and how much they lower customer prices
micro.Feedback: Merger analysis requires weighing competitive harm against genuine efficiencies rather than using one fact mechanically.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: When a cartel raises price, some lost consumer surplus becomes additional producer surplus. What happens to the remaining loss associated with trades that no longer occur?
micro.Choice A: It becomes tax revenue
micro.Choice B: It becomes an HHI increase
micro.Choice C: It is automatically recovered through innovation
micro.Choice D: It becomes deadweight loss
micro.Correct Answer: D — It becomes deadweight loss
micro.Feedback: Foregone mutually beneficial trades destroy total surplus rather than transfer it to another market participant.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: A domestic industry has a high concentration ratio, but buyers can readily switch to imported substitutes when domestic prices rise. What does this imply?
micro.Choice A: The market must be a monopoly
micro.Choice B: High concentration guarantees collusion
micro.Choice C: Domestic concentration alone may overstate the firms’ effective market power
micro.Choice D: Imports are irrelevant to market definition
micro.Correct Answer: C — Domestic concentration alone may overstate the firms’ effective market power
micro.Feedback: Competitive constraints from close substitutes, including imports when relevant, matter to the economic market definition.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: A merger creates a larger research budget but also reduces head-to-head price competition. Which statement is most defensible?
micro.Choice A: The merger must lower HHI because research increases
micro.Choice B: Both innovation benefits and reduced-rivalry costs should be evaluated rather than assuming one dominates
micro.Choice C: A larger research budget proves consumer welfare will rise
micro.Choice D: Reduced rivalry is irrelevant whenever innovation is possible
micro.Correct Answer: B — Both innovation benefits and reduced-rivalry costs should be evaluated rather than assuming one dominates
micro.Feedback: The welfare question is empirical: innovation gains can matter, but so can weaker price and quality competition.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: A merger sharply raises HHI, but entry is easy and several well-funded firms can expand quickly if price rises. What is the strongest economic inference?
micro.Choice A: The concentration increase is relevant, but ease of entry and expansion can limit post-merger market power
micro.Choice B: The HHI increase proves prices will rise
micro.Choice C: Easy entry is irrelevant once concentration increases
micro.Choice D: The merger must increase deadweight loss by exactly the HHI change
micro.Correct Answer: A — The concentration increase is relevant, but ease of entry and expansion can limit post-merger market power
micro.Feedback: Concentration is one piece of evidence; credible entry and expansion can constrain the merged firm.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: Four paving contractors independently face the same asphalt-cost increase. An investigator then finds messages in which their managers agree on a common minimum bid for upcoming jobs. Which evidence most directly supports an antitrust concern?
micro.Choice A: The asphalt-cost increase shared by all four firms
micro.Choice B: The fact that all four firms may earn positive accounting profit
micro.Choice C: The fact that the market has fewer than ten sellers
micro.Choice D: The agreement among competing bidders to set a common minimum price
micro.Correct Answer: D — The agreement among competing bidders to set a common minimum price
micro.Feedback: A common cost shock can explain similar independent price increases. An agreement among competing bidders to set a minimum bid is direct evidence of coordinated pricing. Concentration or profit alone does not establish such an agreement.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: A cartel restriction transfers $9 million of surplus from consumers to producers and destroys another $3 million of mutually beneficial trade. What is the deadweight loss?
micro.Choice A: $12 million
micro.Choice B: $6 million
micro.Choice C: $3 million
micro.Choice D: $9 million
micro.Correct Answer: C — $3 million
micro.Feedback: Transfers change who receives surplus; only the destroyed gains from trade are deadweight loss.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: A platform market is highly concentrated because network effects make a large user base valuable, but users can easily use multiple platforms at once. What is the most careful conclusion?
micro.Choice A: The market must be perfectly competitive because users can switch
micro.Choice B: Network effects can support concentration, while easy multi-homing may still preserve meaningful competitive pressure
micro.Choice C: High concentration proves the platform has unconstrained monopoly power
micro.Choice D: Multi-homing makes network effects disappear
micro.Correct Answer: B — Network effects can support concentration, while easy multi-homing may still preserve meaningful competitive pressure
micro.Feedback: The same structural fact can have different welfare implications depending on switching, multi-homing, and rival expansion.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: Two industries have identical CR4 and HHI values. One has standardized products and transparent prices; the other has differentiated products and rapid innovation. Why might their competitive outcomes differ?
micro.Choice A: Concentration measures do not capture every strategic and product-market feature that shapes rivalry
micro.Choice B: Equal concentration measures guarantee equal prices and profits
micro.Choice C: Differentiation is irrelevant in oligopoly
micro.Choice D: Only the number of firms can affect oligopoly behavior
micro.Correct Answer: A — Concentration measures do not capture every strategic and product-market feature that shapes rivalry
micro.Feedback: Concentration is informative but does not summarize product differentiation, innovation, information, costs, or strategic conduct.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: A concentrated industry has high prices, strong product innovation, and frequent entry by niche rivals. Which analysis is strongest?
micro.Choice A: Conclude the industry is harmful solely because prices are high
micro.Choice B: Conclude the industry is efficient solely because innovation is high
micro.Choice C: Ignore entry because the incumbent firms are large
micro.Choice D: Evaluate market power, innovation benefits, entry conditions, and consumer substitution together
micro.Correct Answer: D — Evaluate market power, innovation benefits, entry conditions, and consumer substitution together
micro.Feedback: Oligopoly welfare requires integrating several margins rather than treating one statistic as decisive.

micro.Question: A merger creates a verifiable 20% marginal-cost reduction but removes the closest rival. Which analysis is strongest?

micro.Choice D: Treat the lower marginal cost as a fixed-cost saving, so it affects profit but provides no possible offset to higher pricing incentives.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Compare the pricing incentive from weaker rivalry with the extent to which marginal-cost savings reach consumers.
micro.Feedback: Oligopoly policy requires evidence about conduct, entry, efficiencies, and consumer effects.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.
micro.Question: A platform has strong network effects but users can easily use several competing platforms at the same time. What follows?

micro.Choice B: Network effects raise concentration pressure, but using several platforms at once may preserve competition

micro.Choice D: Easily using several platforms at once removes the strategic importance of network effects because users face little reason to coordinate
micro.Correct Answer: B — Network effects raise concentration pressure, but using several platforms at once may preserve competition
micro.Feedback: Oligopoly policy requires evidence about conduct, entry, efficiencies, and consumer effects.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.

micro.Choice B: The conduct must be illegal
micro.Choice C: Static price costs and dynamic innovation benefits both require evidence
micro.Choice D: The outcome must be perfectly competitive
micro.Correct Answer: C — Static price costs and dynamic innovation benefits both require evidence
micro.Feedback: Oligopoly policy requires evidence about conduct, entry, efficiencies, and consumer effects.

micro.Learning Objective: OLI.6 — Evaluate cartel welfare, mergers, concentration, innovation, and antitrust tradeoffs.

micro.Correct Answer: D — The pattern alone does not establish collusion
micro.Feedback: Oligopoly policy requires evidence about conduct, entry, efficiencies, and consumer effects.
