micro.Question: A permanent demand increase in a decreasing-cost industry can cause long-run price to:
micro.Choice A: Remain above the short-run price
micro.Choice B: Equal zero

micro.Choice D: Settle below the original level

micro.Question: Which condition represents productive efficiency?

micro.Learning Objective: PC.6 — Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.
micro.Question: Entry stops when:

micro.Choice B: Market output is zero

micro.Choice D: Economic profit has been eliminated
micro.Correct Answer: D — Economic profit has been eliminated

micro.Learning Objective: PC.6 — Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.
micro.Question: Exit stops when:

micro.Learning Objective: PC.6 — Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.
micro.Question: A demand increase first raises price and profit, then entry lowers price. This describes:
micro.Choice A: A shutdown decision only

micro.Question: Why can perfect competition be efficient but not equitable?

micro.Learning Objective: PC.6 — Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.
micro.Question: An external cost is unpriced. Which equality may still hold privately while social efficiency fails?

micro.Choice B: P=min AFC
micro.Choice C: MR=ATC
micro.Choice D: P=private MC
micro.Correct Answer: D — P=private MC
micro.Feedback: Private and social marginal cost can differ.

micro.Learning Objective: PC.6 — Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.
micro.Question: An information problem prevents buyers from evaluating quality. Which result is threatened?
micro.Choice A: The welfare conclusion of the benchmark

micro.Learning Objective: PC.6 — Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.
micro.Question: In a constant-cost industry, horizontal long-run supply means:

micro.Learning Objective: PC.6 — Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.
micro.Question: Use the paired market and firm diagram. Under free entry with identical firms and unchanged input prices and cost curves, which current profit and eventual market adjustment eliminate the incentive to enter?
micro.Choice A: $1,500; entry expands market supply, lowering price and each firm’s output along rising MC until economic profit is zero.
micro.Choice B: $1,800; entry reduces market supply and raises each survivor’s price and output until profit is zero.
micro.Choice C: $1,500; entry reduces market supply and raises each survivor’s price and output until profit is zero.
micro.Choice D: $1,800; entry expands market supply, lowering price and each firm’s output along rising MC until economic profit is zero.
micro.Correct Answer: D — $1,800; entry expands market supply, lowering price and each firm’s output along rising MC until economic profit is zero.
micro.Feedback: The market sets P = 40. The firm chooses Q = 90, with ATC = 20, earning (40−20) × 90 = 1800. Entry adds market supply and lowers the shared price. Each firm’s MR falls and its output contracts along fixed rising MC. Under the stated conditions adjustment ends at P = MC = minimum ATC.

micro.Learning Objective: PC.6 — Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.
micro.Question: Use the paired market and firm diagram to compare the firm’s revenue, variable cost and total cost. Which operating loss and decisions distinguish the short run from the long run?
micro.Choice A: $100; operate because P > AVC, while persistent losses lead to exit and higher market price.
micro.Choice B: $150; operate because P > AVC, while persistent losses lead to exit and higher market price.
micro.Choice C: $150; shut down immediately because P < ATC, even though producing covers avoidable cost.
micro.Choice D: $100; shut down immediately because P < ATC, even though producing covers avoidable cost.
micro.Correct Answer: B — $150; operate because P > AVC, while persistent losses lead to exit and higher market price.
micro.Feedback: The market sets P = 15; rising MC gives Q = 50. AVC = 10 < P = 15 < ATC = 18, so the operating loss is 150 and shutdown would sacrifice a contribution to fixed cost. Persistent losses induce exit and raise price as market supply contracts.

micro.Learning Objective: PC.6 — Analyze entry, exit, long-run equilibrium, industry cost conditions, and efficiency.
micro.Question: Starting with market price in the paired market and firm diagram, which firm output and cost relationships summarize the long-run competitive equilibrium?
micro.Choice A: P = $20, Q = 40; P = MC = minimum ATC gives zero economic profit and no net entry or exit pressure.
micro.Choice B: P = $25, Q = 50; P = AVC alone establishes long-run break-even and removes all entry or exit pressure.
micro.Choice C: P = $20, Q = 40; P = AVC alone establishes long-run break-even and removes all entry or exit pressure.
micro.Choice D: P = $25, Q = 50; P = MC = minimum ATC gives zero economic profit and no net entry or exit pressure.
micro.Correct Answer: D — P = $25, Q = 50; P = MC = minimum ATC gives zero economic profit and no net entry or exit pressure.
micro.Feedback: The market supplies price 25 to the firm. Its rising MC crosses at Q = 50, also the ATC minimum. P = MC gives marginal efficiency; P = min ATC gives productive efficiency and zero economic profit. Covering AVC alone is only a short-run operating criterion.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.8 — Perfect Substitutes and Perfect Complements
micro.Question: The consumer is always willing to trade two units of Y for one X. What preference form fits?

micro.Choice B: Strictly convex preferences with changing MRS
micro.Choice C: A vertical budget line
micro.Choice D: Perfect substitutes with straight-line indifference curves
micro.Correct Answer: D — Perfect substitutes with straight-line indifference curves
micro.Feedback: A constant tradeoff produces a constant MRS and therefore straight, parallel indifference curves.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.8 — Perfect Substitutes and Perfect Complements
micro.Question: X and Y are useful only in fixed one-to-one pairs. What preference form fits?
micro.Choice A: Perfect complements with L-shaped indifference curves
micro.Choice B: Perfect substitutes with straight lines
micro.Choice C: A good and a bad
micro.Choice D: Preferences with constant MRS
micro.Correct Answer: A — Perfect complements with L-shaped indifference curves
micro.Feedback: Extra units of only one component add no benefit, producing right-angle indifference curves around matched pairs.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.8 — Perfect Substitutes and Perfect Complements
micro.Question: For a consumer with perfect-substitute preferences represented by U = 2X + Y, which bundle is equally preferred to (1 X, 0 Y)?
micro.Feedback: Both the original bundle and (0, 2) have utility 2. One unit of X replaces two units of Y.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.8 — Perfect Substitutes and Perfect Complements
micro.Question: A consumer treats X and Y as perfect substitutes at a constant rate. With X horizontal and Y vertical, what shape do the indifference curves have?
micro.Choice A: L-shaped curves.
micro.Choice B: Strictly bowed curves with a changing slope.
micro.Choice C: Upward-sloping curves when both goods are desirable.
micro.Choice D: Straight, downward-sloping lines.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Straight, downward-sloping lines.
micro.Feedback: A constant willingness to substitute implies a constant negative slope.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.8 — Perfect Substitutes and Perfect Complements
micro.Question: X and Y are useful only in one-to-one pairs. A consumer has 4 X and 7 Y and receives one more Y. What happens to the number of useful pairs?
micro.Choice A: It stays at 4.
micro.Choice B: It rises to 5.
micro.Choice C: It rises to 8.
micro.Choice D: It falls to 3.
micro.Correct Answer: A — It stays at 4.
micro.Feedback: X is the limiting good. Extra Y alone cannot create another complete pair.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.8 — Perfect Substitutes and Perfect Complements
micro.Question: A consumer uses X and Y only in one-to-one pairs. Where are the kinks of the indifference curves?
micro.Choice A: On the line X = 2Y.
micro.Choice B: Only on the X-axis.
micro.Choice C: On the line X = Y.
micro.Choice D: At every point on a straight downward-sloping line.
micro.Correct Answer: C — On the line X = Y.
micro.Feedback: A kink occurs where neither component is in excess: X and Y are equal.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.8 — Perfect Substitutes and Perfect Complements
micro.Question: X and Y are useful only in one-to-one pairs. A consumer has 4 X and 7 Y, then loses 4 Y. How many useful pairs are lost?
micro.Choice A: 1 pair.
micro.Choice B: None.
micro.Choice C: 3 pairs.
micro.Choice D: 4 pairs.
micro.Correct Answer: A — 1 pair.
micro.Feedback: Initially X limits the consumer to 4 pairs. After the loss, only 3 Y remain, so Y becomes the limiting good and there are 3 pairs.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.8 — Perfect Substitutes and Perfect Complements
micro.Question: X and Y are useful only in one-to-one pairs. X costs $2, Y costs $3, and income is $20. Which bundle provides the greatest number of complete pairs?
micro.Choice A: 10 X and 0 Y.
micro.Choice B: 0 X and 6 Y.
micro.Choice C: 4 X and 4 Y.
micro.Choice D: 5 X and 2 Y.
micro.Correct Answer: C — 4 X and 4 Y.
micro.Feedback: Each complete pair costs $5. Four pairs exhaust the $20 budget and provide more complete pairs than the alternatives.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.8 — Perfect Substitutes and Perfect Complements
micro.Question: A consumer treats X and Y as perfect substitutes, with U = 2X + Y. X costs $3 and Y costs $1. With positive income and divisible goods, which spending pattern gives the most utility?
micro.Choice A: Spend all income on X.
micro.Choice B: Spend all income on Y.
micro.Choice C: Buy equal quantities of X and Y.
micro.Choice D: Any affordable bundle gives the same utility.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Spend all income on Y.
micro.Feedback: X gives 2/3 utility units per dollar and Y gives 1. With perfect substitutes, all spending goes to the higher-return good.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.8 — Perfect Substitutes and Perfect Complements
micro.Question: A consumer treats X and Y as perfect substitutes, with U = 2X + Y. X costs $2 and Y costs $1. If income is $12 and goods are divisible, which bundles maximize utility?
micro.Choice A: Only (6 X, 0 Y).
micro.Choice B: Only (0 X, 12 Y).
micro.Choice C: Only bundles with equal quantities of X and Y.
micro.Choice D: Every bundle on the budget line 2X + Y = 12.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Every bundle on the budget line 2X + Y = 12.
micro.Feedback: Each good provides one utility unit per dollar. All bundles spending the full $12 yield utility 12.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.8 — Perfect Substitutes and Perfect Complements
micro.Question: A consumer uses X and Y only in one-to-one pairs and spends $24 on them. Initially each good costs $2. If X rises to $4 while Y stays at $2, how does the number of pairs purchased change?
micro.Choice A: It falls from 6 to 4; only purchases of X fall.
micro.Choice B: It remains at 6 because Y’s price is unchanged.
micro.Choice C: It falls from 6 to 4; purchases of both goods fall.
micro.Choice D: It rises from 6 to 8 because X is more expensive.
micro.Correct Answer: C — It falls from 6 to 4; purchases of both goods fall.
micro.Feedback: The cost of a pair rises from $4 to $6. With fixed income, pairs fall from 24/4 = 6 to 24/6 = 4, reducing demand for both complements.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.5
micro.Question: The economist's role in policy analysis is primarily to:
micro.Choice A: Clarify likely tradeoffs and consequences
micro.Choice B: Choose everyone's values
micro.Choice C: Guarantee a policy works
micro.Choice D: Eliminate scarcity
micro.Correct Answer: A — Clarify likely tradeoffs and consequences
micro.Feedback: Economics can analyze consequences and tradeoffs, while value judgments remain separate choices.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.5
micro.Common Misconception: Giving economists authority to choose society’s values.
micro.Question: An economist estimates a policy’s effects, then recommends adoption. What two roles appear?
micro.Choice A: Scientist for the estimate and adviser for the recommendation
micro.Choice B: Adviser for both because policy is mentioned
micro.Choice C: Scientist for both because evidence is used
micro.Choice D: Legislator for the estimate and judge for the advice
micro.Correct Answer: A — Scientist for the estimate and adviser for the recommendation
micro.Feedback: Economists can estimate consequences; recommendations also require value judgments.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.1
micro.Question: A policy improves pay for some workers, reduces job opportunities for others, and may raise consumer prices. Which policy is most likely being described?
micro.Choice A: A nonbinding price ceiling above equilibrium
micro.Choice B: A decrease in CPI caused by quality improvements
micro.Choice C: A tax cut on sellers in a competitive market
micro.Choice D: A binding minimum wage above equilibrium
micro.Correct Answer: D — A binding minimum wage above equilibrium
micro.Feedback: A binding minimum wage helps some workers who keep jobs, can reduce employment for others, and may raise business costs and consumer prices.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.4
micro.Question: A positive statement is best described as:
micro.Choice A: A testable claim about how the world is
micro.Choice B: A claim about how the world should be
micro.Choice C: A statement that is always good
micro.Choice D: A policy recommendation
micro.Correct Answer: A — A testable claim about how the world is
micro.Feedback: Positive statements describe or predict how the world is.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.4
micro.Question: A statement using 'should' is usually:
micro.Choice A: Positive
micro.Choice B: Normative
micro.Choice C: A demand shifter
micro.Choice D: A supply schedule
micro.Correct Answer: B — Normative
micro.Feedback: Normative statements make value judgments about what should happen.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.4
micro.Common Misconception: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
micro.Question: A price-support study predicts more output, then recommends the policy as fair. How should these two claims be evaluated?
micro.Choice A: Test the output prediction separately from the fairness judgment
micro.Choice B: Ignore the prediction once advice appears
micro.Choice C: Treat both parts as positive because evidence exists
micro.Choice D: Treat both parts as normative because policy is involved
micro.Correct Answer: A — Test the output prediction separately from the fairness judgment
micro.Feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.4
micro.Question: An analyst writes: "A congestion charge will reduce downtown car trips by 10%. That reduction is worth the added financial burden on commuters." How are the two claims classified?
micro.Choice A: First normative; second positive.
micro.Choice B: Both positive.
micro.Choice C: First positive; second normative.
micro.Choice D: Both normative.
micro.Correct Answer: C — First positive; second normative.
micro.Feedback: The 10% traffic prediction can be tested against evidence, whether or not it proves true. Saying the reduction is worth the burden ranks competing outcomes; that judgment needs a value premise that traffic data alone cannot establish.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.4
micro.Common Misconception: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
micro.Question: A transit study predicts that a lower fare will increase ridership. Why is this positive?
micro.Choice A: Evidence could test the predicted change
micro.Choice B: The prediction must be socially desirable
micro.Choice C: The result is guaranteed to be true
micro.Choice D: Transit policy contains no value judgment
micro.Correct Answer: A — Evidence could test the predicted change
micro.Feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.4
micro.Common Misconception: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
micro.Question: A council member says parks should receive more funding because access is fair. Why is this normative?
micro.Choice A: It includes a government budget
micro.Choice B: It ranks outcomes using a value judgment
micro.Choice C: It predicts a measurable funding change
micro.Choice D: It must be supported by all voters
micro.Correct Answer: B — It ranks outcomes using a value judgment
micro.Feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.4
micro.Question: Which statement is positive?
micro.Choice A: The city should make rent cheaper.
micro.Choice B: Rent control is unfair.
micro.Choice C: A binding rent ceiling reduces apartment supply
micro.Choice D: The best policy is always lower rent.
micro.Correct Answer: C — A binding rent ceiling reduces apartment supply
micro.Feedback: This is positive because it makes a testable claim about what the policy will do.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.4
micro.Question: An economist says, 'The city should accept some efficiency loss to make housing more affordable.' What makes this normative?
micro.Choice A: It can be tested with rental data alone
micro.Choice B: It uses a value judgment about what policy should do
micro.Choice C: It describes only current prices
micro.Choice D: It states the law of demand
micro.Correct Answer: B — It uses a value judgment about what policy should do
micro.Feedback: The statement recommends what policy should do, so it is normative.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.4
micro.Question: Which statement is positive rather than normative?
micro.Choice A: A binding rent ceiling reduces the quantity of rental housing supplied
micro.Choice B: The city should cap rents to protect tenants
micro.Choice C: Housing is too important to leave to markets
micro.Choice D: Fair rents matter more than landlord profits
micro.Correct Answer: A — A binding rent ceiling reduces the quantity of rental housing supplied
micro.Feedback: The claim that a binding rent ceiling reduces the quantity of rental housing supplied is a testable prediction. The other claims prescribe what the city should do or express judgments about fairness and priorities.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.4
micro.Question: An economist says, 'A higher minimum wage will reduce employment among low-skill workers.' What kind of statement is this?
micro.Choice A: Positive
micro.Choice B: Normative
micro.Choice C: A price floor
micro.Choice D: A circular-flow claim
micro.Correct Answer: A — Positive
micro.Feedback: This is positive because it makes a testable claim about cause and effect.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.4
micro.Common Misconception: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
micro.Question: A commissioner says the city ought to favor safer streets even if travel takes longer. What makes this normative?
micro.Choice A: The ability to measure travel time
micro.Choice B: The ranking of safety against travel time
micro.Choice C: The prediction that streets can change
micro.Choice D: The reference to a city decision
micro.Correct Answer: B — The ranking of safety against travel time
micro.Feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.4
micro.Question: An economist says, 'A rent ceiling below equilibrium will reduce housing quality over time.' Another says, 'The city should accept that cost to help low-income renters.' Which pairing is correct?
micro.Choice A: First is positive; second is normative
micro.Choice B: First is normative; second is positive
micro.Choice C: Both are positive
micro.Choice D: Both are normative
micro.Correct Answer: A — First is positive; second is normative
micro.Feedback: The first is testable. The second recommends what policy should do, so it is normative.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.4
micro.Question: A report predicts that extending library hours will increase weekly visits. Another recommends the extension because access is worth the staffing cost. Which assessment is correct?
micro.Choice A: The visit prediction is testable; the recommendation adds a value judgment
micro.Choice B: Both claims are normative because a public agency is involved
micro.Choice C: The recommendation is positive because staffing costs can be measured
micro.Choice D: The visit prediction is normative until the extension occurs
micro.Correct Answer: A — The visit prediction is testable; the recommendation adds a value judgment
micro.Feedback: Evidence can test the predicted visit change. Calling improved access worth its cost also ranks outcomes; future predictions can be positive before observation.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.4
micro.Question: An evaluator says, "Option A saves more staff time, so it is the best policy." Which reply separates the testable component from the hidden value premise?
micro.Choice A: Measure the time savings, then ask why that objective should outrank other consequences
micro.Choice B: Treat the entire sentence as positive because staff time is measurable
micro.Choice C: Treat the time-saving estimate as normative because it supports a recommendation
micro.Choice D: Conclude more accurate timing data will uniquely determine the preferred policy
micro.Correct Answer: A — Measure the time savings, then ask why that objective should outrank other consequences
micro.Feedback: Time savings can be tested. Moving from that estimate to "best" requires a criterion for weighing time against other outcomes.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.4
micro.Question: A board ranks plans only by the number of people served and selects A. New evidence shows B serves more people but offers less privacy. Which conclusion distinguishes logic from values?
micro.Choice A: Choosing A would necessarily show the new service count is false
micro.Choice B: Its stated rule now favors B; preferring A would require changing or qualifying that rule
micro.Choice C: The privacy difference makes the service-count evidence normative
micro.Choice D: More people served proves B is morally superior under every criterion
micro.Correct Answer: B — Its stated rule now favors B; preferring A would require changing or qualifying that rule
micro.Feedback: A fixed criterion has implications that evidence can change. Preferring privacy can justify a different criterion, but does not refute the service-count evidence.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.4
micro.Question: A forecast says a digitization plan will reduce waiting. A recommendation says it should be adopted only if access for people without internet is protected. Waiting falls but offline access worsens. Which inference is sound?
micro.Choice A: Observed waiting reductions prove the plan satisfies the value criterion
micro.Choice B: The forecast becomes normative because implementation affected access
micro.Choice C: The forecast is supported, while the recommendation's stated condition is unmet
micro.Choice D: The failed access condition refutes the waiting-time forecast
micro.Correct Answer: C — The forecast is supported, while the recommendation's stated condition is unmet
micro.Feedback: The observed waiting result bears on the positive claim. Protecting offline access is a separate condition in the recommendation; success on one outcome does not satisfy it.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.4
micro.Question: A report states that volunteers prefer evening shifts and therefore evening-only service is fair. A representative survey confirms the preference. What remains unresolved?
micro.Choice A: Whether a confirmed preference statement can count as positive
micro.Choice B: Whether using a survey converts the fairness conclusion into a measured fact
micro.Choice C: Whether the fairness judgment proves daytime users have no unmet needs
micro.Choice D: Whether fairness should be judged by volunteer preferences rather than users' access
micro.Correct Answer: D — Whether fairness should be judged by volunteer preferences rather than users' access
micro.Feedback: A preference claim is empirically testable. The move from measured volunteer preferences to fairness requires a value premise about whose interests count.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.4
micro.Question: A rule gives priority to people facing the greatest hardship. New data show that a different group meets that description. What change is consistent with keeping the same normative principle?
micro.Choice A: Change the priority group because the evidence changed who satisfies the criterion
micro.Choice B: Keep the old group because normative principles cannot use evidence
micro.Choice C: Declare hardship measurement normative solely because it informs policy
micro.Choice D: Treat the data as proof that greatest-hardship priority is the only fair principle
micro.Correct Answer: A — Change the priority group because the evidence changed who satisfies the criterion
micro.Feedback: A stable value criterion can lead to a different recommendation when facts change. Evidence identifies its beneficiaries without uniquely establishing the criterion itself.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.4
micro.Question: A researcher predicts that simplifying an application raises completion when eligibility is unchanged. A trial simplifies the form and broadens eligibility; completion rises. Which statement is justified?
micro.Choice A: Only recommendations can be evaluated when two policies change together
micro.Choice B: The prediction is positive, but the joint change does not isolate the form's effect
micro.Choice C: The rise proves the form alone caused every added completion
micro.Choice D: The extra eligibility change makes the original claim normative
micro.Correct Answer: B — The prediction is positive, but the joint change does not isolate the form's effect
micro.Feedback: The conditional causal prediction is testable. Because eligibility changed too, the observation does not by itself identify the effect of form simplification.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.4
micro.Question: Which statement is positive?
micro.Choice A: Investment spending raises GDP, other things equal
micro.Choice B: The government should spend more
micro.Choice C: GDP is the fairest possible measure
micro.Choice D: Every country should maximize GDP at all costs
micro.Correct Answer: A — Investment spending raises GDP, other things equal
micro.Feedback: A positive statement is testable. If investment rises and other components stay fixed, GDP rises.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.4
micro.Question: What is a positive statement?
micro.Choice A: A testable claim about how the world is
micro.Choice B: A claim about how the world should be
micro.Choice C: A statement that is always morally good
micro.Choice D: A policy recommendation
micro.Correct Answer: A — A testable claim about how the world is
micro.Feedback: A positive statement describes or predicts how the world is.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.4
micro.Question: An instructor presents this claim: 'A price ceiling below equilibrium creates a shortage.' What kind of statement is this?
micro.Choice A: Normative
micro.Choice B: Positive
micro.Choice C: A value judgment
micro.Choice D: A policy recommendation
micro.Correct Answer: B — Positive
micro.Feedback: This is positive because it is a testable cause-and-effect claim.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.4
micro.Question: An instructor gives two claims. Claim 1: 'Rent control reduces housing supply.' Claim 2: 'The city should use rent control anyway.' Which pairing is correct?
micro.Choice A: Claim 1 is normative; Claim 2 is positive
micro.Choice B: Both claims are positive
micro.Choice C: Claim 1 is positive; Claim 2 is normative
micro.Choice D: Both claims are normative
micro.Correct Answer: C — Claim 1 is positive; Claim 2 is normative
micro.Feedback: The first claim is testable. The second claim recommends what should happen, so it is normative.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.4
micro.Question: An adviser predicts a wage rule raises employed teenagers’ annual income by $8 million but reduces teenage employment by 3%. She recommends it because the income gain is worth the employment loss. A pilot instead finds a 1% job loss. Which conclusion separates evidence from values?
micro.Choice A: The pilot makes the original employment prediction normative because a positive statement cannot be contradicted by data.
micro.Choice B: The pilot challenges the size of the positive employment prediction; it does not by itself establish the adviser’s tradeoff criterion.
micro.Choice C: The smaller loss proves the recommendation objectively correct, regardless of how the affected teenagers value work and income.
micro.Choice D: The recommendation makes both numerical predictions normative, so neither can be evaluated using pilot evidence.
micro.Correct Answer: B — The pilot challenges the size of the positive employment prediction; it does not by itself establish the adviser’s tradeoff criterion.
micro.Feedback: Predictions about income and employment are testable positive claims even when inaccurate. Calling one outcome worth another introduces a value judgment. New evidence informs the tradeoff but cannot supply the normative weighting by itself.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.4
micro.Common Misconception: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
micro.Question: A report states: (1) a tax reduces cigarette purchases; (2) the tax burden falls heavily on low-income smokers; (3) therefore the tax is unjust. Which classification is correct?
micro.Choice A: All three are positive, because technical wording removes every value judgment
micro.Choice B: Only statement 1 is positive
micro.Choice C: Statements 1 and 2 are positive; statement 3 is normative
micro.Choice D: Statements 2 and 3 are normative
micro.Correct Answer: C — Statements 1 and 2 are positive; statement 3 is normative
micro.Feedback: The first two claims can be tested empirically. The conclusion that the policy is unjust is normative.

micro.Common Misconception: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
micro.Question: Does positive mean good or favorable?
micro.Choice A: Yes; positive means the outcome is desirable
micro.Choice B: Yes; positive claims support the policy being discussed
micro.Choice C: No; it means testable in principle
micro.Choice D: Yes; positive claims are facts that must be true.
micro.Correct Answer: C — No; it means testable in principle
micro.Feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

micro.Common Misconception: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
micro.Question: Does false automatically mean normative?
micro.Choice A: Yes; normative claims are the claims that turn out to be false
micro.Choice B: Yes; positive claims must be factually correct
micro.Choice C: Yes; a claim becomes normative once evidence rejects it.
micro.Choice D: No; a false claim can still be testable
micro.Correct Answer: D — No; a false claim can still be testable
micro.Feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

micro.Common Misconception: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
micro.Question: Is every policy statement normative?
micro.Choice A: No; policy predictions can be positive
micro.Choice B: Yes; any statement about government policy is normative
micro.Choice C: Yes; policy effects cannot be tested with evidence
micro.Choice D: Yes; mentioning a recommendation makes every related claim normative.
micro.Correct Answer: A — No; policy predictions can be positive
micro.Feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

micro.Common Misconception: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
micro.Question: Does technical tone guarantee a positive claim?
micro.Choice A: Yes; technical language makes a statement factual
micro.Choice B: No; technical wording can conceal a value judgment
micro.Choice C: Yes; numerical language removes value judgments
micro.Choice D: Yes; professional wording means the claim can be tested.
micro.Correct Answer: B — No; technical wording can conceal a value judgment
micro.Feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

micro.Common Misconception: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
micro.Question: An economist predicts job losses and recommends against a rule. What additional judgment turns the prediction into policy advice?
micro.Choice A: The existence of a measurable employment effect
micro.Choice B: The fact that the rule is a government policy
micro.Choice C: The recommendation adds a value judgment about the predicted cost
micro.Choice D: The use of an economic forecast.
micro.Correct Answer: C — The recommendation adds a value judgment about the predicted cost
micro.Feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

micro.Common Misconception: Assuming objective wording alone makes a claim positive.
micro.Question: A model predicts a tax effect under stated assumptions. Why is it positive?
micro.Choice A: Because the prediction supports the tax
micro.Choice B: Because the model is written in technical language
micro.Choice C: Because the prediction must be true if the assumptions are stated.
micro.Choice D: Evidence could test the conditional prediction
micro.Correct Answer: D — Evidence could test the conditional prediction
micro.Feedback: Identify what observation could support or contradict the testable component.

micro.Common Misconception: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
micro.Question: A library reports that Sunday hours increased visits. What makes this positive?
micro.Choice A: The increase in visits is a desirable outcome
micro.Choice B: Library officials support Sunday hours
micro.Choice C: The report is written confidently, so the claim must be true.
micro.Choice D: Visit records could test the claimed increase
micro.Correct Answer: D — Visit records could test the claimed increase
micro.Feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

micro.Common Misconception: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
micro.Question: “The library should stay open Sundays because access matters.” Why is this normative?
micro.Choice A: It recommends a choice using a value judgment
micro.Choice B: Sunday visits can be counted
micro.Choice C: The statement concerns a public institution
micro.Choice D: Evidence could show whether Sunday hours increase attendance.
micro.Correct Answer: A — It recommends a choice using a value judgment
micro.Feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

micro.Common Misconception: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
micro.Question: A forecast that later proves false can still be positive when:
micro.Choice A: The forecast was made by an expert
micro.Choice B: Evidence could in principle have tested it
micro.Choice C: The forecast described an outcome people wanted
micro.Choice D: The forecast was stated with certainty.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Evidence could in principle have tested it
micro.Feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

micro.Common Misconception: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
micro.Question: Which claim is normative in a school debate?
micro.Choice A: Average class size fell by two students last year
micro.Choice B: Smaller classes increased per-student spending
micro.Choice C: The district ought to favor smaller classes despite higher costs
micro.Choice D: Enrollment is projected to rise next year.
micro.Correct Answer: C — The district ought to favor smaller classes despite higher costs
micro.Feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

micro.Common Misconception: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
micro.Question: Which claim is positive in a transit debate?
micro.Choice A: The city should make transit more affordable
micro.Choice B: Lower fares are fairer to low-income riders
micro.Choice C: Expanding transit access is more important than balancing the transit budget.
micro.Choice D: A lower fare increased weekday ridership
micro.Correct Answer: D — A lower fare increased weekday ridership
micro.Feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

micro.Common Misconception: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
micro.Question: A report says a fee reduced waste and therefore is fair. What is normative?
micro.Choice A: The claim that the fee reduced waste
micro.Choice B: The measured amount of waste reduction
micro.Choice C: The judgment that the fee is fair
micro.Choice D: The fact that a fee was imposed.
micro.Correct Answer: C — The judgment that the fee is fair
micro.Feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

micro.Common Misconception: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
micro.Question: A weakly supported prediction later fails. What classification remains possible?
micro.Choice A: Normative, because the prediction turned out to be false
micro.Choice B: Normative, because the evidence supporting it was weak
micro.Choice C: Neither positive nor normative until the prediction is confirmed.
micro.Choice D: Positive, because testability does not require truth
micro.Correct Answer: D — Positive, because testability does not require truth
micro.Feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

micro.Common Misconception: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
micro.Question: “Costs rose 8%, so the city should respond.” What is present?
micro.Choice A: A positive measurement plus a normative recommendation
micro.Choice B: A purely positive statement because it includes a measured percentage
micro.Choice C: A purely normative statement because it recommends action
micro.Choice D: Two positive claims because both parts refer to economic conditions.
micro.Correct Answer: A — A positive measurement plus a normative recommendation
micro.Feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

micro.Common Misconception: Assuming objective wording alone makes a claim positive.
micro.Question: A program “works,” but no outcome is named. What is missing?
micro.Choice A: A statement that the program is desirable
micro.Choice B: A measurable claim that evidence could contradict
micro.Choice C: A recommendation about whether the program should continue
micro.Choice D: A larger sample of people who support the program.
micro.Correct Answer: B — A measurable claim that evidence could contradict
micro.Feedback: Identify what observation could support or contradict the testable component.

micro.Common Misconception: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
micro.Question: “Equal access matters more than maximum output.” What is this?
micro.Choice A: A positive claim because access and output can both be measured
micro.Choice B: A positive claim because it compares two economic outcomes
micro.Choice C: A normative ranking of competing values
micro.Choice D: Neither positive nor normative because no policy is named.
micro.Correct Answer: C — A normative ranking of competing values
micro.Feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

micro.Common Misconception: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
micro.Question: A tax study uses the word efficient for a measurable revenue criterion. Is it necessarily normative?
micro.Choice A: Yes; the word efficient always expresses a value judgment
micro.Choice B: Yes; any claim about taxes is normative
micro.Choice C: Yes; a policy criterion cannot be evaluated with evidence.
micro.Choice D: No; the stated criterion can be tested with evidence
micro.Correct Answer: D — No; the stated criterion can be tested with evidence
micro.Feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

micro.Common Misconception: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
micro.Question: A subsidy is predicted to raise enrollment and is therefore recommended. Which split is correct?
micro.Choice A: Both parts are positive because enrollment can be measured
micro.Choice B: Both parts are normative because a subsidy is a policy
micro.Choice C: The forecast is positive; the recommendation is normative
micro.Choice D: The forecast is normative; the recommendation is positive.
micro.Correct Answer: C — The forecast is positive; the recommendation is normative
micro.Feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

micro.Common Misconception: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
micro.Question: “The policy benefits most residents, so it is just.” Where is the normative step?
micro.Choice A: The claim that most residents benefit
micro.Choice B: The number of residents affected by the policy
micro.Choice C: The measured size of the benefits.
micro.Choice D: Calling the distribution just
micro.Correct Answer: D — Calling the distribution just
micro.Feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

micro.Common Misconception: Assuming objective wording alone makes a claim positive.
micro.Question: What could test the claim that a road fee reduces congestion?
micro.Choice A: Traffic counts around comparable fee changes
micro.Choice B: A survey asking whether drivers think the fee is fair
micro.Choice C: A city council vote on the fee
micro.Choice D: A statement from officials that the fee will work.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Traffic counts around comparable fee changes
micro.Feedback: Identify what observation could support or contradict the testable component.

micro.Common Misconception: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
micro.Question: When can “the project has positive net benefits” be positive?
micro.Choice A: Always, because net benefits are measured in dollars
micro.Choice B: When inputs and the net-benefit rule are empirically checkable
micro.Choice C: Never, because the word benefits is inherently normative
micro.Choice D: Only when everyone agrees the project is desirable.
micro.Correct Answer: B — When inputs and the net-benefit rule are empirically checkable
micro.Feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

micro.Common Misconception: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
micro.Question: “The only acceptable policy is universal access.” Why is this normative?
micro.Choice A: Universal access can be measured
micro.Choice B: The statement refers to a policy outcome
micro.Choice C: It embeds a value standard despite objective wording
micro.Choice D: The sentence does not include a numerical prediction.
micro.Correct Answer: C — It embeds a value standard despite objective wording
micro.Feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

micro.Common Misconception: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
micro.Question: A rule lowers costs but is called morally wrong. What can evidence settle?
micro.Choice A: Both the cost effect and whether the rule is morally wrong
micro.Choice B: Only whether the rule is morally wrong
micro.Choice C: Neither claim, because the rule is a policy.
micro.Choice D: The cost effect, but not the moral conclusion by itself
micro.Correct Answer: D — The cost effect, but not the moral conclusion by itself
micro.Feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

micro.Common Misconception: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
micro.Question: A report defines success only as maximum total surplus. What choice is normative?
micro.Choice A: Calculating total surplus from observed prices and quantities
micro.Choice B: Selecting total surplus as the sole ranking criterion
micro.Choice C: Measuring how total surplus changes after the policy
micro.Choice D: Estimating the policy’s effect on output.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Selecting total surplus as the sole ranking criterion
micro.Feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

micro.Common Misconception: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
micro.Question: Two analysts agree that an archive plan preserves more records but delays public access. One recommends it; the other rejects it. What additional finding would show a factual disagreement as well as a value disagreement?
micro.Choice A: They agree on the delay but differ on whether it is acceptable
micro.Choice B: They use the same probabilities but prefer different distributions of access
micro.Choice C: They assign different probabilities to permanent record loss under the alternative
micro.Choice D: They give different ethical priority to immediate public access
micro.Correct Answer: C — They assign different probabilities to permanent record loss under the alternative
micro.Feedback: Probabilities of record loss are empirical assessments. The other differences concern how agreed consequences should be valued.

micro.Common Misconception: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
micro.Question: A report finds that a shuttle saves travelers time but increases neighborhood noise. It recommends adoption using travelers' gains alone. Which critique is precise?
micro.Choice A: Time savings become normative when expressed in money
micro.Choice B: Adding more precise effect estimates removes the need to decide whose welfare counts
micro.Choice C: The effects are testable; excluding neighbors from the recommendation embeds a value choice
micro.Choice D: Noise estimates are normative because neighbors dislike the outcome
micro.Correct Answer: C — The effects are testable; excluding neighbors from the recommendation embeds a value choice
micro.Feedback: Time and noise effects can be measured. Counting only travelers when recommending a policy assigns standing to one group and excludes another, which is a value choice.

micro.Common Misconception: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
micro.Question: Two forecasts disagree about whether a new scheduling rule will shorten next year's queues. Both specify measurable waiting times and comparable staffing. What would change their status as positive claims?
micro.Choice A: The forecast with the larger benefit is positive; the other is normative
micro.Choice B: Both become normative until next year's data exist
micro.Choice C: Agreement by the forecasters is required before evidence can test them
micro.Choice D: Neither disagreement nor the future date changes their testable status
micro.Correct Answer: D — Neither disagreement nor the future date changes their testable status
micro.Feedback: Positive status depends on empirical testability, not agreement, truth, desirability or whether the outcome has occurred. Later evidence can support one forecast over the other.

micro.Common Misconception: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
micro.Question: An analyst rejects a delivery plan because predicted delays exceed her stated acceptable limit. Better evidence places delays below that limit, but she still rejects it on privacy grounds. Which interpretation fits?
micro.Choice A: The factual case changed, and the rejection now requires an additional value criterion
micro.Choice B: The original delay forecast was normative because it supported rejection
micro.Choice C: The unchanged decision proves the new delay estimate is irrelevant to the original argument
micro.Choice D: Privacy concerns establish that the revised forecast is false
micro.Correct Answer: A — The factual case changed, and the rejection now requires an additional value criterion
micro.Feedback: The delay objection no longer follows from the updated evidence and original threshold. A privacy objection can support rejection, but it is a separate normative premise.

micro.Common Misconception: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
micro.Question: A planner defines "optimal" as maximizing visits, then claims the chosen schedule is objectively best. Another schedule serves fewer visitors but reaches people with greater need. Which statement is most defensible?
micro.Choice A: A numerical criterion cannot contain a value judgment
micro.Choice B: Visit maximization identifies an optimum under one criterion, not a uniquely justified social ranking
micro.Choice C: Calling a result optimal makes its criterion empirically true
micro.Choice D: The need difference disproves the measured visit counts
micro.Correct Answer: B — Visit maximization identifies an optimum under one criterion, not a uniquely justified social ranking
micro.Feedback: Optimization can be objective conditional on a criterion. Choosing visits rather than need as the social objective remains a normative judgment.

micro.Common Misconception: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
micro.Question: “A bus lane reduced travel time.” What kind of claim is this?
micro.Choice A: Positive and empirically testable
micro.Choice B: Normative because reduced travel time is desirable
micro.Choice C: Normative because the statement concerns transportation policy
micro.Choice D: Neither, because one observed result cannot be tested.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Positive and empirically testable
micro.Feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

micro.Common Misconception: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
micro.Question: “The city ought to accept higher costs for cleaner air.” What kind?
micro.Choice A: Positive because costs and air quality can be measured
micro.Choice B: Normative because it ranks a tradeoff
micro.Choice C: Positive because the statement describes a policy tradeoff
micro.Choice D: Neither, because the statement contains no numerical estimate.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Normative because it ranks a tradeoff
micro.Feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

micro.Common Misconception: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
micro.Question: When does a false forecast remain positive?
micro.Choice A: Only when the forecast describes a desirable outcome
micro.Choice B: Only when an expert made the forecast
micro.Choice C: When evidence could have tested the forecast
micro.Choice D: Never; a false claim cannot be positive.
micro.Correct Answer: C — When evidence could have tested the forecast
micro.Feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

micro.Common Misconception: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
micro.Question: A report predicts gains and calls them worth unequal losses. What is normative?
micro.Choice A: The judgment that gains justify the losses
micro.Choice B: The prediction that the policy creates gains
micro.Choice C: The estimated size of the gains
micro.Choice D: The measured distribution of gains and losses.
micro.Correct Answer: A — The judgment that gains justify the losses
micro.Feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

micro.Common Misconception: Assuming objective wording alone makes a claim positive.
micro.Question: What best tests “a fee reduces congestion”?
micro.Choice A: A survey asking whether residents support the fee
micro.Choice B: Traffic counts before and after comparable changes
micro.Choice C: A council vote to adopt the fee
micro.Choice D: A statement from officials that congestion will fall.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Traffic counts before and after comparable changes
micro.Feedback: Identify what observation could support or contradict the testable component.

micro.Common Misconception: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
micro.Question: Why is “Policy A is responsible” not automatically positive?
micro.Choice A: The statement mentions a policy
micro.Choice B: The word responsible refers to a measurable outcome
micro.Choice C: Responsible may hide an unstated value standard
micro.Choice D: Any sentence about policy performance is positive.
micro.Correct Answer: C — Responsible may hide an unstated value standard
micro.Feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

micro.Common Misconception: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
micro.Question: School plan A is predicted to raise scores by 6 points and reduce free time by 4 hours weekly. Plan B raises scores by 4 points and reduces free time by 1 hour. A board declares A preferable because each extra score point is worth at least 2 hours of free time. Which statement correctly distinguishes the predictions from the board’s value judgment?
micro.Choice A: The outcome predictions are normative; the board’s numerical weighting is positive, and A’s extra 2 points cost 3 hours.
micro.Choice B: All claims are positive because they contain numbers; A dominates B on both scores and free time.
micro.Choice C: The weighting is normative, so the score and time predictions cannot be tested against observed outcomes.
micro.Choice D: The outcome predictions are positive; the board’s weighting is normative, and A’s extra 2 points cost 3 hours relative to B.
micro.Correct Answer: D — The outcome predictions are positive; the board’s weighting is normative, and A’s extra 2 points cost 3 hours relative to B.
micro.Feedback: Comparative predictions imply A adds 2 score points while costing 3 more hours, or 1.5 hours per extra point. Whether that is worthwhile depends on the board’s stated value criterion, not merely on the accuracy of the predictions.

micro.Learning Objective: IP.6 — Poverty Thresholds and Measurement
micro.Question: A study of hypothetical Economy C reports that the official threshold for a household is $26,000 and measured money income is $27,800. Under that rule, how is the household classified?
micro.Choice A: Below the threshold because every household is poor
micro.Choice B: Exactly at the poverty threshold
micro.Choice C: Above the poverty threshold
micro.Choice D: Classification cannot use an explicit threshold
micro.Correct Answer: C — Above the poverty threshold
micro.Feedback: Compare the specified money-income measure, $27,800, with the $26,000 threshold; the rule is mechanical even though the measure has limitations.

micro.Choice B: Above the threshold because benefits are always counted
micro.Choice C: Exactly at the poverty threshold
micro.Choice D: Classification cannot use an explicit threshold
micro.Correct Answer: A — Below the poverty threshold

micro.Question: A hypothetical poverty rule classifies households as poor only when measured money income is strictly below $30,000. A household has $28,400 of measured money income. How is it classified?

micro.Choice B: Exactly at the threshold.

micro.Learning Objective: IP.6 — Poverty Thresholds and Measurement
micro.Question: A household has $25,800 in measured income against a $27,000 poverty threshold. A cash grant counts dollar for dollar and changes no other income. What is the smallest grant that reaches the threshold?
micro.Feedback: The shortfall is $27,000 − $25,800 = $1,200. Reaching the threshold requires closing that gap.

micro.Learning Objective: IP.6 — Poverty Thresholds and Measurement
micro.Question: A hypothetical poverty measure counts cash income but excludes food vouchers. A household has $25,000 in cash and $3,000 in vouchers; its threshold is $27,000. Replacing the vouchers with $3,000 cash changes no prices. Which conclusion follows?
micro.Choice A: Measured status remains below because transfers never enter cash income.
micro.Choice B: Measured status changes from above to below because vouchers are counted twice.
micro.Choice C: Measured status remains above because the original vouchers already count as cash.
micro.Choice D: Measured status changes from below to above the threshold, though this alone does not measure the change in well-being.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Measured status changes from below to above the threshold, though this alone does not measure the change in well-being.
micro.Feedback: The measure initially counts $25,000 and then $28,000. Classification changes mechanically; the economic value of relaxing spending restrictions is a separate question.

micro.Learning Objective: IP.6 — Poverty Thresholds and Measurement
micro.Question: Two households each have $31,000 measured income. The threshold is $30,000 for the smaller household and $34,000 for the larger. An analyst classifies both as above poverty because their incomes match. What is the error?
micro.Choice A: The analyst should classify both below poverty because their incomes match.
micro.Choice B: The analyst should compare the smaller household with the larger household’s threshold only.
micro.Choice C: The analyst should average the thresholds before classifying either household.
micro.Choice D: The analyst ignores different applicable thresholds; only the smaller household is above its threshold.
micro.Correct Answer: D — The analyst ignores different applicable thresholds; only the smaller household is above its threshold.
micro.Feedback: Each household must be compared with its own specified threshold. Equal measured income need not imply equal classification.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: On a PPF, opportunity cost is measured by:
micro.Choice A: What must be given up to gain more of the other good
micro.Choice B: The money price of the good only
micro.Choice C: The legal maximum price
micro.Choice D: The tax paid by buyers
micro.Correct Answer: A — What must be given up to gain more of the other good
micro.Feedback: Opportunity cost on a PPF is what must be given up to get more of another good.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Common Misconception: Confusing movement toward the frontier with a shift of productive capacity.
micro.Question: An economy moves from inside its PPF to the frontier without new resources. What changed?
micro.Choice A: Productive capacity necessarily expanded
micro.Choice B: Unused resources were employed more efficiently
micro.Choice C: The frontier shifted outward
micro.Choice D: Opportunity cost disappeared
micro.Correct Answer: B — Unused resources were employed more efficiently
micro.Feedback: Moving from inside the PPF to its frontier uses idle or misallocated resources more fully; productive capacity and the frontier remain unchanged.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: A bowed-out PPF shows that as more Good X is produced:
micro.Choice A: The opportunity cost of Good X rises
micro.Choice B: The opportunity cost of Good X falls to zero
micro.Choice C: The economy escapes scarcity
micro.Choice D: The PPF becomes a price floor
micro.Correct Answer: A — The opportunity cost of Good X rises
micro.Feedback: A bowed-out PPF shows increasing opportunity cost as resources are shifted toward one good.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: Why does opportunity cost usually rise along a bowed-out PPF?
micro.Choice A: Resources are perfectly identical in every use
micro.Choice B: Resources are not equally well suited to producing both goods
micro.Choice C: Scarcity disappears at high output levels
micro.Choice D: Prices are fixed by government
micro.Correct Answer: B — Resources are not equally well suited to producing both goods
micro.Feedback: Opportunity cost rises because resources are specialized and become less well suited as they are shifted into the other good.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: An economy is producing inside its PPF. What is the best interpretation?
micro.Choice A: The point is unattainable
micro.Choice B: The point is efficient
micro.Choice C: The point is attainable but inefficient
micro.Choice D: The point eliminates scarcity
micro.Correct Answer: C — The point is attainable but inefficient
micro.Feedback: A point inside the PPF can be produced, but resources are not being used efficiently.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: A workshop makes chairs and desks. Better scheduling lets previously idle machines produce more of both until no further increase in either is possible without reducing the other. Labor, machines and technology are unchanged. How does this appear on its PPF?
micro.Choice A: An outward shift of the frontier.
micro.Choice B: A move from one frontier point to another.
micro.Choice C: A move beyond the unchanged frontier.
micro.Choice D: A move from inside to the unchanged frontier.
micro.Correct Answer: D — A move from inside to the unchanged frontier.
micro.Feedback: Idle machines initially put production inside the PPF. Using existing capacity fully moves production to the frontier. The unchanged resources and technology mean capacity has not expanded, so the frontier does not shift.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: An economy gains more capital and better technology. What happens to its PPF?
micro.Choice A: It shifts outward
micro.Choice B: It shifts inward
micro.Choice C: It becomes a demand curve
micro.Choice D: It creates a binding price floor
micro.Correct Answer: A — It shifts outward
micro.Feedback: More resources or better technology increase productive capacity, shifting the PPF outward.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: A natural disaster destroys factories and equipment. What happens to the PPF?
micro.Choice A: It shifts outward
micro.Choice B: It shifts inward
micro.Choice C: The economy moves to a different point on the same PPF.
micro.Choice D: Opportunity cost disappears
micro.Correct Answer: B — It shifts inward
micro.Feedback: A loss of productive resources reduces what the economy can produce, shifting the PPF inward.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: Moving along a PPF gives up 18 units of Good Y to gain 6 units of Good X. What is the opportunity cost per unit of Good X?
micro.Choice A: 6 units of Good Y
micro.Choice B: 18 units of Good Y
micro.Choice C: 3 units of Good Y
micro.Choice D: 108 units of Good Y
micro.Correct Answer: C — 3 units of Good Y
micro.Feedback: Opportunity cost per Good X is what is given up divided by what is gained: 18 / 6 = 3.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: A PPF move gains 5 units of Good X but gives up 20 units of Good Y. What is the opportunity cost per additional Good X?
micro.Choice A: 5 units of Good Y
micro.Choice B: 20 units of Good Y
micro.Choice C: 0.25 units of Good Y
micro.Choice D: 4 units of Good Y
micro.Correct Answer: D — 4 units of Good Y
micro.Feedback: The economy gives up 20 units of Good Y to gain 5 units of Good X, so 20 / 5 = 4.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: A production possibilities frontier shows:
micro.Choice A: The exact market price of each good
micro.Choice B: Government’s preferred production mix
micro.Choice C: The economy’s current unemployment rate
micro.Choice D: Currently feasible combinations of two goods
micro.Correct Answer: D — Currently feasible combinations of two goods
micro.Feedback: A PPF shows possible production combinations with current resources and technology.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: A point inside the PPF usually means:
micro.Choice A: Resources are not being used efficiently
micro.Choice B: The point is unattainable
micro.Choice C: The economy has no tradeoffs
micro.Choice D: The economy is beyond its resources
micro.Correct Answer: A — Resources are not being used efficiently
micro.Feedback: A point inside the PPF is attainable but inefficient.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: A point outside the PPF is:
micro.Choice A: Efficient but always chosen
micro.Choice B: Unattainable with current resources and technology
micro.Choice C: A price floor
micro.Choice D: A market surplus
micro.Correct Answer: B — Unattainable with current resources and technology
micro.Feedback: A point outside the PPF cannot be reached with current resources and technology.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: Moving along a PPF usually means:
micro.Choice A: Producing more of every good without cost
micro.Choice B: Creating a tax wedge
micro.Choice C: Producing more of one good and less of another
micro.Choice D: Changing only the price level
micro.Correct Answer: C — Producing more of one good and less of another
micro.Feedback: Moving along the PPF shows a tradeoff between two goods.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: An outward shift of the PPF usually represents:
micro.Choice A: A shortage
micro.Choice B: A binding price ceiling
micro.Choice C: A decrease in demand
micro.Choice D: Economic growth
micro.Correct Answer: D — Economic growth
micro.Feedback: An outward shift means the economy can produce more than before.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: If moving from point A to point B on a PPF gives up 6 units of corn to gain 3 units of wheat, the opportunity cost per wheat is:
micro.Choice A: 2 units of corn
micro.Choice B: 3 units of corn
micro.Choice C: 6 units of corn
micro.Choice D: 18 units of corn
micro.Correct Answer: A — 2 units of corn
micro.Feedback: Opportunity cost per wheat is corn given up divided by wheat gained: 6 / 3 = 2.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: A PPF is bowed outward. Moving from low production of Good X to high production of Good X requires giving up larger and larger amounts of Good Y. What principle does this show?
micro.Choice A: Increasing opportunity cost
micro.Choice B: Constant opportunity cost
micro.Choice C: A binding price floor
micro.Choice D: A tax wedge
micro.Correct Answer: A — Increasing opportunity cost
micro.Feedback: A bowed-out PPF shows increasing opportunity cost as resources are shifted toward one good.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: A student says, 'This point is inside the PPF, so it is impossible.' What is the correction?
micro.Choice A: Inside the PPF is unattainable
micro.Choice B: Inside the PPF is efficient
micro.Choice C: Inside the PPF means economic growth
micro.Choice D: Inside the PPF is attainable but inefficient
micro.Correct Answer: D — Inside the PPF is attainable but inefficient
micro.Feedback: A point inside the PPF can be produced, but it wastes or underuses resources.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: A student says, 'This point is outside the PPF, so it is efficient.' What is the correction?
micro.Choice A: Outside the PPF is unattainable with current resources and technology
micro.Choice B: Outside the PPF is inefficient but possible
micro.Choice C: Outside the PPF means unemployment and underused resources.
micro.Choice D: Outside the PPF means a binding ceiling
micro.Correct Answer: A — Outside the PPF is unattainable with current resources and technology
micro.Feedback: Outside the PPF means the economy cannot reach that point with current resources and technology.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: With a constant production tradeoff, a country can produce either 80 units of food or 40 units of machinery. What is the opportunity cost of one unit of machinery?
micro.Choice A: 0.5 unit of machinery per unit of food
micro.Choice B: 2 units of food per unit of machinery
micro.Choice C: 2 units of machinery per unit of food
micro.Choice D: 80 units of food per unit of machinery
micro.Correct Answer: B — 2 units of food per unit of machinery
micro.Feedback: Divide the 80 units of food forgone by the 40 units of machinery gained: 80 / 40 = 2 units of food per unit of machinery. The inverse ratio, 0.5 unit of machinery per unit of food, answers the opposite question; 80 is the total endpoint sacrifice, not the cost per machinery unit.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: A storm destroys factories and equipment. What happens to the economy's PPF?
micro.Choice A: It shifts outward
micro.Choice B: The economy moves along the same PPF only
micro.Choice C: It shifts inward
micro.Choice D: The PPF becomes a demand curve
micro.Correct Answer: C — It shifts inward
micro.Feedback: A loss of productive resources reduces what the economy can produce, shifting the PPF inward.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: Worker training improves human capital and shifts the PPF outward for both goods. Which economic relationship does this illustrate?
micro.Choice A: A price ceiling creates a shortage
micro.Choice B: Human capital raises productive capacity
micro.Choice C: A tax wedge reduces market size
micro.Choice D: A positive statement becomes normative
micro.Correct Answer: B — Human capital raises productive capacity
micro.Feedback: Better worker training improves human capital and can shift the PPF outward.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: A student says, “A point outside the PPF is inefficient because the economy is not producing there.” What is wrong with that statement?
micro.Choice A: A point outside the PPF is always efficient
micro.Choice B: A point outside the PPF shows idle resources
micro.Choice C: It is unattainable with current resources, not merely inefficient.
micro.Choice D: A point outside the PPF means opportunity cost is zero
micro.Correct Answer: C — It is unattainable with current resources, not merely inefficient.
micro.Feedback: Inside the PPF is inefficient. Outside the PPF is unattainable with current resources and technology.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: An economist uses a PPF to show how producing more military goods requires producing fewer consumer goods. What is the model showing?
micro.Choice A: Tradeoffs and opportunity cost
micro.Choice B: Tax incidence
micro.Choice C: A binding price ceiling
micro.Choice D: A market surplus
micro.Correct Answer: A — Tradeoffs and opportunity cost
micro.Feedback: The PPF shows tradeoffs because producing more of one good requires giving up some of another.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: An economy moves from a point inside its PPF to a point on the PPF. What happened?
micro.Choice A: It reached an unattainable point
micro.Choice B: It used idle resources more efficiently
micro.Choice C: It created a tax wedge
micro.Choice D: It shifted demand left
micro.Correct Answer: B — It used idle resources more efficiently
micro.Feedback: Moving from inside the PPF to the frontier means resources are being used more efficiently.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: An economy gets better technology for producing both goods. What happens to its PPF?
micro.Choice A: It shifts inward
micro.Choice B: It becomes a price ceiling
micro.Choice C: It shifts outward
micro.Choice D: It creates a shortage
micro.Correct Answer: C — It shifts outward
micro.Feedback: Better technology increases productive capacity, shifting the PPF outward.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: A point is outside the PPF today but becomes attainable after an increase in capital and technology. What changed?
micro.Choice A: The market price was fixed
micro.Choice B: Demand decreased
micro.Choice C: The economy moved inside the PPF
micro.Choice D: The economy's productive capacity increased
micro.Correct Answer: D — The economy's productive capacity increased
micro.Feedback: More capital and better technology increase what the economy can produce.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: Which list contains all and only the efficient production points labeled in the PPF graph?
micro.Choice A: A, B, C, D, E
micro.Choice B: A, B, C, D, F
micro.Choice C: A, B, C, E, G
micro.Choice D: A, B, D, E, F
micro.Correct Answer: A — A, B, C, D, E
micro.Feedback: A, B, C, D, and E lie on the production possibilities frontier. F lies inside it and is inefficient; G lies outside it and is currently unattainable.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: Refer to the PPF graph. Which point is attainable but inefficient?
micro.Choice A: G
micro.Choice B: F
micro.Choice C: C
micro.Choice D: E
micro.Correct Answer: B — F
micro.Feedback: Point F is inside the PPF, so it is attainable but inefficient.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: Refer to the PPF graph. Which point is currently unattainable?
micro.Choice A: F
micro.Choice B: A
micro.Choice C: G
micro.Choice D: D
micro.Correct Answer: C — G
micro.Feedback: Point G is outside the PPF, so it is unattainable with current resources and technology.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: Refer to the PPF graph. Moving from B to C increases production of Good X by how many units?
micro.Feedback: Point B has 8 units of Good X and point C has 15, so Good X increases by 7 units.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: Refer to the PPF graph. Moving from B to C requires giving up how many units of Good Y?
micro.Feedback: Good Y falls from 45 at B to 35 at C, so the economy gives up 10 units of Good Y.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: Refer to the PPF graph. What is the opportunity cost of moving from C to D?
micro.Choice A: 6 units of Good X
micro.Choice B: 15 units of Good Y
micro.Choice C: 20 units of Good Y
micro.Choice D: 21 units of Good X
micro.Correct Answer: B — 15 units of Good Y
micro.Feedback: Moving from C to D raises Good X from 15 to 21, but Good Y falls from 35 to 20. The opportunity cost is 15 units of Good Y.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: Refer to the PPF graph. What is the opportunity cost per additional unit of Good X when moving from C to D?
micro.Choice A: 6 units of Good Y
micro.Choice B: 15 units of Good Y
micro.Choice C: 2.5 units of Good Y
micro.Choice D: 0.4 units of Good Y
micro.Correct Answer: C — 2.5 units of Good Y
micro.Feedback: Moving from C to D gains 6 units of Good X and gives up 15 units of Good Y, so 15 / 6 = 2.5 units of Good Y per Good X.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: Use the graph. Compare the opportunity cost of Good X over A to B and D to E. Which numerical evidence and conclusion fit the PPF?
micro.Choice A: The costs are 0.5 and 4 Y per X; opportunity cost rises as more X is produced.
micro.Choice B: The costs are 0.625 and 5 Y per X; opportunity cost stays constant as more X is produced.
micro.Choice C: The costs are 0.5 and 4 Y per X; opportunity cost stays constant as more X is produced.
micro.Choice D: The costs are 0.625 and 5 Y per X; opportunity cost rises as more X is produced.
micro.Correct Answer: D — The costs are 0.625 and 5 Y per X; opportunity cost rises as more X is produced.
micro.Feedback: A to B gives up 5 Y for 8 X, so the cost is 0.625 Y per X. D to E gives up 20 Y for 4 X, so the cost is 5 Y per X. This larger sacrifice per additional X shows increasing opportunity cost along the bowed frontier.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: Refer to the PPF graph. If the economy moves from F to C, what has happened?
micro.Choice A: The economy has moved from inefficient production to efficient production
micro.Choice B: The economy has moved from unattainable production to attainable production
micro.Choice C: The economy has reduced both goods
micro.Choice D: The economy has moved outside the PPF
micro.Correct Answer: A — The economy has moved from inefficient production to efficient production
micro.Feedback: Point F is inside the PPF and point C is on the PPF, so the economy moved from inefficient to efficient production.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: A country invests more in capital goods today, sacrificing consumer goods. In a PPF framework, what is the likely long-run implication?
micro.Choice A: More future growth because capital accumulation can expand productive capacity
micro.Choice B: No future effect because PPF choices never matter
micro.Choice C: Immediate elimination of scarcity because future productive capacity will be larger.
micro.Choice D: A binding price floor in the capital market
micro.Correct Answer: A — More future growth because capital accumulation can expand productive capacity
micro.Feedback: Choosing more capital goods today can increase future productive capacity and shift the PPF outward later.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: An economy moves from inside its PPF to a point on the PPF and then later shifts the PPF outward. What sequence is correct?
micro.Choice A: First scarcity disappears, then opportunity cost disappears
micro.Choice B: First efficiency improves, then productive capacity grows
micro.Choice C: First demand shifts, then price controls bind
micro.Choice D: First the economy becomes unattainable, then efficient
micro.Correct Answer: B — First efficiency improves, then productive capacity grows
micro.Feedback: Moving from inside to the frontier is improved efficiency. Shifting the frontier outward is growth.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: A new technology improves only production of medical devices, not food. Which PPF interpretation is best?
micro.Choice A: The entire frontier must shift inward
micro.Choice B: The economy moves inside the PPF
micro.Choice C: The frontier rotates outward on the medical-device axis
micro.Choice D: The law of demand no longer applies
micro.Correct Answer: C — The frontier rotates outward on the medical-device axis
micro.Feedback: Technology that improves only one good expands capacity for that good, rotating the PPF outward along that axis.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: A PPF table shows that moving from Bundle B to Bundle C increases wheat from 40 to 55 but reduces corn from 90 to 60. What is the opportunity cost per additional unit of wheat?
micro.Choice A: 15 units of corn
micro.Choice B: 30 units of corn
micro.Choice C: 2 units of corn
micro.Choice D: 0.5 units of corn
micro.Correct Answer: C — 2 units of corn
micro.Feedback: Wheat rises by 15 and corn falls by 30. Opportunity cost per wheat is 30 / 15 = 2 corn.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: An economy is producing inside its PPF because some labor and capital are idle. Which change moves it toward the frontier without shifting the frontier?
micro.Choice A: Discovering a new technology
micro.Choice B: Putting unemployed resources back to work
micro.Choice C: Increasing the capital stock
micro.Choice D: Expanding the labor force permanently
micro.Correct Answer: B — Putting unemployed resources back to work
micro.Feedback: Using idle resources moves the economy toward the existing PPF. New technology or more resources shift the PPF outward.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: A new technology improves only the production of Good X, not Good Y. What happens to the PPF?
micro.Choice A: It shifts inward equally for both goods
micro.Choice B: It creates a shortage of Good Y
micro.Choice C: It becomes a price ceiling
micro.Choice D: It rotates outward on the Good X axis
micro.Correct Answer: D — It rotates outward on the Good X axis
