micro.Feedback: Technology that helps only one good expands production possibilities for that good, rotating the PPF outward on that axis.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: Refer to the PPF graph. What is the opportunity cost per additional unit of Good X when production moves from A to B?
micro.Choice A: 1.6 units of Good Y
micro.Choice B: 5 units of Good Y
micro.Choice C: 8 units of Good Y
micro.Choice D: 0.625 units of Good Y
micro.Correct Answer: D — 0.625 units of Good Y
micro.Feedback: Moving from A to B gains 8 units of Good X and gives up 5 units of Good Y, so opportunity cost per Good X is 5 / 8 = 0.625.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: Refer to the PPF graph. What is the opportunity cost per additional unit of Good X when production moves from B to C?
micro.Choice A: About 1.43 units of Good Y
micro.Choice B: 0.7 units of Good Y
micro.Choice C: 7 units of Good Y
micro.Choice D: 10 units of Good Y
micro.Correct Answer: A — About 1.43 units of Good Y
micro.Feedback: Moving from B to C gains 7 units of Good X and gives up 10 units of Good Y, so 10 / 7 is about 1.43.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: Refer to the PPF graph. What is the opportunity cost per additional unit of Good X when production moves from D to E?
micro.Choice A: 4 units of Good Y
micro.Choice B: 5 units of Good Y
micro.Choice C: 0.2 units of Good Y
micro.Choice D: 20 units of Good Y
micro.Correct Answer: B — 5 units of Good Y
micro.Feedback: Moving from D to E gains 4 units of Good X and gives up 20 units of Good Y, so 20 / 4 = 5.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: Refer to the PPF graph. Which move has the highest opportunity cost per additional unit of Good X?
micro.Choice A: A to B
micro.Choice B: D to E
micro.Choice C: B to C
micro.Choice D: C to D
micro.Correct Answer: B — D to E
micro.Feedback: The move from D to E gives up 20 units of Good Y to gain only 4 units of Good X, the highest cost per unit among the listed moves.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: Refer to the PPF graph. Compare the opportunity cost per additional unit of Good X from A to B with the cost from D to E. Which calculation and conclusion are supported?
micro.Choice A: A to B costs 0.625 Y per X, while D to E costs 5 Y per X; opportunity cost rises
micro.Choice B: A to B costs 5 Y per X, while D to E costs 0.625 Y per X; opportunity cost falls
micro.Choice C: Both moves cost 1 Y per X; opportunity cost remains constant
micro.Choice D: A to B costs 8 Y per X, while D to E costs 4 Y per X; opportunity cost falls
micro.Correct Answer: A — A to B costs 0.625 Y per X, while D to E costs 5 Y per X; opportunity cost rises
micro.Feedback: The graph shows A to B gives up 5 Y for 8 X, or 0.625 Y per X. D to E gives up 20 Y for 4 X, or 5 Y per X, demonstrating increasing opportunity cost.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: Refer to the PPF graph. What is the opportunity cost per additional unit of Good Y when production moves from E to D?
micro.Choice A: 5 units of Good X
micro.Choice B: 4 units of Good X
micro.Choice C: 0.2 units of Good X
micro.Choice D: 20 units of Good X
micro.Correct Answer: C — 0.2 units of Good X
micro.Feedback: Moving from E to D gives up 4 units of Good X to gain 20 units of Good Y, so 4 / 20 = 0.2 units of Good X per Good Y.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: Refer to the PPF graph. If the economy is at F and moves to B, what happens?
micro.Choice A: It produces more Good X and less Good Y
micro.Choice B: It moves outside the PPF
micro.Choice C: It becomes unattainable
micro.Choice D: It produces the same amount of Good X but more Good Y
micro.Correct Answer: D — It produces the same amount of Good X but more Good Y
micro.Feedback: F and B both have about 8 units of Good X, but B has more Good Y and lies on the PPF.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: Refer to the PPF graph. If the economy moves from F to C, what best describes the change?
micro.Choice A: It gains both Good X and Good Y by using resources more efficiently
micro.Choice B: It gives up Good Y to gain Good X
micro.Choice C: It moves from efficient to inefficient production
micro.Choice D: It moves beyond current resources
micro.Correct Answer: A — It gains both Good X and Good Y by using resources more efficiently
micro.Feedback: F is inside the PPF and C is on the PPF. Moving from F to C increases both goods by using idle or misallocated resources.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: Use the graph. Compare the average opportunity cost of Good X over B to C and C to D. Which costs and explanation best fit the PPF?
micro.Choice A: About 0.63 then 1.43 Y per X; expanding X production uses resources increasingly less suited to producing X.
micro.Choice B: About 1.43 then 2.5 Y per X; expanding X production uses resources increasingly less suited to producing X.
micro.Choice C: About 1.43 then 2.5 Y per X; the change shows that resources are equally well suited to producing X and Y.
micro.Choice D: About 0.63 then 1.43 Y per X; the change shows that resources are equally well suited to producing X and Y.
micro.Correct Answer: B — About 1.43 then 2.5 Y per X; expanding X production uses resources increasingly less suited to producing X.
micro.Feedback: B=(8,45), C=(15,35), and D=(21,20). The costs of additional X are 10/7, about 1.43 Y per X, and 15/6 = 2.5 Y per X. Rising opportunity cost is consistent with moving resources into X production that are increasingly less suited to it, rather than resources being equally suited to both goods.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: Refer to the PPF graph. A proposal values each extra unit of X at 2 units of Y. Comparing the average tradeoff over A to B and D to E, which movement passes that benefit-cost test?
micro.Choice A: A to B passes; D to E fails
micro.Choice B: Both pass because each ends on the frontier
micro.Choice C: D to E passes; A to B fails
micro.Choice D: Neither passes because every frontier movement sacrifices Y
micro.Correct Answer: A — A to B passes; D to E fails
micro.Feedback: A to B forgoes 5 Y for 8 X, or 0.625 Y per X; D to E forgoes 20 Y for 4 X, or 5 Y per X. A benefit of 2 Y per X exceeds only the first average cost.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: Refer to the PPF graph. Starting at B, a planner must choose among labeled frontier points while keeping at least 30 units of Y. What is the greatest attainable X among those choices, and what Y is sacrificed?
micro.Choice A: 25 X at E, sacrificing 45 Y
micro.Choice B: 15 X at C, sacrificing 10 Y
micro.Choice C: 21 X at D, sacrificing 25 Y
micro.Choice D: 8 X at B, sacrificing no Y
micro.Correct Answer: B — 15 X at C, sacrificing 10 Y
micro.Feedback: A, B and C meet the Y floor. C has the most X of those labeled points: 15. Relative to B, Y falls from 45 to 35, a cost of 10.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: Refer to the PPF graph. An economy at F considers B as an immediate target and G as a longer-run target. Which diagnosis fits both?
micro.Choice A: Reaching B expands the frontier; reaching G merely removes unemployment
micro.Choice B: Both targets are currently efficient choices because each is desirable
micro.Choice C: Better resource use can reach B; reaching G requires an expansion of feasible production
micro.Choice D: Both targets require new technology because both are above F
micro.Correct Answer: C — Better resource use can reach B; reaching G requires an expansion of feasible production
micro.Feedback: F is inside the existing frontier, B lies on it and G lies outside. Removing inefficiency can reach B with current capacity; G requires a changed production possibility set.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: Refer to the PPF. Moving from point C to point D increases production of X but reduces production of Y. Suppose each additional unit of X generates a benefit equivalent to 3 units of Y. What is the net benefit, measured in units of Y, from moving from C to D?
micro.Choice D: 3 Y
micro.Correct Answer: D — 3 Y
micro.Feedback: The move gains 6 X and forgoes 15 Y. Its benefit is 6 times 3 = 18 Y; deducting the 15 Y opportunity cost leaves 3 Y.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: Production moves from F to C and then from C to D with resources and technology unchanged. Which explanation, supported by the graph’s output changes, explains why only the second move sacrifices Y for more X?
micro.Choice A: F to C uses idle resources to add 7 X and 15 Y; C to D reallocates fully employed resources, adding 6 X at a cost of 15 Y.
micro.Choice B: F to C uses idle resources to add 7 X and 10 Y; C to D reallocates fully employed resources, adding 6 X at a cost of 15 Y.
micro.Choice C: F to C expands productive capacity to add 7 X and 15 Y; C to D uses idle resources to add 6 X at a cost of 15 Y.
micro.Choice D: F to C expands productive capacity to add 7 X and 10 Y; C to D uses idle resources to add 6 X at a cost of 15 Y.
micro.Correct Answer: A — F to C uses idle resources to add 7 X and 15 Y; C to D reallocates fully employed resources, adding 6 X at a cost of 15 Y.
micro.Feedback: F=(8,20) lies inside the PPF, while C=(15,35) and D=(21,20) lie on it. F to C uses idle resources to add 7 X and 15 Y without expanding capacity. C to D reallocates fully employed resources: gaining 6 X requires giving up 15 Y.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: The first ten generators cost two forgone repairs; the next ten cost six more. A buyer offers four repairs in exchange for each ten-generator block. Blocks must be produced in order. Which production choice yields the most net repairs?
micro.Choice A: Produce only the second block because its opportunity cost is higher
micro.Choice B: Produce neither because any generator production sacrifices repairs
micro.Choice C: Produce one block, gaining two net repairs
micro.Choice D: Produce both blocks because their average cost equals the offer
micro.Correct Answer: C — Produce one block, gaining two net repairs
micro.Feedback: The first block gains 4 - 2 = 2 repairs; the second loses 4 - 6 = -2. Producing both yields zero net gain, so one block is better.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: From an efficient starting point, reallocating crews to the first four school reopenings forgoes 12 bridge repairs; the next four forgo 20 more. A planner uses the first block's cost to estimate all eight. What is the error?
micro.Choice A: The estimate is correct because equal numbers of schools must cost equal repairs
micro.Choice B: The estimate is 12 repairs too high because the first block is already planned
micro.Choice C: The estimate is 20 repairs too low because the first block has no opportunity cost
micro.Choice D: The estimate is 8 repairs too low because the later marginal tradeoff is steeper
micro.Correct Answer: D — The estimate is 8 repairs too low because the later marginal tradeoff is steeper
micro.Feedback: Extrapolating the first block gives 24 repairs for eight schools. Actual cost is 12 + 20 = 32, eight more. The second block has the higher opportunity cost.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: A factory raises both outputs after reorganizing idle workers. Later, training expands the maximum output possible even when all workers are occupied. Which evidence separates the two improvements?
micro.Choice A: The first can occur within existing capacity; the second changes the efficient production boundary
micro.Choice B: Any simultaneous output increase proves the frontier shifted
micro.Choice C: Any training program moves production along an unchanged frontier
micro.Choice D: Both improvements establish that the original output was outside the frontier
micro.Correct Answer: A — The first can occur within existing capacity; the second changes the efficient production boundary
micro.Feedback: Using idle resources can raise both outputs without changing capacity. A higher maximum under full efficient use establishes a frontier expansion.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: A straight-line PPF trades one turbine for three pumps. An observed move gains two turbines while pumps stay unchanged, with technology and resources fixed. Which explanation is consistent with both facts?
micro.Choice A: The straight frontier proves every observed move must lose six pumps
micro.Choice B: The turbine gain by itself proves the PPF shifted outward
micro.Choice C: The observation establishes zero opportunity cost everywhere on the frontier
micro.Choice D: The starting point was inside the frontier, so the move could use idle capacity
micro.Correct Answer: D — The starting point was inside the frontier, so the move could use idle capacity
micro.Feedback: The three-pump tradeoff describes efficient frontier reallocations. An interior starting point can permit output gains without sacrificing the other good; the observation does not erase frontier opportunity cost.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: What does a production possibilities frontier show?
micro.Choice A: The legal maximum price in a market
micro.Choice B: Currently feasible combinations of two goods
micro.Choice C: The amount of tax paid by buyers
micro.Choice D: The demand curve for one product
micro.Correct Answer: B — Currently feasible combinations of two goods
micro.Feedback: A PPF shows possible production combinations given current resources and technology.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: What does a point inside the PPF indicate?
micro.Choice A: Unattainable
micro.Choice B: Efficient
micro.Choice C: Attainable but inefficient
micro.Choice D: A binding price ceiling
micro.Correct Answer: C — Attainable but inefficient
micro.Feedback: A point inside the PPF is attainable, but resources are not being used efficiently.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: A PPF move gives up 12 units of Good Y to gain 4 units of Good X. What is the opportunity cost per Good X?
micro.Choice A: 3 units of Good Y
micro.Choice B: 4 units of Good Y
micro.Choice C: 12 units of Good Y
micro.Choice D: 48 units of Good Y
micro.Correct Answer: A — 3 units of Good Y
micro.Feedback: Opportunity cost per Good X is what is given up divided by what is gained: 12 / 4 = 3.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: On an unchanged efficient frontier, moving from 50 drones and 80 scanners to 65 drones and 50 scanners costs 2 scanners per added drone. The next 10 drones would reduce scanners from 50 to 20. A planner claims a constant cost of 2 and wants 10 more drones only if each is worth at least 2.5 scanners. Which evaluation is correct?
micro.Choice A: The next block costs 3 scanners per drone, so it fails the 2.5 threshold and indicates rising opportunity cost.
micro.Choice B: The next block costs 2 scanners per drone, so it passes the threshold because the previous average applies to every move.
micro.Choice C: The next block costs 0.33 scanner per drone, so it passes the threshold after inverting the ratio.
micro.Choice D: The next block costs 30 scanners per drone, so the frontier must have shifted inward rather than displaying changing tradeoffs.
micro.Correct Answer: A — The next block costs 3 scanners per drone, so it fails the 2.5 threshold and indicates rising opportunity cost.
micro.Feedback: The first cost is (80-50)/(65-50)=2. The next is (50-20)/10=3. At a value of 2.5 scanners per drone, the extra block loses 0.5 scanner-equivalent per drone. Changing slopes can occur along one unchanged bowed frontier.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: A country starts inside its PPF with idle workers. Hiring them raises both outputs until the old frontier is reached. Later, technology improves only scanner production and the country can produce more scanners at the same drone output. Which diagnosis distinguishes the two changes?
micro.Choice A: Both changes shift the frontier outward equally because any rise in both observed outputs proves general capacity growth.
micro.Choice B: The first improves resource utilization; the second expands productive capacity asymmetrically, rather than merely moving along the old frontier.
micro.Choice C: The first is growth and the second is improved utilization because scanner output rises without reducing drones.
micro.Choice D: Neither changes productive capacity because every increase in one output must reduce the other under scarcity.
micro.Correct Answer: B — The first improves resource utilization; the second expands productive capacity asymmetrically, rather than merely moving along the old frontier.
micro.Feedback: Using idle resources can move production to the existing frontier without changing capacity. Sector-specific technology expands feasible production toward scanners, so the later improvement cannot be attributed solely to more efficient use of the old technology.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Question: On one efficient frontier, the first 20 solar units sacrifice 5 food units and the next 20 sacrifice 14. A storage innovation then halves the food sacrifice required for each of those solar blocks, leaving maximum food output unchanged. Which conclusion separates the original tradeoff from the innovation?
micro.Choice A: Original marginal cost falls from 4 to about 1.43 food per solar unit; the innovation merely moves production along the same frontier.
micro.Choice B: Original marginal cost is constant at 0.475 food per solar unit; the innovation eliminates increasing opportunity cost because both blocks improve.
micro.Choice C: Original marginal cost rises from 0.25 to 0.70 food per solar unit; the innovation expands solar capacity, with the two costs falling to 0.125 and 0.35.
micro.Choice D: Original marginal cost rises from 5 to 14 food per solar unit; unchanged maximum food means productive capacity cannot expand.
micro.Correct Answer: C — Original marginal cost rises from 0.25 to 0.70 food per solar unit; the innovation expands solar capacity, with the two costs falling to 0.125 and 0.35.
micro.Feedback: Divide each food sacrifice by 20 solar units: 0.25 and 0.70. Halving sacrifices produces 0.125 and 0.35, still increasing across blocks. The new technology changes the feasible set, unlike movement along the original frontier.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Common Misconception: Treating an inside point as impossible or fully efficient.
micro.Question: A production point lies inside the PPF. How should it be classified?
micro.Choice A: It is unattainable with current resources and technology.
micro.Choice B: It is efficient because it uses fewer resources.
micro.Choice C: It is attainable but inefficient because resources are underused.
micro.Choice D: It proves the economy has experienced long-run growth.
micro.Correct Answer: C — It is attainable but inefficient because resources are underused.
micro.Feedback: A point inside the frontier is feasible, but the economy could produce more of at least one good with existing resources.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
micro.Question: Use the graph. With the resources and technology represented by PPF0, which production combination would require greater productive capacity?
micro.Choice A: 20 pizzas and 120 robots
micro.Choice B: 60 pizzas and 80 robots
micro.Choice C: 80 pizzas and 60 robots
micro.Choice D: 100 pizzas and 0 robots
micro.Correct Answer: C — 80 pizzas and 60 robots
micro.Feedback: At 80 pizzas, PPF0 permits fewer than 60 robots, so that combination lies outside the frontier. The other combinations are A, B, and the pizza-axis intercept, all on PPF0.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Common Misconception: Calling movement to the existing frontier economic growth.
micro.Question: A country puts unemployed workers and idle factories back to work without gaining new technology. How does this appear on its PPF?
micro.Choice A: Production moves to the existing frontier, showing greater efficiency but no growth.
micro.Choice B: The frontier shifts outward, showing growth in productive capacity.
micro.Choice C: Production moves outside the frontier, becoming unattainable.
micro.Choice D: The frontier shifts inward because idle resources were used.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Production moves to the existing frontier, showing greater efficiency but no growth.
micro.Feedback: Using existing resources more fully moves production to the frontier; growth requires the frontier itself to shift outward.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
micro.Question: Which statement correctly distinguishes the move from A to B from the shift of PPF0 to PPF1, using the changes shown in the graph?
micro.Choice A: A to B reallocates existing resources and gives up 40 orders of fries; PPF1 expands capacity and raises maximum burger output by 10.
micro.Choice B: A to B reallocates existing resources and gives up 20 orders of fries; PPF1 expands capacity and raises maximum burger output by 10.
micro.Choice C: A to B expands productive capacity by giving up 40 orders of fries; PPF1 only reallocates existing resources toward 10 more burgers.
micro.Choice D: A to B expands productive capacity by giving up 20 orders of fries; PPF1 only reallocates existing resources toward 10 more burgers.
micro.Correct Answer: A — A to B reallocates existing resources and gives up 40 orders of fries; PPF1 expands capacity and raises maximum burger output by 10.
micro.Feedback: Moving from A to B on PPF0 reallocates existing resources: fries fall from 120 to 80 orders, a sacrifice of 40. Shifting to PPF1 expands productive capacity: the burger-axis intercept rises from 50 to 60. Reallocation changes the output mix within existing capacity; an outward shift expands what can be produced.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. After the shift from PPF0 to PPF1, production remains at B. Which statement combines the capacity change with the observed production choice?
micro.Choice A: Capacity expanded, and PPF1 identifies the preferred output combination; unchanged production at B therefore establishes that welfare has increased.
micro.Choice B: Capacity expanded, but unchanged B is now inside the new frontier; higher welfare is not established by the shift alone
micro.Choice C: Capacity expanded, but unchanged B remains on the efficient frontier; its earlier efficiency establishes that resources are still fully employed.
micro.Choice D: Capacity stayed unchanged because production remains at B; the shift to PPF1 changes the selected output mix rather than the feasible set.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Capacity expanded, but unchanged B is now inside the new frontier; higher welfare is not established by the shift alone
micro.Feedback: The outward frontier makes more output feasible and places the old B inside the new boundary. A capacity change alone does not show that production adjusted or establish a welfare ranking.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Common Misconception: Treating a one-sector technology gain as an equal shift for both goods.
micro.Question: A technological improvement affects only the production of medical equipment, not food. How does the PPF change?
micro.Choice A: The entire frontier shifts inward by the same amount.
micro.Choice B: The medical-equipment intercept moves outward; food stays fixed.
micro.Choice C: The frontier pivots outward toward the food axis only.
micro.Choice D: The economy moves along an unchanged frontier toward more food.
micro.Correct Answer: B — The medical-equipment intercept moves outward; food stays fixed.
micro.Feedback: A productivity gain limited to one good expands the maximum attainable quantity of that good without changing the other intercept.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Common Misconception: Ignoring the link between current investment and future productive capacity.
micro.Question: Country A chooses more capital goods and fewer consumer goods today than Country B, with otherwise similar resources. What is the likely long-run implication?
micro.Choice A: Country A must have a lower future PPF because current consumption is smaller.
micro.Choice B: Country A may gain more future capacity because it produces more capital goods now.
micro.Choice C: Country B necessarily grows faster because consumption creates capital automatically.
micro.Choice D: Neither choice can affect future production possibilities.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Country A may gain more future capacity because it produces more capital goods now.
micro.Feedback: Greater current production of capital goods can expand future capacity, though it requires sacrificing current consumption.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Common Misconception: Treating a sector-specific loss as an equal inward shift or a movement along the same frontier.
micro.Question: A disaster destroys equipment used only to produce electric power, while agricultural capacity is unchanged. What happens to the PPF?
micro.Choice A: It shifts outward equally for both goods.
micro.Choice B: It pivots inward toward the agricultural axis only.
micro.Choice C: Only the electric-power intercept moves inward.
micro.Choice D: It remains fixed because the economy can move along the frontier.
micro.Correct Answer: C — Only the electric-power intercept moves inward.
micro.Feedback: Losing capacity in one sector reduces the maximum output of that good and rotates the frontier inward on that axis.

micro.Question: An economist shows a PPF shifting outward after years of investment in capital and technology. What is the best interpretation?
micro.Choice A: The economy's productive capacity has increased
micro.Choice B: The economy moved inside the PPF because resources are idle
micro.Choice C: The CPI basket became fixed
micro.Choice D: A tax wedge disappeared
micro.Correct Answer: A — The economy's productive capacity has increased
micro.Feedback: An outward PPF shift means the economy can produce more because resources, technology, or productivity improved.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Moving from A to B, what is the opportunity cost per additional pizza?
micro.Choice A: 1 robot
micro.Choice B: 2 robots
micro.Choice C: 0.5 robot
micro.Choice D: 40 robots
micro.Correct Answer: A — 1 robot
micro.Feedback: The move gains 40 pizzas and gives up 40 robots, so each pizza costs 1 robot.

micro.Learning Objective: LO2.2
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. On PPF0, moving from A to B gains 20 burgers. What is the opportunity cost per additional burger?
micro.Choice A: 0.5 order of fries
micro.Choice B: 20 orders of fries
micro.Choice C: 40 orders of fries
micro.Choice D: 2 orders of fries
micro.Correct Answer: D — 2 orders of fries
micro.Feedback: The move gives up 40 fries for 20 burgers, or 2 fries per burger.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.4 — Preference Ranking and Completeness
micro.Question: Refer to the graph above. Assume the consumer prefers more of either good when the amount of the other is unchanged. Which indifference curve contains the most-preferred bundles?
micro.Choice A: IC3
micro.Choice B: IC1
micro.Choice C: IC2
micro.Choice D: All curves are equally ranked
micro.Correct Answer: A — IC3
micro.Feedback: IC3 lies northeast of the other curves and therefore contains bundles with more of at least one good.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.4 — Preference Ranking and Completeness
micro.Question: Refer to the graph above. How does the consumer rank C relative to A?
micro.Choice A: C is strictly preferred
micro.Choice B: A is strictly preferred
micro.Choice C: They are indifferent
micro.Choice D: The graph supplies no ranking
micro.Correct Answer: A — C is strictly preferred
micro.Feedback: C lies on IC2 while A lies on the lower IC1, so C has the higher ordinal rank.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.4 — Preference Ranking and Completeness
micro.Question: A consumer can compare every pair of feasible bundles. Which preference property is illustrated?
micro.Choice A: Transitivity
micro.Choice B: Convexity
micro.Choice C: Completeness
micro.Choice D: Cardinal utility
micro.Correct Answer: C — Completeness
micro.Feedback: Completeness means the consumer can rank any two bundles or regard them as equally preferred.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.4 — Preference Ranking and Completeness
micro.Question: A consumer says, “I have compared A and B and like them equally.” Does this response violate completeness?
micro.Choice A: Yes. Completeness requires a strict preference.
micro.Choice B: Yes. Every bundle must have a different rank.
micro.Choice C: No. Indifference is a valid comparison.
micro.Choice D: No. Completeness applies only when prices are equal.
micro.Correct Answer: C — No. Indifference is a valid comparison.
micro.Feedback: Complete preferences allow A preferred, B preferred, or indifference for each pair.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.4 — Preference Ranking and Completeness
micro.Question: A consumer ranks every pair of feasible bundles except A and B, saying there is no ranking at all for that pair. Are these preferences complete?
micro.Choice A: Yes; almost all pairs are ranked.
micro.Choice B: Yes; an unranked pair is automatically a tie.
micro.Choice C: No; at least one pair cannot be compared.
micro.Choice D: No; completeness requires equal rankings for all bundles.
micro.Correct Answer: C — No; at least one pair cannot be compared.
micro.Feedback: Completeness requires a ranking, including possible indifference, for every pair. No ranking is different from indifference.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.4 — Preference Ranking and Completeness
micro.Question: Use the graph. On IC2, compare the bundles at X = 5 and X = 20. Which Y readings and preference comparison are correct?
micro.Choice A: First Y is between 10 and 15, then between 5 and 10; the consumer is indifferent between the bundles.
micro.Choice B: First Y is between 15 and 20, then below 5; the consumer is indifferent between the bundles.
micro.Choice C: First Y is between 15 and 20, then below 5; the bundle with more X must be preferred.
micro.Choice D: First Y is between 10 and 15, then between 5 and 10; the bundle with more X must be preferred.
micro.Correct Answer: B — First Y is between 15 and 20, then below 5; the consumer is indifferent between the bundles.
micro.Feedback: IC2 is between Y = 15 and 20 at X = 5, and below Y = 5 at X = 20. Points on the same indifference curve have the same preference rank despite their different compositions.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.4 — Preference Ranking and Completeness
micro.Question: A consumer prefers A to B and B to C. What does transitivity require?
micro.Choice A: C must be preferred to A
micro.Choice B: A must be preferred to C
micro.Choice C: A and C must be tied
micro.Choice D: The ranking may cycle without inconsistency
micro.Correct Answer: B — A must be preferred to C
micro.Feedback: Transitivity makes preference rankings internally consistent: A ≻ B and B ≻ C imply A ≻ C.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.4 — Preference Ranking and Completeness
micro.Question: Bundle D contains at least as much of both desirable goods as bundle E and more of one. Under more-is-better, how are they ranked?
micro.Choice A: E is strictly preferred to D
micro.Choice B: They must be indifferent
micro.Choice C: No ranking is possible
micro.Choice D: D is strictly preferred to E
micro.Correct Answer: D — D is strictly preferred to E
micro.Feedback: Monotonic preferences rank a bundle with more of one good and no less of the other above the comparison bundle.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.4 — Preference Ranking and Completeness
micro.Question: A is indifferent to B and B is indifferent to C. What does consistent ranking imply?
micro.Choice A: A is indifferent to C
micro.Choice B: A must be preferred to C
micro.Choice C: C must be preferred to A
micro.Choice D: Indifference can never be transitive
micro.Correct Answer: A — A is indifferent to C
micro.Feedback: Transitivity applies to weak preference and indifference, preventing inconsistent equivalence chains.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.4 — Preference Ranking and Completeness
micro.Question: A consumer strictly prefers A to B, B to C, and C to A. Which diagnosis is correct?
micro.Choice A: The rankings violate completeness because all pairs are ranked.
micro.Choice B: The rankings form a cycle and violate transitivity.
micro.Choice C: The rankings are consistent if the bundles have different prices.
micro.Choice D: The rankings are transitive because each comparison is strict.
micro.Correct Answer: B — The rankings form a cycle and violate transitivity.
micro.Feedback: A > B and B > C require A > C under transitivity, contradicting C > A.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.4 — Preference Ranking and Completeness
micro.Question: Both X and Y are desirable. Bundle A has 6 X and 2 Y; bundle B has 4 X and 5 Y. Does more-is-better alone determine which is preferred?
micro.Choice A: Yes. A is preferred because it has more X.
micro.Choice B: Yes. B is preferred because it contains more units in total.
micro.Choice C: Yes. The consumer must be indifferent.
micro.Choice D: No. Each bundle has more of one good and less of the other.
micro.Correct Answer: D — No. Each bundle has more of one good and less of the other.
micro.Feedback: Neither bundle dominates the other. The ranking depends on the consumer’s willingness to trade X for Y.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.4 — Preference Ranking and Completeness
micro.Question: A consumer is indifferent between A and B and between B and C, but strictly prefers A to C. Are these rankings transitive?
micro.Choice A: No. The two indifferences imply indifference between A and C.
micro.Choice B: Yes. Strict preference can coexist with indifference for the same pair.
micro.Choice C: Yes. Transitivity applies only to strict preferences.
micro.Choice D: No. Indifference itself violates transitivity.
micro.Correct Answer: A — No. The two indifferences imply indifference between A and C.
micro.Feedback: Transitivity carries the indifference relation through B, contradicting the stated strict preference between A and C.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.4 — Preference Ranking and Completeness
micro.Question: A consumer is indifferent between A and B, and strictly prefers B to C. If preferences are transitive, how must the consumer rank A and C?
micro.Choice A: C is strictly preferred to A.
micro.Choice B: A is strictly preferred to C.
micro.Choice C: A and C must be indifferent.
micro.Choice D: Their ranking depends on which bundle costs more.
micro.Correct Answer: B — A is strictly preferred to C.
micro.Feedback: Replacing B with an equally preferred A preserves the strict preference over C.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.4 — Preference Ranking and Completeness
micro.Question: Both goods are divisible and desirable, their prices are positive, and a consumer can spend all income. A chosen bundle leaves enough money to buy more of either good. Can it be the consumer’s most-preferred affordable bundle?
micro.Choice A: Yes. Any affordable bundle is equally preferred.
micro.Choice B: Yes. Leaving income unspent proves the goods are balanced.
micro.Choice C: No. An optimum must contain equal quantities of both goods.
micro.Choice D: No. Buying more of a good without giving up the other would improve it.
micro.Correct Answer: D — No. Buying more of a good without giving up the other would improve it.
micro.Feedback: With more-is-better and no saving option in this two-good choice, unspent income permits a strictly better affordable bundle.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.4 — Preference Ranking and Completeness
micro.Question: A consumer is indifferent between A and B. A costs $20 and B costs $30. Does consistent preference ranking require the consumer to prefer B?
micro.Choice A: No. A higher price does not establish a higher preference rank.
micro.Choice B: Yes. Spending more always gives more utility.
micro.Choice C: Yes. Indifference is possible only at equal prices.
micro.Choice D: No. The lower-cost bundle must be strictly preferred.
micro.Correct Answer: A — No. A higher price does not establish a higher preference rank.
micro.Feedback: Preference ranking describes satisfaction with bundles; prices determine affordability. Different prices do not overturn the given indifference.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.4 — Preference Ranking and Completeness
micro.Question: Preferences are complete and transitive. A consumer prefers A to B and A to C. What can be concluded about B and C from this information?
micro.Choice A: B must be preferred to C.
micro.Choice B: B may be preferred, C may be preferred, or they may be equally preferred.
micro.Choice C: C must be preferred to B.
micro.Choice D: B and C must be equally preferred.
micro.Correct Answer: B — B may be preferred, C may be preferred, or they may be equally preferred.
micro.Feedback: Knowing that both rank below A does not rank them against each other. Completeness requires a ranking but does not tell us which one.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.4 — Preference Ranking and Completeness
micro.Question: A survey records a ranking for every pair of bundles. Is that enough to establish both completeness and transitivity?
micro.Choice A: It establishes both because every pair was compared.
micro.Choice B: It establishes transitivity but not completeness.
micro.Choice C: It establishes completeness, but the rankings must still be checked for transitivity.
micro.Choice D: It establishes neither unless every bundle has a distinct rank.
micro.Correct Answer: C — It establishes completeness, but the rankings must still be checked for transitivity.
micro.Feedback: Pairwise coverage establishes completeness. The comparisons could still form a cycle, so transitivity needs a separate check.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.4 — Preference Ranking and Completeness
micro.Question: Both goods are desirable. Bundle E contains 4 X and 3 Y. A proposed bundle D contains 5 X and an unknown whole-number amount of Y. What is the smallest Y amount that guarantees D is preferred to E under more-is-better?
micro.Choice A: 0 units of Y.
micro.Choice B: 2 units of Y.
micro.Choice C: 4 units of Y.
micro.Choice D: 3 units of Y.
micro.Correct Answer: D — 3 units of Y.
micro.Feedback: D already has more X. At 3 Y it has no less of either good, so it dominates E. With less Y, preferences over the tradeoff are needed.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A maximum legal price is binding only when it is set:
micro.Choice A: Below equilibrium price
micro.Choice B: Above equilibrium price
micro.Choice C: Exactly at zero
micro.Choice D: Above quantity supplied
micro.Correct Answer: A — Below equilibrium price
micro.Feedback: A price ceiling binds only when it is below equilibrium price.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A binding price ceiling usually creates:
micro.Choice A: A shortage
micro.Choice B: A surplus
micro.Choice C: A tax wedge
micro.Choice D: An outward PPF shift
micro.Correct Answer: A — A shortage
micro.Feedback: A binding ceiling keeps price too low, so quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: At a binding price ceiling, Qd = 90 and Qs = 60. What is the shortage?
micro.Choice A: 30 units
micro.Choice B: 60 units
micro.Choice C: 90 units
micro.Choice D: 150 units
micro.Correct Answer: A — 30 units
micro.Feedback: Shortage equals Qd - Qs: 90 - 60 = 30.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: At a binding ceiling, buyers want 120 units and sellers offer 75 units. What happens?
micro.Choice A: A shortage of 45 units
micro.Choice B: A surplus of 45 units
micro.Choice C: A shortage of 195 units
micro.Choice D: No shortage
micro.Correct Answer: A — A shortage of 45 units
micro.Feedback: The shortage is quantity demanded minus quantity supplied: 120 - 75 = 45.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A rent ceiling is set at $900 when equilibrium rent is $1,300. What happens?
micro.Choice A: The ceiling is binding and creates a shortage
micro.Choice B: The ceiling is nonbinding and has no effect
micro.Choice C: The ceiling creates a surplus
micro.Choice D: The ceiling shifts supply right
micro.Correct Answer: A — The ceiling is binding and creates a shortage
micro.Feedback: A ceiling below equilibrium is binding and creates a shortage.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A legal maximum price is above equilibrium. Why is it nonbinding?
micro.Choice A: The market price remains below the legal maximum
micro.Choice B: All ceilings create shortages
micro.Choice C: Sellers must charge the maximum
micro.Choice D: Demand must fall to zero
micro.Correct Answer: A — The market price remains below the legal maximum
micro.Feedback: A ceiling above equilibrium does not stop the market from reaching equilibrium.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A rental schedule lists monthly rent, apartments wanted and apartments offered: $800: 120, 60; $1,000: 100, 80; $1,200: 90, 90. An enforced rent ceiling is $1,000. What shortage follows?
micro.Choice A: 20 apartments
micro.Choice B: 80 apartments
micro.Choice C: 180 apartments
micro.Choice D: 0 apartments
micro.Correct Answer: A — 20 apartments
micro.Feedback: Use the $1,000 row, not the equilibrium row at $1,200. At the ceiling, buyers want 100 apartments and owners offer 80, so the shortage is 100 - 80 = 20. Adding the quantities does not measure unmet demand.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: At a binding cap on storage-unit rents, 150 customers each want one unit and owners offer 110 units. All offered units are rented. A manager reports, "The shortage is 110 units because that is how many were rented." Which correction is accurate?
micro.Choice A: 40 units are unfilled demand; 110 units are rented.
micro.Choice B: 110 units are unfilled demand; 40 units are rented.
micro.Choice C: 40 units are excess supply; 110 units are rented.
micro.Choice D: 260 units are unfilled demand; 110 units are rented.
micro.Correct Answer: A — 40 units are unfilled demand; 110 units are rented.
micro.Feedback: The 110 rentals are actual transactions, not the shortage. Unfilled demand is 150 - 110 = 40 units. Because customers want more than owners offer, the gap is a shortage rather than a surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A legal maximum price is called:
micro.Choice A: A price ceiling
micro.Choice B: A price floor
micro.Choice C: Tax incidence
micro.Choice D: Consumer surplus
micro.Correct Answer: A — A price ceiling
micro.Feedback: A price ceiling is a legal maximum price.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A price ceiling is binding when it is set:
micro.Choice A: Below equilibrium price
micro.Choice B: Above equilibrium price
micro.Choice C: At any seller's preferred price
micro.Choice D: Only on producers
micro.Correct Answer: A — Below equilibrium price
micro.Feedback: A ceiling must be below equilibrium to prevent price from rising to equilibrium.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A binding price ceiling creates:
micro.Choice A: A shortage
micro.Choice B: A surplus
micro.Choice C: More supply than demand
micro.Choice D: A tax wedge
micro.Correct Answer: A — A shortage
micro.Feedback: A binding price ceiling keeps price too low, so quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A city sets rent at $800 when equilibrium rent is $1,200. This rent ceiling is:
micro.Choice A: Binding
micro.Choice B: Not binding
micro.Choice C: A price floor
micro.Choice D: A tax
micro.Correct Answer: A — Binding
micro.Feedback: The ceiling is below equilibrium, so it is binding.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: At a binding price ceiling, quantity demanded is 70 and quantity supplied is 45. What is the shortage?
micro.Choice A: 25 units
micro.Choice B: 45 units
micro.Choice C: 70 units
micro.Choice D: 115 units
micro.Correct Answer: A — 25 units
micro.Feedback: Shortage equals quantity demanded minus quantity supplied: 70 - 45 = 25.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: Which policy would most likely create a shortage?
micro.Choice A: A binding price ceiling
micro.Choice B: A binding price floor
micro.Choice C: A tax wedge
micro.Choice D: An outward PPF shift
micro.Correct Answer: A — A binding price ceiling
micro.Feedback: A binding price ceiling creates a shortage because price is held below equilibrium.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A legal maximum rent of $1,000 is shown. Which classification and equilibrium reading are correct?
micro.Choice A: A binding ceiling; $1,000 is below the $2,000 equilibrium level.
micro.Choice B: A binding ceiling; $1,000 is below the $1,500 equilibrium level.
micro.Choice C: A nonbinding ceiling; $1,000 is below the $2,000 equilibrium level.
micro.Choice D: A binding floor; $1,000 is below the $2,000 equilibrium level.
micro.Correct Answer: A — A binding ceiling; $1,000 is below the $2,000 equilibrium level.
micro.Feedback: The demand and supply curves intersect at $2,000. The legal maximum of $1,000 is a price ceiling. It is below equilibrium, so it prevents the market from clearing at $2,000 and is binding.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A government wants to make a good affordable, so it imposes a price ceiling. Which condition must hold for the policy to actually affect the market?
micro.Choice A: The ceiling must be below equilibrium price
micro.Choice B: The ceiling must be above equilibrium price
micro.Choice C: The ceiling must equal quantity demanded
micro.Choice D: The ceiling must be imposed on sellers only
micro.Correct Answer: A — The ceiling must be below equilibrium price
micro.Feedback: A price ceiling only binds if it is below the equilibrium price.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A binding rent ceiling is imposed below equilibrium. Quantity demanded is 1,200 apartments and quantity supplied is 850. What is the shortage?
micro.Choice A: 350 apartments
micro.Choice B: 850 apartments
micro.Choice C: 1,200 apartments
micro.Choice D: 2,050 apartments
micro.Correct Answer: A — 350 apartments
micro.Feedback: Shortage is Qd - Qs: 1,200 - 850 = 350 apartments.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: Equilibrium rent is $1,400. A ceiling is set at $1,550. What is the immediate market effect?
micro.Choice A: Shortage: the ceiling is binding
micro.Choice B: Surplus: the ceiling is binding
micro.Choice C: No effect: the ceiling is nonbinding
micro.Choice D: Tax wedge: the difference is $150
micro.Correct Answer: C — No effect: the ceiling is nonbinding
micro.Feedback: A ceiling above equilibrium does not constrain the market price.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: The posted price is held below equilibrium, but buyers wait in long lines. What policy most likely caused this?
micro.Choice A: A binding price ceiling
micro.Choice B: A binding price floor
micro.Choice C: A tax on sellers
micro.Choice D: An outward PPF shift
micro.Correct Answer: A — A binding price ceiling
micro.Feedback: A binding price ceiling creates a shortage, so nonprice rationing like waiting can appear.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A rent ceiling is set above the equilibrium rent. What is the likely result?
micro.Choice A: The ceiling is not binding and has no effect
micro.Choice B: The ceiling creates a shortage
micro.Choice C: The ceiling creates a surplus
micro.Choice D: The ceiling shifts supply right
micro.Correct Answer: A — The ceiling is not binding and has no effect
micro.Feedback: A price ceiling above equilibrium does not prevent the market price from reaching equilibrium.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A rent ceiling is set below equilibrium. Quantity demanded is 900 apartments and quantity supplied is 600. What occurs?
micro.Choice A: A shortage of 300 apartments
micro.Choice B: A surplus of 300 apartments
micro.Choice C: A shortage of 1,500 apartments
micro.Choice D: No effect because ceilings are minimum prices
micro.Correct Answer: A — A shortage of 300 apartments
micro.Feedback: The shortage is quantity demanded minus quantity supplied: 900 - 600 = 300.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A binding price ceiling tends to reduce the quality of rental housing because:
micro.Choice A: Landlords have less incentive to maintain units when price cannot rise
micro.Choice B: Tenants always demand less housing at lower prices
micro.Choice C: Quantity supplied rises above quantity demanded
micro.Choice D: The ceiling is above equilibrium
micro.Correct Answer: A — Landlords have less incentive to maintain units when price cannot rise
micro.Feedback: A binding ceiling can create shortages and reduce incentives to maintain quality.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A government policy keeps apartment rents below equilibrium. Which outcome is most likely over time?
micro.Choice A: Shortages and nonprice rationing
micro.Choice B: Surpluses and unsold apartments
micro.Choice C: A rightward supply shift caused by lower rent
micro.Choice D: An increase in quantity supplied
micro.Correct Answer: A — Shortages and nonprice rationing
micro.Feedback: A binding rent ceiling creates shortages, so apartments may be rationed through waiting, search costs, or other nonprice methods.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: The graph shows a $20 price ceiling. Which statement correctly classifies the policy and identifies the competitive equilibrium price?
micro.Choice A: Binding: the equilibrium price is $30, so the legal level is below equilibrium.
micro.Choice B: Binding: the equilibrium price is $25, so the legal level is below equilibrium.
micro.Choice C: Nonbinding: the equilibrium price is $30, so the market still clears at that price.
micro.Choice D: Nonbinding: the equilibrium price is $25, so the market still clears at that price.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Binding: the equilibrium price is $30, so the legal level is below equilibrium.
micro.Feedback: The demand and supply curves intersect at $30. The legal maximum of $20 is a price ceiling. It is below equilibrium, so it prevents the market from clearing at $30 and is binding.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. At a price ceiling of $20, what is quantity demanded?
micro.Choice A: 250 units
micro.Choice B: 150 units
micro.Choice C: 200 units
micro.Choice D: 300 units
micro.Correct Answer: A — 250 units
micro.Feedback: At $20, the demand curve shows quantity demanded of 250 units.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. At a price ceiling of $20, what is quantity supplied?
micro.Choice A: 150 units
micro.Choice B: 250 units
micro.Choice C: 200 units
micro.Choice D: 100 units
micro.Correct Answer: A — 150 units
micro.Feedback: At $20, the supply curve shows quantity supplied of 150 units.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. If the government sets a price ceiling at $20, what shortage results?
micro.Choice A: 100 units
micro.Choice B: 50 units
micro.Choice C: 150 units
micro.Choice D: 400 units
micro.Correct Answer: A — 100 units
micro.Feedback: At $20, quantity demanded is 250 and quantity supplied is 150. The shortage is 250 - 150 = 100 units.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. If the government sets a price ceiling at $40, what is the most likely result?
micro.Choice A: The price ceiling is not binding
micro.Choice B: A shortage of 100 units occurs
micro.Choice C: A surplus of 100 units occurs
micro.Choice D: The equilibrium quantity falls to 150
micro.Correct Answer: A — The price ceiling is not binding
micro.Feedback: A price ceiling above equilibrium is not binding. Since $40 is above the $30 equilibrium price, it does not affect the market.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: At the $1,000 rent ceiling, what shortage is shown?
micro.Choice A: 50 apartments
micro.Choice B: 200 apartments
micro.Choice C: 150 apartments
micro.Choice D: 300 apartments
micro.Correct Answer: B — 200 apartments
micro.Feedback: Read quantity demanded and quantity supplied at the $1,000 ceiling and subtract: 250 − 50 = 200 apartments.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. At the binding $1,000 rent ceiling, what is the maximum number of apartments that can be rented if transactions cannot exceed the number landlords offer?
micro.Choice A: 150 apartments
micro.Choice B: 200 apartments
micro.Choice C: 50 apartments
micro.Choice D: 250 apartments
micro.Correct Answer: C — 50 apartments
micro.Feedback: At $1,000, quantity supplied is only 50 apartments. Even though 250 are demanded, actual transactions cannot exceed the 50 units offered.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A price ceiling is set at $18 when equilibrium price is $25. At $18, Qd = 900 and Qs = 600. Which statement is correct?
micro.Choice A: The ceiling is binding and creates a shortage of 300
micro.Choice B: The ceiling is nonbinding and creates no shortage
micro.Choice C: The ceiling is binding and creates a surplus of 300
micro.Choice D: The ceiling is a price floor because it is below equilibrium
micro.Correct Answer: A — The ceiling is binding and creates a shortage of 300
micro.Feedback: A ceiling below equilibrium is binding. Shortage is 900 - 600 = 300.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A price ceiling is set above equilibrium. Why does it usually have no effect?
micro.Choice A: The market price remains below the legal maximum
micro.Choice B: Because all price ceilings create shortages
micro.Choice C: Because sellers are forced to charge the maximum
micro.Choice D: Because quantity supplied must equal zero
micro.Correct Answer: A — The market price remains below the legal maximum
micro.Feedback: A nonbinding ceiling is above equilibrium, so the market can still reach equilibrium below the legal maximum.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A rent ceiling lowers the money rent but causes long search times, side payments, and poorer maintenance. What is the best interpretation?
micro.Choice A: Lower legal rent can be offset by nonmoney costs.
micro.Choice B: The ceiling eliminated scarcity
micro.Choice C: The ceiling created a surplus of apartments
micro.Choice D: The price ceiling shifted demand left
micro.Correct Answer: A — Lower legal rent can be offset by nonmoney costs.
micro.Feedback: A binding ceiling can lower the legal price but create search costs, rationing, and quality decline.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: Refer to the price-control graph. Officials lower a price ceiling from $50 to $40 and predict that the market price will fall by $10. With demand and supply unchanged, which assessment is correct?
micro.Choice A: Price falls from $50 to $40 because the ceiling sets the transaction price.
micro.Choice B: Price stays $30 because both legal maxima permit the equilibrium price.
micro.Choice C: Price rises from $30 to $40 because sellers charge the highest legal price.
micro.Choice D: Price falls from $30 to $20 because the legal maximum fell by $10.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Price stays $30 because both legal maxima permit the equilibrium price.
micro.Feedback: The intersection is $30 and 200 units. Both ceilings are above $30, so both are nonbinding. Lowering a nonbinding ceiling while it remains above equilibrium changes the legal limit, not the competitive market outcome.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: Refer to the price-control graph. If a price ceiling is set at $10, what shortage results?
micro.Choice A: 200 units
micro.Choice B: 100 units
micro.Choice C: 300 units
micro.Choice D: 400 units
micro.Correct Answer: A — 200 units
micro.Feedback: At $10, quantity demanded is 300 and quantity supplied is 100. The shortage is 300 - 100 = 200 units.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: Refer to the price-control graph. A policy holds the price at $20. What is the full market result?
micro.Choice A: A binding price ceiling with a shortage of 100 units
micro.Choice B: A nonbinding price ceiling with no effect
micro.Choice C: A binding price floor with a surplus of 100 units
micro.Choice D: A nonbinding price floor with no effect
micro.Correct Answer: A — A binding price ceiling with a shortage of 100 units
micro.Feedback: $20 is below the $30 equilibrium, so it is a binding ceiling. At $20, Qd is 250 and Qs is 150, so the shortage is 100.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: Refer to the price-control graph. At $10, what are quantity demanded and quantity supplied?
micro.Choice A: Quantity demanded is 300 and quantity supplied is 100
micro.Choice B: Quantity demanded is 100 and quantity supplied is 300
micro.Choice C: Quantity demanded is 150 and quantity supplied is 250
micro.Choice D: Quantity demanded is 250 and quantity supplied is 150
micro.Correct Answer: A — Quantity demanded is 300 and quantity supplied is 100
micro.Feedback: At a low price of $10, buyers demand 300 units while sellers supply 100 units.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A $50 price ceiling is imposed with demand and supply unchanged. Which statement correctly classifies the policy using the equilibrium shown?
micro.Choice A: Nonbinding: the legal price is above the $30 equilibrium price, so the market stays at equilibrium.
micro.Choice B: Nonbinding: the legal price is above the $40 equilibrium price, so the market stays at equilibrium.
micro.Choice C: Binding: the legal price is above the $30 equilibrium price, so transactions must occur at $50.
micro.Choice D: Binding: the legal price is above the $40 equilibrium price, so transactions must occur at $50.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Nonbinding: the legal price is above the $30 equilibrium price, so the market stays at equilibrium.
micro.Feedback: The graph’s competitive equilibrium price is $30. A $50 maximum is above that price, so the ceiling does not prevent the equilibrium trade. It is nonbinding, and the market remains at $30 and 200 units.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: An enforced $20 price ceiling is imposed. What additional consequence, beyond the lower posted price, follows from the quantities shown in the graph?
micro.Choice A: A shortage of 100 units makes waiting, search, or another form of nonprice rationing necessary.
micro.Choice B: A shortage of 50 units makes waiting, search, or another form of nonprice rationing necessary.
micro.Choice C: A surplus of 100 units leaves sellers competing to dispose of unsold goods.
micro.Choice D: A surplus of 50 units leaves sellers competing to dispose of unsold goods.
micro.Correct Answer: A — A shortage of 100 units makes waiting, search, or another form of nonprice rationing necessary.
micro.Feedback: At the $20 ceiling, buyers demand 250 units and sellers supply 150, leaving a shortage of 100. Because the legal price cannot rise to clear the market, waiting, search, or another nonprice allocation method must ration the available units.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A city caps rent below equilibrium. The advertised rent falls, but apartment searches become longer, maintenance falls, and landlords screen tenants harder. What is the best economic diagnosis?
micro.Choice A: The ceiling lowers the posted price but creates shortage and nonmoney rationing
micro.Choice B: The ceiling lowers the posted price and therefore eliminates scarcity
micro.Choice C: The ceiling raises quantity supplied and creates seller competition
micro.Choice D: The ceiling is nonbinding because landlords still choose tenant quality
micro.Correct Answer: A — The ceiling lowers the posted price but creates shortage and nonmoney rationing
micro.Feedback: The posted money price is only part of the cost. Binding ceilings create shortage and hidden rationing costs.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A legal maximum price is set above equilibrium. A student predicts a shortage. What is wrong?
micro.Choice A: A ceiling above equilibrium is nonbinding and does not create a shortage
micro.Choice B: Any price ceiling always creates a shortage
micro.Choice C: A ceiling above equilibrium creates a surplus
micro.Choice D: A ceiling above equilibrium is actually a price floor
micro.Correct Answer: A — A ceiling above equilibrium is nonbinding and does not create a shortage
micro.Feedback: A price ceiling binds only when it is below equilibrium.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A binding price ceiling on gasoline leads stations to sell out early. Some stations favor regular customers. What is the best interpretation?
micro.Choice A: The shortage creates nonprice rationing
micro.Choice B: The market clears because the legal price is low
micro.Choice C: The ceiling creates a surplus
micro.Choice D: The ceiling increases supply
micro.Correct Answer: A — The shortage creates nonprice rationing
micro.Feedback: When price cannot ration the good, other methods like waiting, favoritism, and side payments can take over.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A rent ceiling causes landlords to convert apartments into short-term rentals outside the regulated market. What does this show?
micro.Choice A: The ceiling reduced regulated rental supply by changing landlord incentives.
micro.Choice B: A ceiling always increases quantity supplied
micro.Choice C: A ceiling eliminates opportunity cost for landlords
micro.Choice D: A ceiling is nonbinding if landlords find loopholes
micro.Correct Answer: A — The ceiling reduced regulated rental supply by changing landlord incentives.
micro.Feedback: A binding ceiling lowers returns in the regulated market and can push suppliers to adjust around the policy.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Relative to the competitive equilibrium, how do quantity demanded and quantity supplied change at the $1,000 ceiling?
micro.Choice A: Quantity demanded -100; quantity supplied +100.
micro.Choice B: Quantity demanded +200; quantity supplied unchanged.
micro.Choice C: Quantity demanded unchanged; quantity supplied -200.
micro.Choice D: Quantity demanded +100; quantity supplied -100.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Quantity demanded +100; quantity supplied -100.
micro.Feedback: At equilibrium both quantities are 150. At $1,000, quantity demanded is 250 and quantity supplied is 50. Demand therefore rises by 100 while supply falls by 100, opening a 200-unit shortage.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: In a city housing market, a binding rent ceiling leaves 80,000 units demanded but only 52,000 supplied. Tenants who secure units save $300 each, while 28,000 households are rationed out. Which conclusion best captures the welfare tradeoff?
micro.Choice A: The ceiling creates winners and losers
micro.Choice B: All renters benefit because the legal price is lower
micro.Choice C: Landlords benefit because quantity supplied rises
micro.Choice D: The market clears because the legal price is lower
micro.Correct Answer: A — The ceiling creates winners and losers
micro.Feedback: Some renters gain lower rent, but others lose access because the ceiling creates a shortage.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A city caps rent below equilibrium to help renters. In the short run, some renters pay less, but many cannot find apartments and landlords reduce maintenance. Which answer best explains the full economic result?
micro.Choice A: The legal price falls, but shortage, rationing, and quality decline create hidden costs
micro.Choice B: The policy eliminates scarcity because rent is lower
micro.Choice C: The policy creates a surplus because quantity supplied rises
micro.Choice D: The market reaches equilibrium because demand and supply adjust immediately
micro.Correct Answer: A — The legal price falls, but shortage, rationing, and quality decline create hidden costs
micro.Feedback: A binding rent ceiling lowers the legal price but creates a shortage, rationing, search costs, and weaker maintenance incentives.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A city creates a low legal parking fee below equilibrium. Drivers spend extra time circling for spaces, miss class, and compete for limited spots. What is the best economic interpretation?
micro.Choice A: The ceiling lowers the money price but raises nonmoney costs through shortage and rationing
micro.Choice B: The ceiling creates a surplus of parking spaces
micro.Choice C: The ceiling is nonbinding because drivers still pay with time
micro.Choice D: The ceiling shifts demand left
micro.Correct Answer: A — The ceiling lowers the money price but raises nonmoney costs through shortage and rationing
micro.Feedback: A binding price ceiling can lower the posted price while raising search and waiting costs.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A binding rent ceiling lowers the rent paid by tenants who retain apartments by $300. At that rent, 28,000 more households want apartments than landlords offer. Which conclusion is warranted?
micro.Choice A: Continuing tenants save on rent, but the shortage does not identify how many former tenants lost housing
micro.Choice B: All 28,000 unmatched households must previously have rented apartments
micro.Choice C: Every household is better off because the legal rent is lower
micro.Choice D: The rent saving proves aggregate consumer surplus increased
micro.Correct Answer: A — Continuing tenants save on rent, but the shortage does not identify how many former tenants lost housing
micro.Feedback: The shortage compares current quantities demanded and supplied; it is not a count of displaced former tenants. Continuing tenants save on rent, but the net effects on all households also depend on lost access, allocation and any search costs.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: Refer to the apartment graph. Under the displayed ceiling, what is the maximum number of rentals and the excess demand, assuming landlords offer the quantity on S0?
micro.Choice A: At most 50 rentals and excess demand of 200 apartments
micro.Choice B: At most 250 rentals and excess demand of 200 apartments
micro.Choice C: At most 150 rentals and excess demand of 100 apartments
micro.Choice D: At most 50 rentals and excess supply of 200 apartments
micro.Correct Answer: A — At most 50 rentals and excess demand of 200 apartments
micro.Feedback: The ceiling is below the $2,000 equilibrium rent. At $1,000, supply is 50 and demand is 250. Supply limits possible rentals to 50, while excess demand is 250 − 50 = 200. Actual matching could be lower; the graph alone establishes a maximum.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: After a binding rent ceiling is imposed, some landlords move units into unregulated short-term rentals. Which lesson about price controls follows?
micro.Choice A: A policy can change incentives and reduce quantity supplied in the regulated market
micro.Choice B: A ceiling increases quantity supplied because landlords must meet the stronger demand at the lower price.
micro.Choice C: A ceiling eliminates opportunity cost for landlords
micro.Choice D: A ceiling is nonbinding if landlords find loopholes
micro.Correct Answer: A — A policy can change incentives and reduce quantity supplied in the regulated market
micro.Feedback: A binding ceiling lowers returns in the regulated market and can push suppliers to adjust around the policy.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Compare a $20 ceiling with a $40 ceiling, assuming efficient matching and no other restrictions. Which policy comparison is correct?
micro.Choice A: $20 permits 150 trades and creates a 100-unit shortage; $40 allows the 200-unit equilibrium
micro.Choice B: $20 permits 250 trades and creates a 100-unit shortage; $40 allows the 200-unit equilibrium
micro.Choice C: $20 permits 150 trades; $40 forces 250 trades and a 100-unit surplus
micro.Choice D: Both ceilings leave the market at 200 trades because both are legal maximum prices
micro.Correct Answer: A — $20 permits 150 trades and creates a 100-unit shortage; $40 allows the 200-unit equilibrium
micro.Feedback: Equilibrium is $30 and 200 units. The $20 maximum binds: Qs = 150 and Qd = 250, so the shortage is 100 and at most 150 units trade. The $40 maximum allows the equilibrium price below it; it does not force the market to charge $40.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A binding rent ceiling reduces the number of apartments rented, eliminating the gains from some mutually beneficial rentals. Which way of allocating the remaining apartments would cause an additional loss of total surplus?
micro.Choice A: Some available apartments go to lower-value applicants while higher-value applicants go without
micro.Choice B: The remaining apartments all go to the highest-value applicants
micro.Choice C: The lower rent transfers money from landlords to continuing tenants
micro.Choice D: Landlords supply exactly the number of apartments willing buyers rent
micro.Correct Answer: A — Some available apartments go to lower-value applicants while higher-value applicants go without
micro.Feedback: A quantity reduction loses gains from missing beneficial trades. A further allocation loss arises if a lower-value recipient displaces a higher-value applicant. A ceiling does not by itself prove that this misallocation occurs.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: At a binding rent ceiling, 4,000 households demand apartments and landlords offer 2,700. A construction program adds 500 apartments at that rent, while new arrivals raise quantity demanded by 200. Assuming all offered apartments are rented, what changes?
micro.Choice A: Rentals rise by 500 and the shortage falls by 300
micro.Choice B: Rentals rise by 500 and the shortage falls by 500
micro.Choice C: Rentals rise by 200 and the shortage falls by 700
micro.Choice D: Rentals rise by 700 and the shortage stays unchanged
micro.Correct Answer: A — Rentals rise by 500 and the shortage falls by 300
micro.Feedback: Initially the shortage is 4,000 − 2,700 = 1,300. Afterward demand is 4,200 and supply is 3,200, so rentals rise by 500 and the shortage is 1,000, down 300. Additional demand partly offsets the construction program.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: Refer to the apartment graph. One tenant keeps the same apartment after the displayed ceiling is imposed but now spends time searching and queuing valued at $1,100 per month. With apartment quality unchanged, which evaluation is correct?
micro.Choice A: The tenant gains $1,000 net, and the market has excess demand of 200 apartments
micro.Choice B: The tenant loses $100 net, and the market has excess demand of 200 apartments
micro.Choice C: The tenant loses $100 net, and all 200 unmatched applicants must be former tenants
micro.Choice D: The tenant gains $100 net, and the market has excess supply of 200 apartments
micro.Correct Answer: B — The tenant loses $100 net, and the market has excess demand of 200 apartments
micro.Feedback: The graph shows rent falling from $2,000 to $1,000, a $1,000 saving. Subtract the stated $1,100 time cost: the continuing tenant loses $100 net. At the ceiling, Qd = 250 and Qs = 50, giving excess demand of 200. The time cost is specified for this tenant, not asserted for every ceiling.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A city sets a price ceiling below equilibrium to make apartments affordable. The legal rent falls, but renters wait longer, landlords reduce maintenance, and some units are rented off-book. What is the strongest economic conclusion?
micro.Choice A: The posted price falls, but shortage shifts part of the cost into waiting, quality loss, and rationing
micro.Choice B: The posted price falls, so the policy removes the main cost renters face in the market
micro.Choice C: The posted price falls, but the shortage means sellers now compete harder for renters
micro.Choice D: The posted price falls, so the market clears through a lower equilibrium rent
micro.Correct Answer: A — The posted price falls, but shortage shifts part of the cost into waiting, quality loss, and rationing
micro.Feedback: A binding ceiling can lower the posted price while creating shortage, search costs, lower quality, rationing, and misallocation.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: Refer to the price-control graph and treat the plotted curves as straight lines. An enforced ceiling rises from $20 to $25. All units sellers offer are purchased, and there are no side payments or other changes. What happens to the shortage and quantity actually traded?
micro.Choice A: Shortage falls by 25 units; quantity traded rises by 50 units.
micro.Choice B: Shortage rises by 50 units; quantity traded falls by 25 units.
micro.Choice C: Shortage falls by 50 units; quantity traded falls by 25 units.
micro.Choice D: Shortage falls by 50 units; quantity traded rises by 25 units.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Shortage falls by 50 units; quantity traded rises by 25 units.
micro.Feedback: At $20, Qd=250 and Qs=150: shortage is 100 and trades are 150. Halfway to the $30 equilibrium, at $25, Qd=225 and Qs=175: shortage is 50 and trades are 175. The smaller gap reflects both lower quantity demanded and higher quantity supplied; trades are limited by the latter.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: Initially Qd=140-2P and Qs=2P, with a price ceiling of $40. Later demand becomes Qd=200-2P while supply stays fixed. What happens to the ceiling’s effect?
micro.Choice A: Initially nonbinding at equilibrium $35; later binding at $40, with Qd=120, Qs=80 and a shortage of 40.
micro.Choice B: Initially binding at $40 with a shortage of 20; later nonbinding because demand growth raises equilibrium above the ceiling.
micro.Choice C: Initially nonbinding at $35; later nonbinding at $50 because a ceiling never changes when only demand shifts.
micro.Choice D: Initially nonbinding at $35; later binding at $40, with a surplus of 40 because sellers supply more than buyers demand.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Initially nonbinding at equilibrium $35; later binding at $40, with Qd=120, Qs=80 and a shortage of 40.
micro.Feedback: Initially 140-2P=2P gives P=35. Later 200-2P=2P gives P=50, above the ceiling. At P=40, demand is 120 and supply 80, so the previously nonbinding maximum becomes binding and creates a 40-unit shortage.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A binding price ceiling reduces the legal price from $100 to $70. At $70, buyers want 500 units and sellers offer 300 units. Which outcome is most likely?
micro.Choice A: A shortage of 200 units and rationing by waiting, favoritism, or side payments
micro.Choice B: A surplus of 200 units and falling inventories
micro.Choice C: No shortage because the legal price is lower
micro.Choice D: A demand decrease because buyers dislike lower prices
micro.Correct Answer: A — A shortage of 200 units and rationing by waiting, favoritism, or side payments
micro.Feedback: At the ceiling, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied by 200 units. Because price cannot rise, the good must be rationed some other way.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A policy lowers the legal price, creates a shortage, reduces product quality, and causes buyers to spend time searching. Which policy best matches this pattern?
micro.Choice A: A binding price ceiling
micro.Choice B: A binding price floor
micro.Choice C: A nonbinding price floor
micro.Choice D: A seller tax with perfectly elastic demand
micro.Correct Answer: A — A binding price ceiling
micro.Feedback: Lower legal price plus shortage and search costs points to a binding price ceiling.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A binding rent ceiling creates a 200-unit shortage. The city allocates apartments to whoever waits in line longest. Which conclusion best completes the analysis?
micro.Choice A: The money price is lower, but time costs rise and apartments may not go to those who value them most
micro.Choice B: The lower money price eliminates the economic cost of housing
micro.Choice C: Waiting lines prove that quantity supplied now exceeds quantity demanded
micro.Choice D: The allocation is efficient because every renter faces the same legal price
micro.Correct Answer: A — The money price is lower, but time costs rise and apartments may not go to those who value them most
micro.Feedback: A binding ceiling lowers the posted price but can replace money costs with waiting, search, quality loss, and inefficient rationing.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: At a binding rent ceiling, Qd=8,000 and Qs=5,600. Of the supplied units, 400 are assigned by waiting list; they are not additional apartments. Later, 300 landlords withdraw units while Qd at the ceiling is unchanged. An official subtracts the 400 waiting-list allocations from the later shortage. What is the correct diagnosis?
micro.Choice A: Shortage rises from 2,000 to 2,300; waiting-list allocation reduces excess demand independently of the supplied apartments.
micro.Choice B: Shortage rises from 2,400 to 2,700; waiting lists allocate existing supply and do not add units or reduce the underlying gap.
micro.Choice C: Shortage falls from 2,400 to 2,100; withdrawals remove potential renters as well as the landlords’ supplied units.
micro.Choice D: Shortage stays 2,400; nonprice allocation prevents a change in the shortage when legal rent is unchanged.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Shortage rises from 2,400 to 2,700; waiting lists allocate existing supply and do not add units or reduce the underlying gap.
micro.Feedback: Initial excess demand is 8000-5600=2400. Supply then falls to 5300, giving 8000-5300=2700. The 400 apartments are already counted in supply, so subtracting them again double counts an allocation as new capacity.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: A rental market has Qd=10,000-2P and Qs=1,000+P. A $2,000 ceiling is introduced. Over time, 500 units are converted out of the regulated market at every rent, while demand is unchanged. Which sequence follows, and what can be inferred about tenants?
micro.Choice A: Equilibrium was $3,000; surplus is initially 3,000 and later 3,500 units, so all tenants necessarily gain from easier apartment access.
micro.Choice B: Equilibrium was $3,000; shortage is initially 3,000 and later 3,500 units, while search and quality costs can offset some tenants’ posted-rent savings.
micro.Choice C: Equilibrium was $2,000; the ceiling is nonbinding initially, and conversion creates a 500-unit shortage only because demand shifts right.
micro.Choice D: Equilibrium was $3,000; shortage falls from 3,000 to 2,500 units, and lower legal rent guarantees every prospective tenant is better off.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Equilibrium was $3,000; shortage is initially 3,000 and later 3,500 units, while search and quality costs can offset some tenants’ posted-rent savings.
micro.Feedback: Set 10000-2P=1000+P to get P=3000 and Q=4000. At P=2000, Qd=6000 and Qs=3000, a shortage of 3000. Conversion lowers supply to 2500 and raises shortage to 3500. Lower posted rent does not ensure access or exclude search and quality costs.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Question: An economist observes that gasoline prices rise after a supply disruption. A city responds with a binding price ceiling. What is the most likely result?
