micro.Choice B: 676 total boxes
micro.Choice C: 42.3 boxes per worker
micro.Choice D: 23 boxes per added worker
micro.Correct Answer: D — 23 boxes per added worker
micro.Feedback: MPL is the change in output divided by the change in labor: (676 − 630) ÷ (16 − 14) = 23 boxes per added worker.

micro.Question: Is a point inside the PPF unattainable?
micro.Choice A: Yes; any point not on the frontier is unattainable
micro.Choice B: Yes; only points on the PPF are feasible
micro.Choice C: Yes; producing inside the frontier requires more resources than the economy has.
micro.Choice D: No; it is attainable but inefficient
micro.Correct Answer: D — No; it is attainable but inefficient
micro.Feedback: A point inside the PPF is attainable with current resources but productively inefficient because some capacity is unused.

micro.Common Misconception: Confusing movement toward the frontier with a shift of productive capacity.
micro.Question: Does moving along a PPF represent economic growth?
micro.Choice A: No; it reallocates production on the same frontier
micro.Choice B: Yes; any movement to a different production mix is economic growth
micro.Choice C: Yes; producing more of one good means productive capacity has increased
micro.Choice D: Yes; moving along the frontier shifts it outward.
micro.Correct Answer: A — No; it reallocates production on the same frontier
micro.Feedback: Movement along one PPF reallocates production between goods; economic growth requires an outward shift of the frontier.

micro.Common Misconception: Confusing movement toward the frontier with a shift of productive capacity.
micro.Question: What shifts a PPF outward?
micro.Choice A: Moving from one point to another on the existing frontier
micro.Choice B: More resources, better technology, or improved productive capacity
micro.Choice C: Reallocating idle resources without changing productive capacity
micro.Choice D: Producing more of one good by giving up some of the other.
micro.Correct Answer: B — More resources, better technology, or improved productive capacity
micro.Feedback: More resources, improved technology, or better institutions can expand productive capacity and shift the PPF outward.

micro.Question: Why can opportunity cost rise along a bowed-out PPF?
micro.Choice A: Because the money price of the expanding good rises
micro.Choice B: Because the economy becomes less efficient as it moves along the frontier
micro.Choice C: Resources differ in suitability across uses
micro.Choice D: Because scarcity disappears for the good produced in larger quantities.
micro.Correct Answer: C — Resources differ in suitability across uses
micro.Feedback: Specialized resources are less adaptable as production shifts toward one good, so each additional unit can require a larger sacrifice.

micro.Common Misconception: Confusing movement toward the frontier with a shift of productive capacity.
micro.Question: With full resource use and constant tradeoffs, an economy can make 100 food units or 50 medical units. Medical-only technology doubles maximum medical output, leaving maximum food unchanged. At 60 food, compare feasible medical output before and after; then assess an observed rise from an interior point to the old frontier.
micro.Choice A: Medical capacity rises from 20 to 50; every output increase from an interior point proves the whole frontier shifted equally.
micro.Choice B: Medical capacity stays 20 because food technology is unchanged; only a move to a new point on the old line is possible.
micro.Choice C: Medical capacity rises from 40 to 80; an interior-to-frontier move reduces efficiency because fewer resources remain idle.
micro.Choice D: Medical capacity at 60 food rises from 20 to 40; the separate interior-to-old-frontier move is improved utilization, not evidence of that technology shift.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Medical capacity at 60 food rises from 20 to 40; the separate interior-to-old-frontier move is improved utilization, not evidence of that technology shift.
micro.Feedback: The old linear frontier is M=50(1-F/100), giving 20 at F=60. The new one is M=100(1-F/100), giving 40. An interior-to-frontier move under old technology improves utilization without identifying a capacity change.

micro.Common Misconception: Confusing movement toward the frontier with a shift of productive capacity.
micro.Question: An economy initially produces 60 units of each good inside a frontier that permits 80 of each together. Reemploying idle labor reaches 80 of each. New machinery then permits 100 of each together. A planner attributes the entire increase to growth in productive capacity. Which counterfactual best exposes the error?
micro.Choice A: Without new machinery, reemployment could still reach 80 of each; only the later extension beyond the old feasible set demonstrates added capacity.
micro.Choice B: Without reemployment, machinery could not affect the frontier, because a frontier is defined by actual rather than possible output.
micro.Choice C: Without new machinery, output must remain at 60 of each, because any increase in both goods requires an outward frontier shift.
micro.Choice D: Without reemployment, the old frontier would automatically move inward to the observed 60-unit bundle.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Without new machinery, reemployment could still reach 80 of each; only the later extension beyond the old feasible set demonstrates added capacity.
micro.Feedback: Initial unused resources explain movement from 60 to 80 under the old feasible set. Machinery changes what can be produced, permitting 100 of each. Observed output growth combines utilization and capacity changes; it cannot all be labeled a frontier shift.

micro.Topic: Property Rights And Resource Use Incentives
micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.9 — Property Rights and Efficient Resource Use
micro.Common Misconception: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
micro.Question: What is required for a legal property right to change resource-use incentives?
micro.Choice A: The resource must become nonrival
micro.Choice B: The right must be sufficiently clear and enforceable
micro.Choice C: All transaction costs must be zero
micro.Choice D: Every user must value the resource equally
micro.Correct Answer: B — The right must be sufficiently clear and enforceable
micro.Feedback: Users respond to rights when boundaries and permissions are clear and violations can be detected and sanctioned.

micro.Topic: Property Rights And Resource Use Incentives
micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.9 — Property Rights and Efficient Resource Use
micro.Common Misconception: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
micro.Question: Why might a private forest owner conserve young trees?
micro.Choice A: Ownership makes harvesting nonrival
micro.Choice B: The owner cannot exclude trespassers
micro.Choice C: Conservation always has zero current cost
micro.Choice D: Future timber value is part of the owner's private opportunity cost of harvesting now
micro.Correct Answer: D — Future timber value is part of the owner's private opportunity cost of harvesting now
micro.Feedback: Secure ownership lets the owner capture future forest value, so cutting a young tree carries a private cost that open-access harvesters may ignore.

micro.Topic: Property Rights And Resource Use Incentives
micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.9 — Property Rights and Efficient Resource Use
micro.Common Misconception: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
micro.Question: A toll is introduced on a congested road. How can this improve resource-use incentives?
micro.Choice A: Drivers face a price connected to scarce road capacity and delay
micro.Choice B: The toll makes road space unlimited
micro.Choice C: The toll guarantees no congestion at any price
micro.Choice D: Drivers stop receiving private trip benefits
micro.Correct Answer: A — Drivers face a price connected to scarce road capacity and delay
micro.Feedback: A toll can make access excludable and require drivers to consider more of the congestion cost associated with scarce road space.

micro.Topic: Property Rights And Resource Use Incentives
micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.9 — Property Rights and Efficient Resource Use
micro.Common Misconception: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
micro.Question: Which claim about assigning property rights is too strong?
micro.Choice A: Enforcement matters
micro.Choice B: Property rights automatically produce perfect efficiency in every setting
micro.Choice C: Monitoring can be costly
micro.Choice D: Rights can improve conservation incentives
micro.Correct Answer: B — Property rights automatically produce perfect efficiency in every setting
micro.Feedback: Rights can align incentives, but unclear boundaries, weak enforcement, ecological spillovers, market power, and transaction costs can prevent a perfect outcome.

micro.Topic: Property Rights And Resource Use Incentives
micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.9 — Property Rights and Efficient Resource Use
micro.Common Misconception: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
micro.Question: An exclusive grazing lease is never monitored, and outsiders continue using the land. What is the main problem?
micro.Choice A: Grazing has become nonrival
micro.Choice B: The lease creates free riding on a public good
micro.Choice C: The right is not effectively enforceable
micro.Choice D: Ownership eliminates the need for boundaries
micro.Correct Answer: C — The right is not effectively enforceable
micro.Feedback: A paper lease does not create practical exclusion when unauthorized grazing cannot be detected or stopped.

micro.Topic: Property Rights And Resource Use Incentives
micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.9 — Property Rights and Efficient Resource Use
micro.Common Misconception: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
micro.Question: How can transferable catch shares reduce a race to fish?
micro.Choice A: Shares eliminate scarcity
micro.Choice B: Shares make fish nonrival
micro.Choice C: Shares require every fisher to use identical equipment
micro.Choice D: Fishers no longer need to capture their allowed share before everyone else
micro.Correct Answer: D — Fishers no longer need to capture their allowed share before everyone else
micro.Feedback: A secure share gives each holder a defined claim, reducing the incentive to race for an unowned portion of the catch.

micro.Topic: Property Rights And Resource Use Incentives
micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.9 — Property Rights and Efficient Resource Use
micro.Common Misconception: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
micro.Question: Why can community-managed access rights sometimes improve stewardship?
micro.Choice A: Users who share enforceable rules also retain more of the benefits from conserving the resource
micro.Choice B: Community rules make depletion impossible
micro.Choice C: Shared management eliminates rivalry
micro.Choice D: Local users face no monitoring costs
micro.Correct Answer: A — Users who share enforceable rules also retain more of the benefits from conserving the resource
micro.Feedback: Collective rights can align use with the group's future resource value when rules and sanctions are credible.

micro.Topic: Property Rights And Resource Use Incentives
micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.9 — Property Rights and Efficient Resource Use
micro.Common Misconception: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
micro.Question: A city converts an open parking district into spaces reserved for permit holders. Which characteristic changes most directly?
micro.Choice A: Parking becomes nonrival
micro.Choice B: Excludability increases
micro.Choice C: Scarcity disappears
micro.Choice D: Every permit holder consumes the same space
micro.Correct Answer: B — Excludability increases
micro.Feedback: Permits let the city deny access to nonholders, creating excludability. Rivalry remains because one occupied space is unavailable to another driver.

micro.Topic: Property Rights And Resource Use Incentives
micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.9 — Property Rights and Efficient Resource Use
micro.Common Misconception: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
micro.Question: What conservation incentive does a long-term water right create that a one-day extraction race may not?
micro.Choice A: The holder stops valuing current water
micro.Choice B: The right makes the aquifer nonrival
micro.Choice C: The holder can benefit from preserving future availability
micro.Choice D: The right removes all uncertainty
micro.Correct Answer: C — The holder can benefit from preserving future availability
micro.Feedback: A durable claim lets the holder capture part of the future value created by restraint, bringing future scarcity into today's private decision.

micro.Topic: Property Rights And Resource Use Incentives
micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.9 — Property Rights and Efficient Resource Use
micro.Common Misconception: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
micro.Question: Why can defining rights be difficult for migratory wildlife?
micro.Choice A: Wildlife is always nonrival
micro.Choice B: Property rights require a market price of zero
micro.Choice C: Migration eliminates social value
micro.Choice D: The resource crosses boundaries and is costly to monitor
micro.Correct Answer: D — The resource crosses boundaries and is costly to monitor
micro.Feedback: Movement across jurisdictions complicates boundaries, monitoring, and enforcement, limiting how completely rights can create exclusion.

micro.Topic: Property Rights And Resource Use Incentives
micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.9 — Property Rights and Efficient Resource Use
micro.Common Misconception: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
micro.Question: A fishing cooperative can exclude outsiders but cannot prevent members from exceeding internal limits. What remains unresolved?
micro.Choice A: Enforcement among authorized users
micro.Choice B: The fish stock has become nonrival
micro.Choice C: Outsider exclusion is the only relevant incentive
micro.Choice D: The cooperative has created a public good
micro.Correct Answer: A — Enforcement among authorized users
micro.Feedback: Excluding outsiders helps, but members still need monitored and enforceable use rules to prevent depletion within the group.

micro.Topic: Property Rights And Resource Use Incentives
micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.9 — Property Rights and Efficient Resource Use
micro.Common Misconception: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
micro.Question: How do clear rights differ from a general request to conserve?
micro.Choice A: A request makes the resource excludable automatically
micro.Choice B: Clear rights specify who may use the resource and who bears gains or losses from stewardship
micro.Choice C: Clear rights eliminate marginal cost
micro.Choice D: A request guarantees penalties for overuse
micro.Correct Answer: B — Clear rights specify who may use the resource and who bears gains or losses from stewardship
micro.Feedback: Defined rights connect authorized use and future resource value to identifiable decision-makers, while a general request may leave access and consequences diffuse.

micro.Topic: Property Rights And Resource Use Incentives
micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.9 — Property Rights and Efficient Resource Use
micro.Common Misconception: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
micro.Question: Which combination is most likely to reduce open-access overuse?
micro.Choice A: Undefined access, no monitoring, and voluntary restraint only
micro.Choice B: More users with identical extraction incentives
micro.Choice C: Clear access rights, feasible monitoring, and credible enforcement
micro.Choice D: A rule that cannot detect violations
micro.Correct Answer: C — Clear access rights, feasible monitoring, and credible enforcement
micro.Feedback: Rights alter behavior most reliably when users know the boundaries, compliance can be observed, and violations carry credible consequences.

micro.Topic: Property Rights And Resource Use Incentives
micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.9 — Property Rights and Efficient Resource Use
micro.Common Misconception: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
micro.Question: Why can property or access rights improve common-resource efficiency?
micro.Choice A: They make the resource nonrival
micro.Choice B: They guarantee zero transaction cost
micro.Choice C: They remove every competing use
micro.Choice D: They make users bear more of the opportunity cost of depletion
micro.Correct Answer: D — They make users bear more of the opportunity cost of depletion
micro.Feedback: Enforceable rights connect current use with forgone future value or lost use by others, reducing the incentive for open-access overuse.

micro.Topic: Property Rights And Resource Use Incentives
micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.9 — Property Rights and Efficient Resource Use
micro.Common Misconception: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
micro.Question: How can enforceable fishing rights reduce overharvesting?
micro.Choice A: Right holders bear more of the loss from depleting the future stock
micro.Choice B: Rights make fish nonrival
micro.Choice C: Rights eliminate every monitoring cost
micro.Choice D: Rights guarantee equal income for fishers
micro.Correct Answer: A — Right holders bear more of the loss from depleting the future stock
micro.Feedback: A secure claim to future harvest gives the holder a reason to preserve stock value rather than race to take fish before others do.

micro.Topic: Property Rights And Resource Use Incentives
micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.9 — Property Rights and Efficient Resource Use
micro.Common Misconception: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
micro.Question: A village assigns each household a monitored groundwater allowance. What incentive changes?
micro.Choice A: Groundwater becomes nonrival
micro.Choice B: Future scarcity disappears
micro.Choice C: Households face a clearer limit on the opportunity cost of withdrawal
micro.Choice D: Every household must pump its full allowance
micro.Correct Answer: C — Households face a clearer limit on the opportunity cost of withdrawal
micro.Feedback: A monitored allowance replaces unrestricted access with enforceable use rights, reducing the incentive to pump before others do.

micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.7 — Cost-Benefit Analysis and Efficient Public-Good Provision
micro.Common Misconception: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
micro.Question: Refer to the emergency-sirens graph. At what quantity do MSB and MC intersect?
micro.Choice A: 40 sirens
micro.Choice B: 20 sirens
micro.Choice C: 30 sirens
micro.Choice D: 60 sirens
micro.Correct Answer: A — 40 sirens
micro.Feedback: MSB intersects MC at 40 sirens, so the marginal social benefit of the 40th siren equals its marginal cost.

micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.7 — Cost-Benefit Analysis and Efficient Public-Good Provision
micro.Common Misconception: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
micro.Question: Which number of sirens and decision rule maximize net social benefits in the graph?
micro.Choice A: 40; stop where marginal social benefit equals marginal cost.
micro.Choice B: 60; stop where marginal social benefit equals marginal cost.
micro.Choice C: 40; expand until total benefit falls to zero.
micro.Choice D: 60; expand until total benefit falls to zero.
micro.Correct Answer: A — 40; stop where marginal social benefit equals marginal cost.
micro.Feedback: MSB intersects MC at 40 sirens and $20,000 per siren. Further sirens have cost above their added benefit even though total benefit remains positive. The decision rule is marginal.

micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.7 — Cost-Benefit Analysis and Efficient Public-Good Provision
micro.Common Misconception: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
micro.Question: Which challenge arises when benefits from flood protection occur decades in the future?
micro.Choice A: Future and uncertain benefits must be estimated and compared with current costs
micro.Choice B: Future benefits are automatically zero
micro.Choice C: Marginal cost stops mattering
micro.Choice D: The project becomes a private good
micro.Correct Answer: A — Future and uncertain benefits must be estimated and compared with current costs
micro.Feedback: Long horizons require forecasts and comparison of benefits and costs occurring at different times, adding uncertainty to valuation.

micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.7 — Cost-Benefit Analysis and Efficient Public-Good Provision
micro.Common Misconception: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. At the efficient emergency-siren quantity, what marginal benefit and marginal cost are shown?
micro.Choice A: $10,000 per siren
micro.Choice B: $20,000 per siren
micro.Choice C: $30,000 per siren
micro.Choice D: $40,000 per siren
micro.Correct Answer: B — $20,000 per siren
micro.Feedback: At 40 sirens, the graph shows 20 on an axis measured in thousands of dollars per siren, so MSB and MC both equal $20,000 per siren.

micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.7 — Cost-Benefit Analysis and Efficient Public-Good Provision
micro.Common Misconception: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. At the efficient 30-mile coastal-protection quantity, what marginal value do both curves show?
micro.Choice A: $15 million per mile
micro.Choice B: $45 million per mile
micro.Choice C: $60 million per mile
micro.Choice D: $30 million per mile
micro.Correct Answer: D — $30 million per mile
micro.Feedback: At Q = 30, the graph shows both MSB and MC at $30 million per mile.

micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.7 — Cost-Benefit Analysis and Efficient Public-Good Provision
micro.Common Misconception: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. What happens to the net marginal benefit of coastal protection as quantity approaches 30 miles from below?
micro.Choice A: It rises because both curves slope upward
micro.Choice B: It stays fixed at $30 million
micro.Choice C: It becomes private benefit rather than social benefit
micro.Choice D: It falls toward zero as MSB approaches MC
micro.Correct Answer: D — It falls toward zero as MSB approaches MC
micro.Feedback: Net marginal benefit is MSB minus MC. The graph's gap narrows as Q rises and reaches zero at the efficient 30-mile intersection.

micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.7 — Cost-Benefit Analysis and Efficient Public-Good Provision
micro.Common Misconception: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
micro.Question: How can free riding bias a survey used to value a proposed public good?
micro.Choice A: Respondents must overstate marginal cost
micro.Choice B: The survey makes the good rival
micro.Choice C: Only nonbeneficiaries answer surveys
micro.Choice D: Respondents may understate willingness to pay if answers affect their expected contribution
micro.Correct Answer: D — Respondents may understate willingness to pay if answers affect their expected contribution
micro.Feedback: People who expect to receive the good regardless of payment may report low values to reduce their expected cost share.

micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.7 — Cost-Benefit Analysis and Efficient Public-Good Provision
micro.Common Misconception: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
micro.Question: Why might voluntary donations be a poor measure of total benefit from a public warning system?
micro.Choice A: Donations include only marginal cost
micro.Choice B: Noncontributors can benefit, so donations omit part of willingness to pay
micro.Choice C: Warning systems are rival
micro.Choice D: Total benefit equals government spending
micro.Correct Answer: B — Noncontributors can benefit, so donations omit part of willingness to pay
micro.Feedback: Observed gifts reflect contributed private payments, not necessarily the full value received by contributors and free riders.

micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.7 — Cost-Benefit Analysis and Efficient Public-Good Provision
micro.Common Misconception: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
micro.Question: A council can afford 20, 30 or 40 miles of protection. Which target in the graph maximizes net social benefit, and what is the economic reason?
micro.Choice A: 40 miles; stop adding protection when marginal social benefit equals marginal cost.
micro.Choice B: 30 miles; any affordable target is equally efficient regardless of marginal benefits and costs.
micro.Choice C: 30 miles; stop adding protection when marginal social benefit equals marginal cost.
micro.Choice D: 40 miles; any affordable target is equally efficient regardless of marginal benefits and costs.
micro.Correct Answer: C — 30 miles; stop adding protection when marginal social benefit equals marginal cost.
micro.Feedback: MSB meets MC at 30 miles. The units between 20 and 30 add positive net benefits, while units beyond 30 cost more than their added benefit. Affordability permits a choice; it does not establish efficiency.

micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.7 — Cost-Benefit Analysis and Efficient Public-Good Provision
micro.Common Misconception: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
micro.Question: Why is cost-benefit analysis difficult when a public good has no ordinary market price?
micro.Choice A: Public goods have no opportunity cost
micro.Choice B: Marginal benefit cannot be positive
micro.Choice C: Analysts lack a direct price signal revealing beneficiaries' willingness to pay
micro.Choice D: Market prices always overstate social value
micro.Correct Answer: C — Analysts lack a direct price signal revealing beneficiaries' willingness to pay
micro.Feedback: Without ordinary purchases and prices, analysts must estimate benefits that market transactions do not directly reveal.

micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.7 — Cost-Benefit Analysis and Efficient Public-Good Provision
micro.Common Misconception: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
micro.Question: An analyst values a public-health information campaign using only benefits to people who completed a survey. What may be missing?
micro.Choice A: The campaign's excludability must be zero
micro.Choice B: Every unobserved benefit is a cost
micro.Choice C: Benefits to affected people who were not identified or surveyed
micro.Choice D: Only the producer's profit matters
micro.Correct Answer: C — Benefits to affected people who were not identified or surveyed
micro.Feedback: Public-good benefits can be dispersed, so failing to identify all affected beneficiaries understates marginal social benefit.

micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.7 — Cost-Benefit Analysis and Efficient Public-Good Provision
micro.Common Misconception: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
micro.Question: Which statement best compares efficient provision of a public good with an ordinary private good?
micro.Choice A: Public goods ignore marginal cost
micro.Choice B: Private goods require vertical summation of all buyers at one quantity
micro.Choice C: Public goods are efficient whenever government supplies them
micro.Choice D: Both use marginal benefit versus marginal cost, but public-good benefit is harder to observe and aggregate
micro.Correct Answer: D — Both use marginal benefit versus marginal cost, but public-good benefit is harder to observe and aggregate
micro.Feedback: The same marginal efficiency principle applies, but nonexcludability, free riding, dispersed benefits, and missing market prices make public-good MSB harder to estimate.

micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.7 — Cost-Benefit Analysis and Efficient Public-Good Provision
micro.Common Misconception: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
micro.Question: A cost-saving method lowers the graphed MC by $15 million per mile at every quantity, leaving MSB unchanged. Treat quantity as continuous. Which revised target and decision rule are correct?
micro.Choice A: 50 miles; equate MSB to the new MC.
micro.Choice B: 40 miles; retain the old MC when evaluating the additional miles.
micro.Choice C: 40 miles; equate MSB to the new MC.
micro.Choice D: 50 miles; retain the old MC when evaluating the additional miles.
micro.Correct Answer: C — 40 miles; equate MSB to the new MC.
micro.Feedback: The graph implies MSB = 60−Q and original MC = 15+0.5 Q, in millions. New MC is 0.5 Q. Equating 60−Q = 0.5 Q gives 40 miles, with both margins at $20 million. The efficiency rule uses the changed cost.

micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.7 — Cost-Benefit Analysis and Efficient Public-Good Provision
micro.Common Misconception: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
micro.Question: Refer to the sirens graph, treating provision as continuous. A proposal installs 60 rather than the quantity that maximizes net social benefit. What excess provision and loss follow, and can positive total benefits alone justify the proposal?
micro.Choice A: 20 excess sirens and $400,000 of lost net benefit; every dollar spent on them is a net loss.
micro.Choice B: 20 excess sirens and $100,000 of lost net benefit; positive total benefits do not establish that the extra sirens are worthwhile.
micro.Choice C: 40 excess sirens and $200,000 of lost net benefit; the marginal-cost value is the target quantity.
micro.Choice D: No excess provision; any quantity with positive MSB maximizes net social benefit.
micro.Correct Answer: B — 20 excess sirens and $100,000 of lost net benefit; positive total benefits do not establish that the extra sirens are worthwhile.
micro.Feedback: MSB = MC at 40. From 40 to 60, the gap MC - MSB rises from 0 to $10,000 per siren. The excess-loss triangle is 0.5 x 20 x 10,000 = $100,000. Extra sirens may have positive benefit while costing even more.

micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.5 — Public Goods and the Free-Rider Problem
micro.Common Misconception: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
micro.Question: A household understates how much it values flood protection during a voluntary fundraising survey. What motive may explain the response?
micro.Choice A: It wants the barrier to become rival
micro.Choice B: It cannot benefit if another household pays
micro.Choice C: It hopes to lower its payment while still receiving protection
micro.Choice D: It is revealing the full social benefit
micro.Correct Answer: C — It hopes to lower its payment while still receiving protection
micro.Feedback: Because protection reaches the household even if it contributes little, understating willingness to pay can reduce its expected share of the cost.

micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.5 — Public Goods and the Free-Rider Problem
micro.Common Misconception: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
micro.Question: Which statement best distinguishes a free rider from someone who receives no benefit?
micro.Choice A: A free rider pays but cannot consume
micro.Choice B: A free rider depletes an open-access resource
micro.Choice C: A free rider benefits but does not pay or contribute
micro.Choice D: A free rider always breaks a law
micro.Correct Answer: C — A free rider benefits but does not pay or contribute
micro.Feedback: Free riding requires receiving a benefit without contributing toward its cost; a person who receives no benefit is not riding on others' provision.

micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.5 — Public Goods and the Free-Rider Problem
micro.Common Misconception: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
micro.Question: Why can a unanimous claim that 'someone else will fund it' be self-defeating for a public good?
micro.Choice A: If everyone withholds payment, a valued project may not be provided
micro.Choice B: Withholding makes MSB equal zero
micro.Choice C: The project becomes rival
micro.Choice D: The project is necessarily overprovided
micro.Correct Answer: A — If everyone withholds payment, a valued project may not be provided
micro.Feedback: Individually attractive free riding can produce a collective outcome in which contributions are too small to finance a project whose total social benefit exceeds cost.

micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.5 — Public Goods and the Free-Rider Problem
micro.Common Misconception: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
micro.Question: In the public-radio graph, how much provision is omitted by relying on Private Benefit rather than MSB, and what explains the difference?
micro.Choice A: 20 hours; free riding can keep voluntary payments below the value of shared benefits.
micro.Choice B: 40 hours; free riding can keep voluntary payments below the value of shared benefits.
micro.Choice C: 40 hours; voluntary payments necessarily capture every nonpayer’s benefit.
micro.Choice D: 20 hours; voluntary payments necessarily capture every nonpayer’s benefit.
micro.Correct Answer: B — 40 hours; free riding can keep voluntary payments below the value of shared benefits.
micro.Feedback: Private Benefit meets MC at 40 hours; MSB meets MC at 80. Between them MSB exceeds cost. Nonexcludability allows nonpayers to benefit, so observed private contributions can understate the relevant social marginal benefit.

micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.5 — Public Goods and the Free-Rider Problem
micro.Common Misconception: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
micro.Question: At 40 hours, how large is the gap between MSB and Private Benefit in the radio graph?
micro.Choice A: $2,000 per hour
micro.Choice B: $6,000 per hour
micro.Choice C: $8,000 per hour
micro.Choice D: $4,000 per hour
micro.Correct Answer: D — $4,000 per hour

micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.5 — Public Goods and the Free-Rider Problem
micro.Common Misconception: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
micro.Question: A public safety website is funded by voluntary gifts. Many users assume enough other people will donate. What is the likely result?

micro.Feedback: When each user relies on others to fund a nonexcludable service, aggregate contributions can be insufficient even when users collectively value it highly.

micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.5 — Public Goods and the Free-Rider Problem

micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.5 — Public Goods and the Free-Rider Problem
micro.Common Misconception: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.

micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.5 — Public Goods and the Free-Rider Problem

micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.5 — Public Goods and the Free-Rider Problem
micro.Common Misconception: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
micro.Question: A shared warning service costs $600 and will be provided only if fully funded. Four households each value it at $200; nonpayers cannot be excluded. Three have irrevocably contributed $150 each. What is the fourth household’s best choice if it cares only about its own net benefit?
micro.Choice A: Contribute the remaining $150: its contribution is pivotal and leaves a $50 net benefit.
micro.Choice B: Contribute nothing: a nonpayer can enjoy the service even if it is never funded.
micro.Choice C: Contribute $200: full willingness to pay is the minimum needed to finish funding.
micro.Choice D: Contribute nothing: total social benefit below $600 makes the service inefficient.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Contribute the remaining $150: its contribution is pivotal and leaves a $50 net benefit.
micro.Feedback: The shortfall is 600 - 3 x 150 = $150. Without that payment the service is not provided; paying leaves 200 - 150 = $50. Nonexcludability creates free-riding incentives, but a pivotal contribution can still be privately worthwhile.

micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.5 — Public Goods and the Free-Rider Problem

micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.5 — Public Goods and the Free-Rider Problem

micro.Learning Objective: PGCR.5 — Public Goods and the Free-Rider Problem

micro.Question: A nonexcludable siren project is worth $300 to each of five households and costs $1,000. One household cannot finance it alone. A binding agreement would collect $200 from each household only if all five sign, with no contracting costs. Which comparison follows?

micro.Correct Answer: B — Uncoordinated funding can fail despite $500 of total gains; the conditional agreement can make every household $100 better off.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.3 — Budget-Line Slope and Opportunity Cost
micro.Question: Good X costs $3 and good Y costs $6. What is the opportunity cost of one unit of X in units of Y?

micro.Choice D: It cannot be found without utility
micro.Correct Answer: A — 3/6 unit of Y
micro.Feedback: The opportunity cost is the relative price Px/Py, so one X uses the income needed for 3/6 unit of Y.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.3 — Budget-Line Slope and Opportunity Cost

micro.Learning Objective: CC.3 — Budget-Line Slope and Opportunity Cost
micro.Question: A budget line has Y on the vertical axis and X on the horizontal axis. X costs $5 and Y costs $10. What is its slope?

micro.Learning Objective: CC.3 — Budget-Line Slope and Opportunity Cost
micro.Question: One unit of X costs 0.4 units of Y. If Y costs $10, what is the price of X?

micro.Question: X costs $7 and Y costs $8. What is the opportunity cost of one Y, expressed in units of X?

micro.Correct Answer: B — 8/7 units of X

micro.Learning Objective: CC.3 — Budget-Line Slope and Opportunity Cost

micro.Choice C: 8 units
micro.Choice D: 6 units

micro.Learning Objective: CC.3 — Budget-Line Slope and Opportunity Cost

micro.Choice B: The reciprocal price ratio in units of Y

micro.Learning Objective: CC.3 — Budget-Line Slope and Opportunity Cost
micro.Question: Starting from bundle B in the graph, cereal rises to $10 per box while income and the yogurt price stay fixed. If the consumer keeps B’s yogurt quantity, what is the most cereal the consumer can afford, and how does the budget change?
micro.Choice A: 1.2 boxes; the budget pivots inward.
micro.Choice B: 1.6 boxes; the budget pivots inward.
micro.Choice C: 1.6 boxes; the budget shifts inward in parallel.
micro.Choice D: 1.2 boxes; the budget shifts inward in parallel.
micro.Correct Answer: B — 1.6 boxes; the budget pivots inward.
micro.Feedback: B contains six yogurts. They cost 6 × $4 = $24, leaving $16 of the $40 income for cereal: 16/10 = 1.6 boxes. Only the cereal intercept changes, so the line pivots rather than shifting in parallel.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.3 — Budget-Line Slope and Opportunity Cost
micro.Question: Initially X costs $6 and Y costs $12. Both prices then double while income stays fixed. Which comparison is correct?
micro.Choice A: The opportunity cost of X doubles; both budget intercepts halve.
micro.Choice B: The opportunity cost of X stays at 0.5 Y; both budget intercepts stay fixed.
micro.Choice C: The opportunity cost of X halves; both budget intercepts double.
micro.Choice D: The opportunity cost of X stays at 0.5 Y; both budget intercepts halve.
micro.Correct Answer: D — The opportunity cost of X stays at 0.5 Y; both budget intercepts halve.
micro.Feedback: Doubling both prices leaves their ratio unchanged, but fixed income buys half as much of either good.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.3 — Budget-Line Slope and Opportunity Cost
micro.Question: X initially costs $5 and Y costs $12. X rises to $6 while Y rises to $18. Has X become more or less costly in units of Y?
micro.Choice A: More costly: the ratio rises because X has a higher dollar price.
micro.Choice B: Unchanged: both prices increased.
micro.Choice C: Less costly: the ratio falls from 12/5 to 3.
micro.Choice D: Less costly: the ratio falls from 5/12 to 1/3.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Less costly: the ratio falls from 5/12 to 1/3.
micro.Feedback: Relative cost depends on Px/Py. It falls from about 0.417 to 0.333 even though the dollar price of X rises.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.3 — Budget-Line Slope and Opportunity Cost
micro.Question: X costs $3 and Y costs $10. A student says that doubling income halves the opportunity cost of X. What is the error?
micro.Choice A: Income changes the price ratio, but the opportunity cost remains 3 Y.
micro.Choice B: The opportunity cost doubles because purchasing power doubles.
micro.Choice C: Income changes affordability, but the unchanged price ratio still makes one X cost 0.3 Y.
micro.Choice D: The student should halve both money prices when income doubles.
micro.Correct Answer: C — Income changes affordability, but the unchanged price ratio still makes one X cost 0.3 Y.
micro.Feedback: Opportunity cost in units of Y is Px/Py = 3/10. An income increase shifts the budget line outward without changing its slope.

micro.Learning Objective: CC.3 — Budget-Line Slope and Opportunity Cost
micro.Question: X initially costs $3 and Y costs $8. After X rises to $6, a shopper says “the opportunity cost of two extra X is still three-quarters of a Y because income did not change.” Which correction is right?
micro.Choice A: Two extra X now cost the income needed for 0.75 Y; unchanged income holds the price ratio fixed.
micro.Choice B: Two extra X now cost the income needed for 1.5 Y; opportunity cost depends on relative prices, not unchanged income.
micro.Choice C: Two extra X now cost the income needed for 2.67 Y; use Y’s price divided by X’s price for each X.
micro.Choice D: Two extra X now cost the income needed for 6 Y; the dollar price is already measured in Y units.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Two extra X now cost the income needed for 1.5 Y; opportunity cost depends on relative prices, not unchanged income.
micro.Feedback: At the new prices one X costs 6/8=0.75 Y, so two X cost 1.5 Y. The former two-X cost was 2×3/8=0.75 Y; income does not determine this ratio.

micro.Choice B: It screens or separates borrowers by willingness and ability to bear default consequences
micro.Choice C: It creates moral hazard intentionally
micro.Choice D: It proves all borrowers have identical risk
micro.Correct Answer: B — It screens or separates borrowers by willingness and ability to bear default consequences
micro.Feedback: Contract terms can elicit private information when different risk types choose differently or face different costs.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.4 — Signaling and Screening
micro.Question: An employer offers two contract packages that induce applicants with different private productivity to choose differently. Who designs the information-revealing action, and what is it called?
micro.Choice A: The informed applicant designs screening.
micro.Choice B: The uninformed employer sends a signal of applicant quality.
micro.Choice C: The applicants disclose all types through a compulsory public test.
micro.Choice D: The uninformed employer designs screening.
micro.Correct Answer: D — The uninformed employer designs screening.
micro.Feedback: Screening is initiated by the less-informed side through offers that reveal private information via choices.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.4 — Signaling and Screening
micro.Question: Evidence indicates that a credential is more costly for low-productivity workers than for high-productivity workers. Why can it be informative?
micro.Choice A: Different costs can make the credential credibly distinguish workers by productivity
micro.Choice B: Any costless claim is automatically credible
micro.Choice C: It directly raises every worker's productivity by definition
micro.Choice D: It eliminates employer uncertainty without inference
micro.Correct Answer: A — Different costs can make the credential credibly distinguish workers by productivity
micro.Feedback: A credible signal must be sufficiently harder for the type that would like to imitate it.

micro.Question: A bank offers borrowers a choice between a low-interest loan with collateral and a high-interest loan without collateral. Borrowers privately know their repayment risk. Which action constitutes screening?

micro.Choice B: The bank’s design of the contract menu
micro.Choice C: The bank’s payment after a default
micro.Choice D: A borrower’s change in effort after the loan
micro.Correct Answer: B — The bank’s design of the contract menu
micro.Feedback: The uninformed bank designs alternatives intended to reveal risk through borrowers’ choices.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.4 — Signaling and Screening
micro.Question: A job applicant independently obtains a credible certificate before approaching employers. Employers did not require or design a menu of choices. Which information mechanism is described?

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.4 — Signaling and Screening
micro.Question: An informed seller voluntarily posts a warranty that is much more expensive for low-quality sellers to honor. Why can it convey quality?
micro.Choice A: All sellers face identical warranty costs and incentives.
micro.Choice B: Low-quality sellers may find imitation less profitable because expected warranty costs are higher.
micro.Choice C: Posting a warranty mechanically improves the physical product.
micro.Choice D: A warranty prevents buyers from learning about defects.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Low-quality sellers may find imitation less profitable because expected warranty costs are higher.
micro.Feedback: Different expected costs can make the observable warranty a credible signal rather than cheap talk.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.4 — Signaling and Screening
micro.Question: In this setting, an insurer offers a high-deductible and a low-deductible plan so customers reveal risk through their choice. What mechanism is this?

micro.Choice B: A Condorcet vote
micro.Choice C: Anchoring
micro.Choice D: Screening by the less-informed insurer
micro.Correct Answer: D — Screening by the less-informed insurer
micro.Feedback: The uninformed side designs a menu that induces different hidden types to self-select.

micro.Question: A policy analyst notes that a credential is more costly for low-productivity workers than for high-productivity workers. Why can it be informative?

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.4 — Signaling and Screening
micro.Question: A job applicant chooses to obtain an unsolicited certificate before applying; an employer separately offers a menu of trial contracts to reveal applicants’ types. Which action is signaling?
micro.Choice A: The applicant’s certificate
micro.Choice B: The employer’s contract menu
micro.Choice C: Both actions are signaling by the informed side.
micro.Choice D: Neither action can convey information.
micro.Correct Answer: A — The applicant’s certificate
micro.Feedback: The informed applicant initiates the certificate signal. The uninformed employer initiates the screening menu.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.4 — Signaling and Screening
micro.Question: An insurer offers plans with different deductibles so applicants reveal risk through their choices. What mechanism is this?
micro.Choice A: Signaling by the insurer
micro.Choice B: Screening by the less-informed insurer
micro.Choice C: A default nudge
micro.Choice D: A Condorcet vote
micro.Correct Answer: B — Screening by the less-informed insurer
micro.Feedback: The uninformed side designs a menu that induces hidden types to self-select.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.4 — Signaling and Screening
micro.Question: A borrower offers collateral as a signal of repayment confidence. Suppose both high-risk and low-risk borrowers face the same expected collateral loss and obtain the same loan benefit. What follows?
micro.Choice A: Collateral necessarily separates types even when their incentives match.
micro.Choice B: The stated costs and benefits do not give the two types different signaling incentives.
micro.Choice C: Equal incentives reveal every borrower to be low risk.
micro.Choice D: Equal incentives convert the signal into perfect lender screening.
micro.Correct Answer: B — The stated costs and benefits do not give the two types different signaling incentives.
micro.Feedback: A separating signal needs an incentive difference that makes mimicking unattractive for one type. The stated identical payoffs provide none.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.4 — Signaling and Screening
micro.Question: A warranty initially costs good sellers $2 and bad sellers $20 to honor. Third-party insurance then makes the warranty cost $3 for either type. Holding the price premium fixed, does the warranty become a stronger or weaker signal of product quality, and why?
micro.Choice A: It strengthens because identical costs reveal quality more accurately.
micro.Choice B: It weakens because the warranty no longer imposes a higher signaling cost on bad sellers.
micro.Choice C: It is unchanged because signaling never depends on imitation incentives.
micro.Choice D: It reverses physical quality, making bad products good.
micro.Correct Answer: B — It weakens because the warranty no longer imposes a higher signaling cost on bad sellers.
micro.Feedback: Equalizing the cost removes the original reason bad sellers would be less willing to mimic the warranty.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.4 — Signaling and Screening
micro.Question: High-productivity applicants value a job at $30,000 more than their alternative and face a $5,000 certificate cost. Low-productivity applicants gain $10,000 and face a $15,000 cost. With the job available only to certificate holders, can certification separate the two types under these payoffs?
micro.Choice A: No; both types gain because the job is valuable.
micro.Choice B: No; both types lose because certification is costly.
micro.Choice C: Yes; low types gain $5,000 while high types lose $25,000.
micro.Choice D: Yes; high types gain $25,000 net while low types would lose $5,000.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Yes; high types gain $25,000 net while low types would lose $5,000.
micro.Feedback: High types have benefit minus cost 30,000 − 5,000 = 25,000; low types have 10,000 − 15,000 = −5,000. Their incentives differ as separation requires.

micro.Learning Objective: IBP.4 — Signaling and Screening
micro.Question: An insurer offers low-premium/high-deductible and high-premium/low-deductible plans before it knows applicants’ risk types. A customer separately provides a costly certified safety record. Which distinction correctly identifies the two information mechanisms?
micro.Choice A: The menu is signaling by the informed insurer; the customer’s record is screening by the uninformed side.
micro.Choice B: Both are screening because neither depends on who initiates the information mechanism.
micro.Choice C: Both are moral hazard because the information concerns actions only after coverage begins.
micro.Choice D: The menu is screening by the less-informed insurer; the customer’s credible record is signaling by the informed side.
micro.Correct Answer: D — The menu is screening by the less-informed insurer; the customer’s credible record is signaling by the informed side.
micro.Feedback: The insurer designs a menu to induce self-selection, a screening device. The informed applicant supplies a credible observable record, a signal. Timing and who initiates the mechanism distinguish them.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.4
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. What can be concluded about the move from D to B?
micro.Choice A: Price falls; quantity rises in the drawing
micro.Choice B: Price and quantity both remain unchanged
micro.Choice C: Quantity falls; the price direction is ambiguous
micro.Choice D: Price rises; quantity is unchanged in the drawing
micro.Correct Answer: D — Price rises; quantity is unchanged in the drawing
micro.Feedback: From D to B, the opposing quantity effects cancel while both shifts raise equilibrium price, so quantity is unchanged and price rises.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.4
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. How do equilibrium price and quantity change from A to B?
micro.Choice A: Price rises 4 dollars; quantity stays 200 thousand
micro.Choice B: Price rises 4 dollars; quantity rises 200 thousand
micro.Choice C: Price falls 4 dollars; quantity stays 200 thousand
micro.Choice D: Price stays 10 dollars; quantity falls 4 thousand
micro.Correct Answer: A — Price rises 4 dollars; quantity stays 200 thousand
micro.Feedback: The quantity effects offset while price rises from 10 to 14 dollars.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.4
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Which statement distinguishes the general prediction for these simultaneous shifts from the particular outcome shown?
micro.Choice A: Price is generally ambiguous; quantity must rise and does so here
micro.Choice B: Price must rise; quantity is generally ambiguous but unchanged here
micro.Choice C: Both price and quantity must remain unchanged after both shifts
micro.Choice D: Price must fall; quantity is generally ambiguous but rises here
micro.Correct Answer: B — Price must rise; quantity is generally ambiguous but unchanged here
micro.Feedback: Demand up and supply down reinforce price but oppose in quantity.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.4
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
micro.Question: Cheaper alternative transportation reduces gasoline demand while refinery costs fall. For the move from B to D, which outcome and explanation fit the graph?
micro.Choice A: Price falls $2 and quantity stays at 200 thousand gallons per day; the two shifts have offsetting effects on quantity.
micro.Choice B: Price falls $1 and quantity stays at 200 thousand gallons per day; the two shifts have offsetting effects on quantity.
micro.Choice C: Price falls $2 and quantity stays at 200 thousand gallons per day; unchanged quantity means neither curve shifted.
micro.Choice D: Price falls $1 and quantity stays at 200 thousand gallons per day; unchanged quantity means neither curve shifted.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Price falls $2 and quantity stays at 200 thousand gallons per day; the two shifts have offsetting effects on quantity.
micro.Feedback: Cheaper alternative transportation reduces gasoline demand, while lower refinery costs increase supply. B is at $6 and 200 thousand gallons per day; D is at $4 and 200 thousand. The $2 price fall accompanies offsetting quantity effects: lower demand reduces quantity, while higher supply increases it. Unchanged equilibrium quantity does not mean the curves stayed fixed.

micro.Correct Answer: A — Labor-market discrimination

micro.Learning Objective: IP.5 — Sources of Income Differences
micro.Question: A safety improvement eliminates a job hazard without changing productivity, worker skills or other job amenities. In a competitive labor market, what happens to the compensating part of its wage?
micro.Choice A: It tends to rise because the job is safer.
micro.Choice B: It stays fixed because compensating differentials depend only on productivity.
micro.Choice C: It becomes an inheritance payment rather than labor income.
micro.Choice D: It tends to fall because the undesirable attribute has been removed.
micro.Correct Answer: D — It tends to fall because the undesirable attribute has been removed.
micro.Feedback: Workers require less compensation for risk when the risk falls, holding other determinants of pay fixed.

micro.Learning Objective: IP.5 — Sources of Income Differences
micro.Question: Two jobs have equal risk and amenities, but one requires scarce technical training. Why is a higher wage in that job not evidence of a compensating differential for danger?
micro.Choice A: Every wage difference is compensation for danger.
micro.Choice B: Training changes wealth but cannot affect earnings.
micro.Choice C: Equal danger implies equal productivity in both jobs.
micro.Choice D: The stated difference is skill scarcity, while risk is held equal.
micro.Correct Answer: D — The stated difference is skill scarcity, while risk is held equal.
micro.Feedback: A risk premium requires a difference in risk. Here skill requirements provide a distinct explanation of the wage gap.

micro.Learning Objective: IP.5 — Sources of Income Differences
micro.Question: A household receives a one-time $60,000 inheritance and saves it. Its annual wage remains $30,000. Which statement correctly separates stocks and flows?
micro.Choice A: The inheritance raises its wage to $90,000 every year.
micro.Choice B: The inheritance raises its asset stock; it does not by itself raise its annual wage flow.
micro.Choice C: Saving the inheritance prevents it from affecting wealth.
micro.Choice D: The inheritance is a debt because it is not earned through labor.
micro.Correct Answer: B — The inheritance raises its asset stock; it does not by itself raise its annual wage flow.
micro.Feedback: Accumulated assets are wealth measured at a point in time. Wages are a flow over a period, and the inherited asset need not change that flow.

micro.Correct Answer: D — A compensating wage differential
micro.Feedback: A riskier or less pleasant job may need to pay more to attract workers.

micro.Learning Objective: IP.5 — Sources of Income Differences
micro.Question: Two households each earn $50,000 from work. One inherits $100,000 and invests it at 4% per year; the other receives no inheritance. Ignoring taxes and other income, how do next year’s labor earnings and total incomes compare?
micro.Choice A: Labor earnings differ by $100,000; total income is equal.
micro.Choice B: Labor earnings are equal; the inheriting household has $4,000 more total income.
micro.Choice C: Labor earnings are equal; total income differs by $100,000 each year.
micro.Choice D: Both labor earnings and total income differ by $4,000.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Labor earnings are equal; the inheriting household has $4,000 more total income.
micro.Feedback: An inheritance is an asset stock; its 4% return produces a $4,000 annual income flow without changing labor earnings.

micro.Learning Objective: IP.5 — Sources of Income Differences
micro.Question: Two households have equal labor earnings. Household A inherits productive assets, while B does not. A proposal equalizes their current labor earnings but leaves asset ownership and returns unchanged. Which evaluation is justified?
micro.Choice A: The proposal eliminates the wealth gap because equal annual earnings imply equal asset stocks.
micro.Choice B: The proposal leaves this wealth gap and associated capital-income gap in place; equal labor earnings do not establish equal economic resources.
micro.Choice C: The proposal removes capital income by holding labor earnings equal.
micro.Choice D: The proposal increases labor productivity in B by transferring ownership of A’s assets.
micro.Correct Answer: B — The proposal leaves this wealth gap and associated capital-income gap in place; equal labor earnings do not establish equal economic resources.
micro.Feedback: A stock of inherited assets can persist and yield income independently of equal labor earnings. A labor-income rule alone does not transfer that stock.

micro.Learning Objective: IP.5 — Sources of Income Differences
micro.Question: A household holds assets of $180,000 and debt of $70,000, including an inherited asset worth $40,000 already included in total assets. What is its net wealth?
micro.Feedback: Net wealth equals assets minus debt: $180,000 − $70,000 = $110,000. Adding the inheritance again would double-count it.

micro.Learning Objective: IP.5 — Sources of Income Differences
micro.Question: A dangerous job pays more than a safe job, but its workers also have more training. After training is controlled for, the wage gap shrinks but remains positive. What does this evidence support?
micro.Choice A: Training explains the entire gap; the remaining difference is evidence against risk compensation.
micro.Choice B: Risk compensation explains the entire gap; the training adjustment is irrelevant.
micro.Choice C: The remaining gap measures inherited wealth rather than labor income.
micro.Choice D: Training explains part of the gap; the rest could reflect compensation for risk, but other explanations may remain.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Training explains part of the gap; the rest could reflect compensation for risk, but other explanations may remain.
micro.Feedback: The observed gap mixes worker characteristics and job attributes. Controlling for training removes one competing explanation but does not establish that no other differences remain.

micro.Learning Objective: FM.2 — Value of Marginal Product, Wages, and Hiring Decisions
micro.Common Misconception: Compares physical marginal product directly with a dollar wage instead of comparing VMP with labor cost.
micro.Question: The monopsonist has chosen to hire 4,000 nurses. In the graph, what hourly wage does it pay, and which curve determines that wage?
micro.Choice A: $20, read from labor supply.
micro.Choice B: $25, read from labor supply.
micro.Choice C: $20, read from marginal factor cost.
micro.Choice D: $30, the marginal cost of hiring the last nurse.
micro.Correct Answer: A — $20, read from labor supply.
micro.Feedback: At 4,000 nurses (40 hundreds), labor supply shows $20 per hour. The $30 MFC includes the extra wage expense associated with expanding employment; it is not the wage paid.

micro.Learning Objective: FM.2 — Value of Marginal Product, Wages, and Hiring Decisions
micro.Common Misconception: Compares physical marginal product directly with a dollar wage instead of comparing VMP with labor cost.
micro.Question: Which employment and decision rule identify the monopsonist’s hiring in the graph?
micro.Choice A: 3,000 nurses; equate marginal factor cost with marginal revenue product.
micro.Choice B: 4,000 nurses; equate the wage on supply with marginal revenue product.
micro.Choice C: 3,000 nurses; equate the wage on supply with marginal revenue product.
micro.Choice D: 4,000 nurses; equate marginal factor cost with marginal revenue product.
micro.Correct Answer: D — 4,000 nurses; equate marginal factor cost with marginal revenue product.
micro.Feedback: MFC and MRP intersect at 40 hundreds, or 4,000 nurses. A monopsonist compares the extra hiring expenditure with the extra revenue generated; supply = MRP is the competitive benchmark instead.

micro.Learning Objective: FM.10 — Factor-Market Equilibrium
micro.Common Misconception: Confuses the equilibrium factor price and quantity or ignores shortage and surplus adjustment.
micro.Question: Why is the minimum wage in the graph binding, and how far above the competitive wage is it?
micro.Choice A: $5 above it; the legal lower bound prevents adjustment to the market-clearing wage.
micro.Choice B: $10 above it; the legal lower bound prevents adjustment to the market-clearing wage.
micro.Choice C: $5 above it; a lower bound binds because any positive minimum wage fixes all wages.
micro.Choice D: $10 above it; a lower bound binds because any positive minimum wage fixes all wages.
micro.Correct Answer: A — $5 above it; the legal lower bound prevents adjustment to the market-clearing wage.
micro.Feedback: The minimum is $20 and equilibrium is $15, a $5 gap. A floor above equilibrium rules out the wage that would clear the market; positivity alone does not make it binding.

micro.Learning Objective: FM.10 — Factor-Market Equilibrium
micro.Common Misconception: Confuses the equilibrium factor price and quantity or ignores shortage and surplus adjustment.
micro.Question: Refer to the minimum-wage graph. Which gap between the market-clearing wage and the legal minimum, and policy conclusion, are correct?
micro.Choice A: $10; the floor is nonbinding, so it does not create a labor surplus.
micro.Choice B: $5; a legal minimum requires pay to fall to that minimum and creates a labor surplus.
micro.Choice C: $10; a legal minimum requires pay to fall to that minimum and creates a labor surplus.
micro.Choice D: $5; the floor is nonbinding, so it does not create a labor surplus.
micro.Correct Answer: D — $5; the floor is nonbinding, so it does not create a labor surplus.
micro.Feedback: Equilibrium is $15 while the legal minimum is $10. Paying the market wage already complies with the floor. The $5 gap therefore creates neither a forced wage reduction nor policy-induced excess supply.

micro.Learning Objective: FM.10 — Factor-Market Equilibrium
micro.Common Misconception: Confuses the equilibrium factor price and quantity or ignores shortage and surplus adjustment.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph above. What labor surplus does the $20 floor create in the textbook model?
micro.Choice A: 400 workers
micro.Choice B: 2,000 workers
micro.Choice C: 6,000 workers
micro.Choice D: 4,000 workers
micro.Correct Answer: D — 4,000 workers
micro.Feedback: Labor supplied is 6,000 and labor demanded is 2,000, leaving a surplus of 4,000 workers.

micro.Learning Objective: FM.10 — Factor-Market Equilibrium
micro.Common Misconception: Confuses the equilibrium factor price and quantity or ignores shortage and surplus adjustment.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph above. A student calls 6,000 workers the employment level at the floor. What graph-based correction is needed?
micro.Choice A: That is labor demanded; supply is 2,000
micro.Choice B: The floor creates 6,000 new jobs
micro.Choice C: That is labor supplied; firms demand only 2,000 workers
micro.Choice D: The competitive equilibrium is 6,000 workers
micro.Correct Answer: C — That is labor supplied; firms demand only 2,000 workers
micro.Feedback: The right intersection measures people willing to work. Actual transactions are limited by the short side, labor demanded at 2,000.

micro.Common Misconception: Confuses the equilibrium factor price and quantity or ignores shortage and surplus adjustment.
micro.Question: Refer to the minimum-wage graph. Which gap between the market-clearing wage and the legal minimum, and policy conclusion, are correct?
micro.Choice A: $10; the floor is nonbinding, so it does not create a labor surplus.
micro.Choice B: $5; the floor is nonbinding, so it does not create a labor surplus.
micro.Choice C: $5; a legal minimum requires pay to fall to that minimum and creates a labor surplus.
micro.Choice D: $10; a legal minimum requires pay to fall to that minimum and creates a labor surplus.
micro.Correct Answer: B — $5; the floor is nonbinding, so it does not create a labor surplus.
micro.Feedback: Equilibrium is $15 while the legal minimum is $10. Paying the market wage already complies with the floor. The $5 gap therefore creates neither a forced wage reduction nor policy-induced excess supply.

micro.Learning Objective: FM.11 — Labor-Market Equilibrium Wage and Employment
micro.Common Misconception: Confuses a firm hiring decision with equilibrium in the market that aggregates many firms and workers.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph above. If employment cannot exceed firms' quantity demanded, what employment level follows at the floor?
micro.Choice A: 2,000 workers
micro.Choice B: 4,000 workers
micro.Choice C: 6,000 workers
micro.Choice D: 8,000 workers
micro.Correct Answer: A — 2,000 workers
micro.Feedback: At $20, firms demand 2,000 workers. Willingness of 6,000 people to work does not create additional jobs.

micro.Learning Objective: FM.11 — Labor-Market Equilibrium Wage and Employment
micro.Common Misconception: Confuses a firm hiring decision with equilibrium in the market that aggregates many firms and workers.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph above. What market outcome remains after the $10 floor is imposed?
micro.Choice A: 4,000 workers at $15 per hour
micro.Choice B: 2,000 workers at $10 per hour
micro.Choice C: 6,000 workers at $10 per hour
micro.Choice D: 4,000 workers at $10 per hour
micro.Correct Answer: A — 4,000 workers at $15 per hour
micro.Feedback: Because the floor is below equilibrium, the intersection at 4,000 workers and $15 remains feasible and unchanged.

micro.Learning Objective: FM.11 — Labor-Market Equilibrium Wage and Employment
micro.Common Misconception: Confuses a firm hiring decision with equilibrium in the market that aggregates many firms and workers.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph above. How many workers seek restaurant jobs at the minimum wage?
micro.Choice A: 600 workers
micro.Choice B: 2,000 workers
micro.Choice C: 6,000 workers
micro.Choice D: 4,000 workers
micro.Correct Answer: C — 6,000 workers
micro.Feedback: The $20 line intersects labor supply at 60 hundreds of workers, or 6,000 workers.

micro.Learning Objective: FM.11 — Labor-Market Equilibrium Wage and Employment
micro.Common Misconception: Confuses a firm hiring decision with equilibrium in the market that aggregates many firms and workers.
micro.Question: Compared with competition in the graph, what wage and employment prevail under the minimum wage, and which side of the market limits actual hiring?
micro.Choice A: $25 and 1,000 workers; firms’ demand limits employment.
micro.Choice B: $20 and 2,000 workers; firms’ demand limits employment.
micro.Choice C: $20 and 2,000 workers; the number wanting work determines employment regardless of firms’ demand.
micro.Choice D: $25 and 1,000 workers; the number wanting work determines employment regardless of firms’ demand.
micro.Correct Answer: B — $20 and 2,000 workers; firms’ demand limits employment.
micro.Feedback: The $20 floor is above the $15 equilibrium. At $20 firms demand 20 hundreds, so 2,000 are employed despite 6,000 willing workers. Actual trade is limited by the short side, labor demand.

micro.Learning Objective: FM.11 — Labor-Market Equilibrium Wage and Employment
micro.Common Misconception: Confuses a firm hiring decision with equilibrium in the market that aggregates many firms and workers.
micro.Question: Refer to the graph above. Which change would make the wage floor binding, holding the curves fixed?
micro.Choice A: Lower it below $10
micro.Choice B: Move it to zero
micro.Choice C: Raise it above $15 per hour
micro.Choice D: Keep it at $10
micro.Correct Answer: C — Raise it above $15 per hour
micro.Feedback: A floor affects the competitive outcome only when it is set above the $15 market-clearing wage.

micro.Learning Objective: FM.11 — Labor-Market Equilibrium Wage and Employment
micro.Common Misconception: Confuses a firm hiring decision with equilibrium in the market that aggregates many firms and workers.
micro.Question: Refer to the monopsony graph. How much lower are wage and employment than under competition, and what hiring rule accounts for the difference?
micro.Choice A: $10 and 4,000 workers lower; monopsony equates MFC with MRP, then pays the supply-curve wage.
micro.Choice B: $5 and 2,000 workers lower; monopsony equates the wage itself with MRP to choose employment.
micro.Choice C: $5 and 2,000 workers lower; monopsony equates MFC with MRP, then pays the supply-curve wage.
micro.Choice D: $10 and 4,000 workers lower; monopsony equates the wage itself with MRP to choose employment.
micro.Correct Answer: C — $5 and 2,000 workers lower; monopsony equates MFC with MRP, then pays the supply-curve wage.
micro.Feedback: MFC = MRP at 40 hundreds, with wage $20 on supply. Competition has supply = MRP at 60 hundreds and $25. Monopsony restricts hiring because marginal factor cost exceeds the wage.

micro.Learning Objective: FM.11 — Labor-Market Equilibrium Wage and Employment
micro.Common Misconception: Confuses a firm hiring decision with equilibrium in the market that aggregates many firms and workers.
micro.Question: Use the graph. A report calls all excess job seekers at the plotted wage floor “jobs lost.” Which figures and correction distinguish these measures?
micro.Choice A: Jobs fall by 1,000; excess labor supply is 2,000 because the higher wage also attracts additional job seekers.
micro.Choice B: Jobs fall by 2,000; excess labor supply is 4,000 because the higher wage also attracts additional job seekers.
micro.Choice C: Jobs fall by 2,000; excess labor supply is 4,000, and both figures measure the same decline in employment.
micro.Choice D: Jobs fall by 1,000; excess labor supply is 2,000, and both figures measure the same decline in employment.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Jobs fall by 2,000; excess labor supply is 4,000 because the higher wage also attracts additional job seekers.
micro.Feedback: Competitive employment is 40 hundreds. At the $20 floor, demand is 20 hundreds and supply 60 hundreds. Jobs lost = (40−20) × 100 = 2,000; excess supply = (60−20) × 100 = 4,000. The second includes new job seekers.

micro.Learning Objective: FM.11 — Labor-Market Equilibrium Wage and Employment
micro.Common Misconception: Confuses a firm hiring decision with equilibrium in the market that aggregates many firms and workers.
micro.Question: A proposal expands hiring from the monopsony outcome toward the competitive outcome in the graph. Which employment increase and welfare argument are correct?
micro.Choice A: 1,000 additional nurses; their marginal product value exceeds opportunity cost, while higher wages are transfers.
micro.Choice B: 2,000 additional nurses; their marginal product value exceeds opportunity cost, while higher wages are transfers.
micro.Choice C: 2,000 additional nurses; the larger wage payments themselves are the extra real resource gains.
micro.Choice D: 1,000 additional nurses; the larger wage payments themselves are the extra real resource gains.
micro.Correct Answer: B — 2,000 additional nurses; their marginal product value exceeds opportunity cost, while higher wages are transfers.
micro.Feedback: MFC = MRP gives monopsony employment of 40 hundreds; supply = MRP gives 60 hundreds. In between, MRP exceeds the opportunity cost on supply. The additional 2,000 hires recover gains from trade; wage transfers alone do not measure those gains.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Question: When only the price of a good changes, what happens on the supply curve?
micro.Choice A: There is movement along the supply curve
micro.Choice B: The supply curve shifts right
micro.Choice C: The supply curve shifts left
micro.Choice D: Demand shifts right
micro.Correct Answer: A — There is movement along the supply curve
micro.Feedback: A good's own price changes quantity supplied, not supply.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Question: The price of handmade tables rises. What is the most precise result?
micro.Choice A: Quantity supplied increases
micro.Choice B: Supply increases
micro.Choice C: Demand increases
micro.Choice D: Supply decreases
micro.Correct Answer: A — Quantity supplied increases
micro.Feedback: Because the good's own price changed, sellers move along the supply curve.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Question: Which event shifts supply?
micro.Choice A: Input costs change
micro.Choice B: The good's own price changes
micro.Choice C: Quantity demanded changes
micro.Choice D: Consumers' income changes
micro.Correct Answer: A — Input costs change
micro.Feedback: Input costs shift supply. The good's own price causes movement along supply.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Question: Steel is an input in car production. If the price of steel rises, what happens to the supply of cars?
micro.Choice A: Supply decreases
micro.Choice B: Supply increases
micro.Choice C: Demand decreases
micro.Choice D: Quantity supplied increases
micro.Correct Answer: A — Supply decreases
micro.Feedback: The repair cue identifies steel as an input. A higher input price raises marginal production cost and shifts car supply left.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Question: Bread's selling price rises, while flour becomes cheaper. Considering each change separately, how does it affect the supply of bread?
micro.Choice A: Higher bread price moves sellers along supply; cheaper flour shifts supply right.
micro.Choice B: Higher bread price shifts supply right; cheaper flour moves sellers along supply.
micro.Choice C: Higher bread price moves sellers along supply; cheaper flour shifts supply left.
micro.Choice D: Both changes move sellers along the same supply curve.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Higher bread price moves sellers along supply; cheaper flour shifts supply right.
micro.Feedback: Bread's own price changes quantity supplied along a supply curve. Flour is a production input: a lower flour price reduces cost at each output level, shifting bread supply right. These are separate mechanisms.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Question: The price of concert tickets falls, and venues offer fewer tickets for resale. Which statement is most precise?
micro.Choice A: Quantity supplied decreased, but supply did not necessarily shift
micro.Choice B: Supply decreased because price changed
micro.Choice C: Demand increased because price fell
micro.Choice D: Supply shifted right because sellers offered fewer tickets
micro.Correct Answer: A — Quantity supplied decreased, but supply did not necessarily shift
micro.Feedback: A change in the good's own price changes quantity supplied, not supply.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Question: A new machine lowers the cost of producing shoes. What happens in the shoe market?
micro.Choice A: Supply increases
micro.Choice B: Supply decreases
micro.Choice C: Demand increases
micro.Choice D: Quantity demanded decreases
micro.Correct Answer: A — Supply increases
micro.Feedback: Better technology lowers production costs, shifting supply right.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Question: Delivery firms face higher diesel prices and also receive higher prices for each delivery. Consider each change separately. Which change reduces delivery supply at every delivery price?
micro.Choice A: Higher delivery prices; they shift delivery supply left.
micro.Choice B: Higher diesel prices; they shift delivery supply right.
micro.Choice C: Higher diesel prices; they shift delivery supply left.
micro.Choice D: Higher delivery prices; they move firms down the supply curve.
micro.Correct Answer: C — Higher diesel prices; they shift delivery supply left.
