micro.Feedback: Diesel is an input. Its higher price raises the cost of making deliveries, so firms offer fewer at each delivery price: supply shifts left. A higher price received per delivery instead increases quantity supplied along a curve.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Question: The law of supply says that, other things equal:
micro.Choice A: As price rises, quantity supplied rises
micro.Choice B: As price rises, demand rises
micro.Choice C: As price falls, quantity supplied rises
micro.Choice D: As price falls, supply shifts right
micro.Correct Answer: A — As price rises, quantity supplied rises
micro.Feedback: The law of supply says price and quantity supplied move in the same direction.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Question: If the price of a good rises, what happens to quantity supplied?
micro.Choice A: Quantity supplied increases
micro.Choice B: Supply decreases
micro.Choice C: Demand increases
micro.Choice D: The supply curve shifts left
micro.Correct Answer: A — Quantity supplied increases
micro.Feedback: A change in the good's own price causes movement along the supply curve.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Question: Which change would shift the supply curve?
micro.Choice A: A change in input costs
micro.Choice B: A change in the good's own price
micro.Choice C: A change in quantity demanded
micro.Choice D: A movement along the demand curve.
micro.Correct Answer: A — A change in input costs
micro.Feedback: Input costs shift supply. The good's own price changes quantity supplied.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Question: If the cost of steel rises for car producers, what happens to the supply of cars?
micro.Choice A: Supply decreases
micro.Choice B: Supply increases
micro.Choice C: Demand decreases
micro.Choice D: Quantity demanded increases
micro.Correct Answer: A — Supply decreases
micro.Feedback: Steel is an input in car production. A higher steel price raises producers' costs, so the car supply curve shifts left.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Question: An improvement in production technology usually causes:
micro.Choice A: Supply to increase
micro.Choice B: Demand to decrease
micro.Choice C: Quantity demanded to fall because price changed
micro.Choice D: A binding price floor
micro.Correct Answer: A — Supply to increase
micro.Feedback: Better technology makes production easier or cheaper, shifting supply right.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Confusing market supply with one firm’s supply or with demand.
micro.Question: Market supply at a given price is the:
micro.Choice A: Sum of the quantities all sellers are willing and able to offer.
micro.Choice B: Quantity supplied by the single largest seller at that price.
micro.Choice C: Average quantity each seller plans to produce at that price.
micro.Choice D: Total quantity buyers are willing and able to purchase at that price.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Sum of the quantities all sellers are willing and able to offer.
micro.Feedback: Market supply horizontally adds the quantities supplied by every seller at each price.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
micro.Question: On the displayed coffee supply curve, what price and quantity are shown at point A?
micro.Choice A: $11 and 225 thousand units
micro.Choice B: $6 and 225 thousand units
micro.Choice C: $6 and 100 thousand units
micro.Choice D: $2 and 100 thousand units
micro.Correct Answer: C — $6 and 100 thousand units
micro.Feedback: At point A, the supply curve pairs a price of $6 with a quantity supplied of 100 thousand units.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
micro.Question: In the displayed hamburger market, the move from S0 to S1 represents:
micro.Choice A: A decrease in supply
micro.Choice B: An increase in supply
micro.Choice C: An increase in quantity supplied caused only by a higher price
micro.Choice D: A decrease in demand
micro.Correct Answer: A — A decrease in supply
micro.Feedback: S1 lies to the left and above S0, showing less quantity supplied at each common price.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
micro.Question: How should the taco supply change from S0 to S1 be classified?
micro.Choice A: A decrease in supply
micro.Choice B: An increase in quantity supplied caused only by a higher price
micro.Choice C: An increase in supply
micro.Choice D: A decrease in demand
micro.Correct Answer: C — An increase in supply
micro.Feedback: S1 lies below and to the right of S0, showing more quantity supplied at each common price.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Question: The price of handmade tables rises, and sellers produce more tables. What happened?
micro.Choice A: Quantity supplied increased
micro.Choice B: Supply increased
micro.Choice C: Demand increased
micro.Choice D: Supply shifted right
micro.Correct Answer: A — Quantity supplied increased
micro.Feedback: A change in the good's own price causes movement along supply, so quantity supplied changes.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Question: The price of a good falls, and sellers produce less of it. What happened?
micro.Choice A: Quantity supplied decreased
micro.Choice B: Supply decreased
micro.Choice C: Demand increased
micro.Choice D: Supply shifted right
micro.Correct Answer: A — Quantity supplied decreased
micro.Feedback: A change in the good's own price changes quantity supplied, not supply.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Question: A new machine lowers the cost of producing shoes. What happens to the supply of shoes?
micro.Choice A: Supply increases
micro.Choice B: Supply decreases
micro.Choice C: Demand decreases
micro.Choice D: Quantity demanded decreases
micro.Correct Answer: A — Supply increases
micro.Feedback: Lower production costs from better technology shift supply right.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Question: Several sellers leave the market. What happens to market supply?
micro.Choice A: Supply decreases
micro.Choice B: Supply increases
micro.Choice C: Demand decreases
micro.Choice D: Quantity supplied rises
micro.Correct Answer: A — Supply decreases
micro.Feedback: Fewer sellers means less market supply at each price.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Question: An input used to make pizza becomes more expensive. What is the likely effect in the pizza market?
micro.Choice A: Supply decreases and price rises
micro.Choice B: Supply increases and price falls
micro.Choice C: Demand increases and price rises
micro.Choice D: Quantity demanded increases because cost rose
micro.Correct Answer: A — Supply decreases and price rises
micro.Feedback: Higher input costs decrease supply, which tends to raise price.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Question: Refer to the supply and demand graph. Which curve shift is shown when equilibrium moves from Price P2, Quantity Q1 to Price P1, Quantity Q2?
micro.Choice A: A rightward shift in supply
micro.Choice B: A rightward shift in demand
micro.Choice C: A leftward shift in demand
micro.Choice D: A leftward shift in supply
micro.Correct Answer: A — A rightward shift in supply
micro.Feedback: The move from D1 with S1 to D1 with S2 lowers price and raises quantity, which matches an increase in supply.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Treating a producer subsidy as a movement along supply or a demand shifter.
micro.Question: The government begins paying producers a subsidy for every unit sold. What happens to market supply, other things equal?
micro.Choice A: Supply shifts left because the subsidy increases firms’ effective production cost.
micro.Choice B: Supply shifts right because the subsidy lowers the effective marginal cost of selling output.
micro.Choice C: Quantity supplied rises along the original curve because only the market price changed.
micro.Choice D: Demand shifts right because the payment is received directly by buyers.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Supply shifts right because the subsidy lowers the effective marginal cost of selling output.
micro.Feedback: A per-unit producer subsidy raises the return from supplying each unit and shifts supply right.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
micro.Question: At a market price of $8, approximately how many units does the displayed coffee supply curve show producers are willing to sell?
micro.Choice A: 100 thousand units
micro.Choice B: 175 thousand units
micro.Choice C: 150 thousand units
micro.Choice D: 225 thousand units
micro.Correct Answer: C — 150 thousand units
micro.Feedback: The supply line passes through quantity 150 thousand at a price of $8.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
micro.Question: Use the graph. A producer claims that the move from A to B proves that supply increased. Which quantity change and diagnosis are correct?
micro.Choice A: An increase of 100 thousand units; this is a change in quantity supplied along the existing curve.
micro.Choice B: An increase of 125 thousand units; any rise in quantity is an increase in the whole supply schedule.
micro.Choice C: An increase of 100 thousand units; any rise in quantity is an increase in the whole supply schedule.
micro.Choice D: An increase of 125 thousand units; this is a change in quantity supplied along the existing curve.
micro.Correct Answer: D — An increase of 125 thousand units; this is a change in quantity supplied along the existing curve.
micro.Feedback: A is at 100 thousand units and B at 225 thousand, an increase of 125 thousand. Both lie on the same supply curve. The higher own price changes quantity supplied; an increase in supply would shift the entire schedule.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
micro.Question: What economic change does the move from A to B in the coffee graph represent?
micro.Choice A: Price rises $5; quantity supplied increases by 100 thousand along the existing curve.
micro.Choice B: Price rises $5; supply increases by 125 thousand because the curve shifts right.
micro.Choice C: Price rises $5; supply increases by 100 thousand because the curve shifts right.
micro.Choice D: Price rises $5; quantity supplied increases by 125 thousand along the existing curve.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Price rises $5; quantity supplied increases by 125 thousand along the existing curve.
micro.Feedback: A is at $6 and 100 thousand units; B is at $11 and 225 thousand. Price rises $5 and quantity supplied rises 125 thousand along the same supply curve. This is an increase in quantity supplied, not a rightward shift of supply.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
micro.Question: Moving from point A to point B on the displayed supply curve changes quantity supplied by:
micro.Choice A: An increase of 125 thousand units
micro.Choice B: A decrease of 125 thousand units
micro.Choice C: An increase of 5 thousand units
micro.Choice D: An increase of 225 thousand units
micro.Correct Answer: A — An increase of 125 thousand units
micro.Feedback: Quantity supplied rises from 100 thousand at A to 225 thousand at B, an increase of 125 thousand.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
micro.Question: At a price of $9 on the displayed hamburger graph, how does quantity supplied change when supply shifts from S0 to S1?
micro.Choice A: It increases from 100 thousand to 200 thousand
micro.Choice B: It decreases from 200 thousand to 100 thousand
micro.Choice C: It decreases from 300 thousand to 200 thousand
micro.Choice D: It stays at 200 thousand
micro.Correct Answer: B — It decreases from 200 thousand to 100 thousand
micro.Feedback: At $9, S0 shows 200 thousand units while S1 shows 100 thousand, a decrease of 100 thousand at the same price.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
micro.Question: Which event is consistent with the shift from S0 to S1 shown in the hamburger market?
micro.Choice A: The price of hamburgers rises and firms move up S0
micro.Choice B: A new cost-saving grill technology is adopted
micro.Choice C: The price of a major meat input rises
micro.Choice D: More hamburger restaurants enter the market
micro.Correct Answer: C — The price of a major meat input rises
micro.Feedback: Higher input costs reduce supply, shifting the supply curve left.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
micro.Question: What economic change does the move from A to B in the tacos graph represent?
micro.Choice A: Price rises $1; quantity supplied increases by 100 thousand along the existing curve.
micro.Choice B: Price rises $1; supply increases by 125 thousand because the curve shifts right.
micro.Choice C: Price rises $1; supply increases by 100 thousand because the curve shifts right.
micro.Choice D: Price rises $1; quantity supplied increases by 125 thousand along the existing curve.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Price rises $1; quantity supplied increases by 125 thousand along the existing curve.
micro.Feedback: A is at $3 and 100 thousand tacos; B is at $4 and 225 thousand. Price rises $1 and quantity supplied rises 125 thousand along S0. The higher quantity supplied reflects movement along the curve, not an increase in supply.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
micro.Question: At a price of $3, the shift from S0 to S1 changes quantity supplied from 100 thousand to approximately:
micro.Choice A: 225 thousand
micro.Choice B: 125 thousand
micro.Choice C: 200 thousand
micro.Choice D: 325 thousand
micro.Correct Answer: A — 225 thousand
micro.Feedback: At $3, point A on S0 is 100 thousand, while S1 crosses the $3 line at about 225 thousand. Supply therefore increases by about 125 thousand units at that price.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Question: A new production method cuts the cost of making solar panels. What happens in the solar panel market?
micro.Choice A: Supply increases, price falls, and quantity rises
micro.Choice B: Supply decreases, price rises, and quantity falls
micro.Choice C: Demand increases, price rises, and quantity rises
micro.Choice D: Quantity demanded decreases because supply rose
micro.Correct Answer: A — Supply increases, price falls, and quantity rises
micro.Feedback: Lower production costs increase supply, which lowers price and raises quantity.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Question: A tax on producers raises the cost of selling bottled water. What is the likely market effect?
micro.Choice A: Supply decreases, price rises, and quantity falls
micro.Choice B: Supply increases, price falls, and quantity rises
micro.Choice C: Demand decreases, price falls, and quantity falls
micro.Choice D: Demand increases because taxes fund public services
micro.Correct Answer: A — Supply decreases, price rises, and quantity falls
micro.Feedback: A tax on producers raises production cost, shifting supply left and reducing quantity.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Question: Producers expect the future price of a product to rise sharply, so they hold inventory back today. What happens to current supply?
micro.Choice A: Current supply decreases
micro.Choice B: Current supply increases
micro.Choice C: Current demand decreases
micro.Choice D: Quantity supplied increases because current price changed
micro.Correct Answer: A — Current supply decreases
micro.Feedback: If sellers expect higher future prices, they may reduce current supply to sell later.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Question: Refer to the supply and demand shift graph. Which movement shows an increase in supply with demand fixed at D2?
micro.Choice A: From P3, Q2 to P2, Q3
micro.Choice B: From P2, Q1 to P1, Q2
micro.Choice C: From P1, Q2 to P2, Q3
micro.Choice D: From P2, Q3 to P3, Q2
micro.Correct Answer: A — From P3, Q2 to P2, Q3
micro.Feedback: With demand fixed at D2, moving from S1 to S2 changes equilibrium from P3, Q2 to P2, Q3.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Calling a price-induced movement along supply an increase in supply.
micro.Question: Demand rises and the market price increases. Firms respond by producing more with the same technology, input prices, and number of sellers. Which statement is correct?
micro.Choice A: Supply shifts right because firms produce more.
micro.Choice B: Quantity supplied rises along an unchanged supply curve.
micro.Choice C: Supply shifts left because the product is now more expensive.
micro.Choice D: Both supply and quantity supplied must increase.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Quantity supplied rises along an unchanged supply curve.
micro.Feedback: A change in the good’s own price changes quantity supplied. The supply curve shifts only when a nonprice determinant changes.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Using only one supply shifter when several operate at once.
micro.Question: Workers accept lower wages, but producers also expect the product’s future price to rise and hold inventory for later sale. What can be concluded about current supply?
micro.Choice A: Supply must rise because lower wages dominate the decision to withhold inventory.
micro.Choice B: Supply must fall because withholding inventory dominates the wage reduction.
micro.Choice C: The net supply shift is uncertain because lower wages and inventory withholding work in opposite directions.
micro.Choice D: Supply stays fixed because wages and expected future prices only move firms along supply.
micro.Correct Answer: C — The net supply shift is uncertain because lower wages and inventory withholding work in opposite directions.
micro.Feedback: Lower wages reduce production costs and increase supply. Holding inventory for a higher expected future price reduces current supply. Their relative sizes determine the net shift.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Treating unequal per-unit cost changes as if they cancel.
micro.Question: A per-unit input cost falls by $4, but a new per-unit tax raises cost by $6. Holding other determinants fixed, what is the likely supply effect?
micro.Choice A: Supply shifts left because net marginal cost rises by $2 per unit.
micro.Choice B: Supply shifts right because any input-cost decline dominates a tax.
micro.Choice C: Supply is unchanged because the two policies offset exactly.
micro.Choice D: Only quantity supplied falls along the same curve.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Supply shifts left because net marginal cost rises by $2 per unit.
micro.Feedback: The combined change raises marginal cost by $2 per unit, reducing supply at each price.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
micro.Question: Use the graph. From A to B, what is the quantity response per $1 price increase, and what economic change does it represent?
micro.Choice A: Quantity supplied rises by 25 thousand units per dollar through movement along the existing supply curve.
micro.Choice B: Quantity supplied rises by 20 thousand units per dollar through movement along the existing supply curve.
micro.Choice C: Supply increases by 25 thousand units per dollar because the price change shifts the curve right.
micro.Choice D: Supply increases by 20 thousand units per dollar because the price change shifts the curve right.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Quantity supplied rises by 25 thousand units per dollar through movement along the existing supply curve.
micro.Feedback: Price rises from $6 to $11 and quantity supplied rises from 100 thousand to 225 thousand. The response is 125/5 = 25 thousand units per $1 price increase. Both points lie on the same supply curve, so quantity supplied increases through a movement along supply; supply itself does not shift.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. At $9, compare S0 with S1. Which event and quantity change are consistent with that comparison?
micro.Choice A: Lower input costs; 100 thousand fewer units supplied.
micro.Choice B: A fall in the product’s own price; 100 thousand fewer units at the same $9 price.
micro.Choice C: Higher input costs; 200 thousand fewer units supplied.
micro.Choice D: Higher input costs; 100 thousand fewer units supplied.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Higher input costs; 100 thousand fewer units supplied.
micro.Feedback: At $9, supply falls from 200 thousand on S0 to 100 thousand on S1. Higher input costs can cause this leftward shift. A change in the product’s own price cannot explain different quantities at the same price.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
micro.Question: Which comparison correctly distinguishes the two changes visible in the taco graph?
micro.Choice A: A to B is an increase in supply; S0 to S1 is movement along supply
micro.Choice B: A to B is movement along S0; S0 to S1 is an increase in supply
micro.Choice C: Both A to B and S0 to S1 are movements caused only by price
micro.Choice D: Both changes are decreases in supply
micro.Correct Answer: B — A to B is movement along S0; S0 to S1 is an increase in supply
micro.Feedback: A and B are points on one curve, so their difference is quantity supplied. Moving from S0 to S1 shifts the entire curve and changes supply.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Question: A product gets more expensive because demand increases. Sellers produce more at the higher price. Students say supply increased. What is the error?
micro.Choice A: They confused an increase in quantity supplied with an increase in supply
micro.Choice B: They correctly identified a supply shift
micro.Choice C: They confused demand with quantity demanded
micro.Choice D: They ignored that equilibrium cannot change
micro.Correct Answer: A — They confused an increase in quantity supplied with an increase in supply
micro.Feedback: Sellers move along the supply curve when price rises. Quantity supplied increases, but supply does not shift.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Assuming one opposing supply shifter automatically dominates the other.
micro.Question: A new machine lowers unit production cost, while a new per-unit environmental fee raises cost. Which conclusion about supply is justified without knowing the size of each change?
micro.Choice A: Supply must shift right because improved technology outweighs any higher per-unit fee.
micro.Choice B: Supply must shift left because a new per-unit fee outweighs any technological saving.
micro.Choice C: Supply must remain unchanged because there is one cost decrease and one cost increase.
micro.Choice D: The net supply shift cannot be determined without comparing the two cost changes.
micro.Correct Answer: D — The net supply shift cannot be determined without comparing the two cost changes.
micro.Feedback: The cost saving increases supply; the fee reduces supply. The net direction depends on the magnitudes, not the number of changes.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Ignoring an offsetting change in the number of sellers or input costs.
micro.Question: Twenty new firms enter a market, but an essential input becomes more expensive for every firm. What is the most careful conclusion about market supply?
micro.Choice A: Entry pushes supply right and higher input cost pushes it left, leaving the net effect uncertain.
micro.Choice B: Market supply must rise because entry outweighs the input-cost increase.
micro.Choice C: Market supply must fall because higher input costs outweigh entry.
micro.Choice D: Market supply stays fixed because both events only change quantity supplied along the curve.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Entry pushes supply right and higher input cost pushes it left, leaving the net effect uncertain.
micro.Feedback: More firms add supply at each price; a cost increase reduces each firm’s supply. Without magnitudes, the combined shift can go either way or be zero.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
micro.Question: Compare the initial point on S0 at $9 with the final point on S1 at $13. Which explanation separates the supply change from the later price change?
micro.Choice A: The supply decrease reduces quantity from 200 to 100 thousand at $9; the price rise moves along S1 to 200 thousand without shifting supply back.
micro.Choice B: The supply decrease reduces quantity from 250 to 150 thousand at $9; the price rise moves along S1 to 250 thousand without shifting supply back.
micro.Choice C: The supply decrease reduces quantity from 200 to 100 thousand at $9; the price rise moves along S1 to 200 thousand because supply shifts back to S0.
micro.Choice D: The supply decrease reduces quantity from 250 to 150 thousand at $9; the price rise moves along S1 to 250 thousand because supply shifts back to S0.
micro.Correct Answer: A — The supply decrease reduces quantity from 200 to 100 thousand at $9; the price rise moves along S1 to 200 thousand without shifting supply back.
micro.Feedback: At $9, S0 shows 200 thousand units and S1 shows 100 thousand. The lower quantity at the same price is a supply decrease. A subsequent price rise to $13 moves along S1 to 200 thousand. Returning to the original quantity does not shift supply back to S0.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
micro.Question: Compare A on S0 with the final point on S1 at $2. Which explanation separates the supply change from the later price change?
micro.Choice A: The supply increase raises quantity from 100 to about 225 thousand at A’s price; the price fall moves along S1 to about 100 thousand without shifting supply back.
micro.Choice B: The supply increase raises quantity from 125 to about 250 thousand at A’s price; the price fall moves along S1 to about 125 thousand without shifting supply back.
micro.Choice C: The supply increase raises quantity from 100 to about 225 thousand at A’s price; the price fall moves along S1 to about 100 thousand because supply shifts back to S0.
micro.Choice D: The supply increase raises quantity from 125 to about 250 thousand at A’s price; the price fall moves along S1 to about 125 thousand because supply shifts back to S0.
micro.Correct Answer: A — The supply increase raises quantity from 100 to about 225 thousand at A’s price; the price fall moves along S1 to about 100 thousand without shifting supply back.
micro.Feedback: A is at $3 and 100 thousand tacos on S0. At that same price, S1 shows about 225 thousand, indicating a supply increase. The later price fall to $2 moves along S1 to about 100 thousand. Quantity returns to its original level, but the supply curve remains S1.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Using the largest or average firm quantity instead of summing quantities.
micro.Question: At $30, three sellers offer 12, 18, and 25 units; at $35 they offer 16, 24, and 30 units. Calculate both market quantities and infer what the comparison represents.
micro.Choice A: Market quantity rises from 55 to 70 units, representing movement along market supply
micro.Choice B: Market supply shifts right from 55 to 70 units because the number of sellers increases
micro.Choice C: Market quantity falls from 70 to 55 units, representing movement down market supply
micro.Choice D: Market supply shifts left by 15 units because individual quantities are aggregated vertically
micro.Correct Answer: A — Market quantity rises from 55 to 70 units, representing movement along market supply
micro.Feedback: Horizontal summation gives 55 units at $30 and 70 at $35. Because only the product's own price changes, the 15-unit increase is movement along the market supply curve.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Forgetting that market supply depends on the number of active sellers.
micro.Question: At a fixed price, 60 identical firms initially supply 8 units each. An input-cost decline raises each surviving firm’s supply to 10 units, but some firms exit. Total supply at that price is unchanged. How many firms exited, and what does the unchanged total imply?
micro.Choice A: 10 firms; the cost and exit effects offset at this price.
micro.Choice B: 12 firms; neither input costs nor firm exit shifted supply.
micro.Choice C: 15 firms; a higher product price offset the firm exits.
micro.Choice D: 12 firms; the cost and exit effects offset at this price.
micro.Correct Answer: D — 12 firms; the cost and exit effects offset at this price.
micro.Feedback: Initial supply is 60 × 8 = 480 units. At 10 units each, 48 firms supply 480, so 12 exited. Opposing supply determinants offset at the stated price; this is not a movement caused by an own-price change.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Applying future price expectations in the wrong time direction.
micro.Question: Producers expect a temporary price spike next month and can store the product cheaply. What pattern is most plausible?
micro.Choice A: Current and future supply both rise because firms expand production immediately and store none of it.
micro.Choice B: Current supply falls as firms hold inventory, while future supply rises when the inventory is released.
micro.Choice C: Current supply rises as firms sell inventory before the expected spike, while future supply falls.
micro.Choice D: Current quantity supplied falls along one curve because the current product price decreases.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Current supply falls as firms hold inventory, while future supply rises when the inventory is released.
micro.Feedback: When storage is feasible, a higher expected future price can reduce current supply and increase supply when the stored goods are later sold.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Treating immediate output response and later firm entry as the same kind of change.
micro.Question: A surge in demand raises the equilibrium price. Firms expand output, and new firms later enter the industry. Which sequence is correct?
micro.Choice A: First supply shifts right; later quantity supplied falls along the curve.
micro.Choice B: Both responses are movements along the original supply curve.
micro.Choice C: First quantity supplied rises along the curve; later entry shifts market supply right.
micro.Choice D: Both responses are supply shifts caused by the good’s own price.
micro.Correct Answer: C — First quantity supplied rises along the curve; later entry shifts market supply right.
micro.Feedback: The higher price first causes a movement along supply. Entry is a nonprice determinant that later shifts market supply right.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Using the higher equilibrium price as evidence of an increase in supply.
micro.Question: A drought reduces crop yields, while the market price of the crop rises because demand is unchanged. What is the best description?
micro.Choice A: Supply shifts right because the higher equilibrium price encourages more production after the drought.
micro.Choice B: Quantity supplied falls along the original supply curve while the curve itself remains unchanged.
micro.Choice C: Demand shifts left because the drought changes buyer preferences rather than production conditions.
micro.Choice D: Supply shifts left, and the higher price causes movement upward along the new supply curve.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Supply shifts left, and the higher price causes movement upward along the new supply curve.
micro.Feedback: The drought is a supply shifter. The resulting higher price determines the quantity supplied on the new, left-shifted curve.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Producers start on S0 at $9. Higher input costs move supply to S1, while a purchase contract permits a price no higher than $11. A buyer expects that allowed price increase to restore the original quantity supplied. Which assessment is correct?
micro.Choice A: It succeeds: S1 supplies 200 thousand at $11, restoring the original quantity.
micro.Choice B: It fails: S1 supplies 150 thousand at $11, still 50 thousand below the original quantity.
micro.Choice C: It fails: S1 supplies 100 thousand at $11, still 100 thousand below the original quantity.
micro.Choice D: It succeeds: raising price to $11 shifts supply back to S0, restoring the original quantity.
micro.Correct Answer: B — It fails: S1 supplies 150 thousand at $11, still 50 thousand below the original quantity.
micro.Feedback: S0 at $9 supplies 200 thousand. S1 supplies only 100 thousand at $9 and 150 thousand at $11. Returning to 200 thousand on S1 would require $13, outside the contract. The allowed price movement offsets only half the quantity reduction caused by the cost-driven shift.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. A technology improvement shifts supply from S0 to S1. At the unchanged price of $3, quantity supplied rises. Half of this increase in quantity is later lost, leaving a parallel supply curve halfway between S0 and S1. What price would now be needed to supply the quantity originally available on S1 at $3, and how would the market reach that quantity?
micro.Choice A: About $2.50; movement down the halfway curve offsets the lost capacity.
micro.Choice B: About $3.00; unchanged desired output prevents a supply shift.
micro.Choice C: About $3.50; movement up the halfway curve offsets the partial supply reversal.
micro.Choice D: About $4.00; movement up S0 offsets the entire improvement.
micro.Correct Answer: C — About $3.50; movement up the halfway curve offsets the partial supply reversal.
micro.Feedback: At $3, S0 supplies about 100 thousand and S1 about 225 thousand. The halfway curve supplies about 162.5 thousand at $3. At 225 thousand, S0 requires $4 and S1 $3, so the halfway curve requires $3.50. A price movement along that new curve restores quantity; it does not undo the partial technology loss.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Averaging firm quantities instead of adding them.
micro.Question: At one price, Firm A supplies 8 units and Firm B supplies 11 units. Market quantity supplied is:
micro.Choice A: 19 units.
micro.Choice B: 8 units.
micro.Choice C: 9.5 units.
micro.Choice D: 11 units.
micro.Correct Answer: A — 19 units.
micro.Feedback: Market supply adds each seller’s quantity: 8 + 11 = 19.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Calling a movement caused by the good’s own price a supply shift.
micro.Question: The price of oranges rises, and growers offer more oranges while all nonprice determinants stay fixed. This is:
micro.Choice A: An increase in supply.
micro.Choice B: An increase in quantity supplied.
micro.Choice C: A decrease in supply.
micro.Choice D: A decrease in quantity supplied.
micro.Correct Answer: B — An increase in quantity supplied.
micro.Feedback: A higher own price causes movement up the existing supply curve.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Confusing lower production cost with a movement along supply.
micro.Question: The price of an important input falls. What happens to supply, other things equal?
micro.Choice A: Supply shifts left.
micro.Choice B: Quantity supplied falls along the curve.
micro.Choice C: Supply shifts right.
micro.Choice D: Demand shifts right.
micro.Correct Answer: C — Supply shifts right.
micro.Feedback: Lower input cost makes production profitable at more output levels, shifting supply right.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Question: According to the law of supply, how are price and quantity supplied related, other things equal?
micro.Choice A: As price rises, quantity supplied rises
micro.Choice B: As price rises, supply shifts left
micro.Choice C: As price falls, quantity supplied rises
micro.Choice D: As demand rises, supply must rise
micro.Correct Answer: A — As price rises, quantity supplied rises
micro.Feedback: The law of supply says price and quantity supplied move in the same direction.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Question: The price of handmade tables rises, and sellers offer more tables for sale. What is the most precise statement?
micro.Choice A: Quantity supplied increases
micro.Choice B: Supply increases
micro.Choice C: Demand increases
micro.Choice D: Supply shifts right
micro.Correct Answer: A — Quantity supplied increases
micro.Feedback: A change in the good's own price causes movement along the supply curve, so quantity supplied changes.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Question: Steel becomes more expensive for car producers. What happens to the supply of cars?
micro.Choice A: Supply decreases
micro.Choice B: Quantity supplied increases because car price changed
micro.Choice C: Demand decreases
micro.Choice D: Supply increases
micro.Correct Answer: A — Supply decreases
micro.Feedback: More expensive steel raises the cost of producing cars at every output level, shifting car supply left rather than changing demand.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Assuming the label of a policy matters more than its net marginal-cost effect.
micro.Question: A subsidy lowers marginal cost by $3 per unit, while a regulation raises marginal cost by $3 per unit. What happens to supply if those are the only changes?
micro.Choice A: Supply shifts right because the subsidy lowers marginal cost by more than the regulation raises it
micro.Choice B: Supply shifts left because the regulation raises marginal cost by more than the subsidy lowers it
micro.Choice C: Quantity supplied rises along the original curve because the product's market price increases
micro.Choice D: The two per-unit effects offset, so supply is unchanged.
micro.Correct Answer: D — The two per-unit effects offset, so supply is unchanged.
micro.Feedback: Equal and opposite per-unit cost changes leave marginal cost, and therefore supply, unchanged.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Failing to remove the exiting firm’s quantity from market supply.
micro.Question: Four firms each supply q=2P units at every price. Demand is Qd=120-4P. One firm exits permanently, with the surviving firms’ schedules unchanged. Which statement correctly compares market equilibrium before and after exit?
micro.Choice A: Price rises from $10 to $12; quantity falls from 80 to 72 as remaining firms move along their unchanged individual schedules.
micro.Choice B: Price stays $10 and quantity becomes 60; unchanged individual schedules prevent equilibrium price adjustment.
micro.Choice C: Price falls from $10 to $8; exit shifts each surviving firm’s individual supply curve right.
micro.Choice D: Price rises from $10 to $12 and quantity rises from 80 to 96 because four firms remain in the aggregate schedule.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Price rises from $10 to $12; quantity falls from 80 to 72 as remaining firms move along their unchanged individual schedules.
micro.Feedback: Before exit supply is 8P, so 120-4P=8P gives P=10, Q=80. Afterward supply is 6P, giving P=12, Q=72. Market supply shifts because a seller exits; survivors respond along unchanged individual supply curves.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Declaring a net shift when opposing determinants are not quantified.
micro.Question: Technology improves while the expected future selling price rises sharply and firms store current output. What is the strongest conclusion about current supply?
micro.Choice A: Current supply increases because improved technology and storing output for future sale both add to current market supply.
micro.Choice B: The net direction is ambiguous without knowing the strength of each effect.
micro.Choice C: Current supply decreases because the expected future price rises sharply, which establishes that withholding outweighs the technology improvement.
micro.Choice D: Quantity supplied moves along one curve because both events change the product's current price.
micro.Correct Answer: B — The net direction is ambiguous without knowing the strength of each effect.
micro.Feedback: Better technology increases current supply, while withholding output for a higher expected future price reduces current supply. The word “sharply” does not quantify the withholding effect relative to the technology effect, so the net direction remains uncertain. Neither determinant is a change in the product’s current price along a fixed curve.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Question: Bakers pay $4 less in flour cost per loaf, but a new energy levy adds $6 per loaf. At the same time, a health report reduces buyers’ willingness to purchase bread. With unknown shift magnitudes, which conclusion is supported?
micro.Choice A: Net unit cost falls $2, shifting supply right; demand shifts left, so price rises while quantity is ambiguous.
micro.Choice B: Net unit cost rises $2, shifting supply left; demand also shifts left, so quantity falls while price is ambiguous.
micro.Choice C: Both changes shift supply left, so price rises and quantity falls with no demand change.
micro.Choice D: Lower flour cost shifts supply right regardless of the levy, so quantity rises and price is ambiguous.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Net unit cost rises $2, shifting supply left; demand also shifts left, so quantity falls while price is ambiguous.
micro.Feedback: The cost changes net to +2 per loaf, reducing supply. The health information reduces demand. Both changes lower equilibrium quantity, but their price effects oppose one another.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Assuming one opposing supply shifter automatically dominates the other.
micro.Question: Evaluate the competing effects of a cost-saving production technology and a new compliance cost. What can be inferred about the net supply shift without relative magnitudes?
micro.Choice A: Supply must increase because technology reduces production cost.
micro.Choice B: Supply must decrease because compliance raises production cost.
micro.Choice C: The net supply direction is ambiguous without relative cost changes.
micro.Choice D: Supply must stay fixed because the two changes cancel by definition.
micro.Correct Answer: C — The net supply direction is ambiguous without relative cost changes.
micro.Feedback: The two cost effects oppose each other. Supply rises if the saving dominates, falls if the added cost dominates, and is unchanged only if they offset.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Question: Several firms leave a market, reducing the quantity offered at each fixed price. Demand is unchanged. At the new equilibrium, surviving firms sell more than each sold before, but total market sales are lower. Which explanation reconciles the observations?
micro.Choice A: Market supply shifted left, raising price; survivors move up their own unchanged supply curves even though fewer firms reduce total output.
micro.Choice B: Market supply shifted right because each survivor sells more; the lower total shows demand must have shifted left too.
micro.Choice C: Market supply is unchanged because survivor technology is unchanged; exit is only a movement along aggregate supply.
micro.Choice D: Each survivor’s supply shifted left, lowering price; fewer sellers then raise each remaining firm’s quantity supplied.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Market supply shifted left, raising price; survivors move up their own unchanged supply curves even though fewer firms reduce total output.
micro.Feedback: Exit reduces aggregate supply at any fixed price. Along unchanged demand, price rises and total quantity falls. Higher price induces more output along each survivor’s own curve, consistent with lower aggregate output.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.4
micro.Question: A hurricane destroys part of the orange crop. What is the likely result in the orange market?
micro.Choice A: Supply decreases, price rises, and quantity falls
micro.Choice B: Demand increases, price rises, and quantity rises
micro.Choice C: Supply increases, price falls, and quantity rises
micro.Choice D: Quantity demanded rises because supply fell
micro.Correct Answer: A — Supply decreases, price rises, and quantity falls
micro.Feedback: A crop loss reduces supply, which raises price and lowers equilibrium quantity.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.4
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. A production improvement shifts supply from S1 to S2 while demand remains D1. Which explanation connects the curve shift to the new equilibrium?
micro.Choice A: Equilibrium moves from P2, Q1 to P1, Q2, so price falls and quantity rises
micro.Choice B: Equilibrium moves from P1, Q2 to P2, Q3, so price and quantity rise
micro.Choice C: Equilibrium moves from P3, Q2 to P2, Q3, so price falls and quantity rises
micro.Choice D: Equilibrium moves from P2, Q3 to P3, Q2, so price rises and quantity falls
micro.Correct Answer: A — Equilibrium moves from P2, Q1 to P1, Q2, so price falls and quantity rises
micro.Feedback: The production improvement shifts supply right to S2. Along unchanged D1, the intersection moves from P2, Q1 to P1, Q2.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.4
micro.Question: Refer to the supply and demand graph with D1, D2, S1, and S2. Starting at D2 and S1, supply increases to S2 while demand stays at D2. What happens?
micro.Choice A: Equilibrium moves from P3, Q2 to P2, Q3.
micro.Choice B: Equilibrium moves from P2, Q1 to P3, Q2.
micro.Choice C: Equilibrium moves from P1, Q2 to P2, Q3.
micro.Choice D: Equilibrium moves from P2, Q3 to P1, Q2.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Equilibrium moves from P3, Q2 to P2, Q3.
micro.Feedback: A supply increase shifts supply right from S1 to S2, lowering price and raising quantity.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.4
micro.Question: Refer to the supply and demand graph with D1, D2, S1, and S2. Starting at D1 and S2, supply decreases to S1 while demand stays at D1. What happens?
micro.Choice A: Equilibrium moves from P1, Q2 to P2, Q1.
micro.Choice B: Equilibrium moves from P2, Q1 to P1, Q2.
micro.Choice C: Equilibrium moves from P2, Q3 to P3, Q2.
micro.Choice D: Equilibrium moves from P3, Q2 to P2, Q3.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Equilibrium moves from P1, Q2 to P2, Q1.
micro.Feedback: A decrease in supply shifts supply left, raising price and lowering quantity.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.4
micro.Question: A storm reduces supply while demand stays the same. Before any price control, what happens in the market?
micro.Choice A: Equilibrium price falls and equilibrium quantity rises
micro.Choice B: Both price and quantity rise
micro.Choice C: Equilibrium price rises and equilibrium quantity falls
micro.Choice D: Both price and quantity fall
micro.Correct Answer: C — Equilibrium price rises and equilibrium quantity falls
micro.Feedback: A decrease in supply shifts supply left, raising equilibrium price and lowering equilibrium quantity.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. What market change is shown from A to B?
micro.Choice A: Supply increases, lowering price and raising quantity
micro.Choice B: Demand increases, raising price and quantity
micro.Choice C: Supply decreases, raising price and reducing quantity
micro.Choice D: Demand decreases, lowering price and quantity
micro.Correct Answer: C — Supply decreases, raising price and reducing quantity
micro.Feedback: Supply shifts left; price rises from 10 to 12 and quantity falls from 200 to 150 thousand.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.3
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
micro.Question: The movie-ticket market moves from A to B after one production cost changes. Which explanation and changes in equilibrium price and quantity match the graph?
micro.Choice A: Higher operating costs reduce supply; price rises $2 and quantity falls 50 thousand
micro.Choice B: Higher operating costs reduce supply; price rises $4 and quantity falls 50 thousand
micro.Choice C: Lower operating costs increase supply; price falls $2 and quantity rises 50 thousand
micro.Choice D: Lower operating costs increase supply; price falls $4 and quantity rises 50 thousand
micro.Correct Answer: A — Higher operating costs reduce supply; price rises $2 and quantity falls 50 thousand
micro.Feedback: A is ($10,200 thousand) and B is ($12,150 thousand). The move follows a decrease in supply, consistent with higher operating costs: price rises $2 and quantity falls 50 thousand.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.4
micro.Question: At a price above equilibrium, quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded. What exists, and what pressure follows?
micro.Choice A: A surplus; price tends to fall
micro.Choice B: A shortage; price tends to rise
micro.Choice C: A surplus; price tends to rise
micro.Choice D: A shortage; price tends to fall
micro.Correct Answer: A — A surplus; price tends to fall
micro.Feedback: A surplus occurs when quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded. Sellers compete, pushing price down.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.4
micro.Question: At a price below equilibrium, quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied. What exists, and what pressure follows?
micro.Choice A: A shortage; price tends to rise
micro.Choice B: A surplus; price tends to fall
micro.Choice C: A shortage; price tends to fall
micro.Choice D: A surplus; price tends to rise
micro.Correct Answer: A — A shortage; price tends to rise
micro.Feedback: A shortage occurs when quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied. Buyers compete, pushing price up.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.4
micro.Question: If the market price is above equilibrium, the market has:
micro.Choice A: A surplus
micro.Choice B: A shortage
micro.Choice C: A binding price ceiling
micro.Choice D: No quantity supplied
micro.Correct Answer: A — A surplus
micro.Feedback: A price above equilibrium creates a surplus because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.4
micro.Question: If the market price is below equilibrium, the market has:
micro.Choice A: A shortage
micro.Choice B: A surplus
micro.Choice C: Excess supply
micro.Choice D: No demand
micro.Correct Answer: A — A shortage
micro.Feedback: A price below equilibrium creates a shortage because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.4
micro.Question: A market price is too low. Quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied. What pressure should occur in an unregulated market?
micro.Choice A: Price should rise
micro.Choice B: Price should fall
micro.Choice C: Supply should vanish
micro.Choice D: Demand must be zero
micro.Correct Answer: A — Price should rise
micro.Feedback: A shortage creates upward pressure on price as buyers compete for limited goods.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.4
micro.Question: A market price is too high. Quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded. What pressure should occur in an unregulated market?
micro.Choice A: Price should fall
micro.Choice B: Price should rise
micro.Choice C: Demand shifts right in response to unsold inventory
micro.Choice D: Supply shifts left before price can adjust
micro.Correct Answer: A — Price should fall
micro.Feedback: A surplus creates downward pressure on price as sellers compete to sell the extra output.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.4
micro.Question: In a market with Qd = 300 - 10P and Qs = 10P, price is initially $12. Diagnose the disequilibrium and calculate the price toward which an unregulated market adjusts.
micro.Choice A: A shortage of 60; price rises toward $15
micro.Choice B: A surplus of 60; price falls toward $9
micro.Choice C: A shortage of 120; price rises toward $18
micro.Choice D: A surplus of 120; price falls toward $6
micro.Correct Answer: A — A shortage of 60; price rises toward $15
micro.Feedback: At $12, Qd = 180 and Qs = 120, so the shortage is 60. Setting 300 - 10P = 10P gives the equilibrium price of $15, toward which the shortage pushes price.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.4
micro.Question: In a market with Qd = 410 - 10P and Qs = -10 + 10P, price is initially $25. Diagnose the disequilibrium and calculate the price toward which an unregulated market adjusts.
micro.Choice A: A surplus of 80; price falls toward $21
micro.Choice B: A shortage of 80; price rises toward $29
micro.Choice C: A surplus of 40; price falls toward $23
micro.Choice D: A shortage of 40; price rises toward $27
micro.Correct Answer: A — A surplus of 80; price falls toward $21
micro.Feedback: At $25, Qs = 240 and Qd = 160, so the surplus is 80. Setting the schedules equal gives P = $21, and seller competition pushes price downward toward it.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.4
micro.Question: Inventories are accumulating because sellers are offering more units than buyers want at the current price. What market condition exists?
micro.Choice A: A situation where quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
micro.Choice B: A situation where quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
micro.Choice C: A point outside the PPF
micro.Choice D: A legal maximum price
micro.Correct Answer: A — A situation where quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
micro.Feedback: A surplus exists when quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.4
micro.Question: At the current price, buyers want 180 units and sellers offer 120 units. What exists, and what pressure follows?
micro.Choice A: A shortage; price tends to rise
micro.Choice B: A surplus; price tends to fall
micro.Choice C: A shortage; price tends to fall
micro.Choice D: A surplus; price tends to rise
micro.Correct Answer: A — A shortage; price tends to rise
micro.Feedback: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, so there is a shortage. Shortages push price upward.

micro.Learning Objective: LO4.4
micro.Question: A market price is above equilibrium. Which result is most likely in an unregulated market?
micro.Choice A: A surplus creates downward pressure on price
micro.Choice B: A shortage creates upward pressure on price
micro.Choice C: Unsold inventories shift demand right
micro.Choice D: Seller competition shifts supply left
micro.Correct Answer: A — A surplus creates downward pressure on price
micro.Feedback: A price above equilibrium creates a surplus, and sellers respond by lowering price.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.1
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. At the binding $1,000 rent ceiling, what is the maximum number of apartments that can actually be rented?
micro.Choice A: 200 thousand apartments
micro.Choice B: 300 thousand apartments
micro.Choice C: 400 thousand apartments
micro.Choice D: 100 thousand apartments
micro.Correct Answer: D — 100 thousand apartments
micro.Feedback: Transactions are limited by the short side, quantity supplied.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.2
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
micro.Question: Refer to the labor graph. Assume all jobs demanded are filled for one hour each. With the displayed floor, what are employment and excess labor supply, and how does payroll compare with the equilibrium without the floor?
micro.Choice A: 150,000 employed, 100,000 excess workers, and payroll $450,000 higher
micro.Choice B: 150,000 employed, 100,000 excess workers, and payroll $150,000 lower
micro.Choice C: 250,000 employed, 100,000 excess workers, and payroll $1,350,000 higher
micro.Choice D: 200,000 employed, no excess workers, and payroll $600,000 higher
micro.Correct Answer: B — 150,000 employed, 100,000 excess workers, and payroll $150,000 lower
micro.Feedback: Without the floor, payroll is 200,000 × $12 = $2,400,000. At $15, firms demand 150,000 workers, so payroll is $2,250,000. Supply is 250,000 workers, so excess labor supply is 100,000. Employment falls by 50,000 and payroll by $150,000 despite the higher wage on remaining jobs.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. A report attributes the smaller market after the tax to the buyer–seller price wedge. Which quantity comparison and explanation support that account?
micro.Choice A: From 100 to 80 units; the wedge between buyer payment and seller receipt removes some mutually beneficial trades.
micro.Choice B: From 100 to 65 units; the wedge between buyer payment and seller receipt removes some mutually beneficial trades.
micro.Choice C: From 100 to 80 units; the tax leaves buyer and seller prices identical, so it creates no wedge.
micro.Choice D: From 100 to 65 units; the tax leaves buyer and seller prices identical, so it creates no wedge.
micro.Correct Answer: A — From 100 to 80 units; the wedge between buyer payment and seller receipt removes some mutually beneficial trades.
micro.Feedback: Original supply meets demand at Q = 100. Supply plus tax meets demand at Q 80. Buyers pay 18 and sellers receive 12 at the taxed quantity, so the wedge prevents trades that would occur without tax.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: At Q = 80 in the tax graph, how much higher is Supply + tax than Supply, and what does this vertical distance mean?
micro.Choice A: $6; sellers need a buyer price $6 above their net supply price to cover the per-unit tax.
micro.Choice B: $4; sellers need a buyer price $4 above their net supply price to cover the per-unit tax.
micro.Choice C: $6; the tax makes sellers willing to receive $6 less net of tax at every quantity.
micro.Choice D: $4; the tax makes sellers willing to receive $4 less net of tax at every quantity.
micro.Correct Answer: A — $6; sellers need a buyer price $6 above their net supply price to cover the per-unit tax.
micro.Feedback: At Q 80 the original supply price is 12 and supply-plus-tax price 18. The vertical gap 6 is the tax. The shifted curve expresses the required buyer price inclusive of tax; it does not change the underlying net-of-tax supply schedule.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: A $7 tax reduces quantity from 500 to 420 units. What does this show beyond tax revenue?
micro.Choice A: The tax shrinks the market by discouraging mutually beneficial trades
micro.Choice B: The tax increases market size because government collects revenue
micro.Choice C: The tax leaves buyers and sellers unaffected if revenue is spent
micro.Choice D: The tax creates a surplus because quantity falls
micro.Correct Answer: A — The tax shrinks the market by discouraging mutually beneficial trades
micro.Feedback: A tax reduces quantity traded, meaning some mutually beneficial exchanges no longer happen.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: Before tax, price is $20 and quantity is 1,000. After a $6 tax, buyers pay $24, sellers receive $18, and quantity is 850. What is tax revenue?
micro.Feedback: Tax revenue equals tax per unit times after-tax quantity: $6 × 850 = $5,100.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: Refer to the tax graph. An analyst calls the government receipt the entire efficiency loss. With no externalities and using the straight curve segments around the two equilibria, which correction is right?
micro.Choice A: Revenue is $480; deadweight loss is $60
micro.Choice B: Revenue is $600; deadweight loss is $60
micro.Choice C: Revenue is $480; deadweight loss is $480
micro.Choice D: Revenue is $240; deadweight loss is $120
micro.Correct Answer: A — Revenue is $480; deadweight loss is $60
micro.Feedback: Buyers pay $18, sellers receive $12 and 80 units trade, so revenue is $6 × 80 = $480. Quantity falls from 100 to 80, giving a lost-gains triangle of 0.5 × 20 × $6 = $60. Revenue transfers surplus to government; the missing trades destroy surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: A linear market has demand P = 30 − Q and supply P = 6 + Q. Compare an $8 tax with a $14 ceiling. Under the ceiling, available units go to the highest-value buyers and lowest-cost sellers, with no search costs. With no externalities, which comparison is correct?
micro.Choice A: Both trade 8 units and retain $128 of total surplus; the ceiling gives consumers $64 more surplus
micro.Choice B: Both trade 8 units, but the tax destroys its $64 revenue and leaves only $64 of total surplus
micro.Choice C: The tax trades 8 units, but the ceiling trades all 16 units demanded at $14
micro.Choice D: Both retain $144 of total surplus because revenue and lower prices are transfers
micro.Correct Answer: A — Both trade 8 units and retain $128 of total surplus; the ceiling gives consumers $64 more surplus
micro.Feedback: Untaxed Q is 12 and TS is $144. With the tax, Q = 8, buyers pay $22 and sellers receive $14: CS = $32, PS = $32 and revenue = $64, totaling $128. The ceiling also supports 8 supplied units; efficient allocation gives CS = $96 and PS = $32. Each loses $16 of gains, but consumers receive $64 more under the ceiling. This equality depends on the stated allocation and cost assumptions.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: Before a tax, price is $20 and quantity is 1,000. Afterwards buyers pay $24, sellers receive $18 and 850 units trade. An analyst says the buyer burden is the entire tax and calculates revenue using the original quantity. Which correction is right?
micro.Choice A: The wedge is $6, buyers bear $4 per unit and sellers $2; revenue is $5,100.
micro.Choice B: The wedge is $4, buyers bear $4 per unit and sellers $0; revenue is $3,400.
micro.Choice C: The wedge is $6, buyers bear $4 per unit and sellers $2; revenue is $6,000.
micro.Choice D: The wedge is $6, buyers bear $6 per unit and sellers $0; revenue is $5,100.
micro.Correct Answer: A — The wedge is $6, buyers bear $4 per unit and sellers $2; revenue is $5,100.
micro.Feedback: The wedge is $24−$18=$6, split into the $4 buyer-price increase and $2 seller-receipt decrease. Only 850 units are taxed, so revenue is $6×850=$5,100.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: A tax produces a $6 wedge and 850 sales, down from 1,000 without tax. A proposed increase would produce an $8 wedge and 600 sales. Which comparison correctly evaluates revenue and lost trades?
micro.Choice A: Revenue falls from $5,100 to $4,800 while lost trades increase from 150 to 400.
micro.Choice B: Revenue rises from $5,100 to $6,800 while lost trades remain 150.
micro.Choice C: Revenue falls from $6,000 to $4,800 while lost trades decrease from 400 to 150.
micro.Choice D: Revenue rises from $5,100 to $6,000 while lost trades increase from 150 to 400.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Revenue falls from $5,100 to $4,800 while lost trades increase from 150 to 400.
micro.Feedback: Revenue uses the quantity remaining under each tax: $6×850=$5,100 versus $8×600=$4,800. Relative to 1,000 untaxed trades, losses are 150 and 400. A higher rate does not guarantee more revenue.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: Untaxed price is $30. A $7 tax makes buyers pay $34 and sellers receive $27. Lawmakers propose collecting the same tax from buyers instead of sellers in the same competitive market, with unchanged demand, supply and enforcement. Which prediction correctly combines the observed burdens with the proposed change?
micro.Choice A: Buyers bear $4 and sellers $3 per unit; collecting from buyers shifts the full $7 burden to buyers.
micro.Choice B: Buyers bear $4 and sellers $3 per unit; changing the statutory payer alone does not change those economic burdens.
micro.Choice C: Buyers bear $3 and sellers $4 per unit; changing the statutory payer alone does not change those burdens.
micro.Choice D: Buyers bear $7 and sellers $0 per unit; collecting from sellers would reverse those burdens.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Buyers bear $4 and sellers $3 per unit; changing the statutory payer alone does not change those economic burdens.
micro.Feedback: The buyer-price increase is $4 and seller-receipt decrease is $3, summing to $7. Moving collection between sides does not change the equilibrium wedge or relative responsiveness in the stated competitive setting.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: In a competitive market, a per-unit tax initially raises buyer price, lowers seller receipts and reduces trades. Several years later suppliers can adjust output much more easily, while demand responsiveness is unchanged. Which statement correctly distinguishes the initial effect from the later burden comparison?
micro.Choice A: Initially buyers bear the full wedge; as supply becomes more elastic, sellers necessarily bear the full wedge.
micro.Choice B: Initially both sides bear part of the wedge; more elastic supply tends to move a larger share onto sellers.
micro.Choice C: Initially both sides bear part of the wedge; as supply becomes more elastic, a larger share tends to fall on buyers.
micro.Choice D: Initially seller receipts rise; later statutory collection determines which side bears the wedge.
micro.Correct Answer: C — Initially both sides bear part of the wedge; as supply becomes more elastic, a larger share tends to fall on buyers.
micro.Feedback: The initial wedge separates a higher buyer price from a lower seller receipt. In the later comparison, suppliers have better adjustment options, so the relatively less responsive demand side tends to bear more of the tax.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: A $10 tax reduces equilibrium quantity only slightly in Market A but sharply in Market B. What is the strongest inference?
micro.Choice A: Market A likely has less elastic demand and/or supply around equilibrium
micro.Choice B: Market A must have more elastic demand and supply
micro.Choice C: Tax revenue must be zero in Market A
micro.Choice D: The statutory side paying the tax differs across markets
micro.Correct Answer: A — Market A likely has less elastic demand and/or supply around equilibrium
micro.Feedback: Less elastic curves produce a smaller quantity response to a given tax wedge.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Relative to the original $10 equilibrium price, how is the $4 tax burden divided?
micro.Choice A: Buyers bear all $4; sellers bear none.
micro.Choice B: Sellers bear all $4; buyers bear none.
micro.Choice C: Buyers gain $2; sellers bear $6.
micro.Choice D: Buyers bear $2; sellers bear $2.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Buyers bear $2; sellers bear $2.
micro.Feedback: Buyer price rises to 12 and seller price falls to 8.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. What percentage of the $8 tax burden is borne by buyers?
micro.Choice A: 25 percent
micro.Choice B: 75 percent
micro.Choice C: 50 percent
micro.Choice D: 100 percent
micro.Correct Answer: B — 75 percent
micro.Feedback: The buyer price rises by $6. Buyers therefore bear $6 of the $8 tax, or 75%.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
micro.Question: The $8 tax is legally collected from sellers. Using the original equilibrium as the benchmark, which division of the economic burden does the graph show?
micro.Choice A: Buyers bear $2 per unit; sellers bear $6 per unit
micro.Choice B: Buyers bear $3 per unit; sellers bear $5 per unit
micro.Choice C: Buyers bear $6 per unit; sellers bear $2 per unit
micro.Choice D: Buyers bear $5 per unit; sellers bear $3 per unit
micro.Correct Answer: A — Buyers bear $2 per unit; sellers bear $6 per unit
micro.Feedback: The original price is $10. After the tax, buyers pay $12 and sellers keep $4. Buyers therefore bear $2 and sellers $6. Legal collection from sellers does not determine the economic division.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.4
micro.Question: Whether a tax is legally collected from buyers or sellers, its economic burden depends mainly on:
micro.Choice A: Relative elasticities
micro.Choice B: Which side writes the check
micro.Choice C: The number of firms only
micro.Choice D: The tax's label
micro.Correct Answer: A — Relative elasticities
micro.Feedback: Legal incidence does not determine economic incidence; elasticities determine who bears more burden.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.4
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
micro.Question: Refer to the concert graph with Demand with tax. The law changes so sellers remit the same tax instead. With demand and supply fixed, which cash-flow description fits the resulting equilibrium?
micro.Choice A: Buyers pay sellers $8; sellers remit $8 and keep $0; 150,000 tickets trade
micro.Choice B: Buyers pay sellers $18; sellers remit $8 and keep $10; 200,000 tickets trade
micro.Choice C: Buyers pay sellers $16; sellers remit $8 and keep $8; 150,000 tickets trade
micro.Choice D: Buyers pay sellers $16; sellers remit $6 and keep $10; 200,000 tickets trade
micro.Correct Answer: C — Buyers pay sellers $16; sellers remit $8 and keep $8; 150,000 tickets trade
micro.Feedback: The graph shows buyer cost $16 and net seller receipt $8 at 150,000 tickets, so the wedge is $8. Switching remittance changes the transaction payment, not these net prices or quantity. Sellers now collect $16, forward $8 and retain $8.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.4
micro.Question: Why do a tax on buyers and an equal tax on sellers lead to similar market outcomes?
micro.Choice A: Both create the same wedge between what buyers pay and sellers receive
micro.Choice B: Only seller taxes reduce quantity
micro.Choice C: Only buyer taxes change demand
micro.Choice D: The legal taxpayer always bears the full burden
micro.Correct Answer: A — Both create the same wedge between what buyers pay and sellers receive
micro.Feedback: Whether the tax is legally placed on buyers or sellers, the market adjusts around the wedge between buyer and seller prices.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.4
micro.Question: A $5 tax is legally placed on sellers. After the tax, buyers pay $3 more than before and sellers receive $2 less than before. What does this show?
micro.Choice A: The legal side pays the government, but buyers and sellers share the economic burden
micro.Choice B: The legal side bears the full burden because sellers are the ones sending in the tax
micro.Choice C: The buyer side avoids the burden because the law places the payment on sellers
micro.Choice D: The seller side avoids the burden because buyers now pay a higher market price
micro.Correct Answer: A — The legal side pays the government, but buyers and sellers share the economic burden
micro.Feedback: Legal assignment does not determine economic burden. Buyers and sellers share the tax through changes in prices.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.4
micro.Question: A $5 tax is placed on buyers instead of sellers. Supply and demand conditions are unchanged. What should happen compared with an equal tax on sellers?
micro.Choice A: The same wedge, quantity reduction, and burden split occur
micro.Choice B: Buyers bear all of the tax because they legally pay it
micro.Choice C: Sellers bear all of the tax because they receive less
micro.Choice D: The tax disappears because sellers are not legally charged
micro.Correct Answer: A — The same wedge, quantity reduction, and burden split occur
micro.Feedback: A tax on buyers and an equal tax on sellers create the same wedge and the same economic outcome. The legal side does not control the burden.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.4
micro.Question: The tax in the graph is currently collected from sellers. If the same per-unit tax were collected from buyers instead, with demand, supply, and compliance unchanged, which buyer price, net seller price, and quantity would result?
micro.Choice A: Buyer price $18; seller price $12; quantity 80
micro.Choice B: Buyer price $20; seller price $14; quantity 80
micro.Choice C: Buyer price $18; seller price $12; quantity 100
micro.Choice D: Buyer price $20; seller price $14; quantity 100
micro.Correct Answer: A — Buyer price $18; seller price $12; quantity 80
micro.Feedback: The graph shows an after-tax buyer price of $18, a net seller price of $12, and 80 units traded. Changing who sends the tax to the government leaves this economic outcome unchanged.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.4
micro.Question: Demand is Qd=100-2Pb and supply is Qs=2Ps, where Pb is the buyer’s total price and Ps is the seller’s net receipt. A $5 unit tax is first remitted by sellers, then by buyers, with unchanged schedules and compliance. Which outcome and interpretation are correct?
micro.Choice A: Seller remittance yields Pb=$25 and Ps=$20, while buyer remittance yields Pb=$30 and Ps=$25; legal assignment fixes who loses.
micro.Choice B: Both systems yield Pb=$27.50, Ps=$22.50 and Q=45; the legal payer changes but the same wedge determines economic incidence.
micro.Choice C: Both systems yield Pb=$25, Ps=$25 and Q=50; changing the remitter cancels the wedge from equilibrium.
micro.Choice D: Both systems yield Pb=$22.50, Ps=$27.50 and Q=45; sellers receive more than buyers pay because the tax is a transfer.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Both systems yield Pb=$27.50, Ps=$22.50 and Q=45; the legal payer changes but the same wedge determines economic incidence.
micro.Feedback: Use Pb=Ps+5 and 100-2Pb=2Ps. Then 90=4Ps, so Ps=22.5, Pb=27.5 and Q=45. The untaxed price was 25, giving each side a 2.5 burden. Remittance changes the payment route, not these equations.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.4
micro.Question: Under a seller-remitted tax, buyers pay $52 and sellers keep $46 per unit. The same tax is reassigned to buyers, with curves unchanged. An invoice then asks buyers to pay sellers $52 plus a separate tax payment. Which correction preserves the original economic outcome?
micro.Choice A: Pay sellers $52 and government $6, for $58 in total
micro.Choice B: Pay sellers $49 and government $3, for $52 in total
micro.Choice C: Pay sellers $46 and government $6, for $52 in total
micro.Choice D: Pay sellers $46 and government nothing, for $46 in total
micro.Correct Answer: C — Pay sellers $46 and government $6, for $52 in total
micro.Feedback: The original wedge is $52 − $46 = $6. Under buyer remittance, the seller transaction payment must be $46, with another $6 sent directly to government. Paying sellers $52 and then adding $6 double-counts the wedge relative to the equivalent equilibrium.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.4
micro.Question: Labor demand is Ld=120-2Wf and supply is Ls=2Ww. Wf is the employer’s total cost and Ww is take-home pay. An $8 per-worker payroll tax is legally moved from firms to workers without other changes. Which prediction refutes the claim that firms’ economic burden disappears?
micro.Choice A: Wf falls to $30 and Ww to $22, with employment 60; legal reassignment removes all employer burden.
micro.Choice B: Wf remains $34 and Ww rises to $34, with employment 52; workers now remit the tax from a higher net wage.
micro.Choice C: Wf remains $34 and Ww $26, with employment 52; each side still bears $4 relative to the untaxed $30 wage.
micro.Choice D: Wf rises to $38 and Ww stays $30, with employment 44; firms bear all tax whenever labor demand slopes down.
micro.Correct Answer: C — Wf remains $34 and Ww $26, with employment 52; each side still bears $4 relative to the untaxed $30 wage.
micro.Feedback: The wedge is Wf-Ww=8 regardless of remitter. Solve 120-2(Ww+8)=2Ww: Ww=26, Wf=34 and L=52. Without tax W=30. Employer and worker burdens are 4 each, unchanged by the statutory relabeling.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: A city taxes ride-share trips. Riders pay higher prices, drivers receive less per trip, and fewer trips occur. What is the best synthesis?
micro.Choice A: The tax wedge is shared and shrinks the number of exchanges
micro.Choice B: The tax affects only riders if they see the fee at checkout
micro.Choice C: The tax affects only drivers if the platform remits it
micro.Choice D: The tax increases quantity because government revenue rises
micro.Correct Answer: A — The tax wedge is shared and shrinks the number of exchanges
micro.Feedback: A tax creates a wedge shared by market participants and reduces the quantity traded.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: Use the graph. A clerk uses only the buyer-price increase as the tax rate and multiplies by the original quantity, reporting $300. Which correction addresses both errors?
micro.Choice A: $6 on 80 units gives $480; use both sides of the wedge and the post-tax quantity.
micro.Choice B: $8 on 70 units gives $560; use both sides of the wedge and the post-tax quantity.
micro.Choice C: $6 on 80 units gives $480; the buyer-price increase alone and the untaxed quantity are the correct definitions.
micro.Choice D: $8 on 70 units gives $560; the buyer-price increase alone and the untaxed quantity are the correct definitions.
micro.Correct Answer: A — $6 on 80 units gives $480; use both sides of the wedge and the post-tax quantity.
micro.Feedback: The graph has Pb 18, Ps 12 and taxed Q 80. Full tax 6 times 80 gives 480, which is 180 above the report. Using only the buyer increase 3 misses the seller burden; using 100 wrongly includes trades that no longer occur.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.4
micro.Question: A student says, 'If sellers legally pay the tax, buyers avoid the burden.' What is wrong?
micro.Choice A: Elasticities, not legal labels, determine burden
micro.Choice B: The statement is always correct
micro.Choice C: Sellers cannot change prices
micro.Choice D: Taxes do not affect buyers
micro.Correct Answer: A — Elasticities, not legal labels, determine burden
micro.Feedback: Legal assignment does not determine who bears the economic burden.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.4
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. At the post-tax quantity of 60 thousand movies, what price do sellers receive?
micro.Choice A: $10.50 per movie
micro.Choice B: $13.50 per movie
micro.Choice C: $7.50 per movie
micro.Choice D: $6.00 per movie
micro.Correct Answer: C — $7.50 per movie
micro.Feedback: At quantity 60 thousand, the shifted demand curve intersects supply at $7.50. That is the amount sellers receive before the buyer remits the tax.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.4
micro.Question: A policy analyst says a tax legally placed on sellers will be paid entirely by sellers. What is wrong with this claim?
micro.Choice A: Legal assignment does not determine economic incidence
micro.Choice B: Sellers always pass the entire tax to buyers
micro.Choice C: Buyers always avoid taxes completely
micro.Choice D: A seller tax is the same as a price floor
micro.Correct Answer: A — Legal assignment does not determine economic incidence
micro.Feedback: Economic tax burden depends on market responses and elasticities, not only on who legally sends payment.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.4
