micro.Question: A tax is legally imposed on sellers, but buyers end up paying most of the burden. What does this show?
micro.Choice A: Economic incidence does not depend only on legal assignment
micro.Choice B: Sellers never pay taxes
micro.Choice C: Buyers must have become the statutory taxpayers when the market price changed.
micro.Choice D: The tax must be a price ceiling
micro.Correct Answer: A — Economic incidence does not depend only on legal assignment
micro.Feedback: Who legally pays the tax does not determine who bears the economic burden.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.4
micro.Question: A tax causes buyers to pay more, sellers to receive less, and quantity to fall. Which statement is false?
micro.Choice A: The side legally assigned the tax must bear the entire burden
micro.Choice B: The tax creates a wedge between buyer and seller prices
micro.Choice C: The market quantity falls after the tax
micro.Choice D: Buyers and sellers can both be worse off per unit traded
micro.Correct Answer: A — The side legally assigned the tax must bear the entire burden
micro.Feedback: The legal assignment does not determine the entire burden. Market elasticities matter.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.4
micro.Question: A tax is legally imposed on sellers, but buyers pay most of the burden. What explains this?
micro.Choice A: Legal assignment does not determine economic burden
micro.Choice B: Sellers always avoid all taxes
micro.Choice C: Buyers became legally responsible for the tax after prices adjusted.
micro.Choice D: The market must have a price ceiling
micro.Correct Answer: A — Legal assignment does not determine economic burden
micro.Feedback: Tax burden depends on market responses, not just who is legally assigned to pay.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.4
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. What per-unit tax wedge is created by the buyer-side tax?
micro.Choice A: $3 per movie
micro.Choice B: $7.50 per movie
micro.Choice C: $21 per movie
micro.Choice D: $6 per movie
micro.Correct Answer: D — $6 per movie
micro.Feedback: At the post-tax quantity, read the buyer price and seller receipt from the graph and take the difference: $13.50 − $7.50 = $6.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.4
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Which side bears more of the buyer-side tax?
micro.Choice A: Neither; the burden is split equally.
micro.Choice B: Buyers bear more of the tax than sellers.
micro.Choice C: Sellers bear more of the tax than buyers.
micro.Choice D: Neither side bears any economic tax burden.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Neither; the burden is split equally.
micro.Feedback: Buyers pay $3 more than the original $10.50 price, while sellers receive $3 less. The legal placement on buyers does not make buyers bear the entire tax.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.4
micro.Question: Refer to the tax graph. If the same per-unit tax is collected from buyers instead of sellers, with demand and supply unchanged, which outcome follows?
micro.Choice A: Buyers still pay $18 in total, sellers keep $12, and 80 units trade
micro.Choice B: Buyers pay $21 in total, sellers keep $15, and 80 units trade
micro.Choice C: Buyers pay $18 in total, sellers keep $18, and 100 units trade
micro.Choice D: Buyers pay $15 in total, sellers keep $9, and 100 units trade
micro.Correct Answer: A — Buyers still pay $18 in total, sellers keep $12, and 80 units trade
micro.Feedback: The graph establishes a $6 wedge at quantity 80, with total buyer payment $18 and net seller receipt $12. Changing the remitter preserves this wedge and equilibrium. Under buyer remittance, buyers pay sellers $12 and government $6; that does not make the economic buyer burden $6.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.4
micro.Question: A seller-side tax shifts the supply curve upward. Which statement best explains why buyers still pay part of the tax?
micro.Choice A: Elasticities determine how the tax is split.
micro.Choice B: Buyers voluntarily pay taxes for sellers
micro.Choice C: The demand curve shifts right by the tax amount
micro.Choice D: The tax creates a price ceiling
micro.Correct Answer: A — Elasticities determine how the tax is split.
micro.Feedback: Legal remittance does not determine economic burden. Prices adjust based on supply and demand elasticities.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.4
micro.Question: A tax is placed on buyers instead of sellers. In a standard supply-demand model, why is the final outcome similar to an equal seller tax?
micro.Choice A: Both taxes create the same buyer–seller price wedge.
micro.Choice B: Only buyer taxes reduce quantity
micro.Choice C: Only seller taxes raise prices
micro.Choice D: The tax disappears if buyers legally pay it
micro.Correct Answer: A — Both taxes create the same buyer–seller price wedge.
micro.Feedback: A buyer tax or seller tax of the same size creates the same wedge and reduces quantity similarly.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.4
micro.Question: Refer to the tax graph. If sellers instead remitted the same tax, with both curves fixed, which bundle would give the total buyer payment, net seller receipt and quantity?
micro.Choice A: $7.50 paid, $13.50 received, and 60,000 units traded
micro.Choice B: $13.50 paid, $7.50 received, and 60,000 units traded
micro.Choice C: $13.50 paid, $7.50 received, and 100,000 units traded
micro.Choice D: $10.50 paid, $4.50 received, and 100,000 units traded
micro.Correct Answer: B — $13.50 paid, $7.50 received, and 60,000 units traded
micro.Feedback: Supply intersects Demand with tax at 60,000 units and $7.50 received by sellers. At that quantity, original demand gives the $13.50 total buyer payment. The $6 difference goes to government. Switching remittance to sellers preserves these total and net prices and quantity.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.4
micro.Question: The movie tax in the graph is currently collected from buyers. Collection shifts to sellers, with the tax, demand, supply, and compliance unchanged. A cinema proposes adding the tax again to the buyer’s current total payment. Which corrected tax-inclusive invoice and burden calculation preserve the competitive outcome?
micro.Choice A: Invoice $13.50; buyers bear $2 and sellers $4
micro.Choice B: Invoice $12.50; buyers bear $2 and sellers $4
micro.Choice C: Invoice $12.50; buyers bear $3 and sellers $3
micro.Choice D: Invoice $13.50; buyers bear $3 and sellers $3
micro.Correct Answer: D — Invoice $13.50; buyers bear $3 and sellers $3
micro.Feedback: The graph shows a $6 tax, a $7.50 net seller receipt, and a $13.50 total buyer price, compared with $10.50 before tax. After the collection change the invoice remains $13.50 including tax; the seller remits $6 and keeps $7.50. Each side bears $3. Adding another $6 would charge the tax twice.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.4
micro.Question: Suppose an equal per-unit tax could legally be collected from either buyers or sellers. In the standard supply-demand model, why is the equilibrium incidence similar either way?
micro.Choice A: Only a buyer tax reduces quantity because it directly affects demand.
micro.Choice B: Either tax creates the same wedge between buyer price and seller price
micro.Choice C: Only seller taxes raise prices
micro.Choice D: The tax disappears if buyers legally pay it
micro.Correct Answer: B — Either tax creates the same wedge between buyer price and seller price
micro.Feedback: A buyer tax or seller tax of the same size creates the same wedge and reduces quantity similarly.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.4
micro.Question: A $6 tax is legally remitted by buyers. Before it, 120 repairs sold for $25 each; afterward, 100 repairs sell, buyers pay $29 in total and firms keep $23. A firm says buyer remittance leaves its sales receipts unaffected. What refutes the claim?
micro.Choice A: Net sales receipts fall by $700, although the seller burden is only $2 per remaining repair
micro.Choice B: Net sales receipts fall by $600, equal to the full government receipt
micro.Choice C: Net sales receipts rise by $400, because buyers pay $4 more per repair
micro.Choice D: Net sales receipts remain $3,000, because firms do not remit the tax
micro.Correct Answer: A — Net sales receipts fall by $700, although the seller burden is only $2 per remaining repair
micro.Feedback: Firms initially receive 120 × $25 = $3,000, then 100 × $23 = $2,300: a $700 decline. Only $200 is the $2 price burden on continuing repairs; $500 reflects lost sales at the old price. Sales receipts are not profit or producer surplus. Legal remittance does not shield firms from price and quantity changes.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.4
micro.Question: Refer to the tax graph. A proposal shifts remittance to sellers while keeping the tax unchanged. Which forecast correctly combines revenue and economic incidence?
micro.Choice A: Revenue stays $600,000; buyers and sellers each bear $3 per unit
micro.Choice B: Revenue stays $360,000; sellers now bear the entire $6 per unit
micro.Choice C: Revenue falls to $180,000; only the new legal remitter has a burden
micro.Choice D: Revenue stays $360,000; buyers and sellers each bear $3 per unit
micro.Correct Answer: D — Revenue stays $360,000; buyers and sellers each bear $3 per unit
micro.Feedback: The wedge is $13.50 − $7.50 = $6 and 60,000 units trade, giving $360,000 in revenue. Relative to the original $10.50 price, buyer and seller burdens are each $3. The same fixed curves and wedge yield the same equilibrium under seller remittance.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.4
micro.Question: A tax is legally imposed on buyers instead of sellers. What does tax-incidence analysis imply?
micro.Choice A: Buyers always bear 100% of the burden
micro.Choice B: Legal assignment alone does not determine the burden
micro.Choice C: Sellers always bear 100% of the burden
micro.Choice D: The tax disappears from the market
micro.Correct Answer: B — Legal assignment alone does not determine the burden
micro.Feedback: Tax incidence depends on market responses, not simply on whether the law says buyers or sellers pay the tax.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: The less elastic side of the market usually bears:
micro.Choice A: More of the tax burden
micro.Choice B: Less of the tax burden
micro.Choice C: None of the tax burden
micro.Choice D: Only the portion of the tax named in the statute.
micro.Correct Answer: A — More of the tax burden
micro.Feedback: The less elastic side adjusts less, so it bears more of the tax burden.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: When demand is less elastic than supply, which side is less able to avoid the tax?
micro.Choice A: Buyers
micro.Choice B: Sellers
micro.Choice C: Neither side
micro.Choice D: Only the government
micro.Correct Answer: A — Buyers
micro.Feedback: If demand is less elastic, buyers bear more of the tax burden.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: A tax causes buyers to pay $5 more and sellers to receive $2 less. Which side likely has less elastic behavior?
micro.Choice A: Buyers
micro.Choice B: Sellers
micro.Choice C: Neither side
micro.Choice D: The government
micro.Correct Answer: A — Buyers
micro.Feedback: The side bearing more of the tax is usually less elastic. Buyers bear $5, so demand is likely less elastic.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: Supply is less elastic than demand. Who is expected to bear more of a tax?
micro.Choice A: Sellers
micro.Choice B: Buyers
micro.Choice C: Both sides bear zero
micro.Choice D: Only the legal taxpayer
micro.Correct Answer: A — Sellers
micro.Feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the tax. If supply is less elastic, sellers bear more.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: Tax incidence means:
micro.Choice A: How the burden of a tax is divided between buyers and sellers
micro.Choice B: The legal maximum price
micro.Choice C: The number of firms in a market
micro.Choice D: The quantity demanded at every price
micro.Correct Answer: A — How the burden of a tax is divided between buyers and sellers
micro.Feedback: Tax incidence is about who bears the burden of the tax, not just who sends the payment.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: The side of the market that is less elastic usually bears:
micro.Choice A: More of the tax burden
micro.Choice B: None of the tax burden
micro.Choice C: Less of the tax burden because it changes behavior less.
micro.Choice D: All of the producer surplus
micro.Correct Answer: A — More of the tax burden
micro.Feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the tax burden because it responds less to price changes.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: If demand is less elastic than supply, who bears more of a tax?
micro.Choice A: Buyers
micro.Choice B: Sellers
micro.Choice C: Neither side
micro.Choice D: Only the government
micro.Correct Answer: A — Buyers
micro.Feedback: Buyers bear more because demand is less elastic than supply.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: If supply is less elastic than demand, who bears more of a tax?
micro.Choice A: Sellers
micro.Choice B: Buyers
micro.Choice C: Neither side
micro.Choice D: Whichever side is legally required to remit the tax.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Sellers
micro.Feedback: Sellers bear more because supply is less elastic than demand.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: A $5 tax causes buyers to pay $3 more than before and sellers to receive $2 less than before. How is the burden split?
micro.Choice A: Buyers bear $3 and sellers bear $2
micro.Choice B: Buyers bear $2 and sellers bear $3
micro.Choice C: Sellers bear all $5
micro.Choice D: Buyers bear all $5
micro.Correct Answer: A — Buyers bear $3 and sellers bear $2
micro.Feedback: The buyer burden is the price increase paid by buyers. The seller burden is the price decrease received by sellers.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: A tax on cigarettes causes only a small drop in smoking even though buyers face a noticeably higher price. What is the most likely explanation?
micro.Choice A: Demand is relatively inelastic
micro.Choice B: Demand is perfectly elastic
micro.Choice C: Supply increased after the tax
micro.Choice D: The tax created a price floor
micro.Correct Answer: A — Demand is relatively inelastic
micro.Feedback: If quantity falls only a little after a tax, demand is likely relatively inelastic.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Common Misconception: Assigning economic tax burden by statutory collection rather than relative elasticity.
micro.Question: In a competitive cigarette market, demand is less price-elastic than supply. A small per-unit tax is collected from sellers. With other market conditions unchanged, which conclusion about the economic burden follows?
micro.Choice A: Buyers bear more because demand is less price-responsive than supply.
micro.Choice B: Sellers bear more because the government collects the tax from sellers.
micro.Choice C: Each side bears half because both participate in the taxed transactions.
micro.Choice D: Buyers bear the entire tax because demand is less elastic than supply.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Buyers bear more because demand is less price-responsive than supply.
micro.Feedback: Buyers bear the larger share because demand is less elastic than supply: buyers adjust quantity less readily when prices change. Collecting the tax from sellers does not determine economic incidence. The stated comparison does not imply that buyers bear the entire tax.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Common Misconception: Assigning economic tax burden by statutory collection rather than relative elasticity.
micro.Question: In a competitive luxury-boat rental market, demand is more price-elastic than supply. A small per-unit tax is collected from renters. With other market conditions unchanged, which conclusion is best supported?
micro.Choice A: Sellers are more likely to bear more of the tax burden.
micro.Choice B: Buyers are more likely to bear more of the tax burden.
micro.Choice C: Buyers and sellers are likely to share the tax burden equally.
micro.Choice D: Sellers are likely to bear the entire tax because they receive payment.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Sellers are more likely to bear more of the tax burden.
micro.Feedback: Supply is less elastic than demand, so sellers are less able to adjust quantity and bear the larger share through lower net receipts. Collecting the tax from renters does not make renters bear the larger share. Relative inelasticity does not imply that sellers bear the entire tax.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: A tax is imposed on a market where demand is perfectly inelastic. Who bears the tax burden?
micro.Choice A: Buyers bear the burden because quantity demanded does not respond
micro.Choice B: Sellers bear the burden because they collect the money
micro.Choice C: The government bears the burden
micro.Choice D: No one bears the burden because quantity does not change
micro.Correct Answer: A — Buyers bear the burden because quantity demanded does not respond
micro.Feedback: If buyers do not change quantity demanded at all, buyers bear the tax burden.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: A $6 tax causes buyers to pay $4 more than before and sellers to receive $2 less than before. Who bears more of the tax burden?
micro.Choice A: Buyers
micro.Choice B: Sellers
micro.Choice C: Both sides bear zero burden
micro.Choice D: Only the government
micro.Correct Answer: A — Buyers
micro.Feedback: Buyers bear $4 of the $6 tax, while sellers bear $2, so buyers bear more.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: If demand is very inelastic and supply is elastic, who likely bears more of a tax?
micro.Choice A: Buyers
micro.Choice B: Sellers
micro.Choice C: Both sides bear exactly zero
micro.Choice D: The side with more firms always bears it
micro.Correct Answer: A — Buyers
micro.Feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the tax burden. Here, that is buyers.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: If supply is very inelastic and demand is elastic, who likely bears more of a tax?
micro.Choice A: Sellers
micro.Choice B: Buyers
micro.Choice C: Only the government
micro.Choice D: No one because demand is elastic
micro.Correct Answer: A — Sellers
micro.Feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the burden. Here, that is sellers.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: Why does the more elastic side of a market tend to bear less of a tax?
micro.Choice A: It can adjust its behavior more easily in response to the tax.
micro.Choice B: A binding price floor absorbs part of the tax.
micro.Choice C: Elasticity affects only the legal assignment of the tax.
micro.Choice D: The more elastic side cannot change quantity when price changes.
micro.Correct Answer: A — It can adjust its behavior more easily in response to the tax.
micro.Feedback: The more elastic side can respond more easily, so it bears less of the tax burden.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: Refer to the tax incidence graph. How much of the tax burden is paid by buyers?
micro.Feedback: Buyers paid $15 before the tax and pay $18 after the tax, so their burden is $3.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: Refer to the tax incidence graph. How much of the tax burden is paid by sellers?
micro.Feedback: Sellers received $15 before the tax and receive $12 after the tax, so their burden is $3.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: Refer to the tax incidence graph. Who bears more of the tax burden?
micro.Choice A: Buyers and sellers share the burden equally
micro.Choice B: Buyers bear all of the burden
micro.Choice C: Sellers bear all of the burden
micro.Choice D: No one bears the burden
micro.Correct Answer: A — Buyers and sellers share the burden equally
micro.Feedback: Buyers pay $3 more and sellers receive $3 less, so the burden is split equally.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: A $12 tax causes buyers to pay $7 more and sellers to receive $5 less. Demand is likely less elastic than supply because:
micro.Choice A: Buyers bear more of the tax burden
micro.Choice B: Sellers bear more of the tax burden
micro.Choice C: The legal tax must have been placed on buyers
micro.Choice D: The tax increased quantity sold
micro.Correct Answer: A — Buyers bear more of the tax burden
micro.Feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the tax burden. Buyers bear $7, so demand is likely less elastic.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: A tax is imposed on a good with elastic demand and highly inelastic supply. Which result is most likely?
micro.Choice A: Sellers bear most of the burden
micro.Choice B: Buyers bear most of the burden
micro.Choice C: Demand increases because the tax is high
micro.Choice D: The legal assignment alone determines burden
micro.Correct Answer: A — Sellers bear most of the burden
micro.Feedback: The less elastic side bears more. If supply is highly inelastic, sellers bear most of the tax.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: A student says, 'The price rose after the tax, so buyers paid the entire tax.' What is the flaw?
micro.Choice A: Buyers bear only the increase above the old equilibrium price.
micro.Choice B: Any price increase means buyers pay everything
micro.Choice C: Sellers cannot bear taxes if buyers pay more
micro.Choice D: Tax incidence is unrelated to prices
micro.Correct Answer: A — Buyers bear only the increase above the old equilibrium price.
micro.Feedback: Buyers bear the part of the tax reflected in the higher price they pay; sellers bear the part reflected in the lower price they receive.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: Before a tax, buyers pay $30 and sellers receive $30. After a tax, buyers pay $34 and sellers receive $27. Who bears more of the burden?
micro.Choice A: Buyers
micro.Choice B: Sellers
micro.Choice C: They split it equally
micro.Choice D: No one bears any burden
micro.Correct Answer: A — Buyers
micro.Feedback: Buyers pay $4 more, while sellers receive $3 less. Buyers bear more of the burden.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: If demand is less elastic than supply, why do buyers bear more of a tax?
micro.Choice A: Buyers are less able to reduce quantity demanded when price rises
micro.Choice B: Buyers legally pay all taxes
micro.Choice C: Sellers are less able to adjust quantity supplied
micro.Choice D: Demand shifts right after the tax
micro.Correct Answer: A — Buyers are less able to reduce quantity demanded when price rises
micro.Feedback: The less elastic side adjusts less, so it bears more of the tax burden.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: If supply is perfectly inelastic and demand is elastic, who bears the tax burden?
micro.Choice A: Sellers bear all of it.
micro.Choice B: Buyers bear all of it
micro.Choice C: No one bears it
micro.Choice D: The government bears it because supply is vertical
micro.Correct Answer: A — Sellers bear all of it.
micro.Feedback: With perfectly inelastic supply, quantity supplied cannot respond to the tax. Sellers therefore bear the entire tax burden through a lower net price received.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: Refer to the tax incidence graph. What is the buyers’ tax burden on the units still traded, excluding surplus lost on missing trades?
micro.Feedback: The per-unit buyer burden is $3 relative to the original $15 price. Multiplying by 80 continuing units gives $240. The full welfare loss for that side also includes surplus lost on trades that no longer occur.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: Refer to the tax incidence graph. On the units still sold after the tax, what is the sellers’ total loss from receiving a lower price? Exclude surplus lost on sales that no longer occur.
micro.Feedback: The per-unit seller burden is $3 relative to the original $15 price. Multiplying by 80 continuing units gives $240. The full welfare loss for that side also includes surplus lost on trades that no longer occur.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: Refer to the tax incidence graph. On the units still traded, what is the combined tax burden on buyers and sellers, equal to government tax revenue?
micro.Feedback: The $6 wedge applies to 80 continuing trades, so the rectangle is $480. This is the combined per-unit incidence times taxed quantity. Lost gains from the missing trades are additional welfare loss and are not government revenue.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: For the units still purchased after the tax, what is the buyers’ total additional payment compared with paying the original price for those same units? Exclude the welfare effect of purchases forgone.
micro.Choice A: $200: $2.50 extra on each of 80 units
micro.Choice B: $300: $3 extra on each of 100 units
micro.Choice C: $240: $3 extra on each of 80 units
micro.Choice D: $250: $2.50 extra on each of 100 units
micro.Correct Answer: C — $240: $3 extra on each of 80 units
micro.Feedback: The graph shows the buyer price rising from $15 to $18 and after-tax quantity falling to 80. The extra payment on purchases still made is ($18-$15)*80=$240. Lost gains on the 20 forgone purchases are excluded.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: Refer to the tax incidence graph. A seller group divides the fall in total sales revenue after paying the tax by the 80 units still sold and calls the result its tax burden per unit still sold. Why is that calculation misleading?
micro.Choice A: The $540 decline in sales revenue includes fewer units sold; the tax burden per unit still sold is $3.
micro.Choice B: The $540 decline in sales revenue is entirely a price effect; the burden on each continuing unit is $6.75.
micro.Choice C: The $240 decline in sales revenue includes fewer units sold; the tax burden per unit still sold is $6.
micro.Choice D: The $300 decline in sales revenue is entirely a quantity effect; the tax burden per unit still sold is $0.
micro.Correct Answer: A — The $540 decline in sales revenue includes fewer units sold; the tax burden per unit still sold is $3.
micro.Feedback: Receipts fall from $15 x 100 = $1,500 to $12 x 80 = $960, a $540 decline. This combines $300 from 20 fewer units valued at the old price and $240 from receiving $3 less on each of 80 continuing sales. The per-unit seller tax burden is $15 - $12 = $3; gross receipts are not a measure of producer surplus.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: Using the original equilibrium price as the benchmark, how is the per-unit tax burden divided in the graph?
micro.Choice A: Buyers bear $3; sellers bear $3
micro.Choice B: Buyers bear $2; sellers bear $4
micro.Choice C: Buyers bear $4; sellers bear $2
micro.Choice D: Buyers bear $1; sellers bear $5
micro.Correct Answer: A — Buyers bear $3; sellers bear $3
micro.Feedback: The original price is $15. Buyers pay $18 after the tax and sellers receive $12, so each side bears $3 of the $6 tax.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: Before tax, price is $20. After tax, buyers pay $24 and sellers receive $18. Which statement correctly splits the burden?
micro.Choice A: Buyers bear $4 and sellers bear $2
micro.Choice B: Buyers bear $2 and sellers bear $4
micro.Choice C: Buyers bear $6 and sellers bear $0
micro.Choice D: Buyers bear $24 and sellers bear $18
micro.Correct Answer: A — Buyers bear $4 and sellers bear $2
micro.Feedback: Buyers pay $4 more than before, while sellers receive $2 less than before.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: A tax is imposed on a good with highly inelastic demand and elastic supply. Which policy outcome is most likely?
micro.Choice A: Buyers bear most of the burden and quantity falls relatively little
micro.Choice B: Sellers bear most of the burden and quantity falls dramatically
micro.Choice C: Buyers bear no burden because sellers legally pay
micro.Choice D: The tax creates a surplus equal to the tax
micro.Correct Answer: A — Buyers bear most of the burden and quantity falls relatively little
micro.Feedback: Inelastic demand means buyers bear more and reduce quantity less in response to the tax.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: Before a tax, price is $40 and 500 units trade. Afterward buyers pay $46, sellers keep $34, and 420 units trade. What is the buyers’ tax burden on the units still traded, as distinct from the entire change in consumer surplus?
micro.Feedback: The per-unit buyer burden is $46 − $40 = $6. On 420 continuing units, its rectangle is $2,520. The full CS change also includes lost gains from the 80 missing trades; the rectangle alone does not measure that entire loss.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: A market moves from $40 and 500 units before a tax to a buyer price of $46, seller receipt of $34, and 420 units afterward. On the units still sold after the tax, what is the sellers’ total loss from receiving a lower price? Exclude surplus lost on sales that no longer occur.
micro.Feedback: The seller loses $40 − $34 = $6 per continuing unit, so the rectangle is $6 × 420 = $2,520. Using 500 applies the burden to trades that no longer occur. The $12 wedge times 420 is total revenue, not the seller share alone.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: A tax is imposed on sellers. Before the tax, price is $20 and quantity is 300. After the tax, buyers pay $24, sellers receive $18, and quantity is 240. Which statement is correct?
micro.Choice A: Tax wedge: $6; buyer burden: $4 per unit; seller burden: $2 per unit; quantity falls by 60 units.
micro.Choice B: Tax wedge: $6; buyer burden: $2 per unit; seller burden: $4 per unit; quantity falls by 60 units.
micro.Choice C: Tax wedge: $6; buyer burden: $0 per unit; seller burden: $6 per unit; quantity falls by 60 units.
micro.Choice D: Tax wedge: $6; buyer burden: $4 per unit; seller burden: $2 per unit; quantity falls by 240 units.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Tax wedge: $6; buyer burden: $4 per unit; seller burden: $2 per unit; quantity falls by 60 units.
micro.Feedback: The tax wedge is $24 - $18 = $6 per unit. Relative to the original $20 price, buyers bear $24 - $20 = $4 per unit and sellers bear $20 - $18 = $2 per unit; these burdens sum to $6. Quantity falls by 300 - 240 = 60 units. The 240 units are the new quantity, not the decrease. Requiring sellers to remit the tax does not make them bear its entire economic burden.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: Refer to the tax graph. A seller argues that its legal duty to remit the tax means it bears the entire revenue rectangle. What do the price changes and continuing quantity show?
micro.Choice A: Each side bears $3 per unit and $240 of the $480 rectangle
micro.Choice B: Sellers bear $6 per unit and all $480 of the rectangle
micro.Choice C: Each side bears $3 per unit and $300 of the $600 rectangle
micro.Choice D: Buyers bear $6 per unit and all $480 of the rectangle
micro.Correct Answer: A — Each side bears $3 per unit and $240 of the $480 rectangle
micro.Feedback: Relative to $15, buyers pay $3 more and sellers receive $3 less. At 80 units, each incidence rectangle is $240, together equaling $480 of revenue. Remitting the money is different from bearing the price burden; these rectangles exclude gains lost on missing trades.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: A $4 tax is placed on concert tickets. Buyers pay $2.50 more than before, sellers receive $1.50 less than before, and fewer tickets are sold. Which statement is strongest?
micro.Choice A: The burden is shared, quantity falls, and the side less able to adjust bears more
micro.Choice B: The burden falls only on sellers because the legal tax is charged to sellers
micro.Choice C: The burden falls only on buyers because the buyer price increased
micro.Choice D: The burden disappears because tax revenue offsets the lower quantity sold
micro.Correct Answer: A — The burden is shared, quantity falls, and the side less able to adjust bears more
micro.Feedback: Legal responsibility for the tax does not determine economic burden. The wedge is shared and quantity falls.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: A market has an $8 tax, a total buyer price of $26 and a net seller receipt of $18. Buyers bear 75% of the per-unit burden. What was the untaxed price, and which side is less price responsive over this change?
micro.Choice A: $20; buyers
micro.Choice B: $24; sellers
micro.Choice C: $20; sellers
micro.Choice D: $24; buyers
micro.Correct Answer: A — $20; buyers
micro.Feedback: Buyer burden is 0.75 × $8 = $6, so the old price was $26 − $6 = $20. Sellers bear the remaining $2, since $20 − $18 = $2. Under the standard tax-incidence comparison, the side bearing more of the wedge is less price responsive.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: Supply is perfectly inelastic at 200 units and demand slopes downward. A $6 tax is imposed in a competitive market with no externalities or collection costs. Which combination follows?
micro.Choice A: Sellers bear $6 per unit, revenue is $1,200, and deadweight loss is zero
micro.Choice B: Buyers bear $6 per unit, revenue is $1,200, and deadweight loss is zero
micro.Choice C: Sellers bear $6 per unit, revenue is $1,200, and deadweight loss is $1,200
micro.Choice D: Buyers and sellers each bear $3, revenue is $600, and quantity falls
micro.Correct Answer: A — Sellers bear $6 per unit, revenue is $1,200, and deadweight loss is zero
micro.Feedback: The vertical supply curve holds quantity at 200. Buyers pay the same demand price at that quantity, so sellers absorb the full $6 wedge through lower net receipts. Revenue is $1,200. With no trades lost and no other distortions in the stated model, tax revenue is a transfer and there is no deadweight loss.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: Demand is less elastic than supply. Which side bears more of a per-unit tax?
micro.Choice A: Sellers bear more because buyers can easily leave
micro.Choice B: The government bears the burden
micro.Choice C: No one bears the burden because taxes do not affect prices
micro.Choice D: Buyers bear more because they respond less to the price change
micro.Correct Answer: D — Buyers bear more because they respond less to the price change
micro.Feedback: The less elastic side of the market bears more of the tax burden because it has fewer good alternatives.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: A tax is placed on a good with very inelastic demand and elastic supply. Which outcome is most likely?
micro.Choice A: Sellers bear most of the burden and quantity rises
micro.Choice B: Buyers and sellers split the burden exactly equally by law
micro.Choice C: Buyers bear most of the burden and quantity falls relatively little
micro.Choice D: The tax has no effect because supply is elastic
micro.Correct Answer: C — Buyers bear most of the burden and quantity falls relatively little
micro.Feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the tax burden. With inelastic demand, buyers bear more and quantity changes less.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: A $6 tax is imposed. Before the tax, buyers paid $20. After the tax, buyers pay $24 and sellers receive $18. How much of the tax burden falls on buyers and sellers?
micro.Choice A: Buyers bear $4 and sellers bear $2
micro.Choice B: Buyers bear $2 and sellers bear $4
micro.Choice C: Buyers bear all $6 and sellers bear $0
micro.Choice D: Buyers bear $24 and sellers bear $18
micro.Correct Answer: A — Buyers bear $4 and sellers bear $2
micro.Feedback: Buyers now pay $4 more than before. Sellers receive $2 less than before. The $6 tax burden is split $4 on buyers and $2 on sellers.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: Demand is much less elastic than supply. A tax is imposed on the good. Who bears more of the tax burden, and why?
micro.Choice A: Buyers bear more because they are less able to reduce quantity demanded
micro.Choice B: Sellers bear more because supply is more elastic
micro.Choice C: Buyers and sellers must split the burden equally
micro.Choice D: Sellers bear more because buyers pay the tax through the market price
micro.Correct Answer: A — Buyers bear more because they are less able to reduce quantity demanded
micro.Feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the tax because it is less able to change behavior in response to the tax.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: Supply is much less elastic than demand. A tax is imposed. What is the likely result?
micro.Choice A: Sellers bear more of the burden because quantity supplied is less responsive
micro.Choice B: Buyers bear more of the burden because demand is more elastic
micro.Choice C: The burden must be equal because the tax wedge is fixed
micro.Choice D: The side required to remit the tax bears more because statutory payment determines the economic burden
micro.Correct Answer: A — Sellers bear more of the burden because quantity supplied is less responsive
micro.Feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the tax. If supply is less elastic than demand, sellers bear more of the burden.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: A $4 tax is placed on a good. After adjustment, buyers pay $2.75 more and sellers receive $1.25 less. Which conclusion is best?
micro.Choice A: Sellers bear more of the burden, so supply is likely less elastic than demand
micro.Choice B: Buyers and sellers split the burden equally because the tax is $4
micro.Choice C: The legal taxpayer must be the buyer because buyers pay $2.75 more
micro.Choice D: Buyers bear more of the burden, so demand is likely less elastic than supply
micro.Correct Answer: D — Buyers bear more of the burden, so demand is likely less elastic than supply
micro.Feedback: Buyers bear $2.75 of the $4 tax. The side bearing more burden is usually less elastic.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: A tax reduces quantity only slightly but raises the buyer price substantially. Which market condition best explains this?
micro.Choice A: Demand is relatively inelastic, so buyers keep purchasing despite the higher price
micro.Choice B: Demand is relatively elastic, so buyers leave the market completely
micro.Choice C: Supply is perfectly elastic, so sellers bear the full burden
micro.Choice D: The tax must be legally assigned to buyers
micro.Correct Answer: A — Demand is relatively inelastic, so buyers keep purchasing despite the higher price
micro.Feedback: When demand is inelastic, buyers do not reduce quantity much, so they can bear much of the tax through higher prices.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: Tax A is on insulin with very inelastic demand. Tax B is on restaurant meals with more elastic demand. Which tax likely creates less quantity reduction but places more burden on buyers?
micro.Choice A: Tax B, because restaurant meals are easier to avoid
micro.Choice B: Tax A, because insulin demand is less elastic
micro.Choice C: Both taxes have identical effects because all taxes create wedges
micro.Choice D: Neither tax affects quantity if sellers legally pay it
micro.Correct Answer: B — Tax A, because insulin demand is less elastic
micro.Feedback: A tax on a good with very inelastic demand causes less quantity reduction and places more burden on buyers.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: In a competitive market, demand elasticity is Ed=-0.25 and supply elasticity Es=1.20 near equilibrium. A small unit tax is introduced. Later, buyers gain substitutes and Ed becomes -1.50 while Es stays 1.20. Which comparison is best, holding the initial price, quantity and tax size comparable?
micro.Choice A: Buyers initially bear more; afterward sellers bear more, and the stronger demand response makes the tax-induced quantity reduction larger.
micro.Choice B: Sellers initially bear more; afterward buyers bear more, and stronger demand response makes the quantity reduction smaller.
micro.Choice C: Buyers bear more in both cases because the negative sign makes demand less elastic than every positive supply elasticity.
micro.Choice D: Burden shares reverse only if the law changes the tax remitter; elasticity changes affect quantity but not economic incidence.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Buyers initially bear more; afterward sellers bear more, and the stronger demand response makes the tax-induced quantity reduction larger.
micro.Feedback: Compare absolute elasticities. Initially 0.25<1.20, so buyers are less responsive and bear more. Later 1.50>1.20, so sellers are relatively less responsive. Greater demand responsiveness also increases the quantity response to a comparable small tax.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: Demand elasticity is -1.80 and supply elasticity is 0.20 in a market. A small tax is imposed on sellers. Over time, sellers gain alternative uses for their resources and supply elasticity rises to 2.40, with demand elasticity unchanged. Compare equal small taxes from the same initial price and quantity. Which evaluation is correct?
micro.Choice A: Buyers initially bear more, but sellers bear more later; the legal seller tax becomes binding only in the long run.
micro.Choice B: Sellers initially bear more, but buyers bear more later; greater supply responsiveness also increases the quantity response to the tax.
micro.Choice C: Sellers bear more in both periods because the statute requires them to remit the tax, regardless of alternatives.
micro.Choice D: Burden becomes exactly equal later because both elasticity magnitudes exceed one, making relative sizes irrelevant.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Sellers initially bear more, but buyers bear more later; greater supply responsiveness also increases the quantity response to the tax.
micro.Feedback: Initially supply magnitude 0.20 is below demand magnitude 1.80, so sellers bear more. Later supply magnitude 2.40 exceeds demand, so buyers bear more. More responsive supply permits a greater quantity adjustment under a comparable small tax.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Question: Before a tax, market price is $40. After a $12 unit tax, buyers pay $43 and sellers receive $31. A reform puts legal remittance on buyers without changing behavior or the tax size. Which combined inference is supported?
micro.Choice A: Buyers bear 75% and sellers 25%; demand is relatively less elastic, and remittance alone reverses the $43/$31 price pair.
micro.Choice B: Buyers bear 25% and sellers 75%; supply is relatively less elastic, and remittance alone leaves the $43/$31 price pair unchanged.
micro.Choice C: Buyers bear 25% and sellers 75%; demand is relatively less elastic, so buyer remittance makes buyers bear the entire $12.
micro.Choice D: Buyers bear 50% and sellers 50%; the $12 wedge must be split evenly once both sides participate in the market.
micro.Correct Answer: B — Buyers bear 25% and sellers 75%; supply is relatively less elastic, and remittance alone leaves the $43/$31 price pair unchanged.
micro.Feedback: Buyer burden is 43-40=3 and seller burden 40-31=9, totaling 12. Shares are 3/12=25% and 9/12=75%. In the standard model the less elastic side bears more, indicating relatively less elastic supply. Legal remittance alone does not alter the wedge equilibrium.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
micro.Question: Using the original equilibrium and the after-tax buyer and seller prices, which burden split and relative-elasticity conclusion fit the graph?
micro.Choice A: Buyers bear $5 and sellers $3; demand is less elastic
micro.Choice B: Buyers bear $2 and sellers $6; supply is less elastic
micro.Choice C: Buyers bear $6 and sellers $2; demand is less elastic
micro.Choice D: Buyers bear $3 and sellers $5; supply is less elastic
micro.Correct Answer: C — Buyers bear $6 and sellers $2; demand is less elastic
micro.Feedback: The original price is $10, the buyer price is $16, and the net seller price is $8. Buyers bear $6 and sellers $2 of the $8 tax. The larger buyer burden indicates less elastic demand over this change.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. Which side bears more of the $8 tax, and what does that imply about relative elasticity?
micro.Choice A: Buyers bear 6 dollars; demand is less elastic
micro.Choice B: Sellers bear 2 dollars; supply is more elastic
micro.Choice C: Buyers bear all 8 dollars; demand is perfectly inelastic
micro.Choice D: Sellers bear $6; supply is less elastic.
micro.Correct Answer: D — Sellers bear $6; supply is less elastic.
micro.Feedback: The seller price falls by $6 while the buyer price rises by $2. Sellers therefore bear more of the tax, consistent with supply being less elastic than demand.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.5
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
micro.Question: The tax in the graph is legally collected from buyers. Which economic burden split and relative-elasticity conclusion match the plotted prices?
micro.Choice A: Buyers bear $5 and sellers $3; demand is less elastic
micro.Choice B: Buyers bear $2 and sellers $6; supply is less elastic
micro.Choice C: Buyers bear $3 and sellers $5; supply is less elastic
micro.Choice D: Buyers bear $6 and sellers $2; demand is less elastic
micro.Correct Answer: D — Buyers bear $6 and sellers $2; demand is less elastic
micro.Feedback: The original price is $10. Buyers now pay sellers $8 and remit the $8 tax, for a total price of $16. Buyers bear $6 and sellers $2. The larger buyer burden indicates less elastic demand; buyers also remain the legal remitters.

micro.Choice D: Revenue is 400,000 dollars; trips fall by 150 thousand
micro.Correct Answer: C — Revenue is 600,000 dollars; trips fall by 50 thousand
micro.Feedback: Four dollars times 150 thousand is 600,000; quantity falls by 50 thousand.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. How much daily tax revenue is generated?
micro.Choice A: 400,000 dollars
micro.Choice B: 1,000,000 dollars
micro.Choice C: 1,200,000 dollars
micro.Choice D: 800,000 dollars
micro.Correct Answer: D — 800,000 dollars

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
micro.Question: What daily tax revenue is shown?
micro.Choice A: 400,000 dollars
micro.Choice B: 800,000 dollars
micro.Choice C: 1.2 million dollars
micro.Choice D: 1.6 million dollars
micro.Correct Answer: C — 1.2 million dollars
micro.Feedback: The 8 dollar wedge applies to 150 thousand trips.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
micro.Question: A proposal halves the per-trip tax shown in the rideshare graph. Keep the straight demand and supply curves fixed. Which revenue change and interpretation are correct?
micro.Choice A: $600,000 to $350,000; extra trips offset part, but not all, of the lower tax rate.
micro.Choice B: $800,000 to $450,000; extra trips offset part, but not all, of the lower tax rate.
micro.Choice C: $800,000 to $450,000; a tax-rate cut leaves the number of trips fixed by definition.
micro.Choice D: $600,000 to $350,000; a tax-rate cut leaves the number of trips fixed by definition.
micro.Correct Answer: B — $800,000 to $450,000; extra trips offset part, but not all, of the lower tax rate.
micro.Feedback: The original tax wedge is 14−10 = 4 at 200 thousand trips; untaxed Q is 250 thousand. Halving the tax to 2 moves quantity halfway to 250, or 225 thousand, under the fixed linear curves. Receipts change 4 × 200,000 = 800,000 to 2 × 225,000 = 450,000. The quantity response partially offsets the rate cut.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. What is the per-trip tax wedge?
micro.Choice A: 2 dollars
micro.Choice B: 4 dollars
micro.Choice C: 8 dollars
micro.Choice D: 20 dollars
micro.Correct Answer: B — 4 dollars
micro.Feedback: Buyers pay 12 and sellers receive 8.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
micro.Question: Which price and quantity changes occur after the tax in the graph, and what economic effect do they represent?
micro.Choice A: Buyer price rises $2, seller receipt falls $2 and quantity falls 50 thousand; a tax separates buyer and seller prices.
micro.Choice B: Buyer price rises $3, seller receipt falls $3 and quantity falls 75 thousand; a tax separates buyer and seller prices.
micro.Choice C: Buyer price rises $2, seller receipt falls $2 and quantity falls 50 thousand; both sides still face the same price after tax.
micro.Choice D: Buyer price rises $3, seller receipt falls $3 and quantity falls 75 thousand; both sides still face the same price after tax.
micro.Correct Answer: A — Buyer price rises $2, seller receipt falls $2 and quantity falls 50 thousand; a tax separates buyer and seller prices.
micro.Feedback: The untaxed point is P = 12, Q = 250 thousand. After tax buyers pay 14, sellers receive 10 and Q = 200 thousand. The wedge changes both prices and reduces the amount traded.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. For the buyer-side tax, what are the wedge and revenue?
micro.Choice A: A 6 dollar wedge and 900,000
micro.Choice B: An 8 dollar wedge and 1.2 million dollars
micro.Choice C: An 8 dollar wedge and 1.6 million
micro.Choice D: A 2 dollar wedge and 300,000
micro.Correct Answer: B — An 8 dollar wedge and 1.2 million dollars
micro.Feedback: Buyers pay 16, sellers receive 8, and 150 thousand tickets are taxed.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: A tax wedge is the difference between:
micro.Choice A: The price buyers pay and the price sellers receive
micro.Choice B: Quantity demanded and quantity supplied
micro.Choice C: Two points on a PPF
micro.Choice D: A price ceiling and a price floor
micro.Correct Answer: A — The price buyers pay and the price sellers receive
micro.Feedback: A tax wedge separates what buyers pay from what sellers receive.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: Buyers pay $18 after a tax and sellers receive $12. What is the tax per unit?
micro.Feedback: The tax wedge is $18 - $12 = $6.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: Before a tax, buyers pay $20 and sellers receive $20. After the tax, buyers pay $24 and sellers receive $18. What is the tax per unit?
micro.Feedback: The tax wedge is buyer price minus seller price: $24 - $18 = $6.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: A tax raises the price buyers pay and lowers the price sellers receive. What else usually happens?
micro.Choice A: Quantity traded falls
micro.Choice B: Quantity traded rises
micro.Choice C: Scarcity disappears
micro.Choice D: The PPF shifts outward
micro.Correct Answer: A — Quantity traded falls
micro.Feedback: A tax creates a wedge and reduces the quantity traded.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: A tax on a good generally causes the quantity sold to:
micro.Choice A: Decrease
micro.Choice B: Increase
micro.Choice C: Stay exactly the same always
micro.Choice D: Become unlimited
micro.Correct Answer: A — Decrease
micro.Feedback: A tax raises the effective cost of trade, so the quantity sold falls.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: A tax creates a wedge between:
micro.Choice A: The price buyers pay and the price sellers receive
micro.Choice B: Demand and consumer income only
micro.Choice C: Two different PPFs
micro.Choice D: Positive and normative statements
micro.Correct Answer: A — The price buyers pay and the price sellers receive
micro.Feedback: A tax drives a wedge between what buyers pay and what sellers receive.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: After a tax, buyers pay $12 and sellers receive $9. What is the tax per unit?
micro.Feedback: The tax wedge is the difference between what buyers pay and sellers receive: $12 - $9 = $3.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: If buyers pay $15 after a tax and sellers receive $10, the wedge is:
micro.Feedback: The wedge is the difference between buyer price and seller price: $15 - $10 = $5.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: In the displayed movie market, how large is the vertical gap between S0 and the parallel “Supply with tax” curve at a given quantity?
micro.Choice A: $4 per movie
micro.Choice B: $2 per movie
micro.Choice C: $10 per movie
micro.Choice D: $14 per movie
micro.Correct Answer: A — $4 per movie
micro.Feedback: At quantity 100 thousand, S0 is at $10 while Supply with tax is at $14. The parallel vertical gap is therefore $4 per movie.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: A tax on gasoline raises the price paid by drivers, lowers the price received by sellers, and reduces gallons sold. Which concept chain is correct?
micro.Choice A: Tax wedge → shared burden → lower quantity traded
micro.Choice B: Price ceiling → shortage → higher quantity traded
micro.Choice C: Demand increase → higher price → higher quantity
micro.Choice D: PPF shift → economic growth → lower price
micro.Correct Answer: A — Tax wedge → shared burden → lower quantity traded
micro.Feedback: A tax creates a wedge between buyer and seller prices, splits the burden, and reduces the quantity traded.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: Before a tax, buyers pay $30 and sellers receive $30. After a tax, buyers pay $34 and sellers receive $27. What is the tax per unit?
micro.Feedback: The tax wedge is the buyer price minus the seller price: $34 - $27 = $7.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: A tax reduces quantity sold from 500 to 420 units. If the tax is $8 per unit, how much tax revenue is collected?
micro.Feedback: Tax revenue uses the quantity sold after the tax: $8 × 420 = $3,360.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: A $10 tax is imposed. Before the tax, price is $50. After the tax, buyers pay $56 and sellers receive $46. What happened to quantity sold?
micro.Choice A: It likely decreased because the tax created a wedge
micro.Choice B: It must have increased because buyers pay more
micro.Choice C: It stayed exactly the same because the tax is split
micro.Choice D: It became zero because all taxes eliminate trade
micro.Correct Answer: A — It likely decreased because the tax created a wedge
micro.Feedback: A tax creates a wedge between buyer and seller prices and usually reduces the quantity traded.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: A tax on sellers shifts the supply curve upward because:
micro.Choice A: The tax raises the cost of selling each unit
micro.Choice B: The tax increases buyers' income
micro.Choice C: The tax makes demand perfectly elastic
micro.Choice D: The tax eliminates opportunity cost
micro.Correct Answer: A — The tax raises the cost of selling each unit
micro.Feedback: A tax on sellers raises the cost of selling each unit, shifting supply upward.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: Before a tax, buyers pay $10 and sellers receive $10. After the tax, buyers pay $12 and sellers receive $8. What is the tax wedge?
micro.Feedback: The wedge is the price buyers pay minus the price sellers receive: $12 - $8 = $4.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: A tax reduces the quantity sold from 100 units to 75 units. What is the best interpretation?
micro.Choice A: The tax shrinks the size of the market
micro.Choice B: The tax eliminates scarcity
micro.Choice C: The tax increases both supply and demand
micro.Choice D: The tax causes quantity sold to rise
micro.Correct Answer: A — The tax shrinks the size of the market
micro.Feedback: A tax raises the cost of exchange and reduces the quantity traded.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: Refer to the tax incidence graph. What is the original equilibrium price and quantity before the tax?
micro.Choice A: $15 and 100 units
micro.Choice B: $18 and 80 units
micro.Choice C: $12 and 80 units
micro.Choice D: $20 and 65 units
micro.Correct Answer: A — $15 and 100 units
micro.Feedback: Before the tax, demand and the original supply curve intersect at $15 and 100 units.

micro.Question: Refer to the tax incidence graph. After the tax, what price do buyers pay?
micro.Feedback: After the tax, the price buyers pay is read from the demand curve at the new quantity, which is $18.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: Refer to the tax incidence graph. After the tax, what price do sellers receive?
micro.Feedback: After the tax, sellers receive $12 per unit after the tax is accounted for.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: Refer to the tax incidence graph. What is the amount of the tax per unit?
micro.Feedback: The tax wedge is the difference between what buyers pay and what sellers receive: $18 - $12 = $6.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: Refer to the tax graph. Which before-and-after quantities describe the change in sales, and why does the tax affect sales?
micro.Choice A: From 100 to 80 units; the wedge between buyer payment and seller receipt removes some mutually beneficial trades.
micro.Choice B: From 100 to 65 units; the wedge between buyer payment and seller receipt removes some mutually beneficial trades.
micro.Choice C: From 100 to 80 units; the 20 units no longer sold become tax revenue.
micro.Choice D: From 100 to 80 units; all buyer payments become a social loss rather than a payment to sellers or government.
micro.Correct Answer: A — From 100 to 80 units; the wedge between buyer payment and seller receipt removes some mutually beneficial trades.
micro.Feedback: The tax lowers sales from 100 to 80. Buyers pay $18 and sellers receive $12, leaving a $6 wedge that prevents mutually beneficial trades. Lost units are not tax revenue; revenue is the tax times units still traded.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: Refer to the tax incidence graph. By how many units does the tax reduce the quantity sold?
micro.Choice A: 20 units
micro.Choice B: 80 units
micro.Choice C: 100 units
micro.Choice D: 180 units
micro.Correct Answer: A — 20 units
micro.Feedback: Quantity falls from 100 to 80, so the tax reduces quantity sold by 20 units.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: Refer to the tax graph. Which quantity change accompanies the wedge between the price buyers pay and the amount sellers receive?
micro.Choice A: From 100 to 80 units; the wedge between buyer payment and seller receipt removes some mutually beneficial trades.
micro.Choice B: From 100 to 65 units; the wedge between buyer payment and seller receipt removes some mutually beneficial trades.
micro.Choice C: From 100 to 80 units; the buyer’s $3 price increase is the entire wedge because the seller’s loss does not count.
micro.Choice D: From 80 to 100 units; using the untaxed intersection as the after-tax quantity measures the sales response.
micro.Correct Answer: A — From 100 to 80 units; the wedge between buyer payment and seller receipt removes some mutually beneficial trades.
micro.Feedback: The original quantity is 100 and the taxed quantity 80. The wedge is $18 − $12 = $6, including the $3 rise in buyer price and the $3 fall in seller receipt from the original $15.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: After the seller-side tax shown, quantity falls to 100 thousand movies. What prices do buyers pay and sellers receive?

micro.Choice B: Buyers pay $14 and sellers receive $10
micro.Choice C: Buyers pay $10 and sellers receive $14
micro.Choice D: Buyers pay $14 and sellers receive $12
micro.Correct Answer: B — Buyers pay $14 and sellers receive $10
micro.Feedback: At the post-tax quantity of 100 thousand, demand gives the buyer price of $14 while the original supply curve gives the seller receipt of $10.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. After the tax is imposed, by how much does quantity traded fall?
micro.Choice A: 20 thousand movies
micro.Choice B: 100 thousand movies
micro.Choice C: 40 thousand movies
micro.Choice D: 240 thousand movies
micro.Correct Answer: C — 40 thousand movies

micro.Question: A market begins in equilibrium. A tax is imposed, and quantity falls from 1,000 to 850. Buyers pay $4 more and sellers receive $6 less. What is the tax revenue?

micro.Choice B: The wedge is $3 and quantity falls from 100 to 80

micro.Question: What is the full per-unit tax in the graph, and why is the increase in buyer price alone insufficient to measure it?

micro.Choice B: $8; buyers pay $4 more and sellers receive $4 less than before.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: Refer to the graph. After the tax is imposed, how much tax revenue is collected?

micro.Question: A tax on luxury goods sharply reduces sales, and the government collects much less revenue than expected. What most likely explains the disappointing revenue?

micro.Choice D: Imposing a tax always increases total revenue regardless of market responses

micro.Question: A luxury tax causes quantity sold to fall sharply and tax revenue disappoints. What is the strongest explanation?
micro.Choice A: A strong response to the tax-related price change sharply reduces trade
micro.Choice B: The tax must be too small to affect purchases and sales
micro.Choice C: Buyers must bear the entire burden, leaving sellers unaffected by the tax
micro.Choice D: Imposing a tax always increases total revenue regardless of market responses
micro.Correct Answer: A — A strong response to the tax-related price change sharply reduces trade
micro.Feedback: If market participants respond strongly, quantity falls sharply and tax revenue may be lower than expected.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: Refer to the movie-tax graph. A report counts only the buyer price increase as the tax rate. Which correction correctly gives the two per-unit burdens and total government revenue?

micro.Choice B: Buyers bear $2 and sellers $2; revenue is $560,000
micro.Choice C: Buyers bear $4 and sellers $0; revenue is $400,000

micro.Feedback: The old price is $12, buyer price $14 and seller receipt $10. Thus the burdens are $2 each, summing to the $4 wedge. Apply that wedge to 100,000 taxed units: revenue is $400,000. The old quantity of 140,000 no longer trades.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: Refer to the movie-tax graph. A review finds that CS plus PS falls by $480,000 after the displayed tax. With no externalities or collection costs, how should that change be reconciled with incidence and total surplus?
micro.Choice A: $480,000 is lost surplus, while the $400,000 revenue is an additional loss
micro.Choice B: $400,000 becomes revenue, $80,000 is lost surplus, and each side bears $2 per unit
micro.Choice C: $560,000 becomes revenue, total surplus rises $80,000, and each side bears $2
micro.Choice D: $400,000 becomes revenue, $80,000 is lost surplus, and buyers bear all $4 per unit
micro.Correct Answer: B — $400,000 becomes revenue, $80,000 is lost surplus, and each side bears $2 per unit
micro.Feedback: Read the old price $12, buyer price $14, seller receipt $10 and taxed quantity 100,000. The $4 wedge raises $400,000. Subtracting that transfer from the $480,000 private loss leaves $80,000 of lost surplus, also 0.5 × 40,000 × $4. Each side bears $2 on each remaining unit.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: A tax is imposed on sellers. Buyers pay a higher price, sellers receive a lower price, and fewer units are sold. What concept ties these effects together?
micro.Choice A: A price floor that creates a labor surplus
micro.Choice B: A tax wedge that shrinks the market
micro.Choice C: Substitution bias in the CPI
micro.Choice D: Discouraged-worker measurement
micro.Correct Answer: B — A tax wedge that shrinks the market
micro.Feedback: A tax drives a wedge between what buyers pay and sellers receive, reducing the quantity sold.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.3
micro.Question: A tax on sellers shifts supply upward, raises the price buyers pay, lowers the price sellers receive, and reduces quantity. What is the best overall description?
micro.Choice A: The tax creates a price floor and expands the market
micro.Choice B: The tax only affects sellers because they mail the check
micro.Choice C: The tax eliminates deadweight loss
micro.Choice D: The tax creates a wedge and shrinks the market
micro.Correct Answer: D — The tax creates a wedge and shrinks the market
micro.Feedback: A tax wedge separates buyer and seller prices and reduces the equilibrium quantity traded.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.4
micro.Question: A $4 tax on buyers and a $4 tax on sellers create the same wedge in the same market. What should happen to the market outcome?
micro.Choice A: The outcome should be equivalent
micro.Choice B: The buyer tax must hurt only buyers
micro.Choice C: The seller tax must hurt only sellers
micro.Choice D: Only the seller tax reduces quantity
micro.Correct Answer: A — The outcome should be equivalent
micro.Feedback: Equivalent taxes on buyers or sellers create the same wedge and market outcome.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.4
micro.Question: A tax levied on sellers and an equal tax levied on buyers are generally:
micro.Choice A: Equivalent in their market effects
micro.Choice B: Completely unrelated
micro.Choice C: Opposite in their effect on quantity
micro.Choice D: Always paid only by sellers
micro.Correct Answer: A — Equivalent in their market effects
micro.Feedback: A tax on buyers or sellers creates the same wedge and similar market effects.

micro.Learning Objective: LO6.4
micro.Question: A seller tax and a buyer tax of the same size create the same wedge in the same market. What does this imply about the market outcome?
micro.Choice A: The market outcome is equivalent even if the legal payer differs
micro.Choice B: The seller tax always hurts sellers more
micro.Choice C: The buyer tax always hurts buyers more
micro.Choice D: Only the tax on sellers reduces quantity
micro.Correct Answer: A — The market outcome is equivalent even if the legal payer differs
micro.Feedback: Equivalent taxes on buyers or sellers create the same wedge and market outcome.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.5
micro.Common Misconception: Assuming higher combined output makes every possible exchange mutually beneficial.
micro.Question: Voluntary trade can benefit both sides when:
micro.Choice A: Each expects to gain from the exchange
micro.Choice B: One side is forced to trade
micro.Choice C: Prices are zero
micro.Choice D: All goods are identical
micro.Correct Answer: A — Each expects to gain from the exchange
micro.Feedback: People voluntarily trade because each expects the exchange to make them better off.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.5
micro.Common Misconception: Treating trade as zero-sum or assigning every task to the fastest producer.
micro.Question: Two neighbors specialize in the chores for which each gives up less valuable alternative work, then exchange help. Why can both benefit?
micro.Choice A: Specialization can raise combined output available to share
micro.Choice B: Exchange makes both neighbors completely self-sufficient.
micro.Choice C: Scarcity disappears once the chores are divided
micro.Choice D: The faster neighbor must perform every chore
micro.Correct Answer: A — Specialization can raise combined output available to share
micro.Feedback: Different opportunity costs can make specialization and voluntary exchange beneficial.

micro.Learning Objective: LO1.1
micro.Question: What is a tradeoff?
micro.Choice A: Giving up one thing to get something else
micro.Choice B: A tax placed on buyers
micro.Choice C: A legal maximum price
micro.Choice D: A measure of total national output
micro.Correct Answer: A — Giving up one thing to get something else
micro.Feedback: A tradeoff exists when choosing one option means giving up another option.

macro.Question: The vertical axis on a standard AD-AS graph measures:
macro.Choice A: The price level
macro.Choice B: Real GDP
macro.Choice C: The unemployment rate
macro.Choice D: The nominal interest rate
macro.Correct Answer: A — The price level
macro.Feedback: AD-AS graphs place the price level on the vertical axis and real output on the horizontal axis.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing output with the price level.
macro.Question: In the standard AD–AS convention, the vertical axis measures:
macro.Choice A: Real GDP
macro.Choice B: The price level
macro.Choice C: Unemployment
macro.Choice D: Money supply
macro.Correct Answer: B — The price level
macro.Feedback: The vertical axis in the AD-AS model measures the price level.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing the AD-AS axes.
macro.Question: In the standard AD–AS convention, the horizontal axis measures:
macro.Choice A: The price level
macro.Choice B: Inflation expectations
macro.Choice C: Real GDP
macro.Choice D: Nominal interest rates
macro.Correct Answer: C — Real GDP
macro.Feedback: The horizontal axis in the AD-AS model measures real GDP or output.

macro.Question: In an AD-AS graph, short-run equilibrium occurs where:
macro.Choice A: Aggregate demand intersects short-run aggregate supply
macro.Choice B: AD intersects LRAS only
macro.Choice C: The price level is zero
macro.Choice D: Unemployment is zero
macro.Correct Answer: A — Aggregate demand intersects short-run aggregate supply
macro.Feedback: The intersection of AD and SRAS determines the short-run equilibrium price level and real output.

macro.Question: If AD falls while SRAS also falls, what outcome is certain?
macro.Choice A: Output falls
macro.Choice B: The price level falls
macro.Choice C: Inflation rises
macro.Choice D: Unemployment falls
macro.Correct Answer: A — Output falls
macro.Feedback: Both a leftward AD shift and a leftward SRAS shift reduce equilibrium output; their price-level effects conflict.

macro.Common Misconception: Reading the wrong intersection.
macro.Question: Refer to the graph. At AD1 and AS2, the economy is at:
macro.Choice A: Y2 and P2
macro.Choice B: Y1 and P1
macro.Choice C: Y3 and P2
macro.Choice D: Y1 and P3
macro.Correct Answer: B — Y1 and P1
macro.Feedback: AD1 and AS2 intersect at Y1 and P1.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring the curve labels.
macro.Question: Refer to the graph. At AD2 and AS2, the economy is at:
macro.Choice A: Y1 and P3
macro.Choice B: Y3 and P2
macro.Choice C: Y2 and P2
macro.Choice D: Y1 and P1
macro.Correct Answer: C — Y2 and P2
macro.Feedback: AD2 and AS2 intersect at Y2 and P2.

macro.Common Misconception: Reading only one axis after an AD shift.
macro.Question: Refer to the graph. If the economy moves from AD1-AS2 to AD2-AS2, what happens?
macro.Choice A: Output rises and the price level rises
macro.Choice B: Output falls and the price level falls
macro.Choice C: Output rises and the price level falls
macro.Choice D: Output falls and the price level rises
macro.Correct Answer: A — Output rises and the price level rises
macro.Feedback: The economy moves from Y1-P1 to Y2-P2, so both output and the price level rise.

macro.Common Misconception: Tracking only one curve shift.
macro.Question: Refer to the graph. If AD rises from AD1 to AD2 while SRAS rises from AS1 to AS2, the final point is:
macro.Choice A: Y1 and P3
macro.Choice B: Y2 and P2
macro.Choice C: Y3 and P2
macro.Choice D: Y1 and P1
macro.Correct Answer: B — Y2 and P2
macro.Feedback: AD2 and AS2 intersect at Y2 and P2.

macro.Common Misconception: Tracking only one curve shift.
macro.Question: Refer to the graph. The economy begins at AD1-AS1. Higher planned spending moves demand to AD2 while lower production costs move short-run supply to AS2. Compared with the starting equilibrium, what happens to output and the price level?
macro.Choice A: Output rises from Y3 to Y2 while the price level stays at P2.
macro.Choice B: Output stays at Y1 while the price level rises from P1 to P3.
macro.Choice C: Output falls from Y2 to Y3 while the price level stays at P2.
macro.Choice D: Output rises from Y3 to Y1 while the price level falls from P2 to P1.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Output rises from Y3 to Y2 while the price level stays at P2.
macro.Feedback: The starting AD1-AS1 intersection is Y3/P2 and the ending AD2-AS2 intersection is Y2/P2. The two rightward shifts reinforce output and offset in the price level in this particular drawing.

macro.Common Misconception: Forgetting both curves must change.
macro.Question: Refer to the graph. Starting at AD1-AS1, which change gets the economy to Y2 and P2?
macro.Choice A: AD rises and SRAS rises
macro.Choice B: AD falls and SRAS rises
macro.Choice C: AD rises and SRAS falls
macro.Choice D: AD falls and SRAS falls
macro.Correct Answer: A — AD rises and SRAS rises
macro.Feedback: Starting from AD1-AS1 at Y3-P2, moving to AD2-AS2 requires AD to rise and SRAS to rise.

macro.Common Misconception: Following only AD or only SRAS.
macro.Question: Starting at AD1-AS2, AD rises to AD2 and SRAS falls to AS1. Why would using the plotted final output as the effect of the demand expansion alone be misleading?
macro.Choice A: Final output is Y1; the supply contraction offsets the demand-driven increase that would otherwise reach Y2.
macro.Choice B: Final output is Y2; the supply contraction offsets part of a demand increase that would otherwise reach Y3.
macro.Choice C: Final output is Y1; that proves the demand expansion has no effect on output even with supply fixed.
macro.Choice D: Final output is Y1 because the two curves shift in ways that always leave output unchanged regardless of size.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Final output is Y1; the supply contraction offsets the demand-driven increase that would otherwise reach Y2.
macro.Feedback: AD2-AS1 is Y1/P3, but demand expansion alone would reach AD2-AS2 at Y2/P2. The unchanged final output combines opposing effects; it does not show an ineffective demand channel.

macro.Common Misconception: Tracking the starting point but not both curve shifts.
macro.Question: Starting at AD2-AS1, AD falls to AD1 while SRAS rises to AS2. Output ends where it began. What does the figure imply about a claim that the supply improvement had no output benefit?
macro.Choice A: The claim is wrong: without the supply improvement, AD1-AS1 would leave output at Y3 rather than Y1.
macro.Choice B: The claim is wrong: without the supply improvement, AD1-AS1 would leave output at Y2 rather than Y1.
macro.Choice C: The claim is right: unchanged final output means each individual shock had zero effect on output.
macro.Choice D: The claim is right: supply improvements affect the price level but cannot affect output in the short run.
macro.Correct Answer: A — The claim is wrong: without the supply improvement, AD1-AS1 would leave output at Y3 rather than Y1.
macro.Feedback: The combined endpoint AD1-AS2 is Y1/P1. Demand contraction without the supply improvement would giveY 3/P2. The supply change has a positive output contribution even though the two effects cancel in the observed total.

macro.Common Misconception: Following only one curve shift.
macro.Question: Starting at AD1-AS2, demand moves to AD2 and supply to AS1. An analyst generalizes the plotted output outcome to every demand expansion combined with a supply contraction. What is wrong with that claim?
macro.Choice A: Output is unchanged at Y1 here, but that requires the two output effects to offset; a different-sized pair need not do so.
macro.Choice B: Output rises to Y2 here, but that requires the demand effect to dominate; a different-sized pair need not do so.
macro.Choice C: Output is unchanged at Y1 here, proving that opposite-direction AD and SRAS shifts always cancel in output.
macro.Choice D: Output is unchanged at Y1 here because neither shift can affect real output, only prices.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Output is unchanged at Y1 here, but that requires the two output effects to offset; a different-sized pair need not do so.
macro.Feedback: The initial and final intersections both have output Y1, while prices rise P1 toP 3. AD expansion raises output and SRAS contraction lowers it; their equality is a feature of these plotted magnitudes, not a universal theorem.

macro.Common Misconception: Missing offsetting output effects from two shifts.
macro.Question: The economy moves from AD2-AS1 to AD1-AS2. Compared with reducing AD alone while holding AS1 fixed, what does the simultaneous supply improvement accomplish?
macro.Choice A: It prevents the fall from Y1 to Y3 and leaves output at Y1, while prices fall farther to P1.
macro.Choice B: It prevents the fall from Y2 to Y1 and leaves output at Y2, while prices fall farther to P2.
macro.Choice C: It leaves output at Y1 because demand contraction has no real effect even without the supply improvement.
macro.Choice D: It leaves output at Y1 by shifting aggregate demand back to AD2, reversing the original demand restraint.
macro.Correct Answer: A — It prevents the fall from Y1 to Y3 and leaves output at Y1, while prices fall farther to P1.
macro.Feedback: AD restraint alone reaches AD1-AS1 at Y3/P2. Adding the AS2 improvement instead gives AD1-AS2 at Y1/P1. The supply gain offsets the demand-related output loss while reinforcing the price decline.

macro.Question: In the AD-AS-LRAS graph, which labeled point represents the original long-run equilibrium before aggregate demand increases?
macro.Choice A: Point C
macro.Choice B: Point A
macro.Choice C: Point B
macro.Choice D: Point D
macro.Correct Answer: A — Point C
macro.Feedback: The original long-run equilibrium is where AD0, SRAS0, and LRAS0 meet. That is point C.

macro.Question: Which labeled point is the original long-run equilibrium in the graph with LRAS0 and LRAS1?
macro.Choice A: Point B
macro.Choice B: LRAS1
macro.Choice C: Point A
macro.Choice D: SRAS1
macro.Correct Answer: C — Point A
macro.Feedback: Point A is where AD0, SRAS0, and LRAS0 intersect.

macro.Question: In the AD-AS graph, which point shows the original equilibrium before aggregate demand rises?
macro.Choice A: Point A
macro.Choice B: Point B
macro.Choice C: AD1
macro.Choice D: AS0
macro.Correct Answer: A — Point A
macro.Feedback: Point A is the intersection of AD0 and AS0.

macro.Question: Which point marks the original equilibrium where AD0 and AS0 intersect?
macro.Choice A: Point B
macro.Choice B: Point C
macro.Choice C: Point A
macro.Choice D: Point D
macro.Correct Answer: C — Point A
macro.Feedback: Point A is the initial intersection of AD0 and AS0.

macro.Question: Which statement best describes the macro outcome shown by the move from A to B?
macro.Choice A: Recession with accelerating inflation pressure.
macro.Choice B: Demand-pull inflation with no long-run growth.
macro.Choice C: Long-run growth with lower price pressure.
macro.Choice D: No change in either output or the price level.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Long-run growth with lower price pressure.
macro.Feedback: Higher LRAS and SRAS support more output alongside a lower price level.

macro.Question: Which description best matches the move from A to B?
macro.Choice A: AD rises; the economy moves upward along fixed AS0.
macro.Choice B: AS rises; the economy moves downward along fixed AD0.
macro.Choice C: AD falls; the economy moves downward along fixed AS0.
macro.Choice D: Both AD and AS shift; output returns to its starting level.
macro.Correct Answer: A — AD rises; the economy moves upward along fixed AS0.
macro.Feedback: With AS0 unchanged, the AD increase causes a movement along the AS curve to a new short-run equilibrium.

macro.Question: Compare point A with point C. Which statement is correct?
macro.Choice A: Real GDP rises to 100; the price level stays at 100.
macro.Choice B: Real GDP falls to 50; the price level stays at 125.
