macro.Choice C: Both events shift AD right because both involve nominal expenditure
macro.Choice D: Both events move along AD because no supply condition changed
macro.Correct Answer: A — Spending plans shift AD right; the price-level rise moves upward along an AD curve
macro.Feedback: A non-price spending change shifts the schedule. The price level is an axis variable, so its change is represented as movement along a given schedule, holding its other determinants fixed.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “AD shifts left by $30; investment dominates regardless of the amounts” in this aggregate demand task.
macro.Question: Planned investment falls $30 while government purchases rise $60. Treat both amounts as total AD shifts after induced effects. Which net shift and reasoning are correct?
macro.Choice A: AD shifts left by $30; investment dominates regardless of the amounts
macro.Choice B: AD is unchanged; one positive and one negative shift must cancel
macro.Choice C: Only a movement along AD occurs; policy cannot shift the schedule
macro.Choice D: AD shifts right by $30; the positive spending effect is larger
macro.Correct Answer: D — AD shifts right by $30; the positive spending effect is larger
macro.Feedback: The total shift is −30+60=+30. Stated total effects can be compared directly; they are not autonomous amounts requiring another multiplier.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Exports and investment both tend to fall; AD shifts left” in this aggregate demand task.
macro.Question: A country initially sells $40 of exports. Foreign income rises while domestic business confidence falls. No magnitudes are given. What can be concluded about aggregate demand when both changes occur?
macro.Choice A: Exports and investment both tend to fall; AD shifts left
macro.Choice B: Exports tend to rise and investment to fall; opposite signs establish exactly unchanged AD
macro.Choice C: Exports tend to rise and investment to fall; the net AD direction is uncertain
macro.Choice D: Exports and investment both tend to rise; AD shifts right
macro.Correct Answer: C — Exports tend to rise and investment to fall; the net AD direction is uncertain
macro.Feedback: Foreign demand supports exports while weaker confidence reduces investment. Competing components require relative magnitudes before assigning a net AD shift.

macro.Common Misconception: Treats the price-level interest-rate effect as decisive despite an opposing money-supply change.
macro.Question: In the liquidity-preference model, a lower price level reduces transaction money demand. At the same time the central bank independently reduces nominal money supply. The relative sizes of the changes are not given, and other investment determinants are fixed. Which interest-rate and investment conclusion is warranted?
macro.Choice A: Lower money demand lowers the rate; lower supply also lowers it; investment must rise
macro.Choice B: Lower money demand raises the rate; lower supply also raises it; investment must fall
macro.Choice C: Lower money demand raises the rate; lower supply lowers it; the changes must cancel
macro.Choice D: Lower money demand lowers the rate; lower supply raises it; investment’s net change is undetermined
macro.Correct Answer: D — Lower money demand lowers the rate; lower supply raises it; investment’s net change is undetermined
macro.Feedback: Lower money demand tends to reduce the equilibrium rate; a lower money supply tends to increase it. Without relative magnitudes, the net rate and therefore interest-sensitive investment cannot be signed. The usual price-level channel is not a guarantee about the outcome when policy also changes.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Both events shift AD right because both involve nominal expenditure” in this aggregate demand task.
macro.Question: Consumer spending plans rise $60 at every price level while an unexpected rise in the price level changes the quantity demanded along AD. How does each change affect the AD curve?
macro.Choice A: Both events shift AD right because both involve nominal expenditure
macro.Choice B: Both events move along AD because no supply condition changed
macro.Choice C: Spending plans shift AD right; the price-level rise moves upward along an AD curve
macro.Choice D: Spending plans move upward along AD; the price-level rise shifts AD right
macro.Correct Answer: C — Spending plans shift AD right; the price-level rise moves upward along an AD curve
macro.Feedback: A non-price spending change shifts the schedule. The price level is an axis variable, so its change is represented as movement along a given schedule, holding its other determinants fixed.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Only a movement along AD occurs; policy cannot shift the schedule” in this aggregate demand task.
macro.Question: Planned investment falls $70 while government purchases rise $140. Treat both amounts as total AD shifts after induced effects. Which net shift and reasoning are correct?
macro.Choice A: Only a movement along AD occurs; policy cannot shift the schedule
macro.Choice B: AD shifts right by $70; the positive spending effect is larger
macro.Choice C: AD shifts left by $70; investment dominates regardless of the amounts
macro.Choice D: AD is unchanged; one positive and one negative shift must cancel
macro.Correct Answer: B — AD shifts right by $70; the positive spending effect is larger
macro.Feedback: The total shift is −70+140=+70. Stated total effects can be compared directly; they are not autonomous amounts requiring another multiplier.

macro.Common Misconception: Failing to separate price-level movement from a spending shift.
macro.Question: The price level falls while firms cut investment. What occurs?
macro.Choice A: Only movement upward along AD
macro.Choice B: Only a rightward AD shift
macro.Choice C: Movement downward along AD plus a leftward AD shift.
macro.Choice D: A rightward SRAS shift only
macro.Correct Answer: C — Movement downward along AD plus a leftward AD shift.
macro.Feedback: The lower price level changes quantity demanded; lower investment shifts AD left.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming offsetting shifters cancel exactly.
macro.Question: Consumer confidence rises and the currency appreciates. The net AD direction is:
macro.Choice A: No change because the effects are equal
macro.Choice B: Ambiguous because consumption rises while net exports fall.
macro.Choice C: Certainly rightward
macro.Choice D: Certainly leftward
macro.Correct Answer: B — Ambiguous because consumption rises while net exports fall.
macro.Feedback: The two components move in opposite directions, and magnitudes matter.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Exports and investment both tend to rise; AD shifts right” in this aggregate demand task.
macro.Question: A country initially sells $80 of exports. Foreign income rises while domestic business confidence falls. No magnitudes are given. What can be concluded about aggregate demand when both changes occur?
macro.Choice A: Exports tend to rise and investment to fall; the net AD direction is uncertain
macro.Choice B: Exports and investment both tend to rise; AD shifts right
macro.Choice C: Exports and investment both tend to fall; AD shifts left
macro.Choice D: Exports tend to rise and investment to fall; opposite signs establish exactly unchanged AD
macro.Correct Answer: A — Exports tend to rise and investment to fall; the net AD direction is uncertain
macro.Feedback: Foreign demand supports exports while weaker confidence reduces investment. Competing components require relative magnitudes before assigning a net AD shift.

macro.Common Misconception: Combining three distinct forces into one curve change.
macro.Question: The price level rises, taxes fall and foreign income declines. Despite the higher price level, the quantity of domestic output demanded increases. What must be true about the two shifts in spending plans?
macro.Choice A: The export-demand loss exceeds the tax-cut stimulus, because a higher price level directly shifts AD right.
macro.Choice B: The two spending shifts exactly cancel, leaving the price rise to increase quantity demanded along AD.
macro.Choice C: The tax-cut stimulus exceeds the export-demand loss by enough to overcome the price-level restraint on quantity demanded.
macro.Choice D: The observation proves the price rise strengthened tax-cut spending rather than causing movement along AD.
macro.Correct Answer: C — The tax-cut stimulus exceeds the export-demand loss by enough to overcome the price-level restraint on quantity demanded.
macro.Feedback: A higher price level reduces quantity demanded along AD. Lower taxes shift AD right, while lower foreign income shifts it left. For quantity demanded to rise despite the price effect, the positive net shift must more than offset that restraint.

macro.Common Misconception: Attributes rising observed investment to the price-level channel when a separate investment shift outweighs its restraint.
macro.Question: With nominal money supply fixed, the price level and borrowing rate both rise. Firms also become more optimistic, shifting desired investment outward at every rate, and observed investment rises. Other influences are unchanged. Which account fits the evidence, and what would investment have done had the price level stayed fixed?
macro.Choice A: The rate channel restrains investment but optimism outweighs it; with the price level fixed, investment would rise even more
macro.Choice B: The rate channel raises investment and optimism restrains it; with the price level fixed, investment would rise even more
macro.Choice C: The rate channel restrains investment and optimism is irrelevant; with the price level fixed, investment would fall
macro.Choice D: The rate channel raises investment and optimism reinforces it; with the price level fixed, investment would remain unchanged
macro.Correct Answer: A — The rate channel restrains investment but optimism outweighs it; with the price level fixed, investment would rise even more
macro.Feedback: At fixed nominal money supply, a higher price level raises money demand and the borrowing rate, restraining investment along its schedule. The separate optimistic shift raises investment enough to offset that restraint. Removing the price-level increase removes the restraint, so investment would rise more. A movement along AD is distinct from an independent spending shift.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Spending plans move upward along AD; the price-level rise shifts AD right” in this aggregate demand task.
macro.Question: Consumer spending plans rise by $100 at every price level. An unexpected price-level increase then leaves the observed quantity of output demanded unchanged. Does the unchanged quantity mean aggregate demand did not shift?
macro.Choice A: Yes. An unchanged observed quantity proves that spending plans did not change at any price level.
macro.Choice B: No. The higher price itself shifted AD left, while higher spending caused movement along the old curve.
macro.Choice C: Yes. Price-level changes and spending-plan changes are both movements along one unchanged AD curve.
macro.Choice D: No. AD shifted right, but movement along the new curve at the higher price offset the increase in observed quantity.
macro.Correct Answer: D — No. AD shifted right, but movement along the new curve at the higher price offset the increase in observed quantity.
macro.Feedback: The $100 fixed-price spending increase is an AD shift. A higher price lowers quantity demanded along the new curve. An unchanged final quantity can conceal both changes; it does not establish an unchanged demand schedule.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing a demand boom with a supply improvement.
macro.Question: The economy begins at natural output. A stock-market boom raises consumption and investment, while expected prices have not yet adjusted. Which conclusion is most accurate?
macro.Choice A: AD shifts right, output rises above potential, and inflation rises in the short run.
macro.Choice B: SRAS shifts right, output rises above potential, and inflation falls in the short run.
macro.Choice C: LRAS shifts right, unemployment falls permanently, and inflation stays fixed.
macro.Choice D: AD shifts left, output falls below potential, and inflation rises in the short run.
macro.Correct Answer: A — AD shifts right, output rises above potential, and inflation rises in the short run.
macro.Feedback: A stock market boom can raise spending and shift AD right, raising output and prices in the short run.

macro.Common Misconception: Reading the graph backward.
macro.Question: Refer to the AD graph with constant price level P. Moving from AD1 to AD2 changes output from:
macro.Choice A: Y1 to Y2
macro.Choice B: Y2 to Y1
macro.Choice C: Y2 to Y3
macro.Choice D: Y3 to Y1
macro.Correct Answer: A — Y1 to Y2
macro.Feedback: At the same price level, output rises from Y1 to Y2 when AD shifts from AD1 to AD2.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing curve position with label order.
macro.Question: Refer to the AD graph with constant price level P. Which curve shows the largest aggregate demand level?
macro.Choice A: AD1
macro.Choice B: AD2
macro.Choice C: AD3
macro.Choice D: P
macro.Correct Answer: C — AD3
macro.Feedback: AD3 is farthest to the right, so it shows the largest AD at price level P.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing productive capacity with aggregate demand.
macro.Question: A rise in economy-wide productivity shifts long-run aggregate supply:
macro.Choice A: Not at all because productivity affects only demand.
macro.Choice B: Left.
macro.Choice C: Right.
macro.Choice D: Up along the same curve.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Right.
macro.Feedback: Higher productivity raises the economy’s sustainable level of output.

macro.Common Misconception: Reversing the effect of higher production costs.
macro.Question: An increase in nominal wages, holding productivity and expected prices constant, shifts short-run aggregate supply:
macro.Choice A: Nowhere.
macro.Choice B: Down along the same SRAS curve.
macro.Choice C: Right.
macro.Choice D: Left.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Left.
macro.Feedback: Higher nominal wages raise firms’ costs and reduce output supplied at each price level.

macro.Question: What change from AS0 to AS1 is shown?
macro.Choice A: A decrease in aggregate supply
macro.Choice B: An increase in aggregate supply
macro.Choice C: An increase in aggregate demand
macro.Choice D: A decrease in aggregate demand
macro.Correct Answer: A — A decrease in aggregate supply
macro.Feedback: When the aggregate supply curve shifts left/up, less output is supplied at each price level, which is a decrease in aggregate supply.

macro.Question: How should AS1 be classified relative to AS0 in the second aggregate-supply diagram?
macro.Choice A: A decrease in aggregate supply
macro.Choice B: An increase in aggregate demand
macro.Choice C: An increase in aggregate supply
macro.Choice D: A decrease in aggregate demand
macro.Correct Answer: C — An increase in aggregate supply
macro.Feedback: A downward/rightward shift of the AS curve means aggregate supply has increased.

macro.Common Misconception: Reversing the real-wage effect.
macro.Question: The price level rises unexpectedly while nominal wages are fixed. In the short run, firms tend to:
macro.Choice A: Increase production because output prices rise relative to wage costs.
macro.Choice B: Leave output unchanged because SRAS is vertical
macro.Choice C: Shift LRAS right immediately
macro.Choice D: Reduce production because real wages rise
macro.Correct Answer: A — Increase production because output prices rise relative to wage costs.
macro.Feedback: Unexpectedly higher output prices lower the real cost of contracted wages.

macro.Common Misconception: Reversing how lower expected prices affect wage and cost setting.
macro.Question: Firms revise expected prices downward after a period of unexpectedly low inflation. Holding actual prices fixed, SRAS tends to:
macro.Choice A: Become vertical.
macro.Choice B: Shift left.
macro.Choice C: Shift right.
macro.Choice D: Move upward along the same curve.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Shift right.
macro.Feedback: Lower expected prices tend to reduce nominal wage and input-cost growth.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing expected-price effects with long-run capacity.
macro.Question: An economy’s expected price level falls while actual price level and productive resources are unchanged. At each actual price level, firms are likely to supply:
macro.Choice A: More potential output, so LRAS shifts right.
macro.Choice B: Less output, so SRAS shifts left.
macro.Choice C: The same output because expectations never matter.
macro.Choice D: More output, so SRAS shifts right.
macro.Correct Answer: D — More output, so SRAS shifts right.
macro.Feedback: Lower expected prices tend to lower nominal input costs and raise short-run supply.

macro.Common Misconception: Reversing the expected-price effect.
macro.Question: If workers and firms expect a higher price level before contracts are set, short-run aggregate supply tends to:
macro.Choice A: Become vertical immediately.
macro.Choice B: Remain fixed because expectations affect only AD.
macro.Choice C: Shift left.
macro.Choice D: Shift right.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Shift left.
macro.Feedback: Higher expected prices tend to produce higher nominal wages and other input costs.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating a production-cost change as an AD shifter.
macro.Question: A temporary payroll-tax reduction lowers firms’ labor costs. Holding other factors constant, SRAS shifts:
macro.Choice A: AD right only.
macro.Choice B: LRAS left only.
macro.Choice C: Left.
macro.Choice D: Right.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Right.
macro.Feedback: Lower per-worker cost raises short-run output supplied at each price level.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing short-run wage rigidity with long-run capacity.
macro.Question: Why can an unexpected rise in the price level increase output in the short run under sticky-wage theory?
macro.Choice A: Household wealth rises and shifts AD
macro.Choice B: Potential output permanently increases
macro.Choice C: Nominal wages immediately rise more than prices
macro.Choice D: Product prices rise before nominal wages fully adjust, lowering real labor cost.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Product prices rise before nominal wages fully adjust, lowering real labor cost.
macro.Feedback: With sticky wages, unexpected price increases can make production temporarily more profitable.

macro.Common Misconception: Focusing on reconstruction spending while ignoring lost capacity.
macro.Question: A hurricane destroys factories and transport infrastructure. Which long-run effect is most likely?
macro.Choice A: LRAS shifts left because productive capacity falls.
macro.Choice B: SRAS shifts right because inputs are scarcer.
macro.Choice C: LRAS shifts right because rebuilding spending rises.
macro.Choice D: Only AD shifts right.
macro.Correct Answer: A — LRAS shifts left because productive capacity falls.
macro.Feedback: Destroyed capital reduces the economy’s potential output.

macro.Question: Refer to the first AS graph. At real GDP of 150, which value is closest to the vertical price-level gap between AS0 and AS1?
macro.Feedback: The hand-drawn curves lie near price levels 150 and 190 at GDP 150. Their gap is roughly 40–45 price-level units, so 40 is the closest offered estimate; the graph does not support exact coordinate arithmetic.

macro.Question: Refer to the second AS graph. At real GDP of 150, which value is closest to the vertical price-level gap between AS0 and AS1?
macro.Feedback: The curves lie near price levels 150 and 110 at GDP 150. Their separation is approximately 40 price-level units, the closest offered estimate.

macro.Question: Assume aggregate demand is unchanged. Based on the AS shift shown, what happens to equilibrium real GDP and the price level?
macro.Choice A: Real GDP increases while the price level decreases
macro.Choice B: Real GDP decreases while the price level increases
macro.Choice C: Both real GDP and the price level increase
macro.Choice D: Both real GDP and the price level decrease
macro.Correct Answer: B — Real GDP decreases while the price level increases
macro.Feedback: An inward/leftward AS shift reduces output and raises the price level.

macro.Question: Which event best matches the shift from AS0 to AS1?
macro.Choice A: Lower wage costs make production more profitable at each price level.
macro.Choice B: Stronger consumer confidence raises planned spending.
macro.Choice C: An increase in input prices raises production costs.
macro.Choice D: A lower price level reduces output along the original supply curve.
macro.Correct Answer: C — An increase in input prices raises production costs.
macro.Feedback: AS1 lies above and left of AS0, indicating less output supplied at each price level. Higher input costs can produce that contraction; lower costs would move supply the other way.

macro.Question: If aggregate demand stays put, what equilibrium effect follows from the supply change in the second AS diagram?
macro.Choice A: Real GDP decreases while the price level increases
macro.Choice B: Both real GDP and the price level increase
macro.Choice C: Both real GDP and the price level decrease
macro.Choice D: Real GDP increases while the price level decreases
macro.Correct Answer: D — Real GDP increases while the price level decreases
macro.Feedback: A rightward shift of AS increases output and lowers the price level.

macro.Question: Which change could explain the shift from AS0 to AS1 in the diagram?
macro.Choice A: Lower input costs increase short-run aggregate supply.
macro.Choice B: Higher expected prices reduce short-run aggregate supply.
macro.Choice C: Higher government purchases increase aggregate demand.
macro.Choice D: A higher current price level raises output along AS0.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Lower input costs increase short-run aggregate supply.
macro.Feedback: AS1 lies below and right of AS0, so more output is supplied at each price. Lower input costs can explain this shift. Higher expected prices would shift SRAS in the opposite direction.

macro.Common Misconception: Allowing one supply shifter to dominate without magnitude information.
macro.Question: Oil prices rise sharply, but firms also adopt a productivity-enhancing technology. What can be concluded about SRAS?
macro.Choice A: Oil costs push SRAS left and productivity pushes it right; magnitudes determine the net shift
macro.Choice B: Oil costs push SRAS right and productivity pushes it right; both raise short-run supply
macro.Choice C: Oil costs push SRAS left and productivity pushes it left; both lower short-run supply
macro.Choice D: Oil costs push SRAS left and productivity pushes it right; opposing signs establish an unchanged curve
macro.Correct Answer: A — Oil costs push SRAS left and productivity pushes it right; magnitudes determine the net shift
macro.Feedback: Higher oil costs push SRAS left, while higher productivity pushes it right.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring the mechanism through which expectations affect costs.
macro.Question: Expected prices rise by 4 percent, but nominal wages are locked in long-term contracts. Compared with a setting where wages adjust immediately, the leftward SRAS shift is likely:
macro.Choice A: Larger.
macro.Choice B: Smaller in the short run.
macro.Choice C: A rightward shift of LRAS.
macro.Choice D: Identical by definition.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Smaller in the short run.
macro.Feedback: If wages cannot yet adjust, expected-price changes have a weaker immediate cost effect.

macro.Common Misconception: Combining long-run capacity and short-run cost changes incorrectly.
macro.Question: A permanent labor-force increase raises productive capacity and tends to expand short-run supply. A simultaneous temporary energy-price spike tends to reduce short-run supply. No relative magnitudes are given. What can be concluded about LRAS and the net SRAS shift?
macro.Choice A: LRAS shifts right; the net SRAS direction is not determined.
macro.Choice B: LRAS shifts right; SRAS necessarily shifts left.
macro.Choice C: LRAS shifts left; SRAS necessarily shifts right.
macro.Choice D: LRAS stays fixed; SRAS necessarily shifts right.
macro.Correct Answer: A — LRAS shifts right; the net SRAS direction is not determined.
macro.Feedback: The labor-force increase raises potential output, shifting LRAS right. The two events exert opposing pressures on SRAS, so their relative effects are needed to determine its net direction. A temporary energy-price spike does not by itself remove productive capacity.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating all policy effects as demand-side or same-direction.
macro.Question: A government permanently improves transportation infrastructure but finances it with a temporary business-energy surcharge. Which supply effects are possible?
macro.Choice A: Only AD can change.
macro.Choice B: LRAS may shift right while SRAS shifts left temporarily.
macro.Choice C: Both LRAS and SRAS must shift left permanently.
macro.Choice D: LRAS must remain fixed because taxes are involved.
macro.Correct Answer: B — LRAS may shift right while SRAS shifts left temporarily.
macro.Feedback: Infrastructure can raise capacity while the temporary surcharge raises current production costs.

macro.Common Misconception: Failing to distinguish capacity growth from current cost reduction.
macro.Question: A permanent tax credit raises capital investment, while a temporary wage subsidy lowers current labor costs. Which supply changes are most likely?
macro.Choice A: LRAS shifts right over time and SRAS shifts right immediately.
macro.Choice B: SRAS shifts left because subsidies raise wages
macro.Choice C: LRAS shifts left and SRAS right
macro.Choice D: Only AD shifts right
macro.Correct Answer: A — LRAS shifts right over time and SRAS shifts right immediately.
macro.Feedback: More capital raises potential output, while the subsidy lowers short-run production cost.

macro.Question: With aggregate demand unchanged, which macro outcome is consistent with the AS shift shown?
macro.Choice A: Lower output with a higher price level
macro.Choice B: Higher output with a lower price level
macro.Choice C: Higher output with a higher price level
macro.Choice D: Lower output with a lower price level
macro.Correct Answer: A — Lower output with a higher price level
macro.Feedback: A leftward shift of AS reduces output and raises prices, the classic stagflation pattern.

macro.Question: For the second AS diagram, what output-price pattern would follow if aggregate demand stayed fixed?
macro.Choice A: Lower output with a higher price level
macro.Choice B: Higher output with a higher price level
macro.Choice C: Higher output with a lower price level
macro.Choice D: Lower output with a lower price level
macro.Correct Answer: C — Higher output with a lower price level
macro.Feedback: Demand-pull expansions raise both price level and output. This graph instead shows more output paired with a lower price level, which is an AS increase.

macro.Common Misconception: Failing to separate permanent capacity from temporary production costs.
macro.Question: A country receives a permanent productivity improvement and a temporary spike in imported input prices. Which graph change best fits?
macro.Choice A: Both curves shift left permanently
macro.Choice B: LRAS shifts left and SRAS right
macro.Choice C: Only aggregate demand shifts
macro.Choice D: LRAS shifts right, while SRAS may shift left initially.
macro.Correct Answer: D — LRAS shifts right, while SRAS may shift left initially.
macro.Feedback: Productivity raises potential output; costly imported inputs can reduce short-run supply.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring how excessive expected inflation enters wage contracts.
macro.Question: Workers expect 6 percent inflation, but actual inflation is 2 percent and wage contracts reflect the higher expectation. What happens to SRAS relative to contracts based on accurate expectations?
macro.Choice A: Contract nominal wages are lower and real labor costs at actual prices are lower; SRAS lies farther right
macro.Choice B: Contract nominal wages are lower and real labor costs at actual prices are higher; SRAS lies farther left
macro.Choice C: Contract nominal wages are higher and real labor costs at actual prices are higher; SRAS lies farther left
macro.Choice D: Contract nominal wages are higher and real labor costs at actual prices are lower; SRAS lies farther right
macro.Correct Answer: C — Contract nominal wages are higher and real labor costs at actual prices are higher; SRAS lies farther left
macro.Feedback: Higher expected prices can produce higher nominal wages and lower short-run supply.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming all supply forces have the same horizon and direction.
macro.Question: A severe storm destroys capital, while emergency deregulation lowers current compliance costs. Which conclusion is strongest?
macro.Choice A: Capital destruction reduces LRAS; cost relief shifts only AD, so the SRAS direction is certainly left
macro.Choice B: Capital destruction reduces LRAS; its adverse SRAS effect competes with lower compliance costs, leaving net SRAS uncertain
macro.Choice C: Capital destruction reduces LRAS; lower compliance costs also reduce SRAS, so both short-run forces shift supply left
macro.Choice D: Lower compliance costs raise LRAS; capital destruction affects only SRAS, so long-run capacity rises
macro.Correct Answer: B — Capital destruction reduces LRAS; its adverse SRAS effect competes with lower compliance costs, leaving net SRAS uncertain
macro.Feedback: Capital destruction lowers capacity; lower compliance cost pushes SRAS right, while storm disruption may push it left.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing movement along SRAS with a curve shift.
macro.Question: Two economies experience the same rise in actual output prices. In A, wages and expected prices remain fixed; in B, wage contracts reset upward with expectations. A student predicts identical output responses because actual prices changed equally. What is missing?
macro.Choice A: A moves along its existing SRAS, while B's higher expected costs also shift SRAS left, restraining its output response.
macro.Choice B: Both actual-price increases shift SRAS right by the same amount, so wage-setting differences cannot matter.
macro.Choice C: Only B moves along SRAS; fixed wages in A force an immediate rightward LRAS shift.
macro.Choice D: B's higher expected wage costs shift SRAS right, reinforcing the output effect of the actual-price rise.
macro.Correct Answer: A — A moves along its existing SRAS, while B's higher expected costs also shift SRAS left, restraining its output response.
macro.Feedback: Actual prices are the vertical-axis variable: changing them moves along a given supply schedule. Changed expectations and wage costs alter that schedule. Equal observed price changes therefore need not imply equal output responses under different contract conditions.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring offsetting supply shifters.
macro.Question: Expected inflation rises, productivity improves, and oil prices fall. What can be concluded about SRAS?
macro.Choice A: Left: expected inflation and productivity shift SRAS left, oil shifts it right
macro.Choice B: Right: all three changes shift the SRAS curve right
macro.Choice C: Unchanged: the opposing SRAS shifts necessarily cancel each other
macro.Choice D: Ambiguous: expectations shift SRAS left, productivity and oil shift it right
macro.Correct Answer: D — Ambiguous: expectations shift SRAS left, productivity and oil shift it right
macro.Feedback: Multiple cost and productivity forces push SRAS in opposite directions.

macro.Common Misconception: Comparing raw percentages that apply to different economic quantities.
macro.Question: For this capacity calculation only, potential output equals usable capital multiplied by output per unit of usable capital; other inputs are sufficient and unchanged. Usable capital falls by 5 percent while output per unit rises by 8 percent. A planner claims that any productivity gain above 5 percent would restore the original LRAS position. Which assessment is correct?
macro.Choice A: Potential output rises by 2.6 percent, but exactly restoring it would require a productivity gain of about 5.26 percent.
macro.Choice B: Potential output rises by 3 percent, and a 5 percent productivity gain would exactly restore it.
macro.Choice C: Potential output falls by 2.6 percent, and an 8 percent productivity gain cannot offset the capital loss.
macro.Choice D: Potential output is unchanged because the two percentage changes cancel exactly.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Potential output rises by 2.6 percent, but exactly restoring it would require a productivity gain of about 5.26 percent.
macro.Feedback: Capacity becomes 0.95 × 1.08 = 1.026 times its original value, a 2.6 percent increase and a rightward LRAS shift. The break-even productivity factor is 1/0.95, or a gain of approximately 5.26 percent. Percentages with different bases cannot simply be subtracted.

macro.Common Misconception: Failing to distinguish immediate movement from later expectation adjustment.
macro.Question: Nominal wages are fixed for one year. The price level rises unexpectedly, then wage contracts reset to reflect the higher expected price level. What sequence is most likely?
macro.Choice A: Initially shift SRAS left; later wage resetting moves up the same curve
macro.Choice B: Initially move up along SRAS; later wage resetting shifts SRAS left
macro.Choice C: Initially move up along SRAS; later wage resetting shifts SRAS right
macro.Choice D: Initially shift SRAS right; later wage resetting moves down the same curve
macro.Correct Answer: B — Initially move up along SRAS; later wage resetting shifts SRAS left
macro.Feedback: Unexpected prices initially raise output along SRAS; higher wage expectations later shift SRAS left.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating permanent productivity and current cost changes as identical.
macro.Question: A permanent improvement in education raises worker productivity, but a new regulation raises current compliance costs. Which statement is most complete?
macro.Choice A: LRAS shifts right; opposing SRAS effects make its net shift uncertain
macro.Choice B: LRAS shifts left; both changes move SRAS to the left
macro.Choice C: LRAS is unchanged; both changes move SRAS to the right
macro.Choice D: LRAS shifts right; compliance costs necessarily outweigh productivity gains
macro.Correct Answer: A — LRAS shifts right; opposing SRAS effects make its net shift uncertain
macro.Feedback: Education raises capacity; compliance costs can reduce short-run supply.

macro.Question: A temporary energy bottleneck and a permanent loss of equipment both reduce short-run aggregate supply. Once energy costs normalize, what additional evidence is needed to predict whether wage adjustment can restore the old output level?
macro.Choice A: Whether the price level initially rose; any price rise proves that LRAS stayed fixed.
macro.Choice B: Whether productive capacity has been restored; lower wage costs alone do not replace the lost equipment.
macro.Choice C: Whether actual GDP fell; any actual output loss permanently lowers potential output by the same amount.
macro.Choice D: Whether demand policy can raise spending; a rightward AD shift by itself restores lost productive capacity.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Whether productive capacity has been restored; lower wage costs alone do not replace the lost equipment.
macro.Feedback: Lower energy costs can reverse a temporary supply restraint. Destroyed equipment may leave productive capacity lower, so restoring the old output level requires evidence that capacity was restored; wage adjustment alone does not replace equipment.

macro.Question: Lower expected prices and a lasting productivity gain both increase short-run aggregate supply. If expected prices return to their original level while the productivity gain remains, what can be predicted?
macro.Choice A: SRAS must return to its original position because expected prices returned, regardless of productivity.
macro.Choice B: SRAS cannot move again because a lasting productivity gain prevents expectation effects.
macro.Choice C: Potential output must fall because higher expected prices erase the physical productivity gain.
macro.Choice D: Some supply increase can remain, and potential output can be higher; the exact final SRAS position depends on the two contributions.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Some supply increase can remain, and potential output can be higher; the exact final SRAS position depends on the two contributions.
macro.Feedback: Returning expected prices reverses only that contribution to SRAS. The productivity gain can still support higher supply and potential output. The final SRAS position depends on the sizes of the original contributions.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The actual price rise shifts SRAS left immediately because higher revenues reduce profitable output” in this short run aggregate supply task.
macro.Question: Nominal wage contracts for 20 workers are fixed. Actual output prices rise unexpectedly while other input prices are unchanged. Which initial response and later qualification are consistent with the sticky-wage account?
macro.Choice A: The actual price rise shifts SRAS left immediately because higher revenues reduce profitable output
macro.Choice B: Lower real labor cost supports movement up SRAS; later wage resetting can shift SRAS left
macro.Choice C: Higher real labor cost supports movement down SRAS; later wage resetting shifts SRAS right
macro.Choice D: The actual price rise immediately shifts LRAS right; nominal contracts determine long-run capacity
macro.Correct Answer: B — Lower real labor cost supports movement up SRAS; later wage resetting can shift SRAS left
macro.Feedback: With wages fixed, higher output prices lower real wage cost and encourage output along SRAS. Later higher nominal wages/expected prices change the schedule rather than repeating the same movement.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Both shift LRAS right because more spending is itself more productive capital” in this long run aggregate supply and potential output task.
macro.Question: An economy has potential output 20. Better production technology raises capacity, while a monetary expansion raises spending. Which long-run comparison separates real capacity from nominal demand?
macro.Choice A: Technology shifts LRAS right; monetary expansion alone need not raise long-run capacity
macro.Choice B: Both shift LRAS right because more spending is itself more productive capital
macro.Choice C: Technology shifts only AD; monetary expansion determines the LRAS position
macro.Choice D: Neither can affect output at any horizon because LRAS is vertical
macro.Correct Answer: A — Technology shifts LRAS right; monetary expansion alone need not raise long-run capacity
macro.Feedback: Technology changes how much real output resources can sustainably produce. A vertical LRAS does not mean its position is immutable; monetary demand alone is a different mechanism.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Both changes shift SRAS right because any higher price encourages production” in this short run aggregate supply task.
macro.Question: A supply reform reduces production costs, while firms expect a higher general price level in future wage bargaining. Which SRAS conclusion is justified without magnitudes?
macro.Choice A: Both push SRAS right; higher expected wages encourage firms to supply more.
macro.Choice B: Both push SRAS left; lower production costs reduce the supply of output.
macro.Choice C: Costs push right, expectations push left; the net shift is exactly zero.
macro.Choice D: Costs push SRAS right, expectations push left; the net shift is uncertain.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Costs push SRAS right, expectations push left; the net shift is uncertain.
macro.Feedback: A lower real input cost improves supply at each output price. Higher expected prices incorporated in wage setting can raise nominal costs and shift SRAS left. Their opposing strengths are unspecified.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “A leftward AD shift is consistent; demand tightening raises output and prices together” in this short run aggregate supply task.
macro.Question: Only one shock occurs in an economy producing 40 units: output falls while the price level rises. AD and LRAS initially remain unchanged. Which short-run diagnosis and policy tradeoff follow?
macro.Choice A: An adverse SRAS shift is consistent; demand tightening can reduce price pressure but worsen the output loss
macro.Choice B: A leftward AD shift is consistent; demand tightening raises output and prices together
macro.Choice C: A favorable SRAS shift is consistent; demand expansion lowers prices and restores output
macro.Choice D: A rightward LRAS shift is consistent; no short-run supply change can produce the observation
macro.Correct Answer: A — An adverse SRAS shift is consistent; demand tightening can reduce price pressure but worsen the output loss
macro.Feedback: A leftward SRAS shift at fixed AD raises prices and reduces output. Tightening AD does not remove the supply problem and can deepen the output loss while reducing prices.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Higher AD shifts LRAS right immediately and must more than reverse the capital loss” in this long run aggregate supply and potential output task.
macro.Question: Potential output is 30 before a disaster destroys capital. A simultaneous rebuilding-demand boom raises spending. Which distinction prevents treating the boom as proof of restored capacity?
macro.Choice A: Higher AD shifts LRAS right immediately and must more than reverse the capital loss
macro.Choice B: Capital loss shifts only AD; the productive frontier cannot change
macro.Choice C: Opposing shocks must exactly cancel both the price and output effects
macro.Choice D: Capital loss shifts LRAS left; higher AD can raise short-run output without proving capacity has recovered
macro.Correct Answer: D — Capital loss shifts LRAS left; higher AD can raise short-run output without proving capacity has recovered
macro.Feedback: Demand and productive capacity are different schedules. Spending can use or strain remaining resources; restoration of capital or productivity requires separate evidence.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Use a rightward LRAS shift for actual prices; expected prices have no supply implication” in this short run aggregate supply task.
macro.Question: Firms face higher actual output prices but unchanged expected prices and input costs. An analyst shifts the entire SRAS curve right. Why should this be shown as a movement along SRAS instead?
macro.Choice A: Use a rightward LRAS shift for actual prices; expected prices have no supply implication
macro.Choice B: Keep output fixed on a vertical SRAS at every horizon because actual prices never affect production
macro.Choice C: Use movement along SRAS for actual prices; a change in expected prices or input costs would shift the curve
macro.Choice D: Use a rightward SRAS shift for actual prices; expected prices only move along it
macro.Correct Answer: C — Use movement along SRAS for actual prices; a change in expected prices or input costs would shift the curve
macro.Feedback: A schedule relates actual prices and supplied output holding its determinants fixed. Changing that axis variable moves along it; changing expected prices/costs changes the schedule.

macro.Common Misconception: Combining capacity and cost changes incorrectly.
macro.Question: A larger permanent labor force adds productive capacity and supports short-run supply, but a temporary oil-price spike pushes short-run supply in the opposite direction. Before their relative sizes are known, which conclusion should an AD-AS analysis carry forward?
macro.Choice A: LRAS shifts right; SRAS necessarily shifts left.
macro.Choice B: LRAS shifts left; SRAS necessarily shifts right.
macro.Choice C: LRAS shifts right; the net SRAS direction is not determined.
macro.Choice D: LRAS stays fixed; SRAS necessarily shifts right.
macro.Correct Answer: C — LRAS shifts right; the net SRAS direction is not determined.
macro.Feedback: The labor-force increase raises potential output, shifting LRAS right. The two events exert opposing pressures on SRAS, so their relative effects are needed to determine its net direction. A temporary energy-price spike does not by itself remove productive capacity.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The actual price rise immediately shifts LRAS right; nominal contracts determine long-run capacity” in this short run aggregate supply task.
macro.Question: Nominal wage contracts for 60 workers are fixed. Actual output prices rise unexpectedly while other input prices are unchanged. Which initial response and later qualification are consistent with the sticky-wage account?
macro.Choice A: The actual price rise immediately shifts LRAS right; nominal contracts determine long-run capacity
macro.Choice B: The actual price rise shifts SRAS left immediately because higher revenues reduce profitable output
macro.Choice C: Lower real labor cost supports movement up SRAS; later wage resetting can shift SRAS left
macro.Choice D: Higher real labor cost supports movement down SRAS; later wage resetting shifts SRAS right
macro.Correct Answer: C — Lower real labor cost supports movement up SRAS; later wage resetting can shift SRAS left
macro.Feedback: With wages fixed, higher output prices lower real wage cost and encourage output along SRAS. Later higher nominal wages/expected prices change the schedule rather than repeating the same movement.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrect inference: The unchanged net curve proves both individual effects were zero.
macro.Question: Lower input costs shift SRAS right, but expected wages rise enough to offset that shift at every price level. An observer sees the original curve and says neither force mattered. Which correction is supported?
macro.Choice A: Both forces shifted LRAS equally, even without any change in real resources.
macro.Choice B: The unchanged net curve can hide two nonzero, opposing supply effects.
macro.Choice C: The unchanged net curve proves both individual effects were zero.
macro.Choice D: Both forces shifted AD instead, since supply curves cannot have offsetting changes.
macro.Correct Answer: B — The unchanged net curve can hide two nonzero, opposing supply effects.
macro.Feedback: The stem explicitly supplies an exact offset. Lower input costs and higher expected wages affect short-run supply in opposite directions; their cancellation does not mean either individual channel was absent.

macro.Common Misconception: Forcing offsetting SRAS shifters into one predetermined direction.
macro.Question: Productivity rises permanently, expected prices rise, and oil prices fall. What is the most accurate result?
macro.Choice A: Higher expected prices lower LRAS; productivity and cheaper oil raise SRAS, so the curves move in opposite directions
macro.Choice B: Productivity leaves LRAS fixed; expected prices and cheaper oil offset in SRAS, so both curves remain unchanged
macro.Choice C: Productivity raises LRAS; higher expected prices oppose productivity and cheaper oil in SRAS, so its net direction is uncertain
macro.Choice D: Productivity raises LRAS; expected prices and cheaper oil reinforce productivity in SRAS, so both curves shift right
macro.Correct Answer: C — Productivity raises LRAS; higher expected prices oppose productivity and cheaper oil in SRAS, so its net direction is uncertain
macro.Feedback: Productivity raises capacity; expected prices and oil prices push SRAS in opposite directions.

macro.Common Misconception: Failing to separate current movement from later expectation adjustment.
macro.Question: Nominal wages are initially fixed when the price level unexpectedly rises; contracts later reset with higher expected inflation. Compare this with contracts that had fully incorporated the higher price level before it occurred. Which difference follows?
macro.Choice A: The surprise initially raises output along SRAS before wage adjustment contracts supply; prior contract adjustment removes that particular temporary cost advantage.
macro.Choice B: Both cases give the same permanent output increase because expected and actual prices have identical supply effects.
macro.Choice C: Prior contract adjustment strengthens the temporary output gain by keeping real wage costs even lower.
macro.Choice D: The surprise immediately shifts LRAS right, so contract timing affects only the final price level.
macro.Correct Answer: A — The surprise initially raises output along SRAS before wage adjustment contracts supply; prior contract adjustment removes that particular temporary cost advantage.
macro.Feedback: With fixed nominal wages, unexpectedly higher output prices initially improve production incentives along SRAS. Later higher expected prices and wages shift supply left. If contracts already reflect the higher level, that initial real-cost surprise is absent.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Capital loss reduces capacity and technology raises it; opposite effects establish unchanged LRAS” in this long run aggregate supply and potential output task.
macro.Question: Capital is destroyed while a new technology raises productivity. Which LRAS conclusion is valid?
macro.Choice A: Capital loss reduces capacity and technology raises it; net LRAS direction requires relative effects
macro.Choice B: Capital loss reduces capacity and technology raises it; opposite effects establish unchanged LRAS
macro.Choice C: Capital loss reduces capacity and technology affects only current costs; LRAS shifts left
macro.Choice D: Technology raises capacity and capital loss affects only current costs; LRAS shifts right
macro.Correct Answer: A — Capital loss reduces capacity and technology raises it; net LRAS direction requires relative effects
macro.Feedback: Lost capital and better technology push potential output in opposite directions.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “NCO rises because risk determines flows independently of returns” in this capital flows and net capital outflow task.
macro.Question: The domestic real interest rate rises, but political risk also rises sharply. What can be concluded about NCO?
macro.Choice A: NCO rises because risk determines flows independently of returns
macro.Choice B: NCO is unchanged because NX = NCO forces the channels to cancel
macro.Choice C: The direction is ambiguous because the two forces push NCO oppositely
macro.Choice D: NCO falls because interest returns determine flows independently of risk
macro.Correct Answer: C — The direction is ambiguous because the two forces push NCO oppositely
macro.Feedback: Higher domestic returns tend to lower NCO, while greater domestic risk tends to raise it; relative magnitudes are needed.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The positive NCO response proves that higher domestic rates increase desired foreign purchases” in this capital flows and net capital outflow task.
macro.Question: Domestic real returns rise while perceived domestic political risk also rises. An analyst observes that NCO increased and concludes that higher interest rates caused capital flight. Holding other determinants fixed, which inference separates the observed change from the interest-rate effect?
macro.Choice A: The positive NCO response proves that higher domestic rates increase desired foreign purchases
macro.Choice B: The identity NX = NCO requires risk and interest-rate effects to have equal size
macro.Choice C: The risk-driven outward shift dominated the rate-induced reduction in NCO; the observation does not reverse the rate mechanism
macro.Choice D: The rate increase must have preceded the risk shock because NCO rose
macro.Correct Answer: C — The risk-driven outward shift dominated the rate-induced reduction in NCO; the observation does not reverse the rate mechanism
macro.Feedback: The return effect lowers NCO, while the domestic risk shock raises it. Positive net change under these two channels shows that risk dominated, not that the partial interest-rate slope reversed. Timing is not identified.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “It falls because the domestic fiscal change receives greater weight” in this open economy policy transmission task.
macro.Question: A government deficit rises while foreign interest rates also rise. What is the direction of domestic NCO?
macro.Choice A: It falls because the domestic fiscal change receives greater weight
macro.Choice B: It rises because foreign rates determine the relevant return by themselves
macro.Choice C: It is unchanged because the NX identity offsets both rate changes
macro.Choice D: Ambiguous because the domestic-rate and foreign-rate channels oppose each other
macro.Correct Answer: D — Ambiguous because the domestic-rate and foreign-rate channels oppose each other
macro.Feedback: The deficit-driven domestic rate rise tends to reduce NCO, while higher foreign returns tend to increase it.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “AD falls because foreign income changes exports while monetary policy changes only investment” in this open economy policy transmission task.
macro.Question: In a short-run comparison before full trade and output adjustment, monetary easing lowers domestic real rates while a foreign recession cuts export demand. Prices are fixed, and NCO is not held fixed across the two shocks. Can the direction of the net change in aggregate demand be determined without knowing the strength of each response?
macro.Choice A: AD falls because foreign income changes exports while monetary policy changes only investment
macro.Choice B: AD is unchanged because depreciation offsets the export-demand shift one for one
macro.Choice C: Ambiguous without the relative strengths of higher NX from depreciation and lower export demand
macro.Choice D: AD rises because the monetary channel determines the exchange rate before exports respond
macro.Correct Answer: C — Ambiguous without the relative strengths of higher NX from depreciation and lower export demand
macro.Feedback: Easing supports domestic investment and, through depreciation, NX. Foreign recession reduces demand for exports. Their short-run AD contributions compete. The fixed-NCO long-run trade-offset result cannot be imposed on this adjustment comparison.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “It is unchanged because monetary policy affects the nominal rate while risk affects the real rate” in this open economy policy transmission task.
macro.Question: Monetary tightening raises the domestic interest rate, while political risk simultaneously rises. What can be concluded about the currency?
macro.Choice A: It is unchanged because monetary policy affects the nominal rate while risk affects the real rate
macro.Choice B: Its direction is ambiguous because lower NCO from returns opposes higher NCO from risk
macro.Choice C: It appreciates because the policy-rate channel is transmitted before portfolios rebalance
macro.Choice D: It depreciates because political risk shifts currency demand rather than supply
macro.Correct Answer: B — Its direction is ambiguous because lower NCO from returns opposes higher NCO from risk
macro.Feedback: Higher returns tend to reduce currency supply and appreciate the currency; higher risk tends to raise supply and depreciate it.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Both rise; e rises exactly 25 percent” in this foreign exchange market task.
macro.Question: Use the dollar market with downward-sloping demand, upward-sloping supply, and e quoted in foreign currency per U.S. dollar. At the original exchange rate, an export-demand shock increases dollars demanded by 70 units and an asset-purchase shock increases dollars supplied by 45 units. What happens to equilibrium e and quantity, and do those two shift amounts identify their exact changes?
macro.Choice A: Both rise; e rises exactly 25 percent
macro.Choice B: e falls and quantity rises; supply determines the rate independently
macro.Choice C: Both rise; curve slopes are needed for exact changes
macro.Choice D: e is unchanged and quantity rises exactly 115 units
macro.Correct Answer: C — Both rise; curve slopes are needed for exact changes
macro.Feedback: At the old rate, excess demand is 70 − 45 = 25 units, so e rises. Both rightward shifts increase equilibrium quantity. Horizontal shift amounts at a common rate sign the change but do not determine exact rate or quantity changes without slopes.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The exchange rate rises and quantity falls” in this foreign exchange market task.
macro.Question: Use the dollar market with downward-sloping demand, upward-sloping supply, and e quoted in foreign currency per U.S. dollar. Demand for domestic currency falls while its supply rises. What is determined?
macro.Choice A: The exchange rate falls, while the quantity direction is ambiguous
macro.Choice B: The exchange rate rises and quantity falls
macro.Choice C: Both the exchange rate and quantity fall
macro.Choice D: Both outcomes are ambiguous
macro.Correct Answer: A — The exchange rate falls, while the quantity direction is ambiguous
macro.Feedback: Both shifts lower the exchange rate. The demand decrease lowers quantity while the supply increase raises it, so quantity depends on relative shift sizes.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The dollar depreciates; rising quantity shows the supply contraction dominated” in this foreign exchange market task.
macro.Question: Use the dollar market with downward-sloping demand, upward-sloping supply, and e quoted in foreign currency per U.S. dollar. Foreign demand for U.S. goods rises while domestic purchases of foreign assets fall. Quantity exchanged nevertheless rises. Which inference uses both the identified rate effect and the observed quantity?
macro.Choice A: The dollar depreciates; rising quantity shows the supply contraction dominated
macro.Choice B: The dollar appreciates; rising quantity proves that dollar supply actually increased
macro.Choice C: The dollar appreciates; at the original quantity, the demand increase exceeds the supply contraction in vertical rate terms
macro.Choice D: The rate remains ambiguous; quantity evidence can never constrain relative shifts
macro.Correct Answer: C — The dollar appreciates; at the original quantity, the demand increase exceeds the supply contraction in vertical rate terms
macro.Feedback: Demand right and supply left both raise e. Evaluated at the original quantity, a larger upward demand-price shift than upward supply-price shift leaves demand above supply there, so their new intersection lies to the right. The given quantity increase supplies this additional restriction.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The rate raises it while foreign risk lowers it” in this capital flows and net capital outflow task.
macro.Question: Domestic rates rise while foreign risk also rises. What is the likely combined effect on domestic NCO?
macro.Choice A: The effects necessarily cancel
macro.Choice B: Both changes tend to reduce it
macro.Choice C: Both changes tend to increase it
macro.Choice D: The rate raises it while foreign risk lowers it
macro.Correct Answer: B — Both changes tend to reduce it
macro.Feedback: Higher domestic returns favor home assets, and riskier foreign assets further discourage purchases abroad.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The exchange rate falls while currency quantity is unchanged” in this foreign exchange market task.
macro.Question: Use the dollar market with downward-sloping demand, upward-sloping supply, and e quoted in foreign currency per U.S. dollar. Demand and supply of domestic currency both increase, with no information about relative shift sizes. What is determined?
macro.Choice A: The exchange rate falls while currency quantity is unchanged
macro.Choice B: Currency quantity rises, but the exchange-rate direction is ambiguous
macro.Choice C: Both currency quantity and the exchange rate rise
macro.Choice D: Currency quantity falls while the exchange rate rises
macro.Correct Answer: B — Currency quantity rises, but the exchange-rate direction is ambiguous
macro.Feedback: Both shifts raise equilibrium quantity. The demand increase raises the rate while the supply increase lowers it, so their relative sizes determine the rate.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Whether both original curves had the same slope sign” in this foreign exchange market task.
macro.Question: Use the dollar market with downward-sloping demand, upward-sloping supply, and e quoted in foreign currency per U.S. dollar. Equilibrium dollar quantity falls, but the final exchange rate is unavailable. If both curves shifted left, what additional evidence determines whether the dollar appreciated?
macro.Choice A: At the original exchange rate, whether the fall in quantity supplied exceeds the fall in quantity demanded
macro.Choice B: Whether both original curves had the same slope sign
macro.Choice C: Whether dollar quantity fell, since that alone determines appreciation
macro.Choice D: Whether demand shifted before supply, regardless of final curves
macro.Correct Answer: A — At the original exchange rate, whether the fall in quantity supplied exceeds the fall in quantity demanded
macro.Feedback: At the old exchange rate, a larger supply contraction creates excess demand, requiring a higher foreign-currency-per-dollar rate. A larger demand contraction creates excess supply. Final quantity alone does not identify the rate.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Quotas increase national saving by the import reduction” in this open economy policy transmission task.
macro.Question: Why does an import quota fail to guarantee higher NX in the textbook model?
macro.Choice A: Quotas increase national saving by the import reduction
macro.Choice B: Foreigners stop demanding domestic currency
macro.Choice C: The quota raises domestic investment by identity
macro.Choice D: Exchange-rate appreciation offsets the direct trade effect when NCO is fixed
macro.Correct Answer: D — Exchange-rate appreciation offsets the direct trade effect when NCO is fixed
macro.Feedback: Trade policy changes currency demand and the real exchange rate, but not the saving-investment balance that sets NCO and NX.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “A fall in national saving that raises NCO” in this open economy policy transmission task.
macro.Question: An import quota directly reduces import demand. In the standard long-run open-economy model with NCO fixed, what offsets this effect?
macro.Choice A: A fall in national saving that raises NCO
macro.Choice B: A currency depreciation that raises exports further
macro.Choice C: A fall in domestic investment equal to the quota
macro.Choice D: A real appreciation that reduces exports and encourages other imports
macro.Correct Answer: D — A real appreciation that reduces exports and encourages other imports
macro.Feedback: The quota raises demand for domestic currency, but appreciation brings NX back to the level fixed by NCO.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “NX rises because lower imports change the trade balance while NCO stays fixed” in this open economy policy transmission task.
macro.Question: A tariff is imposed while national saving and domestic investment remain unchanged. In the textbook open-economy model, what happens to net exports after the economy adjusts?
macro.Choice A: NX rises because lower imports change the trade balance while NCO stays fixed
macro.Choice B: NX falls because appreciation reduces exports by more than the tariff changes imports
macro.Choice C: NX becomes positive because the tariff shifts currency demand right
macro.Choice D: NX is unchanged after currency appreciation offsets the direct import reduction
macro.Correct Answer: D — NX is unchanged after currency appreciation offsets the direct import reduction
macro.Feedback: Unchanged S and I fix NCO = S − I and hence NX. The tariff raises demand for domestic currency, causing real exchange-rate appreciation until exports and other imports adjust enough to preserve that NX balance. This is an exchange-rate change, not a claim that the real interest rate rises.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “A fall in the foreign-currency value of domestic money” in this nominal exchange rates task.
macro.Question: Which change makes imported goods cheaper to domestic buyers when foreign prices are fixed?
macro.Choice A: A rise in foreign prices
macro.Choice B: An appreciation of the domestic currency
macro.Choice C: A depreciation of the domestic currency
macro.Choice D: A fall in the foreign-currency value of domestic money
macro.Correct Answer: B — An appreciation of the domestic currency
macro.Feedback: Appreciation lets each domestic-currency unit buy more foreign currency.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “U.S. exports become cheaper to foreign buyers” in this nominal exchange rates task.
macro.Question: A U.S. traveler benefits directly when the dollar appreciates because:
macro.Choice A: Each dollar buys more foreign currency
macro.Choice B: Each foreign-currency unit buys more dollars
macro.Choice C: U.S. exports become cheaper to foreign buyers
macro.Choice D: Dollar prices of all U.S. goods must fall
macro.Correct Answer: A — Each dollar buys more foreign currency
macro.Feedback: A stronger dollar increases the traveler's foreign purchasing power.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “A U.S. exporter paid only in dollars” in this nominal exchange rates task.
macro.Question: The dollar appreciates against the peso. Holding product prices fixed in their own currencies, which buyer gains purchasing power?
macro.Choice A: A U.S. exporter paid only in dollars
macro.Choice B: Both buyers gain the same foreign purchasing power
macro.Choice C: A U.S. buyer purchasing Mexican goods
macro.Choice D: A Mexican buyer purchasing U.S. goods
macro.Correct Answer: C — A U.S. buyer purchasing Mexican goods
macro.Feedback: A stronger dollar buys more pesos, making peso-priced goods cheaper in dollar terms.

macro.Topic: Apply Exchange Rate To Asset Value
macro.Learning Objective: apply exchange rate to asset value
macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “It becomes equal to its euro coupon” in this nominal exchange rates task.
macro.Question: A foreign bond's value is unchanged in euros, but the euro appreciates against the dollar. What happens to its dollar value?
macro.Choice A: It rises
macro.Choice B: It falls
macro.Choice C: It remains fixed
macro.Choice D: It becomes equal to its euro coupon
macro.Correct Answer: A — It rises
macro.Feedback: Each euro converts into more dollars after the euro appreciates.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “NX = C + I” in this international transactions and identities task.
macro.Question: In the standard open-economy accounts, which identity links trade in goods and services to trade in assets?
macro.Choice A: NX = C + I
macro.Choice B: NCO = G − T
macro.Choice C: S = C + NX
macro.Choice D: NX = NCO
macro.Correct Answer: D — NX = NCO
macro.Feedback: Net exports equal net capital outflow as an accounting identity.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “NCO equals domestic investment” in this international transactions and identities task.
macro.Question: If the trade account is balanced, what must be true of NCO in the same consistent accounts?
macro.Choice A: NCO equals domestic investment
macro.Choice B: NCO equals zero
macro.Choice C: NCO is positive
macro.Choice D: NCO is negative
macro.Correct Answer: B — NCO equals zero
macro.Feedback: Balanced trade means NX = 0, and NX = NCO requires NCO = 0.

macro.Common Misconception: Reverses the sign of exports minus imports or of the identity NX=NCO.
macro.Question: A country records NCO of −$60 billion. What must its net exports equal?
macro.Choice A: −$60 billion
macro.Choice B: $60 billion
macro.Choice D: An amount that cannot be inferred
macro.Correct Answer: A — −$60 billion
macro.Feedback: NX and NCO are equal in the accounts, so negative NCO implies an equal trade deficit.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “P” in this real exchange rates and purchasing power task.
macro.Question: If ε = eP/P*, which variable is the foreign price level?
macro.Choice A: P
macro.Choice B: e
macro.Choice C: ε
macro.Choice D: P*
macro.Correct Answer: D — P*
macro.Feedback: The star identifies the foreign price level in the stated formula.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “e × foreign price level ÷ domestic price level” in this real exchange rates and purchasing power task.
macro.Question: Using e as foreign currency per domestic currency, which formula gives the real exchange rate?
macro.Choice A: e × domestic price level ÷ foreign price level
macro.Choice B: e × foreign price level ÷ domestic price level
macro.Choice C: Domestic price level ÷ e
macro.Choice D: Foreign price level − domestic price level
macro.Correct Answer: A — e × domestic price level ÷ foreign price level
macro.Feedback: With this quotation, ε = eP/P*, the foreign-goods value of a domestic basket.

macro.Common Misconception: Adds equal domestic and foreign inflation rather than using their difference under relative PPP.
macro.Question: Domestic and foreign inflation are both 4 percent. Under relative PPP, the nominal exchange rate should be approximately:
macro.Choice A: 8 percent higher
macro.Choice B: Unchanged
macro.Choice C: 4 percent higher
macro.Choice D: 4 percent lower
macro.Correct Answer: B — Unchanged
macro.Feedback: Equal inflation rates leave the relative price level stable, so PPP predicts little nominal change.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Remain fixed because both countries have inflation” in this real exchange rates and purchasing power task.
macro.Question: Domestic inflation is 3 percent and foreign inflation is 8 percent. Under relative PPP, the domestic currency should:
macro.Choice A: Depreciate about 5 percent nominally
macro.Choice B: Appreciate about 11 percent nominally
macro.Choice C: Remain fixed because both countries have inflation
macro.Choice D: Appreciate about 5 percent nominally
macro.Correct Answer: D — Appreciate about 5 percent nominally
macro.Feedback: The lower-inflation currency tends to appreciate by about the 5-percentage-point inflation differential.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “About a 4 percent appreciation” in this real exchange rates and purchasing power task.
macro.Question: The real exchange rate is unchanged while domestic inflation is 6 percent and foreign inflation is 2 percent. What does relative PPP imply for the nominal rate?
macro.Choice A: About a 4 percent depreciation
macro.Choice B: About a 4 percent appreciation
macro.Choice C: About an 8 percent depreciation
macro.Choice D: No nominal change
macro.Correct Answer: A — About a 4 percent depreciation
macro.Feedback: The nominal rate must fall about 4 percent to offset the 4-point domestic inflation excess.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “S = C + G” in this international transactions and identities task.
macro.Question: Which equation correctly allocates national saving in an open economy?
macro.Choice A: S = C + G
macro.Choice B: I = S + NX
macro.Choice C: NCO = imports − exports
macro.Choice D: S = I + NCO
macro.Correct Answer: D — S = I + NCO
macro.Feedback: National saving finances domestic investment plus net purchases of foreign assets.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “It appreciates about 3 percent” in this real exchange rates and purchasing power task.
macro.Question: Use e in foreign currency per domestic currency and ε = eP/P*. The nominal rate rises 5 percent, domestic prices rise 4 percent, and foreign prices rise 2 percent. Approximately how does the real exchange rate change?
macro.Choice A: It appreciates about 3 percent
macro.Choice B: It depreciates about 7 percent
macro.Choice C: It appreciates about 7 percent
macro.Choice D: It depreciates about 1 percent
macro.Correct Answer: C — It appreciates about 7 percent
macro.Feedback: Using growth-rate approximation, Δε ≈ 5% + 4% − 2% = 7%.

macro.Common Misconception: Adds the domestic inflation differential to nominal depreciation instead of recognizing that it offsets real depreciation.
macro.Question: A currency depreciates 8 percent nominally while domestic inflation exceeds foreign inflation by 3 percentage points. What is the approximate real change?
macro.Choice A: A 5 percent real depreciation
macro.Choice B: An 11 percent real depreciation
macro.Choice C: A 5 percent real appreciation
macro.Choice D: An 8 percent real depreciation
macro.Correct Answer: A — A 5 percent real depreciation
macro.Feedback: The growth approximation gives −8% + 3% = −5%, so the real exchange rate falls about 5 percent.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “It depreciates about 4 percent” in this real exchange rates and purchasing power task.
macro.Question: Use ε = eP/P*, where e is foreign currency per domestic currency, P is the domestic price level and P* the foreign price level. The nominal rate stays fixed, domestic prices rise 6 percent, and foreign prices rise 2 percent. Approximately what happens to the real exchange rate?
macro.Choice A: It appreciates about 4 percent
macro.Choice B: It depreciates about 4 percent
macro.Choice C: It appreciates 8 percent
macro.Choice D: It remains unchanged
macro.Correct Answer: A — It appreciates about 4 percent
macro.Feedback: Faster domestic inflation raises eP/P* by roughly the inflation differential, about 4 percent.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The real rate rises about 13%; add every rate change regardless of quotation” in this real exchange rates and purchasing power task.
macro.Question: Quote e as foreign units per domestic unit and define the real rate ε=eP/P*. The nominal rate falls 4%, domestic inflation is 7%, and foreign inflation 2%. A report calls the nominal depreciation proof of improved price competitiveness. Using the growth-rate approximation, which correction follows?
macro.Choice A: The real rate rises about 13%; add every rate change regardless of quotation
macro.Choice B: The real rate rises about 1%; domestic goods become relatively dearer despite nominal depreciation
macro.Choice C: The real rate falls about 1%; every nominal depreciation guarantees improved competitiveness
macro.Choice D: The real rate falls about 9%; subtract domestic inflation rather than add it
macro.Correct Answer: B — The real rate rises about 1%; domestic goods become relatively dearer despite nominal depreciation
macro.Feedback: Approximate real-rate growth is −4+7−2=+1%. Under this quotation an increased real rate makes domestic goods relatively dearer. Nominal depreciation is outweighed by domestic inflation relative to foreign inflation.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “A decline of exactly 5 percent” in this real exchange rates and purchasing power task.
macro.Question: Initially ε = eP/P* = 1, with e in foreign currency per domestic currency. In year one e rises 12 percent, domestic prices fall 3 percent and foreign prices rise 4 percent. In year two both price levels are fixed. What year-two change in e restores the initial real rate?
macro.Choice A: A decline of about 4.27 percent
macro.Choice B: A decline of exactly 5 percent
macro.Choice C: A rise of about 4.46 percent
macro.Choice D: A decline of about 4.46 percent
macro.Correct Answer: A — A decline of about 4.27 percent
macro.Feedback: Year-one ε factor is 1.12×0.97/1.04=1.04461538. Year two must multiply e by its reciprocal, 1.04/(1.12×0.97), a decline of about 4.27 percent. The recovery percentage uses the new base.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The combination is expected whenever saving is high” in this international transactions and identities task.
macro.Question: A country has positive NCO but a reported trade deficit. Within the same consistently measured period, which statement is correct?
macro.Choice A: At least one reported balance is inconsistent with the accounting identity
macro.Choice B: The combination is expected whenever saving is high
macro.Choice C: Positive NCO mechanically creates a trade deficit
macro.Choice D: The signs can differ whenever exchange rates float
macro.Correct Answer: A — At least one reported balance is inconsistent with the accounting identity
macro.Feedback: The identity NX = NCO requires the two balances to share the same value and sign.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Raise X to $225 billion or lower M to $225 billion; the identity does not select between them” in this international transactions and identities task.
macro.Question: For the same period, a data release reports S = $480 billion, I = $525 billion, X = $210 billion, M = $240 billion, foreign-asset purchases by residents of $70 billion, and domestic-asset purchases by foreigners of $115 billion. If exactly one trade figure is wrong and all other figures are correct, how could the trade figures be corrected, and can we tell which figure is wrong?
macro.Choice A: Raise X to $225 billion or lower M to $225 billion; the identity does not select between them
macro.Choice B: Raise M to $255 billion; the identity proves that imports alone are wrong
macro.Choice C: Raise M to $255 billion or lower X to $195 billion; the identity does not select between them
macro.Choice D: Lower X to $195 billion; the identity proves that exports alone are wrong
macro.Correct Answer: C — Raise M to $255 billion or lower X to $195 billion; the identity does not select between them
macro.Feedback: S − I = −45 and asset NCO = 70 − 115 = −45, but reported NX is −30. Trade must fall another 15: either M rises from 240 to 255 or X falls from 210 to 195. The stated data do not identify which trade entry is erroneous.

macro.Question: Which policy acts automatically to cushion a recession without a new vote by Congress?
macro.Choice A: Unemployment benefits that rise as workers lose jobs
macro.Choice B: A one-time discretionary tax bill
macro.Choice C: A Federal Reserve bond sale
macro.Choice D: A price ceiling
macro.Correct Answer: A — Unemployment benefits that rise as workers lose jobs
macro.Feedback: Automatic stabilizers change with economic conditions; unemployment benefits rise as unemployment rises.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing automatic stabilizers with discretionary policy.
macro.Question: An automatic stabilizer is best described as:
macro.Choice A: A built-in response to the economy
macro.Choice B: A Fed bond sale
macro.Choice C: A permanent shift of LRAS
macro.Choice D: A fixed money multiplier
macro.Correct Answer: A — A built-in response to the economy
macro.Feedback: Automatic stabilizers, such as taxes and transfer payments, respond automatically as conditions change.

macro.Common Misconception: Thinking leverage only increases returns and not risk
macro.Question: Why does leverage make banks riskier?
