macro.Choice D: One workshop must have comparative advantage in both goods
macro.Correct Answer: A — Neither has comparative advantage in desks based on these costs
macro.Feedback: Compute the forgone alternative per unit, then select the lower opportunity cost.

macro.Common Misconception: Repeating a ratio instead of taking its reciprocal.
macro.Question: River can produce 18 X or 6 Y; Hill can produce 12 X or 8 Y. What is each producer’s opportunity cost of one unit of Y, measured in units of X?
macro.Choice A: River: 3 X; Hill: 1.5 X
macro.Choice B: River: one-third X; Hill: two-thirds X
macro.Choice C: River: 12 X; Hill: 18 X
macro.Choice D: River: 2 X; Hill: 3 X
macro.Correct Answer: A — River: 3 X; Hill: 1.5 X
macro.Feedback: River gives up 18/6 = 3 units of X per unit of Y; Hill gives up 12/8 = 1.5 units of X per unit of Y.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating comparative advantage as fixed after productivity or opportunity costs change.
macro.Question: North can make 20 chips or 10 sensors; South can make 12 chips or 12 sensors. A technology change lets North make 40 sensors with unchanged chip capacity. What changes?
macro.Choice A: North gains comparative advantage in sensors and South in chips
macro.Choice B: North keeps comparative advantage in chips because its chip output is unchanged
macro.Choice C: South gains comparative advantage in both goods
macro.Choice D: Equal opportunity costs eliminate specialization
macro.Correct Answer: A — North gains comparative advantage in sensors and South in chips
macro.Feedback: Recompute relative opportunity costs after a change and respect the model limits.

macro.Common Misconception: Including a boundary or a rate outside the two opportunity costs as a strict mutual gain.
macro.Question: Ava’s cost of one crate is 2 sacks; Ben’s is 5 sacks. At exactly 2 sacks per crate, which statement is correct?
macro.Choice A: Ava is indifferent and Ben can gain from buying the crate
macro.Choice B: Both receive positive gains from the trade.
macro.Choice C: Ben is indifferent and Ava captures every gain
macro.Choice D: The rate lies strictly between their opportunity costs
macro.Correct Answer: A — Ava is indifferent and Ben can gain from buying the crate
macro.Feedback: For both producers to be better off, the trading price must be above the lower opportunity cost and below the higher one.

macro.Common Misconception: Including a boundary or a rate outside the two opportunity costs as a strict mutual gain.
macro.Question: One bolt costs East 0.5 panel and West 1.25 panels. What range of trading prices, measured in panels per bolt, makes both producers better off than producing the goods themselves? Exclude prices at which either producer only breaks even.
macro.Choice A: More than 0.5 but less than 1.25 panels per bolt
macro.Choice B: More than 2 but less than 4 bolts per panel.
macro.Choice C: At least 0.5 and at most 1.25 panels per bolt
macro.Choice D: Less than 0.5 panels per bolt only
macro.Correct Answer: A — More than 0.5 but less than 1.25 panels per bolt
macro.Feedback: Both producers gain when the trading price is above East’s opportunity cost of 0.5 panel per bolt and below West’s cost of 1.25 panels per bolt. At either endpoint, one producer only breaks even.

macro.Common Misconception: Using greater output alone to assign comparative advantage.
macro.Question: A consultant completes more audits and presentations than an associate. A manager concludes the consultant should do both. What is missing?
macro.Choice A: The opportunity cost of assigning the consultant to each task
macro.Choice B: Only the consultant’s total output in both tasks.
macro.Choice C: A guarantee that specialization divides gains equally
macro.Choice D: The money price of international exports
macro.Correct Answer: A — The opportunity cost of assigning the consultant to each task
macro.Feedback: Absolute advantage concerns productivity; comparative advantage concerns lower opportunity cost.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming higher combined output makes every possible exchange mutually beneficial.
macro.Question: Specialization raises combined output, but a proposed exchange rate lies above both producers’ costs for the exported good. What follows?
macro.Choice A: Higher output creates potential gains, but this rate will not benefit both sides
macro.Choice B: Every feasible exchange must share the production gain.
macro.Choice C: The higher-cost producer now has comparative advantage
macro.Choice D: Both sides are strictly better off because specialization occurred
macro.Correct Answer: A — Higher output creates potential gains, but this rate will not benefit both sides
macro.Feedback: Specialization creates potential output gains; the trading terms determine whether both sides gain.

macro.Common Misconception: Repeating a ratio instead of taking its reciprocal.
macro.Question: Coast’s opportunity cost of one unit of cocoa is 3 units of tea; Ridge’s is 6 units of tea. What range of trading prices, measured in units of cocoa per unit of tea, makes both producers better off? Exclude break-even prices.
macro.Choice A: More than one-sixth and less than one-third
macro.Choice B: More than one-third and less than one-sixth
macro.Choice C: More than 3 and less than 6
macro.Choice D: At least one-sixth and at most one-third
macro.Correct Answer: A — More than one-sixth and less than one-third
macro.Feedback: Both gain when one unit of cocoa trades for more than 3 but less than 6 units of tea. In cocoa per unit of tea, the range is greater than 1/6 and less than 1/3. At either endpoint, one producer only breaks even.

macro.Common Misconception: Equating positive aggregate gains with equal or universal individual gains.
macro.Question: One machine costs Alpha 2 kits and Beta 6 kits. Compare rates of 3 and 5 kits per machine. Which statement is true?
macro.Choice A: Both work, but 5 shifts more modeled gain to Alpha
macro.Choice B: Only the 3-kit rate lies between the two opportunity costs.
macro.Choice C: Only the 5-kit rate is between costs
macro.Choice D: Both divide the gain equally
macro.Correct Answer: A — Both work, but 5 shifts more modeled gain to Alpha
macro.Feedback: Total gains and their distribution are distinct; terms of trade allocate the modeled surplus.

macro.Common Misconception: Skipping a required link among opportunity cost, specialization, exchange, and the autarky comparison.
macro.Question: A problem gives specialization output and a trading rate but no pre-trade consumption bundle. Can a unique numerical consumption gain be found?
macro.Choice A: No; the autarky comparison is underdetermined
macro.Choice B: Yes; the trading rate determines the pre-trade consumption bundle.
macro.Choice C: Yes; combined output equals each gain
macro.Choice D: No; trade gains can never be measured
macro.Correct Answer: A — No; the autarky comparison is underdetermined
macro.Feedback: A consumption gain is the difference between the post-trade bundle and the pre-trade, or autarky, bundle. Specialization output and an exchange rate do not identify that missing baseline, so different autarky bundles could imply different numerical gains. Gains can be measured when the required consumption information is supplied.

macro.Common Misconception: Skipping a required link among opportunity cost, specialization, exchange, and the autarky comparison.
macro.Question: A technology has increasing rather than constant opportunity cost. Which conclusion is supported?
macro.Choice A: Both producers can gain through specialization without either specializing completely
macro.Choice B: Both producers must always specialize completely.
macro.Choice C: Opportunity cost becomes irrelevant after exchange
macro.Choice D: Absolute advantage fixes every output
macro.Correct Answer: A — Both producers can gain through specialization without either specializing completely
macro.Feedback: With increasing opportunity cost, producing more of a good requires giving up progressively more of the other good. Reallocation can create gains while relative marginal costs differ, but the rising cost can make further specialization unattractive before either producer specializes completely. Absolute productivity alone does not determine that stopping point.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming the static model settles every long-run policy question.
macro.Question: A static two-good model finds gains from specialization. Which conclusion goes beyond that result alone?
macro.Choice A: Every long-run trade policy benefits every worker and industry
macro.Choice B: Lower opportunity cost identifies comparative advantage.
macro.Choice C: Terms inside the bounds can create mutual gains
macro.Choice D: Specialization can raise output under the assumptions
macro.Correct Answer: A — Every long-run trade policy benefits every worker and industry
macro.Feedback: The static model can show gains from specialization under its assumptions, but it does not establish that every long-run trade policy benefits every worker and industry.

macro.Common Misconception: Comparing a post-trade bundle with specialization output instead of the stated autarky bundle.
macro.Question: A can make 12 X or 24 Y and B can make 10 X or 10 Y. After full specialization, B sends A 4 X for 6 Y. A previously consumed 4 X and 12 Y. What is A's gain?
macro.Choice A: The same 4 X and 6 additional Y
macro.Choice B: Four additional X and the same Y
macro.Choice C: Six additional X and 4 additional Y
macro.Choice D: No gain because A exports output
macro.Correct Answer: A — The same 4 X and 6 additional Y
macro.Feedback: Subtract the stated autarky bundle from post-trade consumption good by good.

macro.Common Misconception: Using the wrong autarky bundle or failing to conserve the traded goods.
macro.Question: C can make 16 cloth or 8 wine; D can make 6 cloth or 12 wine. They fully specialize, and C trades 4 cloth for 4 wine. Before trade, C consumed 12 cloth and 2 wine while D consumed 2 cloth and 8 wine. What are the gains?
macro.Choice A: C gains 2 wine; D gains 2 cloth
macro.Choice B: C gains 4 wine; D gains 4 cloth
macro.Choice C: C gains 2 cloth; D gains 2 wine
macro.Choice D: Each gains 2 units of both goods
macro.Correct Answer: A — C gains 2 wine; D gains 2 cloth
macro.Feedback: Derive both post-trade bundles and compare each with its stated autarky bundle.

macro.Common Misconception: Skipping a required link among opportunity cost, specialization, exchange, and the autarky comparison.
macro.Question: A workshop's cost of a motor is 2 batteries; its trading partner's is 5. The workshop exports motors and pays 1 battery in shipping per motor. Measured in motors per battery, what range of trading prices makes both partners better off after shipping costs? Exclude break-even prices.
macro.Choice A: Between 1/5 and 1/3 motor per battery
macro.Choice B: Between 1/5 and 1/2 motor per battery
macro.Choice C: Between 3 and 5 motors per battery
macro.Choice D: Between 1/3 and 1/2 motor per battery
macro.Correct Answer: A — Between 1/5 and 1/3 motor per battery
macro.Feedback: The exporter needs more than 2 + 1 = 3 batteries per motor to cover production and shipping costs. The importer gains when the price is below 5 batteries per motor. Expressing these prices in motors per battery gives a range greater than 1/5 and less than 1/3.

macro.Common Misconception: Comparing a post-trade bundle with specialization output instead of the stated autarky bundle.
macro.Question: After specializing, a workshop has 30 panels. It can trade panels for motors at 3 panels per motor. Its former bundle was 16 panels and 3 motors. Which integer trade leaves it with strictly more of both goods?
macro.Choice A: Trade 12 panels for 4 motors
macro.Choice B: Trade 9 panels for 3 motors
macro.Choice C: Trade 15 panels for 5 motors
macro.Choice D: Trade 6 panels for 2 motors
macro.Correct Answer: A — Trade 12 panels for 4 motors
macro.Feedback: Trading 12 leaves 18 panels and 4 motors, above both former quantities. Nine panels only matches former motors; fifteen leaves too few panels; six leaves fewer motors.

macro.Common Misconception: Using the wrong autarky bundle or failing to conserve the traded goods.
macro.Question: North specializes at 24 fish and South at 12 nets. North trades 8 fish for 4 nets. Their autarky bundles were North 12 fish and 3 nets, South 6 fish and 6 nets. What are their gains?
macro.Choice A: North gains 4 fish and 1 net; South gains 2 fish and 2 nets
macro.Choice B: North gains 8 fish and 4 nets; South gains 8 fish and 4 nets
macro.Choice C: North gains 4 fish and 4 nets; South gains 2 fish and 6 nets
macro.Choice D: North gains 12 fish and 1 net; South gains 2 fish and 2 nets
macro.Correct Answer: A — North gains 4 fish and 1 net; South gains 2 fish and 2 nets
macro.Feedback: Derive both post-trade bundles and compare each with its stated autarky bundle.

macro.Common Misconception: Including a boundary or a rate outside the two opportunity costs as a strict mutual gain.
macro.Question: One printer costs X 3 scanners and Y 7 scanners. X exports a printer at a quoted price of 6 scanners but Y must also use 2 scanners for shipping. What would make both strictly better off?
macro.Choice A: A quoted price strictly between 3 and 5 scanners
macro.Choice B: Any quoted price strictly between 3 and 7 scanners
macro.Choice C: The existing price of 6 because it is below Y's domestic cost
macro.Choice D: A price of 7 because it exactly matches Y's production cost
macro.Correct Answer: A — A quoted price strictly between 3 and 5 scanners
macro.Feedback: X needs a quote above 3. Y's full import cost is quote + 2, which must be below 7. Thus 3 < quote < 5; ignoring shipping overstates the mutual-gain range.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating comparative advantage as fixed after productivity or opportunity costs change.
macro.Question: At constant tradeoffs, Oak can make 24 racks or 8 desks; Pine can make 18 racks or 9 desks. Oak adopts a tool that raises its desk maximum to 16 without changing racks. Which conclusion follows?
macro.Choice A: Oak switches to comparative advantage in desks; a 1.75-rack desk price can then benefit both
macro.Choice B: Pine retains desk advantage because its rack maximum is lower
macro.Choice C: Oak has comparative advantage in both goods because both maxima exceed Pine's
macro.Choice D: The old 2.5-rack desk price still gives Oak positive gains when it imports desks
macro.Correct Answer: A — Oak switches to comparative advantage in desks; a 1.75-rack desk price can then benefit both
macro.Feedback: Oak's desk cost falls from 3 to 1.5 racks; Pine's stays 2. Oak becomes the lower-cost desk maker, and 1.75 lies between their costs. At the old import price Oak could now make desks more cheaply.

macro.Common Misconception: Skipping a required link among opportunity cost, specialization, exchange, and the autarky comparison.
macro.Question: With constant tradeoffs, Ridge can make 24 maps or 12 models. Vale can make 18 maps or m models. Ridge exports models at 1.5 maps each and claims both receive a positive gain. Which value of m makes the claim consistent?
macro.Choice A: No positive m; Ridge loses at the stated export price
macro.Choice B: m = 6; Vale's higher cost suffices for mutual gains
macro.Choice C: m = 9; matching costs makes this price mutually beneficial
macro.Choice D: m = 18; Vale's higher model productivity guarantees mutual gains
macro.Correct Answer: A — No positive m; Ridge loses at the stated export price
macro.Feedback: Ridge sacrifices 2 maps to make a model but receives only 1.5 maps. Regardless of Vale's productivity, Ridge loses on this export; solving only Vale's inequality misses one side.

macro.Common Misconception: Skipping a required link among opportunity cost, specialization, exchange, and the autarky comparison.
macro.Question: Two labs each sacrifice 4 tests for one prototype at constant tradeoffs. One lab doubles its maximum output of both goods. What changes in the pure comparative-advantage model?
macro.Choice A: Its capacity rises, but equal opportunity costs still leave no positive gains for both producers from specialization at any common price
macro.Choice B: It gains comparative advantage in both goods because both maxima double
macro.Choice C: A price of 4 tests now gives both a positive gain on each prototype
macro.Choice D: Doubling capacity halves its opportunity cost of a prototype
macro.Correct Answer: A — Its capacity rises, but equal opportunity costs still leave no positive gains for both producers from specialization at any common price
macro.Feedback: Proportional productivity growth leaves the ratio unchanged. At 4 tests both are indifferent; any other price advantages one direction while making the other party worse off.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring transaction and transport costs.
macro.Question: Specialization creates a gross gain of 24 units of a common consumption good. Shipping uses 5 units and verification uses 7. The proposed division gives one party 15 units of gross gain and assigns it both costs. Does that party gain, and what net gain remains for the other?
macro.Choice A: Yes, it gains 3 units; the other gains 9
macro.Choice B: Yes, it gains 15 units; the other gains 9
macro.Choice C: No, it loses 12 units; the other gains 24
macro.Choice D: Yes, both gain 12 units
macro.Correct Answer: A — Yes, it gains 3 units; the other gains 9
macro.Feedback: Net total gain is 24 - 5 - 7 = 12. The cost-paying party gains 15 - 12 = 3; the other receives the remaining gross 9 and pays no cost.

macro.Common Misconception: Skipping a required link among opportunity cost, specialization, exchange, and the autarky comparison.
macro.Question: An engineer needs 2 hours per design and 1 hour per inspection. A technician needs 6 hours per design and 2 hours per inspection. They move one inspection from the engineer to the technician, who gives up one-third of a design. What net design capacity is freed?
macro.Choice A: One-sixth of a design
macro.Choice B: One-half of a design
macro.Choice C: One-third of a design
macro.Choice D: Five-sixths of a design
macro.Correct Answer: A — One-sixth of a design
macro.Feedback: The engineer saves an hour, enough for half a design. The technician's two hours cost one-third of a design. Net capacity gain is 1/2 - 1/3 = 1/6; the engineer's absolute inspection advantage does not settle assignment.

macro.Common Misconception: Skipping a required link among opportunity cost, specialization, exchange, and the autarky comparison.
macro.Question: Mesa specializes at 30 meals and Bay at 15 repairs, then exchanges 10 meals for 5 repairs. A report says Mesa gains 5 meals and 1 repair, while Bay gains 2 meals and 3 repairs. Which pair of autarky bundles makes all four claims consistent?
macro.Choice A: Mesa: 25 meals, 6 repairs; Bay: 12 meals, 13 repairs.
macro.Choice B: Mesa: 15 meals, 4 repairs; Bay: 8 meals, 7 repairs.
macro.Choice C: Mesa: 20 meals, 5 repairs; Bay: 10 meals, 10 repairs.
macro.Choice D: Mesa: 5 meals, 4 repairs; Bay: 8 meals, 2 repairs.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Mesa: 15 meals, 4 repairs; Bay: 8 meals, 7 repairs.
macro.Feedback: Post-trade bundles are Mesa (20 meals, 5 repairs) and Bay (10 meals, 10 repairs). Subtracting the claimed gains gives autarky bundles (15, 4) and (8, 7). Adding gains to final bundles or treating the exchange itself as consumption gives the distractors.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating comparative advantage as fixed after productivity or opportunity costs change.
macro.Question: Delta can make 24 files or 8 reviews; Echo can make 15 files or 10 reviews at constant tradeoffs. Delta doubles review productivity without changing files. A contract exchanges one review for 2 files. What changes?
macro.Choice A: The cost difference disappears, and the old contract no longer gives both positive gains
macro.Choice B: Delta gains review advantage because 16 exceeds Echo's 10
macro.Choice C: Echo retains review advantage because 15 is below Delta's 24 files
macro.Choice D: Both now receive a positive gain at every price between 1.5 and 3 files
macro.Correct Answer: A — The cost difference disappears, and the old contract no longer gives both positive gains
macro.Feedback: Initially review costs are 3 and 1.5 files, so 2 can benefit both. Delta's new cost is 24/16 = 1.5, equal to Echo's. At 2, a review importer would pay more than domestic cost.

macro.Common Misconception: Repeating a ratio instead of taking its reciprocal.
macro.Question: A lens costs Urban 0.25 sensor and Rural 0.5 sensor. Urban proposes exporting lenses at 3 lenses per sensor, and pays shipping of 0.05 sensor per lens. Which assessment is correct?
macro.Choice A: Both gain: Urban nets more than 0.25 sensor per lens and Rural pays less than 0.5
macro.Choice B: Urban loses because three is larger than both stated opportunity costs
macro.Choice C: Rural loses because the reciprocal price is above 0.5 sensor per lens
macro.Choice D: Both are indifferent because shipping makes the costs equal
macro.Correct Answer: A — Both gain: Urban nets more than 0.25 sensor per lens and Rural pays less than 0.5
macro.Feedback: The quote is 1/3 sensor per lens. Urban nets 1/3 - 0.05, about 0.283, above 0.25; Rural pays about 0.333, below 0.5. Keep price and cost in the same units.

macro.Common Misconception: Skipping a required link among opportunity cost, specialization, exchange, and the autarky comparison.
macro.Question: Lumen specializes at 32 lamps and Shade at 16 rugs. Their autarky bundles were Lumen (16 lamps, 4 rugs) and Shade (8 lamps, 8 rugs). Lumen now sends 18 lamps for 3 rugs, with no exchange costs. A planner says higher combined output proves both receive more of both goods. Which evaluation follows?
macro.Choice A: The claim holds: Lumen gains 2 lamps and 1 rug; Shade gains 10 lamps and 5 rugs.
macro.Choice B: The claim fails: Lumen gains 2 lamps and 1 rug; Shade loses 10 lamps and 5 rugs.
macro.Choice C: The claim holds: each receives half of the combined increase of 8 lamps and 4 rugs.
macro.Choice D: The claim fails: Lumen loses 2 lamps and 1 rug; Shade gains 10 lamps and 5 rugs.
macro.Correct Answer: D — The claim fails: Lumen loses 2 lamps and 1 rug; Shade gains 10 lamps and 5 rugs.
macro.Feedback: Combined output rises from (24 lamps, 12 rugs) to (32, 16), but the exchange leaves Lumen (14, 3) and Shade (18, 13). Lumen has less of both goods; Shade has more of both. Higher total output does not establish mutually beneficial distribution.

macro.Common Misconception: Skipping a required link among opportunity cost, specialization, exchange, and the autarky comparison.
macro.Question: Before specialization, two workshops jointly consume 18 frames and 10 cushions. Specialization produces 23 frames and 13 cushions; transport uses 2 cushions. Which claim follows before the remaining goods are divided?
macro.Choice A: The available bundle rises by 5 frames and 1 cushion, but individual gains depend on the division
macro.Choice B: Both parties necessarily gain 5 frames and 1 cushion each
macro.Choice C: Net cushion gain is 3 because transport is separate from production
macro.Choice D: One party's loss is impossible whenever both aggregate quantities rise
macro.Correct Answer: A — The available bundle rises by 5 frames and 1 cushion, but individual gains depend on the division
macro.Feedback: After transport, 23 frames and 11 cushions remain, a net gain of 5 and 1. Aggregate improvement permits beneficial divisions but does not establish the gains of a particular division.

macro.Common Misconception: Using greater output alone to assign comparative advantage.
macro.Question: A baker makes more bread and cakes than a helper. What must be known before assigning both tasks?
macro.Choice A: Their opportunity costs for bread and cakes
macro.Choice B: Only the baker’s total output in both goods.
macro.Choice C: The price of imported flour
macro.Choice D: Whether the helper likes cake
macro.Correct Answer: A — Their opportunity costs for bread and cakes
macro.Feedback: Absolute advantage concerns productivity; comparative advantage concerns lower opportunity cost.

macro.Common Misconception: Assigning every activity to the absolutely more productive producer.
macro.Question: Nia gives up 2 posters per video; Omar gives up 5. Who should specialize in videos?
macro.Choice A: Nia, because her opportunity cost is lower
macro.Choice B: Omar, because he gives up more posters per video.
macro.Choice C: Both, because gains must be equal
macro.Choice D: Neither, because totals are missing
macro.Correct Answer: A — Nia, because her opportunity cost is lower
macro.Feedback: In the textbook model, specialization follows comparative advantage.

macro.Common Misconception: Computing or comparing the opportunity costs in the wrong direction.
macro.Question: A can produce 16 apples or 8 pears; B can produce 9 apples or 9 pears. Who has comparative advantage in apples?
macro.Choice A: A; one apple costs 0.5 pear
macro.Choice B: B; one apple costs 1 pear
macro.Choice C: A; it has advantage in both
macro.Choice D: Neither; only money costs count
macro.Correct Answer: A — A; one apple costs 0.5 pear
macro.Feedback: Compute the forgone alternative per unit, then select the lower opportunity cost.

macro.Common Misconception: Including a boundary or a rate outside the two opportunity costs as a strict mutual gain.
macro.Question: One file costs Town 3 reports and City 7 reports. Which rate can strictly benefit both?
macro.Choice A: 5 reports per file
macro.Choice B: 3 reports per file
macro.Choice C: 7 reports per file
macro.Choice D: 9 reports per file
macro.Correct Answer: A — 5 reports per file
macro.Feedback: A strict mutual-gain rate lies strictly between the relevant opportunity costs.

macro.Common Misconception: Including a boundary or a rate outside the two opportunity costs as a strict mutual gain.
macro.Question: East can make 12 drones or 18 radios per day; West can make 6 drones or 24 radios. Costs are constant. West offers 1.5 radios per drone, then raises its offer to 2.5. Ignoring exchange costs, which evaluation is correct?
macro.Choice A: East exports drones; the first offer leaves East indifferent, while the second gives East 1 radio and West 1.5 radios of gain per drone.
macro.Choice B: West exports drones; the first offer leaves West indifferent, while the second gives West 1 radio and East 1.5 radios of gain per drone.
macro.Choice C: East exports drones; both offers give positive gains, and the second divides 2.5 radios of gain equally between the two producers.
macro.Choice D: East exports drones; the first offer benefits both, while the second makes West lose because the rate exceeds East’s opportunity cost.
macro.Correct Answer: A — East exports drones; the first offer leaves East indifferent, while the second gives East 1 radio and West 1.5 radios of gain per drone.
macro.Feedback: East gives up 18/12=1.5 radios per drone; West gives up 24/6=4. At 1.5 East is indifferent. At 2.5 East gains 2.5-1.5=1 radio and West saves 4-2.5=1.5 radios.

macro.Common Misconception: Computing or comparing the opportunity costs in the wrong direction.
macro.Question: A can make 12 machines or 24 tools; B can make 6 machines or 12 tools. After training, B can make 6 machines or 24 tools with the same resources. With constant costs, what changes in the case for specialization?
macro.Choice A: Initially costs are equal; after training A has machine advantage, B has tool advantage, and a rate between 2 and 4 tools per machine can benefit both.
macro.Choice B: Initially A has both advantages; after training B has both advantages, and any positive tools-per-machine rate can benefit both.
macro.Choice C: Initially costs are equal; after training B has machine advantage, A has tool advantage, and a rate between 2 and 4 tools per machine can benefit both.
macro.Choice D: Initially costs are equal; after training costs remain equal because B’s machine capacity is unchanged, so no range of trading prices that makes both producers better off appears.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Initially costs are equal; after training A has machine advantage, B has tool advantage, and a rate between 2 and 4 tools per machine can benefit both.
macro.Feedback: Initially both sacrifice 2 tools per machine. Training raises B’s machine opportunity cost to 4 tools while A remains at 2. A should specialize relatively more in machines and B in tools; positive gains for both producers require a rate between 2 and 4.

macro.Common Misconception: Skipping a required link among opportunity cost, specialization, exchange, and the autarky comparison.
macro.Question: Arbor specializes at 28 timber and Basin at 14 tools. Their autarky bundles were Arbor (14 timber, 3 tools) and Basin (6 timber, 7 tools). Basin offers 4 tools for t units of timber. With no exchange costs, which range of t gives each party strictly more of BOTH goods than in autarky?
macro.Feedback: Arbor receives 4 tools and retains 28 - t timber; it needs 28 - t > 14, so t < 14. Basin retains 10 tools and receives t timber; it needs t > 6. Thus 6 < t < 14. At either endpoint one party only matches, rather than exceeds, its autarky timber quantity.

macro.Common Misconception: Equating positive aggregate gains with equal or universal individual gains.
macro.Question: Quartz can make 10 chips or 20 screens; Sable can make 4 chips or 20 screens. Costs are constant. Quartz exports chips and uses resources worth 0.5 screen per chip to arrange delivery. At 5 screens per chip, who receives a positive gain? If the rate falls to 4, what changes?
macro.Choice A: At 5 only Quartz receives a positive gain; at 4 both gain, with Quartz gaining 1.5 screens and Sable saving 1 screen per chip.
macro.Choice B: At 5 both receive a positive gain; at 4 only Sable gains, because delivery raises Quartz’s opportunity cost to 4.5 screens per chip.
macro.Choice C: At 5 only Sable receives a positive gain; at 4 both gain, with Sable gaining 1.5 screens and Quartz saving 1 screen per chip.
macro.Choice D: At 5 neither receives a positive gain; at 4 Quartz loses 0.5 screen, because delivery costs must be added to Sable’s production cost.
macro.Correct Answer: A — At 5 only Quartz receives a positive gain; at 4 both gain, with Quartz gaining 1.5 screens and Sable saving 1 screen per chip.
macro.Feedback: Production costs are 2 and 5 screens per chip. Quartz’s delivered cost is 2.5. At rate 5, Quartz gains 2.5 and Sable is indifferent. At rate 4, Quartz gains 1.5 and Sable saves 1.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating comparative advantage as fixed after productivity or opportunity costs change.
macro.Question: Cedar can make 30 boards or 10 doors; Dune can make 16 boards or 8 doors. A tool doubles Dune’s board capacity without changing door capacity. Costs are constant. A proposed contract keeps Dune exporting doors at 2.5 boards per door. Which revision follows?
macro.Choice A: Reverse the specialization: Dune now exports boards, Cedar exports doors, and a rate strictly between 3 and 4 boards per door can benefit both.
macro.Choice B: Keep Dune exporting doors at 2.5 boards per door, because its door capacity and therefore its door opportunity cost are unchanged.
macro.Choice C: Reverse the specialization but retain 2.5 boards per door, because any rate above Dune’s original cost benefits both after the tool.
macro.Choice D: Stop specialization because Dune’s higher board output gives it absolute and comparative advantage in both goods.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Reverse the specialization: Dune now exports boards, Cedar exports doors, and a rate strictly between 3 and 4 boards per door can benefit both.
macro.Feedback: Initially door costs are 3 boards in Cedar and 2 in Dune, making 2.5 mutually beneficial. After the tool Dune’s door cost rises to 32/8=4 boards. Cedar now exports doors; the mutual-gain interval is strictly 3 to 4.

macro.Common Misconception: Using the wrong autarky bundle or failing to conserve the traded goods.
macro.Question: Orchid specializes at 36 flowers and Reed at 18 baskets. Autarky bundles were Orchid (18 flowers, 4 baskets) and Reed (9 flowers, 9 baskets). They exchange 12 flowers for 6 baskets. Carrier A consumes 1 of Orchid’s received baskets in transport; carrier B consumes 3. No other goods are lost. Which carrier leaves BOTH parties with strictly more of each good than in autarky?
macro.Choice A: Both carriers: Orchid keeps 5 baskets with A and 7 with B.
macro.Choice B: Only carrier B: Orchid keeps 3 baskets with A and 5 with B.
macro.Choice C: Only carrier A: Orchid keeps 5 baskets with A and 3 with B.
macro.Choice D: Neither carrier: Orchid keeps 3 baskets with A and 1 with B.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Only carrier A: Orchid keeps 5 baskets with A and 3 with B.
macro.Feedback: Before transport Orchid has (24 flowers, 6 baskets), and Reed has (12 flowers, 12 baskets). Carrier A leaves Orchid (24, 5), exceeding (18, 4); Reed also gains in both goods. Carrier B leaves Orchid (24, 3), so it fails the more-of-each-good test. This does not rank the mixed bundle under unspecified preferences.

macro.Common Misconception: Equating positive aggregate gains with equal or universal individual gains.
macro.Question: Haven gives up 3 grain per turbine and Isle 7. Haven exports turbines; Isle also uses resources worth 1 grain per imported turbine to transport them. Compare offers of 4 and 6 grain per turbine. Which contract strictly benefits both after transport?
macro.Choice A: Only 4 does: Haven gains 1 and Isle gains 2 grain; at 6 Isle is indifferent after transport.
macro.Choice B: Both do: Haven gains more at 6, while Isle still gains 1 grain because transport does not enter comparative cost.
macro.Choice C: Only 6 does: Haven gains 3 and Isle gains 1 grain; at 4 Haven is indifferent after transport.
macro.Choice D: Neither does: the transport cost makes every rate between production opportunity costs unprofitable for the importer.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Only 4 does: Haven gains 1 and Isle gains 2 grain; at 6 Isle is indifferent after transport.
macro.Feedback: At rate r, Haven gains r-3 and Isle gains 7-r-1. At 4 these gains are 1 and 2; at 6 they are 3 and 0. Strict mutual gain now requires 3<r<6.

macro.Common Misconception: Skipping a required link among opportunity cost, specialization, exchange, and the autarky comparison.
macro.Question: Peak specializes at 40 services and Glen at 20 devices. Autarky bundles were Peak (20 services, 6 devices) and Glen (10 services, 10 devices). Proposal A exchanges 16 services for 8 devices; B exchanges 22 services for 8 devices. Each party prefers more of either good when the other is unchanged; no other preferences or costs are given. Which assessment is justified?
macro.Choice A: A gives both more of both goods; B gives Peak fewer services but more devices, leaving its welfare change undetermined.
macro.Choice B: B gives both more of both goods; A gives Glen fewer devices but more services, leaving its welfare change undetermined.
macro.Choice C: Both give both more of both goods; each party is better off without needing further preference information.
macro.Choice D: Neither gives either more of both goods; each party’s welfare change under both proposals remains undetermined.
macro.Correct Answer: A — A gives both more of both goods; B gives Peak fewer services but more devices, leaving its welfare change undetermined.
macro.Feedback: A leaves Peak (24 services, 8 devices) and Glen (16 services, 12 devices), more of both goods for each. B leaves Peak (18, 8) and Glen (22, 12). Glen gains in both, but Peak trades 2 fewer services for 2 more devices relative to autarky. Its welfare comparison requires preferences; total output alone cannot settle it.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing absolute productivity with comparative advantage.
macro.Question: Comparative advantage belongs to the producer who:
macro.Choice A: Produces the largest amount of every good.
macro.Choice B: Charges the lowest money price after trade.
macro.Choice C: Has the highest income.
macro.Choice D: Gives up less of the alternative good.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Gives up less of the alternative good.
macro.Feedback: Compare opportunity costs, not total output.

macro.Common Misconception: Not using opportunity costs as the trading-price bounds.
macro.Question: A mutually beneficial terms-of-trade price must generally lie:
macro.Choice A: Between the two producers’ opportunity costs.
macro.Choice B: Above both opportunity costs.
macro.Choice C: Below both opportunity costs.
macro.Choice D: At the higher producer’s total output.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Between the two producers’ opportunity costs.
macro.Feedback: A price between the opportunity costs lets both sides save resources.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating trade as necessarily zero-sum.
macro.Question: Trade can benefit both sides because:
macro.Choice A: One side is forced to accept a loss.
macro.Choice B: Specialization can increase combined output and exchange can share the gain.
macro.Choice C: Scarcity disappears after exchange.
macro.Choice D: Both sides must have identical skills.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Specialization can increase combined output and exchange can share the gain.
macro.Feedback: Voluntary specialization and exchange can create mutual gains.

macro.Common Misconception: Using absolute productivity instead of the opportunity cost of the lead's time.
macro.Question: A project lead is faster at every task but delegates data entry. Which concept explains the choice?
macro.Choice A: A price ceiling that limits payment for outsourced data entry
macro.Choice B: Absolute advantage because the lead is faster at data entry
macro.Choice C: Comparative advantage based on the opportunity cost of the lead's time
macro.Choice D: Elimination of scarce time after the work is delegated
macro.Correct Answer: C — Comparative advantage based on the opportunity cost of the lead's time
macro.Feedback: Delegation can be efficient when the lead has a higher opportunity cost of doing data entry.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring the internal resources forgone when the city provides the service itself.
macro.Question: A city can buy snowplow service from a neighboring county for less than the resources required to provide it internally. What does opportunity-cost reasoning suggest?
macro.Choice A: The city should remain self-sufficient even at a higher resource cost
macro.Choice B: The neighboring county cannot benefit from any voluntary contract
macro.Choice C: Money prices make the city's forgone alternatives irrelevant
macro.Choice D: Contracting can free city resources for other services
macro.Correct Answer: D — Contracting can free city resources for other services
macro.Feedback: Buying the service at lower opportunity cost frees scarce city resources for other uses.

macro.Common Misconception: Using total output, wages, or prices instead of opportunity cost.
macro.Question: Mira gives up 1 report to prepare a presentation; Sol gives up 3 reports. Which fact determines comparative advantage in presentations?
macro.Choice A: Mira gives up fewer reports per presentation
macro.Choice B: Sol may complete more total tasks in a day
macro.Choice C: Mira charges a lower money price after exchange
macro.Choice D: Sol has a higher wage in an unrelated job
macro.Correct Answer: A — Mira gives up fewer reports per presentation
macro.Feedback: Comparative advantage belongs to the lower-opportunity-cost producer.

macro.Common Misconception: Inferring comparative advantage from productivity alone.
macro.Question: With the same resources, East Farm can harvest 12 crates while West Farm can harvest 8. What does this establish?
macro.Choice A: East Farm has an absolute advantage in harvesting crates
macro.Choice B: East Farm must have comparative advantage in every crop.
macro.Choice C: West Farm has the lower opportunity cost of harvesting
macro.Choice D: Both farms gain equally from every possible exchange
macro.Correct Answer: A — East Farm has an absolute advantage in harvesting crates
macro.Feedback: Greater output from the same resources establishes absolute, not necessarily comparative, advantage.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming the more productive producer should make everything.
macro.Question: Why can two people gain from trade even when one is better at producing both goods?
macro.Choice A: The less productive person must accept a loss.
macro.Choice B: Absolute advantage guarantees equal output.
macro.Choice C: Their opportunity costs can still differ.
macro.Choice D: Trade removes the need to specialize.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Their opportunity costs can still differ.
macro.Feedback: Different opportunity costs create room for specialization and mutually beneficial exchange.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming specialization reduces total production.
macro.Question: Specialization based on comparative advantage tends to:
macro.Choice A: Make both producers self-sufficient.
macro.Choice B: Require identical opportunity costs.
macro.Choice C: Prevent either side from consuming outside its PPF.
macro.Choice D: Increase the combined output available for exchange.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Increase the combined output available for exchange.
macro.Feedback: When each producer concentrates on the lower-opportunity-cost good, combined output can rise.

macro.Common Misconception: Thinking one side must lose whenever the other gains.
macro.Question: Voluntary trade occurs most directly because:
macro.Choice A: Each side expects the exchange to improve its situation.
macro.Choice B: One side must be forced to surrender a good.
macro.Choice C: Both sides must value the goods equally.
macro.Choice D: Prices must be fixed by a government.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Each side expects the exchange to improve its situation.
macro.Feedback: A voluntary exchange happens when both parties expect to gain.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming trade gains arise even without relative-cost differences.
macro.Question: Two producers have identical opportunity costs for both goods. What does the basic two-good model predict?
macro.Choice A: Both gain automatically from complete specialization.
macro.Choice B: The producer with absolute advantage must import both goods.
macro.Choice C: No gains from specialization based solely on comparative advantage.
macro.Choice D: Any terms of trade will double total output.
macro.Correct Answer: C — No gains from specialization based solely on comparative advantage.
macro.Feedback: Identical opportunity costs leave no comparative-advantage basis for specialization.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming the most productive worker should perform every task.
macro.Question: Maya is faster than Leo at both coding and testing. Why might Maya still assign testing to Leo?
macro.Choice A: Absolute advantage requires Maya to do both tasks.
macro.Choice B: Leo may have the lower opportunity cost of testing.
macro.Choice C: Testing cannot be traded within a team.
macro.Choice D: Maya’s wage automatically determines comparative advantage.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Leo may have the lower opportunity cost of testing.
macro.Feedback: Efficient assignment depends on relative sacrifice, not only speed.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring transaction and transport costs.
macro.Question: Two regions specialize according to comparative advantage, but transport costs exceed the production gains. What is the best conclusion?
macro.Choice A: Comparative advantage is mathematically impossible.
macro.Choice B: Absolute advantage has replaced opportunity cost.
macro.Choice C: The gross gains from specialization may be smaller than the costs of exchange.
macro.Choice D: Trade must still make both regions better off.
macro.Correct Answer: C — The gross gains from specialization may be smaller than the costs of exchange.
macro.Feedback: Comparative advantage identifies production gains, but real exchange costs can erase net gains.

macro.Common Misconception: Preferring self-sufficiency without comparing opportunity costs.
macro.Question: A region can obtain one turbine by giving up 3 tons of grain through exchange or 5 tons by producing it internally. Which reasoning supports exchange?
macro.Choice A: Importing the turbine has the lower opportunity cost in grain
macro.Choice B: Producing internally must be better because it avoids trade.
macro.Choice C: The money price eliminates the need to compare resources
macro.Choice D: Exchange guarantees equal gains for every resident
macro.Correct Answer: A — Importing the turbine has the lower opportunity cost in grain
macro.Feedback: Exchange uses resources worth 3 tons rather than 5, freeing 2 tons for other uses.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring costs of arranging and enforcing exchange.
macro.Question: Two firms specialize and increase combined output by 20 units, but contracting and monitoring cost 25 units. What follows?
macro.Choice A: Comparative advantage does not exist.
macro.Choice B: The specialization creates gross gains but a net loss after transaction costs.
macro.Choice C: The firms must trade because output rose.
macro.Choice D: Transaction costs are transfers and cannot affect net gains.
macro.Correct Answer: B — The specialization creates gross gains but a net loss after transaction costs.
macro.Feedback: Net gains equal production gains minus the real costs of coordinating trade.

macro.Common Misconception: Comparing domestic and foreign choices without a common opportunity-cost measure.
macro.Question: A country can import steel for 4 units of wheat per ton. Producing a ton domestically costs 6 units of wheat. Which statement is best?
macro.Choice A: Domestic steel has lower opportunity cost.
macro.Choice B: The money price alone proves dumping.
macro.Choice C: Importing steel frees 2 units of wheat-equivalent resources per ton for other uses.
macro.Choice D: Importing steel reduces available resources by 2 units per ton.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Importing steel frees 2 units of wheat-equivalent resources per ton for other uses.
macro.Feedback: Importing at a cost of 4 instead of producing at a cost of 6 releases resources worth 2 units of wheat.

macro.Common Misconception: Comparing absolute output instead of opportunity costs.
macro.Question: Rina can make 8 posters or 4 videos in a day. Malik can make 6 posters or 6 videos. Who has the comparative advantage in posters?
macro.Choice A: Malik, because one poster costs him 0.5 video while it costs Rina 1 video.
macro.Choice B: Rina, because one poster costs her 0.5 video while it costs Malik 1 video.
macro.Choice C: Malik, because one poster costs him 1 video while it costs Rina 2 videos.
macro.Choice D: Neither, because one poster costs each of them 1 video at their stated output rates.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Rina, because one poster costs her 0.5 video while it costs Malik 1 video.
macro.Feedback: Rina gives up 4/8 = 0.5 video per poster, while Malik gives up 6/6 = 1 video per poster. Rina therefore has the lower opportunity cost of posters. Using 8/4 reverses the units to posters per video; swapping the producers or assuming equal costs also gives the wrong comparison.

macro.Common Misconception: Using the higher total output as the comparative-advantage test.
macro.Question: Nora can edit 12 pages or design 3 graphics per hour. Eli can edit 8 pages or design 4 graphics. Who has the comparative advantage in graphics?
macro.Choice A: Nora, because she edits more pages.
macro.Choice B: Nora, because one graphic costs her fewer graphics.
macro.Choice C: Eli, because one graphic costs him 2 edited pages rather than Nora’s 4.
macro.Choice D: Neither, because Eli has no absolute advantage in editing.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Eli, because one graphic costs him 2 edited pages rather than Nora’s 4.
macro.Feedback: Eli sacrifices 2 edited pages per graphic; Nora sacrifices 4.

macro.Common Misconception: Choosing specialization from absolute quantities alone.
macro.Question: Farm A can produce 20 crates of apples or 10 crates of pears. Farm B can produce 12 crates of apples or 12 crates of pears. Which specialization pattern follows comparative advantage?
macro.Choice A: Farm A specializes in pears and Farm B in apples.
macro.Choice B: Both farms specialize in apples because apples output is larger.
macro.Choice C: Neither farm specializes because both can produce both goods.
macro.Choice D: Farm A specializes relatively more in apples and Farm B in pears.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Farm A specializes relatively more in apples and Farm B in pears.
macro.Feedback: Farm A gives up 0.5 pear per apple; Farm B gives up 1 pear per apple.

macro.Common Misconception: Failing to place the trading price between the two opportunity costs.
macro.Question: Ava gives up 2 cups of coffee to bake one loaf. Ben gives up 5 cups to bake one loaf. A trade price of one loaf for 3 cups of coffee is:
macro.Choice A: Potentially beneficial to both Ava and Ben.
macro.Choice B: Beneficial only to Ava.
macro.Choice C: Beneficial only to Ben.
macro.Choice D: Outside the mutually beneficial range.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Potentially beneficial to both Ava and Ben.
macro.Feedback: Three cups lies between Ava’s cost of 2 and Ben’s cost of 5 cups per loaf.

macro.Common Misconception: Assigning comparative advantage to the higher opportunity-cost producer.
macro.Question: Country X gives up 3 tons of wheat for one machine. Country Y gives up 7 tons. Which statement is correct?
macro.Choice A: Country Y has the comparative advantage in machines.
macro.Choice B: Country X has the comparative advantage in machines.
macro.Choice C: Country X must also have the comparative advantage in wheat.
macro.Choice D: Comparative advantage cannot be identified from opportunity costs.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Country X has the comparative advantage in machines.
macro.Feedback: Country X sacrifices less wheat per machine.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming higher total output makes every possible trade acceptable.
macro.Question: After specialization, total production rises but one proposed trade leaves a producer worse off. What failed?
macro.Choice A: Comparative advantage ceased to exist.
macro.Choice B: Specialization always lowers total output.
macro.Choice C: The proposed terms of trade were not mutually beneficial.
macro.Choice D: Absolute advantage made exchange impossible.
macro.Correct Answer: C — The proposed terms of trade were not mutually beneficial.
macro.Feedback: Specialization can create gains, but the exchange terms must divide those gains so both sides benefit.

macro.Common Misconception: Calling a boundary rate a strict mutual gain or assuming gains divide equally.
macro.Question: A trade rate equals the exporter’s opportunity cost exactly but remains below the importer’s opportunity cost. Which evaluation is precise?
macro.Choice A: The exporter is indifferent while the importer captures the modeled gain
macro.Choice B: The exporter captures every gain because it supplies the good.
macro.Choice C: Both parties receive positive and exactly equal gains
macro.Choice D: Neither party can gain because the rate is on one boundary
macro.Correct Answer: A — The exporter is indifferent while the importer captures the modeled gain
macro.Feedback: At its own opportunity cost the exporter is indifferent; the importer still saves resources.

macro.Common Misconception: Letting absolute advantage determine both specialization choices.
macro.Question: With constant tradeoffs per day, Fern can make 28 trays or 7 stools; Cove can make 18 trays or 9 stools. Which specialization and exchange can give both positive gains?
macro.Choice A: Fern makes stools, Cove makes trays; 3 trays per stool
macro.Choice B: Fern makes trays, Cove makes stools; 5 trays per stool
macro.Choice C: Fern makes trays, Cove makes stools; 1 tray per stool
macro.Choice D: Fern makes trays, Cove makes stools; 3 trays per stool
macro.Correct Answer: D — Fern makes trays, Cove makes stools; 3 trays per stool
macro.Feedback: A stool costs Fern 4 trays and Cove 2. Cove has stool advantage and Fern tray advantage; a rate strictly between 2 and 4 trays per stool can benefit both.

macro.Common Misconception: Using output levels rather than opportunity-cost bounds.
macro.Question: Two studios have constant daily tradeoffs. Alder can make 21 prints or 7 models; Brook can make 20 prints or 10 models. Which proposal benefits both at the margin?
macro.Choice A: Brook exports models to Alder for 2.5 prints each
macro.Choice B: Alder exports models to Brook for 2.5 prints each
macro.Choice C: Brook exports models to Alder for 3.5 prints each
macro.Choice D: Brook exports models to Alder for 1.5 prints each
macro.Correct Answer: A — Brook exports models to Alder for 2.5 prints each
macro.Feedback: Alder gives up 3 prints per model; Brook gives up 2. Brook can supply models at a rate above 2 that still saves Alder prints compared with making models itself.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing total gains with mutual benefit under a particular exchange.
macro.Question: Two firms specialize and create 40 extra units of combined output. A proposed exchange gives all 40 extra units to one firm. What is the strongest conclusion?
macro.Choice A: Specialization created aggregate gains, but the proposed distribution may not benefit both firms
macro.Choice B: Comparative advantage is disproved whenever gains are unequal.
macro.Choice C: Any increase in combined output makes every exchange mutually beneficial
macro.Choice D: Equal gains are required before specialization can raise output
macro.Correct Answer: A — Specialization created aggregate gains, but the proposed distribution may not benefit both firms
macro.Feedback: Higher combined output creates potential gains; terms of trade determine how those gains are divided.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring the value of the next-best use of time.
macro.Question: A high-productivity surgeon is also the fastest typist in a clinic. The surgeon hires an assistant to type notes. What completes the economic explanation?
macro.Choice A: The assistant must have an absolute advantage in typing.
macro.Choice B: The surgeon cannot have comparative advantage in surgery.
macro.Choice C: The surgeon’s opportunity cost of typing is high because typing displaces valuable surgical time.
macro.Choice D: Specialization matters only in international trade.
macro.Correct Answer: C — The surgeon’s opportunity cost of typing is high because typing displaces valuable surgical time.
macro.Feedback: The surgeon delegates typing because the forgone value of surgical work makes typing costly for the surgeon.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating aggregate efficiency and distribution as the same criterion.
macro.Question: Country A has comparative advantage in software. After trade opens, software employment rises but some hardware workers lose jobs. Which evaluation is strongest?
macro.Choice A: The job losses prove comparative advantage was calculated incorrectly.
macro.Choice B: All workers must gain for trade to be efficient.
macro.Choice C: Comparative advantage predicts no sectoral adjustment.
macro.Choice D: Aggregate gains can coexist with transition costs and distributional losses.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Aggregate gains can coexist with transition costs and distributional losses.
macro.Feedback: Trade can expand total gains while requiring adjustment and creating identifiable losers.

macro.Common Misconception: Forgetting that comparative advantage in one good implies the other producer has it in the other good.
macro.Question: At constant tradeoffs, Iona makes 32 badges or 8 signs daily; Paz makes 18 badges or 9 signs. Paz offers one sign for 3 badges. Express the offered trading price in signs per badge. Which statement correctly identifies the exporter of badges and compares that price with both producers’ opportunity costs?
macro.Choice A: Paz exports badges; 3 signs per badge lies between the relevant costs
macro.Choice B: Iona exports badges; 1/3 sign per badge lies between costs of 1/4 and 1/2
macro.Choice C: Iona exports signs because its badge output is greater
macro.Choice D: Both have sign advantage because 3 exceeds both sign-output ratios
macro.Correct Answer: B — Iona exports badges; 1/3 sign per badge lies between costs of 1/4 and 1/2
macro.Feedback: Iona gives up 1/4 sign per badge and Paz 1/2. Iona exports badges and obtains 1/3 sign each, which is strictly between those costs.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating comparative advantage as immutable.
macro.Question: At constant tradeoffs, Slate can make 36 tiles or 12 sinks; Moss can make 24 tiles or 12 sinks. Slate doubles sink capacity without changing tile capacity. Which contract could now give both positive gains?
macro.Choice A: Slate exports sinks for 1.75 tiles each
macro.Choice B: Moss exports sinks for 2.5 tiles each
macro.Choice C: Slate exports tiles for 0.4 sink each
macro.Choice D: Moss exports sinks for exactly 2 tiles each
macro.Correct Answer: A — Slate exports sinks for 1.75 tiles each
macro.Feedback: Slate's sink cost falls from 3 to 1.5 tiles while Moss's remains 2. Slate now exports sinks; 1.75 lies between their costs. At 2, Moss is indifferent.

macro.Common Misconception: Reversing the opportunity-cost bounds.
macro.Question: With constant tradeoffs, Forge can make 36 panels or 12 motors; Harbor can make 20 panels or 10 motors. Forge imports a motor and pays an additional shipping cost of 0.5 panel per motor. Which quoted panel price gives both positive gains?
macro.Choice A: 3 panels per motor
macro.Choice B: 2.25 panels per motor
macro.Choice C: 2 panels per motor
macro.Choice D: 2.75 panels per motor
macro.Correct Answer: B — 2.25 panels per motor
macro.Feedback: Forge's domestic cost is 3 panels; Harbor's is 2. Harbor requires a price above 2, while Forge requires price + 0.5 below 3. Only 2.25 is strictly between 2 and 2.5.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming the static model settles every long-run policy question.
macro.Question: Suppose learning-by-doing lowers a nation’s future opportunity cost in a good it does not currently produce. What does this imply?
macro.Choice A: Current comparative advantage may not fully describe future comparative advantage.
macro.Choice B: Opportunity costs can never change over time.
macro.Choice C: The nation must already have absolute advantage in that good.
macro.Choice D: Trade eliminates any reason to consider future productivity.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Current comparative advantage may not fully describe future comparative advantage.
macro.Feedback: Investment and learning can alter future relative costs, so dynamic considerations may matter.

macro.Common Misconception: Choosing the wrong opportunity-cost or net-gain criterion.
macro.Question: For one poster, Team A gives up 2 flyers and Team B gives up 5. Another pair of teams each gives up 3 flyers per poster. Which pair has a basis for gains from specialization in this two-good model?
macro.Choice A: Only the first pair, because its opportunity costs differ.
macro.Choice B: Only the second pair, because its opportunity costs match.
macro.Choice C: Both pairs, because having two teams is sufficient.
macro.Choice D: Neither pair, because both activities use scarce time.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Only the first pair, because its opportunity costs differ.
macro.Feedback: The first pair faces different tradeoffs: 2 versus 5 flyers per poster. The second pair has identical opportunity costs, so this model provides no comparative-advantage basis for specialization.

macro.Common Misconception: Choosing the wrong opportunity-cost or net-gain criterion.
macro.Question: Maya voluntarily exchanges her spare notebook for Lee’s spare pen, and Lee voluntarily agrees. Both understand what they will receive. What does their choice suggest?
macro.Choice A: They assign exactly the same value to the notebook and pen.
macro.Choice B: Maya expects a gain, while Lee expects a loss.
macro.Choice C: Each prefers what they receive to what they give up.
macro.Choice D: Lee expects a gain, while Maya expects a loss.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Each prefers what they receive to what they give up.
macro.Feedback: Voluntary acceptance suggests each expects a gain at the time of choice. Maya can prefer the pen while Lee prefers the notebook; their valuations need not be equal.

macro.Common Misconception: Choosing the wrong opportunity-cost or net-gain criterion.
macro.Question: Ana prepares 6 lessons per hour and Ben prepares 4. A coordinator concludes that Ana also has comparative advantage in lessons. What additional information would test that conclusion?
macro.Choice A: How much tutoring each gives up per lesson.
macro.Choice B: How many lessons Ana and Ben produce together.
macro.Choice C: Whether Ana can prepare any lessons at all.
macro.Choice D: Whether the lesson count is measured per hour or per day.
macro.Correct Answer: A — How much tutoring each gives up per lesson.
macro.Feedback: The output rates establish Ana’s absolute productivity advantage. Comparative advantage requires comparing what each sacrifices per lesson, such as tutoring sessions forgone. A higher lesson output by itself does not supply that comparison.

macro.Common Misconception: Choosing the wrong opportunity-cost or net-gain criterion.
macro.Question: Lena gives up 1 report to make a presentation; Omar gives up 3. A manager assigns the next presentation to Omar because his opportunity cost is higher. If either can prepare it, what correction follows?
macro.Choice A: Keep Omar; his assignment preserves 2 more reports.
macro.Choice B: Choose Lena; her assignment preserves 2 more reports.
macro.Choice C: Keep Omar; his assignment preserves 4 more reports.
macro.Choice D: Choose Lena; her assignment preserves 4 more reports.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Choose Lena; her assignment preserves 2 more reports.
macro.Feedback: Making the presentation costs Lena 1 forgone report instead of Omar’s 3. Assigning it to Lena preserves 3 - 1 = 2 reports. A higher opportunity cost is a reason to use that person in the alternative task.

macro.Common Misconception: Choosing the wrong opportunity-cost or net-gain criterion.
macro.Question: Lena gives up 1 report per presentation; Omar gives up 3. Lena offers one presentation to Omar for 2 reports. Ignoring exchange costs, who gains relative to doing the task themselves?
macro.Choice A: Only Lena: she gains 1 report while Omar loses 1.
macro.Choice B: Only Omar: he gains 1 report while Lena loses 1.
macro.Choice C: Neither: each loses 1 report at this rate.
macro.Choice D: Both: Lena receives 1 more report than her cost, and Omar saves 1 report.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Both: Lena receives 1 more report than her cost, and Omar saves 1 report.
macro.Feedback: Lena receives 2 reports for a presentation costing her 1, a gain of 1. Omar pays 2 reports rather than sacrificing 3 to make it himself, a saving of 1. The rate lies strictly between their costs.

macro.Common Misconception: Choosing the wrong opportunity-cost or net-gain criterion.
macro.Question: Nia can produce more of either good per hour than Sol. Yet each loaf costs Nia 2 shirts and Sol 1 shirt in forgone output. With constant tradeoffs and no trade costs, which proposed loaf-for-shirt exchange can benefit both?
macro.Choice A: Nia supplies loaves at 1.5 shirts per loaf.
macro.Choice B: Sol supplies loaves at 2.5 shirts per loaf.
macro.Choice C: Sol supplies loaves at 1.5 shirts per loaf.
macro.Choice D: Nia supplies loaves at 0.5 shirts per loaf.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Sol supplies loaves at 1.5 shirts per loaf.
macro.Feedback: Sol’s cost of a loaf is 1 shirt, below Nia’s 2. At 1.5 shirts, Sol receives 0.5 shirt above cost and Nia saves 0.5 shirt relative to making a loaf. Absolute productivity does not settle this comparison.

macro.Common Misconception: Choosing the wrong opportunity-cost or net-gain criterion.
macro.Question: Specialization frees resources worth 60 units of output, but the proposed shipping plan uses 70 units. A different carrier would use 35 units and require 10 units of extra monitoring. Which plan increases net resources?
macro.Choice A: Both carriers: the original gains 60 units and the alternative gains 95.
macro.Choice B: Only the alternative carrier: the original loses 10 units and the alternative gains 15.
macro.Choice C: Only the original carrier: monitoring makes the alternative lose 45 units.
macro.Choice D: Neither carrier: any positive exchange cost eliminates specialization gains.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Only the alternative carrier: the original loses 10 units and the alternative gains 15.
macro.Feedback: Net resources are 60-70=-10 under the original plan and 60-35-10=15 under the alternative. Real exchange and monitoring costs must be netted against production gains.

macro.Common Misconception: Choosing the wrong opportunity-cost or net-gain criterion.
macro.Question: Opening trade yields consumer gains of $90 million and producer losses of $50 million. Moving displaced workers uses $12 million of real resources. A proposed $20 million domestic transfer to producers costs another $5 million to administer. Which evaluation includes efficiency and distribution?
macro.Choice A: Net national gain is $3 million; producers remain $30 million below their initial position after the transfer.
macro.Choice B: Net national gain is $43 million; producers recover fully because the transfer exceeds adjustment costs.
macro.Choice C: Net national gain is $23 million; producers remain $30 million below their initial position after the transfer.
macro.Choice D: Net national gain is $28 million; producers recover fully because aggregate consumer gains exceed their losses.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Net national gain is $23 million; producers remain $30 million below their initial position after the transfer.
macro.Feedback: The domestic transfer redistributes rather than destroys surplus. Net gain is 90-50-12-5=23. Producers lose 50 and receive 20, leaving a 30 loss. Positive aggregate gains do not establish that compensation is complete.

macro.Common Misconception: Choosing the wrong opportunity-cost or net-gain criterion.
macro.Question: A gives up 6 grain per machine and B gives up 4. Technology lowers A’s cost to 3 while B’s cost stays 4. They had traded at 5 grain per machine. Which conclusion follows under constant costs?
macro.Choice A: Machine comparative advantage stays with B; a rate between 3 and 4 benefits both because only absolute productivity changed.
macro.Choice B: Machine comparative advantage switches to A; the old rate of 5 still benefits both because it exceeds A’s new cost.
macro.Choice C: Neither has machine comparative advantage now; technological progress eliminates the need to compare forgone grain.
macro.Choice D: Machine comparative advantage switches to A; the old rate no longer benefits the importer, and a rate between 3 and 4 can benefit both.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Machine comparative advantage switches to A; the old rate no longer benefits the importer, and a rate between 3 and 4 can benefit both.
macro.Feedback: Before the change B exports machines at a cost of 4 while A saves relative to 6. Afterward A has lower cost, 3 versus 4. If A exports at 5, B would pay more than producing; the new strict interval is 3 to 4.

macro.Common Misconception: Choosing the wrong opportunity-cost or net-gain criterion.
macro.Question: At constant tradeoffs, A makes 30 filters or 10 pumps; B makes 24 filters or 12 pumps. B exports pumps and pays shipping of 0.4 filter per pump. Which price gives both positive gains and gives B the larger per-pump gain measured in filters?
macro.Choice A: 2.8 filters per pump
macro.Choice B: 2.5 filters per pump
macro.Choice C: 2.4 filters per pump
macro.Choice D: 3 filters per pump
macro.Correct Answer: A — 2.8 filters per pump
macro.Feedback: B's net gain is price - 2 - 0.4; A's is 3 - price. At 2.8 the gains are 0.4 and 0.2. At 2.5 A gains more; 2.4 or 3 leaves one party indifferent.

macro.Common Misconception: Choosing the wrong opportunity-cost or net-gain criterion.
macro.Question: Per hour a manager can make 6 sales or complete 12 accounts; an assistant can make 2 sales or complete 8 accounts. Each sale nets $100. Completing 24 accounts through the assistant also requires one hour of the manager’s supervision. Should the manager delegate the accounts, holding total paid hours fixed?
macro.Choice A: Yes: delegation allows 6 additional sales because the assistant’s forgone sales are the only cost to compare.
macro.Choice B: Indifferent: delegation sacrifices 12 sales including supervision, the same as completing the accounts personally.
macro.Choice C: No: delegation sacrifices 18 sales while direct typing sacrifices 8, so direct typing gains 10 sales.
macro.Choice D: No: the manager’s higher speed at both tasks proves delegation always lowers total sales.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Indifferent: delegation sacrifices 12 sales including supervision, the same as completing the accounts personally.
macro.Feedback: Direct typing takes 24/12=2 manager hours, forgoing 12 sales. Delegation takes 24/8=3 assistant hours, forgoing 6 sales, plus 6 sales forgone during manager supervision: also 12. Delegation does not improve the outcome under the specified measure.

macro.Common Misconception: Choosing the wrong opportunity-cost or net-gain criterion.
macro.Question: A trade agreement yields gross national gains of $100 million before $30 million of real adjustment costs. Before adjustment costs, consumers gain $160 million and displaced workers lose $60 million. A $60 million domestic compensation transfer would fully offset that loss but costs $15 million to administer. Which evaluation is correct?
macro.Choice A: Net gain after administration is -$5 million; the compensation payment must be deducted again as a resource loss.
macro.Choice B: Net gain after administration is $70 million; the transfer automatically occurs when aggregate surplus rises.
macro.Choice C: Net gain after administration is $55 million; full compensation is feasible under the stated estimates but requires the transfer to be made.
macro.Choice D: Net gain after administration is $115 million; compensation increases national surplus by the amount workers receive.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Net gain after administration is $55 million; full compensation is feasible under the stated estimates but requires the transfer to be made.
macro.Feedback: Gross gains already net the $60 million worker loss: 160-60=100. National net gain is 100-30-15=55; the domestic transfer is not an additional resource loss. Workers receive compensation only if the policy is implemented.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “It falls because a stronger dollar against the euro makes every other currency cheaper” in this nominal exchange rates task.
macro.Question: The U.S. dollar buys 10 percent more euros but 5 percent fewer yen. From these bilateral changes alone, what follows about the euro price of one yen?
macro.Choice A: It rises because one yen buys more dollars and each dollar buys more euros
macro.Choice B: It falls because a stronger dollar against the euro makes every other currency cheaper
macro.Choice C: It is unchanged because the two dollar quotations use reciprocal units
macro.Choice D: Its direction is indeterminate because one dollar quote rises and the other falls
macro.Correct Answer: A — It rises because one yen buys more dollars and each dollar buys more euros
macro.Feedback: Euros per yen equals (euros per dollar)/(yen per dollar). Its factor is 1.10/0.95 > 1; the yen appreciates against the euro. Both bilateral dollar quotations are needed.

macro.Question: An agency quotes £0.75 per U.S. dollar with no fee, then £0.84 per dollar with a 3 percent fee added to the converted dollar charge. A £420 booking keeps its pound price. What is the new dollar cost, and what fee rate would exactly eliminate the benefit of the better quote?
macro.Choice A: $515; a 10.7 percent fee
macro.Choice B: $515; a 12 percent fee
macro.Choice C: $485; a 12 percent fee
macro.Choice D: $560; a 3 percent fee
macro.Correct Answer: B — $515; a 12 percent fee
macro.Feedback: The old cost is £420/(£0.75/$) = $560. The new pre-fee cost is £420/(£0.84/$) = $500; with 3 percent added it is $515. Break-even requires 500(1+f)=560, giving f=12 percent.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Alder investment rises by less than $15 billion” in this international transactions and identities task.
macro.Question: Two countries initially have S = $700 billion and I = $750 billion. In Alder, saving rises $65 billion while investment rises an unknown amount. In Brin, saving rises $40 billion and investment rises $25 billion. What condition makes Alder end with a smaller trade deficit than Brin but still a deficit?
macro.Choice A: Alder investment rises by less than $15 billion
macro.Choice B: Alder investment rises by more than $50 billion but less than $65 billion
macro.Choice C: Alder investment rises by more than $15 billion but less than $50 billion
macro.Choice D: Alder investment rises by exactly $65 billion
macro.Correct Answer: C — Alder investment rises by more than $15 billion but less than $50 billion
macro.Feedback: Brin ends with NX = −50 + 40 − 25 = −35. Alder ends at NX = −50 + 65 − ΔI = 15 − ΔI. Requiring −35 < 15 − ΔI < 0 gives 15 < ΔI < 50, in billions.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Whether the nominal exchange rate is quoted reciprocally, since taking a reciprocal removes real basket gaps” in this real exchange rates and purchasing power task.
macro.Question: In common currency, identical traded goods have equal prices across two countries, but broad consumer baskets remain differently priced. An analyst predicts that removing shipping costs alone must equalize the broad baskets. Which missing evidence matters most?
macro.Choice A: Whether the nominal exchange rate is quoted reciprocally, since taking a reciprocal removes real basket gaps
macro.Choice B: Whether domestic saving equals investment, since balanced trade is sufficient for broad-basket PPP
macro.Choice C: Whether traded-goods PPP holds, since that alone requires every consumer basket to match
macro.Choice D: Whether remaining basket gaps come from nontraded services, quality differences or local taxes that shipping reform does not remove
macro.Correct Answer: D — Whether remaining basket gaps come from nontraded services, quality differences or local taxes that shipping reform does not remove
macro.Feedback: Traded-goods arbitrage can coexist with broad-basket differences. Shipping reform does not remove nontraded components, basket composition or local taxes; identifying the sources of the remaining gap is necessary.

macro.Common Misconception: Assumes reciprocal exchange-rate percentage changes have equal absolute magnitudes.
macro.Question: A dollar appreciates 25 percent from 0.80 euro per dollar to 1.00. How much does the euro depreciate in reciprocal terms?
macro.Choice A: 25 percent
macro.Choice B: 5 percent
macro.Choice C: 31.25 percent
macro.Choice D: 20 percent
macro.Correct Answer: D — 20 percent
macro.Feedback: The reciprocal moves from $1.25 per euro to $1.00, a $0.25 decline on a $1.25 base, or 20 percent.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Yes; bilateral appreciation and depreciation use the same percentage base” in this nominal exchange rates task.
macro.Question: The dollar rises 20 percent in euros per dollar. Must the euro fall 20 percent in dollars per euro?
macro.Choice A: Yes; both reciprocal quotations rise together
macro.Choice B: No; reciprocal percentage changes have different denominators
macro.Choice C: Yes; bilateral appreciation and depreciation use the same percentage base
macro.Choice D: No; the reciprocal falls 40 percent
macro.Correct Answer: B — No; reciprocal percentage changes have different denominators
macro.Feedback: If the rate moves from e to 1.2e, its reciprocal moves to 1/1.2 of its old value, a 16.7 percent decline.

macro.Common Misconception: Confuses a decimal rate of change with percentage units while reversing the currency quotation.
macro.Question: The pound appreciates from $1.50 to $1.65 per pound. Approximately how much does the dollar depreciate against the pound using reciprocal rates?
macro.Choice A: 0.1 percent
macro.Choice B: 9.1 percent
macro.Choice C: 10 percent
macro.Choice D: 15 percent
macro.Correct Answer: B — 9.1 percent
macro.Feedback: The reciprocal moves from 0.6667 to about 0.6061 pound per dollar, a decline of roughly 9.1 percent.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Wheat prices exclude storage and transport from arbitrage decisions” in this real exchange rates and purchasing power task.
macro.Question: Why does the law of one price support PPP more strongly for wheat than for apartments?
macro.Choice A: Wheat prices exclude storage and transport from arbitrage decisions
macro.Choice B: Apartment rents represent identical tradable units across countries
macro.Choice C: Wheat is easier to trade and arbitrage across locations
macro.Choice D: Housing services respond more directly to exchange-rate quotations
macro.Correct Answer: C — Wheat is easier to trade and arbitrage across locations
macro.Feedback: Cross-border arbitrage is more feasible for standardized tradable goods than for location-specific housing services.

macro.Question: A price-taking firm is one that:
macro.Choice A: Cannot individually influence the market price
macro.Choice B: Sets any price it wants
macro.Choice C: Faces no competitors
macro.Choice D: Always earns zero profit
macro.Correct Answer: A — Cannot individually influence the market price
macro.Feedback: In a competitive market, an individual firm is too small to affect the market price.

macro.Question: A competitive market has:
macro.Choice A: Many buyers and sellers, none with much price control
macro.Choice B: One seller who controls the price
macro.Choice C: Only government buyers
macro.Choice D: No price signals
macro.Correct Answer: A — Many buyers and sellers, none with much price control
macro.Feedback: A competitive market has many buyers and sellers, each with little control over price.

macro.Question: A price taker is a buyer or seller who:
macro.Choice A: Accepts the market price as given
macro.Choice B: Sets the market price alone
macro.Choice C: Creates a legal maximum price
macro.Choice D: Always avoids trade
macro.Correct Answer: A — Accepts the market price as given
macro.Feedback: A price taker accepts the market price because no single buyer or seller controls it.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming a small firm can raise price without losing demand.
macro.Question: A town has many independent sellers of identical notebooks. Customers can compare prices and switch stores at negligible cost. One store raises its price while others do not. Which outcome is most consistent with a competitive market?
macro.Choice A: It loses many customers because comparable alternatives limit its pricing discretion.
macro.Choice B: It keeps most customers because many sellers guarantee each store a loyal share.
macro.Choice C: It raises the market price because one seller’s posted price defines equilibrium.
macro.Choice D: It forces rival prices down because customers cannot compare standardized products.
macro.Correct Answer: A — It loses many customers because comparable alternatives limit its pricing discretion.
