macro.Feedback: Independent rivals, a standardized good and easy comparison make close alternatives available. An individual store has little ability to sustain an above-market price.

macro.Question: An economist points to a wheat farmer selling at the going market price. Why is the farmer a price taker?
macro.Choice A: The farmer's individual output is too small to control the market price
macro.Choice B: The farmer legally sets the national wheat price
macro.Choice C: The farmer faces no competitors
macro.Choice D: The farmer can ignore supply and demand
macro.Correct Answer: A — The farmer's individual output is too small to control the market price
macro.Feedback: A price taker accepts the market price because no single seller has enough influence to set it.

macro.Question: A market has many buyers but only one seller, and that seller has control over price. Is this a competitive market?
macro.Choice A: No, because one seller has market power
macro.Choice B: Yes, because many buyers are enough
macro.Choice C: Yes, because all markets are competitive
macro.Choice D: No, because buyers never matter
macro.Correct Answer: A — No, because one seller has market power
macro.Feedback: A competitive market requires many buyers and sellers, with no single participant controlling price.

macro.Question: A price taker is a seller that:
macro.Choice A: Accepts the market price because its own output is too small to move it.
macro.Choice B: Sets the market price for all firms.
macro.Choice C: Has no production costs.
macro.Choice D: Faces no buyers.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Accepts the market price because its own output is too small to move it.
macro.Feedback: Price takers choose output but cannot materially influence the market price.

macro.Common Misconception: Reversing the effects of entry and switching costs.
macro.Question: A market becomes more competitive when:
macro.Choice A: One seller acquires rivals.
macro.Choice B: Entry and switching become easier.
macro.Choice C: Products lose all substitutes.
macro.Choice D: Buyers receive less price information.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Entry and switching become easier.
macro.Feedback: Easier entry and switching strengthen competitive pressure.

macro.Common Misconception: Failing to apply competition logic to digital markets.
macro.Question: An online marketplace makes prices easy to compare and lets buyers switch with one click. This tends to:
macro.Choice A: Create a monopoly automatically.
macro.Choice B: Make demand for every seller inelastic.
macro.Choice C: Reduce each seller’s ability to charge above rivals.
macro.Choice D: Eliminate all production costs.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Reduce each seller’s ability to charge above rivals.
macro.Feedback: Transparent prices and low switching costs constrain seller pricing power.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing participation with market power.
macro.Question: A price-taking seller is one that:
macro.Choice A: Sets any price without losing customers.
macro.Choice B: Controls the total market supply.
macro.Choice C: Cannot noticeably affect the market price by changing its own output.
macro.Choice D: Faces no competitors.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Cannot noticeably affect the market price by changing its own output.
macro.Feedback: A price taker is too small relative to the market to influence the market price.

macro.Common Misconception: Using the everyday meaning of rivalry instead of the market structure.
macro.Question: Which feature most supports a competitive market?
macro.Choice A: One dominant seller.
macro.Choice B: Legal barriers blocking entry.
macro.Choice C: A unique product with no substitutes.
macro.Choice D: Many buyers and sellers with no single participant controlling price.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Many buyers and sellers with no single participant controlling price.
macro.Feedback: Competitive markets disperse market power among many participants.

macro.Common Misconception: Using temporary profit as conclusive evidence of market power.
macro.Question: Which observation most strongly contradicts the strict competitive-market model?
macro.Choice A: A firm can raise price persistently without losing many customers.
macro.Choice B: A firm earns accounting profit in one month.
macro.Choice C: Market demand changes over time.
macro.Choice D: Some firms have different bookkeeping methods.
macro.Correct Answer: A — A firm can raise price persistently without losing many customers.
macro.Feedback: Persistent price discretion indicates a downward-sloping firm demand curve rather than price taking.

macro.Common Misconception: Reversing the effect of easier switching.
macro.Question: A new technology lowers switching costs to nearly zero. Holding other factors constant, what competitive effect is most likely?
macro.Choice A: Sellers face more elastic demand and less pricing discretion.
macro.Choice B: Sellers gain more market power.
macro.Choice C: Entry becomes legally impossible.
macro.Choice D: Market demand becomes perfectly inelastic.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Sellers face more elastic demand and less pricing discretion.
macro.Feedback: When customers can switch easily, a price increase causes a larger loss of buyers.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating any chosen price as market power.
macro.Question: A wheat farmer sells at the posted market price because charging more would cause buyers to switch. This illustrates:
macro.Choice A: Price-taking behavior.
macro.Choice B: Monopoly pricing.
macro.Choice C: A binding price floor.
macro.Choice D: Perfect price discrimination.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Price-taking behavior.
macro.Feedback: The farmer accepts the market price because close substitutes are readily available.

macro.Common Misconception: Overstating the influence of one small firm.
macro.Question: If one small seller exits a highly competitive market, the market price usually changes little because:
macro.Choice A: Demand becomes perfectly vertical.
macro.Choice B: The seller represents a tiny share of total market supply.
macro.Choice C: The seller owns a patent.
macro.Choice D: All remaining sellers coordinate prices.
macro.Correct Answer: B — The seller represents a tiny share of total market supply.
macro.Feedback: A small participant has little effect on total market supply.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming more concentration increases competition.
macro.Question: Which change would make a market less competitive?
macro.Choice A: More firms entering.
macro.Choice B: Lower switching costs for buyers.
macro.Choice C: A merger that leaves one firm with substantial control over output.
macro.Choice D: Better price information.
macro.Correct Answer: C — A merger that leaves one firm with substantial control over output.
macro.Feedback: Concentration can give firms greater ability to influence price.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring how entry responds to profit opportunities.
macro.Question: Why does easy entry matter in a competitive market?
macro.Choice A: Economic profits attract new sellers, reducing market supply as existing firms divide sales among more rivals.
macro.Choice B: Economic profits attract new sellers, lowering each entrant’s costs until all firms share the same cost curve.
macro.Choice C: Economic profits attract new sellers, raising market demand as buyers redistribute purchases among rivals.
macro.Choice D: Economic profits attract new sellers, increasing competition and making those profits harder to sustain.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Economic profits attract new sellers, increasing competition and making those profits harder to sustain.
macro.Feedback: Profit opportunities attract entrants when entry is easy. Their additional supply puts downward pressure on price and economic profits. Redistributing sales does not itself increase market demand, and entry does not make firms’ production costs identical.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating market structures as all-or-nothing labels.
macro.Question: A restaurant market has many sellers, but each offers a differentiated experience. Which statement is best?
macro.Choice A: The market may be competitive in a broad sense without meeting the strict price-taking benchmark.
macro.Choice B: The large number of restaurants makes each a price taker despite customers’ preferences for particular experiences.
macro.Choice C: Differentiation gives each restaurant the pricing freedom of a sole supplier because other dining experiences are distinct.
macro.Choice D: Competition should be assessed only through price differences, since differences in service quality do not affect buyer choice.
macro.Correct Answer: A — The market may be competitive in a broad sense without meeting the strict price-taking benchmark.
macro.Feedback: Many restaurants can compete for customers even when differentiated experiences give individual sellers some price discretion. Differentiation means the strict identical-product price-taking benchmark need not hold, but competing restaurants can still constrain each other’s prices.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming a small firm can raise price without losing demand.
macro.Question: A firm in a competitive market raises price above the market price while rivals do not. The likely result is:
macro.Choice A: Higher sales because price signals quality.
macro.Choice B: A sharp loss of customers to close substitutes.
macro.Choice C: No change because buyers cannot switch.
macro.Choice D: Automatic market-wide inflation.
macro.Correct Answer: B — A sharp loss of customers to close substitutes.
macro.Feedback: Buyers can switch to other sellers offering the same or similar product.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring how entry barriers protect incumbents.
macro.Question: A licensing rule sharply limits new sellers. What is the most direct competitive effect?
macro.Choice A: The rule guarantees lower prices.
macro.Choice B: The rule creates perfect information.
macro.Choice C: Reduced entry can increase the market power of existing sellers.
macro.Choice D: The rule makes every firm a price taker.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Reduced entry can increase the market power of existing sellers.
macro.Feedback: Barriers can weaken competitive pressure and preserve market power.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming seller count alone determines competitiveness.
macro.Question: A market has many sellers, but buyers face high search costs and cannot compare prices. Why might price-taking be weakened?
macro.Choice A: Many sellers always eliminate market power.
macro.Choice B: High search costs strengthen competition by making buyers compare prices more carefully.
macro.Choice C: Price comparison is unrelated to competition.
macro.Choice D: Information frictions can give individual sellers some pricing discretion.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Information frictions can give individual sellers some pricing discretion.
macro.Feedback: Competition also depends on buyer information and ability to switch.

macro.Common Misconception: Counting labels instead of economic control.
macro.Question: A market appears to have many separate sellers, but four firms own most capacity through subsidiaries. What should an analyst examine?
macro.Choice A: Only the number of storefronts.
macro.Choice B: Whether prices are written in dollars.
macro.Choice C: Whether consumers enjoy variety.
macro.Choice D: Which firms control capacity, rather than the number of brands.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Which firms control capacity, rather than the number of brands.
macro.Feedback: Competitive pressure depends on independent control of capacity and decisions.

macro.Common Misconception: Equating legal permission to enter with practical competitive viability.
macro.Question: A market has free entry but strong network effects favor the largest platform. What is the best conclusion?
macro.Choice A: Legal freedom to enter makes the incumbent face perfectly elastic demand despite its user network.
macro.Choice B: Formal entry may be easy while effective competition remains weak.
macro.Choice C: Network effects remove the incumbent’s advantage because every entrant can start with an equally valuable user network.
macro.Choice D: The incumbent’s user advantage implies formal entry is restricted, so the premise of free entry cannot hold.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Formal entry may be easy while effective competition remains weak.
macro.Feedback: Permission to enter does not ensure that a new platform can attract enough users to compete effectively. When a platform becomes more valuable as its user base grows, the incumbent’s network can be an entry obstacle even without legal restrictions. That advantage does not establish perfectly elastic demand or equal starting networks.

macro.Common Misconception: Listing many traders without explaining why individual price control is limited.
macro.Question: Two exchanges each list hundreds of sellers of standardized grain. On X, buyers can immediately compare prices and switch suppliers. On Y, contracts impose large switching charges. Which claim best separates seller count from effective competition?
macro.Choice A: An individual seller likely has less pricing discretion on Y because switching charges protect buyer choice.
macro.Choice B: The same seller count ensures equal pricing discretion even when switching costs differ.
macro.Choice C: An individual seller likely has less pricing discretion on X because buyers can readily use competing offers.
macro.Choice D: Standardization gives each seller a unique product, preventing price taking on either exchange.
macro.Correct Answer: C — An individual seller likely has less pricing discretion on X because buyers can readily use competing offers.
macro.Feedback: Many sellers support competition when buyers can substitute among their offers. Price transparency and low switching costs on X make an individual price increase harder to sustain. Seller count alone does not establish equal competitive pressure.

macro.Common Misconception: Misidentifying the conditions that limit market power.
macro.Question: Which seller is most clearly a price taker?
macro.Choice A: A patented-drug producer.
macro.Choice B: A small grain farmer selling a standardized crop at a market quotation.
macro.Choice C: A sole local utility.
macro.Choice D: A platform with locked-in users.
macro.Correct Answer: B — A small grain farmer selling a standardized crop at a market quotation.
macro.Feedback: A small grain farmer supplies a tiny share of a standardized market. Buyers can turn to other farmers, so this farmer generally accepts the quoted market price.

macro.Common Misconception: Misidentifying the conditions that limit market power.
macro.Question: What makes sustained economic profit difficult in a competitive market?
macro.Choice A: A single seller restricts output.
macro.Choice B: Buyers face high switching costs.
macro.Choice C: Entry by new firms expands supply.
macro.Choice D: Products become more unique.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Entry by new firms expands supply.
macro.Feedback: Entry adds market supply when existing firms earn economic profit. The resulting competitive pressure makes that profit harder to sustain.

macro.Common Misconception: Misidentifying the conditions that limit market power.
macro.Question: A market has many buyers and sellers and standardized products. What does this imply about an individual seller’s ability to set price?
macro.Choice A: Each seller controls market demand.
macro.Choice B: Each seller can raise price without losing sales.
macro.Choice C: Buyers cannot compare offers.
macro.Choice D: An individual seller faces strong pressure to accept the market price.
macro.Correct Answer: D — An individual seller faces strong pressure to accept the market price.
macro.Feedback: With many sellers offering standardized products, buyers can switch to competing offers. An individual seller therefore has little scope to charge above the market price.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “A 4 percent asset return; no further currency change” in this nominal exchange rates task.
macro.Question: The dollar-per-yen quote rises 10% then falls 10%, and a yen-denominated asset gains 4%. A costless hedge could have fixed the original conversion rate. A dealer says the currency changes cancel, so the hedge would not change the dollar return. Is that claim correct?
macro.Choice A: Yes. The changes cancel exactly, giving 4% with or without the hedge and no remaining quote difference.
macro.Choice B: No. The unhedged return is 3% exactly; a 1% appreciation exactly restores the currency quote.
macro.Choice C: No. The unhedged return is 2.96% versus 4% with the hedge; restoring the original quote alone requires about 1.01% appreciation.
macro.Choice D: No. The unhedged return is 5.04%, so the currency movement improves on the fixed-conversion return.
macro.Correct Answer: C — No. The unhedged return is 2.96% versus 4% with the hedge; restoring the original quote alone requires about 1.01% appreciation.
macro.Feedback: The quote factor is 1.10×0.90=0.99, so the unhedged asset return is 0.99×1.04−1=2.96%. A fixed original conversion preserves the 4% yen return under the stated costless hedge. Restoring the quote requires 1/0.99−1≈1.01%, not an exact 1%.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The foreign-exchange rate becomes the price in the loanable-funds market” in this open economy policy transmission task.
macro.Question: Political risk raises desired NCO. Why does this shift demand for loanable funds right and tend to raise the real interest rate?
macro.Choice A: The foreign-exchange rate becomes the price in the loanable-funds market
macro.Choice B: Government purchases replace domestic investment in the saving identity
macro.Choice C: National saving must finance both domestic investment and the larger NCO
macro.Choice D: Household consumption becomes part of NCO when political risk rises
macro.Correct Answer: C — National saving must finance both domestic investment and the larger NCO
macro.Feedback: National saving finances I + NCO, so a larger desired NCO raises total demand for loanable funds at each real interest rate.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “NCO becomes positive when investment exceeds saving” in this capital flows and net capital outflow task.
macro.Question: Why can a net capital inflow help finance domestic investment above national saving?
macro.Choice A: Domestic investment is subtracted from GDP
macro.Choice B: Foreign purchases of domestic assets provide external financing
macro.Choice C: Imports are counted as domestic saving
macro.Choice D: NCO becomes positive when investment exceeds saving
macro.Correct Answer: B — Foreign purchases of domestic assets provide external financing
macro.Feedback: When I exceeds S, NCO = S − I is negative; the counterpart is net financing from abroad.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Rises” in this nominal exchange rates task.
macro.Question: When the domestic currency depreciates, its purchasing power over foreign goods generally:
macro.Choice A: Rises
macro.Choice B: Remains fixed by definition
macro.Choice C: Becomes equal to domestic inflation
macro.Choice D: Falls
macro.Correct Answer: D — Falls
macro.Feedback: A depreciated currency buys fewer units of foreign currency and therefore less foreign output, other things equal.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “It rises about 6 percent” in this nominal exchange rates task.
macro.Question: A Japanese product's yen price rises 4 percent while the yen depreciates 10 percent against the dollar. Approximately what happens to its dollar price?
macro.Choice A: It rises about 6 percent
macro.Choice B: It falls about 6.4 percent
macro.Choice C: It rises about 14.4 percent
macro.Choice D: It falls about 14 percent
macro.Correct Answer: B — It falls about 6.4 percent
macro.Feedback: The dollar price changes by 1.04×0.90 − 1 = −0.064, so it falls about 6.4 percent.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “It lowers the domestic money supply by identity” in this open economy policy transmission task.
macro.Question: Why does a real currency appreciation tend to reduce aggregate demand, holding its other components fixed?
macro.Choice A: It lowers net exports, a component of aggregate demand
macro.Choice B: It lowers the domestic money supply by identity
macro.Choice C: It raises government purchases
macro.Choice D: It shifts long-run aggregate supply left
macro.Correct Answer: A — It lowers net exports, a component of aggregate demand
macro.Feedback: Relatively expensive domestic goods reduce exports and encourage imports, lowering NX and AD.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Identical to foreign assets” in this capital flows and net capital outflow task.
macro.Question: In the standard model, a higher domestic real interest rate tends to make domestic assets:
macro.Choice A: Identical to foreign assets
macro.Choice B: Unrelated to capital flows
macro.Choice C: More attractive relative to foreign assets
macro.Choice D: Less attractive relative to foreign assets
macro.Correct Answer: C — More attractive relative to foreign assets
macro.Feedback: A higher return draws funds toward domestic assets, other things equal.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Zero NCO and a trade deficit” in this international transactions and identities task.
macro.Question: If national saving is less than domestic investment, which combination is consistent with the identities?
macro.Choice A: Zero NCO and a trade deficit
macro.Choice B: Negative NCO and a trade deficit
macro.Choice C: Positive NCO and a trade surplus
macro.Choice D: Positive NCO and balanced trade
macro.Correct Answer: B — Negative NCO and a trade deficit
macro.Feedback: S − I equals NCO, so S below I makes NCO negative; NX = NCO makes net exports negative as well.

macro.Common Misconception: Does not multiply the dollar amount by the stated yen-per-dollar quotation.
macro.Question: At 150 yen per dollar, $20 buys:
macro.Choice A: 750 yen
macro.Choice D: 170 yen
macro.Correct Answer: C — 3,000 yen
macro.Feedback: Twenty dollars times 150 yen per dollar equals 3,000 yen.

macro.Common Misconception: Does not multiply the dollar amount by the stated yen-per-dollar quotation.
macro.Question: At 120 yen per dollar, how many yen can $75 purchase?
macro.Correct Answer: B — 9,000 yen
macro.Feedback: Multiply $75 by 120 yen per dollar to obtain 9,000 yen.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “It falls by C $7,000” in this nominal exchange rates task.
macro.Question: A Canadian firm compares converting the same US$200,000 receipt at 1.35 versus 1.28 Canadian dollars per U.S. dollar. Ignoring fees, how does its Canadian-dollar revenue change?
macro.Choice A: It falls by C$7,000
macro.Choice B: It rises by C$27,000
macro.Choice C: It falls by C$14,000
macro.Choice D: It rises by C$14,000
macro.Correct Answer: C — It falls by C$14,000
macro.Feedback: Revenue changes from C$270,000 to C$256,000, a decline of C$14,000.

macro.Common Misconception: Multiplies a euro price by euros per dollar instead of dividing to obtain dollars.
macro.Question: A hotel costs 240 euros. At 0.80 euro per dollar, what is its dollar price?
macro.Feedback: Divide 240 euros by 0.80 euro per dollar: the hotel costs $300.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
macro.Question: A higher price can overstate inflation when the product also has:
macro.Choice A: Higher quality
macro.Choice B: Lower quality only
macro.Choice C: No market value
macro.Choice D: No consumer use
macro.Correct Answer: A — Higher quality
macro.Feedback: Some price increases reflect quality improvement.

macro.Common Misconception: Compares total bills instead of their increases, or ignores the stipulated substitute basket.
macro.Question: A household initially buys two apples and two pears at $1 each, costing $4. Apples then cost $3 and pears still $1. The old basket now costs $8, but four pears cost $4 and are stipulated to give this household the same satisfaction. How much does the fixed-basket cost increase overstate the increase needed for that satisfaction?
macro.Choice A: Understates by $4: fixed-basket cost is unchanged; the equally satisfactory basket’s cost rises $4
macro.Choice B: Overstates by $4: fixed-basket cost rises $4; the equally satisfactory basket’s cost is unchanged
macro.Choice C: Overstates by $8: the fixed basket’s entire $8 bill is an increase; substitute cost is unchanged
macro.Choice D: No overstatement: the fixed and equally satisfactory baskets each cost $4 more than before
macro.Correct Answer: B — Overstates by $4: fixed-basket cost rises $4; the equally satisfactory basket’s cost is unchanged
macro.Feedback: The fixed basket’s increase is 8−4=4. The equally satisfactory adjusted basket’s increase is 4−4=0. The fixed basket therefore overstates the needed increase by $4. The supplied satisfaction assumption makes this a cost comparison rather than a claim that arbitrary bundles are equivalent.

macro.Feedback: Substitution and quality improvements often mean CPI overstates true cost-of-living increases.

macro.Question: Suppose beef rises from $10 to $20 and chicken rises from $10 to $12. The CPI basket assumes consumers still buy equal amounts of beef and chicken, but consumers buy much more chicken. What is the main measurement problem?

macro.Question: A CPI basket keeps 10 pounds of beef even after beef becomes expensive and consumers switch to chicken. Which CPI problem is this?
macro.Choice A: Substitution bias
macro.Choice B: Discouraged-worker bias
macro.Choice C: GDP deflator bias

macro.Correct Answer: A — Substitution bias
macro.Feedback: A fixed basket can miss consumer substitution toward cheaper goods.

macro.Question: Why does substitution bias usually cause the CPI to overstate inflation?

macro.Choice B: Consumers never change behavior when prices change
macro.Choice C: The CPI ignores all prices
macro.Choice D: The CPI counts used goods twice
macro.Correct Answer: A — Consumers switch toward relatively cheaper substitutes
macro.Feedback: If consumers substitute, their actual cost of living may rise less than the fixed basket suggests.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
macro.Question: A smartphone costs more than an old flip phone but also provides far more services. Which CPI issue does this illustrate?

macro.Choice B: The CPI counts only unemployment

macro.Choice D: The new product must be an intermediate good
macro.Correct Answer: A — The CPI may miss gains from new variety and improved purchasing power
macro.Feedback: New goods can make consumers better off in ways not fully captured by the CPI.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
macro.Question: Which example would most likely make the CPI overstate the true rise in the cost of living?
macro.Choice A: Consumers switch from expensive beef to cheaper chicken
macro.Choice B: All consumers buy exactly the fixed CPI basket forever
macro.Choice C: Quality falls but prices fall more
macro.Choice D: Imports disappear from stores
macro.Correct Answer: A — Consumers switch from expensive beef to cheaper chicken
macro.Feedback: Substitution toward cheaper goods means the fixed basket may exaggerate cost increases.

macro.Question: Which scenario combines two CPI biases at once?
macro.Choice A: A new streaming service draws consumers from expensive cable
macro.Choice B: A worker becomes unemployed during a recession
macro.Choice C: Exports rise faster than imports
macro.Choice D: Government purchases increase
macro.Correct Answer: A — A new streaming service draws consumers from expensive cable
macro.Feedback: New goods and substitution both complicate CPI measurement.

macro.Choice B: Only GDP deflator bias
macro.Choice C: Only cyclical unemployment
macro.Choice D: Only nominal interest error
macro.Correct Answer: A — Introduction of new goods and substitution bias
macro.Feedback: New goods improve choice, and substitution toward them can reduce actual cost-of-living increases.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring that consumers switch toward relatively cheaper goods.
macro.Question: A statistical agency sees households replacing a newly expensive rail route with an existing bus route. A trial finds the cheaper travel bundle preserves the same commuting service. Which evidence supports substitution bias, and what does it fail to establish?
macro.Choice A: A fixed bundle overstates the cost of that service; the evidence does not quantify bias for the whole CPI

macro.Correct Answer: A — A fixed bundle overstates the cost of that service; the evidence does not quantify bias for the whole CPI
macro.Feedback: The same service can be maintained at lower cost by changing an existing bundle, which is the substitution mechanism. A travel example alone does not measure the full index’s bias or imply that overall prices fell.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
macro.Question: A new pump costs 12% more than the old model and lasts 12% longer with identical annual performance and maintenance costs. Ignoring discounting, which conclusion is supported for this product, and which is not?
macro.Choice A: Cost per service-year is unchanged; economy-wide inflation cannot be inferred
macro.Choice B: Cost per service-year rises 12%; durability is irrelevant to quality
macro.Choice C: Cost per service-year falls 12%; equal percentage changes must be subtracted from price twice
macro.Choice D: Economy-wide inflation is zero because this product has no service-cost rise
macro.Correct Answer: A — Cost per service-year is unchanged; economy-wide inflation cannot be inferred
macro.Feedback: Price per lifetime service-year changes by 1.12/1.12 = 1. The sticker-price rise alone is therefore not pure service-cost inflation for this product. Its example cannot establish the economy-wide price change.

macro.Correct Answer: B — Delayed inclusion can miss gains in purchasing opportunities; that limitation does not make every observed CPI change meaningless
macro.Feedback: New goods can improve purchasing opportunities before an index incorporates them. The limitation is specific; it does not invalidate all price evidence or establish one universal bias size.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The payment exactly preserves utility because any official index equals every household's cost of living” in this cpi bias task.
macro.Question: A $170 payment is indexed to measured CPI. A careful study estimates measured inflation at 5% but the cost of maintaining the recipient's utility at 3%, owing to substitution and new choices. How does indexation affect the payment's purchasing power under these estimates?

macro.Choice B: Real value falls about 2%; measured inflation exceeds estimated cost growth.
macro.Choice C: Real value rises about 8%; add measured and estimated inflation rates.
macro.Choice D: Real value is unchanged; official indexation exactly preserves the recipient's utility.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Real value rises about 1.9%; indexation exceeds estimated cost growth.
macro.Feedback: The relevant factor is 1.05/1.03, about a 1.94% gain relative to the estimated utility-maintaining cost. The conclusion is conditional on the supplied estimates, not an assertion that every index overstates inflation by two points.

macro.Correct Answer: D — It misses cost-saving substitution; the indexed payment can exceed the increase in minimum cost of maintaining utility
macro.Feedback: Pricing the unchanged basket can overstate the cost increase when consumers substitute to maintain utility. Indexing to that measure can overcompensate relative to the minimum cost-of-living increase.

macro.Correct Answer: A — The redesigned bundle preserves the relevant living standard, with comparable quality and coverage

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The payment exactly preserves utility because any official index equals every household's cost of living” in this cpi bias task.
macro.Question: A $250 payment is indexed to measured CPI. A careful study estimates measured inflation at 5% but the cost of maintaining the recipient's utility at 3%, owing to substitution and new choices. How does indexation affect the payment's purchasing power under these estimates?
macro.Choice A: Real value falls about 2%; measured inflation exceeds estimated cost growth.
macro.Choice B: Real value rises about 8%; add measured and estimated inflation rates.
macro.Choice C: Real value is unchanged; official indexation exactly preserves the recipient's utility.
macro.Choice D: Real value rises about 1.9%; indexation exceeds estimated cost growth.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Real value rises about 1.9%; indexation exceeds estimated cost growth.
macro.Feedback: The relevant factor is 1.05/1.03, about a 1.94% gain relative to the estimated utility-maintaining cost. The conclusion is conditional on the supplied estimates, not an assertion that every index overstates inflation by two points.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “It fully reflects the new choices; the indexed payment must exactly preserve every household's utility” in this cpi bias task.
macro.Question: A fixed basket includes 260 units of a food whose price rises sharply. Households switch toward a cheaper substitute while maintaining utility. What does the fixed-basket index miss, and how does that affect a payment fully indexed to it?
macro.Choice A: It fully reflects the new choices; the indexed payment must exactly preserve every household's utility
macro.Choice B: It counts the substitute twice; the index necessarily falls despite the dearer original food
macro.Choice C: It misses cost-saving substitution; the indexed payment can exceed the increase in minimum cost of maintaining utility
macro.Choice D: It misses cost-saving substitution; the indexed payment necessarily falls short of that increase
macro.Correct Answer: C — It misses cost-saving substitution; the indexed payment can exceed the increase in minimum cost of maintaining utility
macro.Feedback: Pricing the unchanged basket can overstate the cost increase when consumers substitute to maintain utility. Indexing to that measure can overcompensate relative to the minimum cost-of-living increase.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Holding service quality constant; comparable-price measurement should ignore quality” in this cpi bias task.
macro.Question: A product originally costs $270. Its replacement costs 20% more but provides twice the measured service, with no other relevant quality changes. How should the price change be interpreted after allowing for the improved service?
macro.Choice A: The comparable price rises 20%; improved service should have no role in measuring a like-for-like price.
macro.Choice B: The price per unit of service falls; counting the entire sticker-price increase as inflation ignores the quality improvement.
macro.Choice C: The comparable price is unchanged; a new version is always treated as having the old price.
macro.Choice D: The price per unit of service doubles; the quality gain should be added to rather than allowed for in the comparison.
macro.Correct Answer: B — The price per unit of service falls; counting the entire sticker-price increase as inflation ignores the quality improvement.
macro.Feedback: The replacement's price per service unit is 1.20/2 = 0.60 of the old level. A like-for-like comparison must adjust for quality rather than automatically calling the full 20% higher price inflation.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Delayed inclusion proves CPI understates every household's inflation by the same fixed amount” in this cpi bias task.
macro.Question: A new product expands choice while the price index still records spending of $240 on older products. How does the delayed inclusion of the new product limit what the CPI tells us?
macro.Choice A: Delayed inclusion proves CPI understates every household's inflation by the same fixed amount
macro.Choice B: Delayed inclusion can miss gains in purchasing opportunities; that limitation does not make every observed CPI change meaningless
macro.Choice C: Delayed inclusion means CPI is a complete cost-of-living measure because consumers previously did not buy the new product
macro.Choice D: Delayed inclusion means actual prices cannot change until the product enters the official basket
macro.Correct Answer: B — Delayed inclusion can miss gains in purchasing opportunities; that limitation does not make every observed CPI change meaningless
macro.Feedback: New goods can improve purchasing opportunities before an index incorporates them. The limitation is specific; it does not invalidate all price evidence or establish one universal bias size.

macro.Question: A fixed basket has two meals at a base price of $4 each and one fare at $12. Meal prices rise 10%; the fare is unchanged. What CPI results, with the base set to 100?

macro.Question: A basket costs $750 when the CPI is 125. One year later the same basket costs $810. Which new index and claim about inflation are correct?

macro.Question: The base-year basket cost is $640, last year’s CPI was 125, and the basket costs $856 now. Which pair gives the current CPI and inflation since last year?

macro.Question: A basket contains 4 units of A and 6 units of B. Base prices are $5 and $10; current prices are $8 and $12. What is the CPI?

macro.Question: A basket has 10 units of food and 1 unit of electronics. Food prices rise 4 percent and the electronics price rises 40 percent. Which conclusion is justified without more information?

macro.Question: A fixed basket contains 3 tickets and 2 repairs. Base prices are $8 and $18; last year the basket cost $72. This year CPI is 135 and tickets cost $9 each. An agency plans to rebase last year's CPI to 100. Would that change the implied repair price or this year's inflation?
macro.Choice A: No. Repairs still cost $27 and annual inflation is 12.5%; rebasing changes index units, not the underlying price ratio.
macro.Choice B: Yes. Repairs fall to $24 and inflation to zero because the new base year removes the earlier price rise.
macro.Choice C: No. Repairs remain $27, but annual inflation is 35% because this year's old index was 135.

macro.Correct Answer: A — No. Repairs still cost $27 and annual inflation is 12.5%; rebasing changes index units, not the underlying price ratio.
macro.Feedback: Base cost is $60, so current cost is $81. Subtracting $27 for tickets leaves $54 for two repairs. Inflation is 81/72−1=12.5%. Rebasing would express the current index as 112.5 with last year 100, preserving both prices and the growth ratio.

macro.Question: An index is rebased: the old series lists last year at 160 and this year at 176, while the new series sets last year to 100. A nominal benefit rose 6% over the period. Which comparison survives rebasing?

macro.Common Misconception: Using the CPI point change instead of the percentage change.
macro.Question: A nominal hourly wage rises from $25 to $27. Basket cost rises from $500 to $540, then falls to $525 while the wage stays $27. Relative to the starting year, what real-wage change remains after both price movements?

macro.Choice B: The next CPI is 120; next inflation is 10%

macro.Correct Answer: D — The next CPI is 132; next inflation is 10%
macro.Feedback: CPI levels are 120 and 132. Inflation is (132−120)/120×100 = 10%, not the 12-point change or the 32% cumulative rise.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Yes; a rising nominal payment guarantees more purchasing power” in this cpi and inflation measurement task.
macro.Question: A fixed-basket index is 125 in the initial period and 130 in the next. A $190 nominal payment rises 3%. Does its purchasing power keep pace?
macro.Choice A: Yes; a rising nominal payment guarantees more purchasing power
macro.Choice B: No; real purchasing power falls exactly 5% because the index rises five points

macro.Correct Answer: C — No; prices rise 4%, and real purchasing power falls about 1.0%
macro.Feedback: Inflation is (130−125)/125 = 4%. The real payment factor is 1.03/1.04, a decline of about 0.96%.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Nominal and real pay both rise 6%; wage changes are independent of prices” in this cpi and inflation measurement task.
macro.Question: A worker earns $210 before a 6% nominal raise. The relevant CPI rises 8%. A report says higher pay alone establishes a real gain. Which correction follows?
macro.Choice A: Nominal pay rises 6%; real pay falls about 1.9%.
macro.Choice B: Nominal and real pay both rise 6%; prices do not enter.
macro.Choice C: Nominal pay rises 6%; real pay rises 14% after adding inflation.
macro.Choice D: Nominal pay rises 6%; real pay falls 8% after ignoring the raise.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Nominal pay rises 6%; real pay falls about 1.9%.
macro.Feedback: Purchasing power changes by 1.06/1.08−1 ≈ −1.85%. A positive nominal raise can accompany a real loss.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The next CPI is 132; next inflation is 12%” in this cpi and inflation measurement task.

macro.Choice B: The next CPI is 120; next inflation is 10%

macro.Choice D: The next CPI is 132; next inflation is 10%
macro.Correct Answer: D — The next CPI is 132; next inflation is 10%

macro.Question: A basket cost is $240 before prices change. Its index rises from 160 to 168. A clerk multiplies the old cost by 1.08. Which corrected cost and reason are right?

macro.Feedback: The price factor is new index/old index = 168/160 = 1.05. An eight-point rise from 160 is 5%, not 8%.

macro.Question: A fixed basket costs $260 in the base year, $312 this year and $343.2 next year. A report treats the increase in CPI index points as the inflation rate. What are next year's CPI and inflation rate?
macro.Choice A: The next CPI is 132; next inflation is 32%
macro.Choice B: The next CPI is 132; next inflation is 10%

macro.Choice D: The next CPI is 120; next inflation is 10%
macro.Correct Answer: B — The next CPI is 132; next inflation is 10%
macro.Feedback: CPI levels are 120 and 132. Inflation is (132−120)/120×100 = 10%, not the 12-point change or the 32% cumulative rise.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “$336; apply the new index as though the old index were 100” in this cpi and inflation measurement task.
macro.Question: A basket costs $200 before its index rises from 160 to 168. A clerk budgets $216 by treating the eight-point increase as 8%. If the index were rebased so the initial value was 100, what would happen to the purchasing-power calculation?
macro.Choice A: The new index would be 108 and the basket would still cost $216; rebasing validates the clerk's method.
macro.Choice B: The new index would be 105, but the basket cost would return to $200 because the old price increase is removed.
macro.Choice C: The new index would be 105 and the basket would still cost $210; the clerk's $6 excess budget would remain.
macro.Choice D: The basket would cost $336 because rebasing requires applying 168% to its old dollar price.
macro.Correct Answer: C — The new index would be 105 and the basket would still cost $210; the clerk's $6 excess budget would remain.
macro.Feedback: The price ratio is 168/160=1.05, so cost is $210. Rebasing gives 105 and leaves that ratio unchanged. An eight-point rise on a 160 index is not 8% inflation; changing the base cannot alter the needed dollars.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Yes; a rising nominal payment guarantees more purchasing power” in this cpi and inflation measurement task.
macro.Question: A fixed-basket index rises from 125 to 130 while a $270 payment rises 3%. The recipient's own cost of living rises only 2%. How can the payment lose purchasing power under one comparison and gain it under the other?
macro.Choice A: It gains against both baskets because a larger nominal payment always buys more goods.
macro.Choice B: It loses 5% against the index basket and gains 1% against the recipient's basket because index points are percentage changes.
macro.Choice C: The payment loses about 1% against the index basket but gains about 1% against the recipient's basket because their price changes differ.
macro.Choice D: The comparisons are inconsistent because one payment must have the same real change under every price measure.
macro.Correct Answer: C — The payment loses about 1% against the index basket but gains about 1% against the recipient's basket because their price changes differ.
macro.Feedback: The index basket rises 4%, giving a real factor 1.03/1.04≈0.9904. The recipient's cost rises 2%, giving 1.03/1.02≈1.0098. Different relevant consumption baskets can yield different real changes without contradiction.

macro.Common Misconception: Uses the CPI base-year cost rather than the previous period as the inflation denominator.
macro.Question: A basket contains 5 units of A and 4 of B. Base prices are $8 and $15; current prices $10 and $18; next prices $11 and $19. A report divides the next cost increase by the base-year cost. Would simply rebasing the index correct its inflation calculation?
macro.Choice A: Yes, any new base fixes the denominator; current CPI is 122 and next inflation is 9%.
macro.Choice B: No. Inflation needs the preceding-period denominator; current CPI is 122 and next inflation is about 7.4%.
macro.Choice C: No, annual inflation must always divide by the original base; current CPI is 122 and next inflation is 9%.
macro.Choice D: Yes, using next year as the base gives the correct annual rate of about 6.9%.
macro.Correct Answer: B — No. Inflation needs the preceding-period denominator; current CPI is 122 and next inflation is about 7.4%.
macro.Feedback: Basket costs are 100,122 and 131. The annual increase is 9/122≈7.4%, not 9/100 or 9/131. Index rebasing rescales levels; the substantive correction is to compare the increase with the immediately preceding cost.

macro.Common Misconception: Treats CPI and the GDP deflator as interchangeable measures of the same set of prices.
macro.Question: The price of a domestically produced aircraft sold to a foreign airline rises. Which index directly includes that domestic export price?
macro.Choice A: The GDP deflator
macro.Choice B: The CPI only
macro.Choice C: Neither price index
macro.Choice D: A consumer import index only
macro.Correct Answer: A — The GDP deflator
macro.Feedback: CPI follows a consumer-basket framework; the GDP deflator follows prices of current domestically produced final output.

macro.Common Misconception: Chooses an index by familiarity rather than by the purpose of the comparison.
macro.Question: Which index is designed for tracking the prices paid for a representative consumer basket?
macro.Choice A: The GDP deflator
macro.Choice B: A real-interest index
macro.Choice C: A domestic-export index
macro.Choice D: The CPI
macro.Correct Answer: D — The CPI
macro.Feedback: Use CPI for consumer purchasing-power questions and the GDP deflator for the price level of current domestic GDP.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignores whether a priced item is imported, exported, consumed, or part of domestic investment.
macro.Question: A domestic firm buys newly produced business software whose price rises. Which index directly covers that final domestic product?
macro.Choice A: The GDP deflator
macro.Choice B: The CPI because every business purchase is consumer spending
macro.Choice C: Neither index because software is intangible
macro.Choice D: The CPI only when the firm imports the software
macro.Correct Answer: A — The GDP deflator
macro.Feedback: The GDP deflator covers newly produced final goods and services made domestically, including business software. The CPI is limited to the consumer basket.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignores whether a priced item is imported, exported, consumed, or part of domestic investment.
macro.Question: Imported prescription-drug prices rise while prices of domestic hospital services are unchanged. Which outcome is plausible?
macro.Choice A: GDP-deflator inflation must exceed CPI inflation
macro.Choice B: Both indexes must change by the same amount
macro.Choice C: Neither index can reflect a medical price change
macro.Choice D: CPI inflation exceeds GDP-deflator inflation
macro.Correct Answer: D — CPI inflation exceeds GDP-deflator inflation
macro.Feedback: Imported prescription drugs can raise the CPI because they are consumer purchases. They are not domestic production, so they do not directly raise the GDP deflator; unchanged domestic hospital prices add no offsetting price increase.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignores whether a priced item is imported, exported, consumed, or part of domestic investment.
macro.Question: Prices of domestically produced aircraft exports rise while imported smartphones bought by households become cheaper. Which combination is plausible?
macro.Choice A: The GDP deflator rises while the CPI falls
macro.Choice B: The CPI rises while the GDP deflator falls
macro.Choice C: Both indexes must rise because one price increased
macro.Choice D: Both indexes must fall because consumers buy smartphones
macro.Correct Answer: A — The GDP deflator rises while the CPI falls

macro.Common Misconception: Ignores whether a priced item is imported, exported, consumed, or part of domestic investment.
macro.Question: Between two years, individual prices do not change, but domestic production shifts toward goods whose current prices are higher relative to their base-year prices. Why can a fixed-base GDP deflator rise?
macro.Choice A: The deflator must be unchanged whenever current-year prices are unchanged
macro.Choice B: The deflator begins including imported consumer goods as domestic output
macro.Choice C: A shift toward goods with higher dollar prices raises every index regardless of base prices
macro.Choice D: Current quantities put more weight on goods with larger price increases since the base year
macro.Correct Answer: D — Current quantities put more weight on goods with larger price increases since the base year
macro.Feedback: The deflator compares current-price and base-price values of current quantities. Changing the output mix toward larger current-to-base price relatives can raise the ratio even with no new individual price changes. High dollar prices alone do not establish that result.

macro.Common Misconception: Treats CPI and the GDP deflator as interchangeable measures of the same set of prices.
macro.Question: Imported home solar panels become cheaper while domestically produced industrial turbines become more expensive. Why can CPI and the GDP deflator move in opposite directions?
macro.Choice A: The indexes cover different goods and use different weighting frameworks
macro.Choice B: Both indexes measure only domestic consumer purchases
macro.Choice C: The CPI excludes imports while the deflator includes them
macro.Choice D: The GDP deflator fixes a household basket while CPI tracks current output
macro.Correct Answer: A — The indexes cover different goods and use different weighting frameworks
macro.Feedback: CPI follows a consumer-basket framework; the GDP deflator follows prices of current domestically produced final output.

macro.Common Misconception: Chooses an index by familiarity rather than by the purpose of the comparison.
macro.Question: A household grant rises from $2,000 to $2,160 as the CPI rises from 125 to 135. Nominal GDP rises 8% and the GDP deflator rises 4%. A report uses the 8% consumer-price increase to adjust both the grant and GDP for inflation, concluding that both real values are unchanged. Which conclusion is correct, and which is mistaken?
macro.Choice A: Both conclusions are valid because identical nominal growth requires identical real growth.
macro.Choice B: The GDP conclusion is valid, but the grant gains about 3.8% because households should use the GDP deflator.
macro.Choice C: Both real values rise 8% because neither consumer nor output prices affect real measurement.
macro.Choice D: The grant conclusion is valid, but real GDP rises about 3.8% because GDP needs its own 4% price change.
macro.Correct Answer: D — The grant conclusion is valid, but real GDP rises about 3.8% because GDP needs its own 4% price change.
macro.Feedback: The grant and CPI each rise 8%, so its purchasing power is constant. Real GDP uses 1.08/1.04−1≈3.8%. The incorrect inference comes from using the consumer price measure for domestic output.

macro.Question: A city buys domestic transit vehicles while households buy imported fuel. Which mapping is correct?

macro.Choice C: Both prices enter only the GDP deflator
macro.Choice D: Imported fuel enters the GDP deflator but not CPI
macro.Correct Answer: A — Vehicle prices enter the GDP deflator; imported fuel can enter CPI
macro.Feedback: Domestic transit vehicles are newly produced domestic output, so their prices enter the GDP deflator. Imported fuel bought by households is in the consumer basket and can enter CPI, but it is not domestic production.

macro.Question: A domestic economy buys $220 of imported household fuel and produces machinery only for export. Fuel prices rise while machinery prices are unchanged. Holding quantities fixed, what happens to the CPI and GDP deflator?

macro.Correct Answer: C — CPI rises; the GDP deflator is unchanged, reflecting their different coverage.
macro.Feedback: CPI covers household consumption including imports. The GDP deflator covers domestically produced final output, including exports; unchanged domestic output prices need not reflect imported fuel inflation.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Use the GDP deflator for both; household consumption excludes imported food” in this cpi versus gdp deflator task.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “CPI falls 4%; the GDP deflator rises 6%” in this cpi versus gdp deflator task.
macro.Question: A country initially produces $200 of export machinery and households buy only imported food. Machinery prices fall 4% and food prices rise 6%, with quantities fixed. An analyst deflates the new nominal GDP using the food-price increase and reports a real contraction. Is that result sound?
macro.Choice A: No. Real machinery output is unchanged; dividing the 4% nominal GDP decline by consumer-price growth uses the wrong price measure.
macro.Choice B: Yes. Real GDP falls about 9.4% because imported food prices determine the prices of all domestic output.
macro.Choice C: No. Real GDP rises 6% because household prices rise while domestic output prices fall.
macro.Choice D: Yes. Any decline in nominal GDP proves real domestic production has declined.
macro.Correct Answer: A — No. Real machinery output is unchanged; dividing the 4% nominal GDP decline by consumer-price growth uses the wrong price measure.
macro.Feedback: Nominal GDP becomes $192, and the deflator factor is 0.96. Dividing 192 by 0.96 returns $200 in base prices. Using 1.06 instead would falsely suggest a 9.4% real decline because CPI covers imported food rather than domestic machinery.

macro.Correct Answer: A — CPI includes imported consumer goods; the GDP deflator covers domestic output
macro.Feedback: Different coverage of imports can cause CPI and GDP deflator movements to differ.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
macro.Question: Why can the CPI overstate inflation while the GDP deflator still moves differently for valid reasons?
macro.Choice A: CPI uses a fixed basket; the GDP deflator uses current output
macro.Choice B: Both measure the exact same goods but use different names
macro.Choice C: The GDP deflator measures unemployment
macro.Choice D: The CPI measures only exports
macro.Correct Answer: A — CPI uses a fixed basket; the GDP deflator uses current output
macro.Feedback: These indexes differ both because of CPI bias issues and because they cover different baskets.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
macro.Question: Which price change affects the CPI but not the GDP deflator directly?
macro.Choice A: A price increase for imported coffee bought by households
macro.Choice B: A price increase for domestically produced tractors
macro.Choice C: A price increase for government services
macro.Choice D: A price increase for domestically produced bread
macro.Correct Answer: A — A price increase for imported coffee bought by households
macro.Feedback: Imported consumer goods are included in the CPI but excluded from the GDP deflator.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
macro.Question: Why can the GDP deflator change differently from the CPI?
macro.Choice A: GDP deflator uses current output; CPI uses a fixed basket
macro.Choice B: They measure exactly the same basket
macro.Choice C: The GDP deflator only counts imports
macro.Choice D: The CPI ignores consumer prices
macro.Correct Answer: A — GDP deflator uses current output; CPI uses a fixed basket
macro.Feedback: The CPI and GDP deflator use different baskets and coverage.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
macro.Question: A domestically produced machine purchased by a business becomes more expensive. Which index is more likely to capture this directly?
macro.Choice A: GDP deflator
macro.Choice B: CPI
macro.Choice C: Unemployment rate
macro.Choice D: Labor force participation rate
macro.Correct Answer: A — GDP deflator
macro.Feedback: Capital goods produced domestically are included in GDP and affect the GDP deflator.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
macro.Question: A country imports most consumer goods but produces mostly capital equipment. Imported consumer prices rise while domestic capital prices fall. Which statement is most accurate?
macro.Choice A: CPI and GDP deflator can move in opposite directions
macro.Choice B: CPI and GDP deflator must move together
macro.Choice C: GDP deflator must include imported consumer goods
macro.Choice D: CPI must include capital equipment bought by firms
macro.Correct Answer: A — CPI and GDP deflator can move in opposite directions
macro.Feedback: Different baskets mean the CPI and GDP deflator can diverge sharply.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
macro.Question: Imported household energy becomes dearer while domestic investment equipment becomes cheaper. An analyst sees rising CPI but a falling GDP deflator and declares one series wrong. What should be checked before accepting that claim?
macro.Choice A: Their coverage: imported consumption enters CPI, while domestic equipment enters the GDP deflator, so the movements can be consistent.
macro.Choice B: Only which series has the larger base-year number; a higher base index must show higher inflation.
macro.Choice C: Whether imports reduced net exports; that makes their prices part of the domestic GDP deflator.
macro.Choice D: Whether nominal GDP rose; if it did, both price indexes must also have risen.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Their coverage: imported consumption enters CPI, while domestic equipment enters the GDP deflator, so the movements can be consistent.
macro.Feedback: Household purchasing power and domestic-production prices use different coverage. More expensive imported energy can raise CPI while cheaper domestically produced equipment lowers the deflator. Conflicting directions do not by themselves establish a data error.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
macro.Question: An economy’s consumer basket has base spending of $40 on imported tea and $60 on domestic services. Tea prices rise 25%; services prices stay fixed. The only other domestic output is exported machinery, whose price falls 10%. With quantities fixed, which conclusion is justified?
macro.Choice A: CPI rises 10%; the GDP deflator falls, but its size needs domestic-output weights
macro.Choice B: Both indexes rise 25% because imports are in consumer spending
macro.Choice C: CPI rises 25%; the GDP deflator falls exactly 10%
macro.Choice D: CPI is unchanged; imported consumer prices are excluded
macro.Correct Answer: A — CPI rises 10%; the GDP deflator falls, but its size needs domestic-output weights
macro.Feedback: The consumer basket rises from 100 to 40 × 1.25 + 60 = 110, a 10% increase. The domestic deflator includes unchanged service prices and lower machinery prices, so it falls; their output weights are needed to measure the decline.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing a fixed consumer basket with current domestic production prices.
macro.Question: Domestic output consists of 10 machines and 100 services. Base prices are $100 and $10; current prices are $120 and $10. Consumers buy the services and imported clothing; the clothing price is unchanged. Which price-index account is supported?
macro.Choice A: GDP deflator 110; CPI unchanged if its fixed basket contains only those consumer purchases
macro.Choice B: GDP deflator 120; CPI rises 20% because domestic machines got dearer
macro.Choice C: GDP deflator 110; CPI must rise by the same 10%
macro.Choice D: GDP deflator 100; business equipment is not final domestic output
macro.Correct Answer: A — GDP deflator 110; CPI unchanged if its fixed basket contains only those consumer purchases
macro.Feedback: Base-price domestic output is 10 × 100 + 100 × 10 = 2,000; current-price output is 2,200, giving deflator 110. The stated consumer prices did not change, so their fixed basket’s CPI is unchanged.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Every household and domestic output price rose in exactly the same proportion” in this cpi versus gdp deflator task.
macro.Question: An economy with nominal output $130 reports a higher GDP deflator but unchanged CPI. Which proposed explanation could reconcile the reports without concluding either index is wrong?
macro.Choice A: Every household and domestic output price rose in exactly the same proportion
macro.Choice B: Only current quantities changed while all current and base-year prices stayed identical
macro.Choice C: Prices of domestic investment goods rose while household-consumption prices stayed fixed
macro.Choice D: Prices of imported household goods rose while every domestic output price stayed fixed
macro.Correct Answer: C — Prices of domestic investment goods rose while household-consumption prices stayed fixed
macro.Feedback: Investment goods are domestic final output but not household consumption. Their prices can raise the deflator while CPI remains unchanged; different scopes can explain the divergence.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Neither rises because imported prices are outside all domestic price statistics” in this cpi versus gdp deflator task.
macro.Question: A domestic economy buys $140 of imported household fuel and produces machinery only for export. Fuel prices rise while machinery prices are unchanged. Holding quantities fixed, what happens to the CPI and GDP deflator?
macro.Choice A: Both rise equally; household fuel belongs in both indexes at equal weight.
macro.Choice B: CPI rises; the GDP deflator is unchanged, reflecting their different coverage.
macro.Choice C: CPI is unchanged; the GDP deflator rises through the import-price component.
macro.Choice D: Both are unchanged; imported consumption is excluded from either price index.
macro.Correct Answer: B — CPI rises; the GDP deflator is unchanged, reflecting their different coverage.
macro.Feedback: CPI covers household consumption including imports. The GDP deflator covers domestically produced final output, including exports; unchanged domestic output prices need not reflect imported fuel inflation.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Use the GDP deflator for the benefit and CPI for GDP; imported food belongs only in the deflator” in this cpi versus gdp deflator task.
macro.Question: A household benefit of $150 must track consumption costs, while an analyst must convert nominal domestic GDP into real output. Imported food becomes dearer and domestic investment equipment becomes cheaper. Which index should be used for each purpose, and must the two indexes move together?
macro.Choice A: CPI for benefits, deflator for GDP; different coverage permits different movements.
macro.Choice B: CPI for both uses; consumer prices also measure domestic capital-goods prices.
macro.Choice C: Deflator for both uses; domestic output prices measure imported household costs.
macro.Choice D: Deflator for benefits, CPI for GDP; imported food belongs to domestic output.
macro.Correct Answer: A — CPI for benefits, deflator for GDP; different coverage permits different movements.
macro.Feedback: The purpose determines index choice. CPI tracks consumption costs; the deflator matches domestic final output. Imports and investment equipment enter these measures differently, so divergent movements are possible.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Both rise equally because every purchase is included in both baskets” in this cpi versus gdp deflator task.
macro.Question: A domestic economy buys $100 of imported household fuel and produces machinery only for export. Fuel prices rise while machinery prices are unchanged. Holding quantities fixed, what happens to the CPI and GDP deflator?
macro.Choice A: Both rise equally; household fuel belongs in both indexes at equal weight.
macro.Choice B: CPI is unchanged; the GDP deflator rises through the import-price component.
macro.Choice C: Both are unchanged; imported consumption is excluded from either price index.
macro.Choice D: CPI rises; the GDP deflator is unchanged, reflecting their different coverage.
macro.Correct Answer: D — CPI rises; the GDP deflator is unchanged, reflecting their different coverage.
macro.Feedback: CPI covers household consumption including imports. The GDP deflator covers domestically produced final output, including exports; unchanged domestic output prices need not reflect imported fuel inflation.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Use CPI for both; imported consumption and domestic investment always have identical weights” in this cpi versus gdp deflator task.
macro.Question: A household benefit of $110 must track consumption costs, while an analyst must convert nominal domestic GDP into real output. Imported food becomes dearer and domestic investment equipment becomes cheaper. Which index should be used for each purpose, and must the two indexes move together?
macro.Choice A: CPI for both uses; consumer prices also measure domestic capital-goods prices.
macro.Choice B: Deflator for both uses; domestic output prices measure imported household costs.
macro.Choice C: CPI for benefits, deflator for GDP; different coverage permits different movements.
macro.Choice D: Deflator for benefits, CPI for GDP; imported food belongs to domestic output.
macro.Correct Answer: C — CPI for benefits, deflator for GDP; different coverage permits different movements.
macro.Feedback: The purpose determines index choice. CPI tracks consumption costs; the deflator matches domestic final output. Imports and investment equipment enter these measures differently, so divergent movements are possible.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Both indexes fall 4% because domestic output determines every index” in this cpi versus gdp deflator task.
macro.Question: A country produces only $120 of export machinery and households consume only imported food. Machinery prices fall 4% while food prices rise 6%, with quantities fixed. Which pair is consistent?
macro.Choice A: Both indexes fall 4% because domestic output determines every index
macro.Choice B: CPI rises 6%; the GDP deflator falls 4%
macro.Choice C: CPI falls 4%; the GDP deflator rises 6%
macro.Choice D: Both indexes rise 6% because households pay that inflation
macro.Correct Answer: B — CPI rises 6%; the GDP deflator falls 4%
macro.Feedback: Under the deliberately distinct baskets, CPI follows imported household food and the deflator follows domestic machinery, even though all machinery is exported.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “CPI falls 4%; the GDP deflator rises 6%” in this cpi versus gdp deflator task.
macro.Question: A country produces only $160 of export machinery and households consume only imported food. Machinery prices fall 4% while food prices rise 6%, with quantities fixed. Would indexing household payments to the GDP deflator preserve their purchasing power?
macro.Choice A: No. Payments would fall 4% while food costs rise 6%, reducing their real value by about 9.4%.
macro.Choice B: Yes. A 4% payment reduction matches the prices of domestic output and therefore household purchases.
macro.Choice C: No. Payments would rise 6% while food prices fall 4%, increasing their real value by about 10.4%.
macro.Choice D: Yes. Exported machinery and imported food have equal weight in both price indexes.
macro.Correct Answer: A — No. Payments would fall 4% while food costs rise 6%, reducing their real value by about 9.4%.
macro.Feedback: The deflator follows domestic machinery, while CPI follows imported food in this deliberately separated economy. A deflator-indexed payment has real factor 0.96/1.06≈0.9057, a 9.4% loss. Domestic-output price changes are the wrong compensation basis for these consumers.

macro.Question: Crowding out happens when fiscal expansion raises rates and reduces:
macro.Choice A: Private investment
macro.Choice B: Currency
macro.Choice C: LRAS
macro.Choice D: Expected output
macro.Correct Answer: A — Private investment
macro.Feedback: Crowding out weakens fiscal expansion by reducing private investment.

macro.Common Misconception: Adding crowding out instead of subtracting it.
macro.Question: Crowding out reduces the effect of fiscal expansion by reducing:
macro.Choice A: Private investment
macro.Choice B: Government spending automatically
macro.Choice C: Money demand
macro.Choice D: Taxes
macro.Correct Answer: A — Private investment
macro.Feedback: Crowding out happens when higher interest rates reduce private investment.

macro.Common Misconception: Adding the crowding-out amount to the multiplier effect.
macro.Question: Aggregate demand would rise by $200 billion before crowding out. If crowding out reduces that increase by $50 billion, how much does aggregate demand rise overall?
macro.Choice A: $150 billion
macro.Choice B: $250 billion
macro.Choice C: $200 billion
macro.Choice D: $50 billion
macro.Correct Answer: A — $150 billion
macro.Feedback: Subtract the reduction caused by crowding out from the increase before crowding out: $200 − $50 = $150 billion.

macro.Common Misconception: Adds crowding out to demand instead of subtracting it.
macro.Question: Fiscal expansion would add $100 to AD before crowding out. Higher rates reduce AD by a total $30 after induced investment effects. What net increase remains?
macro.Feedback: Subtract the already-total offset once: 100−30=70.

macro.Common Misconception: Uses the gross fiscal impulse instead of its net effect on the gap.
macro.Question: A demand gap is $250. Fiscal policy adds $300 gross to AD, while displaced investment reduces AD by a total $80 including induced effects. How much of the original gap remains in this fixed-price planning model?
macro.Choice A: $80 remains
macro.Choice B: $220 remains
macro.Choice C: $30 remains
macro.Choice D: $50 of excess demand appears
macro.Correct Answer: C — $30 remains
macro.Feedback: Net impulse=300−80=220; remaining gap=250−220=30.

macro.Common Misconception: Thinking crowding out makes government spending disappear
macro.Question: Crowding out occurs when expansionary fiscal policy raises interest rates and reduces
macro.Choice A: investment spending
macro.Choice B: government spending automatically
macro.Choice C: money supply by definition
macro.Choice D: the price level immediately
macro.Correct Answer: A — investment spending
macro.Feedback: Crowding out occurs when higher interest rates reduce private investment spending.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing crowding out with the multiplier effect itself
macro.Question: If expansionary fiscal policy raises interest rates, which effect offsets part of the multiplier?
macro.Choice A: Crowding out
macro.Choice B: The Fisher effect
macro.Choice C: Monetary neutrality
macro.Choice D: Commodity backing
macro.Correct Answer: A — Crowding out
macro.Feedback: Crowding out occurs when higher interest rates reduce private investment, offsetting fiscal stimulus.

macro.Common Misconception: Thinking crowding out strengthens fiscal stimulus
macro.Question: Crowding out weakens fiscal expansion because higher government spending can raise interest rates and reduce
macro.Choice A: private investment
macro.Choice B: tax collections automatically to zero
macro.Choice C: the price level immediately
macro.Choice D: the money multiplier to infinity
macro.Correct Answer: A — private investment
macro.Feedback: Crowding out offsets fiscal expansion by reducing private investment when interest rates rise.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring offsetting effects from interest rates
macro.Question: Which situation would make fiscal stimulus less powerful?
macro.Choice A: Strong crowding out
macro.Choice B: A high MPC with no interest-rate effect
macro.Choice C: A large initial increase in government spending
macro.Choice D: A high willingness to consume extra income
macro.Correct Answer: A — Strong crowding out
macro.Feedback: Crowding out weakens fiscal stimulus by reducing private investment.

macro.Common Misconception: Adding crowding out instead of subtracting it
macro.Question: A fiscal package produces a gross $300 billion rightward AD shift in a simplified expenditure model. Crowding out produces a total $80 billion leftward AD offset, including all induced spending effects of the displaced investment. What net AD increase should policy analysis use?
macro.Choice A: $220 billion
macro.Choice B: $380 billion
macro.Choice C: $80 billion
macro.Choice D: $300 billion
macro.Correct Answer: A — $220 billion
macro.Feedback: The two magnitudes are both total AD changes: 300 − 80 = $220 billion. Do not multiply the stated total offset again. This is an AD shift, not a guaranteed equal increase in equilibrium GDP.

macro.Common Misconception: Adding crowding out instead of subtracting it
macro.Question: A fiscal package produces a gross $200 billion rightward AD shift in a simplified expenditure model. Crowding out produces a total $60 billion leftward AD offset, including all induced spending effects of the displaced investment. What net AD increase should policy analysis use?
macro.Choice A: $140 billion
macro.Choice B: $260 billion
macro.Choice C: $200 billion
macro.Choice D: $60 billion
macro.Correct Answer: A — $140 billion
macro.Feedback: The two magnitudes are both total AD changes: 200 − 60 = $140 billion. Do not multiply the stated total offset again. This is an AD shift, not a guaranteed equal increase in equilibrium GDP.

macro.Common Misconception: Thinking crowding out strengthens the fiscal multiplier
macro.Question: If policymakers expect the multiplier shift to close a recessionary gap exactly, but crowding out is stronger than expected, what is the likely result?
macro.Choice A: AD does not shift far enough right to fully close the gap.
macro.Choice B: AD shifts too far right because crowding out magnifies fiscal policy.
macro.Choice C: AD shifts left because government spending is not part of AD.
macro.Choice D: The multiplier becomes infinite.
macro.Correct Answer: A — AD does not shift far enough right to fully close the gap.
macro.Feedback: Stronger crowding out reduces the net AD shift, so stimulus may fall short.

macro.Common Misconception: Forgetting to apply the multiplier before subtracting crowding out
macro.Question: Government purchases increase by $60 billion. MPC = 0.75; use the simple spending multiplier, with no other leakages. Crowding out produces a total $50 billion AD offset, including its induced spending effects. What is the net rightward AD shift?
macro.Choice A: $190 billion
macro.Choice B: $240 billion
macro.Choice C: $110 billion
macro.Choice D: $10 billion
macro.Correct Answer: A — $190 billion
macro.Feedback: Multiplier is 4, so the gross shift is $240 billion. Subtract $50 billion crowding out for a net $190 billion. The offset is already a total AD change and is subtracted after multiplication; the sequence is an analytical decomposition, not a claim about separate calendar stages.

macro.Common Misconception: Adding crowding out instead of subtracting it from the gross multiplier shift
macro.Question: Government purchases increase by $100 billion. MPC = 0.6; use the simple spending multiplier, with no other leakages. Crowding out produces a total $75 billion AD offset, including its induced spending effects. Which sequence separates the direct purchases, gross multiplier prediction, and net AD shift?
macro.Choice A: AD first shifts right $100 billion, then the multiplier pushes the gross shift to $250 billion, then crowding out leaves a net $175 billion shift.
macro.Choice B: AD first shifts right $250 billion, then crowding out increases it to $325 billion.
macro.Choice C: AD first shifts left $100 billion, then the multiplier pushes it left $250 billion, then crowding out leaves $175 billion.
macro.Choice D: AD shifts right $100 billion only because crowding out cancels the multiplier.
macro.Correct Answer: A — AD first shifts right $100 billion, then the multiplier pushes the gross shift to $250 billion, then crowding out leaves a net $175 billion shift.
macro.Feedback: MPC = 0.6 gives multiplier 2.5. The $100 billion initial shift becomes $250 billion, then crowding out reduces the net shift to $175 billion. The offset is already a total AD change and is subtracted after multiplication; the sequence is an analytical decomposition, not a claim about separate calendar stages.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrect inference: MPC: 0.25; the saving share equals the marginal consumption share.
macro.Question: An increase in government purchases of $40 raises AD by $160 before crowding out in the simple model. What MPC does this imply, and does it determine how much aggregate demand will rise after crowding out?
macro.Choice A: MPC: 0.75; the increase before crowding out does not establish the final increase.
macro.Choice B: MPC: 0.25; the saving share equals the marginal consumption share.
macro.Choice C: MPC: 4; the gross spending ratio equals the marginal consumption share.
macro.Choice D: MPC: 0.75; the increase before crowding out establishes the same final increase.
macro.Correct Answer: A — MPC: 0.75; the increase before crowding out does not establish the final increase.
macro.Feedback: The spending multiplier is 4 = 1/(1 − MPC), so MPC = 0.75. This gives the demand increase before crowding out. Later crowding out can reduce the final increase.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “B has zero effect because a lower MPC eliminates every induced round” in this fiscal multipliers and crowding out task.
