macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: Tea is a normal good. At a price of $4, compare D0 and D1. Which income change and quantity change are consistent with the graph?
macro.Choice A: Income falls; quantity demanded falls by 75 thousand
macro.Choice B: Income rises; quantity demanded rises by 100 thousand
macro.Choice C: Income falls; quantity demanded falls by 100 thousand
macro.Choice D: Income rises; quantity demanded rises by 75 thousand

macro.Question: A product gets cheaper because supply increases. Students say demand increased because quantity sold rose. What is the error?
macro.Choice A: They confused an increase in quantity demanded with an increase in demand
macro.Choice B: They correctly identified a demand shift
macro.Choice C: They confused a price floor with a price ceiling
macro.Choice D: They ignored that supply can never change price
macro.Correct Answer: A — They confused an increase in quantity demanded with an increase in demand
macro.Feedback: If price falls because supply increases, buyers move along the demand curve. Quantity demanded rises, but demand itself does not shift.

macro.Question: A product becomes cheaper and sales rise. A follow-up survey finds that buyers now want more at EVERY unchanged price after a favorable health report. A student attributes all extra purchases to movement along the old demand curve. Which correction uses the survey evidence?
macro.Choice A: Demand is unchanged; every increase in sales is a movement along demand.
macro.Choice B: Demand shifts left; lower prices mean buyers want less at each fixed price.
macro.Choice C: Supply must shift left; buyer surveys establish producers’ costs.
macro.Choice D: Demand shifts right; the price change alone cannot explain greater planned purchases at a fixed price.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Demand shifts right; the price change alone cannot explain greater planned purchases at a fixed price.
macro.Feedback: Unlike a supply-driven price fall alone, the survey reports greater demand at fixed prices after new health information. That identifies a demand shift, although the survey alone does not determine the separate supply change or how much of observed sales growth each cause explains.

macro.Question: The price of peanut butter rises. If jelly is a complement, what happens in the jelly market?
macro.Choice A: Demand for jelly decreases
macro.Choice B: Demand for jelly increases
macro.Choice C: Supply of jelly decreases
macro.Choice D: Quantity demanded of jelly increases
macro.Correct Answer: A — Demand for jelly decreases
macro.Feedback: Peanut butter and jelly are complements. If peanut butter gets more expensive, demand for jelly falls.

macro.Question: The price of bus rides rises. If subway rides are substitutes, what happens in the subway market?
macro.Choice A: Demand for subway rides increases
macro.Choice B: Demand for subway rides decreases
macro.Choice C: Supply of subway rides decreases
macro.Choice D: Quantity supplied of bus rides increases
macro.Correct Answer: A — Demand for subway rides increases
macro.Feedback: When the price of a substitute rises, demand for the other good increases.

macro.Question: Consumers expect the price of coffee to fall next month. What happens to current demand for coffee, other things equal?
macro.Choice A: Current demand decreases
macro.Choice B: Current demand increases
macro.Choice C: Current quantity supplied increases
macro.Choice D: Supply shifts left
macro.Correct Answer: A — Current demand decreases
macro.Feedback: If buyers expect a lower future price, they delay purchases, reducing current demand.

macro.Question: The market initially clears at D1/S1. A substitute becomes more expensive, while supply conditions remain unchanged. Which explanation and equilibrium movement fit the graph?
macro.Choice A: Demand shifts right; equilibrium moves from (P2, Q1) to (P3, Q2).
macro.Choice B: Demand shifts right; equilibrium moves from (P1, Q2) to (P2, Q3).
macro.Choice C: Demand shifts left; equilibrium moves from (P2, Q1) to (P3, Q2).
macro.Choice D: Demand shifts left; equilibrium moves from (P1, Q2) to (P2, Q3).
macro.Correct Answer: A — Demand shifts right; equilibrium moves from (P2, Q1) to (P3, Q2).
macro.Feedback: A higher substitute price increases demand for this good, shifting demand right from D1 to D2. With supply fixed at S1, the graph moves from (P2,Q1) to (P3,Q2). Both equilibrium price and quantity rise.

macro.Question: The market initially clears at D2/S2. A close substitute becomes cheaper, while supply conditions remain unchanged. Which explanation and equilibrium movement fit the graph?
macro.Choice A: Demand shifts left; equilibrium moves from (P2, Q3) to (P1, Q2).
macro.Choice B: Demand shifts left; equilibrium moves from (P3, Q2) to (P2, Q1).
macro.Choice C: Demand shifts right; equilibrium moves from (P2, Q3) to (P1, Q2).
macro.Choice D: Demand shifts right; equilibrium moves from (P3, Q2) to (P2, Q1).
macro.Correct Answer: A — Demand shifts left; equilibrium moves from (P2, Q3) to (P1, Q2).
macro.Feedback: A cheaper substitute reduces demand for this good, shifting demand left from D2 to D1. On unchanged S2, equilibrium moves from (P2,Q3) to (P1,Q2). Both equilibrium price and quantity fall.

macro.Question: The price of a substitute for coffee rises. What happens in the coffee market, holding other factors constant?
macro.Choice A: Demand for coffee increases, raising equilibrium price and quantity
macro.Choice B: Quantity demanded of coffee decreases along the same curve
macro.Choice C: Supply of coffee increases because coffee is now profitable
macro.Choice D: Demand for coffee decreases because substitutes are now expensive
macro.Correct Answer: A — Demand for coffee increases, raising equilibrium price and quantity
macro.Feedback: When a substitute becomes more expensive, demand for the original good rises.

macro.Question: The price of peanut butter falls. What happens to the demand for jelly, assuming they are complements?
macro.Choice A: Demand for jelly increases
macro.Choice B: Quantity demanded of jelly falls along the same curve
macro.Choice C: Supply of jelly decreases
macro.Choice D: Demand for jelly decreases because peanut butter is cheaper
macro.Correct Answer: A — Demand for jelly increases
macro.Feedback: A lower price for a complement increases demand for the related good.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: The only change in the donut market is the good’s own price, taking the market from A to B. Which conclusion fits the graph?
macro.Choice A: Quantity demanded rises by 125 thousand along the existing curve; demand is unchanged.
macro.Choice B: Quantity demanded rises by 75 thousand along the existing curve; demand is unchanged.
macro.Choice C: Demand increases by 125 thousand because the lower price shifts the demand curve right.
macro.Choice D: Demand increases by 75 thousand because the lower price shifts the demand curve right.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Quantity demanded rises by 125 thousand along the existing curve; demand is unchanged.
macro.Feedback: A shows 100 thousand donuts and B shows 225 thousand, an increase of 125 thousand. The only change is the good’s own price, so this is an increase in quantity demanded along the existing curve. Demand itself does not shift.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: Use the graph. From A to B, what is the quantity response per $1 price decrease, and what economic change does it represent?
macro.Choice A: Quantity demanded rises by 25 thousand donuts per dollar through movement along the existing demand curve.
macro.Choice B: Quantity demanded rises by 20 thousand donuts per dollar through movement along the existing demand curve.
macro.Choice C: Demand increases by 25 thousand donuts per dollar because the price change shifts the curve right.
macro.Choice D: Demand increases by 20 thousand donuts per dollar because the price change shifts the curve right.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Quantity demanded rises by 25 thousand donuts per dollar through movement along the existing demand curve.
macro.Feedback: A is at $10 and 100 thousand donuts; B is at $5 and 225 thousand. Quantity demanded rises by 125/5 = 25 thousand per $1 price decrease. This is movement along the unchanged demand curve, not a price-induced increase in demand.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: Refer to the graph. At $6, compare D0 with D1. If this is a normal good, which change could explain the difference, and how large is it?
macro.Choice A: A fall in the good’s own price; 75 thousand more units demanded at that price.
macro.Choice B: Higher consumer income; 75 thousand more units demanded at that price.
macro.Choice C: Higher consumer income; 100 thousand more units demanded at that price.
macro.Choice D: A cheaper substitute; 75 thousand more units demanded at that price.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Higher consumer income; 75 thousand more units demanded at that price.
macro.Feedback: At $6, D0 shows 150 thousand and D1 shows 225 thousand: a 75-thousand increase at the same price. Higher income shifts demand right for a normal good; an own-price fall moves along a curve, and a cheaper substitute shifts demand left.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: Refer to the tea graph. Compare D0 with D1 at both $4 and $6. Which inference is supported by the repeated horizontal gap?
macro.Choice A: Demand decreases by 100 thousand units at each shown price, indicating a leftward curve shift
macro.Choice B: Quantity demanded decreases by 100 thousand solely because tea's own price rises
macro.Choice C: Demand increases by 100 thousand units at each shown price, indicating a rightward curve shift
macro.Choice D: Supply decreases by 100 thousand units, causing movement from D0 to D1
macro.Correct Answer: A — Demand decreases by 100 thousand units at each shown price, indicating a leftward curve shift
macro.Feedback: At both $4 and $6, D1 lies 100 thousand units left of D0. A repeated horizontal difference at fixed prices identifies a decrease in demand rather than movement along one curve.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming one of two opposing demand shifters must dominate.
macro.Question: Income rises for a normal good while the price of a close substitute falls. What can be concluded about demand for the normal good?
macro.Choice A: The net demand shift is uncertain because the two effects oppose each other.
macro.Choice B: Demand must rise because income rises for a normal good.
macro.Choice C: Demand must fall because the substitute becomes cheaper.
macro.Choice D: Demand stays fixed; both changes are movements along the original curve.
macro.Correct Answer: A — The net demand shift is uncertain because the two effects oppose each other.
macro.Feedback: Higher income raises demand for the normal good; a cheaper substitute lowers it. Either effect can dominate, or they can offset. Own-price movements do not describe these determinants.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: Refer to the graph. A buyer group starts on D0 at $6. After demand changes to D1, price is $10. Which statement reconciles the demand change with the final quantity?
macro.Choice A: Demand decreased, causing final quantity to be 25 thousand below the starting quantity.
macro.Choice B: Demand increased, so final quantity must be 75 thousand above the starting quantity.
macro.Choice C: Demand increased, yet final quantity is 25 thousand below the starting quantity.
macro.Choice D: Demand was unchanged, and the price increase reduced quantity by 100 thousand.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Demand increased, yet final quantity is 25 thousand below the starting quantity.
macro.Feedback: The initial quantity is 150 thousand and the final quantity is 125 thousand. D1 is right of D0, but movement up the new demand curve offsets more than the 75-thousand rightward shift.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: Compare the initial point on D0 at $6 with the final point on D1 at $4. Which explanation correctly separates the demand change from the price change?
macro.Choice A: The demand decrease cuts quantity from 150 to 50 thousand at $6; the later price fall moves along D1 to 100 thousand, partly offsetting that decrease.
macro.Choice B: The demand decrease cuts quantity from 150 to 75 thousand at $6; the later price fall moves along D1 to 125 thousand, partly offsetting that decrease.
macro.Choice C: Demand is unchanged; the price fall alone changes quantity from 150 to 50 and then 100 thousand along D0.
macro.Choice D: Demand is unchanged; the price fall alone changes quantity from 150 to 75 and then 125 thousand along D0.
macro.Correct Answer: A — The demand decrease cuts quantity from 150 to 50 thousand at $6; the later price fall moves along D1 to 100 thousand, partly offsetting that decrease.
macro.Feedback: At $6, quantity is 150 thousand on D0 and 50 thousand on D1. The lower quantity at the same price is a demand decrease. The subsequent price fall to $4 moves along D1 to 100 thousand, adding 50 thousand and only partly offsetting the demand decrease.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: Use the graph. A report attributes the A-to-B change to stronger tastes for donuts. A survey finds that quantity desired at every fixed price is unchanged. Which diagnosis fits both sources of evidence?
macro.Choice A: The report confuses a movement with a shift: price falls $4 and quantity demanded rises 100 thousand along unchanged demand.
macro.Choice B: The report confuses a movement with a shift: price falls $5 and quantity demanded rises 125 thousand along unchanged demand.
macro.Choice C: The report is supported: price falls $5 and quantity demanded rises 125 thousand because demand shifts right.
macro.Choice D: The report is supported: price falls $4 and quantity demanded rises 100 thousand because demand shifts right.
macro.Correct Answer: B — The report confuses a movement with a shift: price falls $5 and quantity demanded rises 125 thousand along unchanged demand.
macro.Feedback: The unchanged quantities desired at every fixed price rule out a demand shift caused by stronger tastes. A is at $10 and 100 thousand donuts; B is at $5 and 225 thousand. The $5 price fall increases quantity demanded by 125 thousand along unchanged demand, so the report confuses a movement with a shift.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: Refer to the graph. First compare D0 with D1 at a price of $10. Then follow D1 as price falls from $10 to $6. Which option correctly decomposes the two quantity changes into a demand shift and a movement along D1?
macro.Choice A: 50→125 from the price fall; 125→225 from a supply shift.
macro.Choice B: 50→150 from the demand shift; 150→225 from the price fall.
macro.Choice C: 50→25 from the demand shift; 25→225 from the price fall.
macro.Choice D: 50→125 from the demand shift; 125→225 from the price fall.
macro.Correct Answer: D — 50→125 from the demand shift; 125→225 from the price fall.
macro.Feedback: At $10 the shift from D0 to D1 raises quantity demanded from 50 to 125 thousand. Moving down D1 from $10 to $6 raises it again from 125 to 225 thousand, for a total increase of 175 thousand.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: Starting on D0 at $6, demand shifts to D1 at that price and then price falls to $4. What are the separate quantity changes caused by the shift and by the later movement along D1?
macro.Choice A: The shift reduces quantity by 75 thousand; the price fall adds 50 thousand
macro.Choice B: The shift reduces quantity by 100 thousand; the price fall adds 50 thousand
macro.Choice C: The shift reduces quantity by 100 thousand; the price fall adds 75 thousand
macro.Choice D: The shift reduces quantity by 125 thousand; the price fall adds 75 thousand
macro.Correct Answer: B — The shift reduces quantity by 100 thousand; the price fall adds 50 thousand
macro.Feedback: At $6 the shift changes quantity from 150 thousand on D0 to 50 thousand on D1, a decrease of 100 thousand. At $4, D1 shows 100 thousand, so the price fall adds 50 thousand.

macro.Common Misconception: Adding demand shifters mechanically without recognizing opposing effects.
macro.Question: Coffee is a normal good. Consumer income rises, buyers expect coffee prices to fall next month, and the current price of tea, a substitute, rises. What can be concluded about current coffee demand?
macro.Choice A: Demand must rise: two favorable determinants outweigh one unfavorable determinant regardless of their sizes.
macro.Choice B: Demand must fall: an expected future price decline outweighs current income and substitute-price effects.
macro.Choice C: Demand is indeterminate: income and the substitute price raise it, while waiting for a lower future price reduces it.
macro.Choice D: Demand is unchanged: income, expectations, and related-good prices affect only movement along the curve.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Demand is indeterminate: income and the substitute price raise it, while waiting for a lower future price reduces it.
macro.Feedback: The two positive demand effects need not outweigh the negative expectations effect. Counting determinants cannot replace comparing their magnitudes.

macro.Common Misconception: Using demand and quantity demanded as interchangeable terms.
macro.Question: The good’s own price declines while every non-price determinant stays fixed. Which demand-side change occurs?
macro.Choice A: Demand increases through a rightward shift of the curve.
macro.Choice B: Demand decreases through a leftward shift of the curve.
macro.Choice C: Quantity demanded stays fixed because the curve did not shift.
macro.Choice D: Quantity demanded increases through a movement along the existing curve.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Quantity demanded increases through a movement along the existing curve.
macro.Feedback: A change in the good’s own price causes movement along the demand curve and changes quantity demanded.

macro.Common Misconception: Selecting an own-price movement or a supply shifter as a demand shifter.
macro.Question: Which event shifts demand for bus rides to the right?
macro.Choice A: The price of subway rides, a substitute, increases.
macro.Choice B: The price of bus rides decreases while all non-price determinants remain fixed.
macro.Choice C: Bus companies add routes and lower their operating costs.
macro.Choice D: The cost of diesel fuel decreases for bus operators.
macro.Correct Answer: A — The price of subway rides, a substitute, increases.
macro.Feedback: A higher price for a substitute makes bus rides more attractive at every bus fare and shifts demand right.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating all goods as normal or confusing demand evidence with supply.
macro.Question: Income falls and purchases of instant noodles rise. What does this evidence suggest?
macro.Choice A: Instant noodles are a normal good for these consumers
macro.Choice B: Instant noodles are an inferior good for these consumers
macro.Choice C: A lower noodle price caused movement along the demand curve
macro.Choice D: A supply decrease raised purchases despite the income change
macro.Correct Answer: B — Instant noodles are an inferior good for these consumers
macro.Feedback: Demand for an inferior good rises when income falls, holding other determinants constant.

macro.Question: A shop cuts a product’s price and sells more. A separate survey finds the quantity buyers want at every fixed price is unchanged. Which account fits both observations?
macro.Choice A: Movement down the same curve; unchanged fixed-price plans provide no evidence of a demand shift.
macro.Choice B: A rightward demand shift; rising purchases provide evidence of stronger demand despite unchanged fixed-price plans.
macro.Choice C: Movement up the same curve; a lower price reduces the quantity buyers desire at that price.
macro.Choice D: A leftward demand shift; unchanged fixed-price plans provide evidence that consumers now want fewer units.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Movement down the same curve; unchanged fixed-price plans provide no evidence of a demand shift.
macro.Feedback: A price cut raises quantity demanded along the same curve. An unchanged fixed-price schedule rules out attributing the increase to a demand shift.

macro.Question: Coffee buyers remain on the same downward-sloping demand curve. Their quantity demanded falls from 80 to 60 cups per day. With non-price determinants unchanged, which price change is consistent with this movement?
macro.Choice A: A rise in coffee’s own price.
macro.Choice B: A fall in coffee’s own price.
macro.Choice C: An unchanged coffee price.
macro.Choice D: A change in coffee’s production cost with its price unchanged.
macro.Correct Answer: A — A rise in coffee’s own price.
macro.Feedback: Moving to a smaller quantity on the same downward-sloping demand curve requires a higher own price. A demand shift would change the curve rather than move along it.

macro.Question: A household’s income rises. With tablet prices, tastes and all other demand determinants unchanged, it plans to buy fewer tablets. How should tablets be classified for this household over this income range?
macro.Choice A: Normal, because any income change shifts demand.
macro.Choice B: Inferior, because higher income reduces its demand.
macro.Choice C: Normal, because the tablet price has not changed.
macro.Choice D: Inferior, because the tablet price must have risen.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Inferior, because higher income reduces its demand.
macro.Feedback: An inferior good has lower demand when income rises, other things equal. This is an income-driven demand shift; the unchanged tablet price rules out an own-price movement.

macro.Common Misconception: Explaining a full demand-schedule change as movement along one curve.
macro.Question: Electric scooters are normal goods. Household incomes rise, but a close substitute becomes cheaper. At an unchanged scooter price, can we predict the direction of scooter purchases without knowing the strength of each effect?
macro.Choice A: Yes, purchases rise; higher income and the cheaper substitute both push demand right.
macro.Choice B: Yes, purchases fall; higher income and the cheaper substitute both push demand left.
macro.Choice C: No; higher income pushes demand right while the cheaper substitute pushes it left.
macro.Choice D: No change occurs; an unchanged scooter price prevents any change in quantity purchased.
macro.Correct Answer: C — No; higher income pushes demand right while the cheaper substitute pushes it left.
macro.Feedback: Income growth increases normal-good demand, while a cheaper substitute reduces scooter demand. Their unknown relative strengths make the net fixed-price quantity effect ambiguous.

macro.Common Misconception: Claiming certainty when opposing demand shifters act simultaneously.
macro.Question: Movie tickets are a normal good. Income rises, but the price of streaming subscriptions, a substitute, falls. What is the strongest conclusion about movie-ticket demand?
macro.Choice A: Demand rises because higher income and a cheaper substitute both increase demand for movie tickets.
macro.Choice B: Demand falls because the cheaper substitute lowers ticket demand while income does not shift demand for a normal good.
macro.Choice C: Quantity demanded changes along one curve because both events change the ticket price
macro.Choice D: The net shift is uncertain because the two effects oppose each other
macro.Correct Answer: D — The net shift is uncertain because the two effects oppose each other
macro.Feedback: Higher income increases demand for a normal good, while a cheaper substitute reduces demand for movie tickets. The effects oppose each other and their relative sizes are not supplied, so the net shift cannot be determined. These are demand shifters, not changes caused by the ticket’s own price.

macro.Common Misconception: Calling an own-price movement a change in demand.
macro.Question: Concert attendance falls after ticket prices rise. A fan claims demand decreased. Surveys show fans’ planned purchases at each fixed price are unchanged, but later a popular performer joins the tour. Which sequence is supported?
macro.Choice A: The first decline is movement along demand; the later performer change can shift demand right.
macro.Choice B: The first decline is a leftward demand shift; the later performer change is movement down that curve.
macro.Choice C: Both events are movements along demand because each changes the number of tickets sold.
macro.Choice D: Both events shift demand left because ticket price and performer popularity are market conditions.
macro.Correct Answer: A — The first decline is movement along demand; the later performer change can shift demand right.
macro.Feedback: Unchanged fixed-price plans imply the first attendance decline is due to movement along demand. Greater performer appeal changes a nonprice determinant and can shift the demand schedule right.

macro.Question: Streaming subscriptions are normal goods. Incomes rise, a rival streaming service lowers its price, and broadband needed for both services becomes more expensive. A manager credits income alone for rising subscriptions. Which inference is defensible?
macro.Choice A: Income and the rival-price cut push demand right; broadband cost changes supply, so observed growth isolates the two demand effects.
macro.Choice B: Income pushes demand right; rival-price and broadband-cost changes push left, so observed growth need not measure the income effect alone.
macro.Choice C: Income pushes demand left; the rival-price cut and broadband cost push right, so observed growth rules out normal-good status.
macro.Choice D: All three changes push demand right; an unchanged subscription price would show that subscriptions rose along the old demand curve.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Income pushes demand right; rival-price and broadband-cost changes push left, so observed growth need not measure the income effect alone.
macro.Feedback: Income raises normal-good demand. A cheaper substitute and a dearer complement reduce it. Observed growth is the net result and cannot identify the isolated income effect; a fixed own price does not prevent a demand shift.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming one of two opposing demand shifters must dominate.
macro.Question: Tea and coffee are substitutes. Coffee prices rise while consumer income falls, and tea is a normal good. What can be concluded about tea demand without knowing effect sizes?
macro.Choice A: Tea demand rises because the substitute-price effect is larger than the income effect
macro.Choice B: Tea demand falls because the income effect is larger than the substitute-price effect
macro.Choice C: The direction of the tea-demand shift is ambiguous
macro.Choice D: Tea demand is unchanged because tea's own price did not change
macro.Correct Answer: C — The direction of the tea-demand shift is ambiguous
macro.Feedback: The higher coffee price raises demand for tea, while lower income reduces demand for tea because it is normal. Without relative effect sizes, the net shift cannot be determined.

macro.Question: A new health report says blueberries are especially beneficial. What likely happens in the blueberry market?
macro.Choice A: Demand increases, price rises, and quantity rises
macro.Choice B: Supply decreases, price rises, and quantity falls
macro.Choice C: Demand decreases, price falls, and quantity falls
macro.Choice D: Quantity supplied falls because demand rose
macro.Correct Answer: A — Demand increases, price rises, and quantity rises
macro.Feedback: A favorable taste or information change increases demand, raising price and quantity.

macro.Question: Refer to the supply and demand graph. If demand shifts from D1 to D2 while supply remains at S2, what happens to equilibrium price and quantity?
macro.Choice A: Price rises and quantity rises
macro.Choice B: Price falls and quantity falls
macro.Choice C: Price rises and quantity falls
macro.Choice D: Price falls and quantity rises
macro.Correct Answer: A — Price rises and quantity rises
macro.Feedback: Moving from D1 with S2 to D2 with S2 raises equilibrium price from P1 to P2 and raises equilibrium quantity from Q2 to Q3.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
macro.Question: How does equilibrium change as demand moves from D0 to D1?
macro.Choice A: Demand decreases, lowering price and quantity
macro.Choice B: Demand increases, raising price and quantity
macro.Choice C: Supply decreases, raising price and reducing quantity
macro.Choice D: Supply increases, lowering price and raising quantity
macro.Correct Answer: B — Demand increases, raising price and quantity
macro.Feedback: Demand shifts right; price rises from 10 to 12 and quantity rises from 200 to 250 thousand.

macro.Question: A negative AD shock usually causes output and the price level to:
macro.Choice A: Both fall
macro.Choice B: Both rise
macro.Choice C: Output falls and prices rise
macro.Choice D: Output rises and prices fall
macro.Correct Answer: A — Both fall
macro.Feedback: A negative AD shock lowers output and the price level.

macro.Common Misconception: Stops at the short-run demand-shock outcome and does not connect the recessionary gap to long-run self-correction.
macro.Question: Consumer confidence collapses, shifting AD left and leaving real output below potential. With no new policy response, which process becomes relevant next?
macro.Choice A: Weak wage and price pressures can shift SRAS right over time, moving output back toward potential.
macro.Choice B: Aggregate demand must automatically shift right to its original position.
macro.Choice C: LRAS must shift left until it reaches the depressed output level.
macro.Choice D: A permanent adverse supply shock must occur before output can recover.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Weak wage and price pressures can shift SRAS right over time, moving output back toward potential.
macro.Feedback: A negative AD shock can create a recessionary gap; with no policy response, wage and expectation adjustment can shift SRAS right over time.

macro.Question: A sharp fall in consumer confidence is primarily which kind of shock?
macro.Choice A: A negative aggregate-demand shock
macro.Choice B: A positive supply shock
macro.Choice C: A change in LRAS
macro.Choice D: A movement along AD
macro.Correct Answer: A — A negative aggregate-demand shock
macro.Feedback: Lower consumer confidence reduces consumption and shifts aggregate demand left.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing demand shocks with supply shocks.
macro.Question: A negative demand shock usually causes which short-run outcome?
macro.Choice A: Higher output and higher prices
macro.Choice B: Lower output and lower prices
macro.Choice C: Lower output and higher prices
macro.Choice D: Higher output and lower prices
macro.Correct Answer: B — Lower output and lower prices
macro.Feedback: A leftward AD shift lowers output and the price level in the short run.

macro.Common Misconception: Calling lower spending a supply shock.
macro.Question: A recession caused by falling consumer confidence is most directly a:
macro.Choice A: Negative demand shock
macro.Choice B: Positive supply shock
macro.Choice C: Higher expected price shock
macro.Choice D: Long-run productivity shock
macro.Correct Answer: A — Negative demand shock
macro.Feedback: Falling confidence reduces consumption and shifts AD left.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing fiscal demand effects with supply shocks.
macro.Question: A tax increase reduces consumption and aggregate demand. Productive capacity is unchanged, and equilibrium output falls below potential. What kind of gap has opened, and through which curve did the tax increase create it?
macro.Choice A: A recessionary gap caused by a leftward AD shift.
macro.Choice B: An inflationary gap caused by a rightward AD shift.
macro.Choice C: A recessionary gap caused by a leftward LRAS shift.
macro.Choice D: An inflationary gap caused by a movement up an unchanged AD curve.
macro.Correct Answer: A — A recessionary gap caused by a leftward AD shift.
macro.Feedback: Lower consumption shifts AD left. With potential output unchanged, the resulting output shortfall is a recessionary gap.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The deficit proves national saving exceeds domestic investment” in this international transactions and identities task.
macro.Question: A student says a trade deficit proves imports destroyed an equal amount of domestic output. Which correction is best?
macro.Choice A: The deficit proves national saving exceeds domestic investment
macro.Choice B: The deficit records imports above exports; it does not identify the separate response of domestic production
macro.Choice C: The claim is correct because imports are subtracted from GDP
macro.Choice D: A trade deficit means domestic consumption must be falling
macro.Correct Answer: B — The deficit records imports above exports; it does not identify the separate response of domestic production
macro.Feedback: Imports are subtracted to exclude foreign production from GDP. The trade balance alone does not show how domestic output changed.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The statement is correct whenever interest rates rise” in this capital flows and net capital outflow task.
macro.Question: A student says a capital inflow means domestic residents purchased more foreign assets. What is the correction?
macro.Choice A: The statement is correct whenever interest rates rise
macro.Choice B: A net inflow means foreign purchases of domestic assets exceeded domestic purchases abroad
macro.Choice C: A net inflow means both asset-purchase flows were zero
macro.Choice D: A net inflow is the same as positive NCO
macro.Correct Answer: B — A net inflow means foreign purchases of domestic assets exceeded domestic purchases abroad
macro.Feedback: Negative NCO is generated when the foreign acquisition of domestic assets is the larger flow.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The foreign price level must equal one” in this real exchange rates and purchasing power task.
macro.Question: A student argues that equal inflation rates guarantee an unchanged real exchange rate. What is missing?
macro.Choice A: Domestic prices cannot be measured
macro.Choice B: PPP rules out equal inflation
macro.Choice C: The foreign price level must equal one
macro.Choice D: The nominal exchange rate may change
macro.Correct Answer: D — The nominal exchange rate may change
macro.Feedback: Equal inflation stabilizes the price-level ratio, but nominal exchange-rate movements can still change eP/P*.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The student is correct because every lower quotation is depreciation” in this nominal exchange rates task.
macro.Question: A student sees the quotation fall from 1.10 dollars per euro to 1.00 dollar per euro and says the dollar depreciated. What is the error?
macro.Choice A: The student is correct because every lower quotation is depreciation
macro.Choice B: The euro appreciated because its dollar price fell
macro.Choice C: No currency changed because the quotation reached one
macro.Choice D: Fewer dollars are needed per euro, so the dollar appreciated
macro.Correct Answer: D — Fewer dollars are needed per euro, so the dollar appreciated
macro.Feedback: The dollar price of the euro fell, meaning each dollar can obtain more euros than before.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The domestic currency depreciates 10 percent in reciprocal terms; the import costs 9.1 percent more domestically” in this nominal exchange rates task.
macro.Question: A foreign dollar costs 80 domestic currency units initially and 88 later. A report calls this a 10 percent domestic-currency appreciation and says a dollar-priced import became 10 percent cheaper domestically. With its dollar price fixed, which paired correction is accurate?
macro.Choice A: The domestic currency depreciates 10 percent in reciprocal terms; the import costs 9.1 percent more domestically
macro.Choice B: The domestic currency appreciates 10 percent; the import costs 10 percent more domestically
macro.Choice C: The domestic currency depreciates about 9.1 percent in dollars per domestic unit; the import costs 10 percent more domestically
macro.Choice D: The domestic currency depreciates about 9.1 percent; the import costs 9.1 percent less domestically
macro.Correct Answer: C — The domestic currency depreciates about 9.1 percent in dollars per domestic unit; the import costs 10 percent more domestically
macro.Feedback: Domestic currency value changes by (1/88)/(1/80) − 1 = −1/11, about −9.1 percent. A fixed dollar bill multiplied by domestic units/dollar rises by 88/80 − 1 = 10 percent. Reciprocal percentage bases differ.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The interest-rate rise caused the supply increase, reversing the usual NCO slope” in this foreign exchange market task.
macro.Question: Use the foreign-exchange model in which net capital outflow determines a vertical supply curve for domestic currency. The domestic real interest rate rises, while a separate increase in risk makes investors want to send more funds abroad at each interest rate. The final currency-supply curve lies to the right of its original position. With domestic and foreign price levels fixed and demand for domestic currency unchanged, what does this tell us about the two effects on net capital outflow and the exchange rate?
macro.Choice A: The interest-rate rise caused the supply increase, reversing the usual NCO slope
macro.Choice B: Risk outweighs higher interest rates; the currency depreciates, but neither effect's size can be determined separately
macro.Choice C: Vertical supply means NCO is fixed across both equilibria, so the stated curve change is impossible
macro.Choice D: The effects of risk and the higher interest rate cancel exactly because both supply curves are vertical
macro.Correct Answer: B — Risk outweighs higher interest rates; the currency depreciates, but neither effect's size can be determined separately
macro.Feedback: A vertical currency-supply curve fixes the quantity supplied for a given level of net capital outflow, not when that level changes. The rightward shift means the increase caused by risk exceeds the decrease caused by the higher interest rate. With currency demand unchanged, the domestic currency depreciates. The final shift alone does not reveal the size of each separate effect.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
macro.Question: Diminishing returns means extra capital eventually adds:
macro.Choice A: Smaller extra amounts of output
macro.Choice B: Larger extra amounts forever
macro.Choice C: No output from the beginning
macro.Choice D: Only inflation
macro.Correct Answer: A — Smaller extra amounts of output
macro.Feedback: Additional capital still helps, but by smaller amounts as capital becomes abundant.

macro.Common Misconception: Confuses identical physical inputs with equal marginal products.
macro.Question: With labor and technology fixed, successive identical machines raise output by 12, 9 and 6 units. A plan assumes a fourth adds 12. Which revision fits diminishing marginal returns?
macro.Choice A: Expect a gain smaller than 6 if the pattern continues
macro.Choice B: Expect a gain of 12 because the machines are identical
macro.Choice C: Expect total output to fall by 6
macro.Choice D: Expect every previous machine’s output to disappear
macro.Correct Answer: A — Expect a gain smaller than 6 if the pattern continues
macro.Feedback: Diminishing marginal returns concern successively smaller additions to output, not a fall in total output or identical gains from identical inputs.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
macro.Question: Diminishing returns to capital means:
macro.Choice A: Each added unit of capital contributes less extra output
macro.Choice B: Capital always reduces output
macro.Choice C: Technology stops mattering
macro.Choice D: Workers never benefit from machines
macro.Correct Answer: A — Each added unit of capital contributes less extra output
macro.Feedback: Diminishing returns means extra capital still helps, but by smaller amounts as capital accumulates.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing worker training and skills with physical equipment.
macro.Question: Why does capital deepening eventually face limits if technology and human capital do not improve?
macro.Choice A: Each extra machine adds less output as capital accumulates
macro.Choice B: Capital is never useful
macro.Choice C: Natural resources become irrelevant
macro.Choice D: Output per worker must become zero
macro.Correct Answer: A — Each extra machine adds less output as capital accumulates
macro.Feedback: Diminishing returns limit the gains from adding more capital alone.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
macro.Question: A country doubles its capital stock, but output rises by less than double. Which concept is most directly illustrated?
macro.Choice A: Diminishing returns to capital
macro.Choice B: The Rule of 70
macro.Choice C: CPI overstatement
macro.Choice D: Cyclical unemployment
macro.Correct Answer: A — Diminishing returns to capital
macro.Feedback: Diminishing returns means additional capital raises output, but by less and less as capital accumulates.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
macro.Question: Diminishing returns imply that if a country keeps adding capital while labor stays fixed:
macro.Choice A: Each additional unit of capital eventually adds smaller increases in output
macro.Choice B: Each additional unit of capital adds larger increases forever
macro.Choice C: Output must immediately fall
macro.Choice D: Capital stops being counted in GDP
macro.Correct Answer: A — Each additional unit of capital eventually adds smaller increases in output
macro.Feedback: Diminishing returns means extra capital becomes less productive as more of it is added.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
macro.Question: With labor, skills and technology fixed, output at 10, 20 and 30 identical machines is 100, 160 and 200 units. A planner predicts that 40 machines must yield 260. Which assessment follows from the observed pattern?
macro.Choice A: The successive gains are 60 and 40; continued diminishing marginal returns would put the next gain below 40
macro.Choice B: The observed average gain is 50, so 40 machines must yield exactly 250
macro.Choice C: The capital stock doubled once, proving output must double at 40 machines
macro.Choice D: The last gain was 40, so every later ten machines must add exactly 40
macro.Correct Answer: A — The successive gains are 60 and 40; continued diminishing marginal returns would put the next gain below 40
macro.Feedback: Equal capital increments add 60 then 40 units while other inputs are fixed. If the diminishing-returns pattern continues, the next increment adds less than 40; the table alone does not supply an exact future output level.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “It confuses diminishing returns with falling total output; the second machine necessarily destroys output” in this sources of productivity task.
macro.Question: A fixed technology gives an extra 260 units of output from the first additional machine and only 130 from the second. A proposal assumes each later machine adds the first machine's amount. What is the flaw?
macro.Choice A: It ignores diminishing marginal gains; total output can still rise.
macro.Choice B: It ignores declining total output; the second machine reduces production.
macro.Choice C: It ignores labor displacement; the second machine must halve employment.
macro.Choice D: It ignores technical progress; each machine raises future marginal gains.
macro.Correct Answer: A — It ignores diminishing marginal gains; total output can still rise.
macro.Feedback: With other inputs and technology fixed, added capital can increase total output at a decreasing rate. A smaller positive increment is not a fall in total output.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The capital-poor economy must grow faster regardless of investment, institutions or technology access” in this sources of productivity task.
macro.Question: Two economies each employ 270 workers. One has little capital per worker and the other much more, with similar technology and institutions. Which qualification should accompany a catch-up prediction?
macro.Choice A: The capital-poor economy must grow faster regardless of investment, institutions or technology access
macro.Choice B: The capital-rich economy must have higher percentage growth because its output level is higher
macro.Choice C: Equal worker counts require equal output per worker regardless of capital
macro.Choice D: The capital-poor economy may earn higher marginal returns, but investment and effective use of capital are still required
macro.Correct Answer: D — The capital-poor economy may earn higher marginal returns, but investment and effective use of capital are still required
macro.Feedback: Diminishing returns can create catch-up potential when conditions are comparable. Potential is not an automatic growth guarantee without investment and productive use.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Transport affects consumption only and cannot limit production from resources” in this sources of productivity task.
macro.Question: A discovery increases available mineral resources for 280 workers, but extraction technology and transport remain inadequate. Which policy diagnosis best connects resources to productivity?
macro.Choice A: Transport affects consumption only and cannot limit production from resources
macro.Choice B: Resource abundance makes worker skills and institutions irrelevant to long-run output
macro.Choice C: The resource expands potential opportunities, but complementary technology/infrastructure can be the binding constraint
macro.Choice D: The resource alone guarantees an immediate proportional increase in output per worker
macro.Correct Answer: C — The resource expands potential opportunities, but complementary technology/infrastructure can be the binding constraint
macro.Feedback: Natural resources can support production, but usable technology, skills and infrastructure determine whether they can be exploited productively. More resources alone need not raise current output.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
macro.Question: Two equal additions to capital per worker produce output gains of 9 and 6 with skills and technology fixed. A later 9-unit gain occurs after a new production method is introduced. Does that last observation refute diminishing returns to capital?
macro.Choice A: No; the first two gains compare capital with other inputs fixed, while technology changed in the third
macro.Choice B: Yes; any later larger gain refutes diminishing returns regardless of other changes
macro.Choice C: No; diminishing returns means total output must fall after adding capital
macro.Choice D: Yes; introducing technology changes physical capital into a natural resource
macro.Correct Answer: A — No; the first two gains compare capital with other inputs fixed, while technology changed in the third
macro.Feedback: Diminishing marginal returns concerns additional capital with other determinants held fixed. The first two gains fit that pattern. A technology improvement changes the production relationship, so the larger third gain is not a comparable capital-only experiment.

macro.Common Misconception: Confuses diminishing positive gains with negative gains and treats training as machinery.
macro.Question: With worker hours, skills and methods fixed, two equal additions of machines raise output per hour first from 100 to 110, then from 110 to 116. Training then raises it to 124 without more machines. A report says diminishing returns made the second machine addition harmful and that only machines can raise productivity. Which assessment fits all the evidence?
macro.Choice A: Machine gains remain positive but shrink from 10 to 6; training adds human capital and a further gain of 8
macro.Choice B: Machine gains become negative after the first addition; training reverses a loss of 6 with a gain of 8
macro.Choice C: Machine gains rise from 10 to 16; training adds physical capital and a further gain of 8
macro.Choice D: Machine gains remain equal at 10; training adds worker hours rather than output per hour
macro.Correct Answer: A — Machine gains remain positive but shrink from 10 to 6; training adds human capital and a further gain of 8
macro.Feedback: The successive machine gains are 110−100=10 and 116−110=6: diminishing marginal gains are still positive. The further 124−116=8 occurs without new machines and is attributed to worker training, a human-capital improvement.

macro.Common Misconception: Confuses a lower positive inflation rate with a falling price level.
macro.Question: Inflation falls from 5% to 2% but remains positive. Did the price level fall?
macro.Choice A: No; it rose more slowly
macro.Choice B: Yes; any inflation decline lowers prices
macro.Choice C: Yes; disinflation and deflation are identical
macro.Choice D: No; the price level stayed exactly fixed
macro.Correct Answer: A — No; it rose more slowly
macro.Feedback: Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a decline in the price level.

macro.Common Misconception: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
macro.Question: Contractionary disinflation raises unemployment in the short run. Is that necessarily permanent?
macro.Choice A: Yes; every contraction shifts LRPC right
macro.Choice B: Yes; the SRPC never shifts after policy
macro.Choice C: No; unemployment must fall below natural immediately
macro.Choice D: No; unemployment can return toward natural as expectations adjust
macro.Correct Answer: D — No; unemployment can return toward natural as expectations adjust
macro.Feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

macro.Common Misconception: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
macro.Question: Contractionary monetary policy reduces spending and inflation pressure. Which Phillips connection follows initially?
macro.Choice A: Movement toward higher unemployment and lower inflation along SRPC
macro.Choice B: A permanent LRPC shift to higher unemployment after expected inflation adjusts
macro.Choice C: Movement toward lower unemployment and lower inflation along the same curve
macro.Choice D: An upward SRPC shift caused by lower expected inflation during contraction
macro.Correct Answer: A — Movement toward higher unemployment and lower inflation along SRPC
macro.Feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

macro.Common Misconception: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
macro.Question: Expected inflation falls and the economy later returns to natural unemployment. How do the short-run and long-run Phillips curves explain this adjustment?
macro.Choice A: A permanent move along one SRPC only
macro.Choice B: An LRPC shift caused by the price level
macro.Choice C: A sacrifice-ratio shift of aggregate demand
macro.Choice D: A downward SRPC shift followed by long-run return to LRPC
macro.Correct Answer: D — A downward SRPC shift followed by long-run return to LRPC
macro.Feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring the short-run cost of disinflation.
macro.Question: If the Fed reduces money growth to fight inflation, unemployment usually:
macro.Choice A: Falls immediately
macro.Choice B: Rises temporarily
macro.Choice C: Stays permanently at zero
macro.Choice D: Becomes the price level
macro.Correct Answer: B — Rises temporarily
macro.Feedback: Disinflation usually raises unemployment temporarily as the economy moves along the SRPC.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring short-run disinflation costs.
macro.Question: A policymaker wants lower inflation but ignores unemployment during transition. What model warns about this cost?
macro.Choice A: Short-run Phillips curve
macro.Choice B: Money multiplier only
macro.Choice C: M1 definition only
macro.Choice D: Classical dichotomy only
macro.Correct Answer: A — Short-run Phillips curve
macro.Feedback: The short-run Phillips curve shows that reducing inflation can temporarily raise unemployment.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing disinflation with deflation.
macro.Question: Disinflation means that:
macro.Choice A: The overall price level is falling because average prices are declining.
macro.Choice B: Unemployment is falling even though output remains below potential.
macro.Choice C: Inflation is slowing, although the price level may still be rising.
macro.Choice D: Nominal wages are fixed while real wages rise automatically.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Inflation is slowing, although the price level may still be rising.
macro.Feedback: Disinflation is slower price growth; deflation is a falling price level.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring the role of expected inflation in the transition.
macro.Question: Why can a credible anti-inflation announcement reduce the short-run cost of disinflation?
macro.Choice A: It permanently eliminates the natural rate of unemployment.
macro.Choice B: It guarantees that the price level falls immediately.
macro.Choice C: It makes aggregate demand irrelevant.
macro.Choice D: Expected inflation may adjust downward more quickly.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Expected inflation may adjust downward more quickly.
macro.Feedback: When expectations fall sooner, wage and price setting can adjust with less output and unemployment loss.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating the sacrifice ratio as a permanent unemployment rate.
macro.Question: The sacrifice ratio measures the:
macro.Choice A: Cumulative output lost per percentage-point reduction in inflation.
macro.Choice B: The permanent unemployment rate created by a recession.
macro.Choice C: The price-level increase caused by one point of money growth.
macro.Choice D: The share of public spending financed by current taxes.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Cumulative output lost per percentage-point reduction in inflation.
macro.Feedback: The sacrifice ratio summarizes the output cost of lowering inflation.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring the short-run unemployment cost.
macro.Question: If the Fed reduces money growth to lower inflation, the short-run Phillips curve predicts:
macro.Choice A: Lower inflation and temporarily higher unemployment
macro.Choice B: Higher inflation and lower unemployment
macro.Choice C: Lower inflation and lower unemployment immediately
macro.Choice D: No short-run cost at all
macro.Correct Answer: A — Lower inflation and temporarily higher unemployment
macro.Feedback: Disinflation usually moves the economy toward lower inflation and higher unemployment in the short run.

macro.Common Misconception: Skipping the temporary move above natural unemployment.
macro.Question: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at b, which sequence best shows disinflation with temporary unemployment costs?
macro.Choice A: b to d to c
macro.Choice B: b to a to c
macro.Choice C: b to c to d
macro.Choice D: b to d to b
macro.Correct Answer: A — b to d to c
macro.Feedback: Disinflation lowers actual inflation first, moving to d, then expectations fall and the economy returns to c.

macro.Common Misconception: Missing the temporary cost of disinflation.
macro.Question: What does the path b to d to c show about disinflation when expected inflation adjusts gradually?
macro.Choice A: Unemployment temporarily rises from U2 to U3, then returns to U2 as expectations fall.
macro.Choice B: Unemployment temporarily rises from U1 to U2, then returns to U1 as expectations fall.
macro.Choice C: Unemployment rises from U2 to U3 because disinflation permanently raises the natural rate.
macro.Choice D: Unemployment returns from U3 to U2 through a rise in demand along the unchanged upper SRPC.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Unemployment temporarily rises from U2 to U3, then returns to U2 as expectations fall.
macro.Feedback: The path first moves down SRPC2 from b to d, raising unemployment to U3. Falling expected inflation then shifts the short-run curve down, reaching c at the unchanged natural rate U2.

macro.Common Misconception: Skipping the temporary unemployment cost.
macro.Question: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at b, which sequence matches disinflation and expectations adjustment?
macro.Choice A: b to d to c
macro.Choice B: b to c to d
macro.Choice C: b to a to c
macro.Choice D: b to d to a
macro.Correct Answer: A — b to d to c
macro.Feedback: Disinflation moves from b to d in the short run; expected inflation falls and the economy moves to c.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming gradualism automatically produces low transition costs.
macro.Question: A central bank announces a gradual disinflation, but households and firms doubt that the plan will continue. What is the most likely consequence?
macro.Choice A: The natural unemployment rate immediately falls to zero.
macro.Choice B: High expected inflation can prolong the output and job losses.
macro.Choice C: The price level must begin falling throughout the adjustment.
macro.Choice D: Unemployment cannot rise because the disinflation is gradual.
macro.Correct Answer: B — High expected inflation can prolong the output and job losses.
macro.Feedback: If the plan lacks credibility, expected inflation can adjust slowly and make the disinflation more costly.

macro.Common Misconception: Reversing the sacrifice ratios or treating equal inflation reductions as equal output costs.
macro.Question: Country A has a sacrifice ratio of 2, while Country B has a sacrifice ratio of 5. If both reduce inflation by 3 percentage points, which comparison is correct?
macro.Choice A: A loses about 15% of annual GDP cumulatively; B loses about 6%.
macro.Choice B: Both lose about 3% of annual GDP because the inflation reduction is equal.
macro.Choice C: A loses about 6% of annual GDP cumulatively; B loses about 15%.
macro.Choice D: A has no output loss because its sacrifice ratio is below the inflation reduction.
macro.Correct Answer: C — A loses about 6% of annual GDP cumulatively; B loses about 15%.
macro.Feedback: Cumulative output loss equals the sacrifice ratio times the inflation reduction: 2 × 3 = 6 for A and 5 × 3 = 15 for B.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “First d, eventually a; lower expected inflation permanently lowers natural unemployment to U1” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
macro.Question: Starting at b, policymakers reduce inflation to I1 before expectations change. If expectations later adapt to I1 and the natural rate stays fixed, how should the transition be interpreted?
macro.Choice A: The path is b-a-c: unemployment first rises, then returns to its natural rate as the short-run curve shifts down.
macro.Choice B: The path is b-d-c: unemployment first rises, then returns to its natural rate as the short-run curve shifts down.
macro.Choice C: The path is b-d-c: the return occurs because the natural rate falls permanently from U3 to U2.
macro.Choice D: The path stops at d: changing expectations cannot alter unemployment when actual inflation stays at I1.
macro.Correct Answer: B — The path is b-d-c: unemployment first rises, then returns to its natural rate as the short-run curve shifts down.
macro.Feedback: With initial expectations, I1 intersects SRPC2 at d, U3. Lower expectations shift the curve to SRPC1 and allow c at U2. The change in actual unemployment is temporary; LRPC stays fixed.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Credible adjustment moves toward a at U1; unchanged expectations also restore U2 automatically” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
macro.Question: At d after disinflation, actual inflation is held at I1. Compare a credible policy whose lower inflation becomes expected with a policy that leaves expectations at their old level.
macro.Choice A: Lower expectations allow c at U2; old expectations leave d at U3, so commitment alone is not the same as belief.
macro.Choice B: Lower expectations allow a at U1; old expectations leave d at U3, so commitment alone is not the same as belief.
macro.Choice C: Lower expectations allow c at U2; this shows credibility permanently reduces the natural rate.
macro.Choice D: Both cases reach c at U2 immediately, because announcing a fixed actual rate also fixes expectations.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Lower expectations allow c at U2; old expectations leave d at U3, so commitment alone is not the same as belief.
macro.Feedback: At I1, the old SRPC2 implies d/U3. Lowering expected inflation shifts the curve down, allowing c/U2 at the same actual inflation. Holding the target is not identical to having the target believed.

macro.Common Misconception: Skipping the short-run unemployment cost of disinflation.
macro.Question: Compare disinflations from b to the lower sustained inflation rate in the diagram. Supply conditions and natural unemployment do not change. Old contracts initially preserve expected inflation in one case; in the other, credibility and immediate contract adjustment reduce expectations before spending changes. Which comparison fits?
macro.Choice A: Old contracts allow b-d-c; prompt expectation adjustment can allow b-c without the same temporary unemployment increase.
macro.Choice B: Old contracts allow b-a-c; prompt expectation adjustment can allow b-c without the same temporary unemployment increase.
macro.Choice C: Old contracts allow b-d-c; prompt expectation adjustment still requires d because credibility cannot affect wage setting.
macro.Choice D: Old contracts allow b-d-c; prompt adjustment shifts the natural rate to U3 and makes d the permanent endpoint.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Old contracts allow b-d-c; prompt expectation adjustment can allow b-c without the same temporary unemployment increase.
macro.Feedback: The plotted disinflation is from b at I2 to c at I1. With old expectations it can pass through d at U3. If expectations and relevant contracts already adjust, the lower SRPC supports c without that initial gap. This conclusion depends on prompt contract adjustment, not credibility alone.

macro.Common Misconception: Missing the expectation adjustment needed after disinflation.
macro.Question: After moving from b to d, inflation is held at the rate shown at d. Supply conditions and natural unemployment stay unchanged. A forecast predicts a return to the natural rate. Which expectation adjustment is consistent with the diagram?
macro.Choice A: Expected inflation falls, shifting the short-run curve through c; staying on SRPC2 would leave the economy at d.
macro.Choice B: Expected inflation rises, shifting the short-run curve through b; staying on SRPC1 would leave the economy at a.
macro.Choice C: Expected inflation falls, shifting the short-run curve through c; this permanently lowers natural unemployment from U3 to U2.
macro.Choice D: Expected inflation is unchanged; demand growth alone moves d to c along SRPC2.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Expected inflation falls, shifting the short-run curve through c; staying on SRPC2 would leave the economy at d.
macro.Feedback: At the fixed lower inflation rate, c is on SRPC1 at natural unemployment U2, while d remains on SRPC2 at U3. With the supply offset fixed, lower expectations are needed to change the short-run curve.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrect inference: b becomes the endpoint; contract lags prevent eventual inflation adjustment.
macro.Question: During the disinflation from b, a credible announcement immediately lowers expectations, but existing wage contracts adjust gradually. Which endpoint and transition-cost claim fit the diagram?
macro.Choice A: a is the eventual endpoint; gradual contract adjustment can still leave temporary unemployment above U2.
macro.Choice B: c is the eventual endpoint; gradual contract adjustment can still leave temporary unemployment above U2.
macro.Choice C: c is the eventual endpoint; immediate belief alone eliminates all unemployment costs despite the contract lag.
macro.Choice D: d is the eventual endpoint; a contract lag permanently prevents the lower expectations from affecting supply.
macro.Correct Answer: B — c is the eventual endpoint; gradual contract adjustment can still leave temporary unemployment above U2.
macro.Feedback: At lower inflation I1 and unchanged natural unemployment U2, the endpoint is c. Credibility supports the lower SRPC, but contracts can delay cost adjustment, leaving temporary costs before reaching it.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The lower deposit expansion proves rates cannot have fallen, so the reported observations are impossible” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
macro.Question: A banking system receives $350 of reserves. With a required reserve ratio of 10%, the simple model predicts a maximum deposit increase of $3500; actual deposits increase by $1400. Interest rates fall, but firms also expect lower returns on their projects. Why might both deposit growth and investment spending be smaller than the simple model predicts?
macro.Choice A: Leakages can explain a multiplier below ten, and weaker expected returns can further limit investment despite lower rates
macro.Choice B: The lower deposit expansion proves rates cannot have fallen, so the reported observations are impossible
macro.Choice C: Lower rates guarantee the full predicted investment expansion even when expected returns deteriorate
macro.Choice D: The reserve injection raises real productive capacity immediately by the textbook deposit maximum
macro.Correct Answer: A — Leakages can explain a multiplier below ten, and weaker expected returns can further limit investment despite lower rates
macro.Feedback: Observed multiplier=1400/350=4, below the restrictive simple maximum 10. Even if rates fall, the rate-to-investment link can weaken when expected profitability falls. These are distinct constraints at successive stages.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrect inference: Deflation; prices fall; excess unemployment indicates temporary real costs.
macro.Question: A country reduces inflation from 8% to 3% through demand restraint. Prices keep rising, and unemployment temporarily exceeds natural. Which diagnosis includes all three observations?
macro.Choice A: Deflation; prices fall; excess unemployment indicates temporary real costs.
macro.Choice B: Disinflation; prices still rise; excess unemployment indicates temporary real costs.
macro.Choice C: Disinflation; prices still rise; excess unemployment implies no real cost.
macro.Choice D: Disinflation; prices are unchanged; excess unemployment represents permanently lower potential.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Disinflation; prices still rise; excess unemployment indicates temporary real costs.
macro.Feedback: Disinflation lowers the inflation rate, not necessarily the price level. With sticky expectations or contracts, demand restraint can temporarily lower output and raise unemployment.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Actual inflation falls while expected inflation rises by the same amount” in this disinflation and policy task.
macro.Question: Starting at b, policymakers reduce inflation. Why could the economy reach c directly instead of first passing through d?
macro.Choice A: Expectations and contracts adjust promptly, moving the short-run relationship from SRPC1 to SRPC2 before the demand restraint.
macro.Choice B: Expectations and contracts adjust promptly, moving the short-run relationship from SRPC2 to SRPC1 before the demand restraint.
macro.Choice C: Expectations remain fixed, but the lower actual inflation alone moves both unemployment and the short-run curve to c.
macro.Choice D: Demand restraint permanently lowers natural unemployment, shifting LRPC to c before expectations change.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Expectations and contracts adjust promptly, moving the short-run relationship from SRPC2 to SRPC1 before the demand restraint.
macro.Feedback: The graph places c on the lower SRPC at the same natural unemployment rate as b. Reaching c immediately requires lower expected inflation and prompt contract adjustment; demand restraint with old expectations leads to d.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The gradual plan is costless because spreading losses across years removes them from the sum” in this disinflation and policy task.
macro.Question: Two plans each lower inflation four points. A rapid plan loses 8% of one year's output cumulatively; a gradual plan loses 6%. Which comparison is supported, and what is not established?
macro.Choice A: Ratios: gradual 0, rapid 2; spreading losses removes the gradual plan's cost.
macro.Choice B: Ratios: gradual 1.5, rapid 2; timing constraints still matter for selection.
macro.Choice C: Ratios: gradual 2, rapid 1.5; fewer calendar years establish lower cumulative cost.
macro.Choice D: Ratios: gradual 4, rapid 4; equal inflation reductions establish equal costs per point.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Ratios: gradual 1.5, rapid 2; timing constraints still matter for selection.
macro.Feedback: Using the stated cumulative-loss convention: rapid 8/4=2, gradual 6/4=1.5. Timing, uncertainty and other constraints are additional evaluation margins.

macro.Common Misconception: Subtracts a positive but lower inflation rate from the price level.
macro.Question: A price index is 200. Over the next year inflation slows from the previous year’s 6% to 3%, remaining positive. What is the new index, and does this year illustrate disinflation or deflation?
macro.Choice A: 194; deflation
macro.Choice B: 212; disinflation
macro.Choice C: 206; disinflation
macro.Choice D: 200; deflation
macro.Correct Answer: C — 206; disinflation
macro.Feedback: The index rises to 200×1.03=206. A lower but positive inflation rate means prices rise more slowly: disinflation. Subtracting 3% would incorrectly turn it into deflation; using 6% would ignore the new rate.

macro.Common Misconception: Confuses a lower positive inflation rate with a falling price level.
macro.Question: Inflation slows from 6% to 3%, so the price level still rises more slowly. What is this?
macro.Choice A: Disinflation
macro.Choice B: Deflation
macro.Choice C: Hyperinflation
macro.Choice D: A falling real interest rate by definition
macro.Correct Answer: A — Disinflation
macro.Feedback: Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a decline in the price level.

macro.Common Misconception: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
macro.Question: Which short-run effect commonly accompanies contractionary disinflation policy?
macro.Choice A: Higher output and lower unemployment
macro.Choice B: A permanently lower natural unemployment rate
macro.Choice C: An immediate rise in aggregate demand
macro.Choice D: Lower output and higher unemployment
macro.Correct Answer: D — Lower output and higher unemployment
macro.Feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

macro.Common Misconception: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
macro.Question: A central bank reduces aggregate demand to lower inflation. What Phillips movement is expected before expectations adjust?
macro.Choice A: An immediate leftward LRPC shift
macro.Choice B: An upward SRPC shift from lower expected inflation
macro.Choice C: Down and right along the current SRPC
macro.Choice D: Up and left along the current SRPC
macro.Correct Answer: C — Down and right along the current SRPC
macro.Feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

macro.Common Misconception: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
macro.Question: Why can a credible lower-inflation target reduce the short-run cost of disinflation?
macro.Choice A: It causes aggregate demand to expand during contraction
macro.Choice B: It may lower expected inflation and shift the SRPC downward sooner
macro.Choice C: It permanently lowers the natural rate by announcement
macro.Choice D: It guarantees wages and prices adjust instantly
macro.Correct Answer: B — It may lower expected inflation and shift the SRPC downward sooner
macro.Feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

macro.Common Misconception: Confuses a lower positive inflation rate with a falling price level.
macro.Question: Inflation falls from 4% to 1%, but prices continue rising. Which statement is correct?
macro.Choice A: The economy has disinflation, not deflation
macro.Choice B: The economy has deflation because inflation fell
macro.Choice C: The price level must be below its initial level
macro.Choice D: The natural rate must have declined
macro.Correct Answer: A — The economy has disinflation, not deflation
macro.Feedback: Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a decline in the price level.

macro.Common Misconception: Assumes either rapid or gradual disinflation is unconditionally best.
macro.Question: Why might gradual disinflation be chosen instead of a rapid contraction?
macro.Choice A: It always produces zero cumulative output loss
macro.Choice B: It guarantees expected inflation never changes
macro.Choice C: It permanently shifts LRPC left
macro.Choice D: It can spread adjustment and reduce a severe short-run output gap
macro.Correct Answer: D — It can spread adjustment and reduce a severe short-run output gap
macro.Feedback: The preferred path depends on credibility, expectations, adjustment speed, uncertainty, and cumulative costs.

macro.Common Misconception: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
macro.Question: A disinflation announcement is not credible, and wage contracts embed 6% inflation. What makes immediate costless adjustment unlikely?
macro.Choice A: Aggregate demand cannot affect inflation
macro.Choice B: Deflation is required before unemployment changes
macro.Choice C: Expected inflation and nominal contracts may adjust slowly
macro.Choice D: The LRPC must shift left before policy begins
macro.Correct Answer: C — Expected inflation and nominal contracts may adjust slowly
macro.Feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

macro.Common Misconception: Assumes either rapid or gradual disinflation is unconditionally best.
macro.Question: Two paths reach 2% inflation. The rapid path has a deep one-year recession; the gradual path has smaller gaps for several years. What must be compared?
macro.Choice A: The price levels at the start, without output data
macro.Choice B: Their cumulative output losses and inflation reductions
macro.Choice C: Only the largest annual unemployment rate
macro.Choice D: Only the final year’s output level
macro.Correct Answer: B — Their cumulative output losses and inflation reductions
macro.Feedback: The preferred path depends on credibility, expectations, adjustment speed, uncertainty, and cumulative costs.

macro.Common Misconception: Mixes annual and cumulative output loss or omits units.
macro.Question: Inflation falls 3 points while cumulative output loss equals 6% of annual GDP. Unemployment later returns to its natural rate. What is the sacrifice ratio, and is the unemployment increase permanent?
macro.Choice A: The sacrifice ratio is 0.5, and unemployment stays permanently high
macro.Choice B: The ratio is 3, and LRPC shifts right permanently
macro.Choice C: The ratio is 6, and the price level must have fallen
macro.Choice D: The sacrifice ratio is 2, and the unemployment cost was temporary in the model
macro.Correct Answer: D — The sacrifice ratio is 2, and the unemployment cost was temporary in the model
macro.Feedback: The sacrifice ratio is 6/3=2 percent of annual output per percentage-point inflation reduction. The given return to natural unemployment means the unemployment cost is temporary in this model; disinflation alone need not make the price level fall.

macro.Common Misconception: Claims contractionary policy lowers inflation with no short-run output or unemployment cost.
macro.Question: An adverse supply shock has raised inflation and unemployment. Why can disinflation policy face a harder near-term tradeoff than after a demand boom?
macro.Choice A: The LRPC becomes downward sloping during supply shocks
macro.Choice B: Contraction shifts the SRPC downward with no demand effect
macro.Choice C: Contraction can lower inflation pressure while worsening an already weak output position
macro.Choice D: Supply shocks automatically lower the sacrifice ratio to zero
macro.Correct Answer: C — Contraction can lower inflation pressure while worsening an already weak output position
macro.Feedback: Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment.

macro.Common Misconception: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
macro.Question: A credible central bank announces a lower inflation target, expected inflation falls partly, and policy still contracts demand. Which conclusion is most defensible?
macro.Choice A: The downward SRPC shift may reduce but need not eliminate the short-run output cost
macro.Choice B: Credibility guarantees unemployment never rises during the contractionary adjustment
macro.Choice C: The LRPC shifts left because the announced target permanently lowers natural unemployment
macro.Choice D: Disinflation necessarily becomes deflation before expected inflation can decline
macro.Correct Answer: A — The downward SRPC shift may reduce but need not eliminate the short-run output cost
macro.Feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Earlier adjustment must raise the unemployment excursion because lower expected inflation shifts SRPC up” in this disinflation and policy task.
