macro.Choice A: Not in the labor force
macro.Choice B: Unemployed
macro.Choice C: Employed
macro.Choice D: Structurally unemployed
macro.Correct Answer: A — Not in the labor force
macro.Feedback: People not working and not looking for work are not in the labor force.

macro.Common Misconception: Counting discouraged workers as unemployed even after they stop actively searching.
macro.Question: A discouraged worker is usually counted as:
macro.Choice A: Not in the labor force
macro.Choice B: Unemployed
macro.Choice C: Employed
macro.Choice D: Part of GDP
macro.Correct Answer: A — Not in the labor force
macro.Feedback: Discouraged workers are not counted as unemployed because they are not actively looking for work.

macro.Common Misconception: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
macro.Question: A worker has a part-time job but wants full-time work. How is the worker officially classified?
macro.Choice A: Employed, even though the situation may show underemployment
macro.Choice B: Unemployed because the worker wants more hours
macro.Choice C: Not in the labor force because the job is part time
macro.Choice D: Discouraged because the worker is dissatisfied
macro.Correct Answer: A — Employed, even though the situation may show underemployment
macro.Feedback: Part-time workers are counted as employed, even when they would prefer full-time work.

macro.Common Misconception: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
macro.Question: Why does the official unemployment rate miss some labor market pain?
macro.Choice A: It misses discouraged workers and involuntary part-time work
macro.Choice B: It counts all adults as unemployed
macro.Choice C: It includes no employed workers
macro.Choice D: It measures only inflation
macro.Correct Answer: A — It misses discouraged workers and involuntary part-time work
macro.Feedback: The unemployment rate is useful but misses discouraged workers and underemployment.

macro.Common Misconception: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
macro.Question: A person works 5 hours per week for pay but wants 40 hours. How is this person treated in the headline unemployment rate?
macro.Choice A: Counted as employed, even though underemployment is present
macro.Choice B: Counted as unemployed because they want more hours
macro.Choice C: Counted as not in the labor force
macro.Choice D: Counted as discouraged
macro.Correct Answer: A — Counted as employed, even though underemployment is present
macro.Feedback: The official unemployment rate counts part-time workers as employed, even if they want full-time work.

macro.Common Misconception: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
macro.Question: Which change would reduce the unemployment rate without improving the number of people employed?
macro.Choice A: Unemployed workers become discouraged and stop searching
macro.Choice B: Part-time workers become full-time workers
macro.Choice C: Discouraged workers begin looking for jobs
macro.Choice D: New firms hire unemployed workers
macro.Correct Answer: A — Unemployed workers become discouraged and stop searching
macro.Feedback: When unemployed workers stop searching, they leave the labor force and measured unemployment can fall.

macro.Common Misconception: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
macro.Question: A survey classifies people as employed, unemployed, or not in the labor force. Whose difficulty finding enough work is least likely to be captured by the official unemployment rate?
macro.Choice A: A part-time worker who wants full-time work
macro.Choice B: A full-time worker satisfied with their job
macro.Choice C: A retiree who does not want work
macro.Choice D: A student not seeking employment
macro.Correct Answer: A — A part-time worker who wants full-time work
macro.Feedback: Involuntary part-time workers are counted as employed, even though their labor situation is weak.

macro.Common Misconception: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
macro.Question: Which case creates the biggest problem for interpreting the official unemployment rate?
macro.Choice A: A large increase in discouraged workers
macro.Choice B: A worker voluntarily switches jobs and searches for one week
macro.Choice C: A student works part time by choice
macro.Choice D: A retiree remains retired
macro.Correct Answer: A — A large increase in discouraged workers
macro.Feedback: Discouraged workers are excluded from measured unemployment, hiding some labor market distress.

macro.Common Misconception: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
macro.Question: Which case makes the headline unemployment rate look better than the actual labor market experience?
macro.Choice A: A rise in discouraged workers and involuntary part-time workers
macro.Choice B: A rise in full-time employment
macro.Choice C: More unemployed workers actively searching
macro.Choice D: More job openings filled
macro.Correct Answer: A — A rise in discouraged workers and involuntary part-time workers
macro.Feedback: Discouraged and involuntary part-time workers are not fully captured by the headline unemployment rate.

macro.Common Misconception: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
macro.Question: A parent who stays home full-time and is not seeking paid work is classified as:
macro.Choice A: Employed
macro.Choice B: Unemployed
macro.Choice C: Not in the labor force
macro.Choice D: Structurally unemployed
macro.Correct Answer: C — Not in the labor force
macro.Feedback: Someone not working and not looking for paid work is not in the labor force.

macro.Common Misconception: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
macro.Question: A person works one hour for pay during the survey week while looking for full-time work. How is the person classified?
macro.Choice A: Unemployed
macro.Choice B: Employed
macro.Choice C: Not in the labor force
macro.Choice D: Discouraged worker
macro.Correct Answer: B — Employed
macro.Feedback: A person who does any paid work during the survey period is counted as employed.

macro.Common Misconception: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
macro.Question: A worker without a job sends out applications during the last four weeks. How is the worker classified?
macro.Choice A: Employed
macro.Choice B: Unemployed
macro.Choice C: Not in the labor force
macro.Choice D: Retired
macro.Correct Answer: B — Unemployed
macro.Feedback: Actively looking for work while jobless means the person is unemployed.

macro.Common Misconception: Counting discouraged workers as unemployed even after they stop actively searching.
macro.Question: A discouraged worker wants a job but stopped searching because they believe no jobs are available. How is this worker classified in official unemployment statistics?
macro.Choice A: Employed
macro.Choice B: Unemployed
macro.Choice C: Not in the labor force
macro.Choice D: Part of investment
macro.Correct Answer: C — Not in the labor force
macro.Feedback: Discouraged workers are not in the labor force because they are not actively searching.

macro.Common Misconception: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
macro.Question: Which classification is most likely to make the unemployment rate understate labor market weakness?
macro.Choice A: Counting discouraged workers as not in the labor force
macro.Choice B: Counting active job seekers as unemployed
macro.Choice C: Counting paid workers as employed
macro.Choice D: Counting unemployed workers in the labor force
macro.Correct Answer: A — Counting discouraged workers as not in the labor force
macro.Feedback: Discouraged workers are excluded from unemployment, which can hide labor market weakness.

macro.Common Misconception: Counting discouraged workers as unemployed even after they stop actively searching.
macro.Question: A recession causes job loss, and some unemployed workers become discouraged. Why might the unemployment rate understate the recession's damage?
macro.Choice A: Discouraged workers are not counted as unemployed once they stop searching
macro.Choice B: Discouraged workers are counted twice
macro.Choice C: All discouraged workers are counted as employed
macro.Choice D: The unemployment rate includes only retired people
macro.Correct Answer: A — Discouraged workers are not counted as unemployed once they stop searching
macro.Feedback: Discouraged workers leave the labor force, which can hide labor market weakness.

macro.Common Misconception: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
macro.Question: A person has no job, wants work, is available, but has not searched in six weeks because they think no jobs exist. How is this person classified and why does it matter?
macro.Choice A: Outside the labor force; this can understate labor-market weakness
macro.Choice B: Unemployed; all jobless people are counted
macro.Choice C: Employed; wanting work is enough
macro.Choice D: Structurally employed; skills do not matter
macro.Correct Answer: A — Outside the labor force; this can understate labor-market weakness
macro.Feedback: Without active search, discouraged workers are not counted as unemployed, which can understate weakness.

macro.Common Misconception: Counting discouraged workers as unemployed even after they stop actively searching.
macro.Question: A laid-off engineer searches actively for work in the same field. A retired teacher does not want work. A discouraged factory worker wants work but stopped searching. Who is counted as unemployed?
macro.Choice A: Only the laid-off engineer
macro.Choice B: The engineer and retired teacher
macro.Choice C: The engineer and discouraged factory worker
macro.Choice D: All three
macro.Correct Answer: A — Only the laid-off engineer
macro.Feedback: Only jobless people actively searching are counted as unemployed.

macro.Common Misconception: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
macro.Question: A jobless worker applied to three jobs last week. Another jobless worker wants work but last searched two months ago. A third works 3 hours per week but wants full-time work. How are they classified?
macro.Choice A: Unemployed; not in labor force; employed
macro.Choice B: Unemployed; unemployed; unemployed
macro.Choice C: Employed; unemployed; not in labor force
macro.Choice D: Not in labor force; unemployed; employed
macro.Correct Answer: A — Unemployed; not in labor force; employed
macro.Feedback: Recent active search means unemployed; no recent search means not in labor force; any paid work means employed.

macro.Common Misconception: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
macro.Question: A survey has 84 adults working for pay, including 14 seeking more hours; 6 available jobless adults applied last week; 30 jobless adults are not searching. Which official count and limitation are correct?
macro.Choice A: Labor force 90 and unemployment about 6.7%; underemployment among paid workers is not in that rate
macro.Choice B: Labor force 104 and unemployment about 19.2%; add those seeking more hours to unemployment
macro.Choice C: Labor force 120 and unemployment 5%; use every adult in the denominator
macro.Choice D: Labor force 76 and unemployment about 7.9%; exclude part-time paid workers
macro.Correct Answer: A — Labor force 90 and unemployment about 6.7%; underemployment among paid workers is not in that rate
macro.Feedback: All 84 paid workers are employed, including those wanting more hours. Add the 6 active, available seekers for LF = 90; 6/90 ≈ 6.7%. The rate does not measure all of the part-time workers’ unmet demand for hours.

macro.Common Misconception: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
macro.Question: Two districts have the same unemployment rate and population. One has lower participation and a larger share of employed people working part time because full-time work is unavailable. Which additional comparison is best before calling their labor markets equally strong?
macro.Choice A: Compare employment per adult and desired versus actual hours; the headline rate omits both differences
macro.Choice B: Compare only total unemployment; equal unemployment rates guarantee equal counts
macro.Choice C: Count all involuntary part-time workers as unemployed before applying the official definition
macro.Choice D: Exclude discouraged workers from every indicator because they are outside the labor force
macro.Correct Answer: A — Compare employment per adult and desired versus actual hours; the headline rate omits both differences
macro.Feedback: Unemployment divides job seekers by the labor force. Lower participation can lower employment per adult even at the same rate, while involuntary part-time workers remain employed. Additional participation and hours evidence is needed for the broader assessment.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Employment and participation fall in both because fewer people are unemployed” in this unemployment measurement task.
macro.Question: An economy has 170 employed and 17 unemployed adults. Two separate policy evaluations observe the same fall in unemployed people. In A, they find jobs; in B, they stop searching. With adult population fixed, which extra indicator distinguishes the cases?
macro.Choice A: Employment and participation fall in both because fewer people are unemployed
macro.Choice B: Employment rises with unchanged participation in A; employment is unchanged and participation falls in B
macro.Choice C: Employment is unchanged and participation falls in A; employment rises with unchanged participation in B
macro.Choice D: Employment and participation rise in both because measured unemployment falls
macro.Correct Answer: B — Employment rises with unchanged participation in A; employment is unchanged and participation falls in B
macro.Feedback: Job finding moves people within the labor force from unemployed to employed. Discouragement moves people out of unemployment and the labor force without raising employment. The same unemployment change can conceal different labor outcomes.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The unemployment rate must rise because any lost hour makes a worker unemployed” in this unemployment measurement task.
macro.Question: Of 180 employed workers, ten full-time workers lose half their hours but retain paid jobs. No one enters or leaves the labor force. Which observation would reveal the deterioration that the official unemployment rate misses?
macro.Choice A: Hours fall; employment, unemployment and participation remain unchanged.
macro.Choice B: Employment falls by five; two half-time jobs equal one employed person.
macro.Choice C: Unemployment rises by ten; each loss of full-time hours counts as joblessness.
macro.Choice D: Participation falls by ten; paid part-time workers leave the labor force.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Hours fall; employment, unemployment and participation remain unchanged.
macro.Feedback: A paid part-time worker is employed. Head-count employment, UR and LFPR can stay constant while hours and underemployment worsen; hours-based evidence supplies the missing margin.

macro.Common Misconception: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
macro.Question: A jobless adult who had stopped searching accepts a paid part-time job but still wants full-time work. With other adults unchanged, which immediate changes follow?
macro.Choice A: Employment and the labor force rise; involuntary part-time work can remain
macro.Choice B: Unemployment rises because the worker still wants a full-time job
macro.Choice C: Employment rises but the labor force stays fixed because the job is part time
macro.Choice D: Participation falls because part-time employment is outside the labor force
macro.Correct Answer: A — Employment and the labor force rise; involuntary part-time work can remain
macro.Feedback: The worker moves from outside the labor force to employed. Both employment and the labor force rise, while wanting more hours does not change the official employed classification. The hours shortfall remains relevant to labor-market well-being.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Employment and participation rise in both because measured unemployment falls” in this unemployment measurement task.
macro.Question: An economy has 220 employed and 22 unemployed adults. Two separate policy evaluations observe the same fall in unemployed people. In A, they find jobs; in B, they stop searching. With adult population fixed, which extra indicator distinguishes the cases?
macro.Choice A: Employment and participation rise in both because measured unemployment falls
macro.Choice B: Employment and participation fall in both because fewer people are unemployed
macro.Choice C: Employment rises with unchanged participation in A; employment is unchanged and participation falls in B
macro.Choice D: Employment is unchanged and participation falls in A; employment rises with unchanged participation in B
macro.Correct Answer: C — Employment rises with unchanged participation in A; employment is unchanged and participation falls in B
macro.Feedback: Job finding moves people within the labor force from unemployed to employed. Discouragement moves people out of unemployment and the labor force without raising employment. The same unemployment change can conceal different labor outcomes.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Employment is fixed because layoffs and exits cancel; the unemployment rate is fixed” in this unemployment measurement task.
macro.Question: Initially 240 adults are employed and 24 unemployed. A recession causes 12 employed workers to lose jobs and actively search, while an equal number of previously unemployed people stop searching. Which joint result can occur?
macro.Choice A: Employment is fixed because layoffs and exits cancel; the unemployment rate is fixed
macro.Choice B: Employment falls and unemployment head count falls; the unemployment rate necessarily falls
macro.Choice C: Employment and labor-force participation fall; unemployment head count stays fixed and its rate rises
macro.Choice D: Employment falls but participation is fixed; unemployment head count doubles
macro.Correct Answer: C — Employment and labor-force participation fall; unemployment head count stays fixed and its rate rises
macro.Feedback: Layoffs move employed people to unemployment; discouraged exits remove an equal number from unemployment. U is unchanged, E and the labor force fall, so U/LF rises. Equal flows do not cancel employment or participation effects.

macro.Question: Demand shifts to the right while supply remains unchanged. What happens to equilibrium price and quantity?
macro.Choice A: Both price and quantity rise
macro.Choice B: Both price and quantity fall
macro.Choice C: Price rises while quantity falls
macro.Choice D: Price falls while quantity rises
macro.Correct Answer: A — Both price and quantity rise
macro.Feedback: A rightward demand shift creates upward pressure on both equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity when supply is fixed.

macro.Question: Holding demand constant, which equilibrium outcome follows from an increase in supply?
macro.Choice A: Price falls and quantity rises
macro.Choice B: Price rises and quantity falls
macro.Choice C: Both rise
macro.Choice D: Both fall
macro.Correct Answer: A — Price falls and quantity rises
macro.Feedback: An increase in supply lowers equilibrium price and raises equilibrium quantity.

macro.Common Misconception: Reversing shortage and surplus or treating disequilibrium as a curve shift.
macro.Question: At the current price, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied. What market condition exists?
macro.Choice A: A surplus exists because sellers offer more than buyers want.
macro.Choice B: A shortage exists because buyers want more than sellers offer.
macro.Choice C: The market is in equilibrium because both quantities are positive.
macro.Choice D: Demand must shift left before any price adjustment can occur.
macro.Correct Answer: B — A shortage exists because buyers want more than sellers offer.
macro.Feedback: When quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied at the current price, the market has a shortage and upward price pressure.

macro.Question: A new report makes blueberries more attractive to consumers. Production conditions are unchanged. With ordinary downward-sloping demand and upward-sloping supply, what happens to equilibrium price and quantity?
macro.Choice A: Price rises and quantity rises
macro.Choice B: Price falls and quantity falls
macro.Choice C: Price rises and quantity falls
macro.Choice D: Price falls and quantity rises
macro.Correct Answer: A — Price rises and quantity rises
macro.Feedback: The report raises willingness to buy blueberries at each price, shifting demand right. With supply unchanged, the new intersection has both a higher price and a higher quantity.

macro.Question: Plant disease destroys part of the orange crop. Consumers' willingness to buy oranges is unchanged. With ordinary downward-sloping demand and upward-sloping supply, what happens to equilibrium price and quantity?
macro.Choice A: Price rises and quantity falls
macro.Choice B: Price falls and quantity rises
macro.Choice C: Price rises and quantity rises
macro.Choice D: Price falls and quantity falls
macro.Correct Answer: A — Price rises and quantity falls
macro.Feedback: Crop loss reduces the amount growers can supply at each price, shifting supply left. With demand unchanged, oranges become scarcer: equilibrium price rises and quantity falls.

macro.Question: Market equilibrium occurs where:
macro.Choice A: Quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
macro.Choice B: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, creating a shortage
macro.Choice C: Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, creating a surplus
macro.Choice D: The demand curve reaches the price axis
macro.Correct Answer: A — Quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
macro.Feedback: At equilibrium, quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.

macro.Question: A popular endorsement increases demand for a product while production conditions remain unchanged. How does the market's equilibrium price respond?
macro.Choice A: It increases
macro.Choice B: It decreases
macro.Choice C: It remains unchanged
macro.Choice D: It becomes a shortage at every price
macro.Correct Answer: A — It increases
macro.Feedback: The endorsement shifts demand right. With supply unchanged, buyers compete for the product and the equilibrium price rises.

macro.Question: If supply increases and demand does not change, what happens to equilibrium price?
macro.Choice A: It decreases
macro.Choice B: It increases
macro.Choice C: It remains unchanged because demand did not change.
macro.Choice D: It increases because more units are available for sale.
macro.Correct Answer: A — It decreases
macro.Feedback: An increase in supply lowers equilibrium price when demand is unchanged.

macro.Common Misconception: Defining equilibrium as a shortage, surplus, or unrelated quantities.
macro.Question: At the equilibrium price, quantity demanded is:
macro.Choice A: Greater than quantity supplied.
macro.Choice B: Equal to quantity supplied.
macro.Choice C: Less than quantity supplied.
macro.Choice D: Unrelated to quantity supplied.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Equal to quantity supplied.
macro.Feedback: Market equilibrium occurs at the price where buyers’ quantity demanded equals sellers’ quantity supplied.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: What equilibrium price and quantity are shown in the displayed gas market?
macro.Choice A: $3 per gallon and 150 thousand gallons
macro.Choice B: $2 per gallon and 200 thousand gallons
macro.Choice C: $4 per gallon and 100 thousand gallons
macro.Choice D: $3 per gallon and 300 thousand gallons
macro.Correct Answer: A — $3 per gallon and 150 thousand gallons
macro.Feedback: D0 and S0 intersect at a price of $3 per gallon and a quantity of 150 thousand gallons.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: Before either curve shifts, what equilibrium is formed by D0 and S0 in the displayed gas market?
macro.Choice A: $4 and 100 thousand units
macro.Choice B: $4 and 200 thousand units
macro.Choice C: $3 and 150 thousand units
macro.Choice D: $5 and 150 thousand units
macro.Correct Answer: C — $3 and 150 thousand units
macro.Feedback: The original curves D0 and S0 intersect at price $3 and quantity 150 thousand.

macro.Question: A product goes viral while firms' production conditions remain unchanged. How do the resulting demand shift and movement along supply change equilibrium?
macro.Choice A: Price rises and quantity rises
macro.Choice B: Price falls and quantity falls
macro.Choice C: Price rises and quantity falls
macro.Choice D: Price falls and quantity rises
macro.Correct Answer: A — Price rises and quantity rises
macro.Feedback: The viral interest shifts demand right. With supply fixed, the new intersection lies higher and farther right, so equilibrium price and quantity both rise.

macro.Question: Supply for a product decreases while demand stays the same. What happens to equilibrium price and quantity?
macro.Choice A: Price rises and quantity falls
macro.Choice B: Price falls and quantity rises
macro.Choice C: Price rises and quantity rises
macro.Choice D: Price falls and quantity falls
macro.Correct Answer: A — Price rises and quantity falls
macro.Feedback: A decrease in supply raises equilibrium price and lowers equilibrium quantity.

macro.Question: Refer to the supply and demand graph. Which equilibrium is formed by D1 and S2?
macro.Choice A: Price P1 and Quantity Q2
macro.Choice B: Price P2 and Quantity Q1
macro.Choice C: Price P3 and Quantity Q2
macro.Choice D: Price P2 and Quantity Q3
macro.Correct Answer: A — Price P1 and Quantity Q2
macro.Feedback: D1 and S2 intersect at the middle vertical guide and the lowest horizontal guide, which is Price P1 and Quantity Q2.

macro.Question: Refer to the supply and demand graph. Which equilibrium is formed by D1 and S1?
macro.Choice A: Price P2 and Quantity Q1
macro.Choice B: Price P1 and Quantity Q2
macro.Choice C: Price P3 and Quantity Q2
macro.Choice D: Price P2 and Quantity Q3
macro.Correct Answer: A — Price P2 and Quantity Q1
macro.Feedback: D1 and S1 intersect at the left vertical guide and the middle horizontal guide, which is Price P2 and Quantity Q1.

macro.Question: Refer to the supply and demand graph. Which equilibrium is formed by D2 and S2?
macro.Choice A: Price P2 and Quantity Q3
macro.Choice B: Price P1 and Quantity Q2
macro.Choice C: Price P3 and Quantity Q2
macro.Choice D: Price P2 and Quantity Q1
macro.Correct Answer: A — Price P2 and Quantity Q3
macro.Feedback: D2 and S2 intersect at the right vertical guide and the middle horizontal guide, which is Price P2 and Quantity Q3.

macro.Question: Refer to the supply and demand graph. Compared with the equilibrium at D1 and S1, the equilibrium at D2 and S2 shows:
macro.Choice A: The same price but a higher quantity
macro.Choice B: A lower price and a lower quantity
macro.Choice C: A higher price and a lower quantity
macro.Choice D: A lower price and the same quantity
macro.Correct Answer: A — The same price but a higher quantity
macro.Feedback: D1 and S1 gives Price P2 and Quantity Q1, while D2 and S2 gives Price P2 and Quantity Q3, so price is the same and quantity is higher.

macro.Question: Refer to the supply and demand graph. The market begins at D1 and S1. Supply then increases, followed by an increase in demand. What is the final equilibrium?
macro.Choice A: Price P2 and Quantity Q3
macro.Choice B: Price P1 and Quantity Q2
macro.Choice C: Price P2 and Quantity Q1
macro.Choice D: Price P3 and Quantity Q2
macro.Correct Answer: A — Price P2 and Quantity Q3
macro.Feedback: Starting at D1 and S1 gives P2, Q1. A supply increase moves equilibrium to P1, Q2. Then a demand increase moves equilibrium to P2, Q3.

macro.Question: Refer to the price-control graph. What is the market equilibrium price and quantity?
macro.Choice A: $30 and 200 units
macro.Choice B: $20 and 250 units
macro.Choice C: $40 and 150 units
macro.Choice D: $50 and 300 units
macro.Correct Answer: A — $30 and 200 units
macro.Feedback: Equilibrium occurs where supply and demand intersect, which is $30 and 200 units.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: Starting from D0/S0, suppose demand shifts to D1 while supply remains at S0. What intermediate equilibrium does the graph show?
macro.Choice A: $4 and 100 thousand units
macro.Choice B: $4 and 200 thousand units
macro.Choice C: $5 and 150 thousand units
macro.Choice D: $3 and 150 thousand units
macro.Correct Answer: B — $4 and 200 thousand units
macro.Feedback: D1 intersects the unchanged S0 curve at price $4 and quantity 200 thousand. A demand increase alone raises both equilibrium price and quantity.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: At a price of $2 per gallon in the displayed gas market, what imbalance exists?
macro.Choice A: A surplus of 100 thousand gallons
macro.Choice B: A shortage of 100 thousand gallons
macro.Choice C: A shortage of 200 thousand gallons
macro.Choice D: No shortage or surplus
macro.Correct Answer: B — A shortage of 100 thousand gallons
macro.Feedback: At $2, quantity demanded is 200 thousand and quantity supplied is 100 thousand, so the shortage is 100 thousand gallons.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: Refer to the graph. At $4 per gallon, does the gas market have a shortage, a surplus, or equilibrium, and by how much?
macro.Choice A: A shortage of 100 thousand gallons
macro.Choice B: A surplus of 200 thousand gallons
macro.Choice C: A surplus of 100 thousand gallons
macro.Choice D: No shortage or surplus
macro.Correct Answer: C — A surplus of 100 thousand gallons
macro.Feedback: At $4, quantity supplied is 200 thousand and quantity demanded is 100 thousand, so the surplus is 100 thousand gallons.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: Which pair of market changes is shown when the graph moves from D0/S0 to D1/S1?
macro.Choice A: Demand decreases while supply increases
macro.Choice B: Both demand and supply increase
macro.Choice C: Both demand and supply decrease
macro.Choice D: Demand increases while supply decreases
macro.Correct Answer: D — Demand increases while supply decreases
macro.Feedback: D1 is to the right of D0, indicating increased demand. S1 is to the left of S0, indicating decreased supply.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: After both shifts shown in the graph, what equilibrium is formed by D1 and S1?
macro.Choice A: $5 and 150 thousand units
macro.Choice B: $3 and 150 thousand units
macro.Choice C: $4 and 100 thousand units
macro.Choice D: $4 and 200 thousand units
macro.Correct Answer: A — $5 and 150 thousand units
macro.Feedback: The new curves D1 and S1 intersect at price $5 and quantity 150 thousand.

macro.Question: Demand increases while supply decreases, and the observed equilibrium quantity is unchanged. Which inference best reconciles the two shifts with that observation?
macro.Choice A: Equilibrium price rises, and the opposing quantity effects happen to offset
macro.Choice B: Equilibrium price falls, and the two shifts reinforce the quantity effect
macro.Choice C: Equilibrium quantity is unchanged because neither curve shifts
macro.Choice D: Equilibrium price is unchanged because the demand and supply shifts are equal
macro.Correct Answer: A — Equilibrium price rises, and the opposing quantity effects happen to offset
macro.Feedback: A demand increase and supply decrease both raise equilibrium price. Their quantity effects oppose one another, and the observed unchanged quantity indicates that those effects offset in this case.

macro.Question: Demand decreases while supply increases. What can be predicted with certainty?
macro.Choice A: Equilibrium price falls
macro.Choice B: Equilibrium quantity rises
macro.Choice C: Equilibrium price rises
macro.Choice D: Equilibrium quantity falls
macro.Correct Answer: A — Equilibrium price falls
macro.Feedback: Both shifts push price down, but quantity is ambiguous.

macro.Question: Demand and supply both increase. What can be predicted with certainty?
macro.Choice A: Equilibrium quantity rises
macro.Choice B: Equilibrium price rises
macro.Choice C: Equilibrium price falls
macro.Choice D: Equilibrium quantity falls
macro.Correct Answer: A — Equilibrium quantity rises
macro.Feedback: Both shifts increase quantity, but price depends on which shift is larger.

macro.Question: Demand and supply both decrease. What can be predicted with certainty?
macro.Choice A: Equilibrium quantity falls
macro.Choice B: Equilibrium price rises
macro.Choice C: Equilibrium price falls
macro.Choice D: Equilibrium quantity rises
macro.Correct Answer: A — Equilibrium quantity falls
macro.Feedback: Both shifts reduce quantity, but price is ambiguous.

macro.Question: A market initially has Qd = 500 - 10P and Qs = 100 + 10P. Demand then rises to Qd = 600 - 10P. Calculate the new equilibrium price and compare it with the original equilibrium.
macro.Choice A: $25, which is $5 higher
macro.Choice B: $20, so price is unchanged
macro.Choice C: $30, which is $10 higher
macro.Choice D: $15, which is $5 lower
macro.Correct Answer: A — $25, which is $5 higher
macro.Feedback: Initially, 500 - 10P = 100 + 10P gives P = $20. After demand rises, 600 - 10P = 100 + 10P gives P = $25, a $5 increase.

macro.Question: Demand is Qd = 500 - 10P. Supply shifts from Qs = 100 + 10P to Qs = 40 + 10P. Calculate the new equilibrium quantity and infer the effect of the supply decrease.
macro.Choice A: 270; equilibrium quantity falls from 300
macro.Choice B: 300; equilibrium quantity is unchanged
macro.Choice C: 230; equilibrium quantity falls from 300
macro.Choice D: 350; equilibrium quantity rises from 300
macro.Correct Answer: A — 270; equilibrium quantity falls from 300
macro.Feedback: The new equilibrium solves 500 - 10P = 40 + 10P, so P = $23 and Q = 270. Compared with the original Q = 300, the supply decrease lowers equilibrium quantity.

macro.Question: A drought reduces wheat supply while a health trend increases demand for wheat bread. Explain which equilibrium effect is certain and which depends on the relative shift sizes.
macro.Choice A: Price rises; quantity is ambiguous because the shifts have opposing quantity effects
macro.Choice B: Price falls; quantity rises because both shifts increase purchases
macro.Choice C: Price rises; quantity rises because demand determines both outcomes
macro.Choice D: Price is ambiguous; quantity falls because supply determines both outcomes
macro.Correct Answer: A — Price rises; quantity is ambiguous because the shifts have opposing quantity effects
macro.Feedback: The demand increase and supply decrease both raise price. Demand raises quantity while the supply decrease lowers it, so quantity depends on the relative magnitudes.

macro.Question: Production technology lowers costs while consumer interest in the good falls. Explain which equilibrium effect is certain and which depends on the relative shift sizes.
macro.Choice A: Price falls; quantity is ambiguous because the shifts have opposing quantity effects
macro.Choice B: Price rises; quantity falls because both shifts reduce market availability
macro.Choice C: Price falls; quantity rises because supply determines both outcomes
macro.Choice D: Price is ambiguous; quantity falls because demand determines both outcomes
macro.Correct Answer: A — Price falls; quantity is ambiguous because the shifts have opposing quantity effects
macro.Feedback: The supply increase and demand decrease both lower price. Supply raises quantity while the demand decrease lowers it, so quantity depends on the relative magnitudes.

macro.Question: Demand and supply both increase, taking the market from D1/S1 to D2/S2. Which statement distinguishes what theory guarantees from the particular outcome shown?
macro.Choice A: Quantity must rise; price could rise, fall, or stay unchanged. Here price stays P2 and quantity rises from Q1 to Q3.
macro.Choice B: Quantity must rise; price could rise, fall, or stay unchanged. Here price stays P2 and quantity rises from Q1 to Q2.
macro.Choice C: Quantity must rise; price must stay unchanged. Here price stays P2 and quantity rises from Q1 to Q3.
macro.Choice D: Quantity must rise; price must stay unchanged. Here price stays P2 and quantity rises from Q1 to Q2.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Quantity must rise; price could rise, fall, or stay unchanged. Here price stays P2 and quantity rises from Q1 to Q3.
macro.Feedback: A demand increase raises equilibrium price and quantity; a supply increase lowers price and raises quantity. Quantity therefore rises for certain, but price depends on the relative shifts. Here D1/S1 is (P2,Q1) and D2/S2 is (P2,Q3): price stays P2 and quantity rises from Q1 to Q3.

macro.Question: Demand increases from D1 to D2 while supply decreases from S2 to S1. Which statement distinguishes what theory guarantees from the particular outcome shown?
macro.Choice A: Price must rise; quantity could rise, fall, or stay unchanged. Here price rises from P1 to P3 and quantity stays Q2.
macro.Choice B: Price must rise; quantity could rise, fall, or stay unchanged. Here price rises from P2 to P3 and quantity stays Q2.
macro.Choice C: Price must rise; quantity must stay unchanged. Here price rises from P1 to P3 and quantity stays Q2.
macro.Choice D: Price must rise; quantity must stay unchanged. Here price rises from P2 to P3 and quantity stays Q2.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Price must rise; quantity could rise, fall, or stay unchanged. Here price rises from P1 to P3 and quantity stays Q2.
macro.Feedback: Higher demand and lower supply both raise price, but demand raises quantity while lower supply reduces it. Quantity is therefore ambiguous in general. Here D1/S2 is (P1,Q2) and D2/S1 is (P3,Q2): price rises from P1 to P3 while the quantity effects offset at Q2.

macro.Question: Refer to the supply and demand shift graph. Starting from D2/S1, demand decreases to D1 while supply increases to S2. What happens?
macro.Choice A: Price falls and quantity stays the same
macro.Choice B: Price rises and quantity stays the same
macro.Choice C: Price stays the same and quantity rises
macro.Choice D: Price falls and quantity falls
macro.Correct Answer: A — Price falls and quantity stays the same
macro.Feedback: D2/S1 gives P3 and Q2. D1/S2 gives P1 and Q2. Price falls while quantity remains Q2.

macro.Question: Refer to the supply and demand shift graph. If demand and supply both increase, what does this graph show is possible?
macro.Choice A: Quantity rises while price stays the same
macro.Choice B: Quantity rises while price rises because the demand shift has the larger price effect
macro.Choice C: Quantity rises while price falls because the supply shift has the larger price effect
macro.Choice D: Price rises while quantity stays the same because the shifts have equal quantity effects
macro.Correct Answer: A — Quantity rises while price stays the same
macro.Feedback: The graph shows D1/S1 to D2/S2. Both demand and supply increase, quantity rises, and price remains unchanged.

macro.Question: Compare the equilibrium at D1/S2 with the equilibrium at D2/S1. Which outcome is shown when demand increases and supply decreases?
macro.Choice A: Price rises from P1 to P3; quantity stays Q2
macro.Choice B: Price rises from P1 to P3; quantity rises from Q1 to Q2
macro.Choice C: Price rises from P1 to P3; quantity falls from Q3 to Q2
macro.Choice D: Price rises from P2 to P3; quantity stays Q2
macro.Correct Answer: A — Price rises from P1 to P3; quantity stays Q2
macro.Feedback: The graph places D1/S2 at (P1,Q2) and D2/S1 at (P3,Q2). The price increase is from P1 to P3; the two shifts have offsetting quantity effects here.

macro.Question: Refer to the graph. Tastes shift demand from D1 to D2 while supply remains S1. Which explanation uses both intersections to distinguish the demand shift from the market's movement along supply?
macro.Choice A: Demand shifts right, and equilibrium moves along S1 from P2, Q1 to P3, Q2
macro.Choice B: Supply shifts right, and equilibrium moves along D1 from P2, Q1 to P1, Q2
macro.Choice C: Demand shifts left, and equilibrium moves along S1 from P3, Q2 to P2, Q1
macro.Choice D: Supply shifts left, and equilibrium moves along D2 from P2, Q3 to P3, Q2
macro.Correct Answer: A — Demand shifts right, and equilibrium moves along S1 from P2, Q1 to P3, Q2
macro.Feedback: The taste change shifts the entire demand curve from D1 to D2. Because S1 is fixed, the new intersection is also a movement along S1 to a higher price and quantity.

macro.Question: A market price is above equilibrium. What pressure does the market create and why?
macro.Choice A: Downward pressure on price because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
macro.Choice B: Upward pressure on price because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
macro.Choice C: No pressure because high prices clear every market
macro.Choice D: Downward pressure on quantity demanded because demand shifts left
macro.Correct Answer: A — Downward pressure on price because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
macro.Feedback: A price above equilibrium creates a surplus, so sellers have an incentive to lower price.

macro.Question: A market price is below equilibrium. What pressure does the market create and why?
macro.Choice A: Upward pressure on price because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
macro.Choice B: Downward pressure on price because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
macro.Choice C: No pressure because buyers prefer low prices
macro.Choice D: A supply increase because the legal price is low
macro.Correct Answer: A — Upward pressure on price because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
macro.Feedback: A price below equilibrium creates a shortage, so buyers compete and push price upward.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: Refer to the graph. Calculate the disequilibrium at $1 per gallon and explain the price pressure that follows from buyers' and sellers' incentives.
macro.Choice A: A 200-thousand surplus; downward price pressure
macro.Choice B: A 50-thousand shortage; no price pressure
macro.Choice C: A 250-thousand surplus; upward price pressure
macro.Choice D: A 200-thousand shortage; upward price pressure
macro.Correct Answer: D — A 200-thousand shortage; upward price pressure
macro.Feedback: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied by 200 thousand gallons. A shortage gives buyers an incentive to bid price upward toward equilibrium.

macro.Question: A drought reduces supply of wheat while a health trend increases demand for wheat bread. What can be predicted with certainty in the wheat market?
macro.Choice A: Price rises; equilibrium quantity can rise, fall, or stay unchanged.
macro.Choice B: Quantity rises; equilibrium price can rise, fall, or stay unchanged.
macro.Choice C: Price and quantity both rise for every possible size of the shifts.
macro.Choice D: Price and quantity both fall for every possible size of the shifts.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Price rises; equilibrium quantity can rise, fall, or stay unchanged.
macro.Feedback: Reduced wheat supply and greater derived demand for wheat both raise its price. They push equilibrium quantity in opposite directions, so quantities require more information.

macro.Question: Consumer interest in a product falls while new technology lowers production costs. What can be predicted with certainty?
macro.Choice A: Price falls, but quantity is ambiguous
macro.Choice B: Quantity rises, but price is ambiguous
macro.Choice C: Both price and quantity rise
macro.Choice D: Both price and quantity fall
macro.Correct Answer: A — Price falls, but quantity is ambiguous
macro.Feedback: A demand decrease and supply increase both lower price, but quantity is ambiguous.

macro.Question: A celebrity endorsement increases demand for a product at the same time input costs rise. What can be predicted with certainty?
macro.Choice A: Equilibrium price rises
macro.Choice B: Equilibrium quantity rises
macro.Choice C: Equilibrium quantity falls
macro.Choice D: Equilibrium price falls
macro.Correct Answer: A — Equilibrium price rises
macro.Feedback: Demand rises and supply falls. Both raise price, but quantity is ambiguous.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming an unchanged price means the market experienced no shifts.
macro.Question: Demand and supply both increase. The equilibrium quantity rises, but the equilibrium price is unchanged. What does this reveal?
macro.Choice A: Neither curve shifted because an unchanged price proves the market did not move.
macro.Choice B: Demand increased more than supply, so price should have risen instead of staying fixed.
macro.Choice C: The price effects offset, while both shifts raise equilibrium quantity.
macro.Choice D: Supply decreased while demand increased, creating offsetting quantity effects.
macro.Correct Answer: C — The price effects offset, while both shifts raise equilibrium quantity.
macro.Feedback: A demand increase raises price and quantity, while a supply increase lowers price and raises quantity. Equal price effects can cancel while quantity rises.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: Refer to the graph. The market price starts at $2 and can adjust freely. Which pair of quantity changes would eliminate the initial imbalance with both curves fixed?
macro.Choice A: Quantity demanded falls 50 thousand gallons and quantity supplied rises 50 thousand gallons.
macro.Choice B: Quantity demanded rises 50 thousand gallons and quantity supplied falls 50 thousand gallons.
macro.Choice C: Quantity demanded falls 100 thousand gallons and quantity supplied stays fixed.
macro.Choice D: Demand shifts left 50 thousand gallons and supply shifts right 50 thousand gallons.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Quantity demanded falls 50 thousand gallons and quantity supplied rises 50 thousand gallons.
macro.Feedback: At $2, quantity demanded is 200 thousand and quantity supplied is 100 thousand. Price rises to the intersection at $3 and 150 thousand. Each side adjusts by 50 thousand along its existing curve.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: Refer to the graph. A normal-good market moves from the D1/S1 intersection to the D0/S0 intersection. Which pair of events could explain that change, and what happens to price?
macro.Choice A: Consumer income rises and production becomes cheaper; price falls by $2.
macro.Choice B: Consumer income falls and production becomes more expensive; price rises by $2.
macro.Choice C: Consumer income falls and production becomes cheaper; price falls by $2.
macro.Choice D: Consumer income rises and production becomes more expensive; price rises by $2.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Consumer income falls and production becomes cheaper; price falls by $2.
macro.Feedback: The two intersections have the same quantity, 150 thousand, but prices $5 and $3. D1 to D0 is lower demand, consistent with lower income for a normal good. S1 to S0 is higher supply, consistent with lower cost.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: With the curves fixed, compare the gas market at $2 and $4 per gallon. Which imbalances and price pressures would move the market toward the equilibrium shown?
macro.Choice A: At $2, a 50-thousand-gallon shortage pushes price up; at $4, a 50-thousand-gallon surplus pushes price down.
macro.Choice B: At $2, a 100-thousand-gallon shortage pushes price up; at $4, a 100-thousand-gallon surplus pushes price down.
macro.Choice C: At $2, a 100-thousand-gallon shortage pushes price down; at $4, a 100-thousand-gallon surplus pushes price up.
macro.Choice D: At $2, a 50-thousand-gallon shortage pushes price down; at $4, a 50-thousand-gallon surplus pushes price up.
macro.Correct Answer: B — At $2, a 100-thousand-gallon shortage pushes price up; at $4, a 100-thousand-gallon surplus pushes price down.
macro.Feedback: At $2, quantity demanded is 200 thousand gallons and quantity supplied is 100 thousand, so a 100-thousand-gallon shortage puts upward pressure on price. At $4, supply is 200 thousand and demand is 100 thousand, so a 100-thousand-gallon surplus puts downward pressure on price. Both pressures move price toward the $3 equilibrium.

macro.Question: Refer to the graph. The market moves from D1/S1 to D2/S2. An analyst claims that simultaneous demand and supply increases must leave price unchanged. Then part of the supply increase is reversed: supply lies strictly between S1 and S2 at every shown price, while demand stays D2. Which assessment is correct?
macro.Choice A: The original offset is specific to the graph; afterward price is between P2 and P3 and quantity between Q2 and Q3.
macro.Choice B: The original offset is a general rule; afterward price stays P2 and quantity stays Q3.
macro.Choice C: The original offset is specific to the graph; afterward price is between P1 and P2 and quantity exceeds Q3.
macro.Choice D: The original offset is a general rule; afterward price reaches P3 and quantity falls below Q1.
macro.Correct Answer: A — The original offset is specific to the graph; afterward price is between P2 and P3 and quantity between Q2 and Q3.
macro.Feedback: Both initial increases raise quantity, but their opposing price effects need not cancel in general. They happen to cancel at P2 in this drawing. With D2 fixed, partially reversing S2 toward S1 places the new intersection between (P2,Q3) and (P3,Q2). Price rises above P2, and quantity falls from Q3 but remains above Q2 and the original Q1.

macro.Question: A disease reduces berry supply while a nutrition trend raises berry demand. The final quantity is above its original level. Which conclusion follows with ordinary downward demand and upward supply?
macro.Choice A: Price is higher; the demand increase more than offsets the supply reduction’s effect on quantity.
macro.Choice B: Price is lower; greater final quantity proves that supply increased.
macro.Choice C: Price is unchanged; the higher quantity shows that the two shifts offset completely.
macro.Choice D: Price is higher; the observed quantity proves that the supply reduction dominated demand.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Price is higher; the demand increase more than offsets the supply reduction’s effect on quantity.
macro.Feedback: Both shifts raise price. Supply reduction alone lowers equilibrium quantity, so the observed quantity increase requires the demand effect to outweigh that reduction in the final outcome.

macro.Question: Two initially identical device markets face the same increase in demand. Only Market Y also loses a component supplier. Compared with Market X’s final equilibrium, what must be true in Market Y?
macro.Choice A: Y has a higher price and lower quantity, although its quantity relative to the original equilibrium is uncertain.
macro.Choice B: Y has a lower price and higher quantity, although its quantity relative to the original equilibrium is uncertain.
macro.Choice C: Y has a higher price and quantity, because both changes increase demand.
macro.Choice D: Y has the same price and quantity, because both markets face the same demand change.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Y has a higher price and lower quantity, although its quantity relative to the original equilibrium is uncertain.
macro.Feedback: Starting from X’s final equilibrium, the additional supply reduction in Y raises price and lowers quantity. Compared with the common original equilibrium, Y’s demand increase and supply decrease have opposing quantity effects.

macro.Question: Lunch-delivery demand falls while improved routing lowers delivery costs. Final price is lower and the number of deliveries is unchanged. Which explanation is consistent?
macro.Choice A: Demand fell and supply rose; their quantity effects offset at the final equilibrium.
macro.Choice B: Demand and supply both fell; their quantity effects offset at the final equilibrium.
macro.Choice C: Demand and supply both rose; unchanged deliveries reflect offsetting quantity effects.
macro.Choice D: Only demand fell; a fixed upward-sloping supply curve kept deliveries unchanged.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Demand fell and supply rose; their quantity effects offset at the final equilibrium.
macro.Feedback: Lower demand and higher supply both reduce price but have opposite quantity effects. The observed unchanged quantity reflects an offset in this case; it is not a general prediction of those shifts.

macro.Question: Bicycles are a normal good. Income and production-input costs rise, yet equilibrium bicycle sales fall. A manager concludes that bicycle demand must have fallen. Evaluate the conclusion.
macro.Choice A: Incorrect: demand rose, but the supply reduction more than offset its effect on quantity; price rose.
macro.Choice B: Correct: lower equilibrium sales establish a demand decrease even when income rises.
macro.Choice C: Incorrect: supply rose, but demand fell enough to reduce both price and quantity.
macro.Choice D: Correct: higher input costs reduce bicycle demand directly while supply stays fixed.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Incorrect: demand rose, but the supply reduction more than offset its effect on quantity; price rose.
macro.Feedback: Higher income increases demand for a normal good; higher input costs reduce supply. Both raise price. Lower sales can result when the supply effect dominates quantity, so sales alone do not identify a demand shift.

macro.Question: A production improvement increases supply while tastes shift away from the product. An analyst predicts that price and quantity must both fall. What is the precise correction?
macro.Choice A: Price must fall, but quantity falls only if the demand reduction outweighs the supply increase’s quantity effect.
macro.Choice B: Quantity must fall, but price falls only if the production improvement outweighs the taste change.
macro.Choice C: Price must rise, but quantity can rise or fall depending on the relative shifts.
macro.Choice D: Neither direction can be inferred because simultaneous shifts make both variables indeterminate.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Price must fall, but quantity falls only if the demand reduction outweighs the supply increase’s quantity effect.
macro.Feedback: Both changes lower equilibrium price. Lower demand reduces quantity while higher supply increases it, so the analyst needs relative effects to assert a quantity decline.

macro.Question: A coffee shop sees more customers after a celebrity endorsement. At the same time, wages for baristas rise. If the relative sizes of the two shifts are unknown, which equilibrium outcome can be predicted with certainty?
macro.Choice A: Price rises; quantity is ambiguous
macro.Choice B: Quantity rises; price is ambiguous
macro.Choice C: Both price and quantity fall
macro.Choice D: Price falls; quantity rises
macro.Correct Answer: A — Price rises; quantity is ambiguous
macro.Feedback: Demand increases and supply decreases. Both raise price, but quantity depends on which shift is larger.

macro.Question: A new production method makes shoes cheaper to produce. At the same time, a fashion shift makes shoes less popular. What is certain?
macro.Choice A: Price falls; quantity is ambiguous
macro.Choice B: Quantity falls; price is ambiguous
macro.Choice C: Both price and quantity rise
macro.Choice D: Price rises; quantity falls
macro.Correct Answer: A — Price falls; quantity is ambiguous
macro.Feedback: Supply increases and demand decreases. Both lower price, but quantity is ambiguous.

macro.Question: A hurricane disrupts production and reduces supply while households expect prices to rise tomorrow and rush to buy today. What is the strongest prediction for today’s market?
macro.Choice A: Price rises; quantity is ambiguous
macro.Choice B: Quantity rises; price is ambiguous
macro.Choice C: Both price and quantity fall
macro.Choice D: Price falls; quantity rises
macro.Correct Answer: A — Price rises; quantity is ambiguous
macro.Feedback: Expected future price increases raise current demand, while the hurricane lowers supply. Price rises; quantity is ambiguous.

macro.Question: Fewer buyers want a product and several producers exit. Final price is above the starting price. Which interpretation is consistent with both shifts and that observation?
macro.Choice A: Quantity falls; the supply reduction’s upward price effect outweighs the demand reduction’s downward effect.
macro.Choice B: Quantity rises; the demand reduction’s downward price effect outweighs the supply reduction’s upward effect.
macro.Choice C: Quantity stays fixed; an increase in price prevents either curve from shifting.
macro.Choice D: Quantity falls; the higher price proves that demand increased rather than decreased.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Quantity falls; the supply reduction’s upward price effect outweighs the demand reduction’s downward effect.
macro.Feedback: Both lower demand and lower supply reduce equilibrium quantity. Their price effects oppose each other; the observed price increase identifies the dominant price effect in this case.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: Refer to the graph. The market starts at D1/S1 and ends at D0/S0. Demand changes first while supply is initially fixed. Which sequence and explanation fit the graph?
macro.Choice A: First $4 and 200 thousand, then $3 and 150 thousand; demand falls before supply rises.
macro.Choice B: First $4 and 100 thousand, then $5 and 150 thousand; demand falls before supply falls.
macro.Choice C: First $3 and 150 thousand, then $4 and 100 thousand; supply rises before demand falls.
macro.Choice D: First $4 and 100 thousand, then $3 and 150 thousand; demand falls before supply rises.
macro.Correct Answer: D — First $4 and 100 thousand, then $3 and 150 thousand; demand falls before supply rises.
macro.Feedback: The initial D1/S1 intersection is $5 and 150 thousand. Holding S1 fixed, lower demand takes the market to D0/S1 at $4 and 100 thousand. Higher supply then takes it to D0/S0 at $3 and 150 thousand.

macro.Common Misconception: Reversing shortage and surplus conditions.
macro.Question: A market price below equilibrium creates a:
macro.Choice A: Surplus.
macro.Choice B: Balanced market.
macro.Choice C: Leftward demand shift.
macro.Choice D: Shortage.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Shortage.
macro.Feedback: Below equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, creating a shortage.

macro.Common Misconception: Reversing the price adjustment associated with a surplus.
macro.Question: What pressure does a surplus create in an unregulated market?
macro.Choice A: Sellers lower prices to clear unwanted inventories.
macro.Choice B: Buyers bid prices higher because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied.
macro.Choice C: Demand shifts right until buyers absorb every unit offered for sale.
macro.Choice D: Supply shifts left because firms are holding unwanted inventories.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Sellers lower prices to clear unwanted inventories.
macro.Feedback: When quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, sellers compete to clear inventory by lowering price.

macro.Common Misconception: Using the supply-shift outcome for a demand increase.
macro.Question: If demand increases while supply is unchanged, equilibrium price and quantity usually:
macro.Choice A: Both decrease.
macro.Choice B: Both increase.
macro.Choice C: Price rises and quantity falls.
macro.Choice D: Price falls and quantity rises.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Both increase.
macro.Feedback: A rightward demand shift moves the equilibrium up along the supply curve to a higher price and quantity.

macro.Question: At $8, buyers plan to purchase 70 units and sellers plan to sell 110. At $6 both plan 90. No price control prevents adjustment. Which diagnosis and prediction fit the plans?
macro.Choice A: The $8 price creates a 40-unit surplus; price tends toward $6, where planned purchases and sales both equal 90.
macro.Choice B: The $8 price creates a 40-unit shortage; price tends toward $6, where planned purchases and sales both equal 90.
macro.Choice C: The $8 price is equilibrium because 70 buyers can be served; unsold units do not create pressure to adjust.
macro.Choice D: The $6 price creates a 90-unit shortage because buyers’ planned purchases must be added to sellers’ planned sales.
macro.Correct Answer: A — The $8 price creates a 40-unit surplus; price tends toward $6, where planned purchases and sales both equal 90.
macro.Feedback: At $8 supply exceeds demand by 110-70=40. Downward pressure moves toward the $6 price where the two planned quantities are equal.

macro.Question: Demand increases while supply stays the same. What happens to equilibrium price and quantity?
macro.Choice A: Price rises and quantity rises
macro.Choice B: Price falls and quantity falls
macro.Choice C: Price rises and quantity falls
macro.Choice D: Price falls and quantity rises
macro.Correct Answer: A — Price rises and quantity rises
macro.Feedback: The demand increase moves the market to a higher point on the unchanged supply curve, raising both equilibrium price and quantity.

macro.Question: Demand shifts right while supply shifts left at the same time. Which equilibrium change can be predicted with certainty?
macro.Choice A: Equilibrium price rises
macro.Choice B: Equilibrium quantity rises
macro.Choice C: Equilibrium quantity falls
macro.Choice D: Equilibrium price falls
macro.Correct Answer: A — Equilibrium price rises
macro.Feedback: Demand rising and supply falling both push price up, but quantity depends on which shift is stronger.

macro.Common Misconception: Claiming certainty about quantity when the two shifts move quantity in opposite directions.
macro.Question: Demand increases while supply decreases. Which equilibrium outcome is certain?
macro.Choice A: The equilibrium quantity rises.
macro.Choice B: The equilibrium quantity falls.
macro.Choice C: The equilibrium price rises.
macro.Choice D: The equilibrium price falls.
macro.Correct Answer: C — The equilibrium price rises.
macro.Feedback: Both shifts raise price, while demand raises quantity and lower supply reduces quantity.

macro.Common Misconception: Claiming certainty about price when both curves shift left.
macro.Question: Both demand and supply shift left in the same market. Which equilibrium result can be stated without knowing the shift sizes?
macro.Choice A: The equilibrium price rises.
macro.Choice B: The equilibrium price falls.
macro.Choice C: The equilibrium quantity rises.
macro.Choice D: The equilibrium quantity falls.
macro.Correct Answer: D — The equilibrium quantity falls.
macro.Feedback: Both shifts reduce equilibrium quantity, but their price effects oppose each other.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating a surplus as a shortage or confusing movement along curves with shifts.
macro.Question: At the current price, quantity demanded is 400 and quantity supplied is 520. Which explanation diagnoses the imbalance and traces the adjustment along the existing curves without a price control?
macro.Choice A: A surplus pushes price down, raising quantity demanded and lowering quantity supplied until they converge
macro.Choice B: A shortage pushes price up, lowering quantity demanded and raising quantity supplied until they converge
macro.Choice C: A surplus shifts demand right while price remains fixed until inventories clear
macro.Choice D: A shortage shifts supply left while buyers reduce quantity demanded
macro.Correct Answer: A — A surplus pushes price down, raising quantity demanded and lowering quantity supplied until they converge
macro.Feedback: Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded by 120, creating a surplus. Falling price moves the market along both curves: quantity demanded rises and quantity supplied falls toward equilibrium.

macro.Question: A widely reported health study increases consumers’ willingness to buy fresh berries. At the same time, frost destroys part of the berry crop. With ordinary downward-sloping demand and upward-sloping supply, and unknown effect sizes, which equilibrium conclusion is certain?
macro.Choice A: Quantity rises; price may rise or fall because the two changes push price in opposite directions.
macro.Choice B: Price falls; quantity may rise or fall because lower crop output reduces sellers’ willingness to sell.
macro.Choice C: Price rises; quantity may rise or fall because the two changes push quantity in opposite directions.
macro.Choice D: Quantity falls; price may rise or fall because stronger willingness to buy offsets the crop loss.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Price rises; quantity may rise or fall because the two changes push quantity in opposite directions.
macro.Feedback: The health information shifts demand right; crop loss shifts supply left. Both raise price, but demand growth raises quantity while the supply contraction lowers it. Their relative sizes determine the quantity change.

macro.Question: A market has Qd = 180 - 2P and Qs = 20 + 2P. At every price, demand then falls by 24 units and supply falls by 8 units. Which final change and explanation are correct?
macro.Choice A: Price rises $4 and quantity falls 16 units; demand’s larger reduction raises price.
macro.Choice B: Price falls $4 and quantity falls 16 units; demand’s larger horizontal reduction dominates the price effect.
macro.Choice C: Price falls $4 and quantity rises 16 units; both curve reductions expand sales.
macro.Choice D: Price is unchanged and quantity falls 32 units; the horizontal reductions simply add.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Price falls $4 and quantity falls 16 units; demand’s larger horizontal reduction dominates the price effect.
macro.Feedback: Initially 180 - 2P = 20 + 2P gives P = 40 and Q = 100. After the changes, 156 - 2P = 12 + 2P gives P = 36 and Q = 84. Stating horizontal units makes the comparison of shift sizes well defined.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating a surplus as a shortage or confusing movement along curves with shifts.
macro.Question: Unchanged linear schedules give Qd=900 and Qs=1,150 at $10, and Qd=1,100 and Qs=950 at $8. Sellers currently charge $10. An analyst calls the resulting surplus evidence of a supply shift and predicts it will persist even without a price control. Which correction is complete?
macro.Choice A: The surplus is 250 at $10; price must rise to $11.25 and quantity 1,025, while a $10 ceiling would preserve the gap.
macro.Choice B: The surplus is 250 at $10; price can fall to $8.75 and quantity 1,025 along unchanged curves, while a $10 floor would preserve the gap.
macro.Choice C: The shortage is 250 at $10; price can fall to $8.75 and quantity 1,025 only if supply shifts left.
macro.Choice D: The surplus is 150 at $10; price can fall to $8 and quantity 950, while unchanged curves prevent further adjustment.
macro.Correct Answer: B — The surplus is 250 at $10; price can fall to $8.75 and quantity 1,025 along unchanged curves, while a $10 floor would preserve the gap.
macro.Feedback: The schedules imply Qd=1900-100P and Qs=150+100P. Equating them gives P=8.75 and Q=1025. At 10, excess supply is 250. Price adjustment moves along existing curves; a binding floor at 10 could block the fall and sustain surplus.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
macro.Question: With supply fixed at S0, which transition is an increase in demand?
macro.Choice A: D to A
macro.Choice B: A to B
macro.Choice C: C to B
macro.Choice D: D to C
macro.Correct Answer: D — D to C
macro.Feedback: D is D0-S0 and C is D1-S0.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
macro.Question: With supply fixed at S1, which transition isolates increased demand?
macro.Choice A: D to A
macro.Choice B: D to C
macro.Choice C: A to B
macro.Choice D: C to B
macro.Correct Answer: C — A to B
macro.Feedback: A is D0-S1 and B is D1-S1.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The gap identifies an exchange-rate error rather than a possible real-price difference” in this real exchange rates and purchasing power task.
macro.Question: The prices of consumer baskets in two countries remain different even after they are converted to the same currency. What does this suggest about purchasing-power parity?
macro.Choice A: PPP is an imperfect benchmark because baskets and arbitrage conditions differ
macro.Choice B: The gap identifies an exchange-rate error rather than a possible real-price difference
macro.Choice C: The cheaper basket shows that its traded goods face stronger transport barriers
macro.Choice D: PPP applies more closely when broad baskets contain more nontraded services
macro.Correct Answer: A — PPP is an imperfect benchmark because baskets and arbitrage conditions differ
macro.Feedback: Differences in goods, quality, taxes, trade costs, and nontraded services can sustain deviations from PPP.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “A weaker dollar directly lowers every euro price” in this nominal exchange rates task.
macro.Question: The dollar depreciates against the euro, but a U.S. tourist's euro hotel bill falls in dollar terms. Which explanation can reconcile both facts?
macro.Choice A: A weaker dollar directly lowers every euro price
macro.Choice B: Depreciation makes the reciprocal exchange rate irrelevant
macro.Choice C: The hotel's dollar price cannot fall under any circumstances
macro.Choice D: The euro price of the hotel fell enough to offset the weaker dollar
macro.Correct Answer: D — The euro price of the hotel fell enough to offset the weaker dollar
macro.Feedback: The dollar conversion depends on both the euro price and the exchange rate; a sufficiently large hotel-price decline can dominate depreciation.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Replace the nominal quote with its reciprocal and treat the discrepancy as resolved” in this real exchange rates and purchasing power task.
macro.Question: Relative PPP predicts depreciation of a domestic currency, but it depreciates less over the observed interval. The report gives no horizon or evidence about traded-goods price gaps. Which follow-up best distinguishes short-run deviation from persistent limits to PPP?
macro.Choice A: Replace the nominal quote with its reciprocal and treat the discrepancy as resolved
macro.Choice B: Examine the horizon and whether gaps are concentrated in nontraded or costly-to-arbitrage goods
macro.Choice C: Infer that inflation data are wrong because depreciation differed from the benchmark
macro.Choice D: Infer that capital flows cannot matter because PPP already predicts a direction
macro.Correct Answer: B — Examine the horizon and whether gaps are concentrated in nontraded or costly-to-arbitrage goods
macro.Feedback: A short interval can reflect asset-demand or policy forces, while persistent nontradable or trade-cost gaps can limit arbitrage. The discrepancy alone identifies neither measurement error nor the source and persistence of the deviation.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Foreign returns rise relative to domestic returns, raising NCO, and lower domestic risk also raises it; NCO rises” in this capital flows and net capital outflow task.
macro.Question: Domestic rates rise 2 percentage points, foreign rates rise 3 points, and domestic political risk falls. What can be inferred about NCO?
macro.Choice A: Foreign returns rise relative to domestic returns, raising NCO, and lower domestic risk also raises it; NCO rises
macro.Choice B: Foreign returns rise relative to domestic returns, raising NCO, while lower domestic risk reduces it; the opposing channels exactly cancel
macro.Choice C: Foreign returns rise relative to domestic returns, raising NCO, while lower domestic risk reduces it; the net direction is undetermined
macro.Choice D: Domestic returns rise relative to foreign returns, reducing NCO, and lower domestic risk also reduces it; NCO falls
macro.Correct Answer: C — Foreign returns rise relative to domestic returns, raising NCO, while lower domestic risk reduces it; the net direction is undetermined
macro.Feedback: Foreign returns rise one point relative to domestic returns, tending to raise NCO, while safer domestic assets tend to lower it; magnitudes decide the net effect.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Compare the saving decline with the import rise; exports are unnecessary” in this international transactions and identities task.
macro.Question: Imports increased, national saving fell, and domestic investment also fell. A commentator says these observations prove that the trade deficit widened. What additional comparisons would let us check this claim using both saving and investment and the export and import figures?
macro.Choice A: Compare the saving decline with the investment decline, and compare the import rise with the export change
macro.Choice B: Compare the saving decline with the import rise; exports are unnecessary
macro.Choice C: Compare the investment decline with the import rise; saving is unnecessary
macro.Choice D: Compare the levels of saving and exports; their changes are unnecessary
macro.Correct Answer: A — Compare the saving decline with the investment decline, and compare the import rise with the export change
macro.Feedback: ΔNX = ΔS − ΔI, so falling saving and investment alone do not sign the change. Independently, ΔNX = ΔX − ΔM; exports must be compared with imports. Either complete accounting comparison should produce the same answer.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating all reserves as excess reserves.
macro.Question: Excess reserves equal:
macro.Choice A: Actual reserves minus required reserves
macro.Choice B: Deposits plus loans
macro.Choice C: Required reserves minus deposits
macro.Choice D: Currency plus M2
macro.Correct Answer: A — Actual reserves minus required reserves
macro.Feedback: Excess reserves are actual reserves beyond what the bank is required to hold.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating all reserves as lendable.
macro.Question: If actual reserves are $150 and required reserves are $100, excess reserves are:
macro.Feedback: Excess reserves are $150 - $100 = $50.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating all reserves as lendable.
macro.Question: A bank has $900,000 in deposits, a 10% reserve requirement, and $140,000 in reserves. How much can it lend?
macro.Feedback: Required reserves are $90,000, so excess reserves are $50,000.

macro.Common Misconception: Thinking the full deposit can be lent when reserves are required
macro.Question: If a bank receives a new $1,000 deposit and must hold $100 in required reserves, the bank can initially lend
macro.Feedback: The bank can lend excess reserves. $1,000 minus $100 leaves $900 available to lend.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating all reserves as excess reserves
macro.Question: A bank has $500,000 in deposits, $80,000 in reserves, and a 10 percent reserve requirement. Excess reserves equal
macro.Feedback: Required reserves are $50,000, so excess reserves are $80,000 - $50,000 = $30,000.

macro.Common Misconception: Lending the entire deposit despite reserve requirements
macro.Question: A bank receives a new $2,000 deposit and the reserve requirement is 25 percent. How much can the bank initially lend?
macro.Feedback: Required reserves are 0.25 x $2,000 = $500, so the bank can initially lend $1,500.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating all actual reserves as lendable reserves
macro.Question: A bank has $800,000 in deposits, a required reserve ratio of 12.5 percent, and actual reserves of $140,000. How much can it lend before hitting its required reserve level?
macro.Feedback: Required reserves are 0.125 x $800,000 = $100,000. Excess reserves are $140,000 - $100,000 = $40,000.

macro.Common Misconception: Lending required reserves as if they were excess reserves
macro.Question: Use the textbook reserve-constrained model, with no other changes. A bank has $300,000 in deposits and a 10 percent reserve requirement. It currently holds $45,000 in reserves. If it lends all excess reserves, what will its reserves and loans change by? Assume the borrower immediately pays someone at another bank and the entire payment settles in reserves.
macro.Choice A: Reserves fall by $15,000 and loans rise by $15,000.
macro.Choice B: Reserves fall by $30,000 and loans rise by $30,000.
macro.Choice C: Reserves fall by $45,000 and loans rise by $45,000.
macro.Choice D: Reserves rise by $15,000 and loans fall by $15,000.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Reserves fall by $15,000 and loans rise by $15,000.
macro.Feedback: Required reserves are $30,000, so excess reserves are $15,000. Lending those lowers reserves by $15,000 and raises loans by $15,000.

macro.Common Misconception: Lending all reserves instead of only excess reserves
macro.Question: A bank has $1,200,000 in deposits, $210,000 in reserves, and a 12.5 percent reserve requirement. If it lends all excess reserves, how much can it lend?
macro.Feedback: Required reserves are 0.125 x $1,200,000 = $150,000. Excess reserves are $210,000 - $150,000 = $60,000.

macro.Common Misconception: Forgetting to find required reserves before solving deposits
macro.Question: If excess reserves are $25,000, actual reserves are $85,000, and the reserve ratio is 12 percent, what are deposits?
macro.Feedback: Required reserves are actual minus excess: $85,000 - $25,000 = $60,000. Deposits = $60,000 / 0.12 = $500,000.

macro.Common Misconception: Dividing actual reserves by the reserve ratio instead of required reserves
macro.Question: A bank has actual reserves of $96,000, excess reserves of $24,000, and a reserve requirement of 12 percent. What are deposits?
macro.Feedback: Required reserves are actual minus excess: $96,000 - $24,000 = $72,000. Deposits are $72,000 / 0.12 = $600,000.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Reserves become $100, required reserves become $110, and there is a $10 shortfall” in this bank balance sheets reserves and capital task.
macro.Question: A bank has deposits of $1000, reserves of $200, and a required reserve ratio of 10% in a simplified model. A depositor withdraws $100 in currency. Assume no other balance-sheet change. How does the withdrawal affect required and excess reserves?
macro.Choice A: Reserves become $100, required reserves become $110, and there is a $10 shortfall
macro.Choice B: Reserves become $100, required reserves $90, and excess reserves $10
