macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The nominal rate becomes 6% because actual inflation replaces the contractual rate” in this fisher effect task.
macro.Question: A $280 fixed-rate loan has nominal interest 7% when expected inflation is 3%. Actual inflation later turns out to be 6%. Which pair separates the rate-setting prediction from the realized outcome?
macro.Choice A: The nominal rate becomes 6% because actual inflation replaces the contractual rate
macro.Choice B: The expected real return was about 4%; the realized real return is about 1%, without changing the contractual nominal rate
macro.Choice C: The expected real return was about 1%; the nominal contract automatically resets to 10% after inflation is observed
macro.Choice D: Both expected and realized real returns are 4% because the lender chose a fixed nominal rate
macro.Correct Answer: B — The expected real return was about 4%; the realized real return is about 1%, without changing the contractual nominal rate
macro.Feedback: Fisher rate setting uses expected inflation at agreement; ex post purchasing power uses actual inflation. Thus 7−3=4% expected and 7−6=1% realized; the nominal contract remains 7%.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
macro.Question: Refer to the graph. At the $15 minimum wage, what labor surplus is created?
macro.Choice A: 100 thousand workers
macro.Choice B: 50 thousand workers
macro.Choice C: 150 thousand workers
macro.Choice D: 250 thousand workers
macro.Correct Answer: A — 100 thousand workers
macro.Feedback: Labor supplied 250 minus labor demanded 150 equals 100 thousand.

macro.Question: Which group directs open-market operations?
macro.Choice A: FOMC
macro.Choice B: IRS
macro.Choice C: BLS
macro.Choice D: CBO
macro.Correct Answer: A — FOMC
macro.Feedback: The Federal Open Market Committee directs open-market operations.

macro.Common Misconception: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
macro.Question: The FOMC decides that monetary conditions should be easier and authorizes purchases of securities. What connection is being made?
macro.Choice A: The FOMC is choosing a monetary-policy tool that adds reserves
macro.Choice B: The Treasury is using fiscal policy to change government purchases
macro.Choice C: A commercial bank is deciding how much capital to issue to shareholders
macro.Choice D: Households are changing M1 by moving funds from checking to savings
macro.Correct Answer: A — The FOMC is choosing a monetary-policy tool that adds reserves
macro.Feedback: When the FOMC authorizes securities purchases, it is using an expansionary monetary-policy tool that adds reserve balances to banks.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing monetary policy agencies with data or tax agencies.
macro.Question: Which group directs open-market operations?
macro.Choice A: Federal Open Market Committee
macro.Choice B: Congressional Budget Office
macro.Choice C: Bureau of Labor Statistics
macro.Choice D: Internal Revenue Service
macro.Correct Answer: A — Federal Open Market Committee
macro.Feedback: The FOMC directs open-market operations as part of monetary policy.

macro.Common Misconception: Thinking fiat money must have intrinsic value.
macro.Question: Fiat money has value mainly because:
macro.Choice A: People accept it and government supports its use
macro.Choice B: The paper itself is valuable
macro.Choice C: It is always backed by gold
macro.Choice D: It is never used in modern economies
macro.Correct Answer: A — People accept it and government supports its use
macro.Feedback: Fiat money does not need intrinsic value. It works because people accept it.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing fiat money and commodity money.
macro.Question: Which feature distinguishes commodity money from fiat money?
macro.Choice A: Has intrinsic value
macro.Choice B: Cannot be used to buy goods
macro.Choice C: Is created only by banks
macro.Choice D: Is excluded from M1
macro.Correct Answer: A — Has intrinsic value
macro.Feedback: Commodity money has value as a good itself. Fiat money does not.

macro.Common Misconception: Uses a surface cue instead of distinguishing the institution, banking mechanism, policy tool, or control limit.
macro.Question: Customers accept paper currency even though the paper itself has little intrinsic value and cannot be redeemed for a commodity. Which explanation best fits?
macro.Choice A: It is fiat money whose usefulness depends on general acceptance rather than commodity value
macro.Choice B: It is commodity money because the paper can be physically held
macro.Choice C: It is bank capital because it supports financial transactions
macro.Choice D: It is not money unless every note is backed one-for-one by gold
macro.Correct Answer: A — It is fiat money whose usefulness depends on general acceptance rather than commodity value
macro.Feedback: The currency is fiat money: it is accepted as payment even though the paper has little intrinsic value and is not redeemable for a commodity.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating all money as fiat money
macro.Question: Commodity money differs from fiat money because commodity money
macro.Choice A: has intrinsic value
macro.Choice B: is created only through bank lending
macro.Choice C: cannot be used as a medium of exchange
macro.Choice D: is always part of M2 but never M1
macro.Correct Answer: A — has intrinsic value
macro.Feedback: Commodity money has value as a good itself, like gold or silver. Fiat money does not.

macro.Common Misconception: Thinking money must be backed by a commodity to have value
macro.Question: A country uses paper currency that has no intrinsic value, is not convertible into gold, but is accepted for payment. What kind of money is this?
macro.Choice A: Fiat money
macro.Choice B: Commodity money
macro.Choice C: Barter money
macro.Choice D: Reserve money only
macro.Correct Answer: A — Fiat money
macro.Feedback: That is fiat money: it has value because it is accepted, not because the paper itself has intrinsic value.

macro.Common Misconception: Thinking fiat money must have intrinsic value
macro.Question: A student says, 'Money is valuable because the dollar bill itself has valuable paper.' What is the best correction?
macro.Choice A: Fiat money has value because people accept it and the government supports its use.
macro.Choice B: Fiat money has value because its paper is worth more than its face value.
macro.Choice C: Commodity money and fiat money are the same thing.
macro.Choice D: Money only has value if it can be exchanged for gold.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Fiat money has value because people accept it and the government supports its use.
macro.Feedback: Fiat money does not need intrinsic value. Its value comes from general acceptance and government backing.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Both events create new M1 equal to the amounts credited because checking balances rise” in this money functions and measures task.
macro.Question: A customer deposits $100 of currency into checking. A bank later makes a separate loan by crediting a borrower's checking account. Which comparison correctly separates the two events?
macro.Choice A: The currency deposit changes M1 composition; the later loan can create a new deposit and raise M1
macro.Choice B: Both events create new M1 equal to the amounts credited because checking balances rise
macro.Choice C: Neither event can change M1 because every bank deposit merely replaces currency
macro.Choice D: The currency deposit creates new M1; lending changes only the ownership of existing currency
macro.Correct Answer: A — The currency deposit changes M1 composition; the later loan can create a new deposit and raise M1
macro.Feedback: In the first event, public currency falls as checking rises; in the second, a loan asset and deposit liability are created together. The initial transfer and subsequent credit creation must not be conflated.

macro.Question: What makes fiat money valuable?
macro.Choice A: Government acceptance and public trust, not intrinsic commodity value
macro.Choice B: Its gold content alone
macro.Choice C: A fixed reserve requirement
macro.Choice D: Its use only in foreign trade
macro.Correct Answer: A — Government acceptance and public trust, not intrinsic commodity value
macro.Feedback: Fiat money has value because it is accepted in exchange, not because the paper itself is valuable.

macro.Common Misconception: Thinking fiat money must be backed by gold.
macro.Question: What is fiat money?
macro.Choice A: Money backed fully by gold
macro.Choice B: Accepted money with no intrinsic value
macro.Choice C: Money used only by banks
macro.Choice D: Money that cannot lose value
macro.Correct Answer: B — Accepted money with no intrinsic value
macro.Feedback: Fiat money has value because people accept it, not because it has intrinsic value.

macro.Question: A bank gets $1,000 in deposits and must hold $100. How much can it lend?
macro.Feedback: The bank can lend deposits minus required reserves: $1,000 - $100 = $900.

macro.Question: A bank gets $4,000 in new deposits and must hold 25 percent in reserves. First-round lending can be:
macro.Feedback: Required reserves are $1,000, so the bank can lend $3,000.

macro.Common Misconception: Lending required reserves or using the multiplier too early.
macro.Question: A bank receives $5,000 in new deposits, holds 15 percent required reserves, and lends the rest. What is the maximum first-round loan?
macro.Feedback: Required reserves are $750, so the bank can lend $4,250 in the first round.

macro.Common Misconception: Lending required reserves.
macro.Question: A bank receives $2,000 in new deposits and faces a 10 percent reserve requirement. If it lends all excess reserves, its first new loan can be:
macro.Feedback: Required reserves are $200, so excess reserves are $1,800.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Count $115; every sale is separate current output” in this gdp measurement task.
macro.Question: A domestic farm sells grain for $20 to a domestic mill, which sells flour for $35 to a domestic bakery. The bakery sells all bread to households for $60. No inventories change. An accountant adds all three sales to GDP. Which correction reconciles expenditure with value added?
macro.Choice A: Count $115; every sale is separate current output
macro.Choice B: Count $25; only the bakery creates final value
macro.Choice C: Count $95; exclude the farm but retain the mill's intermediate sale
macro.Choice D: Count $60; summing each producer's value added gives the same final-output value
macro.Correct Answer: D — Count $60; summing each producer's value added gives the same final-output value
macro.Feedback: Value added is 20 + (35−20) + (60−35) = $60, equal to the bread's final sale. Adding gross intermediate sales counts embedded production repeatedly.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Current GDP rises $62; the dealer fee is only a transfer” in this gdp measurement task.
macro.Question: A household buys a used domestic machine for $62 through a dealer charging a current service fee of $22. The machine was produced last year. Which pair correctly compares current GDP with the household's total payment?
macro.Choice A: Current GDP rises $62; the dealer fee is only a transfer
macro.Choice B: Current GDP is unchanged; anything connected to a used asset is excluded
macro.Choice C: Current GDP rises $22; the larger payment includes transfer of an existing asset
macro.Choice D: Current GDP rises $84; both the machine and dealer service are newly produced
macro.Correct Answer: C — Current GDP rises $22; the larger payment includes transfer of an existing asset
macro.Feedback: The $62 used asset is not current production. The newly provided dealer service contributes $22, even though the transaction concerns a used asset.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Current GDP includes $103; next year's sale contributes nothing” in this gdp measurement task.
macro.Question: A domestic factory produces $64 of final goods, sells $39, and holds the remainder as new inventory. A report uses sales alone and says GDP will rise when the inventory is sold next year without new production. Which correction is valid?
macro.Choice A: Current GDP includes $103; next year's sale contributes nothing
macro.Choice B: Current GDP includes $25; only unsold goods are counted this year
macro.Choice C: Current GDP includes $64; next year's inventory sale is offset by inventory disinvestment
macro.Choice D: Current GDP includes $39; next year's sale adds the remaining output again
macro.Correct Answer: C — Current GDP includes $64; next year's inventory sale is offset by inventory disinvestment
macro.Feedback: Production, not only sales, is counted: sales 39 plus inventory investment 25 equals 64. A later sale of that inventory is offset by a fall in inventories, avoiding a second count.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Include $107; both ownership and location independently add production” in this gdp measurement task.
macro.Question: A foreign-owned factory produces $66 of final output inside the country and sends $26 of profit to its foreign owners. A domestically owned factory produces $41 abroad. Which output counts in domestic GDP?
macro.Choice A: Include $107; GDP adds domestic location and domestic ownership.
macro.Choice B: Include $66; GDP follows production location rather than ownership.
macro.Choice C: Include $41; GDP follows the owners' nationality rather than location.
macro.Choice D: Include $40; GDP deducts foreign profit remittances from domestic output.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Include $66; GDP follows production location rather than ownership.
macro.Feedback: GDP measures production within the country. Profit remittance concerns cross-border income, not whether the domestic factory produced output. Output made abroad is excluded from domestic GDP.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “$87; subtract the input from final output even though it was never added” in this gdp measurement task.
macro.Question: A producer reports $72 of final output. A supplier's $32 input is already embodied in it. The national accounts also record $47 of unrelated domestic services. Which proposed GDP total counts each unit of current output once?
macro.Choice A: $151; every observed sale is added
macro.Choice B: $87; subtract the input from final output even though it was never added
macro.Choice C: $72; services are excluded when goods have intermediate inputs
macro.Choice D: $119; count final output and unrelated services, without adding its embodied input
macro.Correct Answer: D — $119; count final output and unrelated services, without adding its embodied input
macro.Feedback: The final good already embodies the supplier's contribution. GDP is 72+47 = $119; neither add the input again nor subtract it from final expenditure.

macro.Common Misconception: Counts a government transfer as government purchases before any recipient buys output.
macro.Question: Does a government benefit payment enter G when it is sent?
macro.Choice A: Yes; every government payment enters G
macro.Choice B: Yes; but only if the household saves it
macro.Choice C: No; it enters business investment
macro.Choice D: No; it is a transfer, not a purchase of current output
macro.Correct Answer: D — No; it is a transfer, not a purchase of current output
macro.Feedback: Transfers redistribute income and are excluded from G; a later purchase can enter the appropriate spending component.

macro.Common Misconception: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
macro.Question: Which equation correctly states the expenditure approach to GDP?
macro.Choice A: Y = C + I + G + NX
macro.Choice B: Y = C - I + G - NX
macro.Choice C: Y = wages + CPI
macro.Choice D: Y = exports + unemployment
macro.Correct Answer: A — Y = C + I + G + NX
macro.Feedback: GDP equals consumption plus investment plus government purchases plus net exports.

macro.Common Misconception: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
macro.Question: A household buying groceries is counted under which GDP component?
macro.Choice A: Consumption
macro.Choice B: Investment
macro.Choice C: Government purchases
macro.Choice D: Net exports
macro.Correct Answer: A — Consumption
macro.Feedback: Household spending on goods and services is consumption.

macro.Common Misconception: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
macro.Question: Net exports equal:
macro.Choice A: Exports minus imports
macro.Choice B: Imports minus exports
macro.Choice C: Consumption minus imports
macro.Choice D: Investment plus imports
macro.Correct Answer: A — Exports minus imports
macro.Feedback: Net exports are exports minus imports.

macro.Common Misconception: Treats the subtraction of imports as a claim that imported goods are inherently harmful or absent from spending.
macro.Question: Why are imports subtracted after imported spending may appear in C, I, or G?
macro.Choice A: To remove foreign production from domestic GDP
macro.Choice B: Because imports are inherently harmful
macro.Choice C: To erase the buyer’s spending from every account
macro.Choice D: Because exports must always exceed imports
macro.Correct Answer: A — To remove foreign production from domestic GDP
macro.Feedback: Imports are subtracted because imported final spending may already appear in C, I, or G and foreign production must not enter domestic GDP.

macro.Common Misconception: Excluding unsold current production instead of counting it as inventory investment.
macro.Question: Unsold goods produced this year are counted as:
macro.Choice A: Inventory investment
macro.Choice B: Used goods
macro.Choice C: Imports
macro.Choice D: Transfer payments
macro.Correct Answer: A — Inventory investment
macro.Feedback: Goods produced but not sold are counted as inventory investment.

macro.Common Misconception: Classifies durable household consumption as business investment.
macro.Question: A household buys a newly produced domestic car for $30,000; a firm buys a newly produced domestic machine for $20,000. Which pair enters the expenditure accounts?
macro.Feedback: Household final purchases enter consumption; productive equipment purchased by a firm enters investment.

macro.Common Misconception: Includes the imported appliance without its NX cancellation.
macro.Question: A household buys an imported appliance for $500 and pays a domestic installer $100. Both payments enter consumption. How much does this transaction add to domestic GDP after the import offset?
macro.Feedback: Consumption rises 600, but imports subtract 500 through NX. The domestic installation 100 remains in GDP.

macro.Common Misconception: Excludes unsold current production or counts it twice.
macro.Question: A factory makes $100 of new domestic output and sells $80 this period. The unsold $20 stays in inventory. What current production total is recorded?
macro.Choice A: $80: only sold goods count
macro.Choice B: $120: production 100 plus inventory 20
macro.Choice C: $20: only inventory is new production
macro.Choice D: $100: sales 80 plus inventory investment 20
macro.Correct Answer: D — $100: sales 80 plus inventory investment 20
macro.Feedback: Unsold current production is inventory investment. Final sales 80 plus inventory accumulation 20 record the same 100 produced.

macro.Common Misconception: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
macro.Question: Which of the following is one of the four components of GDP expenditure?
macro.Choice A: Consumption
macro.Choice B: Inflation
macro.Choice C: Unemployment
macro.Choice D: Depreciation
macro.Correct Answer: A — Consumption
macro.Feedback: Consumption is one of the four expenditure components of GDP.

macro.Common Misconception: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
macro.Question: The GDP expenditure identity is:
macro.Choice A: Y = C + I + G + NX
macro.Choice B: Y = C - I + G - NX
macro.Choice C: Y = wages + prices + taxes
macro.Choice D: Y = inflation + unemployment
macro.Correct Answer: A — Y = C + I + G + NX
macro.Feedback: GDP expenditure is consumption plus investment plus government purchases plus net exports.

macro.Common Misconception: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
macro.Question: If C = 10, I = 3, G = 4, and NX = -1, what is GDP?

macro.Common Misconception: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
macro.Question: Net exports are calculated as:
macro.Choice A: Exports minus imports
macro.Choice B: Imports minus exports
macro.Choice C: Consumption minus investment
macro.Choice D: Government purchases minus taxes
macro.Correct Answer: A — Exports minus imports
macro.Feedback: Net exports equal exports minus imports.

macro.Common Misconception: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
macro.Question: A household buys groceries. Which GDP component does this most directly enter?
macro.Choice A: Consumption
macro.Choice B: Investment
macro.Choice C: Government purchases
macro.Choice D: Net exports
macro.Correct Answer: A — Consumption
macro.Feedback: Household spending on goods and services is consumption.

macro.Common Misconception: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
macro.Question: A firm buys new machinery to produce more output. Which GDP component does this enter?
macro.Choice A: Investment
macro.Choice B: Consumption
macro.Choice C: Government purchases
macro.Choice D: Net exports
macro.Correct Answer: A — Investment
macro.Feedback: Business spending on capital goods is investment.

macro.Common Misconception: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
macro.Question: Suppose C = $14T, I = $4T, G = $5T, exports = $3T, and imports = $4.5T. What is GDP?

macro.Common Misconception: Excluding unsold current production instead of counting it as inventory investment.
macro.Question: A U.S. firm builds $100 million of equipment domestically and sells $70 million of it this year, keeping $30 million in inventory. What is counted in GDP?
macro.Choice A: $100 million because unsold output is inventory investment
macro.Choice B: $70 million because only sold goods count
macro.Choice C: $30 million because only inventory counts
macro.Choice D: $0 because business equipment is excluded
macro.Correct Answer: A — $100 million because unsold output is inventory investment
macro.Feedback: Current production counts whether sold or added to inventories, so all $100 million counts.

macro.Common Misconception: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
macro.Question: If consumption is $12 trillion, investment is $4 trillion, government purchases are $5 trillion, exports are $3 trillion, and imports are $4 trillion, what is GDP?
macro.Choice A: $20 trillion
macro.Choice B: $21 trillion
macro.Choice C: $24 trillion
macro.Choice D: $28 trillion
macro.Correct Answer: A — $20 trillion

macro.Common Misconception: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
macro.Question: A household buys a newly built home. In GDP accounting, this is counted as:
macro.Choice A: Consumption
macro.Choice B: Investment
macro.Choice C: Government purchases
macro.Choice D: Net exports
macro.Correct Answer: B — Investment
macro.Feedback: New residential construction is counted as investment, not consumption.

macro.Common Misconception: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
macro.Question: A state government pays workers to repair highways. Which GDP component rises?
macro.Choice A: Consumption
macro.Choice B: Investment
macro.Choice C: Government purchases
macro.Choice D: Net exports
macro.Correct Answer: C — Government purchases
macro.Feedback: Government spending on goods and services is counted as government purchases.

macro.Common Misconception: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
macro.Question: If exports are $800 billion and imports are $1.1 trillion, net exports equal:
macro.Choice A: $300 billion
macro.Choice B: -$300 billion
macro.Choice C: $1.9 trillion
macro.Choice D: -$1.9 trillion
macro.Correct Answer: B — -$300 billion
macro.Feedback: Net exports = exports - imports = 800 - 1100 = -300 billion.

macro.Common Misconception: Excluding unsold current production instead of counting it as inventory investment.
macro.Question: A U.S. firm produces $10 million in goods but sells only $7 million this year. The remaining $3 million is added to inventories. How much is counted in GDP?
macro.Choice A: $7 million
macro.Choice B: $3 million
macro.Choice C: $10 million
macro.Correct Answer: C — $10 million
macro.Feedback: Unsold output is counted as inventory investment, so all $10 million is counted.

macro.Common Misconception: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
macro.Question: Which transaction increases investment in GDP accounting?
macro.Choice A: A household buys groceries
macro.Choice B: A firm buys new delivery trucks
macro.Choice C: The government sends unemployment benefits
macro.Choice D: A consumer buys imported shoes
macro.Correct Answer: B — A firm buys new delivery trucks
macro.Feedback: Business purchases of new capital goods are investment.

macro.Common Misconception: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
macro.Question: Consumption is $9T, investment is $3T, government purchases are $4T, exports are $2T, and imports are $3T. Then households buy $1T more imported goods, with no change in domestic production. What happens to measured GDP?
macro.Choice A: It does not change
macro.Choice B: It rises by $1T because consumption rises
macro.Choice C: It falls by $1T because imports rise
macro.Choice D: It rises by $2T because trade increases
macro.Correct Answer: A — It does not change
macro.Feedback: Imported consumption raises C but lowers NX by the same amount, so domestic GDP is unchanged.

macro.Common Misconception: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
macro.Question: A government spends $100B hiring workers to build bridges and also sends $100B in Social Security payments. If recipients spend all Social Security payments on current domestic goods, what is the maximum direct GDP increase described?
macro.Feedback: Bridge spending is government purchases, and household spending from transfers can count as consumption. The transfer itself is not counted separately.

macro.Common Misconception: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
macro.Question: If C = $15T, I = $4T, G = $6T, imports = $5T, and GDP = $23T, what are exports?
macro.Correct Answer: A — $3T

macro.Common Misconception: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
macro.Question: A household buys a newly built condo for $250,000 and pays $3,000 in property taxes. Which is the best GDP treatment?
macro.Choice A: The condo is investment; the property tax is not current output
macro.Choice B: Both count as consumption
macro.Choice C: The condo is consumption and the tax is government purchases
macro.Choice D: Neither counts
macro.Correct Answer: A — The condo is investment; the property tax is not current output
macro.Feedback: New residential construction is investment. A tax payment is not itself government purchase of a final good or service.

macro.Common Misconception: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
macro.Question: A household buys a newly built house for $300,000, a used car for $15,000, and $5,000 of groceries. What amount is added to GDP from these purchases?
macro.Feedback: The new house and groceries count. The used car resale does not add to current GDP, so GDP rises by $305,000.

macro.Common Misconception: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
macro.Question: A government sends $1,000 unemployment checks to households, and households spend the full amount on groceries. What is the GDP effect?
macro.Choice A: The transfer is excluded; grocery purchases count as consumption
macro.Choice B: Both the transfer and groceries count, so GDP rises by $2,000
macro.Choice C: Neither counts because government is involved
macro.Choice D: Only the transfer counts as government purchases
macro.Correct Answer: A — The transfer is excluded; grocery purchases count as consumption
macro.Feedback: Transfer payments are not purchases of current goods and services, but later household spending can count as consumption.

macro.Common Misconception: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
macro.Question: A U.S. household buys a $40,000 car produced in Germany. In U.S. GDP accounting, what happens?
macro.Choice A: Consumption rises $40,000 and net exports fall $40,000; GDP is unchanged
macro.Choice B: Consumption rises and GDP rises by $40,000
macro.Choice C: Investment rises and imports are ignored
macro.Choice D: Government purchases rise and GDP is unchanged
macro.Correct Answer: A — Consumption rises $40,000 and net exports fall $40,000; GDP is unchanged
macro.Feedback: Imported consumer goods enter consumption but are subtracted through imports in net exports, so domestic GDP does not rise.

macro.Common Misconception: Excluding unsold current production instead of counting it as inventory investment.
macro.Question: A firm produces $500M in goods, sells $450M, and unintentionally accumulates $50M in inventories. Which GDP component includes the unsold goods?
macro.Choice A: Investment
macro.Choice B: Consumption
macro.Choice C: Government purchases
macro.Choice D: Net exports
macro.Correct Answer: A — Investment
macro.Feedback: Inventory accumulation is counted as investment, even when unplanned.

macro.Common Misconception: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
macro.Question: An economy reports C = 46, G = 13, exports = 9, imports = 11, and GDP = 72, all in billions. A separate inventory report records 4 billion of new unsold output. What investment total reconciles the accounts, and how should the inventory figure be treated?
macro.Choice A: I = 15; the 4 of inventories is included within that total
macro.Choice B: I = 19; add inventories after solving the identity
macro.Choice C: I = 7; subtract inventories twice to avoid unsold output
macro.Choice D: I = 37; imports should be added when solving for investment
macro.Correct Answer: A — I = 15; the 4 of inventories is included within that total
macro.Feedback: The expenditure identity gives I = 72 - 46 - 13 - 9 + 11 = 15. Inventory investment is one part of I, leaving 11 in other investment; it is not an extra addition after reconciliation.

macro.Common Misconception: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
macro.Question: A government purchases $18 million of new domestic flood barriers and pays $12 million in household benefits. Recipients spend $7 million on new domestic services and $3 million on imported goods, saving the rest. What GDP contribution and expenditure classification follow?
macro.Choice A: $25 million; G = 18, C = 10, and M = 3
macro.Choice B: $37 million; benefits and recipient purchases both count
macro.Choice C: $28 million; imported purchases count only in C
macro.Choice D: $18 million; spending financed by benefits is excluded
macro.Correct Answer: A — $25 million; G = 18, C = 10, and M = 3
macro.Feedback: The benefit payment itself is a transfer. Recipient purchases enter C = 7 + 3 = 10; M = 3 removes the imported goods. G = 18, so domestic GDP rises 18 + 10 - 3 = 25 million, without counting the transfer again.

macro.Common Misconception: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
macro.Question: A firm produces $10M of goods in December but sells $7M in December and $3M in January. How should the $3M be treated for December GDP?
macro.Choice A: It counts as inventory investment in December
macro.Choice B: It is excluded until January
macro.Choice C: It counts as consumption in December
macro.Choice D: It is subtracted from December GDP
macro.Correct Answer: A — It counts as inventory investment in December
macro.Feedback: Goods produced but not sold are counted as inventory investment in the period produced.

macro.Common Misconception: Excluding unsold current production instead of counting it as inventory investment.
macro.Question: At the start of a year, a producer has $8 million of goods made last year. It produces $30 million this year and sells $34 million, leaving $4 million in inventory. With unchanged prices, no imports and all sales to final users, which GDP account is correct?
macro.Choice A: $30 million: final sales 34 plus inventory investment of -4
macro.Choice B: $34 million: sales determine the production year
macro.Choice C: $38 million: add beginning inventories to new output
macro.Choice D: $42 million: add beginning inventories to final sales
macro.Correct Answer: A — $30 million: final sales 34 plus inventory investment of -4
macro.Feedback: Inventory investment is the change in stock: 4 - 8 = -4. Sales of 34 plus inventory investment of -4 equal current production of 30. Selling previously produced goods does not create output again.

macro.Common Misconception: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
macro.Question: A revision adds $6 billion of imported household appliances to consumption and records $2 billion of previously omitted current domestic installation services. The same imported appliances were missing from M. How should measured GDP change after all corrections?
macro.Choice A: Rise $2 billion; imported spending cancels while domestic installation remains
macro.Choice B: Rise $8 billion; all added consumption is domestic output
macro.Choice C: Fall $4 billion; imports are subtracted without adding their spending
macro.Choice D: Remain unchanged; every correction associated with imports cancels
macro.Correct Answer: A — Rise $2 billion; imported spending cancels while domestic installation remains
macro.Feedback: C rises by 8 billion and M by 6 billion. The net 2-billion increase is the newly measured domestic service. Subtracting imports removes foreign production, not the associated domestic activity.

macro.Common Misconception: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
macro.Question: A firm buys a new domestically produced machine for $1M and a share of stock in another company for $1M. What is the direct effect on GDP?
macro.Choice A: GDP rises $1M; the stock purchase is financial
macro.Choice B: GDP rises by $2M because both are investments
macro.Choice C: GDP does not change because firms made both purchases
macro.Choice D: GDP rises only from the stock purchase
macro.Correct Answer: A — GDP rises $1M; the stock purchase is financial
macro.Feedback: Economic investment in GDP means new capital goods, not financial asset purchases.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “G and C both rise $30; GDP rises $50” in this gdp components task.
macro.Question: Government sends households $30 in transfers. Recipients buy $10 of imported goods and $20 of current domestic services. No other spending changes. Which expenditure-account entry and GDP change are correct?
macro.Feedback: The transfer is not a government purchase. Recipient consumption enters C; imported consumption also enters M. Thus ΔGDP = 30−10 = $20, the domestic services alone.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Both are financial saving; neither is production until resold” in this gdp components task.
macro.Question: A firm adds $35 of current unsold output to inventories while a household buys a newly built domestic home for $105. A student classifies only the firm's inventory as investment. Which correction is needed?
macro.Choice A: Both are financial saving; neither is production until resold
macro.Choice B: Both are investment; their combined GDP contribution is $140

macro.Common Misconception: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
macro.Question: A U.S. household buys a new $30,000 car built in Mexico, while a Mexican household buys a new $40,000 car built in Michigan. What is the net effect on U.S. GDP from these two transactions?
macro.Choice A: U.S. GDP rises by $40,000
macro.Choice B: U.S. GDP rises by $70,000
macro.Choice C: U.S. GDP rises by $10,000
macro.Choice D: U.S. GDP is unchanged
macro.Correct Answer: A — U.S. GDP rises by $40,000
macro.Feedback: Only the car produced in Michigan counts in U.S. GDP. The imported car affects consumption and imports but not domestic production.

macro.Common Misconception: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
macro.Question: A firm imports $500,000 of parts, adds $300,000 of domestic labor and capital services, and sells the final good domestically for $800,000. What is the contribution to domestic GDP?
macro.Feedback: Only domestic value added counts in domestic GDP. Imported inputs are not domestic production.

macro.Common Misconception: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
macro.Question: A country produces only two goods. In 2025 it produces 100 meals at $20 and 50 laptops at $1,000. It imports 10 additional laptops at $900 each for households. What domestic production value is counted in GDP?
macro.Feedback: GDP counts domestic production: 100($20) + 50($1,000) = $52,000. Imported laptops are not domestic production.

macro.Common Misconception: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
macro.Question: A restaurant buys $300 of ingredients and receives $900 from customers for meals, including $100 in tips. Ignoring other complications, how much final restaurant service enters GDP?
macro.Feedback: The $300 of ingredients are intermediate inputs. The full $900 customer payment, including the $100 in tips, is final expenditure on restaurant service.

macro.Common Misconception: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
macro.Question: A firm imports $200,000 of components, adds $150,000 of domestic labor and capital services, and sells the final product domestically for $350,000. How much does this production add to domestic GDP?
macro.Feedback: Only domestic value added counts in domestic GDP. Imported components are not domestic production.

macro.Common Misconception: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
macro.Question: A mill sells $180 of flour made from $70 of current domestic grain. A baker uses all the flour in $310 of bread sold to households. What are the baker’s value added and GDP across the full domestic chain?
macro.Choice A: $130 at the bakery; $310 across the chain
macro.Choice B: $240 at the bakery; $560 across the chain
macro.Choice C: $310 at the bakery; $310 across the chain
macro.Choice D: $130 at the bakery; $490 across the chain
macro.Correct Answer: A — $130 at the bakery; $310 across the chain
macro.Feedback: The baker adds 310 - 180 = 130. Summing domestic value added gives 70 + (180 - 70) + 130 = 310, equal to the final sale. Intermediate sales cannot be added again.

macro.Common Misconception: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
macro.Question: A domestic assembler sells $420,000 of new equipment, using $150,000 of imported parts and $90,000 of current domestic components. A clerk adds all three values as domestic GDP. What correction reconciles final spending with domestic value added?
macro.Choice A: $270,000 total domestic GDP, including $180,000 at assembly
macro.Choice B: $420,000 total domestic GDP, including $330,000 at assembly
macro.Choice C: $510,000 total domestic GDP, including $420,000 at assembly
macro.Choice D: $180,000 total domestic GDP, excluding the domestic component makers
macro.Correct Answer: A — $270,000 total domestic GDP, including $180,000 at assembly
macro.Feedback: Final spending of 420,000 less imported inputs of 150,000 yields 270,000 domestic value added. Assembly contributes 420,000 - 150,000 - 90,000 = 180,000; domestic component makers contribute the remaining 90,000. Do not count their output twice.

macro.Common Misconception: Double-counting intermediate goods instead of counting final value or value added.
macro.Question: A workshop sells $560 of new furniture after buying $140 of domestic lumber. Its wage bill is $250 and rent plus interest is $90. With no other costs or taxes, which value-added and profit account is consistent?
macro.Choice A: $420 value added, including $80 profit
macro.Choice B: $560 value added, including $220 profit
macro.Choice C: $280 value added, including $80 profit
macro.Choice D: $420 value added, including $420 profit
macro.Correct Answer: A — $420 value added, including $80 profit
macro.Feedback: Value added is final output less intermediate lumber: 560 - 140 = 420. Of that, wages and rent/interest absorb 340, leaving profit of 80. Subtracting wages when computing value added would remove income generated by production.

macro.Common Misconception: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
macro.Question: A renovation business bills households $96,000, including $24,000 of imported fixtures. It also brokers an old building for a $6,000 fee; the building sells for $310,000. Ignoring other inputs, what current domestic production and counting rule follow?
macro.Choice A: $78,000; count domestic renovation value and the new brokerage service
macro.Choice B: $388,000; the old building becomes current output when sold
macro.Choice C: $102,000; imported fixtures count because households bought them
macro.Choice D: $72,000; services attached to used assets must also be excluded
macro.Correct Answer: A — $78,000; count domestic renovation value and the new brokerage service
macro.Feedback: Domestic renovation value is 96,000 - 24,000 = 72,000. The current brokerage service adds 6,000, while the old building itself is not new output. Total current domestic production is 78,000.

macro.Common Misconception: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
macro.Question: A used machine changes hands for $40,000 through a broker charging $2,000. A new domestic machine worth $28,000 is produced but remains unsold. An analyst counts only the $40,000 resale as this year’s GDP. What is the corrected contribution?
macro.Choice A: $30,000: brokerage service plus inventory investment
macro.Choice B: $42,000: resale plus brokerage service
macro.Choice C: $70,000: every transaction and unsold machine
macro.Choice D: $2,000: unsold output cannot count until purchased
macro.Correct Answer: A — $30,000: brokerage service plus inventory investment
macro.Feedback: The resale transfers an existing asset; the newly produced brokerage service counts. The unsold new machine is inventory investment when produced. Thus current GDP includes 2,000 + 28,000 = 30,000.

macro.Common Misconception: Counting transactions that are not current domestic production, such as used goods, financial assets, or foreign production.
macro.Question: A U.S. firm earns profits from a factory located in Vietnam. Why is this not part of U.S. GDP?
macro.Choice A: GDP counts production within U.S. borders, not income earned abroad by U.S. residents
macro.Choice B: Profits are excluded from GDP because GDP measures wage income rather than business income earned by firms
macro.Choice C: Foreign production enters U.S. GDP when the resulting goods or services are eventually sold to U.S. consumers
macro.Choice D: GDP assigns production to the owner's home country rather than to the country where the production occurs
macro.Correct Answer: A — GDP counts production within U.S. borders, not income earned abroad by U.S. residents
macro.Feedback: GDP is domestic production. Income earned abroad relates more to national income measures, not U.S. GDP.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Include $55; ownership determines which output belongs to GDP” in this gdp measurement task.
macro.Question: A foreign-owned factory produces $80 of final output inside the country and sends $40 of profit to its foreign owners. A domestically owned factory produces $55 abroad. Which output counts in domestic GDP?
macro.Choice A: Include $80; GDP follows production location rather than ownership.
macro.Choice B: Include $135; GDP adds domestic location and domestic ownership.
macro.Choice C: Include $55; GDP follows the owners' nationality rather than location.
macro.Choice D: Include $40; GDP deducts foreign profit remittances from domestic output.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Include $80; GDP follows production location rather than ownership.
macro.Feedback: GDP measures production within the country. Profit remittance concerns cross-border income, not whether the domestic factory produced output. Output made abroad is excluded from domestic GDP.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Profit is $40; only wages count as costs in the income account” in this gdp measurement task.
macro.Question: A current domestic final sale is $82. Wages are $42, other production income is $15, and profit is the residual. A reviewer claims expenditure exceeds income because profit is omitted from the income account. Which reconciliation is correct?
macro.Choice A: Profit is $40; only wages count as costs in the income account
macro.Choice B: Profit is $57; adding it doubles total income
macro.Choice C: Profit is zero; the expenditure-income gap is genuine output
macro.Choice D: Profit is $25; adding it makes income equal the $82 expenditure
macro.Correct Answer: D — Profit is $25; adding it makes income equal the $82 expenditure
macro.Feedback: The listed non-profit income totals $57. Residual profit is 82−57 = $25, bringing income to $82. Income and expenditure are two views of this same current production.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Subtract the $84 computer; financial transactions contribute $103” in this gdp measurement task.
macro.Question: A household buys a $84 newly produced domestic computer and a $59 existing corporate share. A broker supplies a new service charging $44. Which revision to a report counting all three payments is correct?
macro.Choice A: Subtract the $84 computer; financial transactions contribute $103
macro.Choice B: Subtract both the share and service; only $84 counts
macro.Choice C: Subtract the $59 share transfer; the computer and brokerage service contribute $128
macro.Choice D: Subtract the $44 service; the computer and share contribute $143
macro.Correct Answer: C — Subtract the $59 share transfer; the computer and brokerage service contribute $128
macro.Feedback: The share is a financial-asset transfer. The current computer and brokerage service are production, totaling 84+44 = $128. A service is not excluded merely because it accompanies finance.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Count $199; every sale is separate current output” in this gdp measurement task.
macro.Question: A domestic farm sells grain for $48 to a mill, which sells flour for $63 to a bakery; bread sells to households for $88. The farm buys no intermediate inputs, and no inventories change. An accountant sums value added but omits the farm, reporting GDP of $40. Would excluding the farm be justified because its grain is intermediate?
macro.Choice A: No. The mill and bakery add $40, but the farm adds $48; all value added totals the $88 final sale.
macro.Choice B: Yes. Intermediate producers add nothing to GDP, so only downstream value added counts.
macro.Choice C: No. All three gross sales should be added, making GDP $199.
macro.Choice D: Yes. The farm's $48 has already been counted in the mill's $15 of value added.
macro.Correct Answer: A — No. The mill and bakery add $40, but the farm adds $48; all value added totals the $88 final sale.
macro.Feedback: Mill value added is 63−48=15 and bakery value added 88−63=25. Their $40 excludes the farm's $48 contribution. Intermediate sales are not added on top of final expenditure, but each domestic producer's value added belongs in the production account.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Current GDP rises $140; both the machine and dealer service are newly produced” in this gdp measurement task.
macro.Question: A household buys a machine produced last year for $90 and pays a dealer a $50 current service fee. Suppose the used-machine price were instead $60 while the fee and service stayed the same. How would that change current GDP from this transaction?
macro.Choice A: GDP would fall $30 because every reduction in the total household payment lowers current output.
macro.Choice B: GDP would be $110 because both the used machine and dealer fee count as newly produced output.
macro.Choice C: GDP would be zero because transactions involving used goods exclude even newly provided services.
macro.Choice D: It would not change the $50 contribution; the lower payment changes the price of an existing asset, not current production.
macro.Correct Answer: D — It would not change the $50 contribution; the lower payment changes the price of an existing asset, not current production.
macro.Feedback: The original $140 payment contains $90 for an existing asset and $50 for current service. The counterfactual $110 payment still buys the same $50 service. GDP records that service, not the resale price of last year's machine.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
macro.Question: In GDP accounting, why does total income equal total expenditure?
macro.Choice A: Because one person's spending becomes another person's income
macro.Choice B: Because imports always equal exports
macro.Choice C: Because government sets income equal to spending
macro.Choice D: Because wages are excluded from GDP
macro.Correct Answer: A — Because one person's spending becomes another person's income
macro.Feedback: Every transaction has a buyer and seller, so expenditure becomes income.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
macro.Question: If a customer spends $100 at a business, what happens to the business in the income-expenditure flow?
macro.Choice A: It receives $100 of income
macro.Choice B: It loses $100 of income
macro.Choice C: GDP falls by $100
macro.Choice D: Only imports change
macro.Correct Answer: A — It receives $100 of income
macro.Feedback: The customer's spending is the business's income.

macro.Common Misconception: Adds spending to income instead of reconciling the two ledgers.
macro.Question: Final domestic output sells for $210. Production income records show wages of $140 and rent and interest of $30. With no taxes, depreciation or discrepancy, what profit completes the income account?
macro.Feedback: All income from producing the output sums to 210. The missing profit is 210−140−30=40.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
macro.Question: In the circular flow of income and expenditure, why does total income equal total expenditure?
macro.Choice A: Every dollar spent by a buyer becomes income for a seller
macro.Choice B: Government sets income equal to spending
macro.Choice C: Exports always equal imports
macro.Choice D: Savings are never counted
macro.Correct Answer: A — Every dollar spent by a buyer becomes income for a seller
macro.Feedback: Income equals expenditure because one person's spending becomes another person's income.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
macro.Question: If households spend $500 billion buying goods and services, what happens to sellers' income in the basic income-expenditure logic?
macro.Choice A: It rises by $500 billion
macro.Choice B: It falls by $500 billion
macro.Choice C: It is unchanged
macro.Choice D: It only rises if taxes fall
macro.Correct Answer: A — It rises by $500 billion
macro.Feedback: Spending by buyers becomes income for sellers, so seller income rises by the same amount.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
macro.Question: GDP measures which two sides of economic activity?
macro.Choice A: Total income and total expenditure
macro.Choice B: Taxes and imports
macro.Choice C: Profits and inflation
macro.Choice D: Wages and unemployment
macro.Correct Answer: A — Total income and total expenditure
macro.Feedback: GDP can be measured as total income or total expenditure because those two sides are linked.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
macro.Question: If total expenditure in an economy is $20 trillion, what is total income in the basic GDP accounting identity?
macro.Choice A: $20 trillion
macro.Choice B: $10 trillion
macro.Choice C: $40 trillion
macro.Choice D: It cannot be determined
macro.Correct Answer: A — $20 trillion
macro.Feedback: In the basic circular-flow logic, total expenditure equals total income.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
macro.Question: A student argues that total spending must exceed total income because consumers sometimes borrow to spend. What is the best correction?
macro.Choice A: Borrowed spending still becomes sellers’ income
macro.Choice B: Borrowed spending is excluded from GDP
macro.Choice C: Borrowing makes imports negative
macro.Choice D: Income only counts wages, so the student is correct
macro.Correct Answer: A — Borrowed spending still becomes sellers’ income
macro.Feedback: Borrowing can finance spending, but the expenditure still becomes income for producers.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
macro.Question: A firm produces $600,000 of final output. It pays $350,000 in wages, $100,000 in rent, $50,000 in interest, and keeps $100,000 in profit. What does this example show about GDP measurement?
macro.Choice A: Expenditure on output and income earned from production both equal $600,000
macro.Choice B: Only wages count in GDP, so GDP is $350,000
macro.Choice C: Profit is excluded from GDP, so GDP is $500,000
macro.Choice D: GDP cannot be measured from income
macro.Correct Answer: A — Expenditure on output and income earned from production both equal $600,000
macro.Feedback: The value of final output equals the income generated in producing it: wages, rent, interest, and profit all add to $600,000.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
macro.Question: Suppose expenditure GDP is $22 trillion. Income data show $13 trillion in wages, $3 trillion in rent and interest, $4 trillion in profit, and $2 trillion in other production income. What do these figures show?
macro.Choice A: The income and expenditure approaches both measure GDP at $22 trillion.
macro.Choice B: The income approach measures $20 trillion because other production income is excluded.
macro.Choice C: The expenditure approach measures $24 trillion because other production income is added again.
macro.Choice D: The figures cannot be compared because wages are excluded from the income approach.
macro.Correct Answer: A — The income and expenditure approaches both measure GDP at $22 trillion.
macro.Feedback: The income categories sum to $22 trillion, matching expenditure GDP. The two approaches measure the same current domestic production from different sides.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
macro.Question: A student says GDP can be measured by adding up either total income or total expenditure. Why is that true?
macro.Choice A: Each buyer’s spending becomes a seller’s income
macro.Choice B: GDP only counts income earned by households, not spending
macro.Choice C: The government adjusts income until it equals spending
macro.Choice D: Exports and imports must always be equal
macro.Correct Answer: A — Each buyer’s spending becomes a seller’s income
macro.Feedback: The income and expenditure approaches match because each dollar spent becomes income to someone else.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
macro.Question: Suppose firms sell $900 billion of final goods and households, firms, government, and foreigners buy all of it. What should total income from producing those goods equal?
macro.Choice B: $450 billion
macro.Choice C: $900 billion
macro.Choice D: It depends only on taxes
macro.Correct Answer: C — $900 billion
macro.Feedback: Total expenditure on final output becomes total income earned from producing that output.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
macro.Question: Which example best shows the income-expenditure identity in action?
macro.Choice A: A firm sells a $40 meal and the restaurant receives $40 in revenue
macro.Choice B: A used car is resold and counted twice in GDP
macro.Choice C: A government transfer payment raises GDP directly
macro.Choice D: A household saves money under a mattress
macro.Correct Answer: A — A firm sells a $40 meal and the restaurant receives $40 in revenue
macro.Feedback: The restaurant sale shows spending by the buyer becoming income to the seller.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
macro.Question: If total income generated by current production is $18 trillion, what is total expenditure on that production?
macro.Choice A: $9 trillion
macro.Choice B: $18 trillion
macro.Choice C: $36 trillion
macro.Choice D: Impossible to compare
macro.Correct Answer: B — $18 trillion
macro.Feedback: In GDP accounting, total income and total expenditure are two ways of measuring the same economic activity.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
macro.Question: A country reports $18T in consumption, $5T in investment, $6T in government purchases, $4T in exports, and $5T in imports. Separately, income data show $20T in wages, $4T in rents and interest, and $4T in profits plus other production income. What is the best conclusion?
macro.Choice A: The expenditure and income approaches both imply GDP of $28T
macro.Choice B: The expenditure approach implies $38T while income implies $28T
macro.Choice C: Imports should be added, so GDP is $38T
macro.Choice D: Income cannot be used to measure GDP
macro.Correct Answer: A — The expenditure and income approaches both imply GDP of $28T
macro.Feedback: Expenditure GDP = 18 + 5 + 6 + (4 - 5) = 28. Income also totals 20 + 4 + 4 = 28.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
macro.Question: A firm produces $1M of output, sells $800,000 to customers, and adds $200,000 to inventory. It pays $600,000 in wages, $100,000 in rent, $100,000 in interest, and has $200,000 in profit. Which statement is correct?
macro.Choice A: GDP rises by $1M and income generated also totals $1M
macro.Choice B: GDP rises only by $800,000 because inventories are unsold
macro.Choice C: GDP rises by $1.2M because inventory is added to sales
macro.Choice D: GDP rises by wages only
macro.Correct Answer: A — GDP rises by $1M and income generated also totals $1M
macro.Feedback: Unsold output is inventory investment, so all $1M counts; income payments also total $1M.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating spending and income as unrelated totals instead of two sides of the same transaction.
macro.Question: A production audit reports $74 million of final sales and $6 million of new inventories. Domestic production income is $51 million in wages, $9 million in rent and interest, and unreported profit. With no imports, taxes or depreciation adjustments, which result closes both accounts?
macro.Choice A: $80 million GDP and $20 million profit
macro.Choice B: $74 million GDP and $14 million profit
macro.Choice C: $86 million GDP and $26 million profit
macro.Choice D: $60 million GDP and $20 million profit
macro.Correct Answer: A — $80 million GDP and $20 million profit
macro.Feedback: Current production includes the unsold 6 million, giving expenditure GDP of 80 million. Wages and rent/interest total 60 million, so residual profit is 20 million. Sales alone omit inventory investment.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Count $157; every sale is separate current output” in this gdp measurement task.
macro.Question: A domestic farm sells grain for $34 to a domestic mill, which sells flour for $49 to a domestic bakery. The bakery sells all bread to households for $74. No inventories change. An accountant adds all three sales to GDP. Which correction reconciles expenditure with value added?
macro.Choice A: Count $157; every sale is separate current output
macro.Choice B: Count $25; only the bakery creates final value
macro.Choice C: Count $123; exclude the farm but retain the mill's intermediate sale
macro.Choice D: Count $74; summing each producer's value added gives the same final-output value
macro.Correct Answer: D — Count $74; summing each producer's value added gives the same final-output value
macro.Feedback: Value added is 34 + (49−34) + (74−49) = $74, equal to the bread's final sale. Adding gross intermediate sales counts embedded production repeatedly.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Current GDP rises $76; the dealer fee is only a transfer” in this gdp measurement task.
macro.Question: A household buys a used domestic machine for $76 through a dealer charging a current service fee of $36. The machine was produced last year. Which pair correctly compares current GDP with the household's total payment?
macro.Choice A: Current GDP rises $76; the dealer fee is only a transfer
macro.Choice B: Current GDP is unchanged; anything connected to a used asset is excluded
macro.Choice C: Current GDP rises $36; the larger payment includes transfer of an existing asset
macro.Choice D: Current GDP rises $112; both the machine and dealer service are newly produced
macro.Correct Answer: C — Current GDP rises $36; the larger payment includes transfer of an existing asset
macro.Feedback: The $76 used asset is not current production. The newly provided dealer service contributes $36, even though the transaction concerns a used asset.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Current GDP includes $25; only unsold goods are counted this year” in this gdp measurement task.
macro.Question: A domestic factory produces $78 of final goods, sells $53, and holds the remainder as new inventory. A report uses sales alone and says GDP will rise when the inventory is sold next year without new production. Which correction is valid?
macro.Choice A: Current GDP includes $25; only unsold goods are counted this year
macro.Choice B: Current GDP includes $78; next year's inventory sale is offset by inventory disinvestment
macro.Choice C: Current GDP includes $53; next year's sale adds the remaining output again
macro.Choice D: Current GDP includes $131; next year's sale contributes nothing
macro.Correct Answer: B — Current GDP includes $78; next year's inventory sale is offset by inventory disinvestment
macro.Feedback: Production, not only sales, is counted: sales 53 plus inventory investment 25 equals 78. A later sale of that inventory is offset by a fall in inventories, avoiding a second count.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Current GDP includes $67; next year's sale adds the remaining output again” in this gdp measurement task.
macro.Question: A domestic factory produces $92 of final goods, sells $67, and holds the remainder as new inventory. A report uses sales alone and says GDP will rise when the inventory is sold next year without new production. Which correction is valid?
macro.Choice A: Current GDP includes $92; next year's inventory sale is offset by inventory disinvestment
macro.Choice B: Current GDP includes $67; next year's sale adds the remaining output again
macro.Choice C: Current GDP includes $159; next year's sale contributes nothing
macro.Choice D: Current GDP includes $25; only unsold goods are counted this year
macro.Correct Answer: A — Current GDP includes $92; next year's inventory sale is offset by inventory disinvestment
macro.Feedback: Production, not only sales, is counted: sales 67 plus inventory investment 25 equals 92. A later sale of that inventory is offset by a fall in inventories, avoiding a second count.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrect inference: Include $163; GDP adds domestic location and domestic ownership.
macro.Question: A foreign-owned factory produces $94 of final output inside the country and sends $54 of profit to its foreign owners. A domestically owned factory produces $69 abroad. Which output counts in domestic GDP?
macro.Choice A: Include $163; GDP adds domestic location and domestic ownership.
macro.Choice B: Include $69; GDP follows the owners' nationality rather than location.
macro.Choice C: Include $40; GDP deducts foreign profit remittances from domestic output.
macro.Choice D: Include $94; GDP follows production location rather than ownership.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Include $94; GDP follows production location rather than ownership.
macro.Feedback: GDP measures production within the country. Profit remittance concerns cross-border income, not whether the domestic factory produced output. Output made abroad is excluded from domestic GDP.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Profit is $71; adding it doubles total income” in this gdp measurement task.
macro.Question: A current domestic final sale is $96. Wages are $56, other production income is $15, and profit is the residual. A reviewer claims expenditure exceeds income because profit is omitted from the income account. Which reconciliation is correct?
macro.Choice A: Profit is $71; adding it doubles total income
macro.Choice B: Profit is zero; the expenditure-income gap is genuine output
macro.Choice C: Profit is $25; adding it makes income equal the $96 expenditure
macro.Choice D: Profit is $40; only wages count as costs in the income account
macro.Correct Answer: C — Profit is $25; adding it makes income equal the $96 expenditure
macro.Feedback: The listed non-profit income totals $71. Residual profit is 96−71 = $25, bringing income to $96. Income and expenditure are two views of this same current production.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Subtract the $58 service; the computer and share contribute $171” in this gdp measurement task.
macro.Question: A household buys a $98 newly produced domestic computer and a $73 existing corporate share. A broker supplies a new service charging $58. Which revision to a report counting all three payments is correct?
macro.Choice A: Subtract the $58 service; the computer and share contribute $171
macro.Choice B: Subtract the $98 computer; financial transactions contribute $131
