macro.Common Misconception: Treats union wage setting and efficiency wages as identical mechanisms or ignores their tradeoffs.
macro.Question: A firm deliberately pays above the market-clearing wage to reduce turnover and encourage effort. Which idea best describes the policy?
macro.Choice A: Efficiency wage theory
macro.Choice B: Unemployment insurance
macro.Choice C: A binding minimum wage
macro.Choice D: Cyclical unemployment policy
macro.Correct Answer: A — Efficiency wage theory
macro.Feedback: Unions bargain over wages, while firms may voluntarily pay efficiency wages; both can keep wages above market-clearing levels under some conditions.

macro.Common Misconception: Treats union wage setting and efficiency wages as identical mechanisms or ignores their tradeoffs.
macro.Question: Workers bargain collectively with an employer over wages and working conditions. Which institution is most directly involved?
macro.Choice A: The CPI basket
macro.Choice B: The GDP deflator
macro.Choice C: A discouraged-worker rule
macro.Choice D: A labor union
macro.Correct Answer: D — A labor union
macro.Feedback: Unions bargain over wages, while firms may voluntarily pay efficiency wages; both can keep wages above market-clearing levels under some conditions.

macro.Common Misconception: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
macro.Question: A union wage raises pay for employed members but reduces hiring by firms. Which statement best captures the tradeoff?
macro.Choice A: Insiders gain while some outsiders lose job opportunities
macro.Choice B: All workers must benefit equally
macro.Choice C: The unemployment rate must fall to zero
macro.Choice D: The policy only affects CPI
macro.Correct Answer: A — Insiders gain while some outsiders lose job opportunities
macro.Feedback: Union wage gains can help employed members but reduce opportunities for workers not hired.

macro.Common Misconception: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
macro.Question: A union contract raises wages above the competitive equilibrium. Which workers are most likely hurt?
macro.Choice A: Workers no longer hired at the higher union wage
macro.Choice B: All union workers who keep their jobs
macro.Choice C: Only retired workers
macro.Choice D: Only consumers of imported goods
macro.Correct Answer: A — Workers no longer hired at the higher union wage
macro.Feedback: Above-equilibrium wages can reduce labor demanded, hurting workers who cannot get hired.

macro.Common Misconception: Forgetting that a binding wage floor creates a surplus when labor supplied exceeds labor demanded.
macro.Question: A binding minimum wage above equilibrium creates unemployment because:
macro.Choice A: Quantity of labor supplied exceeds quantity of labor demanded
macro.Choice B: Quantity of labor demanded exceeds quantity supplied
macro.Choice C: All workers leave the labor force
macro.Choice D: Firms hire more low-skill workers
macro.Correct Answer: A — Quantity of labor supplied exceeds quantity of labor demanded
macro.Feedback: A wage floor above equilibrium creates a surplus of labor.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
macro.Question: How can unemployment insurance improve worker outcomes even if it lengthens unemployment spells?
macro.Choice A: It gives workers income support and time to find better job matches
macro.Choice B: It eliminates structural mismatch immediately
macro.Choice C: It forces all firms to hire
macro.Choice D: It lowers the labor force to zero
macro.Correct Answer: A — It gives workers income support and time to find better job matches
macro.Feedback: Unemployment insurance can support job seekers, but may also reduce urgency to accept a job quickly.

macro.Common Misconception: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
macro.Question: A union negotiates wages above the competitive equilibrium. What is the likely effect in that labor market?
macro.Choice A: More workers want jobs than firms want to hire
macro.Choice B: Firms hire every worker who wants a job
macro.Choice C: Labor demand shifts to infinity
macro.Choice D: The unemployment rate is impossible to calculate
macro.Correct Answer: A — More workers want jobs than firms want to hire
macro.Feedback: Above-equilibrium wages can create a surplus of labor in that market.

macro.Common Misconception: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
macro.Question: Efficiency wage theory says firms may pay above-equilibrium wages because higher wages can:
macro.Choice A: Improve effort, retention, or worker quality
macro.Choice B: Guarantee zero unemployment
macro.Choice C: Eliminate all inflation
macro.Choice D: Make GDP equal CPI
macro.Correct Answer: A — Improve effort, retention, or worker quality
macro.Feedback: Efficiency wages can make workers more productive or reduce costly turnover.

macro.Common Misconception: Treats union wage setting and efficiency wages as identical mechanisms or ignores their tradeoffs.
macro.Question: How do a union wage and an efficiency wage differ most directly?
macro.Choice A: A union wage is bargained collectively; an efficiency wage is voluntarily chosen by the firm
macro.Choice B: A union wage is always below equilibrium; an efficiency wage is always legally mandated
macro.Choice C: A union wage affects only prices; an efficiency wage affects only GDP accounting
macro.Choice D: They are identical policies imposed by government in every labor market
macro.Correct Answer: A — A union wage is bargained collectively; an efficiency wage is voluntarily chosen by the firm
macro.Feedback: Unions bargain over wages, while firms may voluntarily pay efficiency wages; both can keep wages above market-clearing levels under some conditions.

macro.Common Misconception: Confuses normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
macro.Question: A state improves job-search assistance while leaving unemployment benefits unchanged. Which outcome is most directly targeted?
macro.Choice A: Higher cyclical unemployment through weaker aggregate demand
macro.Choice B: A larger labor surplus from a binding minimum wage
macro.Choice C: A permanent increase in structural mismatch
macro.Choice D: Shorter frictional unemployment spells through faster matching
macro.Correct Answer: D — Shorter frictional unemployment spells through faster matching
macro.Feedback: Job-search assistance improves worker-firm matching, so it can shorten normal search spells and reduce frictional unemployment.

macro.Common Misconception: Forgetting that a binding wage floor creates a surplus when labor supplied exceeds labor demanded.
macro.Question: A wage floor is $16. At that wage, 112 workers seek jobs and firms hire 88. A demand increase raises desired hiring to 100 while the wage and labor supply stay fixed. What happens to the labor surplus?
macro.Choice A: It falls from 24 to 12; higher labor demand reduces the excess supply
macro.Choice B: It stays at 24 because the statutory wage did not change
macro.Choice C: It rises from 24 to 36 because firms want more labor
macro.Choice D: It disappears because any increase in demand makes a floor nonbinding
macro.Correct Answer: A — It falls from 24 to 12; higher labor demand reduces the excess supply
macro.Feedback: Initially the surplus is 112 - 88 = 24. With hiring demand of 100, it is 112 - 100 = 12. The wage floor can remain binding even as the size of the labor surplus changes.

macro.Common Misconception: Forgetting that a binding wage floor creates a surplus when labor supplied exceeds labor demanded.
macro.Question: A binding minimum wage raises hourly pay for workers who keep jobs but reduces low-skill employment. What is the strongest economic interpretation?
macro.Choice A: Higher wages for some, fewer opportunities for others
macro.Choice B: The policy must help every worker equally
macro.Choice C: The policy eliminates structural unemployment
macro.Choice D: The policy has no effect if firms dislike it
macro.Correct Answer: A — Higher wages for some, fewer opportunities for others
macro.Feedback: A binding wage floor can raise wages for some workers while creating a labor surplus.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
macro.Question: Unemployment insurance increases from 12 weeks to 40 weeks. What is the likely tradeoff?
macro.Choice A: Better income protection, but longer searches and more frictional unemployment
macro.Choice B: Lower income protection and shorter unemployment spells only
macro.Choice C: Immediate elimination of structural unemployment
macro.Choice D: A guaranteed fall in labor force participation to zero
macro.Correct Answer: A — Better income protection, but longer searches and more frictional unemployment
macro.Feedback: Unemployment insurance helps workers smooth income but can reduce urgency to accept work quickly.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
macro.Question: A recession increases layoffs, while unemployment insurance helps workers avoid immediate hardship but lengthens some searches. Which pair of concepts is involved?
macro.Choice A: Cyclical unemployment and frictional unemployment incentives
macro.Choice B: Only structural unemployment
macro.Choice C: GDP deflator and CPI
macro.Choice D: Natural resources and capital deepening
macro.Correct Answer: A — Cyclical unemployment and frictional unemployment incentives
macro.Feedback: The recession creates cyclical unemployment; unemployment insurance affects job-search incentives.

macro.Common Misconception: Confuses normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
macro.Question: Unemployment benefits become more generous while a new matching platform sharply improves the quality and speed of job referrals. What is the best prediction for frictional unemployment?
macro.Choice A: The net effect is ambiguous because the two changes work in opposite directions
macro.Choice B: It must rise because matching services cannot offset the weaker search incentives created by benefits
macro.Choice C: It must fall because unemployment benefits never change search incentives when matching technology improves
macro.Choice D: Only structural unemployment can change because neither policy affects normal search and matching
macro.Correct Answer: A — The net effect is ambiguous because the two changes work in opposite directions
macro.Feedback: More generous benefits can lengthen search by reducing urgency, putting upward pressure on frictional unemployment. Faster and better referrals shorten matching time, putting downward pressure on it. Without their relative magnitudes the net effect is ambiguous.

macro.Common Misconception: Treats union wage setting and efficiency wages as identical mechanisms or ignores their tradeoffs.
macro.Question: A firm raises wages above equilibrium and worker effort rises enough to improve productivity, but fewer workers are hired at the higher wage. Which interpretation is most complete?
macro.Choice A: Higher productivity guarantees every worker seeking a job will be hired despite the higher wage
macro.Choice B: The wage increase must be a legally binding minimum wage rather than a voluntary firm decision
macro.Choice C: The policy can raise worker effort only when cyclical unemployment has already fallen to zero
macro.Choice D: Efficiency-wage benefits can coexist with a labor surplus and fewer job opportunities
macro.Correct Answer: D — Efficiency-wage benefits can coexist with a labor surplus and fewer job opportunities
macro.Feedback: An efficiency wage can raise effort and productivity, but if it is above equilibrium, firms may hire fewer workers, creating a labor surplus.

macro.Common Misconception: Forgetting that a binding wage floor creates a surplus when labor supplied exceeds labor demanded.
macro.Question: In a competitive labor market, employment is 100 at the clearing wage. A binding wage floor produces labor supply of 140 and demand of 95. Assuming everyone seeking work is available and active, which comparison is correct?
macro.Choice A: Employment falls by 5, while the labor surplus is 45; these are different quantities
macro.Choice B: Employment falls by 45 because every person in the surplus previously had a job
macro.Choice C: Employment falls by 40, matching the increase in labor supply
macro.Choice D: There is no surplus because 95 people remain employed
macro.Correct Answer: A — Employment falls by 5, while the labor surplus is 45; these are different quantities
macro.Feedback: Employment changes from 100 to 95, a loss of 5. The new excess of labor supplied over labor demanded is 140 - 95 = 45, including the effect of increased job seeking as well as reduced hiring. The surplus is not the number of pre-existing jobs lost.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
macro.Question: A benefit extension lowers the cost of continued search. A simultaneous placement program improves matching. Average unemployment duration then falls. Which conclusion is warranted from these facts alone?
macro.Choice A: The combined outcome improved duration; it does not show that the benefit extension by itself shortened search
macro.Choice B: The fall proves benefit extensions always shorten search
macro.Choice C: The extension must have been ineffective at protecting income because duration fell
macro.Choice D: The placement program cannot matter because benefits determine every search decision
macro.Correct Answer: A — The combined outcome improved duration; it does not show that the benefit extension by itself shortened search
macro.Feedback: Income support can reduce search urgency while better matching shortens search. Their combined result does not isolate either effect; a credible separate comparison would be needed. The duration result also does not measure the value of income protection.

macro.Common Misconception: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
macro.Question: A negotiated wage rises from $20 to $24 while employment falls from 100 to 90, with hours per worker fixed. What happens to the total wage bill, and what distributional claim is justified?
macro.Choice A: The wage bill rises 8%; retained workers gain hourly pay while some workers lose jobs
macro.Choice B: The wage bill falls 10%; no workers gain from the contract
macro.Choice C: The wage bill rises 20%; the employment change is irrelevant
macro.Choice D: The wage bill rises 8%; this proves every original worker is better off
macro.Correct Answer: A — The wage bill rises 8%; retained workers gain hourly pay while some workers lose jobs
macro.Feedback: The wage bill changes from 20 × 100 = 2,000 to 24 × 90 = 2,160 per common unit of hours, an 8% rise. The aggregate increase does not erase the job losses; gains to retained workers and losses to displaced workers differ.

macro.Common Misconception: Missing how above-equilibrium wages can create unemployment even when they have benefits.
macro.Question: A firm considers raising wages from $18 to $21 per hour. Output per hour is expected to rise from 6 to 7 units through better retention and effort, with other unit costs unchanged. Which cost calculation and caution are correct?
macro.Choice A: Wage cost stays $3 per unit if the productivity forecast holds; the forecast still needs evidence
macro.Choice B: $3.50 per unit is certain because productivity cannot respond to wages
macro.Choice C: $2.57 per unit is certain because the old wage applies to the new output
macro.Choice D: $3 per unit proves the wage policy eliminates unemployment throughout the economy
macro.Correct Answer: A — Wage cost stays $3 per unit if the productivity forecast holds; the forecast still needs evidence
macro.Feedback: The old wage cost is 18/6 = 3 per unit; the proposed cost is 21/7 = 3 if the effort/retention forecast occurs. This makes an efficiency-wage rationale possible, but does not prove the forecast or settle economy-wide unemployment.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Only the union’s name, because unemployment is unrelated to the contract” in this labor market institutions task.
macro.Question: A union agreement raises members’ wages while firms reduce hiring. A report measures only the wage gain of those still employed. Which additional evidence is needed to evaluate the employment tradeoff?
macro.Choice A: Only the union’s name, because unemployment is unrelated to the contract
macro.Choice B: Whether the wage is nominal, because real wages cannot affect labor demand
macro.Choice C: How many workers lose or cannot obtain jobs under the higher wage
macro.Choice D: Only the price level, because hiring cannot change at an agreed wage
macro.Correct Answer: C — How many workers lose or cannot obtain jobs under the higher wage
macro.Feedback: The report conditions on remaining employed and omits workers excluded from jobs. Assessing the tradeoff requires both wage gains and the employment margin.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrect inference: Yes; any above-market wage establishes collective bargaining in both workplaces.
macro.Question: A union negotiates an above-market wage, while a nonunion firm voluntarily offers the same premium to reduce turnover. Does equal observed pay establish the same wage-setting mechanism?
macro.Choice A: No; the union wage is a price ceiling while voluntary pay is a price floor.
macro.Choice B: No; collective bargaining and employer retention incentives can produce the same observed wage.
macro.Choice C: Yes; any above-market wage establishes collective bargaining in both workplaces.
macro.Choice D: Yes; equal wages establish identical productivity and turnover effects in both workplaces.
macro.Correct Answer: B — No; collective bargaining and employer retention incentives can produce the same observed wage.
macro.Feedback: The same wage can arise through different mechanisms. A union bargains on behalf of members; an employer may independently choose efficiency pay to improve retention. The wage level alone does not identify the mechanism or all outcomes.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Longer search proves the reform reduced job-match quality despite better observed retention” in this labor market institutions task.
macro.Question: A benefit reform gives 270 unemployed workers more time to search for good matches. Search duration rises, while later job retention also improves. Which policy assessment recognizes the tradeoff?
macro.Choice A: Longer job searches are costly, but improved retention provides a benefit; both matter for welfare.
macro.Choice B: Longer job searches are costly, and improved retention provides no offsetting benefit, so welfare must fall.
macro.Choice C: Improved retention provides a benefit, and longer job searches have no cost, so welfare must rise.
macro.Choice D: Longer searches raise cyclical unemployment, while improved retention affects only structural unemployment.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Longer job searches are costly, but improved retention provides a benefit; both matter for welfare.
macro.Feedback: Search incentives and match quality can move in opposite evaluative directions. A longer spell need not mean the eventual match is worse; welfare assessment needs both costs and benefits.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Whether retained employees are classified as unemployed when the wage is above equilibrium” in this labor market institutions task.
macro.Question: Above-market wages improve effort among 290 retained employees. A proposal predicts that productivity gains must exactly offset reduced hiring. Which missing comparison is essential?
macro.Choice A: Whether retained employees are classified as unemployed when the wage is above equilibrium
macro.Choice B: Whether the statutory unemployment denominator should exclude workers receiving higher wages
macro.Choice C: Whether every firm uses identical technology, which alone guarantees an exact offset
macro.Choice D: The size of the productivity/turnover benefit relative to the higher labor cost and hiring response
macro.Correct Answer: D — The size of the productivity/turnover benefit relative to the higher labor cost and hiring response
macro.Feedback: The efficiency mechanism can benefit the employer, but it does not algebraically guarantee a particular employment or cost offset. Relative magnitudes determine the net result.

macro.Common Misconception: Keeps the initial nonbinding diagnosis after the equilibrium wage changes.
macro.Question: A competitive labor market initially clears at $15 with a legal minimum of $12. Labor demand then falls so that the new market-clearing wage would be $10. The minimum stays $12; at that wage firms demand 90 workers and 120 offer labor. What changes under the competitive wage-floor model?
macro.Choice A: The minimum stays nonbinding; employment is 120 and there is no labor surplus
macro.Choice B: The minimum changes from binding to nonbinding; employment is 90 and the labor surplus is 30
macro.Choice C: The minimum changes from nonbinding to binding; employment is 90 and the labor surplus is 30
macro.Choice D: The minimum changes from nonbinding to binding; employment is 120 and the labor surplus is 90
macro.Correct Answer: C — The minimum changes from nonbinding to binding; employment is 90 and the labor surplus is 30
macro.Feedback: Initially $12 is below equilibrium and does not bind. After equilibrium falls to $10, the unchanged $12 floor binds. Firms hire the 90 workers demanded at that wage; 120−90=30 workers are the excess supply of labor.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrect inference: Compare the wage with the legal minimum alone; retention costs cannot affect profit.
macro.Question: A firm claims higher pay is profitable because it cuts turnover costs. What comparison tests that claim rather than assuming any wage premium pays for itself?
macro.Choice A: Compare posted wages across firms alone; a higher wage establishes higher profit.
macro.Choice B: Compare added wage expense with reduced turnover costs and any productivity gain.
macro.Choice C: Compare the wage with the legal minimum alone; retention costs cannot affect profit.
macro.Choice D: Compare headcounts alone; wage expense and worker productivity do not affect profit.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Compare added wage expense with reduced turnover costs and any productivity gain.
macro.Feedback: The efficiency-wage claim is behavioral, not an accounting identity. The firm must weigh the extra wage bill against lower hiring/training costs from quits and any productivity benefit; a premium alone does not prove profitability.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “All workers necessarily gain equal income because the legal wage is higher” in this labor market institutions task.
macro.Question: A binding wage floor raises pay for retained workers in a competitive labor market, but firms offer fewer jobs and more people seek work at the higher wage. What do these wage and employment changes tell us about workers' total earnings?
macro.Choice A: Wages rise for workers who keep their jobs, but fewer people work; total earnings depend on the sizes of both changes.
macro.Choice B: Wages rise for workers who keep their jobs, and fewer people work; total earnings rise by the same percentage as wages.
macro.Choice C: Wages rise for workers who keep their jobs, and fewer people work; total earnings fall by the same percentage as employment.
macro.Choice D: Wages rise and more people work; the higher wage shows that labor demand increased.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Wages rise for workers who keep their jobs, but fewer people work; total earnings depend on the sizes of both changes.
macro.Feedback: A binding floor changes the wage paid and the quantity employed along demand. Winners among retained workers do not establish an aggregate earnings gain; employment quantities matter.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The wage is a government price ceiling; it increases labor demand by legal requirement” in this labor market institutions task.
macro.Question: A firm voluntarily pays above the market wage to reduce turnover and improve effort among workers. Which comparison distinguishes an efficiency wage from a union-negotiated wage without denying either employment tradeoff?
macro.Choice A: Firm incentives drive efficiency wages; bargaining drives union wages; only unions can exceed clearing.
macro.Choice B: Bargaining drives efficiency wages; firm incentives drive union wages; either can exceed clearing.
macro.Choice C: Firm incentives drive efficiency wages; bargaining drives union wages; either can exceed clearing.
macro.Choice D: Legal wage floors drive both wage types; neither depends on productivity or bargaining.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Firm incentives drive efficiency wages; bargaining drives union wages; either can exceed clearing.
macro.Feedback: Efficiency wages arise from employer incentives such as effort and turnover; union wages arise from bargaining. They differ in mechanism even if both can leave job seekers unmatched at the wage.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Both observations imply cyclical unemployment rose because matching institutions affect only demand” in this labor market institutions task.
macro.Question: A benefit reform gives 120 unemployed workers more time to search for good matches. Search duration rises, while later job retention also improves. Which policy assessment recognizes the tradeoff?
macro.Choice A: Longer job searches are costly, and improved retention provides no offsetting benefit, so welfare must fall.
macro.Choice B: Longer job searches are costly, but improved retention provides a benefit; both matter for welfare.
macro.Choice C: Improved retention provides a benefit, and longer job searches have no cost, so welfare must rise.
macro.Choice D: Longer searches raise cyclical unemployment, while improved retention affects only structural unemployment.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Longer job searches are costly, but improved retention provides a benefit; both matter for welfare.
macro.Feedback: Search incentives and match quality can move in opposite evaluative directions. A longer spell need not mean the eventual match is worse; welfare assessment needs both costs and benefits.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
macro.Question: A state increases unemployment benefits but also improves job-placement services. What is the most careful prediction?
macro.Choice A: Benefits slow search; placement services speed it
macro.Choice B: Frictional unemployment must rise
macro.Choice C: Frictional unemployment must fall
macro.Choice D: Only structural unemployment can change
macro.Correct Answer: A — Benefits slow search; placement services speed it
macro.Feedback: Two forces move in opposite directions, so the net effect is not automatic.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Whether either channel concerns frictional unemployment; all search is structural by definition” in this labor market institutions task.
macro.Question: Job-search assistance speeds matching for 130 applicants, while reduced search pressure permits others to wait longer for suitable offers. Which unemployment prediction requires more evidence?
macro.Choice A: Whether either channel concerns frictional unemployment; all search is structural by definition
macro.Choice B: Whether faster matching reduces a spell, because matching can affect only wages
macro.Choice C: Whether weaker search pressure raises the natural rate permanently regardless of matching gains
macro.Choice D: The net frictional-unemployment change, because faster matching and longer chosen searches oppose
macro.Correct Answer: D — The net frictional-unemployment change, because faster matching and longer chosen searches oppose
macro.Feedback: Faster matching shortens spells; waiting longer can lengthen them. Both involve the search component, so relative magnitudes are needed for the net rate.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Whether the statutory unemployment denominator should exclude workers receiving higher wages” in this labor market institutions task.
macro.Question: Above-market wages improve effort among 140 retained employees. A proposal predicts that productivity gains must exactly offset reduced hiring. Which missing comparison is essential?
macro.Choice A: Whether the statutory unemployment denominator should exclude workers receiving higher wages
macro.Choice B: Whether every firm uses identical technology, which alone guarantees an exact offset
macro.Choice C: The size of the productivity/turnover benefit relative to the higher labor cost and hiring response
macro.Choice D: Whether retained employees are classified as unemployed when the wage is above equilibrium
macro.Correct Answer: C — The size of the productivity/turnover benefit relative to the higher labor cost and hiring response
macro.Feedback: The efficiency mechanism can benefit the employer, but it does not algebraically guarantee a particular employment or cost offset. Relative magnitudes determine the net result.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “It disappears because any increase in hiring eliminates a binding wage floor” in this labor market institutions task.
macro.Question: At a binding wage floor, 120 workers seek jobs and firms hire 90. A productivity gain raises hiring to 110 with the wage and labor supply unchanged. Which claim about the labor surplus is correct?
macro.Choice A: Surplus falls from 30 to zero; increased demand fully removes the wage-floor constraint.
macro.Choice B: Surplus falls from 30 to 10; twenty additional jobs still leave ten workers unable to find a job.
macro.Choice C: Surplus rises from 10 to 30; productivity gains displace twenty previously employed workers.
macro.Choice D: Surplus stays at 30; the unchanged wage fixes the number of available jobs.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Surplus falls from 30 to 10; twenty additional jobs still leave ten workers unable to find a job.
macro.Feedback: Surplus initially 120−90=30, later 120−110=10. The fixed wage does not prevent labor demand changing; the remaining positive surplus still matters.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrect inference: Lower turnover proves employment increased; retention and hiring measure the same margin.
macro.Question: A nonunion firm pays above the clearing wage to reduce quits. Turnover falls but hiring also falls. What do lower turnover and lower hiring tell us about the effects of the higher wage?
macro.Choice A: The firm can retain more workers while offering fewer jobs; an efficiency wage above the market-clearing wage can leave some willing workers without jobs.
macro.Choice B: Lower turnover proves employment increased; retaining existing workers and hiring new workers measure the same change.
macro.Choice C: Fewer jobs prove a union imposed the wage; a firm cannot voluntarily choose to pay an efficiency wage.
macro.Choice D: Lower turnover eliminates job shortages; an efficiency wage necessarily brings labor supply and labor demand into balance.
macro.Correct Answer: A — The firm can retain more workers while offering fewer jobs; an efficiency wage above the market-clearing wage can leave some willing workers without jobs.
macro.Feedback: An efficiency wage is chosen for productivity or retention incentives. Those benefits do not establish that all willing workers obtain jobs at the higher wage; the effect on hiring must also be considered.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Longer search proves the reform reduced job-match quality despite better observed retention” in this labor market institutions task.

macro.Choice B: Improved retention provides a benefit, and longer job searches have no cost, so welfare must rise.

macro.Choice D: Longer job searches are costly, but improved retention provides a benefit; both matter for welfare.

macro.Feedback: Search incentives and match quality can move in opposite evaluative directions. A longer spell need not mean the eventual match is worse; welfare assessment needs both costs and benefits.

macro.Question: Job-search assistance speeds matching for 180 applicants, while reduced search pressure permits others to wait longer for suitable offers. Which unemployment prediction requires more evidence?
macro.Choice A: Whether faster matching reduces a spell, because matching can affect only wages
macro.Choice B: Whether weaker search pressure raises the natural rate permanently regardless of matching gains
macro.Choice C: The net frictional-unemployment change, because faster matching and longer chosen searches oppose
macro.Choice D: Whether either channel concerns frictional unemployment; all search is structural by definition
macro.Correct Answer: C — The net frictional-unemployment change, because faster matching and longer chosen searches oppose

macro.Choice A: Whether the statutory unemployment denominator should exclude workers receiving higher wages
macro.Choice B: Whether every firm uses identical technology, which alone guarantees an exact offset
macro.Choice C: The size of the productivity/turnover benefit relative to the higher labor cost and hiring response

macro.Feedback: The efficiency mechanism can benefit the employer, but it does not algebraically guarantee a particular employment or cost offset. Relative magnitudes determine the net result.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Profit falls $3,000 because cost savings reduce revenue” in this labor market institutions task.
macro.Question: A firm voluntarily raises wages above market rates. Its wage bill rises $12,000, turnover costs fall $8,000 and improved effort adds $7,000 to revenue. Which evaluation goes beyond looking only at wages?
macro.Choice A: Profit falls $3,000 because cost savings reduce revenue
macro.Choice B: Profit rises $3,000 under these estimates; the efficiency gains exceed the wage cost
macro.Choice C: Profit falls $12,000 because only payroll affects profitability
macro.Choice D: Profit rises $15,000 because higher payroll is not a cost
macro.Correct Answer: B — Profit rises $3,000 under these estimates; the efficiency gains exceed the wage cost
macro.Feedback: Net profit change=−12000+8000+7000=3000. The stated efficiency-wage channels can justify higher pay; that is conditional on the estimates.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrect inference: The efficiency-wage premium must rise; monitoring raises the minimum wage set by law.
macro.Question: Better monitoring lets a firm obtain the same effort at a lower wage. A proposal instead keeps its old above-market wage solely to deter shirking. Which inference follows from the changed constraint?
macro.Choice A: The efficiency-wage premium may become less valuable; monitoring substitutes for part of its incentive role.
macro.Choice B: The efficiency-wage premium must rise; monitoring raises the minimum wage set by law.
macro.Choice C: The union wage must rise; monitoring automatically creates collective bargaining coverage.
macro.Choice D: The market-clearing wage becomes irrelevant; a lower effort cost fixes employment mechanically.
macro.Correct Answer: A — The efficiency-wage premium may become less valuable; monitoring substitutes for part of its incentive role.
macro.Feedback: If monitoring delivers the same effort at lower pay, part of the original anti-shirking reason for a wage premium weakens. The observation does not establish a legal or union wage requirement or a mechanical employment change.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Both observations imply cyclical unemployment rose because matching institutions affect only demand” in this labor market institutions task.
macro.Question: A benefit reform gives 220 unemployed workers more time to search for good matches. Search duration rises, while later job retention also improves. Which policy assessment recognizes the tradeoff?
macro.Choice A: Longer job searches are costly, and improved retention provides no offsetting benefit, so welfare must fall.
macro.Choice B: Longer job searches are costly, but improved retention provides a benefit; both matter for welfare.
macro.Choice C: Improved retention provides a benefit, and longer job searches have no cost, so welfare must rise.
macro.Choice D: Longer searches raise cyclical unemployment, while improved retention affects only structural unemployment.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Longer job searches are costly, but improved retention provides a benefit; both matter for welfare.
macro.Feedback: Search incentives and match quality can move in opposite evaluative directions. A longer spell need not mean the eventual match is worse; welfare assessment needs both costs and benefits.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Whether either channel concerns frictional unemployment; all search is structural by definition” in this labor market institutions task.
macro.Question: Job-search assistance speeds matching for 230 applicants, while reduced search pressure permits others to wait longer for suitable offers. Which unemployment prediction requires more evidence?
macro.Choice A: The net frictional-unemployment change, because faster matching and longer chosen searches oppose
macro.Choice B: Whether either channel concerns frictional unemployment; all search is structural by definition
macro.Choice C: Whether faster matching reduces a spell, because matching can affect only wages
macro.Choice D: Whether weaker search pressure raises the natural rate permanently regardless of matching gains
macro.Correct Answer: A — The net frictional-unemployment change, because faster matching and longer chosen searches oppose
macro.Feedback: Faster matching shortens spells; waiting longer can lengthen them. Both involve the search component, so relative magnitudes are needed for the net rate.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Whether retained employees are classified as unemployed when the wage is above equilibrium” in this labor market institutions task.
macro.Question: Above-market wages improve effort among 240 retained employees. A proposal predicts that productivity gains must exactly offset reduced hiring. Which missing comparison is essential?
macro.Choice A: Whether retained employees are classified as unemployed when the wage is above equilibrium
macro.Choice B: Whether the statutory unemployment denominator should exclude workers receiving higher wages
macro.Choice C: Whether every firm uses identical technology, which alone guarantees an exact offset
macro.Choice D: The size of the productivity/turnover benefit relative to the higher labor cost and hiring response
macro.Correct Answer: D — The size of the productivity/turnover benefit relative to the higher labor cost and hiring response
macro.Feedback: The efficiency mechanism can benefit the employer, but it does not algebraically guarantee a particular employment or cost offset. Relative magnitudes determine the net result.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Whether either channel concerns frictional unemployment; all search is structural by definition” in this labor market institutions task.
macro.Question: Job-search assistance speeds matching for 280 applicants, while reduced search pressure permits others to wait longer for suitable offers. Which unemployment prediction requires more evidence?
macro.Choice A: Whether either channel concerns frictional unemployment; all search is structural by definition
macro.Choice B: Whether faster matching reduces a spell, because matching can affect only wages
macro.Choice C: Whether weaker search pressure raises the natural rate permanently regardless of matching gains
macro.Choice D: The net frictional-unemployment change, because faster matching and longer chosen searches oppose
macro.Correct Answer: D — The net frictional-unemployment change, because faster matching and longer chosen searches oppose
macro.Feedback: Faster matching shortens spells; waiting longer can lengthen them. Both involve the search component, so relative magnitudes are needed for the net rate.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
macro.Question: Consider three labor-market observations: a worker is counted as employed even though they want full-time work, another worker is not counted as unemployed because they stopped searching, and actual unemployment is above the natural rate. What do these observations tell us about labor-market conditions?
macro.Choice A: Part-time employment can hide unmet hours, discouraged exits are outside unemployment, and the excess above natural proves only structural unemployment
macro.Choice B: Part-time employment can hide unmet hours, discouraged exits are outside unemployment, and the excess above natural signals cyclical weakness
macro.Choice C: Part-time employment counts as unemployment, discouraged exits are outside unemployment, and the excess above natural signals cyclical weakness
macro.Choice D: Part-time employment can hide unmet hours, discouraged exits remain unemployed, and the excess above natural signals cyclical weakness
macro.Correct Answer: B — Part-time employment can hide unmet hours, discouraged exits are outside unemployment, and the excess above natural signals cyclical weakness
macro.Feedback: This pulls together underemployment, discouraged workers, and cyclical unemployment.

macro.Question: Why is Fed control of the money supply imperfect?
macro.Choice A: Banks and depositors affect lending and reserves
macro.Choice B: The Fed cannot buy bonds
macro.Choice C: Currency is not money
macro.Choice D: Deposits never change
macro.Correct Answer: A — Banks and depositors affect lending and reserves
macro.Feedback: The Fed influences the money supply, but banks and depositors also affect it.

macro.Common Misconception: Treats the simple multiplier maximum as guaranteed actual expansion.
macro.Question: A reserve injection could support $1,000 of deposits in the simple maximum model. Banks instead retain additional excess reserves. Relative to that maximum, what should an analyst forecast?
macro.Choice A: No reserves remaining because deposits remove reserves from the system
macro.Choice B: Less deposit creation, other conditions equal
macro.Choice C: More deposit creation because excess reserves are loans
macro.Choice D: Exactly $1,000 regardless of lending decisions
macro.Correct Answer: B — Less deposit creation, other conditions equal
macro.Feedback: Additional reserve retention leaves less available for repeated lending and deposit expansion than the restrictive simple maximum assumes.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming the Fed controls every dollar directly.
macro.Question: Why is the Fed's control over the money supply not perfect?
macro.Choice A: M1 and M2 are always equal
macro.Choice B: Currency is not money
macro.Choice C: The Fed cannot buy bonds
macro.Choice D: Banks and depositors also influence lending
macro.Correct Answer: D — Banks and depositors also influence lending
macro.Feedback: The Fed influences the money supply, but banks and depositors affect reserves, lending, and deposits.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming Fed purchases always create full deposit expansion.
macro.Question: The Fed buys bonds, but banks hold the new reserves instead of lending them. What happens to the money multiplier process?
macro.Choice A: It weakens despite higher reserves
macro.Choice B: It strengthens despite no lending
macro.Choice C: It becomes unrelated to banks
macro.Choice D: It eliminates currency from M1
macro.Correct Answer: A — It weakens despite higher reserves
macro.Feedback: Fed purchases raise reserves, but deposit expansion is weaker if banks do not lend those reserves.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring bank behavior in monetary control.
macro.Question: If banks decide to hold more excess reserves, the money creation process becomes:
macro.Choice A: Stronger because lending rises
macro.Choice B: Weaker because lending falls
macro.Choice C: Unchanged because reserves do not matter
macro.Choice D: Infinite because deposits disappear
macro.Correct Answer: B — Weaker because lending falls
macro.Feedback: When banks hold more excess reserves, they lend less, so deposit creation weakens.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming deposits automatically create full lending expansion.
macro.Question: A bank receives new deposits, the Fed pays higher interest on reserves, and banks choose to hold more excess reserves. What is the likely result?
macro.Choice A: Money creation weakens because lending falls
macro.Choice B: Money creation strengthens because deposits rose
macro.Choice C: The multiplier becomes unrelated to reserves
macro.Choice D: M1 falls because deposits are excluded
macro.Correct Answer: A — Money creation weakens because lending falls
macro.Feedback: Deposits increase lending potential, but higher interest on reserves can make banks hold reserves instead of lending them.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring leakage from currency holdings and excess reserves.
macro.Question: The Fed buys bonds during a banking panic, but households increase currency holdings and banks increase excess reserves. What should students infer?
macro.Choice A: Fed control is limited by depositor and bank behavior
macro.Choice B: The money multiplier must rise to its maximum
macro.Choice C: Open-market purchases cannot affect reserves
macro.Choice D: Currency holdings are excluded from M1
macro.Correct Answer: A — Fed control is limited by depositor and bank behavior
macro.Feedback: Fed purchases add reserves, but currency withdrawals and excess reserve holdings can weaken money creation.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating the simple multiplier as automatic.
macro.Question: The Fed lowers reserve requirements, but few households or firms want to borrow and banks are cautious about lending. Why might the actual increase in the money supply be smaller than the simple model predicts?
macro.Choice A: The potential multiplier rises, but actual money creation may remain weak.
macro.Choice B: The actual multiplier must rise fully because reserve rules changed.
macro.Choice C: The money supply must fall because lower reserves reduce deposits.
macro.Choice D: The natural rate must fall because banks can lend more.
macro.Correct Answer: A — The potential multiplier rises, but actual money creation may remain weak.
macro.Feedback: A lower reserve requirement increases lending potential, but actual lending depends on banks and borrowers.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Net AD rises $680 under either plan because the gross multiplier is unchanged” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
macro.Question: A fixed-price fiscal plan raises purchases $170 with MPC 0.75. The resulting rate increase produces a total AD crowding-out offset $340, already including induced effects. Monetary accommodation could remove half that offset without changing the direct spending impulse. Which comparison is correct?
macro.Choice A: Net AD rises $340 without accommodation and $510 with it; the change comes from a smaller offset
macro.Choice B: Net AD rises $680 under either plan because the gross multiplier is unchanged
macro.Choice C: Net AD is negative under both plans because the total offset must be multiplied again
macro.Choice D: Accommodation doubles the purchases impulse and therefore doubles the gross multiplier effect
macro.Correct Answer: A — Net AD rises $340 without accommodation and $510 with it; the change comes from a smaller offset
macro.Feedback: Gross effect=4×170=680. Without accommodation subtract 340, leaving 340; with half the offset subtract 170, leaving 510. Compare total offsets at the same stage.

macro.Common Misconception: Assumes valuable activity must appear in GDP even without a recorded market transaction.
macro.Question: A parent provides full-time unpaid child care at home. How is this usually treated in GDP?
macro.Choice A: The valuable nonmarket service is generally omitted
macro.Choice B: It is counted as government purchases
macro.Choice C: It is counted as business investment
macro.Choice D: It is added to exports
macro.Correct Answer: A — The valuable nonmarket service is generally omitted
macro.Feedback: Unpaid household production and unreported underground activity can be omitted from measured GDP.

macro.Common Misconception: Assumes higher measured production automatically settles the welfare comparison.
macro.Question: Two economies have equal GDP per person, but workers in one have much more leisure. What can GDP alone establish?
macro.Choice A: Their total well-being must be equal
macro.Choice B: The economy with less leisure is necessarily better off
macro.Choice C: Leisure is already fully priced in GDP
macro.Choice D: Their measured output is equal, not their total well-being
macro.Correct Answer: D — Their measured output is equal, not their total well-being
macro.Feedback: Leisure, environmental quality, and health or safety can change independently of measured output.

macro.Common Misconception: Uses an average output measure to infer distribution or every quality improvement.
macro.Question: Average GDP per person rises while nearly all gains go to a small group. Which limitation matters?
macro.Choice A: The higher average establishes that every household received an equal gain
macro.Choice B: Income distribution is already deducted when real GDP is calculated
macro.Choice C: The average does not show how income is distributed
macro.Choice D: GDP cannot measure the value of any recorded market production
macro.Correct Answer: C — The average does not show how income is distributed
macro.Feedback: GDP per person does not show distribution and may incompletely capture product-quality change.

macro.Common Misconception: Assumes valuable activity must appear in GDP even without a recorded market transaction.
macro.Question: A business produces market services but hides the sales from official records. What is the likely measurement issue?
macro.Choice A: Only nonmarket household work can be omitted
macro.Choice B: Underground activity can make measured GDP understate production
macro.Choice C: The hidden sales automatically enter government purchases
macro.Choice D: GDP must overstate output by the same amount
macro.Correct Answer: B — Underground activity can make measured GDP understate production
macro.Feedback: Unpaid household production and unreported underground activity can be omitted from measured GDP.

macro.Common Misconception: Treats GDP as either a complete welfare index or a useless statistic.
macro.Question: Two countries have the same real GDP per person, but one has longer life expectancy, safer streets, and cleaner water. What follows?
macro.Choice A: Equal measured output does not imply equal well-being
macro.Choice B: Both countries must have equal welfare
macro.Choice C: The safer country must have lower real GDP
macro.Choice D: Health and safety are fully included in the GDP average
macro.Correct Answer: A — Equal measured output does not imply equal well-being
macro.Feedback: GDP is a strong measure of market production for its purpose, but it omits some dimensions of welfare.

macro.Common Misconception: Uses an average output measure to infer distribution or every quality improvement.
macro.Question: A software update greatly improves usefulness while its market price is unchanged. What difficulty can arise?
macro.Choice A: GDP may not fully capture the quality improvement
macro.Choice B: Real GDP must fall because price is unchanged
macro.Choice C: The update counts only as a transfer
macro.Choice D: GDP already measures every consumer benefit exactly
macro.Correct Answer: A — GDP may not fully capture the quality improvement
macro.Feedback: GDP per person does not show distribution and may incompletely capture product-quality change.

macro.Common Misconception: Assumes higher measured production automatically settles the welfare comparison.
macro.Question: A factory expands output while causing more pollution. What is the careful conclusion?
macro.Choice A: GDP and welfare must rise by the same percentage
macro.Choice B: Welfare must fall because production increased
macro.Choice C: Pollution is subtracted automatically from nominal GDP
macro.Choice D: GDP rises, while the net welfare effect remains uncertain
macro.Correct Answer: D — GDP rises, while the net welfare effect remains uncertain
macro.Feedback: Leisure, environmental quality, and health or safety can change independently of measured output.

macro.Common Misconception: Equates a change in market spending with the same change in total useful services.
macro.Question: A family replaces unpaid home cooking with otherwise similar restaurant meals. What can happen?
macro.Choice A: GDP is unchanged because meals are identical
macro.Choice B: Real output must double
macro.Choice C: GDP rises because more activity is purchased in markets
macro.Choice D: GDP falls because restaurant work is intermediate
macro.Correct Answer: C — GDP rises because more activity is purchased in markets
macro.Feedback: Moving activity into or out of markets can change GDP even when useful services or consumer benefit move differently.

macro.Common Misconception: Assumes higher measured production automatically settles the welfare comparison.
macro.Question: Production is unchanged, but workplace injuries fall after a safety improvement. What does GDP alone miss?
macro.Choice A: A transfer counted in government purchases
macro.Choice B: A welfare gain from greater safety
macro.Choice C: A decline in all final output
macro.Choice D: A required increase in imports
macro.Correct Answer: B — A welfare gain from greater safety
macro.Feedback: Leisure, environmental quality, and health or safety can change independently of measured output.

macro.Common Misconception: Assumes higher measured production automatically settles the welfare comparison.
macro.Question: Pollution causes more medical and cleanup spending, raising measured output. Why can the welfare conclusion differ from the GDP change?
macro.Choice A: Medical and cleanup services are excluded whenever pollution caused the demand
macro.Choice B: GDP subtracts the environmental damage and then subtracts cleanup spending again
macro.Choice C: Any increase in measured cleanup output proves the original damage improved welfare
macro.Choice D: GDP counts the services produced but not the full damage that made them necessary
macro.Correct Answer: D — GDP counts the services produced but not the full damage that made them necessary
macro.Feedback: Leisure, environmental quality, and health or safety can change independently of measured output.

macro.Common Misconception: Treats GDP as either a complete welfare index or a useless statistic.
macro.Question: Workers choose shorter workweeks, measured output falls, and leisure rises. Which inference is justified?
macro.Choice A: GDP stays unchanged because added leisure replaces every lost unit of production
macro.Choice B: The leisure gain is automatically valued and added to business investment
macro.Choice C: GDP falls, but well-being could rise or fall
macro.Choice D: Both measured GDP and total well-being must decline by the same amount
macro.Correct Answer: C — GDP falls, but well-being could rise or fall
macro.Feedback: GDP is a strong measure of market production for its purpose, but it omits some dimensions of welfare.

macro.Common Misconception: Treats GDP as either a complete welfare index or a useless statistic.
macro.Question: Country A has higher market output but more pollution and inequality; Country B has more leisure and unpaid household production. Which comparison is defensible?
macro.Choice A: Country A must have higher well-being because its recorded market GDP is higher
macro.Choice B: Country B must have higher measured GDP after valuing every hour of leisure
macro.Choice C: GDP is useless because it measures neither legal market goods nor services
macro.Choice D: GDP compares market production, but these facts do not settle overall well-being
macro.Correct Answer: D — GDP compares market production, but these facts do not settle overall well-being
macro.Feedback: GDP is a strong measure of market production for its purpose, but it omits some dimensions of welfare.

macro.Common Misconception: Treats GDP as either a complete welfare index or a useless statistic.
macro.Question: A storm destroys productive assets, followed by a surge in rebuilding services. What distinction is essential?
macro.Choice A: Higher rebuilding output proves the storm created a net gain for every household
macro.Choice B: Current production can rise while lost wealth and hardship leave welfare lower
macro.Choice C: Rebuilding services cannot enter GDP because the storm destroyed assets first
macro.Choice D: The destroyed productive assets are added to current household consumption spending
macro.Correct Answer: B — Current production can rise while lost wealth and hardship leave welfare lower
macro.Feedback: GDP is a strong measure of market production for its purpose, but it omits some dimensions of welfare.

macro.Common Misconception: Equates a change in market spending with the same change in total useful services.
macro.Question: A free translation tool replaces $9 million of paid translation services. Users report more completed translations and less effort; domestic firms produce $2 million of new paid implementation services. No other output changes. Which claim is supported?
macro.Choice A: Measured GDP falls $9 million; the implementation services do not count
macro.Choice B: Measured GDP rises because the number of translations rose
macro.Choice C: Measured GDP falls $7 million; the value of users’ net welfare gain is not determined
macro.Choice D: Measured GDP falls $7 million, proving welfare fell by $7 million
macro.Correct Answer: C — Measured GDP falls $7 million; the value of users’ net welfare gain is not determined
macro.Feedback: The measured output change is -9 + 2 = -7 million. Greater use and convenience can improve welfare despite reduced market spending, but the stated information does not price the total welfare change.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Output per person increased, so welfare must have increased by exactly the same percentage” in this limits of gdp task.
macro.Question: Real GDP per person rises 21% while leisure falls and air quality deteriorates. An analyst calls the GDP increase a complete measure of the welfare gain. Which assessment is justified?
macro.Choice A: Output per person increased, but the net welfare change requires valuing the omitted losses
macro.Choice B: Output per person increased, so welfare must have increased by exactly the same percentage
macro.Choice C: Output per person decreased because environmental damage is automatically deducted from GDP
macro.Choice D: Output per person is unknown because GDP cannot be measured when leisure changes
macro.Correct Answer: A — Output per person increased, but the net welfare change requires valuing the omitted losses
macro.Feedback: Real GDP per person measures average production, not a complete welfare index. Leisure and environmental quality can offset some or all benefits; their values are not supplied.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Every resident has equal income; different health outcomes therefore cannot change the ranking” in this limits of gdp task.
macro.Question: Two countries have the same real GDP per person of $21200. One has greater inequality and poorer health outcomes. Which conclusion respects both the production data and their limits?
macro.Choice A: Every resident has equal income; different health outcomes therefore cannot change the ranking
macro.Choice B: The less equal country has lower real GDP per person once inequality is read into the given measure
macro.Choice C: The data establish neither output nor welfare because all averages exclude distribution
macro.Choice D: Average measured output is equal; distribution and health can still support different welfare rankings
macro.Correct Answer: D — Average measured output is equal; distribution and health can still support different welfare rankings
macro.Feedback: Equal GDP per person establishes equality of average measured production, not individual incomes or a complete welfare ranking. Distribution and health are separate evidence.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Rebuilding is excluded because it replaces old assets; neither GDP nor welfare changes” in this limits of gdp task.
macro.Question: A storm destroys existing homes. Rebuilding produces $23 million of current construction, while families lose housing services during repairs. Which GDP-versus-welfare comparison is correct?
macro.Choice A: Rebuilding is excluded because it replaces old assets; neither GDP nor welfare changes
macro.Choice B: Destruction is automatically subtracted from GDP by the replacement value; GDP equals the net welfare effect
macro.Choice C: Rebuilding adds to current GDP; loss of existing wealth and services prevents treating it as a net welfare gain
macro.Choice D: Destruction and rebuilding both add to current GDP; their sum measures the welfare gain
macro.Correct Answer: C — Rebuilding adds to current GDP; loss of existing wealth and services prevents treating it as a net welfare gain
macro.Feedback: Current reconstruction is production. Destruction of existing assets is a wealth loss, not automatically a negative final purchase; lost services also matter for welfare.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Output per person increased, so welfare must have increased by exactly the same percentage” in this limits of gdp task.
macro.Question: Real GDP per person rises 16% while leisure falls and air quality deteriorates. An analyst calls the GDP increase a complete measure of the welfare gain. Which assessment is justified?
macro.Choice A: Output per person increased, but the net welfare change requires valuing the omitted losses
macro.Choice B: Output per person increased, so welfare must have increased by exactly the same percentage
macro.Choice C: Output per person decreased because environmental damage is automatically deducted from GDP
macro.Choice D: Output per person is unknown because GDP cannot be measured when leisure changes
macro.Correct Answer: A — Output per person increased, but the net welfare change requires valuing the omitted losses
macro.Feedback: Real GDP per person measures average production, not a complete welfare index. Leisure and environmental quality can offset some or all benefits; their values are not supplied.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Every resident has equal income; different health outcomes therefore cannot change the ranking” in this limits of gdp task.
macro.Question: Two countries have the same real GDP per person of $20700. One has greater inequality and poorer health outcomes. Which conclusion respects both the production data and their limits?
macro.Choice A: Every resident has equal income; different health outcomes therefore cannot change the ranking
macro.Choice B: The less equal country has lower real GDP per person once inequality is read into the given measure
macro.Choice C: The data establish neither output nor welfare because all averages exclude distribution
macro.Choice D: Average measured output is equal; distribution and health can still support different welfare rankings
macro.Correct Answer: D — Average measured output is equal; distribution and health can still support different welfare rankings
macro.Feedback: Equal GDP per person establishes equality of average measured production, not individual incomes or a complete welfare ranking. Distribution and health are separate evidence.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Rebuilding is excluded because it replaces old assets; neither GDP nor welfare changes” in this limits of gdp task.
macro.Question: A storm destroys existing homes. Rebuilding produces $18 million of current construction, while families lose housing services during repairs. Which GDP-versus-welfare comparison is correct?
macro.Choice A: Rebuilding is excluded because it replaces old assets; neither GDP nor welfare changes
macro.Choice B: Destruction is automatically subtracted from GDP by the replacement value; GDP equals the net welfare effect
macro.Choice C: Rebuilding adds to current GDP; loss of existing wealth and services prevents treating it as a net welfare gain
macro.Choice D: Destruction and rebuilding both add to current GDP; their sum measures the welfare gain
macro.Correct Answer: C — Rebuilding adds to current GDP; loss of existing wealth and services prevents treating it as a net welfare gain
macro.Feedback: Current reconstruction is production. Destruction of existing assets is a wealth loss, not automatically a negative final purchase; lost services also matter for welfare.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Measured output rises by the former fees because zero price is recorded as additional consumption” in this limits of gdp task.
macro.Question: A formerly paid domestic information service worth $19 million becomes freely available at the same quality. Its paid output disappears from measured GDP, with no replacement market sales. Which inference is supported?
macro.Choice A: Measured output rises by the former fees because zero price is recorded as additional consumption
macro.Choice B: Measured market output can fall while users retain the service; welfare need not fall with the measured amount
macro.Choice C: Measured output must be unchanged because useful free services always receive an imputed market price
macro.Choice D: Measured output falls, so users necessarily lose services worth exactly the former fees
macro.Correct Answer: B — Measured market output can fall while users retain the service; welfare need not fall with the measured amount
macro.Feedback: The market transaction disappears, while usefulness need not. GDP and access to valuable services can diverge when a service becomes free.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Measured market production rises; the full fee therefore measures an equal increase in welfare” in this limits of gdp task.
macro.Question: Households begin paying $20 million for domestic childcare they formerly provided unpaid, with the same hours and quality of care. GDP rises by that fee. Which conclusion and limitation follow?
macro.Choice A: Measured market production rises; unchanged care services mean that rise alone does not establish a welfare gain
macro.Choice B: Measured market production rises; the full fee therefore measures an equal increase in welfare
macro.Choice C: Measured market production is unchanged; shifting an unpaid service into markets cannot affect GDP
macro.Choice D: Measured market production falls; payment replaces household income rather than creating output
macro.Correct Answer: A — Measured market production rises; unchanged care services mean that rise alone does not establish a welfare gain
macro.Feedback: Paid current childcare enters measured production; the same unpaid care was largely outside GDP. Marketization can raise GDP without an equal increase in services or welfare.

macro.Question: In liquidity preference theory, the interest rate balances:
macro.Choice A: Money supply and money demand
macro.Choice B: Taxes and transfers
macro.Choice C: Exports and imports
macro.Choice D: Inflation and unemployment
macro.Correct Answer: A — Money supply and money demand
macro.Feedback: The interest rate adjusts to balance money supply and money demand.

macro.Question: If money demand rises and money supply is fixed, the interest rate tends to:
macro.Choice A: Rise
macro.Choice B: Fall
macro.Choice C: Become zero
macro.Choice D: Become GDP
macro.Correct Answer: A — Rise
macro.Feedback: Higher money demand pushes interest rates up when money supply is fixed.

macro.Common Misconception: Calls an interest-rate-induced movement along a money-demand curve a shift of the curve.
macro.Question: The central bank increases the money supply while income and the price level stay unchanged. The equilibrium interest rate falls. What happens to money demand in the standard diagram?
macro.Choice A: There is a movement down along the existing money-demand curve; the curve itself need not shift.
macro.Choice B: The money-demand curve shifts left because the lower interest rate changes households’ desired money holdings at every possible interest rate, not just at the new equilibrium.
macro.Choice C: The money-demand curve shifts right because the central bank supplied more money.
macro.Choice D: Money demand becomes vertical because the money supply changed.
macro.Correct Answer: A — There is a movement down along the existing money-demand curve; the curve itself need not shift.
macro.Feedback: A change in the interest rate causes movement along a given money-demand curve. Income or the price level can shift the money-demand curve.

macro.Common Misconception: Treats a labeled point on a money-supply line as an equilibrium even when it is not on the active money-demand curve.
macro.Question: At the current interest rate, households want to hold more money than the fixed money supply provides. Which adjustment moves the market toward equilibrium?
macro.Choice A: People try to obtain money by selling interest-bearing assets, putting upward pressure on the interest rate.
macro.Choice B: People buy interest-bearing assets, pushing the interest rate downward.
macro.Choice C: The money-demand curve automatically shifts left until it equals money supply.
macro.Choice D: The central bank must change money supply because the interest rate cannot adjust.
macro.Correct Answer: A — People try to obtain money by selling interest-bearing assets, putting upward pressure on the interest rate.
macro.Feedback: At an interest rate above equilibrium, money supplied exceeds money demanded and asset-market adjustment pushes the rate down; below equilibrium, excess money demand pushes it up.

macro.Question: In the money market, if the interest rate is too low, quantity of money demanded is usually:
macro.Choice A: Greater than money supplied
macro.Choice B: Less than money supplied
macro.Choice C: Equal to zero
macro.Choice D: Equal to LRAS
macro.Correct Answer: A — Greater than money supplied
macro.Feedback: At too low an interest rate, people demand more money than is supplied, pushing rates up.

macro.Common Misconception: Reverses the interest-rate-to-investment link.
macro.Question: Income rises and money demand increases, with money supply fixed. If investment is interest-sensitive, what follow-on pressure results?
macro.Choice A: Higher interest raises investment
macro.Choice B: Investment is unchanged by assumption whenever income changes
macro.Choice C: Higher interest reduces investment
macro.Choice D: Lower interest raises investment
macro.Correct Answer: C — Higher interest reduces investment
macro.Feedback: Greater money demand raises the equilibrium rate; the higher financing cost reduces interest-sensitive investment.

macro.Common Misconception: Confuses demand for money with demand for interest-bearing bonds.
macro.Question: Money demand rises at fixed supply. A firm borrows at the resulting market interest rate. Relative to before the shift, what happens to its financing cost?
macro.Choice A: It falls as the equilibrium interest rate rises
macro.Choice B: It falls because demand for money means demand for bonds rises
macro.Choice C: It stays fixed because money demand cannot affect rates
macro.Choice D: It rises as the equilibrium interest rate rises
macro.Correct Answer: D — It rises as the equilibrium interest rate rises
macro.Feedback: With a fixed quantity of money, higher demand raises its opportunity cost, the interest rate faced by borrowers.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing money market equilibrium with AD-AS equilibrium
macro.Question: Liquidity preference theory says the interest rate adjusts to balance
macro.Choice A: money supply and money demand
macro.Choice B: aggregate supply and aggregate demand
macro.Choice C: tax revenue and government spending
macro.Choice D: exports and imports
macro.Correct Answer: A — money supply and money demand
macro.Feedback: Liquidity preference theory explains the interest rate as the price that balances money supply and money demand.

macro.Common Misconception: Thinking money supply slopes downward like money demand
macro.Question: In liquidity preference theory, the money supply is assumed to be fixed by
macro.Choice A: the central bank
macro.Choice B: household income
macro.Choice C: the price level alone
macro.Choice D: consumer confidence
macro.Correct Answer: A — the central bank
macro.Feedback: In this model, the central bank fixes the money supply.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing money market equilibrium with AD-AS equilibrium
macro.Question: Liquidity preference theory explains the interest rate as the variable that balances
macro.Choice A: money supply and money demand
macro.Choice B: labor supply and labor demand
macro.Choice C: exports and imports
macro.Choice D: taxes and spending
macro.Correct Answer: A — money supply and money demand
macro.Feedback: The interest rate adjusts to balance money supply and money demand.

macro.Common Misconception: Thinking money demand is fixed by the central bank
macro.Question: Which curve shows the amount of money fixed by the central bank?
macro.Choice A: The vertical money supply curve
macro.Choice B: The downward-sloping money demand curve
macro.Choice C: The aggregate demand curve
macro.Choice D: The multiplier curve
macro.Correct Answer: A — The vertical money supply curve
macro.Feedback: The central bank fixes the money supply in this model, so money supply is vertical.

macro.Common Misconception: Thinking higher money demand lowers interest rates
macro.Question: If money demand shifts right while money supply stays fixed, what must happen to restore money-market equilibrium?
macro.Choice A: The interest rate rises.
macro.Choice B: The interest rate falls.
macro.Choice C: Money supply shifts left automatically.
macro.Choice D: Aggregate demand becomes vertical.
macro.Correct Answer: A — The interest rate rises.
macro.Feedback: With fixed money supply, stronger money demand pushes the equilibrium interest rate up.

macro.Common Misconception: Thinking higher money demand lowers the interest rate
macro.Question: Money demand increases while the money supply remains fixed. What is the likely effect on the interest rate and interest-sensitive investment?
macro.Choice A: r rises and investment falls.
macro.Choice B: r falls and investment rises.
macro.Choice C: r rises and investment rises.
macro.Choice D: r falls and investment falls.
macro.Correct Answer: A — r rises and investment falls.
macro.Feedback: With fixed money supply, a rightward shift in money demand raises the interest rate, which lowers investment.

macro.Common Misconception: Missing the investment response after the money-market movement
macro.Question: Money demand shifts left while money supply remains fixed. What chain follows?
macro.Choice A: r falls, investment rises, and AD tends to increase.
macro.Choice B: r rises, investment falls, and AD tends to decrease.
macro.Choice C: r falls, investment falls, and AD tends to decrease.
macro.Choice D: r rises, investment rises, and AD tends to increase.
macro.Correct Answer: A — r falls, investment rises, and AD tends to increase.
macro.Feedback: Lower money demand reduces the equilibrium interest rate, which supports investment and AD.

macro.Common Misconception: Thinking the Fed should reduce money supply when money demand rises
macro.Question: If an increase in Y raises money demand and the Fed wants to prevent r from rising, what should the Fed do?
macro.Choice A: Increase money supply to match the higher money demand.
macro.Choice B: Decrease money supply to reduce money demand.
macro.Choice C: Raise taxes because money supply cannot shift.
macro.Choice D: Reduce government spending to make MD vertical.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Increase money supply to match the higher money demand.
macro.Feedback: If money demand rises, increasing money supply can prevent the equilibrium interest rate from rising.

macro.Common Misconception: Thinking the Fed should reduce money supply when money demand rises
macro.Question: Money demand shifts right while money supply is fixed. If the Fed wants to prevent the resulting interest-rate increase, what should it do?
macro.Choice A: Increase money supply enough to offset the rightward money-demand shift.
macro.Choice B: Decrease money supply to reinforce the money-demand shift.
macro.Choice C: Raise taxes because taxes directly shift money demand left.
macro.Choice D: Do nothing because r must fall when money demand rises.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Increase money supply enough to offset the rightward money-demand shift.
macro.Feedback: A rightward money-demand shift raises r if MS is fixed. Increasing MS can offset that pressure.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Leave supply fixed because higher demand is only movement along the original curve” in this liquidity preference and money market task.
macro.Question: Transaction demand for money increases at every rate in an economy with money supply 20. The central bank wants to hold the interest rate fixed in the standard liquidity-preference model. Which response and curve distinction are correct?
macro.Choice A: Leave supply fixed because higher demand is only movement along the original curve
macro.Choice B: Shift money demand back by redefining the unchanged nominal supply as a demand curve
macro.Choice C: Raise money supply enough to meet the added demand at that rate; the demand curve still shifted
macro.Choice D: Reduce money supply to match the higher demand; the interest rate then stays fixed
macro.Correct Answer: C — Raise money supply enough to meet the added demand at that rate; the demand curve still shifted
macro.Feedback: At the old rate, higher money demand creates excess demand. Increasing supply to meet it can keep the rate unchanged; a fixed observed rate does not prove no demand shift.

macro.Question: In the money market, the equilibrium interest rate occurs where:
macro.Choice A: Money demand equals money supply
macro.Choice B: AD equals SRAS
macro.Choice C: Saving equals investment only
macro.Choice D: Government spending equals taxes
macro.Correct Answer: A — Money demand equals money supply
macro.Feedback: The money-market interest rate adjusts until the quantity of money demanded equals the quantity supplied.

macro.Common Misconception: Stops after finding the new money-market interest rate and does not carry the result into spending and aggregate demand.
macro.Question: Money demand shifts right while money supply is fixed, raising the equilibrium interest rate. How does the higher interest rate affect investment and aggregate demand?
macro.Choice A: Higher borrowing costs reduce interest-sensitive investment and put downward pressure on aggregate demand.
