macro.Common Misconception: Omitting either forgone wages or an explicit cost.
macro.Question: A worker attends a free six-hour workshop instead of a shift paying $24 per hour and pays $12 for parking. Ignoring benefits, what is the opportunity cost?
macro.Choice A: $156 from forgone wages plus parking
macro.Choice B: $144 from forgone wages only
macro.Choice C: $12 because the workshop is free
macro.Choice D: $132 after subtracting parking
macro.Correct Answer: A — $156 from forgone wages plus parking
macro.Feedback: Six hours at $24 equals $144; adding $12 parking gives $156.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring joint resource constraints or choosing only the largest single alternative.
macro.Question: A city assigns its only crew and an $8 million project budget to a rail extension that uses all 12 available crew-weeks. Alternative projects are indivisible and can be sequenced; their resource use and net benefits add. Water repairs need 12 weeks and $8 million, with $24 million net benefit. Drainage needs 5 weeks and $3 million, with $14 million net benefit. Bridge work needs 7 weeks and $5 million, with $15 million net benefit. A hospital upgrade needs 6 weeks and $5 million, with $20 million net benefit. All net benefits already deduct project spending. What is the best feasible alternative forgone by selecting rail?
macro.Choice A: Drainage plus the hospital upgrade, worth $34 million net.
macro.Choice B: Bridge work plus the hospital upgrade, worth $35 million net.
macro.Choice C: Drainage plus bridge work, worth $29 million net.
macro.Choice D: The water-repair project alone, worth $24 million net.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Drainage plus the hospital upgrade, worth $34 million net.
macro.Feedback: Drainage plus the hospital upgrade fits: 11 crew-weeks and $8m, yielding $34m net. Bridge work plus the hospital upgrade would yield $35m but needs 13 weeks and $10m, exceeding both limits. Drainage plus bridge work fits but yields $29m; water repairs yield $24m. The rail choice forgoes the best feasible bundle, worth $34m; do not deduct project spending again.

macro.Common Misconception: Adding alternatives or using the chosen project’s value.
macro.Question: An owned parcel can support a clinic worth $12 million, housing worth $15 million, or parking worth $5 million. Choosing the clinic has an opportunity cost of:
macro.Choice A: $12 million.
macro.Choice B: $3 million.
macro.Choice C: $20 million.
macro.Choice D: $15 million.
macro.Correct Answer: D — $15 million.
macro.Feedback: Housing is the highest-valued forgone use.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating sunk design spending as the current alternative forgone.
macro.Question: A university has already spent $4 million designing a laboratory. It can finish the lab or assign the same construction team to a residence project valued at $11 million. What is the current opportunity cost of finishing the lab?
macro.Choice A: $11 million in forgone residence value
macro.Choice B: $4 million already spent on design
macro.Choice C: $15 million from adding both amounts
macro.Choice D: Zero because laboratory design is complete
macro.Correct Answer: A — $11 million in forgone residence value
macro.Feedback: The design expense is sunk; the residence project is the current best alternative use of the team.

macro.Common Misconception: Counting only the workshop fee or only the forgone earnings.
macro.Question: A consultant can attend a workshop or take one of two mutually exclusive Saturday jobs: one pays $480 with $40 travel cost; the other pays $430 remotely. Workshop admission costs $120, including a $50 nonrefundable deposit already paid, and attendance requires $20 travel. From now, what is attendance’s relevant economic cost?
macro.Choice A: $580: the full $120 workshop fee, $20 travel and $440 net job earnings.
macro.Choice B: $960: $90 of attendance spending plus both jobs’ combined $870 net earnings.
macro.Choice C: $90: only attendance requires a new payment, so foregone work is not a current cost.
macro.Choice D: $530: $90 of avoidable workshop/travel spending plus the best forgone job’s $440 net earnings.
macro.Correct Answer: D — $530: $90 of avoidable workshop/travel spending plus the best forgone job’s $440 net earnings.
macro.Feedback: The remaining fee is 120-50=70; add 20 travel. The best alternative nets max(480-40,430)=440. Relevant cost is 90+440=530. The nonrefundable deposit is sunk and mutually exclusive jobs are not added.

macro.Common Misconception: Using the first unit’s cost or cumulative cost for the next unit.
macro.Question: A factory reallocates a shift from valves to pumps. The first 30 pumps displace 40 valves; the next 30 displace 60 more. It needs 45 pumps. A supplier offers those 45 pumps in exchange for 65 valves. Assume constant tradeoffs within each stated block. Which source uses fewer valve-equivalent resources?
macro.Choice A: Make them internally: apply the first-block ratio to all 45 pumps, for a cost of 60 valves.
macro.Choice B: Make them internally: one pump displaces one valve, for a cost of 45 valves.
macro.Choice C: Use the supplier: internal production sacrifices 70 valves, compared with 65 through exchange.
macro.Choice D: Use the supplier: producing any of the second block requires giving up all 100 valves.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Use the supplier: internal production sacrifices 70 valves, compared with 65 through exchange.
macro.Feedback: The first 30 pumps cost 40 valves. The next 15 cost 15×(60/30)=30 valves, totaling 70. The supplier costs 65, saving 5. Rising opportunity cost requires using the appropriate segment rather than one overall ratio.

macro.Common Misconception: Using personal value or the original ticket price instead of forgone resale value.
macro.Question: A student owns a concert ticket bought for $90. Selling it now would yield $140 less a $10 selling fee. Attending requires $20 parking and rules out a $100 evening job; she can both sell the ticket and work if she skips. What is the relevant economic cost of attending?
macro.Choice A: $160: the $140 posted resale price and parking, excluding the compatible work alternative.
macro.Choice B: $210: the original $90 purchase, $100 forgone earnings and parking.
macro.Choice C: $150: the better of resale or work, plus parking, treating those alternatives as mutually exclusive.
macro.Choice D: $250: $130 net resale value, $100 forgone earnings and $20 parking.
macro.Correct Answer: D — $250: $130 net resale value, $100 forgone earnings and $20 parking.
macro.Feedback: If she skips, selling and working are compatible and yield 140-10+100=230. Attendance also costs 20 parking, for a relevant total of 250. The original purchase price is sunk; net resale value remains a current opportunity cost.

macro.Common Misconception: Selecting the highest-valued infeasible bundle or using gross rather than net alternative value.
macro.Question: A foundation has $10 million and one evaluation team. Health uses the full budget and team and yields benefits valued at $14 million. Education yields $13 million using both resources. Two small programs together yield $16 million within the budget, but need two teams. Hiring a second team costs $3 million beyond the available budget. With no borrowing, what is the best feasible alternative forgone if health is chosen?
macro.Choice A: Education at $13 million; the $16 million package is infeasible under the joint budget and staffing limits.
macro.Choice B: The two-program package at $16 million; a larger benefit makes its extra staffing feasible.
macro.Choice C: Education plus the small programs at $29 million; all rejected benefits belong in opportunity cost.
macro.Choice D: $1 million; opportunity cost is health’s gain relative to education rather than the alternative itself.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Education at $13 million; the $16 million package is infeasible under the joint budget and staffing limits.
macro.Feedback: Opportunity cost is the value of the best feasible forgone alternative. Education fits both constraints; the two-program package would require unaffordable staffing. The difference in benefits is not the opportunity cost.

macro.Common Misconception: Choosing a capacity-infeasible bundle or failing to compare feasible net-return bundles.
macro.Question: A studio selects a film that uses both of its release slots and all 8 available editor-weeks. Its alternatives are indivisible. A documentary uses 1 slot and 3 editor-weeks for $6 million net return. A series uses 1 slot and 5 editor-weeks for $9 million net return. A concert uses 1 slot and 4 editor-weeks, earning $12 million before $2 million of new costs. A festival package uses both slots and 8 editor-weeks for $14 million net return. Projects can be combined when both capacity limits are met, and net returns add. What is the best feasible alternative forgone by selecting the film?
macro.Choice A: The documentary and concert, with $16 million net return.
macro.Choice B: The series and concert, with $19 million net return.
macro.Choice C: The documentary and series, with $15 million net return.
macro.Choice D: The festival package alone, with $14 million net return.
macro.Correct Answer: A — The documentary and concert, with $16 million net return.
macro.Feedback: The concert nets $10m. Combining it with the documentary yields $16m and uses 2 slots and 7 editor-weeks. The series plus concert would yield $19m but requires 9 editor-weeks, so it is infeasible. The documentary plus series yields $15m, and the festival package yields $14m. The best feasible use forgone is the $16m documentary-concert bundle.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming a mandate eliminates opportunity cost or adding rejected projects.
macro.Question: A city has one engineering team for this year. A stadium roof must eventually be repaired, but an approved one-year deferral is feasible at an expected cost of $4 million. Deferring would allow a flood barrier worth $26 million or a transit repair worth $19 million; the same team cannot do both. If the city repairs the roof now, what current alternative value is forgone?
macro.Choice A: $22 million: the flood-barrier benefit net of the feasible deferral cost.
macro.Choice B: $26 million: the flood-barrier benefit with the cost of making that alternative feasible ignored.
macro.Choice C: $41 million: both public-project benefits minus the deferral cost.
macro.Choice D: Zero: an eventual roof requirement removes every feasible current alternative.
macro.Correct Answer: A — $22 million: the flood-barrier benefit net of the feasible deferral cost.
macro.Feedback: The best current deferral plan yields 26-4=22 million; transit would yield 19-4=15. The future repair obligation does not erase a feasible timing alternative, but its associated cost must be included.

macro.Common Misconception: Reversing the output ratio or using the required pump count directly.
macro.Question: A machine can make 420 filters or 280 pumps per day at a constant tradeoff. A contract needs 70 pumps; each forgone filter has net value $8. Buying all pumps externally costs $700 plus $80 delivery and leaves the machine free for filters. Which fulfillment method has the lower relevant cost?
macro.Choice A: Buy externally: $780 is below the $840 value of the 105 filters forgone by making pumps.
macro.Choice B: Make internally: 70 filters are forgone, costing $560 compared with $780 externally.
macro.Choice C: Make internally: owned machine time has zero current cost, so only the external bill is relevant.
macro.Choice D: Buy externally: 210 filters are forgone internally, making its relevant cost $1,680.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Buy externally: $780 is below the $840 value of the 105 filters forgone by making pumps.
macro.Feedback: Each pump sacrifices 420/280=1.5 filters; 70 pumps cost 105 filters worth 840. External fulfillment costs 700+80=780 and saves 60 in resource value. Machine ownership does not remove its alternative use.

macro.Common Misconception: Failing to update opportunity cost when a better feasible alternative appears.
macro.Question: Maintenance uses a weekend that could otherwise produce a certain $40,000 net value. Before the decision, an urgent order becomes available: a 50% chance of $80,000 net value and a 50% chance of zero; it cannot be combined with the regular order. A guarantee costing $6,000 would make the urgent order’s $80,000 certain. For a risk-neutral manager, what is the opportunity cost of maintenance?
macro.Choice A: $74,000: the guaranteed urgent order is the best feasible alternative after its guarantee cost.
macro.Choice B: $120,000: add the regular order and the urgent order’s expected value plus its guaranteed gain.
macro.Choice C: $40,000: the original plan fixes opportunity cost even after a better alternative becomes feasible.
macro.Choice D: $80,000: use the guaranteed receipt while ignoring the resources needed to obtain the guarantee.
macro.Correct Answer: A — $74,000: the guaranteed urgent order is the best feasible alternative after its guarantee cost.
macro.Feedback: The regular and unguaranteed urgent orders each have expected net value 40,000. The guaranteed order nets 80,000-6,000=74,000 and is feasible before maintenance is chosen. Mutually exclusive alternatives are compared, not added.

macro.Question: If output is below natural output, the economy has:
macro.Choice A: A recessionary gap
macro.Choice B: An expansionary gap
macro.Choice C: No output gap
macro.Choice D: A money multiplier
macro.Correct Answer: A — A recessionary gap
macro.Feedback: Output below natural output is a recessionary gap.

macro.Question: If output is above natural output, the economy has:
macro.Choice A: An expansionary gap
macro.Choice B: A recessionary gap
macro.Choice C: No output gap
macro.Choice D: A reserve gap
macro.Correct Answer: A — An expansionary gap
macro.Feedback: Output above natural output is an expansionary gap.

macro.Common Misconception: Confuses a partial recovery with complete gap closure.
macro.Question: Actual output is $19 trillion and potential $20 trillion. If demand increases output by $0.5 trillion without changing capacity, what gap remains?
macro.Choice A: No gap because output rose
macro.Choice B: A $0.5 trillion recessionary gap
macro.Choice C: A $0.5 trillion inflationary gap
macro.Choice D: A $1.5 trillion recessionary gap
macro.Correct Answer: B — A $0.5 trillion recessionary gap
macro.Feedback: New actual output 19.5 remains 0.5 below potential 20.

macro.Common Misconception: Reversing recessionary and expansionary gaps.
macro.Question: A recessionary gap means output is:
macro.Choice A: Above natural output
macro.Choice B: Below natural output
macro.Choice C: Equal to the price level
macro.Choice D: Always at Y2
macro.Correct Answer: B — Below natural output
macro.Feedback: A recessionary gap occurs when output is below natural output.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring LRAS after an AD shift.
macro.Question: Refer to the graph with LRAS. If the economy starts at AD1-AS2 and AD shifts to AD2, what gap appears?
macro.Choice A: Inflationary gap
macro.Choice B: Recessionary gap
macro.Choice C: No output gap
macro.Choice D: Supply gap
macro.Correct Answer: A — Inflationary gap
macro.Feedback: The economy moves to Y2, which is above natural output, so it creates an expansionary gap.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring LRAS when judging gaps.
macro.Question: Refer to the graph with LRAS. If the economy is at Y2, the main short-run concern is:
macro.Choice A: Output is below potential
macro.Choice B: Output is above potential
macro.Choice C: There is no output gap
macro.Choice D: The price level is below zero
macro.Correct Answer: B — Output is above potential
macro.Feedback: Y2 is to the right of LRAS, so output is above potential.

macro.Common Misconception: Missing the output-unemployment link.
macro.Question: Refer to the graph with LRAS. If the economy is at Y3, unemployment is most likely:
macro.Choice A: Below the natural rate
macro.Choice B: Above the natural rate
macro.Choice C: Equal to zero
macro.Choice D: Impossible to infer from output
macro.Correct Answer: B — Above the natural rate
macro.Feedback: Y3 is below natural output, so unemployment is usually above the natural rate.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating any AD increase as long-run equilibrium.
macro.Question: Refer to the graph with LRAS. If the economy moves from AD1-AS2 to AD2-AS2, the short-run result is:
macro.Choice A: An expansionary gap at Y2
macro.Choice B: A recessionary gap at Y3
macro.Choice C: Long-run equilibrium at Y1
macro.Choice D: A leftward SRAS shock
macro.Correct Answer: A — An expansionary gap at Y2
macro.Feedback: The move ends at Y2, which is above natural output, creating an expansionary gap.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “LRAS remains at Y1; wage adjustment shifts AD2 back to AD1 and restores the original price level” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
macro.Question: Demand expands from AD1-AS2 to AD2-AS2. An analyst calls the new output level permanent capacity growth. If demand then stays at AD2, what does the graph imply?
macro.Choice A: Potential remains Y3; rising wage costs move SRAS toward AS1, removing the temporary output gain.
macro.Choice B: Potential remains Y1; wage adjustment closes the gap by shifting AD2 back to AD1.
macro.Choice C: Potential remains Y1; rising wage costs move SRAS toward AS1, removing the temporary output gain.
macro.Choice D: Potential rises to Y2; reaching that output through demand expansion permanently moves LRAS.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Potential remains Y1; rising wage costs move SRAS toward AS1, removing the temporary output gain.
macro.Feedback: LRAS remains at Y1, while AD2-AS2 is at Y2. Above-potential output raises wage and expected-price pressure, shifting SRAS left toward AS1 and returning output to Y1 on fixed AD2.

macro.Learning Objective: FB8 — Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing
macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Every annual deficit becomes an equal surplus in a later year” in this deficits debt and government borrowing task.
macro.Question: What generally happens when the federal government runs persistent deficits?
macro.Choice A: They automatically erase existing debt
macro.Choice B: Every annual deficit becomes an equal surplus in a later year
macro.Choice C: They generally add to accumulated debt
macro.Choice D: Government purchases are removed from measured GDP during deficit years
macro.Correct Answer: C — They generally add to accumulated debt
macro.Feedback: Deficits are recurring gaps that generally require financing and add to the debt stock.

macro.Learning Objective: FB8 — Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing
macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Surplus, lower revenue, larger deficit by definition” in this deficits debt and government borrowing task.
macro.Question: How does financing a government deficit through borrowing affect public debt?
macro.Choice A: Borrowing reduces outstanding debt by the amount of the deficit.
macro.Choice B: Borrowing turns the budget deficit into a surplus without changing debt.
macro.Choice C: Borrowing raises tax revenue, leaving the outstanding debt unchanged.
macro.Choice D: Borrowing adds to the outstanding debt used to finance the deficit.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Borrowing adds to the outstanding debt used to finance the deficit.
macro.Feedback: Borrowing commonly finances a deficit, and repeated borrowing adds to outstanding debt.

macro.Learning Objective: FB8 — Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing
macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “A budget surplus” in this deficits debt and government borrowing task.
macro.Question: A government has outlays above revenues. What commonly finances the shortfall?
macro.Choice A: A budget surplus
macro.Choice B: Lower accumulated debt by definition
macro.Choice C: Government purchases becoming revenue
macro.Choice D: Government borrowing
macro.Correct Answer: D — Government borrowing
macro.Feedback: Borrowing is a common way to finance the annual gap between outlays and revenues.

macro.Learning Objective: FB8 — Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing
macro.Common Misconception: Subtracts deficit-financed borrowing from the initial debt stock instead of accumulating it.
macro.Question: Debt is initially $12 trillion. Three annual deficits of $0.4 trillion are fully financed by borrowing, with no other adjustments. What is debt afterward?
macro.Choice A: $13.2 trillion
macro.Choice B: $10.8 trillion
macro.Choice C: $12.4 trillion
macro.Choice D: $14.4 trillion
macro.Correct Answer: A — $13.2 trillion
macro.Feedback: Three deficits add $1.2 trillion to the starting stock under the simplifying assumptions.

macro.Learning Objective: FB8 — Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing
macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “It counts as mandatory spending in the federal budget” in this deficits debt and government borrowing task.
macro.Question: Why does issuing debt not close a deficit by increasing measured revenue?
macro.Choice A: It counts as mandatory spending in the federal budget
macro.Choice B: It finances the deficit but is not revenue
macro.Choice C: It reduces current federal outlays to zero when issued
macro.Choice D: It represents only borrowing from intragovernmental accounts
macro.Correct Answer: B — It finances the deficit but is not revenue
macro.Feedback: Financing explains how the shortfall is covered, not how revenues and outlays are classified.

macro.Learning Objective: FB8 — Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing
macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “It can leave broader financial conditions permanently unaffected in every case” in this deficits debt and government borrowing task.
macro.Question: Which statement about sustained government borrowing is appropriately conditional?
macro.Choice A: It always eliminates all private investment
macro.Choice B: It can leave broader financial conditions permanently unaffected in every case
macro.Choice C: It can guarantee faster economic growth whenever the government borrows
macro.Choice D: It can raise rates and reduce some private investment
macro.Correct Answer: D — It can raise rates and reduce some private investment
macro.Feedback: The possible effect depends on economic conditions; it is not an unconditional outcome.

macro.Learning Objective: FB8 — Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing
macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Interest rises and private investment rises” in this deficits debt and government borrowing task.
macro.Question: A larger deficit reduces public saving while private saving is unchanged. In a closed-economy loanable-funds model with unchanged investment demand, what pressure does this place on interest and private investment?
macro.Choice A: Interest rises and private investment rises
macro.Choice B: Interest falls and private investment falls
macro.Choice C: Interest rises and private investment falls
macro.Choice D: Interest falls and private investment rises
macro.Correct Answer: C — Interest rises and private investment falls
macro.Feedback: Lower national saving shifts loanable-funds supply left. The higher equilibrium interest rate reduces investment demanded.

macro.Learning Objective: FB8 — Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing
macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Private saving falls but public saving is unchanged, because government purchases are household consumption” in this deficits debt and government borrowing task.
macro.Question: A government raises purchases with net taxes unchanged. Private-saving behavior is unchanged. Which sequence describes the fiscal consequence?
macro.Choice A: Private saving falls but public saving is unchanged, because government purchases are household consumption
macro.Choice B: Public saving rises and the budget moves toward surplus, reducing the need to issue government debt
macro.Choice C: Public saving falls and the budget moves toward deficit, increasing borrowing needs if the shortfall is debt-financed
macro.Choice D: Public saving falls but issuing debt counts as revenue, so borrowing restores the budget balance
macro.Correct Answer: C — Public saving falls and the budget moves toward deficit, increasing borrowing needs if the shortfall is debt-financed
macro.Feedback: With net taxes unchanged, higher government purchases reduce public saving T − G and move the budget toward deficit. Borrowing can finance the shortfall, but debt issuance does not count as revenue or reverse the decline in public saving.

macro.Learning Objective: FB8 — Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing
macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The primary balance is a $120 deficit because interest is added a second time” in this deficits debt and government borrowing task.
macro.Question: The overall deficit is $40, including interest outlays of $80. Define the primary balance as revenues minus noninterest outlays. Which diagnosis follows?
macro.Choice A: The primary balance is a $40 surplus even though the overall budget is in deficit
macro.Choice B: The primary balance is a $120 deficit because interest is added a second time
macro.Choice C: The primary balance is zero because all deficits consist entirely of interest
macro.Choice D: The primary balance equals the outstanding debt stock of $40
macro.Correct Answer: A — The primary balance is a $40 surplus even though the overall budget is in deficit
macro.Feedback: Overall deficit = primary deficit + interest. Primary deficit = 40−80=−40, so there is a primary surplus of 40. Flow definitions matter.

macro.Learning Objective: FB8 — Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing
macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Whether A issues less debt than B, even though their additional borrowing is stated to be equal” in this deficits debt and government borrowing task.
macro.Question: Two packages require the same additional borrowing, leave public saving equally lower, and face the same unchanged private-saving and investment-demand schedules. Package A finances productive public infrastructure; Package B finances transfers. What evidence is needed to decide whether A leaves more total productive capital than before the policy?
macro.Choice A: Whether the public-capital addition exceeds the private-capital formation displaced by the higher real rate
macro.Choice B: Whether A issues less debt than B, even though their additional borrowing is stated to be equal
macro.Choice C: Whether transfers count as current public-capital formation at the moment they are paid
macro.Choice D: Whether a decline in public saving is itself a one-for-one measure of lost private capital
macro.Correct Answer: A — Whether the public-capital addition exceeds the private-capital formation displaced by the higher real rate
macro.Feedback: Both packages create the same initial loanable-funds pressure under the stated schedules. A also adds public productive capital. Its net capital effect depends on that addition relative to displaced private capital formation; borrowing alone does not establish the sign. No project-valuation or AD-AS model is needed for this comparison.

macro.Learning Objective: FB8 — Persistent Deficits and Government Borrowing
macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The saving curve shifts left; the real rate rises and private investment must fall” in this deficits debt and government borrowing task.
macro.Question: A deficit reduces public saving at every real rate. A separate household incentive exactly offsets that reduction in planned private saving at every rate, while an investment tax credit also raises desired investment. In the closed-economy loanable-funds model, what can be concluded relative to the initial equilibrium?
macro.Choice A: The saving curve shifts left; the real rate rises and private investment must fall
macro.Choice B: Both curves are unchanged; exact private-saving offset also cancels the investment tax credit
macro.Choice C: The saving curve is unchanged; the real rate and equilibrium private investment rise
macro.Choice D: The saving curve shifts right; private investment rises but the real rate must fall
macro.Correct Answer: C — The saving curve is unchanged; the real rate and equilibrium private investment rise
macro.Feedback: The public- and private-saving shifts cancel at every rate, leaving national-saving supply unchanged. The tax credit separately shifts investment demand right. With an upward-sloping saving curve, the new equilibrium has a higher real rate and more private investment. A higher rate alone does not prove crowding out when investment demand also changes.

macro.Common Misconception: Shifts the entire SRPC when aggregate demand changes unexpectedly.
macro.Question: A demand increase raises inflation and lowers unemployment while expectations are unchanged. Is this a movement or a shift?
macro.Choice A: A movement along the current SRPC
macro.Choice B: An upward shift of the entire SRPC
macro.Choice C: A leftward shift of the LRPC
macro.Choice D: A downward shift of the entire SRPC
macro.Correct Answer: A — A movement along the current SRPC
macro.Feedback: With expected inflation initially fixed, a demand change moves the economy along the current SRPC.

macro.Common Misconception: Treats the short-run association as a permanent menu of policy choices.
macro.Question: Can a downward-sloping SRPC guarantee permanently lower unemployment from higher inflation?
macro.Choice A: No, because demand never affects unemployment
macro.Choice B: No, because expected inflation adjusts
macro.Choice C: Yes, because the same SRPC is permanent
macro.Choice D: Yes, because natural unemployment becomes zero
macro.Correct Answer: B — No, because expected inflation adjusts
macro.Feedback: On a given SRPC, lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation only in the short run.

macro.Common Misconception: Shifts the entire SRPC when aggregate demand changes unexpectedly.
macro.Question: Aggregate demand expands unexpectedly, raising output and the price level. What short-run change in unemployment and inflation does the Phillips-curve model predict?
macro.Choice A: Lower unemployment and higher inflation along the current SRPC
macro.Choice B: Higher unemployment and higher inflation from an SRPC shift
macro.Choice C: Lower unemployment and lower inflation from an LRPC shift
macro.Choice D: Unchanged unemployment with a downward SRPC shift
macro.Correct Answer: A — Lower unemployment and higher inflation along the current SRPC
macro.Feedback: With expected inflation initially fixed, a demand change moves the economy along the current SRPC.

macro.Common Misconception: Claims disinflation along a fixed SRPC has no unemployment cost.
macro.Question: A contraction lowers inflation from 6% to 4% along a fixed SRPC. In the short run, what unemployment change should accompany that disinflation?
macro.Choice A: Natural unemployment automatically falls 2 points
macro.Choice B: Unemployment rises
macro.Choice C: Unemployment falls
macro.Choice D: Unemployment must stay fixed
macro.Correct Answer: B — Unemployment rises
macro.Feedback: A movement down a fixed downward-sloping SRPC entails higher unemployment as inflation falls. It does not itself change the natural rate.

macro.Common Misconception: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
macro.Question: An adverse supply shock raises inflation and unemployment together. What curve change is indicated?
macro.Choice A: An upward shift of the SRPC
macro.Choice B: Movement up-left along the same SRPC
macro.Choice C: A downward shift of the SRPC
macro.Choice D: A vertical movement along the LRPC
macro.Correct Answer: A — An upward shift of the SRPC
macro.Feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing the Phillips curve with the money market.
macro.Question: The Phillips curve shows a short-run trade-off between:
macro.Choice A: Inflation and unemployment
macro.Choice B: Taxes and spending
macro.Choice C: Money supply and money demand
macro.Choice D: Imports and exports
macro.Correct Answer: A — Inflation and unemployment
macro.Feedback: The short-run Phillips curve shows a trade-off between inflation and unemployment.

macro.Common Misconception: Reversing the Phillips curve axes.
macro.Question: In the standard Phillips-curve convention, the vertical axis measures:
macro.Choice A: Unemployment rate
macro.Choice B: Inflation rate
macro.Choice C: Real GDP
macro.Choice D: Money supply
macro.Correct Answer: B — Inflation rate
macro.Feedback: The vertical axis measures the inflation rate.

macro.Common Misconception: Reversing the Phillips curve axes.
macro.Question: In the standard Phillips-curve convention, the horizontal axis measures:
macro.Choice A: Inflation rate
macro.Choice B: Price level
macro.Choice C: Unemployment rate
macro.Choice D: Money demand
macro.Correct Answer: C — Unemployment rate
macro.Feedback: The horizontal axis measures the unemployment rate.

macro.Common Misconception: Reading the Phillips curve axes backward.
macro.Question: Refer to the graph. Point a has:
macro.Choice A: Lower unemployment and higher inflation than point c
macro.Choice B: Higher unemployment and lower inflation than point c
macro.Choice C: The same unemployment and lower inflation than point c
macro.Choice D: No inflation
macro.Correct Answer: A — Lower unemployment and higher inflation than point c
macro.Feedback: Point a is at U1 and I2, while point c is at U2 and I1.

macro.Question: At point A, what is the unemployment rate?
macro.Choice A: 2.5 percent
macro.Choice B: 8 percent
macro.Choice C: 5 percent
macro.Choice D: 10 percent
macro.Correct Answer: C — 5 percent
macro.Feedback: Point A lies directly above 5 on the unemployment axis.

macro.Question: Relative to point A, what does point B show on SRPC0?
macro.Choice A: Lower unemployment and higher inflation
macro.Choice B: Higher unemployment and lower inflation
macro.Choice C: Lower unemployment and lower inflation
macro.Choice D: Higher unemployment and higher inflation
macro.Correct Answer: A — Lower unemployment and higher inflation
macro.Feedback: Point B is left of A on the unemployment axis and above A on the inflation axis.

macro.Question: How does point B compare with the natural-rate point A in the displayed Phillips-curve graph?
macro.Choice A: Lower unemployment and higher inflation
macro.Choice B: Higher unemployment and higher inflation
macro.Choice C: Higher unemployment and lower inflation
macro.Choice D: Lower unemployment and lower inflation
macro.Correct Answer: C — Higher unemployment and lower inflation
macro.Feedback: Point B is to the right of A on the unemployment axis and below A on the inflation axis.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring the LRPC natural rate.
macro.Question: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which point reflects unemployment below the natural rate with inflation above I1?
macro.Choice A: a
macro.Choice B: b
macro.Choice C: c
macro.Choice D: d
macro.Correct Answer: A — a
macro.Feedback: Point a is at U1 and I2, so unemployment is below the natural rate U2 and inflation is above I1.

macro.Common Misconception: Missing the AD-to-unemployment channel.
macro.Question: The short-run Phillips curve slopes downward because higher AD tends to:
macro.Choice A: Raise output, lower unemployment, and raise inflation
macro.Choice B: Lower output, lower unemployment, and lower inflation
macro.Choice C: Raise unemployment while lowering inflation forever
macro.Choice D: Shift LRPC left immediately
macro.Correct Answer: A — Raise output, lower unemployment, and raise inflation
macro.Feedback: Higher AD raises output and prices, which maps to lower unemployment and higher inflation.

macro.Question: With expected inflation and supply conditions fixed, what short-run tradeoff does a downward-sloping Phillips curve describe?
macro.Choice A: Lower unemployment is associated with lower inflation.
macro.Choice B: Lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation.
macro.Choice C: Unemployment stays fixed at its natural rate at every inflation rate.
macro.Choice D: A change in actual inflation necessarily changes expected inflation by the same amount.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation.
macro.Feedback: Along a given short-run Phillips curve, demand conditions that lower unemployment are associated with higher inflation. A change in expected inflation or supply conditions can instead shift the curve.

macro.Question: At point A, what is the inflation rate?
macro.Choice A: 5 percent
macro.Choice B: 0 percent
macro.Choice C: 6.5 percent
macro.Choice D: 2.5 percent
macro.Correct Answer: D — 2.5 percent
macro.Feedback: The horizontal guide through point A hits the inflation axis at 2.5 percent.

macro.Question: How far below the natural rate is unemployment at point B?
macro.Choice A: 0.5 percentage point
macro.Choice B: 2 percentage points
macro.Choice C: 1 percentage point
macro.Choice D: 3.5 percentage points
macro.Correct Answer: B — 2 percentage points
macro.Feedback: The natural rate is 5 percent at point A on the LRPC, while point B has 3 percent unemployment.

macro.Question: What type of change is the move from A to B?
macro.Choice A: An upward shift from SRPC0 to another SRPC
macro.Choice B: A leftward shift of the LRPC
macro.Choice C: A movement along the same SRPC0
macro.Choice D: A movement along the vertical LRPC
macro.Correct Answer: C — A movement along the same SRPC0
macro.Feedback: Both A and B lie on the same SRPC0, so the graph shows a movement along the curve, not a curve shift.

macro.Question: Point B is to the right of the LRPC. By how many percentage points does its unemployment rate exceed the natural rate?
macro.Choice A: 0.5 percentage point
macro.Choice B: 1 percentage point
macro.Choice C: 4.5 percentage points
macro.Choice D: 2 percentage points
macro.Correct Answer: D — 2 percentage points
macro.Feedback: The natural rate is 5 percent at A, and point B is at 7 percent unemployment.

macro.Question: How should the change from A to B be interpreted?
macro.Choice A: A movement along SRPC0 consistent with weaker demand while expected inflation is unchanged.
macro.Choice B: A movement along SRPC0 consistent with stronger demand while expected inflation is unchanged.
macro.Choice C: A downward shift of SRPC0 caused by lower expected inflation.
macro.Choice D: A rightward shift of LRPC caused by a permanent increase in structural unemployment.
macro.Correct Answer: A — A movement along SRPC0 consistent with weaker demand while expected inflation is unchanged.
macro.Feedback: A and B lie on the same downward-sloping SRPC0, with B showing higher unemployment and lower inflation. That is a demand-related movement along a fixed short-run relationship, not evidence of changed expectations or natural unemployment.

macro.Question: Consumer spending unexpectedly strengthens while expectations, supply conditions and the natural rate remain unchanged. How does A to B represent the short-run response?
macro.Choice A: Unemployment becomes 1 point below natural and inflation rises 2 points; this is movement along the existing SRPC.
macro.Choice B: Unemployment becomes 2 points below natural and inflation rises 1 point because LRPC shifts left.
macro.Choice C: Unemployment becomes 2 points below natural and inflation rises 1 point because expectations immediately shift SRPC upward.
macro.Choice D: Unemployment becomes 2 points below natural and inflation rises 1 point; this is movement along the existing SRPC.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Unemployment becomes 2 points below natural and inflation rises 1 point; this is movement along the existing SRPC.
macro.Feedback: A is (5,2.5) and B is (3,3.5). A demand change with expectations and supply fixed moves along SRPC0. Compare the unemployment coordinate with LRPC at 5, and compare inflation with A; the cyclical gap does not move natural unemployment.

macro.Question: An unexpected fall in investment occurs before expectations adjust. Supply conditions and the natural rate are unchanged. What does the plotted move from A to B imply?
macro.Choice A: Unemployment is 1 point above natural and inflation is 2 points lower; demand weakness moves the economy along SRPC0.
macro.Choice B: Unemployment is 2 points above natural and inflation is 1 point lower; demand weakness moves the economy along SRPC0.
macro.Choice C: Unemployment is 2 points above natural and inflation is 1 point lower; the change establishes a permanent rise in structural unemployment.
macro.Choice D: Unemployment is 2 points above natural and inflation is 1 point lower; lower expected inflation has already shifted SRPC0 downward.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Unemployment is 2 points above natural and inflation is 1 point lower; demand weakness moves the economy along SRPC0.
macro.Feedback: A is (5,2.5) and B is (7,1.5). A demand change with expectations and supply fixed moves along SRPC0. Compare the unemployment coordinate with LRPC at 5, and compare inflation with A; the cyclical gap does not move natural unemployment.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming every inflation change is a movement along one fixed Phillips curve.
macro.Question: Two episodes produce the same increase in inflation. In one, unemployment falls after aggregate demand expands; in the other, unemployment rises after an adverse supply shock. What explains the difference?
macro.Choice A: Both episodes are movements along one SRPC, but they begin from different unemployment rates.
macro.Choice B: Both episodes shift the LRPC because inflation changes the natural rate in opposite directions.
macro.Choice C: The supply shock lowers expected inflation and moves the economy down an unchanged SRPC.
macro.Choice D: The demand expansion moves along an SRPC, while the supply shock shifts the curve.
macro.Correct Answer: D — The demand expansion moves along an SRPC, while the supply shock shifts the curve.
macro.Feedback: Demand changes can move the economy along a given SRPC; supply shocks alter the inflation-unemployment relationship and shift the SRPC.

macro.Question: Later observations put unemployment at the rate shown at A, but inflation stays above A's level. Which evidence would support a higher short-run Phillips curve crossing the same LRPC, rather than a vertical short-run curve?
macro.Choice A: Unemployment remains 2.5%, and wage-setting expectations rise with sustained inflation while labor-market structure and supply conditions stay unchanged.
macro.Choice B: Unemployment remains 5%, and a higher price level alone proves the short-run curve has become vertical.
macro.Choice C: Unemployment remains 5%, and unchanged expectations explain a lasting upward SRPC shift with no other supply change.
macro.Choice D: Unemployment remains 5%, and wage-setting expectations rise with sustained inflation while labor-market structure and supply conditions stay unchanged.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Unemployment remains 5%, and wage-setting expectations rise with sustained inflation while labor-market structure and supply conditions stay unchanged.
macro.Feedback: A is at unemployment 5% and inflation 2.5%. Higher expected inflation can raise SRPC while the same natural rate preserves LRPC. An observed price level or unchanged unemployment alone does not establish that expectations have adjusted.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrect inference: First move along LRPC; later expectations rotate it down, lowering natural unemployment.
macro.Question: An economy starts at natural unemployment. Unexpected demand expansion raises inflation and lowers unemployment; expected inflation and supply conditions initially stay fixed. Which first-stage and later-stage account is consistent?
macro.Choice A: First move along LRPC; later expectations rotate it down, lowering natural unemployment.
macro.Choice B: First shift SRPC down; later inflation falls further, preserving lower unemployment.
macro.Choice C: First move along SRPC; later expectations shift it up, restoring natural unemployment.
macro.Choice D: First shift SRPC up; later expectations shift LRPC left, preserving lower unemployment.
macro.Correct Answer: C — First move along SRPC; later expectations shift it up, restoring natural unemployment.
macro.Feedback: A demand shock with fixed expectations moves along a given SRPC. When higher inflation enters expectations, the curve shifts up; the initial unemployment gain need not persist.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The observations prove the LRPC slopes upward because every pair of data points defines the long-run relation” in this short run phillips curve task.
macro.Question: Inflation and unemployment both rise in a country. Expected inflation or supply conditions may have changed. Which diagnosis avoids calling every observation a movement along the same SRPC?
macro.Choice A: A positive demand movement fits; both variables rise along the fixed downward curve.
macro.Choice B: An upward SRPC shift fits; a movement along the fixed downward curve does not.
macro.Choice C: A downward SRPC shift fits; higher unemployment establishes lower inflation expectations.
macro.Choice D: An upward-sloping LRPC fits; two observed outcomes establish the long-run relation.
macro.Correct Answer: B — An upward SRPC shift fits; a movement along the fixed downward curve does not.
macro.Feedback: Along a fixed downward SRPC, inflation and unemployment move in opposite directions. A shifted short-run relation can produce simultaneous increases; more evidence is needed to isolate supply from expectations.

macro.Common Misconception: Reading the wrong curve at the same unemployment rate.
macro.Question: Refer to the graph. At U3, SRPC2 has inflation rate:
macro.Choice A: I1
macro.Choice B: I2
macro.Choice C: I3
macro.Choice D: I4
macro.Correct Answer: D — I4
macro.Feedback: At U3, the upper curve SRPC2 is at I4.

macro.Common Misconception: Reading the upper curve instead of SRPC1.
macro.Question: Refer to the graph. At U4 on SRPC1, inflation is:
macro.Choice A: I1
macro.Choice B: I2
macro.Choice C: I3
macro.Choice D: I4
macro.Correct Answer: A — I1
macro.Feedback: The lower point at U4 on SRPC1 is at I1.

macro.Question: What natural rate of unemployment is shown by the LRPC?
macro.Choice A: 3 percent
macro.Choice B: 6 percent
macro.Choice C: 5 percent
macro.Choice D: 10 percent
macro.Correct Answer: C — 5 percent
macro.Feedback: The vertical LRPC is drawn at 5 percent unemployment, so that is the natural rate.

macro.Question: What does this LRPC imply about a policy that permanently maintains higher inflation?
macro.Choice A: Long-run unemployment remains 5%; higher sustained inflation does not buy a permanent unemployment reduction.
macro.Choice B: Long-run unemployment remains 2.5%; higher sustained inflation does not buy a permanent unemployment reduction.
macro.Choice C: Long-run unemployment starts at 5% but falls permanently as policy moves upward along LRPC.
macro.Choice D: Unemployment remains 5% at every short-run point because LRPC also fixes the slope of SRPC.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Long-run unemployment remains 5%; higher sustained inflation does not buy a permanent unemployment reduction.
macro.Feedback: LRPC is vertical at unemployment 5%. Once expectations adjust, a higher sustained inflation rate changes the inflation coordinate rather than the natural unemployment rate. Short-run deviations can still occur.

macro.Question: What does the diagram imply about the natural unemployment rate when SRPC changes from SRPC0 to SRPC1?
macro.Choice A: It remains 5%; shifting the short-run inflation relationship does not itself change the long-run unemployment benchmark.
macro.Choice B: It remains 6%; shifting the short-run inflation relationship does not itself change the long-run unemployment benchmark.
macro.Choice C: It becomes 6% because point B always determines the natural rate, even off LRPC.
macro.Choice D: It remains 5%, so unemployment cannot deviate from 5% anywhere on either short-run curve.
macro.Correct Answer: A — It remains 5%; shifting the short-run inflation relationship does not itself change the long-run unemployment benchmark.
macro.Feedback: LRPC stays vertical at 5%. Point B is a short-run observation at 6% unemployment, not a new natural-rate marker. Short-run and long-run unemployment need not coincide.

macro.Question: Which description of point A is correct?
macro.Choice A: A is only on SRPC0 and remains below the natural unemployment rate.
macro.Choice B: A is only on LRPC and remains above the natural unemployment rate.
macro.Choice C: A is on both SRPC0 and LRPC at the natural rate
macro.Choice D: A is the location where SRPC0 turns into a vertical Phillips curve.
macro.Correct Answer: C — A is on both SRPC0 and LRPC at the natural rate
macro.Feedback: Point A is where the short-run curve crosses the long-run curve, so unemployment equals the natural rate there.

macro.Question: Suppose actual inflation is held at B's rate while expectations adjust to it. With supply conditions and the natural rate unchanged, what adjustment does this graph predict?
macro.Choice A: SRPC shifts upward, and unemployment returns to the natural rate of 5%.
macro.Choice B: SRPC shifts downward, and unemployment returns to the natural rate of 5%.
macro.Choice C: SRPC shifts upward, permanently raising the natural rate from 3% to 5%.
macro.Choice D: LRPC shifts left, allowing unemployment to remain at B's 3% once expectations catch up.
macro.Correct Answer: A — SRPC shifts upward, and unemployment returns to the natural rate of 5%.
macro.Feedback: B is above A's inflation rate and left of LRPC. Expectations catch up to the higher actual rate, shifting SRPC upward. At that sustained inflation, unemployment returns to the unchanged natural rate 5%.

macro.Question: Actual inflation is held at B's rate while expectations gradually adjust to it. With the natural rate and supply conditions unchanged, which long-run adjustment fits the figure?
macro.Choice A: SRPC shifts upward, and unemployment returns from 3% toward 5%.
macro.Choice B: SRPC shifts downward, permanently reducing the natural rate from 7% to 5%.
macro.Choice C: SRPC shifts downward, and unemployment returns from 7% toward 5%.
macro.Choice D: LRPC shifts right to 7%, making the demand-induced unemployment increase permanent.
macro.Correct Answer: C — SRPC shifts downward, and unemployment returns from 7% toward 5%.
macro.Feedback: B has unemployment 7 and inflation 1.5, compared with A at natural unemployment 5 and inflation 2.5. Adapting to lower inflation shifts SRPC down; the eventual return to 5 does not change the natural rate.

macro.Question: Compared with point A, what combination is shown at point B?
macro.Choice A: Higher unemployment and more inflation
macro.Choice B: Lower unemployment and more inflation
macro.Choice C: Higher unemployment and less inflation
macro.Choice D: Lower unemployment and less inflation
macro.Correct Answer: A — Higher unemployment and more inflation
macro.Feedback: Point A is at 5 percent unemployment and 3 percent inflation, while point B is at 6 percent unemployment and 6 percent inflation.

macro.Question: At a given unemployment rate, how does SRPC1 compare with SRPC0?
macro.Choice A: SRPC1 shows a lower inflation rate
macro.Choice B: SRPC1 shows the same inflation rate
macro.Choice C: SRPC1 shows a lower natural rate
macro.Choice D: SRPC1 shows a higher inflation rate
macro.Correct Answer: D — SRPC1 shows a higher inflation rate
macro.Feedback: Point B lies on a different short-run Phillips curve, SRPC1, so the graph is showing a curve shift rather than a movement along SRPC0.

macro.Question: At the natural unemployment rate shown, how much higher is inflation on SRPC1 than on SRPC0, and what could explain the difference with supply conditions unchanged?
macro.Choice A: 3 percentage points; higher expected inflation shifts the short-run curve upward.
macro.Choice B: 3.6 percentage points; higher expected inflation shifts the short-run curve upward.
macro.Choice C: 3.6 percentage points; a fall in the natural unemployment rate moves LRPC left.
macro.Choice D: 3.6 percentage points; a change in actual inflation alone moves the economy along SRPC0.
macro.Correct Answer: B — 3.6 percentage points; higher expected inflation shifts the short-run curve upward.
macro.Feedback: At unemployment 5%, SRPC0 gives inflation 3% and SRPC1 gives 6.6%, a 3.6-point gap. With supply conditions unchanged, higher expectations can explain the curve shift. The LRPC stays fixed.

macro.Question: Refer to the graph with SRPC0, SRPC1, A, and B. Use inflation = expected inflation − 0.6 × (unemployment − 5) + s, where s is the number of percentage points a supply shock adds to inflation. Rates are in percent and differences are in percentage points. At B, s is independently measured as +1.1 percentage points. What expected inflation is consistent with B, and could we determine it from the graph alone without knowing s?
macro.Choice A: Expected inflation is 5.5%; without knowing s, only expected inflation plus s is identified
macro.Choice B: Expected inflation is 6.6%; without knowing s, only expected inflation plus s is identified
macro.Choice C: Expected inflation is 5.5%; without knowing s, expected inflation is still separately identified by the curve intercept
macro.Choice D: Expected inflation is 4.3%; without knowing s, expected inflation is still separately identified by actual inflation
macro.Correct Answer: A — Expected inflation is 5.5%; without knowing s, only expected inflation plus s is identified
macro.Feedback: At B, unemployment is 6% and actual inflation is 6%. Thus 6 = expected inflation − 0.6 + 1.1, giving expected inflation of 5.5%. Without knowing the supply shock's contribution s, the graph determines only expected inflation + s = 6.6. The higher curve alone does not show how much expectations changed.

macro.Question: Refer to the graph with A and B on SRPC0. Initially expected inflation is the inflation rate at A, and the economy is at B. Next period expected inflation equals this period’s actual inflation. Hold the natural rate and supply conditions fixed; each one-point expectations change shifts the SRPC vertically by one point with slope unchanged. Compare keeping unemployment at B’s rate with instead keeping actual inflation at B’s current rate. Which next-period outcome follows?
macro.Choice A: Keeping unemployment at B's 3% requires inflation of 5.5%; holding inflation at 4% instead returns unemployment to 5%.
macro.Choice B: Keeping unemployment at B's 3% requires inflation of 4.5%; holding inflation at 3.5% instead returns unemployment to 5%.
macro.Choice C: Keeping unemployment at B's 3% requires inflation of 3.5%; expected inflation cannot alter a point already reached.
macro.Choice D: Keeping unemployment at B's 3% requires inflation of 4.5%; holding inflation at 3.5% instead permanently lowers the natural rate to 3%.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Keeping unemployment at B's 3% requires inflation of 4.5%; holding inflation at 3.5% instead returns unemployment to 5%.
macro.Feedback: Expectations rise from 2.5 to 3.5, shifting the curve up one point. At unemployment 3, inflation therefore rises from 3.5 to 4.5. Alternatively, actual inflation equal to the new expectation gives natural unemployment at 5. A fixed unemployment target and a fixed inflation target are different continuations.

macro.Question: Refer to the graph with B to the right of A on SRPC0. Initially actual inflation is B’s rate and expected inflation is A’s rate. Each period expectations equal the previous period’s actual inflation; each one-point expectations change shifts SRPC vertically by one point with slope unchanged. Natural unemployment and supply conditions stay fixed. Policy holds unemployment at B’s rate for one additional period, then requires inflation to be nonnegative in the following period. What inflation occurs in the additional period, and what is the highest unemployment rate compatible with that later inflation constraint?
macro.Choice A: Inflation stays 1.5 percent, then unemployment can remain at 7 percent.
macro.Choice B: Inflation is 0.5 percent, then unemployment can remain at 7 percent without deflation.
macro.Choice C: Inflation is 2.5 percent, then unemployment can be at most 5 percent.
macro.Choice D: Inflation is 0.5 percent, then unemployment can be at most 6 percent.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Inflation is 0.5 percent, then unemployment can be at most 6 percent.
macro.Feedback: The plotted slope is (1.5 − 2.5)/(7 − 5) = −0.5. Expectations first fall from 2.5 to 1.5, so holding unemployment at 7 gives inflation 0.5. Next expectations are 0.5; nonnegative inflation requires 0.5 − 0.5 × (unemployment − 5) ≥ 0, or unemployment no greater than 6. Maintaining 7 would instead produce −0.5 percent inflation.

macro.Common Misconception: Moves along the SRPC instead of shifting it when expected inflation changes.
macro.Question: Workers and firms begin expecting higher inflation next year. Holding unemployment fixed, what happens to the short-run Phillips curve?
macro.Choice A: It shifts upward
macro.Choice B: It shifts downward
macro.Choice C: The economy moves down one unchanged curve
macro.Choice D: The vertical LRPC shifts left
macro.Correct Answer: A — It shifts upward
macro.Feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward; lower expected inflation shifts it downward.

macro.Common Misconception: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
macro.Question: Two central banks announce the same lower inflation target. One has a stronger record of meeting targets. Under otherwise similar conditions, what can differ?
macro.Choice A: Actual inflation must reach zero with no output cost
macro.Choice B: The less credible bank must cause immediate deflation
macro.Choice C: Expected inflation may fall faster where the announcement is more credible
macro.Choice D: The natural rate must immediately fall only in the credible economy
macro.Correct Answer: C — Expected inflation may fall faster where the announcement is more credible
macro.Feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

macro.Common Misconception: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
macro.Question: Actual inflation is 5% while wage setters expected 3%, temporarily pushing unemployment below natural. What erodes that effect?
macro.Choice A: The price level returns to its initial value automatically
macro.Choice B: Forecasts adjust upward, shifting the SRPC until unemployment returns toward natural
macro.Choice C: The LRPC shifts left because actual inflation is above expected
macro.Choice D: Forecasts adjust downward, moving unemployment farther below natural
macro.Correct Answer: B — Forecasts adjust upward, shifting the SRPC until unemployment returns toward natural
macro.Feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.

macro.Common Misconception: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
macro.Question: A temporary supply disruption raises inflation while existing contracts still reflect the original expected inflation. Wage setters update forecasts using the observed inflation, but the disruption ends before the new contracts take effect. Expected inflation nevertheless remains above its original level. With natural unemployment unchanged, what can be concluded about the final SRPC relative to its original position and its position during the disruption?
macro.Choice A: It must return exactly to its original position because the physical disruption ended.
macro.Choice B: It must lie above the disruption-period curve because any expectations rise exceeds the inflation effect of the supply disruption ending.
macro.Choice C: It must lie below the original curve because the original supply shock was temporary.
macro.Choice D: It remains above the original curve; its position relative to the curve during the disruption depends on the sizes of the two effects.
macro.Correct Answer: D — It remains above the original curve; its position relative to the curve during the disruption depends on the sizes of the two effects.
macro.Feedback: Neither the supply disruption nor the higher expected inflation affected the original curve. The final curve reflects only the higher expected inflation, so it remains above the original curve. Comparing the final curve with the curve during the disruption requires comparing the sizes of those two effects; observed inflation alone does not establish them.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Credibility guarantees every nominal contract instantly resets even though the stem rules it out” in this phillips curve expectations task.
macro.Question: Wage contracts were written for 5% inflation. A credible announcement lowers forecasts to 2%, but those contracts cannot reset this year. Which qualification prevents overstating the announcement's immediate effect?
macro.Choice A: Fixed contracts can preserve current costs; lower forecasts help later adjustment.
macro.Choice B: Fixed contracts immediately reset; credible forecasts eliminate current adjustment costs.
macro.Choice C: Fixed contracts permanently fix forecasts; lower expectations cannot aid later adjustment.
macro.Choice D: Fixed contracts lower natural unemployment; credible forecasts shift the long-run curve left.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Fixed contracts can preserve current costs; lower forecasts help later adjustment.
macro.Feedback: Credibility may affect expectations, but fixed contracts delay the associated nominal adjustment. The timing assumption matters; a forecast change alone does not guarantee a costless immediate disinflation.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Higher forecasts shift SRPC down; repeating inflation permanently lowers unemployment further” in this phillips curve expectations task.
macro.Question: Workers repeatedly observe inflation above their forecasts. Supply conditions and natural unemployment are unchanged. Which adaptation and policy implication follow?
macro.Choice A: Higher forecasts shift SRPC down; repeating inflation permanently lowers unemployment further
macro.Choice B: Higher forecasts move the economy along an unchanged SRPC rather than changing its intercept
macro.Choice C: Higher forecasts shift LRPC left by the same number of points as the forecast revision
macro.Choice D: Higher forecasts shift SRPC up; repeating the same actual inflation no longer produces the original surprise-driven unemployment reduction
macro.Correct Answer: D — Higher forecasts shift SRPC up; repeating the same actual inflation no longer produces the original surprise-driven unemployment reduction
macro.Feedback: Once higher inflation is expected, the short-run curve shifts upward. Maintaining an old actual inflation rate then produces less surprise, so the original temporary unemployment benefit fades.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Expected inflation is exactly 4% whenever actual inflation is 4%” in this phillips curve expectations task.
macro.Question: Use π = πe − (u − 5) + s, where π is actual inflation, πe is expected inflation, u is unemployment, and s is the number of percentage points a supply shock adds to inflation. Rates are in percent. Actual inflation is 4% and unemployment is 6%. Without knowing s, a student reports expected inflation as exactly 5%. What assumption does this answer require, and how would a positive value of s change the answer?
macro.Choice A: Expected inflation is exactly 4% whenever actual inflation is 4%
macro.Choice B: A positive value of s implies a higher expectation estimate at the same inflation and unemployment
macro.Choice C: 5% follows only if s=0; a positive value of s implies a lower expectation estimate
macro.Choice D: 5% is exact for every value of s because actual inflation is given
macro.Correct Answer: C — 5% follows only if s=0; a positive value of s implies a lower expectation estimate
macro.Feedback: Rearranging gives πe = 4 + (6 − 5) − s = 5 − s. Expected inflation is 5% only if s = 0. A positive contribution from the supply shock means lower expected inflation at the same actual inflation and unemployment.

macro.Common Misconception: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
macro.Question: Under rational expectations, wage setters use available information, including credible policy announcements; forecasts can still be wrong when new information arrives. A credible lower-inflation target changes their forecasts before much demand contraction occurs, but some contracts remain fixed. Which assessment follows?
macro.Choice A: Rational expectations guarantee exact forecasts and eliminate every unemployment cost even with fixed contracts.
macro.Choice B: The SRPC can shift downward sooner, reducing the transition cost, while fixed contracts can leave some temporary unemployment increase.
macro.Choice C: Expected inflation must wait for past inflation to decline because announcements cannot enter a forecast.
macro.Choice D: A credible nominal target permanently shifts LRPC left even when labor-market structure is unchanged.
macro.Correct Answer: B — The SRPC can shift downward sooner, reducing the transition cost, while fixed contracts can leave some temporary unemployment increase.
macro.Feedback: Available-information forecasting can incorporate credible policy news before actual inflation falls. It does not imply perfect foresight or instantly flexible contracts. Earlier expectations adjustment can reduce disinflation costs without guaranteeing zero costs.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrect inference: SRPC stays above its original position in both cases; temporary oil shocks permanently fix the curve.
macro.Question: An adverse oil shock ends. Expected inflation also returns fully to its original level, with natural unemployment unchanged. How does this differ from a case where expectations remain elevated?
macro.Choice A: SRPC stays above its original position in both cases; temporary oil shocks permanently fix the curve.
macro.Choice B: LRPC shifts left only when expectations normalize; expected inflation determines natural unemployment.
macro.Choice C: SRPC falls below its original position; removing the shock reverses it into a permanent subsidy.
macro.Choice D: SRPC returns to its original position; persistent expectations would leave it above that position.
macro.Correct Answer: D — SRPC returns to its original position; persistent expectations would leave it above that position.
macro.Feedback: Both the supply offset and expectations contributed to the short-run curve. Removing the shock and restoring original expectations removes both shifts; if expectations stay high, their upward shift remains.

macro.Common Misconception: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
macro.Question: A supply shock raises inflation without a demand boom. Why might a simple expectations-only diagnosis be incomplete?
macro.Choice A: Expected inflation is the only possible SRPC shifter in the introductory model
macro.Choice B: Every inflation increase is movement along a fixed SRPC regardless of its cause
macro.Choice C: Supply shocks shift only the vertical LRPC while leaving SRPC unchanged
macro.Choice D: The shock can shift the SRPC even before expectations adapt
macro.Correct Answer: D — The shock can shift the SRPC even before expectations adapt
macro.Feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Increase the contraction before wages reset because credibility removes every nominal rigidity” in this phillips curve expectations task.
macro.Question: A credible target lowers expectations immediately, but nominal wages cannot reset for one year. Officials propose an equally immediate, large demand contraction and promise no output loss. Which sequencing change would most directly address the stated conflict?
macro.Choice A: Coordinate the restraint with contract adjustment; credibility alone does not instantly change locked-in nominal costs
macro.Choice B: Increase the contraction before wages reset because credibility removes every nominal rigidity
macro.Choice C: Raise expected inflation back to its old level to shift SRPC down immediately
macro.Choice D: Treat the old contracts as lower natural unemployment and use the new natural rate as the target
macro.Correct Answer: A — Coordinate the restraint with contract adjustment; credibility alone does not instantly change locked-in nominal costs
macro.Feedback: A belief change and a contract-cost change can occur at different times. The no-loss promise overlooks that timing mismatch; coordinating adjustment addresses it without assuming an altered natural rate.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The same anticipated inflation permanently lowers natural unemployment; a new surprise is unnecessary” in this phillips curve expectations task.
macro.Question: A government repeatedly uses surprise demand expansion to hold unemployment below natural. Wage setters begin anticipating the next expansion. Compare continuing the same actual inflation rate with generating a fresh surprise.
macro.Choice A: Anticipated inflation preserves the gain; expectations adjustment permanently lowers natural unemployment.
macro.Choice B: Anticipated inflation loses the gain; a fresh surprise must fall below updated expectations.
macro.Choice C: Anticipated inflation preserves the gain; a fresh surprise shifts the long-run curve left.
macro.Choice D: Anticipated inflation loses the gain; a fresh surprise must exceed updated expectations.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Anticipated inflation loses the gain; a fresh surprise must exceed updated expectations.
macro.Feedback: Once the higher rate is expected, the short-run surprise disappears. Repeating the gain requires exceeding the updated expectation; under repeated adjustment this can mean accelerating inflation rather than a stable long-run tradeoff.

macro.Common Misconception: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
macro.Question: An adverse supply shock raises actual inflation, then wage setters incorporate it into next year’s contracts. What are the two stages?
macro.Choice A: An initial SRPC shift followed by reinforcement through higher expected inflation
macro.Choice B: Two movements along one fixed SRPC with no change in the inflation-unemployment relation
macro.Choice C: An LRPC shift followed by lower expected inflation when contracts renew
macro.Choice D: A demand contraction followed by an SRPC shift downward at each unemployment rate
macro.Correct Answer: A — An initial SRPC shift followed by reinforcement through higher expected inflation
macro.Feedback: The supply shock first shifts SRPC upward even with expectations unchanged. Incorporating the higher observed inflation into contracts adds an expectations-driven upward shift. This reinforces inflation pressure rather than describing the disappearance of a demand-created unemployment gain.

macro.Question: The economist's role in policy analysis is primarily to:
macro.Choice A: Clarify likely tradeoffs and consequences
macro.Choice B: Choose everyone's values
macro.Choice C: Guarantee a policy works
macro.Choice D: Eliminate scarcity
macro.Correct Answer: A — Clarify likely tradeoffs and consequences
macro.Feedback: Economics can analyze consequences and tradeoffs, while value judgments remain separate choices.

macro.Common Misconception: Giving economists authority to choose society’s values.
macro.Question: An economist estimates a policy’s effects, then recommends adoption. What two roles appear?
macro.Choice A: Scientist for the estimate and adviser for the recommendation
macro.Choice B: Adviser for both because policy is mentioned
macro.Choice C: Scientist for both because evidence is used
macro.Choice D: Legislator for the estimate and judge for the advice
macro.Correct Answer: A — Scientist for the estimate and adviser for the recommendation
macro.Feedback: Economists can estimate consequences; recommendations also require value judgments.

macro.Question: Policy lags matter because policy may arrive:
macro.Choice A: After conditions have changed
macro.Choice B: Before money exists
macro.Choice C: Only when LRAS shifts
macro.Choice D: Only when M1 equals M2
macro.Correct Answer: A — After conditions have changed
macro.Feedback: Policy can become poorly timed if it takes effect after the economy has changed.

macro.Common Misconception: Assesses policy only at approval rather than implementation.
macro.Question: A stimulus approved during recession arrives after output has returned to potential. With no new negative shock, which risk follows from the implementation lag?
macro.Choice A: It lowers potential output by changing the approval date
macro.Choice B: It can push demand above capacity
macro.Choice C: It automatically reverses direction and contracts demand
macro.Choice D: It is costless because the initial recession justified it
macro.Correct Answer: B — It can push demand above capacity
macro.Feedback: The demand addition arrives after its original gap has closed and can create excess demand.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring timing problems in stabilization policy.
macro.Question: Policy lags matter because stabilization policy may:
macro.Choice A: Arrive after conditions have already changed
macro.Choice B: Eliminate all inflation permanently
macro.Choice C: Stop all supply shocks
macro.Choice D: Make money neutral in the short run
macro.Correct Answer: A — Arrive after conditions have already changed
macro.Feedback: Policy can become destabilizing if it takes effect after the economy has already moved.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring policy timing after recovery.
macro.Question: A government passes stimulus after a recession has ended, and the economy is already above potential. What is the risk?
macro.Choice A: The stimulus may worsen inflation pressure
macro.Choice B: The stimulus must lower output below potential
macro.Choice C: The stimulus shifts SRAS right automatically
macro.Choice D: The stimulus lowers expected prices instantly
macro.Correct Answer: A — The stimulus may worsen inflation pressure
macro.Feedback: Because of lags, stimulus can hit after recovery and add excess demand.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring timing in stabilization policy.
macro.Question: A policy takes six months to pass and another year to affect spending. The main risk is:
macro.Choice A: The shock may reverse before policy hits
macro.Choice B: The money multiplier must equal zero
macro.Choice C: LRAS becomes horizontal
macro.Choice D: M2 stops including near money
macro.Correct Answer: A — The shock may reverse before policy hits
macro.Feedback: Inside and outside lags can make policy arrive after conditions have changed.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring timing problems.
macro.Question: A recession begins, but Congress passes stimulus after the economy has already recovered. This illustrates:
macro.Choice A: Policy lag risk
macro.Choice B: Monetary neutrality
macro.Choice C: A reserve multiplier
macro.Choice D: Commodity money
macro.Correct Answer: A — Policy lag risk
macro.Feedback: Policy lags can make stabilization arrive after conditions have changed.

macro.Common Misconception: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
macro.Question: Expected inflation rises while unemployment is held fixed. What happens to the SRPC?
macro.Choice A: The economy moves up the same SRPC
macro.Choice B: It shifts downward
macro.Choice C: The LRPC becomes horizontal
macro.Choice D: It shifts upward
macro.Correct Answer: D — It shifts upward
macro.Feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

macro.Common Misconception: Calls a change in inflation at fixed unemployment a movement along an unchanged SRPC.
macro.Question: An SRPC predicts 4% inflation at 5% unemployment. Expected inflation then rises 2 percentage points; in this model it shifts the SRPC up one-for-one, with other supply conditions unchanged. At 5% unemployment, what inflation and curve change follow?
macro.Choice A: 6% inflation; an upward shift of the SRPC
macro.Choice B: 6% inflation; movement along the original SRPC
macro.Choice C: 2% inflation; a downward shift of the SRPC
macro.Choice D: 4% inflation; no shift because unemployment is unchanged
macro.Correct Answer: A — 6% inflation; an upward shift of the SRPC
macro.Feedback: At the same unemployment rate, the two-point expectations increase adds two points to predicted inflation: 4+2=6%. Changing inflation at fixed unemployment locates a shifted curve, not movement along the old curve.

macro.Common Misconception: Missing the short-run tradeoff.
macro.Question: In the short run, expansionary policy usually moves the economy toward:
macro.Choice A: Higher inflation and lower unemployment
macro.Choice B: Lower inflation and lower unemployment
macro.Choice C: Higher unemployment and lower inflation
macro.Choice D: No change in either variable
macro.Correct Answer: A — Higher inflation and lower unemployment
macro.Feedback: Expansionary policy raises inflation pressure and lowers unemployment in the short run.

macro.Common Misconception: Reversing contractionary policy effects.
macro.Question: In the short run, contractionary policy usually moves the economy toward:
macro.Choice A: Higher inflation and lower unemployment
macro.Choice B: Lower inflation and higher unemployment
macro.Choice C: Higher inflation and higher unemployment
macro.Choice D: Lower unemployment and higher output
macro.Correct Answer: B — Lower inflation and higher unemployment
macro.Feedback: Contractionary policy lowers inflation but raises unemployment in the short run.

macro.Common Misconception: Reversing movement along SRPC.
macro.Question: Refer to the graph. Moving from point c to point a shows:
macro.Choice A: Lower inflation and higher unemployment
macro.Choice B: Higher inflation and lower unemployment
macro.Choice C: Higher inflation and higher unemployment
macro.Choice D: Lower inflation and lower unemployment
macro.Correct Answer: B — Higher inflation and lower unemployment
macro.Feedback: Moving from c to a raises inflation and lowers unemployment in the short run.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing movement along SRPC with a shift of SRPC.
macro.Question: With supply conditions and expectations unchanged, what does the move from c to b on SRPC1 represent?
macro.Choice A: Stronger demand: actual inflation rises while unemployment falls.
macro.Choice B: Weaker demand: actual inflation falls while unemployment rises.
macro.Choice C: Higher expected inflation: actual inflation rises at unchanged unemployment.
macro.Choice D: Lower natural unemployment: LRPC shifts left as the economy moves along SRPC1.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Stronger demand: actual inflation rises while unemployment falls.
