macro.Choice A: The food bank now faces only a temporary shortage
macro.Choice B: The additional resources reduce the constraint but do not eliminate scarcity.
macro.Choice C: No allocation rule is needed once donations increase
macro.Choice D: Scarcity disappears whenever supply increases.
macro.Correct Answer: B — The additional resources reduce the constraint but do not eliminate scarcity.
macro.Feedback: More resources can ease scarcity while competing needs remain.

macro.Common Misconception: Recognizing a tradeoff without connecting it to the next-best forgone alternative.
macro.Question: A campus uses its only open parcel for a laboratory instead of student housing. Scarcity creates a tradeoff; which concept names the next-best alternative forgone?
macro.Choice A: Opportunity cost
macro.Choice B: Market equilibrium
macro.Choice C: Price elasticity
macro.Choice D: Monetary neutrality
macro.Correct Answer: A — Opportunity cost
macro.Feedback: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative given up when scarcity forces a choice.

macro.Common Misconception: Recognizing limited resources without connecting them to feasible production combinations.
macro.Question: A factory divides fixed labor and machine time between medical devices and water filters. Which model displays the feasible production combinations created by this scarcity?
macro.Choice A: A production possibilities frontier
macro.Choice B: A consumer price index
macro.Choice C: A money-demand curve
macro.Choice D: A Phillips curve
macro.Correct Answer: A — A production possibilities frontier
macro.Feedback: A PPF represents the combinations possible when scarce productive resources have competing uses.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating scarcity as a problem only for poor societies.
macro.Question: A wealthy city can afford more services than before, yet this year it must choose between expanding transit and replacing aging water lines. Why does scarcity remain?
macro.Choice A: Its budget, crews, and construction time are still limited relative to valued projects
macro.Choice B: Wealth makes every desired project physically impossible to complete
macro.Choice C: Higher income automatically creates a temporary market shortage
macro.Choice D: The city faces scarcity only if both projects charge a money price
macro.Correct Answer: A — Its budget, crews, and construction time are still limited relative to valued projects
macro.Feedback: Greater wealth relaxes constraints, but limited resources still have competing uses.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming a zero money price means no scarce resources are used.
macro.Question: A free campus workshop still involves scarcity because:
macro.Choice A: It still uses limited seats, instructor time, and student time
macro.Choice B: A zero price makes every required resource unlimited in supply
macro.Choice C: Only the workshop topic, rather than its inputs, can be scarce
macro.Choice D: Free admission creates a legal ceiling on every campus price
macro.Correct Answer: A — It still uses limited seats, instructor time, and student time
macro.Feedback: A zero admission price does not make space, labor, or time unlimited.

macro.Common Misconception: Naming a want or a price instead of the binding resource constraint.
macro.Question: A hospital has eight nurse-hours available for either a vaccination clinic or follow-up calls. What is the scarce resource?
macro.Choice A: The eight available nurse-hours
macro.Choice B: The number of patients who value care
macro.Choice C: The absence of a money price for calls
macro.Choice D: The hospital building in every future period
macro.Correct Answer: A — The eight available nurse-hours
macro.Feedback: The limited nurse-hours cannot be used fully for both services.

macro.Common Misconception: Recognizing the purchase but not the displaced use of the budget.
macro.Question: A family uses its monthly budget to replace a broken refrigerator, leaving less for a planned vacation. What is the tradeoff?
macro.Choice A: Refrigerator spending leaves less budget for the vacation
macro.Choice B: The refrigerator creates unlimited future income
macro.Choice C: The vacation becomes a temporary market shortage
macro.Choice D: The family no longer faces scarcity after buying an appliance
macro.Correct Answer: A — Refrigerator spending leaves less budget for the vacation
macro.Feedback: Using the fixed budget for one purpose reduces what remains for another.

macro.Common Misconception: Overlooking production time as the constrained resource.
macro.Question: A bakery can use its oven this hour for bread or pastries, but there is not enough oven time for both batches. What choice is forced by scarcity?
macro.Choice A: How to allocate the limited oven time
macro.Choice B: How to eliminate every customer want
macro.Choice C: How to create a legal price ceiling
macro.Choice D: How to make flour an unlimited resource
macro.Correct Answer: A — How to allocate the limited oven time
macro.Feedback: Limited oven time with competing uses requires an allocation choice.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating partial adequacy as proof that a resource is nonscarce.
macro.Question: A reservoir currently contains enough water for all essential uses, but not for every lawn, pool, factory, and farm request. Which conclusion is correct?
macro.Choice A: Water is scarce because not every valued use can be satisfied
macro.Choice B: Water is abundant because essential uses can be satisfied
macro.Choice C: A shortage exists only because the reservoir charges too much
macro.Choice D: Scarcity ends whenever some users receive the resource
macro.Correct Answer: A — Water is scarce because not every valued use can be satisfied
macro.Feedback: Scarcity remains when the available amount cannot satisfy every competing use.

macro.Common Misconception: Equating low marginal copying cost with zero resource use.
macro.Question: Which claim commits the clearest scarcity error?
macro.Choice A: Cheap copying means digital production and distribution use no scarce inputs
macro.Choice B: Higher productivity can relax a binding resource constraint without ending scarcity
macro.Choice C: A zero money price can still require scarce server capacity and user time
macro.Choice D: Allocation rules can change who receives access to a capacity-limited service
macro.Correct Answer: A — Cheap copying means digital production and distribution use no scarce inputs
macro.Feedback: Creation, servers, bandwidth, attention, and time remain scarce even when copying is inexpensive.

macro.Common Misconception: Focusing on one beneficiary while ignoring displaced uses.
macro.Question: During a drought, a city allocates water first to hospitals, then households, and lastly decorative landscaping. The policy most clearly reflects:
macro.Choice A: A market surplus caused by excess supply.
macro.Choice B: A guarantee that the allocation is both perfectly efficient and perfectly equal.
macro.Choice C: A scarcity-driven tradeoff among uses with different social priorities.
macro.Choice D: A claim that water has no opportunity cost.
macro.Correct Answer: C — A scarcity-driven tradeoff among uses with different social priorities.
macro.Feedback: Drought limits the available water, so the city must rank competing uses.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming fairness can remove the underlying constraint.
macro.Question: A hospital has one intensive-care bed and two equally ill patients. Which conclusion follows from scarcity?
macro.Choice A: Any allocation rule leaves at least one valued use of the bed unmet
macro.Choice B: An equal lottery creates enough capacity to treat both patients fully
macro.Choice C: No money price means the intensive-care bed is not economically scarce
macro.Choice D: A medically fair rule removes the physical limit on available treatment
macro.Correct Answer: A — Any allocation rule leaves at least one valued use of the bed unmet
macro.Feedback: Scarcity means not every valued use can be satisfied, regardless of the allocation rule.

macro.Common Misconception: Believing an allocation rule removes scarcity.
macro.Question: A government reserves scarce vaccine doses for people at highest medical risk rather than for those willing to pay most. The rule primarily changes:
macro.Choice A: How the scarce doses are allocated, not whether the doses are scarce.
macro.Choice B: The definition of scarcity itself
macro.Choice C: The number of vaccine doses physically available
macro.Choice D: Whether people still compete for the limited doses.
macro.Correct Answer: A — How the scarce doses are allocated, not whether the doses are scarce.
macro.Feedback: Allocation rules determine who receives scarce goods; they do not erase the resource limit.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming socially valuable projects are costless in resource terms.
macro.Question: An economy can produce more clean energy only by using engineers and materials currently employed elsewhere. Which statement is strongest?
macro.Choice A: The project still trades off against other uses of engineers and materials
macro.Choice B: Government financing makes the engineers and materials no longer scarce
macro.Choice C: Large environmental benefits remove every resource cost from the project
macro.Choice D: Only privately financed energy projects compete for productive resources
macro.Correct Answer: A — The project still trades off against other uses of engineers and materials
macro.Feedback: Benefits do not eliminate the need to redirect scarce labor and materials from other uses.

macro.Common Misconception: Missing the tradeoff because both projects are socially valuable.
macro.Question: A city can fund either a new fire station or several neighborhood parks with the same budget. This illustrates:
macro.Choice A: A tradeoff created by competing uses of a limited city budget
macro.Choice B: An end to scarcity created by collecting and spending local taxes
macro.Choice C: A temporary shortage produced by fixing a public-service price
macro.Choice D: A specialization gain created by assigning each project to a district
macro.Correct Answer: A — A tradeoff created by competing uses of a limited city budget
macro.Feedback: Limited funds force the city to choose among competing uses.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring time as a scarce resource.
macro.Question: A student has three free hours and wants to study, work, exercise, and sleep more. The central economic problem is:
macro.Choice A: The student must choose the option with the highest money return.
macro.Choice B: The student faces no scarcity because time has no price.
macro.Choice C: The student cannot fully satisfy all competing uses of time.
macro.Choice D: Only the work option has a cost.
macro.Correct Answer: C — The student cannot fully satisfy all competing uses of time.
macro.Feedback: Time is scarce, so not every desired activity can be expanded at once.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating efficiency and equality as synonyms.
macro.Question: Which statement best distinguishes efficiency from equality?
macro.Choice A: Efficiency concerns total value; equality concerns its distribution
macro.Choice B: Efficiency requires equal shares; equality requires maximum output
macro.Choice C: Efficiency and equality describe the same resource-allocation goal
macro.Choice D: Efficiency concerns prices; equality concerns physical production
macro.Correct Answer: A — Efficiency concerns total value; equality concerns its distribution
macro.Feedback: Efficiency focuses on the size of the economic pie; equality focuses on its distribution.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming productivity growth eliminates scarcity.
macro.Question: A new technology doubles crop yields. What happens to scarcity?
macro.Choice A: Scarcity disappears because higher crop output satisfies every want
macro.Choice B: Scarcity becomes a shortage because technology changes only prices
macro.Choice C: The crop constraint eases, but land, time, and other wants remain
macro.Choice D: The technology removes the need to choose among all production uses
macro.Correct Answer: C — The crop constraint eases, but land, time, and other wants remain
macro.Feedback: Greater productivity relaxes constraints but does not remove limited resources or competing wants.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing a market shortage with the universal condition of scarcity.
macro.Question: After a storm, a store cannot meet customers' bottled-water purchases at its posted price. A delivery then provides enough water to meet those purchases. Producing and delivering the water still uses materials and truck time that could serve other purposes. What changed, and what remains?
macro.Choice A: The stockout ended; using materials and truck time still involves scarcity.
macro.Choice B: Both stockout and scarcity ended because buyers can obtain water again.
macro.Choice C: Scarcity ended; the stockout remains because producing water still uses resources.
macro.Choice D: Neither condition ended because the store still has a finite water inventory.
macro.Correct Answer: A — The stockout ended; using materials and truck time still involves scarcity.
macro.Feedback: The delivery resolves this store's stockout at the posted price. Scarcity remains because materials and truck time have alternative uses and cannot satisfy every want. Duration is not the defining difference, and finite inventory alone does not imply unmet purchases at the prevailing price.

macro.Common Misconception: Collapsing a temporary supply disruption and a persistent resource constraint.
macro.Question: A delivery disruption leaves a hospital temporarily short of oxygen cylinders, while its limited budget also restricts how many backup systems it can maintain. Which statement is accurate?
macro.Choice A: The disruption is a shortage; the budget tradeoff reflects ongoing scarcity
macro.Choice B: Both conditions are temporary shortages because money is involved
macro.Choice C: Both conditions are scarcity only if oxygen receives a market price
macro.Choice D: The backup budget eliminates scarcity once deliveries resume
macro.Correct Answer: A — The disruption is a shortage; the budget tradeoff reflects ongoing scarcity
macro.Feedback: The disruption leaves fewer cylinders available than the hospital needs under current conditions. The budget constraint requires choices among backup systems and other uses of funds, illustrating scarcity. This particular disruption is temporary; shortages need not be temporary, and scarcity is not limited to the long run.

macro.Common Misconception: Letting urgency obscure the alternative output of a fixed workforce.
macro.Question: A public agency reassigns cybersecurity analysts to clear a benefits-processing backlog. Which consequence must be included even if the backlog is urgent?
macro.Choice A: The forgone security monitoring performed by the same scarce analysts
macro.Choice B: The analysts become nonscarce because both assignments serve the public
macro.Choice C: The backlog creates more analyst-hours by increasing social need
macro.Choice D: Only the agency payroll, not analyst time, has an alternative use
macro.Correct Answer: A — The forgone security monitoring performed by the same scarce analysts
macro.Feedback: Urgency can affect priorities but does not remove the forgone use of analyst time.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring a less visible displaced use when multiple visible goals improve.
macro.Question: A government funds both climate adaptation and transit by postponing courthouse maintenance. Officials call the package “tradeoff-free” because two programs expand. What is wrong?
macro.Choice A: The postponed maintenance is a displaced use of scarce public resources
macro.Choice B: Two expanding programs guarantee that no group bears a cost
macro.Choice C: Deferred maintenance is not a cost until a courthouse closes
macro.Choice D: Public borrowing makes labor and materials immediately unlimited
macro.Correct Answer: A — The postponed maintenance is a displaced use of scarce public resources
macro.Feedback: A package can advance several goals while shifting costs to another use or time.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating national wealth as freedom from physical and time constraints.
macro.Question: A wealthy country can afford either a high-speed rail network or a major hospital modernization program sooner, but construction crews and materials cannot complete both on the same schedule. What does this show?
macro.Choice A: Wealth expands options without eliminating real resource constraints
macro.Choice B: Wealth eliminates scarcity whenever both projects have positive benefits
macro.Choice C: Only lower-income countries face tradeoffs involving public infrastructure
macro.Choice D: The conflict is a temporary shortage caused entirely by incorrect prices
macro.Correct Answer: A — Wealth expands options without eliminating real resource constraints
macro.Feedback: Wealth increases capacity, but real inputs and time remain limited.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating positive benefits as proof that mutually competing projects are jointly feasible.
macro.Question: A state has one construction workforce for unsafe bridges, aging schools, and storm-water upgrades. Which proposal most clearly hides the tradeoff?
macro.Choice A: Complete all projects immediately because each has benefits greater than zero
macro.Choice B: Rank projects by expected benefits, urgency, and displaced work
macro.Choice C: Phase projects as crews and materials become available
macro.Choice D: State which communities wait under each feasible schedule
macro.Correct Answer: A — Complete all projects immediately because each has benefits greater than zero
macro.Feedback: Positive benefits do not create the crews and materials required to do everything at once.

macro.Common Misconception: Restricting tradeoffs to alternatives with explicit money prices.
macro.Question: A parent can accept additional paid work only by reducing caregiving or rest. A colleague says no tradeoff exists because caregiving has no money price. What is the best correction?
macro.Choice A: Time is scarce even when an alternative use is unpaid
macro.Choice B: Only lost wages can count as a scarce-resource sacrifice
macro.Choice C: Unpaid activities use no economically relevant resources
macro.Choice D: A tradeoff exists only when the household budget falls
macro.Correct Answer: A — Time is scarce even when an alternative use is unpaid
macro.Feedback: Nonmarket time has competing valuable uses and remains scarce.

macro.Common Misconception: Counting the new benefit while ignoring displaced classroom users.
macro.Question: A university converts two classrooms into laboratories. Science students gain space, while other departments lose course capacity. Which analysis is most complete?
macro.Choice A: The conversion reallocates scarce space and creates gains and losses
macro.Choice B: The conversion ends scarcity because laboratories are more specialized
macro.Choice C: Only departments charging lab fees face a resource constraint
macro.Choice D: Classroom capacity becomes a shortage caused by a legal price rule
macro.Correct Answer: A — The conversion reallocates scarce space and creates gains and losses
macro.Feedback: The same limited space cannot simultaneously serve both sets of uses.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming improvement in one input removes every remaining constraint.
macro.Question: A faster 3D printer doubles output per hour, but every job still requires one technician and the lab has only two technicians. What changed?
macro.Choice A: One constraint eased, while technician time still limits feasible production
macro.Choice B: All scarcity ended because machine productivity doubled
macro.Choice C: The technician constraint became a price shortage
macro.Choice D: The lab can now complete every desired job without choosing
macro.Correct Answer: A — One constraint eased, while technician time still limits feasible production
macro.Feedback: Technology can shift the binding constraint without eliminating scarcity.

macro.Common Misconception: Analyzing beneficiaries without identifying who loses the reallocated resource.
macro.Question: A transit agency moves buses from a lightly used route to an overcrowded route. Which statement best captures the tradeoff?
macro.Choice A: Crowded-route riders gain capacity while other riders lose service frequency
macro.Choice B: The transfer creates more buses because average ridership rises
macro.Choice C: Public ownership means the routes do not compete for vehicles
macro.Choice D: The agency eliminates scarcity by serving the larger group first
macro.Correct Answer: A — Crowded-route riders gain capacity while other riders lose service frequency
macro.Feedback: Reassigning a fixed fleet benefits one route while reducing capacity elsewhere.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming a resource increase eliminates all unmet wants.
macro.Question: A larger reservoir expands the region’s water supply. Cities, farms, and ecosystems still request more water than is available in dry years. Which statement follows?
macro.Choice A: The expansion relaxes scarcity but does not remove competing uses
macro.Choice B: The expansion eliminates scarcity because total water increased
macro.Choice C: The remaining conflict must be a temporary retail shortage
macro.Choice D: More capacity means allocation rules no longer affect any group
macro.Correct Answer: A — The expansion relaxes scarcity but does not remove competing uses
macro.Feedback: More resources can ease a constraint while valued uses still exceed availability.

macro.Common Misconception: Using a single outcome to judge a multi-dimensional policy.
macro.Question: A policy expands total production, reduces pollution, and requires a small tax increase. Which statement is most defensible?
macro.Choice A: Several goals may improve, while taxes and inputs still have alternative uses
macro.Choice B: Several benefits mean the policy uses no scarce resources or public funds
macro.Choice C: Scarcity matters only when total production falls after the policy change
macro.Choice D: Any tax increase proves the policy reduces both efficiency and equality
macro.Correct Answer: A — Several goals may improve, while taxes and inputs still have alternative uses
macro.Feedback: A complete tradeoff analysis includes gains, resource use, financing, and distribution.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming efficiency and equality are the same criterion.
macro.Question: A policy increases total output but leaves the lowest-income group worse off. Which judgment is most accurate?
macro.Choice A: It may improve total output while worsening the distribution of gains
macro.Choice B: It must improve both efficiency and equality because output increased
macro.Choice C: It eliminates scarcity because the economy can now produce more output
macro.Choice D: It cannot improve efficiency because at least one affected group loses
macro.Correct Answer: A — It may improve total output while worsening the distribution of gains
macro.Feedback: Efficiency and distribution are separate dimensions, so they can move in opposite directions.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating tradeoffs as proof that every objective must worsen.
macro.Question: A reform raises average income and narrows the income gap but requires more administrative resources. Which statement is warranted?
macro.Choice A: Efficiency and equality cannot improve at the same time
macro.Choice B: Publicly funded administrative resources are not scarce
macro.Choice C: The reform may improve both efficiency and equality while still using scarce resources.
macro.Choice D: There is no tradeoff because average income and equality both improve.
macro.Correct Answer: C — The reform may improve both efficiency and equality while still using scarce resources.
macro.Feedback: Some policies can improve multiple outcomes, but resource use and implementation constraints still matter.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating high value as proof of no sacrifice.
macro.Question: A government can increase disaster preparedness by diverting engineers from current infrastructure repairs. The preparedness program is highly valuable. What still follows?
macro.Choice A: Public projects do not compete for scarce inputs
macro.Choice B: Its value does not remove the tradeoff created by limited engineering capacity.
macro.Choice C: Only money, not skilled labor, can be scarce
macro.Choice D: A highly valuable program has no resource cost.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Its value does not remove the tradeoff created by limited engineering capacity.
macro.Feedback: Even high-value projects require scarce labor, time, and materials that could serve other purposes.

macro.Common Misconception: Using efficiency as a complete moral judgment.
macro.Question: An allocation rule maximizes total output but concentrates nearly all gains among a small group. Which conclusion is strongest?
macro.Choice A: The rule may be efficient by one criterion while raising serious equality concerns.
macro.Choice B: Scarcity prevents economists from discussing how gains are distributed
macro.Choice C: High total output automatically makes the allocation equal
macro.Choice D: Any unequal allocation must reduce total output.
macro.Correct Answer: A — The rule may be efficient by one criterion while raising serious equality concerns.
macro.Feedback: Efficiency and equality are distinct criteria and should be evaluated separately.

macro.Common Misconception: Evaluating one time horizon while ignoring the competing use and affected groups.
macro.Question: After a flood, a county can use its emergency fund for temporary housing or immediate levee repairs. Housing aids displaced families now; repairs reduce future risk. What must an economic analysis include?
macro.Choice A: Current beneficiaries, future risk reduction, and the use forgone under either choice
macro.Choice B: Only the number of residents receiving immediate housing assistance
macro.Choice C: Only the engineering estimate for the levee repair project
macro.Choice D: A claim that emergency spending makes the county budget unlimited
macro.Correct Answer: A — Current beneficiaries, future risk reduction, and the use forgone under either choice
macro.Feedback: Scarcity requires comparing both uses, their timing, and who gains or loses.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating a productivity gain as the elimination of all production choices.
macro.Question: Automation reduces the labor needed in a warehouse, but expansion still requires scarce electricity, loading space, and computing capacity. Which conclusion is strongest?
macro.Choice A: Automation changes the constraint mix rather than abolishing scarcity
macro.Choice B: Automation abolishes scarcity because fewer workers are required
macro.Choice C: The remaining limits are shortages caused only by incorrect prices
macro.Choice D: Every expansion becomes feasible once one input requirement falls
macro.Correct Answer: A — Automation changes the constraint mix rather than abolishing scarcity
macro.Feedback: Reducing one input requirement can leave other resources as binding constraints.

macro.Common Misconception: Equating scarcity with poverty and overlooking universal nonmoney constraints.
macro.Question: A low-income household and a wealthy household both have 24 hours in a day, but very different financial options. Which statement correctly distinguishes poverty from scarcity?
macro.Choice A: Poverty concerns limited material means; both households still face scarce time
macro.Choice B: Only the low-income household faces scarcity because wealth removes all constraints
macro.Choice C: Both households are poor because neither can create more hours in a day
macro.Choice D: Scarcity describes temporary stockouts, while poverty describes every tradeoff
macro.Correct Answer: A — Poverty concerns limited material means; both households still face scarce time
macro.Feedback: Poverty and scarcity are different: scarcity persists across income levels.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating the chosen use as proof that forgone uses have no value.
macro.Question: A city can zone a waterfront parcel for housing, a flood barrier, or a public park. A developer claims housing demand makes the other uses economically irrelevant. What is the strongest response?
macro.Choice A: High housing value does not erase the flood and recreation benefits forgone
macro.Choice B: Market demand makes the parcel physically available for all three uses
macro.Choice C: Public benefits matter only when users pay an admission price
macro.Choice D: Choosing housing proves the other uses were not valued by anyone
macro.Correct Answer: A — High housing value does not erase the flood and recreation benefits forgone
macro.Feedback: Scarcity makes the benefits of mutually exclusive uses economically relevant.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating additional financing as immediate creation of specialized capacity.
macro.Question: A factory that builds both emergency generators and defense equipment receives a fixed allocation of skilled machinist-hours. Why does a larger government budget not automatically remove the production tradeoff this quarter?
macro.Choice A: Money cannot instantly create the specialized labor and machine time required
macro.Choice B: Government purchases never use resources that have alternative civilian uses
macro.Choice C: A larger budget converts every physical constraint into an accounting entry
macro.Choice D: Defense production eliminates scarcity whenever national security is valuable
macro.Correct Answer: A — Money cannot instantly create the specialized labor and machine time required
macro.Feedback: Nominal funding cannot instantly expand every real resource needed for production.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring constraints that become more important after another constraint relaxes.
macro.Question: A university can admit more students by enlarging lectures, but laboratory space and advising time remain fixed. What does the enrollment expansion demonstrate?
macro.Choice A: Relaxing one capacity limit can intensify other educational tradeoffs
macro.Choice B: Larger lectures eliminate scarcity throughout the university
macro.Choice C: Advising time becomes abundant when tuition revenue increases
macro.Choice D: Laboratory capacity matters only for programs charging separate fees
macro.Correct Answer: A — Relaxing one capacity limit can intensify other educational tradeoffs
macro.Feedback: The binding limit can move from lecture seats to labs or advising.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring competing uses across time when the resource is renewable.
macro.Question: A fishery can allow a larger catch this season or preserve more breeding stock for future seasons. Which feature makes this a scarcity problem rather than only a biological fact?
macro.Choice A: The limited stock has competing current and future valued uses
macro.Choice B: The fish have no posted price while still in the ocean
macro.Choice C: The catch becomes scarce only after a legal quota is adopted
macro.Choice D: Future fish are unlimited because they have not yet been harvested
macro.Correct Answer: A — The limited stock has competing current and future valued uses
macro.Feedback: The breeding stock cannot simultaneously support maximum current catch and future reproduction.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating a fairness rationale as elimination of the underlying capacity cost.
macro.Question: An evacuation plan dedicates the only outbound bridge to buses carrying people without cars, delaying private vehicles. Which statement is most complete?
macro.Choice A: The rule reallocates scarce road capacity and changes who bears delay
macro.Choice B: Prioritizing vulnerable residents creates additional bridge capacity
macro.Choice C: A fairness goal makes the delay imposed on other users economically irrelevant
macro.Choice D: The bridge is not scarce because evacuees are not charged a toll
macro.Correct Answer: A — The rule reallocates scarce road capacity and changes who bears delay
macro.Feedback: The priority rule affects distribution, but the bridge capacity remains fixed.

macro.Common Misconception: Listing benefits without confronting mutually exclusive uses.
macro.Question: A coastal city can use a limited parcel for flood protection, affordable housing, or commercial development. Which analysis best respects scarcity?
macro.Choice A: Compare feasible parcel uses, incremental benefits and displaced uses, making the distribution of gains and losses explicit.
macro.Choice B: Rank uses by expected cash revenue, counting public benefits only when the city can charge users for them.
macro.Choice C: Rank uses by the number of beneficiaries, treating benefit size and displaced alternatives as secondary tie-breakers.
macro.Choice D: Divide the parcel equally among uses, treating equal area shares as sufficient evidence of equal benefit and efficiency.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Compare feasible parcel uses, incremental benefits and displaced uses, making the distribution of gains and losses explicit.
macro.Feedback: A scarce parcel requires a feasible comparison of valued uses, including nonmarket benefits and distribution. Cash revenue, beneficiary counts or equal acreage alone can miss opportunity costs and competing criteria.

macro.Common Misconception: Reducing a scarcity problem to a single efficiency or fairness rule.
macro.Question: A region faces limited electricity during a heat wave. It can prioritize hospitals, households, or energy-intensive factories. Which response is the most complete economic analysis?
macro.Choice A: Compare marginal benefits and forgone uses across feasible allocations, then show the health, output and distribution tradeoffs.
macro.Choice B: Prioritize immediate health effects, treating displaced production and later income losses as outside the economic comparison.
macro.Choice C: Prioritize measured dollar output losses, treating unpriced household and hospital benefits as equal across allocations.
macro.Choice D: Give each group the same percentage reduction, treating proportional rationing as sufficient evidence of the best allocation.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Compare marginal benefits and forgone uses across feasible allocations, then show the health, output and distribution tradeoffs.
macro.Feedback: Electricity has competing health, household and productive uses. Economic evaluation compares marginal gains and displaced benefits while stating distributional priorities; health-only, cash-only and proportional rules each impose a particular criterion.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming one technological improvement removes all constraints.
macro.Question: A breakthrough makes desalination much cheaper, but coastal land, energy, pipelines, and environmental capacity remain limited. Which statement is best?
macro.Choice A: Cheaper desalination reduces water opportunity cost to zero, leaving land and energy limits relevant only for other industries.
macro.Choice B: Cheaper desalination relaxes one constraint, but land, energy and delivery limits can become the binding sources of tradeoffs.
macro.Choice C: Cheaper desalination makes physical water abundant, so any remaining scarcity must be explained entirely by monopoly pricing.
macro.Choice D: Cheaper desalination expands output proportionally at every stage, so pipelines and environmental limits become less binding automatically.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Cheaper desalination relaxes one constraint, but land, energy and delivery limits can become the binding sources of tradeoffs.
macro.Feedback: A productivity improvement changes which resource limits output. Complementary land, energy, networks and environmental capacity remain scarce and need not expand with desalination technology.

macro.Common Misconception: Using one allocation criterion while ignoring displaced care and distribution.
macro.Question: Following an earthquake, a hospital has one surgical team for trauma cases, routine emergencies, and patients already scheduled. Which policy best acknowledges scarcity without pretending one criterion settles the decision?
macro.Choice A: Compare expected health gains, urgency and displaced treatment under feasible schedules, stating how the priority rule weights them.
macro.Choice B: Treat trauma first in every case, using the emergency label as sufficient evidence that postponed care has lower marginal value.
macro.Choice C: Preserve scheduled order in every case, using earlier commitments as sufficient evidence that urgent arrivals have lower priority.
macro.Choice D: Allocate equal team time to each group, using equal shares as sufficient evidence of both fair treatment and greatest health gain.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Compare expected health gains, urgency and displaced treatment under feasible schedules, stating how the priority rule weights them.
macro.Feedback: The surgical team has competing uses with differences in urgency, benefits and forgone care. No label or equal-time rule settles every dimension without evaluating the feasible alternatives.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming expansion of one input removes complementary-input constraints.
macro.Question: A laboratory has idle testing machines but fully occupied specialist staff. It buys more machines, then shifts specialists from quality checks to testing. Tests rise and errors rise. What best explains the result?
macro.Choice A: The equipment purchase left the staff constraint; reallocation increased tests at a quality cost
macro.Choice B: More tests prove the original equipment constraint was the only limit
macro.Choice C: Idle machines mean the extra tests had no opportunity cost
macro.Choice D: The rise in errors shows there was no expansion in testing
macro.Correct Answer: A — The equipment purchase left the staff constraint; reallocation increased tests at a quality cost
macro.Feedback: Specialist time remained scarce. Reassigning it raised testing by sacrificing quality checks, so the extra machines alone did not remove the tradeoff.

macro.Common Misconception: Using efficiency or equality as a complete allocation rule without examining the other.
macro.Question: During a drought, a river authority must allocate water among cities, farms, and minimum ecosystem flows. Which statement avoids both an efficiency-only and a fairness-only mistake?
macro.Choice A: Compare total and ecological benefits while showing how each feasible rule distributes losses among users.
macro.Choice B: Maximize measured market output while counting ecosystem flows only when the authority can collect a fee.
macro.Choice C: Equalize percentage cuts across users while treating equal reductions as proof of equal welfare losses.
macro.Choice D: Preserve historical allocations while treating prior entitlements as evidence of the highest current marginal benefits.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Compare total and ecological benefits while showing how each feasible rule distributes losses among users.
macro.Feedback: Benefits, ecosystem effects and distribution must be distinguished. Prices, proportional reductions and historical shares can each omit relevant marginal values or impose a distributional rule.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating abundant output at one stage as abundance throughout a system.
macro.Question: A region has surplus generation but a fully used transmission line. A subsidy expands generation again. Delivered power stays flat. Which proposal addresses the observed limit without claiming scarcity disappears?
macro.Choice A: Expand transmission, then reassess other constrained resources and forgone uses
macro.Choice B: Expand generation further because surplus generation measures delivered capacity
macro.Choice C: Declare electricity costless because some generated power goes unused
macro.Choice D: Treat unchanged deliveries as proof that users place no value on power
macro.Correct Answer: A — Expand transmission, then reassess other constrained resources and forgone uses
macro.Feedback: Transmission is the observed bottleneck. Relaxing it may expand deliveries, but construction resources and other constraints still have alternative uses.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming labor-saving technology eliminates choice over the released resources.
macro.Question: Automation frees assembly hours. Managers assign them to inspection, reducing defects, but product development gets no extra staff. Which counterfactual is needed to evaluate the allocation?
macro.Choice A: What those same hours would have achieved in development relative to the inspection gain
macro.Choice B: What the robot cost before the hours were freed, counted as the entire current tradeoff
macro.Choice C: The sum of benefits from inspection and development as if both received the hours
macro.Choice D: Whether inspection has a cash price rather than a nonmonetary benefit
macro.Correct Answer: A — What those same hours would have achieved in development relative to the inspection gain
macro.Feedback: The technology relaxes one constraint; it does not determine the best use of freed labor. Compare inspection with the feasible development alternative.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring intertemporal costs because their effects are delayed or uncertain.
macro.Question: A transit authority postpones track maintenance to accelerate a network extension. The extension raises capacity next year but increases breakdown risk now. Which analysis best captures the dynamic tradeoff?
macro.Choice A: Compare current reliability losses with future capacity gains and their distribution
macro.Choice B: Count only future riders because maintenance creates no new visible service
macro.Choice C: Treat postponed work as costless until a breakdown actually occurs
macro.Choice D: Assume future capacity removes the present scarcity of repair crews
macro.Correct Answer: A — Compare current reliability losses with future capacity gains and their distribution
macro.Feedback: Scarcity links present resource use to future benefits and risks.

macro.Common Misconception: Using the total output result as a complete judgment about distribution.
macro.Question: Route A delivers more meals but skips isolated households. Route B reaches every district but delivers fewer meals. An official calls A superior because total deliveries are higher. What evidence and judgment are still needed?
macro.Choice A: Who loses access, and how that loss is weighed against additional deliveries
macro.Choice B: Only more precise meal totals, because totals establish distributional fairness
macro.Choice C: Only whether either route has positive benefits, because that settles the ranking
macro.Choice D: Proof that isolated households are costly, which makes their access irrelevant
macro.Correct Answer: A — Who loses access, and how that loss is weighed against additional deliveries
macro.Feedback: A higher total establishes a production advantage under that metric. Ranking the routes also requires the distribution of access and an explicit weight on it.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming discovery of one resource makes the complete production system unconstrained.
macro.Question: A mineral discovery expands deposits, but refining staff are fully occupied. Exporting unrefined ore can fund training; keeping it for later refining forgoes that revenue. Which statement follows?
macro.Choice A: More deposits expand options, while refining and the timing of resource use still involve tradeoffs
macro.Choice B: The discovery removes scarcity because the mineral stock increased
macro.Choice C: Keeping the ore has no cost because it remains physically available
macro.Choice D: Export revenue proves immediate export is best under every future-use objective
macro.Correct Answer: A — More deposits expand options, while refining and the timing of resource use still involve tradeoffs
macro.Feedback: The deposit gain does not eliminate the refining constraint. Holding ore preserves a future option but forgoes a feasible current use, including financing training.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring intertemporal costs because their effects are delayed or uncertain.
macro.Question: A machine can make sensors or monitors. A proposal raises both outputs by reducing maintenance time; next period's downtime then rises. Which evaluation avoids a false tradeoff-free claim?
macro.Choice A: Compare current output gains with the future production sacrificed through downtime
macro.Choice B: Count only current outputs because both increased
macro.Choice C: Treat maintenance as irrelevant because customers do not buy it
macro.Choice D: Add current and future output gains without deducting the downtime loss
macro.Correct Answer: A — Compare current output gains with the future production sacrificed through downtime
macro.Feedback: Maintenance uses capacity now to preserve capacity later. Expanding both saleable outputs by reducing it can shift the sacrifice into the future.

macro.Common Misconception: Looking at quality or access alone instead of their competing use of instructional capacity.
macro.Question: A school uses idle rooms for smaller classes, but instructor hours stay fixed. More hours per student reduce enrollment unless other teaching duties shrink. Which condition permits higher enrollment and smaller classes without that sacrifice?
macro.Choice A: Additional effective instructor capacity as well as rooms
macro.Choice B: A larger room budget with instructor hours and productivity unchanged
macro.Choice C: A statement that smaller classes are educationally valuable
macro.Choice D: Reclassifying the displaced teaching duties as unpaid work
macro.Correct Answer: A — Additional effective instructor capacity as well as rooms
macro.Feedback: Rooms and instructor time are separate inputs. Idle rooms alone cannot supply the additional teaching capacity needed for both goals.

macro.Common Misconception: Using a single rule while ignoring cargo capacity and the supplies displaced.
macro.Question: An aid aircraft can carry water filters, antibiotics, or shelter materials after a cyclone. Which decision process best applies scarcity reasoning?
macro.Choice A: Compare marginal relief benefits per constrained cargo unit and identify the urgent needs displaced by each feasible load.
macro.Choice B: Load the items serving the largest headcount, treating differences in treatment benefit and cargo weight as secondary.
macro.Choice C: Divide weight equally across the three supplies, treating equal shares as proof of the greatest total relief benefit.
macro.Choice D: Load the highest-priced supplies first, treating purchase prices as complete measures of local marginal relief value.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Compare marginal relief benefits per constrained cargo unit and identify the urgent needs displaced by each feasible load.
macro.Feedback: Scarce payload requires comparing benefits against space or weight and the supplies forgone. Headcounts, equal weights and purchase prices alone do not identify the best load.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing scarcity with poverty, high prices, or a temporary stockout.
macro.Question: A school has more requests for tutoring than its staff can serve this week. Which fact makes tutoring time scarce?
macro.Choice A: Limited tutor-hours have several valued uses and cannot meet every request
macro.Choice B: The school has permanently run out of every kind of educational service
macro.Choice C: Families differ in income even if every tutoring request could be served
macro.Choice D: The school charges a price below the market-clearing price for tutoring
macro.Correct Answer: A — Limited tutor-hours have several valued uses and cannot meet every request
macro.Feedback: Tutor-hours are limited relative to the competing requests for them.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring the displaced use of a fixed resource.
macro.Question: A community center has one gym available tonight. Scheduling a youth league means canceling an adult exercise class. What does that choice show?
macro.Choice A: Using the fixed gym for one valued activity leaves less access for another
macro.Choice B: The community has permanently exhausted every recreation resource
macro.Choice C: The gym stops being scarce once managers publish the schedule
macro.Choice D: Both groups receive equal access because the choice is publicly announced
macro.Correct Answer: A — Using the fixed gym for one valued activity leaves less access for another
macro.Feedback: Assigning the fixed gym to one activity displaces another valued use.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing efficiency with equality.
macro.Question: Efficiency is primarily about:
macro.Choice A: Giving everyone identical outcomes
macro.Choice B: Eliminating all tradeoffs
macro.Choice C: Getting the greatest total value from available resources.
macro.Choice D: Ensuring that no one ever loses from a change.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Getting the greatest total value from available resources.
macro.Feedback: Efficiency concerns how much total value is produced from scarce resources.

macro.Common Misconception: Naming unmet wants rather than the resource that constrains them.
macro.Question: A classroom has 24 seats and 31 students who want to attend. Which statement identifies the scarce resource?
macro.Choice A: The 24 available classroom seats
macro.Choice B: The seven students without seats
macro.Choice C: The tuition paid by every student
macro.Choice D: The number of courses in the catalog
macro.Correct Answer: A — The 24 available classroom seats
macro.Feedback: Seats are the limited resource relative to enrollment demand.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring the alternative public use.
macro.Question: A town spends its entire emergency fund on flood barriers instead of fire equipment. The central issue is:
macro.Choice A: An elimination of scarcity through public spending.
macro.Choice B: A shortage created by a price floor.
macro.Choice C: A tradeoff among competing uses of limited funds.
macro.Choice D: A gain from comparative advantage.
macro.Correct Answer: C — A tradeoff among competing uses of limited funds.
macro.Feedback: The same limited fund cannot fully finance both priorities.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating efficiency and equality as one measure.
macro.Question: A policy raises total output but widens the income gap. Which pair best describes the possible outcome?
macro.Choice A: Lower efficiency and higher equality.
macro.Choice B: No change in either criterion.
macro.Choice C: Scarcity and shortage become identical.
macro.Choice D: Higher efficiency and lower equality.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Higher efficiency and lower equality.
macro.Feedback: Total output and distribution can move in opposite directions.

macro.Common Misconception: Equating free access with unlimited resources.
macro.Question: Why does a zero-price service still face scarcity?
macro.Choice A: It still uses limited labor, space, equipment, and user time
macro.Choice B: A zero price guarantees enough capacity for every possible user
macro.Choice C: Only services sold for money can require scarce productive inputs
macro.Choice D: Free access removes every competing use of the service resources
macro.Correct Answer: A — It still uses limited labor, space, equipment, and user time
macro.Feedback: Money price and resource scarcity are different issues.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating a priority decision as elimination of the resource constraint.
macro.Question: A county gives more reservoir water to farms during planting season, leaving less for lawn irrigation and some industrial uses. What is the best interpretation?
macro.Choice A: A limited resource is being shifted among competing users
macro.Choice B: The county has eliminated scarcity by choosing agriculture
macro.Choice C: Only users paying the highest price face a water tradeoff
macro.Choice D: The reduced uses prove the reservoir has a temporary leak
macro.Correct Answer: A — A limited resource is being shifted among competing users
macro.Feedback: Prioritizing farms reallocates water and reduces what remains for other users.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming rationing rules remove the constraint.
macro.Question: A city allocates scarce shelter beds by medical vulnerability instead of willingness to pay. What changes?
macro.Choice A: The allocation rule changes, while the limited number of beds does not
macro.Choice B: The vulnerability rule immediately creates enough beds for every applicant
macro.Choice C: The beds stop being scarce because recipients do not bid a money price
macro.Choice D: The rule makes efficiency and equality identical measures of the outcome
macro.Correct Answer: A — The allocation rule changes, while the limited number of beds does not
macro.Feedback: The rule determines recipients but does not create more beds.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming productivity growth eliminates choice.
macro.Question: A technology raises output and reduces input use, yet firms still choose among projects. Why?
macro.Choice A: Remaining capital, skilled labor, time, and wants still create choices
macro.Choice B: Higher productivity guarantees that every available project can be funded
macro.Choice C: Only government agencies continue to face tradeoffs after technology improves
macro.Choice D: Productivity growth changes scarcity into a temporary market shortage
macro.Correct Answer: A — Remaining capital, skilled labor, time, and wants still create choices
macro.Feedback: Productivity relaxes constraints but does not remove all competing uses.

macro.Common Misconception: Using only one criterion in a multi-dimensional judgment.
macro.Question: Which evaluation is most complete for a policy that increases output but harms a vulnerable group?
macro.Choice A: Reject the policy solely because one group loses
macro.Choice B: Assume there is no tradeoff because output rises
macro.Choice C: Evaluate only the change in total output.
macro.Choice D: Assess both the total gains and the distribution of gains and losses.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Assess both the total gains and the distribution of gains and losses.
macro.Feedback: Economic evaluation should separate efficiency from distributional effects.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming positive benefits make mutually exclusive projects jointly feasible.
macro.Question: A space agency has one launch window for a weather satellite or a communications satellite. Both have large benefits. Which claim is least defensible?
macro.Choice A: Large benefits allow both satellites to use the same launch window
macro.Choice B: Choosing either mission forgoes the other mission’s near-term benefits
macro.Choice C: The launch window remains scarce even if the agency receives more money
macro.Choice D: A complete choice compares benefits, timing, and affected users
macro.Correct Answer: A — Large benefits allow both satellites to use the same launch window
macro.Feedback: Value does not allow two missions to occupy one fixed launch window.

macro.Common Misconception: Using one visible quantity without comparing benefits and displaced cargo.
macro.Question: A convoy can carry 800 food rations or 500 water rations, with a linear payload tradeoff. Relief requires at least 320 food and 200 water. Above those minima, an extra food ration adds 1 benefit point and an extra water ration adds 2. Which feasible load maximizes the stated benefit?
macro.Choice A: 320 food and 300 water: it meets both minima and gives 200 additional benefit points.
macro.Choice B: 480 food and 200 water: it meets both minima and gives 160 additional benefit points.
macro.Choice C: 400 food and 250 water: equal payload shares necessarily maximize the benefit measure.
macro.Choice D: 480 food and 300 water: the two separate maxima imply enough capacity for this combined load.
macro.Correct Answer: A — 320 food and 300 water: it meets both minima and gives 200 additional benefit points.
macro.Feedback: The constraint is F/800+W/500≤1. The minima use 0.4+0.4=0.8 of capacity. Remaining capacity yields either 160 food points or 100 water×2=200 points, so choose 320 food and 300 water. The last load requires 1.2 convoys.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating rejection of an alternative as evidence that it had no value.
macro.Question: A city has one waterfront parcel. A flood barrier yields net benefits of $30 million; housing yields $28 million; a park yields $12 million. Housing and the park each require the entire parcel. The city chooses the barrier for a stated safety priority. Which analysis correctly describes the tradeoff?
macro.Choice A: The best forgone feasible use is $28 million housing; the safety priority explains the choice but does not erase that sacrificed value.
macro.Choice B: The forgone value is $40 million because the benefits of every rejected use must be added even when they cannot coexist.
macro.Choice C: The forgone value is zero because the barrier has the largest net benefit and was chosen for public safety.
macro.Choice D: The forgone value is $2 million because the difference between chosen and next-best benefits is the entire displaced use.
macro.Correct Answer: A — The best forgone feasible use is $28 million housing; the safety priority explains the choice but does not erase that sacrificed value.
macro.Feedback: Only one use is feasible. Housing is the best alternative at 28, while the barrier’s advantage over it is 2. A safety criterion may guide the decision, but neither public ownership nor superior benefits makes displaced uses valueless.

macro.Common Misconception: Generalizing one productivity improvement to the entire production system.
macro.Question: A supply chain can deliver at most 10 battery packs weekly because battery assembly is capped at 10, minerals at 15 and transmission installations at 12. Assembly productivity triples with no other capacity change. Demand is 20 packs. Which investment would next expand deliverable output?
macro.Choice A: Transmission capacity: output first rises to 12, then can rise to 15 before minerals become the next bottleneck.
macro.Choice B: Mineral capacity: output first rises to 30, then mineral expansion is needed only after demand reaches 30.
macro.Choice C: More assembly capacity: tripling assembly leaves its old 10-pack limit binding until every stage also triples.
macro.Choice D: No investment: the productivity improvement makes every 20-pack demand feasible despite the other stated limits.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Transmission capacity: output first rises to 12, then can rise to 15 before minerals become the next bottleneck.
macro.Feedback: Deliverable output is the minimum capacity: initially min(10,15,12)=10; afterward min(30,15,12)=12. Raising transmission to at least 15 then makes the mineral constraint binding at 15.

macro.Common Misconception: Equating wealth with unlimited real resources.
macro.Question: A wealthy country has 100 engineer-years available this year. Hospital upgrades require 70 and rail expansion 60; each project must be completed as a whole. Funding covers both, but training extra engineers takes a year. Which plan and interpretation are feasible now?
macro.Choice A: Complete one project now and schedule the other later; the 30-engineer-year shortfall is a current real constraint despite adequate funds.
macro.Choice B: Complete both now by borrowing more money; financing removes the need for the missing 30 engineer-years.
macro.Choice C: Assign 50 engineer-years to each and count both completed; equal resource shares satisfy any whole-project requirement.
macro.Choice D: Complete both now because training expands next year’s workforce, so its future capacity can be used this year.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Complete one project now and schedule the other later; the 30-engineer-year shortfall is a current real constraint despite adequate funds.
macro.Feedback: The two projects need 70+60=130 engineer-years, exceeding the current 100. Money is not the binding constraint and next-year training cannot instantly supply current labor. A feasible schedule must delay at least one whole project.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating an efficiency result as a complete distributional judgment.
macro.Question: A vaccine program compares two feasible allocations of a fixed stock. A is projected to save 120 lives, including 10 in remote communities. B saves 110, including 30 remotely. A charter requires at least 25 remote lives saved. Which evaluation respects both the estimates and the stated constraint?
macro.Choice A: A saves most overall; only B meets the remote constraint, sacrificing 10 total lives for 20 additional remote lives.
macro.Choice B: A meets the charter because its larger total automatically compensates remote communities for receiving fewer doses.
macro.Choice C: B maximizes the stated total because adding its 30 remote lives to 110 produces 140 lives saved.
macro.Choice D: B removes scarcity because satisfying the charter makes the additional 10 projected total lives costless to obtain.
macro.Correct Answer: A — A saves most overall; only B meets the remote constraint, sacrificing 10 total lives for 20 additional remote lives.
macro.Feedback: Remote lives are included in the totals. A has 10 more total lives, while B has 20 more remote lives and meets the threshold. The charter imposes a distributional constraint; it does not change the projections or eliminate the tradeoff.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring either the present or future use of a fixed workforce.
macro.Question: A port has one crew for this month. Routine maintenance prevents a certain $40 million loss this year. A resilience project instead avoids $100 million of storm losses with probability 0.6 next year but leaves the $40 million current loss. At a 20% discount rate, ignoring other effects and using expected present value, which allocation is better?
macro.Choice A: Resilience by $10 million: its expected discounted benefit is $50 million versus $40 million for maintenance.
macro.Choice B: Maintenance by $20 million: the resilience project’s $100 million must be multiplied by the 0.2 discount rate.
macro.Choice C: Resilience by $60 million: compare the full possible $100 million directly with the certain $40 million.
macro.Choice D: Maintenance because future benefits are uncertain; a positive probability makes expected-value comparison invalid.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Resilience by $10 million: its expected discounted benefit is $50 million versus $40 million for maintenance.
macro.Feedback: Expected present benefit of resilience is 0.6×100/1.2=50 million. Maintenance provides 40 now. With the specified criterion and no other effects, resilience leads by 10; it still sacrifices the current protection, rather than offering a tradeoff-free gain.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “It stays fixed because the two changes offset” in this real exchange rates and purchasing power task.
macro.Question: Let e be foreign currency per domestic currency and ε = eP/P*. The domestic currency depreciates nominally while domestic prices grow more slowly than foreign prices. What happens to ε?
macro.Choice A: It stays fixed because the two changes offset
macro.Choice B: It rises because lower domestic inflation raises P/P*
macro.Choice C: It falls because both changes cause real depreciation
macro.Choice D: Its direction is ambiguous because both nominal and real rates change
macro.Correct Answer: C — It falls because both changes cause real depreciation
macro.Feedback: Nominal depreciation lowers e, and slower domestic inflation lowers P/P*. Both factors lower their product ε; they reinforce rather than offset.

macro.Common Misconception: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
macro.Question: Two years have the same unemployment rate, but inflation is higher in the second after wage setters revise expected inflation upward. What changed?
macro.Choice A: The LRPC became downward sloping
macro.Choice B: Aggregate demand alone fixed both outcomes
macro.Choice C: The economy is on a higher SRPC
macro.Choice D: The economy moved up one unchanged SRPC
macro.Correct Answer: C — The economy is on a higher SRPC
macro.Feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

macro.Common Misconception: Shifts the entire SRPC when aggregate demand changes unexpectedly.
macro.Question: Aggregate demand rises unexpectedly while expected inflation is fixed. Which Phillips-curve change best represents the immediate effect?
macro.Choice A: A move up and left along the current SRPC
macro.Choice B: An upward shift of the SRPC at every unemployment rate
macro.Choice C: A rightward shift of the vertical LRPC
macro.Choice D: A move down and right along the current SRPC
macro.Correct Answer: A — A move up and left along the current SRPC
macro.Feedback: With expected inflation initially fixed, a demand change moves the economy along the current SRPC.

macro.Common Misconception: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
macro.Question: Inflation and unemployment both rise after a sharp increase in energy costs. What is the best diagnosis?
macro.Choice A: Aggregate demand causes movement up one unchanged SRPC
macro.Choice B: Lower expected inflation shifts the SRPC downward
macro.Choice C: The natural rate necessarily falls and shifts LRPC left
macro.Choice D: The adverse supply shock shifts the SRPC upward
macro.Correct Answer: D — The adverse supply shock shifts the SRPC upward
macro.Feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

macro.Common Misconception: Stops the causal chain at the initial short-run Phillips movement.
macro.Question: A demand expansion moves the economy to lower unemployment and higher inflation. A year later unemployment returns to its original rate while inflation remains higher. Which sequence fits?
macro.Choice A: A supply improvement followed by movement down the SRPC
macro.Choice B: Movement along an SRPC followed by an upward SRPC shift
macro.Choice C: Two movements along one permanently fixed SRPC
macro.Choice D: An LRPC shift left followed by falling expectations
macro.Correct Answer: B — Movement along an SRPC followed by an upward SRPC shift
macro.Feedback: Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate.

macro.Common Misconception: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
macro.Question: An adverse supply shock raises inflation while output falls. How should the AD-AS result transfer to the Phillips model?
macro.Choice A: Higher inflation and unemployment indicate an upward SRPC shift
macro.Choice B: Higher inflation and lower unemployment indicate movement along SRPC
macro.Choice C: Lower inflation and unemployment indicate a downward SRPC shift
macro.Choice D: Unchanged inflation with lower unemployment indicates an LRPC shift
macro.Correct Answer: A — Higher inflation and unemployment indicate an upward SRPC shift
macro.Feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

macro.Common Misconception: Treats the short-run association as a permanent menu of policy choices.
macro.Question: A policymaker cites the downward-sloping SRPC as proof that permanently higher inflation will secure permanently lower unemployment. What is the decisive flaw?
macro.Choice A: The SRPC actually slopes upward for every demand change
macro.Choice B: Inflation cannot respond to aggregate demand in the short run
macro.Choice C: The natural rate is always zero after an expansion
macro.Choice D: Expected inflation adjusts, so the short-run unemployment gain is not permanent
macro.Correct Answer: D — Expected inflation adjusts, so the short-run unemployment gain is not permanent
macro.Feedback: On a given SRPC, lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation only in the short run.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “At a common unemployment rate, inflation must be equal because natural unemployment is equal” in this short run phillips curve task.
macro.Question: Two countries each employ 160 workers and have identical natural unemployment. Both reduce demand, but one begins with higher expected inflation. Under parallel SRPCs and unchanged expectations during the adjustment, which comparison is supported?
macro.Choice A: At a common unemployment rate, inflation must be equal because natural unemployment is equal
macro.Choice B: The high-expectations country has lower inflation at every unemployment rate because expectations reverse the tradeoff
macro.Choice C: Reducing demand necessarily shifts both LRPCs right by the same amount
macro.Choice D: At a common unemployment rate, the high-expectations country retains higher inflation; equal unemployment does not identify one common SRPC
macro.Correct Answer: D — At a common unemployment rate, the high-expectations country retains higher inflation; equal unemployment does not identify one common SRPC
macro.Feedback: Expected inflation shifts the SRPC vertically. A common natural rate fixes the long-run unemployment benchmark, not the short-run inflation intercept. Compare the curves rather than treating both observations as points on one curve.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrect inference: Yes; any higher actual inflation implies the same unemployment gain regardless of expectations.
macro.Question: An anticipated increase in aggregate demand raises actual and expected inflation together, with no supply shock or labor-market reform. Can we conclude that unemployment initially falls below its natural rate, as it might after an unexpected increase in demand?
macro.Choice A: Yes; expected inflation shifts the long-run curve left and lowers natural unemployment.
macro.Choice B: No; expected demand expansion necessarily reduces actual inflation below its initial rate.
macro.Choice C: No; equal actual and expected inflation supplies no inflation surprise to push unemployment below natural.
macro.Choice D: Yes; any higher actual inflation implies the same unemployment gain regardless of expectations.
macro.Correct Answer: C — No; equal actual and expected inflation supplies no inflation surprise to push unemployment below natural.
macro.Feedback: In the expectations-augmented Phillips model, the temporary unemployment deviation depends on inflation relative to expectations. Equal increases in the two do not supply the surprise that generated the original short-run gain.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrect inference: Expected inflation is 5%; unemployment below 5% places the outcome on LRPC.
macro.Question: Use π=πe−0.5(u−5), with rates in percent. Actual inflation is 4% and unemployment is 3%. What expectation is consistent, and does that outcome locate the economy on LRPC?
macro.Choice A: Expected inflation is 2%; lower unemployment must reduce inflation below expectations.
macro.Choice B: Expected inflation is 3%; unemployment below 5% places the outcome off LRPC.
macro.Choice C: Expected inflation is 5%; unemployment below 5% places the outcome on LRPC.
macro.Choice D: Expected inflation is 4%; actual inflation alone identifies expectations and the long run.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Expected inflation is 3%; unemployment below 5% places the outcome off LRPC.
macro.Feedback: Rearrange to πe=π+0.5(u−5)=4+0.5(3−5)=3%. The natural benchmark is 5%; observed unemployment of 3% is a short-run deviation, not a point on the vertical LRPC.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrect inference: Yes; rising unemployment proves a pure favorable demand shock along an unchanged curve.
macro.Question: Inflation and unemployment rise together. Analysts disagree between an adverse supply shock and higher inflation expectations. Do the two outcomes alone identify which mechanism caused the shift?
macro.Choice A: No; either can worsen the short-run relation, so additional evidence must distinguish the cause.
macro.Choice B: Yes; rising unemployment proves a pure favorable demand shock along an unchanged curve.
macro.Choice C: Yes; rising inflation proves expectations were unchanged during the observation.
macro.Choice D: No; neither mechanism can shift the short-run Phillips curve at all.
macro.Correct Answer: A — No; either can worsen the short-run relation, so additional evidence must distinguish the cause.
macro.Feedback: Both adverse supply conditions and higher expected inflation can shift the SRPC upward. Observing higher inflation with higher unemployment rejects a pure movement along one fixed downward curve, but does not by itself distinguish the two shift causes.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “At a common unemployment rate, inflation must be equal because natural unemployment is equal” in this short run phillips curve task.
macro.Question: Two countries each employ 240 workers and have identical natural unemployment. Both reduce demand, but one begins with higher expected inflation. Under parallel SRPCs and unchanged expectations during the adjustment, which comparison is supported?
macro.Choice A: At a common unemployment rate, inflation must be equal because natural unemployment is equal
macro.Choice B: The high-expectations country has lower inflation at every unemployment rate because expectations reverse the tradeoff
macro.Choice C: Reducing demand necessarily shifts both LRPCs right by the same amount
macro.Choice D: At a common unemployment rate, the high-expectations country retains higher inflation; equal unemployment does not identify one common SRPC
macro.Correct Answer: D — At a common unemployment rate, the high-expectations country retains higher inflation; equal unemployment does not identify one common SRPC
macro.Feedback: Expected inflation shifts the SRPC vertically. A common natural rate fixes the long-run unemployment benchmark, not the short-run inflation intercept. Compare the curves rather than treating both observations as points on one curve.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrect inference: Return to natural unemployment proves nominal demand returned to its old level.
macro.Question: After a demand surprise lowers unemployment, expectations fully catch up while productive capacity is unchanged. A report describes the return to natural unemployment as a reversal of the original demand increase. Which correction is needed?
macro.Choice A: Expectations adjustment permanently lowers natural unemployment below the initial benchmark.
macro.Choice B: Return to natural unemployment requires prices to fall back to their original level.
macro.Choice C: Expectations adjustment can reverse the real gain even if higher demand and inflation persist.
macro.Choice D: Return to natural unemployment proves nominal demand returned to its old level.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Expectations adjustment can reverse the real gain even if higher demand and inflation persist.
macro.Feedback: The upward adjustment of inflation expectations removes the initial surprise. Unemployment can return to natural at a higher sustained inflation rate without reversal of the nominal demand expansion or the price-level increase.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrect inference: Unemployment remains 3%; retaining 3% requires no inflation increase beyond 4%.
macro.Question: Use π=πe−0.5(u−5). Expectations rise from 3% to 4% after a demand surprise. If actual inflation is held at 4%, what happens to unemployment, and what inflation would retain u=3%?
macro.Choice A: Unemployment remains 3%; retaining 3% requires no inflation increase beyond 4%.
macro.Choice B: Unemployment rises to 7%; retaining 3% would require inflation of 3%.
macro.Choice C: Unemployment returns to 5%; retaining 3% would require inflation of 4%.
macro.Choice D: Unemployment returns to 5%; retaining 3% would require inflation of 5%.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Unemployment returns to 5%; retaining 3% would require inflation of 5%.
macro.Feedback: With π=πe=4%, the equation gives u=5%. To retain u=3% when πe=4%, actual inflation must be 4−0.5(3−5)=5%. Updated expectations change the inflation required for the same short-run unemployment target.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrect inference: Yes; any SRPC shift must change unemployment even when policymakers adjust demand.
macro.Question: After an adverse supply shock, policymakers hold unemployment at its former natural rate by supporting demand. Inflation rises. Does unchanged unemployment prove the short-run Phillips relation stayed fixed?
macro.Choice A: No; unchanged unemployment proves natural unemployment permanently fell.
macro.Choice B: Yes; demand support eliminates the supply shock rather than changing the chosen outcome.
macro.Choice C: No; policy can offset the unemployment effect while inflation reveals a worse short-run relation.
macro.Choice D: Yes; any SRPC shift must change unemployment even when policymakers adjust demand.
macro.Correct Answer: C — No; policy can offset the unemployment effect while inflation reveals a worse short-run relation.
macro.Feedback: An outcome reflects both the shock and the response. Supporting demand can hold unemployment at the previous benchmark while accepting higher inflation; that observation is compatible with an upward SRPC shift.

macro.Common Misconception: Treats the short-run association as a permanent menu of policy choices.
macro.Question: A government maintains a fixed unemployment gap below the natural rate through successive demand expansions. Expectations adapt to observed inflation, the Phillips slope is unchanged, and no supply or structural shock occurs. Which distinction explains why a permanently higher but stable inflation rate is insufficient?
macro.Choice A: Maintaining the gap requires only a one-time increase in inflation; expectations adjustment then preserves the lower unemployment.
macro.Choice B: Maintaining the gap shifts LRPC left even though the prompt holds labor-market structure fixed.
macro.Choice C: Maintaining the gap requires continuing positive inflation surprises; once inflation stabilizes and expectations catch up, unemployment returns toward natural.
macro.Choice D: Maintaining the gap requires falling actual inflation while expected inflation rises.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Maintaining the gap requires continuing positive inflation surprises; once inflation stabilizes and expectations catch up, unemployment returns toward natural.
macro.Feedback: A fixed below-natural unemployment gap requires a positive actual-minus-expected inflation gap. Adaptive expectations catch up to a stable inflation rate, eliminating that gap. Continued surprises and a return to natural are alternative policy paths, not simultaneous endpoints.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Both curves shift left” in this loanable funds shifts task.
macro.Question: Refer to the graph above. Which two curves shift between A and B?
macro.Choice A: Saving supply and investment demand both shift right
macro.Choice B: Both curves shift left
macro.Choice C: Only saving supply shifts right
macro.Choice D: Only investment demand shifts right
macro.Correct Answer: A — Saving supply and investment demand both shift right
macro.Feedback: The graph shows dashed S1 to the right of S0 and dashed D1 to the right of D0.
