macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “At point A” in this loanable funds shifts task.
macro.Question: Refer to the graph above. Where do the new saving and investment-demand curves intersect?
macro.Choice A: At point B
macro.Choice B: At point A
macro.Choice C: At the D0 intercept
macro.Choice D: At the S0 intercept
macro.Correct Answer: A — At point B
macro.Feedback: The dashed S1 and D1 curves represent the new saving and investment-demand schedules, and their intersection is labeled point B.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “It rises” in this loanable funds shifts task.
macro.Question: Saving supply and investment demand both decrease. What must happen to equilibrium quantity?
macro.Choice A: It falls
macro.Choice B: It rises
macro.Choice C: It remains fixed
macro.Choice D: Its direction is always ambiguous
macro.Correct Answer: A — It falls
macro.Feedback: Both leftward shifts reduce equilibrium quantity, while their effects on the real rate oppose each other.

macro.Common Misconception: Reads quantity from a different labeled location instead of the specified demand-supply intersection.
macro.Question: Refer to the graph above. With both curves shifted right, what equilibrium quantity is shown at B?
macro.Choice A: 40 units
macro.Choice B: 60 units
macro.Choice C: 80 units
macro.Choice D: 100 units
macro.Correct Answer: C — 80 units
macro.Feedback: Dashed S1 and D1 intersect at B at 80 units.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Quantity falls while the real interest rate remains unchanged” in this loanable funds shifts task.
macro.Question: Refer to the graph above. Given the relative shift sizes drawn, which outcome occurs from A to B?
macro.Choice A: Quantity falls while the real interest rate remains unchanged
macro.Choice B: Quantity remains unchanged while the real interest rate rises
macro.Choice C: Quantity rises while the real interest rate remains unchanged
macro.Choice D: Both equilibrium variables fall
macro.Correct Answer: C — Quantity rises while the real interest rate remains unchanged
macro.Feedback: The marked intersections incorporate the relative curve shifts: equilibrium quantity rises from 40 to 80, while both points remain at a 6 percent real interest rate.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The quantity axis fixes every interest rate” in this loanable funds shifts task.
macro.Question: What can the marked new equilibrium tell us that the directions of the two shifts alone cannot?
macro.Choice A: The real rate is 8%; this is the particular result of the relative supply and demand shifts drawn.
macro.Choice B: The real rate is 6%; this is the particular result of the relative supply and demand shifts drawn.
macro.Choice C: The real rate is 6%; every simultaneous rightward supply and demand shift must leave rates unchanged.
macro.Choice D: The real rate is 6%; the quantity increase proves that only saving supply changed.
macro.Correct Answer: B — The real rate is 6%; this is the particular result of the relative supply and demand shifts drawn.
macro.Feedback: B is at 6%, the same rate as A. Theory alone leaves the rate effect of the two increases ambiguous; their actual sizes and slopes in this figure locate the new intersection.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “It falls” in this loanable funds shifts task.
macro.Question: Saving supply and investment demand both increase. What must happen to equilibrium quantity?
macro.Choice A: It falls
macro.Choice B: It remains fixed
macro.Choice C: Its direction is always ambiguous
macro.Choice D: It rises
macro.Correct Answer: D — It rises
macro.Feedback: Both shifts raise the equilibrium quantity; their competing effects make the real-rate direction depend on relative sizes.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “It falls” in this loanable funds shifts task.
macro.Question: Saving supply falls while investment demand rises. What happens to the equilibrium real interest rate?
macro.Choice A: It falls
macro.Choice B: It remains unchanged
macro.Choice C: It rises
macro.Choice D: It cannot be determined
macro.Correct Answer: C — It rises
macro.Feedback: Both the leftward supply shift and the rightward demand shift put upward pressure on the equilibrium real interest rate, while their quantity effects oppose one another.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The real rate must rise, while quantity is theoretically ambiguous; this graph shows quantity unchanged” in this loanable funds shifts task.
macro.Question: Both saving supply and investment demand increase. Which statement distinguishes the general prediction from the outcome at A and B?
macro.Choice A: Quantity must rise; the rate is generally ambiguous, and the plotted rate rises.
macro.Choice B: Quantity must rise; the rate is generally ambiguous, but the plotted rate is unchanged.
macro.Choice C: Quantity rises and the rate is unchanged; every pair of rightward saving and investment shifts has that rate result.
macro.Choice D: Quantity is generally ambiguous; the unchanged plotted rate means national saving did not rise.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Quantity must rise; the rate is generally ambiguous, but the plotted rate is unchanged.
macro.Feedback: Both shifts raise quantity, but they exert opposing pressures on the rate. A and B are both at 6%, so those pressures offset in this drawing. That particular offset is not a universal rule.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Less household saving and weaker expected profits” in this loanable funds shifts task.
macro.Question: Which pair of events could produce the changes from the solid to the dashed curves?
macro.Choice A: Households plan less saving, and firms expect investment projects to be less profitable.
macro.Choice B: Households plan more saving, while firms expect investment projects to be less profitable.
macro.Choice C: The higher quantity itself shifts both schedules, without any change in saving or investment plans.
macro.Choice D: Households plan more saving, and firms expect investment projects to be more profitable.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Households plan more saving, and firms expect investment projects to be more profitable.
macro.Feedback: S1 is right of S0 and D1 is right of D0. Higher planned saving explains the supply shift, while higher expected project returns explain investment demand. Equilibrium quantity is a result, not a determinant that shifts both curves.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Simultaneous rightward shifts always leave the real interest rate unchanged” in this loanable funds shifts task.
macro.Question: The market changes from A to B after saving and investment plans both change. What explains the interest-rate outcome shown?
macro.Choice A: Investment demand dominates here, raising the rate to 8%; different relative shifts could change the rate.
macro.Choice B: The rate stays at 6% because every equal-direction pair of supply and demand shifts leaves the rate fixed.
macro.Choice C: The opposing pressures offset here, leaving the rate at 6%; different relative shifts could change the rate.
macro.Choice D: The rate stays at 6% because a doubling of quantity prevents any change in the price of loanable funds.
macro.Correct Answer: C — The opposing pressures offset here, leaving the rate at 6%; different relative shifts could change the rate.
macro.Feedback: Both marked equilibria are at 6%, though quantity rises from 40 to 80. Greater saving puts downward pressure on the rate and greater investment demand puts upward pressure on it. Their offset is specific to the drawn shifts.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The real rate falls; investment quantity must fall because only the demand shift affects quantity” in this loanable funds shifts task.
macro.Question: A saving incentive raises planned national saving at every real rate, while weaker expected sales reduce desired investment at every real rate. With upward-sloping saving supply and downward-sloping investment demand, which conclusion and information requirement are correct?
macro.Choice A: The real rate falls; investment quantity must fall because only the demand shift affects quantity
macro.Choice B: The real rate falls; the relative shift magnitudes are needed to determine the investment-quantity change
macro.Choice C: Investment quantity rises; the relative shift magnitudes are needed to determine the real-rate change
macro.Choice D: The real rate rises; investment quantity must rise because the saving incentive finances more projects
macro.Correct Answer: B — The real rate falls; the relative shift magnitudes are needed to determine the investment-quantity change
macro.Feedback: More saving shifts supply right, while weaker sales shift demand left. Both changes lower the real rate. The supply change raises equilibrium quantity and the demand change lowers it, so their relative magnitudes determine the net investment response.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The saving shift is absent because the real rate did not fall” in this loanable funds shifts task.
macro.Question: Refer to the graph above. In general, simultaneous rightward shifts make the real-rate effect ambiguous. What does this particular outcome imply about the depicted shift magnitudes?
macro.Choice A: The saving shift is absent because the real rate did not fall
macro.Choice B: The investment-demand shift dominates, so the real rate must rise above 6 percent
macro.Choice C: Both shifts reduce quantity, but equal magnitudes conceal the decline
macro.Choice D: The rate pressures offset while both shifts raise quantity
macro.Correct Answer: D — The rate pressures offset while both shifts raise quantity
macro.Feedback: A rightward supply shift pushes the rate down and a rightward demand shift pushes it up. The unchanged 6 percent rate shows offsetting rate effects, while both shifts raise quantity from A to B.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Saving supply shifts left and investment demand right; quantity rises while the rate depends on relative shifts” in this loanable funds shifts task.
macro.Question: A deficit lowers saving while new technology raises investment demand. What can be concluded without shift magnitudes?
macro.Choice A: Saving supply shifts left and investment demand right; the rate rises while quantity depends on relative shifts
macro.Choice B: Saving supply shifts left and investment demand right; quantity rises while the rate depends on relative shifts
macro.Choice C: Saving supply shifts right and investment demand right; quantity rises while the rate depends on relative shifts
macro.Choice D: Saving supply shifts left and investment demand left; quantity falls while the rate depends on relative shifts
macro.Correct Answer: A — Saving supply shifts left and investment demand right; the rate rises while quantity depends on relative shifts
macro.Feedback: Supply left and demand right both raise the rate, but they push equilibrium quantity in opposite directions.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “A $30 billion increase at every rate; subtracting the public-saving decline gives the $40 billion supply increase” in this loanable funds shifts task.
macro.Question: Refer to the graph above. Each quantity unit represents $1 billion, and the straight-line shifts summarize all changes in saving and investment behavior. Public saving falls by $10 billion at every real rate, while technology raises investment demand. What private-saving shift is required to reconcile the graph with that fiscal change?
macro.Choice A: Private saving must rise $70 billion: together with public saving falling $10 billion, this gives a $60 billion supply increase.
macro.Choice B: Private saving must rise $50 billion: together with public saving falling $10 billion, this gives the plotted $40 billion supply increase.
macro.Choice C: Private saving must rise $30 billion: subtract the $10 billion public-saving loss from the plotted $40 billion increase.
macro.Choice D: Private saving must rise $10 billion: an unchanged equilibrium rate implies no national-saving change.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Private saving must rise $50 billion: together with public saving falling $10 billion, this gives the plotted $40 billion supply increase.
macro.Feedback: At 6 percent, S0 and D0 each have quantity 40, while S1 and D1 each have quantity 80. Each schedule shifts right by $40 billion. Since national saving combines private and public saving, the private shift must satisfy private change − 10 = 40, giving +$50 billion. The two shifts leave the depicted equilibrium rate at 6 percent.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
macro.Question: Refer to the graph. What can be concluded about the move from D to B?
macro.Choice A: Price falls; quantity rises in the drawing
macro.Choice B: Price and quantity both remain unchanged
macro.Choice C: Quantity falls; the price direction is ambiguous
macro.Choice D: Price rises; quantity is unchanged in the drawing
macro.Correct Answer: D — Price rises; quantity is unchanged in the drawing
macro.Feedback: From D to B, the opposing quantity effects cancel while both shifts raise equilibrium price, so quantity is unchanged and price rises.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
macro.Question: Refer to the graph. How do equilibrium price and quantity change from A to B?
macro.Choice A: Price rises 4 dollars; quantity stays 200 thousand
macro.Choice B: Price rises 4 dollars; quantity rises 200 thousand
macro.Choice C: Price falls 4 dollars; quantity stays 200 thousand
macro.Choice D: Price stays 10 dollars; quantity falls 4 thousand
macro.Correct Answer: A — Price rises 4 dollars; quantity stays 200 thousand
macro.Feedback: The quantity effects offset while price rises from 10 to 14 dollars.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
macro.Question: Refer to the graph. Which statement distinguishes the general prediction for these simultaneous shifts from the particular outcome shown?
macro.Choice A: Price is generally ambiguous; quantity must rise and does so here
macro.Choice B: Price must rise; quantity is generally ambiguous but unchanged here
macro.Choice C: Both price and quantity must remain unchanged after both shifts
macro.Choice D: Price must fall; quantity is generally ambiguous but rises here
macro.Correct Answer: B — Price must rise; quantity is generally ambiguous but unchanged here
macro.Feedback: Demand up and supply down reinforce price but oppose in quantity.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
macro.Question: Cheaper alternative transportation reduces gasoline demand while refinery costs fall. For the move from B to D, which outcome and explanation fit the graph?
macro.Choice A: Price falls $2 and quantity stays at 200 thousand gallons per day; the two shifts have offsetting effects on quantity.
macro.Choice B: Price falls $1 and quantity stays at 200 thousand gallons per day; the two shifts have offsetting effects on quantity.
macro.Choice C: Price falls $2 and quantity stays at 200 thousand gallons per day; unchanged quantity means neither curve shifted.
macro.Choice D: Price falls $1 and quantity stays at 200 thousand gallons per day; unchanged quantity means neither curve shifted.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Price falls $2 and quantity stays at 200 thousand gallons per day; the two shifts have offsetting effects on quantity.
macro.Feedback: Cheaper alternative transportation reduces gasoline demand, while lower refinery costs increase supply. B is at $6 and 200 thousand gallons per day; D is at $4 and 200 thousand. The $2 price fall accompanies offsetting quantity effects: lower demand reduces quantity, while higher supply increases it. Unchanged equilibrium quantity does not mean the curves stayed fixed.

macro.Common Misconception: Rearranges NCO = resident foreign-asset purchases minus foreign domestic-asset purchases with the wrong sign.
macro.Question: National saving is $520 billion, domestic investment is $610 billion, and domestic residents buy $160 billion of foreign assets. How much do foreigners buy in domestic assets?
macro.Choice A: $250 billion
macro.Choice B: $70 billion
macro.Choice C: $160 billion
macro.Choice D: $770 billion
macro.Correct Answer: A — $250 billion
macro.Feedback: NCO = S − I = −$90 billion. Since −90 = 160 − foreign purchases, foreign purchases are $250 billion.

macro.Common Misconception: Rearranges NCO = resident foreign-asset purchases minus foreign domestic-asset purchases with the wrong sign.
macro.Question: Output is $5.0 trillion, consumption $3.1 trillion, government purchases $0.9 trillion, and investment $1.2 trillion. Domestic purchases of foreign assets are $260 billion. How much must foreigners purchase in domestic assets?
macro.Choice A: $660 billion
macro.Choice B: $460 billion
macro.Choice C: $60 billion
macro.Choice D: $260 billion
macro.Correct Answer: B — $460 billion
macro.Feedback: NX = 5.0 − 3.1 − 0.9 − 1.2 = −$0.2 trillion, so NCO is −$200 billion. With NCO = $260 billion − foreign purchases, foreign purchases equal $460 billion.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Foreign purchases remain $300 billion; NX must be −$100 billion despite the fixed NCO figure” in this capital flows and net capital outflow task.
macro.Question: A country reports NCO = −$120 billion and resident purchases of foreign assets of $200 billion. Another report lists foreign purchases of domestic assets of $300 billion. Keeping the first two figures fixed, what should the reported foreign purchases be, and does NX = NCO imply a trade surplus or deficit?
macro.Choice A: Foreign purchases remain $300 billion; NX must be −$100 billion despite the fixed NCO figure
macro.Choice B: Foreign purchases must be $320 billion; NX is +$120 billion because a capital inflow is an export
macro.Choice C: Foreign purchases must be $320 billion; NX is −$120 billion, a trade deficit
macro.Choice D: Foreign purchases must be $80 billion; NX is +$120 billion, a trade surplus
macro.Correct Answer: C — Foreign purchases must be $320 billion; NX is −$120 billion, a trade deficit
macro.Feedback: NCO = resident foreign purchases − foreign domestic purchases. Thus −120=200−F implies F=320. With NX=NCO, NX=−120; the inflow finances a trade deficit rather than changing its sign.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “They must rise by $150 billion” in this capital flows and net capital outflow task.
macro.Question: NCO moves from −$80 billion to $30 billion while domestic foreign-asset purchases rise $40 billion. How must foreign purchases of domestic assets change?
macro.Choice A: They must rise by $150 billion
macro.Choice B: They must fall by $70 billion
macro.Choice C: They must rise by $70 billion
macro.Choice D: They must fall by $110 billion
macro.Correct Answer: B — They must fall by $70 billion
macro.Feedback: NCO rises $110 billion. With domestic foreign purchases up $40 billion, foreign domestic-asset purchases must fall $70 billion to make the net rise $110 billion.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “NCO is −$60 billion and NX is $60 billion” in this international transactions and identities task.
macro.Question: National saving is $300 billion and investment is $360 billion. Which external balance follows?
macro.Choice A: NCO and NX are $60 billion
macro.Choice B: NCO is −$60 billion and NX is $60 billion
macro.Choice C: Both balances are $660 billion
macro.Choice D: NCO and NX are −$60 billion
macro.Correct Answer: D — NCO and NX are −$60 billion
macro.Feedback: S − I = −$60 billion, and the identity makes both NCO and NX equal to that amount.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “NX is −$0.1 trillion and NCO is $0.1 trillion” in this international transactions and identities task.
macro.Question: Output is $2.4 trillion, consumption is $1.5 trillion, investment is $0.4 trillion, and government purchases are $0.6 trillion. What are NX and NCO?
macro.Choice A: Both are $0.1 trillion
macro.Choice B: NX is −$0.1 trillion and NCO is $0.1 trillion
macro.Choice C: NX is $0.5 trillion and NCO is −$0.1 trillion
macro.Choice D: Both are −$0.1 trillion
macro.Correct Answer: D — Both are −$0.1 trillion
macro.Feedback: NX = Y − C − I − G = 2.4 − 1.5 − 0.4 − 0.6 = −0.1 trillion; NX = NCO.

macro.Common Misconception: Subtracts a trade surplus from investment instead of using national saving = investment + net exports.
macro.Question: A country has a $90 billion trade surplus and domestic investment of $260 billion. What national saving is consistent with the accounts?
macro.Choice A: $170 billion
macro.Choice B: $260 billion
macro.Choice C: $440 billion
macro.Choice D: $350 billion
macro.Correct Answer: D — $350 billion
macro.Feedback: NX = NCO = $90 billion, and S = I + NCO = $260 billion + $90 billion = $350 billion.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “NX must rise $35 billion; with exports up $20 billion, imports must fall $15 billion” in this international transactions and identities task.
macro.Question: Private saving rises $40 billion, public saving falls $15 billion, and domestic investment rises $10 billion. The trade accounts report exports up $20 billion and imports up $10 billion. Under S−I=NX, with no statistical discrepancy and all saving/investment figures held fixed, which correction makes the trade figures consistent with saving and investment?
macro.Choice A: NX must rise $35 billion; with exports up $20 billion, imports must fall $15 billion
macro.Choice B: NX must fall $15 billion; with exports up $20 billion, imports must rise $35 billion
macro.Choice C: NX must rise $15 billion; with exports up $20 billion, imports must rise $5 billion
macro.Choice D: NX must rise $10 billion; revise saving down $5 billion despite the instruction to hold it fixed
macro.Correct Answer: C — NX must rise $15 billion; with exports up $20 billion, imports must rise $5 billion
macro.Feedback: National saving rises 40−15=25; subtract investment growth 10 to obtain NX growth 15. Since ΔNX=ΔX−ΔM, 15=20−ΔM implies imports rise 5. The original trade report's $10 billion NX increase fails the identity under the stated constraints.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “National saving is $340 billion, so NCO and NX are $50 billion” in this international transactions and identities task.
macro.Question: Private saving is $420 billion, public saving is −$80 billion, and domestic investment is $390 billion. What follows?
macro.Choice A: National saving is $340 billion, so NCO and NX are $50 billion
macro.Choice B: National saving is −$50 billion, so NCO and NX are −$390 billion
macro.Choice C: National saving is $340 billion, so NCO and NX are −$50 billion
macro.Choice D: National saving is $500 billion, so NCO and NX are $110 billion
macro.Correct Answer: C — National saving is $340 billion, so NCO and NX are −$50 billion
macro.Feedback: National saving is $420 billion − $80 billion = $340 billion. Subtracting $390 billion of investment gives NCO = NX = −$50 billion.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Equal worker counts require equal output per worker regardless of capital” in this sources of productivity task.
macro.Question: Two economies each employ 320 workers. One has little capital per worker and the other much more, with similar technology and institutions. Which qualification should accompany a catch-up prediction?
macro.Choice A: Equal worker counts require equal output per worker regardless of capital
macro.Choice B: The capital-poor economy may earn higher marginal returns, but investment and effective use of capital are still required
macro.Choice C: The capital-poor economy must grow faster regardless of investment, institutions or technology access
macro.Choice D: The capital-rich economy must have higher percentage growth because its output level is higher
macro.Correct Answer: B — The capital-poor economy may earn higher marginal returns, but investment and effective use of capital are still required
macro.Feedback: Diminishing returns can create catch-up potential when conditions are comparable. Potential is not an automatic growth guarantee without investment and productive use.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Equal productivity gains at both points because capital additions are equal” in this sources of productivity task.
macro.Question: Two economies start at A and B on this productivity curve. Each adds the same small amount of capital per worker, with other inputs fixed. Which comparison follows?
macro.Choice A: The gain is larger near A; capital has a higher marginal product there.
macro.Choice B: The gain is larger near B; capital has a higher marginal product there.
macro.Choice C: The gain is larger near A because total output per worker is already higher there.
macro.Choice D: The gain is zero near B because a smaller marginal product means capital adds nothing.
macro.Correct Answer: A — The gain is larger near A; capital has a higher marginal product there.
macro.Feedback: The curve is steeper near A than B, indicating a larger marginal output gain at A. B has higher total productivity, but that does not imply a higher marginal gain from capital.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The resource alone guarantees an immediate proportional increase in output per worker” in this sources of productivity task.
macro.Question: A discovery increases available mineral resources for 330 workers, but extraction technology and transport remain inadequate. Which policy diagnosis best connects resources to productivity?
macro.Choice A: The resource alone guarantees an immediate proportional increase in output per worker
macro.Choice B: Transport affects consumption only and cannot limit production from resources
macro.Choice C: Resource abundance makes worker skills and institutions irrelevant to long-run output
macro.Choice D: The resource expands potential opportunities, but complementary technology/infrastructure can be the binding constraint
macro.Correct Answer: D — The resource expands potential opportunities, but complementary technology/infrastructure can be the binding constraint
macro.Feedback: Natural resources can support production, but usable technology, skills and infrastructure determine whether they can be exploited productively. More resources alone need not raise current output.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Both show falling marginal productivity means falling total productivity” in this sources of productivity task.
macro.Question: Capital deepening initially raises output per worker with technology and other productivity determinants unchanged. Later, output per worker rises again even though capital per worker is fixed. How do the two increases differ?
macro.Choice A: Both are movements along the same curve caused solely by more capital per worker.
macro.Choice B: The first is capital deepening; the later gain requires an improvement in another productive factor or technology.
macro.Choice C: The first is a technology improvement; the later gain is diminishing returns to unchanged capital.
macro.Choice D: Both show that a falling marginal product causes the level of productivity to fall.
macro.Correct Answer: B — The first is capital deepening; the later gain requires an improvement in another productive factor or technology.
macro.Feedback: The first change is a movement along a production relationship as capital per worker rises. The later gain at unchanged capital requires another determinant, such as technology or human capital, to improve.

macro.Common Misconception: Ranks total output using productivity alone, ignoring different total hours.
macro.Question: Two plants each initially produce 100 units in 100 worker hours. New machines raise A’s output per hour 20%; training raises B’s output per hour 15%. A then cuts hours to 80, while B keeps 100 hours. A report predicts A must have the larger total output because its productivity gain is larger. Which comparison is correct?
macro.Choice A: A produces 96 and B produces 115; A’s larger productivity gain is outweighed by its hours reduction
macro.Choice B: A produces 120 and B produces 115; different worker hours cannot change the productivity ranking
macro.Choice C: A produces 80 and B produces 100; only hours matter once the productivity changes are identified
macro.Choice D: A produces 100 and B produces 115; a 20% productivity rise exactly cancels a 20% hours cut
macro.Correct Answer: A — A produces 96 and B produces 115; A’s larger productivity gain is outweighed by its hours reduction
macro.Feedback: Initially each produces one unit per hour. A’s new rate is 1.2 and output is 1.2×80=96; B’s rate is 1.15 and output is 1.15×100=115. Productivity and total output need not rank plants the same way, and equal opposite percentage changes do not cancel multiplicatively.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrect inference: Hourly productivity was unchanged; total output alone measures output per hour.
macro.Question: Training raises output per hour at a factory, but a reduction in operating hours leaves total output unchanged. A report says the training had no productivity benefit. Which correction follows?
macro.Choice A: Hourly productivity was unchanged; total output alone measures output per hour.
macro.Choice B: Hourly productivity fell; a reduction in hours directly lowers output per hour.
macro.Choice C: Physical capital must have increased; training cannot change productivity with fixed output.
macro.Choice D: Hourly productivity improved; fewer hours offset the gain in total output.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Hourly productivity improved; fewer hours offset the gain in total output.
macro.Feedback: Productivity and output are different measures. When output is unchanged and hours fall, output per hour rises. Lower hours can offset the total-output effect of improved skills.

macro.Question: SRAS slopes upward mainly because wages, prices, or perceptions:
macro.Choice A: Do not adjust instantly
macro.Choice B: Never change at all
macro.Choice C: Are always real variables
macro.Choice D: Cancel aggregate demand
macro.Correct Answer: A — Do not adjust instantly
macro.Feedback: Sticky wages, sticky prices, and misperceptions help explain upward-sloping SRAS.

macro.Question: If nominal wages are sticky and the price level rises unexpectedly, firms' real labor costs:
macro.Choice A: Fall, so output rises
macro.Choice B: Rise, so output falls
macro.Choice C: Stay fixed forever
macro.Choice D: Become money demand
macro.Correct Answer: A — Fall, so output rises
macro.Feedback: Sticky nominal wages mean a higher price level lowers real labor costs and can raise output.

macro.Common Misconception: Applying long-run neutrality to the short run.
macro.Question: The short-run aggregate supply curve slopes upward mainly because:
macro.Choice A: Wages, prices, or perceptions do not adjust instantly
macro.Choice B: Money is neutral in every period
macro.Choice C: Taxes cannot change
macro.Choice D: Output is fixed forever
macro.Correct Answer: A — Wages, prices, or perceptions do not adjust instantly
macro.Feedback: SRAS slopes upward because sticky wages, sticky prices, and misperceptions allow price-level changes to affect output.

macro.Common Misconception: Applying long-run neutrality to short-run wages.
macro.Question: Sticky-wage theory explains upward-sloping SRAS because unexpected price-level changes affect:
macro.Choice A: Real labor costs and firm production decisions
macro.Choice B: Only the money multiplier
macro.Choice C: Only net exports
macro.Choice D: The vertical position of LRPC
macro.Correct Answer: A — Real labor costs and firm production decisions
macro.Feedback: When nominal wages are sticky, price-level changes alter real labor costs and production.

macro.Question: Higher production costs shift SRAS:
macro.Choice A: Left
macro.Choice B: Right
macro.Choice C: Into AD
macro.Choice D: Into LRPC
macro.Correct Answer: A — Left
macro.Feedback: Higher production costs reduce SRAS and shift it left.

macro.Question: Lower production costs shift SRAS:
macro.Choice A: Right
macro.Choice B: Left
macro.Choice C: Into AD
macro.Choice D: Into money demand
macro.Correct Answer: A — Right
macro.Feedback: Lower production costs increase SRAS and shift it right.

macro.Question: Oil costs fall while aggregate demand is unchanged. What output/price combination follows from the resulting SRAS shift?
macro.Choice A: Both output and the price level rise
macro.Choice B: Output falls and the price level rises
macro.Choice C: Both output and the price level fall
macro.Choice D: Output rises and the price level falls
macro.Correct Answer: D — Output rises and the price level falls
macro.Feedback: Lower input costs shift SRAS right, increasing output and reducing the price level at the new demand intersection.

macro.Question: Higher expected prices usually shift SRAS:
macro.Choice A: Left
macro.Choice B: Right
macro.Choice C: Nowhere
macro.Choice D: Into AD
macro.Correct Answer: A — Left
macro.Feedback: Higher expected prices raise costs and shift SRAS left.

macro.Common Misconception: Treats higher expected costs as an increase in short-run supply.
macro.Question: Expected prices rise and new wage contracts raise nominal costs. With aggregate demand fixed, apply the SRAS shift to output and the price level.
macro.Choice A: Output rises and the price level falls
macro.Choice B: Output and the price level both fall
macro.Choice C: Output falls and the price level rises
macro.Choice D: Output and the price level both rise
macro.Correct Answer: C — Output falls and the price level rises
macro.Feedback: Higher expected wages/costs shift SRAS left. The intersection with unchanged AD has lower output and higher prices.

macro.Question: A leftward shift of SRAS means:
macro.Choice A: Firms supply less output at each price level
macro.Choice B: Aggregate demand rose
macro.Choice C: Potential output must have increased
macro.Choice D: The money supply fell by definition
macro.Correct Answer: A — Firms supply less output at each price level
macro.Feedback: A leftward SRAS shift reflects higher costs or lower productive capacity in the short run.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating production cost changes as AD shifts.
macro.Question: A decrease in oil prices would most likely shift:
macro.Choice A: SRAS right
macro.Choice B: AD left
macro.Choice C: LRPC right
macro.Choice D: Money demand left
macro.Correct Answer: A — SRAS right
macro.Feedback: Lower production costs shift short-run aggregate supply to the right.

macro.Common Misconception: Reversing AS1 and AS2.
macro.Question: Refer to the graph. Moving from AS2 to AS1 represents:
macro.Choice A: A decrease in short-run aggregate supply
macro.Choice B: An increase in short-run aggregate supply
macro.Choice C: An increase in aggregate demand
macro.Choice D: A fall in money demand
macro.Correct Answer: A — A decrease in short-run aggregate supply
macro.Feedback: AS1 is up and left of AS2, so moving from AS2 to AS1 is a decrease in SRAS.

macro.Common Misconception: Reversing expected price effects on SRAS.
macro.Question: If expected prices rise, short-run aggregate supply usually shifts:
macro.Choice A: Right because real wages fall
macro.Choice B: Left because production costs rise
macro.Choice C: Right because AD increases
macro.Choice D: Left because LRAS moves
macro.Correct Answer: B — Left because production costs rise
macro.Feedback: Higher expected prices push wages and costs upward, shifting SRAS left.

macro.Common Misconception: Reading a positive SRAS shift backward.
macro.Question: Refer to the graph. If the economy moves from AD1-AS1 to AD1-AS2, what happens?
macro.Choice A: Output rises and prices fall
macro.Choice B: Output falls and prices rise
macro.Choice C: Output rises and prices rise
macro.Choice D: Output falls and prices fall
macro.Correct Answer: A — Output rises and prices fall
macro.Feedback: Moving from AS1 to AS2 along AD1 raises output from Y3 to Y1 and lowers the price level from P2 to P1.

macro.Question: If output is below potential because AD is weak, policy that shifts AD right is:
macro.Choice A: Expansionary
macro.Choice B: Contractionary
macro.Choice C: Neutral
macro.Choice D: A supply shock
macro.Correct Answer: A — Expansionary
macro.Feedback: Expansionary policy shifts AD right and can help close a recessionary gap.

macro.Common Misconception: Assumes a delayed policy has the same stabilizing effect regardless of how the economy changes before implementation.
macro.Question: A stimulus is approved during a recession but takes effect only after output has returned close to potential. What risk does the delayed stimulus create?
macro.Choice A: The delayed stimulus can push aggregate demand too far right after the original gap has faded.
macro.Choice B: The delay automatically turns the stimulus into contractionary policy.
macro.Choice C: The policy can no longer affect aggregate demand once recovery begins.
macro.Choice D: The delay directly shifts LRAS left.
macro.Correct Answer: A — The delayed stimulus can push aggregate demand too far right after the original gap has faded.
macro.Feedback: A policy can destabilize the economy if it arrives after the original gap has already narrowed or reversed.

macro.Common Misconception: Choosing tighter policy in a recessionary gap.
macro.Question: A recessionary AD gap can be addressed with:
macro.Choice A: Expansionary monetary or fiscal policy
macro.Choice B: Contractionary policy only
macro.Choice C: Higher taxes only
macro.Choice D: Lower government spending only
macro.Correct Answer: A — Expansionary monetary or fiscal policy
macro.Feedback: Expansionary policy can shift AD right.

macro.Common Misconception: Treats a negative supply shock as if policymakers can simultaneously eliminate its inflation and output effects by shifting AD.
macro.Question: A negative supply shock lowers real output and raises the price level. If policymakers use expansionary demand policy to support output, what tradeoff do policymakers face?
macro.Choice A: It can support output while worsening inflation pressure.
macro.Choice B: It lowers the price level and raises output with no tradeoff.
macro.Choice C: It directly shifts SRAS right and restores productive capacity.
macro.Choice D: It must reduce both output and the price level.
macro.Correct Answer: A — It can support output while worsening inflation pressure.
macro.Feedback: Demand stabilization during a negative supply shock involves a tradeoff: supporting output can worsen price pressure, while reducing inflation can deepen the output loss.

macro.Common Misconception: Choosing expansionary policy during overheating.
macro.Question: During an inflationary boom caused by excessive AD, policymakers may use:
macro.Choice A: Contractionary monetary or fiscal policy
macro.Choice B: Expansionary policy only
macro.Choice C: Tax cuts and bond purchases
macro.Choice D: Higher government spending
macro.Correct Answer: A — Contractionary monetary or fiscal policy
macro.Feedback: Contractionary policy shifts AD left and reduces inflation pressure.

macro.Common Misconception: Targets a historical gap without allowing for recovery during the policy lag.
macro.Question: After a demand recession, falling wages are already shifting SRAS right toward recovery. A stimulus takes a year to arrive. What fact is most relevant to whether it will stabilize output at arrival?
macro.Choice A: Only the size of the gap when the recession began
macro.Choice B: Whether the original shock was measured in dollars
macro.Choice C: Whether the economy has ever used fiscal policy before
macro.Choice D: The expected remaining gap when the stimulus arrives
macro.Correct Answer: D — The expected remaining gap when the stimulus arrives
macro.Feedback: Compare the intervention with conditions at implementation. Existing self-correction can reduce or eliminate the gap before delayed stimulus arrives.

macro.Common Misconception: Not comparing stimulus size to the recessionary gap.
macro.Question: A recessionary AD gap is $300 billion. Policy raises spending by $75 billion and the multiplier is 4. What happens?
macro.Choice A: The gap closes exactly
macro.Choice B: A $75 billion gap remains
macro.Choice C: AD overshoots by $75 billion
macro.Choice D: The gap is unchanged
macro.Correct Answer: A — The gap closes exactly
macro.Feedback: $75 billion x 4 = $300 billion, so the gap closes exactly.

macro.Common Misconception: Stops with an AD shift and does not connect the short-run output response to unemployment and inflation pressure.
macro.Question: Contractionary stabilization policy shifts AD left to cool an overheating economy. Which short-run labor-market effect connects this policy choice to Phillips-curve analysis?
macro.Choice A: Unemployment tends to rise as output weakens while inflation pressure falls.
macro.Choice B: Unemployment must fall because lower AD always increases hiring.
macro.Choice C: Unemployment is unchanged because only the price level responds to AD.
macro.Choice D: The natural rate permanently falls by the size of the AD shift.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Unemployment tends to rise as output weakens while inflation pressure falls.
macro.Feedback: A contractionary stabilization policy that lowers AD can reduce inflation pressure while raising unemployment in the short run, creating the bridge to Phillips-curve analysis.

macro.Common Misconception: Thinking stabilization policy works instantly
macro.Question: A policy lag is a reason stabilization policy can be risky because policy actions may
macro.Choice A: take effect after conditions have already changed
macro.Choice B: instantly fix every shock
macro.Choice C: remove the need for aggregate demand
macro.Choice D: make money supply impossible to change
macro.Correct Answer: A — take effect after conditions have already changed
macro.Feedback: Policy lags matter because by the time policy takes effect, the economy may have already changed.

macro.Common Misconception: Choosing contractionary policy during weak demand
macro.Question: If a recession lowers aggregate demand, a stabilization policy response could be
macro.Choice A: expansionary monetary or fiscal policy
macro.Choice B: lower government spending and lower money supply
macro.Choice C: higher taxes and higher interest rates
macro.Choice D: doing anything that shifts AD left
macro.Correct Answer: A — expansionary monetary or fiscal policy
macro.Feedback: If aggregate demand is too low, expansionary policy can help shift AD right.

macro.Common Misconception: Using expansionary policy when AD is already too strong
macro.Question: If aggregate demand is pushing output above its natural level and raising inflation pressure, policymakers might use
macro.Choice A: contractionary monetary or fiscal policy
macro.Choice B: higher government spending and lower interest rates
macro.Choice C: tax cuts and bond purchases
macro.Choice D: only policies that shift AD right
macro.Correct Answer: A — contractionary monetary or fiscal policy
macro.Feedback: When AD is too high and inflation pressure builds, contractionary policy can shift AD left.

macro.Common Misconception: Thinking stabilization policy is meant to eliminate scarcity
macro.Question: One argument in favor of stabilization policy is that it can help offset
macro.Choice A: shocks to aggregate demand
macro.Choice B: all scarcity forever
macro.Choice C: the need for banks
macro.Choice D: every long-run productivity problem instantly
macro.Correct Answer: A — shocks to aggregate demand
macro.Feedback: Supporters argue stabilization policy can reduce the damage caused by short-run aggregate demand shocks.

macro.Common Misconception: Thinking policy timing is never a problem
macro.Question: One argument against aggressive stabilization policy is that
macro.Choice A: policy lags can cause actions to hit the economy too late
macro.Choice B: monetary and fiscal policy always work instantly
macro.Choice C: aggregate demand never changes
macro.Choice D: interest rates cannot affect spending
macro.Correct Answer: A — policy lags can cause actions to hit the economy too late
macro.Feedback: Critics warn that policy lags can make stabilization efforts arrive after the economy has already changed.

macro.Common Misconception: Thinking late expansionary policy is harmless
macro.Question: If policymakers respond too late to a recession that has already recovered, expansionary policy may
macro.Choice A: overstimulate aggregate demand
macro.Choice B: automatically reduce inflation
macro.Choice C: shift aggregate demand left
macro.Choice D: make money demand disappear
macro.Correct Answer: A — overstimulate aggregate demand
macro.Feedback: If expansionary policy arrives after recovery is underway, it can push aggregate demand too far and create inflation pressure.

macro.Common Misconception: Thinking timing never matters
macro.Question: Why can stabilization policy accidentally destabilize the economy?
macro.Choice A: Policy lags can make action arrive after conditions change.
macro.Choice B: Policy always takes effect instantly.
macro.Choice C: Aggregate demand never responds to policy.
macro.Choice D: The Fed cannot change the money supply.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Policy lags can make action arrive after conditions change.
macro.Feedback: Policy lags can make a policy hit after the original problem has faded, creating a new problem.

macro.Common Misconception: Choosing contractionary policy during a demand slump
macro.Question: If a negative demand shock pushes output below its natural level, stabilization policy would most likely try to
macro.Choice A: shift aggregate demand right
macro.Choice B: shift aggregate demand left
macro.Choice C: reduce output further
macro.Choice D: raise unemployment intentionally
macro.Correct Answer: A — shift aggregate demand right
macro.Feedback: A negative demand shock reduces output, so stabilization policy would typically try to shift AD right.

macro.Common Misconception: Stimulating AD when inflation pressure is already high
macro.Question: If aggregate demand is too high and inflation pressure is building, stabilization policy would most likely try to
macro.Choice A: shift aggregate demand left
macro.Choice B: shift aggregate demand right
macro.Choice C: increase government spending
macro.Choice D: lower interest rates
macro.Correct Answer: A — shift aggregate demand left
macro.Feedback: If AD is too strong, contractionary policy can shift AD left and reduce inflation pressure.

macro.Common Misconception: Thinking stabilization policy is meant to solve every economic problem
macro.Question: A key argument for active stabilization policy is that policymakers can
macro.Choice A: counteract short-run aggregate demand shocks
macro.Choice B: eliminate scarcity permanently
macro.Choice C: make all real variables nominal
macro.Choice D: force velocity to equal zero
macro.Correct Answer: A — counteract short-run aggregate demand shocks
macro.Feedback: Supporters argue that active policy can reduce the damage caused by short-run AD shocks.

macro.Common Misconception: Thinking stabilization policy works instantly and perfectly
macro.Question: A key argument against aggressive stabilization policy is that
macro.Choice A: policy lags can cause poorly timed interventions
macro.Choice B: AD never changes
macro.Choice C: the Fed cannot affect interest rates
macro.Choice D: government spending is not part of aggregate demand
macro.Correct Answer: A — policy lags can cause poorly timed interventions
macro.Feedback: Policy lags can cause interventions to arrive after conditions have already changed.

macro.Common Misconception: Thinking wrong policy timing has no cost
macro.Question: If policymakers misread a temporary shock as a lasting recession, they risk
macro.Choice A: overstimulating aggregate demand
macro.Choice B: making aggregate demand vanish
macro.Choice C: ending the money multiplier
macro.Choice D: turning fiat money into commodity money
macro.Correct Answer: A — overstimulating aggregate demand
macro.Feedback: If policymakers stimulate after the economy is already recovering, they may push AD too far.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating every downturn as only an aggregate demand problem
macro.Question: A pandemic reduces production and also weakens spending. Why is stabilization policy harder here than with a simple demand shock?
macro.Choice A: Because both supply and demand may be affected.
macro.Choice B: Because monetary policy cannot affect interest rates in any economy.
macro.Choice C: Because fiscal policy cannot affect aggregate demand.
macro.Choice D: Because money demand must be zero during pandemics.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Because both supply and demand may be affected.
macro.Feedback: A mixed shock is harder because policy may support demand, but it cannot instantly fix lost production capacity.

macro.Common Misconception: Mixing expansionary and contractionary tools
macro.Question: Which policy mix is most expansionary for aggregate demand?
macro.Choice A: Fed buys bonds and Congress increases government spending.
macro.Choice B: Fed sells bonds and Congress raises taxes.
macro.Choice C: Fed sells bonds and Congress cuts spending.
macro.Choice D: Fed raises interest rates and Congress raises taxes.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Fed buys bonds and Congress increases government spending.
macro.Feedback: Fed bond purchases are expansionary monetary policy, and higher government spending is expansionary fiscal policy.

macro.Common Misconception: Thinking bond sales are expansionary
macro.Question: Which policy mix is most contractionary for aggregate demand?
macro.Choice A: Fed sells bonds and Congress raises taxes.
macro.Choice B: Fed buys bonds and Congress cuts taxes.
macro.Choice C: Fed buys bonds and Congress increases spending.
macro.Choice D: Fed lowers interest rates and Congress increases transfers.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Fed sells bonds and Congress raises taxes.
macro.Feedback: Fed bond sales reduce money supply, and tax increases reduce consumption. Both push AD left.

macro.Common Misconception: Thinking late stimulus is always harmless
macro.Question: A recession is already ending, but expansionary fiscal policy passed months earlier now takes effect. What is the risk?
macro.Choice A: AD may be pushed too far right, creating inflation pressure.
macro.Choice B: AD must shift left automatically.
macro.Choice C: Interest rates must fall to zero forever.
macro.Choice D: The money multiplier becomes zero.
macro.Correct Answer: A — AD may be pushed too far right, creating inflation pressure.
macro.Feedback: Late stimulus can overstimulate demand after recovery is already underway.

macro.Common Misconception: Thinking all rightward AD shifts are good regardless of starting point
macro.Question: If the economy is already near full employment and fiscal policy shifts AD right through the multiplier, what risk becomes more important?
macro.Choice A: Inflation pressure from excessive AD
macro.Choice B: Deflation from collapsing AD
macro.Choice C: A lower price level from higher government spending
macro.Choice D: A smaller price level because MPC is positive
macro.Correct Answer: A — Inflation pressure from excessive AD
macro.Feedback: If the economy is already near capacity, more AD can create inflation pressure instead of useful output gains.

macro.Common Misconception: Not comparing the graph's AD shift with the size of the gap
macro.Question: If the economy initially needed AD to fall by $300 billion and the MS1 to MS2 movement reduces AD by $200 billion, what remains?
macro.Choice A: $100 billion of excess AD remains.
macro.Choice B: The overheating gap closes exactly.
macro.Choice C: AD overshoots by $100 billion.
macro.Choice D: Output rises from Y2 to Y1.
macro.Correct Answer: A — $100 billion of excess AD remains.
macro.Feedback: The graph shows AD shifting left. If AD needed to fall $300 billion but falls $200 billion, $100 billion of excess AD remains.

macro.Common Misconception: Adding both policies in the same direction without checking graph direction
macro.Question: The MS1 to MS2 movement causes AD to shift left by $180 billion. A separate fiscal expansion shifts AD right by $60 billion. What is the net AD change?
macro.Choice A: AD falls by $120 billion.
macro.Choice B: AD falls by $240 billion.
macro.Choice C: AD rises by $120 billion.
macro.Choice D: AD rises by $60 billion.
macro.Correct Answer: A — AD falls by $120 billion.
macro.Feedback: The graph's monetary policy lowers AD by $180 billion. Fiscal policy raises AD by $60 billion. Net AD falls by $120 billion.

macro.Common Misconception: Not matching the leftward AD shift in the graph before adding the fiscal offset
macro.Question: The monetary-policy movement shifts AD left by $160 billion. Fiscal expansion shifts AD right by $160 billion. What is the net AD effect?
macro.Choice A: Zero—equal and opposite shifts.
macro.Choice B: AD falls $160 billion.
macro.Choice C: AD rises $160 billion.
macro.Choice D: AD falls $320 billion.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Zero—equal and opposite shifts.
macro.Feedback: The graph shows monetary policy shifting AD left. A fiscal expansion of the same size shifts AD right by the same amount, so the net AD effect is zero.

macro.Common Misconception: Doubling down on contraction after AD falls
macro.Question: Congress cuts government spending to reduce the deficit. If the Fed wants to stabilize output, what should it do?
macro.Choice A: Increase money supply to lower interest rates and support AD.
macro.Choice B: Decrease money supply to raise interest rates and reduce AD further.
macro.Choice C: Raise taxes to lower consumption further.
macro.Choice D: Do nothing because fiscal policy cannot affect AD.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Increase money supply to lower interest rates and support AD.
macro.Feedback: A spending cut shifts AD left. Expansionary monetary policy can partly offset that.

macro.Common Misconception: Using expansionary policy after a positive demand shock
macro.Question: A stock market boom increases household wealth and pushes output above its natural level. If the Fed wants to stabilize output, it should
macro.Choice A: reduce money supply and raise interest rates
macro.Choice B: increase money supply and lower interest rates
macro.Choice C: increase government spending
macro.Choice D: cut taxes
macro.Correct Answer: A — reduce money supply and raise interest rates
macro.Feedback: A positive AD shock can push output too high, so contractionary monetary policy can stabilize output.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating every downturn like a demand shock
macro.Question: A supply shock reduces output and raises prices. Why is the policy response harder than for a pure demand shock?
macro.Choice A: Stimulating AD may raise output somewhat but can worsen inflation.
macro.Choice B: Stimulating AD always lowers prices and raises output with no tradeoff.
macro.Choice C: Contractionary policy always raises output.
macro.Choice D: Supply shocks only affect money demand.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Stimulating AD may raise output somewhat but can worsen inflation.
macro.Feedback: A supply shock creates a tradeoff: boosting aggregate demand may support output but can add inflation pressure.

macro.Common Misconception: Using contractionary policy against weak demand
macro.Question: A negative AD shock reduces output and the price level. Which policy response best targets the shock without relying on supply-side repair?
macro.Choice A: Expansionary monetary or fiscal policy to shift AD right
macro.Choice B: Contractionary policy to shift AD left
macro.Choice C: Higher taxes and lower government spending
macro.Choice D: A policy that reduces investment spending
macro.Correct Answer: A — Expansionary monetary or fiscal policy to shift AD right
macro.Feedback: A negative AD shock calls for policies that shift AD right if the goal is stabilizing output.

macro.Common Misconception: Stimulating an economy that is already overheating
macro.Question: An economy is above potential output because AD is too high. Which response best reduces the boom without increasing AD further?
macro.Choice A: Contractionary monetary policy or contractionary fiscal policy
macro.Choice B: Expansionary monetary policy and tax cuts
macro.Choice C: Higher government spending and lower interest rates
macro.Choice D: Bond purchases and larger deficits
macro.Correct Answer: A — Contractionary monetary policy or contractionary fiscal policy
macro.Feedback: When AD is too high, contractionary policy can shift AD left and reduce inflation pressure.

macro.Common Misconception: Choosing tighter money during a demand slump
macro.Question: Suppose output is below its natural level because AD is weak. Which Fed action through the money market would move AD in the stabilizing direction?
macro.Choice A: Shift money supply right to lower r and raise investment.
macro.Choice B: Shift money supply left to raise r and lower investment.
macro.Choice C: Shift money demand right to raise r and lower investment.
macro.Choice D: Keep money supply fixed and raise taxes.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Shift money supply right to lower r and raise investment.
macro.Feedback: When AD is weak, expansionary monetary policy shifts MS right, lowers rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

macro.Common Misconception: Stimulating AD when output is already above natural level
macro.Question: Suppose output is above its natural level because AD is too strong. Which Fed action through the money market would move AD in the stabilizing direction?
macro.Choice A: Shift money supply left to raise r and lower investment.
macro.Choice B: Shift money supply right to lower r and raise investment.
macro.Choice C: Shift money demand left to lower r and raise investment.
macro.Choice D: Cut taxes to raise consumption.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Shift money supply left to raise r and lower investment.
macro.Feedback: When AD is too strong, tighter money shifts MS left, raises rates, lowers investment, and shifts AD left.

macro.Common Misconception: Not comparing stimulus size to the original AD shortfall
macro.Question: A recession lowers AD by $300 billion. The government increases spending by $100 billion and MPC is 0.5. Ignoring crowding out, what remains of the AD shortfall?
macro.Choice A: $100 billion
macro.Choice B: $200 billion
macro.Choice D: $300 billion
macro.Correct Answer: A — $100 billion
macro.Feedback: MPC 0.5 gives multiplier 2. A $100 billion spending increase shifts AD by $200 billion, leaving a $100 billion shortfall.

macro.Common Misconception: Missing that Fed bond sales are contractionary
macro.Question: Congress cuts spending during a recession while the Fed also sells bonds. What is the combined AD effect?
macro.Choice A: Both policies shift AD left or reduce support for AD, worsening the demand problem.
macro.Choice B: Both policies shift AD right, stabilizing output.
macro.Choice C: Fiscal policy shifts AD right while monetary policy shifts AD right.
macro.Choice D: Neither policy affects AD.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Both policies shift AD left or reduce support for AD, worsening the demand problem.
macro.Feedback: Cutting spending reduces AD, and Fed bond sales raise rates and reduce investment. That is contraction on top of contraction.

macro.Common Misconception: Thinking expansionary policy is always appropriate
macro.Question: Congress raises spending during an inflationary boom while the Fed buys bonds. What is the combined AD effect?
macro.Choice A: Both policies shift AD right, risking more inflation pressure.
macro.Choice B: Both policies shift AD left, reducing inflation pressure.
macro.Choice C: Fiscal policy shifts AD left while monetary policy shifts AD left.
macro.Choice D: Neither affects AD because output is already high.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Both policies shift AD right, risking more inflation pressure.
macro.Feedback: Spending increases and bond purchases both shift AD right. During an inflationary boom, that pours gasoline on the fire.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating supply shocks like pure demand shocks
macro.Question: A negative supply shock reduces output and raises prices. Why can expansionary AD policy be a blunt tool here?
macro.Choice A: It may raise output somewhat but can worsen the price-level increase.
macro.Choice B: It directly restores lost productive capacity with no inflation risk.
macro.Choice C: It shifts SRAS right automatically.
macro.Choice D: It lowers prices and lowers output at the same time.
macro.Correct Answer: A — It may raise output somewhat but can worsen the price-level increase.
macro.Feedback: AD stimulus can support spending, but it does not fix the supply loss and may worsen inflation.

macro.Common Misconception: Not distinguishing AD shocks from AS shocks
macro.Question: A negative demand shock reduces output and prices. Why is expansionary monetary policy more directly suited to this case than to a pure supply shock?
macro.Choice A: It targets weak spending by lowering r and raising investment.
macro.Choice B: It directly increases labor, capital, and natural resources.
macro.Choice C: It shifts SRAS right by changing the reserve ratio.
macro.Choice D: It lowers AD to reduce output further.
macro.Correct Answer: A — It targets weak spending by lowering r and raising investment.
macro.Feedback: Expansionary monetary policy works through spending, so it is more directly suited to weak AD than to lost productive capacity.

macro.Common Misconception: Thinking late stimulus is harmless because it was originally well-intended
macro.Question: A policy is passed to fight a recession, but because of recognition, implementation, and impact lags, it takes effect after output has already recovered. What is the likely stabilization problem?
macro.Choice A: The delayed policy can push AD too far right and create inflation pressure.
macro.Choice B: The delayed policy must shift AD left automatically.
macro.Choice C: The delayed policy cannot affect AD after recovery.
macro.Choice D: The delayed policy eliminates crowding out.
macro.Correct Answer: A — The delayed policy can push AD too far right and create inflation pressure.
macro.Feedback: Good timing matters. Late expansion can overstimulate AD after the recession has already passed.

macro.Common Misconception: Not dividing the AD target by the multiplier
macro.Question: A contractionary monetary-policy move must reduce AD by $240 billion. If MPC = 0.75, what investment decrease is needed to produce that AD movement?
macro.Choice A: $60 billion
macro.Choice B: $240 billion
macro.Choice C: $80 billion
macro.Choice D: $180 billion
macro.Correct Answer: A — $60 billion
macro.Feedback: The graph shows a leftward AD movement. MPC = 0.75 gives multiplier 4, so investment must fall by $240 billion / 4 = $60 billion.

macro.Common Misconception: Failing to compare the multiplied AD effect to the needed AD change
macro.Question: The Fed pushes r high enough to reduce investment by $90 billion, but AD only needed to move left by $240 billion. If MPC = 0.75, what happens?
macro.Choice A: AD falls $360 billion, overshooting by $120 billion.
macro.Choice B: AD falls $240 billion, closing the gap exactly.
macro.Choice C: AD falls $90 billion, leaving $150 billion.
macro.Choice D: AD rises $360 billion.
macro.Correct Answer: A — AD falls $360 billion, overshooting by $120 billion.
macro.Feedback: The graph shows AD moving left. MPC = 0.75 gives multiplier 4, so a $90 billion investment fall lowers AD by $360 billion, overshooting by $120 billion.

macro.Common Misconception: Calculating the multiplier but ignoring the order: initial shift, multiplied shift, crowding-out offset
macro.Question: At a fixed reference price level, desired spending is $250 billion below the policy target. Government purchases rise by $50 billion and MPC = 0.75. Use the simple spending multiplier with no other leakages. Crowding out produces a total $40 billion AD offset, including its induced spending effects. Which decomposition gives the net AD shift and remaining shortfall at that reference price?
macro.Choice A: Direct AD shift $50 billion; multiplied shift $200 billion; net shift $160 billion; gap $90 billion
macro.Choice B: Direct AD shift $50 billion; multiplied shift $150 billion; net shift $110 billion; gap $140 billion
macro.Choice C: Direct AD shift $50 billion; multiplied shift $200 billion; net shift $200 billion; gap $50 billion
macro.Choice D: Direct AD shift $50 billion; multiplied shift $200 billion; net shift $40 billion; gap $210 billion
macro.Correct Answer: A — Direct AD shift $50 billion; multiplied shift $200 billion; net shift $160 billion; gap $90 billion
macro.Feedback: MPC = 0.75 gives multiplier 4. The $50 billion initial shift becomes $200 billion, then crowding out lowers the net shift to $160 billion, leaving a $90 billion gap. These are horizontal AD distances at the reference price, not actual equilibrium GDP changes; the total offset is not multiplied again.

macro.Common Misconception: Thinking any rightward AD shift is good regardless of the starting gap
macro.Question: At a fixed reference price level, desired spending already exceeds the policy target by $180 billion. Purchases rise by $30 billion and MPC = 0.8. With the simple spending multiplier and no offsets, which interpretation of the policy is correct?
macro.Choice A: The direct $30 billion increase becomes a $150 billion AD shift, raising excess desired spending to $330 billion at the reference price.
macro.Choice B: The policy shifts AD left by $150 billion, reducing excess desired spending to $30 billion.
macro.Choice C: Only the direct $30 billion enters AD, raising excess desired spending to $210 billion.
macro.Choice D: The $150 billion AD shift exactly removes the existing $180 billion excess.
macro.Correct Answer: A — The direct $30 billion increase becomes a $150 billion AD shift, raising excess desired spending to $330 billion at the reference price.
macro.Feedback: The multiplier is 5, so desired spending at the reference price rises by $150 billion. The excess becomes 180 + 150 = $330 billion. An upward-sloping SRAS would divide the equilibrium response between output and prices; these AD distances do not determine the GDP gap.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing the first AD shift with the final multiplied AD shift
macro.Question: At a fixed reference price, desired spending is $400 billion below the policy target. Government purchases rise by $100 billion and MPC = 0.75. Using the simple spending multiplier and ignoring crowding out and other leakages, which decomposition gives the AD shift and remaining horizontal AD gap?
macro.Choice A: AD first shifts right $100 billion, then the multiplier expands the shift to $400 billion, closing the gap.
macro.Choice B: AD first shifts right $400 billion, then falls back to $100 billion, leaving a $300 billion gap.
macro.Choice C: AD first shifts left $100 billion, then left $400 billion, worsening the gap.
macro.Choice D: AD shifts right $100 billion only, leaving a $300 billion gap.
macro.Correct Answer: A — AD first shifts right $100 billion, then the multiplier expands the shift to $400 billion, closing the gap.
macro.Feedback: The multiplier is 4. Direct purchases of $100 billion imply a total $400 billion AD shift, closing the stated horizontal AD gap. Without an SRAS relationship, this does not identify an equal equilibrium GDP increase.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The correct current arithmetic guarantees the program is stabilizing at any arrival date” in this stabilization policy task.
macro.Question: A recessionary output gap is $80. In a fixed-price simple model with MPC 0.75 and no crowding out, a purchases program of $20 would close it. The program cannot begin until after the gap is forecast to close. Which assessment is valid?
macro.Choice A: The correct current arithmetic guarantees the program is stabilizing at any arrival date
macro.Choice B: The program must be too small because a fourfold multiplier never applies to purchases
macro.Choice C: The forecast means the current gap should be counted as an expansionary gap instead
macro.Choice D: The size matches the current gap, but the implementation lag can make it excessive when it arrives
macro.Correct Answer: D — The size matches the current gap, but the implementation lag can make it excessive when it arrives
macro.Feedback: The current calculation is 4×20=80. Timing is separate: a program arriving after recovery can add excess demand even if its initial size was correct.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrect inference: Support: output rises, inflation falls; restraint: output falls, inflation rises.
macro.Question: An adverse supply shock reduces output by 30 and raises inflation. Which policy comparison recognizes the constraint facing demand management?
macro.Choice A: Support: output rises, inflation falls; restraint: output falls, inflation rises.
macro.Choice B: Support: output and inflation fall; restraint: output and inflation rise.
macro.Choice C: Support: output and inflation rise; restraint: output and inflation fall.
macro.Choice D: Support: potential output rises; restraint: potential output falls by reversing the disruption.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Support: output and inflation rise; restraint: output and inflation fall.
macro.Feedback: An adverse supply shock worsens the inflation-output tradeoff. Demand management changes the position on that tradeoff; it does not directly repair the supply cause.

macro.Common Misconception: Not subtracting crowding out after applying the multiplier
macro.Question: At a fixed reference price, AD must shift right by $500 billion to meet the policy target. Monetary policy raises autonomous investment by $50 billion, government purchases rise by $60 billion, and fiscal crowding out reduces autonomous investment by $40 billion. MPC = 0.75; apply the same simple multiplier to each autonomous change, with no other leakages. What AD shortfall remains?
macro.Choice A: $220 billion remains.
macro.Choice B: $100 billion remains.
macro.Choice C: $60 billion remains.
macro.Choice D: $460 billion remains.
macro.Correct Answer: A — $220 billion remains.
macro.Feedback: Net autonomous spending rises by 50 + 60 − 40 = $70 billion. The multiplier is 1/(1 − 0.75) = 4, so AD shifts $280 billion and the remaining horizontal shortfall is 500 − 280 = $220 billion. Subtracting only $40 billion after multiplying the gross impulse would omit the lost induced spending.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Both are discretionary because all budget amounts changed” in this stabilization policy task.
macro.Question: In a recession, existing rules reduce taxes by $40 and raise benefits. Lawmakers later pass a separate increase in government purchases. Recovery begins before the spending increase takes effect. Which of these changes can reverse during recovery without another vote by lawmakers?
macro.Choice A: Taxes and benefits can reverse under existing rules; the purchases remain discretionary despite their delayed arrival.
macro.Choice B: All changes reverse automatically because each originally supported aggregate demand.
macro.Choice C: Only the purchases reverse automatically, because passage during a recession makes them an automatic stabilizer.
macro.Choice D: None can reverse without a new vote, because every change in a budget amount is discretionary.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Taxes and benefits can reverse under existing rules; the purchases remain discretionary despite their delayed arrival.
macro.Feedback: Automatic stabilizers depend on economic conditions under already-enacted rules, so recovery can reverse their recession response. A separately legislated purchases program remains discretionary; its timing does not reclassify how it was authorized.

macro.Common Misconception: Using the investment decrease without applying the multiplier
macro.Question: At a fixed reference price, desired spending exceeds the policy target by $360 billion. Contractionary monetary policy reduces autonomous investment by $50 billion. MPC = 0.8; use the simple spending multiplier with no other leakages. What excess desired spending remains at that reference price?
macro.Choice A: $110 billion
macro.Choice B: $250 billion
macro.Choice C: $50 billion
macro.Choice D: No gap remains; policy overshoots by $110 billion.
macro.Correct Answer: A — $110 billion
macro.Feedback: The investment decline shifts AD left by 50/(1 − 0.8) = $250 billion. Excess desired spending falls to 360 − 250 = $110 billion. This is an AD-distance calculation, not a claim that the equilibrium GDP gap falls one-for-one.

macro.Common Misconception: Forgetting that crowding out reduces the gross multiplier effect
macro.Question: At a fixed reference price level, desired spending is $600 billion below the policy target. Government purchases rise by $100 billion and MPC = 0.8. Use the simple spending multiplier with no other leakages. Crowding out produces a total $150 billion AD offset, including its induced spending effects. Which decomposition gives the net AD shift and remaining shortfall at that reference price?
macro.Choice A: AD first shifts right $100 billion, then gross shift reaches $500 billion, then crowding out leaves $350 billion net and a $250 billion gap.
macro.Choice B: AD first shifts right $600 billion, then crowding out leaves $450 billion net and a $150 billion gap.
macro.Choice C: AD first shifts left $100 billion, then gross shift reaches $500 billion, worsening the gap.
macro.Choice D: AD shifts right only $100 billion because crowding out cancels the multiplier.
macro.Correct Answer: A — AD first shifts right $100 billion, then gross shift reaches $500 billion, then crowding out leaves $350 billion net and a $250 billion gap.
macro.Feedback: MPC 0.8 gives multiplier 5, so gross shift is $500 billion. Net after $150 billion crowding out is $350 billion, leaving a $250 billion gap. These are horizontal AD distances at the reference price, not actual equilibrium GDP changes; the total offset is not multiplied again.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “AD rises $50; fiscal policy must dominate any monetary action” in this stabilization policy task.
macro.Question: Monetary restraint reduces aggregate demand by a total $150 while an already-enacted fiscal program adds a total $100. Output initially equals potential and supply is fixed. Fiscal policy cannot be changed. To leave net demand unchanged, how should the monetary restraint be recalibrated?
macro.Choice A: Reduce its total demand contraction to $100; the current combination leaves a $50 net decline.
macro.Choice B: Increase its total demand contraction to $250, because opposing policies require adding both magnitudes.
macro.Choice C: Keep it at $150, because opposite directions guarantee an exact offset regardless of amounts.
macro.Choice D: Reverse it into a $50 expansion, because a positive fiscal effect always requires positive monetary support.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Reduce its total demand contraction to $100; the current combination leaves a $50 net decline.
macro.Feedback: Current total effects sum to −150+100=−50. With the fiscal total fixed, a monetary total of−100 gives zero net demand change. These are already-total effects, so no additional multiplier is applied.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The forecast means the current gap should be counted as an expansionary gap instead” in this stabilization policy task.
macro.Question: A recessionary output gap is $240. In a fixed-price simple model with MPC 0.75 and no crowding out, a purchases program of $60 would close it. The program cannot begin until after the gap is forecast to close. Which assessment is valid?
macro.Choice A: The forecast means the current gap should be counted as an expansionary gap instead
macro.Choice B: The size matches the current gap, but the implementation lag can make it excessive when it arrives
macro.Choice C: The correct current arithmetic guarantees the program is stabilizing at any arrival date
macro.Choice D: The program must be too small because a fourfold multiplier never applies to purchases
macro.Correct Answer: B — The size matches the current gap, but the implementation lag can make it excessive when it arrives
macro.Feedback: The current calculation is 4×60=240. Timing is separate: a program arriving after recovery can add excess demand even if its initial size was correct.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrect inference: Support: output rises, inflation falls; restraint: output falls, inflation rises.
macro.Question: An adverse supply shock reduces output by 70 and raises inflation. Which policy comparison recognizes the constraint facing demand management?
macro.Choice A: Support: output and inflation rise; restraint: output and inflation fall.
macro.Choice B: Support: output rises, inflation falls; restraint: output falls, inflation rises.
macro.Choice C: Support: output and inflation fall; restraint: output and inflation rise.
macro.Choice D: Support: potential output rises; restraint: potential output falls by reversing the disruption.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Support: output and inflation rise; restraint: output and inflation fall.
macro.Feedback: An adverse supply shock worsens the inflation-output tradeoff. Demand management changes the position on that tradeoff; it does not directly repair the supply cause.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring crowding out and expectations.
macro.Question: The economy is below potential. Fiscal expansion begins, but interest rates rise and inflation expectations increase. Which policy assessment is strongest?
macro.Choice A: The policy may close part of the gap, but crowding out and expectations weaken the case.
macro.Choice B: The policy permanently lowers unemployment because the SRPC becomes the LRPC.
macro.Choice C: The policy shifts SRAS right because higher AD lowers production costs.
macro.Choice D: The policy has no effect because fiscal policy cannot move AD.
macro.Correct Answer: A — The policy may close part of the gap, but crowding out and expectations weaken the case.
macro.Feedback: Fiscal expansion can support AD, but crowding out and rising inflation expectations can reduce or complicate the effect.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring demand effects of spending cuts.
macro.Question: Congress cuts spending to reduce deficits during a recession. What policy concern is most direct?
macro.Choice A: AD may fall further before recovery
macro.Choice B: SRAS must shift right instantly
macro.Choice C: Inflation must rise immediately
macro.Choice D: LRPC must become horizontal
macro.Correct Answer: A — AD may fall further before recovery
macro.Feedback: Cutting spending during a recession can reduce AD further and deepen the downturn.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring the starting output gap.
macro.Question: A fiscal expansion is launched when the economy is already above potential and the central bank does nothing. Which risk is most important?
macro.Choice A: The policy may worsen inflation pressure and force later SRAS adjustment.
macro.Choice B: The policy must lower inflation because government spending reduces prices.
macro.Choice C: The policy shifts LRAS right because output is already high.
