macro.Choice D: The policy lowers expected inflation because unemployment is below natural.
macro.Correct Answer: A — The policy may worsen inflation pressure and force later SRAS adjustment.
macro.Feedback: Stimulus when output is already above potential can worsen inflation pressure.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing demand inflation with supply shock inflation.
macro.Question: High inflation is caused by demand growth rather than a supply shock. Which response is most defensible?
macro.Choice A: Contractionary policy can reduce AD, lower inflation pressure, and cool output.
macro.Choice B: Expansionary policy can reduce AD, lower inflation pressure, and cool output.
macro.Choice C: Contractionary policy shifts SRAS right and raises output above potential.
macro.Choice D: Expansionary policy shifts LRPC left and lowers natural unemployment.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Contractionary policy can reduce AD, lower inflation pressure, and cool output.
macro.Feedback: If inflation is demand-driven, contractionary policy can cool AD and reduce inflation pressure.

macro.Common Misconception: Mixing expansionary and contractionary tools.
macro.Question: Which policy pair is expansionary for aggregate demand?
macro.Choice A: Higher taxes and lower money supply
macro.Choice B: Lower taxes and higher money supply
macro.Choice C: Lower spending and higher taxes
macro.Choice D: Higher reserve requirements and lower spending
macro.Correct Answer: B — Lower taxes and higher money supply
macro.Feedback: Lower taxes and higher money supply both tend to shift AD right.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring policy interactions.
macro.Question: Fiscal stimulus raises AD, but the central bank offsets it with tighter money. Which final outcome is most plausible?
macro.Choice A: AD rises less than fiscal policy alone suggests
macro.Choice B: AD rises more than fiscal policy alone suggests
macro.Choice C: SRAS shifts right because interest rates rise
macro.Choice D: LRPC shifts left because taxes fall
macro.Correct Answer: A — AD rises less than fiscal policy alone suggests
macro.Feedback: Tighter monetary policy can offset fiscal stimulus by raising interest rates and weakening AD.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring fiscal-monetary policy interaction.
macro.Question: Congress expands spending during a recession, but the Fed tightens to fight inflation expectations. Which assessment is strongest?
macro.Choice A: Fiscal stimulus may be offset because higher rates weaken investment and AD.
macro.Choice B: Fiscal stimulus must fully work because monetary policy cannot affect AD.
macro.Choice C: Fiscal stimulus shifts SRAS right because higher rates lower production costs.
macro.Choice D: Fiscal stimulus lowers expected inflation because government spending always reduces prices.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Fiscal stimulus may be offset because higher rates weaken investment and AD.
macro.Feedback: Monetary tightening can offset fiscal expansion by raising interest rates and reducing investment.

macro.Common Misconception: Assumes a policy designed for an old output gap remains correctly sized after self-correction has already reduced the gap.
macro.Question: A recessionary gap begins closing without new policy as wage growth slows and SRAS shifts right. A large discretionary stimulus designed for the original gap is still scheduled to take effect several quarters later. What is the strongest stabilization concern?
macro.Choice A: The delayed stimulus may arrive after much of the gap has self-corrected, pushing AD too far right and creating overheating pressure.
macro.Choice B: The stimulus becomes contractionary once SRAS begins shifting right.
macro.Choice C: Self-correction guarantees the stimulus has no effect on aggregate demand.
macro.Choice D: The delayed stimulus automatically shifts LRAS right by the amount of the original gap.
macro.Correct Answer: A — The delayed stimulus may arrive after much of the gap has self-corrected, pushing AD too far right and creating overheating pressure.
macro.Feedback: Policy lags matter because wages, costs, expectations, and private spending can change before discretionary policy takes effect, creating overshoot risk.

macro.Common Misconception: Treats lower inflation pressure from contractionary demand policy as costless in the short run.
macro.Question: Inflation pressure is being driven by excessive aggregate demand. Policymakers use contractionary stabilization policy and the policy succeeds in lowering aggregate demand. Before inflation expectations fully adjust, which short-run combination is most consistent with the policy mechanism?
macro.Choice A: Higher inflation pressure together with weaker output and higher unemployment.
macro.Choice B: No change in unemployment because stabilization policy affects only the price level.
macro.Choice C: Lower inflation pressure together with weaker output and higher unemployment.
macro.Choice D: Lower inflation pressure together with stronger output and lower unemployment.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Lower inflation pressure together with weaker output and higher unemployment.
macro.Feedback: A contractionary AD policy can reduce inflation pressure while also lowering output and raising unemployment before expectations fully adjust.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrect inference: Monetary contribution: +$80; net AD: +$80; foreign contraction is omitted.
macro.Question: Monetary easing lowers rates and raises investment $40. MPC is 0.5 in a fixed-price model. A foreign recession separately reduces AD by a total $120 after induced effects. Which net conclusion distinguishes a working monetary channel from the economy-wide result?
macro.Choice A: Monetary contribution: +$80; net AD: +$80; foreign contraction is omitted.
macro.Choice B: Monetary contribution: +$80; net AD: −$80; the initial investment effect is omitted.
macro.Choice C: Monetary contribution: +$80; net AD: −$40; foreign contraction outweighs easing.
macro.Choice D: Monetary contribution: +$80; net AD: −$160; the total foreign offset is multiplied again.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Monetary contribution: +$80; net AD: −$40; foreign contraction outweighs easing.
macro.Feedback: Investment contributes 40/(1−.5)=80; subtract the total foreign-demand reduction 120, giving −40. Policy transmission can operate as expected while a larger countershock dominates the net outcome.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Velocity growth is+3%; the nominal rate is 9%” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
macro.Question: Use the growth-rate approximation to the quantity equation, MV = PY. Money growth is 10%, output growth 3%, and inflation 4%. A report assumes stable velocity and predicts a nominal interest rate of 9% with a 2% real rate. What are velocity growth and the nominal interest rate when expected inflation equals actual inflation?
macro.Choice A: Velocity growth is +3%; the nominal rate is 9%
macro.Choice B: Velocity growth is 0%; the nominal rate is 12%
macro.Choice C: Velocity growth is −9%; the nominal rate is 2%
macro.Choice D: Velocity growth is −3%; the nominal rate is 6%
macro.Correct Answer: D — Velocity growth is −3%; the nominal rate is 6%
macro.Feedback: From π=gM+gV−gY, 4=10+gV−3 gives gV=−3. With expected inflation 4 and real interest 2, Fisher gives nominal 6.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The shock is adverse supply, so immediate purchases necessarily reduce inflation while restoring output” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
macro.Question: A negative demand shock creates a $1040 recessionary gap with falling inflation; capacity is unchanged. In a fixed-price planning model MPC is 0.75. An increase in government purchases of $260 can take effect immediately, or the same program can take effect after the gap is forecast to close. Would the program close the recessionary gap if it took effect immediately, and what risk would it create if it took effect after recovery?
macro.Choice A: The shock is adverse supply, so immediate purchases necessarily reduce inflation while restoring output
macro.Choice B: The immediate program matches the current gap; the delayed one risks excess demand after recovery
macro.Choice C: Both programs match every future gap because the multiplier makes timing irrelevant
macro.Choice D: The immediate program is contractionary; the delayed program becomes expansionary solely because time passes
macro.Correct Answer: B — The immediate program matches the current gap; the delayed one risks excess demand after recovery
macro.Feedback: Falling output and inflation under the stated demand shock justify demand support. The immediate simple effect is 260/.25=1040, matching the current gap. An increase sized correctly for the original recession may create excess demand if it takes effect after recovery.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrect inference: SRAS shifts right, SRPC down; output and unemployment remain beyond natural benchmarks.
macro.Question: An economy initially has output 120 above potential and unemployment below natural after a demand boom. Demand then stabilizes while wage setters revise expected inflation upward. A proposal assumes this lower unemployment rate can last permanently. As expectations adjust, how do the short-run aggregate supply and Phillips curves change, and what happens to output and unemployment?
macro.Choice A: SRAS shifts left, SRPC up; output returns toward potential and unemployment toward its natural rate.
macro.Choice B: SRAS shifts right, SRPC down; output remains above potential and unemployment below its natural rate.
macro.Choice C: LRAS shifts right, LRPC left; the demand boom changes productive capacity permanently.
macro.Choice D: Both short-run curves stay fixed; wage expectations affect neither output nor unemployment.
macro.Correct Answer: A — SRAS shifts left, SRPC up; output returns toward potential and unemployment toward its natural rate.
macro.Feedback: Higher expected prices incorporated in wages reduce short-run supply at a given actual price; higher expected inflation raises the short-run Phillips relation. Without real structural changes, the initial demand-induced gain does not establish a new potential output level or natural rate of unemployment.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring the conflict between output stabilization and expectations.
macro.Question: The economy is below potential, but inflation expectations are rising. Which policy judgment is strongest?
macro.Choice A: Stimulus may support output but could validate inflation expectations.
macro.Choice B: Tightening always raises output because expectations matter more than AD.
macro.Choice C: Stimulus shifts LRAS right and lowers expected inflation automatically.
macro.Choice D: Doing nothing guarantees lower unemployment and lower inflation immediately.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Stimulus may support output but could validate inflation expectations.
macro.Feedback: When output is weak but expectations are rising, policy faces a tradeoff between demand support and inflation credibility.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Both inflation and nominal interest fall 4 points in both economies because money growth alone determines them” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
macro.Question: Compare two long-run money-growth cuts of 4 points. In A, output and velocity growth stay fixed and expectations fully adjust. In B, velocity growth rises 4 points while output growth stays fixed. Real interest rates are unchanged. Which comparison follows under the growth and Fisher approximations?
macro.Choice A: Both inflation and nominal interest fall 4 points in both economies because money growth alone determines them
macro.Choice B: A’s real interest falls 4 points; B’s nominal interest falls 8 points
macro.Choice C: Both economies’ real output growth must fall 4 points to absorb the policy
macro.Choice D: A’s inflation and nominal interest fall 4 points; B’s velocity offset leaves both unchanged
macro.Correct Answer: D — A’s inflation and nominal interest fall 4 points; B’s velocity offset leaves both unchanged
macro.Feedback: In A, Δπ=−4, so the expected-inflation component of nominal interest falls 4. In B, ΔgM+ΔgV=−4+4=0; unchanged inflation expectations imply unchanged nominal rates at the fixed real rate.

macro.Common Misconception: Uses the original output-gap estimate even after newer data show a much smaller gap.
macro.Question: A government authorizes $75 billion of extra purchases when the required rightward AD shift is $300 billion. Before payment, the required shift at the same reference price falls to $100 billion. The simple spending multiplier is 4; no crowding out or other leakages apply. One third of the authorized purchases must now occur, while the rest can still be cancelled. Which implementation decision meets the revised target without overshooting?
macro.Choice A: Pay the entire remaining $50 billion; the original authorization still matches the revised target.
macro.Choice B: Pay another $25 billion and cancel $25 billion; the unmultiplied purchases must equal the revised target.
macro.Choice C: Cancel all $75 billion; a revision of the target eliminates the unavoidable payment.
macro.Choice D: Cancel the remaining $50 billion; the unavoidable $25 billion already produces the required $100 billion AD shift.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Cancel the remaining $50 billion; the unavoidable $25 billion already produces the required $100 billion AD shift.
macro.Feedback: The unavoidable purchases are 75/3 = $25 billion, producing 25 × 4 = $100 billion of AD. The remaining authorization is $50 billion and should be cancelled under the stated target. Full implementation would create a $300 billion shift and a $200 billion overshoot. Policy must be evaluated when it takes effect.

macro.Question: A short recession causes tax receipts to fall and unemployment-benefit payments to rise automatically. Congress also approves an infrastructure stimulus, but construction begins after the economy has already recovered. Which comparison is strongest?
macro.Choice A: The infrastructure program cannot affect aggregate demand once the recession has ended.
macro.Choice B: The automatic stabilizers cushion the downturn and recede with conditions, while the delayed discretionary program can add demand after the original gap has faded.
macro.Choice C: Both responses have the same implementation timing because each changes the government budget.
macro.Choice D: The automatic stabilizers become contractionary during the recession, while delayed infrastructure is always stabilizing.
macro.Correct Answer: B — The automatic stabilizers cushion the downturn and recede with conditions, while the delayed discretionary program can add demand after the original gap has faded.
macro.Feedback: Automatic stabilizers respond as income and employment change without new legislation; discretionary programs can arrive later and may outlast the original gap.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Initial expected inflation is 6%; final natural-rate inflation is 9% because the temporary offset persists” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
macro.Question: Use inflation = expected inflation − (unemployment − 5) + s, where s is the number of percentage points a temporary supply shock adds to inflation. Rates are in percent. With s = +2 and unemployment at 6%, actual inflation is 6%. Before the shock ends, expected inflation rises by 1 percentage point and stays at that higher rate. What was expected inflation initially, and what will inflation be after the shock ends and unemployment returns to its natural rate of 5%?
macro.Choice A: Initial expected inflation is 5%; final inflation at natural unemployment is 6% after the supply shock ends
macro.Choice B: Initial expected inflation is 6%; inflation at the natural unemployment rate is 9% because the temporary supply shock persists
macro.Choice C: Initial expected inflation is 3%; inflation at the natural unemployment rate is 4% because the unemployment gap is subtracted twice
macro.Choice D: Initial expected inflation is 5%; inflation at the natural unemployment rate is 8% because it still includes the former supply shock's effect
macro.Correct Answer: A — Initial expected inflation is 5%; final inflation at natural unemployment is 6% after the supply shock ends
macro.Feedback: Initially, 6 = πe − 1 + 2, so expected inflation is 5%. Expectations then rise to 6%. After the supply shock ends and unemployment returns to 5%, inflation equals expected inflation, or 6%. Ending the supply shock does not necessarily return expectations to their original rate.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Becomes equal to taxes” in this open economy policy transmission task.
macro.Question: A government deficit reduces public saving. If private saving is unchanged, national saving:
macro.Choice A: Becomes equal to taxes
macro.Choice B: Falls
macro.Choice C: Rises
macro.Choice D: Stays fixed
macro.Correct Answer: B — Falls
macro.Feedback: National saving is private plus public saving, so a lower public component reduces the total.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Foreign saving” in this open economy policy transmission task.
macro.Question: In the standard open-economy model, a larger government budget deficit first reduces:
macro.Choice A: Foreign saving
macro.Choice B: Net exports by accounting definition
macro.Choice C: The domestic price level
macro.Choice D: National saving
macro.Correct Answer: D — National saving
macro.Feedback: A larger deficit lowers public saving and therefore national saving when private saving is unchanged.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “A fall in foreign demand for domestic exports” in this open economy policy transmission task.
macro.Question: Which event most directly initiates capital flight?
macro.Choice A: A fall in foreign demand for domestic exports
macro.Choice B: A balanced government budget
macro.Choice C: A decline in domestic import prices
macro.Choice D: A sharp rise in perceived domestic political risk
macro.Correct Answer: D — A sharp rise in perceived domestic political risk
macro.Feedback: Greater perceived risk prompts investors to move assets abroad.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Foreign purchases of domestic goods” in this open economy policy transmission task.
macro.Question: Capital flight begins with an increase in desired:
macro.Choice A: Foreign purchases of domestic goods
macro.Choice B: Domestic tax revenue
macro.Choice C: Foreign-asset purchases
macro.Choice D: Domestic consumption only
macro.Correct Answer: C — Foreign-asset purchases
macro.Feedback: Political or economic risk can prompt residents and investors to move portfolios toward foreign assets.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “The matching service changes cyclical unemployment and the closure changes only measured participation” in this unemployment types task.
macro.Question: A matching service shortens unemployment spells among otherwise qualified job seekers. At the same time, an industry closes permanently and displaced workers need new qualifications. Which conclusion is defensible?
macro.Choice A: Frictional falls, structural is unchanged; their net natural-rate effect is downward.
macro.Choice B: Frictional is unchanged, structural rises; their net natural-rate effect is upward.
macro.Choice C: Frictional falls, structural rises; their net natural-rate effect is uncertain.
macro.Choice D: Both components fall; faster matching also removes the new qualification mismatch.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Frictional falls, structural rises; their net natural-rate effect is uncertain.
macro.Feedback: Better matching reduces search friction, while a durable skills mismatch raises structural unemployment. Natural unemployment includes both, so opposing changes do not determine the net effect.

macro.Common Misconception: Incorrectly concludes “Both groups face cyclical unemployment because neither is currently employed” in this unemployment types task.
macro.Question: A regional study follows 100 jobless workers after national demand recovers. Former miners still lack skills for local health-care vacancies, while new graduates are interviewing for matching jobs. Which diagnosis and response pair is appropriate?
macro.Choice A: Both groups face cyclical unemployment because neither is currently employed
macro.Choice B: Both groups face structural unemployment because job search always requires new skills
macro.Choice C: Miners face structural mismatch suited to retraining; graduates face frictional search suited to matching assistance
macro.Choice D: Miners face cyclical unemployment suited only to demand stimulus; graduates face structural unemployment suited to changing industries
macro.Correct Answer: C — Miners face structural mismatch suited to retraining; graduates face frictional search suited to matching assistance
macro.Feedback: The persistence of a skill mismatch after demand recovers identifies a structural problem. Graduates searching for suitable existing matches illustrate frictional unemployment. Each remedy should address its actual mechanism.

macro.Question: Automation raises output per worker and lowers production costs, but some workers in the old process lose jobs and need retraining. Which statement best describes the combined effect?
macro.Choice A: Productivity must fall when workers are displaced, even if output per worker rises and unit costs fall
macro.Choice B: Productivity can rise while displaced workers face only frictional search, even when their old skills no longer fit vacancies
macro.Choice C: Productivity and potential living standards can rise while displaced workers face a structural skill mismatch requiring adjustment
macro.Choice D: Productivity can rise while displaced workers face only cyclical unemployment that disappears as soon as the new machines operate
macro.Correct Answer: C — Productivity and potential living standards can rise while displaced workers face a structural skill mismatch requiring adjustment
macro.Feedback: Technology can raise productivity and living standards over time while displacing some workers whose skills no longer match the market.

macro.Question: When only the price of a good changes, what happens on the supply curve?
macro.Choice A: There is movement along the supply curve
macro.Choice B: The supply curve shifts right
macro.Choice C: The supply curve shifts left
macro.Choice D: Demand shifts right
macro.Correct Answer: A — There is movement along the supply curve
macro.Feedback: A good's own price changes quantity supplied, not supply.

macro.Question: The price of handmade tables rises. What is the most precise result?
macro.Choice A: Quantity supplied increases
macro.Choice B: Supply increases
macro.Choice C: Demand increases
macro.Choice D: Supply decreases
macro.Correct Answer: A — Quantity supplied increases
macro.Feedback: Because the good's own price changed, sellers move along the supply curve.

macro.Question: Which event shifts supply?
macro.Choice A: Input costs change
macro.Choice B: The good's own price changes
macro.Choice C: Quantity demanded changes
macro.Choice D: Consumers' income changes
macro.Correct Answer: A — Input costs change
macro.Feedback: Input costs shift supply. The good's own price causes movement along supply.

macro.Question: Steel is an input in car production. If the price of steel rises, what happens to the supply of cars?
macro.Choice A: Supply decreases
macro.Choice B: Supply increases
macro.Choice C: Demand decreases
macro.Choice D: Quantity supplied increases
macro.Correct Answer: A — Supply decreases
macro.Feedback: The repair cue identifies steel as an input. A higher input price raises marginal production cost and shifts car supply left.

macro.Question: Bread's selling price rises, while flour becomes cheaper. Considering each change separately, how does it affect the supply of bread?
macro.Choice A: Higher bread price moves sellers along supply; cheaper flour shifts supply right.
macro.Choice B: Higher bread price shifts supply right; cheaper flour moves sellers along supply.
macro.Choice C: Higher bread price moves sellers along supply; cheaper flour shifts supply left.
macro.Choice D: Both changes move sellers along the same supply curve.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Higher bread price moves sellers along supply; cheaper flour shifts supply right.
macro.Feedback: Bread's own price changes quantity supplied along a supply curve. Flour is a production input: a lower flour price reduces cost at each output level, shifting bread supply right. These are separate mechanisms.

macro.Question: The price of concert tickets falls, and venues offer fewer tickets for resale. Which statement is most precise?
macro.Choice A: Quantity supplied decreased, but supply did not necessarily shift
macro.Choice B: Supply decreased because price changed
macro.Choice C: Demand increased because price fell
macro.Choice D: Supply shifted right because sellers offered fewer tickets
macro.Correct Answer: A — Quantity supplied decreased, but supply did not necessarily shift
macro.Feedback: A change in the good's own price changes quantity supplied, not supply.

macro.Question: A new machine lowers the cost of producing shoes. What happens in the shoe market?
macro.Choice A: Supply increases
macro.Choice B: Supply decreases
macro.Choice C: Demand increases
macro.Choice D: Quantity demanded decreases
macro.Correct Answer: A — Supply increases
macro.Feedback: Better technology lowers production costs, shifting supply right.

macro.Question: Delivery firms face higher diesel prices and also receive higher prices for each delivery. Consider each change separately. Which change reduces delivery supply at every delivery price?
macro.Choice A: Higher delivery prices; they shift delivery supply left.
macro.Choice B: Higher diesel prices; they shift delivery supply right.
macro.Choice C: Higher diesel prices; they shift delivery supply left.
macro.Choice D: Higher delivery prices; they move firms down the supply curve.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Higher diesel prices; they shift delivery supply left.
macro.Feedback: Diesel is an input. Its higher price raises the cost of making deliveries, so firms offer fewer at each delivery price: supply shifts left. A higher price received per delivery instead increases quantity supplied along a curve.

macro.Question: The law of supply says that, other things equal:
macro.Choice A: As price rises, quantity supplied rises
macro.Choice B: As price rises, demand rises
macro.Choice C: As price falls, quantity supplied rises
macro.Choice D: As price falls, supply shifts right
macro.Correct Answer: A — As price rises, quantity supplied rises
macro.Feedback: The law of supply says price and quantity supplied move in the same direction.

macro.Question: If the price of a good rises, what happens to quantity supplied?
macro.Choice A: Quantity supplied increases
macro.Choice B: Supply decreases
macro.Choice C: Demand increases
macro.Choice D: The supply curve shifts left
macro.Correct Answer: A — Quantity supplied increases
macro.Feedback: A change in the good's own price causes movement along the supply curve.

macro.Question: Which change would shift the supply curve?
macro.Choice A: A change in input costs
macro.Choice B: A change in the good's own price
macro.Choice C: A change in quantity demanded
macro.Choice D: A movement along the demand curve.
macro.Correct Answer: A — A change in input costs
macro.Feedback: Input costs shift supply. The good's own price changes quantity supplied.

macro.Question: If the cost of steel rises for car producers, what happens to the supply of cars?
macro.Choice A: Supply decreases
macro.Choice B: Supply increases
macro.Choice C: Demand decreases
macro.Choice D: Quantity demanded increases
macro.Correct Answer: A — Supply decreases
macro.Feedback: Steel is an input in car production. A higher steel price raises producers' costs, so the car supply curve shifts left.

macro.Question: An improvement in production technology usually causes:
macro.Choice A: Supply to increase
macro.Choice B: Demand to decrease
macro.Choice C: Quantity demanded to fall because price changed
macro.Choice D: A binding price floor
macro.Correct Answer: A — Supply to increase
macro.Feedback: Better technology makes production easier or cheaper, shifting supply right.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing market supply with one firm’s supply or with demand.
macro.Question: Market supply at a given price is the:
macro.Choice A: Sum of the quantities all sellers are willing and able to offer.
macro.Choice B: Quantity supplied by the single largest seller at that price.
macro.Choice C: Average quantity each seller plans to produce at that price.
macro.Choice D: Total quantity buyers are willing and able to purchase at that price.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Sum of the quantities all sellers are willing and able to offer.
macro.Feedback: Market supply horizontally adds the quantities supplied by every seller at each price.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: On the displayed coffee supply curve, what price and quantity are shown at point A?
macro.Choice A: $11 and 225 thousand units
macro.Choice B: $6 and 225 thousand units
macro.Choice C: $6 and 100 thousand units
macro.Choice D: $2 and 100 thousand units
macro.Correct Answer: C — $6 and 100 thousand units
macro.Feedback: At point A, the supply curve pairs a price of $6 with a quantity supplied of 100 thousand units.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: In the displayed hamburger market, the move from S0 to S1 represents:
macro.Choice A: A decrease in supply
macro.Choice B: An increase in supply
macro.Choice C: An increase in quantity supplied caused only by a higher price
macro.Choice D: A decrease in demand
macro.Correct Answer: A — A decrease in supply
macro.Feedback: S1 lies to the left and above S0, showing less quantity supplied at each common price.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: How should the taco supply change from S0 to S1 be classified?
macro.Choice A: A decrease in supply
macro.Choice B: An increase in quantity supplied caused only by a higher price
macro.Choice C: An increase in supply
macro.Choice D: A decrease in demand
macro.Correct Answer: C — An increase in supply
macro.Feedback: S1 lies below and to the right of S0, showing more quantity supplied at each common price.

macro.Question: The price of handmade tables rises, and sellers produce more tables. What happened?
macro.Choice A: Quantity supplied increased
macro.Choice B: Supply increased
macro.Choice C: Demand increased
macro.Choice D: Supply shifted right
macro.Correct Answer: A — Quantity supplied increased
macro.Feedback: A change in the good's own price causes movement along supply, so quantity supplied changes.

macro.Question: The price of a good falls, and sellers produce less of it. What happened?
macro.Choice A: Quantity supplied decreased
macro.Choice B: Supply decreased
macro.Choice C: Demand increased
macro.Choice D: Supply shifted right
macro.Correct Answer: A — Quantity supplied decreased
macro.Feedback: A change in the good's own price changes quantity supplied, not supply.

macro.Question: A new machine lowers the cost of producing shoes. What happens to the supply of shoes?
macro.Choice A: Supply increases
macro.Choice B: Supply decreases
macro.Choice C: Demand decreases
macro.Choice D: Quantity demanded decreases
macro.Correct Answer: A — Supply increases
macro.Feedback: Lower production costs from better technology shift supply right.

macro.Question: Several sellers leave the market. What happens to market supply?
macro.Choice A: Supply decreases
macro.Choice B: Supply increases
macro.Choice C: Demand decreases
macro.Choice D: Quantity supplied rises
macro.Correct Answer: A — Supply decreases
macro.Feedback: Fewer sellers means less market supply at each price.

macro.Question: An input used to make pizza becomes more expensive. What is the likely effect in the pizza market?
macro.Choice A: Supply decreases and price rises
macro.Choice B: Supply increases and price falls
macro.Choice C: Demand increases and price rises
macro.Choice D: Quantity demanded increases because cost rose
macro.Correct Answer: A — Supply decreases and price rises
macro.Feedback: Higher input costs decrease supply, which tends to raise price.

macro.Question: Refer to the supply and demand graph. Which curve shift is shown when equilibrium moves from Price P2, Quantity Q1 to Price P1, Quantity Q2?
macro.Choice A: A rightward shift in supply
macro.Choice B: A rightward shift in demand
macro.Choice C: A leftward shift in demand
macro.Choice D: A leftward shift in supply
macro.Correct Answer: A — A rightward shift in supply
macro.Feedback: The move from D1 with S1 to D1 with S2 lowers price and raises quantity, which matches an increase in supply.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating a producer subsidy as a movement along supply or a demand shifter.
macro.Question: The government begins paying producers a subsidy for every unit sold. What happens to market supply, other things equal?
macro.Choice A: Supply shifts left because the subsidy increases firms’ effective production cost.
macro.Choice B: Supply shifts right because the subsidy lowers the effective marginal cost of selling output.
macro.Choice C: Quantity supplied rises along the original curve because only the market price changed.
macro.Choice D: Demand shifts right because the payment is received directly by buyers.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Supply shifts right because the subsidy lowers the effective marginal cost of selling output.
macro.Feedback: A per-unit producer subsidy raises the return from supplying each unit and shifts supply right.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: At a market price of $8, approximately how many units does the displayed coffee supply curve show producers are willing to sell?
macro.Choice A: 100 thousand units
macro.Choice B: 175 thousand units
macro.Choice C: 150 thousand units
macro.Choice D: 225 thousand units
macro.Correct Answer: C — 150 thousand units
macro.Feedback: The supply line passes through quantity 150 thousand at a price of $8.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: Use the graph. A producer claims that the move from A to B proves that supply increased. Which quantity change and diagnosis are correct?
macro.Choice A: An increase of 100 thousand units; this is a change in quantity supplied along the existing curve.
macro.Choice B: An increase of 125 thousand units; any rise in quantity is an increase in the whole supply schedule.
macro.Choice C: An increase of 100 thousand units; any rise in quantity is an increase in the whole supply schedule.
macro.Choice D: An increase of 125 thousand units; this is a change in quantity supplied along the existing curve.
macro.Correct Answer: D — An increase of 125 thousand units; this is a change in quantity supplied along the existing curve.
macro.Feedback: A is at 100 thousand units and B at 225 thousand, an increase of 125 thousand. Both lie on the same supply curve. The higher own price changes quantity supplied; an increase in supply would shift the entire schedule.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: What economic change does the move from A to B in the coffee graph represent?
macro.Choice A: Price rises $5; quantity supplied increases by 100 thousand along the existing curve.
macro.Choice B: Price rises $5; supply increases by 125 thousand because the curve shifts right.
macro.Choice C: Price rises $5; supply increases by 100 thousand because the curve shifts right.
macro.Choice D: Price rises $5; quantity supplied increases by 125 thousand along the existing curve.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Price rises $5; quantity supplied increases by 125 thousand along the existing curve.
macro.Feedback: A is at $6 and 100 thousand units; B is at $11 and 225 thousand. Price rises $5 and quantity supplied rises 125 thousand along the same supply curve. This is an increase in quantity supplied, not a rightward shift of supply.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: Moving from point A to point B on the displayed supply curve changes quantity supplied by:
macro.Choice A: An increase of 125 thousand units
macro.Choice B: A decrease of 125 thousand units
macro.Choice C: An increase of 5 thousand units
macro.Choice D: An increase of 225 thousand units
macro.Correct Answer: A — An increase of 125 thousand units
macro.Feedback: Quantity supplied rises from 100 thousand at A to 225 thousand at B, an increase of 125 thousand.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: At a price of $9 on the displayed hamburger graph, how does quantity supplied change when supply shifts from S0 to S1?
macro.Choice A: It increases from 100 thousand to 200 thousand
macro.Choice B: It decreases from 200 thousand to 100 thousand
macro.Choice C: It decreases from 300 thousand to 200 thousand
macro.Choice D: It stays at 200 thousand
macro.Correct Answer: B — It decreases from 200 thousand to 100 thousand
macro.Feedback: At $9, S0 shows 200 thousand units while S1 shows 100 thousand, a decrease of 100 thousand at the same price.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: Which event is consistent with the shift from S0 to S1 shown in the hamburger market?
macro.Choice A: The price of hamburgers rises and firms move up S0
macro.Choice B: A new cost-saving grill technology is adopted
macro.Choice C: The price of a major meat input rises
macro.Choice D: More hamburger restaurants enter the market
macro.Correct Answer: C — The price of a major meat input rises
macro.Feedback: Higher input costs reduce supply, shifting the supply curve left.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: What economic change does the move from A to B in the tacos graph represent?
macro.Choice A: Price rises $1; quantity supplied increases by 100 thousand along the existing curve.
macro.Choice B: Price rises $1; supply increases by 125 thousand because the curve shifts right.
macro.Choice C: Price rises $1; supply increases by 100 thousand because the curve shifts right.
macro.Choice D: Price rises $1; quantity supplied increases by 125 thousand along the existing curve.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Price rises $1; quantity supplied increases by 125 thousand along the existing curve.
macro.Feedback: A is at $3 and 100 thousand tacos; B is at $4 and 225 thousand. Price rises $1 and quantity supplied rises 125 thousand along S0. The higher quantity supplied reflects movement along the curve, not an increase in supply.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: At a price of $3, the shift from S0 to S1 changes quantity supplied from 100 thousand to approximately:
macro.Choice A: 225 thousand
macro.Choice B: 125 thousand
macro.Choice C: 200 thousand
macro.Choice D: 325 thousand
macro.Correct Answer: A — 225 thousand
macro.Feedback: At $3, point A on S0 is 100 thousand, while S1 crosses the $3 line at about 225 thousand. Supply therefore increases by about 125 thousand units at that price.

macro.Question: A new production method cuts the cost of making solar panels. What happens in the solar panel market?
macro.Choice A: Supply increases, price falls, and quantity rises
macro.Choice B: Supply decreases, price rises, and quantity falls
macro.Choice C: Demand increases, price rises, and quantity rises
macro.Choice D: Quantity demanded decreases because supply rose
macro.Correct Answer: A — Supply increases, price falls, and quantity rises
macro.Feedback: Lower production costs increase supply, which lowers price and raises quantity.

macro.Question: A tax on producers raises the cost of selling bottled water. What is the likely market effect?
macro.Choice A: Supply decreases, price rises, and quantity falls
macro.Choice B: Supply increases, price falls, and quantity rises
macro.Choice C: Demand decreases, price falls, and quantity falls
macro.Choice D: Demand increases because taxes fund public services
macro.Correct Answer: A — Supply decreases, price rises, and quantity falls
macro.Feedback: A tax on producers raises production cost, shifting supply left and reducing quantity.

macro.Question: Producers expect the future price of a product to rise sharply, so they hold inventory back today. What happens to current supply?
macro.Choice A: Current supply decreases
macro.Choice B: Current supply increases
macro.Choice C: Current demand decreases
macro.Choice D: Quantity supplied increases because current price changed
macro.Correct Answer: A — Current supply decreases
macro.Feedback: If sellers expect higher future prices, they may reduce current supply to sell later.

macro.Question: Refer to the supply and demand shift graph. Which movement shows an increase in supply with demand fixed at D2?
macro.Choice A: From P3, Q2 to P2, Q3
macro.Choice B: From P2, Q1 to P1, Q2
macro.Choice C: From P1, Q2 to P2, Q3
macro.Choice D: From P2, Q3 to P3, Q2
macro.Correct Answer: A — From P3, Q2 to P2, Q3
macro.Feedback: With demand fixed at D2, moving from S1 to S2 changes equilibrium from P3, Q2 to P2, Q3.

macro.Common Misconception: Calling a price-induced movement along supply an increase in supply.
macro.Question: Demand rises and the market price increases. Firms respond by producing more with the same technology, input prices, and number of sellers. Which statement is correct?
macro.Choice A: Supply shifts right because firms produce more.
macro.Choice B: Quantity supplied rises along an unchanged supply curve.
macro.Choice C: Supply shifts left because the product is now more expensive.
macro.Choice D: Both supply and quantity supplied must increase.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Quantity supplied rises along an unchanged supply curve.
macro.Feedback: A change in the good’s own price changes quantity supplied. The supply curve shifts only when a nonprice determinant changes.

macro.Common Misconception: Using only one supply shifter when several operate at once.
macro.Question: Workers accept lower wages, but producers also expect the product’s future price to rise and hold inventory for later sale. What can be concluded about current supply?
macro.Choice A: Supply must rise because lower wages dominate the decision to withhold inventory.
macro.Choice B: Supply must fall because withholding inventory dominates the wage reduction.
macro.Choice C: The net supply shift is uncertain because lower wages and inventory withholding work in opposite directions.
macro.Choice D: Supply stays fixed because wages and expected future prices only move firms along supply.
macro.Correct Answer: C — The net supply shift is uncertain because lower wages and inventory withholding work in opposite directions.
macro.Feedback: Lower wages reduce production costs and increase supply. Holding inventory for a higher expected future price reduces current supply. Their relative sizes determine the net shift.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating unequal per-unit cost changes as if they cancel.
macro.Question: A per-unit input cost falls by $4, but a new per-unit tax raises cost by $6. Holding other determinants fixed, what is the likely supply effect?
macro.Choice A: Supply shifts left because net marginal cost rises by $2 per unit.
macro.Choice B: Supply shifts right because any input-cost decline dominates a tax.
macro.Choice C: Supply is unchanged because the two policies offset exactly.
macro.Choice D: Only quantity supplied falls along the same curve.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Supply shifts left because net marginal cost rises by $2 per unit.
macro.Feedback: The combined change raises marginal cost by $2 per unit, reducing supply at each price.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: Use the graph. From A to B, what is the quantity response per $1 price increase, and what economic change does it represent?
macro.Choice A: Quantity supplied rises by 25 thousand units per dollar through movement along the existing supply curve.
macro.Choice B: Quantity supplied rises by 20 thousand units per dollar through movement along the existing supply curve.
macro.Choice C: Supply increases by 25 thousand units per dollar because the price change shifts the curve right.
macro.Choice D: Supply increases by 20 thousand units per dollar because the price change shifts the curve right.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Quantity supplied rises by 25 thousand units per dollar through movement along the existing supply curve.
macro.Feedback: Price rises from $6 to $11 and quantity supplied rises from 100 thousand to 225 thousand. The response is 125/5 = 25 thousand units per $1 price increase. Both points lie on the same supply curve, so quantity supplied increases through a movement along supply; supply itself does not shift.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: Refer to the graph. At $9, compare S0 with S1. Which event and quantity change are consistent with that comparison?
macro.Choice A: Lower input costs; 100 thousand fewer units supplied.
macro.Choice B: A fall in the product’s own price; 100 thousand fewer units at the same $9 price.
macro.Choice C: Higher input costs; 200 thousand fewer units supplied.
macro.Choice D: Higher input costs; 100 thousand fewer units supplied.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Higher input costs; 100 thousand fewer units supplied.
macro.Feedback: At $9, supply falls from 200 thousand on S0 to 100 thousand on S1. Higher input costs can cause this leftward shift. A change in the product’s own price cannot explain different quantities at the same price.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: Which comparison correctly distinguishes the two changes visible in the taco graph?
macro.Choice A: A to B is an increase in supply; S0 to S1 is movement along supply
macro.Choice B: A to B is movement along S0; S0 to S1 is an increase in supply
macro.Choice C: Both A to B and S0 to S1 are movements caused only by price
macro.Choice D: Both changes are decreases in supply
macro.Correct Answer: B — A to B is movement along S0; S0 to S1 is an increase in supply
macro.Feedback: A and B are points on one curve, so their difference is quantity supplied. Moving from S0 to S1 shifts the entire curve and changes supply.

macro.Question: A product gets more expensive because demand increases. Sellers produce more at the higher price. Students say supply increased. What is the error?
macro.Choice A: They confused an increase in quantity supplied with an increase in supply
macro.Choice B: They correctly identified a supply shift
macro.Choice C: They confused demand with quantity demanded
macro.Choice D: They ignored that equilibrium cannot change
macro.Correct Answer: A — They confused an increase in quantity supplied with an increase in supply
macro.Feedback: Sellers move along the supply curve when price rises. Quantity supplied increases, but supply does not shift.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming one opposing supply shifter automatically dominates the other.
macro.Question: A new machine lowers unit production cost, while a new per-unit environmental fee raises cost. Which conclusion about supply is justified without knowing the size of each change?
macro.Choice A: Supply must shift right because improved technology outweighs any higher per-unit fee.
macro.Choice B: Supply must shift left because a new per-unit fee outweighs any technological saving.
macro.Choice C: Supply must remain unchanged because there is one cost decrease and one cost increase.
macro.Choice D: The net supply shift cannot be determined without comparing the two cost changes.
macro.Correct Answer: D — The net supply shift cannot be determined without comparing the two cost changes.
macro.Feedback: The cost saving increases supply; the fee reduces supply. The net direction depends on the magnitudes, not the number of changes.

macro.Common Misconception: Ignoring an offsetting change in the number of sellers or input costs.
macro.Question: Twenty new firms enter a market, but an essential input becomes more expensive for every firm. What is the most careful conclusion about market supply?
macro.Choice A: Entry pushes supply right and higher input cost pushes it left, leaving the net effect uncertain.
macro.Choice B: Market supply must rise because entry outweighs the input-cost increase.
macro.Choice C: Market supply must fall because higher input costs outweigh entry.
macro.Choice D: Market supply stays fixed because both events only change quantity supplied along the curve.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Entry pushes supply right and higher input cost pushes it left, leaving the net effect uncertain.
macro.Feedback: More firms add supply at each price; a cost increase reduces each firm’s supply. Without magnitudes, the combined shift can go either way or be zero.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: Compare the initial point on S0 at $9 with the final point on S1 at $13. Which explanation separates the supply change from the later price change?
macro.Choice A: The supply decrease reduces quantity from 200 to 100 thousand at $9; the price rise moves along S1 to 200 thousand without shifting supply back.
macro.Choice B: The supply decrease reduces quantity from 250 to 150 thousand at $9; the price rise moves along S1 to 250 thousand without shifting supply back.
macro.Choice C: The supply decrease reduces quantity from 200 to 100 thousand at $9; the price rise moves along S1 to 200 thousand because supply shifts back to S0.
macro.Choice D: The supply decrease reduces quantity from 250 to 150 thousand at $9; the price rise moves along S1 to 250 thousand because supply shifts back to S0.
macro.Correct Answer: A — The supply decrease reduces quantity from 200 to 100 thousand at $9; the price rise moves along S1 to 200 thousand without shifting supply back.
macro.Feedback: At $9, S0 shows 200 thousand units and S1 shows 100 thousand. The lower quantity at the same price is a supply decrease. A subsequent price rise to $13 moves along S1 to 200 thousand. Returning to the original quantity does not shift supply back to S0.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: Compare A on S0 with the final point on S1 at $2. Which explanation separates the supply change from the later price change?
macro.Choice A: The supply increase raises quantity from 100 to about 225 thousand at A’s price; the price fall moves along S1 to about 100 thousand without shifting supply back.
macro.Choice B: The supply increase raises quantity from 125 to about 250 thousand at A’s price; the price fall moves along S1 to about 125 thousand without shifting supply back.
macro.Choice C: The supply increase raises quantity from 100 to about 225 thousand at A’s price; the price fall moves along S1 to about 100 thousand because supply shifts back to S0.
macro.Choice D: The supply increase raises quantity from 125 to about 250 thousand at A’s price; the price fall moves along S1 to about 125 thousand because supply shifts back to S0.
macro.Correct Answer: A — The supply increase raises quantity from 100 to about 225 thousand at A’s price; the price fall moves along S1 to about 100 thousand without shifting supply back.
macro.Feedback: A is at $3 and 100 thousand tacos on S0. At that same price, S1 shows about 225 thousand, indicating a supply increase. The later price fall to $2 moves along S1 to about 100 thousand. Quantity returns to its original level, but the supply curve remains S1.

macro.Common Misconception: Using the largest or average firm quantity instead of summing quantities.
macro.Question: At $30, three sellers offer 12, 18, and 25 units; at $35 they offer 16, 24, and 30 units. Calculate both market quantities and infer what the comparison represents.
macro.Choice A: Market quantity rises from 55 to 70 units, representing movement along market supply
macro.Choice B: Market supply shifts right from 55 to 70 units because the number of sellers increases
macro.Choice C: Market quantity falls from 70 to 55 units, representing movement down market supply
macro.Choice D: Market supply shifts left by 15 units because individual quantities are aggregated vertically
macro.Correct Answer: A — Market quantity rises from 55 to 70 units, representing movement along market supply
macro.Feedback: Horizontal summation gives 55 units at $30 and 70 at $35. Because only the product's own price changes, the 15-unit increase is movement along the market supply curve.

macro.Common Misconception: Forgetting that market supply depends on the number of active sellers.
macro.Question: At a fixed price, 60 identical firms initially supply 8 units each. An input-cost decline raises each surviving firm’s supply to 10 units, but some firms exit. Total supply at that price is unchanged. How many firms exited, and what does the unchanged total imply?
macro.Choice A: 10 firms; the cost and exit effects offset at this price.
macro.Choice B: 12 firms; neither input costs nor firm exit shifted supply.
macro.Choice C: 15 firms; a higher product price offset the firm exits.
macro.Choice D: 12 firms; the cost and exit effects offset at this price.
macro.Correct Answer: D — 12 firms; the cost and exit effects offset at this price.
macro.Feedback: Initial supply is 60 × 8 = 480 units. At 10 units each, 48 firms supply 480, so 12 exited. Opposing supply determinants offset at the stated price; this is not a movement caused by an own-price change.

macro.Common Misconception: Applying future price expectations in the wrong time direction.
macro.Question: Producers expect a temporary price spike next month and can store the product cheaply. What pattern is most plausible?
macro.Choice A: Current and future supply both rise because firms expand production immediately and store none of it.
macro.Choice B: Current supply falls as firms hold inventory, while future supply rises when the inventory is released.
macro.Choice C: Current supply rises as firms sell inventory before the expected spike, while future supply falls.
macro.Choice D: Current quantity supplied falls along one curve because the current product price decreases.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Current supply falls as firms hold inventory, while future supply rises when the inventory is released.
macro.Feedback: When storage is feasible, a higher expected future price can reduce current supply and increase supply when the stored goods are later sold.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating immediate output response and later firm entry as the same kind of change.
macro.Question: A surge in demand raises the equilibrium price. Firms expand output, and new firms later enter the industry. Which sequence is correct?
macro.Choice A: First supply shifts right; later quantity supplied falls along the curve.
macro.Choice B: Both responses are movements along the original supply curve.
macro.Choice C: First quantity supplied rises along the curve; later entry shifts market supply right.
macro.Choice D: Both responses are supply shifts caused by the good’s own price.
macro.Correct Answer: C — First quantity supplied rises along the curve; later entry shifts market supply right.
macro.Feedback: The higher price first causes a movement along supply. Entry is a nonprice determinant that later shifts market supply right.

macro.Common Misconception: Using the higher equilibrium price as evidence of an increase in supply.
macro.Question: A drought reduces crop yields, while the market price of the crop rises because demand is unchanged. What is the best description?
macro.Choice A: Supply shifts right because the higher equilibrium price encourages more production after the drought.
macro.Choice B: Quantity supplied falls along the original supply curve while the curve itself remains unchanged.
macro.Choice C: Demand shifts left because the drought changes buyer preferences rather than production conditions.
macro.Choice D: Supply shifts left, and the higher price causes movement upward along the new supply curve.
macro.Correct Answer: D — Supply shifts left, and the higher price causes movement upward along the new supply curve.
macro.Feedback: The drought is a supply shifter. The resulting higher price determines the quantity supplied on the new, left-shifted curve.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: Refer to the graph. Producers start on S0 at $9. Higher input costs move supply to S1, while a purchase contract permits a price no higher than $11. A buyer expects that allowed price increase to restore the original quantity supplied. Which assessment is correct?
macro.Choice A: It succeeds: S1 supplies 200 thousand at $11, restoring the original quantity.
macro.Choice B: It fails: S1 supplies 150 thousand at $11, still 50 thousand below the original quantity.
macro.Choice C: It fails: S1 supplies 100 thousand at $11, still 100 thousand below the original quantity.
macro.Choice D: It succeeds: raising price to $11 shifts supply back to S0, restoring the original quantity.
macro.Correct Answer: B — It fails: S1 supplies 150 thousand at $11, still 50 thousand below the original quantity.
macro.Feedback: S0 at $9 supplies 200 thousand. S1 supplies only 100 thousand at $9 and 150 thousand at $11. Returning to 200 thousand on S1 would require $13, outside the contract. The allowed price movement offsets only half the quantity reduction caused by the cost-driven shift.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the graph or confuses a curve shift with movement along a curve
macro.Question: Refer to the graph. A technology improvement shifts supply from S0 to S1. At the unchanged price of $3, quantity supplied rises. Half of this increase in quantity is later lost, leaving a parallel supply curve halfway between S0 and S1. What price would now be needed to supply the quantity originally available on S1 at $3, and how would the market reach that quantity?
macro.Choice A: About $2.50; movement down the halfway curve offsets the lost capacity.
macro.Choice B: About $3.00; unchanged desired output prevents a supply shift.
macro.Choice C: About $3.50; movement up the halfway curve offsets the partial supply reversal.
macro.Choice D: About $4.00; movement up S0 offsets the entire improvement.
macro.Correct Answer: C — About $3.50; movement up the halfway curve offsets the partial supply reversal.
macro.Feedback: At $3, S0 supplies about 100 thousand and S1 about 225 thousand. The halfway curve supplies about 162.5 thousand at $3. At 225 thousand, S0 requires $4 and S1 $3, so the halfway curve requires $3.50. A price movement along that new curve restores quantity; it does not undo the partial technology loss.

macro.Common Misconception: Averaging firm quantities instead of adding them.
macro.Question: At one price, Firm A supplies 8 units and Firm B supplies 11 units. Market quantity supplied is:
macro.Choice A: 19 units.
macro.Choice B: 8 units.
macro.Choice C: 9.5 units.
macro.Choice D: 11 units.
macro.Correct Answer: A — 19 units.
macro.Feedback: Market supply adds each seller’s quantity: 8 + 11 = 19.

macro.Common Misconception: Calling a movement caused by the good’s own price a supply shift.
macro.Question: The price of oranges rises, and growers offer more oranges while all nonprice determinants stay fixed. This is:
macro.Choice A: An increase in supply.
macro.Choice B: An increase in quantity supplied.
macro.Choice C: A decrease in supply.
macro.Choice D: A decrease in quantity supplied.
macro.Correct Answer: B — An increase in quantity supplied.
macro.Feedback: A higher own price causes movement up the existing supply curve.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing lower production cost with a movement along supply.
macro.Question: The price of an important input falls. What happens to supply, other things equal?
macro.Choice A: Supply shifts left.
macro.Choice B: Quantity supplied falls along the curve.
macro.Choice C: Supply shifts right.
macro.Choice D: Demand shifts right.
macro.Correct Answer: C — Supply shifts right.
macro.Feedback: Lower input cost makes production profitable at more output levels, shifting supply right.

macro.Question: According to the law of supply, how are price and quantity supplied related, other things equal?
macro.Choice A: As price rises, quantity supplied rises
macro.Choice B: As price rises, supply shifts left
macro.Choice C: As price falls, quantity supplied rises
macro.Choice D: As demand rises, supply must rise
macro.Correct Answer: A — As price rises, quantity supplied rises
macro.Feedback: The law of supply says price and quantity supplied move in the same direction.

macro.Question: The price of handmade tables rises, and sellers offer more tables for sale. What is the most precise statement?
macro.Choice A: Quantity supplied increases
macro.Choice B: Supply increases
macro.Choice C: Demand increases
macro.Choice D: Supply shifts right
macro.Correct Answer: A — Quantity supplied increases
macro.Feedback: A change in the good's own price causes movement along the supply curve, so quantity supplied changes.

macro.Question: Steel becomes more expensive for car producers. What happens to the supply of cars?
macro.Choice A: Supply decreases
macro.Choice B: Quantity supplied increases because car price changed
macro.Choice C: Demand decreases
macro.Choice D: Supply increases
macro.Correct Answer: A — Supply decreases
macro.Feedback: More expensive steel raises the cost of producing cars at every output level, shifting car supply left rather than changing demand.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming the label of a policy matters more than its net marginal-cost effect.
macro.Question: A subsidy lowers marginal cost by $3 per unit, while a regulation raises marginal cost by $3 per unit. What happens to supply if those are the only changes?
macro.Choice A: Supply shifts right because the subsidy lowers marginal cost by more than the regulation raises it
macro.Choice B: Supply shifts left because the regulation raises marginal cost by more than the subsidy lowers it
macro.Choice C: Quantity supplied rises along the original curve because the product's market price increases
macro.Choice D: The two per-unit effects offset, so supply is unchanged.
macro.Correct Answer: D — The two per-unit effects offset, so supply is unchanged.
macro.Feedback: Equal and opposite per-unit cost changes leave marginal cost, and therefore supply, unchanged.

macro.Common Misconception: Failing to remove the exiting firm’s quantity from market supply.
macro.Question: Four firms each supply q=2P units at every price. Demand is Qd=120-4P. One firm exits permanently, with the surviving firms’ schedules unchanged. Which statement correctly compares market equilibrium before and after exit?
macro.Choice A: Price rises from $10 to $12; quantity falls from 80 to 72 as remaining firms move along their unchanged individual schedules.
macro.Choice B: Price stays $10 and quantity becomes 60; unchanged individual schedules prevent equilibrium price adjustment.
macro.Choice C: Price falls from $10 to $8; exit shifts each surviving firm’s individual supply curve right.
macro.Choice D: Price rises from $10 to $12 and quantity rises from 80 to 96 because four firms remain in the aggregate schedule.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Price rises from $10 to $12; quantity falls from 80 to 72 as remaining firms move along their unchanged individual schedules.
macro.Feedback: Before exit supply is 8P, so 120-4P=8P gives P=10, Q=80. Afterward supply is 6P, giving P=12, Q=72. Market supply shifts because a seller exits; survivors respond along unchanged individual supply curves.

macro.Common Misconception: Declaring a net shift when opposing determinants are not quantified.
macro.Question: Technology improves while the expected future selling price rises sharply and firms store current output. What is the strongest conclusion about current supply?
macro.Choice A: Current supply increases because improved technology and storing output for future sale both add to current market supply.
macro.Choice B: The net direction is ambiguous without knowing the strength of each effect.
macro.Choice C: Current supply decreases because the expected future price rises sharply, which establishes that withholding outweighs the technology improvement.
macro.Choice D: Quantity supplied moves along one curve because both events change the product's current price.
macro.Correct Answer: B — The net direction is ambiguous without knowing the strength of each effect.
macro.Feedback: Better technology increases current supply, while withholding output for a higher expected future price reduces current supply. The word “sharply” does not quantify the withholding effect relative to the technology effect, so the net direction remains uncertain. Neither determinant is a change in the product’s current price along a fixed curve.

macro.Question: Bakers pay $4 less in flour cost per loaf, but a new energy levy adds $6 per loaf. At the same time, a health report reduces buyers’ willingness to purchase bread. With unknown shift magnitudes, which conclusion is supported?
macro.Choice A: Net unit cost falls $2, shifting supply right; demand shifts left, so price rises while quantity is ambiguous.
macro.Choice B: Net unit cost rises $2, shifting supply left; demand also shifts left, so quantity falls while price is ambiguous.
macro.Choice C: Both changes shift supply left, so price rises and quantity falls with no demand change.
macro.Choice D: Lower flour cost shifts supply right regardless of the levy, so quantity rises and price is ambiguous.
macro.Correct Answer: B — Net unit cost rises $2, shifting supply left; demand also shifts left, so quantity falls while price is ambiguous.
macro.Feedback: The cost changes net to +2 per loaf, reducing supply. The health information reduces demand. Both changes lower equilibrium quantity, but their price effects oppose one another.

macro.Common Misconception: Assuming one opposing supply shifter automatically dominates the other.
macro.Question: Evaluate the competing effects of a cost-saving production technology and a new compliance cost. What can be inferred about the net supply shift without relative magnitudes?
macro.Choice A: Supply must increase because technology reduces production cost.
macro.Choice B: Supply must decrease because compliance raises production cost.
macro.Choice C: The net supply direction is ambiguous without relative cost changes.
macro.Choice D: Supply must stay fixed because the two changes cancel by definition.
macro.Correct Answer: C — The net supply direction is ambiguous without relative cost changes.
macro.Feedback: The two cost effects oppose each other. Supply rises if the saving dominates, falls if the added cost dominates, and is unchanged only if they offset.

macro.Question: Several firms leave a market, reducing the quantity offered at each fixed price. Demand is unchanged. At the new equilibrium, surviving firms sell more than each sold before, but total market sales are lower. Which explanation reconciles the observations?
macro.Choice A: Market supply shifted left, raising price; survivors move up their own unchanged supply curves even though fewer firms reduce total output.
macro.Choice B: Market supply shifted right because each survivor sells more; the lower total shows demand must have shifted left too.
macro.Choice C: Market supply is unchanged because survivor technology is unchanged; exit is only a movement along aggregate supply.
macro.Choice D: Each survivor’s supply shifted left, lowering price; fewer sellers then raise each remaining firm’s quantity supplied.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Market supply shifted left, raising price; survivors move up their own unchanged supply curves even though fewer firms reduce total output.
macro.Feedback: Exit reduces aggregate supply at any fixed price. Along unchanged demand, price rises and total quantity falls. Higher price induces more output along each survivor’s own curve, consistent with lower aggregate output.

macro.Question: A hurricane destroys part of the orange crop. What is the likely result in the orange market?
macro.Choice A: Supply decreases, price rises, and quantity falls
macro.Choice B: Demand increases, price rises, and quantity rises
macro.Choice C: Supply increases, price falls, and quantity rises
macro.Choice D: Quantity demanded rises because supply fell
macro.Correct Answer: A — Supply decreases, price rises, and quantity falls
macro.Feedback: A crop loss reduces supply, which raises price and lowers equilibrium quantity.

macro.Question: Refer to the graph. A production improvement shifts supply from S1 to S2 while demand remains D1. Which explanation connects the curve shift to the new equilibrium?
macro.Choice A: Equilibrium moves from P2, Q1 to P1, Q2, so price falls and quantity rises
macro.Choice B: Equilibrium moves from P1, Q2 to P2, Q3, so price and quantity rise
macro.Choice C: Equilibrium moves from P3, Q2 to P2, Q3, so price falls and quantity rises
macro.Choice D: Equilibrium moves from P2, Q3 to P3, Q2, so price rises and quantity falls
macro.Correct Answer: A — Equilibrium moves from P2, Q1 to P1, Q2, so price falls and quantity rises
macro.Feedback: The production improvement shifts supply right to S2. Along unchanged D1, the intersection moves from P2, Q1 to P1, Q2.

macro.Question: Refer to the supply and demand graph with D1, D2, S1, and S2. Starting at D2 and S1, supply increases to S2 while demand stays at D2. What happens?
macro.Choice A: Equilibrium moves from P3, Q2 to P2, Q3.
macro.Choice B: Equilibrium moves from P2, Q1 to P3, Q2.
macro.Choice C: Equilibrium moves from P1, Q2 to P2, Q3.
macro.Choice D: Equilibrium moves from P2, Q3 to P1, Q2.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Equilibrium moves from P3, Q2 to P2, Q3.
macro.Feedback: A supply increase shifts supply right from S1 to S2, lowering price and raising quantity.

macro.Question: Refer to the supply and demand graph with D1, D2, S1, and S2. Starting at D1 and S2, supply decreases to S1 while demand stays at D1. What happens?
macro.Choice A: Equilibrium moves from P1, Q2 to P2, Q1.
macro.Choice B: Equilibrium moves from P2, Q1 to P1, Q2.
macro.Choice C: Equilibrium moves from P2, Q3 to P3, Q2.
macro.Choice D: Equilibrium moves from P3, Q2 to P2, Q3.
macro.Correct Answer: A — Equilibrium moves from P1, Q2 to P2, Q1.
macro.Feedback: A decrease in supply shifts supply left, raising price and lowering quantity.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
macro.Question: Refer to the graph. What market change is shown from A to B?
macro.Choice A: Supply increases, lowering price and raising quantity
macro.Choice B: Demand increases, raising price and quantity
macro.Choice C: Supply decreases, raising price and reducing quantity
macro.Choice D: Demand decreases, lowering price and quantity
macro.Correct Answer: C — Supply decreases, raising price and reducing quantity
macro.Feedback: Supply shifts left; price rises from 10 to 12 and quantity falls from 200 to 150 thousand.

macro.Common Misconception: Misreads the relationship shown in the graph
macro.Question: The movie-ticket market moves from A to B after one production cost changes. Which explanation and changes in equilibrium price and quantity match the graph?
macro.Choice A: Higher operating costs reduce supply; price rises $2 and quantity falls 50 thousand
macro.Choice B: Higher operating costs reduce supply; price rises $4 and quantity falls 50 thousand
macro.Choice C: Lower operating costs increase supply; price falls $2 and quantity rises 50 thousand
macro.Choice D: Lower operating costs increase supply; price falls $4 and quantity rises 50 thousand
macro.Correct Answer: A — Higher operating costs reduce supply; price rises $2 and quantity falls 50 thousand
macro.Feedback: A is ($10,200 thousand) and B is ($12,150 thousand). The move follows a decrease in supply, consistent with higher operating costs: price rises $2 and quantity falls 50 thousand.

macro.Common Misconception: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
macro.Question: Actual inflation repeatedly exceeds the rate workers expected. Which forecast adjustment is likely?
macro.Choice A: Expected inflation falls
macro.Choice B: Expected inflation becomes permanently zero
macro.Choice C: Expected inflation cannot respond
macro.Choice D: Expected inflation rises
macro.Correct Answer: D — Expected inflation rises
macro.Feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.

macro.Common Misconception: Reverses the expectations shift or equates credibility with a lower natural rate.
macro.Question: A disinflation target becomes more credible, lowering expected inflation before demand is reduced further. What change in the short-run Phillips relation can ease reaching the target?
macro.Choice A: A downward SRPC shift allows lower inflation at a given unemployment rate
macro.Choice B: An upward SRPC shift allows lower inflation at a given unemployment rate
macro.Choice C: A rightward LRPC shift automatically removes all output cost
macro.Choice D: No relation can change until unemployment reaches zero
macro.Correct Answer: A — A downward SRPC shift allows lower inflation at a given unemployment rate
macro.Feedback: Lower expected inflation shifts SRPC down. That can reduce the needed demand contraction, without guaranteeing a completely costless transition.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating supply shocks as movement along the same SRPC.
macro.Question: An adverse supply shock shifts the short-run Phillips curve:
macro.Choice A: Up and right
macro.Choice B: Down and left
macro.Choice C: Nowhere
macro.Choice D: Into LRAS
macro.Correct Answer: A — Up and right
macro.Feedback: An adverse supply shock worsens the tradeoff by shifting the SRPC up and right.

macro.Common Misconception: Thinking inflation and unemployment always move opposite ways.
macro.Question: A surge in oil prices can cause inflation and unemployment to:
macro.Choice A: Both rise
macro.Choice B: Both fall
macro.Choice C: Move in opposite directions only
macro.Choice D: Become zero
macro.Correct Answer: A — Both rise
macro.Feedback: A negative supply shock can raise inflation and unemployment together.

macro.Common Misconception: Missing the worse tradeoff after SRPC shifts upward.
macro.Question: Refer to the SRPC graph. At inflation I3, comparing SRPC1 and SRPC2 shows:
macro.Choice A: SRPC2 has higher unemployment
macro.Choice B: SRPC2 has lower unemployment
macro.Choice C: Both curves have U3
macro.Choice D: Both curves have U1
macro.Correct Answer: A — SRPC2 has higher unemployment
macro.Feedback: At the same inflation rate, the higher SRPC shows higher unemployment.

macro.Common Misconception: Compares points with different unemployment rates, so movement and shift effects are mixed.
macro.Question: Refer to the SRPC graph. Which labeled move isolates an upward SRPC shift at unemployment U3?
macro.Choice A: The move from point c to point f
macro.Choice B: The move from point a to point f
macro.Choice C: The move from point b to point e
macro.Choice D: The move from point c to point a
macro.Correct Answer: A — The move from point c to point f
macro.Feedback: Points c and f share unemployment U3; moving from c on SRPC1 to f on SRPC2 isolates higher inflation at the same unemployment rate.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating SRPC shifts as ordinary movement along a curve.
macro.Question: Refer to the SRPC graph. A shift from SRPC1 to SRPC2 is most consistent with:
macro.Choice A: Higher expected inflation or adverse supply shock
macro.Choice B: Lower expected inflation or favorable supply shock
macro.Choice C: Higher money supply with expectations fixed
macro.Choice D: Lower unemployment at every inflation rate
macro.Correct Answer: A — Higher expected inflation or adverse supply shock
macro.Feedback: The upward SRPC shift reflects higher expected inflation or a worsened supply-side tradeoff.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating supply shocks as AD movements.
macro.Question: A student says an oil shock causes only movement along the SRPC. What is the correction?
macro.Choice A: It shifts SRPC because costs and prices change directly
macro.Choice B: It shifts only AD because spending changes directly
macro.Choice C: It shifts only LRPC because inflation changes
macro.Choice D: It moves only along LRAS because output changes
macro.Correct Answer: A — It shifts SRPC because costs and prices change directly
macro.Feedback: A supply shock shifts the SRPC because it directly changes firms' costs and inflation pressure.

macro.Common Misconception: Calling an upward SRPC shift an improvement.
macro.Question: Refer to the SRPC graph. The economy moves from SRPC1 to SRPC2. Which statement should be rejected?
macro.Choice A: The tradeoff improved because higher inflation now buys lower unemployment at every point.
macro.Choice B: The tradeoff worsened because inflation is higher at a given unemployment rate.
macro.Choice C: Expected inflation may have increased and shifted the curve upward.
macro.Choice D: An adverse supply shock may have raised both inflation pressure and unemployment risk.
macro.Correct Answer: A — The tradeoff improved because higher inflation now buys lower unemployment at every point.
macro.Feedback: An upward SRPC shift worsens the tradeoff because inflation is higher at the same unemployment rate.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating supply shocks as normal AD movements.
macro.Question: An adverse supply shock affects the Phillips curve by:
macro.Choice A: Shifting SRPC up and right
macro.Choice B: Moving down along the same SRPC
macro.Choice C: Shifting LRPC to zero unemployment
macro.Choice D: Eliminating expected inflation
macro.Correct Answer: A — Shifting SRPC up and right
macro.Feedback: An adverse supply shock worsens the inflation-unemployment tradeoff.

macro.Common Misconception: Confusing supply shocks with AD shocks.
macro.Question: Which event shifts both SRAS left and SRPC up-right?
macro.Choice A: Oil price surge
macro.Choice B: Tax cut
macro.Choice C: Open-market purchase
macro.Choice D: Consumer confidence boom
macro.Correct Answer: A — Oil price surge
macro.Feedback: An oil price surge raises production costs and worsens the inflation-unemployment tradeoff.

macro.Common Misconception: Treating the Phillips curve as fixed under every shock.
macro.Question: A policymaker says, 'Inflation is high, so unemployment must be low.' What is the best correction?
